## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III; a Chronological Reissue of all the Monuments of Catholic Tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, carefully corrected by comparison with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is easy for the reader to discover which Fathers have commented on the texts of the individual books of Scripture, and in which places of their works they have done so.**

**The most accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others, if the following are taken into consideration: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reissued works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but for the first time gathered in our library from works dealing with every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The stated figures read: “two hundred volumes of the Latin edition, for one thousand francs; [the] Greek-Latin [edition], eight hundred and one thousand three hundred” (the relation of the latter figures is unclear in the supplied text). The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are provided in it only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of the Lord 860  
## Florus the Deacon of Lyons

[Column 0009]

## Historical Notice

*(From Galland, Library of the Ancient Fathers, volume XIII.)*

[Column 0009A] Wandelbert called our Florus “Master” and described him as a subdeacon of the Church of Lyons, saying:

“I made particular use of the help and assistance of the holy and renowned Florus, subdeacon of the Church of Lyons, who, just as he is known in our time to excel in the knowledge of Scripture through singular zeal and diligence, is likewise recognized as abounding in no small supply and genuine knowledge of authoritative books.”

This easily explains why the name “Master” adhered to him. Later he is also called a deacon. Trithemius writes that he was a monk of Saint-Trond in the diocese of Liège; whether rightly or wrongly, as Oudinus argues [Column 0009B, volume I, p. 1806], makes no difference. He held Augustine in the highest esteem. He wrote various works, whose catalogue may be found in Fabricius [Column 0009B, *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, volume II, p. 63, Padua edition] and Cave [Column 0009B, under the year 837].

He wrote against John Scotus in the year 852, in the name of his Church of Lyons, having been selected for this purpose, as Mauguin thinks [Column 0009B, *Historical Dissertation*, chapter 10, p. 156], because in a certain sermon mentioned by Hincmar [Column 0010A, *On Predestination*, chapter 6] he had given a notable specimen of his doctrine concerning foreknowledge and predestination. In that work he did not, indeed, corrupt the writings of Eriugena, as Matthew of Westminster maintains [Column 0010B, under the year 883], but he sometimes seems not to have sufficiently grasped the meaning of his opponent, as Usserius rightly interprets [Column 0010B, *History of Gottschalk*, chapter 9].

We have thought it appropriate to present from his writings only the little book on the Election of Bishops, which the distinguished scholar Baluze published in his *Agobard*, p. 254, although we do not see it commonly mentioned by bibliographers. Masson had published a fragment of it, and Baronius took it from him; Peter de Marca also reproduces it, though somewhat differently, in his *Concordia* [Column 0010B, Book VIII, chapters 14, sections 2 and 3].

Cave admits that he does not know how long our author survived after writing against Eriugena. But since Matthew of Westminster, mentioned above, refers to him under the year 883, we have thought it by no means inappropriate to place him under that year.

[Column 0009]

## Bibliographical Notice

*(Fabricius, Library of Medieval and Later Latin Literature.)*

[Column 0009C] Drepanius Florus, apparently no different from Master Florus, the deacon of Lyons, whose writings Cave discusses under the year 837. In addition to his observations, I have the following few items to add.

1. Besides his Commentary on Paul’s Epistles, drawn from Augustine and published under Bede’s name, Florus also wrote another similar work on the same Epistles, drawn from Cyprian, Hilary, and other Fathers. It is preserved in manuscript in the library of the Grande Chartreuse; Baluze discusses it in a letter to Tournemin [Column 0009D, *Journal des Savants*, year 1716, p. 234 ff.].

2. A minor work on the Celebration of the Mass, collected from the words of the holy Fathers Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Gregory, Fulgentius, Severianus, Vigilius, Isidore, Bede, and Avitus, and from ancient books of the mysteries, was reprinted from the edition of Peter Francis Chifletius in the Lyon Library of the Fathers, volume XV, p. 62. More recently it was published from a codex of Queen Christina of Sweden, much more completely and accurately, on p. 579 of volume IX of the *Monuments* of Edmond Martène and Ursin Durand, Paris, 1733, folio.

[Column 0010C] 3. Besides nine poems, frequently published in George Fabricius’s *Christian Poets* and in the Libraries of the Fathers, and separately brought to light by Andreas Rivinus [Column 0009D, with several poems of Theodulf and Jonah, bishops of Orléans; Modoinus, bishop of Autun; and Laidradus and Agobard, bishops of Lyons], Leipzig, 1653, octavo, with notes, and besides the six poems published by Mabillon in volume I of the *Analecta*, p. 388 ff. (new edition, p. 412), concerning each of which Polycarpus Leyserus writes carefully in his *History of the Poets of the Middle Ages*, p. 244 ff., the distinguished Martène and Durand recently supplied other poems from the Bigot manuscript in volume V of the *Anecdota*. These are in hexameter verse:

- *On the Gospel of Matthew*, p. 595;
- *The Deeds of Christ the Lord*, p. 601;
- *On the Gospel of John*, p. 603;
- *Prayer to Christ, with a Commemoration of the Ancient Miracles of Christ our God*, p. 608 [Column 0009D, described in the books of the Old Testament];
- *Epigram of the Book of Homilies for the Whole Year, Arranged from Treatises of Various Fathers*, p. 612;
- *The Third Letter to Modoinus, Bishop of Autun*, p. 616.

[Column 0010D] **Note:** The first letter, in George Fabricius and others, begins: “Hail, Father, may you pour forth thanks from a cheerful heart.” The second, in Mabillon, begins: “To you, distinguished Modoinus, I send greetings.” On this Modoinus, see the Sammarthani, volume II of *Gallia Christiana*, p. 36.

The letter begins:

“Greetings, holy parent, venerable priest of Christ,

powerful shepherd in the citadel of Mount Augustus.”

[Column 0011A] The title is on the apse of the memorial of Saint Justus, p. 618.

[Column 0011B] *Dunum* means a Celtic mountain or hill, as the Greeks call it βοῦνον (*bounon*) and θῖνα (*thina*). See Du Cange.

4. A minor work against Amalarius, chorepiscopus of Lyons, *On the Tripartite Body of Christ*, appears in volume IX of Martène and Durand’s *Monuments*, p. 641.

I discussed Amalarius’s error above, in volume I. Florus wrote this work in the form of a letter:

“To the most blessed, most reverend, and most pious shepherds of Christ’s flock; to the rulers of the Church of God; to the preachers and defenders of the Catholic faith:

To Drogo, master of the sacred council and most illustrious pontiff; to Hetti, bishop of Trier; to Aldric, most reverend bishop of Le Mans; to Raban, venerable abbot and from the First Province of Lyons; to Alberic, bishop of Langres; and to Fora, bishop of Chalon, most reverend men:

Florus, an unworthy son of the Catholic Church and a very humble servant of your piety and fatherhood.”

Then follows, on p. 649, a work on the same matter, dealt with in the council of bishops at the palace of Quierzy; and on p. 656, *Florus’s Letter to the Council of Thionville against the Books of Amalarius*.

5. *Against the Erroneous Definitions of John Scotus.* He wrote in the name of the Church of Lyons. It appears in Gilbert Mauguin’s *Defences of Grace and Predestination from Ninth-Century Writers*, volume I, pp. 585 and 738, Paris, 1650, quarto, and in volume XV of the Lyon edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 611.

It should be investigated whether Prudentius Galindo, bishop of Troyes, was another Florus distinct from ours; other writings of his against the same Scotus have been published by the same Mauguin [Column 0012A]. See also what Menetrier argued against the view attributing that work to our Florus, in the *Literary Memoirs of Trevoux* for 1705, pp. 344 ff.

6. The additions to Bede’s *Martyrology* by another, still earlier Florus— a monk of Saint-Trond, of the Benedictine order and of the diocese of Liège, around the year 760—are well known. They were published with Bede by Henschenius in the *Acts of the Saints*, before volume II of March, and most recently with Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, edited by John Smith, Cambridge, 1722, folio. Add Charles Cointe, volume IV of the *Annals of the Franks*, p. 470 ff.

He also added certain elegiac verses at the end of an old commentary on the Psalms, preserved in a thousand-year-old manuscript codex in the Ambrosian Library at Milan. Muratori, publishing this poem in volume III of the *Antiquities*, p. 856, holds that its author was the very deacon of Lyons, the light of his age; yet he equally judges that the author of that commentary [Column 0012B] is very different from Saint Jerome, whose name it bears there.

Moreover, in the poem addressed to Abbot Eloardus, Florus relates that he revised that commentary. Usserius in his *History of Gottschalk* and Cave likewise attribute to the same Florus the commentary known to them from a codex of Elne, but from the poem reported by Muratori we learn of no other service performed by him than that of a corrector. Nevertheless, Muratori himself also seems to have vindicated that work for Jerome rather than Florus.

[Column 0011]

# Florus the Deacon’s Book on the Election of Bishops, Collected from the Sayings of the Fathers

*(From Galland, cited above.)*

[Column 0011C] **I.** It is evident to all who administer priestly office in the Church of God what things, in episcopal ordination, the authority of the sacred canons and ecclesiastical custom, in accordance with the disposition of divine law and apostolic tradition, command to be observed.

Namely, when a pastor has died and the see is vacant, one man from the clergy of the Church—whom the common and unanimous agreement of that clergy and of the entire people has chosen, and whom they have publicly, formally, and solemnly designated—should be consecrated by the legitimate number of bishops and thus be able lawfully to occupy the place of the deceased bishop. There should be no doubt that what has been celebrated by the Church of God in so holy an order and through such legitimate observance has been confirmed by divine judgment and disposition.

**II.** These are the things that are found established both in the Councils of the Fathers and in the decrees of the pontiffs of the apostolic see; they are also found approved and confirmed by the Church of Christ from the beginning.

Thus blessed Cyprian the martyr, when defending the episcopate of Saint Cornelius, bishop of the city of Rome, against certain proud and envious detractors, advanced the following as testimony to the holiness and legitimacy of his ordination, saying (Letter 111):

“Cornelius was made bishop by the judgment of God and of his Christ, by the testimony of all the clergy, by the vote of the people, and by the agreement of the ancient and good priests; when no bishop had previously been made there, and when the rank of the priestly chair was vacant.

When that chair had been occupied and confirmed by the agreement of all of us, if anyone should then wish to be made bishop, it is absolutely necessary that he should not possess ecclesiastical ordination, since he does not maintain the unity of the Church through agreement. After the first, there cannot be a second. For whoever wishes to exist after the one who was consecrated through election is no longer a second bishop, but no bishop at all.”

[Column 0012D] **III.** In accordance with these words of blessed Cyprian, it is clear that all the bishops of the Churches of God thereafter were ordained and lawfully presided over the whole people, without any consultation of secular power, from the time of the apostles and for nearly four hundred years afterward.

Once Christian rulers began to exist, it is clear from reason that the same ecclesiastical freedom remained, for the most part, in episcopal ordinations. For when a single emperor held the monarchy of the whole world, it could not have happened that all those who were to be ordained bishops, from every extensive region of the world—namely, Asia, Europe, and Africa—were brought before his notice.

Rather, that ordination was always valid and unimpaired which the holy Church celebrated according to apostolic tradition and the form of religious observance.

**IV.** As for the custom that later arose in certain kingdoms, whereby episcopal ordination was carried out after consultation with the ruler, this certainly serves to increase brotherly harmony, for the sake of peace and concord with secular power. It does not, however, complete the truth or authority of sacred ordination, which can be conferred upon each person not by royal power but solely by God’s will and by the agreement of the Church’s faithful.

For the episcopate is not a human office but a gift of the Holy Spirit, as the apostle shows when he speaks to the bishops, saying (Acts 20:28):

“Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood.”

Hence he also says in the Letter to the Hebrews (chapter 5:4–6):

“And no one takes this honor upon himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was. So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but the one who said to him, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’ And again: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.’”

In these words of the Apostle it is demonstrated most clearly that, for attaining and assuming this office, God’s grace is sufficient for each person, when joined with faith and devotion to that grace; but without these, it cannot be granted to anyone by human decision.

Therefore any ruler commits a grave offense if he supposes that he can bestow by his own favor what divine grace alone distributes, since he ought to add the ministry of his power to the execution of such a matter, not place it above that ministry.

**V.** Finally, to provide some examples of this matter, I think that, in the ordination of blessed Martin—when he was brought out of the monastery on another pretext, seized by the people, and led to the Church, and immediately consecrated by the bishops who had been invited for this purpose—none of the princes of this world was consulted.

There was likewise once such a religious and venerable custom in the Church of Lyons, as ancient history relates: when the bishop had died, the whole Church gathered together, and after observing a common three-day fast and celebration with united prayer, they appointed without hesitation as bishop whomever the Lord revealed to them, whether from their own clergy or from elsewhere.

The holy book of the Life of blessed Eucherius, bishop of that city and an outstanding teacher, clearly testifies that this was fulfilled in his case. Although he was born of a most noble senatorial family, he renounced this world and distributed all his possessions among the poor for the love of Christ. He then withdrew into a cave in the region of Provence, where he remained hidden, fasting and devoting himself to God alone and to prayers. Through such a revelation he was pointed out, found, and placed in episcopal governance.

From this it is established with complete certainty that throughout the period when almighty God wished to demonstrate such goodness or grace in that Church, his grace alone, together with the devoted faith of the Church, was effective and sufficient for the consecration of its rulers.

**VI.** In the Roman Church also, to the present day, we see pontiffs lawfully consecrated without consultation of the ruler, solely by judgment concerning the disposition of the matter and by the vote of the faithful. They likewise ordain and appoint priests, according to ancient custom and with the same freedom, in all the regions and cities subject to them.

No one there is so absurd as to think that the grace of divine sanctification is lessened because no authority of secular power accompanies it.

**VII.** We say all this not because we think the power of rulers should in any respect be diminished, or because we seek to persuade anyone to think anything contrary to the religious custom of the kingdom. We say it so that it may be demonstrated most clearly that, in a matter of this kind, divine grace is sufficient, whereas human power, unless it agrees with that grace, is of no value.

Accordingly, in the sacred canons of the Fathers, where many circumstances are mentioned without which episcopal ordination must be regarded as invalid, nothing concerning this matter is found to have been inserted.

[Column 0015]

# Florus the Deacon’s Minor Work on the Explanation of the Mass

More complete and corrected from a manuscript of the library of the Queen of Sweden.

*(Martène, Enlarged Collection, volume IX.)*

## Preliminary Observation

[Column 0015A]

What has until now been read in abbreviated form in the *Library of the Fathers*—Master Florus’s minor work on the canon of the Mass—now appears for the first time complete and fully arranged, from a very ancient codex of the Queen of Sweden, written at least in the tenth century and therefore close to the author’s own age. While living in Rome, Mabillon had it copied from this codex.

For when he had carefully compared it with the published version, he observed that not even a fourth part of Florus’s exposition was contained in the *Library of the Fathers*. He therefore rightly considered it worthy of publication, and this seems also to have been the wish of the late Cardinal Bona, who himself had examined the codex of the Queen of Sweden.

Florus flourished around the year 840, during the reign of Charles the Bald among the Franks. He was, as is commonly said, a deacon of the Church of Lyons, or, as Wandelbert prefers, a subdeacon. Wandelbert, like Walafrid Strabo, praises him wonderfully for his outstanding learning and tireless diligence in reading and writing.

Thus he says in the preface to his *Martyrology*:

“I made particular use of the help and assistance of the holy and renowned man Florus, subdeacon of the Church of Lyons, who, just as he is known in our time to excel in the knowledge of divine Scripture through singular zeal and diligence, is likewise recognized as abounding in no small supply and variety of authoritative books.”

This passage of Wandelbert refutes the opinion of John Trithemius, who asserted that Florus was a monk of the monastery of Saint-Trond, unless perhaps he entered the monastic profession toward the end of his life.

Since Florus was thoroughly versed in the reading of the holy Fathers, whose books he possessed in excellent abundance, he composed this work and others published by him chiefly from their sayings and opinions. Very often he reproduces their complete words continuously; sometimes he expresses only their meaning.

After the Explanation of the Mass, we wish to append another work by the same Florus against Amalarius, which Mabillon once copied from two very ancient manuscripts—one belonging to Pelterius, the other to Achilles de Harlay—written eight hundred years ago.

### 1. Beginning of the Work on the Celebration of the Mass

[Column 0015C] “Collected as fully as possible and arranged in order from the words of the holy Fathers Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Gregory, Fulgentius, Severianus, Vigilius, Isidore, Bede, and Avitus, as the individual initial letters of their names, marked externally, show in their respective places; but certain words have necessarily also been taken from ancient books of the mysteries.

The fact that these same names are not inserted everywhere throughout the sequence of the minor work was caused by the necessity of avoiding the frequent interruption, which would have been absurd and inconvenient, of the wording and meanings themselves.

In this little exposition, however, it is not so much the words—which are sufficiently simple—that are presented and commended, as the meaning and celebration of the mystery itself: namely, with what faith it must be celebrated and with how much devotion it must be embraced.”

[Column 0015C] **Note:** By “the celebration of the Mass” (*actio missarum*), liturgical authors understand the canon of the Mass. “The canon itself is called the celebration,” says Walafrid Strabo in Book 1 of *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 22, “because the Lord’s sacraments are accomplished in it. The canon is also called the same celebration because in it there is the legitimate and regular accomplishment of the sacraments.” And the *Micrologus*, chapter 12, says: “The prayer which, because of the regular accomplishment of the sacraments, we call the canon or celebration, in the Roman manner—who composed it, we do not clearly read.”

### 2. *(Augustine, on Psalm 33, section 4.)*

In the mystery of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, which the holy Church offers throughout the whole world for the salvation of that same world, humility is commended to us above all.

[Column 0016B] For that same Lord Jesus Christ made one way for us through humility [Note: In Augustine it reads *viam* (“way”), apparently better], because through pride we had departed from God. Yet we could not return to him except through humility, and we had no one whom we could propose to ourselves for imitation.

All human mortality was swollen with pride; and even if some humble man in spirit existed, as there were prophets and patriarchs, the human race disdained to imitate humble men.

Therefore, so that a human being would not disdain to imitate a humble human being, God became humble, so that, at least in this way, the pride of the human race would not disdain to follow the footsteps of God.

As we read, there were previously sacrifices of the Jews according to Aaron, involving animal victims. But this was not yet the sacrifice of the body and blood of the Lord in mystery—the sacrifice that has now been spread throughout the whole world.

Let us therefore set before our eyes two sacrifices: the one according to the order of Aaron, and the other according to the order of Melchizedek.

For it is written:

“The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:4).

This is plainly said of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Who, then, was Melchizedek? Certainly, as we read, he was king of Salem. Salem was formerly that city which afterward, as learned men have reported, was called Jerusalem.

Therefore, before the Jews reigned there, Melchizedek was there, the priest who is written of in Genesis as “priest of God Most High.”

He met Abraham when Abraham had rescued Lot from the hands of his pursuers, struck down those by whom Lot was being attacked, and rescued his brother. After the rescue of his brother, Melchizedek met him.

So great was Melchizedek, by whom Abraham was blessed. He brought out bread and wine and blessed Abraham, and Abraham gave him tithes.

Consider what he brought forth and whom he blessed. Later it was said:

“You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

David spoke this in the Spirit, long after Abraham. But Melchizedek lived in the time of Abraham.

Of whom else, then, does he say, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,” except of the one whose sacrifice we know?

### 3.

For the sacrifice of Aaron has been taken away, and the sacrifice according to the order of Melchizedek has begun.

Our Lord Jesus Christ therefore willed that our salvation should be in his body and blood. From what did he commend his body and blood? From his humility.

For if he had not been humble, neither would he be eaten nor drunk.

Consider his height:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

Behold the eternal food. Angels eat it; eternal powers eat it; heavenly spirits eat it. They eat and are nourished, while that which satisfies and gladdens them remains whole.

But what could a human being do in relation to that food? Where would there be a heart so suitable for such food?

It was therefore necessary that that table should become milk and reach little children.

But how does milk come to you? How does food become milk unless it passes through flesh? A mother does this: what the mother eats, the infant eats. But because the infant is not yet capable of eating bread, the mother makes that very bread flesh and feeds the infant from the bread through the usefulness of her breast and the nourishment of milk. [Note: In Augustine: “and through the humility of the breast and the liquid of milk,” etc.]

How, then, did the Wisdom of God feed us from that very bread? Because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

See, therefore, the humility: human beings eat the bread of angels.

And it is written:

“He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels” (Psalm 77:24),

that is, the eternal Word by which the angels are nourished, which is equal to the Father—man ate it, because, although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized (Philippians 2:6).

The angels are nourished by it; but he emptied himself so that human beings might eat the bread of angels, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being.

He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross, so that from the cross the flesh and blood of the Lord might now be commended to us as a new sacrifice.

### 4. (AUGUSTINE, *On Psalm 64*, 1)

Therefore our priest, sent by the Lord God, took from us what he might offer to God. He offered those holy firstfruits of the flesh from the Virgin’s womb as a whole burnt offering to God. He stretched out his hands upon the cross, so that he might say: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Psalm 140:2). For we know that the Lord hung upon the cross toward evening, and our impieties were atoned for; otherwise they would have swallowed us up. Rightly we sang to him in the psalm: “And you will atone for our impieties” (Psalm 64:4).

You are the priest, you are the victim, you are the one who offers, you are the offering. He himself is the priest who has now entered within the veil. Of all who have borne flesh, he alone intercedes there for us. As a figure of this, in that first people and in that first temple, one priest entered the Holy of Holies (Hebrews 9:7), while the whole people stood outside; and he who alone entered within the veil offered sacrifice for the people standing outside.

For the Jews did not understand what was being done among that people; but now they do understand. Of them it was said: “As long as Moses is read, a veil is placed over their heart” (2 Corinthians 3:15). There the veil is a figure; but the figure will be removed, and the truth will appear. But when will the veil be removed? Hear the Apostle: “But when it shall turn to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away” (ibid., verse 16).

Therefore, with our sins and impieties atoned for through that evening sacrifice, we turn to the Lord, and the veil is removed. For this reason, when the Lord was crucified, the veil of the temple was torn. Thus we neither circumcise the flesh of the foreskin according to the rite of the Mosaic law, nor abstain from the meats which that same law calls unclean; nor do we observe their Sabbaths, new moons, and feast days in a carnal manner; nor do we sacrifice animals to God; nor do we celebrate the Passover in the same manner with a sheep and unleavened bread. And if there were any other ancient sacraments, all of which the Apostle calls “shadows of things to come,” because they signified things that were to be revealed in their own time, we receive them as revealed, so that, once the shadow has been removed, we may enjoy their bare light.

For by putting off the old person, we too are circumcised in the stripping away of the body of the flesh; and the foods which they forbid in animals, we avoid in our conduct; and we present our bodies as a living, holy, pleasing sacrifice to God. To him, in our desires, we intelligently pour out our souls in place of blood, and by the blood of Christ, as of an immaculate Lamb, we are cleansed from every iniquity. Because of the likeness of sinful flesh, he is also represented by a goat in the ancient sacrifices; nor does one who recognizes in him the greatest victim deny that he is a bull in the flesh of the cross.

When we find rest in him, we truly keep the Sabbath; the observance of the new moon is the sanctification of a new life; our Passover is Christ; and our unleavened bread is the sincerity of truth, having no leaven of oldness. Whatever else was foreshadowed for them by those ancient signs reaches its fulfillment in this one, whose kingdom will have no end.

For in him everything had to be fulfilled, who came not to abolish the law and the prophets but to fulfill them. Accordingly, he did not nullify those ancient signs of realities by censuring them, but changed them by fulfilling them, so that the signs announcing that Christ had already come would be different from those which had foretold that he was to come.

Therefore, since, as it is written in the Song of Songs, “the day has breathed forth” (Song of Songs 2:17), let the shadows be removed; let the spiritual meaning now shine forth; let the carnal observance now cease. Let us hear the Lord rejecting the ancient sacrifices of the Jews and openly promising the new sacrifice of Christ through the prophet Malachi, saying:

“I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord, and I will not accept an offering from your hand. For from the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name is great among the nations, and in every place sacrifice is made and a pure offering is offered to my name, because my name is great among the nations, says the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 1:10).

Certainly the Jews cannot deny here that he not only refuses to receive sacrifice from their hands, but that they do not even offer themselves to him with their hands. For there is one place established by the law of the Lord where he commanded them to offer sacrifices with their hands, and apart from that place he entirely prohibited it.

Thus, having lost this place on account of their merits, they do not dare to offer elsewhere the sacrifice which was permitted to be offered there alone. Behold, what the prophet said has been fulfilled in every respect: “I will not accept an offering from your hands.” Nor was this foretold and fulfilled in such a way that the prophetic sentence permits them to reply.

For although we do not offer flesh with our hands, we offer praise with our heart and mouth, according to what is said in the psalm: “Offer to God the sacrifice of praise” (Psalm 49:14). In this way the one who says, “I have no pleasure in you,” contradicts them.

Moreover, lest the Jews suppose that, if they do not offer, and God does not receive sacrifice from their hands, no sacrifice is offered—although he does not need it, since he needs none of our goods—nevertheless, because there is no sacrifice without one, and because sacrifice is useful not to him but to us, let them hear the Lord himself bearing witness. Indeed, let them open their eyes and see that from the rising of the sun to its setting, sacrifice is offered—not in one place, as had been established for them, but in every place; not to just any god, but to the God of Israel who foretold these things.

Thus elsewhere he says to his Church: “And your Redeemer, the God of Israel, shall be called the God of the whole earth” (Isaiah 54:5).

This pure sacrifice is offered to the God of Israel, not by one Jewish nation, from whose hands he foretold that he would not receive it, but by all the nations, which say: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord.” It is not offered in one place, as had been commanded in the earthly Jerusalem, but everywhere, even unto that Jerusalem; not according to the order of Aaron, but according to the order of Melchizedek.

For this was said to Christ, and was foretold beforehand concerning Christ alone: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:4).

What does “the Lord has sworn” mean except that he has confirmed it with unshakable truth? And what does “he will not repent” mean except that he will not change this priesthood for any other reason? For God does not repent as a human being does; rather, “repentance” is said of God whenever he changes something instituted by him which was believed to be permanent.

Therefore, when he says, “He will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,” he sufficiently shows that he did repent—that is, that he wished to change the priesthood which he had established according to the order of Aaron—as we see fulfilled with respect to both. For the priesthood of Aaron now exists in no temple, whereas the priesthood of Christ endures eternally in heaven.

The Apostle magnificently commends this priest and this priesthood when, distinguishing the grace of the Gospel from the ceremonial observances, he writes to the Hebrews:

“Those priests indeed were made many, because they were prevented by death from continuing; but he, because he remains forever, has an everlasting priesthood. Hence he is able to save forever, himself approaching God, since he always lives to intercede for them.

“For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens. He does not have daily need, like the priests, first to offer sacrifices for his own sins and then for those of the people. For he did this once for all by offering himself” (Hebrews 7:28).

And again:

“We have such a high priest, who has taken his seat at the right hand of the Majesty in the heavens, a minister of the holy places and of the true tabernacle which God established, and not man” (Hebrews 8:1).

Therefore, our holy fathers in the Old Testament offered victims to the one God and Creator of all, who himself willed that they be offered to him. Through their likeness he promised the true victim, through which he reconciled us to himself by the forgiveness of sins in Christ Jesus our Lord. Thus a likeness was offered to him, while the reality of the sacrifice was promised, to which the very reality, once restored, was to be offered in the passion of Christ’s body and blood.

The flesh and blood of this sacrifice were promised before Christ’s coming through victims by way of likeness; in Christ’s passion they were rendered through the reality itself; after Christ’s ascension they are celebrated as a memorial through the sacrament.

Accordingly, the first sacraments, which are observed and celebrated according to the law, were anticipatory signs of Christ who was to come. When Christ fulfilled them by his coming, they were done away with—and were done away with because they had been fulfilled. For he did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it.

Other things were instituted: greater in power, better in usefulness, easier in practice, fewer in number, as the righteousness of faith was revealed and those called into the liberty of the children of God were freed from the yoke of servitude, which was suited to a people hardened and devoted to the flesh. Such things in the Church are Christ’s baptism, Christ’s Eucharist, and Christ’s seal.

**Note:** That is, the sacrament of confirmation. Hence among the Greeks, when the bishop confirms, he uses this formula: “The seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit”; and the *Gelasian Order* has: “The sign of Christ unto eternal life. Amen.”

For this reason, by a most careful order of division, the Church of the living God, which is “the pillar and foundation of the truth,” distinguishes the times of Christ who was to come and who has come. Having set aside the sacrifices by which Christ, destined to suffer, was promised, it offers this sacrifice by which Christ, who has already suffered, is displayed.

He is therefore the true priest because he offered himself as a true victim for us, as the Apostle testifies, saying:

“Be imitators of God, therefore, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma” (Ephesians 5:1–2).

Thus forgiveness of sins takes place in that priest and sacrifice: that is, through the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus. Through him, once our sins have been cleansed, we are reconciled to God.

For human beings are separated from God only by sins. In this life, their cleansing does not occur through our own power but through divine mercy, by his forgiveness and not by our strength. For even whatever small virtue is called ours has been granted to us through his goodness.

### 5.

Therefore grace was granted to us through the Mediator, so that, defiled by the flesh of sin, we might be cleansed through the likeness of the flesh of sin—namely, through that which we were and were not.

For we were human beings, but we were not righteous; in his incarnation, however, there was human nature, but it was righteous, not sinful. This is the mediation by which a hand was extended to those who had fallen and were lying prostrate.

This is the seed arranged through angels, in whose proclamations light was also given, because the worship of the one God was commanded and this coming Mediator was promised.

Through the use of the sacrament in faith, the righteous of ancient times also merited cleansing by living piously, as the blessed Apostle Peter plainly testifies to certain people who were seeking justification in the law, saying:

“Why do you test God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear? But through faith in the Lord Jesus we believe that we are saved, in the same manner as they also were” (Acts 15:10–11).

Thus the entire multitude of human beings, for whose liberation from the dominion of demons Christ came, possesses in him the most merciful cleansing of mind, spirit, and body.

For this reason he assumed the whole human being without sin, so that he might heal from the plague of sins the whole of that which constitutes a human being.

The grace of God could not have been commended more graciously than by this: that the one and only Son of God, remaining unchangeably what he was in himself, should assume a human being and grant human beings the hope of his love through a human mediator. Through this mediator, human beings might be united to him who was so far removed from them: the immortal from mortals, the unchangeable from the changeable, the righteous from the impious, the blessed from the wretched.

And because he naturally implanted in us the desire to be blessed and immortal, he, remaining blessed and assuming mortality, granted us what we love and taught us, by enduring what we fear, to despise it.

By this grace of God, through which he has shown toward us his great mercy, we are governed in this life by faith, and after this life, by the vision itself of unchangeable truth, we are brought to the fullest perfection.

### 6.

This grace of our cleansing and redemption, which the Lord and Savior commended to us in the sacrament of his body and blood, he proclaimed long before he suffered among the peoples; but on the day before he suffered—that is, on the night when he was betrayed—he delivered it to his disciples at supper.

For the blessed evangelist John, immediately after the miracle of the five loaves by which five thousand people were fed, relates that he withdrew to the mountain, avoiding the crowds which, moved by wonder at so great a sign, wanted to seize him and make him king.

Then, as night came, he walked upon the sea, came to Capernaum, and there, on the following day, when the crowds encountered him and, among other questions, asked, “What shall we do, so that we may perform the works of God?” he answered them: “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent.”

When they replied, “What sign, then, do you perform, so that we may see and believe you? What do you work? Our fathers ate manna in the desert, as it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat,’” Jesus said to them:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is the one who descends from heaven and gives life to the world.”

And shortly afterward:

“I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst.”

And again:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: Whoever believes in me has eternal life. I am the bread of life. Your fathers ate manna in the desert, and they died. This is the bread descending from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he may not die. I am the living bread which came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world.”

And again, after some intervening words:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day. For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him. Just as the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me.”

After this the Evangelist added: “He said these things while teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum” (John 6:28, 35, 47, 54, 59).

All this, as the text of the Gospel according to John itself shows, plainly took place a full year before the Lord’s passion. For, as the same evangelist writes, when the miracle of the five loaves occurred, “The Passover was near, the feast of the Jews” (ibid., verse 4). Nevertheless, he records that the Lord came to his passion not at that Passover, but at the Passover of the following year.

For this reason, at that paschal supper when the Lord was betrayed, the blessed John mentions nothing about the mystery of his body and blood. Evidently he had explained it more fully and sublimely in the preceding portions of his Gospel, and he knew that what had been handed down at the same supper, in commemoration of the Lord’s passion for the salvation of the faithful, had been carefully commended by the other three evangelists.

Matthew’s words are these:

“While they were eating, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat; this is my body.’ And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: ‘Drink from it, all of you. For this is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins’” (Matthew 26:26–28).

Mark says:

“While they were eating, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, gave it to them, and said: ‘Take; this is my body.’ And taking the cup and giving thanks, he gave it to them. And they all drank from it. And he said to them: ‘This is my blood of the New Testament, which is poured out for many’” (Mark 14:22–24).

Luke’s account is expressed in these words:

“Taking the cup, he gave thanks and said: ‘Take this and divide it among yourselves. For I tell you that from now on I shall not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.’ And taking bread, he gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying: ‘This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which is poured out for you’” (Luke 22:17–20).

The blessed Paul, recalling the mystery of that most holy supper, says among other things:

“For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread, and giving thanks, broke it and said: ‘This is my body, which will be delivered for you; do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the New Testament in my blood. Do this whenever you drink it in remembrance of me’” (1 Corinthians 11:23–25).

How great and ineffable is this mystery of salvation and sacrament of devotion, foretold with such solemn testimony and commended with such truth, that the Lord asserted this to be his body and blood before his body and blood were delivered for us! For no one can comprehend the sacraments of the Lord’s passion and of his body and blood according to the majesty of the reality.

### 7. (FULGENTIUS, Letter 14 to Ferrandus, no. 43)

It must also be carefully noted that at the same supper the Lord both ate the Jewish Passover, which had to be removed,

**Note:** In Fulgentius one reads *offeri*, “to be offered,” but whether one reads *offeri* or *auferri*, “to be removed,” either reading is sound. Certainly the reading offered by our Florus does not seem to be rejected: for at the Lord’s supper the Passover of the Jews was reaching its end and had to be removed.

and gave the sacrament of his body and blood, which had to be instituted for the salvation of the faithful.

“Desiring, I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.” Therefore he ate the Passover by which he was signified as destined to suffer, before he voluntarily suffered for us. He ate the Passover of the Jews, by which Christ was promised, in order to come to our Passover, which is Christ sacrificed.

### 8. (AUGUSTINE, Letter 54 to Januarius)

The Gospel plainly says that, while they were eating, Jesus took bread and blessed it. For it had also said above: “When evening had come, he was reclining with the twelve.” And while they were eating he said: “One of you will betray me.” Afterwards he delivered the sacrament.

From this it is perfectly clear that, when the disciples first received the body and blood of the Lord, they did not receive them fasting. Nevertheless, the universal Church must in no way be criticized because the sacrament is always received by those who are fasting.

For it pleased the Holy Spirit that, in honor of so great a sacrament, the Lord’s sacrament should enter the mouth of a Christian before any other food. For this reason that custom is observed throughout the world. It does not follow that, because the Lord gave it after the meal, the brothers should therefore gather to receive that sacrament after eating or dining, or that they should mix it with their meals, as those whom the Apostle rebuked and corrected were doing.

For he says: “When you come together, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper” (1 Corinthians 11:18), calling that very reception of the Eucharist the Lord’s supper.

“For each one,” he says, “takes his own supper beforehand to eat” (ibid., verse 21). Hence he says that it was received unworthily by those who did not distinguish it from other foods by the singular reverence due to it.

Immediately after saying that he eats and drinks judgment upon himself, he added: “not discerning the body of the Lord” (ibid., verse 29).

For the Savior, in order to commend more forcefully the greatness of that mystery, wished to impress it last upon the hearts and memory of the disciples, from whom he was about to depart for his passion. Therefore he did not prescribe in what order it should thereafter be received, so that he might preserve this place for the apostles, through whom he had determined to order the Churches.

### 9. (CYPRIAN, Letter 63 to Caecilius)

Nor, because the Lord offered the cup after supper, should we therefore celebrate the sacrifice of the Lord’s day after supper.

It was fitting for Christ to be offered toward evening, so that the very hour of the sacrifice might display the setting and evening of the world, just as it is written concerning the paschal lamb in Exodus: “And the whole assembly of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it toward evening” (Exodus 12:6).

And again in the Psalms: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Psalm 140:2).

### 10. (AUGUSTINE, Letter 149 to Paulinus, no. 16)

We celebrate the Lord’s resurrection in the morning.

But when the Apostle speaks about this sacrament, he says: “Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you may not come together for judgment.” Immediately he adds: “I will arrange the rest when I come” (1 Corinthians 11:33–34).

From this it may be understood that, since it would have been too much to set out for them in the letter the entire order of what was to be done—the order which the whole Church throughout the world observes—he indicates that it had been established in such a way that none of these variations alters it.

Likewise, when he writes to Timothy: “Therefore, first of all I ask that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made” (1 Timothy 2:1), he is understood to have established what every, or nearly every, Church practices.

By “supplications” we understand those made in the celebration of the sacraments, before that which is on the Lord’s table begins to be blessed; by “prayers,” those made when it is blessed and sanctified and broken for distribution. Nearly every Church concludes this entire blessing with the Lord’s Prayer.

“Intercessions,” or, as some manuscripts have it, “petitions,” are made when the people are blessed. For then the bishops, as advocates, present those entrusted to them to the most merciful power by the laying on of hands.

When these things have been completed, and the people have partaken of so great a sacrament, thanksgiving brings everything to a close; the Apostle also commended it as the last of these things in the words he used.

The chief reason for saying this was that, after these matters had been briefly prescribed and indicated, what follows should not be thought deserving of neglect: “for all human beings, for kings, and for all who are in positions of authority, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all devotion and chastity” (1 Timothy 2:2).

No one, in accordance with the weakness of human thought, should suppose that these things ought not to be done for those from whom the Church was suffering persecution, since the members of Christ were to be gathered from every kind of human being.

Accordingly, he adds and says: “For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (ibid., verse 3).

And lest anyone say that there could be a way of salvation in good conduct and the worship of the one almighty God, or in participation in the body and blood of Christ, he says:

“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus.”

Thus what he had said—“he wills all human beings to be saved”—is not to be understood as accomplished in any other way than through our mediator, God, who was always the Word, but became the human being Christ Jesus when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

For this reason Christ is called the mediator between God and human beings: God and human being between immortal God and mortal humanity, reconciling humanity to God; true king, true priest.

Therefore a human being asks to be ruled by Christ the King; and if he should sin, he is expiated by the same priest, Christ.

### 11.

**Note:** Here alone the editions begin.

When the faithful have first assembled together and are standing in the house of God, after the singing of divine praises, after the reading of the Apostles and the Gospels, and sometimes also after the sermon and address of the teachers, with the confession of the Creed and the people’s offering also added, and the consecration of the sacraments begun—in all of which the minds of those standing there are prepared to think about and desire divine and heavenly things—the priest stands at the altar.

About to celebrate the divine mysteries, he prays by greeting the Church and greets it by praying, saying:

### 12. “The Lord be with you.”

This word of greeting is shown to have been composed not by human judgment but taken from the authority of divine Scripture, where it is frequently found both in the singular and in the plural.

In the singular, as the angel said to blessed Mary: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you” (Luke 1:28); and as he likewise said in greeting to Gideon: “The Lord is with you, strongest of men” (Judges 6:12).

In the plural, however, as it is read in the Book of Ruth—which, like the other books of sacred Scripture, certainly contains divine and mystical meanings—that Boaz greeted the reapers by saying: “The Lord be with you.” They in turn answered him: “May the Lord bless you” (Ruth 2:4).

Likewise, in the historical account of the Book of Chronicles, a prophet sent by God is found to have greeted Asa, king of Judah, with his army, invoking God’s aid as they returned victorious from battle. For he said: “The Lord is with you, because you were with him.” And he added: “If you seek him, you will find him; but if you abandon him, he will abandon you” (1 Chronicles 28:9).

From this it is clear that, just as nothing worse can happen to a human being than to abandon God and be abandoned by God, so conversely nothing is better than to possess God and be with God.

And since to greet means nothing other than to wish salvation, this is the true greeting: the wishing of true salvation—that is, wishing that the Lord be with his Church as in his temple, according to what the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Corinthians 3:16).

The Church has the Lord dwelling with it, illuminating, guiding, and protecting it, so that he may be its God and it may be his people, as the prophet promised, saying: “I will dwell and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people” (2 Corinthians 6:16).

Thus, while through so great a gift of blessedness the Church of God both possesses the Lord and is possessed by God, so that it is itself the Lord’s inheritance and the Lord is its portion of inheritance, what the Psalmist says is fulfilled in it:

“Blessed is the nation whose Lord is its God, the people whom he chose as his inheritance” (Psalm 32:12).

For this is the supreme good of a human being: to possess God and to be possessed by God; to love him alone, serve him alone, and cling to him alone, so that the devoted soul may say to him: “But for me, it is good to cling to God” (Psalm 72:28).

And again: “My soul has clung to you” (Psalm 62:9), so that, clinging to the Lord, it may become one spirit with him, as the Apostle says: “Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17).

The Apostle himself also greets in this way in his letters, sometimes saying: “The Lord be with all of you”; sometimes: “May the God of peace be with all of you”; and sometimes: “May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen” (Galatians 6:18).

At other times, distinguishing the persons and invoking the whole Trinity, he greets them thus: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you” (2 Corinthians 13:13).

In all these expressions, when he writes to the faithful, he wishes for them what the priest standing at the altar wishes for the Church: namely, that, while possessing God, they may not be abandoned by him.

Rightly, therefore, after receiving so salutary a greeting from the priest, the Church itself prays in return and, by praying, greets the priest again, saying:

### 13. “And with your spirit.”

For the Church could find nothing better to wish for the priest than what the priest wishes for the Church: namely, that the same Lord who deigns to be with the Church may also deign to be with the priest’s spirit.

Thus, in both, that gracious promise of the Lord may be fulfilled, by which, as he was about to ascend into heaven, he promised all the faithful, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

This is the great good which the priest and the Church wish and ask for one another: that, just as we are illuminated by his grace, strengthened by his presence, and fortified by his protection, we may perceive him always remaining with us, as he promised.

The Apostle also greets in this way on several occasions, in the plural, as we mentioned above, when he says: “The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen” (Galatians 6:18).

In the singular, when he greets Timothy, he says: “The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.”

And rightly it is wished that the Lord be with a human being’s spirit, because the human being was created in spirit and rational mind according to the image and likeness of God. There the human being is capable of divine grace and illumination, so that, insofar as it is granted to him, he may perceive the sweetness of his goodness and the splendor of his presence, so that what the Psalmist says may be fulfilled in him:

“Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33:9).

And again: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened, and your faces will not be ashamed” (ibid., verse 6).

For when the human spirit has been sanctified by God’s indwelling, the human being also becomes a temple in the body. Hence the Apostle says: “Your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit whom you have from God” (1 Corinthians 6:19).

Likewise, the episcopal greeting to the people, “Peace be with you,” or “Peace to you,” was not invented by human judgment but was likewise taken from the authority of sacred Scripture.

For in the Old Testament the angel is found to have said to the prophet Daniel: “Do not fear, man of desires; peace to you. Be strong and courageous” (Daniel 10:19).

And in the New Testament, that is, in the Gospel, the Lord is almost always read to have greeted the Apostles in this way, saying: “Peace to you.”

He also commended this same form of greeting to those Apostles, saying: “Whatever house you enter, greet it, saying: ‘Peace to this house.’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, your peace will return to you” (Matthew 10:13).

Rightly, therefore, the successors of the Apostles, that is, the bishops of the Churches, use this greeting when greeting the house of God, where all ought to be sons of peace:

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9).

Thus, with the greeting of peace resting upon them, it may be fruitful both for those who give the greeting and for those who receive it.

The peace which is invoked for the faithful either through an angel, through the Lord, or through the pastors of the Churches is not worldly or passing, but divine and eternal. It reconciles us to God, fortifies us by his protection against the temptations of the devil and the adversities of the world, and joins us in tranquil love to our neighbors.

For the Lord commended this peace to his Church, saying:

“Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you.”

And immediately he added:

“Not as the world gives do I give to you” (John 14:27).

Again he says concerning it:

“I have spoken these things to you so that you may have peace in me. In the world you will have distress, but take courage: I have conquered the world” (John 16:33).

The Apostle also implores this peace for the faithful, saying:

“And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:7).

This peace must be preserved in times of suffering and faithfully maintained everywhere, but with all the greater attention and devotion at that hour when one stands in the house of the Lord and in God’s presence, and the vows and offerings of all are presented upon the sacred altars.

For we cannot otherwise make the divine majesty favorable to us unless we sincerely strive to fulfill what the Lord specifically commands concerning this matter:

“If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:23–24).

### 14. (GREGORY, *Homily 8 on Ezekiel*)

In this matter we must consider, since every fault is expiated by an offering, how serious is the fault of discord, for which the offering is not accepted.

Therefore, even if our neighbor is far away and greatly separated from us, we must go to him in mind, submit our spirit to him, and appease him through humility and goodwill. Thus, when the Creator sees such an offering of our mind, he may release us from sin, because he accepts the offering in place of the fault.

We have learned from the voice of Truth that a servant who owed ten thousand talents, when he repented, received remission of his debt from the Lord. But because he did not forgive his fellow servant, who owed him one hundred denarii, the debt was ordered to be exacted from him—the very debt which had already been forgiven him.

From these words it is evident that, if we do not forgive from the heart what is committed against us, the debt which we were rejoicing had already been forgiven us through repentance is demanded again.

15. (St. Cyprian.) Above all, it is necessary that, when we stand at prayer, when such holy and venerable mysteries are celebrated before the eyes of God, we devote ourselves to prayer with our whole heart. Let every carnal and worldly thought depart, and let the mind think of nothing except that very thing for which it is praying. Therefore, before that most sacred prayer, after the preface has been spoken, the priest also prepares the minds of the brethren by saying: “Lift up your hearts,” so that when he receives the response, “We have them with the Lord,” they may be reminded that they ought to think of nothing other than the Lord; that the breast may be closed against the adversary and opened to God alone; and that it may not allow God’s enemy to approach during the time of prayer. For he frequently slips in and penetrates, and, subtly deceiving us, turns our prayers away from God, so that we have one thing in our heart and another on our lips. When we pray, it is not the sound of the voice but the mind and understanding that ought to pray with sincere intention, as though there were anything else we ought more fully to consider than the one with whom we are speaking.

How do we ask to be heard by God when we ourselves do not hear? We wish God to remember us when we ourselves do not remember ourselves—that is, when we pray, to offend God’s majesty by negligence in prayer; to be awake in our eyes but asleep in our heart, although a Christian ought, even while his eyes sleep, to keep watch in his heart, as it is written in the person of the Church speaking in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5:2).

Therefore the Apostle carefully and prudently admonishes us, saying: “Be constant in prayer, keeping watch in it” (Col. 4:2), teaching and showing that those are able to obtain from God what they ask who, as he himself sees, keep watch in prayer.

What, then, does it mean to have our hearts above, except to seek the things that are above and to set our minds on the things that are above? To seek them, namely, by loving them; to set our minds on them by understanding them, as the Apostle likewise admonishes in the same passage, saying: “If you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on those that are on earth” (Col. 3:1).

The Psalmist shows us that this ascent of our hearts to God—from the valley of weeping, that is, from the humility of affliction—takes place not by our own strength but by God’s help, saying: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has set ascents in his heart in the valley of tears” (Ps. 83:6). For an ascent cannot be beneficial unless we first remember that we must ascend from the valley of humility.

A valley is a depressed place in the earth. The Lord himself taught that we must ascend from the valley of weeping when he deigned to humble himself for us even unto death on the cross and to suffer. Let us not abandon this example. The martyrs understood this valley of weeping, and from it they ascended in order to be crowned. Holy love lifts us toward things above and sets us aflame for eternal things.

The soul bound by earthly love has, as it were, birdlime on its wings and cannot fly. But when cleansed of its affections and of the most filthy things of the world, it is like a bird with outstretched wings: released by its two wings, namely, the two commandments of love of God and love of neighbor, it flies to the Lord. It ascends by flying because it ascends by loving—to that heavenly Jerusalem, the mother of us all, which is in heaven.

From her we are pilgrims in this life, and we sigh for our return to her, miserable and laboring until we return to her. Nor did our fellow citizens, the angels, abandon us in our pilgrimage; rather, they announced to us that the King himself would come to us. And he came to us, and among us he was despised by us; afterward he remained with us and taught us to be despised, because he was despised; he taught us to endure, because he endured; he taught us to suffer, because he suffered; and he promised that we would rise again, because he rose again, showing in himself what we ought to hope for.

If, therefore, the prophets and ancient fathers, before the Lord Jesus Christ came in the flesh, before he died, rose again, and ascended into heaven, nevertheless sighed for that city, how much ought we to desire the place to which he himself went before us and from which he never departed?

The ancient priests, who cared less for the elegance of speech than for the salvation and edification of the people, used to say “Lift up your hearts” not in elevated but in ordinary language, for the sake of the uneducated and the country people, so that so great a matter might be commended more fully to everyone’s understanding.

The priest still admonishes us and says:

16. “Let us give thanks to our Lord God.” [Note: [Col. 0029D] See the sermon of St. Augustine, Sermon 227, addressed to the infants, on the Sacraments.]

Thanksgiving is always owed by us to the Father of lights, from whom, as Scripture testifies, without any doubt every good gift and every perfect gift descends. No one is blessed by God’s gifts who is ungrateful to the giver, because even this—that we are commanded to have our hearts above amid the sacred mysteries—we are able to do only with his help, by whose command we are admonished.

And therefore it follows that, for this great good of a heart lifted above, we should not attribute glory to ourselves, as though it resulted from our own strength, but give thanks to our Lord God. For we are immediately reminded: “This is fitting; this is just.” We must always remember where these words come from, by what actions and with how great a holiness they are commended; we must retain and possess what we receive, and give thanks to the giver.

Although receiving and possessing are ours, nevertheless we possess what we have received, because Truth says through the Apostle to the proud man who gloried impiously in what he had, as though he had it from himself: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7.)

Rightly, therefore, in that true and unique sacrifice of the Lord we are admonished to give thanks to our God, so that a person may acknowledge that, if he lives well in any respect, he has it through God’s grace, and that he will not obtain from any other source the perfection of his love of righteousness, because thought makes a person devout.

This is that wisdom called piety, by which the Father of lights is worshiped, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes. He is worshiped through the sacrifice of praise and acts of thanksgiving, so that his worshiper may glory not in himself but in him.

“For,” says the same Apostle, “we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God” (1 Cor. 2:12), so that we may know the things given to us by God. And what is the spirit of this world except the spirit of pride, by which the foolish heart of those who knew God but did not glorify him as God by giving thanks was darkened?

Let us therefore consider these things and always render thanks to God for all his benefits. Among all his works, there is nothing that we ought either to consider more willingly or to praise more sweetly than this: that Christ became humble and willingly descended to the human being who, having fallen, had been cast down to the depths, so that the one who lay there might at least believe that he could be raised up.

Finally, in order to lift our hope into heaven, he first lifted up our flesh; and so that we might not doubt that what he promised us would follow, he has already gone there before us with what he received from us.

17. (Fulgentius, Letter 14 to Ferrandus, no. 44.) Therefore, especially in the sacrifice of Christ’s body, we begin with thanksgiving, so that we may show Christ as given to us in truth, not as still to be given; and, in giving thanks to God, may recognize in the offering of Christ’s body and blood that Christ is no longer to be slain for our iniquities, but has been slain; nor are we to be redeemed by that blood, but have been redeemed.

For true is the preaching of blessed Peter, who says: “You were redeemed from your vain manner of life inherited from your fathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood, as of a spotless and undefiled Lamb, Christ” (1 Pet. 1:18).

Thus, when the priest rightly admonishes us and says, “Let us give thanks to our Lord God,” the Church responds:

18. “It is worthy and just.”

For what could be more worthy of God, or what more just thing could be rendered to him by us, than that we should return due thanks for God’s such great mercy, to which we cannot make an adequate return, hearing the Apostle exhort and say: “Giving thanks to God the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the inheritance of the saints in light; who has delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins” (Col. 1:12–14)?

“For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son,” and that Son tasted death by the grace of God for all. We are therefore delivered through this grace from the power of darkness—that is, from the devil and his angels—and transferred into the kingdom of the Son of God’s love, so that we may become a chosen race, a royal priesthood, possessing in that same Son, through his blood, redemption and the forgiveness of sins.

What more worthy thing can we do than what the blessed Apostle Peter admonishes, saying: “Declare the mighty works of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light; once you were no people, but now you are God’s people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy” (1 Pet. 2:9)?

The priest therefore confirms this response of the Church and, with his mind lifted toward God, proclaims with the whole Church acknowledging it with him:

19. “Truly it is worthy and just, fitting and salutary.”

What is just is also fitting; but the repetition of the expression confirms the truth, for justice and equity are one and the same thing, as we sing of the Lord in the Psalter: “He will judge the world in justice and the peoples in equity” (Ps. 95:10).

“Salutary” is said of what is health-giving and what confers salvation. Truly, then, it is worthy that we should give thanks without ceasing, in accordance with God’s great benefits; just, in accordance with our obedience; fitting, by the very weight of reason; and salutary, through the evident fruit of salvation, by which those who praise God are saved and the ungrateful are rejected by his judgment.

For those who faithfully praise God are truly saved, as is sung in the Psalm: “Praising, I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies” (Ps. 17:4).

But the ungrateful are rejected, as the Lord himself clearly shows in the Gospel. Of the ten lepers cleansed by his power, he praised the one who returned humbly to him and gave thanks with a loud voice, and he saved him through the grace of faith, saying: “Was no one found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner?” And immediately he added mercifully: “Rise, go your way; your faith has saved you” (Luke 17:18–19).

As for the other nine, although they believed that they could be cleansed through him when they cried out with one voice, saying, “Jesus, Teacher, have mercy on us,” nevertheless, because they proved ungrateful toward so great a power, he showed that he regarded them as faithless, saying: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine?” (Matt. 25:12.)

For God’s not knowing is rejection; hence he will also say to some: “Truly I tell you, I do not know you.” From this it is clearly shown how great an evil it is to neglect the thanksgiving owed to God, when he rejected, as though they were faithless, even those whom he had cleansed as believers, because of the guilt of this neglect.

We ought always and everywhere to give thanks—that is, at every time and in every place—so that what we sing in the Psalm may be fulfilled in us: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33:2). And again: “Bless the Lord, my soul, in every place of his dominion” (Ps. 102:22).

20. (Augustine, Exposition II on Psalm 33, no. 4.) Who, then, is the one who blesses and gives thanks to the Lord at all times, except the humble in heart? Our Lord taught this very humility in his body, because when he commends his body and blood, he commends his humility.

Be humble if you wish to bless the Lord at all times, with his praise always in your mouth. Job also blessed the Lord not only when everything was abundant for him, when we read that he was rich. Everything was taken away at one moment, and he fulfilled what is written in this Psalm, saying: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away. As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened.” Then he added: “Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

Behold the example of one who blesses at all times. He did not have what he could hold on to, but he had what he could praise. In the praise of his God he rested as though amid an abundance of possessions. God was his consolation, so that he would not be endangered by the loss of his property.

For did he lose God, even though he lost what God had given? It is greater to possess the one who gives than the things he gives. If the things he gives are beautiful, how much more beautiful is the one who gives them? If they are great, how much greater is the giver himself?

And certainly, the things God gives in this earthly life either leave us while we are alive or are left by us at death. But God himself, an eternal possession, always present, never abandons the one who possesses him.

Let the vows of the faithful therefore be pure; let temporal good become worthless, and let the eternal come. Let the devout soul cling to God, suspended toward him in prayer, and, joined to him through spiritual embraces, desire what he himself gives along with himself.

How much will God give us if he does not wish to give us himself? If worldly goods are available, let them provide the material for acts of mercy; if they are lacking, let their absence provide a faithful opportunity for patience.

Through such devotion, thanks are given to God in every place, because he who is present everywhere recognizes his praiser everywhere. Even when the mouth is at rest and the tongue is silent, the faithful soul blesses him through the hidden affection of the heart, performing in silence what is sung in the Psalm: “Bless the Lord, my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name” (Ps. 102:1).

Therefore, whoever seeks a holy and suitable place in which to pray and give thanks to God, cleanse your inner self, drive every evil desire from it, and prepare for yourself a secluded place in the peace of your heart, wishing to pray in a temple. Pray within yourself, and always act so that you may be God’s temple. For God hears in the place where he dwells.

21. “It is truly worthy and just, fitting and salutary, that we should always and everywhere give thanks to you.”

He then adds to whom the prayer is directed, saying: “Lord, holy Father, almighty, eternal God,” and by whom the same prayer is directed, adding: “Through Christ our Lord.”

When he says “Lord,” therefore, this refers to the subjection of creation, of which it is also sung in the Psalm: “For all things serve you” (Ps. 15:1).
