And elsewhere: “I said to the Lord: You are my God, for you have no need of my goods.” For what does “my goods” mean except “those given by you”? How could one from whom every good is given need any good? Therefore he is truly Lord, who does not need his servant. And what servant does he need?

What he adds, “holy Father,” refers either specifically to the generation of the only-begotten Son, in which he is coeternal and coequal with the Father—of which the Prophet also says: “Who can recount his generation?” (Isa. 35:8)—or generally to the adoption of all the children of God.

Its grace is so great that, although he had one unique Son, he did not wish him to be alone; rather, so that he might have brothers, he adopted those who would possess eternal life with him. For them he himself, praying to the Father in the same words, said: “Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me” (John 17:11).

Thus the address “holy Father” is proper to the only Son by nature and common to all adopted children by grace. Through that grace he also granted that those who pray should say: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. 6:9).

He is truly almighty and eternal God: almighty in the power by which he created, sustains, and governs all things. Scripture truly says: “Nothing is impossible for you.”

22. (The same author, in the same work.) Yet he is so almighty that he never overturns the ordinances of his own reason. True eternity also belongs to him: for him, to be is perpetual being. Without beginning, and therefore receiving no end, he likewise admits no change.

The whole prayer and thanksgiving, which we owe always and everywhere, is directed and offered to God the Father through Christ our Lord, as through the mediator and reconciler of God and human beings. Of him the Apostle says: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a redemption for all” (1 Tim. 2:5).

Although in the nature of his divinity he is one with the Father, by assuming our nature he became our mediator with the Father. He is therefore mediator between God and human beings because he is God with the Father and human with human beings—not a human mediator apart from divinity, nor a divine mediator apart from humanity.

Divinity without humanity is not mediator; humanity without divinity is not mediator. Rather, between divinity alone and humanity alone, the mediator is the human divinity and divine humanity of Christ. He also offered himself in his passion for us, so that we might be the body of so great a head, according to the form of a servant.

He offered this form, and in this form he was offered, because according to this form he is mediator. In this form he is priest; in this form, sacrifice.

Through him, therefore, the Church offers her petitions and praises to God the Father, knowing that through him alone she can receive what she asks and through him alone can be pleasing in what she praises, as he promises in the Gospel, saying: “Truly, truly, I tell you, whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John 16:23).

This is the grace of mediation through which the Church is heard, in accordance with which the Apostle also exhorts us, saying: “Through him, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Heb. 13:15), that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name.

For this same mediator between God and human beings—God above us, human for our sake—intercedes for us with the Father through his humanity; through his divinity he hears and grants together with the Father, as he himself testifies, saying: “Because I am going to the Father, and whatever you ask in my name, I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son” (John 14:12).

Regarding this mediation and advocacy, the blessed Apostle John also says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:2), because the one who intercedes for us with the Father through his humanity is the same one who, through his divinity, makes propitiation for us with the Father.

Thus the priest prays for the Church, and the Church prays for the priest, just as the Apostle prays for the people and the people pray for the Apostle, who says: “Pray together for us also, that God may open for us a door for the word” (Col. 4:3).

The Church also prayed for Peter when he was in chains, just as Peter prayed for the Church, because all the members pray for one another. The head intercedes for all; of him it is written: “He is at the right hand of God, and he also intercedes for us” (Rom. 8:34).

23. (Gregory, Moralia, Book XXII, no. 42.) For the only-begotten Son’s interceding for a human being means that, before the coeternal Father, he presents himself as human; and his praying for human nature means that he has assumed that same nature into the height of his divinity.

The Lord therefore intercedes for us not by voice but by compassion, because, by assuming what he did not wish to be condemned in the elect, he preserved it. Since, by rising again, he raised above the angels what he had placed in the tomb by dying, the priest rightly adds and says:

[Col. 0034C] 24. “Through whom your majesty is praised by the angels.”

For this is the ineffable glory of our Savior and mediator, who, as the Apostle says, after making purification for sins, “sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high, having become as much superior to the angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs” (Heb. 1:3–4).

Explaining the greatness of this name elsewhere, he says: “Therefore God highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Phil. 2:9).

Thus, through the same mediator, not only the Church of human beings on earth but also the Church of angels in heaven praises, worships, and trembles before the majesty of God the Father.

25. (Augustine, Sermon 340, no. 11.) The whole and one Church must be understood in this way: not only that part which journeys on earth from the rising of the sun to its setting, praising the name of the Lord and, after the captivity of the old condition, singing a new song, but also that part which has remained united to God in heaven ever since it was created and has experienced no evil of its fall.

This latter part remains blessed in the holy angels, and rightly assists its pilgrim portion, because the two will be one in the fellowship of eternity, and even now they are one through the bond of love.

This Church that journeys on earth has been redeemed from every sin by the blood of the Mediator who had no sin; [lacuna] is not his. “If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Rom. 8:32).

For Christ did not die for the angels. Yet human redemption itself is also redemption for the angels, because through Christ we are restored to friendship after the enmity that sins created between human beings and the holy angels; and through the redemption of human beings the losses caused by the angelic fall are repaired.

For this reason the Apostle says that all things in Christ are being restored, both those in heaven and those on earth (Eph. 1:10). The things in heaven are restored in him when what fell from there among the angels is restored to human beings. The things on earth are restored when the human beings predestined for eternal life are renewed from the oldness of corruption.

Thus, through that singular sacrifice in which the mediator was sacrificed, heavenly things are reconciled with earthly things and earthly things with heavenly things, because, as the Apostle says: “In him all the fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether on earth or in heaven” (Col. 1:19–20).

Of him the same Apostle says elsewhere: “He is the head of the body, the Church” (ibid., verse 18). And again: “You have been filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power” (Col. 2:10).

All the righteous who have existed from the beginning of the world therefore have Christ as their head. They believed that he would come, whereas we already believe that he has come; and they too were healed through faith in him, just as we are.

Thus he is the head of the whole city, Jerusalem, with all the faithful counted from beginning to end, together with the legions and armies of angels, so that there may be one city under one king and one province under one emperor, happy in perpetual peace and salvation, praising the Lord without end in a blessed consummation.

The difference among these three orders of spirits—that is, angels, dominions, and powers—which are said to praise, worship, and tremble before the divine majesty, is as follows.

26. (Gregory, Homily 34 on the Gospels, no. 8 and following.) Angels, which in Latin are interpreted as “messengers,” indicate their office to us by their very name, because, sent by God, they announce his will to human beings.

Thus we read in the Old Testament that angels were sent to Abraham, Lot, Jacob, Moses, Joshua, Daniel, and Tobiah; and frequently in the New Testament as well. Hence the Psalmist says: “Bless the Lord, you his angels, mighty in strength, who do his word, obeying the voice of his command” (Ps. 102:20).

And again: “He makes his angels spirits” (Ps. 103:4), as though he were plainly saying that the one who always has them as spirits also makes them angels—that is, messengers—whenever he wills.

“Dominions” are also called those ranks of angels that excel through marvelous power, because the other orders are subjected to them for obedience.

“Powers” are likewise called those who have received this more powerfully than others in their order, so that opposing powers are subjected to their dominion. By their power they are restrained from being able to tempt human hearts as much as they wish.

These blessed and exalted heavenly spirits therefore praise the majesty of God through Christ our Lord, as they are joyfully addressed in the Psalm: “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights. Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers” (Ps. 148:1–2).

Of them God also speaks in the Book of Job, saying: “When the stars were made, all my angels praised me with a loud voice” (Job 38:7).

They also worship that same divine majesty, as is said to God in Ezra’s hymn of confession: “You alone, Lord God, have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, and all that is in them; you give life to all these things, and the armies of heaven worship you” (2 Esd. 9:6).

They also tremble, as is said figuratively of them in the Book of Job: “The pillars of heaven tremble and are terrified at his command” (Job 26:11).

27. (The same author, Moralia, Book XVII, no. 44.) For even the powers of heaven, which behold God without ceasing, tremble in the very contemplation of him.

Yet their fear is not fear that it may be punitive for them, but fear of wonder. Since, then, there is such devotion among those who praise in heaven, such reverence among those who worship, and such trembling among those who wonder, let the human being to whom it was said, “Why is earth proud?” consider these things and hear the Apostle’s admonition: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. 2:12).

The priest continues in the praises of God and says:

28. “The heavens, the powers of the heavens, and the blessed Seraphim celebrate together with a shared exultation.”

What is implied is what was already said above: “your majesty.” For not only do the angels, dominions, and powers, as stated earlier, praise, worship, and tremble before it; the heavens, the powers of the heavens, and the Seraphim also celebrate it together—that is, they celebrate it in common, praising it with harmonious devotion and shared joy.

For a celebration is an assembly of people in praise, and we call something “celebrated” when it is performed in a celebrated—that is, very numerous—assembly.

That blessed people of angels therefore celebrates and celebrates together the majesty of God. Of its indescribable multitude it is written: “A thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7:10), because God’s face is always present before them, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Their angels in heaven continually see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 18:10).

When he is contemplated and loved without weariness, he is also praised; the pure joy of the chosen citizens is enacted, and all rejoice with one another in their assembly.

This is the eternal house of God, of which it is sung in the Psalms: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; for ever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83:5). And again: “As the dwelling place of all who rejoice is in you” (Ps. 86:7).

Thus it is rightly said here that they celebrate the majesty of God with a shared—that is, united—exultation, because, as has already been said, they praise without interruption and rejoice in him, both in him and in one another.

This is plainly read concerning the Seraphim themselves in Isaiah: “They flew one toward the other and said: ‘Holy, holy, holy,’” and so forth (Isa. 6:3).

29. (Augustine.) They rightly praise the one whom they serve and attend, and give glory to God in the highest, because to him they owe that they are, to him they owe that they live, to him they owe that they live justly, and to him they owe that they live blessedly. Let us not suppose that the human being alone belongs to God’s grace.

What was an angel before he was made? What is an angel if he abandons the one who created him?

The heavens therefore praise and celebrate together this creator of all things, just as the sun and moon, all the stars and the light, praise him. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light. Praise him, heavens of heavens, and let all the waters above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148:3–4).

30. (Augustine.) In the hymn of the three young men, all the elements are likewise summoned to the praise of God—not because mute elements possess the understanding to praise, but because everything rightly contemplated produces praise, and the heart, filled with consideration of creation, pours forth a hymn to the Creator.

Since it would have been lengthy, in this thanksgiving, to list individually all the orders of angels—nine of which are found in Scripture—the Powers are placed after the heavens. By this name all heavenly spirits are sometimes generally called, as in the Psalm: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32:6). And again: “The Lord of hosts is himself the King of glory” (Ps. 24:10).

Properly, however, among the orders of angels, the spirits through whom signs and miracles more frequently occur are called Powers.

Finally, the Seraphim are placed last. They are the highest order of angelic spirits, and truly blessed are they, since through their singular closeness to their Creator they burn with incomparable love.

Hence “Seraphim” is interpreted as “burning” or “kindling,” because the more subtly they behold the splendor of the divinity, the more powerfully they blaze with love for it.

31. (Vigilantius.) It should also be known that cherubim and seraphim, pronounced with the letter *m*, are, according to the character of the Hebrew language, masculine and only plural in number.

But if they are said with the letter *n*, as in the Psalms and hymns, and as they are used in the present thanksgiving, they change into the neuter gender according to Greek declension, as when we say “shining stars,” “beautiful groves,” and “pleasant shores.” Thus we also understand “blessed seraphim” in the neuter gender and plural number.

This must be understood with the greatest care: when the holy angels and the other powers of heaven are said to praise, tremble before, and celebrate the majesty of God the Father with common exultation “through Christ our Lord,” this must not be taken as though they offer these services of veneration and glorification to God the Father alone and not also to the Son and the Holy Spirit.

For we must hold and know with the most certain faith that, just as the entire holy Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—has one divinity and undivided majesty, so it is owed equal honor and undivided glorification in all things. In no way can either the Father without the Son, or the Son without the Father and the Holy Spirit, be praised, worshiped, or honored by any service of divine worship.

32. (Vigilantius.) For there is no distance within the Trinity. Whether someone worships the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are there; whether someone entreats the Son and the Holy Spirit, the Father is undoubtedly found there as well, because when you invoke either the Father or the Son, you embrace the whole unity of the Godhead, the whole Trinity.

For if it is truly and faithfully believed that the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, as Isaiah speaks to this same Son, saying: “In you is God, and there is no God besides you” (Isa. 45:14), and as the Gospel says: “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 10:38), no one can doubt that sacrifice is offered by us to the Son also, just as to the Father, since he remains consubstantially in that same Father.

Since they remain in one another in such a way that they cannot be separated, whatever you offer to one, consider it offered to both.

Finally, the Son says: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. I and the Father are one” (John 14:9; 10:30). Thus the vision of the Son is contemplation of the Father; the honor or glory of the Father [is likewise that of the Son], as the same Son says: “That all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.”

### 33. (AUGUSTINE)

What if some are found who honor the Father but do not honor the Son? “It cannot be,” he says. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him. But lest you honor the Father as greater and the Son as lesser, the Son himself corrects you and recalls you, saying that all should honor the Son, not less, but just as they honor the Father.

Whatever, then, we render to the divinity in obedience to the heavenly commandments—whether in the rite of sacrifices, in the supplication of prayers, or in any other kind of generosity—is owed equally to the Father and the Son, as though the Father possessed no honor of veneration privately that did not also belong to the dignity of the Son and the Holy Spirit. For if the sacrament of regeneration, baptism, pertains equally to them, since that blessed grace of second birth is celebrated in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, no one can doubt that the sacrifices of the mysteries are likewise possessed by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit with a common honor of dignity, because the Trinity itself is joined together by the inseparable unity of the Godhead.

But that prayer should be directed to the Father alone was ordained by the holy apostles, with the Holy Spirit ordering this through them. They were striving to uproot the errors of many gods by preaching one God; therefore they decreed that, under the sacrament of the Trinity, supplication in the rite of sacrifices should be made to one person. Otherwise those who preached one God in order to eradicate the errors of false gods might be accused by those ignorant of the ineffable mystery of the Father and the Holy Spirit of having fallen into a plurality of divinity.

It was therefore most rightly established that, since the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit exist as one Godhead, one nature, one equality, and, finally, one power, one person among them should be invoked in the sacrifice, in order to preserve the mystery of their unity. Nor could any other person have been chosen except the first, in whom the other two naturally remain and exist.

But when we invoke through the Son, saying to the Father, “Through Jesus Christ, your Son,” this is understood, as has already been said above, in that respect in which he performed the office of a priest on our behalf: when he offered to God the Father the spotless offering of his flesh upon the altar of the cross. Hence the chosen vessel says: “Consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, who is faithful to him who made him” (Heb. 3:1). Having therefore been made a priest for us, he must intercede; but, as we have said, in that respect in which he bears human nature.

Accordingly, the apostle applied this mystery of his intercession not to his divinity but to his humanity, saying: “For there is one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:3).

That prayer and worship are to be offered to the Son just as to the Father, Isaiah shows by saying: “The nations will entreat him, and his name will be glorious” (Isa. 11:10). Again, when he introduces God the Father speaking to the Son:

“The labor of Egypt, the commerce of Ethiopia, and the Sabaeans, tall men, shall pass over to you and shall be yours. Behind you they shall follow, bound in chains; they shall worship you and entreat you, because God is in you, and there is none besides you” (Isa. 45:14).

Likewise in Joel: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Joel 2:32). The apostle teaches that this was said of the Son when, reproaching the unbelief of the Jews, he says: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. How, then, shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” (Rom. 10:13).

David also, entreating the Son as the confessor of the highest thrones, says: “You who sit upon the cherubim, appear before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. Stir up your power and come, and save us” (Ps. 79:3).

Hear also how the Holy Spirit commands a sacrifice of praise to be offered to the Son, to the Father, and to himself, where the indivisible Trinity is demonstrated more clearly together with the distinction of the persons. The same Holy Spirit therefore says in the psalm:

“Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High; and call upon me in the day of your trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall honor me” (Ps. 49:14).

Behold: the Holy Spirit urges the worshipers of truth to offer a sacrifice of praise to God the Son, vows to the Most High Father, and to himself the offering of invocation and glorification.

### 34. (AUGUSTINE)

For the Apostle says of him: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought with a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:15).

Which God does he mean except the Holy Spirit, whose temple he had said our bodies are?

### 35. (VIGILIUS)

Glory, therefore, is owed to the Holy Spirit. But that the angelic powers praise and glorify the Son together with the Father is shown to us in Deuteronomy, where the heavenly host is invited to venerate the Son in these words:

“Rejoice, heavens, together with him, and let all the angels of God worship him. Rejoice, nations, with his people, and let all the sons of God glorify him.”

In the Apocalypse also, blessed John, after he had seen the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders before the Lamb, who opened the sealed book, fall down saying, “You are worthy to receive the book and to open its seals, because you were slain and redeemed us for God by your blood,” added the voices of the heavenly host rejoicing with our redemption, and said:

“And I saw and heard the voice of many angels around the throne; and their number was thousands upon thousands, saying with a loud voice: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and divinity and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing” (Rev. 5:9–12).

“After this,” he says, “I saw, and behold, a great multitude which no one could number, from every nation and tribe and people and language, standing before the throne and in the sight of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands. And they cried out with a loud voice, saying: Salvation belongs to our God who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb” (Rev. 7:9–10).

Behold: the chorus of the saints offers a sacrifice of praise indiscriminately to the Father and the Son. The multitude of angels confirms their voices by worshiping and answering “Amen,” as the same book immediately continues:

“And all the angels stood around the throne, and they fell upon their faces before the throne and worshiped God, saying: Amen” (ibid., v. 11).

Blessed Peter also proclaims the Holy Spirit in the same sublimity of glory, saying: “To the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, upon whom angels long to gaze.”

The priest continues and says:

### 36.

“Together with whom we ask that you command our voices also to be admitted.”

(GREGORY, *Moralia*, book II, no. 10.) The voices of the angels in praise of the Creator are the very wonder of intimate contemplation. What, then, ought our voices to be, when we ask that they be admitted into the presence of God together with the angelic praises—that is, that they be allowed to enter—so that we may say: “Let it enter into your presence.” And again: “Let my prayer come before you, into your holy temple.”

Such voices and such a cry are not in the sound of the mouth but in the desire of the heart. For it is not our words but our desires that make voices before the most secret ears of God. If we ask for eternal life with our mouth but do not desire it, we have kept silent while crying out. But if we desire it from the heart, even when we are silent with our mouth, we cry out while keeping silent.

Thus Moses was silent from the clamor of words, yet, though silent, he was heard by the ear of divine mercy. Why, then, is he told: “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. 14:15).

There is therefore, within desire, a secret cry that does not reach human ears and yet fills the hearing of the Creator. And because that heavenly city consists of angels and human beings—and we believe that as many of the human race ascend to it as there are elect angels who have remained there, as it is written: “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God”—the holy Church, which is to be joined to them in heaven and is to remain with them in the praises of God, already praises God on earth with the very voices with which the holy angels praise him in heaven.

It does this not through proud presumption but through humble confession, desiring thus to believe and confess the majesty of God in the world as it is seen and praised by the angels in heaven.

This confession is not confession of sin, concerning which we are commanded: “Confess your sins to one another” (Jas. 5:16). The Psalmist says: “I said: I will confess my iniquity against myself” (Ps. 31:5). Rather, it is confession of praise and thanksgiving, such as is understood in the psalm where we sing: “Let them confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders to the children of human beings” (Ps. 106:8).

It is also the kind of confession offered by the Lord Jesus, who had no sin whatsoever, to God the Father in the Gospel, saying: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to infants” (Matt. 11:23).

By this one confession—that is, by praise and thanksgiving—they are already joined with the angels, praising him for heavenly and earthly things as the one who made heaven and earth, saying:

### 37.

“Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; heaven and earth are full of your glory.”

These are the voices of the angels praising this hymn of God’s glory in heaven. The prophet Isaiah testifies that he heard it when he saw the glory of God and heard the seraphim praising him with these words. Blessed John likewise introduces them in the Apocalypse under the figure of the four living creatures.

For in Isaiah it is written of the seraphim praising in this way:

“And they cried out to one another and said: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory” (Isa. 6:3).

In the Apocalypse, however, it is written of the four living creatures:

“And they had no rest day or night, saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty, who is and who was and who is to come” (Rev. 4:8).

It is therefore evident that, in these words of divine praise which the Church chants in imitation of the heavenly powers according to Isaiah, one expression has been added from the Apocalypse. For in Isaiah only “Lord of hosts” is read, whereas in the Apocalypse we find “Lord God almighty.” Therefore, by the authority of both Scriptures joined together, we say: “Lord God of hosts.”

Likewise in Isaiah we read: “The whole earth is full of his glory,” as though the angels say this not to God himself but about him to one another. We, however, addressing our voice to him, say: “Heaven and earth are full of your glory.” This has not been presumed by human judgment but has been taken and added from another Scripture, where God himself speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, saying: “I fill heaven and earth.”

Whatever Scripture says in the praises of God may rightly be said both to him, in thanksgiving, and about him, in exhorting or instructing others.

### 38. (JEROME)

“Sabaoth” is one of the ten names of God among the Hebrews, and in Latin it is interpreted as “of hosts” or “of powers,” as it is frequently used in the prophets: “Thus says the Lord of hosts.” And in the psalm: “The Lord of powers is himself the King of glory” (Ps. 23:10).

He is rightly called the Lord of hosts and the Lord of powers because the entire army of the heavenly host, all the powers above, and the angelic authorities are subject to his command and serve his will.

### 39. (GREGORY, *Moralia*, book XVII, no. 19)

We rightly call the angelic spirits an army, because we know that they contend against the powers of the air. Yet they carry out these battles not by labor but by command, because whatever they desire to do against unclean spirits they are able to accomplish through the help of him who governs all things.

Concerning this army, when our King was born, it is written: “Suddenly there appeared with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army” (Luke 2:13).

[Note: In Gregory, the reading is *agendo* (“by doing” / “in carrying out”), rather than *agendum* (“what is to be done”).]

### 40. (AMBROSE)

What, then, does the threefold repetition under one name of holiness in this angelic hymn signify? If the repetition is threefold, why is the praise one? If the praise is one, why is the repetition threefold? Is it not because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one in holiness?

He did not say it once, lest he separate the Son; not twice, lest he pass over the Holy Spirit; not four times, lest he join a creature to them. And, to show that the Godhead is one, after saying three times, “Holy, holy, holy,” he added in the singular: “Lord of hosts.”

Holy, therefore, is the Father; holy is the Son; holy is the Spirit of God. The whole Trinity, that is, is worshiped and praised by the angels. The seraphim glorify it, together with all the heavenly powers and virtues.

They add to this hymn of the angels words taken from the Gospel, spoken by the crowds praising God and our King as he came to Jerusalem, saying:

### 41.

“Hosanna in the highest; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; hosanna in the highest.”

Thus the full praise is completed from prophetic and evangelical Scripture, when, after praise and glory to the holy Trinity, thanksgiving is also added for the coming of the Savior. He, who is one within and from that very Trinity, became human and came into the world for our salvation, and completed that salvation by dying and rising again.

“For he died because of our offenses, and rose again because of our justification” (Rom. 4:25). Therefore, rightly giving him thanks, we say “Hosanna,” that is, “salvation in the highest.”

### 42. (VIGILIUS)

This is what is sung in the psalm: “Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people” (Ps. 3:9).

This is what the chorus of the saints resounds in the Apocalypse with great devotional praise: “Salvation belongs to our God, who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb” (Rev. 7:10).

We rightly add: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” in accordance with what he said in the Gospel to the unbelieving Jews: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you have not received me” (John 5:43).

The crowds take up this verse of praise from Psalm 117, which was plainly sung concerning the Lord. When the crowds say “Hosanna,” that is what is said there: “O Lord, save me! O Lord, grant prosperity!” Immediately it continues: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 117:25–26).

What is added in the course of that same praise—“Hosanna,” that is, “salvation,” or “saving power,” in the highest—plainly teaches that the Lord’s coming in the flesh is the salvation not only of the human race on earth but also of the angels in heaven. For as we are led toward the things above, the number of the angels, which had been diminished when Satan fell, is filled up.

Hence Paul says: “To restore all things in Christ, those in heaven and those on earth, in him” (Eph. 1:10).

Rightly, therefore, “Hosanna in the highest” is sung in praise of him whose entire dispensation of incarnation appeared for the fulfillment of the glory of the heavenly homeland.

After these praises and thanksgivings for so great a grace of our redemption, which is enacted and commended in that divine mystery, the whole Church becomes silent. When every verbal disturbance has ceased, and only the intention directed toward God and the devotion of the hearts remain, joined with the vows and desires of all, the priest begins to pour out the prayer by which the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood is consecrated.

For it is fitting that at that hour of so sacred and divine an action, the entire mind, by God’s grace separated from earthly thoughts, should spiritually enter the heavenly and eternal sanctuary of God: the Church with the priest, and the priest with the Church.

And because God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth (John 4:24)—for the Father also seeks such worshipers—let him entreat that same God the Father and say:

### 43.

“You, therefore, most merciful Father, … these most holy and undefiled sacrifices.”

The prayer is directed, like the other prayers, according to the rule of faith and the custom of the Church to the most merciful Father. His clemency and mercy toward us sinners and unworthy people have been so great that the Apostle commends them, saying:

“He did not spare even his own Son, but handed him over for us all; how will he not also, together with him, graciously give us all things?” (Rom. 8:32).

And again:

“But God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ. Through this grace we have received the spirit of adoption,” which the Apostle commends by saying: “You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry: Abba, Father” (Rom. 8:15).

Therefore, in this Spirit of adoption, who pleads for us with inexpressible groanings—for he makes those whom he deigns to fill groan and plead with an inexpressible desire—the priest, together with the Church, cries out not with the voice but with the heart, saying:

“You, therefore, most merciful Father, we humbly beseech and implore.”

This supplication and inclination of the heart toward God must possess such reverence and humility that it can imitate what the Apostle says about his own supplication:

“For this reason I bend my knees before the Father, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named” (Eph. 3:14–15).

In this bending of the knees, not bodily prostration but a supplicant disposition and contrition of heart are understood. Of this the Psalmist says:

“A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 51:17).

Accordingly, it is said: “We humbly beseech and implore,” and this is done through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord. Through him, as the true mediator and eternal priest who sits at the right hand of the Father and intercedes for us, all our supplication and petition must be directed to God.

But for what does the priest say to God the Father, “We beseech and implore,” except for what follows—namely, that he may receive as acceptable and bless the gifts, holy offerings, and sacrifices offered to him?

It belongs to priests to offer and invoke the majesty of God; it belongs to God graciously to receive and bless what is offered. Thus, in the Law, he commands the priests, saying:

“Thus shall you bless the children of Israel, and you shall say to them,”

and after the words of blessing he adds:

“They shall invoke my name over the children of Israel, and I shall bless them” (Num. 6:23, 27).

What could be clearer? They shall invoke, and I shall bless. Yet above he had said to them, “Thus shall you bless.” They do so by entreating; he by bestowing.

So also, in the offering of the divine sacrifice, priests perform the ministry of offering and supplicating, but God bestows the gift of blessing through the one true priest. Through him he both sanctifies what has been offered and accepts what has been sanctified. They therefore say:

### 44.

“That you may accept and bless them,”

as though they were saying in humble supplication:

“We ask that you sanctify these things by your Spirit and bless them by your mouth, so that what is performed through the ministry of our humility may be accomplished through the effect of your power.”

What follows—“These gifts, these offerings, these holy and undefiled sacrifices”—does not refer to different things. Rather, one and the same reality is praised and commended under different names because of its greatness.

What is offered upon the divine altars is called “offerings,” as the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you offer your gift at the altar” (Matt. 5:23). They are also called “gifts” or “sacrifices,” as the Apostle shows, saying:

“Every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters relating to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins” (Heb. 5:1).

But, as has been said, this very repetition of words commends so great a sacrament and stirs up pious devotion. For these are truly holy and undefiled sacrifices—that is, inviolate and uncontaminated—which no words can adequately praise and which are offered in the mystery of the Lord’s body.

As a figure of this, the spotless victims of the old Law, without any defect, were commanded to be offered. Such was found in Christ alone, without any sin whatsoever.

The priest continues and says:

### 45.

“First, what we offer to you … your servant, our pope.”

(AUGUSTINE, on Psalm 130.) It was entirely fitting that the holy offering should begin in this way, namely, with a prayer for the holy Catholic Church of God, spread throughout the whole world.

For it is the universal body redeemed by the Lord’s blood. It is the inheritance promised and given to him by the Father, as the Father himself speaks in the psalm:

“I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8).

This unity of Christ’s body is the temple of God, to which the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Cor. 3:17)—all who believe in Christ and believe in such a way that they love him. For to believe in Christ is to love Christ.

They are like living stones from which the Lord’s temple is built. This is the temple in which God is asked and hears. Whoever prays to God outside the temple is not heard with regard to that heavenly peace; he is not heard with regard to eternal life, which is granted only to one who prays in the temple of God.

The one who prays in the peace of the Church prays in the unity of Christ’s body, and Christ’s body consists of the many who believe throughout the whole world. Therefore the one who prays in the temple is heard, because he prays in spirit and in truth, rightly from the Church and for the Church.

In it the divine offering begins, as though it were said to God concerning it and within it:

“Hear us, God our Savior, hope of all the ends of the earth and of the distant seas” (Ps. 65:5).

For it is this unity that cries out to the Lord from the ends of the earth—that is, from east and west, north and south—and says from the ends of the earth:

“To you I cried when my heart was troubled” (Ps. 61:2).

### 46. (ISIDORE, *Etymologies*, book VIII, chapter 1)

Hence the Church is called *ecclesia* in Greek, which is translated into Latin as “assembly” or “convocation,” because it calls everyone together to itself. It is called “catholic,” that is, “universal.”

For it is not confined, like the gatherings of heretics, to certain parts of the regions; rather, spread throughout the whole world, it is extended and diffused everywhere.

Hence “universal” derives its name from “one,” because it is gathered into unity. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel:

“Whoever does not gather with me scatters”—

that is, whoever is not gathered into my unity, being separated from me, is dispersed into the destruction of dispersion.

For this reason, then, in that offering it is first requested that God deign to pacify the Church throughout the whole world: that her unity not be torn apart by heresies and schisms, nor her tranquility disturbed by the adversity of persecutions.

That God may grant this peace to his Church both inwardly and outwardly, the Apostle himself also prays, saying:

“The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 4:7).

He also urges the whole Church to pray when he says:

“First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made.”

And shortly afterward:

“That we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety” (1 Tim. 2:1–2).

The almighty God is therefore asked to deign to guard, unite, and govern the Church. For he is the true guardian of his people, that is, of the true Israel, concerning whom it is sung in the psalm:

“Behold, he neither slumbers nor sleeps, who guards Israel” (Ps. 121:4).

And again:

“Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain” (Ps. 127:1).

To unite seems to mean the same as to pacify; to guard, the same as to govern. For God both unites his Church by pacifying it and pacifies it by uniting it; he governs it by guarding it and guards it by governing it.

He unites it by pacifying it when he joins the hearts of all the faithful in his peace, when through the unity of faith, hope, and charity he makes the minds of all the faithful one will, and when, through the Holy Spirit’s charity poured out in it, what is written is fulfilled:

“The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32).

And again:

“Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity” (Ps. 133:1).

He also governs that same Church by guarding it when, amid all dangers, he mercifully guides and directs it. Praying to him in the psalm, we say:

“Save your people, and bless your inheritance; shepherd them and lift them up forever” (Ps. 28:9).

### 47.

But when, after the general commemoration of the Church, the words “together with your servant, our pope” are added, the unity of the ecclesiastical body is commended more powerfully.

For, as blessed Leo writes, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior of the human race, established the worship of divine religion—which God’s grace willed to shine throughout all peoples and nations—in such a way that he placed the sacrament of this office principally in blessed Peter, the chief of the apostles, and willed his gifts to flow from him, as from a kind of head, into the entire body. Thus anyone who dared to depart from Peter’s firmness would understand himself to be excluded from the divine mystery.

Having taken him into the fellowship of indivisible unity, he willed that he be called by the name of what Christ himself was, saying:

“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18).

Hence it is clear, as blessed Pope Pelagius again teaches, that those who, through any disagreement, do not regularly commemorate the apostolic pontiff during the sacred mysteries are separated from communion with the whole world.

The mystery continues:

### 48.

“And with our bishop, and with all the orthodox and worshipers of the apostolic faith.”

Just as the commemoration of the universal Church, on account of the unity of fellowship and peace, is joined to the commemoration of the apostolic pontiff, so it is fitting and religious that individual Churches add the commemoration of their own bishops. Through that prayer of the Lord’s offering they thereby show that they preserve unity of spirit with them in the bond of peace.

*Orthodoxoi* (ὀρθόδοξοι) in Greek means “those of right glory” or “right praise” in Latin, because, corrupted by no heresy, they glorify God with the confession of the right faith.

These same people, therefore, are worshipers of the catholic and apostolic faith: catholic, that is, universal, which the whole Church everywhere preserves; and apostolic, the faith which the teaching of the apostles founded throughout the world.

### 49.

They cannot be called worshipers of this faith except those who believe rightly and love truly. For each person worships what he loves most.

Thus the Apostle says of certain lovers of appetite and the belly: “Their god is their belly” (Phil. 3:19).

The worshiper of truth, therefore, is the one who joins love to faith, so that by loving God, whom he rightly believes in, he worships him and, by worshiping him, merits his favor.

This is the faith that the Apostle commends, saying:

“In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any power, but faith working through love” (Gal. 5:6).

Religion is not to be sought amid the confusion of pagans, nor amid the refuse of heretics, nor amid the weakness of schismatics, nor amid the blindness of Jews, but only among those who are called Christians, Catholics, or orthodox—that is, guardians of integrity and followers of what is right.

### 50.

When this prayer has been completed, in which the universal Church, together with the apostolic pontiff and all the orthodox, is first commended to God, the customary conclusion is added:

“Through Christ our Lord.”

For neither the prayer nor the offering of the Church can otherwise be offered to God, nor can he receive the Church—[that is, the Church consisting of all the faithful]—for whom God is entreated, except through the one mediator between God and human beings, who intercedes for us.

What the Church offers, it offers through him. That God may deign to pacify, guard, and unite the same Church, he grants through him. Through him our vows rise to God; through him divine gifts descend to us.

For he himself commends this in the Gospel, saying:

“Because I go to the Father, and whatever you ask in my name, I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son” (John 14:12–13).

The Church preserves this form of petition in all its prayer.

The mystery continues.

### 51.

“Remember, Lord, your male and female servants, and all who stand around, whose faith and devotion are known and manifest to you.”

When the words first say, “Remember, Lord, your male and female servants,” and then add, “and all who stand around,” it is clear that a certain place is intended where, after some people have been named individually, the commemoration of the others who are present in the Church is also added.

At this point, either the priest is free to name individually and commend to God whomever he wishes, or else it was an ancient practice that the names of those making offerings were recited there.

Blessed Pope Innocent seems to indicate this in a certain letter, where he says:

“It is superfluous that, although you have not yet offered someone’s sacrifice to God, you should mention his name beforehand, even though nothing is unknown to him. First, therefore, the offerings must be commended, so that then the names of those whose names are to be declared may be recited among the sacred mysteries, not among the other things which we mention beforehand, so that we may open a way for the prayers that will follow to the mysteries themselves.”

This prayer is therefore made to God the Father, that he may deign to remember his male and female servants—that is, those of either sex who serve him—not only those who are named but also all who stand around.

And it is said concerning all and on behalf of all together: “whose faith and devotion are known and manifest to you”—that is, you alone see in the conscience of each person how rightly they believe and how devoutly they love you.

For you are the one who searches hearts and reins, and it has truly been said to you:

“You alone know the hearts of the children of human beings.”

Among your worshipers you seek especially the offering of faith and devotion: faith, when through your lawgiver you say, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4); devotion, when he immediately adds: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart” (ibid., 6:5).

To offer this faith and devotion to God is truly the sacrifice of salvation: to attend to his commandments.

The mystery continues.

### 52.

“Who offer you this sacrifice of praise and render their vows to you, the eternal, living, and true God.”

In these words it must be considered that the entire Church offers that sacrifice of praise to God, since it is said of the whole multitude of the faithful who stand around: “Who offer you.”

What is fulfilled specifically through the ministry of priests is performed generally through the faith and devotion of all. For the blessed apostle Peter says to the whole Church:

“You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2:9),

to offer spiritual and acceptable sacrifices to God through Jesus Christ.

He therefore calls the whole Church a holy priesthood, although in the Law only the house of Aaron possessed the name and office. This is because all the faithful are members of the high priest; all are marked with the oil of gladness and united to the body of him who is the supreme King and true priest.

As king, he grants them a kingdom; as high priest, he cleanses their sins by the offering of his blood.

Moreover, even in the same law of the Old Testament, the mystery of this spiritual priesthood, by which the whole Church is consecrated, is clearly commended. The lamb to be slaughtered at Passover—“Christ, who was sacrificed for you”—is commanded to be sacrificed not by priests alone but generally by the entire people, when the Lord says:

“The whole assembly of the children of Israel shall slaughter it toward evening” (Exod. 12:6).

The same Law commends this lamb, slaughtered at the Passover solemnity, as victim, offering, and sacrifice, when the Lord commands and says:

“You shall not sacrifice the blood of my victim over leaven, nor shall the victim of the solemnity of Passover remain until morning” (Exod. 34:25).

And again:

“No one who is unclean in soul, or who is far away on a journey among your people, shall keep the Passover for the Lord in the second month” (Num. 9:10).

And shortly afterward:

“But if anyone is clean and was not on a journey, yet did not keep the Passover, that person shall be cut off from his people, because he did not offer the sacrifice to the Lord at its appointed time” (ibid., 9:13).

The priests of the Church therefore offer; through them and in them the whole Church offers to God the sacrifice of praise, which he himself commanded to be offered by his worshipers, saying:

“Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High” (Ps. 50:14).

### 53. (AUGUSTINE)

Not because He seeks praise from us as one in need, but so that through it He may provide for our salvation, as He says again in the same psalm: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me, and there is the way by which I shall show my salvation” (ibid., 33). For what is God’s salvation except the Son of God, the Savior of the world? He, therefore—the priest, the victim, and the sacrifice—fulfilled the sacrifice of praise, granting forgiveness for evil works and bestowing the grace to do good.

[Col. 0048D] For this reason the Lord’s sacrifice of praise is offered by His worshipers: so that “he who glories may glory in the Lord.” This sacrifice of praise—that is, the offering of the Lord’s Passion—in which we acknowledge no merits of our own but praise God’s grace alone, is offered because “the love of God has appeared among us”: God sent His only-begotten Son into the world so that we might live through Him, not because we loved God, but because He first loved us and sent His Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins.

The devotion of the faithful offers this sacrifice for themselves and for all who belong to them—whether by kinship, familiarity, or any other condition—within the profession of the same faith, both for the living and for the dead. [Col. 0049A] The hope with which the faithful do this is then added: not for any temporal gain, but solely for the redemption of their souls, for the hope of their salvation and security—that is, for the hope of eternal salvation. “For in hope we were saved.” And not only for eternal salvation, but also for temporal security, that is, bodily health. For *incolumitas* means wholeness of health. Both kinds of salvation, of soul and of body, come from Him of whom the psalm sings: “Salvation belongs to the Lord.”

“To You,” he says, “they render their vows,” to the eternal, living, and true God, in accordance with what is said in the psalm: “And pay your vows to the Most High”—the vows, namely, of faith and devout dedication, through which we vow and return ourselves to God. Whoever rightly considers what he has vowed to God and what vows he ought to fulfill is required, and obligated, to vow and return himself.

[Col. 0049B] But just as one must consider what he offers, so one must also consider where he offers it, because outside the Catholic Church there is no place for the true sacrifice. Hence, in the mystery, the text appropriately continues:

### 54. “In communion and venerating the memory, first of all … and of all your saints.”

(AUGUSTINE.) Whom does he mean by “in communion and venerating the memory” of the blessed Mother of God, of the apostles and martyrs, and of all the saints, except the priest himself who offers, together with all those standing around who offer the one sacrifice of praise with him?

In order that this sacrifice may be acceptable and pleasing to God, neither the priests nor the Church together with the priests offer it anywhere except in the communion and fellowship of the saints, among whom the same almighty God willed the foundation of His Church to stand, as the Apostle says: “You are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. II, 19).

[Col. 0049C] In their communion and in the veneration of their memory, as in the true temple of God, the devotion of the faithful offers its vows and gifts to God. Therefore they enter into communion with their memory as children of their fathers and followers of those who preceded them. For what does “in communion” mean except holding communion and fellowship? And what does it mean to venerate their memory except to follow their footsteps with piety and humility?

[Col. 0049D] The blessed apostle John invites us to this fellowship when he says: “What we have seen and heard, we announce to you.” And as though we were to ask what benefit that announcement would bring us, he says: “So that you too may have fellowship with us.” And lest anyone think that this fellowship should be despised as merely human, he immediately adds: “And your fellowship may be with the Father and with His Son Jesus Christ.” He plainly shows that whoever desires to have fellowship with God must first be joined to the fellowship of the Church, learn that faith, and be instructed in its sacraments—the faith that the apostles received from the Truth Himself, who was present in the flesh.

For its sake the holy martyrs suffered, and upon it the Catholic Church is founded; and the birth of the blessed and glorious Virgin became the beginning of salvation.

### 55. (AUGUSTINE, Sermon 186)

[Col. 0050A] She is truly believed always to have been a virgin, because even if her integrity had been violated when the Lord was born, He would no longer have been born of a virgin. The whole Church would then—God forbid—be falsely confessing that He was born of the virgin Mary, although, for the salvation of the human race, it was granted as a singular gift to the true man that, from the very moment He began to be conceived in the Virgin’s womb and to become man, He should also be true God. Therefore that same glorious Mary, ever a virgin, must be believed and confessed to be the true Mother of God.

She is therefore placed first in this venerable communion of the saints, through whom both they and we were deemed worthy to receive the author of life. Alongside her is mentioned the fellowship of the blessed apostles and martyrs—not only those named here, but also all those whose number and names we cannot know. [Col. 0050B] Yet if we piously cling to these few who are named, we are joined, in their communion, even to those whom we cannot know.

The mystery continues:

### 56. “By whose merits and prayers grant …”

For on account of the merits and intercessions of the exalted righteous, whom we seek as intercessors and patrons, the Lord has mercy and is propitiated toward our weakness, so that in all things—whether adversity or prosperity—we may neither fail in the former nor be deceived in the latter, but be fortified by the help of His protection.

### 57. (VIGILIUS)

Finally, when Hezekiah was exhausted by his enemies and invoked His help, He said to him: “I will save this city and protect it for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant” (4 Kings XXXI, 6). And Moses, thus entreating God, sought to appease Him: “Let your anger cease,” he said, “and be appeased concerning the wickedness of your people. Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants, to whom you swore by yourself, saying: ‘I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven’” (Exod. XXXII, 13).

[Col. 0050C] There is no doubt that the petitions of the faithful are known by the spirits of the righteous. For those who see the glory of almighty God within cannot in any way be thought to be ignorant of anything that exists outside.

The Church therefore requests the intercession of the holy martyrs; yet she does not raise altars on which sacrifices are offered to the martyrs, but to the one God who is both the God of the martyrs and our God.

(AUGUSTINE, *The City of God*, Book XXII, chapter 10.) At that sacrifice, the human beings of God who conquered the world by confessing Him are named in their proper place and order; yet they are not invoked by the priest who offers the sacrifice. For he sacrifices to God, not to them, although he sacrifices in their memorials, because he is God’s priest, not theirs.

[Col. 0050D] The sacrifice itself is Christ’s. It is not offered to them, because they themselves are part of it.

The mystery continues:

### 58. “Therefore, this offering of our service … through Christ our Lord.”

In these words the unity of the offering Church is shown, when in that most sacred offering a common service is presented to God by both the priests and the whole household of God.

(Ibid., Book X, chapter 19.) This is a service owed to no one else—not to the holy angels, nor to the holy souls—but to the one living and true God, concerning whom we are commanded: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him alone shall you serve” (Matt. IV, 10).

Although it is performed or offered by a human being, the sacrifice is nevertheless a divine reality. Hence elsewhere the divine law commands: “Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be destroyed, except to the Lord alone.”

[Col. 0051A] Therefore those immortal and blessed beings established in the heavenly dwellings, who mercifully love us because we are mortal and miserable, so that we may become immortal and blessed, do not wish us to sacrifice to them, but to Him whose sacrifice they too, together with us, have asked to be. For with them we are one city, a part of which journeys as a pilgrim among us, while another part assists us in them.

The Church therefore prays that God, appeased, may accept this offering, which she brings to Him alone in the service owed to Him. This is the true offering, in which the Son is offered, the Father is reconciled, and, appeased by the life-giving offering, He may order our days in His peace, so that although we have affliction in the world, we may have peace in Him.

[Col. 0051B] When the course of this mortality has been completed, may He deign to rescue us from eternal damnation and number us among His chosen flock.

(GREGORY.) For the predestination of the everlasting kingdom itself has also been arranged by the Almighty in such a way that the elect reach it through labor, so that by asking they may merit to receive what almighty God determined before the ages to give them.

The mystery continues.

### 59. “Which offering, O God, in all respects …”

The Almighty is entreated to make the offering placed upon His sacred altars and commended by such prayers, through the power of the One who descends, into a legitimate and perfect Eucharist, so that in every respect it may be *ascripta*—that is, received and counted among the things pleasing to Him—and also *rata*—that is, established with immovable and perpetual firmness. For that is called *ratum* which is firm and unshaken by an immovable reason.

[Col. 0051C] By the operative power of the same Holy Spirit, may it also be rational and through all these things uniquely grateful and acceptable to God, so that, although taken from the simple fruits of the earth, by the ineffable power of divine blessing it may become the body and blood of the only-begotten Son of God, as He Himself testifies: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John VI, 56). Thus, through this food and drink, what He promises may be fulfilled in the minds of those who receive it: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me” (ibid., 58).

This, therefore, is the true and eternal victim, because its power is true and eternal, and through it true and eternal salvation is accomplished. It belongs to the new and eternal Testament.

[Col. 0051D] This is the rational victim—full of reason, full of mystery—which formerly was enacted through tangible ritual in the ancient sacrifices, but is now celebrated through spiritual understanding and presented in the purity of faith, in accordance with the Apostle’s command concerning our rational service. For when the Apostle said this, he was surely speaking of a spiritual sacrifice.

Hence elsewhere he says: “It was necessary that the copies of the heavenly things should be cleansed with these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these” (Heb. IX, 23). For in order that the hearts of the faithful might become heavenly, and that, just as they had borne the image of the earthly, they might also bear the image of Him who is from heaven—and that, as is the heavenly One, so they might become heavenly—they had to be cleansed not by the blood of irrational animals, but by the rational blood of Christ. As the same Apostle testifies, Christ “through the Holy Spirit offered Himself immaculate to God.”

[Col. 0052A] This is renewed for us daily in the sacrament of the body and blood of the Son of God.

(AUGUSTINE, Book XX against Faustus, chapter 13.) This body and this blood are not gathered from ears of grain and grape shoots, but through a definite consecration become mystical. He is not born anew when the created substance of bread and wine is transferred into the sacrament of His flesh and blood through the ineffable sanctification of the Spirit.

If this were not so, although it would still be bread and a cup, it would be food for nourishment, not the sacrament of religion by which Christ filled the divine altar.

The Lord therefore invited His servants and prepared food for them—Himself. Who would dare to eat his Lord? And yet He says: “Whoever eats me lives because of me” (John VI, 58). When Christ is eaten, life is eaten. He is not killed in order to be eaten; rather, when He is eaten, He gives life to the dead. He nourishes but is not diminished. Christ is eaten, yet, once eaten, He lives, because He rose after being killed.

[Col. 0052B] Nor, when we eat Him, do we divide Him into parts. Indeed, in the sacrament He is eaten in parts, yet He remains wholly and undivided in heaven; He remains wholly and undivided in His own heart.

The mystery continues.

### 60. “Who, on the day before He suffered, took bread … until ‘whenever you do this, you shall do it in memory of me.’”

Thus, so that the universal Church might celebrate the perpetual memory of the Lord and Redeemer, the Lord Himself handed this on to the apostles, and the apostles handed it on generally to the whole Church.

[Col. 0052C] In these words—without which no language, no region, no city, that is, no part of the Catholic Church, can perform or consecrate the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood—the Lord Himself handed it on to the apostles, so that the universal Church might celebrate the perpetual memory of its Redeemer; and the apostles handed it on generally to the whole Church.

Therefore it is always, and will always be, consecrated by Christ’s power and words. It is His speech that sanctifies the heavenly sacraments. He speaks daily in His priests. They perform the office; He acts with the majesty of divine power.

For He is the true Melchizedek, who fulfilled through the offering of His body and blood these holy sacrifices that Melchizedek once prefigured in mystery. Through the power of the Spirit, the Paraclete, and through heavenly blessing, He makes the holy body and blood His own.

[Col. 0052D] When He says concerning the bread, “Take and eat from this, all of you,” and similarly concerning the cup, “Take and drink from it, all of you,” this commends unity and peace: through participation in Christ by this mystery, we may all be one in Him, as the Apostle affirms: “There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal. III, 28).

Elsewhere he commends this unity in participation in the sacrament, saying: “The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? And the bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?” (1 Cor. X, 16). “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, all of us who share in the one bread.”

[Col. 0053A] The Church’s unity in Christ is so great that, just as there is one faith, one baptism, and one altar, of which Isaiah says, “There shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt” (Isa. XIX, 19), so everywhere there is one bread of Christ’s body and one cup of His blood.

Hence, by tradition, when the Church consecrates the mystery of the Lord’s sacred body and blood with these words, she expressly says that the Lord said to the apostles: “Take and eat from this, all of you; for this is my body.” Likewise, after supper had ended, He took “this glorious cup.”

Let every faithful person attend to what is meant by “this”: namely, that the cup which the Catholic priest sacrifices is none other than the cup that the Lord handed on to the apostles. Therefore, what is to be believed and held concerning the blood must likewise be believed and held concerning the body.

[Col. 0053B] When he calls it the “glorious cup,” the expression is plainly taken from the psalm: “And your cup, making drunk—how glorious it is!” (Ps. XXII, 5). It is truly glorious, since the immaculate blood, covered by no stain of sin, is offered through it. By this cup the affection of the faithful is made drunk, so that it may put on joy because of the remission of sin. By this intoxication the soul is not confounded, but consecrated.

### 61.

Again, when these words say “of the new and eternal Testament,” it is clear that in the Gospel one reads only, “The cup of my blood of the New Testament.” But the addition “eternal” is contained both in the prophetic and in the apostolic writings.

[Col. 0053C] For in Isaiah we read God’s promise to the faithful: “I will make with you a covenant”—that is, an everlasting testament. And in Ezekiel, where He promises the Church: “I will establish with you an everlasting covenant” (Ezek. XVI, 80). The Apostle says: “By one offering He has perfected forever those who are sanctified” (Heb. X, 14). And again: “The God of peace, who brought up from the dead the shepherd of the sheep, our Lord Jesus Christ, by the blood of the eternal Testament” (Heb. XIII, 20).

(AUGUSTINE.) Christ’s blood is therefore the new testament because it is the new love by which He loved us unto death in the final times of the ages. This love renews us, so that we may be new human beings and heirs of the New Testament, as the Apostle also teaches when he says: “How much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered Himself immaculate to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God?” And therefore He is “the mediator of the New Testament” (Heb. IX, 14).

[Col. 0053D] Through this blood of the New Testament, which was poured out for the remission of sins, He cleansed—that is, renewed—the conscience of the faithful. And, in accordance with the same Apostle, those faithful become heirs according to the hope of eternal life and receive the promise as those called to an eternal inheritance.

Therefore that blood is of the New and eternal Testament because those whom it renews from oldness it leads to an eternal inheritance.

[Col. 0054A] For this reason the prophet Zechariah, as though speaking to the Lord Himself, says: “You also, by the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there was no water” (Zech. IX, 10). Through the outpouring of this blood, the righteous of old, bound by the hope of the future redemption, were led out from the prison of hell; and through the same blood all believers are rescued from the bonds of sins, from the pit of misery, and from the mire of filth.

### 62.

Again, when this text says “the mystery of faith,” and this expression is not found in those words of the Lord by which He handed on the mystery of His body and blood, it seems to have been taken from another passage of the Gospel. There, according to John, speaking of this same sacrament to certain disciples who did not believe, He says: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life, but there are some among you who do not believe” (John VI, 64–65).

[Col. 0054B] He shows that He has spoken of a great mystery when He says: “The words that I have spoken are spirit and life.” But when He adds, “There are some among you who do not believe,” He shows that this mystery belongs only to faith and to the faithful, who hear those words faithfully. For them the words are spirit and life, because, when spiritually understood, they give them life.

(AUGUSTINE, Book I *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 24.) Or perhaps these words are taken from the Apostle, where he says: “Holding the mystery of faith in a pure conscience” (1 Tim. III, 9). For just as the sacrament of the Holy Trinity, so also the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion and death, which is continually celebrated in that offering, is equally necessary for salvation and must equally be received and retained in a pure conscience.

This is also celebrated in baptism, as the same Apostle teaches when he says: “All who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into His death.”

Everything, therefore, that is done in this offering of the Lord’s body and blood is a mystery. One thing is seen, another is understood. What is seen has a bodily form; what is understood has a spiritual fruit.

[Col. 0054C] It must also be known that, in accordance with the observance handed down from the apostles and maintained by the Catholic Church, it is not permitted to offer the same cup of the Lord’s blood unless it is mixed with water. For wine was the mystery of our redemption, when He said: “From now on I shall not drink of this fruit of the vine” (Mark XIV, 25). And from His side, pierced by the lance, water came forth together with blood, showing that wine had been expressed, together with water, from the true vine of His flesh.

These are the sacraments of the Church, without which one does not enter into the life that is truly life. That blood was poured out for the remission of sins; that water tempers the saving drink. It provides both the washing and the drink.

[Col. 0054D] ### 63.

The Lord Himself commends to us with what piety and love this entire mystery of the Lord’s offering must be enacted and received when He says: “Whenever you do this, you shall do it in memory of me” (Luke XXII, 19).

Explaining this, the Apostle says: “Whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes” (1 Cor. XI, 26).

The offering of that bread and cup is therefore a commemoration and proclamation of Christ’s death. It is enacted not so much through words as through the mysteries themselves, by which that precious death is impressed upon our minds more deeply and powerfully.

For what is the commemoration of Christ’s death except the commending of His love? The blessed evangelist John commends this love to us when he says: “Jesus, knowing that His hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved His own who were in the world, loved them to the end” (John XIII, 1)—that is, that love carried Him even to death, because He loved them so greatly that He died for them.

[Col. 0055A] He testified to this when He said: “No one has greater love than this, that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (John XV, 13).

Therefore, as He was going to His Passion and was about to depart from the world through the glory of His resurrection and ascension, He handed this final sacrament to His disciples, so that He might impress more firmly upon their minds the memory of such great love, through which alone we are saved. He did this so that we might always remember both what we are and how greatly we are loved by Him: what we are, so that we may not glory in ourselves; how greatly we are loved, so that we may hope in Him.

[Col. 0055B] The Apostle carefully imposes and inculcates both points when he says: “Why, while we were still weak, did Christ die at the appointed time for the ungodly?” (Rom. V, 6). And shortly afterward: “But God commends His love toward us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more, therefore, now that we have been justified by His blood, shall we be saved from wrath through Him. For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by His life” (Rom. VIII, 9, 10).

He commended that this should be done and continually repeated until He comes at the end of the age. Then there will be the rest of the saints—not still in the sacrament of hope, through which the Church is joined together in the present age while she drinks what flowed from Christ’s side, but in the perfection itself of eternal salvation, when the kingdom will be handed over to God the Father, so that in the clear contemplation of unchangeable truth we may have no need of bodily mysteries.

[Col. 0055C] (GREGORY.) For this singular victim saves the soul from eternal destruction: through the mystery it restores to us the death of the Only-Begotten. Although, having risen from the dead, He no longer dies and death will no longer rule over Him, nevertheless, living immortally and incorruptibly in Himself, He is again sacrificed for us in the mystery of the sacred offering. There His body is received; His flesh is distributed for the salvation of the people. His blood is no longer poured into the hands of unbelievers.

From this, therefore, let us consider what kind of sacrifice this is for us: a sacrifice that, for our absolution, continually imitates the Passion of the only-begotten Son.

The mystery continues:

[Col. 0055D] ### 64. “Therefore, remembering, we your servants … as far as ‘the cup of everlasting salvation.’”

Because our Lord and Savior commended the mystery of His death—which He undertook for our salvation and for the salvation of all—with such devotion to the memory of the faithful that through the offering and participation of His body and blood He made that same death life-giving, it is fitting and salutary that, since our Lord and Savior willed us to proclaim His life-giving death in the participation of His body and blood until He comes, the priests and the people—that is, the whole Church—should remember His blessed Passion by frequently celebrating these venerable mysteries.

[Col. 0056A] It was truly blessed, because, undertaken without sin, it erased the sins of the whole world. And because, as the Apostle says, He was not only “put to death for our trespasses,” but also “raised for our justification” (Rom. IV, 25), let us also remember His resurrection from the dead. And since, rising from the dead and taken up into heaven, He sits at the right hand of God, let us also remember His glorious ascension.

This is our entire salvation and life: to remember these things without ceasing.

Remembering, therefore, the Lord’s Passion, resurrection, and ascension, both the priests and the faithful people offer to God’s glorious—that is, exalted and splendid—majesty, not something of their own, but from His gifts and bestowals, in accordance with what is written: “And what we have received from your hand, we have given to you.”

In the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood, they offer truly a pure victim, a holy victim, an immaculate victim. This threefold repetition is a praise of so great a mystery.

[Col. 0056B] This victim, which we call a pure, holy, and immaculate victim—that is, the holy bread of eternal life and the cup of everlasting salvation—is eternal life for those who receive it, as the Lord says: “Whoever eats this bread will live forever” (John VI, 59).

What pure, holy, and immaculate victim does the Church offer except the one she received from the Lord—that is, the holy bread of eternal life and the cup of everlasting salvation?

For in this bread there is eternal life for those who receive it, as the Lord Himself, the living bread and bread of life, says of Himself: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John VI, 51).
