And again: “The bread of God is the one who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world” (ibid., 33). Elsewhere He says: “Whoever eats this bread will live forever” (ibid., 59).

[Col. 0056C] And He explains that this is the bread of His body when He says: “And the bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (ibid., 52).

Therefore the cup of His blood is also the cup of eternal salvation, because that blood was poured out for many for the remission of sins, so that He might save His people from their sins.

Of this the psalm sings: “I will receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXV, 13). This cup is saving for the one who receives it, both in receiving the sacrament and in imitating the Passion, as it was received by the holy martyrs.

The manna signified this bread; the altar of God bestowed this bread.

The faithful know the body of Christ: if a person is in the body of Christ, he will receive the Spirit of Christ. Just as our body cannot live without the spirit, so no one will possess the Spirit of life unless he is found in the body of Christ.

[Col. 0056D] Whoever wishes to live, let him draw near, believe, and live from God and in God. Let him be incorporated, so that he may be given life. For this is to eat that food and drink that drink: to remain in Christ and to have Him, remaining in us, as He Himself says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John VI, 57).

The mystery continues.

### 65. “Upon which, with a merciful and serene countenance … as far as ‘the immaculate victim.’”

God is entreated to look with a merciful—that is, an appeased and serene—countenance upon these gifts of life and salvation that are offered to His glorious majesty.

[Col. 0057A] This does not mean that His countenance is ever made serene, as though He were Himself the Father of lights, concerning whom blessed James says: “With whom there is no change or shadow caused by alteration” (James I, 17). Blessed John also testifies: “God is light, and there is no darkness in Him at all” (1 John I, 5).

Rather, He who is always in the light makes His countenance serene over us and illuminates it when He declares His mercy toward us, as we pray in the psalm: “May He illuminate His countenance over us and have mercy on us” (Ps. LXVI, 2).

Conversely, concerning certain people who are unworthy of His mercy, He Himself says: “I will hide my face from them” (Deut. XXXI, 17). And again, to those toward whom He shows Himself appeased, He promises: “I will not turn my face from you” (Jer. III, 12).

Hence blessed Daniel also entreats Him in these very words: “Hear, O Lord, the prayers of your servant; illuminate your face over your sanctuary, and in your mercy look upon this people over whom your name has been invoked” (Dan. IX, 17).

[Col. 0057B] God must not be thought to have a face or countenance in human form, because, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “God is spirit, and those who worship Him must worship in spirit and truth” (John IV, 24). Rather, the face and countenance of God mean His presence.

For what is God’s face illuminated over us except His presence made manifest, when we feel His mercy and goodness present with us? Likewise, God’s looking upon us is His visitation in mercy, as we pray in the psalm: “God of hosts, restore us; look down from heaven, see, and visit this vineyard” (Ps. LXXIX, 15).

[Col. 0057C] The almighty God is therefore entreated, having been made appeased and merciful, to look graciously with a serene countenance—that is, with the presence of His goodness and mercy made manifest—upon the gifts of His Church and to regard them as accepted and pleasing, as He regarded the gifts of His righteous servant Abel.

Abel’s faith, righteousness, and acceptance of his offering are commended both in the Old Law, where it is written, “And God looked upon Abel and his gifts” (Gen. IV, 4), and in the Gospel, where we read, “From the blood of righteous Abel” (Matt. XXII, 35), and in the Apostle, where he writes: “By faith Abel offered God a greater sacrifice than Cain, through which he received testimony that he was righteous” (Heb. XI, 4).

He is called a child of God not on account of his age, but on account of his simplicity and purity. Likewise, concerning David, who died an old man, the Gospel says: “In the house of David his servant” (Luke I, 69).

[Col. 0057D] “And as the sacrifice,” he says, “of our patriarch Abraham”—namely, the sacrifice by which he offered his only-begotten son Isaac as a burnt offering to God. It was so accepted that he deserved to hear: “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord: because you have done this thing and have not spared your only-begotten son for my sake, I will bless you” (Gen. XXII, 12), and so forth.

That patriarch belongs not only to the Israelite people according to the flesh, but also to us according to faith.

The text further adds: “And that which your high priest Melchizedek offered to you.” Concerning him Scripture plainly says: “Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine. For he was priest of God Most High, and he blessed Abraham” (Gen. XIV, 18).

His priesthood and sacrifice are so greatly magnified that the Apostle says of him: “First, Melchizedek, which is interpreted ‘king of righteousness,’ then also king of Salem, which is ‘king of peace,’ without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, made like the Son of God, he remains a priest forever” (Heb. VI, 3).

[Col. 0058A] What is added after all this—“a holy sacrifice, an immaculate victim”—seems to refer back to what was said above: “Upon which may you deign to look with a merciful and serene countenance,” so that it may complete the petition that follows.

The almighty God is therefore entreated in all this to regard the Church’s sacrifice as acceptable as the sacrifice of righteous Abel, of the patriarch Abraham, and of the high priest Melchizedek. For in those ancient sacrifices there was an image of this true sacrifice; and at that time the one God, author of both Testaments and of both sacrifices, was pleased by it, according to the most orderly arrangement of the ages, as a prefiguration of the truth that was to come. Now He is pleased by the same sacrifice in the fulfillment of that truth.

[Col. 0058B] For in Abel’s sacrifice—which was offered from the firstborn of the sheep and their fat and was preferred to Cain’s sacrifice, which was offered from the fruits of the earth—the faith of the New Testament was prefigured. By this faith, innocence, praising God through grace, is preferred to the earthly works of the Old Testament.

In the sacrifice of Abraham’s only and beloved son, the sacrifice of the One concerning whom the Father says, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. XVII, 5), was prefigured. Hence the Apostle says: “He did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all” (Rom. VIII, 32).

[Col. 0058C] The sacrifice of Melchizedek was so true a signification of Christ’s sacrifice that it was foretold concerning it: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4).

The mystery continues:

66. “We earnestly beseech you, almighty God,” etc. Who could sufficiently comprehend these words of the mystery, so profound, so wondrous and awe-inspiring? Who could speak anything worthy of them? They are more to be revered and feared than investigated. Blessed Gregory, however, a suitable interpreter of so great a mystery, speaks of them in one place almost ineffably, as of an ineffable reality (Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book IV, 60):

“For what believer,” he says, “could doubt that, at the very hour of the oblation, at the priest’s voice the heavens are opened; that in this mystery of Jesus Christ the choirs of angels are present; that the highest and the lowest are joined; that earthly things are united to heavenly things; and that one reality is made from visible and invisible things?”

The same teacher also subtly shows elsewhere how God’s sublime altar in the presence of His divine majesty is to be understood, explaining the psalm verse: “Appoint the solemn day in the crowded gathering, even to the horn of the altar” (Ps. 117:27). “The solemn day,” he says, “is the union of our heart with the Lord. But the solemn day is appointed in the crowded gathering when the mind is continually moved by devout love toward Him, as though we were saying to Him: ‘How long shall we do these things? How long shall we be afflicted by tribulation?’” Immediately he added the limit to which this must continue, saying: “even to the horn of the altar.” For the horn of the altar is the exaltation of the inward sacrifice. When we have reached it, there is no longer any necessity for us to make a solemn day to the Lord out of our lamentation. [Col. 0059A]

Blessed Augustine likewise speaks of the same sublime altar. Explaining the psalm verse, “I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will encompass Your altar, O Lord” (Ps. 25:6), he briefly states: “‘Among the innocent I will make my works clean,’ he says, ‘by which I will embrace Your sublime things.’”

Elsewhere (on Ps. 42, no. 5), explaining the verse, “And I will enter to the altar of God, to God who gives joy to my youth,” he says of the same matter:

“There is an invisible altar to which the unjust does not approach; only he approaches it who approaches this one securely. There he will find his life who here discerns his case; whatever sacrifice there is, he who enters will himself be taken up as a burnt offering.”

He repeats in other words what this altar is when he says, “to God who gives joy to my youth.” Elsewhere the same teacher, explaining the same verse as blessed Gregory, says:

“For in that eternal house there is a sacrifice of praise, an eternal priest, and an eternal altar: the peaceful mind itself of the righteous. Therefore, let that solemn day on which the Lamb was slain not suffice on earth; but appoint it in the dense thickets as everlasting, searching into high and secret things, until you arrive there, your minds exalted by God, even to His divinity. And what else shall we sing there but praises? What else shall we say there but: ‘You are my God, and I will confess to You; You are my God, and I will exalt You’?” (Ps. 117:28). “We shall not say this with a clamor of words, but the love clinging to Him itself cries out this utterance: Love itself is the voice.”

These things concerning the sublime altar of God in the presence of His divine majesty have necessarily been set forth here from the words of the holy Fathers, so that no one thinking carnally may suppose that there is a bodily altar in heaven, made from a heavenly or super-heavenly body. Rather, according to the understanding of the spiritual Fathers, we should understand God’s sublime altar to be rational and intelligible, existing in an elect and rational creature—namely, angelic and human nature.

In the holy angels, from the moment they were created, it has been exalted in the contemplation of its Creator and united most closely to itself through the spirit of peace; thus it exists as the true and sublime altar of God. From it God receives an everlasting sacrifice of praise and an offering of jubilation. To the unity of this altar the whole multitude of the elect is joined now through faith and, in the future, through the vision of divine contemplation.

But while they live in this mortality, before they actually enter that altar of God, before they reach the horn of the altar, they are still situated, as it were, in lower places. They are aided by the heavenly powers, so that through their intervention they may be heard and, as if from the sublimity of the altar, may be received. Thus we read that the angel Gabriel appeared to Daniel as he prayed and entreated, and said to him: “From the beginning of your prayers the word went forth, and I came because of your words; and no one is my helper in all these things except Michael the archangel, your prince” (Dan. 9:23).

And in the prophet Zechariah we read, for the consolation and deliverance of God’s people, of an angel pleading and saying: “O Lord of hosts, how long will You not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which You have been angry? This is already the seventieth year” (Zech. 1:12). And the Lord answered the angel with good words, words of consolation.

Likewise, the angel Raphael says to Tobiah: “When you were praying with tears and burying the dead, I offered your prayer to the Lord; and now the Lord has sent me to heal you,” etc. (Tob. 12:12).

Therefore, in this prayer and sacred offering of consecration something incomprehensible and ineffable takes place—something far more wondrous than all these things: through angelic ministries and supplications, as though from the sublime altar of the divine majesty, offerings are presented before God’s sight at that hour of the oblation. At that time Christ, with the heavenly ministers standing beside Him, is to be believed present in order to consecrate what has been set before Him.

On this subject it seems appropriate to set down the words of blessed Ambrose from his *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke* (Book I, no. 28):

“Do not doubt,” he says, “that the angel is present when Christ is present and Christ is sacrificed. For Christ has been sacrificed as our Passover. Therefore it is not without reason that, when Zechariah was praying, an angel appeared at the right side of the altar of incense, because the coming of the true Priest was already being announced and the heavenly sacrifice was being prepared, in which the angels would minister.”

These things must therefore be contemplated in such a way that we strive to attain something by that contemplation than which nothing is better or higher.

67. Likewise, what follows: “So that all of us, whoever have received from this participation in the altar the most holy body and blood of the Son, may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace.” These gifts—these are the gifts established above all glory. By them almighty God refreshes His faithful, gives them life through the glorious body of His Son, sanctifies them, and prepares them for eternity. Through them He fills the hearts of the faithful with every heavenly blessing and grace, granting chastity to their bodies, faith to their minds, and purity to their thoughts.

Through these gifts mercy protects His own, strengthens them with hope, and fortifies them with love, so that, receiving God within themselves through so great a participation in the Lord, they may deserve to become His temple.

What it means, then, to be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace through participation in the body and blood of the Son of God, and how greatly this good should be hungered and thirsted for, let us hear blessed Ambrose teaching and exhorting us sweetly:

“Christ is food for the Church; Christ is drink. The flesh of God is food, and the blood of God is drink. Christ is offered to us daily. This food does not fatten the body, but strengthens the human heart. This is the bread of life: whoever therefore eats life cannot die. Come to Him and be satisfied, because He is bread. Come to Him and drink, because He is the fountain. Come to Him and be enlightened, because He is light. Come to Him and be freed, because where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. Come to Him and be absolved, because He is the forgiveness of sins.

“The body of the Lord Jesus is the plea for divine reconciliation and eternal protection. Take this defense for yourself; receive the Lord Jesus as the guest of your mind. Where His body is, there Jesus is. When the adversary sees that your dwelling has been occupied, through the splendor of heavenly wisdom he will understand that the place has been closed against his schemes by Christ.

“Who is this one, you ask? Hear Him Himself saying: ‘I am the bread of life; whoever comes to Me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in Me shall never thirst’” (John 6:35).

The mystery continues.

68. “Remember also, O Lord, Your servants and handmaids who have gone before us with the sign of faith,” etc., “that You may grant them a place of refreshment, light, and peace, we beseech You.”

The devout mother Church also prays for her deceased and commends them through the intercession of the sacred offering, firmly believing that the precious blood which was poured out for many for the remission of sins benefits not only the salvation of the living but also the absolution of the dead, as blessed John testifies, saying: “The blood of His Son Jesus cleanses us from every sin” (1 John 1:7).

For the faithful depart from the body and go to the Lord, but they are not preceded by the Church, because they go before with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace. They have the sign of faith because they have been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit and marked with the cross and passion of Christ.

They sleep as those who will truly be raised in the resurrection. They sleep in the sleep of peace because they have not been separated from the unity and fellowship of Christ and the Church by heresies, schisms, or mortal sins. Even if they were at some time involved in these, they were healed through repentance and reconciled through the prayer of the Church, and, through the mystery of forgiveness, restored to the fellowship; thus they died in peace through the mercy of Him who does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.

For the souls of the devout dead are not separated from the Church. Otherwise, their memory would not be made at the altar in commemoration of Christ’s body; nor would it benefit anyone, in dangers, to hasten to His baptism lest life end without it; nor would reconciliation benefit one who, through a perverse or evil conscience, had been separated from that same body. Why are these things done, except because the faithful dead are also His members?

Although they do not yet reign with Christ together with their bodies, their souls nevertheless already reign with Him. Thus we read in the Apocalypse: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. From now on the Spirit says that they may rest from their labors, for their works follow them” (Rev. 14:13).

This is the true sabbath-rest of the faithful, that is, their repose, of which the Apostle says: “Therefore a sabbath-rest remains for the people of God” (Heb. 4:9). For whoever has entered into His rest has rested from his works, just as God also rested from His.

Thus the Church now reigns with Christ among the living and the dead. For this reason, as the Apostle says: “Christ died so that He might be Lord both of the living and of the dead” (Rom. 14:9). Hence elsewhere he says: “God has not appointed us for wrath, but for the acquisition of salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with Him” (1 Thess. 5:9).

By these words he intended those who are awake to be understood as the living, and those who are asleep as the dead, just as he says again: “Whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s” (Rom. 14:8).

69. (Gregory.) For it is clearer than light that the souls of the perfect righteous, as soon as they leave the confines of this flesh, are received into heavenly dwellings. The Truth Himself also attests this, saying: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matt. 24:28), because where our Redeemer Himself is bodily, there undoubtedly the souls of the righteous will also be gathered.

And Paul desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ. Therefore, whoever does not doubt that Christ is in heaven cannot deny that Paul’s soul is in heaven, since he also speaks of the dissolution of his body and his dwelling in the heavenly homeland, saying: “We know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5:1).

70. (Vigilius.) It must be noted that this is true of apostles, martyrs, confessors, and other such men. For there are souls of certain righteous people which, although they are in blessed rest, are delayed from the heavenly kingdom in certain dwellings. In the harm caused by this delay it is shown that they lacked something of perfect righteousness.

But some, predestined to the lot of the elect because of the good works of faith, are nevertheless received after death for chastisement in the severe flames of purgatorial fire because of certain evils with which they departed from the body. They are cleansed from the stain of their vices either by a lengthy purification lasting until the day of judgment, or, having been released from their punishments earlier through the prayers, almsgiving, fasts, tears, and offerings of the saving sacrifice made by faithful friends, they themselves attain the rest of the blessed.

The sacred sacrifices offered for those dead therefore benefit those who, while living here, obtained that the good works performed here by others on their behalf would also help them after death.

Among these matters, however, we must consider that the safer course is for each person to do for himself while alive the good that he hopes will be done for him after death by others. For it is more blessed to depart free than to seek freedom after chains.

Because of those words, “who have gone before us with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace,” it was the custom of the ancients—as it is also practiced by the Roman Church—for the names of the dead to be recited immediately from the diptychs, that is, from tablets. After the reading of the names, the following words were added:

“To them and to all who rest in Christ, grant, we beseech You, a place of refreshment, light, and peace.”

To them, namely, whose names are mentioned, and to all the others who rest in Christ, grant a place of refreshment, where they do not feel the heat of punishments; and of light, concerning which the Psalmist says: “That I may please God in the light of the living” (Ps. 55:14); and of peace, concerning which the righteous Simeon says: “Now You dismiss Your servant, O Lord, according to Your word, in peace” (Luke 2:29). It is the peace in which the souls of the holy martyrs rest, as Scripture says: “They seemed in the eyes of the foolish to have died, but they are in peace” (Wis. 3:2–3).

71. This devout and religious observance—which the whole Church throughout the world undoubtedly received from apostolic tradition and keeps uniformly and solemnly—is also strongly commended by the Scripture of the Old Testament and by the custom diligently preserved by the Fathers.

For we read in the books of the Maccabees that the very brave man and high priest Judas sent twelve thousand drachmas of silver to Jerusalem to be offered for the sins of those who had fallen in battle, considering that those who had received their death with piety had an excellent reward stored up for them. There it is also added to the praise of his faith that, with a holy and salutary thought, he prayed for the dead, that they might be released from sin.

The mystery continues.

72. “To us also, Your sinful servants,” etc., “through Christ our Lord.”

A commendation for the spirits of the dead through the offering of piety, so that they may deserve to obtain a place of refreshment, light, and peace in the blessed dwellings of the elect.

Then almighty God is fittingly prayed also to lead the other faithful who remain and live—that is, the priests and the people—to the same blessedness through the power and grace of God and through the help of the venerable sacrament.

For this is the voice of the whole Church, that is, of priests and people, who with humility and contrition of heart say to God: “To us also, Your sinful servants.” Although we ought at all times to recognize from the heart that we are sinners, this must nevertheless be done and confessed with particular attention when, in that sacred mystery, the grace of forgiveness and the remission of sins are celebrated.

With humility and contrition of heart we must say to God: “To us also, Your sinful servants,” because, as it is written, even if we have sinned, we are His, knowing His greatness. We hope not from any of our merits but from the multitude of His mercies, and from the heart we sing in the psalm: “According to the multitude of Your mercies, blot out my iniquity” (Ps. 50:3).

At this point the words of the Apostle must be recalled and carefully impressed upon us: “Every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed for human beings in matters pertaining to God, so that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins; he is able to have compassion on those who are ignorant and erring, since he himself is surrounded by weakness, and for this reason he must offer for sins both on behalf of the people and on his own behalf” (Heb. 5:1–3).

Blessed Gregory, exhorting us concerning this in one place, says:

“But it is necessary that, when we do these things, we ourselves sacrifice to God in the contrition of our hearts, because those who celebrate the mysteries of the Lord’s passion must imitate what they perform. For then the victim will truly be offered to God on our behalf, when He has made us ourselves a victim.”

Almighty God is therefore prayed to grant not only to the dead, whose commemoration was made above, but also to us sinners who hope in the multitude of His mercies, some portion and fellowship with His holy apostles and martyrs and with all the saints, according to our measure. We are now joined to them through the communion of faith; in the future may we also receive fellowship with them in life and eternal blessedness.

We ask that God’s mercy bring us into their fellowship, so that He may be not an assessor of our merits but a giver of forgiveness; so that, because we cannot be joined to the fellowship of the saints through merit, we may be joined to it through indulgence.

For if we are assessed and weighed according to divine judgment, no one will rise to the fellowship of the apostles and martyrs.

At the end of this prayer, as also in the preceding prayers, the words “through Christ our Lord” are added, and immediately the conclusion of the entire consecration follows, saying:

73. “Through whom You always create all good things,” etc.

Through Him almighty God not only created, at the beginning of the world, all these good things that are consecrated on the sacred altars, bringing into being what did not exist—for through His only-begotten Word He spoke, and it came to be: “Let the earth bring forth green plants bearing seed, and fruit trees producing fruit” (Gen. 1:11)—but He also continually creates these same good things by propagating and renewing them, so that every year new crops and new wines may arise.

In that creation, certainly, the grass of grain and the wood of wine also came forth. But concerning this work of governing, propagating, and renewing creation, the only-begotten Son Himself says in the Gospel to the Jews who were indignant that He healed on the Sabbath: “My Father is working until now, and I am working.” It was as though He were saying: “The Father did not work only during the first six days, as you suppose, but He is working until now—not by instituting a new kind of creation, but by propagating what He created in the beginning, so that it may not perish.”

(Vigilius.) “And I am working,” He says—that is, “until now,” ordering, governing, and increasing all things with Him. In these words He most clearly proclaimed Himself equal to God the Father, because where there is one and the same operation, there is undoubtedly also equal majesty.

Through Him, as has been said, God the Father continually creates all these good things. Once created and offered before His sight, He sanctifies them, so that what was simple creation may become sacrament. By sanctifying them He thus gives them life, so that they may be mysteries of life, so that life may be received in them, and so that they may supply vital substance to those who receive it.

By sanctifying and giving life to them, He ineffably blesses them, because He enriches them with every heavenly blessing and grace. Thus sanctified, given life, and blessed, He grants them to us through the same One who sanctifies, gives life, and blesses together with Him, and who has given us such a salutary refreshment from His body and blood.

(Augustine.) “Let those who eat, eat; and let those who drink, drink. Let them hunger and thirst; let them eat life and drink life. To eat that is to be refreshed. But you are refreshed in such a way that the source of your refreshment does not fail. What is it to drink that, except to live? Eat life, drink life; you will have life, and life is complete.

“But this will be so—that is, the body and blood of Christ will be life for each person—if what is visibly received in the sacrament is spiritually eaten in the very truth and spiritually drunk.”

74. Through Him, therefore, as has been said, God the Father ineffably blesses all these good things by sanctifying and giving them life, because He enriches them with every heavenly blessing and grace and prepares them for us.

“Through Him, and with Him, and in Him, to God the Father almighty, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, is all honor and glory.”

“Through Him,” namely, as through the true Mediator of God and human beings; “with Him,” as one equal to Him; “in Him,” as truly consubstantial with Him.

All honor and glory belong to God the Father through the Son, and with the Son, and in the Son, in the unity of the Holy Spirit. Proceeding from the Father and the Son, the Spirit possesses unity of divinity with the Father and the Son and is therefore worshiped and glorified together with them.

In the Father authority is indicated; in the Son, birth; in the Holy Spirit, the community of the Father and the Son; and in the three, equality throughout all ages of ages.

This is what blessed Jude the Apostle distinctly and deliberately sets forth at the end of his Epistle, saying: “To the only God our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, magnificence, dominion, and power before every age, and now, and throughout all ages of ages” (Jude 25).

The age began—that is, temporal mutability began—with the creation of the creature. The present ages run on, passing away in the course of mutable things. The future ages will follow, enduring eternally in the unchangeable state of things.

Yet because all these things are fixed in God’s eternal wisdom, without any beginning or mutability whatsoever—for, as we read in the Gospel, “What was made in Him was life” (John 1:3)—the phrase “ages of ages” is rightly understood to mean ages remaining in the unshaken stability of God’s wisdom, the causes of those ages that pass away with time.

Or “ages of ages” may simply be understood either as the continuation of what precedes or as things joined together in continuous intermingling. They are called “ages of ages” until the whole powerful age, woven from the ages of different times, reaches its end and the future age succeeds it—an age that has no end, where God will be seen and praised without end.

“Amen,” which is answered by the whole Church, is interpreted as “truly,” not wherever and however it may be said, but in a mystical religious sense.

(Augustine.) The faithful therefore give this response for the consecration of so great a mystery, just as they respond in every lawful prayer, and by responding they give their assent.

The priest then adds and says: “Let us pray.”

75. “Instructed by saving precepts,” etc.

It was entirely fitting that this whole most holy action should be concluded with the Lord’s Prayer [Note: Thus Saint Augustine, *Sermon* 227, addressed to the newly baptized: “Behold, when the sanctification has been completed, we say the Lord’s Prayer, which you received and returned. After it, ‘Peace be with you’ is said, and Christians kiss one another with a holy kiss.], and that the petitions of the faithful—which the Lord taught us either for the sake of the future life or for the present life—should be commended more effectively through the same remembrance of His passion.

The whole Church is therefore admonished, and the priest says, “Let us pray.” The Church prays with the priest, not with the voice but with the heart: the lips are closed, but the conscience is open; there is silence, yet the breast cries out, and He who has mercy hears with His ears.

For when Susanna was being condemned by unjust judges, she was silent and prayed. Her mouth was not heard by human beings, but her heart cried out to God. Surely, because her voice did not proceed from the mouth of her body, she did not therefore deserve to be heard? She was heard, but when she prayed no human being knew.

The priest therefore prays together with the Church, turning toward the Lord, and says: “Instructed by saving precepts,” etc.

What is supremely saving for us is this: God the Father has bestowed such grace upon us through His only-begotten Son that, thinking upon and loving such goodness, we should act in such a way that we are no longer children of the world but children of God.

Commanded, therefore, by saving precepts and formed by divine instruction, we presume to say to God—not with the rashness of presumption, but with the devotion of obedience:

76. “Our Father, who are in heaven,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0066D] We have four sermons of St Augustine addressed to candidates for baptism on the Lord’s Prayer, namely 56, 57, 58, and 59, as well as two among the spurious works, 64 and 65, in which the doctrine expounded here is presented more fully.]

We say the Lord’s Prayer for the advancement of our salvation. Through it the only-begotten Son instructed us and commanded us, through the bath of regeneration and the Spirit of adoption, to call ourselves children of God. He Himself, by divine rather than human instruction, gave us the form of prayer, so that we might dare to say to God: “Our Father, who are in heaven.”

(Augustine.) We believe that God is everywhere and that the divine presence is everywhere, but not that the grace of His indwelling is everywhere. Because of this indwelling, wherever His grace is recognized through love, we do not say, “Our Father, who are everywhere,” although this too is true. Rather, we say, “Our Father, who are in heaven,” so that in prayer we may commemorate His temple, which we too ought to know.

(Severianus.) To the extent that we exist, to that extent we belong to His fellowship and the family of adoption.

Nor did the Son omit Himself in this prayer; rather, He joined Himself to the unity of the Father, since He commanded that He Himself also be prayed to in the Father. For when you ask the Father, you invoke the name of the Son.

77. “Hallowed be Your name.”

This does not mean that we wish God to be hallowed by our prayers, but that we ask God for His name to be hallowed in us. For by whom is God, who Himself sanctifies, sanctified? Yet He Himself says: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. 11:44).

We ask and pray that, having been sanctified in baptism, we may persevere in what we have begun to be. We are also admonished to desire that His name, which is always holy, may be held holy among human beings as well—that is, that it may not be despised. This benefits not God but human beings.

78. “Your kingdom come.”

By this petition we stir up our desire for the future kingdom, so that it may come to us and we may deserve to reign in it. That is, we ask that what we do not doubt will come for all the saints may come also to us, so that we may deserve to recognize His kingdom.

79. “Your will be done, as in heaven so on earth.”

This does not mean that God should do what He does not will, but that we may be able to do what God wills, so that, like the holy angels, we too may do His will.

By heaven and earth we may also understand spirit and flesh, since the spirit is known to be from heaven and the flesh from earth. But the spirit seeks heavenly things, while the flesh desires earthly things. Therefore we ask that, with these two in agreement, we may do God’s will.

It may also be understood in this way: the faithful, who are now called heavenly because of the gift of faith, are understood to pray for unbelievers who are still on earth, so that God’s will may be done concerning them by turning them to Him; so that earth may imitate heaven, a human being may imitate an angel, and an unbeliever may imitate a believer.

Accordingly, we pray and ask that we may make petition for the salvation of all.

80. “Give us this day our daily bread.”

By this petition we ask for a sufficient supply of daily nourishment, signifying the whole by the name “bread,” since by “bread,” in Greek and in Latin, is meant that whole sacrament of the faithful. This sacrament is necessary even in the present time, yet not for attaining the happiness of this time, but that eternal happiness.

For Christ is the bread of life, and we ask that He be given to us daily, so that we who are in Christ and daily receive the Eucharist may not, through the intervention of some serious offense, be separated from the body of Christ. He Himself says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever” (John 6:41).

Therefore, just as it is clear that those who truly and worthily receive His body live, so conversely we must fear that those who are separated from the body of Christ may perish in everlasting death, Christ declaring: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (ibid., 54).

And therefore we ask that our bread—that is, Christ—be given to us daily, so that we who remain and live in Him may not depart from His sanctification and body, without which we cannot live forever.

81. “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

Here we are admonished what we should ask and what we should do in order to deserve to receive. After the support of food, forgiveness of sin is also requested, so that the one who is fed by God may live in God.

We are admonished that we are sinners, because we are compelled to pray for our sins, lest anyone please himself as though he were innocent. We are instructed and taught that we sin daily, since we are commanded to pray daily for our sins.

God plainly added a law, binding us by a definite condition and pledge, so that we should ask for our debts to be forgiven according to the way in which we forgive our debtors. We know that we cannot obtain the forgiveness we ask for our sins unless we have done the same toward our debtors, as the Gospel says: “In the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Luke 6:38).

And elsewhere: “When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may also forgive you your sins” (Mark 11:25).

Finally, no excuse remains for you on the day of judgment, since you will be judged according to your own sentence, and what you have done to others you yourself will suffer.

Likewise, what we have done to others, He will do to us, saying in the Gospel: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins; but if you do not forgive, neither will God forgive you your offenses” (Matt. 6:14–15).

82. “And do not lead us into temptation.”

We ask that, deprived of His help, we may neither, having been deceived, consent to some evil temptation nor, when afflicted, yield to it.

In this petition it is shown that the adversary can do nothing against us unless God has first permitted it. Therefore we ask that, strengthened by His help, we may remain thus firmly bound, so that, when tempted, we are not subjected to the evil enemy.

83. “But deliver us from evil.”

Here we are admonished to consider that we are not yet in that good in which we suffer no evil. This petition extends so broadly that a Christian placed in any temptation or tribulation utters his groans and pours out his tears for this.

When we say, “Deliver us from evil,” nothing remains that we ought still to ask beyond this, once we have requested God’s protection against evils.

“Amen,” the seal of the Lord’s Prayer, interpreted as “truly” or “faithfully,” is an affirmation of the truth. Following the Apostle’s tradition, the Church customarily gives the same response to other prayers as well, as the Apostle writes to the Corinthians:

“If you bless in the spirit, how will the one who fills the place of the unlearned say ‘Amen’ over your blessing, since he does not know what you are saying?” (1 Cor. 14:16).

From this it is shown that one cannot respond, “It is true,” to what is said unless one has first understood it.

After the Lord’s Prayer, which the whole Church pours forth to God as the completion of the perfect mystery, the priest follows in the conclusion of that same prayer and says:

[Col. 0068C]

84. “Deliver us, we beseech You, O Lord, from all evils,” etc.

In these words, past evils from which we ask to be delivered are to be understood as our sins already committed. Although the act of sin has now ceased in us, guilt nevertheless remains unless it is erased by divine forgiveness.

Therefore divine Scripture admonishes us, saying: “My son, you have sinned; do not add again to it, but pray also concerning your past sins, that they may be forgiven you” (Ecclus. 21:1).

Present evils arise because we sin daily; hence we need to say: “Forgive us our debts.” Our daily sins may also be understood as those occurring in the soul, as well as the illnesses and afflictions that often arise in the body from outside, and countless calamities such as famine, pestilence, the sword, and other things of this kind.

Whenever we suffer these things, we ought to implore the help of Him who alone in His mercy heals both souls and bodies. He knows when to apply to His children—whom He prepares for an eternal inheritance—both the scourge of correction and the sweetness of consolation.

What else are future evils to be understood as except whatever may happen to us that is contrary to salvation and peace, whether through the temptations of the devil or through the adversities and miseries of the world?

Above all, we must pray to escape those evils: to be delivered from the coming eternal condemnation, which will undoubtedly come upon the wicked.

The priest therefore prays—or rather, the whole Church with the priest—that what was said at the end of the Lord’s Prayer, “But deliver us from evil,” may be granted to us through God’s mercy, so that we may be delivered from all evils—that is, from those which have happened to us in the past, those which happen to us in the present, and those which we fear may happen to us in the future.

Thus the Lord, knowing our weakness, placed as we are amid such dangers, mercifully admonishes us, saying: “Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation” (Matt. 26:41). And again: “Watch, therefore, praying at all times, so that you may be worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of Man” (Luke 21:36).

The priest follows and says:

**85.** And with the intercession of the blessed and glorious [Virgin], etc. The Lord, when the Israelite people were being held captive in Babylonian servitude, said among other things through the prophet Jeremiah: “And pray for the peace of the city to which I have caused you to be carried away, because in its peace there will be peace for you” (Jer. XXIX, 7). Likewise the Apostle exhorts the people [Col. 0069B] of the Church, saying: “I desire, therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and for all who are in high position, so that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all godliness” (1 Tim. II, 1).

Accordingly, following this pattern divinely established through the prophet and the Apostle, the faithful people, in their pilgrimage through this world—as captives, so to speak, in Babylon and longing for their heavenly homeland—also pray for temporal peace, lest they be hindered from spiritual and eternal peace. Thus, with persecutions, seditions, and hostilities removed through God’s mercy, the Church may lead a quiet and tranquil life in complete peace. And she prays for this, according to a general observance, without interruption at every Sunday offering, in which, in accordance with the apostolic command, she offers God her supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings [Col. 0069C]. She asks this of God through the intercession, first of all, of the Mother of God, through whom salvation arose for the human race, and of the blessed apostles Peter, Paul, and Andrew, so that she may be deemed worthy to obtain it.

In this petition, the intercession of the other saints is not omitted; rather, in commemorating these, the assistance of all is sought. For just as they all exist joined and united to one another in God, so they all desire one thing and pray for the salvation of human beings, so that all may likewise be held together in the One and likewise not be neglected in the One. For the saints do not love those who choose them if they find them deserters of their companions; and whoever thinks that this should be done will offend those to whom he turns more than those from whom he turns away [Col. 0069D]. For they rejoice in unity, and in Christ they are one.

**86.** What the Church therefore says—“Graciously grant peace in our days”—she does plainly according to the example found in Isaiah. For when that same prophet had foretold to King Hezekiah, our king, the evils of the captivity that was to come, he replied, moved to compunction: “The word of the Lord that he has spoken is good; let peace and truth only be in my days” (Isa. XXXIX, 8). In this way he humbly left the future to God’s judgment, while pleading for the present insofar as it concerned his own salvation and that of his people: “Let peace and truth,” he said, “be in my days”—peace, lest the tranquility of the kingdom be disturbed by enemies; and truth, so that in that very peace the worship of God and the truth of religion might be preserved [Col. 0070A]. Hence the Apostle also placed both together when he commanded that these things be prayed for: “So that we may lead,” he said, “a quiet and tranquil life in all godliness.” For quiet and tranquility belong to peace, while godliness belongs to the religious worship of God. Thus the Church also prays that peace may be established in our days; and after us others, and after them still others, will likewise pray for it until the consummation of the world.

**87.** When she asks for peace itself, she adds that, aided by the power—that is, by the help and protection—of God’s mercy, we may always be free from sins insofar as this concerns the inward devotion of religion, and that, insofar as it concerns inward peace, we may also be secure from every disturbance. For the peace in which service is rendered not to divine religion but to worldly desire belongs not to the just but to the wicked, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “For I was jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. LXXII, 3).

There follows what is customarily added at the conclusion both of this and of nearly all ecclesiastical prayers:

**88.** “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son,” etc. (Fulgentius, *Letter* 14 to Ferrandus, §36). As has often been said, the Catholic Church celebrates this with sound reason, on account of that sacrament: Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and human beings, who became human, a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, entered once for all through his own blood into the holy places—not those made by human hands, but into heaven itself, where he is at the right hand of God and intercedes for us [Col. 0070C].

Through him, therefore, we offer the sacrifice of praise and prayer, through whose death we were reconciled when we were enemies. For Christ, while remaining in the form of God, the only-begotten God to whom, together with the Father, we offer sacrifices, took the form of a servant and became a priest, through whom we may offer a living, holy sacrifice pleasing to God. Yet we could not have offered a sacrifice if Christ had not become a sacrifice for us.

When we say, “your Son,” and add, “who lives and reigns with you as God in the unity of the Holy Spirit,” we commemorate that unity which the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit possess by nature. Here it is shown that this same Christ fulfilled the priestly office for us, he whose unity with the Father and the Holy Spirit is natural [Col. 0070D]. When we say “in the unity of the Holy Spirit,” we show that the Holy Spirit has one nature with the Father and the Son. What else, then, is unity of nature than that the Trinity is one God—and that this One is also shown to be one kingdom? Where the unity of the kingdom is natural, one power of reigning remains.

Therefore Christ our Lord lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages, as he himself speaks in the Apocalypse, saying: “I am the first and the last; and I was living, and I was dead; and behold, I am living forever and ever” (Rev. I, 17). To him it is said in the Psalm: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.” And again: “Your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages” (Ps. CXLIV, 13). Concerning him the angel also says in the Gospel to blessed Mary: “And of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke I, 33).

**89.** When this prayer has been completed, the priest mixes the Lord’s offering, so that the Lord’s cup may contain the fullness of the sacrament. As though through the union of this same mystery, he invokes peace upon the Church, saying: “May the peace of the Lord be always with you.” To this great blessing the Church responds: “And with your spirit” (Augustine, Sermon 227).

What is the peace of the Lord, then, if not the peace of Christ? Christ’s peace has no temporal end, and it is the perfection of every devout action and intention. For the sake of this peace we believe in and hope in him, and through love of him we are kindled as much as he grants. For this peace, finally, we endure every tribulation courageously, so that in it we may reign happily without tribulation [Col. 0071B].

True peace creates unity, because “whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit.” Having therefore invoked peace, the whole Church, beginning with the priest, gives one another the kiss of peace, so that, with all united in true peace, they may become God’s dwelling place, as it is said in the Psalm: “And his place was made in peace” (Ps. LXXV, 13). And what the Psalmist says elsewhere may be fulfilled in the Church: “God is in his holy place; God makes those of one mind dwell in a house” (Ps. LXVII, 17) (Vigil).

The Church preserves this also by apostolic tradition. The same apostles frequently say to her: “Greet one another with a holy kiss” (Rom. XVI, 16)—that is, with a true kiss, a peaceful kiss, a dove-like kiss, not a false and treacherous one such as Joab used to kill Amasa, or Judas to betray the Savior, or those who speak peace with their neighbor while evil is in their hearts [Col. 0071C]. Those greet one another with a holy kiss who do not love in word or with the tongue, but in deed and truth.

**90.** Amid all this, all sing, and by singing they pray, saying: “Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world,” etc. (Augustine). For no one takes away sins except the one of whom it was said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world,” for whom no human good is impossible and no evil is incurable (Vigil).

The apostle Peter shows this when he says: “You were redeemed from your futile way of life inherited from your fathers, not with corruptible things, silver or gold, but with the precious blood, as of an undefiled and spotless Lamb, Christ” (1 Pet. I, 18). And in the Apocalypse the apostle John says: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. I, V), when he gave his blood for us upon the cross; or when each one of us, in the mystery of his most holy Passion, was washed with the waters of baptism. Indeed, he takes away the sins of the world and washes us from our daily sins in his blood when the memory of that same blessed Passion is recalled at the altar [Col. 0072B].

**91.** After this, when the Eucharist—that is, the good grace—has been received, and thanksgiving has been celebrated—for by God’s grace he tasted death for everyone—all respond: “Amen” (Augustine, Sermon 272). This is the clear voice of Christ’s blood, which the blood itself expresses through the mouth of the faithful who have been redeemed by that same blood.

**92.** When everything has been completed, absolution is given to the people who stand by and observe, while the deacon calls out: “Go, the dismissal has taken place.” *Missa*, therefore, is understood as nothing other than dismissal—that is, absolution—which the deacon declares after everything has been celebrated, when the people are dismissed from the solemn observance.

Hence the canons also speak of the “dismissal of the catechumens,” when, after the reading of the Gospel, the sacred mysteries begin to be celebrated, at which no one may be present unless regenerated in the baptismal font. At that point, when the deacon called out, those same catechumens were sent out—that is, dismissed outside. The dismissal of the catechumens, therefore, took place before the celebration of the sacraments; the dismissal of the faithful takes place after their completion and participation.

[Col. 0071]

# THE LITTLE WORKS OF FLORUS THE DEACON AGAINST AMALARIUS

(According to Martène, in the same place.)

## I. The letter of FLORUS begins, full of all truth, against the false-speaking inventions of AMALARIUS, formerly choir-bishop of Lyon, concerning the tripartite Body of the Lord.

**1.** To the most blessed, most reverend, and most devout shepherds of Christ’s flock, rulers of the Church of God, preachers and defenders of the Catholic faith: DROGO, master of the sacred council and most illustrious bishop; HETTI, bishop of Trier; ALDRIC, most reverend bishop of Le Mans; RABAN, venerable abbot; and, from the province of Lyon, ALBARIC, most reverend bishop of Langres; FLORUS, an unworthy son of the Catholic Church and a very little servant of your piety and fatherhood [Col. 0072D].

I beg you, most gentle and kind servants of Christ, to receive with devout and kindly affection, for love of Christ himself and of the pious mother, God’s Church, my lowly person, grieving and suffering with the dangers of God’s Church and humbly yet confidently reporting her needs to you. The person who speaks is indeed insignificant and unworthy; but the matter he speaks of belongs to the Lord, the cause belongs to the Lord—a cause certainly worthy of being commended by better men and fit to be brought for examination before your judgment, as it should have been long ago.

But since those who are more severely beaten usually cry out more loudly, and those compelled by the greatest need make their requests more insistently, they are considered worthy of pity rather than indignation. May it therefore be safe and permitted for me, the least of all under your fatherly care, to cry out sorrowfully amid the blows suffered by the Church, to complain of her disasters and miseries, and to implore from you the help of fatherly assistance.

**2.** For this reason, blessed lords and fathers, who excel in the height of your dignity, in the sincerity of your faith, in the fear of God, and in the integrity of your knowledge, and who are bound by a particularly close tie to the Church of Lyon, I have believed that this complaint ought above all to be brought to you [Col. 0073B]: so that, the more you surpass others through the abundance of God’s gift, the more earnestly and religiously you may struggle for the defense of the divine faith and truth.

Remember the Holy Spirit, who through Solomon cries out to people such as you are by Christ’s grace: “Rescue those who are being led to death, and do not cease to free those who are being dragged to destruction” (Prov. XXIV, 11). If you say, “Our strength is not sufficient,” he who examines the heart understands, and nothing escapes the Savior of your soul; he will repay each person according to his works.

For recently, in the Church mentioned above, an insane and empty error—hostile to faith and truth, contrary to religion and salvation—was introduced by its prelate, Amalarius. At first, after a synod of priests had been assembled, with everyone sitting around him as though listening to a teacher, he attempted to sow it by word of mouth. Indeed, with his whole purpose and effort, by proposing, explaining, and pressing it for three entire days, he impressed and handed it on to everyone, as though, being a minister of the New Testament, he wished indelibly to imprint everything he asserted upon tablets of fleshly hearts [Col. 0073C].

Then he also handed over for reading and copying a large codex extending through four volumes, composed and arranged by himself. He claimed that it was called the *Official*, as though it discussed the sacred offices with the greatest prudence and completeness. Yet it is so crammed with madness and errors that it would plainly seem worthy of ridicule and spitting even to the most ignorant.

He also brought forth an *Antiphonary*, supposedly arranged and corrected by himself, into which he inserted such things from his own imagination that, in view of his shameless audacity, the brow of the reader is struck with shame and blushes [Col. 0073D].

Most recently he arranged a new volume and had it elegantly bound at Lyon and decorated with silk ribbons. Carrying it to the palace, he is said to intend to present it either to the prince or to the master of the council. In it he is wrapped in such inept language, such absurd ideas, and such elaborate and unheard-of fantasies that you would think him to be raving like a madman. He calls the book of this most tasteless babbling the *Embolus* of his little works—and entirely correctly: it is indeed like a camel’s growing and swelling hump, an accumulation [variant: an augmentation] of his many errors.

**3.** To set out a few points individually seems both tiresome to your seriousness and unsuitable to the language of my petition. I fear that I might make it longer through trivial matters, so that it would appear burdensome in serious and necessary matters. Certainly the books themselves are scattered almost everywhere and known to almost everyone; nor do I doubt at all that they are condemned more severely by the judgment of serious and prudent men than my small capacity could comprehend or my speech exaggerate.

Nevertheless, lest I seem to ask for the aid of healing in vain if I conceal or fear to expose the wound, I will briefly repeat a few matters. As heavenly fellow-physicians, heal what is sick through the antidote of faith or through the scalpel or cautery of the most sincere truth; cut away what is rotten; burn away what is diseased; and provide together for the health of Christ’s body [Col. 0074A].

Far be it, far be it from the judgment of your seriousness that, in refuting errors and absurdities of this kind, the mind of any devout and faithful person should be held back by regard for a person, by the disguise of flattery, or by fear of human offense or danger. When the matter of faith, the cause of the Church, and the business of Christ are at stake, let faith alone, the mother Church alone, the lover of truth alone—or rather Truth, Christ—be kept before one’s eyes.

**4.** The teacher himself, the eminent Amalarius, teaches that Christ’s body is three-formed and tripartite, so that there are three bodies of Christ: the first, which he himself assumed; the second, in us who walk upon the earth; the third, in those who lie buried. He asserts that for this reason three parts ought to be made in the mystery of the sacrifice: one of the chalice for Christ, a second on the paten for the living, and a third on the altar for the dead [Col. 0074C].

He says that the bread is Christ’s flesh and the blood his soul, so that Christ may be whole. He says that it is uncertain whether Christ’s body taken from the altar remains in our body until the day of burial, or is invisibly received into heaven, or flows out with the blood when we cut a vein, or passes into the place of excrement along with the other things that enter the mouth.

His letter is in his book the *Official*, written to some bishop whom I do not know, and it contains this. There he also discusses spittle and phlegm in the most filthy manner. Although he is of such sordid mind and such rotten doctrine, he boasts that he is spiritual and judges everything, while calling others carnal and animal.

He calls the Lord’s chalice a tomb; the priest Joseph of Arimathea and the archdeacon Nicodemus, as though they were Christ’s gravediggers; the deacons, leaning backward, the apostles as though contracting themselves during the Lord’s Passion and wishing to hide; the subdeacons, standing upright facing forward; and the women, standing freely [Col. 0074D].

He attributes one part of the mystical prayer by which the Lord’s body is consecrated to Christ praying on the Mount of Olives, another to him hanging on the cross, and, after certain other foolish divisions, another to him dying. When the priest bows, this means: “And bowing his head, he gave up his spirit” (John XIX, 30).

**5.** He refers the proper fasts of the year to the four humors by which the human body is nourished, and asserts that the fasts are performed on their account. He says that two readings ought to be read at Mass on Wednesday because of the two heavenly bodies created on that day—to use his pagan terms, Phoebus and his sister Phoebe [Col. 0075A].

He also says that holy David, always strong and warlike in the Lord, burned in Mars in the pagan manner. He proclaims Mars to be the worst demon, inventor [variant: instigator] of tumults and wars, even citing a pagan poet who says: “Impious Mars rages throughout the whole world.”

In the Gospel of the Greater Litany, he understands the bread to mean the fruits of the earth; the fish, things born from the waters; and the egg, animals that are generated on earth from both sexes. Preferring such a fantasy of his own understanding to the Gospel’s meaning, he asserts that litanies are celebrated by the faithful at that time for the preservation of such things. “For then,” he says, “the crops are advancing, the fish are coming, and the chicks are trampling the fields.”

He further adds certain monstrous interpretations, with their heads downward and their feet upward, like the antipodes, so that in these matters the thing itself comes first and the figure follows. Yet the shadows of the law, according to the Apostle, signify future good things [Col. 0075B].

When the Gospel is taken from the altar, the altar itself signifies Jerusalem, from which the Gospel proceeded. The place of the altar signifies the place where Jacob, sleeping, saw angels. When the Roman pontiff gives alms on the Saturday before Palm Sunday, he signifies the woman who anointed the Lord.

**6.** As for the sacred garments of priests and ministers, the vessels of the divine ministry, the singers’ tablets, the bronze bells, and even the fringes, colors, and forms of the garments and footwear, as well as the sacred offices and the distribution of the Psalms—what inept, foolish, and utterly laughable things occur! It is as though he alone were permitted, after the Law and the Prophets, after the Gospels and the Apostles, to establish typical and mystical matters in the Church, so that anyone who dared to celebrate something else according to simple usage and custom would be considered a transgressor of his mysteries [Col. 0075C].

He says that in inventing such fantasies he follows the authority of Saint Augustine, because Augustine commands that obscure and ambiguous matters be examined and turned over for as long as necessary, until understanding leads to the love of God or neighbor, on which two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend.

Blinded by an excessive desire for novelties, he does not consider that Augustine was speaking of investigating the meanings of the sacred Scriptures. The books in which Augustine discusses these matters are entitled *On Christian Doctrine*; in them rules are given solely for understanding sacred Scripture. Much is discussed there about things and much about signs; yet nothing at all is said about the kinds of meanings this man seeks. Indeed, in the books addressed to Januarius, Augustine distinguishes the entire variety of ecclesiastical observances according to three categories, asserting that all of them have been handed down either by the authority of sacred Scripture, by the general tradition of the Church, or by the manifold customs of different places [Col. 0075D].

Of the first, he shows that there are very few, but that they are extremely easy in observance and outstanding in significance. He likewise asserts that the second are to be venerated with equal religious devotion. Regarding the third, however, he seeks no significance at all and no mystery; instead he follows the most sincere and weighty judgment of Blessed Ambrose and offers it for observance as though it were a heavenly oracle. When Ambrose was consulted about such matters, he replied: “When you come to any Church, observe its custom, if you do not wish to be a scandal to another or to have anyone become a scandal to you.”

In the same books addressed to Januarius, he says: “Whatever is established by human authority and held as though it were a sacrament and mystery is not to be approved in any way; rather, he expressly asserts that it must unquestionably be cut away” [Col. 0076A].

**7.** What, then, will this young teacher do with his mysteries? By what means will he defend so many inventions of his vanity? There is no authority of sacred Scripture, no general tradition of the Church concerning such matters, and no rule; the teaching of the Fathers is opposed to him. He gives the *Book of the Roman Order* such authority that he attempts to expound it almost word for word; yet immediately he contradicts himself by asserting that it was unknown to the Roman archdeacon whose traditions he boasts of following [Col. 0076B].

And if he drags the meaning of Scripture toward his fables and attempts to support his inventions of error from it, who does not know that it is characteristic madness of heretics always to cloak their lies with the appearance of truth, turning, as Isaiah says, silver into dross and mixing the strength of heavenly wine with the earthly foolishness of water?

May your fatherhood forgive me, unworthy and insignificant as I am, if in devoted petition I bring forward something necessary for the faith and beneficial to the Church. According to the command of the Law, the ox that gores with its horns must plainly be shut up, and its mouth must be restrained with the everlasting bridle of silence. Indeed, since it may already have attacked either a man or a woman—that is, either someone who considers himself strong or someone who is truly weak in faith—and has caused scandal, it must be buried beneath the points [reading uncertain: “spikes” or “stones”] of divine judgments, and its flesh—that is, its doctrine and opinions—must in no way be eaten.

For whenever he is challenged or warned about these matters, he does not readily and humbly submit, as is the custom of the devout. Instead, raising his horns more boastfully and arrogantly, he multiplies his madness, loudly claiming that all Germany thinks this way, all Italy, and Rome itself; that he has been at Constantinople, in Istria, or in Lucania, and that for this reason he possesses unique authority in such matters [Col. 0076C].

Nor is it enough for him to be entangled in such errors and fantasies himself, unless he also disgraces almost the whole world by making it his accomplice. Under the fictitious authority of many pontiffs, he persists in confirming his most foolish—or rather blasphemous—opinion concerning the division of the most holy Eucharist.

We do not criticize the custom of any Church, nor do we arrogantly prefer one to another; all are plainly united in Christ by the bond of peace and distinguished by the distribution of the Holy Spirit. Rather, we condemn the profane interpretation which is manifestly most hostile to sacred Scripture, the Catholic faith, and the unity of the Church [Col. 0076D].

Truly, no one has ever been permitted to call Christ’s body three-formed or tripartite, since the Apostle always proclaims it one and unique, saying: “One bread, one body are we, though many” (1 Cor. X, 17). And again: “We, though many, are one body in Christ” (Rom. XII, 5). And elsewhere: “One body and one spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling” (Eph. IV, 14) [Col. 0077A].

Truly, all the elect have one body under Christ, their one head: nourished by one Spirit, inseparably united to its head, strengthened and compacted by the indissoluble connection of its members, distinguished only by the variety of graces, neither divided by mortality nor dissolved by death itself.

For the fact that this teacher of such fictions is still living in mortal condition, while his father perhaps has died and been returned to dust, does not mean that they are divided either from Christ, if they have deserved to be his members, or from one another, insofar as concerns the grace of the unity of Christ’s body, by the obstacle of mortality or death. The condition of mortality and death belongs to the punishment of the ancient transgression, not to the ineffable unity of spiritual renewal [Col. 0077B].

Only love joins this unity together; only iniquity cuts it apart. The Apostle bears witness: “Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. VI, 17), while the Prophet cries out in opposition: “Your iniquities have divided between you and your God” (Isa. LIX, 2).

**8.** Saint Augustine rebuked Tichonius because, in the *Book of Rules*, he had called one of the seven parts of the Lord’s body “bipartite.” Changing the irreligious name, Augustine asserted that it ought rather to be called the body of the Lord, true and simulated, or the mixed body of the Lord. Thus the holy Father taught that there is now, in Christ’s body, a mingling resulting from the one catch of good and bad fish.

**9.** He rejected division, because the indissoluble unity of the sacrament admits no division whatsoever [Col. 0077C]. Yet with what miserable anxiety is he shaken and constrained, when he fears that Christ’s body may be defiled by the filth of human corruption, and therefore babbles in extraordinary vanity that it is either invisibly received into heaven or placed in our body as though in a container!

He adds “until the day of burial,” evidently fearing that even then, unless Christ’s body were separated from us by some unknown invisible means, it might be dissolved into dust by the condition of our body. But what honor does he confer upon it if he supposes that it flows out from an incision in a vein? It is astonishing that he does not suppose it to flow out simultaneously through the discharge of the nostrils as well. Do we not see in what filthy animals and places human blood is poured out and exposed?

Let such absurd and filthy thoughts about the saving and heavenly mystery be far from a faithful mind! That bread of the most holy offering is truly Christ’s body—not in visible material or appearance, but in spiritual power and efficacy [Col. 0077D].

For Christ’s body is not generated for us in a field, nor does his blood arise in a vineyard or flow from a winepress. Simple bread is made from grain, and simple wine is poured from clusters of grapes. To these the faith of the offering Church is added; the consecration of the mystical prayer is added; the infusion of divine power is added. Thus, in a marvelous and ineffable manner, what is naturally bread and wine from earthly growth becomes spiritually the body of Christ—that is, the mystery of our life and salvation.

In this mystery we see one thing with the eyes of the body and another through the perception of faith. We taste not only what we receive with the mouth, but what we believe with the mind. Hence we also faithfully ask that what we touch with our mouth we may receive with a pure mind [Col. 0078A].

This food, therefore, belongs to the mind, not to the belly. It does not decay but remains unto eternal life, because it grants eternal life to those who receive it devoutly. The person who receives it devoutly is one who, illuminated by the spirit of faith, hungers and thirsts in that visible food and drink for the power of intelligible grace; and spiritually receives the gift of forgiveness and salvation … No pollution whatsoever in this mystery must be imagined or feared.

For Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, is received in it. This Wisdom, as Scripture bears witness, is the radiance of eternal light and a certain emanation of God’s brightness; nothing defiled enters into it; and it reaches everywhere by reason of its purity [Col. 0078B].

Christ’s body, therefore, as has been said, is not present in visible appearance but in spiritual power. Nor can it be defiled by bodily refuse, since it is accustomed to cleanse the faults of souls and bodies.

**10.** I beg you, most blessed Fathers, to recall with your most devout hearts and to consider with all fear and trembling how great was the vigilance concerning faith and the care for truth among the ancient Fathers, and with what zeal they uprooted the seeds of disbelief and the scandals of impiety, so that the Church of Christ, the bride redeemed and adorned by the blood of her Bridegroom and Lord, the Lamb, might be found without spot or wrinkle.

I say nothing of Sabellius and Arius, who sinned against faith in the supreme, indivisible, and coeternal Trinity. I pass over Nestorius and Eutyches, whom it is commonly known to have held impious opinions concerning the faith of the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten. Nor do I touch upon those who, while holding the same faith in the Trinity, withdrew from the Church through the spirit of obstinate schism [Col. 0078C].

I come to those whom ancient sincerity cast out because they had wandered in the worship and celebration of the sacred holy things, or in certain superstitious observances. The Cataphrygians, who celebrate deadly mysteries, and the Manichaeans, who celebrate filthy mysteries, are rightly condemned. Let the Adamites also be considered rightly expelled from the Church because of their shamelessness. Naked men and women practiced mysteries in imitation of Adam and called their Church paradise. Yet how far does the superstition of nakedness differ from the observance of superstitious worship?

The Artonites—so called in Greek from bread and cheese—should rightly be judged outsiders, because in their mysteries, like imitators of Cain and Abel, they offered bread and cheese instead of the evangelical bread and wine. Likewise the Aquarians, because they offered water alone contrary to the evangelical command. Yet it must be piously considered that both these groups were rejected solely because, in the mystery of the sacrifice, contrary to the evangelical and apostolic ordinance, they presumed either to change something or to add or subtract something [Col. 0078D].

These practices, therefore, rightly disapproved in sacred matters, appear to have been justly punished, since by them so great a mystery was impiously violated. I ask: what did the Euchites, called by the Greek term *Euchitae* from praying, deserve? What did the Dactylici, called from a finger, or the Ascitae, called from a wineskin, do wrong, so that they should be excluded from the Church?

Prayer is good, yet the first were rejected because of an excessive excess of prayer. Silence too is good; but because of their excessive superstition regarding silence, so that they placed a finger upon their lips, the second group was cast out [Col. 0079A].

What, then, did the Ascitae do? What would now be considered so trivial, so unworthy of concern, or even so laughable? Going around an inflated and covered wineskin like drunkards, they called themselves new wineskins filled with evangelical wine.

Therefore, most blessed Fathers, care must be taken, and paternal vigilance must provide, lest perhaps even now the ancient enemy—who goes about like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour, who often raises a great evil from a small one and kindles new fires from sparks—should, through these new fantasies, nourish seeds of error in the hearts of the simple and ignorant.

Care must also be taken lest the divine books be violated by their utterly unskilled author. For he is constantly comparing them with the Hebrews, and, since he has no familiarity at all with their language or letters, he frequently, as I hear, twists what is correct [Col. 0079B].

In this matter too the Fathers exercised such great caution that they rejected among the books not to be received the Gospels which blessed Jerome records as having been falsified by Hesychius or Lucian. How much more suspect, then, ought the emendation of this man to be, since the facts themselves show that in so many matters he tramples upon the Scriptural command: “Do not move the ancient boundaries which your fathers established” (Prov. XXII, 28).

**11.** These are the matters, most holy Fathers, which I have judged that I ought to make known to your gentleness, out of fear of God, for the honor of the faith, and out of love for you—or rather, for the whole Church.

Now I, unworthy as I am, pray and beg you by our Lord Jesus Christ, who loved his Church and entrusted [variant: handed over] himself for her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word, so that he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind. May you be inflamed with zeal for the truth and, together with the holy council, attack this most tasteless error. May you drive the plague of this superstition not only from this Church of ours, which lies exposed to plunder, devastation, and trampling, but also from the other Churches of Christ [Col. 0079C].

Believe me, lords most worthy of all reverence, for this wretched and miserable Church laments nothing so much as the loss of truth, which she does not hear, and the growth of the many errors which she is compelled to endure.

You see, most holy Fathers, for whom and against whom I make my petition: for the Church of Christ, to which I owe faithfulness and charity unto death; against the fabricator of lies and cultivator of perverse doctrines, who, in the time of most prudent bishops and of a most religious prince, has attempted with reckless and sacrilegious audacity to inflict upon the Church of the living God—who is the pillar and foundation of truth—so many scandals of error and superstition, against the truth of Scripture, against the authority of the ecclesiastical Fathers, and against every order of reason [Col. 0079D].

These errors undoubtedly have a truncated beginning, a rotten middle, and a ruinous end.
