For either he will humbly confess his error, so that he may offer suitable satisfaction; or, if he prefers to assert stubbornly and shamelessly the inventions of his madness—which is not in his interest, nor do we desire it—he has examples of those who preceded him in such matters, as we have shown above, whose outcome he should fear [Col. 0080A].

**THE END.**

## II. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, the little work begins concerning the case of faith recently conducted before the council of bishops at Quierzy.

1. The matter very recently conducted at the palace of Carisiacum, in a general and highly renowned council of bishops, concerning certain questions of faith and ecclesiastical observances, was so memorable and salutary that, although it has been made known to nearly everyone, it nevertheless deserves most fully to be committed to writing for the benefit and edification of the faithful and to be diligently commended to the minds of all. [Col. 0080B]

2. For when, in the most sacred priestly assembly, the splendor of faith and truth is revealed under the inspiration of the Lord, who promised that he would be present in the midst of those gathered in his name, the divine gift ought not to be concealed. Rather, for the enlightenment of the Church and the praise of God’s name, it should be declared openly and clearly to everyone, as the Lord himself says: “Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house. Let your light so shine before men that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:15).

With this intention, therefore, and as God observes it, I shall endeavor, although with limited eloquence, to convey as briefly as I can the aforesaid matter, which was conducted laudably and profitably, to others [or, according to another reading, “to letters”], and, with the help of Christ the Lord, to impress it upon pious ears. I considered this especially necessary for us—that is, for the entire clergy of the Church of Lyon—so that those whose faith has hitherto been shamefully afflicted by the fables of an ill-omened and fanciful error may now, aided and strengthened by paternal support, rejoice that they have escaped and prevailed. [Col. 0080C]

3. The author of this unheard-of and execrable error, Amalarius, is known to everyone. He went so far in presumption that, spurning the truth of Scripture and trampling upon the authority of the holy Fathers, he violated the purity of the Catholic faith by a damnable doctrine and dared to envelop and discolor the simple observance of the Church with clouds of deceit. [Col. 0080D]

He has disseminated this pestilential vanity of his vanities far and wide for a long time—not so much with a living voice as with a dead one, but also through the monuments of numerous books—wherever he could, like a sower by night inserting weeds among the wheat of the Lord’s field. He abuses the testimonies of Scripture to support his senile absurdities and fits the opinions of orthodox Fathers to his fables.

4. The present Church perceived, indeed lamented, this evil when, in a very celebrated assembly of priests, with chorepiscopi and archdeacons present, as well as several others from the clergy, he presumed to teach such absurdities contrary to the faith that everyone’s ears recoiled. Later, he also forced upon the whole of our parish a copy of his detestable little works, as though it were to be read and recopied. A few days ago, moreover, the utterly demented man brought here another book of his, filled with the phantoms of his inventions.

All these things—more worthy of hatred and oblivion than of narration—I would gladly now pass over in silence, unless the order and cause of the matter whose explanation I have undertaken required me to touch upon them, even in a brief recollection. For the end of a question cannot properly be understood unless its beginning has first been carefully learned. [Col. 0081A]

5. The aforementioned teacher therefore asserts, among other things, that Christ’s body is threefold and tripartite—or rather, that there are three bodies of Christ. He supposes that the body of Christ which is received by the faithful in the sacrament either enters heaven invisibly, remains in the bodies of those who receive it until the day of burial, flows out with the blood through the cutting of the veins, or slips into the privy. [Col. 0081B]

He asserts that the deacons, when they stand bent before the altar, signify the apostles fearing and hiding during the Lord’s Passion; the subdeacons, the women standing fearlessly beside the cross; the priest, Joseph of Arimathea; the archdeacon, Nicodemus; the chalice, the tomb; the offering of the Lord’s body, the crucifixion; the wood itself, the teachers; the wood from which he hangs, the cross; the rope by which he is drawn, faith; the bell by which it sounds, the tongue; the hand of the one drawing it upward, the contemplative life; and when it is lowered, the active life.

He turns the exorcisms of catechumens, which are simply to be recited as an expression of spiritual cleansing, with excessive carnality toward the five bodily senses. [Col. 0081C]

6. He indicates that these same senses should be touched—eyes as well as ears and noses. He compares the Antiphonary with John’s Apocalypse. He says that all these and countless other absurdities are revealed by the Holy Spirit, arrogating to himself the testimony of the Apostle Peter, who says: “For prophecy was never brought forth by human will, but holy men of God spoke as they were inspired by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21).

From this it is plain that, pitiably deceived, he wishes both himself to be believed a prophet and his most empty and laughable doctrine—alas!—to be believed prophecy.

But, to explain briefly what has been begun: when the contagion of such a doctrine began to be spread in this Church for the overthrow of the simple, the shepherd, concerned for the salvation of the flock entrusted to him, made the matter known to the religious prince amid much bitterness of grief, complaining and lamenting that a great wound of the Church and an execrable stain upon the faith were being nourished under the presumption of such novelties, unless God’s providence, owed to him, should come swiftly to its aid.

The pious prince’s care, ardently and laudably attentive to God’s affairs, had summoned the reverend Fathers, the bishops, to the aforesaid palace on account of the Church’s many concerns. He caused the matter to be brought before their council for investigation and examination. When, in their hearing, such foolish and profane inventions of new ideas were recited—and the very man who had produced them from the boldest vanity of his heart was also present—the religious ears recoiled at the blasphemous statements. They demanded of him whether the doctrine was truly his own. He could not deny it, since it had been published by him almost everywhere in numerous books.

They asked where he had read these things. Then, pressed by the greatest difficulty, he replied that he had read within his own spirit the matter, which had been taken neither from Scripture nor even presumed by the heretics themselves—for he had absolutely nothing else to say. But the venerable synod, immediately abhorring so proud and foolish a response, said: “Truly, that was the spirit of error.”

For they remembered that the blessed Apostle had said: “In the last times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy” (1 Timothy 4:1). Ezekiel likewise says of such men: “Woe to the foolish prophets who follow their own spirit and see nothing!” (Ezekiel 13:3). And again: “They see vanity and divine lies, saying, ‘Thus says the Lord,’ when the Lord has not spoken” (Ezekiel 22:28).

Therefore God also testifies through the same prophet that such presumptuous men have been deceived by his judgment, saying: “And when the prophet is deceived and has spoken a word in my name which I did not command him, I, the Lord, have deceived that prophet” (Ezekiel 14:9).

Terribly declaring in the council that all such men, empty of God’s Spirit and puffed up by their own spirit, must be completely excluded from the assembly of the saints, he says: “They shall not be among my people, nor shall they be inscribed in the records of the house of Israel, nor shall they enter the land of Israel” (Ezekiel 2:10). And while that man remained silent, confused by the exposure of the deceptions of his lies, the venerable synod spoke at length.

It was decided that this doctrine was utterly damnable and must be wholly rejected by all worshipers of the Catholic faith, as the Apostle commands and says: “Do not be led away by various and strange doctrines” (Hebrews 13:9). This doctrine is different from the sincerity of the true faith and altogether foreign to the Church, since none of the orthodox Fathers knew it and no reasoning of truth supports it; rather, a recent and alien error introduced it.

The shadows and figures existed in the ceremonies of the Old Testament; the new coming of Christ shines with truth and consists in purity of faith and simplicity of observance, as the Apostle testifies: “The old things have passed away; behold, new things have come. But all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:17–18).

All things, therefore—both old and new, both the type of the Law and the truth of the Gospel—stand by the authority of one and the same God, not of any human being or angel. Hence, after the ministers of both Testaments had been enlightened by the divine Spirit and supported by divine authority—ministers in and through whom God clearly both accomplished and spoke those things which he judged appropriate for the salvation of his people at different times—it was and is permitted to no one to establish new kinds of figures or sacramental mysteries.

Therefore the Church’s reasonable service, whether in the adornment of vestments or in the varied ministry of vessels, must be offered to God purely and simply, in the simplicity of truth and purity of faith, far from every superstitious phantom and with every vanity of obscure doctrine removed. In these things there should be the honor of religion, reverence for divine worship, and the joy of Christian devotion—not figures or mysteries of vanity. [Col. 0082A–D]

But when he presumed, with unheard-of audacity, to call Christ’s body threefold and tripartite—or rather, to assert that there are three bodies of Christ—the priests of the Lord so execrated this that, as was shown above, they did not hesitate to say that it had been taken from spirits of error and doctrines of demons. As though detesting Satan together with the angel of the Lord, who attempts to oppose Jesus, the great and true priest, and driving him away with their breath, they said: “May the Lord rebuke you, Satan; may the Lord who chose Jerusalem rebuke you” (Zechariah 3:2). [Col. 0083A–B]

7. As for the Lord’s body, which is received by the faithful in the mystery, far be it that anyone should approach it with so filthy or superstitious a mind as to allow any of those things which the author of this doctrine has most foully fabricated to occupy his soul and thoughts!

Therefore, with every desire and prayer of piety, we must implore divine mercy so that, once the stain of such phantoms and impurities has been removed not only from our ears but also from our hearts, … he may cleanse our minds with the everlasting purity of his own. Thus, contemplating so divine and glorious a mystery with a pure understanding and receiving it with pure devotion, may we obtain the grace of incorruptible purification.

For when the Lord says: “I am the true vine” (John 15:1); and: “My Father gives you the true bread from heaven” (John 6:32); and: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (ibid., 56); and: “He who eats me will also live because of me” (ibid., 58)—just as nothing pertaining to eternal life is to be desired in food except true refreshment of the soul, so nothing at all is to be contemplated except what is spiritual and immortal.

What wonder is it, then, if, by the grace of faith and divine power, such food is received in such a way that what is mortal is swallowed up by life? “This,” says the Lord, “is the bread descending from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he will not die” (ibid., 50).

But what belongs to the power of the sacrament, and what belongs to the visible sacrament? The one who eats inwardly, not outwardly; the one who eats in the heart, not the one who presses with the tooth. For to believe in him is to eat the living bread. Whoever believes eats; he is nourished invisibly, because he is also reborn invisibly.

These are sacraments; they are called sacraments because in them one thing is seen and another is understood. What is seen has a bodily appearance; what is understood has a spiritual fruit.

Therefore the incorruptible power and most effective strength of the venerable mystery remains in the minds of the faithful, cleansing sins, purifying consciences, and perfecting the grace of redemption and salvation. Hence the blessed John says: “And the blood of his Son Jesus cleanses us from every sin” (1 John 1:7).

Paul, too, the chosen vessel, says: “How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God, cleanse your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?” (Hebrews 9:14).

And Peter, prince of the apostles, says: “Knowing that you were not redeemed with perishable gold or silver from the futile way of life handed down by your fathers, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of an immaculate and unblemished Lamb” (1 Peter 1:18–19).

We were not redeemed with something perishable, then. The faithful person receives this for life, the unworthy person for punishment. This is the price of redemption and the provision of salvation which each of the faithful, at the hour of death, earnestly asks to receive. He presumes that through it he will obtain forgiveness of sins, be protected at death from the attacks of evil spirits, and be admitted to the delights of paradise.

And when the dust returns to its earth, from which it came, the spirit, nevertheless trusting in the consolation of this gift and fortified by the protection of this grace, returns to the Lord who gave it, without losing the incorruptible grace of Christ’s body when it lays down its corruptible body.

These things, insofar as God granted me the ability, I have taken care to record in this brief little page concerning the council of venerable bishops recently held for the edification of God’s Church and the confirmation of the Catholic faith. I have explained their words and meaning with whatever words I could, together with the testimonies of Scripture, and have refuted the recently devised and execrable error.

I bring this to the knowledge of all who wish to read or hear it, so that, rejecting and condemning the fabulously vain vanity and vain fabulism of the profane doctrine, and casting far away both the books and the most deceitful words of the empty-talking teacher, we may draw the streams of faith and knowledge from the purest fountain of Scripture, from the most sincere teaching of the Fathers, and from the authority of the venerable council.

Let us carefully preserve the treasure of faith once delivered to us and flee “the oppositions of knowledge falsely so called” and the profane novelties of words, concerning which the Apostle says to his faithful disciple: “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words and the oppositions of knowledge falsely so called, which some promising have fallen away from the faith” (1 Timothy 6:20–21).

Since this pseudoknowledge and profane novelty of words brings about the destruction and shipwreck of faith, let us avoid it as a kind of Scylla and Charybdis, and fear it with the deepest dread of heart, lest perhaps we have already begun to belong to that time about which the Apostle cries out with the same terrifying warning: “For there will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but will heap up teachers for themselves according to their own desires, itching in their ears; and they will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth, but will turn to fables” (2 Timothy 4:3–4).

Immediately he adds: “But you, keep watch”—namely, lest, while the servants of the master of the house sleep, the enemy sow weeds in the midst of the wheat.

Let us hear the same Apostle speaking to another beloved disciple: “Avoid foolish questions, genealogies, contentions, and disputes about the Law, for they are useless and vain” (Titus 3:9). He immediately adds: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition, knowing that such a one is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment” (ibid., 10–11).

Elsewhere he says: “But if anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the doctrine according to piety, he is proud, knowing nothing, but is diseased” (1 Timothy 6:3–4).

In these words concerning questions and disputes about words, does the Apostle not seem, as if by pointing with his finger, to identify the empty-talking presumptuous man of our time, who, despising the sound words of the Lord Jesus and trampling upon the doctrine of piety, wanders wholly diseased and restless among new questions and useless inventions?

For our Lord Jesus Christ, who is truth itself and the true one, graciously explained in the Gospel the most true mystery of his body and blood, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves. For my flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him. As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so he who eats me will also live because of me” (John 6:54, 56–57). [Col. 0085A–B]

“For the bread of God is the one who descends from heaven and gives life to the world; and the bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world.”

Behold the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ; behold the doctrine of piety; behold the words of eternal life, concerning which he himself says: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (ibid., 64). And Peter says to him: “Lord, you have the words of eternal life” (ibid., 69).

Let us therefore hear the words of life from the mouth of life. He says that his flesh is eaten by the faithful and his blood is drunk; he confirms that this food is truly his flesh and that this drink truly exists as his blood; he asserts that he himself is eaten by his faithful and testifies that, without this food, no one can truly live through this world. He declares this to be the bread descending from heaven—that is, the flesh which he himself gave for the life of the world.

This heavenly bread, because it is heavenly—or rather, because the super-heavenly Word, of our race indeed but of heavenly origin, became flesh and dwelt among us—was made flesh. The Mother of God conceived that flesh not by the will of a man but through the coming upon her of the Holy Spirit and the overshadowing of the power of the Most High.

Therefore, concerning this bread, the prophet had formerly said: “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels” (Psalm 77:25). For the Word of God, remaining in the highest heavens as the bread of angels, became flesh so that man might eat the bread of angels.

How, then, does this presumptuous advocate of profane novelty and, insofar as he is able, violator of such great piety divide the one heavenly bread into three, asserting that Christ is one thing there, living believers another, and the already dead a third? He says that Christ is contained in a portion of the chalice, the living in fragments of the paten, and the dead are reckoned in a certain third portion of the altar.

Thus, in sacrilegious error, he becomes entangled in the very place where the Lord Jesus Christ asserts that he himself is eaten by the faithful and that his flesh is truly food and his blood truly drink. He insists, by contrast, that the living and the dead are eaten.

The Apostle refutes this error, speaking against it directly: “The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? And the bread which we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 10:16). [Col. 0086A]

But this man teaches, on the contrary, in a council of priests: “That blood is the soul of Christ.” What could be more profane than this novelty?

The Apostle, removing every suspicion of division, constantly cries out: “We, though many, are one body in Christ” (Romans 12:5). And again: “Be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling” (Ephesians 4:3–4).

And once more, testifying that Christ and the Church—head and body—are one Christ, he says: “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ” (1 Corinthians 12:12).

Therefore, rebuking the Corinthians who had been wrongly divided and were tearing apart the fabric of the Lord’s body by schisms, he cries out: “Is Christ divided?” (1 Corinthians 1:13).

Asserting that this unity is also signified in the holy sacrifice and mystery, he says: “One bread, one body; we are many, and all partake of the one bread” (1 Corinthians 10:17).

Thus all, both ancient and modern, both living and sleeping, are one bread in Christ, incorporated and united with Christ, yet all of us partake of the one bread to receive the grace of life and salvation—namely, the one who descended from heaven and gives life to the world.

Thus all the saints are living stones, but made alive through him, concerning whom the Apostle Peter says: “Coming to him, the living stone, you yourselves are also built up as living stones” (1 Peter 2:4–5).

Thus all become light, as the Lord says: “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14), but they are illuminated by him of whom the Evangelist says: “Behold, the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9).

Thus they also constitute one bread, drawing their living substance from participation in him who says: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6:41).

All the faithful indeed participate in and share with one another through the fellowship and sharing of the Spirit, through the unity of faith, hope, and charity, as the Apostle says: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the charity of God, and the sharing of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:13).

Yet all this participation and sharing, which exists for them not exactly from one another but toward one another, tends toward him and is nourished from him alone, who is the fountain of life. Of him the blessed John says: “What we have seen and heard, we proclaim to you, so that you also may have fellowship with us, and our fellowship may be with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ” (1 John 1:3).

For Christ Jesus is the head and summit of the Church. Therefore the Church is joined and bound to him for the exchange of eternal life, and the whole Church converges upon him, so that the entire body may be watered and live from the fountain of its head. The Apostle says: “Speaking the truth in charity, let us grow in all things into him who is the head, Christ; from him the whole body, joined and knit together through every supporting joint, according to the working in the measure of each individual member, produces the growth of the body for its building up in charity” (Ephesians 4:15–16).

And again: “Let no one deceive you” (Ephesians 5:6), walking in humility and the worship of angels, which he has not seen, vainly puffed up by the sense of his flesh, and not holding the head, from whom the whole body, supplied and joined together, grows with a growth from God.

The Lord Jesus himself signified this ineffably marvelous unity of the Church—that is, of his body—when, declaring himself the head of all, he said: “I have other sheep which are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one fold and one shepherd” (John 10:16).

For this gathering and unity of his body he accepted death, as the Evangelist testifies: “Jesus was about to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad.”

For this unity he deigned, on the night when he was betrayed, to entreat God the Father, saying: “Holy Father, keep in your name those whom you have given me, so that they may be one as we are” (John 17:11). And shortly afterward: “I pray not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, so that all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us” (John 17:20–21). And: “The glory which you have given me I have given them, so that they may be one as we are one, I in them and you in me, so that they may be perfected into one” (John 17:22–23).

This is the ineffably wonderful unity of the Lord Jesus and his body, which no one is permitted to violate or divide. The Law commands concerning the paschal lamb: “You shall not break a bone of it” (John 19:36).

Indeed, insofar as he is able, the one who breaks the power and strength of so great a bond truly breaks a bone of our Lamb.

The mystery of this unity, formerly prefigured in Adam and Eve and revealed in the last times in Christ and in the Church, was prophesied by Adam and explained by the Apostle, who says: “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Ephesians 5:31). “This mystery is great,” he says; “but I speak of Christ and the Church.” The Lord Jesus himself, recalling this in the Gospel, added: “Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh. What God has joined, let no man separate” (Matthew 19:6).

Do we wish to know with what vigilance we must guard against the one who attempts to violate and dissolve this unity, and how great a sacrilege he presumes? Let us hear the blessed Apostle John, who says: “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God. By this the Spirit of God is known: every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God, and this is the antichrist” (1 John 4:1–3).

Let this man, too, hear it—he who walks vainly, puffed up by the sense of his flesh, following not the Spirit of God but his own spirit, and, insofar as he is able, dissolves and scatters Jesus by dividing him into three parts, three forms, and three bodies.

Let him hear it, I say, and fall silent in eternal silence: “Every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God, and this is the antichrist” (1 John 4:3).

Let us also hear the Apostle Paul, strengthening us in the truth of the faith once delivered and saying: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel besides what you received, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:9).

8. May your affection, venerable lords, forgive me, unworthy as I am, because I speak these things neither from the arrogance of pride nor from the prompting of any malice, but from love for this Church, my lady and my nurturer. To her I owe, insofar as God deigns to inspire me, not only a word of exhortation but every service of charity and devotion—especially at this time, when, because our sins demand it, she is afflicted by so grievous a calamity that she has a bishop without power and a teacher without truth. [Col. 0088A]

Now, as a fitting conclusion to the discourse, I have decided to set forth a few opinions of the ecclesiastical Fathers. By these, as by towers and fortifications, we may defend ourselves against all the deceptive inventions which the foolish fabulist attempts to force upon this Church.

May what the Apostle desires and implores come about in us by divine grace: “I beseech you, brothers, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you, but that you be perfected in the same understanding and in the same judgment” (1 Corinthians 1:10). And again: “Therefore, as you received Jesus Christ the Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in him and confirmed in the faith” (Colossians 2:7).

Thus, elsewhere: “If there is any consolation in Christ, any comfort of charity, any fellowship of the Spirit, any affection and compassion, complete my joy by being of the same mind, having the same charity, united in spirit and thinking the same thing, doing nothing through contention or vainglory” (Philippians 2:1–3). And elsewhere: “And if you think differently in anything, God will reveal this also to you” (Philippians 3:15).

Nevertheless, let us remain in the measure to which we have attained, thinking the same thing and remaining in the same rule.

That the bread received in the mystery is the body and flesh of Christ—or rather, that it is Christ and the Lord himself—we find in Saint Cyprian’s book On the Lord’s Prayer, in the passage concerning “our daily bread” [invenimus = “we find”].

9. Christ is the bread of life, and this bread is not everyone’s, but is our Lord’s. Just as we say “Our Father,” because he is the Father of those who understand and believe, so we call him “our bread,” because Christ is bread for us who touch his body [Latin printed *corpus eorum*, apparently for *corpus eius*].

We ask daily that this bread be given to us, so that we who are in Christ and daily receive his Eucharist as food for salvation may not, if some more serious sin intervenes, be separated from Christ’s body while being barred from the heavenly bread because we have been excluded and do not communicate.

He himself proclaims and says: “I am the bread of life who descended from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:41, 51).

Therefore, when he says that whoever eats of his bread will live forever, so that it may be clear that those who touch his body live, so, conversely, we must fear and pray lest, when someone is excluded and separated from Christ’s body, he remain a stranger to salvation. He threatens and says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54).

And therefore we ask daily that our bread—that is, Christ—be given to us, so that we who remain and live in Christ may not depart from his sanctification and body.

Also from Saint Jerome’s treatise on Psalm 80.

10. Do you wish to receive the Lord’s foods? Do you wish to eat the Lord himself and your Savior? Hear what he says: “Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80:11). Open wide your mouths: he himself is both Lord and bread. He encourages us to eat, and he himself is our food. However much you open your mouth, so much will you receive.

Also from a homily of Saint Augustine.

11. In the mystery of the altar the Lord is received, and he cannot be divided by any division. What sort of invitation from the Lord did you hear? Who invited us? Whom did he invite? And what did he prepare?

The Lord invited servants and prepared food for them—himself. Who would dare to eat his Lord? And yet he says: “He who eats me lives because of me” (John 6:57).

When Christ is eaten, life is eaten. He is not killed in order to be eaten; rather, when eaten, he gives life to the dead. He refreshes but is not diminished.

Therefore, brothers, let us not fear eating this bread, lest perhaps we consume it and afterward find nothing left for us to eat. Christ is eaten; when eaten, he lives, because he rose after being killed. Nor, when we eat, do we divide him into parts.

Indeed, this is how it takes place in the sacrament, and the faithful know how they eat Christ’s flesh. Each person receives his portion; hence the graces themselves are also called portions. He is eaten in portions in the sacrament, yet he remains wholly intact in heaven; he remains wholly intact in your heart.

For he was wholly with the Father when he came into the Virgin. He filled her, yet did not depart from him. He came into the flesh so that human beings might eat him, and remained wholly with the Father so that he might nourish the angels.

What you know—and both those who know and those who do not know must know—is this: when Christ became man, man ate the bread of angels. How, then, by what means, through what path, by what merits, and with what dignity could man eat the bread of angels, unless the Creator of angels became man?

Also from Saint Gregory on the same matter, from a homily for the Nativity of the Lord.

12. Therefore, although he remained eternal, he appeared as temporal; the place where he descended is foreign to him. And because it is said through the prophet, “All flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6), when he became man he turned our grass into grain—he who said of himself: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone” (John 12:24).

Therefore, when he was born, he was laid in a manger, so that he might refresh all the faithful—namely, the holy living creatures—with the grain of his flesh, lest they remain hungry for the nourishment of inner understanding.

Also from the same author, in another homily on the same matter.

13. “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10:11). He did what he taught; he displayed what he commanded. The good shepherd laid down his life for the sheep, so that in our sacrament he might change his body and blood and satisfy with the nourishment of his flesh the sheep whom he had redeemed.

From the same author on this matter, from the books of the Dialogues.

14. For this singular victim saves the soul from eternal destruction: by the mystery of the Only-Begotten’s death, it restores that soul to us. Although, rising from the dead, he no longer dies and death no longer has dominion over him, nevertheless, living in himself immortally and incorruptibly, he is again sacrificed for us in this mystery of the sacred offering.

For there his body is received, his flesh is distributed for the salvation of the people, and his blood is now received not into the hands of unbelievers but into the mouths of the faithful. [Col. 0090A–B]

The mystery of Christ’s garment—that is, of his body—which ought not to be divided; from Saint Cyprian’s book On the Unity of the Church.

15. The Lord says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). And again it is written concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: “These three are one” (John 5:7). Whoever believes this truth, proceeding from divine steadfastness and adhering to the heavenly sacraments, is shown that this sacrament of unity, this bond of inseparably abiding concord, cannot be divided in the Church. This is demonstrated when, in the Gospel, the tunic of our Lord Jesus Christ is not divided or torn at all. Rather, when they cast lots for Christ’s garment to determine who might rather put on Christ, the intact garment is received, and the tunic, undamaged and undivided, is possessed.

Scripture speaks and says: “As for the tunic, because it was seamless, woven from the top throughout, they said to one another: ‘Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it, to determine whose it shall be’” (John 19:23). He was wearing the unity that came from above—from heaven and from the Father—which could not be torn at all by the one who received it, but retained its entire and solid integrity inseparably. He cannot possess Christ’s garment who tears and divides Christ’s Church.

Conversely, when, at Solomon’s death, his kingdom and people were divided, the prophet Ahijah met King Jeroboam in the field and tore his garment into twelve pieces, saying: “Take ten pieces for yourself, for thus says the Lord: ‘Behold, I am tearing the kingdom from Solomon’s hand, and I shall give you ten scepters; and two scepters shall belong to him, for the sake of my servant David and Jerusalem, the city that I have chosen, in order to place my name there’” (1 Kings 11:31). When the twelve tribes of Israel were divided, the prophet Ahijah tore his garment.

But because Christ’s people cannot be divided, his tunic, woven throughout and held together, was not divided among those who possessed it. Undivided, joined, and interwoven, it displayed the concord of our people, who have put on Christ; by the garment’s sacramental unity and sign, it declared the unity of the Church. Who, then, could be so wicked and faithless, so deranged by the madness of discord, as either to believe that God’s unity, the Lord’s garment, the Church of Christ, can be torn, or to dare to tear it?

16. That priest truly acts in Christ’s place who imitates everything Christ did and then offers a true and complete sacrifice to God the Father in the Church if he begins to offer it in the manner in which he sees Christ himself offering it. No one, therefore, should suppose that the custom of certain persons must be followed; for one must ask whom they followed. In the sacrifice that Christ offered, only Christ must be followed. Certainly, we must obey and do what Christ did and commanded to be done, when he himself says in the Gospel: “If you do what I command you, I shall no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:15).

Christ alone must be heard. The Father also bears witness from heaven, saying: “This is my most beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him” (Matthew 17:5). Therefore, if Christ alone is to be heard, we must not consider what someone else before us thought should be done, but what Christ, who existed before all, first did. For we must follow not human custom but God’s power.

When God speaks through the prophet Isaiah and says: “But they worship me in vain, teaching the commandments and doctrines of men” (Matthew 15:9), the Lord again repeats this same point in the Gospel, saying: “You reject the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition” (Mark 7:9). Elsewhere he says: “Whoever breaks one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:19).

If it is not permitted to break even the least of the Lord’s commandments, how much less is it lawful to violate such great and weighty commandments, so intimately pertaining to the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion and our redemption, or to alter them through human tradition into something other than what was divinely instituted?

The entire redeemed city—that is, the assembly and fellowship of the saints—offers a universal sacrifice to God through the great Priest, who also offered himself for us in his Passion, so that we might be the body of so great a Head, according to the form of a servant. He offered this form; in this form he was offered, because according to it he is mediator. In this form he is priest; in this form he is sacrifice.

When, therefore, the Apostle exhorted us to present our bodies as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1), he added shortly afterward: “For just as in one body we have many members, though all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another” (ibid. 4–5). This is the sacrifice of Christians: the many are one body in Christ. It is shown that, in the very thing that it offers, the Church itself is offered.

### The diversity of Churches consists in the unity of faith, from the books of Saint Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Faith*

17. There is one episcopate, of which each bishop holds a share in its entirety. There is one Church, which extends more widely through the multitude by the increase of its fruitfulness, just as the sun has many rays but one light, and a tree many branches but one strength, founded upon tenacious charity.

And when many streams flow from one spring, although the multiplicity [al., totality] may appear dispersed through the abundance of the overflowing supply, unity is nevertheless preserved in its source. Tear a ray of sunlight away from the sun’s body: the unity of the light does not permit division. Break a branch from a tree: it cannot produce fruit. Cut off a stream from its spring: once cut off, it dries up.

Thus the Lord’s Church, suffused with light, extends its rays throughout the whole world; yet it is one light, diffused everywhere, and the unity of the body is not separated. It extends its branches throughout the whole earth in abundant fruitfulness and spreads its flowing streams widely and generously. Yet there is one head, one source, and one mother, rich in the succession of her fruitfulness. From her offspring we are born; with her milk we are nourished; by her spirit we are animated.

### Places are not to be loved for their own sake, but places for the sake of good things, from the letter of Saint Gregory written to Augustine, bishop of the English

18. Your Fraternity knows the custom of the Roman Church, in which you remember having been nurtured. But I am pleased that, whether in the Roman Church, in the Churches of Gaul, or in any other Church, you have found something that could please almighty God more, and that you carefully choose it and pour it into the Church of the English, which is still new to the faith, as a special form of instruction gathered from the many Churches.

For things are not to be loved for the sake of places, but places for the sake of good things. Therefore, from each of the Churches, choose whatever is devout, religious, and right, and, gathered together as though into a bundle, establish these things as a custom among the minds of the English.

### In ecclesiastical garments and worship no superstitious mystery should be given precedence, from the letter of Saint Pope Celestine written to the bishops of Gaul

19. We have learned that certain priests of the Lord serve superstitious ritual rather than purity of mind or faith.

And shortly afterward: Wearing a cloak and girding their loins, they believe that they will fulfill the faith of Holy Scripture not through the spirit but through the letter. For if these commands were given so that they might be observed in this way, why are the things that follow not likewise performed, so that burning lamps are held in the hands together with a staff?

These things have their own mystery, and for those who understand, their meaning is so clear that they ought to be observed according to a significance greater than is appropriate to their outward form. For the girding of the loins indicates chastity; the staff, pastoral governance; the burning lamps, the radiance of good works, concerning which it is said: “Let your works shine” (Matthew 5:16).

Perhaps those who live in more remote places and dwell far from others have this form of worship because they follow custom rather than reason. Hence the custom in the Gallican Churches: the practice of so many years and of so many bishops is being changed into another form of dress.

We must be distinguished from the common people and from others by doctrine, not by clothing; by conduct, not by dress; by purity of mind, not by ritual. For if we begin to pursue novelty, we shall trample upon the order handed down to us by our fathers in order to make room for needless superstitions. We must not therefore lead the unformed minds of the faithful toward such things. They must be taught rather than entertained; precepts must not be imposed upon their eyes but poured into their minds.

### Likewise Saint Jerome on the simple dress of ministers and priests, from the books of the dialogues of Atticus and Christobolus

20. You add that the glory of clothing and ornaments is contrary to God. What enmity against God is there, I ask, if I have a cleaner tunic? If bishops, presbyters, deacons, and the rest of the ecclesiastical order proceed in a white garment while administering the sacrifices?

Beware, clerics; beware, monks, widows, and virgins: you are in danger unless the crowd sees you filthy and clothed in rags. I say nothing of secular people, against whom open war is declared, and enmity against God, if they use costly and shining garments.

In the priesthood of the Church, it is not the mystical adornment of garments but the splendor of souls that must be sought, as the consecration itself of a bishop demonstrates. It runs as follows:

> “O God, who, speaking to your servant Moses with the utterance of intimate fellowship, instructed him among the other teachings of heavenly worship concerning the form of priestly clothing, and commanded the chosen Aaron to be clothed in mystical vesture amid the sacred rites, so that succeeding generations might derive the meaning of understanding from the examples of those who came before, lest the instruction of your teaching be lacking to any age—since among the ancients the very appearance of the symbols possessed reverence, while among us the realities themselves provide more certain evidence than the riddles of figures:
>
> “For the former priesthood’s dress is the adornment of our mind, and it is no longer the honor of garments that commends priestly glory to us, but the splendor of souls. For those things that then pleased the bodily eyes demanded, rather, that the things contained within them should be understood.
>
> “Therefore, we ask that you grant this grace to this servant of yours, whom you have chosen for the ministry of the high priesthood: that whatever those coverings signified by the gleam of gold, the brilliance of jewels, and the variety of their manifold workmanship may shine forth in his character and actions.”

### False books, and books discordant with the sincerity of the faith, are to be used for reading in no way; rather, they should be handed over to the fire, from the letter of Saint Pope Leo to Turibius of Astorga

21. Care must therefore be taken, and priestly diligence must provide above all, that false books, and those discordant with sincere truth, be used for reading in no way. Apocryphal writings which, under the names of the apostles, contain a seedbed of many falsehoods must not merely be prohibited; they must also be completely removed and burned in the fire, because, although some things in them may appear to have the appearance of piety, they are never free from poisons.

22. These things, venerable lords, I have diligently collected both from the sacred Scriptures and from the sayings of the holy Scriptures, and I have set them before your Reverence to be heard and read, so that, meditating upon these and similar matters, we may speak, fortified by the firmness of faith and truth, against the author of this novel presumption, who, like a soothsayer and conjecturer, judges matters that he does not know. Let us speak with the Church:

> “The wicked have told me tales, but not as is your law, O Lord” (Psalm 118 [119]:85).

And let us understand how true is what the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of Solomon, saying: “There are abundant crops in the newly cleared fields of the fathers, and they are gathered by others without judgment” (Proverbs 13:23).

Nor should he so abuse our misfortune and humiliation as to presume to say to us, as though we were the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead, in the words of Nahash, king of the Ammonites—whose name is interpreted as “serpent”—the enemy of truth:

> “On this condition will I make a covenant with you: that I may put out the right eyes of all of you and make you a reproach to Israel” (1 Kings 11:2).

For he truly attempts to put out the right eye who strives to extinguish the light of right faith.

It is more useful for us to wish upon him what is said figuratively through Solomon:

> “The eye that mocks a father and despises the birth of his mother, let the ravens of the valleys dig it out, and the young of the eagle eat it” (Proverbs 30:17).

For he truly mocks the Father who divides the unity of the Son, as the Son himself bears witness: “Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (John 5:23). And he utterly despises the birth of his mother, the Church, who refuses to venerate with sincere purity the mystery of redemption by which he is born from her womb into life.

The evangelical command is fitting for such an eye, which promises to guide toward light but, on the contrary, is darkened by the gloom of error:

> “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you” (Matthew 5:29).

This wicked eye desires to take away the inheritance of the fathers. He strives to change their vineyard into a garden of vegetables—that is, to weaken their strong, fruitful, and purest sayings by replacing them with cheap tales that quickly wither and fall away. But let the sons of the stoned martyr answer him with Naboth:

> “May the Lord be gracious to me, that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers” (1 Kings 21:3).

If, on account of the honorable freedom of this reply, we should be exposed to disgrace by false witnesses or even overwhelmed with stones, let us have the most merciful God as our comforter and avenger, saying:

> “If I do not requite you for the blood of Naboth and of his sons, which I saw yesterday, says the Lord—on this field, says the Lord—”

**Here ends the work.**

## III. Letter of Florus, deacon of Lyons, to the council at the estate of Theodonius against the books of Amalarius

To the holy and venerable council assembled at the estate of Theodonius.

Hear, most blessed and most reverend Fathers, summoned by God and united in God, laboring and destined to labor for God with his help, and, after blessed labor, destined to rest in him and with him. Hear in such a way that God may hear you, and remember the Apostle, who exhorts the rulers of the Church and says:

> “Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to govern the Church of the Lord, which he acquired with his own blood” (Acts 20:28).

The matter concerns the faith and catholic truth, which the prelate of the Church of Lyons does not cease to corrupt and subvert with tongue and pen. He confirms that you yourselves, the venerable eyes of Christ’s Church, are so far partners and accomplices in his errors and falsehoods that, at a public assembly of our Church, he dared to boast that he had brought you by his persuasions in a general synod to the point that you would all sign his most foolish books with your own hands and thus wish to think and observe unanimously.

I replied to him through the elders, saying that I could in no way believe such a thing of men so distinguished; indeed, I would rather have the three fingers with which we write cut off at the root before I, unworthy as I am—“a dead dog and a tiny flea”—would confirm errors of this kind by my own signature.

I added that if those books were examined and judged in a sound council, they would certainly be anathematized. Yet he ordered our chorepiscopus to have them transcribed as exceedingly useful to everyone. When I had reread part of them and seen that they were full of lies and ravings, I urged that this should not be done at all and advised that the books be returned to their author as quickly as possible. I feared, of course, that Christ’s sheep—that is, simple people—might, from reading them, be sprinkled with the most empty itch of curiosity and scorched by the burning pustules of dreadful error.

I myself collected and arranged in order, and explained in my own words, some of the matters that he proposed, discussed, and commended in a general council of presbyters—matters from which his vanity may be exposed to contempt, indeed to execration.

But lest anyone think that I am making false assertions, let his book be brought forward. It will strip its foulness bare before public readers and hearers. From it you will recognize as most certainly spoken by him the matters that I submit for your most sincere examination and judgment, especially when you read many things still more insane.

The chorepiscopi are witnesses; the archdeacons are witnesses; all the presbyters of Lyons who were present are witnesses. From them I learned that these things were immediately mocked and rejected—indeed, lamented and wept over—when, accustomed to divine streams, they were forced to drink from a muddy pool, murmuring over the most wicked bread of doctrine, concerning which the book of Ecclesiasticus says:

> “The city will murmur over the most wicked bread” (Ecclesiasticus 31:29).

His wickedness is truly attested. He does not teach divine things but composes and fabricates his own; and, according to Solomon, “like a soothsayer and conjecturer, he judges what he does not know” (Proverbs 23).

Come to our aid, therefore, most pious Fathers; come to the aid of our souls. “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Corinthians 5:6). And according to an ancient father, if anything false is admitted into the faith, rot enters from the serpent’s poison, worms of corruption are born, and nothing whole will remain.

Almighty God is my witness that I do not exaggerate these matters under the impulse of anger, as though I had been injured. From the very beginning, while he still displayed himself as somewhat flattering toward me, I began to grieve over and detest them. I do not act against divine ordinance or the pious provision of the emperor, as he perhaps boasts, as though I were a rebel—for my insignificance could never even conceive such a thing—but out of hatred for error and love of truth, and because I grieve over the wounds of my mother Church, whose breasts nourished me from infancy, and in which, unworthy as I am, I have exercised both an office of administration and the ministry of teaching and preaching.

Certainly, let me live in utter poverty, or even die, if that is pleasing: only let the putrid wound be exposed; let the putrid discharge be exposed. And let all who are wasting away from this contagion, with Christ’s help and your ministrations as physicians, rejoice in the health they desire once their heavy lethargy has been driven away.

# Florus the Deacon’s Martyrology

(See the *Martyrology* of the venerable Bede, volume 94 of this *Patrologia*, p. 798; and, for the year 876, the *Martyrology* of Usuard, in which Florus’s additions are published.)

## Sermon of Florus the Deacon on Predestination

[Note: Concerning Florus and his sermon, Hincmar says the following in book 6, p. 27, of his work *On Predestination*: “We find that this chapter, when we compared sources, was excerpted for the most part from a written work of Florus, a minister of the Church of Lyons, which we formerly received at Bonoil from the venerable Heribold, bishop of Auxerre. Therefore, in any case, it is not found to be entirely alien to reason. For it does not speak against the catholic faith concerning God’s foreknowledge,” and so forth.

The same author says in the preface to the same work: “At the head of the indexes of the following work, we thought it worthwhile to place in full the sermon of Florus, which, through Heribold, formerly the venerable bishop of Auxerre, we transcribed at a synodal assembly at Bonoila; and which, after our return from the turmoil at Brion, a certain cleric offered us from the archives of Ebo, as he himself said, the venerable bishop of Grenoble. For it proceeds cautiously both in construction and in the truth of its meaning, except in two places where we do not believe that he spoke as we find it written in the copy we received from the archives of the venerable Ebo, since in other places he spoke so catholically, as will be clear to readers.

“Especially because, in the same written copy—which we received through the hands of the aforementioned Heribold, just as he had received it from the aforesaid Florus—we found one version, while in the copy we received later we found another. For this reason we suspect that someone altered it. Before we begin writing out that sermon, we shall carefully identify those passages in particular.

“Where it says: ‘But those whom he foreknew and foresaw would become evil and impious through their own fault, he predestined to eternal damnation by a just judgment,’ the little roll that we received from Heribold reads: ‘But because he foreknew and foresaw that they would become evil and impious through their own fault, he predestined them to eternal damnation, by which they would be punished through a just judgment.’

“And where it is written: ‘For he did not predestine anyone to be evil, but truly predestined every evil person so that he would not be unpunished,’ we find in the roll that we received from the aforesaid Heribold: ‘But he truly predestined punishment, so that every evil person would not be unpunished.’ This is what he himself demonstrates later when he says: ‘He both foreknew their punishment, because he is God, and predestined it, because he is just.’

“We leave the rest to the judgment of the catholic reader. But for this reason we thought it necessary to include this sermon in full: because from it the compiler of the immediately following chapters attempted to construct two chapters—on Foreknowledge and Predestination—in a confused and disordered sequence, and with a wholly false meaning, as anyone who reads both this sermon and those chapters will plainly understand.”]

*(Bibliotheca Patrum maxima.)*

(See concerning this work L. Cellotius, S.J., in *The History of Gottschalk*, book 1, chapter 26.)

Almighty God, because he is most truly true and the only God, foreknew everything in his eternal and unchangeable knowledge before it came to be, as Scripture testifies, saying:

> “Eternal God, knower of hidden things, who know all things before they come to pass” (Daniel 13:42).

Without doubt, therefore, he foreknew both the good things that the good would do and the evil things that the wicked would commit. But in the good he himself, by his grace, made them good; in the wicked, however, he did not himself make them evil—far be it from us to say so—but merely foreknew that they would become such through their own fault.

For God’s foreknowledge did not impose necessity upon them, so that they could not be anything else; rather, God, in his omnipotent majesty, foresaw only what they would become by their own will. Therefore Scripture, impressing upon us his undefiled justice, says of him:

> “He commanded no one to act wickedly, and he gave no one permission to sin.”

Whatever the wicked and unjust do wickedly, and whatever span of this life God granted them for doing good, they turn instead toward the practice of evil. The fault is theirs, not God’s, and therefore they are rightly condemned by his justice.

The same almighty God also foreknew their eternal damnation, but because of the merit of those whom he foresaw would persevere in their own wickedness—not because of any iniquity of his own, far be it from us to say so. He established nothing unjustly, and he will repay each person according to his works (Romans 2:6): eternal good to those who do good, and everlasting evil to those who do evil.

Thus he entirely foreknew the good: that they would become good through his grace and receive eternal rewards through that same grace—that is, that they would live well in the present age and be happily rewarded in the future. Both, however, come from God’s gift of mercy.

Hence the Apostle calls them “vessels of mercy,” saying:

> “In order to show the riches of his grace upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory” (Romans 9:23).

Conversely, he foreknew that the wicked would become wicked through their own wickedness, and he foreknew that, through his justice, they would be condemned to eternal punishment.

He foreknew this concerning Judas the traitor: that he would betray him, as the Gospel says, even though he was one of the Twelve (John 6:72). He also foreknew his eternal damnation when he said:

> “But woe to that man by whom the Son is betrayed. It would have been better for that man if he had not been born” (Mark 14:21).

Thus also, concerning the impious Jews, he undoubtedly foreknew that their impiety would come, concerning which he foretold in the psalm:

> “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm 68 [69]:22).

He also foreknew their subsequent damnation, concerning which he added in the same psalm:

> “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous” (ibid. 29).

But in these people and in all the wicked, the former proceeds from their own depravity; the latter proceeds from divine equity.

The same must be understood entirely concerning God’s predestination. In the good, he predestined both their future goodness itself as a gift of his grace and their eternal reward for that same goodness, so that by his gift they would become good and by his gift they would be rewarded.

Hence the Apostle says:

> “He predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, toward himself” (Ephesians 1:5).

And elsewhere:

> “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29).

He therefore predestined his elect both to be received now into the adoption of God’s sons through the grace of baptism and, in the future, to be made conformable to the image of God’s Son, renewed and glorified according to that image by the same grace of God.

He predestined them entirely to be good here—not from themselves but from him—and blessed there—not through themselves but through him. In both cases, therefore, he foreknew and predestined the good that would be his in them and through them.

In the wicked and impious, however, almighty God did not predestine wickedness and impiety—that is, he did not predestine them to be wicked and impious so that they could not be anything else. But those whom he foreknew [Heribold manuscript: “but because he foreknew them”] and foresaw would become wicked and impious through their own fault, he predestined to eternal damnation by a just judgment—not because they could not be anything else, but because they did not want to be anything else. They themselves therefore became the cause of their own destruction.

God, however, is the just judge and just ordainer of that damnation. He did not predestine anything unjust but something just; nevertheless, he predestined both crowns for the just and punishments for the unjust, because both are just.

Commending this justice to us, the Apostle says:

> “Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath? By no means” (Romans 3:5).

And because God now grants patience to all, so that they may turn to repentance, while those who perish perish through their own contempt and hardness—because they have despised God’s great goodness—he says again elsewhere:

> “Do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering, not knowing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s just judgment, who will repay each according to his works” (Romans 2:4–6).

Another Scripture also testifies, saying:

> “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living. But the impious summoned it with their hands and words; considering it their friend, they wasted away, and they made covenants with it, because they are worthy to belong to its portion” (Wisdom 1:13, 16).

Almighty God is therefore not the cause of death or destruction for any human being. Rather, the impious themselves summon death and destruction upon themselves with their hands and words. By acting wickedly and persuading others to act even more wickedly, they bring damnation upon themselves and upon others.

Loving the way of iniquity and destruction, they turn aside from the straight path and hasten toward everlasting damnation—as though they had joined right hands with one another—in a shared agreement of wickedness, as if by vow and covenant. Allied with death and enemies of eternal life, they store up wrath for themselves according to their hardness and impenitent heart on the day of wrath.

On that day of God’s just judgment, because each person receives according to his works, no one is condemned through a prejudgment of God but through the merit of his own iniquity.

For he did not predestine anyone to be evil, but truly predestined every evil person so that he would not be unpunished [Heribold manuscript: “but truly predestined punishment, so that every evil person would not be unpunished”]. For every just law is itself without crime, lest it be unjust; yet it punishes the criminal, so that it may truly be just.

Whoever therefore says that those who perish were predestined to destruction and therefore could not turn out otherwise must likewise say of the righteous that they are saved because they were predestined to salvation and therefore could not be anything else. Whoever says these things so confusedly and foolishly removes from the former the merit of damnation and from the latter the merit of salvation.

What else does he accomplish by this than imposing upon those who perish a necessity of destruction and upon those who are saved a necessity of salvation? Thus neither are the former justly condemned, because they could not be just, nor are the latter justly rewarded, because they could not be anything other than just. In both cases, therefore, destruction and salvation would proceed not from the judgment of one’s own actions but from the prejudgment of divine predestination.

And where would there be the saying:

> “He will repay each according to his works” (Romans 2:6)?

And again:

> “Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath? By no means” (Romans 3:5).

For the cause of the destruction of those who perish is plainly attributed to God if he predestined them to destruction in such a way that they could not be anything else. To think or say this is a horrible blasphemy.

But the faith of the Catholic Church, whose children and followers we must be, firmly teaches us to hold what we briefly set out above according to the authority of Holy Scripture: almighty God foreknew the wickedness of the wicked because it proceeds from them; he did not predestine it because it does not proceed from him. But he both foreknew their punishment because he is God and predestined it because he is just, so that in them there might be the merit of their own damnation and in him the power and judgment of one who justly condemns.

For God predestines only what he himself will do; but he foreknew many things that he himself will not do, such as all evils. The wicked do those evils; he does not.

The wicked themselves perish not because they could not be good, but because they did not want to be good. Through their own fault they persevered as vessels of wrath prepared for destruction (Romans 9:22), and they remained in the mass of the condemned either by original or actual merit.

In the good, as has been sufficiently shown above, almighty God both foreknew and predestined that they would be good in the present life through his grace and blessed in the future. He is the author and giver of both their goods—that is, of both their present and future good—and therefore he is undoubtedly the foreknower and predestiner of both.

For they themselves, from themselves, could not only have been something else but were something else before they were made righteous from among the wicked by him who justifies the ungodly.

Whether in those who are saved or in those who perish, the will itself is rewarded and the will itself is condemned. In the former, because it has been healed by the grace of the Lord Savior so that from evil and perverse it might become good and upright, it is unquestionably crowned most worthily. In the latter, because it refuses to receive healing through the Savior, it will most justly experience everlasting damnation through that same judge.

In brief, this is everything that must be held concerning free choice according to the truth of the catholic faith: God created every human being with free choice. But because through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned (Romans 5:12), free choice in the whole human race was so vitiated and corrupted through the merit of that transgression, and so blinded and weakened, that it is sufficient for a person to do evil—that is, to fall into iniquity—and can be free only for this.

But it cannot rise and grow strong in doing good—that is, in the practice of virtue and the fruit of good works—unless it is restored, enlightened, and healed through faith in the one Mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, and through the gift of the Holy Spirit.

The Savior himself promises this in the Gospel, saying:

> “If the Son makes you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

And the Apostle says:

> “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:17).

Thus, liberated, enlightened, and healed by this grace of Christ and the Spirit of Christ, human free choice may gratefully say the words of the Psalmist:

> “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Psalm 26 [27]:1).

Whoever, therefore, desires to receive this grace of freedom, so as to become truly free for living well and piously, must not presume upon his own powers but faithfully entrust himself to the one by whom he must be healed and strengthened. Concerning him the same Psalmist says:

> “The steps of a man will be directed by the Lord, and he will desire his way” (Psalm 36 [37]:23).

Let him pray to him and entreat him, saying:

> “Direct my steps according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me” (Psalm 118 [119]:133).

And again:

> “Lord, lead me in your way, and I shall walk in your truth” (Psalm 5:9).

And other similar passages.

I have written these things to you briefly in reply to what you commanded. Now I faithfully beseech and exhort you, grounded in the simplicity and sincerity of the true faith, to close your ears against the wicked tongue of that most vain and wretched man. Prepared for contention and obstinate against the truth, he, unhappy man, puffed up by a diabolical spirit, preferred to separate himself from Christ’s Church and priests rather than abandon his profane and empty words.

# Floro the Deacon, under the Name of the Church of Lyons: A Book against the Erroneous Definitions of John Scotus Eriugena

[Note: There is considerable disagreement among theologians concerning the true author of the following book. Some attribute it to Florus, a master or deacon; others to Remigius, archbishop of Lyons; others to Ebbo, bishop of Grenoble. For a resolution of this question, consult Father Louis Cellot, S.J., *History of Gottschalk*, book II, chapter 24; book III, chapter 15; and book IV, chapters 14 and 15.]

[Note: It should be observed above all that the Church of Lyons directs its argument chiefly against the manner of speaking used by John Eriugena, who seemed especially inclined to favor the Pelagians, so that any less-educated person could easily be deceived by him and fall into heresy. I considered it worthwhile to state this at the outset, so that the innovators of our own age may see how greatly the ancients recoiled from the novelty not only of doctrines but also of names themselves, knowing what Jerome once wrote, as quoted by the Master in book IV, distinction 13, at the end: “By words improperly uttered I fell into heresy.” Likewise, in his book against the errors of John of Jerusalem, he says that ambiguities of wording must not be admitted in the Church: “He who believes purely,” he says, “should speak purely.”

But who this Eriugena was may be learned from Matthew of Westminster, under the year 883: “In that same year there came to England Master John, a Scot by nation, a man of penetrating intellect and exceptional eloquence. Long before, having left his homeland and crossed into the regions of Gaul, he approached Charles the Bald, and, being received by him with great favor, became his constant companion at table and in the bedchamber.”

After recounting several further details about the good fortune of his intellectual gifts, he adds: “At the request of that same king he translated the *Hierarchy* of Dionysius the Areopagite from Greek into Latin, and published another book which he entitled περὶ Φύσεος μερίσμου—that is, *On the Division of Nature*—which, he says, is extremely useful for unraveling various nearly insoluble questions. If, however, he is to be forgiven in certain matters in which he departed from the path of the Latins while fixing his eyes too intently upon the Greeks, he was nevertheless considered a heretic by some. For a certain Florus—what sort of man he was is unknown—wrote against him and, by corrupting his writings, condemned them. Indeed, in the aforementioned book there are very many passages which, unless carefully examined, are judged foreign to the Catholic faith.”

He immediately adds a letter of Pope Nicholas [in fact, Marinus] of Rome to Charles the Bald: “It has been reported to our apostolate that a certain man named John, a Scot by nation, has recently translated into Latin the work of Dionysius the Areopagite, which he composed in Greek concerning the divine names and the celestial orders. This work ought to have been sent to us according to the custom of the Church and approved by our judgment, especially since it is frequently reported that the same John, although formerly praised as a man of extensive learning, does not think soundly in certain matters. Because of this infamy, John left Francia and went to England, where, after several years, he breathed out his soul in severe and bitter torment, having been pierced with writing-styles by the boys whom he taught. For some time he lay in a humble grave in the basilica of Saint Laurence. But when a ray of heavenly fire miraculously fell upon that grave, the monks, encouraged by such revelations, transferred him to a larger church and honorably placed him on the left side of the altar.”

So far Matthew of Westminster. William of Malmesbury adds to all this an epitaph [book II, chapter 4], whose verses are indeed rough and lacking the polish of modern times, but not altogether inelegant by ancient standards:

> This tomb encloses the holy sophist John,  
> who, while still living, was enriched with wondrous doctrine;  
> at last, through martyrdom, he deserved to ascend  
> into Christ’s kingdom, where all the saints reign forever.

Baronius, under the year 883, says that no one has disclosed the reason why he suffered such things that he could be called a martyr. Genebrardus, however, in the French-language *Liturgy of Saint Dionysius*, asserts that the boys attacked him so savagely because of the error of the Sacramentarians. If this is true, then, since in martyrs the cause ought to be considered more than the punishment, he should not be enrolled among the martyrs—especially since Lanfranc, in his book *On the Truth of the Body and Blood of Christ*, counts him among the Sacramentarians and says that his little book *On the Sacrament of the Altar* was condemned at the Council of Vercelli. We leave the examination of all this to the reader’s prudence. Genebrardus’s addition is certainly suspect to me, since it is supported by no author or witness.

As for the version of Scripture used by the Church of Lyons, it is uncertain whose it was. It is certain, however, that it differs greatly from the Vulgate, since it contains no testimony that does not differ from it. Perhaps that Church had fashioned a version of its own, since it was abundantly supplied with exceptionally learned men. For, according to Augustine (*On Christian Doctrine*, book II, chapter 11) and Isidore (*Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 12), Greek translators can be counted, but Latin translators cannot: whenever someone obtained a Greek codex and seemed to possess even a little ability in both languages, he dared to translate it.]

*(From the Great Library of the Fathers.)*

# [Col. 0101] In the Name of Our Lord Jesus Christ Begins the Little Book of Florus against the Absurdities and Errors of a Certain Most Vain Man, Called John, concerning Divine Predestination and Foreknowledge and the True Freedom of the Human Will

## Preface

There have come into our hands—that is, into the hands of the Church of Lyons—the writings of a certain empty and talkative man who, claiming to dispute about divine foreknowledge and predestination by human and, as he himself boasts, philosophical arguments, has dared, without offering any reasoning and without adducing the authority of Scripture or the holy Fathers, to define solely on the basis of his own presumption what ought to be held and followed.

These writings are very easily judged and rejected by faithful readers trained in sacred doctrine, with God’s help, because they are utterly vain, full of falsehood and error, and opposed to the faith and truth of God. Indeed, they are held in contempt and ridicule. But because, as we have heard, this same man is admired by many as though he were a learned scholar, and because by talking or writing in this manner he leads some into hesitation and makes others followers of his error, as though he were saying something important, while by his empty verbosity and inflated loquacity he most dangerously occupies all his hearers and admirers, so that they do not humbly submit to the divine Scriptures and the authority of the Fathers but instead follow his fantastic ravings, we have judged it altogether necessary, in the spirit of charity and in fulfillment of the duty belonging to our place and order, to answer his insolence, with the Lord as our guide.

Thus all who wish to read these things faithfully, with fear of God and concern for their salvation, may truly recognize how necessary it is, especially in these most dangerous and final times, to cling firmly to the immovable truth of holy Scripture, to obey humbly the most firmly established authority of the orthodox holy Fathers, and to close and block their ears against undisciplined and utterly vain verbosity. They should also dread with their whole mind that saying of the Lord which we already see almost fulfilled: “Do you suppose that when the Son of Man comes he will find faith on the earth?” (Luke XVIII, 8).

And the Apostle, in whom the same Lord was speaking, solemnly warns us, saying: “For there will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but, according to their own desires, they will heap up teachers for themselves, itching in their ears; and they will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth, but will turn to fables” (II Timothy IV, 4–5).

Therefore, elsewhere also, speaking in the person of his beloved and chosen disciple, he most diligently warns every faithful person, and especially the pastoral order, saying: “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words and the oppositions of ψευδωνύμου γνώσεως—that is, of knowledge falsely so called. By promising this, some have fallen away from the faith” (I Timothy VI, 20–21).
