Accordingly, after setting forth the statements which he arranged in nineteen chapters of his little work, we undertake, as the Lord deigns to grant us the ability, to answer—not according to our own judgment, but according to the holy Scriptures and the most blessed Catholic Fathers.

## Chapter One

In the first chapter he proposed definitions of the following kind:

1. That every question can be resolved by the fourfold *quadrivium* of the rules of all philosophy.

2. That there are not two predestinations.

[Note: The Church of Lyons argues especially against Scotus that there are two predestinations: one of the good and another of the wicked, provided that the latter is not the cause of the wickedness of their guilt, but only of punishment or of the preparation of punishment, just as the former is the cause and preparation of grace.]

To this the faith of the Church replies in opposition that the truth of God’s eternal judgment and ordering, expressed by the term “predestination,” is not to be sought from philosophers but from God’s apostles and prophets; nor is it to be sought in the quadrivium of worldly doctrine, but in the one true way which says of itself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6).

The blessed prophet Jeremiah exhorts and invites us to this way, saying: “Stand upon the ways, and see, and ask concerning the ancient paths, which is the good way, and walk in it, and you will find refreshment for your souls” (Jeremiah VI, 16). And the prophet Isaiah promises this way to the Church herself, saying: “And there shall be a way there, and it shall be called the holy way. No lion shall be there, nor shall any savage beast ascend by it; and this shall be a straight way for us, so that fools shall not wander on it” (Isaiah XXXV, 8).

Therefore, whoever chooses to be foolish in this world for Christ’s sake and strives to obey the Apostle, who says, “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this world, let him become foolish so that he may be wise” (I Corinthians III, 18), should hold continually and unwaveringly to this true way, this good way, this straight way, which is the Lord Christ himself.

They should flee the craftiness and deception of human wisdom, of which the same Apostle says: “For it is written: I will catch the wise in their craftiness” (ibid., 19); and again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain” (Psalm XCIII, 11). Therefore, the question of divine predestination has not been solved by this kind of philosophy and empty deceit; rather, it has been confused and entangled and heaped up with various falsehoods and errors.

We truly call the predestination of God’s eternal counsel and judgment—whether in the rewarding of the just or in the condemnation of the wicked—one predestination, because of the one and simple divine knowledge in which all things were simultaneously and eternally ordered and determined in advance. But because of its twofold efficacy, by which some are mercifully delivered and others justly condemned, we do not hesitate to call it twofold. Faithfully, with the Psalmist, we say to the Judge of all:

> “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Psalm C, 1).

And we faithfully hear the same Judge declaring in the Gospel that the mystery of this predestination had been eternally established with the Father and was wondrously fulfilled openly in the blinding of some and the illumination of others, when, exulting in the Holy Spirit, he says:

> “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, because this was pleasing before you” (Matthew XI, 25, 27).

For what could have been said more plainly concerning both sides than that by his coming he declares the proud blinded and the humble illuminated? This is what is meant by: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to little ones.”

And what could be firmer and stronger concerning the just and merciful predestination of both than what he immediately adds in thanksgiving: “Yes, Father, because this was pleasing before you”?

And because the Father gave all judgment to the Son, and because he, together with the Father in the eternal counsel, established and determined all these things which he distinguishes and judges in the world at their appointed times, he immediately adds concerning himself: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (ibid., 27)—that is, all things that are to be delivered and condemned, and all who are justly to be blinded and mercifully illuminated, as he says elsewhere:

> “For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John IX, 39).

As the Lord and Savior himself praises this just judgment of God and refers it with thanksgiving to the glory of the Father, so all divine Scripture and the entire holy Catholic Church, in the psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs which it customarily offers to God, faithfully celebrate it with praise and thanksgiving as just, holy, and pious, saying with the Psalmist:

> “The Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works” (Psalm CXLIV, 17).

And the legislator says in the song of Deuteronomy:

> “Give greatness to our God. God’s works are true, and all his ways are judgments: God is faithful, and there is no iniquity in him; the Lord is just and holy” (Deuteronomy XXXII, 3–4).

Likewise, in the psalm, after it had been said generally both of the elect who are to be delivered and of the reprobate who are to be condemned:

> “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth. He will do the will of those who fear him; he will hear their prayer and save them. The Lord guards all who love him, and he will destroy all sinners” (Psalm CXLIV, 18–20),

the just judgment of both sides is commended by abundant and general praise when it immediately adds:

> “My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord, and let all flesh bless his holy name forever and ever” (ibid., 21).

So also in another psalm, after first offering praise to God and then recalling in his praises the just judgment of God concerning both sides, he says:

> “Praise the Lord, O my soul. I will praise the Lord during my life; I will sing to my God as long as I exist” (Psalm CXLV, 1);

and shortly afterward:

> “He keeps truth forever, executes judgment for those who suffer wrong, gives food to the hungry,”

and so on, until he says:

> “He will receive the orphan and the widow, and he will destroy the way of sinners” (ibid., 7–9).

Therefore, in the Apocalypse, after that final judgment and the rewarding of the just and condemnation of the wicked, the saints offer God such praise and thanksgiving concerning both matters. The same book says:

> “And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones in the sight of God fell upon their faces and worshiped God, saying: We give you thanks, Lord God almighty, who are and who were, because you have taken your great power and have reigned. And the nations were angry, and your wrath has come, and the time has come for the dead to be judged, to give reward to your servants the prophets and the saints and to those who fear your name, the small and the great, and to destroy those who corrupted the earth” (Revelation XI, 16–18).

There are many such passages, found in manifold ways throughout the holy Scriptures, so that nothing is better for a faithful person than faithfully to acknowledge and praise God’s just judgment concerning both sides, saying:

> “You are just, O Lord, and your judgment is right” (Psalm CXVIII, 137).

The holy Fathers and teachers of the Church also earnestly urge that this be done. Thus the blessed Pope Leo exhorts us in one passage, saying:

> “Nothing concerning God’s judgments ought to displease us. For what else is it than to criticize him in some respect if we do not give thanks to him in all things?”

And blessed Augustine, when expounding the words of the psalm to the people where it is written, “As smoke fails, so let them fail; as wax melts before the fire, so let sinners perish from the face of God” (Psalm LXVII, 3), asks: Who will boast that he has a pure heart, or who will boast that he is clean from sins? Accordingly, when Scripture says, “As wax melts before the fire, so let sinners perish from the face of God,” who does not tremble, who does not leap up in fear?

“What, then, shall we do, and what hope is there for us? For these words are not sung in vain. Or when the Prophet says these things, does he wish them upon human beings, rather than foresee what is to come? In the words, the form of a wish does indeed appear, but the foreknowledge of one announcing what is to come is understood. For just as certain things in Scripture are narrated as having already happened when future events are being foretold, so certain things are spoken as though they were the wishes of one desiring them. But those who rightly understand what they hear recognize the vision of one announcing what is to come.

[Note: Many passages were missing here; they have been restored from the Corbie manuscript.]

“Thus, just as future events are signified by words in the past tense, so the mind of the one who announces what is to come must be understood beneath the form of a wish.”

So also concerning Judas, the betrayer of the Lord, the Prophet seems to wish for him what he foretold would come to pass. And concerning the Jews he says:

> “Let their table become a snare, a trap, and a stumbling-block” (Psalm LXVIII, 23),

which the Apostle without hesitation explains as having been foretold concerning them (Romans XI, 9). Likewise, the Apostle Peter recalls the things concerning Judas that were foretold under the same figure.

Nor are future things called past without reason. For, if they are certain to God, they are regarded as though they had already happened; and the Prophet seems to speak as one wishing for what he foresees with certainty will come. As far as I can see, this shows nothing other than that we ought not to be displeased by the sentence of God once known, since he has established it as fixed and immovable.

Therefore, in the Acts of the Apostles, when a certain prophet named Agabus foretold that the Apostle Paul would suffer many things from the Jews in Jerusalem and would even be handed over to chains, and when, upon hearing this, the brothers tried to dissuade him and prevent him from going there, he said:

> “What are you doing, weeping and troubling my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but also to die for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts XXI, 10 and following).

And when the brothers saw the man’s unshakable steadfastness in enduring all things, they said:

> “Let the will of God be done” (ibid., 14).

Did the apostles, then, by saying, “Let the will of God be done,” wish that he should suffer such things? Or did they rather submit their minds most devoutly to the sublime and divine decree?

So also, when the Prophet says, “As wax melts before the fire, so let sinners perish from the face of God,” he sees with complete certainty that this threatens sinners, and he approves what God has determined, lest he himself displease God.

[Note: The future is narrated as though it were past to establish the certainty of prophecy; and, to remove suspicion of an evil disposition in the prophets themselves, things that they foretell and announce as future are presented as though they were desired—not because they actually wished sin or eternal condemnation upon anyone, for that conflicts with the charity in which they abounded, but because they had shown those things from far beforehand, or because, when they saw the decree of divine justice for their punishment, their desire was directed not so much toward their destruction as toward the decree of divine justice. Innumerable testimonies in Isaiah and in the royal prophet are explained in this way.]

After these words, the most blessed teacher, lest the predestination of the divine judgment—so fixed and immovable—should seem to anyone to impose a necessity of doing evil, and so that it might instead inspire salutary fear, enabling those who hear to flee the coming wrath through repentance and correction, and thereby escape what is most certainly impending upon those who remain in their sins because of their wickedness, exhorts them as follows:

> “What, then, shall we do, brothers, except that while there is time we change our life and correct our deeds, if there are any such, so that what will undoubtedly come upon sinners may not find anyone upon whom to come—not because we shall not exist, but so that it may not find us as those upon whom it was foretold that it would come?”

Thus the most faithful teacher both asserted the immovable truth of divine predestination, even in the condemnation of sinners, and sincerely taught that they would escape punishment if they corrected themselves and changed for the better. For that divine predestination exercises just judgment in punishing sinners, but takes away from no one the remedy of salvation if he converts, since its promise is true and faithful. Through the prophet it not only promises but also swears, saying:

> “As I live, says the Lord God, I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live” (Ezekiel XXXIII).

## Chapter Two

In the second chapter he presents eight predefinitions to us, saying:

1. That God’s predestination and foreknowledge are his essence, just as are his will, wisdom, and truth.

2. That foreknowledge and predestination are one and the same.

3. That a human being cannot reach God, whom he had freely abandoned without difficulty, without the effort of labor and the gift of cooperating grace.

4. That predestination in God exists according to substance, and cannot be constituted relatively.

5. That, just as it is impious to multiply into two, three, or more the essences, wisdoms, knowledges, powers, and all the other things said of God, so one who asserts two predestinations is bound by the guilt of impiety.

6. That there is one divine predestination, just as there is one divine operation, wisdom, and will.

7. That no one is compelled by the necessity of predestination, just as no one is compelled by the will.

8. That whatever is understood concerning the divine will ought also to be held concerning God’s predestination.

Behold how many things he has proposed—or rather, how many things he has defined as though all were to follow them and no one were permitted to judge them—without any testimony from divine Scripture and without any attestation from the teaching of the Fathers. But we, with the Lord’s help, shall carefully examine each point and discern what ought to be thought concerning them according to the rule of faith.

He says: “Predestination and foreknowledge are God’s essence, just as are his will, wisdom, and truth.”

As for the will, we do not doubt that it is spoken of essentially in the Lord, because in his supreme and simple essence to will is not one thing and to be another, but what it is to be is what it is to will. Therefore, his will is such that he himself is his will.

The same applies to wisdom and truth: he possesses wisdom in such a way that he himself is his wisdom; he possesses truth in such a way that he himself is truth. In that simple nature of the Godhead, possessing is not one thing and being another; rather, what it is to possess is what it is to be, and what it is to be is what it is to possess.

Accordingly, if, as blessed Augustine says, we call him eternal, immortal, incorruptible, immutable, living, wise, powerful, beautiful, just, good, blessed, and spirit, the last of these—that is, “spirit”—seems to signify substance alone, while the others signify qualities of that substance. But it is not so in that ineffable and simple nature. Whatever seems to be said there according to qualities must be understood according to substance or essence.

Far be it from us to say that “spirit” is predicated of God according to substance, while “good” is predicated according to quality; both are predicated according to substance, and so are all the other things we have mentioned.

Since this is so, and since these three things—will, wisdom, and truth—are in God in such a way that they plainly display the nature of God, who is supreme will, supreme wisdom, and truth, possessing all power, surpassing every understanding, and remaining immutable above all things, it is clear according to the rule of God that they are to be understood as being said of God substantially.

The same is clear concerning knowledge: it must be understood essentially in God, because for him to be is not one thing and to know another; rather, what it is for him to be is what it is for him to know. Nor is possessing knowledge for him anything other than being knowledge itself, just as possessing wisdom is the same for him as being wisdom.

Whether, however, just as God is said substantially to be knowledge, he may also be said substantially to be foreknowledge, let whoever can judge according to reason and the rule of faith. It nevertheless seems to us that, just as it is truly said of God, “For him to be is not one thing and to know another,” it cannot likewise be said of him except either falsely or in a highly unusual manner: “For him to be is not one thing and to foreknow another.”

That one may rightly and ordinarily say, “God is knowledge,” just as one rightly and ordinarily says, “God is wisdom,” is beyond doubt. But to say, “God is foreknowledge,” as we have already said, is either untrue or extremely unusual.

The reasoning is similar, or even more difficult, concerning what he has defined: that God is predestination substantially. For who has ever heard it said of God that, for him, being is not one thing and predestining another, but that predestining is being, just as it is truly said of him: “For him, being is not one thing and knowing another; rather, to be is to know”?

Thus we are being compelled by such novel expressions to say that, just as God is knowledge, God is wisdom, and God is truth, so God is predestination. But it seems to us better and more suitable to the true faith and ecclesiastical teaching that, although these three things appear to exist among us—knowledge, foreknowledge, and predestination—and although we distinguish them by certain properties, knowledge should be spoken of absolutely, while foreknowledge and predestination should be referred to the providence of future things.

Among these two, foreknowledge is understood as concerning the foreknowing of good and evil things, while predestination concerns the establishing and ordering of good things alone. It was necessary for these things to be spoken of and distinguished in this way so that, for us, who are temporal and mortal, both the fullness of knowledge in God and his governance of creatures might, through such a distinction—or, if one may say so, distribution—be conveyed and commended with greater clarity.

Nevertheless, it is more suitable for us to understand these three things in God under the one name “knowledge,” because whatever we understand in some way and recognize distinctly in these three is simultaneously present in his supreme, one, and simple knowledge.

His knowing is perfect and complete, and cannot be diminished, increased, or changed by any variation among things. Therefore, what we try to recognize by distinguishing his knowledge from his foreknowledge and predestination is not, in his perfect and immutable knowledge, one thing and another, or one way and another, but exists eternally in one and the same manner.

For this reason, we believe that the proper moderation of ecclesiastical discipline has observed that it is right and customary to say that God has foreknowledge and predestination with respect to his works, as the creator and judge of all things. It is also right and customary to say that foreknowledge and predestination exist in God—that is, in his eternal, perfect, and immutable knowledge.

But it is unusual, and not even correct, to say that God is foreknowledge or predestination. For his knowledge is spoken of in relation to himself, whereas foreknowledge and predestination are referred to creatures. Thus what is shown in these terms is rather his operation, which is carried out in or toward creatures, than his essence or substance.

For “the foreknowledge and predestination of God” or “foreknowledge and predestination in God” are spoken of in the same way as “the ordering or disposition of God” or “ordering or disposition in God.” Yet we have never heard anyone speak so absurdly or contentiously as to say that, just as God possesses ordering and disposition, so God himself is ordering and disposition, or that he ought to be described and defined in this way.

The origin of this entirely novel and contentious definition is clear. He fears that if foreknowledge and predestination, like God’s governance, are not understood substantially of God but are understood as referring to the ordering of his creatures, then he will be unable to call predestination twofold or to admit that it can be plural.

There is therefore no dispute among us as to whether predestinations may be spoken of in the plural or may not be so spoken, provided that we hold faithfully and firmly that, by one and the same judgment and counsel of divine foreknowledge and predestination, two things are most certainly to be fulfilled: namely, that the just are predestined to eternal glory, and that the wicked who persevere in their wickedness until death are destined for eternal punishments.

Scripture says this most plainly. Concerning the just:

> “And all who had been appointed to eternal life believed” (Acts XIII, 48).

Concerning the wicked, who are justly to be condemned:

> “God endured with much patience the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction” (Romans IX, 22).

Thus both things are carried out in the elect and the reprobate by one and the same effect of divine predestination and judgment. It is like one and the same ray of the sun invigorating healthy eyes while irritating diseased ones; and like one and the same fire causing the mud placed near it to harden while melting wax.

Let him also acknowledge that this is how one ought to think of God’s predestination, just as one thinks of his justice. Although justice is one and always remains in the same manner, it plainly receives a twofold distribution when, through it, rewards are bestowed upon the worthy and punishments inflicted upon the unworthy.

Certainly, he himself asserts that God’s will, or the will in God, is said essentially, just as are wisdom and truth—which is entirely true. For even if he said that God is justice substantially, he would be speaking most truly.

Why, then, are these two things—which are said to exist substantially in God, or even to be God substantially, namely his will and his truth—read in Scripture in the plural? Thus we find in the Psalm, where the Lord himself says:

> “He has magnified all my wills among them.”

And elsewhere:

> “I have found David, son of Jesse, a man according to my heart, who will do all my wills.”

Again, we read in the psalm:

> “The Lord has loved justices.”

And again:

> “For truths have been diminished by the children of men.”

And in another place:

> “For the Lord seeks truths.”

Although God’s light and God’s truth are not different things, but are believed to be simply and truly one in God—so that what is God’s light is God’s truth, and what is truth is light—nevertheless, after the Psalmist had said:

> “Send forth your light and your truth,”

he immediately continued in the plural:

> “They themselves have led me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your tabernacles.”

Why is this, unless it is because God’s will, justice, and truth, although they are truly one and simple in his nature, become multiple for us in the distribution of his gifts and in the ordering of his creatures? Thus the Holy Spirit himself, although he is one and simple as a Person of the Trinity, is called, because of this same distribution of gifts, the manifold grace of God and the sevenfold Spirit?

[Note: Up to this point the material is missing in the Thuan manuscript and in the printed editions.]

We repeat all these things so that those who read them may consider that there ought to be no quarrel or dispute about number—whether God’s predestination may be spoken of in the plural or, for some true reason, may not—provided that it is most certain that its effect is twofold: either in the elect, mercifully predestined to life, or in the reprobate, justly predestined to punishment.

Blessed Augustine teaches that, just as the wisdom of the Lord is rightly spoken of, so also are his prudence and knowledge. He says:

> “What human being, then, can comprehend that wisdom by which God knows all things—that wisdom, I say, which is the same as prudence and the same as knowledge—when we cannot even comprehend our own?”

After several intervening remarks, he continues:

> “And do we suppose that God’s providence is memory and understanding, since he does not look upon things individually by thinking about them, but embraces in one eternal, immutable, and ineffable vision all things that he knows—things which we, with such great weakness of mind, can scarcely comprehend? In this difficulty and distress, I am moved to cry out to the living God: ‘Your knowledge has been made wondrous by me; it has prevailed, and I cannot attain to it’” (Psalm CXXXVIII, 6).

[Note: Augustine preferred to call God “knowledge” rather than “providence.” His reasons are not given here, but they are as follows: either because providence includes a relation to governed things, whereas knowledge is simply the cognition of all things; or because providence, considered as an act, exists only in time, while knowledge exists from eternity; or because providence, which is said to be the genus of predestination, is the preparation of means for attaining a fitting end, whether natural or supernatural. Nevertheless, speaking absolutely, because of the supreme simplicity and identity of the divine attributes, God may no less be called providence than knowledge. Hence the ancients commonly called God θεία πρόνοια, “divine providence.”]

Behold how that eminent teacher, thinking and speaking exceptionally about God, confidently said that God is prudence and openly confessed that God is knowledge. But when he came to consider whether God should similarly be called providence—which is indeed God’s and is in God, but is referred to the governance of creatures—he did not rashly wish to define anything about the matter. Rather, as though caught in great difficulty and distress, he preferred to end the same discussion by turning his wonder and prayer into an exclamation addressed to God.

Following his example, we too ought to reflect and say how devoutly we should think about God, how moderately and carefully we should speak, and how cautiously and reverently we should define.

After this, the disputant just mentioned, following his custom, adds as though defining the matter: “Foreknowledge and predestination are one and the same thing.”

But, rejecting the error of this novelty, let us hold fast the most certain and firm rule of faith, and, with God’s help, faithfully distinguish the cases in which foreknowledge can be spoken of without predestination being involved. For almighty God, just as he foreknew good things, also foreknew future evils—that is, the sins of human beings and angels.

[Note: Let the Calvinists read and reread the manifest condemnation of their position, since in impious and intolerable blasphemy they dare to attribute the causality of all sins to God. The most upright truth can disapprove and condemn iniquity; it cannot produce it.—Augustine, *Letter* 105, to Sixtus.]

Yet the just and holy God could not predestine those evils to occur. His predestination, moreover, concerns either the condition and governance of creatures—which is certainly good and just—or, especially and above all, his works and judgments, which he exercises or will exercise upon rational creatures, namely angels and human beings: while by grace he justifies and blesses some of them, and by justice abandons and condemns others. For their good things—that is, those of holy human beings and holy angels—are his gifts or rewards; and their evils—that is, eternal punishments—are his just vengeance, since he orders all things justly.

Therefore his predestination is always concerned with good things, always with his works, which—as has been said—he exercises upon rational creatures either mercifully or justly. It must be understood as that which he both foreknew by predestining and eternally predestined by foreknowing. Hence it is clear that God’s predestination does not exist without foreknowledge; but foreknowledge exists both with predestination in God’s good and just works, and without predestination in the evil works of human beings and wicked angels.

The blessed Augustine, that aforementioned Father, very briefly demonstrates the whole matter as follows (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 10):

[Note: If I am not mistaken, Augustine was the first to define predestination in this way, as may be seen in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 10. The same point is found in what he writes in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 14: predestination is “the preparation of God’s benefits by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered.” Augustine speaks continually in this way whenever he denies that predestination is made on the basis of foreseen merits. From this it is plainly evident that he does not disagree with the other Fathers who assert that we were predestined on the basis of the foreknowledge of works; for they are speaking of predestination to glory, whereas Augustine is speaking of predestination to grace.—Vásquez, on question 23 of the First Part of Thomas Aquinas; Suárez, *Opusculum on Predestination*.]

“Predestination is the preparation of grace; grace, however, is the gift itself. Thus, when the Apostle says, ‘Not from works, lest anyone should boast; for we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works,’ this is grace. But what follows—‘which God prepared that we should walk in them’—is predestination, which cannot exist without foreknowledge; foreknowledge, however, can exist without predestination.

“For by predestination God foreknew those things which he himself was going to do. Hence it is said, ‘He made the things that are to come.’ But he is also able to foreknow things which he himself does not do, such as all sins. For there are certain things which are sins in such a way that they are also punishments for sins. Hence it is said, ‘God gave them over to a reprobate mind, so that they might do things that are not fitting’ (Isaiah 45:11, according to the Septuagint). There is not God’s sin in this, but his judgment.

“Accordingly, God’s predestination, which is directed toward good, is—as I have said—the preparation of grace; grace, however, is the effect of that predestination itself.”

Again, in another place (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 14):

“This is the predestination of the saints,” he says, “nothing other than the foreknowledge and preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered. But the rest—where are they left except in the mass of perdition by the divine judgment?”

From all these words of the holy Doctor it is perfectly clear that, in the sacred writings, foreknowledge and predestination must be understood distinctly and properly. Things separated from one another by so great a difference must not be understood as one and the same, as this man defines them.

Nevertheless, the same Doctor also shows that predestination itself—which never exists without foreknowledge—is sometimes signified by the name “foreknowledge,” saying:

[“Sometimes that same predestination is also signified by the name ‘foreknowledge,’ as the Apostle says: ‘God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew’ (Romans 11:2). Here, what he says—‘whom he foreknew’—is not correctly understood unless it means ‘whom he predestined’; the context of the passage demonstrates this.

“He was speaking of the remnant of the Jews who were saved while the others perished. Therefore, after saying, ‘God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew,’ he subsequently added: ‘What Israel sought, it did not obtain; but the election obtained it, while the rest were hardened’ (ibid., verse 7).

“Thus, in this election and in this remnant, which was saved through the election of grace, he wished the people whom God did not reject to be understood as those whom he foreknew. For this reason, no one who understands these matters is permitted to deny or doubt that, when the Apostle says, ‘God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew,’ he intended to signify predestination. For he foreknew the remnant which he himself was going to bring about according to the election of grace. This, therefore, means ‘he predestined.’ For there is no doubt that, if he predestined, he foreknew; but to predestine is to foreknow what he himself was going to do.”]

Behold what must follow for anyone who desires, according to the pious understanding of the holy Father, to think soundly, purely, and sincerely about divine foreknowledge and predestination.

That definition of the new disputant, however—by which he defines these two things, distinguished from one another by so great a difference and separated with such care, as one and the same thing—must rightly be rejected entirely because of its falsehood and deceitfulness. For whether he wished to define the matter in this way in order to show that these things are, as he had already proposed, substantially one in God, his assertion is empty and frivolous; or whether he wished to teach that these things are to be understood indiscriminately, confusedly, and indifferently in Scripture, it is a most manifest error.

The same disputant adds and says that a human being cannot reach God, whom he had abandoned by free will without labor, without strenuous effort and the gift of cooperating grace.

In these words, when he says that the first human being abandoned God by free will, he is speaking of a free will which, in the one abandoning God and abandoned by God, was no longer free for the good—that blessed freedom of good nature created by God and of grace given by God, which the Apostle commends when he says: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:17). Rather, it was free only for evil, and captive under the domination of sin.

Concerning this most wretched freedom and servitude, the Apostle says to believers who have been converted: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness” (Romans 6:20). And again: “Do you not know that, to whomever you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey—whether of sin leading to death, or of obedience leading to righteousness?” (ibid., verse 16).

Hence the Lord also says: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:33). And the blessed apostle Peter says: “By whatever a person is overcome, by this he is also enslaved” (2 Peter 2:19).

The blessed Paul likewise does not conceal the captivity of sin, saying: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin which is in my members” (Romans 7:23).

Thus, as has been said, the human being, abandoning God and abandoned by God, became free from righteousness, which he had refused to serve, and a slave of sin leading to death, because he refused to be a slave of obedience leading to righteousness. Consequently, he began to have in his members a law warring against the law of his mind and taking him captive to the law of sin.

Having therefore lost the grace of true freedom, by which he could cleave to God and say, “But it is good for me to cling to God” (Psalm 72:28), he clung, through the unhappy freedom of his will, to sin, and became sin’s slave and captive.

He cannot escape and be freed from this servitude and captivity except through the one who says: “If the Son makes you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36). Therefore, when the human being abandoned God, he plainly lost the freedom of the good and remained free only for evil. We do not know, then, why such freedom should be proclaimed in him rather than erased and guarded against.

[Note: With the Pelagians, Erigena removed prevenient grace and seemed to establish cooperative grace alone. Augustine sharply refutes this, as Bellarmine teaches, book VI, chapter 15, conclusion 4.]

But when he says that a human being cannot reach God without strenuous effort and the gift of cooperating grace, the Catholic faith holds otherwise. It certainly believes, in accordance with evangelical and apostolic truth, that a person is saved and comes to God through no good work and no preceding good merit, but solely through the benefit of divine grace.

As the Lord himself says: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). And the Apostle most diligently impresses this upon believers, saying: “To the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness” (Romans 4:5). And again: “We hold that a person is justified by faith without the works of the law” (Romans 3:28).

And lest those who come to God should even attribute faith itself to themselves and think that they were saved through the merit of their own work rather than by God’s free gift, he shows elsewhere that faith itself is also God’s gift, when he says: “By grace you have been saved, through faith”; and immediately he adds: “And this is not from yourselves; it is God’s gift, not from works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9).

Therefore God also says through the prophet, as the Apostle himself recalls: “I was found by those who were not seeking me; I appeared openly to those who were not asking about me” (Isaiah 65:11). Or, as it is read in our edition: “Those who previously did not ask have sought me; those who did not seek me have found me.”

Behold the most manifest grace without works, through which people who do not seek God not only come to God but also reach him. Thus countless thousands of infants, who certainly could have performed no good work, reach God without any doubt through the sole faith of the Church and the grace of regeneration, when at such an age they have been reborn from water and the Spirit, released from the bond of original sin, and have then died.

To think otherwise—that is, to say that a human being cannot reach God without the exertion of his own effort—is not Catholic but Pelagian.

A certain definition of this kind is found in the little book entitled *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* (Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 21). But, as we have said, this too—like several other statements in the same book—is entirely an error of the Pelagians.

Therefore, whoever reads it for the sake of certain other useful matters should, upon finding such a meaning there, carefully remember the Apostle’s words: “Test everything; hold fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21).

After this, he adds and says that predestination in God is according to substance and cannot be relative.

What seems to us better or more suitable concerning this has already been said above, as best we could. Yet since he has added here that predestination cannot be spoken of relatively to God, it is plainly not related to God in the same way that, within the holy Trinity, the Father is related to the Son, the Son to the Father, and the Holy Spirit to both; or the begetter to the begotten, the begotten to the begetter, and the one proceeding to both.

Nor is it related in the same way as, when the Word of God is understood, the Son is related to the Father, whose Word he is. And when that same Son is called the image, he is similarly related to the Father, whose image he is. And when he is called the radiance of glory, he is related to the eternal light from which he comes and whose radiance he is. For he is “the brightness of eternal light” (Wisdom 7:26), as Scripture testifies.

Nor is it related in the same way as, when the gift of God is understood properly as the Holy Spirit, he is related to the Father and the Son, whose gift he is.

These things in that holy and supreme Trinity are related to one another in such a way that they are distinct there, and one cannot be said of the other. For there is one Father, the begetter; one Son, the begotten; and one Holy Spirit, proceeding. There is one Word, image, and radiance of the Father, namely the only-begotten Son. There is one gift of God the Father and the Son, namely the Holy Spirit.

These things are understood individually there in such a way that the property of each person cannot pass over to another. For example, the Father can never be called the Son, nor can the Son naturally be understood as the Father, nor can the Holy Spirit be called the Father or the Son.

It is clear, therefore, as we have said, that predestination is not related to God in the same way that the Father is related to the Son, the Son to the Father, and the Holy Spirit to the Father and the Son. For predestination is not, properly speaking, a person in the Trinity, so that it could be naturally related to another.

Nevertheless, this same predestination is entirely related to God—that is, to the Trinity as a whole—which is wholly the predestining agent of whatever things have been predestined. For predestination is undoubtedly related to the one who predestines, just as governance is related to the one who governs, arrangement to the one who arranges, and ordering to the one who orders.

No one has ever been so absurdly and improperly contentious as to say that God, who arranges all things, is arrangement; that God, who governs all things, is governance; or that God, who orders all things, is ordering. We think that no one would say that the one who predestines all things to be predestined is predestination, since all these things—as we have already said, namely arrangement, governance, ordering, and predestination—are to be understood as referring more properly to the works or operation of the Creator.

But even if this man should try, through a new contention, to assert that God is substantially predestination in the same way that he is truth, goodness, and justice, so that predestination would seem to be spoken of only in the singular, just as God, truth, goodness, and justice are spoken of only in the singular, he still cannot establish by this argument that God’s predestination may substantially be called God, or that God may substantially be called predestination.

Nor can he eliminate the twofold effect and distribution of its work: either in the preparation of the just for life or in the preordination of the impious to destruction. For justice is most truly called God, and yet, when God is understood substantially as justice, it is not correctly expressed in the plural. Nevertheless, the justice of God—which is also God—undoubtedly has a twofold effect, either in rewarding the good or in condemning the wicked.

Therefore, when predestination is correctly spoken of relatively to God who predestines, just as arrangement is related to the one who arranges, governance to the one who governs, ordering to the one who orders, operation to the one who operates, and creation to the one who creates—and even if something could be demonstrated by reason that would require God’s predestination, or predestination of God, to be spoken of substantially—the twofold effect of predestination, declared by the immovable truth of Holy Scripture, cannot in any way be nullified.

What, then, is the purpose of this argument, so utterly superfluous—or even deceitful?

He continues and says: “Just as it is impious to assert two essences, wisdoms, knowledges, virtues, and all the other things that are said of God—or to double, triple, or multiply them—so anyone who asserts two predestinations is bound by the guilt of impiety.”

To these words we reply that it is indeed true that essence, wisdom, knowledge, and virtue, when they are said of God—or when God himself is so described that he is understood to be essence, wisdom, knowledge, and virtue—are not to be expressed in the plural. For the Trinity is not three essences but one essence; not three wisdoms but one wisdom; not three knowledges but one knowledge; not three virtues but one virtue.

Yet when these things are related to God’s different arrangement or operation toward creatures, some of them are plainly expressed even in the plural and in multiplicity, as in the passage: “For God is the Lord of knowledges” (1 Samuel 2:3). And if he is the Lord of knowledges, surely they are not the knowledges of another but his own.

How, then, is this to be understood except that knowledge itself, which is naturally one and simple in him, becomes multiple for us when it is related—as has been said—to the arrangement or ordering of creatures?

Thus God is called virtue, yet in the same sense we read: “Declaring the praises of the Lord and his virtues” (Psalm 148:2). And just as God is rightly called virtue, so the same God is rightly called power; yet in the Psalm we sing: “Who will speak of the powers of the Lord?” (Psalm 105:2).

If, then, God is one knowledge, one virtue, and one power, and yet, in accordance with the truth and authority of Scripture itself, we rightly speak of God in the plural and multiplicative number as “the Lord of knowledges,” “the powers of the Lord,” and “his virtues,” why does this disputant call impious what proceeds from the fountain of truth and piety?

If, however, those things which are most truly substantially in God may, not impiously but piously, be spoken of God in the plural according to a certain manner of expression, how can the person who wishes, by the same reasoning, to speak of God’s predestination in the plural—because of its twofold efficacy—be bound by the guilt of impiety?

Nevertheless, we reject neither this on account of the truly twofold efficacy of predestination, nor do we consider that it must invariably be expressed in the plural. For it must certainly be understood that, just as there is one justice of God, so there is one predestination of God, which operates in multiple ways.

He adds and says: “There is one divine predestination, just as there is one divine operation, wisdom, substance, and will.”

In these words he is attempting to do what he attempted above: namely, to make us believe that, just as God is substantially wisdom, substantially will, and himself the supreme substance, so that same God is predestination and operation.

We have already shown in several ways what we hold should be thought concerning predestination. But concerning the one operation of God which he adds here—apparently wishing operation itself to be understood as God—we must carefully consider what should be thought about this matter according to the rule of faith.

We rightly speak of God’s operation, certainly with reference to the creatures upon whom he has operated, and we may rightly speak of an operation proceeding from God, since, as the Apostle says: “From him, through him, and in him are all things.”

But can we rightly speak of operation in God, when God operates nothing in himself, but every creature that he has made and in which he continues to operate is outside him—that is, outside his nature?

Nevertheless, in another sense a creature may also be said to be in him, because it certainly subsists in his power and might. Hence the Apostle says what has already been quoted: “In him are all things”; and elsewhere: “For in him we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28).

Since, therefore, God operates nothing in himself—that is, in his substance—but all his operation is understood to take place in creatures, which are not of the same nature or substance as he, how can one rightly speak of operation in God?

And if one cannot rightly speak of operation in God, how much less can God himself rightly be called operation?

Nevertheless, almighty God arranges all things with himself and in himself, and likewise operates all things with himself and in himself, because, in order to do these things, he does not go outside himself or depart from himself. For his willing is his doing.

Rather, he calls the things that he operates toward himself, so that, from the one who supremely is, each may receive being according to its own mode; and thus what the Apostle says may come to pass: “He calls those things which are not as though they were” (Romans 4:17).

Therefore he operates nothing outside himself, since by his sole and eternal will, without any effort, labor, or craftsmanship, he operates all things. Nor does he operate anything in himself, since in the perfection and eternity of his substance he accomplishes nothing, increases nothing, diminishes nothing, and changes nothing.

Yet, because his willing is his doing, it does not follow that his willing and his doing are one and the same. For this signifies not the unity of the Creator and the creature, but the power of the Creator alone.

How, then, can operation in God—or God himself, as this man asserts, substantially understood as operation—be understood? Perhaps God is called operation not because someone operates him or in him, but because he himself operates all things.

But since this is highly unusual, is not taken from the authority of Holy Scripture, and is exceedingly dangerous to the faith—lest, when God is called operation, someone should believe that he was made by another, according to the impious error of the Arians, who thought this concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit—such presumption of excessive verbosity must certainly be restrained and suppressed. Among the other novelties of speech, it must be avoided, as the Apostle most earnestly warns (1 Timothy 6:20).

Yet we, who understand divine operation simply in his works and creatures, read that this same operation is set forth in Scripture in the plural, as the Apostle plainly says: “There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God, who operates all things in all” (1 Corinthians 12:4–6).

Since, therefore, God’s operation is so openly expressed in the plural and understood in multiple ways in God’s creatures, what usefulness does an argument of this kind have?

It is useful for nothing, as the Apostle says, “except for the subversion of those who hear” (2 Timothy 2:14).

Nevertheless, he continues and says: “Nothing is compelled by the necessity of predestination, just as nothing is compelled by the will.”

Both parts of this statement—that nothing is compelled by God’s predestination and that nothing is compelled by his will—are plainly false. For by the goodness of God’s predestination the elect are often compelled by various scourges, hardships, and tribulations, either to be converted to God or to live according to God.

Thus the apostle Paul was compelled while he was still Saul (Acts 9): struck down by the terror of a heavenly voice, blinded by a divine blow, and restrained from his error and cruelty by such terror that he might be converted to God.

And yet, after he had been converted, after he had become an apostle and a teacher of the nations, he was still disciplined and still buffeted, lest he be exalted by the greatness of his revelations (2 Corinthians 12:7).

By the judgment and equity of that same divine predestination, the reprobate are also compelled—not, indeed, to live wickedly and impiously, but to undergo eternal punishment for their own iniquities and impieties.

Similarly, by the goodness of God’s will—in which God’s eternal predestination certainly exists—the elect are scourged temporarily for correction or testing, while by the severity of that same divine will the reprobate are scourged eternally for punishment.

For almighty God, as the Apostle says, “with manifest mercy and hidden judgment, has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9:18).

Both are present in God’s predestination, and both in God’s will—namely, goodness and severity. Concerning these the same Apostle says: “See, then, the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but goodness toward you, if you continue in goodness” (Romans 11:22).

### CHAPTER III

In the third chapter he set forth definitions of the following kind:

1. God’s predestination, like his essence, compels no one and imposes no necessity.

[Col. 0120B]

2. There are not two predestinations.

3. Death, sin, and misery are not from God.

4. Predestination, like charity, is not twofold, double, or multiple, and admits no plurality.

Of these four propositions we have already treated above, insofar as the Lord granted us ability.

That is, the first, in which he says that God’s predestination, like his essence, compels no one and imposes no necessity;

the second, in which he says that there are not two predestinations;

and the fourth, in which he defined that predestination, like charity, is not twofold, double, or multiple and admits no plurality.

The only exception is that above he did not name charity among the examples which he wished to be understood as concerning God’s substance.

And plainly, as the blessed apostle John teaches, “God is charity” (1 John 4:16). Thus, according to the rule of true faith, we may most correctly say that there is the charity of God, that charity exists in God, and that God is charity.

Yet because this charity is substance in God, like truth, justice, and goodness, when it is understood of God it is not called twofold, because it is substantially one and simple in him. For this reason it cannot there be called double or triple, since the divine substance—that is, the deity itself, the truth itself, the charity itself, God the Trinity—is not doubled or tripled.

For it is not less in one than in three, nor greater in two or three than in one. Rather, as great as the deity, truth, and charity are in one person of the Holy Trinity, so great are they in two and in three: perfect in each, perfect in all.

For the Father is perfect God, the Son is perfect God, and the Holy Spirit is perfect God; and these three are one perfect God.

In us, however, this charity is not substance but God’s gift, as the Apostle says: “Because the charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

Therefore in us it can be twofold and double, because of the two commandments of charity—namely, of God and of neighbor—which certainly produce in us a twofold affection, so that we love God with our whole heart and our neighbor as ourselves (Matthew 22:37, 39).

And because through this gift of charity God performs manifold and countless good works in his saints, it is also called manifold in Scripture. For it is the grace of God concerning which the blessed apostle Peter says: “As each has received grace, ministering it to one another as good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (1 Peter 4:10).

Who does not know that charity is without plurality, since it is found expressed neither in the plural number nor as plural, whether in God or in us, in Scripture?

But concerning his statement that predestination does not admit the plural number, just as charity does not, enough has already been said above, and it should not be repeated constantly. The same applies to what he says in the first of these propositions, where he compares God’s predestination with God’s substance—or rather, says that it is God’s substance. This too has already been treated above, as best we could.

And if he asserts that God’s predestination itself compels no one and imposes no necessity, then, if he means that by his predestination almighty God compels no one to evil, so that he may be evil and unable to be anything else, he is entirely correct.

But if he has inserted this cautiously and obscurely in order to say that predestination itself compels no one and imposes no necessity, without adding what it compels one to do or what kind of necessity it imposes—and thereby denies that the wicked, who persevere in their wickedness to the end, are to be punished by the eternal judgment of God’s just predestination, as appears more truly from everything he said above—then he plainly accepts divine predestination in part and denies it in part.

Thus, by the same predestination, he would have God prepare the just for the kingdom but not preordain the reprobate for punishment.

[Col. 0121C]

3. The third proposition which he put forward and defined remains: that death, sin, and misery are not from God.

Concerning sin, certainly, he spoke correctly, as the Catholic faith everywhere maintains: sin is not from God, because God neither willed nor commanded nor impelled the human being to sin. Rather, before the human being sinned, God prohibited sin, terrified him with the punishment of death so that he would not sin, and, after he had sinned, justly punished him as a rebel against and opponent of his own will.

Therefore sin is not from God, who created the human being upright and without sin, as Ecclesiasticus says: “This alone I have found: God made the human being upright, but they themselves became entangled in countless questions” (Ecclesiasticus 7:30).

Rather, the beginning of sin came from the one who also first sinned in heaven; afterward he deceived the human being so that he would sin, and by deceiving him killed him in paradise.

The blessed apostle John testifies to this, saying: “The devil sins from the beginning” (John 3:8). And the Lord himself teaches, saying: “He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him” (John 8:44).

By not standing in the truth, he destroyed himself; by offering sin to the human being, he killed the human being. And just as he was the first sinner, so he also became the first murderer, because “the soul that sins shall die” (Ezekiel 18:4).

Hence he is also said in Scripture to possess the power of death (Hebrews 2:14)—not because death invaded and overwhelmed the whole human race by his authority, but because it did so through his malicious envy.

Therefore Scripture says: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world; and those who belong to his party imitate him” (Wisdom 2:24).

The Lord destroyed this impious dominion by his death, as the Apostle says of him: “So that through death he might destroy the one who held the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14).

For he is the Lamb of God who took away the sin of the world (John 1:29).

Therefore this disputant rightly said that sin is not from God. Yet he inserted this point needlessly when defining divine predestination, since no believer says that God predestined sins.

What he added, namely that death and misery likewise are not from God, plainly contradicts Scripture, which says: “Good and evil, life and death, poverty and honor are from God” (Sirach 11:14). But since Scripture also says, “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living” (Wisdom 1:13), we must carefully inquire how both statements are to be understood faithfully—namely, both that God did not make death and that death and life are from God.

Both, then, can rightly be understood in this way: God did not make death, because he created man immortal, had he not sinned. Yet death is from God because he condemned sinful man to a just death. Thus death is not from him by creation, and yet it truly is from him by retribution.

Just as this bodily death, which is also understood as the first death, is from God because it was justly inflicted by him upon sinful man, so also the second death, in Gehenna, is justly to be inflicted by him upon the man who persists in sins. Therefore both this death and that one—that is, the first, which separates the soul from the body, and the second, through which, as has been said, both soul and body are destroyed in Gehenna—are from God, since both are just and are inflicted or to be inflicted upon man by God’s just judgment.

For this reason the same Scripture elsewhere says of the present bodily death: “Do not fear the sentence of death; remember what things came before you, and what things are to come upon you” (Sirach 41:5). “This sentence is from the Lord upon all flesh.” And again: “Fire, hail, famine, and death—all these things have been created for vengeance” (Sirach 39:35).

How, then, were famine and death created? Certainly not with some form or formation by which they were brought into existence as created things, but they were prepared in the hidden ordering of God for his vengeance, so that their manifestation might seem, as it were, to be a kind of creation.

Again the same Scripture says: “Death, bloodshed, strife, and the sword; famine coming upon them, destruction, and scourges: all these things have been created for the wicked, and because of them the cataclysm came” (Sirach 40:9–10).

Since, therefore, the death of man, coming from a just and divine retribution, is so openly said and so truly understood in Scripture to be from God, blessed Elijah, praying to God for the dead son of the widow with whom he was staying, said: “Lord, have you also afflicted this widow, with whom I am in some fashion sustained, so as to kill her son?” (1 Kings 17:20). And the Lord plainly says in the Gospel: “Fear him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna” (Luke 12:5). Let the manifest truth of Scripture, therefore, be understood, and let vanity fall silent.

Thus, just as death is the punishment of sin, so also all the misery of labors, tribulations, and calamities that followed upon man after sin—because they were and are inflicted by divine ordering and judgment—Scripture rightly says to be from God, as the testimonies we have cited plainly demonstrate.

Therefore, just as sin itself, which is contrary to God’s justice, truly is not from God, so the punishment of sin—namely, death—and all that calamity and misery which followed it, because they belong to God’s just judgment and are inflicted by his just retribution, are rightly understood, with Scripture bearing witness, to be from God.

Even if the devil and the other wicked angels do anything in this matter, they are servants of divine retribution and vengeance, not judges or authors, as the history in the blessed book of Job plainly shows. It demonstrates most fully that the devil was not permitted to do any of these things—not merely to strike Job with a most grievous wound from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, or to kill his children by the collapse of the shaken and falling house, or to consume his numerous household either by the sword of marauding robbers or by fire descending from heaven—but not even to touch his livestock and animals, unless the Lord had first permitted it, saying: “Behold, all that he has is in your hand; nevertheless, do not stretch out your hand against him” (Job 1:12). And again: “Behold, he is in your hand; nevertheless, preserve his life” (Job 2:6).

Accordingly, when all these things had happened to that holy man, filled with divine wisdom, he did not attribute them to the devil, since the devil had been the executor of that calamity. Rather, he faithfully and humbly referred everything to God and to his just judgment, with thanksgiving, saying: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:12).

Similarly, in the Gospel, when the legion of demons was being driven out of the man it had possessed, the demons did not have power to enter the herd of pigs and destroy it unless permission was granted by him to whom, grieving and trembling, they said: “If you cast us out, send us into the herd of pigs.” And he said to them: “Go” (Matthew 8:32).

For this reason, in the Psalm where the plagues and calamities with which Egypt was struck for its impiety—God justly taking vengeance, with Moses his servant acting as mediator and minister—are recounted, Scripture plainly refers all these things to God, even if some of them were inflicted upon the Egyptians through the ministry of evil angels:

“He turned their rivers into blood,  
and their rainwaters, so that they could not drink.  
He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them;  
the frog, and it destroyed them.  
He gave their fruits to the rust,  
and their labors to the locust.  
He struck their vineyards with hail,  
and their mulberry trees with frost.  
He delivered their cattle to the hail,  
and their possessions to the fire.  
He sent upon them the anger of his indignation:  
indignation, anger, and tribulation,  
a sending through evil angels” (Psalm 77:44–49).

And in another Psalm, when he recalled the assault of fires and hail, storms and tempests, by which so many shipwrecks, overturnings, and devastations occur in the world, referring everything likewise to God, he said: “Fire, hail, snow, ice, and storm wind, which carry out his word” (Psalm 148:8).

## CHAPTER IV

In the fourth chapter he sets forth five definitions in the following order.

1. Three heresies: first, that of the Pelagians, concerning free choice without commending grace; second, that of grace alone; third, the Gotteschalcian heresy, which also attributes necessities to predestinations.

[Note: For who Gotteschalcus was, see Pithoeus in the *Annals*, Trithemius in the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, and Flodoard, Book III, chapter 13—or rather Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, who was then living and had often seen and heard Gotteschalcus. His words to Nicholas I are as follows:

“I wish,” he says, “to disclose briefly to you how, before I had been ordained bishop, this Gotteschalcus—a monk of the monastery of the metropolitan church of Rheims, called Orbais, in the diocese of Soissons, as the abbot and monks with whom he lived testify—was a man exalted in spirit, impatient of quiet, desirous of novel expressions, inflamed by an insatiable ambition for honor, insolent and disorderly. In order to acquire fame through an empty display of spirit, he chose and collected certain articles of all false doctrines.”

And later:

“The same Gotteschalcus, having been initiated into the priestly order by the dean of Rheims—although this promotion was contrary to ecclesiastical constitutions—left the monastery contrary to his rule and traveled through very distant lands in order to pour out the poison of his false doctrine. The Church of Lyons relates how he went to the remotest regions of Germany for the sake of evangelical preaching, and began his sermons from the ineffable mystery of predestination. Forced to return to Gaul, he was condemned by the bishops at the Council of Mainz and, by their decree, violently beaten with whips. Finally, by decree of the same council, he was confined as though in a prison in a monastery of the diocese of Rheims.”

Hincmar lists the articles condemned at that council: namely, that just as God had predestined some to eternal life, so he had predestined others to eternal death—understand this as being without any foreknowledge of evil works; that God does not wish all men to be saved, but only those who are saved; that the Lord Jesus Christ was not crucified or died for the redemption of the whole world, but only for those who are saved; and that the devil cannot snatch away anyone for whom the Lord Jesus Christ shed his blood. These are the principal articles, among many others, condemned by the Council of Mainz. Serrarius should be read, Book I, chapter 33, of the *History of Mainz*.]

2. That the substance of man consists of three things: being, willing, and knowing; and that he did not lose these through sinning.

3. That no nature can perish, and that he did not lose free will—that is, his nature.

4. That freedom remained to man after sin, but that he lost its vigor and power.

5. That nature can always make a beginning, but can complete nothing except through grace.

Concerning the three heresies he mentions, he knows well and the Church condemns the first—that of the Pelagians, who said that free choice, without God’s grace, could suffice for man’s salvation—following the voice of the Lord, who commends his grace in all things and says: “He who remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit, because without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

In saying, “He who remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit,” he declares the benefit of grace, which those who remain in him receive from him, so that they may bear fruit for God, just as a branch receives nourishment from the root of the vine. But when he adds, “Because without me you can do nothing,” he most plainly shows that man’s free choice, without the help of that same grace, can accomplish nothing toward the fruit of a good work.

As for the second heresy, which he says is that of grace alone—what heresy has existed, or does exist, in the Church that has preached God’s grace alone in such a way as to deny or destroy man’s free choice—we have no knowledge.

For those most ancient and most impious heretics, Marcion, Valentinus, and Mani, who introduced either two or three principles and therefore asserted two natures, whether of angels or of men—one good and the other evil—the one so good that it could not be anything else, and the other, conversely, so evil that it likewise could not be anything else—said nothing at all about God’s grace. They foolishly attempted to defend nature alone as naturally good or naturally evil.

The Catholic Church, however, faithfully instructed and fortified by the teachings of the Law and the Gospel, acknowledges and proclaims only one principle of all heavenly and earthly creatures, visible and invisible: the holy Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God, from whom all things are, through whom all things are, and in whom all things are.

It holds that no nature exists except from him, the best Creator, and therefore that every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good; that evil is not a nature of nature, but a defect of nature.

Yet because this nature was made mutable in angelic and human creation, and by its own fault could fall from the good in which it was created into evil, it can also rise from the evil into which it has fallen and be restored to good—so far as concerns the human race that is saved by God’s mercy.

But as for the portion of the angels who are evil and eternally condemned, they fell from God through pride in such a way that they no longer deserve to be restored by any remedy. They were deprived not only of the good will in which they had been created, but, by the terrible judgment of the Creator, even of the possibility of possessing that good will.

Since, then, those heretics mentioned above either defended nature alone as immutably good or accused it as immutably evil—and therefore it is unclear how they could have preached anything concerning grace or free choice—while the Church of God holds the position we have recalled in the briefest terms, what is this second heresy, so unknown, so novel, and unheard-of, which, after denying free choice, preaches grace alone?

Unless, as it seems to us, this disputant is secretly accusing the blessed Augustine as though he were a heretic, because, in clear accord with the truth of Scripture, he shows and teaches that man can be saved by God’s grace alone, and that human choice can contribute nothing to that eternal salvation unless it has first been reformed, healed, illuminated, and restored by the same grace.

Or perhaps he calls heretics those who now think and teach concerning God’s grace according to Augustine’s venerable and Catholic doctrine, as though they understood his words inadequately—on the assumption that Augustine himself did not think so about free choice, and that they do not rightly understand his words, and therefore err because of his expressions, understanding them differently from the one who wrote them.

For this reason it seems to us that he has very cunningly and craftily introduced a heresy of grace alone, while giving no indication whatever of its author or followers.

If this is so, what else is he doing but accusing the Church of our time, together with those who incite him to such things, with viperine subtlety?

And if there are such people in those regions of his kingdom where this opponent of the truth is not merely left unrebuked or silenced, but is even held in the highest praise and honor—people who favor him in such matters, especially ecclesiastical men—who could worthily grieve over and shudder at this contagion and pestilential evil, which rises from those regions so wildly and shamelessly, so impudently and boldly, against the other regions of God’s Church, which are quiet, peaceful, and tranquil among themselves?

There this monster and portent, which ought long ago to have been kept from the ears of the faithful, sits, argues, and piles up so many lies of error and so many insults against the faith of truth; and no vigilance on the part of the Church’s shepherds either corrects it in such people or drives it out.

Finally, so that we may plainly recognize that he was not speaking of some more ancient heresy that preached grace alone, he did not place this heresy before the Pelagian one, but afterward—that is, from the time of Saint Augustine until now.]

[Note: He asserts that no one taught that we are saved by grace alone without free choice, because if there ever were such people, they were perpetually regarded by the Church as heretics, so that the word “no one” excludes Catholics, but not those whom the Church condemned. Or at least, since no one ever explicitly taught this, certain people merely abolished free choice, as Simon Magus is described in Clement’s Book III of the *Recognitions*; Bardesanes, in Augustine’s chapter 33 of *On Heresies*; and Mani, one hundred years after Bardesanes, from whom the Manichaeans arose, in the same work, chapter 70. Thus our innovators may see that their perverse doctrine of salvation by grace alone, without the concurrence and cooperation of free choice, was unheard-of throughout all preceding ages.]

Nor can any such heresy be found in the Church during the whole period between him and us, unless he is accusing either Augustine himself, as we have already said, or us who follow him, of this error.

He sets forth the third heresy as one that attributes necessities and force to predestinations. He does not conceal, as it seems to him, its author, calling it “Gotteschalcian,” after a certain wretched and most unhappy monk named Gotteschalcus, who was condemned long ago—though we do not know by what procedure there—and has for many years been confined in a prison-like dungeon.

If he dared to teach anything so serious and dangerous against the Catholic faith that he was punished by a synodal judgment with so great and severe a condemnation, then surely, according to the ancient custom of the Church, for the sake of caution—lest more people be infected by so great an error—that error ought to have been reported to the other Churches established in the various regions of the kingdom through synodical and ecclesiastical letters, if not at the beginning, when so great an evil was discovered, or at the end, when it was condemned with such severity, then at least afterward, for the information of all the brethren and fellow bishops.

If this had been done according to the ecclesiastical custom, as we have said, always observed by the Fathers, we would now know better, and would be more prepared to refute and convict what he proposes that Gotteschalcus taught when he says that he imposed necessity and force upon predestination.

When, therefore, he accuses him of speaking of “predestinations” in the plural, it is clear, as we have already demonstrated in many passages above, that what displeases him is not so much the plural number of the term “predestination” as the genuinely plural effect of predestination—namely, as we have frequently said and shown from the holy Scriptures, both the preparation of the elect for life and the foreordination of the reprobate to punishment.

To deny this against the faith of the Church, he undertook such extensive and tedious labor that he tries to persuade us, by novel arguments, that predestination is God’s substance, indeed that God himself is predestination, and that therefore it ought not to be understood in the plural.

According to this view, predestination is to be understood only with respect to the elect, and not at all with respect to the reprobate. Taking this as his opportunity to empty predestination of the reprobate to eternal punishment of its force, he rushed into such audacity that he attempted to assert, plainly against the faith and the truth of Scripture, that just as sin is not from God, so its punishment—that is, all the misery and death that followed upon sinful man—is not from God.

Yet God plainly and justly condemns and judges, and misery consisting of labors and sweat was inflicted upon sinful man, as was also the final death of all those labors, when the Lord said to him concerning the miseries of a laborious life:

“Cursed is the earth in your work;  
in labors you shall eat from it;  
it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you,  
and you shall eat the plants of the earth;  
in the sweat of your face you shall eat bread” (Genesis 3:17–19).

There he immediately added the ultimate punishment of death:

“Until you return to the earth from which you were taken;  
for you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (ibid., 19).

But to the woman who had sinned before her husband, he immediately imposed, in addition to that punishment which she shared with her husband, the punishment proper to her own sin, saying: “I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions; in pain you shall bear children,” and so forth.

By denying, then, the just predestination of the reprobate according to divine judgment, he descended to the point of asserting that all human miseries, and death itself, are not from God—that is, that they do not pertain to God’s judgment.

If he is asked where death and misery come from, if they are not from God, what remains except that he must answer, against all truth, either that they come from no one or that they come from the devil? To say that they come from no one is utter madness. The devil merely persuaded men to sin; it was not he but the just Judge who inflicted the punishment of sin.

When he says that the aforementioned Gotteschalcus imposed necessity and force upon predestination, if he means that the predestination of the reprobate to destruction imposes force and necessity upon some of them toward evil—that is, makes them inevitably evil, so that they cannot possibly be anything else—this is entirely foreign to the Catholic faith.

For it would be exceedingly absurd and impious to say that almighty God, who wishes no one to be evil, compels and forces anyone to be evil, and compels someone to be unjust, although it is written: “The just Lord has loved justices” (Psalm 10:8).
