What takes place in all the reprobate concerns their sins and their final punishment, and was enacted in the first sinful man by the first judgment. Just as that man was not compelled to sin by any impulse, compulsion, or predestination of God, but sinned solely by his own will, yet unwillingly and against his will received the judgment and condemnation of that sin—which was the first punishment of man—so also the entire multitude of the reprobate, descended from that condemnation, is not compelled by God’s predestination to sin, since God has predestined no sins.

Nevertheless, by the just and eternal judgment of that same divine predestination, they are compelled to undergo punishment. They receive from God the force and necessity of a just condemnation, which had no force or necessity compelling the commission of iniquity.

For those who will stand on the left at the judgment and be punished with eternal fire will not willingly accept such punishment, but unwillingly and against their will, grieving and trembling irredeemably, will be hurled there at the command of the divine majesty and through angelic ministry, as the Lord plainly says in the Gospel:

“So it will be at the consummation of the age: the angels will go out and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and will cast them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 13:40–42).

To these reapers—that is, the angelic ministers—when the harvest comes, that is, the consummation of the age, the Judge himself will say: “Gather the weeds and bind them into bundles to burn; but gather the wheat into my barn” (ibid., 30).

Behold what force and necessity the Church of God, in accordance with evangelical truth, believes divine predestination to impose upon the reprobate: the force and necessity of judgment, not the force and necessity of sin.

Anyone who says that God has imposed or imposes upon man the force and necessity of sinning plainly and horribly blasphemes against God, since by compelling him to sin he necessarily confirms God to be the author of sin.

This, then, is how we think concerning the predestination of the reprobate according to God’s truth: we faithfully confess him to be the author not of their sin, but of their just punishment. Therefore, what this man raves—that the preaching of this predestination imposes a necessity of sinning—we consider so slanderous and empty that its character should be clear to everyone from what has been said.

After this he adds: “The substance of man consists of three things, namely being, willing, and knowing; and he did not lose these through sinning.”

We, however, say that the substance of man is nothing other than what divine Scripture demonstrates at the beginning of human creation, saying: “Then the Lord God formed man from the dust of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul” (Genesis 2:7).

This is the substance of man, by which he subsists and lives, as the learned and the unlearned alike know: namely, soul and body vitally joined to one another—the body from the dust of the earth, and the soul from God’s breathing. From these he is constituted, and thus man became a living soul.

Since divine authority teaches this and Catholic truth holds it, what is the point of this superfluous claim that the substance of man consists of three things, namely being, willing, and knowing, when it is evident that the substance of man consists not of three things but of two—namely, as we have already said, soul and body?

But this man, passing over the body, which naturally belongs to the substance of man, says that the substance of man is being, willing, and knowing. These things certainly exist in the soul alone, as though the substance of man were nothing but the soul.

Nevertheless, he seems to have taken the opportunity for saying this from the discussions of Saint Augustine in his books *On the Trinity*. But far be it from us to suppose that so great a teacher ever spoke so absurdly and incompetently as to define, when the substance of man is soul and body, the substance of man as being, willing, and knowing.

He did not say—as anyone who reads and carefully weighs his statements in those same books will plainly be able to understand—that the substance of man consists of these three things, namely being, knowing, and willing. Rather, he spoke of these three as existing in the substance of man—not the external but the internal substance, that is, in the rational mind, where man was created in the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1:26).

He teaches that these things are naturally and substantially implanted by God in that rational and intellectual mind. Hence, in those same discussions he most correctly says that these three belong to one substance with the mind itself and are in the mind itself.

For the mind, just as it substantially has being, so it substantially has willing—that is, it has, substantially and naturally, the capacity to know and the capacity to will.

This is indeed a great good of nature, created well and wonderfully by the best Creator. But if the human mind possesses only this—that it can exist, can know, and can will—and does not possess, from the gift of that same Creator, the ability to exist well and blessedly, to know its author piously and rightly, and, by loving him, to will to be with him, what benefit will it gain from possessing being, knowing, and willing, if it does not possess that gift of its Creator?

For it will have being unhappily, knowing deceitfully, and willing ruinously and wickedly. The angelic nature likewise, condemned in the devil and his angels, certainly possesses these three things in its spiritual substance—being, knowing, and willing—but its being is punitive, while its knowing and willing have been wholly turned toward error and evil.

What, then, is the point of this man’s boasting that human nature did not lose these things through sinning—that is, that it could exist, know, and will—when it entirely lost the goodness and blessedness of all these things, beginning to exist in misery instead of blessedness, losing divine knowledge, and losing heavenly willing?

This remained only insofar as the Creator’s grace afterward helped and raised it up, so that it might recognize the goods it had lost, grieve over what it recognized, and, through grief and repentance, implore divine assistance—and thus recover, through divine goodness, what it had lost through its own fault.

Therefore the Creator’s ineffable mercy did not remove from man, even after sin, these natural goods of his—being, knowing, and willing—so that there might be someone toward whom mercy could be shown.

For if, after sin, God had not wished him to exist, then being would have perished along with him and in him, and likewise knowing and willing. He therefore wished him to exist, so that there might be one toward whom he could show mercy; he wished him to know, so that there might be one whom he could illuminate with his knowledge; he wished him to will, so that there might be one whom he could bless through his love.

Thus the devil, who wished to destroy God’s creature, remained defeated, while the Creator’s goodness and mercy remained unconquered.

But why this man proposed these things will become clearer from his subsequent propositions.

Immediately after these two connected propositions he added: “No nature can perish, nor did he lose free will—that is, his nature.”

In these words, when he defined that no nature can perish—a statement he evidently made generally concerning the nature of all things—from where did he learn this, or how did he show it to be true?

For it is manifest that, just as every nature of things could subsist from nothing by the Creator’s will, so that what previously did not exist might exist, so also, if he wills it, it can perish and return to nothing, so that it may no longer exist.

Scripture also demonstrates this when it speaks of the greatness and power of the Creator: “He is higher than heaven—what will you do? Deeper than hell—how will you know? Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea. If he overturns all things or confines them into one, who will resist him? Or who can say to him, ‘Why do you do this?’” (Job 11:8–10).

Certainly, when the almighty Creator was preparing, because of the excessive wickedness and impiety of men, to destroy the world by the flood, Scripture testifies that he said: “I will destroy man whom I have created from the face of the earth, from man to animals, from creeping thing to birds of the air” (Genesis 6:7). And again: “The earth is filled with iniquity because of them, and I will destroy them together with the earth” (ibid., 13).

Thus, in that great and terrible flood, a large part of the world’s nature was destroyed and changed for the worse, as it had been said: “I will destroy them together with the earth.” Almost the entire nature of the animals that existed in the world—that is, both human beings and beasts—was destroyed by the waters.

Even the souls of the wicked, who deserved to perish in so terrible a punishment, were preserved and passed into something greater, namely infernal punishment; only those were saved who, in such a very small number, were delivered by God’s mercy in the ark.

If the Creator’s marvelous power so willed, could he not easily destroy the whole nature of the world, and of earthly or heavenly things, just as it is plainly recorded in the Books of the Maccabees that certain holy men, preparing to fight against their enemies, said: “But we trust in almighty God, who can by a single nod destroy both those who are coming against us and the whole world” (2 Maccabees 8:18)?

But this man must also be asked what he thinks will happen in that final conflagration of the world, of which the blessed apostle Peter says: “In it the heavens will pass away with great force, while the elements will be dissolved by heat” (2 Peter 3:10). What, then, will he think will happen to the nature of the four elements of the world?

If they will remain as they now are, how is this apostolic statement true? But if for the most part they will be changed or perish, how is this definition true, that no nature can perish?

Certainly the four seasons by which the year proceeds and returns—the spring, summer, autumn, and winter—have the proper and distinct quality of their nature. But when there is a new heaven and a new earth, and the course of the sun, moon, and stars has ceased, by which days and nights now continually succeed one another for the refreshment and rest of mortals, and therefore those four successive seasons, which are accomplished by the course of the sun, cannot exist as they now do, how will their nature not perish?

He must also be asked what he believes will happen when heaven and earth are renewed by fire and wonderfully transferred into another quality suited to the immortal bodies of the saints. What, I ask, does he believe will then happen to the whole nature of birds, four-footed animals, reptiles, and aquatic creatures?

If these are to be believed to be entirely consumed in that immense conflagration, since the renewed world will receive nothing mortal, how will it be true that no nature can perish? Especially since it is written even of that sea of such immense extent, in that wondrous transformation of things: “And the sea is no more.”

If he had said that human nature could not perish, he might in some fashion be heard—not because God could not dissolve it if he wished, but because our Lord’s promise cannot fail, since he himself promised, saying: “Even the hairs of your head are all numbered” (Matthew 10:30). And elsewhere: “Not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke 21:18).

But since he says generally that no nature can perish, let him consider what has happened by the divine and terrible judgment even in rational nature—that is, in the devil and his angels. They have lost not only the will to do good, but even the ability to will the good itself.

After saying that no nature can perish, he immediately reveals whom he meant by all these statements when he adds: “Nor did man lose free will—that is, his nature.” It is as though, by that false and deceptive argument in which he says that no nature can perish, he had proved to us that man did not lose free will through sinning, because, according to him, his free will is itself his nature.

We, however, in accordance with the truth of the Catholic faith, say that the nature of the first man was created by the good Creator wholly good and endowed with a good will. For Scripture says: “God created man upright” (Ecclesiastes 7:30).

Yet this was so arranged that, although a good and free will existed in him as a natural good, he could truly remain in the state in which he had been created only by needing and receiving the help of divine grace.

Hence the voice spoken in his person is understood in the Psalm, where he says: “In my prosperity I said, ‘I shall never be moved’” (Psalm 29:7–8). Immediately afterward, speaking of his fall, he adds and says sorrowfully to God: “You hid your face from me, and I became troubled.”

What he possessed in prosperity—good will and blessed freedom before sin—was from God, and he says to him: “Lord, by your will you gave strength to my beauty.” But when God turned his face away from him, and he became troubled because God no longer illuminated him with his countenance, this was the consequence and punishment of sin.

This man, however, who praises the good of nature in him so highly without the help of divine grace, insists that he did not lose free will through sinning, even calling that free will his nature. He is plainly entangled in Pelagian error.

He asserts that man possessed free will by nature alone, both before sin and after sin, that he did not lose the same free will through sinning, and that this free will is his nature. Yet he was free only so long as he remained good and piously subject to God. Once he sinned by despising God and proudly transgressing his commandment, he immediately came under the yoke of sin.

For, as the Lord himself says: “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34, 36). Thus what had previously been free toward the good, after that miserable ruin, could not by itself remain free except toward evil.

From this deepest evil of condemnation it cannot in any way rise to the freedom of a good will, unless he liberates it who says: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free.”

This man, however, who thinks that the human being did not lose free will by sinning because he was created with that same good and free will, and therefore naturally possessed that disposition toward the good will, ought to know [Col. 0132D] that almighty God created every rational creature—human beings and angels, that is—with a good and upright will for this purpose: that, so long as it preserved its proper order, remaining devoutly subject to God and assisted by his grace, its dignity might remain in it—that is, both the good of nature and the gift of grace itself. But if, through pride against the Creator and by presuming upon itself rather than upon him, it abandoned the order of its subjection and obedience, then immediately, by the just judgment of the Creator himself, it would be deprived of the gift of grace, and its nature would be turned to the worse. Hence it is written in the Psalm: “A human being, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to foolish beasts and became like them” (Ps. LXXXIV, 13, 21). Before sin he was indeed in the honor of the good nature created by God; he was in the honor of the grace bestowed upon him by God. But he did not understand from whom he had this honor of divine goodness and grace, when, abandoning the Creator, he presumed upon himself and, at the serpent’s suggestion, desired to be like God, as though subject to no Lord. Thus, deservedly abandoned by the Creator himself, he was wholly changed for the worse, both in soul and in body. In soul, because, having lost the freedom of righteousness and the freedom of the good will, and being weighed down under the dominion of sin, he ceased to seek the things above and desired lowly things, as an irrational beast, with the sense of cattle. In body, because, condemned to the condition of death, so that he would be dissolved into the earth and dust from which he had been taken, after the manner of beasts, he received the sentence of a just judgment. Behold to what great evil human nature was brought down, wholly changed for the worse by the merit of sin, having lost its freedom toward the good and being free only to desire evil—unless it is healed and restored by the grace of him who came to seek and save what had perished (Luke XIX, 10).

But how greatly the angelic nature was corrupted in the devil and his angels, and horribly changed for the worse, after losing free choice toward the good, so that they are not only unable to rise toward it in any way but are no longer even able to will it, having been turned toward evil alone by a malice that will never change—who could worthily dread this, much less explain it in words? For even bodily nature itself may be healthy or sick: that which is strong and vigorous through the good of health is turned for the worse by the loss of that health and is burdened and afflicted by the disease of sickness. But this man, who does not believe that free will and free choice toward the good are a good belonging to the human mind, but identifies them with the mind itself—who does not believe that they are in the mind, but identifies them with the mind itself—seems to take his opportunity, as we have already said above, from certain words of Saint Augustine in the books *On the Trinity* (book X, chapters 11 and 12). Augustine says there, with complete truth, that the mind, the mind’s knowledge by which it knows itself, and the mind’s will by which it wills and loves itself, are naturally one substance: it exists by being, knows itself by knowing, and wills itself by loving. Truly all of this—that is, the mind, its knowledge, and its love of itself—are substantially one. Nevertheless, he does not say that the two latter—that is, the mind’s knowledge and will, by which it knows and loves itself—are the human mind, but that they are in the human mind; and therefore this man’s argument is plainly erroneous. [Col. 0133D]

When free choice is discussed, by which a human being’s free will desires either good or evil, the issue is not that will by which the mind loves itself, [Col. 0134A] but that will by which it loves the highest good when it is upright—that is, God—or the lowest good when it is perverse—that is, the world. For although this will is one in nature with the will by which the mind loves itself, it nevertheless differs greatly in disposition: as much as there is a difference between love of oneself and love of God, and between love of oneself and love of the world. By one will it loves itself; by the other it either loves God above itself or the world beneath itself. This will, as we have said, is one in nature, but is made different by its disposition. In love of itself it is singular; in love of good or evil things, by which it is drawn or torn apart, it is manifold. Therefore, since that natural will of which blessed Augustine speaks—that is, the will by which the mind loves itself—has nothing to do with free choice and free will, by which good or evil things are desired, but belongs solely to the mind and is referred to the mind itself, this man adds freedom to it with insufficient discernment, or with excessive stupidity, and calls it free choice or free will. Blessed Augustine says nothing of the sort—and far be it from him to have said it. For who does not know that this will of the mind, by which it wills and loves itself, is naturally common to all human beings, and that it is always free in choosing to love itself? What mind is there among human beings—apart from the minds of the mad and insane—whose will does not naturally desire both the mind in which it exists and itself to exist, to live, and to remain unharmed? In this respect the will of all minds is free. For what could be freer than such a will, which loves the mind in which it exists to exist, loves it to live, and loves it not to perish? Or what could be more superfluous and pointless than to call such a will free, when it can never be otherwise in loving itself or the mind to which it belongs? Or to call the same will free choice, when there can be choice only among different things that must be distinguished, judged, chosen, or rejected? The will of the mind, however, finds no diversity within itself: it always loves itself equally and always adheres to itself in natural peace and unity. [Col. 0134C]

Let him therefore cease to say, when free choice is being discussed—the choice by which a human being loves either good things for salvation or evil things for his own ruin—that such a will of the mind is nature. For although it too is the will of the mind, by which it loves both itself and these other things, it loves itself with one disposition—one so natural that it never changes—and it loves these other things with another disposition, one that changes and varies entirely as it turns toward loving good things or evil things. [Col. 0134D]

[Note: The Church of Lyons, as far as I can conjecture, does not understand the mind of John Scotus Eriugena. For Eriugena does not initially say that will and soul are of the same nature, but only that the will of the mind and soul acts in loving itself as nature, not as free will. Secondly, Eriugena thinks both devoutly and in a Catholic manner when he says that freedom remained in human beings after sin, although they lost its vigor and power. The Church of Lyons, however, accuses him of taking freedom as opposed to slavery to sin, in accordance with John VIII: “Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin.” Eriugena nevertheless understands it as the capacity for either alternative, both good and evil, which, according to Augustine, certainly remained in human beings after sin; thus the dispute at this point seems to be about a word. — Bellarmine, *On Grace and Free Choice*, book V, in various chapters.]

For if that will of the mind, by which the mind loves not itself but other things, whether good or evil, [Col. 0135A] by which it is either made blessed or afflicted with misery, were human nature, as this man says, it would be either good alone or evil alone, and could not be changed from one into the other. This will, then—that is, this disposition of the human will—according to the truth of the divine Scriptures, was implanted in human beings by the good Creator as good and upright when they were created; and, with God’s grace cooperating, it remained good and upright in them so long as they obediently obeyed their Creator. But since human nature itself was created mutable by the immutable Creator, and this disposition of the human mind is likewise mutable, it stood in the good, with God’s grace assisting, and fell into evil when that same grace was abandoned, by God’s hidden judgment. And, as has been said very often, what had been free toward the good, after losing that blessed freedom, began to exist under the wretched slavery of sin.

**[Col. 0135B] 4.** He adds, as though defining the matter: “Freedom remained in human beings after sin, but they lost its vigor and power.” We need not linger over these words, because, as we have already said repeatedly above, the one who before sin was of free will, and of a good nature, and by the gift of grace was destined to love, desire, seek, find, and contemplate the highest and eternal good for which he had been created, fell through sin [or: “by sin”] from so great a good and became a slave of sin, as the Lord himself testifies, saying: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII, 34). Blessed Peter the apostle likewise says: “By whatever anyone is overcome, to that he is enslaved” (II Peter II, 19). Thus, after losing the gift of grace and having the good of nature wounded, corrupted, [Col. 0135C] and deformed, he fell so miserably from such great happiness that he could have no return to loving and enjoying that good to which he ought to have adhered, except through the aid of the most merciful reconciler and mediator and through the price of his blood, by which we are redeemed from so great a captivity, so that we may recover our former freedom and from enemies become friends. Concerning this mediator it is written: “For there is one God and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all” (I Timothy II, 5); and again: “While we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Romans V, 10).

Therefore, whoever says that, after that most unhappy ruin of transgression, by which human beings lost their former freedom, became slaves of sin, became slaves of the one by whom they were overcome, became enemies of God, and needed one mediator and reconciler through whom they might receive redemption from slavery and reconciliation with God—whoever, I say, after so great and wretched a fall claims that such a person had or has freedom to desire, love, and merit the true good unless he is redeemed, justified, reconciled, and restored through the grace of the true mediator, is entirely opposed to the faith of the Church, teaches contrary to evangelical and apostolic truth, and, insofar as lies within him, wholly nullifies the cross of Christ and the death of Christ. For if, after that sin, human beings could have or recover true freedom of mind by any means other than through the redemption of the cross and death of Christ, then, as the Apostle says of certain people who thought they could be justified in another way, “Christ died for nothing” (Galatians II, 21), and this is the wisdom of the word in which “the cross of Christ is emptied of its power” (I Corinthians I, 17). Truly, if human beings could have true freedom after that sin, they did not need redemption, they did not need a redeemer, and Christ’s coming and death were superfluous. [Col. 0135D]

But when this man says that the sinner did not lose freedom, but only the vigor and power of freedom, he speaks incorrectly because he thinks incorrectly. He did not retain the good of freedom in part and lose it in part; rather, just as he lost the vigor and power of freedom, so he lost freedom itself, so that he could no longer by himself be free for the true good from which he had fallen. He remained free for evil, because just as by free will he abandoned the good, so by free will he adhered to evil. Thus, after that condemnation, a human being possesses free choice by which he can and does incline himself toward evil by his own will; he possesses free choice by which he can rise toward the good. But that he actually rises toward the good is not the result of his own power, but of the grace of the merciful God. He possesses free choice so that he can will well, live well, and adhere to God; but that he should will well, live well, and adhere to God is not the result of his own power, but of the grace of the merciful God. For one who is gravely ill may be said to be able to receive health, but in order to receive health he needs medicine. And one who is dead might be said to be able to rise again and to live, but not by his own power—only by God’s. So too human free choice, once wounded and once dead, can be healed, but not by its own power—only by the grace of the merciful God. And therefore everyone is rightly admonished, and the word of God is rightly preached to all, because they have the ability to believe and the ability to turn to God, so that those who hear may come to life again through the external admonition of the word and God’s inward raising of them. Thus it is rightly said of such a person: “He was dead and came to life again; he was lost and was found.”

Concerning this capacity of human nature—which nevertheless has no power apart from the generosity of divine grace—blessed Augustine teaches as follows (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 5):

> “To be able to have faith, just as to be able to have charity, belongs to human nature; but to have faith, just as to have charity, belongs to the grace of the faithful.”

But when the will to believe is prepared by the Lord for some and not prepared for others, it must be distinguished what comes from his mercy and what from his judgment. “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10). “His ways are unsearchable” (Romans XI, 33). Unsearchable, therefore, are both the mercy by which he freely liberates and the truth by which he justly judges.

**5.** After this man had vainly and deceitfully said that freedom remained in human beings after sin, he added another conclusion and said: “Nature can always make a beginning, but can complete it only through grace.” If he says this as though human nature, through its own free choice, can always begin the good, but can complete it only through God’s grace—so that the beginning of every good is always attributed to human beings, while only its completion is attributed to God, with human beings claiming the first part of good action and God the second—then this meaning is entirely Pelagian and contrary to evangelical and apostolic truth. For the Lord himself, to show that the beginning of our good does not come from us but from him, says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XV, 16). The Apostle says to the faithful: “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Christ Jesus” (Philippians I, 6); and again: “To you it has been granted for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (ibid., 29). Blessed John the Apostle says: “Not that we loved God, but that he first loved us and sent his Son as an expiation for our sins” (I John IV, 10). And again blessed Paul the apostle says: “Let us run with endurance the race set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith” (Hebrews XII, 1–2).

If, then, we truly wish to be Catholics, we must faithfully attribute everything to divine grace, both the beginning and the end of our good work. For, as is most clearly demonstrated by the testimonies of Holy Scripture quoted above, the Lord chooses his saints; they do not choose him. God both begins and completes the good work in his faithful. From him the faithful receive both the beginning of faith and the completion of martyrdom, since they suffer for him. He first loved his saints, so that they too might be able to love him. Our faith has the Lord Jesus as its author, because he begins it in us, and it has him as its finisher, because he brings it to completion. Let us therefore hold these things faithfully, so that, founded upon the true faith, we may be safe from heretical error. Or, if this man’s words have another sound and acceptable meaning, let the one who wrote them demonstrate it.

## CHAPTER V

In the fifth chapter he sets out propositions of the following kind.

1. No one is compelled by God’s foreknowledge and predestination.

2. God foreknows even things that he would not bring about, but predestines only things that he would bring about.

3. Just as God’s foreknowledge and predestination are not the cause of sin, so neither are they the cause of its punishment or of death.

4. Just as God compels no one to sin, so neither does he compel anyone to live well.

5. If any cause precedes the will—that is, nature—in thinking or doing good or evil, that cause is not nature.

Of these five propositions, three have already been treated sufficiently above, insofar as we were able, and need not be repeated needlessly: the first, second, and fourth. Two therefore remain, which he has now set out for the first time.

In the third proposition he says: “Just as God’s foreknowledge and predestination are not the cause of sin, so neither are they the cause of its punishment or of death.” To these words we reply: if God’s foreknowledge and predestination are not the cause of anyone’s sin, as is entirely true, then that same divine foreknowledge and predestination are not unjust or in any way blameworthy when he foreknew and predestined the impious who persist in their impiety to be condemned to eternal punishments. For by his foreknowledge and predestination almighty God is not the cause of their sin, but the just avenger of sin. He does not drive them to sin, but justly delivers them over to undergo punishment.

As the true and truthful God, he therefore foreknows the future sins of human beings. Hence Scripture says: “Eternal God, who know the hidden things, who know all things before they come to be” (Daniel XIII, 42). He does not compel anyone to sin through his foreknowledge, but, by his eternal providence, justly orders or condemns the sinners themselves. Nor did he, through his predestination by which he decreed to punish the impious, make them impious, as has already been said; rather, he justly decreed that those who persist in their impiety should not go unpunished.

But when this man adds and defines that, just as God by his foreknowledge and predestination is not the cause of anyone’s sin, so neither is he the cause of the punishment and death owed to sin, the distinction must be made faithfully. Human beings, by sinning, were and are themselves the cause of their punishment and the cause of their death. Yet because almighty God is a just judge, although the cause of punishments and death lies not in his foreknowledge and predestination but in human merits, eternal justice is nevertheless present in that foreknowledge and predestination: by it punishment and death are inflicted upon those who remain in their impiety. Therefore, by the argument he proposes, God’s predestination is not destroyed—the predestination by which he inflicts eternal punishments upon the impious. For even if the cause of punishments is not in his predestination, justice and the judgment by which punishments are justly inflicted are there.

The fifth proposition is this: “If any cause precedes the will—that is, nature—in thinking or doing good or evil, that cause is not nature.” Here he plainly speaks against the truth. For if no cause precedes the human will in thinking or doing good, whence does the good will exist in human beings—that is, the devout disposition enabling them to think or do something good? Human beings do not have a good will from themselves, the will of which it is said: “Peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke II, 14). Nor do they have from themselves the effectiveness of good work, of which it is said: “But glory and honor and peace for everyone who works good” (Romans II, 10). They have these from him of whom the Apostle says to the faithful: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good pleasure” (Philippians II, 13).

He himself, in his mercy, precedes the human will, as the Psalmist says: “My God, his mercy will precede me” (Ps. LVIII, 11). He himself inspires human beings with the grace of thinking rightly, as the Apostle says: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (II Corinthians III, 5). He therefore is the cause of our good will; he is the cause of our desiring and accomplishing what is good; he is the cause of the mercy and grace by which we can not only will well, act well, and bring good to completion, but also think well. And he does not do these things only in the present in his elect; before the foundation of the world he also predestined them by his grace to be holy and blameless before him, as the Apostle testifies, saying: “As he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless in his sight in love” (Ephesians III, 4).

Since, then, such a great and such a cause—which is certainly the cause of all good, whether in creating or rewarding his creatures—is for us the best and eternal cause of the good will, his grace preceding us so that we may be able to will and act well, how can this man say that no cause precedes our good will and good works? Or, if some cause does precede them, through which they come to be, how can he say that this cause is not nature, when almighty God, who is the cause of our good will, is himself above all the highest and best nature? Whoever does not believe that this highest and most effective cause—and likewise the highest and best nature—precedes our will so that we may be able to will and act rightly plainly resists the truth and is shown to belong to Pelagian error. For if this blessed cause did not precede human wills, there would be no predestination of the good, no redemption of the miserable, and no reward for pious works.

But as for thinking or doing evil, far be it from us to say that this highest and best cause precedes our will! Yet a cause does precede it—not an efficient cause, but a deficient one: namely, abandonment of the highest good and desire for an inferior good, when the soul falls away from the love of God and covets the things that are beneath it. When the will of human nature has fallen into these things, it becomes evil, having no other cause of its being evil than, as has been said, its defection from the highest good. Such a defection of the will made the angels evil when they abandoned God, and likewise made the human being evil when he disobeyed God. Such a defect is plainly not any nature; nevertheless, it is a defect of the human or angelic nature, abandoning its Creator and flowing downward toward itself or even toward the lowest creature. This is the origin of every evil will, every perverse desire, and every evil work.

Although God is not the cause of our evil wills, nor is any subsisting nature their cause, but rather the disposition of a rational creature declining from love of its Creator, he is nevertheless the judge and avenger of our thoughts and the eternal predestiner of just vengeance and judgment. This is what the man attempts to nullify through such lengthy circumlocutions and arguments.

As for his constant insistence that the will itself is nature, we have already pointed out above that he took the occasion for this error from the words of Saint Augustine. Augustine treats of the will of the human mind by which it loves itself—a will that is always good because it loves its own nature and cannot be otherwise or otherwise directed. This man, however, contentiously transfers Augustine’s discussion to the will at issue when free choice is being treated. For, as we have said, one and the same will of the mind is one thing when it naturally loves itself and another when, assisted by grace, it loves God, or, corrupted by its own fault, loves the world. It is one will and another not in nature but in the diversity of its disposition. Therefore it can be good or evil according to what it loves, whether rightly or wrongly.

## CHAPTER VI

In the sixth chapter he defines the following:

1. No sin and no punishment for sin arises from anywhere except from the human being’s own will, which misuses free choice for evil.

2. It is utterly foolish to doubt that the human will is according to nature.

3. Nor can it be doubted that it is the rational substance itself.

It is not sufficiently apparent why he has set out these three definitions or what he wished to establish from them, unless perhaps his principal intention in all these arguments is either to defend free choice according to nature—which is plainly Pelagian—or to destroy, insofar as he can, the predestination of God’s just judgment—which is Ciceronian. For Cicero, as blessed Augustine recalls in the books *On the City of God* (book V, chapter 9), and demonstrates from Cicero’s own words, attempted to nullify the ordering of divine providence so completely that he denied not only predestination but even God’s foreknowledge altogether, wishing by this sort of reasoning to defend human free choice. Thus, while he wished to make his hearers free, he made them sacrilegious: they would consider themselves so absolved by the freedom of their own choice that they were in no way subject to the providential dispensation or predestination of God, denying to God what belongs supremely and properly to God—that is, foreknowledge of all future things and the predestination of his arrangements. What is this other than saying that God is not God? For how is he truly God if he has no foreknowledge of future things?

There is now great reason to fear and guard against the possibility that, through arguments and disputes of this kind, while accepting God’s predestination in one respect and denying it in another, and wishing, as it were, to make human beings free, we may make them sacrilegious. For this too belongs to our faith: we must believe that God’s predestination, which is certainly just, is complete and perfect in both directions. Since denial of this is contrary to the faith, it is certainly sacrilegious. Therefore, since, as we have said, his chief intention is either to defend free choice according to nature or to deny in part the predestination of God’s justice, he may have set out these three arguments as a defense of free choice.

When he says, then, “No sin and no punishment for sin arises from anywhere except from the human being’s own will, which misuses free choice for evil,” this is indeed true, because sin was committed by the human being’s own will, and the punishment of sin—that is, death, misery, and punishment—followed as the due consequence of sin. Yet there is a very great difference between sin and the punishment of sin: the human being alone committed the sin, but he both deserved the punishment of sin and God inflicted it by judging justly. Therefore, by this argument the man does not at all establish or demonstrate what he wishes—namely, that no punishment of sin, no misery, and no punishment inflicted upon sinners comes from God—and therefore that the eternal punishments of the wicked could not have been predestined by God, because punishment, like sin, does not come from him.

Yet, as we have already shown above, Scripture cries out most clearly against this error: “Good and evil, life and death, poverty and honor are from the Lord” (Ecclesiasticus XI, 14). This does not refer to the evils that human beings commit by sinning and acting wickedly, of which God is in no way the author, but to those evils that, because of sins, are inflicted upon human beings by God’s just judgment—such as famine, slaughter, hostilities, devastations, and other hardships and disasters. Concerning these the prophet Amos says: “Shall there be evil in a city which the Lord has not done?” (Amos III, 6). The Lord himself says through the prophet Isaiah: “I am the Lord, making peace and creating evil” (Isaiah XLV, 7). Hence he threatens certain people with such evils, saying: “I will bring evils upon them in the year of their visitation” (Jeremiah XI, 23). And again: “I will gather evils upon them and exhaust my arrows against them” (Deuteronomy XXXII, 23).

God is said to create all these things, not by creating some nature, but by determining, establishing, and inflicting them through his just judgment. How we ought rightly to distinguish and understand, according to this meaning, the statement that “God did not make death” (Wisdom I, 13), and yet that “death is from God” (Ecclesiasticus XI, 14), blessed Augustine explains and demonstrates most clearly when he says:

> “It is God’s just judgment that each person should perish through his own sin, since God did not make sin, just as he did not make death. Yet the one whom he judges worthy of death, he kills. Hence it is written: ‘God did not make death’; and it is written: ‘Death and life are from God.’ Anyone who distinguishes divine judgments from divine works plainly sees that these two statements are not contradictory. For it is one thing not to have established mortality by creating, and another to punish the sinner by judging.”

But this man adds and says: “It is utterly foolish to doubt that the human will is according to nature.” It is indeed true that the will of the rational soul is according to nature and exists within the nature of that rational soul. But, as has often been said already, this same natural will must be understood in one way when it wills and loves itself and is referred to itself—a will that no one doubts is always naturally good—and in another way when it either devoutly loves the Lord or perversely loves the world and is referred to those things that it loves either above itself or beneath itself. Therefore such a will, when it is not referred to its own mind as it naturally inheres in it, but to one thing or another outside its substance, can be good or evil—not by nature but by disposition: either by rightly loving higher things, through which it is blessed, or by perversely desiring lower things, through which it is corrupted. In this matter it is no longer nature alone, but either a virtue or a vice of nature: a virtue from the infusion of divine grace, a vice from the corruption of one’s own will.

This is the free choice of the human mind, when the human disposition is inclined to desire one thing or another. That disposition is not outside nature, because it moves by spontaneous will in either direction; yet it does not belong to nature alone. To be moved toward good, it is aroused and directed by divine grace; to be moved toward evil, it is corrupted by its own desire. We have thought it necessary to demonstrate this point briefly and carefully, insofar as we were able, so that it might be knowingly distinguished and understood how absurdly and deceitfully this man attempts everywhere to assert merely natural freedom of choice, on account, that is, of that will of the human mind by which it naturally loves itself.

He does not notice—or certainly conceals—that this sort of will has nothing to do with the discussion of free choice, but that the issue is the will which, in another manner and with another disposition, is moved either to love good things or to seek evil things, either assisted by divine grace or corrupted by its own fault. Accordingly, it is clear that his contentious and obstinate purpose, by which he attempts to defend free choice as natural, is plainly empty and ineffective. For although free choice consists in human nature and in the will of the human mind, and human beings naturally have the ability to will good, to live rightly, and to be blessed, nevertheless, that they should will the good, live rightly, and become blessed is not from their own power but solely from the generosity of divine grace.

But because this man wishes to constrain us by such an argument either to deny God’s predestination in part or, by affirming that predestination perfectly, to appear to abolish free choice—as Cicero too argued, attacking and denying divine foreknowledge, claiming that if God’s foreknowledge truly existed, free choice could not exist among human beings, or that if free choice existed among human beings, God’s foreknowledge did not exist—therefore that most impious and detestable blasphemer of God chose to defend human free choice and to deny God’s foreknowledge in every respect. Anyone who carefully considers the matter can easily understand how largely this man appears to follow and imitate Cicero in his discussion. For whoever denies God’s foreknowledge also denies God’s predestination, which cannot exist without foreknowledge.

So that we may understand more clearly and plainly how both things are entirely true—namely, both divine predestination and human free choice—and how neither is at all destroyed by the other, we consider it wholly necessary and salutary to add here the very words of Saint Augustine, in which he defends both against Cicero’s impious argument and teaches most pleasingly that both must be held (*On the City of God*, book V, chapter 9):

> “He constrains the religious mind within such narrow limits that it must choose one of two alternatives: either that something lies within our will, or that there is no foreknowledge of future things. For he considers that both cannot exist; rather, if one is confirmed, the other is removed. If we choose foreknowledge of future things, the freedom of the will is removed; if we choose the freedom of the will, foreknowledge of future things is removed. He himself therefore chose, from the two, free choice of the will; and, in order to confirm it, he denied foreknowledge of future things. Thus, while he wished to make people free, he made them sacrilegious. But the religious mind chooses both, confesses both, and confirms both by the faith of piety.”

Again, after some intervening material:

> “The Spirit of life, therefore, who gives life to all things, and the creator of every body and every created spirit, is God himself—the Spirit, of course, who was not created. In his will resides supreme power, by which he assists the good wills of created spirits, judges the evil, and orders them all; to some he grants powers, to others he does not grant them. For just as he is the creator of all natures, so he is the giver of all powers, but not of wills. Evil wills do not come from him, since they are contrary to nature, which does come from him.”

And after some further material:

> “God is the cause of things who makes but is not made; other causes both make and are made. How, then, can the order of causes that is certain to God, who foreknows it, mean that nothing lies within our will, when our wills occupy a great place within that very order of causes?”

Item, a little later:

> “But in denying,” he says, “that the order of all causes is most certain and fully known to God’s foreknowledge, we detest him more than we do the Stoics. For either he denies that God exists, or, if he confesses that God exists while denying that God foreknows the future, he is still saying nothing other than what that fool said in his heart: ‘There is no God’ (Psalm 13:1). For he who does not foreknow all future things is certainly not God. Therefore our wills have as much power as God willed and foreknew that they would have; and consequently, whatever power they have, they have most certainly. (Chapter 10) And what they are going to do, they themselves will most certainly do, because he foreknew that they would have the power and would do it.”

[Note: When he says that the will will do what God foreknew, he does not wish to impose necessity upon the will by foreknowledge—for that would be heretical—but only to say that it will infallibly do it and that it will undoubtedly occur, given that God foreknew it in this way, since his foreknowledge cannot be mistaken.]

> “For if that is to be called our necessity which is not in our power, but accomplishes what it can even against our will—as is the necessity of death—it is clear that our wills, by which we live rightly or wrongly, are not subject to such a necessity. For we do many things which, if we did not wish to do them, we certainly would not do; and first among these is willing itself. For if we will, it exists; if we do not will, it does not exist. We would not will if we did not wish to will.
>
> “But if necessity is defined as that according to which we say that something must be or must happen in a certain way, I do not know why we should fear that it takes away the freedom of our will. For neither do we place God’s life and God’s foreknowledge under necessity if we say that God must always live and foreknow all things. Nor is his power diminished when it is said that he cannot die or be deceived; indeed, he cannot do these things in such a way that, if he could do them, he would actually have less power. For he is rightly called Almighty, although he cannot die or be deceived. He is called almighty because he does what he wills, not because he suffers what he does not will. If that happened to him, he would in no way be almighty. Thus, it is precisely because he is almighty that he cannot do certain things.
>
> “Similarly, when we say that, whenever we will, we must will by free choice—and we are certainly speaking truthfully—we do not thereby subject free choice itself to the necessity that removes freedom. Our wills, therefore, themselves do whatever we do by willing, and this would not happen if we did not will it. It is not therefore the case that nothing is in our will because God foreknew what would be in our will; for he who foreknew this did not foreknow nothing. Moreover, if he who foreknew what would be in our will foreknew not nothing but something, then surely, with him foreknowing it, something is in our will.
>
> “Consequently, we are in no way compelled either to abolish free choice while retaining God’s foreknowledge, or, while retaining free choice, to deny God—an impious act—to be foreknowledgeable of future things. We embrace both; we faithfully and truthfully confess both: the one so that we may believe rightly, the other so that we may live rightly. But one lives badly if one does not believe rightly about God. Therefore, far be it from us to deny his foreknowledge, so that we may will freely, by whose assistance we are or shall be free.
>
> “Accordingly, rewards have justly been established for good deeds and punishments for sins. For a person does not sin because God foreknew that he would sin; rather, there is no doubt that he sins when he sins because he whose foreknowledge cannot be deceived foreknew that he himself would sin—not fate, not fortune, nor anything else. If he does not wish to sin, he certainly does not sin; but if he does not wish to sin, God also foreknew this.”]

The most blessed teacher set forth these matters with the greatest clarity for our instruction and confirmation, against the errors of human presumption and argumentation. Elsewhere, too, he speaks in this way about the same subject:

> “[God compels no one to sin, yet he foresees those who will sin by their own will. Why, then, should the just one not judge what he does not compel to happen, although he foreknows it? Just as no one, by his memory, compels past events to have happened, so God does not, by his foreknowledge, compel future events to happen. And just as a person remembers certain things that he has done, yet did not do everything that he remembers, so God foreknew all things of which he is himself the author; but of those things of which he is not the wicked author, he is the just avenger.”]

Again, concerning the immutable reason of mutable things in God, and concerning his eternal and universal predestination and foreknowledge, he says elsewhere:

> “[God’s anger is not a disturbance of his mind, but a judgment by which punishment is inflicted for sin. His thought and reconsideration concerning things that are to be changed are an immutable reason. For God does not repent of any deed of his, as a human being does; rather, his decision concerning absolutely all things is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain.”]

# CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0145A]

In the seventh chapter he sets forth the following definition.

## 1. Free choice is to be counted among God’s intermediate gifts; therefore it could sin.

Here it must be said briefly, and a distinction must be made: although this man says that free choice is a gift of God, he asserts that it is merely natural, in the manner of the Pelagians. The faith of the Church, however, makes a significant distinction between the gifts of nature and the gifts of grace.

What Almighty God gave human beings naturally was a rational and intellectual mind, and within that mind memory, understanding, and will. What he also gave naturally to the human body was substance, form, appearance, soundness, and the senses of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching, while the soul gives it life and sensation. These are plainly gifts and endowments of nature, which God implanted in human beings at the first creation and gave naturally in creating them.

But what God gives human beings by his grace—faith, hope, charity, piety, a good will, the capacity for good works, and other gifts of this kind—are gifts of his grace, gifts of the Holy Spirit, concerning which the Apostle says: “But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing them to each one as he wills” (1 Corinthians 11:12).

He also explains that the following was said in the Psalm: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings” (Ephesians 4:8; Psalm 67:19). For this reason the Catholic faith, the true faith, also counts free choice itself among the gifts of grace.

For although God implanted it naturally in human beings when he created them good and endowed them with a good will, even then they needed the grace of the Creator in order to remain in the good in which they had been created. Having lost its freedom through the first sin, and having been weakened, corrupted, and as though crushed by a certain ruin on account of that sin, free choice is entirely unable to rise to that eternal and supreme good for which human beings were created unless it is healed, restored, illuminated, and liberated by God’s grace. Nor can it become free in any other way unless it is made free by God’s grace, through him who says: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36), so that what the Apostle says may be fulfilled in us: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:17).

Therefore, as we have said, it is an insane and Pelagian error if anyone thinks that free choice—which was lost in Adam through sin, with both the gift of nature and the gift of grace lost—can be free in any other way than by being liberated through the grace of Christ.

[Note: Erigena is censured for counting free choice among God’s intermediate gifts, namely, between nature and grace; for in this way he prepares the way for Pelagianism. If freedom is some intermediate gift above nature, it follows that the aids of grace are not necessary for rising from sin or for acting piously. But if by free choice Erigena understands free actions, he can be excused to some extent, since these are said by St. Thomas (First Part, question 57, article 4) to occupy an intermediate rank between natural and supernatural things; hence he says that they cannot be known naturally by angels.]

[Note: Throughout this discussion, “free choice” is understood either as actual conversion to the good or as freedom from the slavery of sin; and thus it is everywhere taught to be good and upright, raised by a good will toward heavenly and divine things. It is therefore unsurprising if he asserts it to be solely a gift of grace and to have perished utterly in Adam. Yet if it is taken as a capacity, or with respect to civil and human actions, it ought to be called a gift of nature.]

But what this man says—that free choice is a good and upright thing, raised by a good will toward heavenly and divine things, such as it was created in the first human being, so that it was without any sin and could refrain from sinning if it wished—and that such a good, so great a good, is to be counted not among God’s supreme gifts but among his intermediate gifts, differs greatly from the truth.

For, as we have said, the good of free choice in that first human being was so great and of such a kind as is found in none of the saints in the present life. Although they possess free choice, already liberated and healed by the grace of Christ, their healing is nevertheless such that, as long as they live mortal lives, they cannot be without sin. Even though they strongly wish and desire not to sin, they still cannot refrain from sinning.

[Note: When he says that even the best people in the state of fallen nature cannot avoid sinning, this must be understood collectively, not distributively—that is, even if there is no individual sin that they are unable to avoid, nevertheless, because they lack a very special grace and because of the corruption of nature resulting from sin, they cannot avoid falling into some sin. Thus teaches St. Thomas, First Part of the Second Part, question 109, article 8.]

Hence they daily need to plead and truthfully say to the heavenly Father: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

According to the manner in which human beings then lived in paradise—free from sin and possessing in their own will the freedom not to sin, so long as they piously submitted themselves to God to be ruled and assisted—free choice was therefore not an intermediate but a supreme gift. It could nevertheless still have been perfected into something better if the human being had remained obedient to God, so as to receive such great strength that he could no longer sin.

But the fact that such free choice could sin in that first human being was caused by abandoning God and presuming upon oneself. While neglecting to remain under God and wishing to be under his own power, he lost the gift of divine grace, lost the good of nature, and found himself under the condemnation of misery.

# CHAPTER VIII

In the eighth chapter he sets forth these definitions.

1. The substantial trinity of the inner human being consists in essence, will, and knowledge.

2. For him, being is not one thing and willing another, nor willing one thing and knowing another; rather, these three constitute one nature, and the whole nature of the soul is will.

3. Free will is the nature of the human being, together with its free movement and its power of moving; this is free choice, the gift of the Creator.

4. Just as an animal body could die because it was not yet perfected—that is, spiritual—so free will, still animal in its condition and therefore mortal, could sin because it was not yet perfected. This perfection of freedom would certainly have been fulfilled after the commandment had been kept, when the will to sin would have been entirely removed from it.

5. This movement was granted to no animal except the human being.

6. There is such a distinction between human free choice and his substance that nature is in rational will, whereas free choice is in its freedom—whether in the naturally free movement of the will or in the gift of understanding.

7. These three things—freedom, movement, and understanding—constitute free choice among themselves. Thus, just as the substance in which it exists is threefold—for it exists, wills, and knows—so that other reality also becomes threefold: free, moving, and understanding.

What he says, therefore, namely, that the substantial trinity of the inner human being consists in essence, will, and knowledge, he took partly from the discussions of St. Augustine in his books On the Trinity and partly devised on his own.

For blessed Augustine, discussing the holy and supreme Trinity (Book IX, chapter 2, and Book XV, chapter 7), and the human mind in which the human being was created in the image and likeness of God, drawing its likeness toward God so that through that image of the Trinity which exists in the human mind he might raise us, to some extent, to contemplate the Trinity who is God, says the following:

These three things—being, knowing, and willing—are found in the human mind in such a way that they are three distinctly, yet are one in substance. The mind naturally exists, naturally knows itself, and naturally wills itself—that is, loves itself—and at that point its knowledge and will are referred to nothing other than itself.

Although these three are then understood distinctly as existing in the mind—namely, being, knowing itself, and willing itself—yet being itself is by nature the essence of the mind, and it naturally knows itself and naturally wills itself. It exists as a whole; and just as it exists as a whole, so it knows itself as a whole, wills and loves itself as a whole. Therefore, whatever its essence is, such also are its knowledge and its will.

By this comparison the blessed teacher urges us to rise from the likeness of our mind to contemplate the true Trinity who is God. Just as these three—being, knowing oneself, and willing oneself—are found in the human mind in such a way that each is properly distinguished, yet they are substantially and naturally one, and just as the mind’s knowledge and love of itself are as great as the mind itself, because it knows and loves itself wholly, so by this image and likeness of God we should raise our understanding to the Trinity of the Lord itself.

We should recognize in that blessed and supreme Trinity three things that are distinct and proper—namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—yet these three are essentially and naturally one and are equal, so that the Father is recognized as being as great as the Son and as great as the Holy Spirit. Thus, as though through a mirror and in an enigma of our mind, we learn to understand the holy Trinity: distinct in persons, united in substance, and equal in nature and power.]

But after reading these statements, which were spoken so usefully and beneficially for the illumination of our faith, this man was not content with the restraint and piety of the holy teacher, lest he exceed the boundaries established by him. Instead, he added on his own that these three things contemplated in the human mind constitute a substantial Trinity.

A substantial or substantive Trinity—that is, one that exists substantially in persons—can be found nowhere except in the one God. Hence the same teacher carefully warns against error in these matters and teaches in the same books that these three are not the human being, but belong to the human being or exist in the human being.

By contrast, in the holy Trinity, those three things that are distinctly recognized there neither should nor can be said to exist in one God as though they were something belonging to God; rather, they truly are the one God. For we do not say that the Trinity is in God, but that the Trinity itself is God. Thus the holy teacher himself says (On the Trinity, Book XV, chapter 6):

> “[In the human being we find a trinity: the mind, the knowledge by which it knows itself, and the love by which it loves itself. But these three are in the human being in such a way that they are not themselves the human being. For the human being is, as the ancients also defined, a mortal rational animal. Those things, therefore, excel in the human being; they are not themselves the human being, who is one person—that is, each individual human being.
>
> “The human being has those three in the mind, or has a mind; and therefore those three are not the human being, but are the human being’s or are in the human being. Even if the body is removed and the soul alone is considered as thinking something, its mind is like its head, eye, or face—but these are not to be conceived as bodies. It is therefore not the soul, but what excels in the soul, that is called the mind. Can we, however, say that the Trinity is in God in such a way that it is something belonging to God and is not itself God?”]

But after wrongly saying that the substantial Trinity is contained in the essence, will, and knowledge of the mind, this man adds something even worse, saying of the human mind itself: “For him, being is not one thing and willing another, nor willing one thing and knowing another; rather, these three constitute one nature, and the whole nature of the soul is will.”

By contrast, faith holds most firmly that no creature—neither angelic nor human—is of such a simple nature or essence that its being is the same as its understanding, since it can exist without understanding. Nor is its being the same as its willing, since it can exist without willing. Nor is its being the same as its knowing, since it can exist without knowing. Nor is its being the same as its loving, since it can exist without loving.

Only the divine nature possesses that supreme and ineffable simplicity, such that whatever it truly is said to be, that is what its being is. For example, its being is the same as its understanding, because in it essence is not one thing and understanding another; rather, what is essence is understanding, and what is understanding is essence.

Similarly, its being and its being wise are not different, because in it essence is not one thing and wisdom another; rather, what is essence is wisdom, and what is wisdom is essence. Concerning this the same blessed teacher speaks as follows:

[Col. 0149A]

> “[If it is asked how that substance can be both multiple and simple, we must first observe why the creature is multiple, whereas it is in no way truly simple.”

And a little later:

> “[The soul also, he says, has one quality when it is skillful, another when it is untrained; one when it is keen, another when it is forgetful; one thing is desire, another fear; one thing joy, another sadness. Since these can exist separately from one another, and since some things can be greater and others lesser, innumerable features, and features innumerable in number, can be found in the nature of the soul. It is therefore plainly not a simple but a multiple nature, for nothing simple is mutable. Every creature, however, is mutable.
>
> “God, on the other hand, is spoken of in many ways: great, good, wise, blessed, true, and whatever else seems not unworthy to be said of him. Yet his greatness is the same as his wisdom. For he is great not by bulk but by power. His goodness is the same as his wisdom and greatness; and his truth is the same as all of these. In him being blessed is not one thing and being great, wise, true, or good another, nor is being itself something different. Nor, because he is a Trinity, should he therefore be thought to be threefold. Otherwise the Father alone, or the Son alone, would be less than the Father and the Son together.”]

Again, when he was speaking of the Son alone, he said of him:

> “[There is the first and supreme life, for which living is not one thing and being another, but being and living are the same; and there is the first and supreme intellect, for which living is not one thing and understanding another, but what it is to understand is the same as living and being. All things are one in it, like a perfect Word lacking nothing, a certain art of the almighty and wise God, full of all the reasons of living and immutable things. And all things are one in it, just as it itself is one from the One with whom it is one.”]

Since these things are so, how did this man dare to say of the creature that is the human mind: “For him, being is not one thing and willing another, nor willing one thing and knowing another, but these three constitute one nature, and the whole nature of the soul is will”?

By contrast, the holy teacher whom he appears to follow—and whose caution and moderation he presumes, with excessive shamelessness, to exceed through his own levity and vanity—shows that there is such a great distance among the three things found in the human mind as a certain likeness of the Trinity, namely, being, knowing, and loving, that he says of them as follows (On the Trinity, Book X, chapters 11–12):

> “[Whether we speak of the mind in the human being, together with its knowledge and love, or of memory, understanding, and will, we remember nothing of the mind except through memory, understand nothing except through understanding, and love nothing except through will.”]

Behold, according to the truth taught by the holy man, how great is the distance and difference within the human mind itself among these three things that naturally belong to it and are in it: namely, between memory of itself, understanding of itself, and love of itself. It remembers itself through memory alone, understands itself through understanding alone, and loves itself through love alone.

Memory can therefore do one thing, understanding another, and love another. What memory can do, understanding cannot do; nor can memory do what understanding can do. Nor can the will do what memory and understanding can do. And if the essence of the mind is considered distinctly, whatever it can do substantially in these three cannot be done without them.

This man, however, says the opposite: that for the mind being is not one thing and willing another, nor willing one thing and knowing another. If this is accepted, what else is asserted by such a novel and unheard-of presumption than that, just as God is of a simple nature, so the human mind too should be believed to be of a simple nature?

For if what being is for the human mind is the same as willing, then plainly essence is not one thing and will another; rather, essence itself is will, and will itself is essence. Likewise, if willing is not one thing for the human mind and knowing another, then will is not one thing and essence another; rather, will itself is knowledge, and knowledge itself is will.

From this incredible reasoning it follows that, as this man also says, just as the mind is wholly essence, so it is wholly will and wholly knowledge. And just as it is most truly believed of God—and can truly be said of him alone—that what he has, he is: he has justice, but he himself is justice; he has wisdom, but he himself is wisdom; he has goodness, but he himself is goodness—so, I say, it follows that the same should be said of the human mind: what it has, it is. It has will, but it itself is will; it has knowledge, but it itself is knowledge, so that, as we believe of God, being and having are not different for it.

[Note: Jerome remembers this error in his letter to Marcellinus and Anapsychia, and Augustine in Letter 28 to the same Jerome. Philosophers and Gnostics fell into it, according to Augustine, On Heresies, 6; Cerdon, according to Theodoret, Book II of Heretical Fables; and the Manichaeans, according to Augustine, Against Fortunatus. Priscillian also held it, according to the First Council of Braga, canon 5. All these groups posited no other soul in the human being than the soul of the whole world, or at least a part of it; consequently, they were compelled to acknowledge that the human soul is God or a part of God. They are refuted by Augustine and Jerome in the passages cited, and likewise by St. Thomas, First Part, question 9, article 1.]

Thus, according to this author—or rather, deceiver—against the whole truth of faith, against the authority of Holy Scripture, against the integrity of the teachings of the Fathers, and indeed against every divine and human reason, a creature has been invented, namely the human mind, which is of a simple nature and therefore immutable, just as God is of a simple and immutable nature.

By contrast, truth cries out, and St. Augustine himself, as we showed above, plainly affirms that every creature is multiple and in no way truly simple. He also says again: “Nothing mutable is simple, whereas every creature is mutable.”

Let this man therefore choose one of two alternatives. If the nature of the mind is simple, as he attempts to assert, then it is not mutable, because, as the teacher says—and says most truly—nothing mutable is simple. But if the nature of the mind is mutable, as every creature is truly mutable, then it is not simple.

Far be it, then, that blessed Augustine, who affirms that every creature is mutable and multiple and in no way simple, should have thought or written such things about the nature of the human mind as to assert that it is not merely like God but equal to God, if he had said that it was of an immutable and simple nature!

Let anyone who wishes and is able read with the greatest diligence and examine with the greatest attention what he says about this matter in his books On the Trinity. He will find that he said that the three things found in the human mind, which have often been mentioned, are one because of the unity of the substance of the mind in which they exist; that they are one mind and one substance.

He will find him saying that these things are substantially present in the mind, and that the mind is a substance, its knowledge of itself a substance, and its will concerning itself a substance. He will also find him saying that the mind knows itself wholly and wills or loves itself wholly.

Yet nowhere there will he find him saying that the mind itself is knowledge or that the mind itself is will, since it has already been shown above from his own words that knowledge, by which the mind alone knows itself, is one thing, and will, by which the mind alone loves itself, another.

Why, then, when the mind knows itself wholly, did he not say that the mind itself is knowledge? And when it wills itself wholly, why did he not say that the mind itself is will? It is because the mind itself is a creature and is not simple; being is one thing for it, knowing another, and willing another.

But if someone—or this man who said it—should object: how, then, are these three one, one mind, and one substance, if one thing is there and another? Let him recognize that these three can be called substantially one because they are one and are in one substance. Yet they are potentially distinct, because, as the teacher himself shows, memory can do one thing in the mind, understanding another, and will another.

By contrast, in the divine Trinity we can say “one person, another person, and another person”; but we cannot in any way say “one thing, another thing, and another thing,” because of the unity of the supreme simple nature. Supreme simplicity is therefore found where “one thing and another” can never be found.

There is an ancient disputant who, while discussing the incorporeal nature of the soul, is reported to have said among other things:

> “And when the soul wills, if it wills as a whole, it is wholly will.”

Here he asserted carefully and cautiously that the soul can sometimes, in a certain respect, be called wholly will when it wills as a whole, since it plainly wills not outside itself but within itself and in relation to itself. He did not therefore define it absolutely as being will, but stated the matter conditionally and cautiously: “If it wills as a whole, it is wholly will.”

From this it must unquestionably be understood—or rather, each person must naturally recognize it in himself—that if it does not will as a whole, it is not wholly will. For one and the same thing can be willed in part and not willed in part; indeed, something that the whole soul wills can be entirely unwilled by it.

Therefore, in view of the mutable and variable movement of the will, the nature of the soul should not be said absolutely and definitively to be wholly will. For plainly it is not so—not when it wills in part, nor when it entirely ceases to will what it had willed—although it always naturally possesses the capacity to will within itself. Its nature and substance remain, while its willing, according to what it seeks or rejects, either remains the same, changes, or perishes.

Let this man therefore cease saying that the whole nature of the soul is will, that is, that the soul itself is will. For it is not of a simple nature, as God is, so that what being is for it should be the same as willing, nor is being one thing for it and having a will another.

Since these matters are so, let such an impious and profane invention be driven away from the ears of the faithful. Let those who admire and willingly listen to such a teacher remember that they are Christians. Let them remember that they must preserve within themselves the Catholic faith, the true faith concerning God, whole and inviolate.
