Let them remember that the deposit of the teaching of the Fathers must be guarded with the greatest fidelity, and that impious presumptions of speech must be avoided with every intention of piety.

The Apostle strongly commends this when he says:

> “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words and the oppositions of falsely named knowledge, which some professing have fallen away from the faith—or suffered shipwreck concerning the faith” (1 Timothy 6:20–21).

Let us learn not to have itching ears—that is, ears greedy for and desirous of empty and childish tales. Concerning this evil the Apostle says:

> “For there will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears. They will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth, but they will turn toward fables” (2 Timothy 4:3–4).

What remains, then, for those who say or accept such things—namely, that the human mind is made equal to God, so that, like God, it too is of a simple nature—except that, like the worst ancient heretics, they blasphemously declare God and the soul to be of the same nature?

After this, the man says:

> “Free will is the nature of the human being, together with its free movement and its power of moving; this is free choice, the gift of the Creator.”

But we, as we have already said, and as the truth of the matter plainly demonstrates, do not say that the human being is will, but that will belongs to the human being. For being is one thing for him and willing another; therefore the human being is not will, but will belongs to the human being.

This man nevertheless shows that, through the Pelagian error, he understands free choice to belong to human nature alone and to be a gift of nature rather than a gift of grace. He calls it “the free movement of the human will and the power of moving.” In this he plainly shows that he believes the human will not only to possess a naturally free movement by which it is moved toward desiring good or evil, but also a free power by which it accomplishes good or evil.

By contrast, against all such errors, the Catholic faith holds that, although free choice was naturally upright and sound in the human being before sin, it was nevertheless perverted on account of sin—or rather, lost—and now has neither movement, that is, desire, toward a good will, nor the power to fulfill that good will, except through hidden grace, given and inspired by him of whom the Apostle most truly says:

> “For it is God who works in us both the willing and the accomplishing, according to his good will” (Philippians 2:13).

As we have already said, the human being has naturally received from the Creator the capacity to will and even the capacity to be able to do what is good. But to will this and to be able to do this does not come from himself; it comes only from him who works in the hearts of the faithful both the willing and the accomplishing, according to his good will.

Hence comes that ecclesiastical and most faithful definition which blessed Pope Celestine sets forth in his Decrees, saying (Celestine, Letter to the Gallican Bishops, chapter 8, §19):

> “[God works in the hearts of human beings and in free choice itself in such a way that holy thought, pious counsel, and every movement of a good will come from God, because through him we are able to do some good, without whom we are able to do nothing.”]

And again:

> “[All the endeavors, all the works, and all the merits of the saints must be referred to the glory and praise of God, because no one pleases him from any other source than that which he himself has given.”]

From this apostolic and ecclesiastical definition it is most certainly demonstrated that free choice in a human being can do nothing toward desiring or accomplishing the good unless it has been liberated by the grace of Christ.

It is nevertheless free for evil, because when it sins it is not compelled by any necessity but is corrupted by its own will.

He then adds and says: “Just as an animal body could die because it was not yet perfect—that is, spiritual—so the will, still free by reason of its animal condition, because it was mortal, could sin, since it was not yet perfect. That perfection of freedom would indeed have been attained after the commandment had been kept, when the will to sin would have been taken away from it.” What else, then, should be said about an animal and a spiritual body than what the Apostle teaches when he says: “If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual one,” just as it is written: “The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit” (I Cor. XV, 44–45). And above, when he was speaking about the resurrection of the dead, he said: “It is sown an animal body; it shall rise a spiritual body” (ibid., 44).

How, then, are an animal body and a spiritual body to be distinguished in these words, except that an animal body is vivified through the soul alone, mortally and corruptibly? Such was Adam’s body even before sin, because although it had not yet been destined for death and corruption, it could nevertheless be corrupted and die on account of sin. Thus, indeed, it happened in him and happens in all his offspring, by the just judgment and punishment of the one who said: “Until you return to the earth from which you were taken, because you are dust and to dust you shall return.” A spiritual body, however, is so called not because it ceases to be a body and becomes spirit—for although spiritual, it is nevertheless truly called a body by the Apostle—but because the body will then be spiritual when it is vivified by the spirit immortally and incorruptibly. Such a body the last Adam, that is, the Lord Jesus Christ, displayed in himself at the resurrection, through which he transferred the mortal body he had assumed into immortality and incorruption; and by that same grace of incorruption he will display it in his saints on the last day.

Then also, according to the same Apostle, “this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality,” so that “what is mortal may be swallowed up by life”; and, as he himself says, the saying that is written may be fulfilled: “Death is swallowed up in victory” (ibid., 53–54). Thus the body that is now sown as an animal body in death will then rise as a spiritual body (ibid., 44), needing no nourishment to sustain it, subject to no disturbance to corrupt it, dissolvable by no death, but vivified by the spirit alone with eternal immortality. Such, too, would Adam’s future body have been, without death intervening, had God rewarded his obedience and he had not sinned.

It is therefore true that Adam’s body was still animal and had not yet been changed into the immortality that was to be given him if he had remained obedient to God in piety: thus, if he had not sinned, he could have avoided death, and if he had sinned, he could have died. It is clear that he could die for this reason: he had not yet been endowed with immortality.

But as for the will in that man—whether it was still animal, that is, living and understanding according to the appetite of the human soul and not according to the spirit of God, so that it was not yet in the inner man, that is, in the spirit of his spiritual mind, but was still animal, sensing animalishly and not spiritually—the Apostle does not demonstrate this in such a way. He says that the great mystery that was to come in Christ and in the Church had been prophesied by that very man, when, filled with the divine Spirit, he said: “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” [Col. 0154C] (Eph. V, 31). Explaining these words, the Apostle added: “This is a great mystery; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (ibid., 32).

How, then, was his will not spiritual for living rightly—a will assisted and enlightened by the spirit—which had also been elevated by prophetic grace? Yet even a spiritual will could sin when it fell into a worse condition. The same Apostle shows that spiritual persons too can be tempted—that is, overcome by some temptation to sin—when he says: “Brothers, if a man is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. VI, 1).

Thus that man’s will, although spiritual, could be tempted and could be overcome by temptation. If, by obeying, he had reached that fullness of blessedness where he could no longer sin, the will to sin would not have been taken away from him, as this man says—for there was no such will in him to be removed—but the good will that was in him would have been perfected by such great happiness that it could not be changed into evil.

For three states of the human will can properly be understood. The first man was created with such a good will that, if he wished, he could avoid sinning. Now, however, even holy people, because they are born from that corrupted propagation, cannot avoid sinning even if they wish to. Therefore they truly say to God each day: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. VI, 12). But in that blessedness which is to be given them, they will be established by such strength that they can no longer sin [Col. 0155A], just as they will be clothed with such a grace of incorruption that they can never die.

It is astonishing why this man wished to add and say: “This movement, that is, of free choice, has been granted to no animal except man.” Yet it is manifest that wherever there is no rational nature, as among all brute and irrational animals, there can be no rational will for desiring good or evil; rather, they are led in everything they do solely by natural, brutish, and senseless appetite. Hence whatever they do, insofar as it concerns them, can be called neither good nor evil, neither vices nor virtues.

Unless perhaps he compared the movement of human free choice with the appetite of brute animals for this reason: just as that irrational appetite is driven solely by the impulse of nature, so this movement of human free choice is led by the mere instinct of its nature toward whatever it chooses. How contrary this is to the truth has already been demonstrated above repeatedly.

This disputant went so far in presuming to abuse the understanding and ears of his audience that he dared, like some fabricator and potter of lies, to mold a new definition of free choice, as though it were something earthen and muddy, and to set it before the eyes of those looking upon it as though it were something great. For afterward he added and said:

“Let there therefore be such a difference between the free choice of man and his substance that his nature consists in rational will, while free choice consists in his freedom, or in the movement of a naturally free will, or in the gift of understanding.”

[Note: [Col. 0155D] Erigena should not be accused in this matter, since distinguished theologians have placed freedom in will and reason.—Durand, in II, dist. 24, where he teaches that the faculty belongs to will and reason, though more properly to reason.]

Behold what kind of free choice he teaches: plainly Pelagian, not Christian! Its nature, namely, is rational will, while its effect consists in the freedom of its natural [Note: [Col. 0155D] These words are to be understood according to ordinary power. Thus God, as punishment for the sin of the damned, has determined that he will no longer cooperate with them through special assistance. Through extraordinary assistance, however, it is certain that they have not been deprived of this; for it is not incompatible with God’s power that he could provide them with sufficient and effective aids by which they would infallibly be liberated from damnation and sin. Thus teaches St. Thomas, as do the other doctors. In the same sense what follows must likewise be explained, namely, that the demons and all the damned together lost through sin the ability to will the good. Although this may seem to extend to all sinners who still survive in this life, their situation differs from that of the damned, because God still wills to cooperate with the former and assist them with sufficient aids.] will; and from, or in, natural will alone it possesses freedom, movement, and the gift of understanding.

We, however, according to the truth of the faith, recognize free choice in man as follows: although it has been naturally implanted by God in the rational mind, and was bestowed as good and upright in the first creation, nevertheless, having been corrupted through the guilt of sin and stripped of its natural strength, it can have no freedom toward the true good, no movement of good will, and no light of understanding unless it has been restored by the grace of him who said: “If the Son makes you free, then you shall be truly free” (John VIII, 36); and who, by his inspiration, moves the hearts of those whom he wills toward faith, as the prophet says: “And I will move all nations, and the Desired One of all nations shall come” (Hag. II, 8). To him we appeal daily, saying: “Give me understanding, and I shall learn your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII, 73). And again: “Give me understanding, and I shall live” (ibid., 144). Giving thanks to the giver of this understanding, we also say: “I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding” (Ps. XV, 7).

This, then, is truly free choice: not, as this defender of Pelagian error asserts, a gift of nature, but a gift of grace; and free because liberated by the grace of Christ.

After naming those three things—freedom of choice, movement, and understanding—which he asserts consist wholly in the power of nature, this man proceeds to produce, from the free choice he himself fabricates, something like a new image composed of three parts or members, and says:

“These three things—namely, the free, movement, and understanding—compose free choice among themselves. Thus, just as the substance in which it exists is threefold—for it is, wills, and knows—so that too becomes threefold, namely, free, moving, and understanding.”

He says all this so that he may contend that free choice consists in these things alone—that is, in nature itself and in what belongs to nature itself. Just as three things naturally belong to the human mind—being, willing, and knowing—so, when the two latter, will and knowledge, are understood as belonging only to themselves and not to another thing, free choice, proceeding from the mind itself and existing in it, likewise derives freedom, movement, and understanding from it alone and from nowhere else. Thus, by such a choice, man is naturally free, moving, and understanding.

He does not say that the human mind has those three things in itself, but that it is threefold in its simple nature. And in the same way, that free choice is threefold—who has ever heard such obstinate impiety of error? He labors to enclose and fortify free choice, as it were with certain boundaries, so that he confines it altogether within the power of human nature alone and entirely excludes God’s grace from it.

What, then, should be answered to one to whom so many answers have already been given above on this subject? Only this: if he wishes either to be or to appear Christian, let him cast away this insane and deadly error. The more subtly he seems to himself to follow and assert it, the more unhappily he is enclosed and blinded by the devil. Let him cast aside the false and deceitful arguments of human inventions and humbly submit himself entirely to the truth of Holy Scripture, to the authority of the Church Fathers, and to the simplicity of faith, lest, while entrusting his freedom to himself and alienating it from Christ, he deserve truly to be alienated from Christ.

“For cursed is the man who trusts in man, makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord” (Jer. XVII, 5). “But blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his confidence” (ibid., 7).

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0157B]

[Note: [Col. 0157D] Throughout that chapter he attacks Erigena for introducing a most pestilential error, which with unrestrained license loosens the reins on every vice and crime. In this most wretched age our sectarians introduce this error much more broadly, driving every obligation of the law from the necks of the faithful. This is the liberty of the flesh, not of the spirit; of the children of the devil, not of God; in a word, ἀταξία (*ataxia*, disorder), more wretched than any servitude.]

In the ninth chapter he sets forth these definitions:

1. Foreknowledge and predestination are transferred to God by analogy with temporal things.

2. All predestination is foreknowledge.

If, then, on the basis of the use of temporal things—which vary through the distinction of three times, namely past, present, and future—these terms belong more properly to temporal matters, where so many future things are awaited, since foreknowledge and predestination properly concern future things, then with God, just as nothing is past, so nothing is future, because in his eternal knowledge everything is eternally present. Therefore these two terms are applied to God more by transference than properly.

How, then, has this man so often defined foreknowledge and predestination above as existing not merely in God and belonging to God—which we too admit—but as being God’s very substance and essence? If he is so self-contradictory in his argument that he later destroys what he previously affirms, why is it necessary for us to demolish his vanity, when he so aptly demolishes himself? But if some rule of sophistical disputation, which he alone follows, is such that in secular wisdom what is affirmed in one place may lawfully be overturned in another, who does not see how contemptible and utterly rejectable it is, since there is no firmness of truth in it, but only such shameless, brazen, and wanton license of falsehood?

As for what he says—that all predestination is foreknowledge—it is partly true. For all predestination of future things takes place not without foreknowledge, through which those future things are foreknown. But if this was said because predestination does no more in or concerning future things than foreknowledge does, it is manifestly false. For by foreknowledge future things themselves are merely foreknown; by predestination they are also established, predetermined, and decreed. Therefore the predestination of the wicked to eternal punishment did not merely foreknow what they would suffer, but also established and predetermined it by a just and eternal judgment.

## CHAPTER X

In the tenth chapter he sets forth four definitions in this manner:

1. That God foreknows or predestines sins, or the death or punishments of human beings or angels, must be understood in the opposite sense.

2. Every evil is sin and its punishment; and these are nothing.

[Note: [Col. 0157D] In our own age Quintin and Copin, the Flemish *Sudores* (“Sweaters”), revived this heresy from the depths; for this reason Catholics called them Libertines—that is, because they said that sin was nothing except an empty and false opinion. They also said that those who kill, commit adultery, or steal ought not to be reproved; that Christ was nothing except something composed of the Spirit of God and opinion; and that angels, demons, and souls were nothing. Although Calvin claims to detest them and published pamphlets against them, it is nevertheless certain that they emerged from his school as from the Trojan horse.—Bellarmine, *On the Loss of Grace*, Book II, chapter 1.]

3. Sin and its consequences, established in death and misery, are nothing other than corruptions of integral and blessed life, so that each is opposed to its corresponding opposite: sin to integrity, death to life, misery to blessedness. Those things exist; these do not exist at all.

4. Every defect, privation, or sin of a perverse will, and its end—death and the misery of eternal punishments—are altogether nothing; and therefore they are neither foreknown nor predestined.

Behold to what this diabolical disputation has come: a man who wishes to appear Christian overturns and destroys, by pagan and diabolical arguments, insofar as he can, all faith in the divine foreknowledge and predestination by which God foreknew and predestined that the wicked would be condemned. He not only empties out God’s just judgment and his eternal and unchangeable decree concerning their condemnation, but also contends that sin and every punishment and condemnation consequent upon sin are nothing. Therefore, since they are nothing, they could neither be foreknown nor predestined by God.

Thus, wherever such things are read as having been foreknown and predestined in Holy Scripture or in the teachings of the Fathers, they must be understood in the opposite sense—that is, as meaning that God did not foreknow or predestine them at all. What else is this than openly to rave? For who among the faithful has ever presumed either to think or say that what the truth has said is not truth; that what the faith has taught is false; or that what all the faithful believe is nothing?

This man maintains that these things—sin, every punishment, misery, and calamity, whether temporal or eternal—are nothing because they do not possess in themselves an essence by which they exist or subsist, as we see the earth, waters, and fires possess a substance by which they exist or subsist, together with grass, trees, and everything of that kind. We also know and believe that human souls and the spirits of good or evil angels possess a substance by which they exist and subsist.

Therefore, with the audacity of diabolical presumption, he asserts that God could know, foreknow, and predestine only the substances of things; but that those things contrary and punitive to these substances, because they have no substance by which they exist, could in no way be foreknown or predestined by God—and consequently could not even be known.

Therefore he did not foreknow the sin of the first man, because sin has no substance by which it exists; nor did he foreknow the punishment of sin, namely death, misery, and everlasting punishment, because these likewise do not substantially exist in themselves. Where, then, is what the faith holds most firmly and immovably: that almighty God is truly foreknowing of all future things? Where is what he foretells through his prophets in the Holy Scriptures—that so many sins of human beings, so many punishments, disasters, and miseries of sinners are to come?

Where also is what the only-begotten Son of God himself, who is eternal Truth, foreknows and foretells concerning so many persecutions of his Church, so many upheavals of wars, so many pressures of labors and terrors, earthquakes and pestilences, and famines, and urges his own to endure with the utmost patience?

Why has this impious man dared to utter such an obvious lie—or rather, such unheard-of and impious blasphemy—while opposing with sacrilegious mouth and impious words the faith of the whole holy Church, the truth of the heavenly Scriptures, and the majesty of almighty God?

What else is he doing than imitating and assisting the devil’s plan and deception, when he tries to persuade people that the things God most truly and certainly foretells and threatens the wicked will suffer—namely, eternal punishments—are nothing? He flatters sinners with wicked lips and a deceitful tongue, just as the serpent did at the beginning, in order to remove from the human heart the fear of death that God had threatened and to provoke it to the pleasure of sinning: “You shall surely not die” (Gen. III, 4).

In the same way, this imitator of the serpent, by saying that the eternal torments which God announces to sinners are nothing, does nothing other than remove salutary fear from the hearts of those who hear him and make them unrestrained and headlong in sinning.

Therefore it must be held with the most steadfast and immovable faith that almighty God foreknows all future things, both good and evil. He foreknew not only the natures of all things before he created them, but also whatever could be contrary and punitive to those natures. He did so not because these things exist substantially, but because they harm, by way of punishment, the substances created by him.

Scripture confirms this faith when it says: “Eternal God, who are the knower of hidden things, who know all things before they come to pass” (Dan. XIII, 42). The Lord himself also terrifies his faithful in the Gospel concerning these matters, saying: “I will show you whom you should fear: Fear him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna; yes, I say to you, fear him” (Luke XII, 5).

But this man, to the contrary, says that all the punishments of eternal torments, both of human beings and of evil angels, which have been threatened and prepared for them, are altogether nothing.

If the eternal punishment of evil angels and the worst human beings has not been predestined, what is the meaning of what the just Judge and condemner of them himself foretold that he would say at that judgment: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41)?

If it has indeed been prepared and predestined, was it predestined for condemned angels and for those who are to be condemned, but was it neither prepared nor predestined for the wicked, who are likewise to be punished in that same eternal fire?

The blessed Enoch, the most ancient patriarch—who walked with God and disappeared because the Lord took him—also prophesied before the Flood concerning the punishments and eternal penalties predestined for the wicked. The blessed Apostle Jude bears witness to this when, speaking about the most impious heretics who began to attack the Church of God in the times of the apostles, he says:

“Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied concerning these men, saying: ‘Behold, the Lord comes with his holy myriads to execute judgment against all and to convict all the impious concerning all their works of impiety by which they acted impiously, and concerning all the harsh things which impious sinners have spoken against him’” (Jude 14–15).

The blessed Apostle Peter also announces in these words the judgment of condemnation of impious, wicked, and blaspheming people, so wonderfully foretold from the beginning of the world and to be most certainly fulfilled at the end of the world:

“There were indeed false prophets among the people, just as there will also be false teachers among you, who will introduce destructive sects and deny the Lord who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction” (II Peter II, 1).

Of them he adds shortly afterward: “For them judgment long ago does not cease, and their destruction does not sleep” (ibid., 3).

If, then, we seek the eternal predestination of this judgment with God, let us listen attentively to what he says: “For them judgment long ago does not cease.” That is, they are not judged for the first time now, nor will they be judged for the first time when they depart from the body for eternal punishment. Their judgment of condemnation was decreed long ago; it was predestined from eternity long ago; and it has long been prepared for them without ceasing.

But if we ask what punishment is inflicted upon them by that judgment, he says: “Their destruction does not sleep.” Again, concerning these same impious and blasphemous people, the same Apostle says: “These are waterless springs and mists driven by storms, for whom the gloom of darkness is reserved” (II Peter II, 17).

How is it reserved for them except because it was prepared for them from the beginning and is to be rendered at the end? The blessed Apostle Jude confirms this in almost the same words when he says:

“These are clouds without water, carried about by winds; autumn trees, twice dead, uprooted; wild waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, for whom the storm of darkness has been reserved forever” (Jude 12–13).

Against these dreadful and terrifying things, which almighty God threatens through his prophets and apostles to the wicked and sinners, this man says: “All evil, sin, and its punishment do not exist.” Again he asserts: “Integrity of nature, life, and blessedness exist.” Conversely, he says, sin, death, and misery do not exist at all.

He further adds that every defect, privation, or sin of a perverse will, and its end—death and the misery of eternal punishments—are altogether nothing; and therefore they are neither foreknown by God nor predestined.

Regarding all these matters, if something must be said individually, the faith plainly knows that evil, which is contrary to good—as vice is to virtue, darkness to light, and weakness to health—does not exist substantially. For, as was said above, it does not possess in itself a substance by which it exists and subsists, as do heaven, earth, water, air, fire, and the rest of creation, whether bodily or spiritual.

But the abandonment of the highest good, to which a rational creature, angelic or human, ought to cling if it is to be blessed, has received the name “evil.” By abandoning the highest good, therefore, rational creation—whether in angels or in sinful human beings—fell away from that good, was deprived of the good, and this became its greatest evil.

Whether, then, we say that evil is abandonment of good, or falling away from good, or privation of good, we speak most correctly, just as vice is the abandonment of virtue, darkness the privation of light, and weakness nothing other than the loss of health. Likewise, sin plainly has no substance by which it exists and subsists in itself; rather, abandonment of justice and falling away from justice have received that name.

Similarly, death has no substance by which it exists and subsists in itself; it is the loss of life that has received this name. Likewise, what is called punishment has no substance by which it exists in itself, but pain and the torment arising from pain have received this name. This is nothing other than the disturbance or loss of natural tranquility and repose, for punishment acts so that the tranquility and repose of nature are disturbed or lost through pain and torment.

All these things—evil, sin, punishment, death, and misery, which itself is nothing other than the loss of happiness—although they possess no substance by which they exist or subsist in themselves, nevertheless necessarily occur in or through some substance. For the abandonment of good, which is called evil, and the abandonment of justice, which is called sin, plainly occur in a mind, whether angelic or human.

Likewise, the loss of life, which is called death, the loss of tranquility or natural repose, which is called punishment, and the loss of happiness, which is called misery, are found to occur in both soul and body.

The soul dies through the abandonment of its life, which is God to it; and the body dies through the loss of its life, which is the soul to it. What else, then, are these two things—the death of the soul and the death of the body—in either case except the loss either of happiness or of tranquility?

The punishment that is felt in torment and pain plainly occurs either in the soul or in the body. When it occurs in the body, it is inflicted chiefly through another body: when the body is beaten with whips, wounded with swords, or afflicted by any kind of torment [Col. 0162A]. The same will occur in eternal punishments, where the bodies of the condemned will be tortured by fire and sulfur.

All the pains and torments inflicted upon bodies by bodies nevertheless take place in the body in such a way that, through the body, they are also experienced by the soul. For the soul can suffer and be tormented without the body, as the soul of that rich man condemned in hell was tormented when he said: “I am tormented in this flame” (Luke XVI, 24). The body, however, cannot suffer without the soul.

To almighty God, then, of whom it is written: “To the Lord God, before they were created, all things were known; so also, after they were completed, he regards all things” (Sirach XXIII, 29); and again: “From age to age he regards them, and nothing is new in his sight” (ibid., XXXIX, 21); and again, when Scripture was speaking about human beings: “All their works are as the sun in the sight of God; no thought escapes him, and no word is hidden from him” (ibid., XVII, 26)—to this most almighty and ineffable Creator, to whom all things were known in his eternal knowledge before they were created, and who, after he had completed all things, regards what has been made not otherwise but as he saw it was to be made, seeing everything not outside himself but within himself—

to this Creator, then, nothing is new in his sight, not even when something is created for the first time, because it has always been eternal in his knowledge. All human works are as exposed to him as in the brightest sun; no human thought escapes him, and no word of theirs is hidden from him.

This wondrous Creator and governor, just as he has always known in his eternal foreknowledge the nature, form, and order of all things that were to exist, so he also eternally foresaw the condition of those things, whether their progress toward better things or their decline toward worse things. As the most just disposer of his work, he both foreknew and predestined what rewards were owed to those progressing toward him and what punishments were owed to those falling away from him, and he foretold that he would fulfill them.

Therefore, whether evil and sin—in which there is a falling away from good—or death and punishment, which are justly owed to that falling away, have always existed in the foreknowledge of the Creator. He alone truly recognizes the measure of progress and decline in his creatures, and he alone is their just judge in both progress and decline.

Thus death, sin, and every punishment and misery that follow sin are nothing, because they possess no substance by which they exist in themselves. Yet, because they do great harm to the rational creature whose decline and corruption these names signify, they are truly experienced in its substance, whether bodily or spiritual. What does not exist as substance is nevertheless wholly destructive in its harmful effects.

Let such blasphemy, therefore, cease, and let almighty God be acknowledged as the creator of all natures, the truest knower of their conditions, and their most just disposer.

## CHAPTER XI

In the eleventh chapter this man proceeds and says:

[Col. 0163A]

1. There is no predestination of God except concerning those who have been prepared for eternal blessedness.

2. It is abusively and metaphorically said that God foreknows and predestines: by analogy, he foreknew what he was going to do; in the opposite sense, “he foreknew what he was not going to do” means “he did not know.” Similarly, by analogy, “he predestined those whom he prepared for grace.” In the opposite sense, “he predestined the wicked to destruction or eternal punishment.” For if they have been predestined, they will necessarily perish and suffer unavoidable punishments. But if this is so, how will the world be judged justly, when the necessity of predestination compels it to perish?

3. The Holy Scriptures are found to place foreknowledge and predestination together, or absolute predestination alone, only among those whom God elected to possess eternal blessedness.

4. The Apostle placed foreknowledge and predestination among the saints alone; Augustine, on several occasions, placed them among the reprobate in the opposite sense.

First of all, as to his assertion that there is no predestination of God except concerning those prepared for eternal blessedness: whether he has said this from his own opinion or heard it from others, we nevertheless truly know that this is an error widespread among many in the present age. They do not think that God's predestination, except in the case of the elect, is found in the Scriptures; nor do they think that the blessed Apostle Paul himself set forth predestination in his Epistles except concerning the elect alone, as he says in what follows. But we must humbly yield and obey the truth; we must not contentiously defend what has once been impressed upon us, but rather investigate Holy Scripture more diligently—not only the apostolic writings, but also the prophetic writings, from which all apostolic authority derives. As the blessed Paul himself clearly declares at the beginning of his Epistle to the Romans, saying that he was set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures (Romans 1:1). At the end of the same Epistle, he confirms that the whole mystery of evangelical preaching—in which is contained also the most profound mystery of God's foreknowledge and predestination—has been revealed through the prophetic Scriptures, saying: “Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal ages, which now has been made manifest through the Scriptures of the Prophets,” etc. (Romans 16:25–26). Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles he speaks of himself: “To this day I stand, bearing witness to small and great alike, saying nothing beyond what the Prophets and Moses said would happen” (Acts 26:22). Since, then, the Apostle himself shows and confirms that he was set apart for that Gospel of God which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures; testifies that all the mystery which he proclaims in the Gospel has been made manifest through the Scriptures of the Prophets; and says nothing beyond what is written in the Law and the Prophets: it is clear that the profundity of this matter—that is, of divine foreknowledge and predestination—must be investigated more diligently not only in the Apostle, who confirms all his preaching from the prophetic Scriptures, but also in the Scriptures of the prophets themselves. Whatever is found in both with a firm declaration of truth must be followed by us faithfully and in every way, without any contentious dispute.

First, then, let us hear what the Apostle himself says about this matter—he who testifies that he says nothing beyond what is written in the Law and the Prophets. Let us not be so absurd or contentious that, when the matter itself, namely the truth of predestination, is evident, we deny that something has been said concerning predestination merely because the word “predestination” is nowhere found there. Rather, whether predestination is explicitly expressed there or the truth of predestination itself shines forth with complete certainty, let it be received with one and the same faith.

He therefore first speaks of the predestination of the elect alone in this way: “For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Romans 8:29–30). If, after these words, he had said absolutely nothing about the portion of the reprobate, we should nevertheless have had to understand, by contrast, what ought to be believed about them—namely, that from the predestination of the elect to glory we should also recognize a predestination of the reprobate to punishment.

Thus, in the Creed, we seem to confess only “eternal life,” which is the reward of the saints; nevertheless, by contrast, we must likewise believe and understand without doubt “eternal death,” which is the condemnation of the wicked. The Apostle himself teaches us this rule for understanding the Scriptures. When, discussing the resurrection, he had said, “It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:44), lest he appear to have spoken of a spiritual body without scriptural authority, he immediately added what ought truthfully to be understood by contrast, saying: “If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual body” (ibid.). Immediately confirming both, he adduces the testimony of Scripture and says: “As it is written: The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit” (ibid., 45).

Likewise, when God had first said to the first man, “You shall not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; on whatever day you eat from it, you shall surely die” (Genesis 2:17), he certainly threatened the disobedient with death. But does faith not recognize what ought to be understood by contrast—that is, that he had prepared life for the obedient?

Again, when God speaks to Abraham: “The male whose flesh of his foreskin has not been circumcised on the eighth day shall perish from among his people, because he has made my covenant void” (Genesis 17:14), it is clear that this male, who was not circumcised on the eighth day, would perish from among his people because he had made God’s covenant void. Certainly this was not in his mother’s womb, nor in that very early infancy when he could in no way have done anything good or evil, but in paradise, in Adam’s transgression, in whom all sinned, as the Apostle says (Romans 5:12)—all who descend from that condemned origin. Therefore, just as the one who was not circumcised on the eighth day is plainly declared destined to perish on account of the guilt of the first transgression, so by contrast it must faithfully be understood that the one who had been circumcised duly and lawfully would be absolved from that guilt.

We have said this so that we may clearly understand that, even if the Apostle had remained silent in that discussion of predestination about the portion of the reprobate, our faith nevertheless ought, by contrast, to have noticed and understood what should be believed about them. But he is not silent. Immediately after setting forth a likeness concerning both the elect and the reprobate, he adds, speaking together of the two twins of Isaac and Rebekah:

“For when they had not yet been born, nor had done anything good or evil—so that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not from works but from him who calls it was said: The elder shall serve the younger. As it is written: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Romans 9:11–13; Malachi 1:1–2).

In this example, therefore, the predestination of the elect to life is plainly declared in Jacob, loved and chosen without any merits, who was nevertheless likewise held liable to original sin, since he was a brother and came from the same mass condemned in Adam. In Esau, however, hated solely on account of the guilt of original sin, the predestination of the reprobate to destruction is declared.

The same applies to what is added shortly afterward concerning both portions: “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens” (Romans 9:18). And then he adds: “Does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (ibid., 21). Of these vessels of honor and dishonor he immediately adds: “But if God, wishing to show his wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory?” (ibid., 22–23).

In all these passages it is most clearly recognized that the Apostle treated not only the predestination of the elect, which he placed first, but throughout the whole course of this discussion the predestination of both portions, whether to life or to death, using both examples and prophetic testimonies: in Jacob he presents the form of the elect, and in Esau the form of the reprobate.

In these two portions, then, God has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills: he has mercy by mercifully helping, and hardens by justly abandoning. Like a potter working with clay from the same entirely condemned mass, he makes one vessel for honor by mercifully liberating it, and another for dishonor by justly condemning it. Thus two orders arise from these: some are vessels of wrath, and others vessels of mercy—the former fitted for destruction, the latter prepared for glory. The vessels fitted for destruction are so fitted both by their own merit and by God’s just judgment; those prepared for glory are prepared not by any merit of their own, but solely by the gift of divine grace.

Since, then, the Apostle says so openly, “vessels of wrath fitted for destruction” and “vessels of mercy prepared for glory,” and since from the same mass one vessel is made for honor and another for dishonor, who would not understand that in these words the divine predestination of both portions is most plainly displayed? The elect are predestined to life without any merit of their own, solely by God’s goodness; the reprobate are predestined to destruction not by any prejudice on God’s part, but solely by their own merit, whether original or actual. Divine predestination does not impose upon them the necessity of perishing, any more than it imposes the necessity of sinning; it imposes only the necessity of suffering just punishments. Thus those who remain in sins by their will are tormented in punishments by necessity.

Even if that entire lengthy discussion of the Apostle on this subject—from this passage to the end, where he says, “For God has enclosed all in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all” (Romans 11:32)—is carefully and faithfully considered, anyone will undoubtedly find him discussing the predestination of both portions, whether within the one people of the Jews, among those who were blinded and those who deserved to be saved according to the election of grace, or among both Jews and Gentiles: the former, like natural branches, were broken off, while the latter, like a wild olive, were grafted into the good olive tree (ibid., 17). He will find the Apostle arguing this both in his own words and especially through prophetic testimonies.

Yet concerning these prophetic testimonies, which the blessed Apostle put before us with such authority that he wished to teach nothing at all about the depth and obscurity of this matter—that is, God’s predestination of both portions—except from their firmness and evident testimony, one point above all must be considered with every attention to piety. Although nowhere in them does the word “predestination” explicitly and properly sound, nevertheless, because the realities pertaining to both predestinations appear and are declared most clearly, the Apostle confidently adopted these testimonies for the confirmation and teaching of so great a matter, and handed them on to the Church to be held and understood in this way.

By his authority and example he thus forms and instructs us, so that we do not argue contentiously and pointlessly among ourselves about the word “predestination” in the utterances of the holy prophets, or—God forbid—even quarrel; rather, wherever the reality itself is most clearly declared, we ought with peaceful and devout understanding unquestionably both to recognize and to affirm divine predestination.

The first prophetic testimony that he brought forward concerning this matter is from Genesis, where he says: “For this is the word of promise: At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son” (Romans 9:9). Although predestination may not seem to sound there, promise clearly does. Yet the promise is rightly understood only if that very promise is faithfully taken as the predestination of Abraham’s chosen offspring—that is, of those who are counted as God’s children and are separated by divine grace from the children of the flesh.

As the Apostle himself explains in the same passage: “Not those who are children of the flesh are children of God, but those who are children of the promise are counted as offspring” (ibid., 8).

In the second place he again set forth a testimony from Genesis, concerning the two twins of Isaac and Rebekah, to whom it had been said: “The elder shall serve the younger” (Genesis 25:23). Although predestination may seem not to sound there at all, the reality of predestination itself is nevertheless demonstrated there so profoundly and magnificently that the Apostle warns and earnestly arouses us to attend vigilantly and faithfully to the entire oracle divinely given to Rebekah concerning these same twins.

We must consider that they were not condemned from their mother’s womb, had not yet done anything good or evil in their own lives, and certainly had been conceived from one intercourse; yet the almighty God distinguished them from one another by so great a difference that, without any preceding good or evil merits of theirs, solely by his goodness and judgment he preferred one of them and subjected the other to servitude.

And lest we should think that this was too little, as though it appeared to have been said merely about human and worldly matters—“The elder shall serve the younger”—as if it were to be fulfilled in them only with respect to temporal circumstances, while among their descendants one would be raised to royal power and rule over the other, who was subject and served him, the Apostle further raises our understanding to consideration of a greater matter by adding a testimony from the prophet Malachi.

There God himself speaks concerning these same twins, distinguished not temporally but eternally, separated by a great difference not only in temporal matters but also in eternal ones: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Malachi 1:2).

Therefore this prophetic testimony cannot rightly be understood otherwise than by faithfully joining it to the testimony taken from Genesis, so that just as it was said there, “The elder shall serve the younger,” so also what God says through the prophet—“Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated”—may be understood as having occurred before they were born and before they had done anything good or evil. Both are to be understood as having been preceded by God’s just judgment: both God’s love for Jacob and God’s hatred of Esau.

Since these two things—God’s love for the one and hatred for the other—preceded both their birth and the whole merit of their lives, according to the true and apostolic understanding, and since no evil could be charged against the latter, because he had not yet done any, nor any good credited to the former, because he had performed none, they are understood to have been done justly in this way: the almighty God, who had eternally established and predetermined in his judgment both the election of one and the reprobation of the other, foresaw the original guilt arising from Adam’s transgression, to which both were equally held liable; by mercifully loving one, he would liberate him, and by justly hating the other, he would reject and condemn him.

Thus we may faithfully understand the deeper and more hidden ordering of divine judgment, and, enlightened by apostolic understanding, perceive more profoundly that universal condemnation of the whole human race in Adam. From it the almighty God liberates those whom he wills by his grace alone, and condemns those whom he does not will by his eternal equity.

Although in this prophetic testimony—“Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated”—the word “predestination” does not sound, the truth of the matter itself nevertheless appears so clearly in the election of both portions, or in the election of one and the reprobation of the other, that nothing stronger or more explicit could have been said than that, through the pattern of these twins, the almighty God is shown by his own testimony to have loved some with his eternal mercy and hated others by his eternal judgment.

This prophetic testimony and apostolic understanding—by which God’s love and hatred toward the two twins, while they were still in their mother’s womb, are understood as proceeding from God’s mercy and judgment—also wonderfully correspond with and agree with a passage from the prophet Isaiah.

There the almighty God is shown as the helper of the chosen people from the womb, and conversely as the condemner of the reprobate people, likewise as transgressors from the womb. The same prophet first says to the chosen people: “Thus says the Lord, who made and formed you, your helper from the womb” (Isaiah 44:2). Then, after some intervening material, speaking from God’s person to the reprobate people, he adds: “And I called you a transgressor from the womb” (Isaiah 48:8).

Thus what the Apostle demonstrated and declared through the form of those twins appears most clearly to be held in the two classes of human beings, namely the elect and the reprobate. The latter are accused by divine judgment as transgressors from the womb, while God is likewise shown as the helper of the former from the womb, so that from the same mass, originally and entirely condemned, some vessels may be made in the mother’s womb for honor and others for dishonor (Romans 9:21, 15).

Likewise, in the third prophetic testimony, which he set forth in this way—“For he says to Moses: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion” (Exodus 33:19)—the word “predestination” is plainly not expressed. Yet the reality is so evident that it cannot in any way be doubted.

The almighty God has mercy on all who have been equally condemned through that first transgression—not because of any preceding good merits, but solely by his grace—and he shows compassion to those to whom he grants compassion. The others, to whom he has not willed to confer this grace, are manifestly hated and condemned by his just and eternal judgment.

After this he set forth the fourth prophetic testimony, also from Exodus, as he had done with the third, adding: “For Scripture says to Pharaoh: For this very purpose I raised you up, so that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth” (Romans 9:17).

Although the name “predestination” is not explicitly expressed there, the predestination of the wicked to eternal destruction on account of the merit of their iniquity is nevertheless displayed so openly that anyone who hears and understands these words faithfully cannot doubt it.

That impious, harsh, and untamable king of the Egyptians was raised up by divine judgment—whether from the mass of the condemned origin or to the power of royal honor—for this one purpose: he who was worthy of eternal destruction in and of himself was, with God adding iniquity to his iniquity [or: with him adding it], to increase his contempt for the Lord. Thus, through the great and extraordinary plagues, he deserved to be scourged by God’s wondrous power, and finally, together with all his similarly impious people, to be destroyed by eternal drowning and ruin.

In this way they most justly received what they deserved, while the power of the almighty God became more gloriously known to all, whether in their scourging or in their destruction, and many others were led by the punishment of one person to knowledge of God and to their own salvation.

The blessed Ambrose, treating this matter with complete clarity, says:

> “The Lord is just in dangers, just in losses, and just in punishments—not only because each person justly pays the price of his guilt, but also because, while one person is punished, many are corrected. Ananias in the Acts of the Apostles committed the crime of defrauding the price he had received from the sale of a field, although he could have offered nothing and escaped the crime. But lest anyone should think that the apostles could be deceived with impunity, or that the gift of mercy could be polluted by the fraud of treachery, he was delivered over to eternal death and, by a just terror, brought all others into devotion to the faith. Pharaoh, drowned with his people in the waves, is an example for worldly conduct, so that no one may persecute the people of God. In the end, God could have made him obedient to his will, but through his punishment he wished everyone to be corrected. Therefore the Lord says to him: ‘For this very purpose I raised you up, so that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth’ (Romans 9:17). Certainly the Lord was not seeking an increase of his own praise, but of our correction.”

Thus far the blessed Ambrose.

After presenting these two testimonies—the first concerning the mercy conferred upon the elect, the second concerning the judgment inflicted upon the reprobate—the Apostle, as though concluding both and teaching that both occur through God’s merciful and just will, adds: “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens” (ibid., 18).

Then, against the boldness and presumption of human beings, who, failing to recognize their own weakness and failing to consider their own merits, nevertheless do not fear to criticize the divine judgments that they do not understand, he sets forth a fifth testimony from the prophet Isaiah, saying: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to him who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’” (Isaiah 45; Romans 9).

Here too the word “predestination” is not expressed at all. Nevertheless, the justice of predestination in both directions is defended so clearly and perfectly that it compels anyone who listens faithfully to recognize with complete truth that the almighty Creator is the true potter, and that all human beings, formed by him from the clay of the earth, are his work.

For this reason, with the utmost justice, the work cannot judge its potter; rather, the potter judges his work. He alone knows how, by his eternal purpose, to form each vessel of his great creation with kindness and to assign and order it for whatever uses please him, which are certainly just and fitting.

To make this still clearer, he adds a sixth testimony from the prophet Jeremiah and says: “Does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Romans 9:21).

There, in the prophet Jeremiah, we read that the Lord said to him: “Rise and go down to the house of the potter, and there you will hear my words” (Jeremiah 18:2 and following). When the prophet had entered, behold, the potter was making a work from clay with his hands, and suddenly the work he was making was spoiled. Immediately he turned and made it into another vessel, just as it pleased him.

Then the prophet was ordered to go and cry out to the people in God’s person: “Can I not do with you, house of Israel, as this potter does?” says the Lord. “Behold, as clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand,” and so forth (ibid., 7).

Through this prophetic reading God plainly shows both that he is the potter and that the whole human race is in his hand like clay in the hand of a potter, so that he may make from it different vessels, as it pleases him.

From one mass—that is, from the same mass, entirely condemned in Adam—he makes vessels distinct and diverse according to his judgment: from it one is made for honor and another for dishonor. Even the vessel which, according to its own merit and divine judgment, is being shaped for destruction, if it is suddenly spoiled through repentance between the potter’s hands, so that it is no longer fitted for destruction, is immediately formed and made by the potter’s wisdom and goodness into another vessel, so that it may be for honor and please the eyes of its creator.

Although in all these words predestination is not found explicitly expressed in its proper form, the power and truth of predestination itself, in both directions—namely, of the elect and the reprobate, of vessels for honor and vessels for dishonor—are nevertheless revealed with such great light and distinguished with such great clarity that nothing more certain or more evident can be found.

We have thought it necessary to set all these matters before readers with such careful and diligent consideration so that, following this pattern of apostolic understanding, we may not labor excessively over the word “predestination” in all the prophetic Scriptures, since the very truth of the realities pertaining to divine predestination is presented there so clearly and in so many ways that human weakness can scarcely find or comprehend them all.

Of these matters we have necessarily attempted to add some examples here, especially those that are clearer and more evident, so that from them those who hear peacefully and faithfully may be more readily instructed, and contentious persons—if they do not refuse to accept the truth—may be corrected more quickly.

For now we say nothing about the predestination of the elect, since the prophetic testimonies brought forward so brilliantly by the Apostle, as we have shown, are entirely sufficient for understanding it, believing it faithfully, and grasping it completely. By the Lord’s generosity, none of us should doubt it.

We repeat only a few of the many clear testimonies concerning that predestination of just judgment by which he foreordained and predestined the impious to destruction, since there is much hesitation about it among many people.

We read in the Book of Genesis that the almighty God had foretold, long beforehand, the destruction of the whole human race—with the exception of those who were to be saved by his mercy in the ark—because of their excessive iniquities and impieties: they would perish generally in the present age, being destroyed by the punishment of the Flood, and in the future they would be punished by eternal damnation. He spoke in this way to the holy patriarch Noah:

“The end of all flesh has come before me. The earth is filled with iniquity because of them, and I will destroy them together with the earth” (Genesis 6:13).

Concerning this universal destruction of all, the same Scripture says shortly above:

“And God said: My spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh. His days shall be one hundred and twenty years” (ibid., 3).

And shortly afterward:

“God, seeing that the wickedness of human beings was great on the earth, and that every thought of the human heart was directed toward evil at all times, repented that he had made man on the earth” (ibid., 5–6).

A little later it adds:

“I will wipe out,” he said, “the human being whom I created from the face of the earth, from human beings to animals, from creeping things to the birds of the sky. For I repent that I made them” (ibid., 7).

What could be more evident than such a prediction and predestination concerning the destruction of all the impious, with whom the world was then filled? God wished to announce it long beforehand to the holy and chosen patriarch, and established and predetermined it within himself in the eternal and inward ordering of his counsel. It is shown that he established and predetermined these things not through an angel or through some prophet of that time, but within himself.

Yet the most kindly judge and creator did not leave even those whom, as is shown, he had deservedly predestined to such dreadful ruin and destruction on account of their iniquities and impieties without the goodness and piety of his mercy. He granted them time and opportunity for repentance, so that within the one hundred and twenty years they might either satisfy God by worthy repentance or, if according to their hardness and impenitent heart they were storing up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath, perish without excuse.

Thus he predestined them to destruction on account of the merit of their impiety, yet he did not in any way compel them by predestination to sin—those whom he waited for so many years in order that they might repent.

[Note: This is a grave question, debated by few and resolved by fewer. The passage in 1 Peter 3 is cited in support of the negative position: “Christ died once for our sins, the just for the unjust, so that he might offer us to God; put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit. In this spirit he came and preached to those spirits who were in prison, who had formerly been disobedient when they were awaiting God’s patience in the days of Noah.” To this is added chapter 4: “For this reason the Gospel was preached even to the dead, so that they might indeed be judged according to human standards in the flesh but live according to God in the spirit.”

From these passages it is inferred that not all who perished in the Flood were eternally condemned. Moreover, at least the infants, whose original sin was remitted through the remedy of the law of nature, did not perish eternally.

Nevertheless, the Church of Lyon upholds the affirmative position here, perhaps because, when all flesh had corrupted its way, as stated in Genesis 9, and refused to heed Noah’s warnings—indeed, when he seemed to them to be speaking as though in jest—the Flood suddenly came upon them, after God had waited one hundred and twenty years for their repentance.

In my judgment, Bellarmine explains the whole matter very well in Book 4 of *On Christ*, chapter 13:

> “I say that Christ preached in hell to all the good spirits, but that those who had been disobedient in the days of Noah were expressly mentioned because there was greater doubt about whether they had been saved or not, since they had been punished by God and submerged in the waters of the Flood. Peter therefore indicates that even among those disobedient people there were some who repented at the end of their lives; and although they perished with respect to the body, they were nevertheless saved with respect to the soul. Jerome also teaches this in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, when discussing chapter 6—‘My spirit shall not remain in man’—where he says that God punished many of them temporally with the waters of the Flood and ought not to punish them eternally in Gehenna. The words of chapter 4 also seem to convey this meaning: ‘For this reason the Gospel was preached to the dead, so that they might indeed be judged according to human standards in the flesh but live according to God in the spirit’; that is, so that outwardly they might be judged and considered condemned according to human standards, because their bodies had been killed, yet live in spirit according to God—that is, so that their souls might be saved.”

Thus far Bellarmine.

It follows that the Church of Lyon wrongly condemns all those who were drowned in this way as eternally damned, unless we wish to say that “all” was used to mean the greater part only, or at least that the conclusion is not a matter of faith. Hence Augustine, in Letter 99 to Evodius, preferred to interpret Saint Peter’s passage differently rather than admit the conversion of those people and Christ’s preaching in the underworld. See Bellarmine, cited work.]

Concerning the unhappy obstinacy and terrible condemnation of these people, the book of Ecclesiasticus also speaks sorrowfully and mournfully, adding their destruction to that of those who were brought out of Egypt by Moses but, because of their unbelief, could not enter the land of promise, and whose corpses were strewn in the wilderness. It says: “The ancient giants, who were destroyed while trusting in their strength, did not seek atonement for their sins; he did not spare their sojourning, but abhorred them because of their pride. He did not have mercy on them, destroying the whole nation that exalted itself in its sins. Likewise the six hundred thousand footmen who gathered in the hardness of their heart; and if there had been one stiff-necked person, it would have been astonishing if he had escaped. For mercy and wrath are with him: mighty in forgiveness and pouring out wrath. As is his mercy, so also is his correction: he judges a person according to his works” (Ecclesiasticus 16:8–13).

Such also is the prediction and predestination of God speaking to Abraham concerning the future oppression, affliction, and deliverance of his offspring, and conversely the condemnation and destruction of their oppressors. He said to him: “Know beforehand that your offspring will be a stranger in a land not its own; they will subject them to slavery and afflict them for four hundred years. But I will judge the nation whom they will serve; and after this they will go out with great possessions. But you will go to your fathers in peace, buried in a good old age. In the fourth generation they will return here; for the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet complete up to the present time” (Genesis 15:13–16).

What is clearer than this predestination? By it Abraham’s offspring is foretold to be a sojourner in a foreign land for the course of so many years, to be subjected to slavery and afflicted, gloriously to be delivered from that very affliction, and at the appointed time—that is, in the fourth generation—to return to the land promised to its fathers; while the most blessed patriarch himself is to be joined to his fathers in peace and a good old age. Conversely, the nation and king of the Egyptians, who were to oppress them, are destined by God’s eternal judgment to everlasting destruction.

Similar, or even much clearer, is that foreannouncement and predestination concerning the destruction of the Amorites—indeed, of the seven most wicked nations. Speaking to Abraham, the almighty God most plainly declared that, on account of their impiety, he had resolved and predetermined long beforehand to destroy and blot them out, when he said: “For the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet complete up to the present time.” For he had promised that same most holy patriarch that, once they had been destroyed, he would give their kingdoms and lands to his offspring as a possession.

Yet the just and merciful judge did not will to do this merely because of his goodness and promise to Abraham, as though he were a respecter of persons—far be it. Rather, in the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering, he waited and delayed through so many ages, granting time for repentance, so that, if the multitude of those nations persisted in their impieties and filled up the measure of their sins, they might most justly be punished in the fullness of their iniquities. In their place Abraham’s offspring, which was to serve God, would succeed—not through respect of persons, nor by any merit of God’s justice and equity, but by divine goodness alone.

When the time was now drawing near—both for the destruction of those nations on account of their iniquities and for the introduction of Abraham’s offspring into their lands through God’s mercy—God speaks to that offspring of Abraham, that is, to the people Israel, concerning their sins and their imminent, just destruction: “Do not defile yourselves with all these things by which all the nations whom I am driving out before you have been defiled, and by which the land has been polluted; I will visit its crimes upon it, so that it may vomit out its inhabitants” (Leviticus 18:24–25). And shortly afterward: “For the inhabitants of the land who were before you committed all these abominations and polluted it. Take care, therefore, lest it likewise vomit you out when you have done the same things, as it vomited out the nation which was before you” (ibid., 27–28).

Already, however, concerning the final destruction of those same nations, by which they undoubtedly perished both in the present age and in the age to come, Scripture speaks in general terms as follows: “For it was the Lord’s decision that their hearts should be hardened, and that they should fight against Israel, fall, and not deserve any mercy, but perish, just as the Lord had commanded Moses” (Josh. XI, 20).

What could be found clearer concerning the predestination of the ungodly to everlasting destruction than this: that almighty God, who had secretly determined this future in his judgment, both foretold these things to Abraham long beforehand and repeatedly threatened them during the intervening periods; and finally Scripture confirms that it was his decision—that is, his purpose and judgment—that they should not deserve any mercy, but should perish utterly and eternally in their ungodliness and contempt?

Concerning these divine judgments, the Book of Wisdom likewise speaks to God, saying: “For who shall say to you, ‘What have you done?’ or who shall stand against your judgment? Or who shall come before you as an avenger of unrighteous men? Or who shall charge you if the nations that you made have perished?” [Col. 0173D] “For there is no other God besides you, who cares for all, so that you may show that you do not judge unjustly; neither king nor tyrant shall inquire in your presence concerning those whom you have destroyed. Since you are just, you dispose all things justly” (Wis. XII, 12–15).

Likewise, when the same Scripture distinguishes between the divine goodness shown toward his own people and the just severity shown toward their enemies, namely the Egyptians, whom he had destined for eternal destruction, it says: “Showing how you exalted your own people and destroyed their adversaries. For when they were tested—and indeed, when they were disciplined with mercy—they learned how the ungodly, judged with wrath, suffered torments. These you tested as a father admonishing them; but those, as a stern king interrogating them, you condemned” (Wis. XI, 9–11).

And again: “For it was necessary that destruction should overtake those who exercised tyranny without excuse, while to these it was necessary only to show how their enemies were being destroyed” (Wis. XVI, 4).

And again: “Then the trial of death touched the righteous also, and a disturbance of the multitude occurred in the wilderness, but your wrath did not remain long; for that trial alone was sufficient as a punishment of wrath” (Wis. XVIII, 20, 25); “but upon the ungodly wrath came without mercy, even to the very end” (Wis. XIX, 1).

A little later, concerning the eternal destruction of those same Egyptians in the Red Sea, it says: “For while they still held mourning in their hands and lamented at the tombs of the dead, they adopted another thought of folly; and those whom they had cast out while begging them to leave, they pursued as fugitives. For a worthy necessity was leading them to this end, and they were losing the memory of what had happened, so that punishment might fill up whatever was lacking in their torments; and while your people passed over wonderfully, they themselves encountered a new death” (ibid., 3–5).

Similarly, in the Book of the Prophet Daniel, the succession, times, and eternal destruction of the four great and principal kingdoms of the future are manifested according to the judgment of divine predestination: either under the appearance of four metals in the statue seen by the king in a dream, or under the variety of the four beasts ascending from the sea, or through the open prediction of kings and wars, extending to the times, the killing, and the destruction of Antichrist himself, and to Christ’s coming for judgment, by the marvelous foreknowledge [Col. 0174D] and ordering of God.

Who would be capable of adequately estimating how many and how dreadful evils those kingdoms, together with the kingdom of Antichrist, would inflict throughout the world, and especially how greatly they would oppress and attack the Church of God? Nevertheless, so that all these things might be understood as having been accomplished—or as destined to be accomplished—by the eternal judgment of divine foreknowledge and predestination, they were, as we have said, most wondrously foretold in their order, distinguished according to their times, and destined to end at their appointed limits; long beforehand they were recognized and recorded through prophetic revelation.

If we also wish to find in the prophetic words the very term “predestination,” which is nothing other than the decree and foreordination of divine judgment, there is a remarkable and memorable passage in the Prophet Isaiah. There he speaks historically about the destruction of the Babylonian and Assyrian kingdom, but mystically about the destruction, at the end of the age, of the entire city of the devil. He introduces almighty God swearing—that is, confirming his words by the unchanging truth of his will—and says:

“The Lord of hosts has sworn, saying: ‘If it is not as I have thought, so shall it be; and as I have considered in my mind, so shall it come to pass’” (Isa. XIV, 24, 26, 27).

And shortly afterward:

“This is the counsel that I have counseled concerning the whole earth; and this is the hand extended over all the nations. For the Lord God of hosts has decreed, and who can invalidate it? His hand is extended, and who can turn it back?”

Behold, the predestination of the destruction of the reprobate is here plainly declared: that is, the destruction of all the nations opposed and hostile to the people of God, through the consideration, counsel, and decree of the divine mind, and through the extending of his hand, by which all works destined to be fulfilled and completed are signified. This is declared with the testimony of an oath—that is, with the immutable firmness of the divine counsel.

In that vision also of the great tree, whose appearance reached to the ends of the earth, which the king saw in his dream being cut down at God’s command, and by which the height of worldly power was signified—a height frequently overturned and scattered by divine judgment because of its pride—it is shown that these things were accomplished through the predestination, decree, and sentence of the divine counsel, by the ministry of the holy angels.

Thus the king himself says in the account of the same dream:

“I saw in the vision of my head upon my bed; and behold, a watcher and a holy one descended from heaven. He cried out loudly and said: ‘Cut down the tree and chop off its branches; shake off its leaves and scatter its fruit,’ and so forth” (Dan. IV, 10, 11).

And shortly afterward:

“In the sentence of the watchers the decree was made, and the word of the holy ones and the petition, until the living know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever he wishes” (ibid., 14).

For these things were not done only on account of Nebuchadnezzar, but for the terror and humiliation of all worldly powers who read or hear them, so that all may tremble and all may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, by whose power and judgment the authority to reign is granted to some and to others.

Because this is ordered and carried out through angelic ministries, it is said that in the sentence of the watchers a decree was made, and that the word of the holy ones and the petition are fulfilled in such matters. They receive authority for this, so that their word in such things is like the word of those who command. Yet a petition is also added, so that whatever they are to accomplish in the world may be obtained from God through prayer.

This predestination and foreordination of divine judgment is also briefly shown in the Prophet Ezekiel, where, in the person of the whole Jewish kingdom and priesthood, which deservedly was to be destroyed in the latter times, when Christ the Lord came, it is said to the reprobate king:

“But you, profane and wicked prince of Israel, whose day has come at the time of iniquity that has been foreordained, thus says the Lord: ‘Remove the turban; take away the crown’” (Ezek. XXI, 25).
