It is clear that the crown signifies the kingdom and the turban the priesthood. We see that both were taken away from that people when Christ the Lord came, and this occurred when the day foreordained for them arrived, at the time of iniquity.

There is a similar passage in the same prophet, where the Lord speaks to the sharpened and polished sword, prepared for the slaughter and destruction of the ungodly:

“That you may be given over the necks of the wounded ungodly, whose day has come at the time of iniquity that has been foreordained” (ibid., 29).

Thus both kinds of predestination are displayed most clearly by the Apostle in his Epistles and by the prophets in the ancient Scriptures: through them nothing is arranged unjustly or disorderly, but everything is ordered with justice and reason.

Faithfully following this apostolic and prophetic authority, blessed Augustine did not fear to call the predestination found in God’s just judgments and arrangements truly predestination—not, as this man says, to simulate it deceitfully. This man attempts to hand down to us two extremely false and deceptive rules, I scarcely know what they are, namely, “from similarity” and “from contrariety,” so that whatever is affirmed as though truthfully by one may be utterly destroyed by the other as though it were false.

Thus he wants whatever is said simply and truthfully, either in the Holy Scriptures or in the teachings of the Fathers, concerning this predestination that pertains to the lot of the reprobate, to be understood freely according to contrariety: so that what was done may be regarded as not done, and what was said as not said.

Who has ever heard of such madness? Surely he must be driven far from the ears of everyone who dares to think—and even to write—so open and ungodly a lie against the truth of Scripture and the purity of the teaching of the Fathers. And although he has said and written so much through his exceedingly deceptive arguments, at the very end he almost remembered, as if in a dream, the Holy Scriptures, the Apostle, and Augustine.

Yet that his definition—namely, that nothing is said in the Holy Scriptures and by the Apostle concerning the predestination of the wicked to eternal punishment—is an open lie, we think has been sufficiently demonstrated above.

Concerning God, according to his ridiculous rule, which everyone ought to spit upon, he says: “He foreknew what he was not going to do,” in place of “he did not know.” Who has ever heard such a thing—that wherever we read that God foreknew something, we should understand “he did not know”?

Both alternatives are plainly false: either “he foreknew” must be understood as “he did not know,” or what God was not going to do must be said to mean that he did not know it. But he who truly and by his eternal knowledge foreknew everything he was going to do likewise foreknew everything he was not going to do.

For example, he foreknew that he would raise Lazarus, and he did so; he foreknew that he would not raise Judas, and he did not do so. But this man says: “He predestined the wicked to destruction or eternal punishment,” in place of “he did not predestine”; that is, wherever we read “he predestined,” we are, in unheard-of madness, to understand “he did not predestine.”

He also raises the question: “How will the world be judged justly when the necessity of predestination compels it to perish?” May it be far from any of us to say such a thing. For it is the clearest blasphemy to say that God, by the prejudgment of his predestination, compels anyone to sin and, by sinning, to perish.

Rather, by the just judgment of his predestination, those whom he has decreed to punish because they persevere in sins he recalls from their sins and inspires those who hear with a saving fear, so that they may be corrected through fear and, once corrected, may not be condemned.

## CHAPTER XII

In the twelfth chapter he sets forth definitions of the following kind:

1. Every foreknowledge of God is predestination, and every predestination is foreknowledge.

2. Every predestination of God is altogether a preparation of grace, and every grace is a gift. Therefore all divine predestination is a preparation of his gifts.

3. Punishment justly tortures the wicked, and it is not a gift; otherwise, if it were a gift, it would not torture but would certainly liberate. Therefore there is no predestination of punishment. If there were, it would not be punishment but grace. Yet it is punishment; therefore it is not its predestination.

[Col. 0177C] Consequently, predestination must always be understood as referring to the gifts of divine generosity.

4. Those predestined to punishment must always be understood by contrariety, just as “the elect” means “the non-elect,” and “the children of God” means “those who are not children.”

Anyone who carefully reads and faithfully understands what we said above, by the Lord’s generosity, according to the rule of faith, can easily judge and destroy these four exceedingly long and empty propositions, woven together as though by the artifice of syllogisms.

For who does not understand how blasphemous and ungodly is what he put first, saying: “Every foreknowledge of God is predestination”? Faith plainly holds that almighty God foreknows everything—that is, good and evil, what he himself is going to do and what he is not going to do. But he predestines only the good things that he himself is going to do, either mercifully by freeing and rewarding the elect, or justly by condemning the reprobate, because whatever is just is certainly good.

Therefore, if, according to this man’s definition, every foreknowledge of God is predestination, then everything he foreknew—including evil—he predestined himself to do. Far be it from us to say so! For he merely foreknew evils; he did not predestine them in any way, because he himself was not going to do them, whereas he himself established and foreordained that everything he predestined should occur.

Similarly, the beginning of his second proposition starts from falsehood and therefore ends in falsehood. For he says: “Every predestination of God is altogether a preparation of grace.” That this is not so was sufficiently shown above through apostolic and prophetic testimonies, where we clearly found and demonstrated that God’s predestination must be understood in two ways: either with respect to the merciful rewarding of the good, or with respect to the just condemnation of the evil.

Therefore, as the words of blessed Augustine that we cited above most clearly teach, when God’s predestination is understood in relation to the good, only then is it to be understood as a preparation of grace.

In his third proposition, likewise, what he attempts to affirm is utterly false: namely, that there is no predestination of punishment. For if punishment had not been predestined for the devil and his angels, and for all the reprobate who are to be punished with them, the Truth would never have said: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41).

What he places at the end of this third proposition—“Predestination must always be understood as referring to the gifts of divine generosity”—is likewise false. For predestination is found and truthfully understood not only in the generosity of God’s gifts but also in the judgments of just condemnation.

His fourth proposition, which runs as follows—“Those predestined to punishments must always be understood by contrariety”—belongs to that madness about which we have said enough above. He wants us to understand “the predestined” as meaning “the non-predestined.”

What he added by way of example—“just as the elect means the non-elect, and the children of God means those who are not children”—will be treated more fully in the following chapter, where he explains at greater length what he thinks about these matters.

Nevertheless, we must recall and recognize that blessed Augustine, as the words cited above demonstrate, at one point said that in Scripture God’s foreknowledge signifies predestination (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, ch. 18). Taking these words as an opportunity for his argument against Augustine’s entirely truthful statement, in which Augustine taught that the expression should sometimes be understood in this way, this man added the word “every” and removed “sometimes.” Thus he produced a thoroughly false definition, saying: “Every foreknowledge of God is predestination.”

Likewise, because blessed Augustine, as we cited above, defined God’s predestination as a preparation of grace (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, ch. 10)—something understood, according to Augustine’s meaning, only with respect to the elect—this man added the word “every” and produced a thoroughly false definition by saying: “Every predestination of God is altogether a preparation of grace.”

## CHAPTER XIII

In the thirteenth chapter he says:

1. “The elected Judas” is to be understood by contrariety as “the non-elected Judas,” and “the children of God” as “those who are not children”; thus the same person is called a friend who had never been anything but an enemy.

2. It is futile to seek children of God apart from his elect; it is futile to suppose that his elect exist apart from those predestined by him.

3. It is impious to suppose that anyone is predestined by God apart from his elect; it is superfluous to regard God’s elect as existing apart from his children; and they are not predestined if they are not children of God.

4. Concerning those predestined to punishments, destruction, or torment, nothing else is to be understood except that they are not predestined, but have not been separated from the condemned mass by the merit of original and personal sin; and therefore they have been permitted to live impiously and are to be punished by eternal fire.

In these words, he understands Judas to have been counted by the Lord among the elected apostles when he says: “Did I not choose you twelve?” (John VI, 71). Thus the others are to be understood as truly elected, while Judas, by contrariety—that is, ironically—is said to have been called elected.

It is better to understand the passage in such a way that the Truth is recognized as having spoken truly: all twelve are to be understood as having been elected by the Lord, but in different ways—the others eternally for the kingdom, Judas temporarily for the ministry.

For he was elected for a time, among the others, to apostolic ministry; he was sent to the office of preaching. Perhaps he also received the gift of miracles. Hence blessed Peter says of him in the Acts of the Apostles: “For he was numbered among us and obtained a share in this ministry” (Acts I, 17).

When they had appointed two men and prayed that God would show which of them should be appointed in place of the one whom Judas had forfeited through his transgression, they prayed as follows: “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen to receive a share in this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas transgressed, so that he might go to his own place” (ibid., 24–25).

Thus he was elected by the Lord so that, through a certain temporal dispensation, he might be joined to the apostles and receive with them a share in the ministry and apostleship. It is therefore said of him that he had transgressed from that apostolic rank.

Yet the Lord did not do this as though ignorant of the future. He had always known, in his eternal foreknowledge, both the persevering faith of the other apostles and Judas’s future fall and ruin. Blessed John the Evangelist testifies to this when he says: “For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who believed, and who it was who would betray him” (John VI, 65).

Therefore, when the Lord had said what we mentioned above—“Did I not choose you twelve?” (ibid., 71)—as one truly foreknowing the future, he immediately added: “And one of you is a devil.”

The Evangelist, explaining of whom he had spoken, immediately added: “Now he was speaking of Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot; for he was going to betray him, though he was one of the twelve” (ibid., 72).

He also knew the place of Judas’s condemnation in eternal punishments, for he had been destined and predestined there on account of the merit of his ungodliness. Hence the apostles said: “So that he might go to his own place” (Acts I, 25).

The Lord himself also said: “Woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed; it would have been better for that man if he had not been born” (Matt. XXVI, 24).

Nevertheless, as has been said, he wished Judas to receive for a time the ministry and place of apostleship, so that, when Judas had made evil use of so great a kindness of the Lord, the Lord might, conversely, make good use of his great evil for our great good.

By this example he taught that there would be evil men mixed into his Church, just as Judas was for a time mixed into that company of apostles, and that such men would share with the Church not only in the sacraments and divine ministries but also in the place of governance.

In this way he offered his people an example of patience, showing how patiently he would tolerate the wicked, just as he both truly knew this man and endured him with marvelous patience. He did this so that true believers would not think themselves defiled by association with such people or suppose that their ministries, insofar as they are performed according to God, should be rejected.

The blessed apostles were not defiled by Judas’s false fellowship, nor was his ministry, insofar as it was performed according to God, rejected. When his misery finally reached the evil of betrayal, the Lord transformed the great evil of one man into the good of the whole world: through this betrayal the true Lamb was himself offered, the one who took away the sin of the world.

Thus the good Lord chose Judas for good in such a way that he granted him his own good things and transformed Judas’s evils into our good. The fact that Judas transgressed and perished was due to his own wickedness; the fact that he was chosen among the good was due to the Lord’s goodness.

If he had remained in goodness, as the Apostle says: “See, then, the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness” (Rom. XI, 22).

Therefore, insofar as the temporal ministry of apostleship is concerned—the ministry about which the Lord was speaking when he said, “Did I not choose you twelve?” (John VI, 71)—this man too can properly be said to have been chosen among the others.

But insofar as the eternal election to blessedness is concerned, only those were elected of whom the Lord said when distinguishing between Judas and the others: “I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen” (John XIII, 18).

[Col. 0180C] Thus the statement, “Did I not choose you twelve?” can rightly and truly be understood even with Judas included, while he is separated as a reprobate by the statement: “I know whom I have chosen.” There is no necessity to understand either expression by contrariety.

That both statements are true is demonstrated by clear reasoning. For it is also written concerning Saul, when he was to be chosen for the kingdom—someone who would be useful in many ways and who perhaps received his election for that purpose—the Scripture says: “There was a man from the tribe of Benjamin, named Saul, chosen and good, and there was no better man among the children of Israel than he” (1 Sam. IX, 2).

Yet afterward he was most unhappily rejected and cast off, and perished. Nevertheless, he is said to have been chosen temporarily for a certain temporal usefulness of the kingdom; through both mystical anointing and the casting of lots, he was set over God’s holy people by the prophet.

As for the Gospel Scripture, we have not read anywhere that it specifically calls Judas a son. For when the Lord says concerning the apostles, “The children of the bridegroom cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them” (Luke V, 34), no necessity compels us to understand that the statement cannot rightly have been spoken only of the others, with Judas excluded.

It is certainly to those others alone, after Judas had perished, that what the Lord adds applies: “But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days” (ibid., 35).

But if anyone wishes Judas himself also to be understood as included among the children in these words of the Lord,

[Note: [Col. 0179D] He teaches that Judas was a son because of a certain degree of faith in Christ the Lord and because he shared in the sacraments. From this two heresies of the innovators are refuted: the first, in which they say that the Church consists only of the predestined; the second, in which they say that the wicked do not receive the body and blood of Christ the Lord. The contrary is plainly inferred in that passage, because Judas participated in that sacrament at the Supper.]

then, manifestly, on account of some faith he had in the Lord and his fellowship in the sacraments, through which he was joined to the holy apostles, he could be called a son—not by contrariety, but rightly and consistently.

Similarly, when the Lord said to Judas, who was already betraying him and identifying him with a kiss, “Friend, for what purpose have you come?” (Matt. XXVI, 50), the words may properly be understood not as referring to what was then happening, but as recalling what Judas had previously been called: that he had once been, in a certain sense, a disciple and friend, but had suddenly been changed into so cruel and ungodly an enemy.

Even if this is understood as having been spoken ironically, as some have understood it, that does not make this new and foolish disputant’s rule valid. For it is one thing, according to human custom, to signify ironically something that is true—when, for example, in indignation or reproach we say to a wicked man, “You are a good man,” or to someone acting badly, “You are doing well,” or to an enemy, “Friend,” and many similar expressions.

It is another thing, according to this man’s diabolical rule, to deny openly through falsehood what is true: when someone, on account of the merit of his ungodliness, is truthfully said by divine judgment to have been predestined to punishment, this man teaches in his new madness that the statement “predestined” means “not predestined.”

In this most perverse and false sense Scripture never speaks, God forbid, about matters pertaining to the faith; no ecclesiastical teacher ever spoke thus, nor did any truthful man.

But if no one, according to God’s just judgment, has been predestined—not for sinning, God forbid, but for suffering punishment for sins—what is the meaning of what the apostles said in their prayer to the Lord concerning Judas: “From which Judas transgressed, so that he might go to his own place”? (Acts I, 25.)

What is the meaning of Solomon’s words: “The Lord has made everything for its own purpose, even the wicked for the evil day”? (Prov. XVI, 4.)

What is the meaning of what is read in the Book of Job: “For the wicked is kept for the day of destruction, and he shall be led to the day of wrath”? (Job XXI, 30.)

Why does Scripture say concerning the Egyptians, who were to be destroyed and perish eternally in the Red Sea: “For a worthy necessity was leading them to this end”? (Wis. XIX, 4.) It plainly shows that the necessity of divine judgment was leading them to destruction, and yet that this was worthy of them because of the merits of their ungodliness and contempt.

What also is the meaning of what is written elsewhere: “And whoever turns from righteousness to sin, God has prepared him for the sword”? (Sir. XXVI, 27.)

The angel likewise spoke concerning Antichrist, who was still to be revealed and destroyed at the end of the age, to blessed John in the Apocalypse: “The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to ascend from the abyss, and it is going to destruction” (Rev. XVII, 8).

If this was not predestined by God, how does the same angel say: “These words of God are most trustworthy and true”? (Rev. XXI, 5.)

If Antichrist, the man of sin and son of destruction (2 Thess. II, 3), together with all his followers, was not predestined to the judgment of eternal condemnation, how does the Apostle speak so openly concerning him: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the manifestation of his coming”? (ibid., 8.)

And concerning all those who are to be deceived by him and perish eternally with him, he adds shortly afterward: “Because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved, therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie, and all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity” (ibid., 10–11).

How is it said in the Prophet Ezekiel, to the sword sharpened and polished for the slaughter and destruction of the ungodly: “That you may be given over the necks of the wounded ungodly, whose day has come, at the time of iniquity that has been foreordained”? (Ezek. XXI, 29.)

Why does the same prophet, concerning the Jews who were to lose both kingdom and priesthood and perish in their unbelief, say under the person of the ungodly king: “But you, profane and wicked prince of Israel, whose day has come at the time of iniquity that has been foreordained, thus says the Lord: ‘Remove the turban; take away the crown’”? (ibid., 25–26.)

For it is clear, as we have already said above, that the crown signifies the kingdom and the turban the priesthood.

If anyone objects that in these two prophetic examples predestination has not been placed, but foreordination, let him recognize that predestination is truly nothing other than the foreordination of a future matter.

The Apostle plainly shows this when he says: “According to the foreordination of the ages, which he made in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Eph. III, 11).

Where in Latin we read *praefinitionem* (“foreordination”), the Greek has πρόθεσιν (*prothesin*), which is properly translated into Latin as *propositum*, “purpose.”

[Note: [Col. 0181D] He says that in Sacred Scripture *praefinitio* (“foreordination”) is the same as *praedestinatio* (“predestination”), because in Greek it is called πρόθεσις (*prothesis*), which signifies “purpose.” It cannot be referred so much to foreknowledge as to the decree of the divine will, which predestination includes. Below he refutes what John Scotus Eriugena used to object: if God predestined the wicked to punishments, predestination would have to compel and lead human beings to sin. Let our innovators take careful note of this, since they so impiously and cruelly attribute causality for sins to God.]

The same word is also used in the Epistle to the Romans, where the same Apostle says: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose” (Rom. VIII, 28).

The Apostle himself almost explains that God’s purpose is nothing other than God’s predestination. For after saying “those who are called according to his purpose,” he immediately adds: “For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. VIII, 29).

From all this we must most correctly understand that God’s purpose, God’s predestination, and God’s foreordination are one and the same.

This foreordination—that is, predestination—is most clearly placed in the good in the Apostle’s words, and in the evil in the prophet’s words cited above: here it designates those foreordained to life, while there it designates those foreordained to destruction.

For such are the vessels of wrath, as the Apostle himself says (Rom. IX, 22), “prepared for destruction”—or, as others have translated it, “made complete for destruction”—both by their own merit and by the just judgment of God.

Concerning these people, when this man says that they were left in the condemned mass on account of original sin, permitted to live wickedly, and finally destined to be punished with eternal fire, he says—although unwillingly and while contradicting himself—nothing other than that they were predestined by divine judgment to eternal fire.

For if that whole mass has been condemned, it was certainly condemned by God’s just judgment; and, having been condemned, it was without doubt condemned to eternal destruction and punishment.

What else is this than that the same mass, condemned by divine judgment, was condemned to everlasting destruction? Thus, while attempting to resist the truth, he is compelled, unwillingly and unknowingly, by an invincible argument to confess the very truth.

## CHAPTER XIV

In the fourteenth chapter he says:

1. That Augustine’s words prove that “the predestined” refers only to the just, when he says: “For we do not know who belongs to the number of the predestined and who does not belong.” And again: “We are unable to distinguish the predestined from the non-predestined.” Likewise: “Those who fall and perish were not among the number of the predestined.”

2. That punishment is predestined for sinners, but that the sinners themselves are only foreknown, not predestined.

3. That this may also be inferred from human laws, which do not determine a person to sin; rather, by determining punishments for those who are going to sin, they seek nothing other than to restrain those inclined to sin by frightening them with the severity of punishments. Thus they bring about for their transgressors no less mercy than vengeance.

To these words we reply—indeed, from the words of blessed Augustine (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, chs. 10, 16)—that it is proved that “the predestined” can also be spoken of the unjust.

When Augustine was defining what predestination is, he said: “The predestination of God that is in the good is a preparation of grace.” He would certainly never have added “that is in the good” if he did not know that predestination also exists in the evil, as he himself plainly demonstrates from the Book of Acts.

He cites the passage where it is said: “For in truth, in this city, they gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, Herod and Pontius Pilate, together with the nations and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your counsel predestined to take place” (Acts IV, 27–28).

He then adds: “For the hand and counsel of God predestined to take place from the hostile Jews all that was necessary for the Gospel on our behalf.”

Therefore, both from the words of the divine book and from the words of blessed Augustine, it is plainly established that the predestination mentioned here was not for the good of those who carried out such great and terrible acts against the Lord at the time of his Passion, but for a great and deadly evil—although God turned that evil to our good.

If anyone thinks that blessed Augustine inserted this testimony from the aforementioned book as though through an error, because in our copies we read, “Which your hand and counsel decreed to take place,” let him recognize instead that Augustine placed it truly, explicitly, and precisely as it stands in the Greek.

The very word—that is, προώρισεν (*proōrisen*, “predestined” or “foreordained”)—is also found here in the Greek, where Augustine wrote: “Which your hand and counsel predestined to take place.”

The same Greek word is also found in the Epistle to the Romans, where the Apostle says: “Those whom he predestined, these he also called” (Rom. VIII, 30).

From this it is clear that he properly translates the same Greek word into Latin as *praedestinavit*, “predestined.” It can also, according to the sense, be translated as “decreed” or “foreordained,” so that we may understand with complete certainty that “predestined” means nothing other than “decreed and determined.”

This has already been demonstrated most clearly both from the words of the Prophet Isaiah, where he says, “For the Lord God of hosts has decreed” (Isa. XIV, 27), and from the words of the Book of Daniel: “In the sentence of the watchers the decree was made” (Dan. IV, 14).

[Col. 0184B] What benefit, then, does it bring him that he lies with such great concentration and insistence, claiming that blessed Augustine defined every predestination as the preparation of grace, when Augustine in no way said “every,” but defined only that predestination which is toward good in this way, as though he himself had said that only the just should be called predestined? Nowhere is he found to have said this. Rather, the words that he used concerning the predestination of the just alone—by which some are, of course, predestined and others are not predestined, some belong to the number of the predestined and others do not—this man, with less obstinacy and shamelessness, presents as though that holy teacher ought always to have spoken simultaneously about both predestinations, that is, of the good and the wicked; or as though it followed that, when he discusses only the predestination of the good, he immediately appears to deny the predestination of the wicked. For Augustine most clearly mentions and demonstrates this in many passages (*On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, ch. 13). As an example, we offer here one testimony, where he says:

“That Psalm censures a certain people among whom there was not even one who did good” (Ps. XIII, 3), “while they wish to remain sons of men and not be sons of God, by whose grace a human being becomes good, so as to do good.”

Here we must understand that “good” to which he refers there when he says: “God looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see whether there was anyone who understood and sought God” (ibid., 2). Thus, there was no one who did this good, which is to seek God—not even one—but this was among that class of human beings predestined [Col. 0184D] to destruction. For upon them God’s foreknowledge looked and pronounced its sentence.

But what use is it to bring this example of God’s predestination of the wicked against this man, when, in his customary madness, he is ready to say to his listeners: whenever they hear in the words of this holy teacher the statement “a class of human beings predestined to destruction,” they should understand its opposite, “not predestined”? Thus those are deceived who seek the truth not in the Scripture of truth, but in fabricators of falsehood.

**2.** He adds further and says: “Punishment is predestined for sinners, but the sinners themselves are merely foreknown, not predestined.” Concerning this matter we have said enough both in this chapter and in the preceding one, clearly demonstrating by many testimonies [Col. 0185A] that sinners who have persisted in their sins are predestined by God’s just judgment to punishments.

It is astonishing in what sense or by what reasoning it can be understood that God predestined punishments for sinners, but did not predestine the sinners to those punishments. For when he predestined and prepared punishments for them, he was not ignorant of who would have to be punished and tormented by them. This man himself also acknowledges this when he says that they were foreknown. If, therefore, God knew with complete certainty who would justly be punished and tormented by those punishments, what else did he do, when he prepared utterly certain punishments for utterly certain persons, except predestine them with complete certainty to those punishments? For only those whom he foreknew would suffer them will suffer them. What, then, is it to have foreknown them by immutable foreknowledge for punishments, if not to have immutably predestined them to punishments? [Col. 0185B] There was no reason to fear that what he most certainly foreknew would justly occur, he would not predestine as something he would justly do.

**3.** Human laws, however, have a different condition. They establish certain penalties for those who sin, while nevertheless being entirely ignorant of who will sin in such a way as to be justly tormented by one penalty or another. Therefore, they can prepare and predestine punishments for sinners, knowing that those punishments are just; but they cannot predestine to punishments the sinners themselves, whom they utterly do not know.

If they knew with complete certainty which persons would be deserving of those penalties, they could justly do both things: just as they establish penalties for sinners, so they could also predestine the sinners themselves to certain and just punishments by a definite judgment. Thus, in the very examination of a trial, when they have established with certainty that particular defendants are guilty of a capital crime, they read out from the laws the death sentence established and decreed for them, and by an open judgment condemn them to death. This is made possible for them by the certain knowledge supplied by judicial examination, so that, just as they dare to assign punishments to sinners, they also dare to predestine sinners to punishments.

If, therefore, both things can rightly and justly be done in human judgment, when that judgment is informed and shaped by certain knowledge—so that punishments are decreed for sinners and sinners for punishments by a just and irreproachable judgment—while nevertheless none of such defendants is compelled to sin either by the laws themselves or by the judges themselves, but is punished justly only because he has sinned, how much more must we believe that this is altogether the case in divine judgment, since eternal knowledge knows both the punishments themselves that are justly owed to sinners and the sinners themselves to whom they are owed? Although God himself is the author or cause of no one’s sin, he nevertheless most justly predestines both the punishments for sinners that he knows to be utterly just and the sinners—never unknown to him, but perfectly known through eternal truth—to eternal punishments.

None of us says what this man so frequently objects: that God by his predestination compels anyone to sin. Rather, God predestines sinners only to undergo punishment for what they have sinned, just as the laws themselves, by decreeing punishment, do not compel anyone to sin, but do not leave unpunished what was sinned spontaneously and voluntarily, exacting the just penalty of condemnation.

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0186A]

In the fifteenth chapter he sets forth definitions such as these:

1. Sins and their punishments are nothing.

2. God foreknew and predestined sins or punishments; “not to have foreknown” means “not to have predestined” and “not to have prepared”—as in the example of Judas, who was chosen instead of not chosen, a friend instead of not a friend, a son instead of not a son.

3. Punishments are evil and therefore not from God, from whom evil does not come; God does not punish what he has made, nor remove natural gifts from them.

4. Pain is the absence of health, darkness of light, silence of shouting, sadness of joy, labor of rest. In this way sins or punishments are foreknown or predestined.

5. In grieving, it is not pain itself but health itself that is known; and one would not know health if one did not have some conception of it.

6. The memory of health remains in the senses, while health itself resides in that substance which God created.

Of these six propositions, the first—that sins and punishments are nothing—has already been treated above as well as we could manage. For although sins can be called “nothing,” because they have no substance by which they exist or subsist in themselves, nevertheless abandoning justice—which is to sin—cannot occur except in some substance and through some substance, whether spiritual or bodily.

It occurs spiritually when truth, justice, and goodness are abandoned in the mind itself, and their opposites enter in: falsehood, iniquity, and wickedness. Although these have no subsisting nature, they are nevertheless great vices, or maladies of the nature—that is, of the mind itself—which they dominate and whose health and integrity they violate. Thus the mind itself, bent and crushed by them, is changed from free into servile and from healthy into infirm, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII, 34).

The Psalmist, sorrowfully and miserably imploring, says: “I said, ‘Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you’” (Ps. XL, 5).

But because these evils begin in the mind while being exercised especially through the body, the evil of the spiritual nature—that is, of the mind—passes into the evil of the bodily nature, that is, into the body itself. Thus, like a kind of pestilence, it stains and corrupts everything together, so that the soul, serving the sin that dominates it, brings its own body into the same servitude. The members of the body consequently become “weapons of iniquity for sin,” through which iniquity and sin themselves rule more powerfully and violently over both.

Therefore the Apostle says to the faithful: “Do not present your members as weapons of iniquity for sin, but present yourselves to God as those who are alive from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness for God” (Rom. VI, 13).

To this great and deadly sickness, which claims and wounds the whole human being, only that one true physician can apply a remedy and bring health who says of himself: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. IX, 12), and of whom it is written: “He himself will save his people from their sins” (Matt. I, 21). Of him the Apostle also says: “The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1 Tim. I, 15).

This man, then, who so persistently says and repeats that sins are nothing, what else is he trying to do, at the devil’s prompting, except make them seem insignificant in the hearts of his listeners, so that they do not grieve, do not recognize the magnitude of the evil that holds them, and do not take care to say with the Psalmist:

“Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy, and according to the multitude of your mercies blot out my iniquity. Wash me more and more from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. L, 2–5).

Let this deceiver, then, be removed from the ears and hearts of the faithful, and against so great [Col. 0187B] a misery let the great mercy of God be implored sorrowfully and simply. Against the multitude of such miseries, let the multitude of his mercies be sought, so that iniquity may be blotted out, the human being may be washed from that iniquity, and may be cleansed from the sin by which he had been made filthy and unclean.

Let him recognize his iniquity and not suppose that his sin is nothing. Let him not put it behind his back, but, always keeping it before his eyes, let him implore the one who said: “I have blotted out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist” (Isa. XLIV, 22).

Likewise, he attempts to diminish, reduce, and nullify the punishments owed to sins, insisting that they are always nothing. Although these punishments have no substance of existence in themselves, they are nevertheless inflicted through bodily natures—that is, through eternal fire, a lake of sulfur, and worms that never cease—upon both the bodies and the souls of the condemned, while tormenting souls and bodies together. Therefore, although they do not exist substantially, they do exist perpetually and miserably in the souls and bodies of those whom they torment without end.

Accordingly, let us not take pleasure in hearing from this wretched seducer that the punishments of sinners are nothing. Rather, let us hear what Truth most truly says:

“The rich man also died and was buried in hell. And lifting up his eyes, while he was in torments, he saw Abraham from afar, and Lazarus in his bosom. And crying out, he said, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame’” (Luke XVI, 22–24).

A little later, when he was pleading for his brothers, he said: “So that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torments” (ibid., 28).

Behold the unhappy—and most unhappily condemned—rich man: as soon as he died in body, his soul was buried in hell. There the soul itself was held in torments, and there it was tormented especially in the part by which it had sinned most, namely, the tongue. It was tormented in a flame burning and scorching it on every side.

And just as he had not given Lazarus, the beggar covered with sores and lying at his gate, the crumbs from his table, so he himself did not deserve to obtain from Lazarus even a drop of water from his finger by which he might be slightly refreshed. He begs for his brothers, so that they too may not come into that place of torments.

If, then, according to the voice of Truth, hell is a place of torments, and the souls of the wretched, stripped of their bodies, are buried there and remain in torments, and are tormented by the very things through which they sinned, so that judgment for them is without mercy because they did not show mercy (Jas. II, 13)—

Let every faithful person hear these things and be afraid. While there is still time, let him flee from the coming wrath, of which blessed John the Baptist said: “Who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke III, 7–8).

The Lord himself frequently calls this place of torments “the outer darkness,” “the furnace of fire,” and “the eternal fire prepared for the devil and all the impious,” where there will be pain without end, and from the pain an everlasting weeping of the eyes and gnashing of teeth (Matt. XXV, 41).

The prophet Isaiah also speaks of such punishment for the unhappy condemned: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be quenched; and they will remain, to the satisfaction of sight, before all flesh” (Isa. LXVI, 24).

Blessed Job also tearfully implores God, saying:

“Will not the shortness of my days soon come to an end? Leave me, then, so that I may lament my sorrow a little, before I go and do not return to the land that is dark and covered with the shadow of death; a land of misery and darkness, where the shadow of death, no order, and everlasting horror dwell” (Job X, 20–22).

And blessed John says in the Apocalypse: “They were cast into the burning lake of fire and sulfur, which is the second death, and they will be tormented day and night for ever and ever” (Rev. XX, 14). And as he says elsewhere: “The smoke of their torments will rise for ever and ever” (Rev. XIV, 11).

Let us believe these things faithfully, fear them truthfully, and drive this empty talker and seducer altogether from our ears. For, as the Apostle says, “bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. XV, 33). Hence another Scripture also warns us: “Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to an evil tongue” (Sir. XXVIII, 28).

**2.** Immediately after this, he adds his impious and frenzied rule by which he attempts to persuade us that, when we hear that something was done, we should understand that it was not done, and when we hear that something was said, we should understand that it was not said. He then adds and says:

“To have foreknown and predestined sins or punishments means not to have foreknown, not to have predestined, and not to have prepared them.”

This is most clearly contrary to faith and truth. If God did not foreknow all the future sins of angels and human beings, he would not be the foreknower of future things. And what else does this foolish man now leave us to conclude except what he says in his heart: “There is no God” (Ps. XIII, 1)? If God did not foreknow the punishments justly owed to sinners, how does he threaten them so constantly, so solemnly, and so terribly both in the Gospels and in the other Scriptures?

But this man says that sins and punishments are nothing because they do not possess a substance by which they exist in themselves. Therefore, he says, God could neither know nor foreknow what is nothing. As though God were ignorant of whatever does not exist, and of whatever he himself did not make to exist essentially and naturally, although by his omnipotent knowledge and foreknowledge he knows not only everything he made, but also what he did not make [Note: [Col. 0189D] When he says that God knows with equal certainty what he would not do and what he would do, and what was not going to happen and what was, he sufficiently and more than sufficiently argues that, wherever God’s knowledge is under discussion, no conjectural knowledge should be attributed to him. For although such knowledge is powerful and, as the jurists say, “most compelling,” it nevertheless cannot exclude uncertainty in every respect. Hence, with regard to conditional futures, we ought rather to admit in God a middle and conditional knowledge. — Fonseca, Molina, Suárez, Mascarenhas, in disputations and minor works on that knowledge.] He knows what he would do, and so he has always known what he would not do.

Thus he could in no way fail to know both what he willed to exist and what he did not will to exist. And what he did not will to possess a nature or substance of existence, he undoubtedly knew to be a great evil for the nature of an angelic or human subsistent being when it is changed for the worse by sin and tormented endlessly by punitive suffering.

As for his claim that God did not predestine punishments or sins: with respect to sins, this is indeed true, because he predestined only what he himself was going to do. All these things are certainly good and just. But with respect to punishments, it is manifestly false. He not only predestined them but also prepared them, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel:

“Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41).

He adds the example of Judas, quite absurdly and inappropriately, as was shown above.

Immediately afterward he adds and says: “Punishments are evil and therefore are not from God, from whom evil does not come.”

This contradicts what God himself testifies through the prophet: “I am the Lord, making peace and creating evil” (Isa. XLV, 7). Hence it is also written elsewhere: “If there is evil in a city, has the Lord not done it?” (Amos III, 6). And again: “Good things and evil, life and death, poverty and honor, are from the Lord” (Sir. XI, 14).

It must therefore be carefully and faithfully distinguished that one kind of evil is vice, opposed to good. This evil is not from God, but was either invented by the devil or committed by a human being. Another kind of evil signifies some affliction, whether temporal or eternal: hunger, pestilence, hostilities, devastation, death, and those things called eternal punishments. All these are from God, because they are prepared or inflicted only by his just ordering and just judgment.

This man, however, who insists that those eternal punishments are not from God must be compelled to say from whom he thinks they come: whether from the devil, for whom they have been prepared; or from human beings, who will be tormented there along with the devil; or from no one, so that they exist coeternal with God without any author.

After this he adds: “God does not punish what he has made, nor remove natural gifts from them.”

If this is considered more carefully, it is clear that the things God made in rational creatures, whether angelic or human, are spirit without a body in angels, and soul and body in human beings.

The natural gifts that God naturally gave these rational creatures, this man wants to be understood as the things about which he spoke at length above: that the human or angelic mind naturally possesses memory, understanding, will, existence, knowledge, and desire; that it naturally remembers itself, understands itself, loves itself; naturally possesses existence, so that it exists; knowledge, so that it knows itself; and desire, so that it loves itself.

He also asserts that free choice is merely a natural gift of the Creator, as he sufficiently demonstrated above in his own words.

Thus he says that God does not punish what he has made—that is, neither the angelic spirit in wicked angels nor spirit and body in condemned human beings.

And how can he say that eternal fire has been prepared for the devil and his angels if angelic spirits are not to be punished by that fire? How can he elsewhere say of human beings and to human beings: “Rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. X, 28), if neither soul nor body—which God made—will be punished by that torment of Gehenna?

But both spirits and bodies truly will be punished in Gehenna, as true faith believes and Truth itself testifies—not because God made them, but because they themselves did what God did not make, what God hates, and what he does not allow to remain unpunished: sins.

These sins cannot exist or be punished without their authors. They do not subsist by themselves, so as to be punished in themselves; rather, they are present in the depraved minds of angels or human beings, committed by those minds, clinging to them, and condemned together with them and in them.

Thus it is also true that Scripture says in praise of God: “For you love all things that are, and hate nothing that you have made” (Wis. XI, 25). And the Lord says: “He who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. X, 28).

For God loves his creature insofar as it is a nature and was created by him, and he hates it insofar as it has been corrupted. Hence it is written: “You hate all who work iniquity; you will destroy all who speak falsehood. The Lord abhors the man of blood and deceit” (Ps. V, 7–8). The prophet also says of certain people: “They became abominable, like the things they loved” (Hos. IX, 10). And again: “Likewise, both the impious person and his impiety are hateful to God” (Wis. XIV, 9).

Thus God loves all things that are and hates nothing that he has made, yet he does not allow these things, once rationally created and corrupted, depraved, and ruined, to remain unpunished and disordered.

The nature that did not wish to be blessed under God and from God, but desired to be free in itself and through itself, is justly ordered and punished in punishments. Thus what did not wish to submit while willing must submit unwillingly, and what could there have been eternally blessed becomes here eternally miserable. For it is impossible to escape the hand of God, as Scripture itself says (Tob. XIII, 2); what did not submit by choice must therefore submit by necessity.

But what benefit will those natural gifts bring to the rational natures established in that eternal condemnation, if, as this man says, they are not removed? It is clear that they will remain in them not for any fruit of blessedness, but solely to increase their torments: they will remember themselves, to suffer eternal pain from an evil conscience; they will understand that they are always miserable and always condemned; they will love themselves, so that they may grieve more deeply and endlessly over the loss of what they love.

[Note: He maintains that free choice is absent in the damned, in the same sense in which he previously taught that it is not found in sinners and in the state of fallen nature.] But how, or of what kind, will free choice exist in those whose will will no longer be able to abandon their iniquity or perform any good? As Scripture says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it diligently, for there is no work, reason, wisdom, or knowledge in the underworld, where you are going” (Eccl. IX, 10).

What benefit will it bring them always to be unhappily existent, to know their condemnation, and to wish—but be unable—to escape their punishment? Everything, therefore, that was given here for the purpose of doing good and earning the Lord’s grace will serve there, however slight its traces may remain, for punishment [Col. 0191B] and not for consolation.

But if the memory, understanding, and will of a rational creature are referred not to itself but to the Creator, what will memory do in those who have been wholly abandoned by God and separated from that eternal and true light? What, I ask, will memory do in them where no one can say: “I remembered God, and I was delighted” (Ps. LXXVI, 4), and where what is written will be fulfilled: “For in death there is no one who remembers you” (Ps. VI, 6)?

There will be no illumination of understanding by which God is known, sought, and found. There will be no loving devotion by which God is loved, desired, and enjoyed. For they themselves will be the outer darkness, having already been placed outside that light, whose illumination they will not enjoy.

They will be that dreadful night of which our Lord, the true light, says: “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world. The night comes when no one can work” (John IX, 4–5). As long, therefore, as he is in the world by illuminating grace, he is the light of those liberated from their darkness. But when he withdraws the grace of his illumination from those condemned to eternal blindness, what will remain for them except dreadful night, perpetual night, in which no one can work?

But if something similar is considered concerning the bodily senses—which are themselves certainly natural gifts of the Creator—[Note: He suggests that the faculty of sight will not operate in the damned, perhaps because the place of hell is so dark that visible forms cannot reach their eyes. St Basil teaches that God withdrew light from hellfire and left in it only the power to burn; nevertheless, it is probable that the damned will see demons and their other companions in punishment, since that sight will strike them more bitterly and grievously. Therefore, when the Church of Lyons deprives them of the sense of sight, this must be understood of a pleasant and delightful vision.] what benefit will sight bring there, where there will be no sight of light? Or, if it exists for a time, it will serve not for consolation but for more vehement pain: namely, so that they may see some good which they can no longer possess or earn.

Thus the rich man, condemned to the same infernal punishments, was able to see Abraham and Lazarus for a time (Luke XVI, 23), but for an increase of pain, not for the consolation of deliverance. This should be believed to have occurred before the final judgment, according to the hidden ordering of the Creator; afterward, however, nothing of this kind is read to occur.

What will hearing do there, where an ever-dreadful crash and sad, innumerable groaning will always be heard? What will smell do, where, according to what God threatens through the prophet, “there will always be stench instead of a sweet odor” (Isa. III, 24)? What will taste do, where there will be eternal hunger and thirst?

Concerning the city of the devil—that is, the whole multitude of the condemned—it is openly written in the Apocalypse: “In one day her plagues will come, death and mourning and famine, because God is strong, who has judged her” (Rev. XVIII, 8). The Gospel clearly speaks of thirst and the ever-burning tongue in the condemnation of that rich man.

What will the touch of the whole body do, where it can have no pleasure or sweetness, but where perpetual pain, eternal burning, and eternal torment will be felt?

What benefit, then, is there in what this man says, as though to console fools: that God does not punish what he has made, nor remove natural gifts from them? For God eternally punishes the corrupted nature for what it has done wickedly; and if he permits it to retain any natural gifts in that condemnation, all of them will serve to increase punishment, not to provide consolation.

What, then, does he mean when he adds: “Pain is the absence of health, darkness of light, silence of shouting, sadness of joy, labor of rest; thus sins or punishments are foreknown or predestined”?

If by these words he wished to persuade us that, just as we recognize pain in ourselves through the absence of health, recognize darkness through the absence of light, recognize silence through the absence of speech, feel sadness through the absence of joy, and feel labor through the absence of rest, so God foreknew sins or predestined punishments—so that he could know or foreknow sins only as the privation of justice, and recognize or predestine punishments only as the privation of blessedness—if, I say, this is what he thought and wished to persuade us of, what could be more terrible than such a thought, by which divine power is reduced to the level of human weakness?

For God’s power, always remaining the same, knows all things in itself and does not need to know anything outside itself. Nor does it know things made in one way and things not made in another, since it does not know the former through their presence or the latter through the absence of other things. Rather, by its eternal and unchangeable knowledge, it sees equally what it willed to exist and what it did not will to exist.

It does not recognize sins through the privation of justice. Rather, since he himself is supreme justice, he sees unchangeably in justice itself what is discordant or at variance with it [al.: in him]. Likewise, he does not recognize punishments through the absence of blessedness. Rather, since he himself is supreme blessedness, he sees unchangeably in himself the depth of punishments into which those who depart from his tranquility must be plunged.

Thus he sees whatever disagrees with justice not through the privation of justice, but in justice itself. Nor does he recognize punishments through the privation of blessedness; rather, in blessedness itself he sees what pain and labor will befall the one who is separated from his tranquility.

[Col. 0193A] He adds further and says: “In grieving, it is not pain itself but health itself that is known; and one would not know health if one did not have some conception of it.”

In these words he appears to affirm that the pain of eternal punishments cannot be known—that is, recognized—by the mind of the one suffering, because pain itself has no substance by which it exists or subsists. Therefore, since pain is substantially nothing, it is not pain itself that is recognized by the one who suffers, but rather health is recognized by comparison with it. Health exists naturally in the body and is contrary to pain itself. One who is wholly suffering in punishments would not know that health at all unless knowledge of it remained in his memory.

And as though to confirm these absurd and foolish claims by presenting some sort of reasoning, he adds and says: “The memory of health remains in the senses, while health itself resides in that substance which God created.”

Perhaps by this he means that, in the senses of one who is always suffering in that condemnation, the memory of health arises as though from the recollection produced by pain itself—namely, in the senses by which either body or soul feels those pains. Health itself, however, can supposedly be understood as remaining in that condemnation because the substance of the human being whom God created is not consumed or destroyed in the perpetuity of soul and body, but endures eternally as though in a certain health of its own fullness.

He seems to say all this so that, through that everlasting pain of punishments, he may assert that neither knowledge of health, nor memory of it, nor health itself perishes in those who are to be tormented.

On the contrary, all these things—the knowledge and memory of health in the mind that is always suffering, and the preservation of that nature which can never be destroyed—do not contribute to any grace or pleasantness of salvation, but rather to an accumulation of pain. Thus the condemned person suffers not only through the sensation of body and soul, but also, while remembering and recognizing the good of health that he has utterly lost, is punished in that very memory and knowledge.

Let the madman, then, say that health exists amid eternal and every kind of pain, when what he thinks and supposes remains there as evidence of health is nothing other than material for pain. Thus, while the one being tormented never comes to an end, neither do the torments themselves come to an end:

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0193D]

In the sixteenth chapter he proposes twelve definitions, saying:

1. No nature is punished by nature.

2. The punishments of sins are nothing other than the sins themselves.

3. In the eternal fire there is no punishment other than the absence of blessed happiness.

4. No one there exists who does not naturally have implanted in him a conception of the blessedness that is absent, together with a desire for it. The wretched will possess a conception and knowledge of happiness and truth; and therefore they are not wretched and are not punished.

5. In the devil and impious human beings, nothing is punished except the perversity of their own will; it is not nature that sinned, but the will.

6. In the first human being, it was not the generality of nature that sinned, but the individual will of each person.

7. If that nature were to sin, since it is one, it would certainly perish in its entirety.

8. Therefore no nature is punished, because it is from God and does not sin; rather, the voluntary movement of desire is punished.

9. Therefore the impious do not suffer punishments for what God made, but for what pride wickedly invented.

10. The desire of the perverse will is tormented when it is not permitted to possess the things it wickedly or unworthily desires.

11. Evil does not come from any good.

12. The person who here changes free choice of the will—which is a gift of natural understanding, that is, the mind’s acuity—into uses of shamefulness will there be justly deprived altogether of enjoying the honor of truth and will not avoid the darkness of eternal ignorance.

In the first of these statements—“No nature is punished by nature”—he seems to have spoken in this way because every nature, having been created by God, the good author, is good insofar as it is nature. For example, the nature of the soul or of the body is good; and the nature of fire, insofar as it is nature, is likewise good.

Since both are naturally good, this man seems rightly to say and define that no nature is punished by another nature, since, according to his reasoning, two goods cannot be contrary to one another, lest one good nature become a punishment for another good nature.

By the most evident fallacy of this kind of argument, he seeks to overthrow in the hearts of his listeners the firmest truth of the faith. All the faithful unquestionably believe and confess that, through the nature of eternal fire and in that nature, the nature of evil spirits and the nature of ruined human beings—that is, their souls and bodies—will be condemned, punished, and tormented without end by God’s just and eternal judgment:

“He who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna,” and he who, “after he has killed, has authority to cast into Gehenna” (Matt. X, 28).

Nor is the certainty of faith concerning only those eternal punishments in which the angelic nature and human nature alike will be tormented by the nature of eternal fire—fire which, given here to human beings by the goodness of the Creator as a comfort, will there be turned against them as a punishment by the just severity of the Judge. No, I say, it is not only concerning these that faith is certain that this will come to pass; it is also established, in the common judgment of human beings, as utterly certain that nature is never punished except by nature. Thus the nature of the body is either punished by itself—as when it falls away from health and succumbs to sickness and weakness, while the good of health is diminished in it and it suffers the evil of weakness from itself—or by the withdrawal of another nature that serves it for sustenance or some other comfort: for example, when the nature of food, drink, light, clothing, or anything of that kind is withdrawn from it as a punishment. As a result, it wastes away and grows weak from hunger and thirst, is afflicted by the horror of darkness, or is tormented by the hardship of cold. Or certainly the human body itself is punished by the nature of another thing: [Col. 0195A] thus the bodies of robbers are indeed punished by the force of whips, swords, and various tortures, which are inflicted as punishments upon their own nature by other natures. Since these things are so, and nature is never punished except either by itself in itself, or by the withdrawal of the usefulness of another nature, or by violence inflicted upon it, how can this man say that no nature is punished by nature? His purpose is thereby, insofar as he can, to destroy the truth of eternal punishments, where the natures both of spirits and of bodies, in accordance with evangelical and apostolic truth, will be tormented by the nature of eternal fire day and night for ever and ever (Apoc. XIV, 10).

But if he says this because natures do not harm one another except through their qualities—as, for example, fire and water, whose proper qualities are that water is naturally moist and fire naturally dry—and therefore the moisture of water can extinguish fire, while the dryness of fire can dry up water’s ignited moisture, so that these things do not seem to oppose one another because they are natures, but because in their qualities they are contrary to one another: if, I say, he says this for that reason, let him know that in our faith there is no difference between saying that natures are punished by natures and saying that the natures themselves, through their natural qualities, are mutually punitive; for one and the same Creator created both—the nature and the quality inherent in the nature. Therefore both together are most rightly called one nature, with one distinguished from another by its proper quality by the all-wise Creator.

Moreover, although the nature of an angelic or human spirit is immortal, nevertheless, by the power of the Creator and of God the just Avenger, it will be bound punitively and eternally to that corporeal and eternal fire, just as here, by the same power of the supreme Creator, the human spirit is bound to an earthly body and cannot be released except by the will and judgment of him who bound it. The nature of the human body in that eternal fire of the damned will likewise be immortal for punishment, so that it will never be released by death from enduring eternal punishments; it will be capable of suffering yet incorruptible, so that it will be afflicted without end by every kind of pain, torment, and punishment. Scripture terrifyingly announces that this punishment must be avoided with every effort, saying: “Humble your spirit greatly, because the vengeance of the flesh of the ungodly is fire and worms” (Eccli. VII, 19). And again: “For the almighty Lord will take vengeance upon them; on the day of judgment he will visit them. He will give fire and worms to their flesh, so that they may burn and feel it for ever” (Judith XVI, 20–21).

Long ago someone proposed a similar question concerning the mutual opposition of natures. Since we consider it necessary, for the admonition and strengthening of readers, to insert here briefly how he proposed it and how blessed Augustine destroyed it with the clearest reasoning—especially because the one who proposed it was either Pelagius himself or some Pelagian, as this man also is—we shall give the question as blessed Augustine recalls it:

“Why is it that he asks: ‘Who made the spirit of man?’ and answers himself, without doubt, ‘God’? And again he asks: ‘Who created the flesh?’ and likewise answers, ‘Again, I believe, God.’ He asks a third time: ‘Is God, who created both, good?’ He answers: ‘No one doubts it.’ He asks further: ‘And is each of the things that the good Creator created good?’ To this he answers: ‘It must be confessed.’ Then he concludes: ‘If, therefore, both spirit and flesh are good, as having been created by a good Creator, how can two good things be contrary to one another?’”

After this, blessed Augustine adds his contrary response, saying:

“I omit saying that his entire line of reasoning would be thrown into confusion if someone asked him: ‘Who made heat and cold?’ For he would doubtless answer, ‘God.’ Let him himself then conclude whether these can either be called not good or fail to appear contrary to one another. Perhaps here he says: ‘These are qualities of substances, not substances.’ That is so; it is true. But they are natural qualities and unquestionably belong to God’s creation. Substances are said to be contrary to one another—not in themselves, but through their qualities—as water and fire are, and so forth.”

These are the points that the holy teacher develops in order to convict and overthrow the madness of that wicked man.

Since, then, the terror and truth of eternal punishments are commended to our faith so openly and in so many ways, in order to instill the most salutary fear and arouse us to continual amendment, how has this man dared to add and say that the punishments of sins are nothing other than the sins themselves? For faith holds with complete certainty that there are other punishments for sins, which souls suffer in the present precisely because of the merit of their sins, when they have been abandoned by God, abandoned by the light of justice, from the contemplation of truth, and from the illumination of charity, and sometimes even handed over to a depraved mind. Divine Scripture most clearly testifies that these punishments are inflicted in the present upon sinners and lovers of bodily pleasures. Thus God says of certain people: “My spirit will not remain in these men for ever, because they are flesh” (Gen. VI, 3). Thus the ungodly will say at the end, grieving and groaning: “The light of justice did not shine for us, and the sun did not rise for us” (Wis. V, 6). And Scripture says of these same ungodly: “Their wickedness blinded them” (Wis. II, 21). And, generally, of those who hate their brothers: “Everyone who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes” (I John II, 11). And it is written of certain people: “Since they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a depraved mind, to do what is improper” (Rom. I, 28).

The sins themselves are punishments of sinful souls, because through them the health of those souls is corrupted and violated, and their conscience becomes wretched, troubled, and full of anxieties. Thus sins themselves become the punishments of sinners by the just and terrible judgment of God; yet, on account of those same sins, other exceedingly severe punishments are immediately imposed in the present, as was shown above. Of all these present punishments, by which the souls of sinners are continually struck and punished, blessed Moses testifies most clearly in Deuteronomy, [Col. 0197A] saying of almighty God: “Showing mercy to thousands of those who love him” (Deut. V, 10), “and repaying those who hate him immediately, so that he destroys them and delays no longer, promptly giving them what they deserve” (Deut. VII, 10).

There are, therefore, even in the present, exceedingly severe punishments of souls: their own sins; the exceedingly severe punishment of the soul is its very abandonment by God, by which sinners are continually repaid according to the merits of their sins. But there remain for the future those punishments of eternal torments of which it is written, in the Lord’s words: “The rich man also died, and was buried in hell” (Luke XVI, 13). And again: “Lest the adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be thrown into prison. Amen I say to you: you will not come out from there until you have paid the last farthing” (Matt. V, 25–26). And elsewhere, when speaking of the wicked servant who refused to forgive his fellow servant the debt that had also been forgiven him, he said: “Then his master, angered, handed him over to the torturers until he should repay the whole debt” (Matt. XVIII, 34).

Since Scripture testifies so openly to these punishments of sinners—whether in their sins themselves, or in their abandonment by God, inflicted upon them immediately in the present according to the merit of their sins; or in the external punishments of various scourges, divinely inflicted upon sinners for the present; or in the damnation of eternal torments, reserved for the end after all these things—and since the faith of the Church holds this so firmly, let all who are deceived by such falsehoods and illusions through this most vain man hear what the Apostle solemnly declares to all the faithful, saying: “Let no one deceive you with empty words; for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience” (Eph. V, 6).

In explaining these words of the Apostle, blessed Jerome adds:

“The words that deceive and trip people up are empty and void; but those that build up their hearers are full, abundant, and rich. Since, then, there are many who say that punishments are not destined for sins, nor torments to be applied from outside, but that the sin itself and the consciousness of the offense serve as the punishment, while the worm does not die in the heart and fire is kindled in the soul—like a fever, which does not torture the sick person from outside, but, seizing the bodies themselves, punishes what it possesses without the infliction of external torment—he called these persuasions and fraudulent snares empty and void words. They seem to possess a kind of rhetorical flower and to flatter sinners. But while they give them confidence, they drive them all the more toward eternal punishments. For God is angry about nothing so much as when a sinner, proud, erect, and stiff-necked, is not bent into weeping and does not ask mercy for his offense.”

Thus speaks the holy teacher, both refuting the error of the ancient heretics concerning this matter and overthrowing, by apostolic truth, the fraudulent lies and inventions of this man.

Yet this man dares still greater and more detestable things, and adds, saying: “In eternal fire there is no other punishment than the absence of blessed happiness.” Here he is rightly asked why evil angels and wicked human beings are to be sent into eternal fire, if they will suffer from that fire no punishment and no torment. Is it merely for this reason: that those who now dwell either in the air or on earth may begin to have a new dwelling place in the fire, where, as it is written concerning the three holy boys condemned to the furnace of Babylon, the fire had no power over their bodies, the hair of their heads was not singed, and the smell of fire did not pass through them? What remains, then, except that, just as Scripture says of them—“An angel of the Lord descended with Azariah and his companions into the furnace, shook the flame of the fire out of the furnace, and made the middle of the furnace like a blowing wind laden with dew; the fire did not touch them at all, nor distress them, nor cause them any harm” (Dan. III, 49–50)—so he should strive, in wondrous madness, to assert the same concerning these people?

If it were so—if such a miracle could ever occur—would it be counted among the great and marvelous works divinely accomplished: that so innumerable a multitude of apostate angels and ruined human beings should be in the midst of immense and seething flames, yet the fire should not touch them at all, forgetting the force of its power, so that the devil and his angels might be preserved unharmed? Who has ever heard of such a thing, or who could endure the madness of such great impiety?

For if there will be no punishment in the eternal fire of the damned, then consequently there will be no glory in the eternal reward of the just. The one who most truly promised this glory, saying, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV, 34), most truly threatened that punishment, saying, “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., 41). He also added, with immovable truth, concerning both: “Then these will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (ibid., 46).

If, therefore, we ask what that kingdom is which was prepared for the righteous from the foundation of the world, let us faithfully hear that it is eternal life. If we ask what we must believe the fire to be into which wicked human beings and angels are to be sent, let us likewise faithfully hear that it is everlasting punishment. There can be no greater glory than eternal life, nor greater punishment than everlasting torment: the former belongs to those placed in the kingdom, the latter to those condemned in the eternal fire.

[Col. 0198D] Concerning this punishment of eternal fire, blessed John plainly testifies in the Apocalypse, saying: “They were thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, and they will be tormented day and night for ever and ever” (Apoc. XX, 9–10). And elsewhere: “The smoke of their torments will rise for ever and ever” (Apoc. XIX, 3). Therefore condemned angels and human beings will never be able to be at rest or free from punishments in the eternal fire, since, as the Truth says, “They will be tormented day and night for ever and ever,” and the smoke of their torments will rise for ever and ever. Such punishment also overtakes them now. Concerning them, Scripture says, in likeness to that rich man dressed in purple who was condemned: “They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they go down to the underworld” (Job XXI, 13). Thus they too, as it is written of him, immediately begin to be in torments, to be tortured in flame, and to be assigned to the place of eternal torments.

As we have heard, this man is accustomed to say, whenever someone begins to oppose him in conversation concerning such matters according to the truth of the faith: “What do you want? Reason is defeating you.” What sort of reason is this, then—empty of all reason, alien to all truth, and frenzied and fantastic with the spirit of the most impious error? He wants people to abandon the truth of Christ and follow his fantastic and demonic shadows.

But after saying that those condemned in eternal fire feel no other punishment than the absence of blessed happiness, he nevertheless adds what amounts to a kind of happiness for them, saying: “In it”—that is, in the absence of blessed happiness—“there is no one who does not naturally possess within himself an awareness of the absent happiness and a desire for it.” He adds that the wretched will possess an awareness and knowledge of happiness and truth, and therefore will not be wretched or punished.

By these words he plainly tries to assert that all who will be in that damnation—which he considers nothing other than the absence of the happiness enjoyed by the saints—will naturally possess within themselves knowledge and desire of that very happiness in which they will not participate. Repeating and reinforcing this point, he says that they will possess knowledge and awareness of truth and happiness, and therefore will not be wretched, nor be punished.
