Thus, according to his meaning, because they will possess knowledge, awareness, and desire of the happiness and truth whose absence will condemn them, they will somehow not be wretched though wretched, and not punished though punished. For insofar as they will be in the absence of happiness and blessedness, they can be called wretched and condemned; but insofar as they will possess awareness, knowledge, and desire of that happiness and truth which will be absent from them, they can be said not to be wretched or condemned.

But the faith of the Church truly knows that no condemnation of a rational creature can be greater than separation from God: being enlightened by none of his illumination, visited by none of his grace, saved by no deliverance, and blessed by none of his vision and contemplation.

Angels and human beings condemned to such great misery, completely excluded from possession of happiness and truth—even if they felt no external punishment or torment—what benefit would it be to them to possess, as this man promises them, knowledge, awareness, and desire of happiness and truth? Indeed, possessing even the smallest awareness of truth would serve them more for torment, while they could never attain its foreknowledge; possessing some desire for eternal happiness, yet never rejoicing in its possession. Therefore, far be it from us to believe that those utterly separated from God are not most wretched, or to say that those completely excluded from eternal happiness are not punished.

Truly wretched and truly condemned for eternity will be those who will always be exiles from truth and happiness, illuminated by no light of truth and consoled by no delight of happiness. Yet, in addition to this complete and supreme misery, external punishment will also be present for them without end, so that inwardly they may be tortured by the unhappiness of conscience and outwardly by the fire of Gehenna. The Psalmist briefly indicates both punishments, speaking to the very Judge of the living and the dead: “Let your hand be found by all your enemies; your right hand will find all who hate you. You will set them like a furnace of fire at the time of your appearing; the Lord in his anger will trouble them, and fire will devour them” (Ps. XX, 9–10).

Blessed Augustine explains this very briefly and very fully in these words:

“‘You will set them,’ he says, ‘burning inwardly with the conscience of their impiety at the time of your manifestation. Then, troubled by the Lord’s vengeance after the accusation of conscience, they will be given over to eternal fire to be devoured.’”

Since these things are so, we must carefully ask what, according to the rule of true faith, we ought to think about those who will be punished by that eternal damnation, so that from the condition of those who will be eternally condemned there we may understand how much the Lord deigns to grant, why no amendment can then be possible, and why no deliverance can come from there.

First, therefore, we must consider what the Catholic faith holds most firmly: no human being who departs from the body through death can acquire for himself any good merit by which he might either abandon the iniquity in which he died or himself be changed for the better. For although there are some who—as the piety of the faith itself teaches—receive forgiveness of sins after death, assisted by the prayers, offerings, and almsgiving of the Church, and, having been cleansed by certain purgatorial punishments, deserve to be joined to eternal blessedness [Note: [Col. 0199D] Let the innovators of our age take heed: purgatory, as well as suffrages for the dead, is here firmly established and sealed in the Church], this does not furnish them with any good merit added after death, but rather with merit acquired before death. Their merit in bodily life was evidently such that even after death they deserved to be assisted by such remedies.

The Apostle plainly shows this when he says: “For we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to the body according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (II Cor. V, 10). What belongs to the body, whether good or evil, is what the soul did while it was in the body. For just as, before the body, the soul could perform neither good nor evil, since it did not yet exist, so after laying aside the body it cannot do anything good or evil, since the time for acting and working ended with the death of the body.

Indeed, those who are bound only by the guilt of original sin and thus depart from the body without a saving remedy are condemned according to the evils belonging to the body [Note: [Col. 0200D] He appears to place original sin in the body, as certain Scholastics did—Durandus and the Master in Book II, distinctions 30 and 31—where he says that through the sin of the first parent the body was first infected through the seed, and that the body conceived from the seed was again infected, and then the soul was infected through the body, just as precious liquid is poured into a polluted vessel. Although these opinions are now judged rash, they do not expressly conflict with the faith. We therefore prefer to assert that the Church of Lyon intended only to condemn the opinion of those who maintained that the soul contracted the original stain before union with the body], because in the body and together with the body they contracted that original debt on account of which they deserved to be condemned eternally.

All, therefore, must be manifested, as the Apostle says, before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive and carry away what belongs to the body (II Cor. V, 10)—that is, what he did or contracted in the body. For certainly he could do nothing before the body, nor can he do anything after the body, since for each person there is no longer a time for acting, but only for receiving according to his actions.

It must therefore be certain to our faith that none of those who will be punished with eternal damnation on the day of judgment will have carried away from this life any such merit by which he might justly be freed from that eternal destruction. For if any one of them had prepared such merit for himself in the present life, he would certainly never be handed over by that just Judge to eternal damnation. But all who are to be punished by that damnation undoubtedly carried away from here such merit that, by just judgment, they deserve never to be absolved from it and never to be delivered.

But in order that that damnation, just as it is just, may also deserve to be eternal, the reason will be that no amendment of past things can then be available, and no improvement of future things can be earned. There will indeed be repentance for past evils there, and there will also be a desire for liberation and rescue; yet it will have no effect.

Where, then, will the mercy of God be at that time? He will be moved neither by so great and so prolonged a repentance to forgive, nor by any desire of the damned, or even by the groans of those who plead, to deliver them. And how will the Just One disregard these things? How will he fail to regard such great pain of conscience and such great affliction of his creature? What, I ask, will be the reason that nothing salutary, nothing acceptable, can be done there? If it could be done, it would never be rejected by such great mercy or such great justice.

Why, then, can it not be done, except because, when God has wholly withdrawn from them, there can be in them no special grace by which the piety of faith, hope, and charity might be granted to them, so that by such piety they might repent of past things and desire future things—that is, by piously believing, piously hoping, and loving?

And because, as has been said, they will be utterly separated from God and preserved for eternal punishments solely by the power of his omnipotence, they will never be participants in the Holy Spirit, even if there should be some faith there—whether arising from memory of past things that they heard or learned here, or from the terror and manifestation of present things that will then appear: namely, when the power and authority of God and of his Christ are manifested to all, both in the majesty that will appear in his judgment and in the eternal reward of the righteous and eternal damnation of the wicked.

These things will certainly be unknown to no one, unacknowledged by no one, and worshipped by all—even if only under the necessity imposed by terror. For then every creature, subjected generally to the Creator, whether through piety, as in the holy angels and holy human beings, or through necessity, as in the evil angels and ungodly human beings, will perfectly fulfill what the Apostle recalls as having been written by the prophet, saying: “As I live, says the Lord God, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to the Lord” (Rom. XIV, 11).

Hence, in that same judgment, what Scripture foretold would happen to the ungodly will also plainly occur: “They will repent among themselves, and groan in anguish of spirit: ‘These are the ones whom we once held in derision and as an object of reproach. We foolishly considered their life madness and their end without honor. How then have they been counted among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints? Therefore we have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not shine for us, and the sun did not rise for us’” (Wis. V, 3–6), along with the other words they will utter on that day, filled with manifold grief.

If, therefore, from so great a manifestation of divine power and of Christ the Lord, and from the terror of so great and so manifest an eternal Judge, there should be some faith in those who once believed, or even in unbelievers who will be compelled to believe by such present majesty and terror, so that in their lamentation they say, as we have already recalled, “We have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not shine for us, and the sun did not rise for us” (ibid., 6), nevertheless such faith in those who, as has been repeatedly said, will be utterly abandoned by God and illuminated by none of his grace will certainly not arise from the piety of love, but from the necessity of terror.

Blessed James the Apostle testifies that such faith exists also in demons, saying: “The demons believe, and they tremble” (Jas. II, 19). Such faith, therefore, will avail them not for salvation but for confusion, so that, as it is written in the Psalm, “They may be ashamed and troubled for ever and ever, and may be confounded and perish” (Ps. LXXXII, 18).

There can no longer be any hope in them, condemned by an eternal sentence and utterly despairing of their deliverance. Likewise, there can be no charity in them by which they might piously love God and their neighbor according to God, or in God, or for God, since God himself, who is charity, will have abandoned them and that grace of the Spirit will not be present with them, of which the Apostle says: “Because the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. V, 5). At the same time, the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the charity of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit will have withdrawn from them.

Even if that rich man, already condemned in the underworld, seemed to have loved his brothers whom he had left behind in the flesh according to God, since he anxiously worked and pleaded on their behalf so that they would not come into that place of torments (Luke XVI, 27), nevertheless this was not truly done according to God. It was forced from him not by the impulse of divine charity, but either by terror of his present condemnation or by human affection.

Since, therefore, through God’s illumination and the gift of the Holy Spirit, there can no longer be in them the piety of faith and charity, nor any expectation of good hope, their repentance for past things and their desire for future things will not be accepted by the just and merciful Judge, because these things will not then arise from piety and the love of divine grace, but only from the necessity of tribulation and anguish.

Thus, when the light of divine illumination has been wholly withdrawn from them, and they have been completely excluded and alienated from that joy promised to the good and faithful servant by the Lord’s words, “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV, 21), they will remain outside the light of God. This will mean being cast into the outer darkness and into that dreadful night of which the Lord says: “The night is coming when no one can work” (John IX, 4). And elsewhere he mercifully warns, saying: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John XII, 35).

Therefore those who will be in such darkness and such a night will no longer be able to perform anything piously or fruitfully—anything that the just Judge might accept, or by which they themselves might deserve to be freed from that eternal damnation. And because there can be no pious repentance, there will consequently be no forgiveness of offense, and therefore no end to punishment.

Whatever recollection of truth or blessedness may be in them will be only as great as the human mind can reach, however faintly; it will not be of the kind that is ordinarily inspired by God’s grace. For then what Scripture says terrifyingly to each person will be fulfilled: “Only affliction will give understanding to what is heard” (Isa. XXVIII, 19). And again: “For there is neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge in the underworld, where you are hastening” (Eccl. IX, 10).

For there will be no work there by which any good merit may be acquired; no reason either to excuse oneself justly or to make worthy satisfaction; no wisdom arising from the illumination of truth; and no knowledge in the practice of any virtue. How, then, according to this man, will they possess knowledge and awareness of the truth, whose illumination and contemplation they will be deprived of eternally?

[Note: [Col. 0203D] He says that the damned are not carried by desire toward blessedness, but later explains himself as follows: “They do not have desire,” he says, “that is, the piety of desire, because through self-love, without any regard for God, they desire blessedness itself.”]

How will they possess desire for that same truth and blessedness, when there will be in them no love of piety by which truth might truly be loved or true blessedness genuinely desired? Perhaps they will be able to possess some knowledge of truth insofar as they recognize themselves to be worthy of such punishments, recognize themselves to have been condemned by just judgment, and recognize that they will never be freed from the eternal and just judgment [or, “Judge”]. But all this will profit them for torment, not for the consolation of comfort. In the same way they may perhaps possess some desire for their own blessedness [f., here the word “not” may be understood], so that they might deserve to be drawn out of those torments and refreshed by some peace or rest.

To know and desire God’s own truth and God’s own blessedness is a gift belonging to the pious, those illuminated by God’s Spirit, not to the ungodly condemned to perpetual blindness and unhappiness. For even if some of those who once believed and knew may there remember to some extent that truth or blessedness, this memory will benefit them only in making them grieve more, repent more, and recognize more justly that they have been condemned. They will desire to have time for amendment, so that they might escape punishment, but they will not possess the piety of that desire by which they might deserve God.

[Note: [Col. 0203D] Erigena was approaching the heresy of Pelagius by wishing the damned to enjoy natural blessedness. Indeed, he held a far worse view than Pelagius, because what Pelagius had established only concerning infants dying without baptism, he himself maintained concerning adult sinners. — Bellarmine, Book I, *On Purgatory*, chapter 9.]

Let this man, therefore, cease to say that those who will not be illuminated by God, who will be alienated from the life of God and consoled by no sweetness of truth or blessedness, are neither wretched nor condemned. For this is true and eternal misery: to be alienated from the blessed life. No greater condemnation can exist than to be utterly excluded and rejected by God and no longer able to possess any hope or recourse to God.

Let every believer therefore consider how vain and insane this man’s endeavor is: he seeks to maintain that those who can never be blessed in God may be blessed from themselves—that is, not by some grace of God, but by certain goods of nature, as he supposes. Even if almighty God leaves these goods in them, they will serve as testimony to his goodness and as testimony, for them, to his just condemnation, so that they too may recognize that the truth of the just judgment has been fulfilled in them and may thus be condemned even by their own judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0204D] Much was missing here; it has been restored from the manuscript Codex Corbeiensis.]

This horrifically ineffable and ineffably horrible damnation of the wicked and impious, without any consolation of divine mercy and without any illumination of truth, blessed Augustine briefly impresses upon us and warns us by every means to avoid, saying:

> “The lower hells must be avoided—that is, the more severe punishments after this life, where there can be no recollection of truth; and because there is no reasoning there, there is therefore no activity of reason, since the true Light does not suffuse it, the Light which enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1:9). Let us therefore hasten and walk while the day is present, lest darkness overtake us. Let us hasten to be freed from the second death, where no one remembers God, and from hell, where no one will confess to God.”

Again, when he was expounding the words of the Psalm where it says, “But in hell, who will confess to you?” (Psalm 6:6), he acknowledged, he says, that the rich man was confessing in hell—the man of whom the Lord says that he saw Lazarus at rest, while he himself was suffering in torments (Luke 16:23)—confessing to such an extent that he even wished his own people to be warned to restrain themselves from sins, on account of the punishments which they do not believe exist in hell. Thus, although he confessed in vain that those torments had deservedly befallen him, he nevertheless wished his own people to be instructed so that they would not fall into them.

What, then, does “But in hell, who will confess to you?” (Psalm 6:6) mean? Is “hell” to be understood as that place into which the impious will be hurled after judgment, where, because of the deeper darkness, they will no longer see any light of God to which they might confess anything? For this man, even now, with his eyes raised, although an immense depth lay between them, could nevertheless see Lazarus established in repose; and by comparison with him he was compelled to confess his own merits.

In these words of the holy teacher, it may not be necessary to understand two hells: one into which the souls of the damned are now hurled, and another into which those same punished souls will be hurled after judgment together with their bodies. Rather, one and the same hell may be understood, now somewhat milder in the torments of souls, but after judgment more savage and more horrible in the torments of souls together with bodies.

For our Lord also appears in the Gospels to signify both punishments of hell—namely, that of the present age and that of the future—under the single name of Gehenna. Concerning the present punishment he says: “Fear him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna” (Luke 12:5); and concerning the future: “Rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matthew 10:28).

The holy Fathers of the Church are also frequently found to have understood the same eternal fire as being imposed upon condemned impious persons both before and after judgment. Yet the aforementioned teacher indicates that there is such a great difference between the two condemnations that, now, through certain divinely arranged visions and manifestations, the light of God can to some extent be perceived there; through that light, at least, the damned are compelled to confess their crimes. While they behold something of the divine light, they have, by the very regard of that vision granted to them, someone to whom they may confess.

Then, however, when they have already been overwhelmed by greater and irremediable darkness, they will deserve to behold nothing of that kind by which they might be stirred to any confession. Thus the statement written about them will be understood with complete truth: “For there is no one in death who remembers you; and in hell, who will confess to you?” (Psalm 6:6).

Therefore the prophet Isaiah, foreseeing this irremediable damnation and most earnestly warning that it must be foreseen and avoided, says that there will then be no place for finding God and no grace for calling upon God: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isaiah 55:6). He plainly shows that he cannot in any way be found in that damnation, nor can he be appeased by any invocation or supplication from the wretched damned, as though he were far away and utterly alienated from them.

[Note: [Col. 0205D] Up to this point was omitted in the manuscript Codex Thuaneus.]

This man adds further and says that in the devil and in impious human beings only the perversity of their own will is punished, and that it was not nature that sinned, but the will.

Here again is something new and unheard-of. What he says is that, in the devil and in impious human beings condemned to eternal destruction, God does not punish their nature, but only their perverse will, because, according to his view, their nature did not sin, but their will did.

Yet the faith of the Church truly knows and most firmly holds that rational nature, whether in angels or in human beings, just as it possesses reason naturally implanted in it by God, also possesses will naturally implanted in it by God; and that the whole of this—that is, nature together with its reason, or nature together with its will—is at the same time one nature. Thus this rational nature cannot exist without will, nor will without nature.

[Note: [Col. 0205D] He argues against Erigena personally, since Erigena maintained that only the will, and not nature, sinned—as though the will could do something that the human being did not do. He rightly asserts that Erigena raves and is insane in this matter.]

Whatever this nature wills, therefore, cannot be alien to nature itself and referred to the will alone. For when this nature wills something, it certainly does not will it in one part of itself while not willing it in another; rather, the whole of it wills. Whether, then, it is moved toward the good, it acts in this entirely by its will; or, conversely, toward evil, it likewise acts in its entirety. Thus, whether it is moved toward good or toward evil, it is moved as a whole.

When it is moved toward the good, this is its virtue; when it is moved toward evil, this is its vice. And therefore, just as through virtue the whole of it becomes better when it is moved toward good, so through vice the whole of it becomes worse when it is moved toward evil.

It is not, then, improved through virtue by the will alone, but in its entirety; nor is it made worse through vice by the will alone, but in its entirety. Thus, through virtue, not the will alone but the whole nature itself is made good; and, conversely, through vice, not the will alone but the whole nature itself is made evil—not by losing the goodness of its substance, but by being corrupted and perverted through the vice of its own will.

When this nature acts rightly, it acts as a whole, because the whole of it wills this. And when it acts perversely, it likewise acts as a whole, because the whole of it wills this. It is therefore just in God that, for good deeds, the whole of it should be glorified, and conversely, for evil deeds, the whole of it should be condemned.

For if, among wicked angels and impious human beings, it was not nature that sinned but the will, then among holy angels and devout human beings their nature likewise did not act rightly or merit anything good; only the will did so. And if, among those wicked angels and impious human beings, not the whole nature but only the will will be condemned, then among these—that is, among holy angels and human beings—not the whole nature but only the will will be glorified.

But faith holds with complete certainty and without doubt that the whole nature of the holy angels has already been blessed and glorified; likewise, the whole nature of holy human beings is to be blessed and glorified. Accordingly, the contrary must also be held without any doubt: that among wicked angels and impious human beings not the will alone but their whole nature will be condemned, because the whole of it sinned.

Against all faith and the truth of God, however, this man introduced such an argument in order to say that evil angels and evil human beings will be condemned in the will alone. In this way he could make room for his insane deception and could say, as he had already said above, that in the eternal fire there will be no other punishment than the absence of blessedness.

Thus, according to his view, the angelic or human nature will suffer no external punishment there, because it did not sin; only the will will be punished inwardly in its conscience, because, as he says, only the will sinned. And it will be punished not by any external torment of punishment, but only by the absence of blessedness, which it will not possess, and by the prohibition of its perverse desire, which it will not be permitted to fulfill.

How contrary all this is to the faith and the truth, and how much it favors the devil’s will by flattering human beings, so that they may neither truly acknowledge that they sinned, since their nature is defended as having not sinned, nor truly acknowledge that they will be punished, since not their nature but only their will is said to be condemned—this is manifest to all who care for their salvation, reject heretical inventions and ravings far from themselves, and faithfully follow evangelical and apostolic truth.

But so that anyone who reads what we have said against his insane and impious definition may be instructed more certainly and firmly, we add here the words of blessed Augustine, in which he teaches most clearly and fully concerning this matter, saying:

> “There is nothing that is called evil if there is no good; but a good entirely free from every evil is an integral good. When evil is present, however, the good is corrupted or defective; and evil can never exist where there is no good at all. Thus a remarkable conclusion follows: since every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good, when a corrupt nature is called a bad nature, nothing else seems to be meant than that what is good is evil, and that nothing is evil except what is good; nor would anything be evil if the thing itself that is evil were not a nature.”

A little later he says:

> “We must beware lest we fall into that prophetic statement where it is written: ‘Woe to those who call good evil and evil good; who call darkness light and light darkness; who call bitter sweet and sweet bitter’ (Isaiah 5:20). Yet the Lord says: ‘The evil person brings evil things out of the evil treasure of his heart’ (Matthew 12:35). What, then, is an evil person except an evil nature, since a human being is a nature? Further, if a human being is some good because he is a nature, what is an evil person except an evil good? Nevertheless, when we distinguish these two things, we find that he is not evil because he is human, nor good because he is wicked, but good because he is human and evil because he is wicked. Whoever, then, says that it is evil to be human, or that it is good to be wicked, falls into that prophetic statement: ‘Woe to those who call good evil and evil good’ (Isaiah 5:20). For he condemns God’s work, which is the human being, and praises the human being’s vice, which is iniquity. Every nature, therefore, even if it is defective, is good insofar as it is nature and evil insofar as it is defective.”

Behold, the venerable teacher does not say that only the corrupted or defective will of a human being is evil, but that the defective nature of a human being is a bad nature; and he confirms that the thing which is evil is a nature. He calls an evil person an evil nature. For he says:

> “What, then, is an evil person except an evil nature?”

He did not say that an evil person is merely an evil will, but an evil nature. Obviously, when a human being is evil, he is evil not by his will alone but by his whole nature.

Yet he faithfully teaches that, when we say “an evil person,” we must distinguish between God’s work and the human being’s vice: being human is God’s work, while being wicked is the human being’s vice. Thus nature, even if it is defective, is good insofar as it is nature and evil insofar as it is defective.

In all these statements, therefore, he says not, as this man asserts, that only the will is good insofar as it is nature; rather, he says that nature itself is good insofar as it is nature, while nature itself is evil insofar as it is defective.

This teaching must therefore be followed faithfully, understood in a Catholic manner, and held with the greatest firmness, so that we may know with complete certainty that neither the will alone of the wicked angel nor that of the evil human being is evil when they sin, but their whole nature; and that their whole nature will suffer eternal evils when they are condemned.

This man adds further and says:

> “It was not the generality of nature that sinned in the first human being, but the individual will of each person. If that nature had sinned, since it is one, it would certainly have perished in its entirety.”

In these words he attempts most openly to affirm not only that nature does not sin in other human beings, but only the will; he also asserts that, similarly, nature did not sin in the first human being, but only the will. Therefore, according to him, the nature of the human race in general did not sin in him, because his nature did not sin; only the particular and individual will of each person sinned in him, since, according to this man’s view, he too sinned solely by his will.

He maintains that if the whole nature of the human being had sinned, it would certainly have perished in its entirety. But now, because only the will sinned, only it was corrupted, while nature remained unharmed.

What, then, shall we say in response to these elaborate and unheard-of fantasies, except that we should oppose them with the testimonies of God’s Scriptures? Through these testimonies we may know most truly and hold most faithfully that the whole nature sinned in that human being, perished in its entirety, and was transmitted to his descendants in its entirety, subject to sin and destruction.

The Apostle teaches this most plainly, saying:

> “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12).

He did not say, “Through the will of one human being sin entered the world,” but “through one human being.” Nor did he say, “and so it passed into the wills of all,” but “so it passed into all human beings.” Nor did he add, “in whom the wills of all sinned,” but “in whom all sinned.”

Through one human being, therefore, sin entered the world—that is, through the whole and complete nature by which the human being consists. And just as the whole of that nature was corrupted by sin in him, so the whole of it passes into all human beings, corrupted by sin, so that from that wholly sinful origin the whole nature of all human beings might be drawn forth as sinful. For in that entire human being who sinned, the whole nature of all human beings sinned.

Therefore all, as the same Apostle says, were made not by will but by nature children of wrath. He says:

> “And we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians 2:3).

All who are born from that corrupted root truly become children of wrath by nature—not of the kind that nature was when created by God, but of the kind it became through that man by sinning.

On behalf of all of them the Psalmist says:

> “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” (Psalm 50:7).

Behold: a sinful nature conceived in iniquities and begotten in sins.

Our Lord Jesus Christ came to seek and save this nature, which perished wholly in Adam and was transmitted wholly lost to his descendants—not partially, that is, not in the will alone, but entirely. As he himself says:

> “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what had perished” (Luke 19:10).

And because the whole of it had perished, he came to save the whole of it. Therefore he assumed it in its entirety—that is, both the human soul and the human body—in order to save it wholly through his death and resurrection: justifying the soul from sins and raising the body from the dead.

As the Apostle says:

> “He died on account of our offenses and rose again for our justification” (Romans 4:25).

Whoever, then, says that human nature did not perish in its entirety is attempting, insofar as it lies within him, to empty the sacrament of the divine Incarnation of its meaning. For the Lord assumed it in his Incarnation without reason if it did not wholly need salvation, if it did not wholly need a Savior.

It is astonishing how this man can say that, in that first human being, the individual wills of each of us sinned, when those wills did not yet exist at all, and that the nature of all of us did not sin, when that nature was certainly present in him.

But when he says, “If the whole nature of that human being had sinned, it would certainly have perished entirely,” it follows, according to his view, that if only the will sinned in him, only the will perished. And if it perished, it certainly needs one who liberates, saves, and restores it, so that it may be sound and free through him who says:

> “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

How, then, does this man, throughout his entirely vain argument, defend free choice as arising from the power of nature and not from the gift of grace? And if, according to him, only the will perished while nature remained safe, then—far be it from us—the Truth did not speak truly when it said of itself:

> “He made the whole human being sound on the Sabbath” (John 7:27).

### 8.

This man adds and says:

> “Therefore nature is in no way punished, because it is from God and does not sin; rather, the voluntary lustful impulse is punished. Accordingly, in the impious, it is not what God made that suffers punishment, but what pride viciously discovered. The lust of the perverse will is tormented when it is not permitted to possess what it wrongly or unworthily desires.”

What he says—that nature is in no way punished because it is from God and does not sin—is contrary to faith and truth in two ways.

For sinful angelic or human nature, as has been demonstrated above in many ways, is punished by the just judgment of God and by eternal damnation. Since evil can neither be nor ought to be left unpunished, it must necessarily be punished where it is found and by what perpetrates it—that is, in the very natures in which the sins were committed and which have been corrupted and perverted by sinning. Therefore they are justly condemned on account of these things.

The angelic or human nature itself, although it is from God not by generation but by creation, not by birth but by origin, can nevertheless sin, and it does sin.

Catholic faith therefore confesses both truths, because it knows both to be true: that nature is truly punished on account of sin, and, conversely, that the nature itself truly sins. This man denies both, since he confirms neither that nature is punished nor that nature sins.

According to his assertion, therefore, there is no nature created by God that does not sin, just as there is no nature that alone is begotten by God. But true faith holds most firmly that every rational nature, both angelic and human, insofar as it depends upon itself, can sin, just as it plainly sinned both in the fallen angels and in human beings who fell through transgressing the commandment.

That this same nature does not sin in the elect angels is due to divine grace and divine goodness, so that they are good by nature and persevere in goodness by grace.

The only nature that can never sin is that which is from God in such a way that it is what God is—not created from nothing, but begotten or proceeding from him. This is undoubtedly the only-begotten Son of God and the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, since this man says that no other nature does not sin, he attempts, with manifest blasphemy, to make the creature equal to the Creator. What else remains for him except to say that the angelic or human spirit is of the same nature as God, as the impious ancient heretics said?

Those heretics introduced two natures, separately opposed to one another: one good, which could not be evil, and another evil, which could not be good. This man, however, by a new and unheard-of kind of error, says of the same angelic or human spirit both that nature does not sin—that is, cannot be evil—and that the will sins—that is, can be evil.

Therefore, after saying that nature does not sin and is not punished, in order to confirm that only the human will sins, he immediately added:

> “But the voluntary lustful impulse is punished.”

### 9.

Repeating and emphasizing this very point, he continued and said:

> “In the impious, it is not what God made that suffers punishment, but what pride viciously discovered.”

By these words, as by those above, he confirms that the nature of impious angels or human beings will never suffer punishment; rather, what a proud will viciously admitted is to be punished in the will alone.

### 10.

And as though we were asking him what the future punishment of this defective will would be, he added, as if explaining it:

> “The lust of the perverse will is tormented when it is not permitted to possess what it wrongly or unworthily desires.”

Behold what sort of torment he says awaits the evil will in impious angels and human beings: not eternal fire, not any external punishment, but merely this—that, because they are oppressed and restrained, they cannot fulfill what they wrongly desire.

Thus he confirms not only that the nature of evil angels or human beings will never sin and will never be punished, but also that the will itself—which he concedes sins in them—will feel no punishment and suffer no penalty except the kind that all wicked human beings suffer in this life, when they are not at all permitted to fulfill what they perversely desire, whether divine judgment stands in the way or some other necessity compels them.

It is therefore clear that he entirely denies every punishment, every torment, and every suffering of the future damnation which almighty God so frequently and so terribly threatens. For this reason, as contrary to our faith and hostile to truth, his teaching must be driven far from the ears and far from the hearts of the faithful.

### 11.

After these numerous and serious claims, he adds a very brief definition and says:

> “Evil is from no good.”

So that we may understand this carefully, we must first consider that something good can be evil. Thus angelic or human nature is certainly good in its own mode and kind. But this good of nature can become evil through vice, so that it remains good insofar as it is nature and begins to be evil insofar as it is corrupted. In this way there is no doubt that a good can be evil.

But when this occurs—that is, when a good begins to be evil—it has no preceding cause from which it comes about as a consequence. For if, for example, we ask what causes this or that nature to be some good, we certainly find that the supreme good, God, is the cause, and that every good comes from the supreme good.

If we ask from where this or that wise and just person is wise and just, we likewise find that God is supreme wisdom and supreme justice. He is therefore himself the supreme and most certain cause from which everyone who is truly wise is wise and everyone who is truly just is just.

Thus, for someone to be good, wise, or just, there is a preceding and efficient cause: supreme wisdom and supreme justice.

But can we say in the same way, if we are asked from where a good begins to be evil, that there is some supreme evil outside every angelic or human nature, and that whatever is evil in those creatures comes from that supreme evil? Could an evil angel and an evil human being thus have a preceding and efficient cause of their evil by which they became evil from good?

For an angel, just like a human being, was certainly good and began to be evil. From where, then, did he have a preceding cause by which he became evil? Could the good God have been the cause by which the angel became evil? Far be it from us, because the supremely good God could not be the cause of evil.

Likewise, far be it from us to say that there is some supreme evil and that it is the preceding cause by which a good angel became evil. For if we say this, we plainly introduce two principles contrary to the truth of faith: a principle of good and, similarly, a principle of evil.

But, as we have said, far be it from us to do this, because there is absolutely no nature of evil, nor does evil exist substantially in such a way that it could be the principle of anything. Rather, evil is called a falling away from the good, just as darkness is a deficiency of light and sickness a deficiency of health.

From where, then, did this falling away from the good—called evil—come to be in the devil, who sinned first? It did not come from God, because God is not the author of evil. It did not come from some substance of evil, because there is no substance of evil.

But if someone says that this happened through the devil’s own will, so that he became evil from good, it must be asked whether that will which brought this about in him was good or evil. If it was good, how could a good will be the cause of an evil will? But if an evil will brought this about in him, so that he became evil from good, who made the evil will through which this happened?

Since this can in no way be discovered, we must truly confess that no efficient cause preceded that evil will by which the good angel became evil. Rather, the cause was deficient, because, as has been said, a falling away from the good is called evil.

The same applies to the sinful human being, who became evil from good. The cause could not have been God’s will, nor the nature of evil, which plainly does not exist; nor could it have been the person’s good will, which could not be the cause of evil; nor his evil will, whose author, if sought, cannot be found.

If it is said that the devil’s evil will made the human being’s will evil, then, just as the human being was able to consent to the one giving evil advice, so he was also able not to consent. Since both alternatives were in his power, no one compelled him, no one forced him, and no one could prevail over him by persuasion, except that inwardly, through a voluntary falling away, he fell and became evil from the good.

The same occurs in other human beings. Thus it is clear that the good itself—that is, good nature—is from God; but for this good of nature to be made evil through vice is from no source, because it has no efficient author. Rather, it is a deficient fall.

This, then, is rightly understood and said concerning rational angelic or human nature: in these creatures, the good of nature becomes evil from no author, or is understood to be evil from no author. For, as has often been said, this evil of the rational creature began neither from God nor from any author of evil, but from its own falling away from the good.

But this man, who asserts that neither angelic nor human nature sins, but only the will of that nature, appears to have established this definition in order to show that the good of the will itself becomes evil or is evil, while nevertheless defending nature itself as alien to this evil.

His reasoning is that nature could not be the author of the evil belonging to its will, which was changed from good into evil, because, for a good to begin to be evil, it is from no source. It has its efficient cause from no author; rather, there is a falling away from the good, and this is the evil in question.

Thus, according to his view, the statement “evil is from no good” is understood to mean that the good of the angelic or human will did not become evil because its nature was the author; and therefore nature remained free from guilt. For when the good of its will began to be evil, this happened from no source, and therefore not from nature itself.

He took the opportunity for this most fraudulent argument from the words of Saint Augustine in his books On the City of God. What Augustine wisely argued for the building up of the faith and the destruction of heretics, especially the Manichaeans, this man cunningly turned against that very faith. In everything, he acts especially in this way: from the most subtle arguments of that holy Father, he steals and appropriates what Augustine said to confirm piety, using it instead to confirm his own error.

### 12.

He adds further and says:

> “He who here changes by the free choice of his will—which is the gift of natural understanding, that is, the sharpness of the mind—the use of that gift toward shameful purposes, will there most justly be destroyed, so that he may not enjoy the honor of truth at all, and will not escape the darkness of eternal ignorance.”

In these words he speaks not of angelic or human nature itself, nor of its will, as he usually does, but rather of its understanding. For three things are considered in a rational mind: being, knowing, and willing.

He now seems to have sufficiently discussed two of these—being and willing—in both natures. He therefore adds something concerning knowing, that is, concerning understanding itself. Thus, while nature remains safe and free from every punishment, according to his view, not only the will of that nature but also its understanding is to be punished in the future damnation—not by any external punishment or torment, but only by an inward loss.

For he says that whoever in this life changes by the free choice of the will the gift of natural understanding—which ought to have been possessed for the exercise of seeking, finding, and contemplating truth—turning it instead toward other uses, that is, occupying the sharpness of understanding with vain, useless, or even harmful things, will in that damnation be punished in this way: the free will of the human being, which here misused the good of understanding, will not enjoy the light of truth at all; it will most justly lose the good of understanding itself and encounter the darkness of eternal ignorance.

If this is so, then this is already a great punishment of the human will: that the will which in this life misused the good of understanding by its free choice should in that damnation lose the good of understanding itself, enjoy no light of truth, and be condemned to the darkness of eternal ignorance.

This punishment of the perverse human will, which loses the light of understanding, will be so punitive for understanding itself that it appears justly to be lost, with the darkness of eternal ignorance taking its place.

We do not reject this punishment of the human mind in the future damnation. For, as we read in the Gospel (Matthew 25:24), when the useless servant is condemned—the servant who did not want to exercise profitably and increase the one talent of understanding that he had received, but either tied it up in a cloth or hid it in the earth, that is, made it fruitless by living luxuriously and immersing himself in earthly cares—when, I say, that useless servant is condemned, the Gospel truth itself makes clear that it will first be said:

> “Take the talent away from him” (ibid., 28);

and then it will be added:

> “Cast the useless servant into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (ibid., 30).

Therefore no punishment should be feared by the faithful person as much as this: in that damnation to be stripped of the light of God’s understanding and cast into the outer darkness, where there will be no illumination and no contemplation of truth for those condemned to eternal blindness.

Since this is so, how could this man earlier have promised those who will be in so great and so severe a damnation of eternal blindness, and who will always suffer the absence of truth and blessedness, knowledge and understanding of that very blessedness and truth? He even affirmed that because of this knowledge they are neither wretched nor damned.

Let him therefore hold to what he said here with at least some degree of truth, and reject what he inserted there pointlessly and vainly.

## CHAPTER XVII

In the seventeenth chapter he sets forth seven definitions as follows:

1. God is not the author, maker, or predestiner of punishments.

2. God’s predestination concerns only those things that are good, whereas foreknowledge concerns both good and evil. This distinction arises not from nature but from customary modes of expression.

3. Just as it is said that God is everywhere by the presence of his power but not everywhere by the grace of his indwelling, so it may be said of him that he is everywhere by foreknowledge but not everywhere by predestination. Yet truth cries out most plainly concerning God: Wherever God is present, he will certainly be there by indwelling; likewise, wherever there is foreknowledge, there will necessarily be predestination.

4. Just as God’s presence and indwelling are found only in those things that have been made by him, so his foreknowledge and predestination concern only those things that he himself would make. And just as his presence and indwelling are said, conversely, to be absent from those things that are neither from him nor made by him, since he is not in them, so his foreknowledge and predestination are, conversely, said to be absent from those things that he neither made nor gave, because they are nothing.

5. The eternal fire was made to burn the devil and his angels, not human beings, after he had been cast down from the ethereal realm. Since he could not suffer punishment in an ethereal body, an aerial body was added to him, in which he might feel the fire.

6. That fire is not a punishment, nor was it prepared or predestined for punishment. Rather, the fire, which had been predestined to exist in the totality of all good things, became the dwelling-place of the impious. In it, without doubt, they will dwell no less blessed than wretched.

7. There is no misery except eternal death; eternal death is ignorance of truth; and there is no misery except ignorance of truth. Wherever truth is unknown, there is no life.

[Col. 0215A] Therefore, what he placed first—that God is not the author, maker, or predestiner of punishments—he plainly said contrary to the faith, as we have already frequently shown above. For those punishments which will be inflicted in eternal damnation upon the devil and his angels and all impious human beings are not unjust, since each of those condemned there is tortured and tormented according to his merit and according to the measure of his iniquity. The just and eternal Judge fulfills in them what is written about him in the Psalm: “For he will repay each according to his works” (Ps. 61:13).

Thus there is one fire of Gehenna, yet it torments those delivered over to it in different ways, just as there is one heat of the sun, yet it is not felt equally by all, but differently by different people according to the constitution of their bodies. The punishments themselves, however, never end because it is just before God that those who never wished to put an end to their sins should never have an end to their torments; that those who were unwilling to be subject to him through piety should all be subjected to him by necessity, so that no creature may remain opposed to its Creator; and that all who here did not assent to the truth but believed in iniquity may there be utterly restrained from iniquity and be unable to deny the manifest truth of the divine judgment, the divine majesty, the power of God, and of his Christ.

Thus the impious themselves, who have always been strangers to the worship of God, will be compelled to confess that very truth and, groaning and repenting too late, will say: “Therefore we went astray from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not shine for us, and the sun did not rise for us” (Wis. 5:6). Hence almighty God himself, when through his prophets he threatens dreadful and eternal punishments, frequently adds at the end of his threat: “And they shall know that I am the Lord” (Exod. 29:46); that is, they will say by necessity, to their own shame, what they never wished to know through piety and devotion for their salvation.

The devil himself, the author and instigator of that wickedness, together with all his attendants, the unclean and condemned angels, will there receive an end to his tyranny, which he has not ceased to exercise from the beginning against God and against the salvation of the whole human race, when, as it is written, “with all looking on he shall be hurled down” (Job 40:28).

For all these reasons, and for others that lie hidden in God’s secrets, hell is even called useful in the Holy Scriptures, just as the punishment of human laws is useful, by which the guilty are punished so that the rest may live in peace. For Scripture says, speaking of the evil tongue: “Hell is more useful than it” (Ecclus. 28:25).

Since, then, those eternal punishments of condemned angels and human beings are so just and so well ordered, why should God not be their author—not because he is the cause of such great evils, but because he is the just disposer and judge of just torments? Or how is he not the author of those punishments of whom the Gospel plainly says: “He can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Luke 12:5); and: “After he has killed, he has power to cast into Gehenna” [Col. 0216A] (Matt. 10:28); and who will say at the very judgment: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41)?

If those punishments, and the place of torments, are to be believed to exist in some part of created things—that is, in some part of the world—who else could have made them, since he made all things? Of him Scripture plainly says: “He who lives eternally created all things together” (Ecclus. 18:1). Since that eternal fire is truly a creature—for it must not be believed to be coeternal with God—and since this creature was made for just and proper purposes, whoever says that either it or any other creature is not from God, the one and only author of the whole creation, is plainly entangled in the heretical impiety either of the Manichaeans or of other most wicked heretics.

And therefore, since that eternal fire must truly be numbered among creatures, it undoubtedly has the same author and maker as every other creature. Of him it is also written: “For in six days God made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and on the seventh day he rested” (Exod. 20:11). Let this man say, then, in what part of the universe he thinks hell exists—that is, the place of those eternal torments: whether in heaven, or on earth, or in the sea, or in the other things that are in them. Wherever he thinks it exists, it is necessary that it was made by him “who made heaven, earth, and the sea, and all that is in them” (ibid.).

Since this is so, why should almighty God himself, who is the author and maker of all things, not rightly and truthfully be understood or believed also to be the predestiner [Col. 0216C] of such just and well-ordered punishments? Although those suffering and enduring the punishments regard them as evil, they are not evil in the sight of that eternal Judge, because they are just, and nothing just can be called evil.

He therefore both predestined and prepared that eternal fire of which the Truth itself says: “Which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41); and of which Solomon says: “Judgments are prepared for scoffers, and striking hammers for the bodies of fools” (Prov. 19:29). For if these punishments were not predestined by God, the just Judge, for the impious and wicked, how is it that, concerning them as still future and yet to come, blessed John says in the Apocalypse: “And they will be tormented day and night for ever and ever” (Rev. 20:10); and again: “And the smoke of their torments will rise for ever and ever” [Col. 0216D] (Rev. 14:11)?

How also does blessed Peter say of certain most wicked people: “For them the gloom of darkness has been reserved forever” (2 Pet. 2:17)? And blessed Jude the Apostle says similarly of the same people: “For them,” he says, “the storm of darkness has been kept forever” (Jude 13). Certainly we all agree that God predestined everything that he himself was going to do, and no one except him will carry out such great, just, and eternal judgments. If, therefore, they belong to his works and cannot be carried out by another, it is altogether certain, and there should be no doubt, that they have as their predestiner the one whom they have as their author and maker.

But if this man says that God is not the author [Col. 0217A] and maker of punishments because, as he is accustomed to say, punishment is nothing, since it has neither substance nor a nature existing and subsisting in itself, just as neither evil, sin, nor death does—and therefore that God could not have predestined things that do not exist substantially—we must firmly oppose him by the clearest truth of the matter.

For the word “punishment” does not signify some subsisting thing or nature, as do the words “heaven,” “earth,” and “sea.” When we say these words, they immediately indicate certain natures of things through their signification. Although, therefore, the word “punishment” does not signify in this way some thing subsisting in itself, it nevertheless signifies a great evil that is carried out through subsisting natures of things.

Thus, when “death” itself is mentioned, it signifies no substance of its own, since it has no nature of existing in itself; yet by this name a most serious evil is signified and understood, an evil recognized in the division of substances—that is, of soul and body. In the same way almighty God predestined punishment—not so that it would exist as a nature in itself, but in truly existing natures and substances, to which the great evil signified and understood by that name is truly and substantially inflicted.

2. After this he says: “God’s predestination applies only to things that are good, whereas his foreknowledge applies to good and evil things.” He says that this distinction arises not from nature but from customary usage in speech.

We hold and embrace this distinction between God’s foreknowledge and predestination because the holy Fathers have handed it down in this way, and truth itself demonstrates it to be true. God, who foreknows all future things, eternally foreknew everything that was going to happen—that is, both good and evil things—but eternally predestined only the good things that he himself was going to do, whether by his gratuitous mercy or by his just judgment.

Therefore it is entirely correct to understand God’s foreknowledge as applying both to good and evil things, but his predestination as applying only to good and just things, which he not only foreknew but also established, predetermined, and decreed as future. Yet he mentions this distinction in order to contend that God could have foreknown evil things but could not have predestined them, failing to understand the distinction regarding evil that we explained above: namely, that one kind of evil is opposed to the good—this is vice—and God is not its author; whereas another kind of evil is opposed to peace, rest, or health, and this never occurs except with God as its author and judge, as he speaks through the prophet: “I am the Lord, making peace and creating evil” (Isa. 45:7).

Hence we also find in another prophet: “If there is evil in a city, which the Lord has not done” (Amos 3:6). And again: “Good things and evil, life and death, poverty and honor, are from the Lord” (Ecclus. 11:14).

God is therefore not the predestiner of that evil which is understood in vice or sin, because he is not its author. But of this evil which is understood in some affliction, torment, or punishment, whether temporal or eternal—since these things, as Scripture teaches, are from him and are ordered and inflicted by his judgment—he is plainly both author and predestiner, because he foreknew them as future and justly predestined them to be carried out. Since this is so, he accomplished nothing by bringing this distinction forward except to deny the truth and display his ignorance.

As for his claim that this distinction between divine foreknowledge and predestination arises not from nature but from customary usage in speech, it seems to us more correct and more truthful that it arises from nature and according to nature. For although in God’s nature “there is no change or shadow of alteration” (Jas. 1:17), so that for him knowing, foreknowing, and predestining are not different things, but his one, simple, and eternal knowledge comprehends all things together and equally—things which in temporal realities are carried out and manifested in different ways—nevertheless, since these matters, namely God’s foreknowledge and predestination, most truly refer to the state and arrangement of his creatures, they have no distinction within God’s eternal and immutable knowledge, because there everything is one and simple knowledge, varied neither by time nor changed by the diversity of things.

Yet this distinction does exist, and is recognized, in temporally passing realities, since among them some things are present or past, in which the human understanding properly recognizes knowledge, while others are future, with which foreknowledge or predestination is properly understood to correspond. And because among future things another difference appears—some being good and others evil—there arises again another distinction: predestination is recognized in good things alone, whereas foreknowledge is understood in both, that is, in good and evil things.

Thus this distinction between foreknowledge and predestination, although it does not arise from nature or according to the nature of the immutable Godhead, nevertheless arises from nature and according to the nature of the administration and ordering of mutable creation. We spoke more fully about this above, that is, in the second chapter of this disputation. Therefore we will in no way permit things that are so rightly and truthfully distinguished according to their proper characteristics, and that have been handed down to us in this way by the Fathers, to be disturbed and confused by anyone’s novel presumption, so that someone may presumptuously say indiscriminately and confusedly, as this man does, that all foreknowledge is predestination. This is most plainly blasphemous: for if God can foreknow even evil things, it would follow—God forbid—that he predestined them.

Although predestination, since it does not exist without foreknowledge, may not unreasonably also be called foreknowledge.

3. Yet this man, wishing to contend that this distinction arises not from the truth and proper nature of things but solely from our customary manner of speaking, adds an example contrary to his own assertion. He says: “Just as what is said of God—that he is everywhere by the presence of his power but not everywhere by the grace of his indwelling—so it can be said of him that he is everywhere by foreknowledge but not everywhere by predestination; and wherever there is foreknowledge, there will necessarily be predestination.”

The truth cries out most plainly concerning God: wherever God is by presence, there he will certainly be by indwelling. Behold, he affirms that this religious expression of ecclesiastical discipline—by which we distinguish and discern, saying that God is everywhere through the presence of his majesty but not everywhere through the presence of his indwelling—does not arise from the proper nature of things but solely from customary human speech. In this way he destroys the salutary meaning of the whole divine Scripture, in which almighty God is presented to us as being generally everywhere through the presence of his majesty, but specially through the grace of indwelling.

Regarding the general presence of his majesty, he himself says: “I fill heaven and earth.” And the Prophet says to him: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings at dawn and dwell at the ends of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Ps. 138:8–10).

Regarding the grace of his indwelling, by which he is not everywhere but in his temple—that is, in the holy and rational angelic or human creature, which alone is capable of his knowledge and understanding, illumination, and grace—Scripture sometimes speaks through the figure of the heavens, by which the heavenly life of angels or holy human beings is understood, and sometimes by expressly mentioning his particular temple.

Thus Scripture says: “He who dwells in the heavens will mock them” (Ps. 2:4); and: “To you I lifted my eyes, who dwell in the heavens” (Ps. 122:1); and: “Look down from your sanctuary, from your high dwelling-place in the heavens” (Deut. 26:15); and: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. 6:9).

There is also what the Apostle says: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16). And again: “For you are the temple of the living God, as God says: ‘For I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people’” (2 Cor. 6:16; Lev. 26:12).

Since, then, there is truly, and entirely according to the nature of things, such a great distance and distinction between the presence of the divine majesty—which is generally and powerfully presented to every creature—and the grace of indwelling—which is specially and mercifully granted only to the rational and elect creature, which is capable of receiving his illumination [the manuscript reading *inminationem* is uncertain], understanding, and sweetness—why does he try, in his rashness, to empty out this so divine a meaning, and one so necessary for our faith and salvation, to such an extent that he says the truth cries out that wherever God is by presence, there he is also by indwelling?

On the contrary, the truth of God’s Scripture always distinguishes and differentiates these matters so carefully that it commends God’s indwelling only in his temple, whether heavenly or still established on earth, through the goodness of his grace [Col. 0219D] [Note: Let the innovators take heed that God dwells in temples and consecrated places in a special manner, as Chrysostom clearly demonstrates against the Anomoeans [Col. 0220D].].

God is indeed sometimes said to dwell in a handmade temple consecrated to his name by religious devotion, because of the grace of its consecration, the more familiar worship of his majesty, and the more celebrated effect of supplication and being heard. The Lord himself shows this in the Gospel, saying: “And he who swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it” (Matt. 23:21).

Yet Scripture plainly says: “The Most High does not dwell in handmade things” (Acts 7:48). Hence Solomon, speaking in his prayer about the very temple that he had built and consecrated to him, says: “If heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house that I have built?” (2 Chron. 2:6).

From this we understand that in such a handmade temple, dedicated and consecrated to his name, God may rightly be said to dwell through a certain gracious condescension and through the sanctification of heavenly mysteries; but he does not dwell there through the immensity of his majesty or through that grace which he grants only to the elect and rational creature [Col. 0220B].

A certain holy and glorious martyr says of him: “The whole world is his temple.” If by these words he simply intended the whole world consisting of heaven and earth, this is correctly understood: in the whole world he can be religiously worshiped and adored everywhere, since true worshipers no longer worship the Father with the Jews in Jerusalem or with the Samaritans on that mountain, but everywhere in spirit and truth (John 4:23).

But if he intended “the whole world is his temple” in the sense that, according to the customary usage of Scripture, he called the whole human race the whole world, then the whole world is plainly God’s temple [Note: [Col. 0220D] Supply: “God dwells.”]—in those who are converted and gathered to God from the whole world, that is, from the entire human race, and become his temple [Col. 0220C].

Therefore the same most blessed martyr, after saying, “The whole world is his temple,” added: “He must be dedicated in our mind and consecrated in our heart.”

Accordingly, it is not merely from customary usage in speech, but from the very truth and proper nature of things, that almighty God is said to be everywhere through the presence of his majesty, but not everywhere through the grace of his indwelling: he presents the presence of his majesty generally to the whole creation, but grants the grace of his indwelling only to the elect rational creature.

What, then, does he mean when he asserts that it can be said that God is everywhere by foreknowledge but not everywhere by predestination, and that wherever there is foreknowledge there will necessarily be predestination? Who ever spoke in such a way as to say that God is everywhere by foreknowledge? His foreknowledge exists only with him, to whom alone it is known.

Or what necessity is there to say that he is everywhere by predestination, when his predestination also exists only with him, because it is known to him alone? His statement that “wherever there is foreknowledge, there will necessarily be predestination” is equally empty, because no one says this. As some of the ancient Fathers said, it is merely a novelty of expression and nothing else.

We say that God is everywhere in majesty, everywhere in power, everywhere in might, because all this—majesty, power, might—is himself, who is everywhere. But there is no reason to say that he is everywhere by foreknowledge or everywhere by predestination, since nowhere is God said to be by either foreknowledge or predestination.

Therefore his statement that God’s foreknowledge and predestination concern only those things that he himself was going to do is plainly false, because his foreknowledge can also concern evil things that he was not going to do.

Further, what he says—that just as his foreknowledge and indwelling are in things that are neither from him nor made by him—is utterly vain. Where has he ever read, or heard the faithful say, that God is said to have presence and indwelling in things that are neither from him nor made by him?

And what are these things which, as he writes, are neither from him nor made by him? If there are any such things, then there is some creature that is neither from God nor made by God. This is certainly not Christian but Manichaean, since the Gospel cannot lie where it is written: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

The same is true of what he immediately adds: “God’s foreknowledge and predestination are declared, on the contrary, in those things which he neither made nor gave.” He says that they are declared “on the contrary,” so that, according to his novel and insane rule, what is declared should be understood as not truly being declared.

It is therefore false that he tries to assert—that those eternal punishments are nothing and were not really made—for in both respects he contradicts the truth. They were truly foreknown by God as future, and they will truly be inflicted by God upon those who have deserved them. Since Scripture so plainly shows that these punishments were made, foreknown, and predestined, let such a rule instead be crushed and perish—a rule by which it is insanely asserted that things made must be understood as though they were not made.

5. He added further, saying: “The eternal fire was made to burn the devil and his angels, not human beings.” This is perhaps why he and others seem either to inquire or to assert that the eternal fire was prepared not for the punishment of human beings but solely for the punishment of the wicked angels: for at that judgment the Lord did not say that he would say to those who will be on his left, “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for you,” but “which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.”

Thus, because he did not say, “which has been prepared for you,” but said, “which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41), the fire may appear to have been prepared only for wicked spirits, that is, for the devil himself and his angels.

Hence some people are found to have held the opinion that the fire in which the souls of the condemned are now tormented in hell is one fire, while that eternal fire is another, into which human beings will be sent only then, when, after being raised again with their bodies, they will be compelled to go together with the devil and his angels into that same eternal fire.

But whether there is one fire in which only souls are now tormented and in which then, after receiving their bodies, they too will be tormented; or whether this fire is one and that fire another—we should believe the truthful Scripture. It teaches that the punishment of eternal fire, and the outer darkness which will undoubtedly be there, are reserved not only for the angels who did not preserve their principality but abandoned their dwelling-place, whom God delivered over, even as they fell from the heavenly places, to be judged and tormented, but also for impious human beings.

Hence, as we have already mentioned, blessed Peter the Apostle says of certain impious people condemned to that final destruction: “For them the gloom of darkness has been reserved forever” (2 Pet. 2:17). And blessed Jude the Apostle says similarly of the same people: “For them the storm of darkness has been reserved forever” (Jude 12).

Therefore, just as that gloom and storm of eternal darkness have been prepared and reserved for impious and wicked human beings, so also that eternal fire, which must unquestionably be understood together with them, has been prepared and reserved for them as well [Col. 0222B].

For this reason, when the Lord says of the same eternal fire, “which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41), let us understand it faithfully: what was said principally of him—that is, of the devil—should consequently be understood also of his body, concerning whom Scripture says: “But they imitate him who are on his side” (Wis. 2:25). Thus the punishment principally prepared for him should also be understood as prepared and reserved consequently for these others, as the apostolic words mentioned above most plainly demonstrate.

5. This man adds and says: “After he had been hurled down from the ether, where in an ethereal body he could not feel punishments, an aerial body was added to him, in which he might feel the fire.”

On this matter let us listen not to this man’s importunate and inconsiderate definition, but rather to the pious, measured, and most cautious words of blessed Augustine—words that inquire rather than define.

“The upper part of the air,” he says, “because of its pure calm, is joined in common peace to the heaven adjoining it and is called by its name. Perhaps the transgressing angels were in that region, before their transgression, together with their prince—now the devil, then an archangel. For some of our people do not think that they were heavenly or super-heavenly angels. It is not surprising if, after their sin, they were thrust down into this darkness, where there is nevertheless air and it is woven together with thin moisture.

“But if those transgressors bore heavenly bodies before they transgressed, neither is it surprising if those bodies were changed through punishment into an aerial quality, so that they could now suffer something from fire—that is, from an element of the higher nature—and were not permitted to occupy even the higher and purer spaces of the air, but this dark region. By its nature it is, as it were, a prison for them until the time of judgment. Yet whether anything more must be carefully sought concerning these transgressing angels…”

Behold the teacher of piety: presuming nothing rashly, but treating each matter cautiously and humbly. He says that the transgressing angels, with their prince—now the devil, then an archangel—were either in the upper part of this air, that is, in the ethereal heaven, before they sinned, or perhaps dwelling in the heavenly regions, if they were heavenly or super-heavenly angels with the others.

And if they were only in the ethereal heaven, he says that after their sin they were cast down and thrust from that pure and perpetually serene calm into this lower and dark region of the air. Similarly, if before their transgression they bore heavenly bodies, like the other angels, he says that those bodies could have been changed, or could have become changed through the punishment of that condemnation, into an aerial quality, so that they could now suffer from the fire the punishment owed to them.

This holy teacher therefore did not define whether they had dwelt before their transgression in the ethereal heaven or even in the starry heaven; rather, he does not deny that either possibility could have occurred. Wherever they fell from after their transgression—whether, that is, from the higher or the lower heaven—and even if they had previously borne heavenly bodies, he does not consider it unreasonable that those bodies were changed through punishment into an aerial quality. He does not suppose that other bodies were added to them from the air, namely aerial bodies.

He therefore does not define, as this man does, that the devil was thrust from the ether into the air, since he could also have fallen from the heavenly regions. Nor does he define that the devil had an ethereal or heavenly body; rather, if he had one, it was changed through punishment into something worse. Nor does he say that an aerial body was added to him, as though he were clothed in two bodies, one heavenly or ethereal and the other aerial.
