Instead, he says that his own heavenly body, if he had one, was changed through punishment into an aerial quality, so that it was no longer a heavenly or ethereal body but an aerial body, in which he could feel the punishment and torment of fire.

Elsewhere, reconsidering the same matter and deliberating with the utmost caution and reserve, he says:

“[If the fire will not be incorporeal but corporeal and harmful by its touch, so that bodies can be tormented by it, how will the punishment of wicked spirits also be in it, unless demons too have certain bodies of their own, as learned men have thought, formed from this thick and moist air, whose movement is perceived when the wind blows? If this kind of element could suffer nothing from fire, it would not burn when heated in baths; for in order to burn, it is itself first burned, and by suffering it causes suffering.

“But if someone insists that they have no bodies at all, this matter need not be pursued through laborious investigation or contested in contentious debate. For why should we not say that, although in wondrous ways, nevertheless by true ones, incorporeal spirits too can be afflicted by the punishment of corporeal fire? If human spirits, which are certainly themselves incorporeal, can now be enclosed within corporeal limbs, then they can also be indissolubly bound by the chains of their bodies hereafter.

“Therefore the spirits of demons—or rather the demons themselves, though incorporeal spirits—will cling to corporeal fires to be tormented, receiving punishment from the fires;” and so forth, as he discusses this matter at greater length.]

This, then, is the caution that the blessed teacher displays in his inquiries. Matters of this kind should be understood and treated in this way, and nothing should be believed concerning them rashly or falsely.

6. This man continues and says: “That fire is not a punishment, nor was it prepared or predestined for punishment; rather, the fire that had been predestined to exist in the universe of all good things became the dwelling-place of the impious, in which, beyond doubt, the blessed will dwell no less than the wretched.”

When he says in these words that the eternal fire is not a punishment, he plainly contradicts the Truth itself—that is, the Judge of the living and the dead—who foretold that he would say at that judgment: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41).

And so that we may understand that the eternal fire is an everlasting punishment and torment, immediately afterward, after a few intervening words concerning the wretched who will be eternally condemned and tormented there, he adds: “Then these will go into eternal punishment” (ibid., 46).

He also contradicts blessed Paul the Apostle, who says: “At the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ from heaven with the angels of his power, when he gives vengeance in a flame of fire to those who do not know God and who do not obey the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ; they will suffer eternal punishment in destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty” (2 Thess. 1:7–9).

[Col. 0224B] He also contradicts blessed John the Apostle, who says in the Apocalypse concerning the same lake of fire and sulfur: “And they will be tormented day and night for ever and ever” (Rev. 20:10); and again: “And the smoke of their torments will rise for ever and ever” (Rev. 14:10).

He contradicts the Scripture that says: “He will give fire and worms to their flesh, so that they may burn and feel it forever” (Judit[h] 16:21). And again: “Humble your spirit greatly, for the vengeance of the flesh of the impious is fire and worms” (Ecclus. 7:19).

Since these things are so, and since they must be held faithfully for terror and continual amendment, how does this man dare—or why is he permitted to have such an impious and harmful freedom—as to say in the Church, for the subversion of his hearers and the nurturing of deadly security, that the eternal fire is not a punishment? The Lord testifies that it is everlasting punishment, and the truth of apostolic teaching most plainly declares that it is the fire and flame of vengeance, eternal punishment in destruction, torment by day and night, and smoke of torments rising for ever and ever.

Therefore we must believe these things altogether without doubt and most truly, so that through such terror the pleasure of sinning may be restrained and put to death in us, and the care to act well and please God may be aroused and strengthened. The Lord himself shows that this is especially necessary for us, saying: “I will show you whom you should fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna” (Luke 12:5); and again: “Rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28).

Hence elsewhere Scripture shows the usefulness of this fear and, by contrast, the evil of security, saying: “The fear of the Lord drives out sin” (Ecclus. 1:27); for one who is without fear cannot be justified.

But what this man says—that the same eternal fire was not prepared and predestined from the beginning as a punishment, but only so that, within the totality of creatures which were created good by the good Creator, it too might, as it were, occupy its own place—must in no way be accepted by our faith. Rather, this must be maintained: that almighty God, who created all things whatsoever from the beginning for definite causes and definite, necessary purposes, established nothing pointlessly or superfluously [Col. 0225A], but willed each thing created by his omnipotence to have its own proper function or usefulness: light for the use of day; darkness for the repose of night; the firmament of heaven as the seat of the luminaries; the separation of the waters above the heavens for the regulation of the stars; herbs and shrubs for the sustenance of living creatures; the greater luminary to rule the day; and the lesser luminary to rule the night, together with the stars—and so forth in the same manner.

Therefore, just as he immediately assigned all these things, created and ordered from the beginning, to their proper functions, services, and uses, so too we must believe that, by his just providence and provident justice, he immediately prepared and predestined that eternal fire, created from the beginning among the other creatures, for those uses [Col. 0225B] to which the Lord shows it to have been prepared, when he says to the impious and condemned: “Go into the eternal fire,” and adds, “which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41). That is, for the everlasting punishment of both kinds of creature, angelic and human.

For from the very words in which he will say, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV, 34), we may rightly understand, by contrast, that the eternal fire itself was likewise prepared from the foundation of the world for the everlasting punishment of impious angels and human beings.

Nor is there any injustice with God because he prepared [Col. 0225C] and predestined that fire of everlasting punishment for so great a multitude of the impious, so long before they existed at all. For if, in the construction of a new city, a dreadful and terrifying prison-house is built at once together with the city itself, this cannot be called injustice, but rather a provision of mercy and justice: so that those who dwell in the city, seeing the penal and gloomy prison of condemnation, may either be mercifully deterred from sinning, or, if they do not avoid sins, may be punished justly and without excuse.

Thus that fire too, created for everlasting punishment, must be believed to have been established both mercifully and justly: either so that human beings may be corrected by its terror, or, if they refuse correction, may be punished all the more justly.

Concerning the creation of this eternal fire—which we must certainly understand among those works of God when, in six days, he made heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them, and on the seventh ceased from every work that he had done [Col. 0225D] (Exod. XX, 11)—holy Pope Gregory, explaining the words of the blessed Job, where it is written concerning the impious man, “A fire that is not kindled shall devour him” (Job XX, 26), says:

> “In a very remarkable way the fire of Gehenna has been expressed in a few words. For corporeal fire, in order to be fire, requires corporeal fuel; when it must be maintained, it is undoubtedly nourished by piled-up wood, and it cannot exist unless kindled, nor continue unless fed. But, by contrast, although the fire of Gehenna is incorporeal, it burns corporeally [Col. 0226A] those cast into it; it is neither kindled by human effort nor nourished by wood. Once created, it endures unquenchable; it does not require kindling, and it does not lack heat.”

The same most blessed teacher, still explaining the following words concerning the same impious man, “He shall be afflicted, having been left in his tabernacle” (ibid., 26), adds what should faithfully be understood concerning the punishments of that eternal fire:

> “For the tabernacle of the wicked is the flesh, because he gladly dwells in it and, if possible, desires never to leave it. When he receives that flesh again in the resurrection, he will burn with it after being handed over to the fires of Gehenna. Then he will desire to be taken out of it; then he will begin to wish to avoid what he loved. But because he preferred that same flesh to God, God’s judgment brings it about that he is tormented by fire all the more through it. Thus, for the increase of his torment, [Col. 0226B] he is unwillingly taken out of the body here, and there he is unwillingly held in the body.”

Again, when he was explaining the words of the same book in which it is written concerning the same impious man, “He will repay everything that he has done, yet he will not be consumed according to the multitude of his devices; so shall he endure” (Job XX, 18), he says:

> “For in torments he pays back the unlawful desires that he preserved here; handed over to avenging flames, he is always dying, because he is always kept in death, yet he is not consumed in his torments. For if the life of the dying man were consumed, his punishment too would end with his life; and because he devised many things for guilt, he is tormented in punishment by new devices.”

This holy teacher speaks terrifying things terrifyingly and true things truly, so as to arouse the minds of his hearers to fear, spur them toward amendment, and compel them, as though awakening them, from deadly [Col. 0226C] security to concern for their salvation.

But this man, still speaking empty things emptily and false things deceitfully, says that the eternal fire itself, which had been created solely for this purpose, as he wishes, became a dwelling-place for the impious within the universe of all good things. He did not say that it became the torment, punishment, or penalty of the impious, but [Note: [Col. 0225D] This criticism concerns only the name. For Eriugena did not want the fire of hell to be a repose and quiet, peaceful dwelling-place for the damned themselves.] a dwelling-place, he says, for the impious. Thus, according to his meaning, just as a dwelling-place is for each person his own house, where he sits and lives in peace, so that fire too is not a torment of condemnation for the impious, but a tranquil dwelling-place.

Therefore he adds concerning the same fire, saying: “In it, without doubt, the blessed will dwell no less than the miserable.” Here too he said that they will dwell in that fire, not that they will be tormented, punished, or anything of that kind, altogether denying [Col. 0226D] the most genuine punishments of eternal torments, which all Scripture proclaims with such terror and commends with such insistence.

When he says, “In it, without doubt, the blessed will dwell no less than the miserable,” he plainly strives to affirm that both groups—that is, the blessed and the miserable—will dwell in one eternal fire after the resurrection. He is following, evidently, the foolishest and most vain persuasion of secular philosophers, who suppose that after the dissolution of the body the souls of the pious will dwell either in the ethereal heaven, [Col. 0227A] or in that circle which they call the Milky Way, or in the spheres of the stars. He calls all these things—the ethereal heaven itself, the firmament of heaven in which that Milky Circle appears, and the stars themselves—eternal fire, just as he does the fire of Gehenna.

For he thinks that all these things, which are established above the three elements of the world—that is, earth, water, and air—exist from the fourth element, fire. Thus he supposes that this same fourth element of the world is, among the dead, the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt. XXV, 41) and for all impious human beings, while in the heavenly regions there is an eternal fire in which the dwelling-place of the blessed will be after the resurrection. (The Latin says *apud inferos*, “in the lower regions” or “in hell,” not “among the dead.”)

Behold what kind of blessedness he promises to the saints and elect of God: that those who, while still mortal [Col. 0227B], dwelt in the first element of the world—that is, on earth—should, once made immortal, dwell in the fourth and higher element of the world, which he calls eternal fire; and that their reward should be to dwell in an element that is, indeed, luminous, tranquil, and pure, but still merely an element.

The Lord, however, does not promise his people eternal blessedness in the elements of the world, but in heavenly and super-heavenly goods: “Where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God” (Col. III, 1), exalted above all the heavens and interceding for us (Rom. VIII, 34).

Concerning the sublimity of this blessedness the Apostle says:

> “For Jesus has not entered into a holy place made with hands, copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God for us” (Heb. IX, 24).

So that his saints may be able to reach this dwelling-place, he himself entreats [Col. 0227C] the Father in the Gospel, saying:

> “Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am they also may be with me, so that they may see my glory, which you have given me” (John XVII, 24).

Concerning this blessed and angelic dwelling-place of the saints, the Apostle again says:

> “We know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (II Cor. V, 1).

Hence he himself also said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I, 23). And concerning all the elect in general, after the resurrection, he promises, saying:

> “We shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (I Thess. IV, 16).

Concerning this glorious and most blessed dwelling-place of the righteous, the Psalmist says: “The upright shall dwell with your countenance” (Ps. CXXXIX, 14).

[Col. 0227D] Let this, then, be the dwelling-place sought; let this be desired—not in the elements of the world, but in the face of God, in the vision of Christ’s glory, and in the fellowship of the blessed and super-heavenly angels, when the saints will be, as the Truth itself promises, “equal to the angels of God in heaven” (Luke XX, 36).

The dwelling-place—or rather, the confinement—of the blessed will not therefore be in one fiery element of the world. Nor will they be enclosed there as the impious are in the eternal fire. Rather, they will have all the elements of the world under their authority, subjected to them with such happiness and ease, and so suited to their immortal condition, that wherever they wish and in whatever manner they wish, they will immediately be able to exist; and they will see and possess all these things not so much as the reward of blessedness as for the increase of their happiness and for the praise [Col. 0228A] and glory of the Creator.

For Scripture promises them this power and glory, saying:

> “The kingdom, and the power, and the greatness of the kingdom under the whole heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High; his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all kings shall serve him and obey him” (Dan. VII, 27).

### 7.

After this, he adds and says: “There is no misery except eternal death; eternal death is ignorance of the truth; and there is no misery except ignorance of the truth. Where truth is unknown, there is no life.”

What is said in these words could be good if the good itself were not spoken wrongly—that is, with a bad meaning. For it is true that, for a just and wise person, every labor, every adversity, and every misery that can occur in this mortal life [Col. 0228B], if it does not break him and change him for the worse but exercises him without weariness, cannot be misery for him. It does not make him miserable; rather, it purifies and tests him and, as gold in a furnace, makes him purer. Such a man counts nothing as misery except ignorance of the truth, insofar as he is still held back from contemplating it and is, in a certain way, repelled by his own weakness.

He fears not the outward death of the body, but that inward death of the soul, which is nothing other than complete ignorance of supreme truth. All unbelievers are dead in this respect, since they neither believe nor acknowledge God’s truth. Concerning them the Lord says: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. VIII, 22); and the Apostle says: “Alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them” (Eph. IV, 18).

[Col. 0228C] The life of the faithful, however, is itself the knowledge of the truth: here they know it through faith, and in the future they will know it by direct vision. Here too they receive life through faith in the truth, as it is written: “The just person lives by faith” (Rom. I, 17); and there they will have eternal life through knowledge and vision of that same truth, as the Lord says:

> “This is eternal life: that they know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII, 3).

Therefore, whoever reaches this knowledge through true faith and eternal contemplation will undoubtedly have eternal life itself as the eternal vision of Truth. But those who are separated from it, whether through unbelief or through final condemnation, what will such separation and such ignorance of the truth be for them except eternal death?

[Col. 0228D] According to this meaning he reads what was said by the teachers; but what he has read well in them, he turns to evil and perverts it, so as to adapt it, as far as he can, to his own error and lies. For he says these things for no other reason than that, by such an argument—violently and wickedly appropriated from good to evil—he may appear to demonstrate and confirm that there will be no other future misery for either the evil angels or the lost human beings condemned in eternal fire except ignorance and, as he has already said above, the absence of truth itself; and that this ignorance and absence of truth alone will be their eternal misery, their eternal [Col. 0229A] death.

In this way he contends that they will be free from every misery of punishments and torments inflicted from without, and from every death of penal condemnation. Yet however much he contends and tries to contradict, apart from that death which they suffer inwardly through ignorance and absence of truth, they will also suffer outwardly, as the Apocalypse says: “The lake of fire and sulphur, which is the second death” (Apoc. XX, 10, 14).

They will truly suffer eternal misery, when God, the just and mighty judge, “will give fire and worms into their flesh, so that they may burn and feel forever” (Judith XVI, 21). For those whom the enormity of their punishments will compel to die will always be in death, and the severity of divine judgment will never permit them to be extinguished.

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0229B]

In the eighteenth chapter he says:

1. The error concerning predestination arose from ignorance of the disciplines which Wisdom itself wished to be its companions and investigators, and from ignorance of Greek letters.

2. The verb *ὁρῶ* (*horō*), which is interpreted as “I see,” “I define,” and “I determine,” is similarly compounded in *προορῶ* (*prohorō*), “I foresee,” “I predefine,” and “I predestine”; and therefore predestination and predefinition are nothing other than foreseeing.

3. God neither foresaw nor predestined death and punishments, because they are nothing.

4. He left sinners in the mass of original sin [Col. 0229C]; he abandoned those who were left; he made those abandoned by the light suffer darkness, and those abandoned by life suffer death.

5. Nor does he leave or abandon what God made in them—otherwise their nature would return to nothing, if supreme Being were not in them—but he rejected what he did not make in them, namely, pride.

6. God always dwells in that nature which he created for himself.

7. God’s wisdom predestined in his laws limits beyond which the malice of the impious cannot advance; nor does it permit anyone’s malice to extend indefinitely, as it wishes, since the divine laws impose a limit on its progress.

8. The sole desire of all the impious and of the devil’s wickedness is to withdraw from him who is supreme Being. [Col. 0229D] So much so that their nature would return to nothing if divine law permitted it. But since an impediment arising from the eternal laws prevents it from falling as far as it would wish, it suffers from that impediment, is tormented by suffering, punished, and tortured, and thereby becomes miserable through deprivation of empty pleasures. That impediment, by which they are prevented from reaching what they lustfully desire, becomes for them a penal destruction and the most just torment of their wretched craving.

9. The number of both parties was predestined.

10. The impious serve God unwillingly—not the nature which he made in them and does not punish in them, but the evil will which he did not make in them and which he punishes in them. In the fact that they serve him unwillingly, they are punished in themselves by their own punishment. [Col. 0230A] Those whom he does not justly free from it, he in a certain way prepares for it, by permitting them to prepare themselves for it.

When in these words he says, “The error concerning predestination arose from ignorance of the disciplines which Wisdom itself wished to be its companions and investigators, and from ignorance of Greek letters,” he naturally admonishes his hearers to learn from him, as from a highly learned and philosophical man, the knowledge of the liberal disciplines, and perhaps also to learn from him in the same way proficiency in Greek letters. For he asserts that Wisdom itself has those teachings of the liberal arts joined to it as companions and associates, so that whoever wishes to reach knowledge of Wisdom necessarily requires those liberal disciplines, [Col. 0230B] in order through them to investigate what is true.

If, then, among others ignorance of secular literature produced error concerning the truth of divine predestination, what did this man, who boasts of being learned in those subjects, investigate about this matter through them? What truth did he discover? What did he argue in his long discourse that was supported by the firmest reasoning and worthy of all acceptance?

Nothing else is found there except the fruitless labor of vanity, the entanglement of boundless error, and the most open assault upon the truth. He despises the Scriptures of truth and, being ignorant even of the histories contained in the divine utterances, does not meditate on them day and night, nor strive to correct, direct, and shape his faith according to their rule. Instead, he spends his days and nights reading human vanities and desires to fill his belly with the pods of swine [Col. 0230C] (Luke XV, 16), yet derives no nourishment from them. He wastes away and perishes in the most wretched hunger, under the domination of the most wicked master, who sent him into his farm to feed swine (ibid., 15).

Let him therefore return to himself, arise, and come to the father, so that he who was starving outside may find bread within. There let him feast on the banquet of the fattened calf, sacrificed for the salvation of the world; there let him hear the symphony and the choir (ibid., 25)—that is, the wondrous harmony of the heavenly Scriptures and the sweet concord of the faithful, who, all possessing the same wisdom and established in the same understanding and judgment, honor God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ with one mind and one voice.

Placed, then, in this house through God’s mercy and the grace of faith, let us faithfully hear and retain [Col. 0230D] what the steward of eternal bread—that is, of the divine word—teaches us:

> “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish so that he may be wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written: ‘He catches the wise in their craftiness.’ And again: ‘The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile’” (I Cor. III, 18, 20).

Let us also hear that most wise man who says:

> “I am the most foolish of men, and the wisdom of men is not with me. I have not learned wisdom, nor do I possess the knowledge of the holy” (Prov. XXX, 2, 3).

We do not say this as though no truth were found even in those human writings, or as though those disciplines had no usefulness for investigating [Col. 0231A] truth. Rather, every faithful person must first learn with the utmost vigilance the truth of faith from the authority of God’s Scriptures, so that if it should later become necessary to read or know something from those same human writings, everything may be judged by that divine authority and the truth of faith.

If anything there does not disagree with its rule, it may be accepted without danger; but whatever is found to be discordant with it must be rejected as deadly. Whoever thinks that, without knowledge of true faith, without the most faithful authority of Holy Scripture, and without the most diligent instruction of the teaching of the Fathers, he can investigate the truth of God and the integrity of faith through human writings and disciplines alone, is undoubtedly mocking and deceiving himself. While he wishes to appear an inventor of truth, he becomes a teacher of error.

[Col. 0231B] This order of piety must be observed with such attention that even the sacred writings in the books of the Law and the Prophets cannot in any way be useful or salutary to readers unless either the faith of Christ precedes in the reader’s heart, through which they may be truly understood, or the faith of Christ itself is faithfully sought in them and found through God’s illumination.

Hence the Apostle, admonishing and instructing his faithful and beloved disciple, says:

> “And because from infancy you have known the sacred writings, which can instruct you for salvation through faith, which is in Christ Jesus” (II Tim. III, 15).

What else does this mean than that, through the faith which is in Christ Jesus, the sacred writings themselves can instruct a person for salvation, because without his faith no saving instruction can be found there?

Therefore this man erred so greatly and conceived and wrote so many false [Col. 0231C] and deceptive things because he was ignorant of the Holy Scriptures. He did not humbly and faithfully seek the truth of faith in them, but arrogantly and vainly believed that he could discover it through human and foolish arguments. Thus he did not discover it; rather, he attacked it faithlessly and disastrously.

Whoever, then, desires to escape human error concerning the truth of divine predestination and to discover what he ought to hold according to the truth should, as we have already said, read carefully and faithfully the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic writings. He must not dare to defend his own understanding against them, but must humbly submit himself to their authority and truth, lest he try, to his own destruction, to kick against the goad.

Since we have already set forth much on this matter from those divine writings, [Col. 0231D] let us mention only one passage briefly here, so as not to weary our readers, from the letter of the blessed apostle Jude. Speaking of the most impious heretics who have attacked and will continue to attack the Lord’s Church from apostolic times until the end of the age, and wishing to show that they had been handed over to a depraved mind by God’s eternal and just judgment, so that they would dare to speak such great and terrible things against God, and that finally, by the same divine judgment, they would be condemned to eternal destruction, he says:

> “For certain men have slipped in among you, who long ago were designated for this judgment: impious men, transferring the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ into licentiousness, and denying the only ruler, our Lord Jesus Christ” (Jude 4). [Col. 0232A]

Showing also how long ago, and how many ages earlier, this had been foretold and prophesied concerning them, he adds after much else:

> “Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied concerning these men, saying: ‘Behold, the Lord came with his holy myriads to execute judgment against all and to convict all the impious concerning all their impious works and concerning all the harsh things that impious sinners have spoken against him’” (ibid., 14–15).

He most clearly adds concerning their eternal condemnation and the dreadful punishment prepared and reserved for them:

> “Wandering stars, for whom the storm of darkness has been reserved forever” (ibid., 13).

For what could be clearer concerning the predestination of the impious to condemnation in the eternal judgment than that these impious men were designated for this judgment so long ago and so many ages earlier, both by divine [Col. 0232B] judgment and by prophetic oracle? (ibid., 4.)

We must not be so foolish as to suppose that, because the most blessed patriarch and prophet Enoch, the seventh generation from Adam, prophesied this, almighty God then established and predestined something that had not previously existed in his eternal judgment and purpose. For in his immutable eternity there can be no new will and no recent disposition. Rather, what had been eternally determined with him, he willed to be both prophesied and fulfilled in time, in the most fitting order: for the judgment and condemnation of those who were going to dare and commit such things, but for the testing and exercise of his Church, which he also determined to be more diligently instructed and more excellently glorified through such contradictions and attacks [Col. 0232C], just as the Apostle says:

> “For there must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (II Cor. XI, 19).

If, then, we seek God’s just and eternal predestination of the wicked to judgment and condemnation, let us hear that certain impious men were designated for this judgment. They were designated not merely temporally by prophetic speech, but altogether eternally by divine judgment, because what had been eternally fixed with God was foretold and designated temporally through the prophet.

If we seek whether punishment and penalty have been prepared for them by God’s eternal judgment, let us hear what is said of them: “For whom the storm of darkness has been reserved forever.” [Col. 0232D] Let us therefore faithfully assent to the divine truth, neither stripping the impious of punishments nor the punishments of the impious of their divine preparation.

“But you, beloved, building yourselves up upon your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God; and convict some who are judged, but save others by snatching them from the fire, and have mercy on others with fear” (ibid., 20, 23).

For he does not say, “Convict those who are to be judged,” but “those who are judged,” thereby showing that what was going to come upon those persisting in their impiety in its proper time had already, as has been said, come upon them terribly through the predestination of the divine and eternal judgment—so that those who would be condemned by future punishment had already been condemned by a present divine sentence.

[Col. 0233A] After this we must turn to the matter in which, wishing to appear to teach something from his knowledge of the Greek language, he adds and says:

> “Behold the Greek verb *ὁρῶ* (*horō*), which is interpreted as ‘I see,’ ‘I define,’ and ‘I determine’; similarly compounded, *προορῶ* (*prohorō*) means ‘I foresee,’ ‘I predefine,’ and ‘I predestine.’ Therefore predestination and predefinition are nothing other than foreseeing.”

In these words he is right to say that *ὁρῶ* can be rendered in Latin as *video*, “I see.” But how should this “seeing” be understood? Is it simply and only as when we see many things casually, things that present themselves spontaneously to our sight? Or does it mean seeing with a definite and fixed gaze, by which we know with certainty that something exists, or by which our gaze is directed toward something with such intensity that, as though toward a target for an arrow, action follows upon that very gaze?

Scripture says [Col. 0233B] something similar about a smith working iron or any other metal: the eye of the craftsman is directed toward the likeness of the vessel being fashioned, attending to it with such intensity that, as though according to the rule or line of his gaze, he permits nothing in it to be otherwise than he has planned.

Thus the expression *ὁρῶ*, that is, “I see,” should rather be understood in such a way that it denotes a kind of vision directed toward a definite object, so that toward that object the movement of the observer, the shooting of an arrow, the act of shaping, or something similar is directed most precisely and without deviation.

From this verb, *ὁρῶ*, comes *ὅραμα* (*horama*), which is “vision” in Latin. The ancients defined this vision—for example, a dream or some revelation—in this way: a vision is present when someone sees something [Col. 0233C] that will occur in exactly the same manner in which it appeared.

Hence, especially in the Scriptures, the vision of any divine revelation—which is seen in the spirit in such a way that it cannot possibly occur otherwise—is said in Greek to be shown or seen in *ὁράματι* (*horamati*).

Therefore, when “I see” is used in this evident sense, it is most certainly understood as “I define” or “I determine,” as he himself correctly stated. When the expression is compounded by the addition of a preposition and becomes *προορῶ* (*proorō*), it is correctly understood as “I predefine” or “I predestine,” both of which have one meaning. It can also be interpreted as “I foresee.” This providence, when referred to God, is entirely certain, and what he foresees will come to pass exactly as he has foreseen.

Thus from the verb *ὁρῶ* there also appears to be derived the Greek word *ὄρισμος* (*horismos*), meaning “determination,” [Col. 0233D] and, with the preposition added, *προορισμός* (*proorismos*), that is, “predestination.” No one has ever dared to interpret these two words as “vision” or “foreseeing”; rather, as we have said, they mean “determination” and “predestination.”

Similarly, from the same verb *ὁρῶ* there appears to be derived *ὄρισεν* (*horisen*), “he determined,” and, with the preposition added, *προώρισεν* (*proōrisen*), that is, “he predestined.”

Now *προορῶ* (*proorō*), as we said above, can also be interpreted as “I foresee,” as in the Psalm where we say in Latin, “I was always setting the Lord before me” (Ps. XV, 8); in Greek it reads, *προορῶμεν τὸν Κύριον* (*proorōmen ton Kyrion*). This foreseeing certainly indicates something definite and predetermined.

The blessed Jerome rendered it in his edition as: “I set the Lord before me always.” This [Col. 0234A] plainly pertains to something determined.

That what is determined is properly directed toward a definite gaze or purpose, Scripture shows when it says: “Or like an arrow sent into a designated place” (Wis. V, 12). The Apostle also says of himself: “I pursue toward the designated goal, toward the prize of the heavenly calling of God” (Phil. III, 14), and so forth.

Explaining this, the blessed Jerome says:

> “He says that he has not yet apprehended and is by no means perfect, but, like an archer, directs his arrows toward the intended object and the target. The Greeks significantly call this *σκοπός* (*skopos*), lest the arrow, deviating to another side, reveal an inexperienced archer.”

Let him not, therefore, mock our ignorance by altering something in the Greek words through a novel interpretation and, as far as he can [Col. 0234B], emptying their force, so that what all the ancients interpreted in the Holy Scriptures as predestination, predefinition, providence, or purpose, he now wishes to call, by an unusual and absurd name, “foreseeing.”

Although this foreseeing too, like foreknowledge, is entirely certain in God, nevertheless we in no way permit the meaning of predestination to be weakened or destroyed by the novelty of this expression. For God can foresee and foreknow even those things which he himself will not do; but nothing is understood to be predestined by him except what he himself will do, whether by his mercy or by his judgment.

Therefore let what he said, and as though defined, be altogether far from us: that God’s predestination and predefinition are nothing other than foreseeing. For this meaning is plainly impious, [Col. 0234C] as though God had merely foreseen what each person would do or what each person would suffer for his deeds, and had predestined or predefined nothing concerning the one who was going to act well or badly in his eternal judgment.

He adds further and says: “God neither foresaw nor predestined death and punishments, because they are nothing.”

How empty this is, and how contrary to the truth, has already, as we think, been sufficiently and repeatedly demonstrated above.

Then he goes on, speaking about God:

“He left sinners in the mass of original sin; he abandoned those whom he had left; he torments those abandoned by the light in darkness; he destroys those abandoned by life through death.”

He does not leave or abandon what God made in them; otherwise their nature would return to nothing, if the highest essence were not in them. Rather, he despised what he did not make in them—that is, pride. Therefore, if in saying that God left sinners in the mass of original sin he had said “the rejected,” or “those to be punished,” or “those to be condemned,” he would certainly have spoken truly. For they—namely, the rejected, those to be punished and condemned—remain in that mass, generally condemned in Adam, because the omnipotent Potter did not separate them from it, since from one and the same mass he makes one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Rom. IX, 21).

But what he now says—that God left sinners in the mass of original sin—cannot altogether be true, since the one who says, “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. II, 17), certainly separated sinners from it and delivered them. And of him the Apostle says: “This saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners” (I Tim. XV).

Nevertheless, since he did not say, “He left all sinners in that mass”—which would plainly be false—but said indefinitely, “He left sinners in that mass,” what was said can be understood as applying only to some; let the statement stand, whatever its force.

But when he adds concerning those same people left in the mass of sin, “He abandoned those whom he had left; he torments those abandoned by the light in darkness; he destroys those abandoned by life through death,” he wants them understood as abandoned by God and, through being abandoned, deserted in this sense: because they have been deserted by the true light, they are tormented in their minds by the darkness of their blindness; and because they have been deserted by true life, they are destroyed in their souls by a particular death.

And this, he would have it, is their only punishment and penalty in that eternal condemnation: that, without any external torment being inflicted, they are punished solely by blindness of mind and death of soul, just as above he repeatedly attempted to maintain.

And, so that he may appear to show that some great good remains for them in that condemnation, he further says of them: “Nor does he leave or abandon what God made in them; otherwise their nature would return to nothing, if the highest essence were not in them; but he despised what he did not make in them, namely, pride.”

See what sort of good he proclaims to have remained in them—indeed, the sort of good God deigns to bestow even upon insensible elements: by the omnipotent power of his essence he gives them being, so that they continue to exist and their nature is not reduced to nothing; by that same power he sustains them and makes them remain.

But these things—that is, the elements of the world—are preserved in their natural substance insofar as they exist; they remain for the praise of the Creator and for the use or honor of rational creation. The nature of the condemned and lost is likewise preserved by the omnipotent power of God, so that it does not perish; and by God’s just judgment, what is preserved benefits it only as punishment, so that its suffering may never end. The Creator may also rightly be praised, since he did not will the good of nature that he had created to be wholly destroyed.

[Note: The elements will not be consumed with respect to their substance and their proper qualities—for they are certain principal parts of the world itself, which will then rather be perfected—but with respect to the qualities mixed into them. At that time they will be made entirely pure and suited to the future condition of the blessed. Thus, when St. Peter says, in II Peter, chapter III, that the heavens will pass away and the elements will be dissolved by heat, this should not first be understood of those heavenly bodies to which it is certain that the conflagrating fire will not extend, but of the aerial heaven—that is, the entire expanse of the air. It is said to pass away because of renewal and greater perfection; likewise, the elements are to be dissolved by heat, that is, purified.—Augustine, *On the City of God*, book XX, chapters 6 and 18.]

But when he says, “Otherwise their nature would return to nothing, if the highest essence were not in them,” if he had said, “Their nature would return to nothing if the highest essence did not grant them being, or did not preserve their being,” he would certainly have spoken truly, because everything that exists received its existence from that supreme and divine essence.

Now, since he has said, “unless the highest essence were in them,” he seems to attribute so much to those who will be condemned in that destruction that they appear even to be God’s temple.

[Note: God is more perfectly united with the condemned than with temples if the order of their actions is considered; but, if the special benefits bestowed upon people praying in a temple are considered, he is more in temples than in hell or with the condemned. This does not deny that the Trinity is present in the condemned, since God will be everywhere by essence, presence, and power. He therefore means only that God is not present in them as an indwelling grace, but only through the manifestation of his justice.]

For if the highest essence will be in them—and the highest essence is God, who says of himself, “I am who I am” (Exod. III, 14)—then God will be in them, and they may be called God’s temple, so that God may say of them, “I will dwell in them.”

Indeed, they will be more than a temple, if the highest essence will be in them, so that they may appear, in a certain manner, to be united with God by an essential union. But this is something that must be believed uniquely of the one and only Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus: the Word of God, who is God, united him to himself by an essential and natural conjunction—that is, received him into the unity of his person.

If, however, he means that the highest substance will be in them by the power of its operation, acting so that their substance may not be abolished and perish, but not by any grace of indwelling through which they might enjoy some good in him and from him, then let him change his unusual and arrogant expression. Let him not say that the highest essence is in impious human beings condemned to eternal destruction, but rather that the highest essence is present to them by the power of its operation, not by the graciousness of indwelling.

There is, however, a great question—one to be investigated with faithful reverence, insofar as divine grace grants the ability—concerning how the omnipotent God is to be believed always to exist or be present everywhere in the whole of creation, and at times also to exist within it or dwell in it. At this point we propose the question rather than explain it, so that pious and faithful people may seek the truth of this matter piously and faithfully, and, with the same God assisting, truly discover it.

This man, being insufficiently experienced both in ecclesiastical expression and in Christian piety, adds further concerning those same impious condemned people and says: “God always dwells in that nature which he created for himself.”

In these words he evidently wants the nature that God created for himself to be understood as human nature, which God made in the rational mind according to his image and likeness. He says that God always dwells in this nature of the rational mind: in the present age and in the future; in believers who are faithful to him and in unbelievers and pagans who, by their very unbelief, are alienated from him; in the elect, whom he made his temple; and in the reprobate, whom he condemned to eternal destruction.

This is plainly contrary to faith and truth. For if it could be true, then one could rightly say that God the Father dwells even in the most unbelieving Jews and pagans who, insofar as natural goodness and their creation by God are concerned, have been made according to God’s image and likeness; and likewise that Christ dwells in them, and the Holy Spirit also dwells in them. The same would have to be said of those lost through eternal condemnation: that God the Father will dwell in them, that Christ will dwell in them, and that the Holy Spirit will dwell in them.

What could be said or imagined that is more horrible than this impious and detestable meaning?

This absurdity is followed by another consequence. If angels, who are certainly preeminently rational creatures, are rightly believed to have been created according to God’s image and likeness—for they received nothing less in their nature than human beings did—then it would also have to be said that God the Father, God forbid, and his Christ, and the Holy Spirit dwell in the devil and his angels, who share one nature with the holy angels.

Yet, as we showed above from the Scriptures, this gift of his blessed and gracious indwelling is to be believed to be bestowed upon the elect and faithful rational creation alone. For the Lord promises the pious and faithful, saying: “I and the Father will come to him, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 23). And concerning the indwelling of the Holy Spirit he likewise promises them, saying: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to remain with you forever” (John XIV, 16–17). Shortly afterward he adds concerning him: “But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.”

Of such people God himself says: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (II Cor. VI, 16). And the Psalmist says: “They will rejoice forever, and he will dwell in them” (Ps. V, 12). Elsewhere they say: “If the Lord had not been with us—let Israel now say—if the Lord had not been with us” (Ps. CXXIII, 1).

Thus also the blessed apostle John, distinguishing between God as the inhabitant of the pious and the devil as the inhabitant of the impious, says to the faithful: “You are from God, little children, and you have conquered them, because greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world” (I John IV, 4).

If this man desires correction, let him faithfully learn these things from the Scriptures, and let him not quarrel against God’s truth with human and empty arguments, but submit himself to it with gentle piety.

But since he repeats everything he says about those who were left in the mass of original sin for no other reason than to assert that they are bound only by the bond of original sin and were not predestined to punishment by any judgment of God, we must ask him and the others who think likewise whether it happened by some judgment of God that so great a multitude of the human race became subject to that original sin and, consequently, liable also to eternal death—or whether it did not.

For if this happened not by any judgment of God, but only through the natural course of a corrupted origin, then sin was naturally transmitted from that first human being to them in such a way that no condemnation for his sin was transmitted to them. In that case, only the origin of sin, and not the just punishment of sin, proceeded from Adam into them.

But the Apostle plainly says that “through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings” (Rom. V, 12). Therefore, truly, through one man and from one man, not only sin but also the punishment of sin—death—entered the world.

By whose judgment, unless by that of the one who had said to the human being: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. II, 12)? Eating from that forbidden tree was certainly the sin; but the punishment of the sin was what was added immediately afterward: “You shall die by death.”

God did not threaten him only with that first bodily death, but also with the death that came about through sin in the soul, because “the soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVIII, 4), and also with the second death that will occur in eternal condemnation, to which the guilt of that first sin draws every human being unless he is delivered by the grace of Christ.

When God therefore spoke these words, he did not merely wish to instill terror in the hearer; rather, by that threat he revealed what he had established by his eternal judgment: namely, that by his just and eternal judgment, if the human being committed that sin, he would first inflict death upon the soul, then dissolve the body through death, and finally condemn him to the second death.

This entire condemnation—of both soul and body—would thereafter, together with the sin itself, be transmitted to all descendants. Therefore he transmitted throughout the whole offspring of that human being the judgment of his eternal counsel and justice, which he had judged should begin in that first and single human being. Thus, by that just judgment of his, whoever from that mass condemned in Adam was not separated by the grace of Christ was held predestined to eternal condemnation by the first sentence of divine judgment.

Therefore he did not merely leave the reprobate in the mass of original sin, as though he had established and defined nothing concerning them. He also judged that his eternal and just judgment, which had gone before in the root, should be followed in the offspring, and that what began in the parent should necessarily be fulfilled in the descendants.

Among the faithful there is absolutely no doubt that, before the human being sinned, the omnipotent God foreknew that he would sin. And just as he foreknew the sin, so he also predestined what that person would suffer by his just judgment. What he began by judging that person justly, he fulfilled in all his descendants by the same foreknowledge, the same predestination of judgment, and the same justice of condemnation.

But these statements—that God left the reprobate in that mass of condemnation and did not predestine anything concerning their condemnation—he appears to have taken from a little book that the Greeks call the *Hypognosticon*, which many holy men also believe, on the basis of its false title, to be by Saint Augustine.

The style itself and the meaning demonstrate that this little book is not by that same holy Augustine. It is contrary not only to the writings of Saint Augustine but also to the faith. It also contains testimonies taken from the new edition that we use, whereas Augustine, disputing against heretics and dealing with matters of faith, continually refutes the contradictors from the old edition and instructs the faithful from it.

He further adds and says: “The wisdom of God predestined in its laws modes beyond which the malice of the impious cannot advance,” and so on, up to the point where he says, “the most just torment of desire.”

In these words certain true premises have been set forth so that a false conclusion might be constructed from them. For it is plainly true that the wisdom of God, in the hidden laws of his ordering, predestined and fixed a limit and measure for the malice of the impious, whether angels or human beings, so that their malice could not proceed and extend as far as they desired, if it is restrained by a definite measure and boundaries under God’s hidden laws.

The devil and wicked human beings always have the will to act or inflict harm wickedly, but they do not always have the power, except insofar as and whenever God permits them. Even when the devil maliciously and wickedly desired to harm the blessed Job, God imposed a limit upon him; he could not harm him as much as he wished, but only as much as he was permitted.

And concerning impious people who attempt malicious and wicked deeds but, because God imposes a limit upon them, are wholly unable to accomplish them, Scripture plainly says: “They devised plans which they were unable to establish” (Ps. XX, 12). Again: “He frustrates the thoughts of the wicked, so that their hands cannot accomplish what they had begun” (Job V, 12).

What this man adds and says—that neither the devil’s malice nor that of all the impious desires anything except that, by sinning and acting wickedly, they may withdraw from God, who is the highest essence—is plainly true. For, as has been said, by sinning and acting wickedly, what else do they do except withdraw from God, become far from him, and perish? As it is written of them: “For those who distance themselves from you will perish” (Ps. LXXII, 27).

He further says that the wicked desire of both the devil and impious human beings is so inclined and eager toward evil that, if divine power permitted them, they would plunge so deeply into sins that their very nature could rightly be destroyed. This is certainly a strained statement, but perhaps not entirely false.

Likewise, what he adds is true: because of the difficulty and impossibility imposed upon them by divine power and providence, which prevents them from falling into as deep an abyss of malice as they desire, there is in their minds—that is, in the minds of both evil spirits and the worst human beings—the labor of striving and the torment of thinking in many ways about what they cannot accomplish.

Such labor certainly becomes torment, punishment, and anguish to their minds, so that they are tortured and punished by their own evil will.

But when, after all this, he adds and says that from this inner torment and punishment of the mind, while it cannot fulfill its desires because God resists it, the soul becomes wretched, suffering the poverty of its empty pleasures, this is indeed true: that this perverse desire of the mind makes that same mind wretched both when it is fulfilled and when it is not permitted to be fulfilled.

But the mind is much more wretched when it is permitted such things than when it is restrained from them by divine power. For it is more unhappy to be able to do evil than merely to wish it and be unable to do it.

Hence that secular philosopher’s statement concerning someone is true: “O wretched man, to whom it was permitted to sin!” The person who said this spoke truly, because if the one of whom it was said had been forbidden to sin, he would have been less wretched, having only the will to sin. But when he was permitted to sin—through that most unhappy permission—he was far more wretched both in the desire and inclination of an evil will.

When this man explains why he has set all these things forth, he adds at the end and says that the difficulty and impossibility by which impious angels or human beings, with God resisting them, are prevented from reaching what they eagerly and perversely desire becomes for them, in that eternal condemnation, only the punishment of destructive death and the most just torment of wretched desire.

Thus, he says, they suffer only this death and torment in their minds, because they are no longer permitted to fulfill what they had perversely desired, and no external punishment or torment is inflicted upon them from that eternal fire. This is an utterly manifest lie, contrary to faith and truth, as has already been shown frequently above.

### CHAPTER XIX

In the nineteenth chapter, that is, the final chapter, he says:

1. “This eternal fire is itself the fourth element of the world, in which the bodies of the saints are changed into an ethereal quality, while the bodies of the impious are to pass into an aerial quality.

2. “And in it the marvelous joy of the natures among themselves is perfected, while the ineffable torment of evil wills is perfected.

3. “And thus the bodies of all the impious, angels and human beings, will suffer the penalties of eternal fire, in such a way that the integrity of their substance will not perish at all, their beauty will not be lacking at all, and their natural soundness will remain; thereafter all the goods of nature will shine forth in marvelous order for the adornment of the whole, except for blessedness, of which they will be deprived.

4. “While the quality of the higher corporeal fire struggles with the bodies of the lower air, the natural power being preserved, the striving of the unhappy souls will suffer eternal hardships from their bodies.

5. “Thus, indeed, that same fire will become glory for all bodies, while for the souls to be condemned their own iniquity will accumulate inwardly and punishment will accumulate outwardly.”

In these fantastic words, filled with every delirium of madness, he sets aside the simplicity of the faith and apostolic confession by which the whole Church believes and confesses that our Lord Jesus Christ rose from the dead on the third day, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come from there to judge the living and the dead; that at his coming there will be a resurrection of the flesh; and that eternal life will be given to the saints.

I say, setting aside this most simple and pure confession of piety, nowhere mentioning Christ’s coming from heaven, nowhere recalling the resurrection from the dead, he confuses everything and attempts to obscure it with various inventions, so that in his writings we can recognize neither the truth of the resurrection, nor the truth of divine judgment and eternal punishment, nor any mention of the future life of the saints.

For he says that in that eternal fire, which he supposes to be the fourth element of the world—placed by the natural order above the earth, the waters, and the air—the bodies of the saints will be changed into an ethereal quality, while the bodies of the impious will pass into an aerial quality.

He is manifestly at odds with and contrary to apostolic teaching, which says that the resurrection of all and the transformation of the saints will take place not in a fourth element of the world, nor in some fiery furnace, but in this earthly dwelling where the bodies of both the righteous and the wicked lived and died. Their transformation will occur with marvelous and ineffable speed—that is, as the Apostle himself says, “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye,” than which nothing in bodily motion is swifter.

For he says: “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed. In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet; for the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (I Cor. XV, 51–52). In these words he plainly describes the general resurrection of all.

But he distinguishes this very general resurrection of all by a particular distinction when he says, “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed.” And when he adds, “The dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed,” he shows that all will rise through receiving their bodies, but that not all will be changed through the glorification of the righteous.

For the wicked will rise merely incorruptible, not glorified. They will be incorruptible only in the sense that they will no longer be able to be dissolved by death. But, as they endure and suffer eternal punishments and torments, they will be entirely corruptible, and they will be corrupted without end by those very punishments, so that, as Scripture says, “fire and worms will be given to their flesh, that they may burn and feel forever” (Judith XVI, 21).

The righteous, however, in whose person the Apostle says, “We shall be changed,” will rise incorruptible, so that they may no longer be dissolved by any death. They will have this special property: that their bodies will be changed for the better. The same Apostle states this and plainly explains what that change will be: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (I Cor. XV, 53).

That is, this very body now borne by the saints as corruptible and mortal will, through the power of the resurrection, become incorruptible and immortal; it will be clothed with incorruption and immortality.

The incorruption of the saints will be so great and so complete that it can no longer be touched by any pain, labor, distress, or need. Through the immortality given to them, death will be swallowed up in their bodies, so that not only will death itself in some manner be destroyed there, but also the cause of death—that is, the sting of sin, by whose piercing death came into being from the beginning—will be utterly crushed.

That sting of sin, however, will never be removed from the bodies of the condemned; therefore they will never truly be free from death.

Concerning this most blessed transformation of the righteous the Apostle further says: “But when this mortal has put on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: Death is swallowed up in victory. Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death? The sting of death is sin; but thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid., vv. 54–57).

Therefore the bodies of the righteous will not rise first and afterward, as this man says, be changed in the fiery element as in a furnace. Rather, in that very moment and twinkling of an eye in which they rise, they will be changed by divine power and clothed with the glory of incorruption and immortality.

Concerning the transformation of the wicked condemned to eternal punishments, whose bodies this man says—through a new and unheard-of kind of error—will be changed into an aerial quality, the Apostle says absolutely nothing. Therefore we too must disregard such a fantasy rather than listen to it, lest we become people with itching ears, turning away from the truth in hearing and turning instead to fables.

For how, according to him, will they pass into an aerial quality? If they become aerial from earthly bodies, there will be no true resurrection, because the same bodies that fell through death will not rise. Those bodies were earthly; these will be aerial.

But if the nature of the earthly bodies remains and they nevertheless receive the quality of air, so that they are changed by the subtlety of air and winds, the Church’s faith does not accept this novelty, because, as has already been said, the Apostle says nothing about the transformation of the impious.

As for his statement that the bodies of the saints will be changed into an ethereal quality, if he believes that this transformation will occur while the nature of their bodies remains—so that the very bodies that fell in death and were raised in the resurrection will be glorified with heavenly brightness, becoming radiant instead of obscure—it is sufficient for us, concerning this marvelous illumination of theirs, to hold what the Lord says will occur in them: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII, 43).

But if he says that those same bodies will be changed into an ethereal quality in such a way that they lose their nature and earthly bodies become heavenly, he plainly contradicts the truth of the resurrection and therefore must not be heard.

Whoever desires to think simply, purely, and truly about the resurrection of the saints and the nature of spiritual bodies should faithfully hear and retain what the blessed Augustine teaches most sincerely about these matters:

> “The need to eat and drink will be removed from such bodies, and therefore they will be spiritual—not because they will cease to be bodies, but because they will subsist through the life-giving Spirit. For just as those bodies that possess a living soul but do not yet possess a life-giving spirit are called animal bodies, although they are not souls but bodies, so those bodies will be called spiritual bodies. Yet far be it from us to believe that they will become spirits. Rather, they will retain the substance of flesh but will suffer none of the slowness or corruption of the flesh, because the Spirit will give them life. Then the human being will be heavenly, not earthly—not because the body fashioned from earth will no longer be the same body, but because, by a heavenly gift, it will then be such that it is suited to dwell in heaven, not by losing its nature but by changing its quality. Accordingly, when the soul has received this body, no longer animal but spiritual through the future transformation, and when it has been made equal to the angels, it will possess the perfect measure of its nature, obeying and commanding, being made alive and giving life, with such ineffable ease that what was once a burden will become its glory.”

This man then adds and says: “And in it the marvelous joy of the natures among themselves is perfected, while the ineffable torment of evil wills is perfected.”

That is, to speak according to his meaning, the marvelous joy of the natures alone will be perfected there, since according to him they did not sin at all. The joy of the natures will consist in this: that the nature of the earthly body, as he supposes, will pass into an aerial quality in the impious, while in the saints it will pass into a still higher glory, that is, into an ethereal quality. The ineffable torment of the evil wills—which alone, he says, sinned—will then arise when they are tormented by their own evil conscience.

But how empty and false all this is has already been sufficiently demonstrated.

### 3

After these statements he adds and says:

“And thus the bodies of all the impious, angels and human beings, will suffer the penalties of eternal fire, in such a way that the integrity of their substance will not perish at all, their beauty will not be lacking at all, and their natural soundness will remain; thereafter all the goods of nature will shine forth in marvelous order for the adornment of the whole, except for blessedness, of which they will be deprived.”

It is exceedingly astonishing how in these words he says that the bodies of all the impious, angels and human beings, will suffer the punishment of eternal fire, since above he so openly and repeatedly denied this everywhere.

In this passage he either confessed it falsely and deceitfully, in which case he is abominable before God because he holds a lie concerning his faith in his heart while wishing to display truth with his mouth, as it is written: “You will destroy all who speak lies; the man of blood and deceit the Lord abhors” (Ps. V, 7–8).

Or, if he truly confessed it, overcome by the actual truth of the matter and by fear of offending the Church, lest he be judged wholly unbelieving, then such a confession is entirely empty and worthless, since it is preceded by so great and repeated a denial.

We, however, are not permitted in matters belonging to the faith of God to say one thing now and another later. What the Church has once received from the very mouth of the Lord and his apostles must be believed and confessed, and it must be retained with inviolable and immutable truth, so that what the Lord commanded may be fulfilled most truly in us: “Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes; No, no’” (Matt. V, 37). That is, by immovable truth our truth must be confirmed through confession, and our falsehood rejected through confession.

And yet how faithfully this man believes in the punishments of eternal fire, he makes perfectly clear in what follows. For after saying that the bodies of wicked angels and human beings will suffer the punishments of eternal fire—in such a way that we can understand the manner in which he believes this will occur—he immediately adds:

“This will happen in such a way that the integrity of their substance, that is, of the wicked angels and human beings, will in no way perish; that their beauty will in no way be lacking; and that their natural soundness will remain in them.”

Observe what good things he grants them amid the punishments of eternal fire: namely, integrity of nature, beauty, and soundness. He says that they will retain the integrity of their nature because their entire nature, in soul and body, will remain forever. But how, or where, can they possess beauty? Let every faithful person consider this. Beauty belongs either to the soul or to the body.

What faithful person could believe that there can be any beauty of souls where there will be the loss of every virtue and the foulness of every vice? For the soul is beautiful through virtue, or deformed through vice. And what beauty of bodies can exist where they will be darkened and obscured by eternal horror and sorrow, by the eternal burning of fire, and by the eternal tearing of worms?

What natural soundness, moreover, can exist in those condemned angels and human beings, as this man says, when their nature is preserved intact for this sole purpose: that it may never be released from its natural structure, but may be tortured more completely, in its entirety, without end?

But not content with such folly and absurdity arising from his corrupted understanding, he adds at the end the most manifest error of heretical impiety, so that what he harbored in his heart for the assault upon the truth and the subversion of his hearers, he might also spew forth from his mouth.

For he immediately adds concerning those same natures of condemned demons and human beings that thereafter—that is, after those punishments of eternal fire—“they will shine forth with all the goods of nature in wondrous order”: namely, that in soul they will be endowed and illumined with the natural goods of memory, understanding, and free will; and that in body they will shine and excel both in the liveliness of the five natural senses and in the beauty of perfect form.

He says that they will therefore be exempted from punishments and adorned with every natural good, so that, shining with such beauty, they may contribute to the adornment of the universe: that is, so that, among the other earthly or heavenly creatures of the world, they too may remain as part of the world’s adornment, although they had been in the punishment of condemnation.

And afterward, lest he seem entirely to contradict the faith of the Church and evangelical and apostolic truth, he added, saying, “except for blessedness, of which they will be deprived”—that is, the demons and human beings, released from their punishments, will shine with all natural goods in such a way that, except for the blessedness of the vision of God, which alone will be denied them, they will appear to lack nothing good.

Observe what this man dares to think, what he dares to say, and what he even dares to write: a man who wishes to appear Christian and strives for nothing else than to oppose Christian truth and to introduce into the Church’s integrity the dogmas of the heretics, with whom he has unhappily joined himself.

For the Church of Christ denies and detests both propositions, because both are heretical and wholly opposed to the truth: namely, both the liberation of demons and human beings from those everlasting punishments, and the existence of some intermediate place where those demons and human beings might remain in repose and in the abundance and brightness of every good, so that they would be neither in the condemnation of eternal fire with the devil nor in blessedness with God.

The Church holds with complete certainty that after that universal judgment no one can exist except either in eternal blessedness or, conversely, in everlasting misery. Those who have once been sent away at that judgment either to punishment or into the joy of eternal life will never afterward be able to exist anywhere else or in any other condition.

The Lord most certainly shows this concerning both parties—that is, the condemned, who will be on the left, and the blessed, who will be on the right—when he pronounces an irrevocable sentence, saying: “Then these will go away to eternal punishment, but the righteous to eternal life” (Matthew 25:46).

For if that eternal punishment will at some time have an end, then eternal life too will at some time have an end—which God forbid. But if eternal life will have no end at all, then without doubt that punishment, namely eternal punishment, can never have an end.

There will therefore not be some people placed in the middle, as this man deliriously imagines, so that they are neither blessed nor wretched, yet nevertheless possess some repose outside the Father’s house. For the Lord clearly says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14:2), showing that outside his Father’s house—that is, outside the fellowship of the holy angels and elect human beings, which he himself inhabits forever—there is no place and no dwelling of rest.

For all that multitude and diversity of dwelling places exists only in the paternal house, where, just as one star differs from another in brightness in the one heaven, so in that one and the same house there will be a diversity of dwelling places according to the diversity of merits.

After this, the man adds and says:

“While the corporeal fire above struggles in its nature with the bodies of the air below, its natural force being preserved, let the intention of the unhappy souls suffer eternal hardships from their bodies.”

Observe how he believes—or, if he believes it at all—that the punishments of eternal fire will be carried out. He supposes that the fire which is the upper element of this kind will punish the bodies of demons, which he thinks are aerial, and the bodies of wicked human beings, which above he said would pass into an aerial quality but now openly calls aerial, just like those of the demons themselves.

He supposes that the natures of both elements—that is, of fire, which he thinks is the eternal fire in the punishments of the condemned, and of air, which he believes exists in the bodies of demons and lost human beings—will struggle and clash with one another in that prison of condemnation, producing eternal hardships of punishment for the unhappy souls of human beings and demons through their aerial bodies.

For, he says, even in that furnace of eternal fire these two elements, fire and air, will preserve their natural force, so that just as in this world the air, which is the lower element, is vaporized and heated by the heat of the sun’s higher fire, affecting our bodies severely through its vapor and heat, so in that furnace of punitive fire everlasting, while the fire inflames by its natural force the aerial bodies of demons and human beings, the souls within them will feel and suffer eternal hardships of affliction from the very heat and burning of their bodies.

Let this man, who thinks and writes such things, now say how the unhappy souls of both kinds of creature, angelic and human, will at some time be rescued from those punishments and shine forth, as he himself says, with all natural goods, if, through the force of that fire, their aerial bodies are cruelly inflamed and they suffer eternal hardships.

For if they are released from those punishments, they will certainly be free from hardships; but if they remain in everlasting hardships, they will never merit liberation.

Yet, while explaining further the manner in which he thinks that this punishment—so fabricated and contrived with such labor—will come about, he adds and says:

“Thus, namely, the very same fire will become glory for all bodies, while punishment will be heaped upon the souls condemned within by their own iniquity and upon their bodies externally.”

In these words he seems to assert that the same eternal fire will increase the punishment both of souls condemned inwardly through the consciousness of their own iniquity and of their bodies externally by inflaming and heating them—so that they are tortured not only inwardly by conscience but also afflicted externally by fiery punishment—and yet that this same fire will confer a kind of glory upon their aerial bodies.

We suppose that, just as this fire which shines in the stars illuminates the dark and shadowy nature of the air by its infusion and makes it bright with its radiance—although the air is naturally dark unless it is illuminated either by the sun’s rays during the day or by the rays of the moon and stars at night—so he imagines that the aerial bodies of demons and human beings will be illumined and glorified by the radiance of that eternal fire, just as the blackness of iron is changed into a shining quality by the heat of a furnace.

How, then, did he say above: “The aerial bodies of angels and human beings will suffer the punishments of eternal fire”? For if that eternal fire will be their punishment, it will certainly not be their glory; but if it will be their glory, it will not be their punishment.

Driving away and repelling far from us such crooked and serpent-like evasions, such laborious and destructive winding paths, let us hold to the simplicity of faith, believing that the bodies of condemned human beings are real bodies—that is, earthly bodies—and that in them they will suffer real and eternal punishments, those who will have been condemned to that condemnation.
