For the statement of Truth is utterly true, and in the Gospel it says: “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, while those who have done evil will come forth to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:28–29).

At that voice of the Son of God, all who are in the tombs will come forth, because they will receive the same bodies that had been placed in the tombs and will rise in those same bodies, possessing in them either the resurrection of life or the resurrection of judgment, so that in them they may either possess eternal life or suffer eternal death.

It is good for us, and altogether necessary for our salvation above all things, that, founded upon the truth and simplicity of faith, we should fear and, with the Lord’s help, avoid the evil that the Apostle declares he fears for the Church betrothed to Christ and endowed with the virginity of a chaste faith, saying:

“For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2–3).

Hence elsewhere also he admonishes us, saying: “Avoid foolish and old-womanish fables” (1 Timothy 4:7). And again: “Avoid profane and empty words, for they advance greatly toward impiety, and their speech spreads like cancer” (2 Timothy 2:16–17).

For this reason blessed Peter the apostle, with the same devotion and concern, admonishes the faithful, saying: “Therefore, beloved, since you know these things beforehand, guard yourselves, lest, carried away by the error of the foolish, you fall from your own steadfastness. Rather, grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (2 Peter 3:17–18).

Let these things not become for us like jokes or matters of play, since the Apostle also calls the play of Ishmael with Isaac a persecution. Therefore, wherever we recognize such things, we ought to be stirred against them by zeal for the faith, under the guidance and assistance of him who says in the Psalm: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Psalm 68:10).

He also made a whip from cords and drove out the violators of God’s house with their merchandise, because they had made that paternal house a den of thieves (John 2:15).

For they truly turn the house of the Lord—which is the Church of the living God, “the pillar and foundation of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15)—into a den of thieves. Truly they are thieves who, under the pretext of the Christian name and as though established in the Church, attempt to conceal their faithlessness and, through crafty and malicious disputations, lie in wait for the lives of the faithful.

And because this man, to whose words we have responded as best we could with the Lord’s help, takes pride in philosophical rules and syllogistic arguments, let us finally hear faithfully and obediently the most blessed bishop and confessor of Christ, Hilary, refuting and addressing such men in these words:

“It was necessary for those who claim to possess religious knowledge of divine matters, wherever the truth of evangelical and apostolic preaching prevailed, to cast aside the crooked questions of philosophy and to follow instead the faith that is in God. For faith’s protection would easily strip a weak understanding of the sophistry of syllogistic questioning, when a deceptive proposition deprived a simple answer—one accommodating and responsive to the question—of its force by the final question of its own reasoning, so that what had been lost in profession would no longer be held in the conscience.”

Again, that same glorious confessor, while explaining the Apostle’s words, “See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ,” says:

“Philosophy must be guarded against, and the studies of human traditions must not so much be avoided as refuted. For they must not be granted such power that they seem to conquer rather than deceive. Since we preach Christ as the power of God and the wisdom of God, it is fitting that we should not so much flee human doctrines as refute them, and should both obstruct and instruct, lest the simpler be stripped by them.

“For since God can do all things, and God can do all things wisely, and neither reason opposes his power nor power his reason, those who preach Christ to the world ought, through knowledge of wise omnipotence, to oppose the religious and imperfect doctrines of the world.”

Thus blessed Hilary.

But what punishment and condemnation await not only the authors but also the supporters of falsehood, and with what devout intention one must withdraw from such people, so that each of the faithful, washed and cleansed by the purity of faith, may deserve fellowship in the tree of life—let us hear our Lord himself, threatening and promising at once, with equal terror and sweetness, in the Apocalypse:

“The one who conquers will possess these things, and I will be his God, and he will be my son. But for the timid, the unbelieving, the accursed, and all liars, their portion will be in the pool burning with fire and sulfur, which is the second death” (Revelation 21:7–8).

And again:

“Her gates will not be shut by day, for there will be no night there. And they will bring into her the glory and honor of the nations. Nothing defiled will enter it, nor [anyone] committing abomination in the blood of the Lamb and falsehood” (ibid., verses 25–27).

And again:

“Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have authority over the tree of life and may enter the city through the gates. Outside are dogs, sorcerers, the sexually immoral, murderers, idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood. I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify these things to you in the churches” (Revelation 22:14–16).

[Col. 0249]

## Various Poems of Florus the Deacon

[Note: Among Florus’s verses, the first place is occupied by two poems which the distinguished Adrian Valesius, royal historiographer, copied in his own hand from an ancient Petavian manuscript and, with his notes, generously made available to me.]

*(From the Analecta of Mabillon and the Thesaurus of Martène.)*

### I. Lament on the Division of the Empire after the Death of Louis the Pious

[Note: This poem concerns the various disasters that befell Gaul after the division of the empire following the death of Louis the Pious. In the Petavian manuscript the poem bears this title: “The book of Manno, offered at the tomb of Saint Oyend as a vow for a good memory.” This book therefore belonged to the monastery of Saint Oyend, or Eugendus, in the Jura region, now called Saint-Claude; and it was offered by Manno, provost of that monastery, at whose request Ado, archbishop of Vienne, confirmed the church of Velnense to the same abbey in the year 870, as is clear from the letters published in volume XII of the *Spicilegium*, p. 135.]

Mountains and hills, forests and rivers, springs,

Steep crags, and valleys sunk in depth,

Mourn the race of the Franks, which, raised high

By Christ’s gift to imperial power, now lies buried in the dust.

Let the elements themselves, pierced with grief, take up this sorrow:

The stretches of earth, the waters of the sea, the stars of heaven,

The blasts of the winds, and finally the drops of rain;

Let human beings grieve, because human hearts have grown hard.

All things resound, encompassed by divine scourges;

All things are ravaged by the hardships of dreadful disaster.

Every good of peace is torn apart by bitter hatred;

Every glory of the kingdom is darkened by wicked fury.

[Col. 0249C] Behold, the honor of the Church has been cast down and lies buried.

The laws of the priests have been utterly overturned and have collapsed.

The love and fear of the divine law have now departed,

And the decrees of all the canons are now trampled underfoot.

Famous cities are harassed by continual conflicts;

The basilicas of Christ are stripped of their ancient honor.

There is now no honor for the martyrs; even at the altars

No one shows fear, and there is no reverence for sacred things.

The wretched populace suffers from continuous plundering;

The divided nobility rages toward mutual slaughter.

The earth is drenched with blood; everything seethes with robbery,

And the frenzy of crimes runs loose, with its reins broken.

Adultery blazes; perjuries are feared by no one.

Innocent blood is poured out, with no avenger remaining;

The fear of kings and laws has now departed from mortals.

With closed eyes, people now go toward the Tartarean fire.

Who could adequately describe the torn-apart enclosures of the monks,

Or the sacred servants of the Lord undergoing

The yoke of lay domination in disgrace,

Or the rulers of the Church being subjected to the danger of arms and slaughter?

Peoples lie bereft of bishops, and more and more episcopal chairs have lain utterly without a teacher for many years.

[Col. 0250C] At that time the terror of the prince compelled this through miserable disaster;

Now dark pride drives some people toward such evil.

[Note: Our annals are silent about what calamity then befell the city of Narbonne. I would suppose that the same thing happened there as at Reims, because Bartholomew favored the party of Lothair against the emperor Louis and was therefore expelled from his see; from this arose the long deprivation of that church, lasting until the ordination of Berarius.]

Still Narbonne wastes away, sad from its ancient wound;

[Note: That is, what happened to the church of Reims after Ebbo was deposed: the see remained vacant for ten years, namely until the year 844, when Hincmar was appointed in his place while Ebbo was still alive.]

The sad walls of Reims likewise mourn.

[Note: Namely, the elder Hilduin, Abbot Wala, Bernard of Vienne, Bishop Agobard of Lyon, and others who were carried away into various exiles.]

Exile afflicts distinguished and learned men;

Wrongdoing occupies its seat through savage gold.

A distinguished kingdom flourished beneath a radiant diadem:

There was one prince, and the people likewise were one.

Law and judge together adorned all the cities;

Peace held the citizens, and virtue terrified the enemies.

The nourishing care of the priests flourished in emulation,

Administering devout laws to the peoples through frequent councils.

From here and there, among sacred clergy, common people,

And distinguished princes, the word of salvation resounded widely.

Young men everywhere learned the divine books.

The hearts of children absorbed the literary arts.

A vigilant censor often drove away foul crimes:

Fear called some, and love others, to righteous covenants.

It was even a concern to unite foreign peoples to the faith

And to impose upon the conquered the bridles of salvation.

Thus the pagan hand entered beneath the yoke of religion;

[Note: Thus Prudentius writes in the preface to the *Cathemerinon*: “Let him fight against heresies.” Florus violates many other rules of poetry; but one must be indulgent toward his age.]

Thus the rising heresy, crushed beneath their feet, groaned.

[Col. 0251B] From this the Frankish people became exceedingly renowned throughout the whole world,

And the fame of their virtues penetrated to the farthest boundaries.

From every direction foreign kingdoms, barbarian, Greek, and Latin,

Sent their legates from afar to this court.

For even the Roman people yielded to this people,

And renowned Rome, mother of kingdoms, likewise yielded.

There the prince of this kingdom received the diadems of power

Through the apostolic gift, trusting in Christ’s protection.

O fortunate kingdom, if only it knew its blessings,

Whose citadel is Rome, whose author is the key-bearer of heaven,

The eternal guardian and ruler of heaven forever,

Who is able to raise an earthly kingdom into heaven.

But now so great a summit has fallen from so great a height,

Like a flowered crown once cast down from a head,

Whose radiance had been woven from fragrant grass.

It is trampled beneath the feet of all; stripped of its diadem,

It has lost both the name and the glory of empire,

And the united kingdom has collapsed into a threefold division.

There is now no one at all who is considered emperor.

In place of a king there is a petty ruler; in place of a kingdom, fragments of a kingdom.

Through frequent councils, plots for causing harm are devised;

In continual assemblies, the laws of salvation are ravaged.

The common good is annulled; each person protects his own.

Everything is a matter of concern; God alone is forgotten.

The pastors of the Lord, accustomed to come together as one,

Attend no synods because of disputes over worldly affairs.

There is now no public assembly of the people; all justice has departed.

In vain may an envoy return here, where there is no court.

What should the peoples do whom the mighty Danube washes,

Whom the Rhine, the Rhône, the Loire, or the Po water?

Those whom concord long held bound together,

Now, with the treaty broken, sad divisions afflict.

Often heavenly signs foretold this evil to us,

When so many fiery, terrifying ranks, like daylight,

Shone dreadfully through the middle of the darkness of night

And flashed in different regions with baleful fire.

When, in the middle of the day, while the peoples were observing

Festal fasts and devout prayers throughout the churches,

The sun covered its shining face with mournful rust

And made the stars radiate in the heavens as an ominous sign.

We know what monstrous, deadly war followed this:

By which Christ-worshipers attacked one another with accursed steel,

And a kinsman’s sword broke the bonds of pious fellowship;

While wild beasts and birds alike devoured the pious limbs.

[Note: Namely, in the years 837 and subsequently 840 and 842.]

When dread comets so often burned in the sky,

Threatening disaster and destruction to the human race.

Among them, one flashed with a flaming mane

And shone for almost an entire month with a savage light.

After it came the terrible devastation of regions, the upheaval of kings,

The frenzy of war, and the division of the kingdom;

These shake the wretched world with unbroken terrors.

What end, or what wrath of God, will follow such great evils?

Such questions scarcely anyone turns over with a trembling heart,

Scarcely recalls, scarcely breathes forth sighs of grief over them.

[Col. 0252B] People rejoice amid the savage wounds of the exhausted kingdom,

And they call it peace where there is no favor of peace.

A wall stands threatening sudden and mighty collapse,

Long leaning, and full of cracks on every side.

[Note: This is imitated from Ezekiel, chapter 13, verses 12 and following. What follows concerning the prophecy of Amos is taken from chapter 8, verses 1 and 2.]

It is smeared with flowing mud, soon to fall.

There is no mixture of straw here; all its parts totter.

Now we see the fearful vision of the holy prophet Amos

Being fulfilled among us, in the order he lamentingly foresaw.

Now the Lord abandons the wall; he prepares

To lay down the trowel, and in anger wishes to apply no plaster.

Now also he sees the hook for gathering fruit,

By which the whole tree will be stripped bare of its fruits.

Now the oak remains naked of its covering of leaves;

Now the Lord’s splendid garden grows yellow without springs.

[Col. 0252C] Behold, thirst and hunger, which that same prophet foresaw,

Are consuming the lands, sent upon them by the Lord’s judgment.

The nourishment and rains of the heavenly word are now lacking.

The East and the North, the seas on every side, cry out this evil.

The Gospel voice thundering from the divine mouth.

Who does not now see and grieve that the ruin of the godly is at hand?

When the Son of Man comes from the citadel of heaven,

Will he, do you think, find traces of faith on earth?

Foxes have made hidden burrows in human hearts,

And unclean birds have made nests in heaven.

This fraud and arrogance of the terrible enemy prevails widely;

There is no place for Christ where he may rest even his head.

Amid these things may that little flock groan and trust,

For whom the Father preserves the joys of the eternal kingdom,

And may it draw tears from its eyes by night and by day,

Persisting at the gates and knocking with prayers for life.

May it ask with longing heart for the true loaves—

The three that the Gospel page of the Word recalls.

True faith, confessing the triune God through the ages,

Enjoys these foods and feeds its faithful friend with them.

It will not receive a stone if it ever asks for bread;

Nor, instead of a fish, will it feel the head of a poisonous serpent;

Nor, instead of an egg, will the deceitful scorpion mock it,

Gentle in appearance, but savage in the wound of its tail.

[Col. 0253A] For that devout Father, who is regarded as the fountain of goodness,

As the sun shines spontaneously and as a fountain flows abundantly,

And as gentle rain freely drips from the clouds,

So, with willing grace, gives every good thing to his children,

Who nevertheless seek him with the true devotion of faith;

Who embrace with pure love what they thirst for in hope;

Who know how to despise the goods and evils of the changing world,

And pursue God with steadfast strength.

O almighty Lord, grant us to see in our minds

So many evils, so many disasters, and so many dangers worthy of tears.

Grant us to groan, and make us grieve over them with all our hearts,

And to seek your power with unceasing prayers.

You who rule Israel, whose eye, seeing all things,

Does not sleep forever; who by everlasting law

Raise up the fallen and yourself strike down the proud,

Granting pardon to the suppliant and hastening ruin upon the arrogant.

You, holy Father, strike us here with a father’s scourge;

Correct us firmly with your rod and staff.

Let every evil in the world become our purification.

May those who always love you grow through every trial,

So that, rescued from the black waves of the sea,

And, with you as our guide, having now reached the harbor of peace,

We may gather sweet fruit from a sorrowful seed

And sing again forever your triumphs in praise.

[Note: This second poem was written to Moduin, bishop of Autun, who is called “the powerful shepherd of Mount Augustodunum” in another poem of Florus, which the Petavian manuscript likewise contained (see below, col. 000). This is Bishop Muatwinus, whom Walafrid Strabo also celebrated in verse, and the same man to whom Bishop Theodulf addresses Book IV, poem 6. Here Moduin is more severely reproached because he mistreated his foster-mother, that is, the Church of Lyon, in whose bosom he had grown up, dragging the clergy of that church into the secular tribunal contrary to the prescriptions of the canons. It is surprising to consider what legal authority Moduin, a suffragan of the Church of Lyon, could have had over his metropolitan see. Since he enjoyed great influence with Louis the Pious, it was easy for him, while Archbishop Agobard was in exile, to invade the rights of that church. Certainly, how well Moduin was regarded by Louis is shown by the aforementioned poem of Theodulf, from which we understand that Moduin attempted to persuade Theodulf to acknowledge and confess the crime imposed upon him by the emperor; Theodulf, being innocent, refused. Walafrid provides clearer evidence of Moduin’s authority, calling him the governor of Gaul.]

## To Moduin, Bishop of Autun: On the Unjust Harassment of the Church of Lyon

To you, distinguished Moduin, I, the insignificant, send greetings,

The lowly to the great, the humble to the eminent.

I am small, but I shall speak of great things, because he is very great

Whose cause is now treated in a little poem.

A divine cause will be sung to you; lend, I beg,

Attentive ears and devout hearts.

Remember: whoever burdens his ears harshly

Makes his prayers hateful before the law of the Lord,

And brings empty words to Christ’s altars,

Bearing a hard heart toward the voice of the poor.

What, I ask, has our sacred foster-mother,

This same Church, our mother, deserved from you?

That, carrying a furious hatred in a savage breast,

You should not fear to plot such things against her?

You tear apart the laws; you overturn the sacred rights of the canons,

While, alas, you subdue the maternal womb.

Nor, madman, do you hesitate to strike Christ with your heel,

From whose goad you bear a bloody back.

You bear a bloody back, yet you do not correct your furrow;

Like a bull with lowered horns, you toss your swollen neck against the Lord.

While your madness drives you to seek with your own sword

The furious evil within your own entrails, you yourself do not know what you are doing.

Nothing is more just than envy, which immediately gnaws at

And tortures the very one who gives it birth.

From ancient times the venerable honor of the Church,

Under supreme princes and devout bishops,

Has flourished resplendently through the course of many years,

Nurturing the beloved pledges of the fathers beneath devotion.

And like a hen, it has covered its devout offspring

With the mystical shelter of its wings against worldly snares.

You recognize, unless I am mistaken, which bird is designated

By that name in the holy Gospel.

That grieving bird still cries out, chattering,

And brings forth devout groans from my mouth.

[Col. 0254B] Before she cuts you with her heel, before she beats you with her wings,

Before she strips you with her eyes, she calls to you in this way, out of devotion:

“O my son Moduin—for you too are our pledge,

Nourished in our bosom—

What, I ask, have I done to deserve that for so long

You should drive our pledges from their secure dwelling places?

Why do you heap sorrows upon me? Why do you cut short my joys?

Why do you not allow me to rejoice in my offspring?

Devotion and ancient faith had enclosed me

With a strong defense and surrounded me with reliable aid.

Even those who had been hawks and ravenous kites,

Accustomed to tear my offspring apart,

Were suddenly changed by devotion into peaceful doves

And eagerly sought the shelter of my breast.

Having laid aside their savage nature and grim name,

They pleased me in both name and nature.

They clung to my hospitality, following my small provisions,

And living on harmless delights.

The fierce beaks and claws with which they once

Used to ravage me, they turned sweetly to my service.

They repel hostile birds by their courage and their words;

They protect me with vigilant devotion and care.

Do you recognize, I ask, the riddles of your venerable mother?

Do you understand what my mystical words signify?

Or, pitiable man, do you refuse to recognize my voice,

And does my bristling appearance displease your eyes?

Our groaning gave birth to you; your little nest

Received you at your birth; this warmth nourished you;

Drawing you into the light, it snatched you from dark prisons

And granted you to enjoy life, light, and salvation.

[Col. 0254D] Remain, then, with your mother; do not abandon your dear brothers.

Their love alone is certain salvation for you.

Why do you persecute her? Why do you tear away her dear pledges?

This form of ours did not give you your own form.

Strike, then, the foul hook of your accursed beak,

And cease, savage one, to live on the flesh of your kin.

Use with us the simple foods, sweetly,

And seek gentle nourishment with a gentle heart.

The laws of rulers are devout; the commands of fathers are devout:

They are what have protected and governed me from the beginning.

Why do you mix darkness with light, or wormwood with honey?

These things will always remain separate for you.

From the time when the conspicuous worship of Christ

Shone through the ages and the plague of idolatry fled the city,

The ancient laws have never harassed my ministers,

Nor has sacred property been burdened by the weight of the world.

A distinct twofold order has always continued here:

[Note: Namely, that of clergy and laity, who have always had different tribunals. Monks too were included within the clerical order before that time.]

And each part flourished under its own judges.

[Col. 0255B] Due reverence was accorded to the sacred orders;

Its own law governed each of the laymen.

Why do you now wish to overturn my ancient boundary?

Why do you tear down the wall set before me?

Why do you strive to tear up the ancient limits of my estate

And make the fields open to everyone?

Hear what Solomon declares with truthful mouth,

And beware lest you be stabbed by your own sword.

The destroyer of a hedge will perish by the bite of the serpent,

And whoever carries stones by his own labor will be crushed by them.

Crush yourself; destroy yourself; for you will not be able to strip me,

Since I am everywhere and always supported by God’s aid.

After the evangelical shields, after the flashing weapons

Of the apostolic mouth, after the devout laws of God,

Constantine protects me with his revered voice;

[Note: The Gallican Church used the Theodosian Code, and its freedom and immunity rested upon the laws of the emperors—formerly its own, the Roman emperors.]

Theodosius also protects me with his devout voice.

Honorius, sweetly clinging to the gentle Arcadius,

Praises, honors, and loves me with gentle speech.

Why should I speak of ancient things? Behold, in our own age,

With what devotion does the peaceful prince honor me?

For my sake he has often labored in venerable councils

And pressed proud necks beneath a powerful yoke.

He joined recent edicts to ancient laws,

And everywhere increased ancient goods with new goods,

Lest a savage storm should suddenly overwhelm me

In shipwreck across the sea of the world and its turbulent rocks.

Truly the sacred mysteries of Christ shine brightly,

Those that signify the blessed deeds of the fathers of old.

Now mighty Samson, when he wished to enter

A foreign marriage, attacked a lion with terrible mouth.

[Col. 0255D] When he had slain it, as though he were tearing apart

A tender young goat limb by limb, he took sweet honeycombs from its mouth.

He took honeycombs and sweet honey from the lion’s mouth;

The one that had once roared now, behold, tastes sweetly.

[Col. 0256A] The power of the world roared when Christ came,

As he himself sought to bind the pagan people to himself.

It roared with dreadful terror, issued savage laws,

And terrified the devout throughout the whole world.

Yet in his servants, through mighty strength,

While overcoming the world, he destroyed its terrible powers.

So that what had lived wickedly might die,

And impiety, once dead, might bring forth sweet faith from its mouth;

And what it had once prepared to tear apart with ravenous roaring,

It might now proclaim in sweet speech as a hymn.

And now the lamb of Christ, who had then departed as a grim lion,

Should himself ask forgiveness for his sins.

Thus Christ subjected the heights of the world to himself

And everywhere drew all things into his service.

But if you do not know the devout laws of the devout men of old,

Cease tearing apart the good that you do not know.

And calmly accept what this page, in brief words,

Suggests as a second peaceful instruction:

[Note: Florus had written another letter or another poem on this subject to Moduin, perhaps the very one that survives in the Petavian manuscript, now belonging to Christina, the most serene queen of Sweden. There is also another poem to Moduin in the collection of various epigrams printed by Morel in 1550, beginning with these verses:

“I offer, Father, flowing thanks from a joyful heart,

Because you open kindly lips to your Florus.”

But the whole of that letter aims to encourage Moduin to study the sacred writings.]

When you have read through everything with a serene countenance,

and have yourself seen the path that you did not know,

then, trembling beneath Christ’s fear, with faithful devotion

correct what you yourself perceive to be wrong.

Indeed, even if no laws anywhere forbade such things,

is it fitting for a bishop to have done them?

To overthrow a work well constructed through such great labor and so many years,

and voluntarily to open a path to crime?

To say, “Believe me, no honor is owed to the sacred

orders: let the court summon everyone everywhere.”

[Note: [Col. 0256D] These are the words of Moduinus, whom Florus introduces as speaking in this way: “Except for bishops and abbesses, let all the other clerics and priests acknowledge the lay court.”] For unless a mother governs a women’s monastery,

and a holy bishop [governs], all the rest will be dust.

[Col. 0256C] If you are the father of the clergy, do not despise the clergy;

nor, while raising yourself thus, cast them down.

Since these things are not holy love but swollen

fury, breathing smoky vapor, belches them from its mouth—

if you read these things with a devout mind, if with a pure heart

you receive them, the sacred potion benefits you.

It is indeed somewhat bitter; but if you endure it, it is health-giving.

Zeal and love are present together in the hen.

I judge, prudent man, that you are moved by no gall

when you see Florus loving you in this way.

For the wounds of devoted love are always better

than deceitful kisses pressed by feigned lips.

And if, though previously unknown, you begin to become notorious to everyone for evil,

you will always be an infamous tale.

## III. Hymn for the feast of Saints John and Paul

[Note: [Col. 0256D] This poem, or hymn, lends support to the Acts of Saints John and Paul.]

[Col. 0256D]

The sun has brought to the world the day of John and Paul,

who bear red garlands of martyrdom stained with blood.

[Col. 0257A] A single bloodshed joined these men in brotherly covenant;

a single death and a single faith soon made them brothers.

In former times, while guarding the walls of the Roman kingdom,

they often struck down barbarian companies with the sword;

now, watching over Christ’s purest sheepfolds,

they repel demonic threats by force and by prayers.

The frenzied tyrant Julian, the despiser of Christ,

devoted them to death for the sake of the sacred law.

He had previously professed the worship of the one God with his lips,

until he climbed to the summit of imperial power.

But when his earthly authority had grown strong under wretched circumstances,

he preferred the idol to the true God.

Then, rending Christ’s servants and feeding upon innocent blood,

he raged everywhere in horrifying ways.

But when Christ looked down from his heavenly citadel

[Col. 0257B] and heard the prayers of the devout blood,

he immediately appointed for the wretched man the disaster

of a fatal hour, so that he would fall beneath an enemy’s hostile sword.

After the Church had been devastated, he had summoned the Persians to war,

and, surrounded by many thousands, he marched in his savagery.

Suddenly, however, he came into the dry fields

of a deserted countryside, and everywhere lost his battle formations.

There was no food, no spring, and no flowing river there,

but the whole ground lay parched beneath excessive heat.

And as he roamed, roaring, through mountains, valleys, and fields,

seeking wherever even a little drop of liquid might flow,

he fell by a fitting error upon opposing ranks,

and, his breast pierced by a dark spear, he expired.

But still frenzied and rebellious even in death,

he growled and challenged the Most High Lord in these words:

[Col. 0257C] “Drink now, Christ, the blood of ours that you seek,

and, greedy one, be satisfied at last with my death.”

He indeed paid such penalties beneath the just judge,

and afterward sought the blind darkness of Tartarus.

But the Lord’s witnesses, washed in consecrated blood,

seek the lofty stars with laurel-bearing heads.

A radiant robe clothes them in peaceful adornment,

and bright purple surrounds them with royal covering.

Like fruitful olive trees in a flourishing paradise,

he continually waters them with the life-giving stream.

They are the shining lampstands in the eternal temple,

the offspring of light and the glory of devotion.

Always standing in the heavenly King’s sublime court,

they bear devout prayers for the peoples.

Look favorably upon us through their prayers, Christ,

[Col. 0257D] and cleanse whatever obscenity you see within us.

## IV. Inscription of the little book offered at the altar of Saint Stephen, dedicated to our most holy and glorious fosterer and patron, blessed Stephen the protomartyr

[Note: [Col. 0257D] This is the title of a little book offered at the altar of Saint Stephen, namely in the cathedral church of Lyon, which is dedicated to blessed Mary and to Saints Stephen and John. In the Petavian copy, from which our [Col. 0258D] Acherius once had these verses transcribed, there are two gaps or blank spaces—not for verses, but for titles to be inserted between them.]

To you, first witness of devout Christ, most steadfast,

we offer this little book, glowing with varied flowers.

Here your first crown shines forth, bestowed after your battles:

[Col. 0258A] your honor and your name gleam, and your rewards proclaim them.

That holy old man Gamaliel once made your bones,

previously unknown to the world, public through his reverent speech from heaven;

and, father, he marked your limbs in radiant gold,

depicting your martyrdom with a splendid bloom of roses.

Joining himself also to the lot of his grandson Nicodemus,

the kindly man duly comes forth in twin golden baskets,

with white roses scarcely tinged with delicate blood;

and commends the virginal limbs in a shining basket of pure

silver, with the fragrance of a saffron flower.

Your praise follows, and your flowering virtue follows—

powerful in Christ’s virtue and overflowing with devotion,

giving joy to the sorrowful, restoring strength to the weak,

and bringing back to life those lying beneath harsh death,

almost buried, because you are held to be a witness of life.

[Col. 0258B] You, Christ’s first and enduring witness, with death trampled underfoot,

carrying the lofty standard with the thunderbolt-like weapons of your tongue

and with flashing signs, struck down hostile camps

and carried away the beautiful palm from death.

A venerable host follows you for the sacred name,

afflicted in a thousand ways and glorified by a thousand triumphs.

Martyr among martyrs, you are the standard and rule for all;

you lead purple battle-lines and rose-colored companies.

Their circle gleams with the purple of blood;

the stars shine with their flower-bearing crowns;

the pure temples of God are adorned with their tombs;

all seasons gleam with the insignia of their festivals;

all their hardships yield to their sacred prayers.

The holy John sees these men in the region of heaven,

[Col. 0258C] illustrious after the harsh battles of so many labors.

To them blessed victory gives eternal palms,

and provides immortal coverings of white robes.

Christ, merciful, denies none of them their gifts—

those whom he himself chose and separated from the world’s lot,

and planted for God, so that with ever-glad strength

they might leap upward to heaven as they grow,

bearing perpetual fruits in vigorous virtue,

and might soon receive, through favorable divine power,

whatever they wish to ask of the Father above,

and grant it to the devout. Among these,

desiring to be counted as needy and mourning the wounds of my heart,

I, Florus, trembling and with a humbled breast,

sang these things, so that through Christ I might be saved

by the merits of so great a fosterling,

and that he might absolve me through the prayers of the purple-robed nobles.

[lacuna]

[Col. 0258D] Through the outstanding merits and blessed prayers of the saints,

whose perpetual triumphs this book commemorates,

grant, almighty Father, forgiveness; grant, Christ, healing,

to those who, with suppliant prayers and faithful mind,

entrust themselves through the ages to such great patrons,

who, after the devil’s defeat, with radiant crowns above the stars,

conspicuous, are worthy to obtain from you whatever they have sought.

[lacuna]

Christ, I pray, mercifully grant forgiveness to your sluggish fosterling.

I am slow, but no one has come to you too late.

[Col. 0259A] Long error has held us back through past years;

I ask that this punishment be sufficient for my merits.

Little life remains, and age is more inclined toward death:

now, as an old man, I can no longer sin; I do not wish to, being yours.

## V. Verses by the same author. Where the bones of Saint Cyprian are buried at Lyon

[Note: [Col. 0259D] Concerning the translation of the relics of Saint Cyprian and others into the church at Lyon in the time of Charlemagne, see the verses of Agobard, bishop of Lyon, and the Chronicle of Ado of Vienne.]

Here, in this chest, lies the rich treasure of Christ,

purer than silver, more precious than burnished gold,

and brighter than all the light of sparkling gems.

Here indeed rests Cyprian, a most gentle teacher with distinguished speech,

an exceptional bishop and most celebrated martyr,

shining like a bright Lucifer sent from great Carthage,

and resting in a beautiful destiny.

[Col. 0259B] A twin star is added to him, radiant with light:

the martyr Speratus together with the martyr Pantaleon,

whose head, together with the sacred bones of the former, is powerful here.

Gaul, rejoicing under Charles, prince of the Franks,

received them together, enriched by Libyan treasures.

May faithful prayer therefore make these men our patrons,

so that, when Christ comes amid flashing heavens

and brings bright diadems to his martyrs,

eternal light may receive us through their merits.

## VI. Inscription of the apse

[Note: [Col. 0259D] Here the ancient arrangement of an altar in an apse of the church [Col. 0260D] is described: the relics of the martyrs were placed beneath the altar, while above stood an image of Christ hanging from the cross, with the Eucharist hanging in a small vessel, and images of the saints set around it.]

Beneath, a venerable hall gleams for the martyrs;

above, Christ the King presides on high for the martyrs.

Mystical creatures of wondrous forms stand around,

[Col. 0259C] proclaiming the triune Godhead with hymns night and day.

The apostolic choir likewise stands near, radiant in speech,

which will come with Christ when he arrives as judge at the appointed time.

And living Jerusalem, shining with the Lamb’s illumination,

sets four rivers of paradise in motion from a single spring.

John the Baptist, glory of the clergy, adorns the altar with sacred relics

and cleanses the hearts that make their petitions.

[Col. 0259]

# Religious poems

## Martenius’s notice concerning the poems that follow

The poems presented here were extracted from a very ancient Bigotian manuscript, whose script seems to approach the author’s period. Although these poems are not of great importance, they should by no means be despised—especially the epigram on the book of Homilies for the entire year, [Col. 0259D] from which we learned how few feasts of the saints were then celebrated or possessed a proper office. For, apart from the feasts of Saints Stephen, John the Evangelist, the Innocents, John the Baptist, Peter and Paul, the Maccabees, and Andrew, which had a place in the book of Homilies, if any others happened to occur, they had no office outside the class of the common offices.

## I. On the Gospel of Matthew

Matthew, called from the tax office to the profits of heaven,

was the first to write the mysteries of the evangelical kingdom.

[Col. 0260A] Let devoted love sing these things; let it resound in a sweet voice.

Christ is born at Bethlehem from the holy Virgin,

and the Magi arrive, led by a heavenly star.

Joseph is commanded to migrate to Egypt with the child.

The children are slaughtered, bloody victims of the king’s jealousy.

Jesus is recalled from Egypt to the city of Nazareth.

John immerses the peoples in the waters of the Jordan.

Christ also humbly receives John’s baptism.

Then, fasting for forty days,

he defeats the assaults of the wicked devil when tempted.

He calls Peter, Andrew, James, and John while they are fishing.

They soon obediently submit to his gracious commands,

throwing aside their nets and leaving both boat and father.

Having taken these men with him, he travels throughout Galilee,

[Col. 0260B] and everywhere cures the various illnesses of the people.

He teaches his disciples the commandments and gives laws to the blessed.

He warns against the anger that must be avoided after blood has been shed.

He teaches that pleasing gifts to God consist in restoring brotherly peace,

and that adultery of the heart must be shunned with a chaste breast.

If eyes habitually cherished, or right hands, cause offences,

they are commanded to be cast far away; a wife joined to a man

is always held an adulteress unless she is established to be adulterous.

He forbids oaths, because they are close to perjuries;

he establishes that “Yes” and “No” are to be maintained with truthful speech.

Let the other cheek be willingly offered to one who strikes.

And let devoted, gracious love itself love enemies,

so that the work of devotion may be done without the left hand knowing the right,

and so that prayer may desire to please the Father alone.

Let a pure mind practice joyful fasts before God,

[Col. 0260C] and not seek fleeting praise with a gloomy face.

Let treasure be stored up in heaven, where no thief is present.

The eye of the body is the simple intention of the deed.

If this intention remains pure, it illuminates all the limbs,

and the things done for love of the light will not become dark.

No one can serve two masters equally,

nor please both Mammon and God with a divided mind.

The worries of clothing and food must be driven from the mind.

If the Father’s abundance feeds the birds of heaven,

and paints the soft lilies with the flower of the field,

when has he ever denied kindly gifts to his own children?

Therefore let each person’s own care be enough for him;

let tomorrow not torment them, since such things are uncertain for mortals.

The righteousness of God must be sought; the rest will be given freely.

Let no one condemn another’s hidden things as judge,

[Col. 0260D] seeking to draw the splinter from his brother’s eye,

while first removing the beam from his own eye.

Long-standing anger drags on; the lighter splinter is noticed.

Let the one who wishes to heal through devotion cleanse his mind of anger.

Indeed, when hatred has extinguished it, the little eye sees nothing rightly.

Who would wish to expose a pearl to be trampled by pigs,

or to give what is holy to dogs to be torn apart?

The mysteries of peace benefit the gentle and the pure.

Let faithful devotion ask, so that it may be able to receive the gifts.

Let thirsty love seek, so that it may soon bring back what it desires.

[Col. 0261A] Let devout work and earnest effort knock; then the closed things will open.

False prophets must always be avoided and cursed,

those whom the black ferocity of wolves drives beneath sheep’s clothing.

They carry the sacraments of faith, but live in death.

A house must be built on the foundation of true rock.

While all earth is removed from the foundation below,

and Christ’s commands are carried out with proven devotion,

the foundation of shifting sand must be completely avoided,

lest the force beneath cause the lightly placed house to collapse;

thus, unmoved, it will withstand rains, winds, and rivers.

The dark rains of errors pour down in a cloud,

the alternating winds of the world, adverse and prosperous.

Lust of the flesh creeps over the earth like a muddy river.

Jesus likewise cleanses the leper as he descends from the mountain,

[Col. 0261B] saying, “If you wish, you can bring healing even to me.”

When he said, “I wish,” the loathsome disease immediately fled.

With powerful virtue he saves the servant exhausted by paralysis,

the centurion’s boy,

Peter’s mother-in-law lying with a deadly fever,

and many others besides.

He rejects the deceitful scribe and declares that he nowhere has

a place where he may lay his head to rest.

He says that foxes have a den here [or: he says this],

but that another has neglected the body of his dead father [text corrupt: “dolosis”],

and commands him to follow himself and leave the dead to bury their dead.

He commands the winds and calms the sea’s waters by his order.

He drives a legion of demons from a human body,

and plunges them with the pigs into the sea’s grim waves.

He commands the man freed from paralysis to carry his pallet.

[Col. 0261C] He calls Matthew and teaches him to despise the profits of the world,

and, graciously deigning to join publicans to his own table,

he declares that the sick need a physician rather than the healthy.

Mystically commending the height of true fasting,

he sets before disciples zealous for the sacred discipline of John

the parable of the cloth, the wine, and the wineskins.

A woman exhausted by a flow of blood long without cessation

departs cleansed by touching the sacred garment.

The girl who had already been joined to death is restored to life.

Soon the sight long lost is restored to the blind.

Jesus drives out the mute and deaf demon.

He orders the apostolic light to go and teach the peoples.

Peter and Andrew, James together with John,

Bartholomew, Thomas, Matthew, and likewise Philip,

[Col. 0261D] James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon, and Iscariot—

these are the men whom the Word sent to proclaim salvation,

to cure the sick, and to drive out the dark demons.

Yet one of them perished, because he betrayed him.

John, shut up in prison, directs a message to Christ.

He rebukes the cities which, although they saw so many wonders,

did not repent in their sorrow because of their monstrous hardness.

Exulting, Jesus praises the Father’s mysteries

and declares that his yoke is gentle and most merciful.

The disciples pluck ears of grain as they pass on the Sabbath.

He heals the withered right hand by the strength granted to him.

After the demon has been cast out, he restores the blind and mute man.

He shows that Satan cannot drive out Satan.

To the crowd that tests him he promises the sign of Jonah.

[Col. 0262A] He recognizes as mothers, brothers, and sisters

only those who follow the Father’s commands.

He speaks many parables in varied language,

pouring forth mysteries hidden from the world’s beginning

and fulfilling the sayings of the ancient prophet in sacred order.

He presents a farmer whose cultivated field abounds in threefold fruit,

who gathered thirtyfold produce from the tilled fields,

and rejoiced when it increased sixtyfold and a hundredfold.

He speaks of the darnel that the enemy had scattered in the pure crop,

of the grain of the smallest mustard seed growing broadly,

and also of the leaven through which the whole mass gains strength.

He explains to the disciples the riddles of the darnel and the crop.

He adds the parable of the hidden treasure,

and also of the pearl gleaming with precious light.

And the net cast into the sea, containing every kind of swimmer,

[Col. 0262B] which draws everything to the shore, where careful separation is made:

the vessels receive the good, while the different [ones] are cast out.

John the Baptist is beheaded at Herod’s command,

and his head is carried on a platter to criminal celebrations.

The disciples come and bury his holy limbs in a tomb.

Five thousand men are filled by Christ’s power

from five loaves and two fish.

They also filled twelve baskets with fragments.

Jesus walks across the waves; the waters of the sea grow warm;

with his gentle right hand he allows Peter, who is sinking, to stand.

At Gennesaret he cures the ailments of many among the people.

The Pharisaic error murmurs about the washing of hands.

He teaches that the true washing is inward, in the heart.

The Canaanite woman obtains salvation for her daughter.

On the mountain of Galilee he cures crowds of afflicted people.

[Col. 0262C] Soon he fills four thousand with seven loaves.

He teaches that the Pharisee’s leaven must be avoided.

Peter’s happy confession glorifies Christ,

and he receives from Christ the keys of the heavenly kingdom.

He commands each person to bear his own cross.

He testifies that some will not see harsh death

until they see Christ shining in his own kingdom

with blessed sight and stand in awe of heaven.

Before three disciples on the mountain he immediately shows himself

clothed in the light of heavenly form.

They see Elijah and Moses standing with him.

At once a luminous cloud surrounds the trembling disciples,

and a clear voice of the Father comes from heaven, testifying:

“This is my Son; hold to his commands.”

Afterward, returning to them on the mountain, he declares that Elijah

[Col. 0262D] has already come, yet has not been received;

in these words they understood him to mean the righteous John.

Soon he cures the boy, and the lunatic disease flees.

He wishes living faith to be like mustard.

He pays the imperial tax from the mouth of a fish.

He commands the faithful to be humble like a child.

He teaches that the offending eye must be torn out from its own place.

He shows that the same applies, with the danger of the foot and hand.

The faithful, even the least, must never be despised,

for angelic guardianship watches over them.

For the one who causes harm is drowned in the abyss beneath a crushing stone.

A brother must be forgiven with every merciful heart,

so that God may forgive and not repay harshness with harshness.

The bond of marriage must be preserved in faithful justice.

[Col. 0263A] He praises eunuchs who seek the kingdom of heaven.

He loves innocent children and blesses them.

He teaches that the gates of life are opened with difficulty to the rich.

Those who leave everything will receive a hundredfold fruit.

He tells, in varied form, the parable of those who cultivate vineyards,

by which he teaches that the last are often made first.

To the sons of Zebedee, eager for the summit of honor,

the sad cup that must be drunk is first presented.

As the Lord passes by, he gives light to two blind men.

The colt is brought with its mother for Jesus to sit upon.

He drives the merchants from the temple and cleanses the Father’s court.

The rejoicing children piously resound with “Hosanna” to Christ.

Because the leafy fig tree perhaps lacked fruit,

he commanded it, and the condemned tree immediately withered:

[Col. 0263B] Christ loves those who bear fruit and hates those without fruit.

The chief priests ask where he has obtained such great authority,

but, confounded by John’s testimony, they depart,

neither willing to speak the truth nor deserving to hear the truth.

He adds the parable of perhaps two sons,

who resist their father’s commands in different ways.

And with justice he prefers prostitutes to proud scribes.

The vineyard is again described as entrusted to farmers,

who killed those sent to them by a cruel death,

and finally impiously killed the Lord’s own son.

The parable invites many to the king’s banquet,

but because they rejected the invitation, fitting vengeance soon followed.

The man without a proper garment is himself plunged into fitting darkness.

He teaches that divine things must be rendered to God and royal things to the king,

that in the age to come marriage unions of the flesh will cease,

[Col. 0263C] and that Christ is both David’s Lord and his Son.

He commands that those learned in the law, seated in Moses’ chair,

be obeyed in what they say, but that their examples be avoided.

Christ rebukes them because they destroy those whom they win over.

He rebukes them because they violate what is especially sacred: an oath.

He rebukes them because they polish the cup and strive to swallow the camel,

following the smallest points while despising the greatest matters of the law.

He rebukes them because they labor to cleanse the cup and bowl outwardly,

but do not strive to wipe away the hidden stain within,

although the creator of the human being is one both outside and within.

He laments that they are like whitewashed tombs,

which are beautiful outside but dreadful within:

[Col. 0263D] outwardly they shine to the eyes, but within their hiding places are wholly foul.

They build splendid monuments for the holy prophets,

but prove by this nothing other than that they are heirs

of the prophets’ blood, because those prophets had refused to believe in the Lord.

He mourns Jerusalem and says that he is leaving the temple,

and suddenly threatens that everything will fall into ashes,

and thereafter denies that his face will be seen by them.

He explains the signs that are known to precede the final days,

and recalls that false Christs and false prophets will arise,

with everything full of errors.

He discloses the terror and times of his own coming,

the falling of the stars and the darkening of all the stars of heaven.

By examples he urges vigilance and warns against the thief.

[Col. 0264A] He warns that the lamps of the virgins must not be lacking in their vessels,

but must rather always be nourished with rich olive oil.

He commands that the talents received be increased through faithful interest.

When he sits upon the dreadful throne of judgment,

he says that the sheep will stand at his right and the goats at his left:

the latter will go into the flames, the former to the pastures of life.

The chief priests seek to kill the Lord Christ.

A blessed woman pours ointment over Jesus.

Judas seeks worthless gifts in order to betray Christ.

At supper the Lord identifies him with a grieving voice.

He himself gives the mysteries of his body to the holy disciples.

He foretells that Peter will deny him three times during the night.

He prays that the hour of the approaching cup may pass away,

but rather that the Father’s appointed will may be done.

Judas gives the kiss as the sign by which to hand over the master.

[Col. 0264B] By an insane plan it was decided to produce false witnesses against Christ;

the lying tongue contradicts itself.

Jesus, condemned, is mocked everywhere with insults.

Peter denies him and soon laments with bitter tears.

Bound, he himself is handed over to Pilate to be killed.

They bought the potter’s field with the price of blood.

Pilate allows the people to destroy Christ.

The sacred Passion of devout Jesus is completed in due order.

Soon the elements tremble; the temple tears its curtains.

He undergoes death; “Away with you, Tartarus!” he says.

He rises from the tomb and shines with glorious power.

He gives commands to the disciples and consecrates baptism.

To him be praise and power, to him supreme glory throughout the ages,

with God the Father, blessed in the heavenly seat,

and with the Holy Spirit, his equal companion; and let the stars proclaim it.

[Col. 0264C] Amen.

## II. The deeds of Christ the Lord

Innocent children, bless Christ the King.

May the lofty name of the Lord be blessed forever.

From the rising of the sun to its setting, let the sweet hymn resound.

Let us sing to the Lord, to whom belongs great glory through Christ,

who alone by his power struck down the horse of the wicked rider

and at the same time plunged the defeated into the abyss.

Behold, God the Savior flashes with wondrous light;

he himself is salvation for us, he himself is strength forever.

Let devoted faith trust; let all fear be absent.

Let us drink the sweet waters of Jesus from the springs,

and echo in order the deeds of glorious Christ.

Let the sky, the earth, and the surface of the sea resound with these things.

[Col. 0264D] These four blessed ones sang them with one voice.

Four rivers of paradise rise from one spring,

and with their abundant flood make the whole world fertile.

Here, then, is paradise; here golden apples are plucked

from the flowering crown of the tree of life.

The dreadful serpent is absent; blessed delight abounds.

As holy Zechariah carries the sacred burning incense,

an angel stands beside him and promises the joy of a son,

who would prepare the hearts of the peoples for the Lord Christ.

Holy Gabriel, radiant in speech, is sent to Mary.

He announces that Christ will come from the untouched Virgin,

to whom eternal sovereignty belongs and whose glory shines forever.

The revered Virgin greets Zechariah’s wife.

Immediately John leaps in his mother’s womb,

[Col. 0265A] and through his joy announces the Christ whom he cannot voice.

Soon the gracious Spirit also fills his mother.

She exclaims that the Lord’s mother is present.

With modest mouth she sings the praises of God.

John is born, and his father’s tongue speaks.

He himself also spends his blessed childhood in the forests,

until at the appointed time he reveals himself to Israel.

Christ is born at Bethlehem from the holy Virgin.

The shepherds keep watch, and an angel addresses them;

the heavenly hosts sing of the King who has been born.

He himself humbly receives the mysteries of the ancient law,

sanctifies the devout rite of the fathers at the appointed time,

thus bringing the old things to an end and causing the new to arise.

Most holy Simeon receives him joyfully in his arms,

and, while he is offered to God and devout gifts are presented in the temple,

[Col. 0265B] declares that this is the Lord of light and the King of salvation.

Anna also, devoted to God and widowed from her husband,

now advanced in years and venerable in religious devotion,

recognizes him, gives thanks, and prophesies to the peoples.

Behold, the Magi arrive from the farthest shores of the East.

They say that they have seen the star which shines as the herald of the King

and commands that the newborn Christ be worshiped.

Joyfully they proceed under the star’s radiant guidance;

they find the child, reverently prostrate themselves in worship,

eagerly offer gifts, and confess in devotion that this is Christ.

At an angel’s instruction Jesus is taken to Egypt.

The children are slaughtered, bloody victims of the king’s jealousy.

Immediately afterward, the dreadful fate of a deserved death overtakes him.

Again Jesus is brought from Egypt to Nazareth,

from which he received the name Nazaraean forever,

[Col. 0265C] as the harmonious voice of the ancient prophets had previously sung.

John goes before him, proclaiming with a great cry,

austere in food and shaggy in his garment of hair,

washing the limbs of believers in the flood of the Jordan.

The Jewish leaders, supposing that he is Christ,

come in astonishment and ask who he wishes to be.

With a submissive voice he declares himself Christ’s herald.

He cries out that this man is the Lamb of God, that he takes away the sins of the world;

he proclaims that he must be followed by all with willing devotion,

and shows with his finger that he is present.

Jesus himself also deigns to be baptized in the sacred river,

and, though exalted, thus dedicates the humble way.

He sanctifies the waters and consecrates a great example.

The heavens open; soon the Spirit in the form of a dove

flies down and, gentle, rests upon peaceful Jesus.

[Col. 0265D] The Father himself proclaims his beloved Son from heaven.

Immediately the gracious Spirit carries him into the wilderness’s solitude

and presents him to be tested by the devil’s assaults.

By prayer and fasting he conquers the tyrant who must be conquered.

The devil, giving proud advice, suggests that he turn stones into loaves,

that Christ, having fallen from the highest summit,

either trust in angelic hands or possess kingdoms.

Showing his own humility, he prefers to walk the humble path

and obey God’s commands above all things.

Thus, victorious over the devil, he gives commands to the angelic ministers.

When he returns, he shines among the peoples with wondrous power.

He turns water into wine and reveals the honor of his divinity.

The disciples believe and follow him as Lord and God.

Joyfully, during the feast of Passover, he drives thousands of merchants

[Col. 0266A] from the temple with a small whip.

The peoples marvel, and the hearts of many believe.

He foretells that the venerable temple of his own body

will be destroyed by bloody hands in the death he undertakes,

and promises that he himself will restore it in three days.

He reveals to Nicodemus the mystical gifts of baptism,

and bathes believing peoples in his own baptism.

They flock from everywhere and receive the gifts of life.

The holy Baptist rejoices and summons everyone.

For he declares that Christ is the bridegroom and himself the bridegroom’s friend;

he confesses that Christ must increase and he himself must decrease.

He says, “That man is the Son of God; whoever believes in him

possesses blessed eternal life throughout the ages.

Whoever denies him has God’s anger ruling over him forever.”

Meanwhile he [Col. 0266B] rebukes Herod, who seeks a shameful marriage,

and chooses to suffer death rather than be silent about the truth.

For this reason the just man is condemned to a dark prison.

Then Jesus withdraws into the region of the Galileans.

He rescues the ruler’s son from the threshold of death,

and moves about within the walls of the city of Capernaum.

He calls Andrew and Peter, James and John,

who carry fishing nets over the waters.

They soon leave everything and follow the Lord’s devout commands.

## III. On the Gospel of John

Let us sing John’s Gospel with a sweet voice,

and let the deeds of the Lord be set to music in clear order.

May love be joyful for us, and may our joys be holy.

[Col. 0266C] The only-begotten Word always remained with the Father.

He is the light, the power, and the wisdom of the Father,

the life of human beings, shining above the heavens among angelic hosts.

Through him the Father himself made both the world and the ages,

establishing everything that exists from heaven’s summit

down to the lowest depths of the black abyss.

He is brighter than the stars and more beautiful than the sun itself,

prior to every light that night and shadow obscure.

He conquers darkness and shines amid the very shadows.

An exceptional man, John, comes with glorious virtue,

sent from heaven to become a witness concerning the light.

He was not the light, but shone as the herald of the light.

The true light was present and illumines human hearts.

It freely sheds light upon minds turned away from it and sunk in darkness,

deigning to visit the world.

[Col. 0266D] He himself was present in the world, and he himself had made the world;

yet the world did not recognize him with its blind heart.

He came to his own, and his own proud people rejected him.

But those who, believing in his sacred name,

received him with humble mind and faithful devotion,

he granted to become, as those born of God, glorious forever.

They were not born from blood, nor created from flesh,

nor produced by any human desire;

rather, the divine Spirit brought them forth as a divine offspring.

The Father’s Word also became flesh and dwelt in him,

mercifully taking on our nature’s mortal body,

so that he might recall us to everlasting life.

From this there arose and shone upon the eyes of the mind a new light;

from this his sublime glory became clear to us,

[Col. 0267A] so that we might recognize the Father’s only-begotten Son.

He is renowned as full of truth and possessed of supreme grace.

For, true God with the Father, he graciously took up our mortal condition

and did not know how to abandon what was proper to him.

The truthful witness, John, cries out and says:

“After me a man will come who will teach things greater than I;

he was before me, and he must be preferred to me.

From his eternal fountain we are all watered.

Through Moses the terrifying letter of the law was given beforehand;

through Christ, gracious Grace will now be present, Jesus.”

No mortal ever sees the face of God.

Only the one who remains in the Father’s lofty bosom knows him.

He reveals worthy things to the worthy.

Upon him, with the radiant face of a heavenly dove,

the Spirit came and rested in his eternal seat:

[Col. 0267B] “This is the Son of God; his glory shines for me.”

While he speaks such things to the peoples and proclaims such things,

behold, priests came from Jerusalem asking

whether John himself wished to be believed to be Christ.

Immediately he denied it: “I am not the one you think,” he said.

“I am the voice of one crying out; I announce that Christ is present,

whose sandal I am not worthy to touch.”

John also saw Christ pass by before him.

“Behold,” he said, “the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world.”

Two disciples were standing there, and they follow Jesus.

One of them was Andrew, Peter’s brother.

He found his brother and said, “We have found the Messiah.”

They come to Christ and soon carry away Christ’s gifts.

He himself chooses worthy men; he himself calls Philip.

[Col. 0267C] Philip, rejoicing in devotion, immediately announces to Nathanael

the Christ whom the Law and the holy prophets sang.

Nathanael hastens. When Christ saw him approaching,

he said, “Behold, a true Israelite has come here,

one in whose heart there is no deceit, whose breast is pure.”

“I saw you from far away beneath the covering of the fig tree,

when you had recently taken your place in the leafy shade.”

Philip had not yet given him faithful words,

when, astonished at Christ’s lofty foreknowledge,

he said, “Truly, behold, this is the exalted Son of God.

This is the true King of Israel forever.”

Christ promises greater things to the believer.

“You will see,” he says, “the heights of heaven opened,

and angelic choirs serving Christ forever.”

Invited with his holy mother to a certain wedding feast,

[Col. 0267D] he suddenly changes the nature of water into wine.

The disciples believe and are awed by the divine deeds.

He drives thousands of merchants from the sacred temple.

He declares that the temple of his own flesh will be destroyed,

and that he himself will raise it again in three days by a heavenly sign.

He reveals to Nicodemus the mystical gifts of baptism,

and himself washes the crowds by immersing them in his baptism.

They eagerly gather and receive the devout gifts of salvation.

When the holy Baptist John learned this,

he proclaims that his own joys have been fulfilled and summons everyone:

he rejoices that he himself decreases and that Christ increases.

At the well of Samaria he speaks mystically to a woman.

He reveals the water of life and declares that he himself is the Christ.

The townspeople recognize that salvation has come into the world.

[Col. 0268A] In his own homeland he says that a prophet is without honor,

and brings the ruler’s son back from the jaws of death,

restoring life by his word to one who was absent from the scene of death.

He raises from the waters of the pool at Bethsaida in Jerusalem

a man long afflicted by paralysis and now almost lying in death.

The sick man leaps up rejoicing and carries his own pallet.

He speaks many mysteries of life to the Jews,

saying that he and the Father do everything equally.

He firmly declares that those who believe Moses must believe him absolutely.

With wondrous power he feeds five thousand men

from five loaves and two fish.

The fragments gathered up fill twelve baskets.

At this the astonished people seek to make him their king.

He flees and goes up the mountain, where he worships alone.

Christ does not accept the honors of a mortal kingdom.

[Col. 0268B] The disciples struggle at sea while the wind resists.

Christ arrives peacefully, walking upon the dark waves.

Soon the boat reaches the desired harbor, freed from danger.

He speaks to the peoples about the gift of the ancient manna.

He declares that he has come as the living bread of heaven,

and that whoever receives it will never experience death forever.

Many disciples withdraw because of this speech.

Peter remains joyfully attached to Christ with his companions,

among whom Christ condemns one under the name of the devil.

The festival day had arrived on which the shelters had been commanded.

He teaches the peoples and promises rivers of living water:

“These are the Spirit of God, whom he gives to believers.”

A great dispute about Christ arises among the proud.

They harass Nicodemus and unjustly pressure the officers.

With insolent speech they curse the simple crowds.

[Column 0268C] An adulterous woman is brought to the Lord Christ.

He, overflowing with generous compassion toward the wretched,

Frees her alike from the sentence of death and from her guilt.

Then with clear voice he proclaims himself the light of the world:

All who follow him will escape death’s darkness;

The light of life will shine for them through all eternity.

Christ, the serene preacher, declares himself to be the Beginning,

Who shines within and speaks to pure minds.

Everyone who sins is held to be a slave of sin.

He teaches that the foul devil is the father of falsehood,

That he was the savage author of human death from the beginning,

And that, in his deception, the wretched one did not stand in the true light.

Christ confesses that he himself existed before Abraham.

The latter eagerly desired to see Christ.

He saw him and, exulting, rejoiced with a joyful heart.

[Column 0268D] He smears the eyes of the man born blind with healing spittle and clay,

And illuminates the blind man at Siloam with its pure waters:

He enlightens the blind man, because it is the baptism of salvation.

He shows that he is the gracious door for the chosen sheep.

Through him those who enter proceed to the pastures of life.

His blood redeemed the sheep from eternal death.

As Jesus walks through the splendid courts of the temple,

While the Jewish people themselves ask who he is,

He confesses in a clear voice that he and the Father are one.

The fourth day had shut Lazarus in the cave of the tomb.

His sisters stood nearby, weeping in mournful tones;

A great crowd was present, bringing sorrowful consolation.

He raises his eyes and offers the Father a gift of praise;

He calls out to the dead man, and at once he emerges from the tomb:

[Column 0269A] He is freed from his bonds and returns to his sweet home.

Holy Mary pours ointment over Jesus:

The whole house is filled with a pleasant fragrance,

As the blessed Church gives off its scent throughout the world.

The gentle King Jesus sat upon a peaceful little donkey.

The crowd offers songs of praise with palm-bearing hands.

Thus he enters Jerusalem and approaches the holy walls of the temple:

The Gentiles were seeking to see the renowned Jesus.

He immediately declares that he is the grain of wheat,

Which, dying in the earth, rises again with abundant fruit.

As he prays, a clear voice from the heavens answers from the Father:

“I have glorified you,” he says, “Son, and I will glorify you.”

The people were terrified by the majesty of the divine voice.

Many of the rulers, seeing such great wonders,

Believed in their hearts, but feared to confess it with their mouths;

[Column 0269B] It was not divine glory but the glory of the world that drew them.

He washed the feet of his venerable disciples during the night,

Poured water into a basin, and carried towels for drying.

O what humility! What clemency there is in Christ!

By a morsel of bread he marks out Judas as the wicked one.

Three times he foretells that he will be denied by Peter.

He prescribes for his own disciples the sign of love.

By this he wished his followers to be known, if the hearts of their brothers,

Joined to one another by mutual charity, were vigorous,

With the same love with which he himself first loved us from heaven.

He teaches that he is in the Father and that the Father is to be honored in him.

There is one majesty, and equal glory belongs to both.

Whatever the Son does is wholly the Father’s action.

He promises that he will soon send the Paraclete to them,

When, having conquered death, he rises again from the tomb,

[Column 0269C] And, glorious, will have penetrated the heights of heaven.

He calls himself the true vine, and urges his faithful,

Like branches, to remain in him,

Lest they lie barren and be consigned to unending fire.

In his mercy Jesus commends the disciples to the Father.

He is betrayed by Judas and, innocent, handed over to Pilate.

Beaten with whips, he himself is given to the people to be killed.

He went out, most gently carrying his own cross.

The Passion is completed when Christ tastes vinegar.

He is placed in the tomb; having destroyed death, he rises again.

At the tomb Mary poured out tears of love,

Believing that Jesus’ body had been stolen by treachery.

Suddenly he shines forth and gives her commands of salvation.

The holy companions return from the tomb rejoicing;

In the midst of their journey Jesus, shining, meets them:

[Column 0269D] He graciously says, “Hail”; they kiss his feet.

That Peter wept very bitterly for the crime of having denied Christ.

The merciful one immediately appears to him,

Comforts the sorrowful man, and strengthens the heart of the trembling disciple.

Two men happened to be going to visit a certain village.

Suddenly Jesus meets them in the guise of a traveler.

When invited, he enters their dwelling and makes himself known in the breaking of bread.

The disciples happened to be sitting in a locked room, afraid.

Suddenly Jesus, radiant, stands among them.

They recognize the Lord and examine the marks of the nails.

Thomas had been absent when that divine teacher had shown himself to his companions,

Displaying the holy wounds in his side;

Christ appears again, and Thomas confesses him to be Lord and God.

[Column 0270A] Peter and his companions had been fishing and had caught nothing in the waters.

Christ stands on the shore and orders the nets to be cast.

A great catch is made, and the glorious one eats with them.

On the mountain of Galilee, as he himself had promised,

The holy ones reverently worship the glorious Jesus,

And he says that all things in heaven and on earth have been subjected to him.

At the last meal, joining himself to his holy disciples,

He commands that the Gospel shine throughout the whole world through them,

And that all who believe be washed in holy baptism.

Then he went to the summit of the Mount of Olives.

The holy ones stand by; he blesses them from heaven,

And, while they watch, enters the starry dwelling.

He sits at the right hand of God, higher than the angelic powers themselves,

And from there he will come in splendor,

To judge the whole world according to eternal laws.

[Column 0270B] Let heaven and earth praise him, and Tartarus itself in its depths,

The Lord of all, powerful with the Father throughout the ages;

Let the stars cry out to him together with the Holy Spirit.

Amen.

## IV. PRAYER, WITH COMMEMORATION OF THE ANCIENT MIRACLES OF CHRIST OUR GOD

O eternal power of God, whom the mechanism of the universe

Receives as its author, whom earth and heaven serve,

The beginning of all things, through whom the Father made everything.

When, with the eternal Spirit resting upon the vast waters,

You once shone with new light upon the waters oppressed by dreadful darkness,

And created night and day,

So that gentle light might reveal the various labors of human beings,

[Column 0270C] And nighttime rest might restore their exhausted limbs.

You fitted two dwelling places, dividing the waters,

Driving some into the sea and storing others above the stars.

So that the dry earth could produce fruit

And cherish all living creatures with free nourishment,

You set the sphere of the moon and sun, and the shining stars,

In their various functions upon the lofty heights.

By your sole command you brought forth from the womb of the earth

All cattle and every creeping creature into the light.

You also formed bodies that breathe in the waters,

Giving the winds to the birds and enriching the sea with fish.

By the life-giving draught of sacred breath you raise up

A body taken from the body of inert earth;

Calling it human, you command it to rule throughout the whole world,

And fill it with the laws of every rational order.

[Column 0270D] So that the race created on earth by one maker

Might be governed in heaven by one ruler.

O eternal power of God, whom the mechanism of the universe

Receives as its author, whom earth and heaven serve.

You did not allow the first man to remain alone,

But created for him the chaste consolation of an excellent wife,

Whom neither the earth bore nor a mother’s womb brought forth,

But your right hand fashioned from the man’s rib.

You punished the sin of both with a merciful death,

And condemned the serpent’s tongue to the dust,

The tongue that taught the wretched to despise the commands of the Thunderer

And to seek for itself the highest name of the divine power.

O eternal power of God, whom the mechanism of the universe

Receives as its author, whom earth and heaven serve,

[Column 0271A] You turn the death of a righteous man, slain by his brother’s hand,

Back upon the author of the crime under a just law of punishment.

You took one of the first mortals of the earliest age,

Ignorant of death, away to the secrets of life.

Meanwhile, however, all people were polluting

The beautiful world with seething vices and a thousand crimes.

You enveloped the whole world in mighty waves,

Depriving earth-dwellers of the earth and rivers of their banks.

You preserved a certain righteous man, together with his offspring and household,

From the waters of the Flood in a vessel-bearing ark,

So that the race on earth, rising from a single seed,

Might fall in one death and rise again from one stock,

And that the cleansed earth might shelter a purified human race,

Nor would those unworthy of life enjoy the gift of life.

O eternal power of God, whom the mechanism of the universe

[Column 0271B] Receives as its author, whom earth and heaven serve,

Seeking to join lofty friends to yourself,

You first called one without blemish from the midst of the fires.

He left behind the boundaries of his homeland and its mournful kingdoms,

And grew into mighty nations in a foreign land.

For the golden law tells that the firstborn, whom a slave woman bore,

Fathered twelve leaders;

He whom the free mother bore later in birth

Received twins born of one wife.

One of them founded the Idumeans from a mingled bloodline;

The other propagated the Hebrews from a twelvefold stock.

This man had two wives according to the ancient custom,

And as many slave women, taken as wives;

From them he brought forth the ancient nation and mighty people,

And joined his descendants to the bright stars.

[Column 0271C] Yet again, when the impious race polluted

The world, washed by the waters, with unspeakable crime,

You prepared to destroy it, and overthrew the walls of Sodom with flames

And the dwellings of Gomorrah with sulfurous fire,

Indeed, together with their wretched inhabitants, the neighboring cities as well,

Reducing them to ashes and plunging them into the deep abyss.

By judgment, the fruits that grew in those places

Are beautiful on the outside but filled with ashes within.

Nevertheless, your hand rescued a certain righteous man from those places
