And led him out of the sinful city, saved from the flames.

His two daughters followed him with their wretched mother,

And they sought the mountains, lest they perish in so great a destruction.

But the utterly unhappy wife, suddenly struck by the crash,

Looked back and, having experienced the punishment, remained behind.

Here the daughters, left alone with their father,

Thinking that mortals had perished, used such deception:

They mixed wine for the old man and, on two successive nights,

Lay with their father in turn and conceived.

From this, after the savage conflagrations, two brothers were born,

And they increased the human race while Sodom was perishing.

One is called Ammon, the other Moab by a different name,

And from the beginning they founded two nations.

O eternal power of God, whom the mechanism of the universe

Receives as its author, whom earth and heaven serve.

You set a certain righteous man, separated from the crime of his brothers,

Over the people of Memphis, and feed the needy world.

You lead back to their ancestral dwelling the holy people

Groaning under a harsh burden, by marvelous power.

For their sake you punish Egypt with ten successive blows,

[Column 0272A] Sending portents from heaven and from earth, and you divide the waters,

Making a purple sea firm with hardened waves,

And lead the rejoicing people along dry paths.

At night a column of fire was their guide, going before them;

And in the midst of the heat, a cloud freely gave them shade.

Heavenly bread provided them with food, and every night

A flowing sweetness filled the fields with nectar.

Whatever food a guest might desire, whatever flavors he might seek,

He joyfully received in a single meal.

Rocks supplied drink, while rods, soft when struck,

Break their hardness and provide abundant streams.

The plentiful quail served flesh-laden meals,

And learned to pour themselves of their own accord onto the tables that had become hateful.

O eternal power of God, whom the mechanism of the universe

Receives as its author, whom earth and heaven serve,

[Column 0272B] You enveloped the holy mountain in gloomy lightning,

And gave forth a terrifying voice from the sacred cloud.

You handed over the precepts of the heavenly law

To the prophet summoned to you, and honored your servant with friendly speech.

You established a high priest who could appease the Thunderer with prayers,

Who could proceed in holy vestments,

Enter beyond the barriers of the veil into the dreadful recesses,

And alone contemplate the secrets of the eternal Father.

Meanwhile, disturbed by the ranks, a confused murmur

Roars through the camp, and dense complaints echo throughout it.

The prophet is reviled, the priest himself is despised,

And, amid a tumult inflamed beyond measure, they are nearly stoned.

They prepare to return to Egypt, fashioning empty idols,

And spend the solemn day in games and song.

At last, anger stirred by just fury,

You restrain such unlawful attempts under such a law.

Some you destroy with flames and heavenly fire;

Others you plunge into the sulfurous waters of Erebus.

Those whom the earth retains, the fiery power of heaven punishes;

Those whom the earth swallows, the underworld devours alive.

Thus nature greedily devours your enemies,

Thus the whole world serves you as the avenger of crimes,

And does not allow anyone to draw breath for life

Whom it sees not believing in you with all his heart.

Yet from these flames and so great a slaughter

Two young men, adorned by the power of faith, are preserved.

A new offspring and an age ignorant of crime,

Accompanying them into the kingdom, received the rewards of faith in you.

For you command seven nations and seven mighty kingdoms

To serve them, and you give them a rich land;

[Column 0272D] A land that pours forth streams of milk and rivers of honey,

And whose fertile soil produces balsams from the sacred branches,

Which the Father himself always regards with a kindly gaze,

And waters with heavenly streams at appointed seasons.

O eternal power of God, whom the mechanism of the world

Receives as its author, whom earth and heaven serve.

You restrain the rushing waves and lead the holy ark

With so many thousands across a dry riverbed.

You once reduced a great city to eternal ruins by cries [or trumpet-blasts; the reading is uncertain], while its people perished.

But a certain prostitute survived, whom sustaining faith

Granted to live alone, with her father and household.

And, not to linger over more, the subject earth rests,

And what belongs to God is held under various destinies.

[Column 0273A] It is governed by twelve judges, whom your Spirit fills

And strengthens with wondrous power.

So that, with great strength, they could overcome savage lions,

And, though bound, could break strong chains;

Now shut up in a city and, under cover of night, surrounded by many soldiers,

They climb the mountains through doors torn away.

Now they lay low grim battle formations and camps threatening with steel,

Not with a sword but with the jawbone of a worthless ass;

Indeed, with a plowshare they scatter vast hosts.

And a tool suited for cultivating the earth resists weapons.

Thus they repel enemies; thus they terrify powerful scepters,

And defend their own people with the protection of faith.

They exercise the ancestral laws and divine ordinances of peace

Among the peoples, worthy of respect for their merits and honor.

Equally ready for arms, equally devoted to the laws,

[Column 0273B] Equally hostile to outsiders and equally affectionate toward citizens,

They were free from deceitful fraud, and desire lay weakened and defeated.

The virtue of justice itself flourished even amid wars.

O eternal power of God, whom the mechanism of the universe

Receives as its author, whom earth and heaven serve;

You make a holy boy, anointed with sacred chrism,

A king to be feared, chosen from among shepherds.

He, powerful now with a stone, now with a sword,

Sent the giants’ masses that struck the stars down into Tartarus.

Those whom no wars previously could overthrow,

This one boy’s hand crushed, under your guidance,

Preserving your own and destroying foreigners everywhere;

He ruled the nation of Abraham’s descendants with wondrous governance.

O eternal power of God, whom the mechanism of the universe

Receives as its author, whom earth and heaven serve.

[Column 0273C] You pour a holy breath upon pious hearts,

And proclaim future things in wondrous ordered forms.

You promise birth from a virgin womb and salvation for the world,

And abundant joys to the sorrowful earth.

Such things the divine prophecies reveal through signs,

And all things give present confirmation to future events.

Even now, the sun, driven rapidly along its swift axis,

Halts its flying horses and prolongs the day, delaying the night.

Now it turns its chariot backward from the western shores,

And bends its falling torches toward the eastern risings.

A bronze serpent, suspended high upon a pole,

Drives poison from the veins and puts the dreadful serpents to flight.

In a chariot of flame, the prophet is lifted to heaven in mortal flesh,

And is not harmed at all by the fire.

A stone is cut from the summit of a lofty mountain,

[Column 0273D] And by a single blow it soon crushes four forms:

Bronze, gold, silver, and iron together with fragments of clay

Are dissolved and carried into the air like straw.

But the stone, growing into an enormous mountain,

Becomes one and occupies the whole world with its vast mass.

From the heat of a dreadful furnace, with flame overflowing,

Three men are handed over at the command of the wicked king.

A gracious angel appears in the middle of the furnace,

Sends forth dewy breaths of air, and parts the flames with the wind.

They, with rejoicing hearts, offer magnificent praises

To the parent of the stars, the earth, and the sea.

They remain cheerful even when the tyrant himself summons them,

And come forth from the midst of the fire with joyful faces.

The satraps marvel; barbarian hearts marvel

At their unharmed hair and their unscorched garments.

They are terrified in their shaken minds that the threatening fires

Have yielded to the flames of faith and that the earth-shaking furnaces have failed.

The wandering prophet, swallowed by a sea-monster,

Drew life-giving breath beneath the deep waters;

After three days and three nights had passed,

He emerged unharmed from the deepest waters to the heavens above.

O eternal power of God, whom the mechanism of the universe

Receives as its author, whom earth and heaven serve.

You clothe with flesh, sinews, and skin

The corpses cast upon the broad field,

The dry fields that were covered with bare bones,

And restore their ancient bodies with new life.

You are seen going with the fiery clouds of heaven,

Holding all peoples, languages, and tribes.

Having set the seats of judgment, you inspect

The opened books of their hearts,

And divide mortals into two companies.

Those rescued from death and shining with the light of life

You join to the angelic assemblies in the heavenly halls;

Those seized in the swift whirlwind of flames

You plunge into eternal fires and the abyss of darkness.

There the voices of joy and songs of praise resound;

Here pain and groaning echo throughout all ages.

Therefore, I beg you, mighty Christ, rescue me,

Cleansed from the stain of sin by your merciful divinity [the transmitted reading is uncertain].

O eternal power of God, whom the mechanism of the universe

Receives as its author, whom earth and heaven serve,

May highest honor, glory, and triumph be yours;

May a kingdom remain without end, and grace endure forever.

May mortal tongues sing of you, and may the heavenly host

Resound, and may the whole world echo in praise.

May the fearful breast sing of you, the trembling hearts sing of you, the voice sing of you;

May the devout mind sing of you, and may all the inward parts resound.

## V. EPIGRAM OF THE BOOK OF HOMILIES FOR THE WHOLE YEAR

Arranged from the treatises of various Fathers.

O prudent reader, whose concern for life is unceasing,

Read through this book with a devoted heart,

Collected at last from the sayings of the ancient Fathers,

Whom integrity and right faith lifted to the stars;

It shines forth and gleams throughout with the lamp of teaching.

It reveals the sacred mysteries of the light-bearing day,

On which the timeless Word, begotten of the eternal Father,

Not from the stain of man but from the power of the Thunderer,

Wonderfully assuming the form of our nature,

[Column 0274D] Emerged from the Virgin’s womb as a bridegroom from his chamber

And brought new joys to the sorrowful world.

The most renowned martyr clings to him with radiant lips,

Gazing toward heaven and upon Christ born of the Virgin,

Seeing him standing above the heavens at the Father’s right hand,

While, full of the holy Spirit, he rebukes the stony hearts

And, battered by a mass of stones, prays:

“Receive, I beg you, illustrious King Jesus, my spirit,

And, with knees bent, spare those for whom I implore your mercy.”

Thus, renowned for faith, powerful with the thunderbolt of doctrine,

Made sacred by a precious death amid terrifying signs,

Having himself received the lofty gift of his own name,

He takes the heavenly crown in return for the praise he has won.

The flower of virginity follows the flower of martyrdom,

[Column 0275A] That holy John who reclines in Christ’s embrace.

The greatest herald throughout the ages of the eternal Word,

Who, as God with the Father, eternally made all things:

Heaven, earth, sea, Tartarus, stars, winds,

And whatever the immense circuit of heaven encloses,

And whatever dwells beyond the heavenly axes,

And, for Christ’s sake, a blessed exile of the waters of Patmos.

From there, suddenly snatched to the heights of heaven,

He saw seven golden lampstands, struck with awe,

And in their midst Christ, the Beloved, walking,

Clothed in a sacred robe, with a golden belt

Girding his breasts, covering his shining chest.

His venerable head blooms with snow-white hair;

His dreadful eyes gleam with flaming light,

And his face shines forth like the radiant sun.

[Column 0275B] His fiery feet glow like refined bronze,

Which powerful fire tests in a swift furnace,

And his shining right hand is adorned with seven stars;

A dreadful two-edged sword proceeds from his mouth.

At this sight he fell as though dead. The other comforted him as he trembled

With gentle speech, raised him with his merciful right hand,

And led him through all the sacred things of heaven,

Which, though described in the sacred volume, no one can comprehend

Unless the Holy Spirit opens the inner ear.

This book next joins, in order, the praises of the infants

Who were the first to be killed for Christ by a cruel fate,

And now enjoy Christ’s eternal kingdom and peace.

It teaches what the mystical circumcision of the eighth day signifies,

Revealing the ancient riddles of the Law.

It passes to the distinguished solemnity of the day

[Column 0275C] On which the piety of the Magi honored the poor cradle

Of our King Christ with three gifts:

It taught that he is God through frankincense, marked him as King in gold,

And depicted the mortal man through bitter myrrh,

Whom the starry radiance from heaven had shown to them.

It joins to these the renowned festival of abundant light,

On which the tender Christ, carried to the threshold of the sacred temple,

Was pleasing in the divine sight through twin turtledoves,

Or through the double offspring of pigeons;

And, embraced by the holy old man,

Christ, the glory of the Jewish people and the light of the whole world,

Is proclaimed.

From there it links the forty-day fast,

Which the Lord completed in a period joined to the moon,

Conquering the raging anger of the ancient demon,

Whom the two prophets, fighting for an equal number of days,

Could not overcome while fasting.

Three times the wicked one rose against him with dreadful weapons;

Three times, pierced by Christ’s powerful spear, he yielded.

Hence that sacred custom flourishes throughout the whole world,

Near the solemn festivals of Easter, on which the Lamb,

Slain, strikes the savage throat of the dark wolf,

So that the seasons of fasting may be celebrated with equal devotion,

And bodies may be disciplined with restrained nourishment,

For Christians over whom the fury of the hostile enemy hangs.

This is followed by the renowned praise of the life-giving wood,

By which the obligation of the ancient guilt was wondrously erased.

While the human race, because it had touched the forbidden tree,

Had been burdened by the harsh dominion of perpetual death,

Through the tree it receives the new joys of eternal life,

[Column 0276A] When Christ, stretching out his sacred palms upon the cross,

Wiped away the dreadful sins of the former Adam with his pious act.

Hereafter the wondrous festival of the true Easter shines forth,

On which Christ, rising from the tomb after conquering death,

Transferred dying limbs into perpetual life,

Subdued the author of death and destroyed death itself,

Rescued the ancient righteous from the prison of Erebus,

And, bringing many back with himself in renewed flesh,

Displayed the happy gifts of the age to come.

After this comes the glorious and splendid ascension of Christ,

As he shines while returning to the heights of the heavenly temple.

Neither did great Enoch, whom the hand of the Thunderer carried away,

Nor holy Elijah, suddenly lifted up in a fiery chariot,

Manage to penetrate there by rapid flight;

[Column 0276B] But Christ could, who, coming from the highest heaven of his own accord,

Voluntarily assumed mortal limbs,

And, when he wished, returned to heaven by his own power.

There he sits exalted at the right hand of the Father’s citadel,

And from there he will come at the final age of the world,

Surrounded by angelic hosts and a whirlwind of fire,

To return punishment to the wicked and rewards to the righteous.

To these are attached the brilliant feasts of the heavenly gift,

Promised by Christ and sent from heaven,

When the Holy Spirit, springing from heaven like a violent whirlwind,

Came upon believing hearts,

And, standing above the heads of God’s disciples in the form of fire,

Was seen burning with many-forked tongues.

He kindled the lukewarm, strengthened the weak with power,

Taught the ignorant, and poured out the gifts of languages.

[Column 0276C] In addition to these are placed the pious sayings of the sacred Fathers

And saints, O reader; fit them to the glorious festivals,

So that the members may always cling to their heavenly head.

First of all sits the exceptional Baptist John,

Born in old age to parents wonderfully worn out,

And prophesying Christ, conceived of the Virgin,

Before he came forth from his mother’s womb into the air of life.

No one born of woman is considered greater than he;

He diligently showed the Lamb of God to the world,

And, changing the crooked path into a straight course,

He showed everyone by what road they might seek the lofty kingdoms of heaven,

After the stains of ancient error had been removed.

Next shines the most renowned feast of Peter and Paul,

Whom the mad fury of the ill-fated Nero killed at Rome,

Those distinguished teachers of the Church in the devotion of faith,

[Column 0276D] Eminent in doctrine, shining with the light of signs,

Unconquered in virtue, though by different forms of death.

For the cross directed Peter’s footsteps toward heaven,

And, rejoicing, recalled him to his own Christ.

But Paul’s neck, severed by the dreadful sword,

Clothed the radiant teacher in the purple of blood,

And, after a thousand battles, sent him purple-clad to heaven.

Next the poem follows the Maccabean struggles with worthy praises

And adorns them with beautiful speech:

The seven brothers, born of one mother,

Bravely overcame the savage fury of Antiochus.

After undergoing many different torments inflicted by his madness,

They deserved heavenly crowns together with their devout mother.

The devout mother, who then, pregnant with seven pledges,

And tortured by the sevenfold death of her sons,

Accompanied the punishment of her offspring with a blessed death,

Gave the ancient week to the new Ogdoad,

Overcame the savage king through her devotion,

And now, embracing Christ with her splendid crown,

Shines, encircled by the seven crowns of her sons.

[Column 0277A] From that point the page brings forth the shared and sweet honors of the martyrs,

Whom, washed in blood, a white robe accompanies,

Famous with palm-bearing hands.

The most beautiful order of confessors follows them,

Whom the ardent strength of faith raised to heaven.

Soon, in their order, the praises of virgins resound,

Wise choirs, bright with the lamp of virtues,

No less richly supplied with inward oil.

They enter the starry bridal chambers and are joined to Christ,

[Column 0277B] Whose right hand binds them with eternal love.

From here, whenever the foundations of a sacred temple rise

And a new building is constructed for God on high,

And the altar is anointed by the touch of divine chrism,

The things collected from the sayings of ancient prophets

That pious usage requires to be read at the proper time follow.

Then holy Andrew is sung with the praise of a wondrous triumph,

And, already near his Christ, clings to the one

For whom he had longed in the desired death of the cross,

To whom he had clung with faithful mind

And for whom his whole heart had burned with fervent love.

Neither clubs, nor the horror of a savage prison,

Nor a hundred threats, nor cruel chains broke him.

For two days he thundered from the height of the sacred wood,

Terrifying mortal hearts with heavenly speech

And cleansing them at the same time. Neither the tyrant himself,

[Column 0277C] Nor the savage arms of the executioners nor the crowd present

Could tear him away from his beloved embrace of the wood,

Until, surrounded on every side by a shining cloud,

Invisible to mortal eyes, he cast off his limbs,

Going radiant toward Christ along a radiant path.

Near the very end the proclamation of Christ’s coming thunders

In a terrible speech, in which the swift cycle of the years,

Led forth from Christ’s life-giving birth,

May always run toward Christ’s life-giving rising.

For he is the beginning; he is regarded as the end of all things.

He is Alpha before all things, and Omega, standing as the last of all.

Therefore, excellent reader, read these venerable sayings of the Fathers attentively

And store them in your remembering heart.

Practice them in your deeds and declare them in faithful speech.

Do not fear here the arrows smeared with deadly poison,

Nor the chaff scattered by frivolous tongues instead of nourishment.

The whole little book shines with Catholic splendor.

It contains throughout the sure sayings of weighty men.

Here the right faith will be revealed to you in clear speech.

Here certain hope will raise your mind to heaven,

And sincere love will cleanse your devout breast.

With faith as guide, rich in hope, pure in love,

May you ascend in swift flight to the heavenly kingdoms,

[Column 0278A] Where, joined to the angelic assemblies throughout all ages,

You may sing perpetual hymns with joyful throats,

Bearing the unconquered palm granted by Christ,

And shine with an eternal crown bestowed by him.

## VI. TO MODOINUS, BISHOP OF AUTUN

Hail, holy father, venerable priest of Christ,

[Note: [Column 0277] That is, of Autun. For the ancients call a mountain *dunus*.]

Powerful shepherd in the citadel of the August mountain.

The sacred order that shines through gleaming merits illumines you,

And devotion to doctrine raises you lovingly to the heights.

By it the brilliance of illustrious birth and the torrent of speech

Are surpassed, and the stars grow dim before the great sun.

I received the snowy garment from your gift,

And bright linens sufficient for wiping the mouth.

At the same time, a most sweet letter, delivered into my hands,

[Column 0278B] Waters our hearts with its own dew.

How great a fervor of sincere love burns there,

And how great a devout mind sparkles with light!

What trumpet or lyre, melodious in breath and strings,

Could adequately express it and summon forth worthy praise?

My blood does not so fervently quicken my breast,

Nor do such abundant streams flow from my mouth,

That I could worthily repay you, holy father, devout prophet, illustrious priest,

With an offering of praise.

That devout Father and creator of heaven and earth,

King of the angelic host and maker of humankind,

Whose clear footsteps you follow with a devout heart,

While, exalted, you look upon and cherish the humble—

He, I say, is able to return to you

[Column 0278C] Worthy recompense for your merits

And to multiply your harvest a hundredfold:

So that what you now scatter across the earth with generous seed,

You may then reap more abundantly in the Elysian region.

Meanwhile, may life be yours, and abundant joys of salvation,

Long days, and the lofty summit of honor.

May there be love of the divine law, a clear trumpet of teaching,

Excellent conduct, and a heart shining with integrity.

May the flock entrusted to you flourish,

And may it crush with the heel the savage throat of the grim lion,

Strong in faith.

So that, when the supreme Shepherd, surrounded by a heavenly army,

Shines forth from the lofty axis of the celestial pole,

He may place you among the well-kept lambs at his right hand,

Restoring worthy rewards for your labors.

Then, like a chosen ram in a gleaming cloud,

Distinguished by the emblem of a golden fleece, may you go forth.

[Column 0278D] May snow-white sheep and shining lambs accompany you,

To receive the perpetual pastures of life.

## VII. TITLE ON THE APSE OF THE MEMORIAL OF SAINT JUSTUS

Holy house of Christ, preeminent hall of the devout,

Hospitable dwelling of the saints, diligent mother of virtues,

This is what you see, where, for one who prays rightly,

Abundant grace lies open, heaped up through so many patrons.

Their shared glory distinguishes them by their individual titles.

They shine in the vaulted heaven like various stars.

[Column 0279]

# EXPOSITION OF FLORUS THE DEACON ON THE EPISTLES OF BLESSED PAUL, COLLECTED FROM THE WORKS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE

[Note: [Column 0279]

A major dispute once arose among critics concerning the author of the *Exposition on the Epistles of Saint Paul*, compiled from Saint Augustine. Some attributed that work to the Venerable Bede, while others attributed it to Florus, the deacon of Lyons. The most learned Mabillon settled the dispute by composing an investigation of the matter. In the *Prolegomena to the Works of the Venerable Bede*, we published this dissertation of Mabillon.

When we were preparing to send Florus’s work to the press, two obstacles presented themselves. For, as can be understood from the title, this exposition of the Epistles of the divine Paul was compiled solely from the works of Saint Augustine. On the one hand, we have already published the works of the holy Doctor in their entirety, and they comprise sixteen volumes, from volume thirty-two through volume forty-seven of the *Patrology*. Therefore, if the commentary of the deacon of Lyons were to be reprinted in full, we would once again have to publish, at least in part, the works of Saint Augustine. Moreover, that was especially to be avoided, [Column 0279B] lest we seem to add volumes to volumes by committing the same material to type twice. [Column 0279C] On the other hand, we could not pass over the labor of the most learned Florus; at the very least, its outline had to be preserved.

It seemed to us that we had achieved our purpose if, by citing the opening and closing words of the passages of Saint Augustine selected by Florus for the explanation of the text of blessed Paul, readers were referred to the page of our edition for each citation. In this way we avoided repeating the same material twice, while Florus’s commentary was preserved intact, insofar as that was possible. Therefore, let readers not be annoyed by the many cross-references to our edition of Saint Augustine.

The same procedure had to be followed for the text of Saint Paul’s Epistles. We thought it superfluous to reproduce every verse in full. Thus, for the sake of brevity, we reprinted only the first and last words of the verses. EDITOR.]

[Column 0279]

“It is said thus in the Psalms, . . . of Jesus Christ.” (St. Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book XII, vol. VIII, col. 1001 and following.)

To all who are in Rome, beloved by God, called as saints. Concerning the commendation of God’s grace . . . the debt should be repaid. [Col. 0281A] (St. Augustine, Letter to Sixtus, vol. II, col. 877.)

Grace to us and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ. The grace of God by which . . . and the prophets. (St. Augustine, Book I of the *Retractations*, vol. I, col. 623.)

First of all . . . throughout the whole world. For blessed is the one . . . not God. (St. Augustine, *On the Sheep*, vol. V, part I, col. 315.)

For God is my witness . . . just as also among the other nations, Greeks and barbarians. But I say to you, do not swear . . . it is of the evil one. (St. Augustine, Book I of *The Sermon on the Mount*, vol. III, part I, cols. 1255 ff.)

I am debtor both to the wise and to the foolish, and therefore I am ready to preach the gospel also to you who are in Rome. You perfected the sun and the moon. The spiritual sun, . . . [Col. 0281B] I am debtor. (St. Augustine, on Psalm 73, vol. IV, part I, col. 941.)

For I am not ashamed . . . to the Jew first and also to the Greek. An objection was raised . . . so freely. (St. Augustine, on Psalm 68, vol. IV, part I, cols. 856 ff.)

For the righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith. This is understood as the faith by which those things are believed which . . . of the most excellent truth. (St. Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels*, question 2, vol. III, part I, cols. 1352 ff.)

The same . . . the following statements teach. (St. Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, vol. X, part I, cols. 211 ff.)

III, cols. 1390 ff.)

The chief philosophers among the nations, etc., up to “they established.” [Col. 0282A] (St. Augustine, *On the Trinity*, vol. VIII, col. 1034.)

For they established idols even in such forms, etc., up to “let them be destroyed.” (Id., *Sermons*, vol. V, part I, cols. 1022 ff.) Id., *On Baptism*, vol. IX, cols. 454 ff.)

Although a Christian may be instructed by letters, etc., up to “he caused it to be understood.” (Id., *The City of God*, vol. V, col. 234.)

The demons, therefore, who are worshiped in temples through some art I do not know, etc., up to “the providence of God.” (Id., *The City of God*, vol. VII, col. 252.)

The appearance of the limbs, etc., up to “was accustomed to see.” [Col. 0282B] (Id., on Psalm 113, vol. IV, part II, cols. 1483 ff.)

The more intelligent among them saw these things, etc., up to “overturned.” (Id., Book IV of *The City of God*, vol. VII, cols. 136 ff.)

A brief recapitulation of everything the Apostle said above against the worshipers or makers of idols. “Because, although they knew God,” etc., up to “Christ will illuminate you.” (Id., *On Nature and Grace*, vol. X, part I, cols. 258 ff.)

Again, a brief recapitulation of the same words. “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven.” Of whom, etc., up to “than the Creator.” (Id., Sermon on the Kalends of January, vol. V, part I, col. [Col. 0282C] 1021 ff.)

But woe to you if you have loved created things and abandoned the Creator (from a sermon on the Second Epistle of John). They are beautiful to you, but how much more beautiful is the one who fashioned them! Let your charity pay attention. Let Satan not creep in upon you, saying what he usually says: “Let us enjoy ourselves in God’s creation. Why did God make it, unless for our enjoyment?” And they become drunk, perish, and forget their Creator, while they use created things not temperately but with desire, and the Creator is despised. Of such people the Apostle says: “They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever.” God does not forbid you to love these things, but he forbids you to love them as your blessedness; rather, he bids you approve and praise them so that you may love the Creator. [Col. 0286A] (Id., on Psalm 117.) Where, then, is your boasting? It has been excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith. This is the law of faith by which we believe and pray that what we cannot fulfill by ourselves may be granted to us through grace, lest, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish our own, we fail to submit to God’s righteousness. Thus, in the law of works there is the righteousness of God commanding; but in the law of faith there is the mercy of God assisting.

For we hold that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law. Is he the God of Jews only? Is he not also the God of the Gentiles? Indeed, of the Gentiles also. (Id., Sermon on the Sacrifice of Isaac, on Galatians IV.) Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, and he was called God’s friend. What he believed in God, inwardly in his heart, belongs to faith alone. But that he [Col. 0286B] led his son to be sacrificed, that he fearlessly armed his right hand, that he would already have struck him if he had not been restrained by a voice—this is certainly great faith, but also a great work. And God praised the work itself when he said, “Because you have obeyed my voice.” Why, then, does the Apostle Paul say: “We hold that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law”? And elsewhere he says: “There is a faith that works through love.” How does faith work through love, and how is a person justified by faith apart from works of the law? Someone believed, received the sacraments of faith, and died; he lacked time for working. What shall we say? That he was not justified? Certainly we say that he was justified, believing in the one who justifies the ungodly. Therefore this person was justified and did not work. The Apostle’s statement is fulfilled: [Col. 0286C] “I hold that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law.” The thief who was crucified with the Lord believed in his heart for righteousness and confessed with his mouth for salvation. For the faith that works through love, even if there is nothing outward in which it can work, is nevertheless preserved fervent in the heart. For there were certain people under the law who gloried in the works of the law, which perhaps they performed not from love but from fear; and they wanted to appear righteous and to be preferred to the Gentiles, who had not performed the work of the law. But the Apostle, preaching faith to the Gentiles, when he saw that those who approached the Lord were justified by faith—so that those who had believed might now do good works, not so that they might deserve to believe because they had done good works—cried out confidently and said that a person can be justified by faith apart from works of the law, so that those who did what they did from fear might not have been righteous, since faith works through love in the heart even if it does not emerge outwardly in a work. The Apostle, preaching, etc., up to “he shows this in many places.” (Id., from the book *Eighty-Three Questions*, vol. VI, cols. 87 ff.)

And to the one who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness according to the purpose of God’s grace. (Id., to Boniface, Pope of the City.) If a person wishes to ask what he deserved before grace in order to receive it, he can find his evil deeds, not good ones—even if the grace of the Savior finds him possessing only one day of life on earth. For if a person performs some good deed in order to deserve grace, the reward is not reckoned to him according to grace but according to debt. But if he believes in the one who justifies the ungodly, so that his faith may be reckoned as righteousness—for “the righteous lives by faith”—then, before grace justifies him, that is, before the ungodly person is made righteous, what is he except ungodly? If debt were exacted from him, what would be rendered to him according to his merit except punishment? Therefore, if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. For debt is paid to works, whereas grace is given freely, and from this it also receives its name. ## CHAPTER VIII

“Perhaps the Lord called the sackcloth the mortality of his flesh,” etc., through “the sins being blotted out.” (The same author, *On Psalm 34*, vol. IV, pt. I, col. 335.)

“What does the Pelagianist say? Hear what he says. He appears to confess that Christ came in the flesh, but upon examination he is found wanting. For Christ came in the flesh: what likeness of sinful flesh would there be if it were sinful flesh? These are the Apostle’s words: ‘God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh.’ Not ‘in the likeness of flesh,’ as though the flesh were not flesh, but ‘in the likeness of sinful flesh,’ because it was flesh, but it was not sinful flesh. Yet this Pelagius attempts to make all other flesh, that of every infant, equal to Christ’s flesh. It is not so, beloved; the likeness of sinful flesh would not be commended as something great in Christ unless all other flesh were sinful flesh.

“What, then, does it profit you to say that Christ came in the flesh while you try to make him equal to the flesh of all infants? I say to you what I say to the Donatists: he is not the same. Behold, I see the Church, the mother, bearing witness with her own breasts. Mothers come running with their little children; they present to the Savior those who are to be saved, not to Pelagius those who are to be condemned. Every woman, running in devotion with her little child, says: ‘Let him be baptized so that he may be saved.’ Pelagius answers:

‘What is to be saved? There is nothing in him to be healed; he has no defect; he has drawn nothing from the inherited condemnation.’ [Col. 0296C] If he is equal to Christ, why does he seek Christ? Behold, I say to you: the Bridegroom, the Son of God, who came in the flesh, is the Savior of adults and children, the Savior of the great and of infants—and he is Christ himself. But if you say that Christ the Savior is the Savior of adults and not of infants, he is not the same. If he is not the same, then you too deny that Christ came in the flesh.

“What a great thing this merchant has brought here! Coming from his own region, has this merchant found in our region what abounds here? Being born and dying—the earth is full of these wares: being born and dying. He was born and died. But by what route was he born? He came to this region, but not by the route by which we do. For he came from heaven, from the Father, and yet he was born mortal; he was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary. Were we born in this way? We are from Adam and Eve: she through the desire of the flesh; but he not through that desire. For Mary was a virgin, without a man’s embrace, without the heat of desire; and because she was not to suffer that heat, it was said to her: ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you’ (Luke 1).

“Thus the Virgin Mary did not have intercourse and conceive, but believed and conceived. For he was born mortal for mortals. Why mortal? Because he was in the likeness of sinful flesh—not in sinful flesh, but in the likeness of sinful flesh. What does sinful flesh possess? Death and sin. What did the likeness of sinful flesh possess? Death without sin. If it had sin, it would be sinful flesh; if it did not have death, it would not be the likeness of sinful flesh. Such was the Savior who came. He came and died, but he killed death. He brought to an end in himself what we feared. He took it upon himself and killed it, just as the supreme hunter took hold of and killed a lion. For the wisdom of the flesh is death, but the wisdom of the Spirit is life and peace. ‘You will revive us, and we will call upon your name. You will be sweet to us,’ etc., through ‘the reward of the justified.’” (The same author, *On Psalm 79*, vol. IV, pt. I, cols. 1027 ff.)

“For the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God; it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be. Nor should anyone use this as an excuse for the impossibility of not sinning,” etc., through “it is manifest.” (The same author, from *On Nature and Grace*, vol. X, pt. I, col. 255.)

“Thus he said that the world cannot receive the Holy Spirit, just as it was also said: ‘The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be.’ It is as if we were to say: ‘Injustice cannot be righteousness.’ For by ‘the world’ in this passage he means lovers of the world; and this love is not from the Father. ‘The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be.’ Since love fulfills the law, etc., through “punishment follows the conquered.” (The same author, *Exposition of the Letter to the Galatians*, vol. “For by hope we were saved,” etc. The holier each person is and the fuller of holy desire, the more abundant are his tears in prayer. Is this not the voice of a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem: “My tears have become my bread day and night,” etc.; “Every night I will wash my bed; I will drench my couch with my tears,” etc.; “My groaning is not hidden from you,” etc.; “My sorrow has been renewed”? For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness … up to “are not subject to the righteousness [Col. 0306D] of God.” The spirit of Elijah is called the spirit of God, of which Elijah became a participant and thereby was able to do those things; so also the righteousness of God is called [righteousness] which is ours, but given by God. Speaking of this, and reproving the Jews, the Apostle says: “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own,” that is, as though prepared by themselves for themselves. Against such people he says: “For what do you have that you did not receive?” (I Corinthians IV). “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they are not subject to the righteousness of God” (Romans X). He said this of the Jews, who, presuming upon themselves, rejected grace and therefore did not believe in Christ. He says that they sought to establish their own righteousness, the righteousness from the law—not because the law was established by them, but because they established their own righteousness in the law, which is from God, when they believed that they could fulfill that same law by their own powers. They were ignorant of God’s righteousness—not the righteousness by which God is righteous, but the righteousness that comes to a human being from God.

[Col. 0317]

# ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0317]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0317A]

The Corinthians are Achaeans, and they likewise heard the word of truth from the Apostle; and they were led astray in many ways by false apostles. Some were led astray by the verbose eloquence of philosophy, while others were induced by the sect of the Jewish law. The Apostle recalls them to the true faith and evangelical wisdom, writing to them from Ephesus through Timothy.

## CHAPTER I

Paul, called an apostle of Jesus Christ, etc., up to “called saints in Christ Jesus.” Paul was first called Saul—that is, at first, “proud”—etc., up to “he healed more than all.” (St. Augustine, *Sermon on the Gospel concerning the Canaanite Woman*, vol. V, part I, col. 484 ff.)

With all who call upon, etc., up to “the Lord Jesus Christ.” They devour my people as though eating bread, etc., up to “they call upon God.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 52*, [Col. 0317C] vol. IV, part I, col. 617.)

And very merciful toward all, etc., up to “those who call upon you.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 80*, vol. IV, part II, col. 1038 ff.)

The Lord is near to all who call upon him, etc., up to “calls upon God in truth.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 144*, vol. IV, part II, cols. 1882–1883.)

My faith calls upon you, Lord, etc., up to “when I call upon him.” (Id., *Confessions*, book I, vol. I, col. 661.)

I give thanks to my God, etc., up to “the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.” On whatever day I call upon you, etc., up to “let him himself be ours.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 55*, vol. IV, part I, col. 657.)

God is faithful, etc., up to “of Jesus Christ our Lord.” God is faithful, who made himself our debtor, etc., up to “might be given freely.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 109*, vol. IV, part II, col. 1445 ff.)

I beseech you, etc., up to “in the same knowledge.” There were many apostles, and to one it is said, “Feed [my sheep],” etc., up to “they will be saddened.” (Id., *Sermon on the Lord’s Passion*, vol. V, part I, col. 279 ff.)

For it was reported to me, etc., up to “but I belong to Christ.” The Apostle acted so that no one might boast, etc., up to “against another.” (Id., *Book on the Predestination of the Saints*, vol. X, part I, col. 967 ff.)

Woe to those who hate unity, etc., up to “Paul is with you.” (Id., *Tractate 12 on the Gospel according to John*, vol. III, part II, col. 1489.)

No one knows the Son except the Father, etc., up to “they had found the door.” (Id., *Tractate 47 on the Gospel according to John*, vol. III, part II, cols. 1734 ff.)

[Col. 0318B] Learn how much you should presume upon God, etc., up to “the mysteries of God.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 35*, vol. IV, part I, col. 547 ff.)

The daughters of the apostles’ churches, etc., up to “to seek glory.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 44*, vol. IV, part I, col. 508 ff.)

For those who are eminent in the Church, etc., up to “heaven and earth.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 71*, vol. IV, part I, col. 904.) And I say to you: “You are Peter,” etc., up to “you were baptized.” (Id., *Sermon on the Gospel*, vol. V, part I, col. 479 ff.)

He was divided, etc., up to “were you baptized?” The Lord’s baptism is divine, because the Lord is God. But Jesus Christ could, etc., up to “the power to baptize.” [Col. 0318C] (Id., *Tractate 5 on the Gospel according to John*, vol. III, part II, col. 1417 ff.)

Therefore those oxen were magnifying the Lord, not themselves, etc., up to “God gives the increase.” (Id., *Tractate 10 on the Gospel according to John*, vol. III, part II, col. 1471.)

I write to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven, etc., up to “they were making schisms.” (Id., *Sermon on the Epistle of John*, tractate 2, vol. III, part II, col. 1992.)

This was their own detestable vice. But what they knew, etc., up to “they did not believe.” (Id., *Book on the One Baptism*, vol. IX.)

See how that great soldier of Christ, [Col. 0318D] etc., up to “not sex.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 54*, vol. IV, part I, col. 509.)

You wonderfully enlighten from the everlasting mountains, etc., up to “enlightened by the Lord.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 75*, vol. IV, part I, col. 961 ff.)

I give thanks to my God, etc., up to “I baptized another of you.” If the Lord Jesus had wished, he could, etc., up to “and be baptized more greatly.” (Id., *Book V on Baptism*, vol. IX, col. 184 ff.)

For he did not send me, etc., up to “the cross of Christ be emptied.” Wretched darkness in the human mind. Whoever knows how he ought to tame a lion, etc., up to “for righteousness to everyone who believes.” (Id., *Book on Nature and Grace*, vol. X, part I, col. 270.)

Do not suppose, I say, that I can be led so far by my own praises [Col. 0319A], etc., up to “for which an account is rendered.” (Id., *Book Against Felicianus*, vol. VIII, col. 1157.)

For the word of the cross, etc., up to “I will reject the prudence of the prudent.” If we are wise according to the Scriptures, etc., up to “is said to be attainable.” (Id., *Book on Nature and Grace*, vol. X, part I, col. 250.)

I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, etc., up to “confessing their misery.” (Id., *Book X of The City of God*, vol. VII, col. 307.)

Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the investigator of this age? We have heard the Son of God saying: “I confess to you, Father,” etc., up to “were handed over by my Father.” (Id., Sermon on the Gospel reading, vol. III, part II, col. 1389 ff.)

Has God not made the wisdom of this world foolish? [Col. 0319B] In the Scriptures wisdom is sometimes spoken of, etc., up to “because they are vain.” (Id., *Book on Pastors*, vol. V, part I, col. 286.)

Let the Christian mind indeed be troubled, not by misery, etc., up to “has lost the sense of pain.” (Id., *Tractate 60 on the Gospel according to John*, vol. III, part II, col. 1798.)

For because, in the wisdom of God, etc., up to “to save those who believe.” When the Son of God was manifested in the flesh, etc., up to “might dwell in us.” (Id., *Book on the Trinity*, vol. VIII, col. 997.)

Because the Jews demand signs, etc., up to “and the wisdom of God.” “You have made all things in wisdom, Lord,” etc., up to “and the wisdom of God.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 103*, vol. IV, part II, col. 1377.)

[Col. 0319C] God made all things by the Word. All things were made through him, etc., up to “nothing was made.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 18*, vol. IV, part II, cols. 158 ff.)

For if only the Son understands there, etc., up to “what the Father is.” (Id., *Book XV on the Trinity*, vol. VIII, col. 1065 ff.)

For God calls many of his sons who are predestined, etc., up to “and the calling of God.” (Id., *Book on the Predestination of the Saints*, vol. X, part I, col. 983.)

Because what is foolish, etc., up to “is stronger than human beings.” For we do not approach him who is present everywhere, etc., up to “my lack of understanding.” (Id., *Book on Christian Teaching*, vol. III, part I, col. 23 ff.)

What is foolishness in Christ, etc., up to “they had crucified him.” (St. Augustine, *Tractate on Psalm 68*, vol. IV, [Col. 0319D] part I, col. 849.)

Jesus weak in the flesh, etc., up to “is our strength.” (Id., *Tractate on the Gospel according to John V*, vol. VII, part II, col. 1513.)

Consider the calling: … which things he would destroy. The Lord Christ was humbled, etc., up to “they set them in the stronghold of shame.” (Id., *Sermon on the Five Resurrections*, vol. V, part II, col. 1729.)

But why were the ignoble chosen first, etc., up to “except through pride.” (Id., *Sermon on the Three Rods*, vol. V, part II, col. 1731 ff.)

But perhaps someone might say, etc., up to “it will not be false.” (Id., *Words of the Gospel*, vol. V, part I, col. 1023.)

The Lord our God Jesus Christ descended, etc., [Col. 0320A] up to “might be diminished.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 65*, vol. IV, part I, col. 788.)

This Peter, who speaks in this way, was a fisherman, etc., up to “may be emptied.” (Id., *Sermon on the Words of the Epistle of Blessed Peter*, vol. V, part I, col. 256 ff.)

So that no flesh might boast in his presence. See how he took glory away from us in order to give glory, etc., up to “let him boast in the Lord.” (Id., *Book on Rebuke and Grace*, vol. X, part I, col. 933 ff.)

From him, however, you are, etc., up to “sanctification and redemption.” The Son was made for us wisdom by God, etc., up to “is particularly indicated.” (Id., *Book VII on the Trinity*, vol. VIII, col. 937.)

That righteousness, moreover, which lives, etc., up to “complete righteousness.” (Id., Letter to Consentus on the Trinity, vol. II, col. 461.)

As it is written: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.” For the one who boasts only in the Lord, etc., up to “has been commanded.” (Id., *Book XI on Genesis Literally*, vol. III, part I, col. 141.)

And to hear this command obediently, etc., up to “possesses it vainly.” (Id., *Book on the Gift of Perseverance*, vol. X, part II, col. 1015.)

When he had said, “Praise”—which those who do good can certainly do deservedly—he added, “In his holy name,” etc., up to “and let them rejoice.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 104*, vol. IV, part II, col. 1391.)

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0320C] And when I came to you, etc., up to “the rulers of this age who are being destroyed.” See the lovers of truth, who do not receive the name of the Lord their God in vain, etc., up to “not food for minds.” (Id., *Sermon on the Decalogue to the People*, vol. V, part I.)

Our mind requires purification, etc., up to “and this crucified one.” (Id., *Book on the Trinity*, vol. VIII, col. 821.)

He spoke to them, etc., up to “they speak to human beings.” (Id., *Book II on the Trinity*, vol. VIII, col. 837.)

For this is to evangelize Christ, etc., up to “lives well through the Gospel.” (Id., *Book on Faith and Works*, vol. VI, col. 206 ff.)

But we speak God’s wisdom, etc., up to “they crucified the Lord of glory.” This Christian grace—for everything has been handed over to Christ by his Father—was hidden from all, etc., up to “those trembling at his words.” (Id., Sermon on the Gospel reading from John, vol. V, part I, col. 776 ff.)

Unless he himself were also the Son of Man, etc., up to “when he was speaking on earth.” (Id., *Book XIII on the Trinity*, vol. VIII, col. 1028 ff.)

Christ is one person, God and man, etc., up to “when he was speaking on earth.” (Id., *Book II Against Maximinus*, vol. VIII, col. 781.)

As it is written, etc., up to “those who love him.” Our hope is not of this present time, etc., up to “from the foundation of the world.” (Id., Sermon on the Same Words of the Apostle, vol. V, part I, col. 705 ff.)

But those who received peace, etc., up to “let us not lose what we are.” (Id., *Tractate on the Gospel according to John II*, vol. III, part II, col. 1393 ff.)

But he revealed to us, etc., up to “even the deep things of God.” For the Spirit searches all things, etc., up to “you would not do it.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 52*, vol. IV, part I, col. 616.)

For who knows, etc., up to “except the Spirit of God.” Human nature consists of body, etc., up to “through the grace of God.” (Id., *Book of Questions on Numbers*, question 18, vol. III, part I, col. 725.)

When someone has reached that age at which he can already be capable of reason, etc., up to “you may be able to receive.” (Id., *Book of Questions on Numbers*, question 83, vol. VI, col. 32 ff.)

No human being has within himself, etc., up to “have been given to us.” (Id., *Tractate 32 on the Gospel according to John*, vol. III, part II, col. 1644.)

For what has been born from the father returns to the father, etc., up to “I have now given it to you.” (Id., *Book IX on the Trinity*, vol. VIII, col. 921.)

For no one knows what is happening in a human being, etc., up to “we are known.” (Id., *Book to Paulina on Seeing God*, vol. II, col. 602.)

But this is eternal life: that they may know you, etc., up to “and the kidneys of God.” (Id., *Book II Against Maximinus*, vol. VIII, col. 771.)

[Col. 0321C] But we have received the Spirit, etc., up to “which have been given to us by God.” The Lord says that a servant does not know what his master is doing, etc., up to “let him boast in the Lord.” (Id., *Tractate 85 on the Gospel according to John*, vol. III, part II, col. 1849 ff.)

The more you know that these are gifts of God, etc., up to “you recognize that they are commended.” (Id., from the *Book on the Gift of Perseverance*, vol. VI, col. 442 ff.)

For whoever has, to him it will be given, etc., up to “are unhappy.” (Id., *Tractate on the Nativity of the Martyr Massylus*, vol. V, part I, col. 1287.)

The things that we also speak, etc., up to “comparing spiritual things.” It is understood that Jesus’ disciples were concerned with carnal things, etc., up to “prove them to be altogether so.” (Id., *Tractate 102 on the Gospel according to John*, vol. III, part II, [Col. 0321D] col. 1897 ff.)

The day is yours. Who are these, etc., up to “the moon consoling the night.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 73*, vol. IV, part I, col. 940.)

But the natural person, etc., up to “is examined spiritually.” In that very condition of mortality of ours from which we are born of Adam, etc., up to “all will be written.” (Id., *Book I on Baptism*, vol. IX, col. 122 ff.)

But what sort of person is the carnal and natural man, etc., up to “by every wind of doctrine.” (Id., *Book III on Baptism*, vol. IX, col. 146 ff.)

Therefore whoever lives from the body is a carnal person, etc., up to “will suffer nothing.” (Id., *Book of Questions*, question 88, vol. III, part II, col. 1881 ff.)

[Col. 0322A] This Spirit, which they do not possess, etc., up to “to nourish them, not with food.” (Id., from the *Sermon on the Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit*, vol. V, part I, col. 461.)

In the book entitled *Against the Donatists*, after recalling the testimony of the apostle Judas, etc., up to “and was found.” (Id., *Book II of the Retractations*, vol. I, col. 642.)

But the spiritual person judges, etc., up to “we have the mind of Christ.” Just as we are all rational souls, etc., up to “is not permitted.” (Id., *Book on True Religion*, vol. III, part I, col. 147 ff.)

Therefore spiritual persons—whether those who rule or those who obey—etc., up to “has the authority to correct.” (Id., *Book XIII of the Confessions*, vol. I, col. 859 ff.)

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0322B] And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal. There is, however, a question whether spiritual people possess anything in doctrine, etc., up to “I belong to Christ.” (Id., *Tractate 98 on the Gospel according to John*, vol. III, part II, col. 1880 ff.)

The Son of Man—that is, the new man—is brought forth by repentance of the old man, etc., up to “you walk according to man.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 8*, vol. IV, part I, col. 113 ff.)

To those who listened willingly, etc., up to “grow so that you may receive.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 38*, vol. IV, part I, col. 415.)

As to little children, etc., up to “for you are still carnal.” Where it says “not yet” or “not even now,” certainly there is no despair, etc., up to “the counterfeit will flee.” (Id., *Sermon on the Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit*, vol. V, part I, col. 462 ff.)

Not all whom the Church gives birth to belong to her unity, etc., up to “would belong to the bond.” (Id., *Book I on the Baptism of Infants*, vol. IX, col. 117.)

What did Simon want except to be praised for miracles, etc., up to “he desired to build.” (Id., Sermon on New Year’s Day, vol. V, part I, col. 1024.)

Therefore neither the one who plants, etc., up to “God gives the increase.” All the people of that kingdom will be taught by God, etc., up to “God gives the increase.” (Id., *Tractate 26 on the Gospel according to John*, vol. III, part II, col. 1609 ff.)

Some suppose that when they exhort certain people to righteousness and piety, etc., up to “he was working secretly.” (Id., *Book on the Good of Widowhood*, vol. VI, col. 444 ff.)

The one who plants … according to his own labor. I do not know whether Scripture contains the saying “that they may be one,” etc., up to “and we are one.” (Id., *Book VI on the Trinity*, vol. VIII, col. 926.)

For you are God’s … you are his building. God the Father is most plainly called a farmer, etc., up to “he is our farmer.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 66*, vol. IV, [Col. 0323C] part I, col. 802.)

According to grace … which is Christ Jesus. Christ is the certain and distinctive foundation of the Catholic faith, etc., up to “must be shown.” (Id., *Enchiridion*, vol. VI, col. 233.)

When a foundation is laid in the earth, etc., up to “where we may be built.” (Id., *Tractate on Psalm 121*, vol. IV, part II, col. 1621.)

As the foundation of a bodily structure, etc., up to “it grows from its beginning.” (Id., *Sentences of Prosper*, vol. X, col. 1868.)

But if anyone builds upon it … he will receive a reward. Blessed Peter the Apostle, knowing this, etc., up to “will be tormented in eternal fire.” (Id., *Book on Faith and Works*, [Col. 0323D] vol. VI, col. 212 ff.)

Before the day of the dedication of the house arrives, let us see that our head has already been dedicated, etc., up to “at the right hand of the Father.” (St. Augustine, *On Psalm 26*, vol. IV, col. 204.)

For wood, hay, and straw may not unreasonably be understood as worldly things, etc., up to “in eternal fire.” (Id., *Enchiridion*, vol. VI, cols. 264 ff.)

Let no one who has committed wicked deeds make promises to himself, etc., up to “through a suitable foundation.” (Id., *On Psalm 80*, vol. IV, part II, col. 1043 ff.)

Lord, do not rebuke me in your indignation, up to “lest they suffer more serious things.” (Id., *On Psalm 36*, vol. IV, part I, col. 389 ff.)

Scripture cries out that the Holy Spirit is God, etc., up to “in your body.” (Id., *On the Trinity*, vol. VIII, col. 938 ff.)

You already know your price; you already know to whom you approach, etc., up to “which you are.” (Id., Sermon on the Words of the Lord on the Mount, vol. III, part I, col. 1276.)

There are two commandments and two kinds of sins, etc., up to “is wounded through lack of self-restraint?” (Id., Sermon on the Conversion of the Apostle, vol. V, part I, col. 1271 ff.)

We recognize the true temple of God, etc., up to “he died for you.” (Id., *On Psalm 94*, vol. IV, part II, col. 1220 ff.)

Let no one deceive himself, etc., up to “because they are vain.” You do not know God’s thoughts, because they are just, etc., up to “who are wise.” (Id., *On Psalm 93*, vol. IV, part I, col. 1202.)

Those who wished, with wondrous vanity, to be blessed here and to become blessed by themselves, truth mocked, etc., up to “the wisdom of this world.” (Id., *The City of God*, vol. VII, col. 618.)

Do not boast, and do not speak lofty things, etc., up to “and do not come from him.” (Id., *The City of God*, vol. VII, col. 528 ff.)

Therefore let no one boast in human beings, for everything is yours—whether Paul, Apollo, Cephas, the world, life, death, things present, or things future. For everything is yours, but you are Christ’s. [Col. 0325A] Christ, however, is God’s. If they are counted from the head, one finds one, two, three, four, etc., up to “in the name of a reward.” (Id., vol. VI, col. 39.)

When it is said, “For God is Spirit,” up to “the very connection.” (Id., Sermon on Faith and the Creed, vol. VI, col. 192.)

## CHAPTER IV

Thus let a person regard us, etc., up to “who may be found.” Clearly, he is a steward of eternal salvation, etc., up to “the measure of faith.” (Id., Letter to Audax, vol. II, col. 1076 ff.)

But it is of very little concern to me, etc., up to “the one who judges me is the Lord.” For each person will render an account for himself, etc., up to “except the spirit of man.” (Id., vol. VI, col. 46.)

[Col. 0325B] But it is of little concern to me, etc., up to “God is greater than I.” (Id., *On Psalm 36*, part I, col. 394.)

The holy preachers of the word of God are themselves also an abyss, etc., up to “he himself did not know.” (Id., from the *Tractate on Psalm 41*, vol. IV, part I, col. 473.)

It is of little concern to me, etc., up to “for your salvation.” (Id., *On Psalm 142*, vol. IV, part II, col. 1851; and Sermon 50, *On the Words of the Gospel*, vol. V.)

Therefore do not judge before the time, etc., up to “one is puffed up against another on behalf of another.” Often in these matters our belief is deceived, etc., up to “human temptation is pardonable.” (Id., *On John*, vol. III, part II, col. 1859.)

The judgment has not yet been revealed. It is night, etc., up to “your heart is night.” (Id., *On Psalm 100*, vol. IV, part II, [Col. 0325C] col. 1291.)

For we mortals do not know the hearts of mortals, etc., up to “he will be enlightened by God himself.” (Id., *Enchiridion*, vol. VI, col. 288.)

Our knowledge of ourselves is more certain within, where, etc., up to “nor will he then be able.” (Id., *To Italica*, vol. II, col. 318 ff.)

Thus God will be known and seen by us, etc., up to “they will praise you for ever and ever.” (Id., *The City of God*, vol. VII, col. 801.)

For who distinguishes you? etc., up to “as those appointed for death.” The Apostle forbids it, saying: “Let no one boast in man,” etc., up to “do not boast in the Lord.” (Id., Letter to Valentinus, vol. II, col. 969 ff.)

[Col. 0325D] All proceeding from one into condemnation are distinguished, not by their own merits, etc., up to “let nothing of ours exist.” (Id., *Book on Rebuke and Grace*, vol. X, col. 923 ff.)

Therefore I said to you, he says, that no one can come to me, etc., up to “which you have not received.” (Id., *On John*, vol. III, part II, col. 1618 ff.)

His mercy will go before me. Consider what was said: “He will go before me,” etc., up to “my God is my mercy.” (Id., *On Psalm 58*, vol. IV, part I, col. 712 ff.)

For in rebuking the Apostle’s pride, he does not say, “You do not have,” but says, etc., up to “nor ungrateful.” (Id., *On Psalm 85*, vol. IV, part II, col. 1084.)

[Col. 0326A] For we have become a spectacle to the world, etc., up to “the refuse of all things until now.” “You have made me a reproach,” he says, “to the fool,” etc., up to “if I am not broken.” (Id., *On Psalm 38*, vol. IV, part I, col. 426.)

I do not write these things to shame you, etc., up to “but in truth.” What the Psalmist says, etc., up to “to be what belongs to God.” (Id., *On Psalm 77*, vol. IV, part I, col. 992.)

What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness? I will visit their iniquities with a rod, etc., up to “the robber perish.” (Id., *On Psalm 88*, vol. IV, part IV, col. 1331 ff.)

## CHAPTER V

It is heard altogether, etc., up to “of our Lord Jesus Christ.” [Col. 0326B] What cruelty did Moses either command or commit, etc., up to “so that they might learn not to blaspheme.” (Id., *Book Against Faustus*, vol. VIII, col. 452.)

Great and holy men who already knew very well, etc., up to “so that the soul may be saved.” (Id., *On the Sermon of the Lord on the Mount*, vol. III, part I, col. 1262 ff.)

Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole mass? What does such great fury of separation mean, etc., up to “they depart from the unity of the Church.” (Id., *Book on the One Baptism*, vol. IX, col. 608 ff.)

Cleanse out the old leaven, etc., up to “Christ has been sacrificed.” Passover, brothers, is not, as some suppose, a Greek name, etc., up to “our passing-over.” (Id., *On John*, vol. III, part II, col. 1784 [Col. 0326C] ff.)

# ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

## ARGUMENT

After the Corinthians had performed their penance, the apostle writes them a consolatory letter from Troas through Titus; praising them and exhorting them to better things, showing that they had indeed been saddened but had been corrected.

## CHAPTER I

## ARGUMENT

The Ephesians are Asians. Having received the word of truth, they persisted in faith. The Apostle praises them highly, writing to them from Rome, from prison, through Tychicus the deacon.

# ON THE LETTER TO THE PHILIPPIANS

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0381D]

The Philippians are Macedonians. After receiving the word of truth, they persevered in the faith and did not accept false apostles. The Apostle praises them highly, writing to them from Rome, from prison, through Epaphroditus.

# ON THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0389B]

The Colossians, like the Laodiceans, are Asians, and they too had been forestalled by false apostles. The Apostle himself did not visit them; nevertheless, he corrects them by letter. For they had heard the word from Archippus, who had also received the ministry among them. Therefore, the Apostle, already imprisoned, writes to them from Ephesus through Tychicus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte.

“He who rescued us,” etc., up to “of the Son of his love.” Whoever you are who read these things, and the grace of God, etc., up to “deliver us from evil.” (The same author, *Tractates on Psalm CV*, vol. IV, part II, cols. 1416 ff.)

# ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0393D]

The Thessalonians are Macedonians who, after receiving the word of truth, persevered in faith even amid the persecution of their fellow citizens. Moreover, they neither accepted false apostles nor what was said by the false apostles. The Apostle praises them highly, writing to them from Athens through Tychicus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte.

## CHAPTER I

“Paul and Silvanus,” etc., up to “the living and true God.” The Jews’ assembly is properly accustomed to be called a synagogue, etc., up to “was seeking.” (The same author, *Tractates on Psalm LXXXI*, vol. IV, part II, col. 1047.)

“And to await,” etc., up to “from the coming wrath.” The wrath of God is not disturbance, etc., up to “punishment for sin.” [Col. 0394D] (The same author, *Sentences of Prosper*, vol. X, part II, col. 1872.)

## CHAPTER II

“And a mother loves to nourish her little child,” etc., up to “and we shall praise him.” (The same author, sermon on the words of the Gospel, vol. V, part I, cols. 156 ff.)
