“For when they say, ‘Peace,’” etc., up to “and they will not escape.” “But,” you say, “our punishment compels us to confess that the end is already present,” etc., up to “the powers of heaven will be shaken.” (The same author, same work, cols. 918 ff.)

“But you, brothers,” etc., up to “nor of darkness.” Those who presume upon their desires, etc., up to “but now you are light in the Lord.” (The same author, *Tractates on Psalm CXX*, vol. IV, part II, col. 1606 ff.)

Therefore let us not sleep, etc., up to “and be at peace with them.” Many, when they sleep, do not make room for the Lord, etc., up to “they saw that riches would pass away.” (The same author, *Tractates on Psalm CXXXI*, col. 1719.)

We ought to perform deeds worthy of the light, that is, as in the light, [Col. 0396B] etc., up to “works in Christ.” (The same author, *Tractates on Psalm LXI*, col. 740.)

“But we ask you,” etc., up to “with one another and toward all.” As far as it depends on us, we ought to wish all to be saved, etc., up to “is neglected through concealment.” (The same author, *On the Good of Perseverance and Grace*, vol. X, part I, cols. 918 ff.)

When a person sees someone living badly, etc., up to “righteous in mercy.” (The same author, sermon on the words of the Gospel, vol. V, part II, cols. 1732 ff.)

“Rejoice always.” “Come, let us exult in the Lord,” etc., up to “to insult the world.” (The same author, *Tractates on Psalm XCIV*, vol. IV, part II, col. 1217.)

“Mercy and truth go before your face,” etc., up to “they will exult in your name.” [Col. 0396C] (The same author, *Tractates on Psalm LXXXVIII*, col. 1228.)

“Blessed will you be,” he says, “when they curse you,” etc., up to “immortality.” (The same author, book II of *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, vol. III, part I, col. 1236.)

“Pray without ceasing.” The Lord says: “It is necessary always to pray and not to grow weary,” etc., up to “it is the cry of the heart.” (The same author, *On Heresies*, vol. VIII, cols. 40 ff.)

“In everything give thanks,” etc., up to “for all of you.” The true humility of the faithful is to be proud in nothing, etc., up to “or kind.” (The same author, *Sentences of Prosper*, vol. X, part II, col. 1866.)

“Do not extinguish the Spirit,” etc. Not because he can be extinguished, but because, insofar as it lies with them, they are extinguishers, etc., up to “may he always shine in you.” (The same author, *Tractates on Psalm LXXVI*, col. 993.)

[Col. 0396D] “May the God of peace himself,” etc., up to “Amen.” Although properly speaking “spirit” is also used not for the whole soul, etc., up to “may he bring this to life.” (The same author, book II *To Victor Vincentius*, vol. X, part I, cols. 496 ff. and 485 ff.)

“And I,” he says, “if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things,” etc., up to “draws everything after himself.” (The same author, *Tractate 53 on the Gospel according to John*, vol. III, part II, col. 1733.)

There are three things of which a human being consists: spirit, soul, and body, etc., up to “and we shall be changed.” (The same author, sermon on faith and the Creed, vol. VI, cols. 193 ff.)

It is one thing to be without sin, etc., up to “declares that he is not so.” (The same author, *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, vol. X, part I, col. 304.)

[Col. 0397]

# ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0397A]

The Apostle writes a second epistle to the Thessalonians and makes known to them matters concerning the last times and the overthrow of the adversary. He writes this epistle from Athens through Titus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte.

## CHAPTER I

“Paul and Silvanus and Timothy,” etc., up to “the love of each one of you for one another.” He said this lest, perhaps, because of so great a good, etc., up to “you may have it from yourselves.” (The same author, *On Grace and Free Will*, vol. X, part I, col. 904.)

“So that we ourselves,” etc., up to “rest with us.” The afflictions and persecutions of the righteous, etc., up to [Col. 0397B] “for the completion of purification.” (The same author, *Tractate 13 Against Faustus*, vol. VIII, cols. 291 ff.)

“At the revelation,” etc., up to “who believed.” If the condition of those who do not know is worse than that of those who know the law, etc., up to “who are ignorant of God.” (The same author, *On Grace and Free Will*, vol. X, part I, cols. 884 ff.)

“Because it was believed,” etc., up to “of the Lord Jesus Christ.” The salvation of this religion, through which alone true salvation is truly promised, etc., up to “with his holy calling.” (The same author, book II of *Retractions*, vol. I, col. 643.)

## CHAPTER II

“But we ask you, brothers,” etc., up to “deceive you in any way.” When he said, “Do not be quickly shaken in mind,” etc., up to “the last day of this age.” (The same author, letter to Hesychius the bishop concerning the end of the world, [Col. 0397C] vol. II, cols. 905 ff.)

Therefore the Lord’s coming must be loved and awaited, as you rightly exhort, etc., up to “certainly did not believe.” (The same author, same work, cols. 909 ff.)

“For unless he comes,” etc., up to “of iniquity for those who perish.” “We ask you,” he says, “brothers, by the coming of the Lord,” etc., up to “who will judge most justly.” [Col. 0398A] (The same author, book XX of *The City of God*, vol. VII, cols. 685 ff.)

“Do you not retain,” etc., up to “by the manifestation of his coming.” These apostolic words are indeed obscure and have been spoken mystically, etc., up to “here it is entirely silent.” (The same author, letter to Hesychius the bishop, vol. II, col. 908.)

Because they have charity, etc., up to “in every good work and word.” When the Jews think that this prophecy pertains to their visible kingdom, etc., up to “and the whole nation not perish.” (The same author, *Tractates on Psalm CV*, vol. IV, part II, col. 1418.)

“For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world and will not be,” etc., up to “rather than what he will have to suffer.” (The same author, letter to Hesychius the bishop, vol. II, col. 915.)

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0398B]

“Finally, brothers,” etc., up to “wicked people.” Could the Apostle Paul finally have prayed for the unbelieving Jews, etc., up to “commands him to do so.” (The same author, letter to Vitalis, vol. II, col. 988.)

“For faith is not possessed by all,” etc., up to “to imitate us.” To be able to have faith, etc., up to “by which he judges justly.” (The same author, *Sentences of Prosper*, vol. X, part II, col. 1887.)

“For we were not in idleness,” etc., up to “they should eat bread.” “No,” they say, “it is not about this bodily work,” etc., up to “they are commanded to do it by proclamation.” (The same author, *On the Work of Monks*, vol. VI, cols. 549 ff.)

“But you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good.” For the needs of the saints, etc., up to “lest they be unfruitful.” (The same author, same work, col. 561.)

[Col. 0398C] “But if anyone,” etc., up to “with all of you. Amen.” Let us love our enemies and rebuke them, etc., up to “does not cut off love.” (The same author, *Tractates on Psalm LIV*, vol. IV, part I, col. 635.)

With a proud eye and an insatiable heart I used to feast upon this, etc., up to “they themselves will be filled.” (The same author, *Tractates on Psalm C*, col. 1290.)

[Col. 0397]

# ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0397D]

He instructs Timothy and teaches him about the ordering of the episcopate, the diaconate, and the whole of ecclesiastical discipline, writing from Laodicea through Tychicus the deacon.

## CHAPTER I

“Paul, an Apostle of Jesus Christ,” etc., up to “which is in faith.” What this person understands by “profane and old-womanish fables,” etc., up to “the Catholic reader understands.” (The same author, *Against the Beginning of the Law and the Prophets*, vol. VIII, cols. 637 ff.)

The end of the commandment, etc., up to “with sincere faith.” The manifold abundance of the divine Scriptures, [Col. 0398D] etc., up to “holds fast in conduct.” (The same author, Sermon on the Praise of Charity, vol. V, part II, col. 1533.)

“You shall love,” he says, “the Lord your God with all your heart,” etc., up to “are joined by a certain lot.” (The same author, On Christian Doctrine, book I, vol. III, part I, cols. 29 ff.)

The whole matter, therefore, is this: that the fullness of the Law and of all the divine Scriptures should be understood, etc., up to “so that it may be perfect.” (The same author, ibid., col. 36.)

All the divine commandments, therefore, are referred to charity, [Col. 0399A] etc., up to “there will be nothing left to surpass.” (The same author, Handbook, vol. VI, cols. 288 ff.)

“Love—but see what you love,” etc., up to “and with sincere faith.” (The same author, Tractate on Psalm XXXI, vol. IV, part I, col. 260.)

Whatever, therefore, is conceived healthfully in the mind, etc., up to “will be a snare for the beloved.” (The same author, Tractate on Psalm CXL, vol. IV, part II, col. 1816.)

For when he said “charity,” he added “from a pure heart,” etc., up to “our hope be deceived.” (The same author, On Christian Doctrine, book I, vol. III, part I, col. 36.)

From whom some have departed, etc., up to “about whom they make assertions.” What trouble and sorrow the reckless cause prudent brothers, etc., up to “they reach food.” (The same author, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, vol. III, part I, cols. 261 ff.)

[Col. 0399B] “Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully. For the law is not laid down for the just”: though it is good, etc., up to “unless divine grace comes to our aid.” (The same author, On the Spirit and the Letter, vol. X, part I, cols. 209 ff.)

The law is good for the one who uses it lawfully, etc., up to “healing through grace.” (The same author, Letter to Anastasius, vol. II, cols. 593 ff.)

Knowing this, etc., up to “what has been entrusted to me.” He lives for God who is under God; but he lives for the law who is under the law. One lives under the law insofar as one is a sinner—that is, insofar as one has not been changed from the old man. For he lives by his own life.

And therefore the law is above him, because whoever does not fulfill it is beneath it, etc., up to “rejoicing in the established good.” [Col. 0399C] (The same author, Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, vol. III, part II, cols. 2115 ff.)

“I give thanks to him,” etc., up to “of whom I am the first.” The Apostle Paul, having been made an announcer of Christ from a persecutor, etc., up to “a persecutor and an abuser.” (The same author, Sermon on the Conversion of Paul, vol. V, part I, cols. 1268 ff.)

But for this reason he received mercy, etc., up to “into eternal life.” Because God loves mercy and truth, etc., up to “he will be able to deny what is owed.” (The same author, Tractate on Psalm LXXXIII, vol. IV, part II, col. 1067.)

But mercy, etc., up to “in unbelief.” “Great is your mercy”; and from great mercy, etc., up to “but great mercy.” (The same author, on Psalm L, [Col. 0399D] vol. IV, part I, col. 588.)

“Faithful is the saying,” etc., up to “into eternal life.” There was no reason for Christ the Lord to come except sinners, etc., up to “you have turned [him] in his weakness.” (The same author, Sermon 9 on the Same Apostolic Words, vol. V, part I, cols. 945 ff.)

“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners,” he says, etc., up to “run to him to be healed.” (The same author, ibid., Sermon 10, cols. 951 ff.)

“We have heard the blessed Apostle Paul saying: ‘The saying is human and worthy of all acceptance,’” etc., up to “to come to me without the little ones.” (The same author, ibid., Sermon 8, col. 940 ff.)

“To the King,” etc., up to “the good warfare.” “The Lord will send forth from Zion the rod of your power.” It is most clearly apparent, brothers, etc., up to “there will be no end of his kingdom.” [Col. 0400A] (The same author, Tractate on Psalm CIX, vol. IV, part II, col. 1453.)

If, in those voices that were made in Exodus, etc., up to “no one had acted imperiously.” (The same author, On the Trinity, book II, vol. VIII, col. 866.)

The invisible God is being discussed among us, etc., up to “we shall see him as he is.” (The same author, Against Maximinus, vol. VIII, cols. 762 ff.)

Having faith, etc., up to “not blaspheme.” What sort of thing is this of the Apostle? Is it not, in fact, remarkable, etc., up to “he is excluded from Satan’s work.” (The same author, On Nature and Grace, vol. X, part I, col. 262.)

There is no creature, whether one that remains in the truth, giving [Col. 0400B] glory to God, etc., up to “he kept for himself.” (The same author, Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, vol. III, part II, cols. 2128 ff.)

## CHAPTER II

“I exhort, therefore,” etc., up to “to come to the knowledge of the truth.” As long as the two cities are mixed together, etc., up to “with him through appearance.” (The same author, City of God, book XIX, vol. VII, cols. 656 ff.)

As Jerusalem signifies the city and fellowship of the saints, etc., up to “you are God’s building.” (The same author, On Catechizing the Uninstructed, vol. VI, cols. 337 ff.)

These matters are plainly very difficult to distinguish, where he says: “I exhort,” etc., up to “and dwelt among us.” (The same author, Letter to Bishop Paulinus, vol. II, cols. 635 ff.)

When we hear and read in the sacred writings that he wishes all human beings to be saved, etc., up to “whatever he did not do.” (The same author, Handbook, vol. VI, cols. 280 ff.)

As with what was said, “All will be made alive in Christ,” etc., up to “unless they are made by his willing.” (The same author, on Psalm CXII, from the Letter to Vitalis, vol. II, col. 985 ff.)

But God wills all human beings to be saved and, etc., up to “under God’s power.” (The same author, On the Spirit and the Letter, vol. X, part I, col. 238.)

Since, therefore, we do not know which of us are going to be saved, etc., up to “because he makes us willing.” (The same author, On Nature and Grace, vol. X, part I, col. 255.)

“For there is one God,” etc., up to “for all.” Since [Col. 0400D] Christ himself is the wisdom of God through whom all things were created, etc., up to “who is the truth in eternal things.” (The same author, On the Harmony of the Gospels, book I, vol. III, part I, col. 870.)

You are truth, presiding over all things, etc., up to “by serving us.” (The same author, Confessions, book X, vol. I, cols. 867 ff.)

If all human beings, as long as they are mortal, must also be miserable, etc., up to “who is alive in higher things.” (The same author, City of God, vol. VII, cols. 268 ff.)

Whether the Apostle Peter, as some try to excuse him through misguided partiality, etc., up to “how is he a member?” (The same author, Tractate 63 on the Gospel according to John, vol. III, part II, col. 1810.)

[Col. 0401A] “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” You have the majesty to which you pray, etc., up to “mercy.” (The same author, Tractate on Psalm XXIX, vol. IV, part I, cols. 216 ff.)

God presented himself in such a way to human beings that he even sent bread from heaven, etc., up to “which you could not.” (The same author, Tractate on Psalm CXXXIV, vol. IV, part II, col. 1741 ff.)

To call the Lord Jesus Christ “mediator” according to the human being, etc., up to “imitated them by loving.” (The same author, Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, vol. III, part II, col. 2122.)

For neither would we be freed through him, the one mediator of God and human beings, etc., up to “if it cannot be said.” (The same author, Handbook, vol. VI, cols. 249 ff.)

[Col. 0401B] “I, the Lord, will be their God,” etc., up to “and the divine humanity of Christ.” (The same author, On the Sheep of Ezekiel, vol. V, part I, col. 310.)

Whose testimony, etc., up to “in faith and truth.” The Lord Jesus said to those who had believed in him, etc., up to “that which is seen.” (The same author, Tractate 40 on the Gospel according to John, vol. III, part II, cols. 1690 ff.)

“I desire, therefore, that men,” etc., up to “through good works.” Our Lord raised his hands on the cross for us, etc., up to “to be raised to God.” (The same author, on Psalm LXII, vol. IV, part I, col. 755.)

“Woman,” etc., up to “in silence.” What was said—“Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you”—etc., up to “and guilt will increase.” (The same author, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book XI, vol. III, part I, col. 450.)

[Col. 0401C] For Adam, etc., up to “was in transgression.” If Adam was already spiritual, although in mind and not in body, etc., up to “he would have forbidden through envy.” (The same author, ibid., cols. 452 ff.)

That proud angel, and therefore envious, etc., up to “entangled in the devil’s snares.” (The same author, City of God, book XIV, vol. VII, cols. 419 ff.)

“She will be saved,” etc., up to “with sobriety.” In this sex, male and female, the Apostle Paul speaks of some hidden matter, etc., up to “sanctification is not found.” (The same author, On the Trinity, book XII, vol. VIII, col. 1004.)

“My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God,” etc., up to “perform your works.” (The same author, Tractate on Psalm LXXXIII, vol. IV, part II, col. 1060 [Col. 0401D] ff.)

What peace? That which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, etc., up to “peace upon Israel.” (The same author, Tractate on Psalm CXXVII, vol. IV, part II, col. 1688.)

## CHAPTER III

“Faithful is the saying: If anyone,” etc., up to “the pillar and foundation of the truth.” Nor should anyone thereby be idle, etc., up to “necessity overwhelm it.” (The same author, City of God, book XIX, vol. VII, col. 647.)

“And plainly great,” etc., up to “was taken up in glory.” What was hidden becomes known to angels not only in God, etc., up to “the truth itself cries out.” (The same author, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book V, vol. III, part I, col. 335.)

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0402A]

“But the Spirit,” etc., up to “who have known the truth.” Hear, then, what you confess that you do not see, etc., up to “lying demons.” (The same author, Against Faustus, book XXX, vol. VIII.)

Hence also that commandment which says, “You shall not commit adultery,” etc., up to “if you give it to the Manichaean.” (The same author, ibid., col. 310.)

But when the Lord, having been invited, came to the wedding, etc., up to “good wine until now.” (The same author, Tractate on the Gospel according to John, vol. III, part II, cols. 1458 ff.)

Since every creature, etc., up to “which you have attained.” In the Old Testament, where certain foods of the flesh are forbidden, etc., up to “nevertheless the authority was commended.” [Col. 0402B] (The same author, Against Faustus, vol. VIII, cols. 233 ff.)

“All things are clean to the clean”; “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness,” etc., up to “is recited for confirmation.” (The same author, On the Epistle to Titus, book I, vol. VIII, cols. 236 ff.)

But foolish [disputations], etc., up to “which now is and which is future.” See the holy love songs. See the Song of Songs, etc., up to “wealth and honor.” (The same author, Tractate on Psalm CXLIII, vol. IV, part II, col. 1868.)

“Faithful is the saying,” etc., up to “who hear you.” “What is man, that you remember him, or the son of man,” etc., up to “proclaims that they are blessed.” (The same author, Tractate on Psalm VIII, vol. IV, part I, col. 113.)

## CHAPTER V

“An elder,” etc., up to “is acceptable before God.” [Col. 0402C] What was that like, when your innermost teacher taught you in the school of your heart, etc., up to “as though she had been begotten by everyone.” (The same author, Confessions, book IX, vol. I, col. 773.)

“But the woman who is truly a widow,” etc., up to “night and day.” Every soul that understands itself to have been abandoned without any help, etc., up to “help is at hand for it.” (The same author, Tractate on Psalm CXXXI, vol. IV, part II, cols. 1725 ff.)

Strive in prayer, conquer this world, etc., up to “fear no losses.” (The same author, Letter to Proba on Prayer to God, vol. II, col. 506.)

However great a happiness in temporal goods may surround you, etc., up to “is nourished by incorruption.” (The same author, ibid., cols. 496 ff.)

Let spiritual delights, therefore, succeed carnal delights in holy chastity, etc., up to “so that God may be gained.” [Col. 0402D] (The same author, On the Good of Widowhood, vol. VI, cols. 447 ff.)

“You who lift me up from the gates of death,” etc., up to “through the gates of death one arrives.” (The same author, Tractate on Psalm IX, vol. IV, part I, col. 123.)

The life that is in sins is usually called death in the Scriptures, etc., up to “to touch a dead person.” (The same author, Against the Manichaeans, vol. III, part I, col. 212.)

“But if anyone,” etc., up to “if she has raised children.” Since the two chief commandments are those concerning love of God and love of one’s neighbor, etc., up to “worse than an unbeliever.” (The same author, City of God, book XIX, chapter 14, vol. VII, cols. 642 ff.)

When Jesus therefore saw his mother and the disciple [Col. 0403A] standing whom he loved, etc., up to “the disciple received her as his own.” (The same author, Tractate 119 on the Gospel according to John, vol. III, part II, cols. 1950 ff.)

If your household property has any money, etc., up to “worse than an unbeliever.” (The same author, Letter to Laetus, vol. II, col. 1059.)

“If she has shown hospitality,” etc., up to “followed afterward.” We say, brothers, that humility comes from the Most High, etc., up to “the feeling of humility.” (The same author, Tractate 58 on the Gospel according to John, vol. III, part II, col. 1794.)

“Younger women,” etc., up to “they have made void.” For in the marriage bond, if chastity is preserved, etc., up to “whether they are absent.” (The same author, Letter to Julian on Holy Widowhood, vol. VI, cols. 437 ff.)

“Make vows and pay them to the Lord your God,” etc., up [Col. 0403B] to “so that you may make and fulfill vows.” (The same author, Tractate on Psalm LXXV, vol. IV, part I, cols. 967 ff.)

What was lawful for each person before making a vow, etc., up to “they made faith void.” (The same author, Letter to Pollentius, vol. VI, col. 468.)

Likewise, etc., up to “it ought not to be.” Let no one deceive you. If you do not wish to be deceived, etc., up to “one will be taken and one will be left.” (The same author, Tractate on Psalm XCIX, vol. IV, part II, cols. 1279 ff.)

“But I desire younger women,” etc., up to “back after Satan.” He commends the good of marriage (*nuptiarum bonum*) with apostolic authority and sobriety, etc., up to “to fall and perish.” (The same author, Letter to Julian on Holy Widowhood, vol. VI, col. 437.)

“If any believing woman,” etc., up to “let it be sufficient.” The Lord also had a money box, etc., up to “may suffice for widows.” (The same author, Tractate 64 on the Gospel according to John, vol. III, part II, col. 1803.)

“Those who preside well,” etc., up to “on the evidence of two or three witnesses.” For we are workers, etc., up to “you will give.” (The same author, Tractate 17 on the Gospel according to John, vol. III, part II, col. 1530.)

“Does this concern oxen for God,” etc., up to “fulfills his office.” (The same author, Tractate on Psalm CXXVI, vol. IV, part II, col. 1675.)

Let us hear Christ the Lord and Paul his servant, etc., up to “to be a mortal wound.” (The same author, Sermon 83 on Gospel Verses, vol. V, part I, cols. 510 ff.)

“Lay hands quickly,” etc., up to “your infirmities.” As the most steadfast truth stands, etc., up to “you may be hindered.” [Col. 0403D] (The same author, On Widowhood, vol. VI, col. 444.)

The sins of certain people, etc., up to “cannot be hidden.” He calls those things manifest concerning which it is clear that they are done in the mind, etc., up to “by which they may be made manifest.” (The same author, Sermon on the Mount, book II, vol. X, part I, col. 1297.)

## CHAPTER VI

“Whoever are under the yoke,” etc., up to “that godliness is gain.” What is commanded concerning the Hebrew slave, etc., up to “had refused.” (The same author, Questions on Exodus, question 177, vol. III, part I, col. 624.)

[Col. 0404A] “Godliness with sufficiency is great gain.” Whoever wishes this sufficiency, wishes it not improperly, and wishes no more, etc., up to “one must live.” (The same author, Letter to Proba on Prayer to God, vol. II, cols. 498 ff.)

“For we brought nothing,” etc., up to “let us be content.” Recall, rich man, your beginnings, etc., up to “let us be content with these.” (The same author, Sermon on Gospel Words, vol. V, part I, col. 412.)

“For those who desire,” etc., up to “into destruction and perdition.” See what has been said to the rich, etc., up to “so that he may not desire.” (The same author, Tractate on Psalm CXXXVI, vol. IV, part II, col. 1769.)

“For the root of all evils,” etc., up to “a good confession.” Consider what they abandoned, etc., [Col. 0404B] up to “not riches, but greed.” (The same author, Sermon on Gospel Words, vol. V, part I, col. 412.)

“The beginning of every sin is pride,” etc., up to “be sent into eternity.” (The same author, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book II, vol. III, part I, cols. 436 ff.)

“Incline my heart to your testimonies,” etc., up to “and not toward avarice.” (The same author, Tractate on Psalm CXXVIII, vol. IV, part II, cols. 1530 ff.)

“That you may keep the commandment,” etc., up to “Lord of lords.” I have shown that it does not follow, etc., up to “the nature of the Father did not make.” (The same author, Against Maximinus, book II, vol. VIII, cols. 766 ff.)

He is of one and the same substance with the Father, etc., up to “both the Son and the Holy Spirit.” (The same author, On the Trinity, vol. VIII, cols. 825 ff.)

[Col. 0404C] “Who alone possesses immortality.” Whatever passes from better to worse, etc., up to “where there is no mutability.” (The same author, Tractate 23 on the Gospel according to John, vol. III, part II, col. 1588.)

What the Apostle says—“Who alone possesses immortality”—etc., up to “he himself is the same.” (The same author, On the Trinity, vol. VIII, cols. 854 ff.)

True eternity and true immortality are not, etc., up to “change was made.” (The same author, Sentences of Prosper, vol. X, part II, col. 1859.)

“And dwells in light,” etc., up to “Amen.” For everything that can be seen by the eyes of the body, etc., up to “as he is.” (The same author, Letter to Italica, vol. II, col. 319.)

It has been said: “God dwells in inaccessible light,” [Col. 0404D] etc., up to “by his gifts.” (The same author, Tractates on Psalms CXVIII and XXXIII, vol. IV, part II, cols. 1514 ff.)

[Col. 0411]

# On the Epistle to the Hebrews

## Argument

[Col. 0411B]

First, it must be explained why the apostle Paul, when writing this epistle, did not follow his usual practice of identifying either his name or the dignity of his office. The reason is that, in writing to those who had believed from the circumcision, he did not wish to place before them the merit of his office, since he was the apostle of the Gentiles and not of the Hebrews; and, knowing their pride, he himself demonstrated humility. In a similar way, the apostle John, out of humility, did not place his name at the beginning of his epistle, for the same reason. This epistle, therefore, is said to have been composed by the Apostle for the Hebrews and sent in the Hebrew language; Luke the evangelist, preserving its meaning and arrangement, composed it in Greek after the Apostle Paul’s departure.

“They stopped the mouths of lions,” etc., up to “their dead by resurrection.” We should understand that the plural number is used for the singular: “they stopped the mouths of lions,” when only Daniel is meant. Likewise, “they were sawn in pieces” is said in the plural, although tradition reports this of Isaiah alone. Similarly, in the Psalm, what is said—“The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together”—is explained in the Acts of the Apostles as the plural number being used for the singular. # Appendix to the Works of Florus the Deacon

(Some attribute to our Florus certain poems, reprinted under the name of Florus of Drepane in the *Bibliotheca maxima Patrum*. See these, if you wish, in volume LXI of the *Patrologia*, col. 1981.)

# Chapters Collected from Law and Canon

(In Acherius, *Spicilegium*.)

These materials were collected by Lord Florus, a prudent man, from Law and Canon.

[Col. 0419C] Chapter of laws received into the Canon concerning the coercion of the Jews and concerning the authority and binding force of the judgment and testimony of bishops: the emperors Theodosius and Caesar Valentinian to Almaghius, illustrious man and prefect of the Gauls.

Because it is not fitting for religious peoples to be corrupted by any superstitions, we decree that all Manichaeans and all heretics or schismatics, whether astrologers or members of any sect hostile to Catholics, must be expelled from the very sight of the various cities, lest some of the inhabitants be defiled by contact with these criminals. We also deny Jews and pagans the right to bring actions or serve in the army; we do not wish persons of the Christian law to be subject to them, lest, under the pretext of dominion, they alter the sect of the venerable religion. Therefore we order that all persons belonging to this unhappy error be excluded, unless timely correction should come to their aid. Issued on the seventh day before the Ides of July at Aquileia, during the third consulship of Theodosius Augustus and Caesar Valentinian.

Constantine to Felix, prefect of the praetorium.

[Col. 0419D] For we have decreed, as the form of our edict declares, that the decisions issued by bishops in any kind of matter, without distinction of age, must always be preserved inviolate and unimpaired; that whatever has been settled by the judgment of bishops should always be held sacred and venerable. Whether bishops have judged between minors or between adults, we wish this to belong to you, who hold the highest judicial authority, and to all other judges for execution. For many matters that the authority of sacred religion investigates and brings forth cannot be produced in court because of the snares of deceptive prescription. All cases, whether handled under praetorian law or civil law, once settled by the decisions of bishops, are confirmed by the perpetual force of stability, and it is not lawful to reopen thereafter a matter decided by a bishop’s judgment.

Moreover, all judges must accept without hesitation testimony given even by a single bishop, and no other witness is to be heard when the bishop’s testimony has been offered by either party. What has been confirmed by the authority of truth is sound; what a holy man, with an unblemished conscience, has brought forth is incorrupt. What we once decreed in a salutary edict, we now confirm by this perpetual law.

From the Council of Carthage.

He judges himself unworthy of fellowship with the Church who, by thinking ill of the universal Church, seeks secular assistance, although the Apostle commands that the cases of private Christians be brought before it and determined there.

That no cleric is to be compelled to give testimony. From the Council of Carthage.

[Col. 0420D]

A cleric may not be summoned to court to give testimony, since a legal representative is otherwise present, and no ecclesiastical person whatsoever should be compelled to give testimony.

Also there.

Whoever has sought from the emperor a hearing of public judgments shall be deprived of his own rank.

The emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius.

[Col. 0421A]

By a continuing law we have decreed that bishops, and those who serve the needs of the Church, must not be dragged before the courts of either ordinary or extraordinary judges. They have their own judges, and have nothing in common with these public courts under the laws.

The emperor Theodosius and Caesar Valentinian.

We restore, with willing devotion, the privileges of all churches and clerics: whatever each bishop has obtained from the deified emperors shall be preserved with perpetual solidity, and no presumption is to dare to disturb anything in which we confess that greater benefit has been conferred upon us.

That clerics are ordered to be reserved for episcopal hearing.

Therefore we reserve all clerics—whom an unhappy presumption had indiscriminately declared should be brought before secular judges—for episcopal hearing. For it is not lawful that ministers of the divine gift be subjected to the judgment of temporal [Col. 0421B] powers.

The emperors Honorius and Theodosius Augustus.

Let the churches be free for the duties of divine preaching, of which they are rightly conscious. Let all spend every moment of every hour in celebrating prayers. Let them rejoice in being protected forever by our generosity, since we rejoice in their devotion and eternal dedication to worship.

The emperors Honorius and Theodosius.

Bishops, presbyters, deacons, and all ministers of the Christian law of lower rank ought to be accused and heard only by bishops, not by anyone else.

Theodosius and Valentinian Augustus.

We indeed dare to speak carefully, seized by even greater fear concerning the holy and venerable priests, the secondary priests, and even the Levites; and we name them with all fear, before whom the earth bows its head.

And shortly afterward.

[Col. 0421C]

That the Church consists in its priests.

Concerning those under accusation, they say:

If anyone should walk with a bishop, or with a presbyter, or even with a deacon, whether in a street, in a field, or in any place whatsoever, we order that he be detained or bound in no way. For the Church consists in its priests.

K. These most Christian kings, who speak of the Church with such reverence, did not hear in vain: “And now, kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling” (Psalm 2:11–12). It is a remarkable and true judgment that the Church consists not so much in stones as in priests. Therefore it is now justly and religiously decreed that the reverence shown to the altar and the temple be shown equally to priests; and just as no one is permitted to seize or touch a person guilty of a crime or even liable to death beside a temple or altar, so no one should dare to drag away or touch a bishop, presbyter, or deacon at his side, wherever they may be.

Also there, from the Council of Carthage, concerning how a bishop, presbyter, and deacon ought to be cleared.

If any bishop—as we do not wish—should fall into some accusation, and should be under such pressing necessity that he cannot assemble many people, lest he remain under accusation, he shall be heard by twelve bishops; a presbyter by six bishops together with his own bishop; and a deacon by three.

Also there.

Any bishop, presbyter, deacon, [Col. 0422A] or cleric against whom a charge has been brought in the Church, or against whom a civil case has been initiated, if, abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, he wishes to be cleared in public courts, shall lose his position—even if a judgment has been issued in his favor—in a criminal case; in a civil case, however, he shall lose what he has won, if he preferred to retain his position.

From a bishop’s letter to the emperor concerning Jews who had been baptized.

After, with the help of divine grace and through the protection of your piety, we began to labor for the enlightenment of the Jews in accordance with the authority of divine law and the decrees of the ecclesiastical Fathers, many of them—men and women, elderly people and young men, adolescents and children—were converted to the Lord by that same divine grace, and among them, separately, some slaves, both male and female. When their number began to increase, and the joy of Mother Church over the salvation of those converted grew day by day, the converts began inviting those who were still opposed to the truth they had come to know, especially children and the innocent, since the others, being hardened by long-standing evil, were more stubborn. The boys and adolescents therefore began to desire that what they saw in these people should come to be true in themselves, especially, as I believe, because every Sabbath the word of the Lord is preached in the synagogue by our brothers and priests.

When the impious parents perceived this, they began secretly, especially by night, to send them toward the lower parts of the province—that is, to the city of Arles—where a great number of them were transferred from the cities of Cabilonum, Matacum, and Vienne. When this had been sorrowfully reported to me by those Jews who had believed, I ordered that those who remained be brought into my presence, without injury or harm, under the supervision of the Church, so that if there were any among them who desired our faith, the door of Mother Church might be open to them, after they had been rescued from the hands of the impious.

Immediately, therefore—marvelous to say!—six little boys, before anyone had begun to exhort them, threw themselves at the feet of our priests and declared that they wished to be baptized, begging that they be brought to me. When they had been brought, they were received amid the rejoicing of all, likewise supplicating and entreating. Afterward, forty-seven others, who made the same profession, were also brought forward. I entrusted all of them, in the sight of God and the Church, to good and faithful brothers for instruction, to be baptized at the solemn celebration of the general washing at Easter and nurtured for the Lord. The others, in whom I recognized no good desire or request, I returned unharmed to their parents.

It belongs to your goodness, your orthodox Christianity, and your piety to ensure that these too may be raised peacefully as children of the Church, without interruption or harassment by the wicked; and that those who were cruelly transferred by the impious to Arles lest they be saved may, through the bishop of that Church—carefully admonished by your serenity and zealously encouraged to undertake the divine work—obtain a similar grace, with the Lord’s help. For if, in temporal matters, it is a great work of almsgiving to rescue by force someone who has been oppressed, or to snatch him from the jaws of some beast, how much greater a reward should be hoped for by one who, when an appropriate power and opportunity are granted, is able to win for salvation a person oppressed either by impious men or by evil spirits so that he cannot come to God. The apostle James bears witness to this when he exhorts and says: “If anyone should wander from the truth and someone should turn him back, he ought to know that whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (James 5:19–20).

[Col. 0423]

# Florus’s Letter to the Empress Judith

[Col. 0423A] Begins. [Note: [Col. 0423B] D. Ravaisson published this letter from a manuscript codex of the library of Avranches, formerly belonging to the monastery of Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea, in an appendix to a book entitled *Rapport au ministre sur les bibliothèques de l’Ouest* (“Report to the Minister on the Libraries of the West”). The historical books discussed here, fragments of which Labbe published in volume III, page 190, of the *Bibliotheca Manuscriptorum*, may reasonably be questioned as works of our Florus. EDITOR.]

Letter of Julius Florus to Judith, empress and wife (so the text; read “mother”) of Charles the Bald, concerning the following books.

Lady Augusta and most fortunate Judith, since nothing is found among human affairs whereby you might increase still higher, for, if the matter concerns a husband, who is nobler as emperor or wiser in divine or secular disciplines than Louis, the unconquered Caesar? Nor is it surprising that such offspring was produced by the most excellent Augustus Charles. But if the matter concerns bodily beauty, then, to state without the shadow of flattery what is true, you surpass in beauty all queens whom the sight or hearing of our humble station has encountered. If, however, it concerns offspring, is not Charles the glory of the world and the delight of humankind? By the elegance of his body, his excellent character, and his swift pursuit of wisdom, he surpasses his own immature age by overcoming it, so that his grandfather seems not to have died but rather, after the darkness of sleep has been driven away, to illuminate a new world. For in his grandson immortal intellect, together with the name, and dignity and virtue shine forth.

Therefore, since nothing is lacking in temporal affairs whereby you might be deprived of increase, you are enlarged by your devotion to the study of wisdom, so that you may be found more excellent than the empresses of former ages. Accordingly, the wisdom bestowed on you by God and the knowledge of your natural intellect have left me astonished among your other hearers. When I came to know your eloquence in divine and liberal studies, I was struck with wonder; and, deliberating with myself how I might offer to your graciousness some small gift gathered through my labor, I therefore completed in writing a work beginning with Augustus Octavian and the birth of our Lord and Savior and continuing down to the kingdoms of the Franks and Lombards, after the Roman emperors or rulers had disappeared from Italy and the Gallic and Gothic kings who had succeeded them had likewise been driven out.

I divided this work into five books. In these, as in a mirror, through the exhortation and command of your most holy devotion, Charles, the most glorious son of your excellence, will be able to contemplate what ought to be done and what ought to be avoided. For it is fitting that you, a venerable lady, should educate your only son, the king of our joy and of the new age, remembering Bathsheba, who likewise instructed the wisest king of ancient times, as he himself says:

> “For I too was my father’s tender and only son before my mother. And she taught me and said: ‘Let your heart receive my words; keep my commandments, and you shall live. Acquire wisdom, acquire prudence; do not forget, and do not turn aside from the words of my mouth. Do not abandon her, and she will guard you; love her,’ and so forth.”

He too, however, as we trust in the Lord’s mercy, will obey your sacred commands, and among the other admonitions of maternal affection he will not disdain to entrust these little books to his memory. Enlightened by the deeds of emperors, the triumphs of saints, and the magnificent teachings of learned men, he will find more carefully what ought to be done and more subtly what ought to be avoided.

Accordingly, the love of your affection compelled me, my ever-august Lady, to write these little books; they now await the judgment of your graciousness and immortal wisdom. If, by your judgment, they attain praise, it will be credited eternally to your memory, since your most sacred name, Judith, is interpreted as “judging” or “praising.”

**In the year of the Lord 862. B. Servatus Lupus, priest and abbot of Ferrières.**

[Col. 0423]

## Historical Notice on Servatus Lupus

*(In Baluze’s notes on the letters of Lupus.)*

The memory of Lupus was holy among the people of Ferrières. Certainly, his works show that he was a man of ancient character. He was born, so far as conjecture permits us to determine, in the fourth province of Lyon, undoubtedly of a distinguished family, during the reign of Louis the Pious. From childhood he devoted himself to literary studies.

Having become a Benedictine monk in the monastery of Ferrières, he was sent by his abbot Aldric—later bishop of Sens—to Germany, while already a deacon, for the sake of study, to Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, who was at that time the most celebrated interpreter of Sacred Scripture. There, through the affability of his character, he won the friendship of many and brought back to Gaul a great reputation for learning and piety.

In the year 838, on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, not long after his return from Germany, he was presented to the emperor Louis the Pious by the empress Judith and admitted among the crowd of courtiers. He was thereby brought near to the expectation of high office, and shortly afterward was ordained priest.

At length, because Odo, abbot of Ferrières, had become notorious for atrocious crimes and had provoked against himself the anger of Charles the Bald, king of the Franks, he was removed by the king’s authority from the administration of that monastery, which was entrusted to Lupus.

[Note: [Col. 0423C] Ferrières: an ancient and noble monastery in the diocese of Sens, made still more noble because it once had Lupus as its abbot. In the *Life of Louis the Pious* it is written that he restored “the monastery [Col. 0424C] of Saint Mary and Saint Peter at Ferrières, which was formerly called Bethlehem; in whose court his father Pippin killed a lion; and he himself was solemnly consecrated king by Stephen, pope of Rome, [Col. 0425] in the same church.” There, by Ansegisus, archbishop of Sens, shortly after Lupus’s lifetime, [Col. 0426] Louis and Carloman, sons of King Louis the Stammerer, were crowned.]

Thus Lupus, going there by Charles’s command, was elected by the monks on the tenth day before the Kalends of December in the year 842. On the day before the Kalends, Charles confirmed the gift of the abbacy to him. Odo, however, had not yet obeyed the prince’s commands. Therefore Lupus, to whom Charles had delegated the task of expelling Odo, compelled him forcefully to withdraw.

This furnished material for new rumors, as though Lupus had laid snares for Odo and had become abbot of Ferrières through fraud and force rather than canonically. He cleared himself of that charge in a letter written to Jonah, bishop of Orléans.

In the year 844 he served as Charles’s envoy in Burgundy. At the end of that same year a synod of bishops was held at the royal palace of Verneuil, and our Lupus was present. His reputation was then so great that, although Hincmar was present, the entire synod nevertheless asked Lupus to write down the canons decreed there.

In the year 847 he attended the assembly at Meerssen, near Utrecht, where the emperor Lothair, Louis the king of Germany, and Charles the Bald, king of the Franks, had gathered for the sake of peace. During that period, namely in the year 849, as I believe, he was sent by Charles to Pope Leo IV. In the year 843 he attended the Council of Soissons, in whose second session he read the volume containing the acts of the deposition of Ebbo, archbishop of Reims.

He lived down to the time of Pope Nicholas I and died after the year 861. Among his intimate associates were the most distinguished men of his age: Hincmar of Reims, Rabanus of Mainz, Wenilo of Sens, Heribald of Auxerre, Pardulus of Laon, Prudentius of Troyes, Jonah of Orléans, Odo of Beauvais, Aeneas of Paris, Einhard, abbot of Seligenstadt, Hilduin, Louis, and Hugh of Saint-Denis, Ratbert of Corbie, Ratramnus, monk of Corbie, Gottschalk, monk of Orbais, and many others.

All this, and much more besides, can be gathered abundantly from Lupus’s own letters and from other records of that age.

[Col. 0425]

## Bibliographical Notice

**Servatus Lupus**, priest and, from the year 838 [Note: [Col. 0425C] Baronius, under the year 838, no. 6.], abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter called Bethlehem or Ferrières, in the diocese of Sens in Gaul and of the order of Saint Benedict, calls Rabanus Maurus his teacher in Letter 40. At the request of Lupus, who was still a deacon, Rabanus composed a *Collectarium* on the Epistles of Paul.

Abbot Lupus attended the Council of Soissons in the year 853 and was still alive after the year 861, as Cave correctly noted. In the year 849 [Note: [Col. 0425C] Sigebert, chapter 94 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.] he wrote a book and collection of testimonies [Note: [Col. 0425C] Of Pope Celestine; several of Augustine; then of Jerome, Philip on Job, Pope Gregory, Fulgentius of Ruspe, John the deacon of Rome, Bishop Isidore, Bede, and John of Constantinople, or Chrysostom—rejecting what Faustus of Riez wrote for the contrary position.] on three questions: free will; the predestination of the good and the wicked; and the blood of Christ poured out for all, since God wills all to be saved, although not all are saved because of their own fault.

B. Sirmond published it in 1650, after Donatus Candidus’s defective edition in Belgium in 1648. It was reprinted in Sirmond’s works, volume II, p. 1227, and by Gilbert Manguin, Paris, 1650, quarto, in the second part of the first volume of *Writers of the Ninth Century on Predestination and Grace*, under the spurious title *Lupus Servatus, priest of Mainz*. Ludovicus Cellotius, in his *History of Gottschalk*, Paris, 1655, folio, should also be consulted.

The twelve chapters of the Second Council held at the royal palace of Verneuil in 844, which Lupus says he rendered in his own style and sent to Hincmar in Letter 42, were published in the volumes of the Councils, in Sirmond’s *Councils of Gaul*, volume III, p. 17, and by Charles Le Cointe, volume VIII of the *Annals of the Franks*, p. 742.

A book of 130 letters, from the edition of Papirius Masson, Paris, 1588, octavo, and in the Cologne edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, volume IX, but corrected against a manuscript, in volume II of André du Chesne’s *Writers on the Affairs of the Franks*, p. 726.

[Note: In these, Letters 128 and 129 are the two letters to Charles the Bald and Hincmar of Reims, which Sirmond had published together with the book on the Three Questions.]

*Life of Saint Maximin, bishop of Trier*, written in 839 for Waldon: published by Surius on 29 May, but omitted by Henschenius from volume VII of the May collection, because he says that he found older Acts belonging to an anonymous writer of Saint Maximin, from which Lupus copied his work; in that writer’s account of Maximin’s miracles, Lupus is called “bishop.”

[Note: From this Life Baronius cites certain material concerning Charles Martel in his entry for the year 741, no. 15; hence some writers came to say that the deeds of Charles Martel were transmitted by Lupus. On Maximin, see Tillemont, volume VII of the *Memoirs*, pp. 247, 694 and following.]

*Life of Saint Wigbert*, abbot of Fritzlar in Hesse, addressed to Bunus, or Bruno, [Note: [Col. 0426C] See Vossius, II, 35, p. 317.] abbot of Herveld, or Hersfeld; published by John Busaeus, S.J., at the end of the letters of Hincmar of Reims and of the *Constitutions of Charlemagne*, Mainz, 1602, quarto, p. 339. Written in the year 836.

Two homilies for the feasts of Saint Wigbert, together with two hymns, were published under Lupus’s name by the same Busaeus in the *Paralipomena of the Little Works of Peter of Blois, John Trithemius, and Others*, Mainz, 1604, octavo.

Stephen Baluze reviewed these writings of Lupus and furnished them with learned notes, Paris, 1664, octavo. This edition was reprinted in the *Library of the Fathers*, Lyon, 1672, volume XV, immediately at the beginning. Lupus was then published again—although the title gives Antwerp—as an octavo edition of 1710, based on Baluze’s second recension. See the *Acta Eruditorum*, 1715, p. 205.

Baluze attributes the *Life of Saint Maximin* to this writer; all the others, however, judge that it should be attributed to another Lupus, the bishop of Châlons, who flourished toward the end of the ninth century. See the authors of the *History of French Literature*, volume V, p. 267.

Likewise, those learned men judge from the difference of style that the two homilies on the solemnity of Saint Wigbert belong to another author. They also believe that there is only one homily, divided into two; for one of them begins, “It remains,” which unmistakably demonstrates that it is a continuation of a sermon.

George Hickes published in Anglo-Saxon and Latin Lupus’s sermon—certainly by a younger Lupus, perhaps Wulfstan [Note: [Col. 0426C] See Humphrey Wanley’s *Catalogue of Old Northern Books*, pp. 140 ff., in volume II of Hickes’s *Thesaurus*.], archbishop of York and bishop of Worcester, mentioned below—on the incursion of the Danes in 1094, in his *Epistolary Dissertation*, volume II of the *Northern Treasury*, pp. 99, 106, Oxford, 1703, folio. Cave noted that another sermon for the feast of Saint Judoc survives in manuscripts in the libraries of England.

## Works of Blessed Servatus Lupus, Priest and Abbot of Ferrières, of the Order of Saint Benedict

[Col. 0427]

Stephen Baluze of Tulle gathered them into one collection, corrected the letters against a very ancient manuscript, and supplied them with notes.

*(According to the edition issued in 1710 and enlarged and corrected in many places by Baluze himself in later labors.)*

## Preface of Stephen Baluze

A hundred and twenty years have now passed since the distinguished Papirius Masson published the letters of Lupus, abbot of the monastery of Ferrières, transcribed from the ancient parchments of that monastery, which Peter Daniel, bailiff of the shrine of Saint Benedict on the Loire, had made available to him.

Certainly there is no doubt that we owe very much to Masson’s learned diligence, by which he brought certain books of ancient writers out of darkness—works that we might perhaps still lack. Yet it would have been desirable that he had applied the same diligence to publishing them that he had applied to seeking out the ancient writings, and that he had not placed his entire confidence in copyists and scribes.

For I believe that the blame must be assigned twice over for the fact that the ancient authors published by Masson have been so horribly disfigured. It cannot be supposed that Masson was so negligent or careless as to depart from the manuscripts he used in almost every line. Yet it is certain that no authors were treated more carelessly than those whom Papirius Masson published.

The works of Agobard, archbishop of Lyon, and the *Acts of the Conference at Carthage between Catholics and Donatists* may serve as examples. The ancient copy of the *Acts*—the very one used by Masson—now exists in the Colbertine Library. It differs so greatly from Masson’s edition that it afterward had to be reprinted according to the testimony of that same manuscript, through the work of the most learned Peter Pithoeus, a man highly experienced in such matters, and was finally corrected and published by us much more successfully in the first volume of our collection of Councils.

The manuscript of Agobard used by Masson is preserved in the royal library. I myself handled this manuscript, compared it with the printed edition, and discovered that Masson’s edition differs enormously from the ancient codex.

Nor was I the first to note this; it was observed by the distinguished Francis Juretus. In his notes on Letter 91 of Ivo of Chartres, when he quoted the passage from Agobard’s letter to the emperor Louis the Pious—“to reckon those things for which you contend as dung”—Juretus remarked that he had seen this written in an ancient manuscript of Papirius Masson. For the printed edition falsely offers “those rejected things.” I too have found Juretus’s observation entirely correct.

Thus, as we have said, it would have been desirable for Masson to have applied somewhat greater care to these editions of his.

From the same negligence it has come about that we possess Lupus’s letters so foully corrupted, so wretched and ruined, that if Lupus were to come back to life today, he would scarcely, I think, recognize himself in them.

For this reason, when the learned André Duchesne acquired an ancient manuscript of Lupus’s letters, he prepared and published a new edition. To state the matter as it is, he removed a very large number of errors, though not all of them. There still remained many more passages in need of correction.

At last, Reader, I have arrived as the latest editor of the works of Lupus, abbot of Ferrières. It therefore seems necessary to preface this new edition with a few remarks and to speak briefly with you about my undertaking.

When I first devoted myself to the studies now pursued by learned men, I believed that I had been given this task above all: to turn them, if I could in any way, to the public use. From childhood I have always had a great concern for antiquity. I therefore always loved examining the shelves of libraries, believing that I might happen by chance upon something that could usefully be published for the public; or, if that could not be achieved, that I might at least find ancient manuscripts of authors already published, with whose help what had already been printed could be renewed and restored.

This has already been attempted, I believe with sufficient success, in the cases of Salvian of Marseille and Vincent of Lérins, whom we published in better and more correct form.

Finally, in the year 1664, the most learned man and my dearest friend, Nicolas Cocquelin, doctor and fellow of the Sorbonne, gave me for use a very ancient manuscript of the highest quality, containing the letters of Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, now preserved in the Colbertine Library.

I immediately compared this manuscript eagerly with the printed edition and saw that the editions differed from it so greatly that I no longer doubted that Lupus’s letters had to be printed anew.

Therefore, if you see anything in this edition that differs from earlier ones, and I do not state in the notes that the corrections are mine, know that the alteration in question derives from the ancient manuscript. The exception is when passages from ancient writers quoted by Lupus have occasionally been restored from better editions or ancient manuscript codices—for example, one passage from Augustine, another from Justin or Trogus Pompeius, and another from some other writer.

Since I believe that Lupus the abbot is none other than Servatus Lupus the priest, whose writings have been published separately, we have taken care to add them here as well, so that, Reader, you might have in the same volume all the writings that learned men attribute to Lupus of Ferrières.

As for the author, I have nothing to say at present, since you have a summary of his life at the beginning of my notes, and I have illustrated his life here and there in the notes themselves. Moreover, after this preface you have testimonies of distinguished writers, which should be more than sufficient for you.

Farewell, Reader; and if you think that anything needs correction, let me know. We shall take care that it be corrected.

[Col. 0429]

## Tributes to Blessed Lupus

### Rudolph, priest and monk, in the *Life of Rabanus, abbot of Fulda*

He also composed, at the urging of the deacon Lupus, a *Collectarium* on the Epistles of Paul, gathering statements from various little works of the holy Fathers and arranging them in order; he completed it in thirty books.

### Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz, in a letter to Samuel, bishop of Worms

Because I have heard that you wish to possess a part of the labor that I have undertaken, as far as I could, in explaining the Sacred Scriptures, and especially the Epistles of Blessed Paul the Apostle, I have sent to Your Holiness a certain *Collectarium* from the little works of the holy Fathers on those same Epistles, which I recently completed at the request of Lupus, then a monk and deacon.

### The same Rabanus, in a letter to Lupus

To his venerable brother and fellow soldier, Lupus, minister of Christ, Rabanus, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings in the Lord.

After your long-desired presence, etc. For the remainder, see the works of Blessed Rabanus Maurus, volume CXI of this *Patrologia*, column 1273.

### Gottschalk, in a letter to Ratramnus, monk of Corbie, speaking of Lupus’s book on the Three Questions

> In truth, I strove to give these three their proper meaning,
>
> to Mateaudus, to Jonah, and to Lupus, whose mouths shine,
>
> earnestly asking that they labor to report what is true.
>
> Yet no one, except one, has as yet given me an answer:
>
> for, cautious and clever alike, he is moderate,
>
> weighing now the three answers of his little book,
>
> so that, once full distinction has been removed from neither side,
>
> it agrees with neither.

[Note: He censures Lupus’s book as equivocal and agreeing with neither side. For although, among other things, when treating the question of Christ’s blood and seeming to have proved that it was not poured out for all, he shortly afterward retracts this and teaches, on the testimony of Paul and Chrysostom, that it was poured out for all. From this it plainly appears that Lupus, as though vainly boasting of his own party, and the supporters of Gottschalk—whom Gottschalk himself indicates did not satisfy him in this book—were mistaken. Sirmond.]

### From the Acts of the Council of Soissons, held in the year 853

When the venerable bishops were seated in synod in the name of the Lord—Hincmar, archbishop of the church of Reims; Wenilo of Sens; and others—and when the priests and abbots were likewise seated—Dodo, abbot of the monastery of Saint Savin; Lupus, abbot of the monastery of Bethlehem, which is called Ferrières; and others.

Likewise, from the second session of the same council:

That volume—that is, the *Acts of the Deposition of Ebbo, archbishop of Reims*—was revealed before the synod and the glorious prince Charles by Lupus, venerable priest and abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter, which is called Bethlehem or Ferrières.

### From the *Life of Saint Faro, bishop of Meaux*, written by Hildegarius, his successor, chapter 118

We recorded in this insertion a very remarkable event made public through a third person, so that it might also be a memorial for future generations. For this statement will not emerge from the depths of my mind on the basis of someone’s uncertain report; we received it from the mouth of the man to whom the event was miraculously shown. He is called Lupus by name, adorned with the light of wisdom, and now a pastor through the sanctity of his religious life in the most famous monastery of Ferrières, where the company of monks in Christ, together with him, is revered throughout the world.

When he was flourishing in the green season of life—that is, in youthful—devotion to wisdom, and for this reason was treated with the greatest affection by his abbot, whose name was Odo, whose spiritual love made him most worthy of reverence to all, since, on account of his promising beginnings, he was already being regarded as the second hope of that place, it happened once that the aforementioned abbot took him as his companion on a journey to reach the palace commonly called Frankfurt.

When he had already completed part of the planned journey, while the remaining portion still demanded his effort, the young Lupus suddenly suffered a very sharp bodily pain in the groin, when the journey was nearly halfway completed. The pain became so intense that, once the road had been traversed, it brought him down with severe weakness at a consecrated place called by the name of Saint Trudo. There, grievous torment was inflicted upon all his limbs, and he was laid low by acute suffering.

By now an exceedingly severe illness was troubling him to the very extremity. And behold, the most merciful bringer of salvation, Faro, appeared at the chamber where empty sleep weighed upon and wearied his afflicted limbs.

When the shadows of night had been dispelled, Christ’s friend Faro appeared there, renowned for the snowy whiteness of his body and the milk-white hair of his face. With him came a boy of distinguished appearance, carrying a flask of oil and walking with a lighted wax candle, as though guiding his steps. Fixing his gentle gaze upon the young man, he stood beside the middle of the bed and addressed him in these mild words:

“Do you recognize me?” he said. “If you do not, the city of Meaux has me as its bishop and patron, and the inhabitants, as the passing ages run their course, will cause my name—which is Burgundofaro—to pass down through the succession of generations. For the author of your healing has sent me to you. Have faith that you will regain health through this anointing of my oil.”

When the young man had directed his eyes and gaze toward him, the bishop of God gently brought his hand, moistened with the liquid oil, to the wound. He passed over all the painful limbs with the softest touch, until the boy’s hand-held flask was emptied of oil.

“Run,” the renowned man said to the boy, “to my monastery at Meaux, for it abounds in this liquid; from it refill this little vessel.”

Blessed Faro said these things so that the face of the healer and the truth of the event might be recognized. The young man awoke from his empty sleep and, freed from the oppressive burdens of sorrow, drew breath. And—what is marvelous to relate—having summoned those who were present, he understood that these things were true, not empty dreams, when in the clear light they examined his limbs and saw them sweating, wet with the greasy substance of the oil.

### Sigebert, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 94

Lupus Servatus composed a book on three questions: free will; the predestination of the good and the wicked; and a certain excessive assertion concerning the blood of Christ, or its redemption extending even to the salvation of the wicked. For on this matter a certain disturbance of the faith arose in the year of the Lord 849.

### John Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Lupus Servatus, priest, to whom Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, is said to have written eight books on Paul the Apostle’s Epistle to the Romans, was a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures and, in secular matters, abundantly skilled in proportion to the age in which he lived. He wrote several little works of his own intellect. There survives his volume on the Three Questions, together with certain letters and other works.

### Papirius Masson, in his preface published in 1588

Ferrières still retains its ancient name. It is a monastery in Gaul, in the diocese of Sens, also called Bethlehem, situated only four miles from the town of Montargis, on the road to Lyon, beside the river Loing, which flows into the Seine.

That Lupus was abbot of this monastery is sufficiently clear both from the Council of Soissons held in the time of Charles the Bald, in the year 853, and from this book of letters. He also presided over the monastery or coastal cell of Saint Judoc, situated at the mouth of the Canche between the towns of Étaples and Montreuil. He now complains, now rejoices, in several letters that this monastery had been taken from him by the king and assigned to Count Odulfus, and later restored to him.

These letters are not without importance because of the dignity of the matters and of the persons to whom they are addressed. For Lupus writes to the apostolic lord, Pope Benedict III, and mentions a letter of his predecessor Leo to Nomenoius. He writes to the greatest princes: the emperor Lothair, Charles of Gaul, and King Æthelwulf of England; but many more letters are addressed to Charles, because he ruled over Sens and the Frankish people in Gaul.

He also writes to the learned men of his age: Einhard and Rabanus, whom he honorably calls his teachers; Jonah, bishop of Orléans, whose books on the worship of images, dedicated to the same Charles, survive; Hincmar, the most learned metropolitan of Reims; Hilduin, who wrote the *Areopagitica*; and, not to mention many others, Marcward, abbot of Prüm.

Prüm, commonly called Prom, is a monastery in the territory of Trier, and Lupus appears to have held that man in high esteem. Lupus himself was sent to Germany by Aldric, the predecessor of Wenilo, bishop of Sens, for the sake of study, since letters were then flourishing in that province. He afterward became a seeker of the best books and requested that books from Germany, Italy, England, and Gaul be sent to him for copying, as will appear in many places.

For the rest, since I possessed with me the only copy of these letters on ancient parchment, brought from the monastery of Ferrières by Peter Daniel, and since, on account of its antiquity, it was corrupted in many places and in some places torn and incomplete, it will not be possible for learned men to regard this book as complete and uncorrupted.

Nevertheless, we preferred that it should be read in whatever condition it might be found rather than not exist at all. Perhaps other copies will be discovered. Yet this much I know: it is not to be found anywhere in the entire province of Sens, where there are many monasteries and numerous churches, and where Lupus was born of highly respectable parents.

It will, however, be of great use to those who wish to know the calamities of that age, which were no milder than those of our own.

### Bellarmine, in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*

Lupus, abbot of the monastery of Ferrières in Gaul, wrote a book of letters, which survives. Since among others he writes to Pope Benedict III, it is inferred that he flourished at that time; this is also clear from the Council of Soissons, held in the year 853 at Saint-Médard, which this Lupus, the abbot, attended, as the acts of the council testify.

[Col. 0429]

# Letters of Blessed Servatus Lupus, Abbot of Ferrières

## 1. First Letter: To Einhard

[Note: To Einhard. He had been notary of the emperor Charlemagne and was, so far as that age permitted, an exceedingly learned man.]

To the most beloved Einhard, Lupus sends greetings.

For a long time I have hesitated, most desired of men, whether I should dare to write to Your Excellence. Although other reasonable considerations also kept me from this undertaking, I was especially deterred by the fear that, while wishing to win your friendship, I might incur your offense.

For it might seem that I had begun with a wholly rash and unusual procedure: I had started with the office of friendship itself, although I had not even reached the beginnings of acquaintance. Yet, as I burned intensely with this desire, the easy, modest, and truly philosophical disposition of your mind gave me hope of obtaining so great a thing.

But, so that I may seem to offer some reason for my action, I shall say nothing of the opinions of secular writers concerning friendship, lest, since you have applied yourself to them with exceptional dedication, I should justly receive that second Horatian saying, well worn on the lips of the learned:

Do not carry firewood into the forest. HORACE, *Satires*, Book I, satire 10.

Certainly our God, far from leaving any occasion for despising friends, prescribed that we should love our enemies. Therefore, I ask you, patiently and kindly turn your attention while I recall my thoughts more deeply, so that you may know that I am undertaking this neither improperly nor with youthful frivolity.

The love of letters was innate in me from almost the beginning of childhood, and I have no distaste for their superstitious leisure, as most people now call it. Had there not been a scarcity of teachers, and had the studies of earlier generations not nearly perished through long neglect, perhaps, with the Lord’s generosity, I could have satisfied my eagerness. Indeed, when the revival of learning began through your memorial of the most famous Emperor Charles—who ought to show letters such favor that they procure for him everlasting remembrance—it raised its head somewhat, and it became sufficiently clear that the celebrated saying rested upon truth:

> Honor nourishes the arts, and all are kindled toward the studies that bring glory.

**[Note: “Loving one’s enemies.” See what we noted on Book III of Salvian’s *On the Government of God*. We shall return to this in the notes on the letters of Ruricius, bishop of Limoges.]**

**[Note: “The most famous.” This epithet is also attributed to Charlemagne in the *Life of Louis the Pious*, which begins as follows: “Charles, the most famous of kings, second to none in his time,” etc. Likewise, in the *Life of King Alfred of the Anglo-Saxons*, written by Asser of Menevia: “He visited that great and most famous Charles, king of the Franks.” Besides the author of Louis the Pious’s life and Asser of Menevia, who attribute this epithet to Charlemagne, I have also noticed it attributed to him by Hericus, a monk of Auxerre, in a letter to Charles the Bald. “Above all,” he says, “this prepares eternal remembrance for you: that you not only represent equally the zeal of your most famous grandfather Charles for the immortal disciplines, but surpass it with incomparable ardor; while what he drew from buried ashes you advance everywhere through the manifold encouragement both of benefactions and of authority, indeed—to compare lofty things with lofty things—you drive it up to the stars.” Hericus seems plainly to have had this letter of Lupus before his eyes. An old codex of the monastery of Val-Dieu, cited by Jean Chapeauville in his *Annotations on the First Volume of the History of the Bishops of Liège*, p. 154, reads: “In the times of Gerbald and Walcand, bishops of Liège, Charles, the most famous Roman emperor, built very many churches from their foundations.”]**

Now those who strive to learn anything are regarded as burdensome; and, as though placed in some elevated position, every earnest student is publicly scrutinized by the ignorant, who, whenever they detect some fault in him, attribute it not to human weakness but to the nature of his disciplines. Thus, while some cannot attain the palm deserved by wisdom and others fear a reputation they do not deserve, they have abandoned so noble a work.

To me it is sufficiently evident that wisdom should be sought for its own sake. Having been entrusted with its pursuit by the holy metropolitan bishop Aldric,

**[Note: Aldric. At that time abbot of Ferrières after Adalbert; later archbishop of Sens before Wenilo, as will be said in Letter 29.]**

I obtained a teacher of grammar and received instruction in that art from him. Since proceeding from grammar to rhetoric and then, in order, to the other liberal disciplines is nowadays merely a story, after I had begun to wander somewhat through the volumes of authors, the compositions produced in our own age displeased me because they strayed from the gravity of Cicero and the other authors, a gravity imitated even by distinguished men of the Christian religion. Thus your work came into my hands,

**[Note: “Your work.” That is, Eginhard’s book on the *Life of Charlemagne*, which is in everyone’s hands. From this passage of Lupus, learned men have rightly concluded that those who deny Eginhard’s authorship of the book on Charlemagne’s life are mistaken.]**

in which you set forth in the clearest language the famous deeds of the emperor I have mentioned—allow me to say this without suspicion of flattery. There I found elegance of thought, the sparing use of conjunctions that I had noticed in the authors, and sentences neither obstructed nor entangled in exceedingly long periods, but completed within moderate limits. I embraced the work.

Therefore, both because of the opinion I had already formed of you—an opinion worthy of a wise man—and especially because I had experienced the eloquence of that book, I subsequently desired to find some opportunity to address you in person. In this way, just as your integrity and wisdom had made you renowned to my smallness, so my love for you and my devotion to the disciplines might commend me to your greatness.

Nor shall I cease wishing for this so long as I know that you remain safe in this life.

**[Note: “Safe.” For *incolumes*, plural accusative. The reference is to Eginhard. It was a known practice among the ancients, who used their ears according to judgment and choice, sometimes inflecting plural accusatives of the third declension with *-is*, sometimes with *-es*, as Valerius Probus observes in Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, Book XIII, chapter 19. I believe the ancients varied these inflections for no other reason than to avoid similar endings, which Lucilius, in the same Gellius, Book XVIII, chapter 8, very wittily calls tasteless, inert, and childish. In the memory of our fathers, moreover, several highly learned men revived this ancient usage in writing. See Priscian, Book V.]**

I am led to hope that this may happen all the more because, moving from Gaul here into the trans-Rhenish region, I have become nearer to you.

**[Note: “Nearer to you.” For Lupus, who had gone to Germany for the sake of study, was staying with Rabanus at the monastery of Fulda. Eginhard, meanwhile, lived at the monastery of Seligenstadt. Both monasteries were situated in the diocese of Mainz.]**

For the aforesaid bishop sent me to the venerable Rabanus,

**[Note: Rabanus. A monk and abbot of Fulda, and eventually archbishop of Mainz, a most learned man, whose many distinguished works of intellect remain. Lupus’s Letter 40 is addressed to him; there he calls him his teacher.]**

so that through him I might gain entrance to the divine Scriptures.

**[Note: “The divine Scriptures.” Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, was at that time their most celebrated interpreter. Lupus, however, was then a deacon. He was extraordinarily devoted to the study of sacred letters. This was why he asked Rabanus to write commentaries on Paul’s Epistles; Rabanus undertook that work only after Lupus had returned from Fulda to Gaul. See Rabanus’s letter to Lupus, published among the encomia.]**

When I learned, therefore, that his messenger was about to come from here to you, at first I proposed to send certain obscurities of wording for you to clarify. Then it seemed preferable that I should also send this letter. If you receive it graciously, I shall congratulate myself as one who has obtained a most desired gift.

But once I have crossed the boundary of modesty, I also ask this: would you lend me here, where I am staying, certain of your books? Although it is much less to ask for books than for friendship, these are the works:

Cicero’s book on rhetoric, which I do possess, but in most places it is corrupt. I therefore collated it with the copy found there, and found the one I had considered more reliable to be more corrupt.

Likewise, three books by the same author on rhetoric, in the form of a discussion and dialogue concerning the Orator. I believe you possess them, because in your inventory of volumes, after the mention of the book *Ad Herennium* and with certain other works inserted, I found written: “Cicero on rhetoric.” Likewise: “Explanation of Cicero’s books.” In addition: “Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*.”

**[Note: “The inventory of volumes.” Below, in Letter 80, *breves* also means the inventories that you were supposed to send from the resources of your monastery. A letter sent from the Council of Carthage to the bishops of Numidia, both Mauritanias, Tripolitania, and the province of Proconsular Africa, in 397, says: “We have appended to this letter an inventory of the regulations, in which everything seems to have been included, and certain matters more carefully safeguarded, so that by reviewing in summary what has been decreed, we may take care to observe it more diligently.” Hence, in the Code of the Canons of the African Church, chapter 94, which lists matters requiring action, the heading reads *Inventory of Matters*.
