Charlemagne, in the Capitularies of 813, says: “Concerning the things that were handed over to Queen Hildegard, we wish written inventories to be made, and those inventories themselves brought to us.” Book III of the Capitularies, chapter 82: “Let there be inventoried not only the benefices of bishops, abbots, abbesses, counts, and our vassals, but also those of our treasury.” Thus they called *breves* what ordinary people call rolls and inventories, as Sirmond observes in his notes on the Capitularies of Charles the Bald. Hence *inbreviāre* in those same Capitularies means to enter and describe in inventories or labels. Hence also *inbreviator*, the recorder or describer of royal stipends, in the document concerning the examination of Willebert, bishop of Châlons.]**

And many others in the aforementioned inventory. If God grants me favor with you, I eagerly wish, once these works have been sent back, to receive them here for copying while I remain in this place.

**[Note: “Of Aulus Gellius.” In our own age and the preceding one, there was a major dispute among learned men over whether one should write *A. Gellius* or *Agellius* as a single word. In this old codex it is expressly written *A. Gellius* everywhere, in the two places where this author is cited.]**

Please relieve my embarrassment by granting my request, and, as I search out the bitter roots of letters, fill me now with their most delightful fruits. Encourage me with that eloquence of yours; if I deserve this, gratitude for such great benefits will remain with me throughout my life. It is unnecessary to say what recompense you may in due course receive from them.

My mind suggested that many more things should be written, but I ought not to detain your intellect any longer with my foolishness. I know that it is occupied either with external affairs of practical importance or intent upon the innermost and hidden principles of philosophy.

## 5. LETTER II. TO THE SAME

### [Col. 0436B]

To his most desired teacher Eginhard, Lupus.

I was deeply shaken by the grievous news of the death of your revered wife,

**[Note: “Your wife.” From this passage, as well as from the letters that follow, learned men have long inferred that support may be found for the account of Eginhard’s marriage to Imma, daughter of Charlemagne, preserved in the Chronicle of the monastery of Lorsch. It reads as follows:

“Eginhard, archchaplain and notary of the Emperor Charles, while serving commendably in the royal court and being loved by everyone, was loved even more ardently by the emperor’s daughter Imma, who had been betrothed to the king of the Greeks. Some time passed, and the mutual love between them grew daily through increase. Fear and royal displeasure held them both back, lest they undertake so grave an attempt to meet. But illicit love conquers all. At length, when the distinguished man was burning irretrievably with love and did not dare address the maiden’s ears through an intermediary, he finally, taking courage from himself, secretly made his way at night toward the girl’s chamber. Knocking quietly there and being admitted, as though he intended to speak with the young woman on royal business, he immediately reversed the pretext and, alone with her alone, using secret words and exchanging embraces, satisfied the love he desired.

“Meanwhile, when daylight was approaching and he wished to return through the silence of night by the way he had come, he suddenly discovered that a considerable amount of snow had fallen. Fearing that the footprints of a man might reveal and betray him, he was afraid to go outside. Anxiety and fear over what they had done compelled both of them to remain inside. As they wavered in great anxiety and deliberated what should be done, the exceedingly graceful young woman, whom love made bold, at last proposed that she should receive him by bending forward beneath the burden of him seated upon her, and carry him to the place adjoining his lodging before dawn. Having set him down there, she would return more cautiously by the same footprints.

“The emperor, it is believed by divine prompting, spent that night sleepless. Rising at daybreak and looking from a distance out of the palace, he saw his daughter scarcely able to walk with an unsteady step beneath the aforementioned burden, and, after setting down the load she had carried at the agreed place, hastily returning. After observing these things for a long time, the emperor, moved partly by astonishment and partly by grief, yet judging that it had happened not without divine providence, restrained himself and meanwhile suppressed what he had seen in silence.

“Eginhard, conscious of what had happened and certain that his lord the king could not remain ignorant of it for long, at last, having found a plan amid his troubles, approached the emperor on bended knees and asked for his dismissal, asserting that such and such great services as his had not received adequate rewards. Hearing this, the king concealed both the circumstances and the outcome of the affair and remained silent for a long time. Then, assuring him that he would answer his request as soon as possible, he fixed a day, and immediately ordered his chief counselors, the leading men of his kingdom, and all his other intimates to be summoned from every direction and assembled.

“When the splendid gathering of people of various ranks had assembled, he began by saying that imperial majesty had been gravely insulted and despised through the unworthy union of his daughter and his notary, and that he was consequently agitated by no small disturbance. They were struck with profound astonishment, and some still doubted because of the novelty and magnitude of the matter. The king then made it clearer to them, recounting from the beginning what he himself had learned with his own eyes and asking their counsel and judgment about it.

“They, however, holding different opinions among themselves, delivered various harsh judgments against the perpetrator of this deed: some condemning him to punishment without precedent, others to exile, and others to destruction in some other manner, as each was moved. But certain men among them, the more merciful because they were wiser, deliberated among themselves and earnestly begged the king to examine the matter himself and determine it according to the wisdom divinely granted to him.

“When the king had weighed the disposition of each toward him and considered which counsel should be preferred among the conflicting opinions, he addressed them as follows:

“‘You are not unaware that the human race is subject to various vicissitudes, and that it often happens that certain affairs, begun under contrary auspices, eventually obtain a better outcome. Therefore, we must not despair. Rather, concerning this matter, which by its seriousness and novelty surpasses our understanding, we must await and seek the mercy of divine providence, which is never deceived in its ordering and knows how to make good use even of evils.

“‘Accordingly, I shall not exact from my notary punishment for so sad an act, punishment by which the disgrace of my daughter would seem more likely to be increased than diminished. We therefore judge it more fitting and more honorable for the glory of our empire that, forgiving the error of youth, I unite them in a lawful marriage and overlay this disgraceful affair with the appearance of honor.’

“When the king’s decision was heard, incomparable joy arose, and his greatness of spirit and gentleness were extolled with the highest praises. Meanwhile Eginhard, ordered to appear, entered. The king greeted him unexpectedly and addressed him with a pleasant expression:

“‘A complaint has long been brought to our ears by you that our royal generosity has not yet adequately repaid your services. But, to tell the truth, your own negligence is chiefly to blame for this. Although I bear alone so many and such great affairs, if I had known any of your wishes, I would have pursued your services with fitting honor. But, so that I may not detain you with a long speech, I shall satisfy your complaints with a most ample gift; and so that I may find you thereafter as faithful and well-disposed toward me as before, I shall give you in marriage, according to your right, my daughter—your bearer, of course—who once, girded high, showed herself sufficiently accommodating in carrying you.’

“Immediately, at the king’s command, his daughter was brought in with a large retinue. Her face suffused with rosy modesty, she was handed by her father into the hands of the aforementioned Eginhard, together with a very large dowry consisting of several estates, countless gifts of gold and silver, and other valuable furnishings.”

Thus far the account from the Chronicle of Lorsch. See a similar story concerning the sister of the Emperor Henry II in Radulf of Diceto, p. 470; Henry of Knighton, p. 2326; and the *Belgian Chronicle*, p. 107. On Eginhard’s marriage, see also Bernard of Mallinckrodt, in his treatise *On the Chancellors of the German Empire*, p. 22.]**

and I wish more than ever that I could now be present with you, so that I might lighten your sorrow either by sharing your grief or by consoling you continually with thoughts drawn from the divine utterances.

But until God makes this possible, I suggest that, remembering the human condition we have contracted through the due consequence of sin, you bear what has happened with moderation and wisdom. For you ought not yield to this misfortune, you who have always overcome the comforts of gentler fortune with steadfast courage.

**[Note: “Of gentler fortune.” Lupus rightly admonishes Eginhard to bear patiently the calamity he has recently suffered, since he has always endured good fortune with a courageous spirit. Those who bear favorable fortune well are harder to find than those who bear adversity well. In favorable circumstances most people grow insolent and exalted; in adversity everyone is recalled to temperance and moderation. Thus says my countryman Marc-Antoine Muretus, *Various Readings*, Book V, chapter 15. Hence Galba’s words to Piso, the future emperor, in Tacitus, *Histories*, Book I: “So far you have endured only adverse fortune. Prosperity tests the spirit with sharper goads, because we endure misery but are corrupted by happiness.” And in Quintus Curtius, Book X, Alexander rebukes soldiers who were beginning a mutiny: “You have begun to rave amid the prosperity that surrounds you, forgetting the condition from which you were stripped by my favor; by heaven, you deserve to grow old in that same state, since it is easier for you to govern adverse fortune than favorable fortune.” See Saint Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, Book I, chapter 3.]**

Therefore, having invoked God, now display those powers of endurance to which you would reasonably summon any dear person found in a similar situation. I wish you prosperous health.

## LETTER III. EGINHARD TO LUPUS

### [Col. 0437B]

Eginhard sends greetings to his Lupus.

The grief I suffered first from the death of my once most faithful wife and now of my most beloved sister and companion has stripped away and shaken off all my pursuits and all my cares, whether they concern my own affairs or those of my friends.

**[Note: “Most beloved sister.” From this I think it may be concluded that Eginhard was made abbot while his wife was still alive. Since they then abstained from marital relations, he called her once his most faithful wife; but after she had died, his most beloved sister, companion, and housemate. Eginhard, Letter 32: “Imma, most beloved sister, be her helper and I commend my soul to you.”]**

Nor does it seem possible for it to end, because memory retains the manner of her death so tenaciously that it cannot be torn away from it.

To this is added the fact that the pain itself repeatedly increases and festers the wound once received: our prayers, namely, were permitted to accomplish nothing, and the hope we placed in the merits and intercession of the martyrs completely frustrated our expectation.

**[Note: “Of the martyrs.” That is, the holy Marcellinus and Peter, who lie in the monastery of Seligenstadt, of which Eginhard was abbot, having been transferred there through Eginhard’s efforts. See the notes on Letter 60.]**

Thus it happens that the words of those who offer consolation—words that usually heal the grief of others—rather cause the wound of our heart to break open and bleed afresh. They tell me to bear calmly the troubles of a misfortune they do not themselves feel, and they think I should rejoice over something in which they cannot display even a trace of joy or gladness.

For what mortal is there whose mind is sound and judgment sane, who would not lament his lot and judge himself unhappy and most wretched when, placed in affliction, he finds the one whom he had believed would favor his prayers turned away and inexorable? Did such things seem to you sufficient to move so insignificant a little man to sighs and tears, to incite him to groaning and lamentation, and even to cast him into the abyss of despair?

They certainly would have done so, had I not been supported by the help of divine mercy and suddenly turned to inquire what our greater and better predecessors had decreed should be held and preserved in such causes or circumstances.

**[Note: “In such causes or circumstances.” I believe the words *causis aut* are superfluous and represent a copyist’s admonition. Since he could not determine which should rather be read—*causis* or *casibus*—he included both, leaving the judgment to the reader. See the notes on Letter 122.]**

There were excellent teachers at hand, not merely not to be rejected but to be heard and followed in every respect: the glorious martyr Cyprian, and the illustrious interpreters of the sacred divine Scriptures, Augustine and Jerome. Encouraged by their judgments and salutary counsels, I tried to raise upward the heart weighed down by profound sorrow, and I began carefully to consider within myself what I ought to think about the death of my most beloved companion,

whose mortality I saw to have been brought to an end rather than her life.

**[Note: “Whose mortality.” Adapted from Pliny, Letter 1 of Book II, where he speaks of the death of Verginius Rufus as follows: “If indeed it is permissible either to weep or even to call it death, by which the mortality of so great a man was ended rather than his life.”]**

I also tried to demand of myself whether I could bring it about by reason that what a long passage of time ordinarily accomplishes might take place in me: namely, that the wound which an unexpected death, not yet anticipated by our mind, inflicted upon us should begin to form a scar and to heal through the medicine of spontaneous consolation.

But the magnitude of the wound resists any easy remedy. Although the treatments offered by the doctors mentioned above, as most skilled and at the same time most gentle physicians, are exceedingly salutary for mitigating severe pain, the wound, which still draws blood, does not yet admit the time for healing.

Perhaps you are surprised and say that a grief arising from such an occasion ought not to have lasted so long or endured so continuously—as though it were in the power of the grieving person to bring to an end what, when it began, he neither controlled nor foresaw.

The magnitude or duration of pain and sorrow nevertheless seems measurable by the extent of the losses that have occurred. I feel these losses daily in every action, every undertaking, the entire administration of the household and family, and in arranging and ordering everything that pertains either to divine or human duty. How, then, can a wound that has inflicted so many and such great troubles, whenever it is repeatedly touched, fail rather to break open and be renewed than to heal and become firm?

For I believe—and I am not afraid that this opinion will prove false—that this pain and anxiety, which arose in me from the death of my most beloved companion, will remain with me forever, until the very span of time that God wishes to grant me for this wretched and temporal life reaches its appointed end.

Yet I have so far found it more beneficial than harmful, since it restrains and holds back my mind, rushing toward joy and prosperity, as though with certain brakes and reins, and recalls my thoughts to the remembrance of death—thoughts that longing and forgetfulness of old age had enticed toward hope and love of a long life.

I see that not much time remains for me to live, although I utterly do not know how much that should be. But this I hold with complete certainty: the newly born can quickly die, and an old man cannot live long.

**[Note: “An old man cannot live long,” etc. Lupus repeats this very statement below, in Letter 84. It is taken from Jerome’s letter to Principia, in which he describes Marcella’s character. After she had buried her husband when she was still very young and could not endure longing for the deceased, she decided to refrain from a second marriage. Marcella was so noble, so beautiful in appearance, and so gracious that it is entirely clear that she undertook a laborious and difficult task when, content with that nobility and age, she wished to remain in a single marriage. Thus, while many suitors courted her, a certain very wealthy old man, captivated by the woman’s beauty, began to demand marriage and was prepared to pay a great price for lawful embraces with her. When the woman could not otherwise drive away the suitor, she excused herself on account of her old age, saying that she was not strong enough to endure so many deaths within so short a period, since he would soon die because he was old. When he replied, Jerome says, that old men can live long and young men can die quickly, she made an elegant joke: a young man can indeed die quickly, but an old man cannot live long.]**

Therefore, I judge that it will be far more useful and blessed to spend the brevity of this uncertain period in mourning rather than in joy. For if, according to the Lord’s saying, those who lament and mourn will be blessed and happy (Matthew 5), then, conversely, those who do not fear to bring their days to an end in perpetual and uninterrupted joy will become unhappy and wretched.

I give and offer thanks to your affection because you have deigned to console me through your letters. You could not have given a greater or more certain sign of your love for me than by extending the hand of encouragement to one who is sick and lying low, and by urging me to rise—one whom you could not have failed to know was prostrate in mind and weighed down by sorrow.

Farewell well, my dearest and most desired son.

## 9. LETTER IV. TO EGINHARD
I read with a mind deeply stirred the letter of Your Eminence, which grievously lamented the calamity that had recently befallen you, and I felt no ordinary pain at seeing your spirit exhausted by the anguish of such prolonged sorrow. Although friends far superior to me attempted to relieve this great grief, they nevertheless achieved nothing, as your letter makes sufficiently clear, because they did not admit a sufficiently serious consideration of your misfortune—indeed, some of them advised you to rejoice over the death of your once most beloved wife. Since, in my opinion, that has little relevance to consolation, I have not been afraid, relying not so much on the confidence of my age or on my talent, which I recognize to be slight, as on the greatness of my affection for you, to forge these words—whatever their worth may be—for your comfort.

For I am conscious that I suffered grief both on your account and on account of that most noble woman herself at her death.

**[Note: “Of the most noble woman.” Namely, Eginhard’s wife. Since Lupus presents her as born of illustrious parents, a strong argument may be drawn from this for confirming the account of the Lorsch Chronicle.]**

Your letter, which cruelly aggravated that grief, compelled me, I confess, to make it break out afresh. Hence I should by no means despair that the Lord has reserved for me some consolation which has not yet been granted to others, so that I may persuade you of it. A remedy is often sought in humble things when what is most precious and most skillfully prepared has long been attempted in vain.

Thus, by returning your letters to me, you divided the support of your—as it seems to you—justified grief into two parts. The first, and by far the greatest, is that your vows and the hope which you had placed in the intercession of the holy martyrs have deceived you as though they had been fruitless. The second, which comes close after the first, is that, because of the misfortune that has brought you so much difficulty in your daily affairs, you are compelled to bear the burden of domestic and divine matters entirely upon your own shoulders—a burden which the faithful companionship of that memorable woman had made light.

Both matters are truly weighty, and either could easily crush anyone beneath its mass, except a wise person who has learned to bear adversity with moderation. First, I shall attempt not to overthrow or wholly remove the argument I have proposed—for that would be entirely impossible even for accomplished orators, had they been present, and I see that it is much more impossible for me—but to weaken it and make it appear feeble when examined by reason.

You are certainly moved and affected by this: that your empty vows have frustrated you, and that the hope placed in the martyrs—or rather, in God—has mocked you. But is it really entirely certain to you that what you asked so earnestly would have contributed to the welfare of yourself and your wife? If this had been sufficiently clear to you, it would indeed seem to be a vast fuel for a sharper and justified grief, since the divine judgment would then appear not to have chastised you as a son but to have raged against you as an enemy.

Even so, you should not have descended into the abyss of despair; rather, the offended divinity should have been bent by constant prayers and submissive patience. But since God wills all people to be saved, and since no one asks in the name of Him who is called the Savior except one who seeks what is beneficial to his own salvation, and since you asked in the name of the Savior with full faith, who would not think that you were not heard with regard to your temporal request, but were heard with regard to eternal salvation?

I, for my part, would firmly believe that provision was made both for you and for your wife, even through her premature departure. You ask how. Plainly, although married couples are joined from two bodies into one structure and may live in the greatest harmony, they do not die by one death; and, so far as the ordinary order of nature is concerned, one must survive the other. Hence your wisdom already understands that, when the divine sentence pronounced upon humanity—“You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3)—may be postponed for a while but cannot be avoided forever, faithful spouses should wish that, whichever of them is to remain, the survivor may be the one who is both stronger in bearing calamity and more capable, according to Christian custom, of managing what is justly required.

Virtue must not be judged by difference of sex but by the mind. Otherwise I do not see how religious spouses can be bound to each other in sincere love. Since sound reason persuades us that these things are so, it is therefore clear—and probable—that God granted something great not only to that venerable woman but also to you, when He Himself, though by a hidden judgment that was nevertheless far from unjust, placed before you what you would have had to choose.

Certainly, although she had learned much from your companionship, and although by her exceptional prudence, dignity, and integrity—qualities that confer great dignity upon human life—she far surpassed not only the members of her own sex but also a multitude of men, and although, though female in body, she had advanced in spirit toward manhood, she would never, had she survived, have fully attained the summit of your wisdom; nor would she ever, through any advancement, have equaled that strength and that steadfastness which everyone especially admires in you.

Had she lived longer, she could never have contributed as much to your salvation as you could contribute to hers and to your own eternal salvation.

Therefore, since, while we remain in this fragile body, we cannot be so free from every disturbance that we are not at some time shaken by some affliction, I wish that what philosophers have thought can happen to the wise may happen to you: that the wisdom of your mind may gradually soften the adversities that, at first sight, appear to overthrow the uncultivated multitude of mortals—or rather, may attune your mind to the divine will.

Furthermore, since the divine word shines upon the darkest shadows of this life, according to the saying, “Your word is a lamp for my feet and a light upon my paths” (Psalm 118), we must look carefully at how it shapes this same life. In the Lord’s Prayer we say every day: “Your will be done”—that is, not our will, which, ignorant of what is beneficial to it, is accustomed to be deceived, but Yours, which, because it belongs to God, foresees what is to come.

Our Savior also, when His Passion was imminent, said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26). In this way He strengthened by divine power the weakness of the assumed human nature—or rather, of His own members—for which reason He had descended to utter this prayer: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will.”

The Teacher who neither deceives nor can be deceived taught us by His own example that, when adversity presses upon us, we should try to drive it away by our prayers, yet should also profitably embrace, even against our own wishes, the accomplishment of His will in these matters.

Recall, I beg you, Paul, whose eminence was so great that, having been caught up into the third heaven, he heard “unspeakable words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter”; yet he prayed that the angel of Satan, by whom he was troubled, might be removed from him. He did not obtain what he wanted, but what was beneficial.

Call David to mind also, and how he afflicted himself in order to obtain life for his son. Yet, although he was so great a prophet, when he had been overcome by such dreadful grief he did not even obtain a divine answer.

“Whatever was written,” however, “was written for our instruction, so that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Romans 15). Consider, then, how David, having experienced the futility of the persistence of his prayers, received consolation through reason and humbly submitted to the justice of God.

You are not of such deeply rooted strength.

Accept as your answer what was said to the Apostle: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12). He too, instructed by this oracle, laid aside the grief expressed in his written prayer, if any had arisen in him, having learned that something else was required.

The books of sacred Scripture abound in commands and examples of this kind. Since, as the distinguished poet says—“We do not sing for deaf ears” (Virgil, *Eclogues* 10)—and since the narrowness of a letter prevents me from discussing them, I pass them by for your consideration. It will be enough to have touched upon those matters alone which, once this wound has been acknowledged, may, as far as my judgment permits, soften and soothe its swelling, with the Lord’s gracious assistance.

As I turn many things over in my mind, another thought also occurs to me: this judgment of God may appear to be the clearest proof of His mercy rather than of His anger. For since He scourges every son whom He receives (Hebrews 12), He may be thought not to have permitted your affection to remain divided between Himself and your love for your wife, but to have recalled you to loving Him alone. And if, in loving her body immoderately, you had granted it more than was just, He may have punished this by taking that body away.

Moreover, when He says through the prophet, “Affliction shall not rise up a second time” (Nahum 1)—which the translation of the Seventy renders as: “God does not judge twice for the same thing”—He deigned to correct in you what you had done in excess as a human being, since no one is free from defilement, so that He might not later decree something more severe against you.

Therefore you should embrace the immense mercy of God, who judged you worthy of His correction, rather than fear His anger while enduring the blows of His discipline. Solomon says:

“My son, do not reject the discipline of the Lord, and do not grow weary when He reproves you. For whom the Lord loves, He chastises, and He takes pleasure in him as a father does in a son” (Proverbs 3).

Finally, those whose sins He does not visit here, and whom He permits to flourish according to their desires, are the ones against whom His anger rages after death. Of such people we read in the Psalter:

“They are not in the labor of mortals, nor are they scourged with human beings” (Psalm 72).

And in Job:

“They spend their days in prosperity, and in an instant they descend to the underworld” (Job 21).

Furthermore, my mind suggests to me that God wished to make you learn through experience how unhappy is the person who is separated forever from Him, in whom alone there is perpetual and true delight, if the momentary separation of even a most faithful and beloved human being afflicts one so terribly.

Since these things appear probable, I beg you to erase from your heart, as far as you can, the grief of which we are speaking, and say with Job:

“The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away. As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1).

And, walking with the Apostle in the praises of God, say:

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation” (2 Corinthians 1).

The other part of the undertaking remains. It must be treated briefly, lest, by saying too much, I become a burden when I desire to be a consolation. You have said that the wound of your grief is renewed—or rather, persists—because the doubled burden of daily administration reminds you of what good you have lost, and therefore seems incapable of coming to an end.

I myself would concede that this is entirely true. I strongly approve what you placed among your other arguments: that a person cannot end grief at will, since he cannot foresee it or escape what is impending. I recognize this as a sufficiently Catholic statement. For a person’s way is not in his own power; human steps are directed by the Lord, and human free will is altogether in need of the assistance of God’s grace.

But what has happened cannot be made not to have happened. Grief cannot recall what has once passed, nor does a person possess within himself the means of obtaining aid from himself. Therefore, when we are caught in any kind of distress, the more truly we feel our weakness, the more swiftly we ought to flee for help to divine mercy, as to the safest harbor.

The saying is elegant: “Divine assistance must be present when human assistance ceases.” Nor is the labor long, provided that we make the attempt. For He who says, “Come to me, all you who labor” (Matthew 11), helps those who strive to reach Him, instructs those who come to Him, and without doubt crowns those who remain in Him.

Therefore, when you said that the grief you mentioned would remain with you as long as you lived, I understand that the intensity of your love, hardened by long habit, expressed this. But, as far as I dare, I urge you not to leave your mind imprisoned in such obstinacy. It will benefit neither the woman whose death gave rise to it if it becomes immoderate, and it will harm you greatly unless it is laid aside.

Rather, entrust your entire care and healing to the Lord, for whom what our nature judges most difficult is exceedingly easy. For “who has hoped in the Lord and been deceived?”

I beg you: pour out your whole heart in prayer to God. He who instructed us to ask wishes to grant what He commands: “Ask, and you shall receive” (John 16). Ask that He Himself inspire you with the desire to pray, and let Him Himself grant the effect of obtaining what you ask.

Say what that illustrious and equally gracious author Augustine says (*Confessions* 10.29, 31, 37):

“Give what You command, and command what You will.”

For God both precedes and follows us by His grace, so that we may be able and willing to do some good. We learn this clearly in the Psalms, where it is written:

“My God, His mercy shall go before me” (Psalm 58).

And likewise:

“Your mercy shall follow me all the days of my life” (Psalm 22).

Yield to the Holy Spirit, who admonishes you through David:

“Cast your care upon the Lord, and He Himself will nourish you” (Psalm 54).

And say confidently to the Lord:

“You are my refuge from the tribulation that has surrounded me” (Psalm 31).

Then, already rejoicing in the praises of God with the Apostle, you will be able to repeat:

“I can do all things in Him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4).

“For worldly sorrow produces death” (2 Corinthians 7)—without doubt spiritual death, but, as you know very well, often also bodily death. Therefore let us grieve over the miseries of the vices by which we are oppressed, and strive to separate ourselves from their false sweetness with as much bitterness as we can; and let us bear moderately this sojourn of life, in which no one lives without complaint.

For the rest, while awaiting forgiveness from God, let us rejoice in Him with full faith.

Finally, the saying promised in the Gospel—“Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5)—is understood not of those who mourn the loss of loved ones and temporal advantages, but of those who grieve after being separated at the outset from the deadly pleasure of vices, until they receive consolation through the virtues and the grace of the Holy Spirit; or of those who are profitably afflicted on account of their own sins or those of their neighbors. This is rightly understood in reference to the postponement of that blessed life for which we sigh with all our prayers.

Therefore, while once you were asking eternal refreshment for your wife, who, as we believe, did not suffer death but laid it aside, ask the Lord our God for patience, perseverance in good works, and progress; and He will very quickly pour consolation into your heart, so that you may hear the Apostle exhorting you:

“Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Philippians 4).

For my part, because you have deigned to share your anxieties with me, I shall try to pray more attentively both for her and for you. I believe that God may be appeased by your humility—not because of my merit, but because of yours—since, without regard to your greatness, you did not disdain to discuss such serious matters with my insignificance.

As best I could, by human reasoning and by divine authorities, I have shown how you should patiently bear the fact that you were not heard according to your request, and how the wound of grief that seemed incurable might be mitigated. It will belong to your wisdom and customary graciousness to read with an equally devout mind what has been poured out with a pious intention—not to instruct, but to remind—and, if any usefulness can be found in it, to reckon it to the account of your friendship.

### 18. Booklet on the Veneration of the Cross

**[Note: “On the veneration of the cross.” This book of Eginhard’s no longer exists. Whether it was written on the occasion of Claudius of Turin’s condemnation of the veneration of the holy cross, as Baronius thinks, I leave for others to investigate. In this matter we can proceed only by conjecture.]**

I have embraced, as was fitting, the booklet on the veneration of the cross, which you dedicated to me and which, in my judgment, is exceedingly useful. Would that, following my request, you would not find it burdensome to explain all the things that I sent you from the beginning for clarification, or that I have left unresolved even this year! Certainly, this labor seems useful not only to me but to many.

Nevertheless, for this work that you have now sent me unexpectedly, and for the others through which you have already instructed me, I give and offer the greatest thanks. I shall anxiously await what God may deign to inspire in your most indulgent piety.

I have decided to depart from here in the middle of May, if life accompanies me. At that time, God willing, I shall come to you, as I told you, if you remember, and spend several days with you, both to return your books to you and to learn and enjoy for a while whatever I need from you, as well as to shape myself by the example—most pleasing to me—of your gravity and integrity.

For empty rumor has falsely told you that I would be leaving at this time. Even if that happened—which I emphatically do not wish—it would not prevent me from hastening to you. So great is my love for you that I could in no way return to my homeland without greeting you and without seeking the patronage of the holy martyrs.

I desire that you, mindful of me, may fare well in the Lord and prosper in every success, my most desired lord and father, who in every respect have deserved so well of me.

## EPISTLE V. TO THE SAME PERSON

Lupus sends eternal greetings to his most faithful father Eginhard.

It is impossible to say easily how grateful I am that you remember me, especially since the height of Your Eminence has stooped so far that on this occasion I have been deemed worthy of the gift of your spontaneous greeting. I should have wished to be refreshed by your letters, to learn how much the heat of this well-known matter has cooled, and to discover whether anything might have been persuaded to you from my insignificance.

For my part, as I promised, I pray to the Lord specially and daily for the eternal refreshment of that most beloved woman, and I do not cease, with watchful perseverance, to ask for whatever I believe may be beneficial to you either in the present life or in the life to come. Whether I am accomplishing anything, you perhaps can judge.

Nevertheless, I have no doubt that I should place the fruit of these prayers in divine mercy and, although late as far as the impatience of your desire is concerned, should undoubtedly await it as timely because of the weight of that justice.

I beg you to read book 21, title 27, of Saint Augustine’s *City of God*, and see whether that man of divine genius did not think about the same calamity in a manner equal to what I have written. I had never read those passages before; but when I later ran through them, I was greatly astonished that my thoughts had been so similar to his that they seemed entirely to have taken their color from him.

For the rest, I have been forced to postpone for a while the time of my journey to my homeland—and therefore to you. For when the venerable man Marcwardus, through whom my return is to be arranged, was being sent as an ambassador to Italy, and had first summoned me to a meeting as his closest friend, he had advised me to leave here on the day I had indicated to you and make my way to Your Holiness.

**[Note: “Marcwardus.” This spelling is consistent in the old manuscript, whereas Masson’s edition always has *Marcwadus*. Regino also calls him *Marcwardus*—for that is how it should be written, rather than *Marcunardus*—and he too was abbot of Prüm:

“In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 829, Tancradus, the second abbot of the monastery of Prüm, died; and Marcunardus succeeded him in the administration, a prudent man and devoted to sacred religion.”

Likewise Thegan, chorepiscopus of Trier, says in his work *On the Deeds of Louis the Pious*, chapter 53:

“After this the emperor sent his ambassadors to Lothar, Marcwardus, the venerable abbot, with his other faithful men.”

Moreover, Marcwardus is a Germanic name, as is clear from the Fulda Annals under the year 880 and from Lambert of Hersfeld under the year 1073:

“The king,” he says, “celebrated Christmas at Bamberg. There he took from Duke Berthold of the people of Chartres, who was absent, the duchy without a legitimate investigation and gave it to a certain Marcwardus, his relative.”

And in the year 1150 Marcwardus was living as abbot of Fulda, as Christopher Brower teaches in *The Antiquities of Fulda*. Eigil succeeded Marcwardus as abbot of Prüm in 853, as we shall say in Epistle 55.]**

But the illustrious abbot Rabanus, after returning from the palace, could not determine with certainty whether Marcwardus would be there at that time on account of the embassy entrusted to him. For that reason he urged me to postpone my return until the Nones of June, since the solemnity of Saint Boniface would not permit him to be absent—unless perhaps the authority of an imperial command, however weighty, should also overrule him.

**[Note: “The abbot.” This is Rabanus, abbot of Fulda. Lupus was then staying in the monastery of Fulda.]**

Therefore, when Marcwardus, after his return, sent to ask me when I especially wished to return, I asked him, because of the matter mentioned above, to arrange for horses to be brought here on the day before the Nones of June, so that, with Christ’s favor, I could set out to you on the eighth day before the Ides of that same month. He will certainly fulfill this, if his life accompanies him.

I therefore do not dare to specify the exact day on which I shall come to you; but I confirm that, God willing, I shall certainly come during the week that begins with the Nones of June.

Would that I might then be worthy to find your spirit relieved of every troubling care, so that you might not only have leisure, in accordance with your customary graciousness, to discuss with me whatever seemed friendly, but so that, whenever my own counsel or that of others failed me, your wise advice might also be present.

How much I defer to you, how much I honor you, and finally how much I believe myself either to have been helped or to be destined to be helped by you—to avoid the bite of flattery, I do not wish to say more. God will see to it, by whose grace this very thing has been brought about.

### 21

Meanwhile, deign to consider with the paternal affection with which you have always cherished me the matters I have appended, so that, having anticipated them, you may explain them to me more easily.

In the first book of Boethius’s *Arithmetic*, chapter 4, he says:

“But what has been stated according to the contrary affections of two kinds”—from this passage up to the words that follow shortly afterward, “In extent there is the greatest and smallest quantity”—is less clear to me than I could wish.

In the same book, chapter 21, he says that it is not difficult for diligent students, beyond the parts that he himself has expressed, to discover the remaining multiples of the superpartients according to the method he has demonstrated.

If, through you, I fully understand what he said somewhat earlier, where he writes, “And these will be called, according to their proper parts, double super-bipartients,” and what follows, it will surely not be difficult for me.

The same outstanding author, in the second book of the same work and likewise in its second chapter, says: “And, as Nichomachus says, an unusual—or, as I have found it elsewhere, *enmusitaton*—productive theorem,” and so forth. I do not know whether I have correctly understood what property or force those Greek words possess.

In the same book, chapter 25, from the place where it is written, “Every cube also which grew from the surface of squares into the depth of a solid body,” up to the statement, “But eight angles, each of which contains three such figures as the earlier squares from which the cube itself was produced,” I cannot grasp the form of the matter, to use his own words, and I very greatly need to gain its meaning through you.

I also desire, with God’s grace going before and with your instruction, to enter upon the calculation of Victorius.

Moreover, in words such as *aratrum*, *salubris*, and similar forms, whose penultimate syllable seems to be lengthened not only by position but also by nature, there is great hesitation, and I confess that I am still struggling with it. Should nature be followed, so that the penultimate syllable is pronounced long, as it is in these words? Or should we follow what Donatus says: “If the penultimate syllable is long by position, it receives the accent,” as in *Catullus*?

This is so, however, only if it is long by position and not because of a mute followed by a liquid, for that changes the accent, as in *pharetra*. When a syllable is long both by nature and by such a position, should the common syllable yield to its natural quantity and the accent be transferred to the antepenultimate?

For so far I have been unable to find anything solid in the authorities from which either of these views might be established or rejected. It will therefore belong to your wisdom to resolve this ambiguity and to strengthen either view with some very powerful evidence.

The difficulty is increased by the fact that I find the penultimate syllable always lengthened in verse in a word such as *aratrum*. Yet if a syllable that is naturally long may also be common, it is clear that the plural nominative, accusative, and vocative *aratra* could have been placed in a dactyl.

There are many other matters to ask about, which I have noted and which I shall investigate more conveniently in person, if God and you permit. I beg you, by the affection that you have always freely shown me, that, until I come to you, you deign to draw more carefully from the hidden storehouses of your memory whatever you know to be necessary for me and from which I have no one to learn except you, and to reveal it to me freely by right of love and friendship. Thus, by planting in me the seeds of your intellect, you may transmit its fruit to very many people.

### 23

It is said that the royal scribe Bertcaudus possesses a written measurement of the ancient letters, at least of those that are largest and which some people consider to be called uncials. Therefore, if it is in your possession, please send it to me by this painter when he returns, though the sheet must be most carefully secured with a seal.

I would have sent Aulus Gellius, had the abbot not detained him again, complaining that he had not yet had him copied for himself. Nevertheless, he said that he would write to you that he had taken the aforementioned book from me by force.

But he will himself return both it and all the other books that I enjoy through your generosity to you through me, if God wills.

The obscure matters in the law, especially the Greek names, and the other Greek expressions from Servius that I sent you at the beginning—would that you would now at least not find it burdensome to explain them.

Farewell, most illustrious teacher and sweetest father, and may you always prosper in every success.

## EPISTLE VI. TO REGINBERTUS

Lupus and Adalgus send eternal greetings to their dearest and most desired Reginbertus.

Your letter has come down heavily upon me, Lupus, because, having apparently stripped my mind of all brotherly feeling and natural affection, I had been so disdainful as to refuse even to alleviate your misfortune with consoling words, when there had been no opportunity to provide any other assistance. From this I concluded that my letters, which I sent through Abbot Marcward from the regions beyond the Rhine nearly twenty-four years ago, had never been delivered to you—though this was not due to his negligence. For when he failed to find you, he left the letters shown to our countryman Bodo, whom he believed faithful to us, to hand over to you. If Bodo had done so, you would have learned that, moved by brotherly affection, I had felt compassion not only for your difficulties but had already been considering a plan for restoring your fortunes.

[Note: Bodo. So the old manuscript reads. Masson’s edition has Bordoni. I strongly suspect that this is the man whom Rabanus of Mainz says renounced the Christian faith in his own time in order to turn to Judaism. Thus Rabanus writes in chapter 42 of his book Against the Jews:

“How much their abominable association and poisonous conversation contributes to impiety, while, as the Apostle says, their speech spreads like cancer, everyone can observe in the case of one man whom they deceived in a marvelous and dreadful way. For something we do not remember ever having happened before has occurred: a palace deacon, nobly brought up, trained in the duties of the Church, and well regarded by the prince, was seduced by their diabolical arguments and enticements. He abandoned the palace, abandoned his homeland and parents, and completely abandoned the Christian kingdom. Now, in Spain, associated with Jews among the Saracens, he has been persuaded by the impious to deny Christ, the Son of God; to profane the grace of baptism; to accept bodily circumcision; and to change his name, so that he who was formerly called Bodo is now called Eliezer. Thus, wholly transformed into a Jew both in superstition and in appearance, every day, bearded and married, he blasphemes Christ and his Church in the synagogues of Satan with the others.”]

Lupus shows that Bodo had been his countryman. Since we see that Christians living in Spain, who had been grievously afflicted by Bodo’s cruelty, sent a tearful letter to Charles the Bald and to the bishops established in his kingdom, asking that the aforesaid apostate be reclaimed, we infer that he originated in that part of the Frankish kingdom which fell to Charles the Bald. Otherwise, why would they not rather have demanded him from the Emperor Lothar or from Louis, king of Germany? Accordingly, when we see in the Annals of Saint-Bertin that Bodo was descended from the Alamannic people, we must interpret this as meaning that, although born of Alamannic parents, he was born in Gaul.

It is preferable to transcribe the entire passage from the same Annals under the year 839:

“Bodo, a deacon descended from the Alamannic people, and from almost the cradle instructed by the palace teachers in the Christian religion and to some extent imbued with divine and human letters, had in the preceding year asked and obtained from the Emperors permission to travel to Rome for the sake of prayer, after being richly supplied with gifts. Enticed by the enemy of the human race, he abandoned Christianity and turned to Judaism. First, after entering into a treacherous and destructive agreement with the Jews whom he had brought with him, he did not fear cunningly to contrive that they should be sold to pagans. After they had been sold, he retained with him only one man, said to be his nephew; and, having denied—as we say with grief—the faith of Christ, he professed himself a Jew. Thus circumcised, with his hair and beard growing, and having changed his name, or rather usurped the name Eleazar, he also girded himself with a military belt and took the daughter of a certain Jew in marriage. His aforementioned nephew was likewise compelled to convert to Judaism. Finally, bound to the Jews by the most wretched desire, he entered the Spanish city of Zaragoza in the middle of August. How grievous this was to the Emperors and to all those redeemed by the grace of the Christian faith was plainly shown by the difficulty with which the Emperor could not easily be persuaded to believe it.”

From this passage, as we also noted earlier and learn from Rabanus, we learn that deacons at that time were accustomed neither to grow their hair nor their beards and abstained from marriage.

Furthermore, reader, you should be informed concerning Bodo, the palace deacon, that this miserable event befell him in the year 838, as is recorded in the Brief Chronicle of the Monastery of Saint Gall, edited by Duchesne: “Puoto, a deacon from the palace, fell into Judaism between the eighth and ninth hours on the vigil of the Lord’s Ascension.”

Afterward he was so stubborn a defender of Jewish perfidy that no one seems ever to have been more hostile to Christians. The Annals of Saint-Bertin bear witness to this under the year 838:

“Bodo, who a few years earlier had abandoned Christian truth and gone over to the perfidy of the Jews, advanced so far in wickedness that he decided to stir up against all the Christians living in Spain the minds both of the king and of the Saracen people, so that they would either abandon the religion of the Christian faith and turn to the madness of the Jews or the folly of the Saracens, or else all be killed. Concerning this matter, a petition from all the Christians of that kingdom was tearfully sent to King Charles, to the bishops of his kingdom, and to the other orders of our faith, asking that the aforesaid apostate be reclaimed, lest he continue to be either an obstacle or a cause of death to the Christians living there.”

From this we learn, therefore, that Bodo had been a deacon of the palace of Charles the Bald. Furthermore, from a letter of Hincmar of Reims concerning Saint Denis, written to King Charles, we learn that he had been a cleric of Abbot Hilduin of Saint Denis.]

But let us set aside these matters, whose fulfillment was prevented either by fraud or by negligence; the present is more urgent. We rejoice, however it may be, that the face of a happier fortune has begun somewhat to open before you. Nor do we wish you to abuse its generosity; rather, we want you to devote all its fruit to the advantage of yourself and your people. You will understand better how you ought to do this if you learn what concerns us.

Last year, through the efforts of friends, I was brought into the presence of the Emperor [Note: The Emperor. That is, Louis the Pious. The event therefore took place in the year 837. December of the following year had the second indiction.] and was received most kindly by him and by the Empress [Note: The Empress. Judith, the last wife of Louis the Pious and mother of Charles the Bald.]. And now, that is, on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, in the first indiction, I am advancing toward the palace, summoned by the Empress, who has very great influence; and many think that some advancement in dignity will soon be granted to me.

If this should happen through the overflowing grace of God, do not doubt that you will immediately be summoned, so that, with the Emperor’s permission, we may live together and enjoy the most delightful exercise of our common studies. But if the outcome should mock our hopes, write back whether you would like me, through my friends,* to obtain from the Emperor that a place be restored to you in your monastery, while with me a place for study be granted to you for as long as either of us wishes.

Since matters stand thus, I urge you not to neglect divine Scripture, whose frequent use is also salutary knowledge. Above all, I ask you to keep this in mind and embrace it always with firm memory:

“Remember your Creator in the days of your youth,”

and what follows (Ecclesiastes XII).

I would have sent the book you requested if a suitable carrier had not been lacking. But I desire, if life accompanies us, to share with you that book and all the others I shall receive through God’s providence; and I shall ceaselessly care for your interests no less than for my own, since I have now laid aside childish concerns. My mind is held by love of useful pursuits. In discovering these, I confess that I am greatly assisted by the persistence of our brother Adalgus, who has deserved so well of us and whose name I have used to adorn the opening of this letter also.

## LETTER VII. TO THE SAME

Do you think it would have been fair, when I had made you the most faithful guardian of my affairs, for me to allow myself to remain for so long excluded from yours? Yet no one—not even you—could doubt how great a concern for you possesses me, if God grants us health and the opportunity I anticipate in my mind.

For what I wrote—that you cannot now study with me in the way you had planned, but that, when you come to me and learn about those matters of ours that cannot be contained in letters, you will approve it—your prudence will confirm. Nevertheless, if no change in my situation should occur, it is better for you to be in good health and to make progress, as well as you can, in the reading of Virgil. You will have an abundance of leisure; and, with my eager care directed toward you, you will make progress by using yourself as your own teacher, though not so profitably as laboriously.

For, with God’s generosity, I both can and ardently desire to be present for you. I have written to Anduinus and Ebrorum concerning your return, which I have disguised under the term “visitation.” But once you have come, our deliberation will easily determine whether you should remain or return.

Nevertheless, present yourself to me on the Kalends of July without any reconsideration. The business that threatens does not permit the greatest delay. Farewell.

## LETTER VIII. TO ADALGARD

[Col. 0451C]

To the singularly and uniquely beloved Adalgard, Lupus sends greetings in the Lord.

In obedience to your wish, although reluctantly, I have composed this letter myself. If it should prove shorter than you wished, you must blame yourself, because you imposed upon me, who was already inextricably entangled, two tasks at the same time and under the same extreme pressure.

But, so as not to delay you long, I think one should understand in matters of this kind what Priscian says: in other cases, and very rarely, not absolutely in just any words, but according to the context of his discussion, he calls them anomalous.

For Servius is the authority for the fact that certain forms lengthen the penultimate syllable in the first or second person. In the verse where Virgil made a shortening, he says:

“We shall have done it—you know—and it is necessary to remember it too much.”

Virgil, *Aeneid*, book VI.

“R,” he says, “he shortened because of the requirements of the meter.”

Likewise Juvencus:

“Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor be willing to do so,”

although some write that they distinguish the perfect subjunctive from the future.

In my opinion he expressed that this occurs very rarely in other anomalous forms, on account of *voluerimus*, *ritis*, *ederimus*, *ritis*, and any other forms of this kind; in these we unquestionably lengthen the penultimate syllables.

Priscian himself asserts that *doceberis* must be pronounced with *e* in the penultimate syllable. He says that, just as in the active voice, so also in the passive, the inflection of the present tense teaches the inflection of the other tenses—except the perfect and those forms that arise from it—which, he says, is formed according to each of the three conjugations.

Therefore, just as the passive present of the third conjugation is formed from the active by inserting *r*, while, as he carefully warns, the *i* is changed into *e*—that is, *legeris*, not *legiris*—so likewise, because the active form is *docebo*, the third-conjugation form *docebaris* retains the same derivation and changes the active *i* into *e*.

I understand that much could be said about this and the preceding question. But the brevity appropriate to a letter compels me to leave it unsaid.

I give you very great thanks for applying brotherly labor to the correction of Macrobius. Yet I would much prefer to see the book from which you sent me a leaf. It is truly venerable and executed with the most exact diligence.

I congratulate you no less on the commentary on Boethius. I still do not know, however, whether it contains the whole work, whether it is yours, or whether you compared it with someone else’s. I would like you corrected once and for all in this matter: never write or tell me anything ambiguous that you yourself know clearly, nor, in the manner of Apollo’s oracles, obscure your meaning through some indirectness.

For you did not make clear whether the book of the *Tusculan Disputations* had been written for us, what Agio was doing, which books you had found, or—what concerns me greatly—whether you had gained any advantage from this retreat.

As for the army and the others, they are proceeding in their usual manner; nothing new has happened to them, except that through the intervention of Bosonius and Frosm. I both recovered the book and, despite everyone’s opposition, was admitted into the association. Farewell.

## LETTER IX. TO LEOT

Lupus the abbot sends greetings to his beloved Leot [Note: To Leot. Thus precisely the manuscript reads, whereas Masson printed “to Leotericus.” Perhaps this letter too was written to Leotald, to whom the fifteenth letter is addressed. I neither affirm nor reject this possibility.].

The machinations of our enemies, which you desired to learn about fully from my letters, proved so numerous, so cunning, and so inflated that, if they were set out in full, they would require the length of a book. For that reason I spared the writer on this occasion; but I did not deny you and all well-wishers the sequence of God’s beneficence. Rather, I postponed it, as I believe, to a more suitable time.

I did not, however, conceal the outcome, for which both I and all who are devoted to me must give and return immense thanks to God.

If Guichard desires to know the truth and therefore seeks our work, I think it should not be denied him. Yet one must prudently beware lest, while he pretends a desire to learn, he should cunningly search out an opportunity to do harm. Farewell.

## 29. LETTER X. TO MARCWARD

The meaning of your letter ought not to have been other than it was, since long ago such a fervor of charity affected us that not even the slightest suspicion of its cooling could remain.

The matter which you disclosed to my humble self in confidence—how welcome it is, God, I think, looks upon with approving eyes, and it will be faithfully explained to you by the one who conveyed it.

I do not need to offer elaborate thanks for your generosity in the gifts sent to me and to the brothers, since you know for certain that, just as we have experienced your benevolence toward us in a singular way, so we perceive in our minds a particular dignity belonging to it.

As for God’s working in me what you have advised, it will be for you to obtain this through continual prayers: namely, that he who has implanted concern for us in you may grant you the joy of hearing of our progress.

What I wish you to do concerning Suetonius Tranquillus and Josephus will be explained by Eigel, the faithful interpreter of our affairs.

Greet all the brothers on behalf of my humble self, and especially Gerungus, Fulcoldus, and Ansboldus; and please ask them to remember us kindly.

[Note: Gerungus. It is clear from this that he was a monk, since Lupus calls him “brother.” Whether he was the man who at that time was a monk of Fulda and afterward abbot of Hirsau is not yet fully certain to me, although my inclination leans strongly in that direction, since monks sometimes changed their monasteries.

In any event, Gerungus, a monk of Fulda, became abbot of Hirsau in the year 854 and died in the year 885, on the Kalends of August, at the age of seventy-one. He was buried at Hirsau in the basilica of Saint Aurelius, as Trithemius records in the *Chronicle of Hirsau*. He had formerly been a pupil of Strabo of Fulda, from whom he had learned secular letters, that is, the humanities.

The inscription of a letter by that same Strabo to the same Gerungus is especially noteworthy. Strabo dedicated to him a book on arithmetic and measurement in these words: “To Gerungus the abbot, most reverend in merit, a father in age, a son in letters, a disciple in learning, and a master in grace.” The year before last we restored a similar heading in Salvian’s letter to Salonius, on page 215.

It should also be noted here that this Gerungus appears not to be different from the man who under the Emperor Louis the Pious was chief master of the doorkeepers of the sacred palace. Concerning him, see the *Annals of Einhard* under the year 822 and the letters of Frotharius, bishop of Toul. That he later became a monk is shown by Wandalbert the deacon, book II of the *Miracles of Saint Goar*, chapter 20.]

## 30. LETTER XI. TO KING LOTHAR, CONCERNING THE CELL OF SAINT JODOCUS

Most excellent Lord Emperor, we brothers from the monastery of Ferrières, oppressed this year by many and great difficulties, are ashamed that we are compelled so often to trouble Your Highness’s majesty.

Yet, remembering that we have prayed and continue to pray faithfully for you, and holding fast to your promise of assistance, we do not despair of obtaining what we ask.

The cell of Saint Judocus, which Charles the Great once entrusted to Alcuin for the distribution of alms to pilgrims, your father of blessed memory granted to us on the condition, as his edict attests, that whatever remained of the alms should pass to our use.

[Note: The cell of Saint Judocus. The monastery, or maritime cell, of Saint Judocus about which the present passage speaks, was situated not far from the mouth of the Quent River, commonly called the Canche, directly opposite the town of Étaples, which lies on the bank of the river. The Reverend Father Philippe Labbe believed that this cell had been situated not far from Quentovic, in the county of Ponthieu. The Sammarthani, however, wrote that it was Quentovic itself.

I follow their opinion because of the authority of Alcuin, who in letter 93 places the cell of Saint Judocus at a place called Vicus. “Martin,” he says, “remained ill at Vicus, at Saint Jodocus.” He clearly speaks of the same place in letter 12 to Charlemagne: “On my return from Wicus, because of necessary matters,” and so forth.

The place was therefore simply called Vicus; sometimes, because it was situated on the Quent River, it was called Quentovic, that is, “Vicus of the Quent,” just as Briva, a town in Limousin, is called Briva-Curretia by Gregory of Tours, book III of the *History*, chapter 10, because it lies on the Curretia River.

Wilibald taught us this in the *Life of Saint Boniface, Archbishop of Mainz*, chapter 5, where he says that the saint, setting out from England, arrived with his companions at the river Cuent, or Quent, and then stopped for a short time at Cuentawic, or Quentawicum. These are Wilibald’s words:

“With a full and favorable wind, they quickly see the mouth of the river called CUENT, now entirely free from every danger of shipwreck, and safely reach dry land. They also made camp at CUENTAWIC until the multitude of their companions, arriving afterward, had gathered together.”

The author of the *Chronicle of Fontenelle* mentions the port of Quentawich in these words: “In the year 844 the Northmen ravaged the port of Quentawich with a disastrous assault.” Lupus mentions this disaster in letter 43, as we shall note there.

Today Quentawicus, like many other towns of Gaul, has abandoned its old name and retains the name of Saint Judocus. It is commonly called Saint-Josse-sur-Mer.]

[Col. 0454A]

Rhuodingus obtained this from you by deception [Note: Rhuodingus. It is clear from this that the letter was written before the division of the empire among the sons of Louis the Pious. For Charles the Bald later gave the cell of Saint Judocus to Count Odulfus, as is clear from several of Lupus’s letters and from a charter of Charles.], and when we demanded from you the lawful gift of your father, he brings against us the charge of fraud.

Therefore, after examining your father’s edict, and out of reverence for blessed Peter and blessed Mary [Note: Blessed Mary. Although this monastery is called the monastery of Saint Peter of Ferrières because it is dedicated to Saint Peter, this passage, as well as the *Life of Louis the Pious*, teaches us that it was also dedicated to the most blessed Virgin Mary. Thus the author of Louis’s *Life* writes: “The monastery of Saint Mary and Saint Peter at Ferrières, which formerly was called Bethlehem.”] and Paul, before whom we intercede with our common Lord for you, we ask you to deign to settle this matter so that not only may the present invader of that cell be justly rebuked, but also that all opportunity for posterity to bring accusations against us may be removed.

For even if our lord, formerly your father, had not granted us this possession, we have worked and continue to work so zealously for you that, if we were to ask Your Highness for that same cell or something greater, we would unanimously trust that it ought not to be denied us.

May God himself inspire your prudence so that, just as this scandal began in your time, so through you it may also receive its firmest conclusion. By this benefaction, may we and our descendants strive to implore him all the more earnestly for you and your sons; and may he grant you to rule on earth in such a way that you may possess the eternal kingdom in heaven.

## LETTER XII. TO PARDULUS

[Col. 0455A]

To the most illustrious bishop Pardulus, Lupus sends abundant greetings.

When I recall that you are among the king’s most intimate associates, I am not at all surprised, when I weigh both the merit of your loyalty and the distinction of your wisdom without envy. Indeed, I rejoice greatly because I believe that the fallen affairs of the Church will be lifted up through your industry.

Therefore, relying on our familiarity, I urge and admonish you not to neglect the grace you have received from God. For, as you know very well, you have received from the Lord a talent that must be returned with interest.

See how great an opportunity for willing profit is placed before you. The monks of Saint Columba, fortified by the privilege of ancient and present bishops [Note: The privilege of bishops. Namely, Gallican bishops, for this was the ancient custom. At that time the authority of the Apostolic See was invoked less frequently. Yet not long afterward, at the request of our kings, the Roman pontiffs granted the protection of the Apostolic See to very many monasteries.

I think this was done so that those whom the princes had removed from monastic affairs by royal authority might be restrained by religious fear. Thus Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, sought certain privileges from the Apostolic See—not because they were necessary, but so that carnal and animal men, frightened by them, might conduct themselves more reverently toward Hincmar and the Church of Reims, as Hincmar writes to Pope Nicholas.

Likewise Ivo, bishop of Chartres, writing to Paschal II in letter 94, asks that the authority of that pope support a certain concession made to his Church by the count of Chartres. Yet he openly teaches that it was new and unusual to invoke the authority of the Apostolic See in such matters. “It is not improper,” he says, “if against new kinds of disease unusual medicines are discovered and applied.” Thus he sought to overturn ancient customs so that, by means of such a barrier—that is, a Roman privilege—he might restrain those who afterward attempted to violate the concession made by the count of Chartres.]

and supplied with the edicts of kings and emperors, both ancient and recent, have gained some hope of recovering their rights. They seek the harbor of royal piety, where they desire to find a safe refuge through your intercession.

Please deign to read what they bring and bring it about that they may be graciously heard by the king. With the praiseworthy acumen of your prudence, do not hesitate to point out that those who ruled successfully before him judged it advantageous both to themselves and to their country when they granted the petitions of God’s servants.

Bring help to the needy, give relief to those who labor, and let the memorial of at least some of God’s servants be yours.

[Note: Restored liberty. That is, the liberty of the monastery of Saint Columba. It had lost this under Louis the Pious, having been subjected by his authority to the archbishop of Sens.

Clarius, a monk in the *Chronicle of Saint Peter the Living at Sens*, speaking of Archbishop Jeremiah, says under the year 814:

“Moreover, the king added to him the abbey of Saint Columba, which his predecessors had recently lost, so that it should be under the protection of the archbishop of the city of Sens.”

Later, however, in the twenty-third year of his reign, on the fourth day before the Nones of April, Louis restored its liberty to the same monastery, disregarding a charter issued in favor of the Church of Sens, which he says had been obtained through the deception of certain persons.

Afterward, undoubtedly under Charles the Bald, this monastery again lost its liberty. Lupus therefore asks Pardulus, relying on the influence he possessed with Charles, to obtain from him the restoration to the monks of Saint Columba of the liberty that had been confirmed by so many royal edicts and by so many episcopal privileges.

Charles the king granted Pardulus’s requests, in accordance with Lupus’s petitions, so that the monastery of Saint Columba might again be withdrawn from the authority of the archbishop of Sens, as is clear from Charles’s *Proclamation against Wenilo*.

At that time Wenilo, having defected from Charles to Louis, king of Germany, obtained from Louis a charter concerning the abbey of Saint Columba, together with letters to the royal agents ordering them to restore the same abbey—that is, to subject it again to the archbishop of Sens by royal authority. This indicates that at that time it had not been subject to the archbishop of Sens. That was our conjecture.

Later, however, the highly learned Dom Claude Chantelou, a Benedictine monk, communicated to me Charles’s charter concerning this matter, which removes every reason for doubt. For, with the counsel of his nobles—namely, bishops and dukes—he granted this monastery of Saint Columba the fullest liberty.

The charter was issued at the palace of Compiègne on the Nones of December, in the eighth year of the reign of the most glorious King Charles, in the eleventh indiction—that is, in the year 848—which appears to be the date of Lupus’s present letter.

From what has been said, it can sufficiently be gathered that the liberty of monasteries at that time depended upon the will of princes. They granted it and afterward, if circumstances demanded, revoked it at their discretion.

Thus Charles the Great subjected the monastery of Sens in the Vosges to the jurisdiction of Angilram, archbishop of Metz, and of his successors. For this place had depended from its beginning upon imperial authority, as Richerius, a monk, says in book II, chapter 1, of the *Chronicle of Sens*.

Likewise Charles’s son, Louis the Pious, subjected the monastery of Glanfeuil to the monastery of Fossés, as Juretus noted in his annotation on Ivo of Chartres’s letter 159.

Likewise King Rudolf had subjected the monastery of Tulle to the monastery of Saint Savin of Poitiers. He later freed it from that yoke for no other reason than that he judged this expedient for religion.

Likewise Henry I subjected the abbey of La Chaise-Dieu to the bishop of Clermont, as is clear from his charter.]

It should meanwhile be noted that these are the words Clarius uses [Col. 0456D] to indicate that the monastery of Saint Columba had once again been made subject to the archbishop of Sens: “that it might be under the protection of the archbishop of the city of Sens.” From this we learn what our kings intended when, in their diplomas, they ordained that monasteries to which they themselves granted liberty should be their own property and should always be placed under royal defence and protection. Charles the Bald, in a diploma for the monastery of Saint Grata in the diocese of Urgell, says:

“Therefore we have ordered these letters of our authority to be drawn up for the aforesaid abbot and his monks of the said monastery, by which we wish it to be made known to our faithful that the aforesaid monastery, with the aforementioned cell and all their appurtenances and possessions, just as it belonged to our lord and father, is our own property (thus the monastery of Vendôme is called the freehold of Blessed Peter because it has been subject to the Apostolic See from the beginning), and remains always under our defence and protection; so that no bishop, [Col. 0457A] count, or travelling royal envoy may exercise there any lordship, tyrannical power, or authority, except as canonical authority commands.”

Diplomas of this sort are nearly innumerable. Thus, when our kings made such provisions, by the terms “protection” and “defence” they drew to themselves the cases of monasteries, which they forbade bishops to touch, excepting matters concerning violations of the canons; these they reserved for episcopal jurisdiction. Proof of this is to be sought in Book II of the *Capitularies*, chapter 8:

“We also especially command abbots and laymen that in the monasteries which they hold through our bounty, they carry out, with the counsel and instruction of bishops, those matters which pertain to the religious life of canons, monks, and nuns; and that in this they willingly hear and [Col. 0457B] obey their wholesome admonition.”

Previously, indeed, by a general law promulgated throughout all provinces, monasteries were wholly in bishops’ power, so that if anything there had been done contrary to the rule, it was corrected by bishops. But thereafter our kings gradually assumed responsibility for monasteries, and by royal authority investigated the condition of the monks to whom they had granted royal protection.

Thus in the *Capitularies* of Charles the Bald we read that he sent envoys into the provinces who, together with bishops and possessors of monasteries—whom he also assigned to the same responsibility—should examine, in the king’s stead, the monks’ life and morals and report everything to him; as is clear from chapter 1 of the seventh session of the Synod of Soissons, later repeated in the capitulary of Compiègne. And, not to seek examples from afar, this Lupus of ours, as he himself attests in Letter 63, was an envoy together with Heribold, bishop of Auxerre, and Prudentius of Troyes [Col. 0457C] to restore to life the monasteries established in Charles’s kingdom.

Perhaps for this reason the most learned Francis Florens sharply censured interpreters of canon law, especially the author of the *Gloss*, because they said that exemptions granted by kings to monasteries extended only to temporal matters, not spiritual ones. By no dissimilar practice, the Roman pontiff today very often appoints visitors and commissioners to ascertain the ailments of monasteries.

Thus monasteries, to use the language of our age, were in those times immediately subject to royal authority and referred to it without intermediary. Since monasteries needed that protection in order more easily to meet the opposition of either bishops or any others whatsoever, those who newly founded monasteries immediately placed them under the protection and defence of princes.

From the countless examples which might be produced on this point, I shall give only one, from which the pattern of the rest may be understood.
