In the year 867 Raymond, count of Toulouse, [Col. 0457D] when founding the monastery of Vabres in Rouergue, decreed that it should remain for ever under the king’s protection and immunity, as Catel records in his *History of the Counts of Toulouse*, p. 69.

But princes, whose authority in this matter was otherwise supreme, thought it followed from this institution by founders that the entire ordering of such monasteries belonged to them, both in appointing abbots and in arranging monastic affairs and shaping the monks’ morals. This was why they appointed abbots there at their discretion, whether from the monastic or the lay order.

Hence the Synod of Pavia, held in 850, earnestly admonished Emperors Lothair and Louis to entrust monasteries to suitable men according to the ordinance of their founders. For canon 16 reads:

“It must be laid before the most blessed emperors that those who placed monasteries and hospitals under the defence of the sacred palace are shown to have done so because they believed that they could be protected better by no one than by the highest powers. And if they give them, contrary to the decrees of their founders, to persons to whom they may not be given, they themselves become assailants who ought to have been defenders.” [Col. 0458A]

Christian devotion then turned to the See of Peter; and, in place of the protection of princes, it became customary, as before, to implore the protection of the Roman pontiffs. Hence John of Salisbury, in the *Policraticus*, book VII, chapters 19 and 21, when speaking of monastic exemptions, joins apostolic privilege with royal privilege.

Thus the monastery of Cluny, founded by William, duke of Aquitaine, was placed under the protection of the apostles Peter and Paul and under the defence of the Roman pontiff. Thus the monastery of Vendôme was offered by Geoffrey Martel, count of Anjou, to Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, [Col. 0458B] and his Roman Church as a freehold and patrimony, though with the consent of Henry, king of the Franks.

Roman pontiffs therefore later followed the piety of ancient kings when they extended their own protection and defence to monasteries in order to free them from episcopal power. I do not particularly approve, however, of those who derive that authority from divine law, from Christ’s words to Peter, “Whatever you bind,” and so forth. It was taken, as I have said, from royal custom, like very many other things.

For example, princes say:

“And whenever the aforesaid abbot, or his successors, shall depart this life by divine calling, so long as the monks themselves can find among themselves men capable of governing that congregation according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, they shall have, by this our authority, licence to elect abbots from among themselves.”

Roman pontiffs say:

“Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any artifice of subreption or violence, except one whom the brothers by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers’ counsel, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict.”

It is so true that the condition of monasteries formerly depended on our kings that, by the authority of Henry I, the church of Chaise-Dieu among the Arverni was raised to the dignity of an abbey without any mention of the supreme pontiff. For that king’s letters on this matter are in the possession of the most distinguished Antoine Vion d’Hérouval, who, with his customary readiness and inclination toward these studies, most willingly consented to their being added to these notes of ours.

They read as follows:

“In the name of the Lord God eternal and of our Saviour Jesus Christ. Henry, by the grace of God king of the Franks. If royal solicitude attends to those things which are known to pertain to the restoration of the holy Catholic Church, it is undoubtedly shown to prepare a great estate for the royal eminence, and not only strengthens the stability of the kingdom in the present, [Col. 0458D] but also obtains in the future the reward of eternal recompense.

“For this reason we wish it to be known to the attention of all the faithful of God and ours, present and future, that the venerable and God-worthy Robert, canon and treasurer of Brioude, sent and commended by letter by our most beloved and intimate lord Rencon, bishop of the Arverni, came before our clemency and made known that he wished, by the command and authority of our liberality and with his bishop’s permission, to raise to the rank and honour of an abbey a certain church, called Casa-Dei, situated in a wilderness in the territory of the Arverni and enlarged by him in revenues.

“Therefore, taking common counsel with the magnates and chief men of our palace, we decreed to grant his requests; and, for the remission both of our sins and of those of our fathers, by a diploma of our confirmation we authorized it and ordered and permitted an abbey to be made [Col. 0459A] and subjected it to the church of the Arverni, on this condition: that, by the command and will of the bishop of the Arverni and by the request and election of the monks of that place, an abbot be provided for that place, and that a God-worthy administrator be installed without any sale or gift.

“Moreover, on the Assumption of the blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary, the abbot of that place, with three or four monks and with the canons, shall celebrate the solemnity of the feast day at the seat of the mother church of the Arverni and shall pay one pound of incense as an annual due.

“We have also assigned, by the authority of our power and confirmed by royal seal, the gifts granted to the aforesaid church for the love and fear of God: namely, in the same estate a church consecrated in honour of the holy martyrs Agricola and Vitalis; in the territory of Brioude, a church in honour of Saint Andrew of Comps with all its appurtenances; in the village of Triniac, the church of Saint Germanus the martyr, with that village and all its appurtenances; in the territory of Fournols, a church with the estate itself and all its appurtenances, the church of Bellepommer with the estate itself and all its appurtenances, and the chapel of Château-Bullion; in the village of Lucidiac, three churches with the village itself and all its appurtenances; in the estate of Saint-Dominin, two churches and half the estate itself; in the fortress of Mont-Vascon, a chapel; in the estate of Saint-Victor, two churches; in the territory of Besse, the church of Saint Desiderius, bishop and martyr; in the territory of Lyon, in the estate called Sauxillanges, the church of Saint Mary, with the estate itself and all its appurtenances; and also very many holdings of estates, cultivated and uncultivated lands, [Col. 0459C] woods, vineyards, waters, and pastures.

“But whoever presumes to bring any dispute or claim against this donation, or attempts to take away anything from the aforesaid property conveyed or to be conveyed to that church, let his petition be void by our command, and let the fellow-countrymen of the bishop exact full punishment on behalf of the brothers serving that church.

“Let the aforesaid church moreover have licence, by command of our majesty, to increase and grow. And whatever its governors, with ecclesiastical right preserved, acquire in any part of our kingdom, whether in estates, holdings, or any goods, we have marked with the confirmation of our majesty; and we have conveyed and authorized both future goods to be acquired and past goods already acquired.

“We further command that no layman shall have any customary right to take anything in that place, nor presume to inflict any annoyance upon that abbot; but let him permit the abbot to arrange everything, and not doubt that this has been ordered by us.

“We also command that, if anyone presumes to bring any claim against [Col. 0459D] this conveyance, the governors of that place shall have recourse to royal aid, with ecclesiastical authority preserved, and rejoice that they have received full redress.

“And in order that this diploma may rest upon stronger attestation, we have confirmed it below with our ring and commanded the bishop of the Arverni and the other bishops of our kingdom to authorize it.

“Done publicly at the palace of Victriac, at the request of the lord and venerable Hugh, bishop of Nevers, in September, on the eleventh lunar day, in the second indiction, in the year 1052 from the Incarnation of the Lord, the twenty-first of the reign of the lord and most unconquered King Henry.

“Sign of Aymon, archbishop of Bourges; sign of Arnulf, archbishop of Tours; sign of Agobert, bishop of Chartres; sign of Odo, the king’s brother; sign of Rencon, bishop of the Arverni; sign of Robert, duke of Burgundy; sign of Herbert, bishop of Auxerre; sign of William, duke of Aquitaine; sign of Guy, archbishop of Reims [Col. 0460A]; sign of Isambard, bishop of Orléans; sign of Helmuin, bishop of Autun; sign of William, duke of the Normans; sign of Mainard, archbishop of Sens; sign of Enzelin, bishop of Paris; sign of Wido, bishop of Chalon; sign of Count Ralph; sign of Count Theobald; sign of Rainaud, chamberlain.

“Seguinus the clerk wrote this in place of Baldwin, royal chancellor, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October.”

Moreover, what I noted a little earlier—that in the age of Charles the Bald the entire administration of monasteries belonged to princes, even with respect to the shaping of monks’ morals—should be understood to mean that princes took the greatest care that monks should live according to the Rule and not depart from it, and that whatever they did outside it should be corrected through the care of royal envoys, as is clear from Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 122, and from Letter 63 of Lupus.

Further, by royal right they regulated their reading and singing, as may be gathered from the same chapter 122 and also chapter 80 of the same book. And Louis the Pious, in chapter 85 of that book, decreed that the Rule of Canons, which he himself had ordered to be compiled from the sayings of the holy Fathers, should without doubt be maintained by all living under that profession, and should henceforth in every way be observed both by canons and by canonesses living canonically.

These matters concern general observance. The observance of the individual chapters of the Rule belonged to the care of abbots, as is clear from chapter 73 of the same book of *Capitularies*.

From that observation it follows that the liberty of monasteries formerly depended on the will of princes, who granted it and afterwards, if circumstances so required, revoked it at their discretion; I have adduced several examples of this. [Col. 0460C] The example of Charles the Bald should also have been added: after he had subjected the monastery of Manglieu to the bishop of the Arverni, he nevertheless revoked the diploma concerning that subjection and thus granted liberty to the monastery,

“so that the monks themselves and all their possessions may remain from this day forward in the immunity of us and our successors. We further command by this present diploma of our high authority that the said place may never fall away from the protection of us or our successors,”

and so forth. This diploma is printed in the *Proofs of the Liberties of the Gallican Church*, chapter 38, § 7.

Restored freedom. In view of your occupations, I submit the matter more sparingly than your remarkable capacity, which fully understands the effect of so great a benefit, might desire. I wish you, remembering me kindly, to enjoy happiness.

## LETTER XIII. TO KING AETHELWULF

[Col. 0459A]

To King Aedilulf (Aethelwulf), who exalts the praise and glory of God with great praises

[Note: [Col. 0460C] To Aethelwulf, king of the English, whom others call Edelwulf and Ethel wulf. Those who call him Edilnulf and Edelbold depart still farther from the truth. It is sufficiently certain that Aethelwulf, king of the English, married Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald. Although there survive acts concerning her blessing when Aethelwulf took her as his wife, and likewise concerning her blessing when she was anointed queen, the time when this occurred has not yet been recorded. The author of the *Annals of Saint Bertin* teaches that it happened in the year 856. These are his words:

“King Edilwulf of the Western English, returning from Rome, takes Judith, daughter of King Charles, who had been betrothed in July, as his wife at the palace of Verberie on the Kalends of October; and when Ingmar, bishop of Reims at Durocortorum, blesses her and places a diadem upon her head, he gives her the title of queen—something previously unfamiliar to himself and his people. After the marriage had been completed on both sides with royal ceremony and gifts, he returned by ship with her to Britain, the dominion of his kingdom.”

Concerning this same Judith, those Annals report under the year 858:

“King Edilwulf of the Western Saxons dies, and his son Adalbold takes his widow Judith as his wife.”

Finally, after Aethelbald’s death, she married Count Baldwin, without the consent of her father, Charles the Bald. Hence serious storms broke out against Baldwin and Judith, which at last subsided in 863. For then Charles “allowed his daughter Judith,” as the same Annals say, “at the request of the lord apostolic, and with the counsel of his faithful, to be lawfully joined in marriage to Baldwin, whom she had followed.”

Flodoard, *History of Reims*, book III, chapter 12:

“Concerning the improper union of Count Baldwin and Judith. This Judith, daughter of King Charles, had formerly been joined in marriage to King Edilnulf of the English, who was also called Edelbold, and had been distinguished by the dignity and blessing of queenship.”

In the book of the *Capitularies* of Charles the Bald there survive the blessings of this Judith, daughter of Charles: first, when she was blessed as the bride of Aethelwulf, and then as queen.]

Lupus, the last of all God’s servants, abbot of the monastery

[Note: [Col. 0460D] of Saint Judoc. See the notes to Letter 11.]

of Saint Judoc, sends present happiness and the salvation of eternal blessedness.

Since we have learned of the good reputation of your rule, [Col. 0461A] and have heard of the strength bestowed upon you by God against the enemies of Christ, we pray the almighty God, who granted you that strength, to make you invincible against all the enemies of the Christian name—he who by his incomprehensible, yet nevertheless just, power always orders all things.

But because the sea separates my smallness from your excellence

[Note: [Col. 0461C] *Continens.* Lupus meant to say that he was separated from Aethelwulf, king of the English, by the sea. He used *continens* for “sea,” with a very improper meaning. For *continens* properly means land adjoining the sea. Hence Sicily is said to have been torn away from the mainland, according to the old story. See Freinshemius on Quintus Curtius, book IV, chapter 11, at the passage “that you are on the mainland.”]

and I wish to make myself known to you by my service, especially since I learned from Felix

[Note: [Col. 0461C] *Felice.* See the following letter.]

—who was responsible for your correspondence

[Note: [Col. 0461D] *Epistolarum officio.* Felix was therefore Aethelwulf’s notary, or perhaps his chancellor.]

—of your zeal in the worship of God. Command whatever you believe possible for me, and you will find me ready to serve in every respect.

But in order to stir you to win God’s favor, we point out to you an opportunity for striving which will undoubtedly provide hope in the present and a reward in the future age. The church in our monastery, which is

[Note: [Col. 0461D] *Mediterraneum,* that is, built far from the sea. Thus, in the margin of the old manuscript, this gloss was added eighty years ago in place of an explanation: “removed from the sea or rivers.” Through the ignorance of copyists it was later incorporated into the text in Masson’s edition. The manuscript lacked these words, and we have judged that our edition ought likewise to lack them, for that reason. They are also absent from Duchesne’s edition.]

inland and is called Ferrières, bearing the name Bethlehem bestowed upon it by its founder,

[Note: [Col. 0461D] *To cover with lead.* After Lupus had built the church of the monastery of Ferrières, and the building had reached the point at which nothing there was lacking except a roof, he wrote to Aethelwulf, the most devout king of the English, and to Felix, formerly the royal notary, asking them to supply him with lead from England, which could be used to cover the church. In the same way Stephen, abbot of Saint Geneviève in Paris, later bishop of Tournai, while engaged in repairing his church, asked Bishop Waldemar of Seleucia to relieve him of part of the expense so that he could purchase English lead for roofing that sacred building. For he writes to him in Letter 165:

“We have begun to repair them”—that is, the walls of the basilica of Saint Geneviève—“having already procured a framework of timber, to be placed above the renewed walls and beneath a leaden roof. With a certain blush, we beg and ask that you send us something from your benevolent and beneficent generosity, so that we may buy lead—not Roman, but English. Churches are roofed with English lead and stripped with Roman lead.”

Here Stephen rubs the Roman Curia with satirical salt, because, as they say, it was accustomed to give not coals but lead in exchange for gold, and at an immense price. Hence the words of Peter of Blois, writing to King Henry II of England in Letter 41:

“Your envoys have returned from the Roman Curia, unloaded of silver but loaded with lead.”]

and which we are striving, after God, to cover with lead, having consecrated it in honor of blessed Peter and all the other apostles: we ask you, if you are willing, to become a participant in this work.

Be helpers, then, in completing it for the honor of God—not out of regard for our merit, but in view of the divine reward. [Col. 0462A] For although we are intercessors for you without your generosity, we shall be more eager if we receive a gift that will benefit both you and us solely as a remedy for the soul. Nevertheless, as we have already indicated, we shall be ready for everything possible that you may entrust to us.

May almighty God make you and your descendants rulers of your realm for a very long time, for the propagation and preservation of his faith, and eventually heirs of eternal blessedness.

## LETTER XIV

[Note: [Col. 0462C] *To Felix.* The printed edition reads, “To Felix, the royal scribe,” which I think was added by Masson. For in the old manuscript nothing is written in the title of this letter except the words “To Felix.” And indeed, when this letter was written, that man was not a royal scribe, although perhaps he was among King Aethelwulf’s closest associates. For in the preceding letter Lupus said: “I learned from Felix, who performed the office of your correspondence,” which refers to the past.]

### TO FELIX

To his dearest friend Felix, Lupus, abbot of the monastery of Ferrières and of Saint Judoc, sends greetings.

Although several years have passed since, by the grace of God, we first came to know one another in the monastery of Fara

[Note: [Col. 0462D] *In the monastery of Fara.* This is what the manuscript explicitly reads. In the margin of the book, however, someone wrote eighty years ago, “in Ferrières.” The person who then read these letters of Lupus did not yet know where the monastery of Fara was located. It is regrettable that this error misled the learned Papirius Masson, who rejected the genuine reading and retained the spurious one. Thus he printed, “in the monastery of Ferrières,” a reading also retained by André Duchesne. The monastery of Fara is situated in the diocese of Meaux, in the district of Brie; it is commonly called Farmoutier-en-Brie. It took its name from Fara, a most devout woman by whom it was founded in the time of King Dagobert.]

and no opportunity has subsequently arisen, as I wished, for us to speak together as friends, nevertheless, because the fervor of charity has cooled in neither of us, I ask that, through your diligence, my request may obtain its effect with your admirable Aethelwulf.

Since you have praised his great generosity, I ask by letter that, because I have resolved to cover with lead the church of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, in the monastery of Ferrières, for the long-lasting preservation of the roof, he may deign, for the increase of his good works, to grant us from the same metal of lead as much as God inspires him to give for the work mentioned.

If, through the overflowing mercy of God and your cooperation, I obtain this, it will once again be your concern to have his benefaction conveyed to Étaples

[Note: [Col. 0463C] *Stapulas.* This is a town on the coast of the River Canche, not far from the ocean, and therefore near the monastery of Saint Judoc, which lies on the opposite bank of the river. Moreover, it may be inferred from this that the letter was written before the recovery of the cell of Saint Judoc. For if it had then been recovered, the port of Quentovic would have been more convenient because of the monastery’s proximity. After the cell was recovered, Lupus did not ask for certain books from England to be brought to Étaples, but to the cell of Saint Judoc; he had requested them from a certain abbot of York, as is clear from Letter 62. Étaples has preserved its ancient name. Today the place is called Étaples.]

. For our part, as we expressed in the letter sent to the aforementioned king, we shall always be ready to pray for him and promptly to carry out whatever he may entrust to us.

I wish you happiness.

## LETTER XV

[Note: [Col. 0463D] *To Leotald.* Perhaps a priest of Langres residing in the castle of Dijon. He is mentioned in the *Chronicle of Saint Benignus of Dijon* under the year 844 in these words:

“In his days Leotald the priest, one of the clerics residing here, gave part of his inheritance in this borough and in the district of Tremolo.”

A little above it likewise says:

“Baldo the provost and the other clerics with him exchanged land with Leotald the priest. Leotald gave two small pieces of land. One is near the castle of Dijon, the other in a place called Petraficta. The brothers gave Leotald the priest land in the district of Tremolo.”

Perhaps Letter 9 of Lupus was also addressed to this same Leotald; its title in the old manuscript is “TO LEOT.,” for which Masson printed “To Leotericus.”]

### TO LEOTALD

Lupus, abbot, sends greetings to his Leotald.

I was not unaware that you held in your mind what you expressed in your letter, since almost everything is known to me, and frequently before my eyes, concerning the ways in which a brotherly spirit customarily responds to goodwill.

Since you asked to be made more certain of my condition, know that, by God’s mercy, I am well for the present, and that nothing, so far as I know, obstructs my plans, which I always wish to season with justice.

Therefore be of good courage, and pray more earnestly during this holy season for our common salvation.

I think that *pater patratus* was the name of a priestly rank, since the man who held it merited such veneration from his fellow citizens that he was said to have become their father; through him they did what

[Note: [Col. 0464C] *In Servius you read this.* Namely, in his commentaries on Books IX and X of the *Aeneid*. I shall quote Servius’s actual words from Book X, so that the reader may understand what Lupus was indicating:

“For whenever men or animals had been carried off from the Roman people by some nation, the *pater patratus* also went out with the fetiales—that is, the priests who preside over the making of treaties. Standing before the boundary, he declared the cause of war in a loud voice; and if they refused to restore what had been carried off or to surrender the perpetrators of the wrong, he threw a spear, which was the beginning of battle; and thus, according to the custom of war, it was permitted to seize property.”]

you read in Servius: namely, that they first terrified the enemies whom they were preparing to overcome by force with the power of religion.

## LETTER XVI

[Note: [Col. 0464D] *To Orsmarus.* The title of the letter indicates which see he held, namely, Tours. Elsewhere he is called Ursmarus, as in the *Capitularies* of Charles the Bald and elsewhere. But the distinction is of no importance.]

### TO ORSMARUS, METROPOLITAN OF TOURS

To the most reverend Orsmarus, metropolitan, Lupus sends greetings in the Lord.

After the report of my brother and your most faithful friend made your reputation known to me, I have always burned with an extraordinary desire to experience what I had joyfully tasted in advance through his diligence. I give and shall continue to give the greatest thanks to your holiness, because you did not disdain voluntarily to vie in kindness—receiving that aforementioned brother in an episcopal manner and treating him graciously, while inviting my smallness to your affection with the most sincere feeling.

Your prudence will easily gather whether I say this with a pure mind, if ever, by the grace of God, I obtain the opportunity to demonstrate it.

Meanwhile, since we have now learned how much we ought to expect from you, we earnestly beg you to send us, through the messenger whom we have dispatched for this purpose, Boethius’s commentaries on Cicero’s *Topics*, which Amalric keeps in the library of Saint Martin in a parchment codex—or, as some think more correct, a *chartinacius* codex—having obtained them from him for us.

[Note: [Col. 0464D] *Armario.* A library. This explanation is entirely certain. Although it would be easy to establish it by many testimonies, I refrain from citing them. For this reason the keeper of a library was called an *armarius*. See Du Cange’s Latin Glossary.]

We also advise you that, whenever anyone asks to whom you will lend the aforementioned codex, you should conceal our names and answer that you wish to send it to certain of your relatives who are earnestly requesting it.

If we are fortunate enough to receive it through you, we shall treat it with the greatest care and return it at the proper time.

Deign to make us informed by letter of your safety and of the prosperity that is so welcome to us, and likewise take care that we have not sent to you in vain.

## LETTER XVII

[Note: [Col. 0464D] This title was added from Masson’s edition. The old manuscript had nothing written here.]

### TO JUNETUS

Although the vast expanse of the earth separates us in different places, nevertheless, because the charity of him who makes us dwell as one in the household of the Church through faith joins us in harmonious religion, it is right that the things which, prompted by usefulness, we write to you in turn should be received with brotherly respect.

Accordingly, your brother came to us after long wanderings and simply explained the nature of his offense. We judged it pointless to set this down in writing, since anyone wishing to know it will learn it without difficulty from both his actions and his words.

Sympathizing with his misfortune and rejoicing in his conversion, we have resolved to send these letters of our lowliness to your holiness. Through them we implore you not to disdain, in response to our intercession, to remit the punishment for his excesses.

For he reports that he has incurred a penalty sufficiently proportionate to his rashness, so that, if he happens to have enemies, they may be sated with the injury caused by his so great, so grievous, and finally so fruitless wandering.

For, yielding to the deception of wicked men, he was led almost to the farthest parts of Gaul; deprived of every resource, he now returns from there to you with great shame, as you see.

Therefore may your clemency, moved by our prayers, graciously pardon his fault and hasten to open to him, now repentant, the embrace of your compassion.

## LETTER XVIII. TO CERTAIN BROTHERS OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT-AMAND

[Note: [Col. 0465C] Of Elnone, in the diocese of Tournai.]

[Col. 0465B]

To his dearest brothers, Lupus sends greetings in the Lord.

[Note: “The care of you.” I agree with Donatus Candidus, who inferred from this passage that Lupus had at some point been entrusted with the care of the monks of Saint Amand. It is clear that Lupus was then abbot of another monastery—namely, Ferrières—when the monastery of Saint Amand was entrusted to him. In those times princes readily assigned several monasteries to one abbot. But because Lupus was burdened with a double responsibility, and because those monks were displeased that an abbot was being given to them who would rarely be present among them, that monastery was entrusted by the prince to someone else, with Lupus readily and willingly consenting that the gift granted to him be transferred to another. He understood, of course, that he already had enough duties at home, and that one who had undertaken the care of even a single monastery could scarcely suffice for himself, much less for two.]

You saw that I neither eagerly sought the care of you nor received it presumptuously, since I readily perceived that my smallness was being burdened, not advanced, by a double responsibility. And now it is evident that I am willingly laying down that same care, nor do I begrudge it in the least to anyone who undertakes it. For what is possessed without the allure of pleasure is lost without pain; and, in accordance with the blessed Apostle (Philippians 1), whether in truth or on occasion, Christ is proclaimed, and in this I rejoice and shall rejoice.

Therefore, it seems to me that I ought to obey him to whom you have given the order, and attend the general assembly, which will begin to be held on the first day of July at a certain estate in the Paris region called Bonogilo. [Note: “Bonogilo.” A village in the Paris district, called Bonoilum in the Capitularies of Charles the Bald and by Hincmar in the preface to his later refutation of Gottschalk. Sirmond thinks that Hincmar speaks of the very assembly at Bonoilum whose acts survive in those same Capitularies, while Lupus speaks of another, earlier one. It is nevertheless possible that the assembly was summoned for the Kalends of July but was not held until August; for many things, especially in a state in the utmost disorder, very often arise that require the discussion of serious business to be deferred. That assembly at Bonoilum was held, as I have said, in August 856, in the presence of King Charles the Bald.] [Note: “To oppose the king’s sacred commands.” That is, to disregard the orders of the prince, which he had communicated in written letters. Lupus considered this dangerous in his own time, because of the suspicion of secession and factionalism; for Gaul was miserably divided. He therefore advises the monks of Elnone to attend the assembly at Bonogilo, lest they bring misfortune upon themselves. There was reason to fear that this deed might disturb Charles the Bald’s suspicious mind if they neglected to be present.]

For I consider it dangerous, especially at this time, to oppose the king’s sacred commands. If life accompanies me, you will find my insignificance at the assembly without difficulty. But if this letter was delivered to you later than you wished, know that yours was brought to me on the ninth day before the Kalends of July, and that mine was handed over on the following day. I wish you happiness, and ask that you remember me kindly.

## LETTER XIX. TO HERIBOLD, BISHOP

[Note: “To Heribold.” The title of the letter in Masson’s edition added “of Auxerre” (*Antissiodorensem*). In this edition we have chosen to omit the name of the see out of respect for antiquity, and because it was absent from the manuscript. He was a man of great renown in those times, being archchaplain of the sacred palace. See what we note on Letter 37.]

[Col. 0466A]

Lupus to the most excellent bishop Heribold.

A certain monk of yours, named John, is staying with us in our monastery. He was summoned by one of our brothers because of a certain necessity, but was afterward retained by me, since this benefits us, while, as we have heard, his own monastery is suffering from want. Learning that you had ordered the brothers to gather from everywhere, I have sent these lines to your Excellency, asking that you allow him to remain with me for a while. I also humbly implore you, as far as I dare, in accordance with your innate kindness and the diligence imposed upon you by your office, to provide for that place, lest the shortage of brothers not only obscure your good works but also provoke the displeasure of our God, toward whose judgment we hasten daily, and hasten an irrevocable punishment. Your prudence sees, even without admonition, how carefully ecclesiastical affairs and the care of souls must be handled. Therefore provide for both yourself and those brothers, so that God may be glorified both for your indulgence and for their relief; he will soon repay each according to his merits. Farewell, dearest lord, and deign especially to remember me in your sacred prayers.

## LETTER XX. TO ALTUIN

[Note: “To Altuin.” See the notes on Letter 34.]

To his dearest brother Altuin, Lupus sends abundant greetings.

Your letter was delivered to me on the third day before the Kalends of May. Its expression of affection toward me made clear how favorably disposed you are, entirely as I had understood and most firmly retained in my heart. For since we lived abroad for some time in such harmony, pleasure, and perhaps profit, how could a love consolidated by such long familiarity be shaken?

As for the illness which you heard had befallen me, know that divine grace, as always and in all things, added nothing harmful but very much beneficial to my situation. It caused no inconvenience except fear alone. A pustule arose in my right groin and merely threatened impending death. [Note: “In the right groin.” That this illness befell Lupus while he was still young, at the monastery of Saint Trond, when he was traveling to Frankfurt with his abbot Odo, is attested by Hildegarius, bishop of Meaux, in his *Life of Saint Faro*, whose words are transcribed among Lupus’s eulogies.]

Yet it produced such an abundance of prayers wherever rumor had spread news of my misfortune that I dare suppose it was brought about for me as a divine favor. After returning from the regions across the Rhine, where I found the condition of our place, I decided to fulfill my obligations; and, with God’s mercy favoring me, I enjoy the firmest tranquility. My leisure is exceedingly agreeable to me because it affords useful opportunities for reading. You see, then, that I am planning no journeys out or returns. Therefore, if you consider conversation with me necessary, you will have to wait until late summer because of the shortage of fodder, when, without the care of the horses hindering you, you may be able to spend several days with us.

Meanwhile, I shall briefly complete what you asked of me—only those matters concerning which I seem to have acquired some knowledge.

I have no doubt that a common syllable formed from a mute and a liquid occurs only in words that are naturally short. First, because nature almost always takes precedence over art. Second, because pronunciations of this kind persuade me that it is so. *Peccator* (“sinner”) produces the feminine *peccatrix* (“female sinner”); *amator* (“lover”), *amatrix* (“female lover”); *venator* (“hunter”), *venatrix* (“female hunter”); and many similar forms, in which no one has ever doubted that the accent belongs on the penultimate syllable. For if we followed positional length, we would pronounce the feminine forms with the acute accent on the antepenultimate syllable. Who does not understand how absurd—even barbarous—that would be?

Finally, wherever nature has lengthened a syllable, I nowhere find it shortened in any poet’s testimony, although I have diligently sought this for a long time. It therefore seems to me, and to certain learned and exceptionally diligent men who have considered such matters with me, that *salubris*, *aratrum*, and similar words must unquestionably be pronounced with the accent on the penultimate syllable.

How *bibliothecam* should be pronounced is shown by Martial’s verse:

> “Which my entire library cannot contain.”

In the moral verses said to have been published by Alcuin, *statera* is similarly positioned:

> “Let neither your bushel nor your balance be double.”

Only someone who pays insufficient attention to the fact that *blasphemus* is written with *p* and *h* would fail to recognize that it is Greek. Accordingly, a certain Greek repeatedly assured me that the Greeks pronounce *blasphemus* with a shortened penultimate syllable, and our Eginhard confirmed the same point. Yet Aurelius Prudentius, who is celebrated most enthusiastically by many, placed the word as follows:

[Col. 0468A]

> “… divider of God, blasphemously …” [Note: Prudentius, at the beginning of the *Hamartigenia*.]

From this, then, the practice spread far and wide of giving *blasphemus* and *blasphemo* the accent on the penultimate syllable.

[Note: “*Nundinas* in Theodulf.” The works of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, were published by the most distinguished man Jacques Sirmond. The verse of Theodulf in which he lengthens the penultimate syllable of *nundinis* is found in Book II, poem 357:

[Col. 0468D]

> “Abounding in grain, resources, market-days, beautiful things, and goods.”

From this testimony of Lupus, Sirmond correctly concluded that the learned man who denied that this poem had been composed by Theodulf was mistaken. His reason was that Alcuin mentions the poem in *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 14, and that Alcuin certainly did not live into the time of Emperor Louis the Pious. But, as Sirmond also observes there, others have already noted that the book *On the Divine Offices* is not by Alcuin.]

I read *nundinas* in Theodulf’s poem with the penultimate syllable lengthened. Whether this should be accepted on the authority of that poem or of the rules belongs to him to judge.

We pronounce *loquelam* and *querelam* with one *l*, following Capri’s orthography. [Note: “*Loquelam* with one *l*.” This shows that there were once people who wrote *loquella*. Indeed, in many ancient manuscript codices I have often read *loquella*, *querella*, and *medella*.] As for *medelam*, we would pronounce it without hesitation, like *suadelam*, if the similarity of the conjugation were not confused by the difference of gender, and if the respectable agreement of nearly all copies did not oppose us. For that reason, let us leave the matter undecided and not rashly alter our usage until something more substantial is found, either by us or by those who dissent from us.

The *sistrum* is a musical instrument which, as you wrote, Isis was represented as carrying in her hand, thereby signifying the Nile’s rising and falling. Thus Virgil, with his customary subtlety revealing that Cleopatra used to arrogate to herself a fictitious power of this kind, says (*Aeneid* VIII):

> “… she summons her troops with the ancestral sistrum.”

We pronounce *fialas* with a shortened penultimate syllable for the reason that vessels are called *fialae* because they are made of glass, which the Greeks call *hyalos* (*hialin*). You have *hialin* in Virgil (*Georgics* IV):

> “They were gathering glass, stained with rich color.”

Likewise in Martial:

> “What have you to do with joining a spoon to a glass vessel?”

Regarding the comets that have been seen, it seems more appropriate to fear than to discuss them. Since divine authority nowhere speaks about them, we may—and indeed may fear—that what the pagans discovered by experience when they appeared is true. They handed down that comets portend pestilence, famine, or wars. Hence the Mantuan poet, when Caesar’s death and civil wars were impending, includes among the portents he lists (*Georgics* I):

> “… nor did the dreadful comets burn so many times.”

Josephus also reports that, before Jerusalem was destroyed, a star in the form of a sword stood over that same city for an entire year.

But to give us some hope that we may experience gentler events, Pompeius Trogus reports that the future greatness of King Mithridates was foretold by a comet in these words (Justin, Book XXXVII, chapter 2):

> “For both in the year in which he was born and in the year in which he first began to reign, a comet-star shone for seventy days on each occasion, so that the entire sky seemed to be ablaze. It occupied a quarter of the sky by its size, surpassed the brightness of the sun with the rays of its lightning, and, when it rose and set, consumed a period of four hours.”

[Note: “This April.” Lupus is undoubtedly speaking of the comet that appeared in 838 “around the Easter festival,” as the author of the *Life of Louis the Pious* says, “in the sign of Virgo.” The same author writes that it passed through the signs of Leo, Cancer, and Gemini, and finally, in the head of Taurus beneath the feet of the Charioteer, “laid down a fiery globe and the long hair” which it had previously extended in every direction. Easter that year fell on the Kalends of April. Louis consulted experts in astronomy about what they thought of the portent. When one of them tried to evade the prince’s question, Louis said: “There is one thing you are still suppressing in silence. For they say that this portent signifies a change of kingdom and the death of a prince.” An example of this popular belief appears in Tacitus, Book XIV of the *Annals*: “Among these events a comet also shone forth, about which there is a popular belief that it portends a change of king.” Another example is supplied by the author of the *Life of Saint Leodegarius of Autun*, published by Duchesne, chapter 7: “For then we clearly recognized that God’s anger had come to pass, so much so that a star even appeared in the sky which astrologers call a comet; at its rising they assert that the earth is disturbed by famine, and that with a change of kings or an upheaval of peoples the blow of the sword is imminent.” Rigord gives another example in his *Life of Philip Augustus*, king of the Franks: “At the time when Philip, the magnanimous king of the Franks, began to fall ill, a dreadful comet appeared in the west, portending his death and the weakening of the kingdom of the Franks.” Thus the comet that appeared in 1264 was thought to portend a change in the kingdom of Sicily and the death of Pope Urban IV, as reported by William of Puylaurens, chapter 49, and in the *Chronicle of an Unknown Author* published by Catel. Hence Lucan’s line in Book I of the *Civil War*:

> “A comet changing kingdoms for the earth.”]

I also saw this April, shortly after midnight, a rather dim star beneath Leo that extended a ray as far as the Virgin’s spike. After carefully observing it for several days, I contemplated the same star, but afterward I no longer saw the ray; then the star itself also disappeared.

The book you requested was sought after my return by many people to whom it ought not to have been lent. Therefore, I almost decided to send it away somewhere, lest it be lost. Perhaps you will obtain it from me when you come. Although I saw that this cleric could be entrusted with it because he is loyal to you, I was surprised that you had not noticed that this was not sufficiently safe, since he was on foot.

As for the fact that you did not make me fully certain about our bishop, I was displeased, since no matter tires me as much as that one. I am now almost angry because you did not write what our Probus is doing—whether, as he used seriously to say, he is pursuing the liberal arts in order in the wilds of Germany, or whether, as I think more likely, he is composing the satire he has begun, [Note: “Our Probus.” A priest of Mainz, concerning whom the *Annals of Fulda* report under the year 859: “The devout priest Probus, whose chaste conduct and devotion to sacred learning illuminated the Church of Mainz, died on the seventh day before the Kalends of July.” Trithemius repeats these words in his *Hirsau Chronicle*, except that he adds that Probus was a monk at the monastery of Saint Alban. I believe this Probus to have been the author of the *Life of Saint Patrick*, which appears among Bede’s works, Volume III. Nor do I agree with Possevino, who writes that Probus, the author of that Life, was Irish by birth. The same Probus is also mentioned in Lupus’s Letter 34.]

[Note: “Cicero and Virgil.” Even among the ancients there were people who believed that the souls of pagans who had nevertheless led holy lives were placed in heaven. They considered it unjust, evidently, if Christ’s blood were said to have been shed in vain for those pagans, who lacked nothing except recognition of the faith. Probus held this view. Whether seriously or jokingly is uncertain. One might say that Erasmus himself was inclined toward this opinion, so much so that in one dialogue, speaking through another person, he says that he can scarcely restrain himself from wishing well to the holy souls of Maro and Flaccus, and from sometimes exclaiming: “Holy Socrates, pray for us.” Zwingli, writing to Francis I, king of the Franks, says that if he governed the supreme affairs entrusted to him by God like David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, he would first see God himself in his substance, and then the assembly of the saints, including Hercules, Theseus, Socrates, Aristides, and the rest. I, however, am restrained from adopting their opinions by the authority of the Church, which denies any hope of salvation to one who is outside the Church; and I greatly approve that famous saying of Augustine, repeated by everyone, who said of such men that they are praised where they are not, but tormented where they are. It nevertheless seemed necessary to record these things in order to illuminate this passage of Lupus. See also Collius, *On the Souls of Pagans*.]

he admits Cicero, Virgil, and the other men whom his opinion regards as most worthy into the company of the elect, lest the Lord have shed his blood in vain and spent his time in hell, if that prophetic saying is true:

> “I shall be your death, O Death; I shall be your bite, O Hell” (Hosea 13).

Farewell, dearest, and continue kindly in our affection. Deign to greet the provost and your congregation on my behalf, and ask them to pray to the Lord for me, my father, and my mother.

## LETTER XXI. TO JONAS

[Note: “To Jonas.” Bishop of Orléans, as the title in Papirius Masson’s edition also stated. The old codex, however, lacked these words. He was a great man in those times, and distinguished monuments of his intellect survive. His books in defense of sacred images against Claudius, bishop of Turin, were published long ago. As I think, the first edition of his books against Claudius appeared at Cologne in 1554, but without any preface by the editor. It was reprinted by Christophe Plantin in 1565, “cleansed,” as the first page says, “of innumerable errors.” Finally, in 1687, an ancient and elegant copy of that work came into my hands—indeed, I believe, the very copy that Jonas presented to Charles the Bald. At the beginning was placed an apology, or reply, of Claudius, bishop of Turin, against Theodemir, the abbot; it was precisely the same text that was published after Dungal’s book and begins, “Your letter.” I noticed that the Plantinian edition was extremely corrupt and mutilated. Dungal’s book also, to mention this in passing, is very incomplete and corrupt. The excellent and most learned man Lucas d’Achery, a Benedictine monk, devoted to public use the three books of that same Jonas *On Lay Formation*, as well as his little work *On Royal Formation*, after they had long lain hidden in corners of libraries.]

[Col. 0470B]

To Jonas.

I am accustomed to wonder greatly that you took offense at the meaning of my letter. If it is considered a little more carefully, it will be clear that it not only detracted nothing from your dignity but even bestowed very much upon it, since what great necessity compelled us to do was, with your permission, obtained through entreaty. So far was I from intending to injure you that, with sincere affection, I wish you always to make your rank and preaching equal to the integrity of your life, and that nothing in it should appear capable of darkening the reputation of your holiness.

This is why I explained to you what was being said by your relative Agius, namely, that many people were criticizing his excessive extortion: since he was boasting that he had done this with your approval, those who wished to see the matter clearly would recognize that, once he was restrained by you, he had done all those things outside your authorization. [Note: “Agius.” He later became bishop of Orléans after Jonas. Sirmond correctly inferred from Canon 10 of the council held at the palace of Ver that Agius’s ordination was not initially approved by Charles the Bald, but that it was later confirmed at the synod’s request, since Agius is subsequently frequently mentioned as bishop. See what we note below on that canon of Ver.]

Although I had uselessly omitted a complaint about the loss he had previously caused, and although, urged on by those who had suffered the greatest damage, I had complained to our lord about the loss he later inflicted, and although he replied that he wished the law to be preserved in that matter, I ceased pursuing the affair out of consideration for your reverence, at the urging of the illustrious man Heribold and the venerable Fulco, who preferred that I bear the losses of great estates rather than the loss of your friendship.

But, to tell you truthfully what I wish you to receive in an episcopal manner: in your city and in the little estates we held outside it, not even enough was left to us for the household to live on and the fields to yield their rent. We had there a not inconsiderable supply of wine and grain, and also some salt. Sold, these would have provided us with clothing and, for the military expeditions required in this troubled period of the state, at least some means of obtaining silver. I now suffer such anxiety over these matters that only this saying occurs to me: “You are my refuge from the tribulation that surrounds me” (Psalm 31).

On one side, the poverty of the brothers troubles me; on the other, the money that must be spent on journeys afflicts me severely; and since nearly all our possessions have been taken away or devastated on every side, I can find help nowhere except in God and in the support of friends.

[Note: “Our former abbot.” Odo, namely, abbot of Ferrières before Lupus. He relinquished the government of the monastery by order of Charles the Bald, a circumstance that also displays royal authority in the disposition of monasteries. Charles then appointed Lupus abbot there. See the notes on the first letter.]

I also hear that certain false stories have been reported to you about our former abbot. To prevent them from gaining further influence with you, I shall explain to your holiness as truthfully as possible what happened. [Note: “Our lord.” That is, King Charles the Bald.] Our lord ordered that he not be permitted to remain in our monastery, having made statements about him that are better left unspoken. [Note: “Lest he be in the monastery.” This is the meaning of the passage. Odo, abbot of Ferrières, had incurred King Charles’s anger by being guilty of atrocious deeds. The issue was undoubtedly the violation of the loyalty owed to the prince under whose rule one lived. Odo was more favorably disposed toward Lothar, as can be inferred from Letter 26. For that reason, and perhaps for others, Charles removed him from the administration of the monastery of Ferrières. In those times they thought that an abbot who was negligent regarding the prince’s affairs should be deposed for that negligence. Thus the bishops assembled at the synod of Vermer, held in 846, say when confirming the privileges of the monastery of Corbie: “If it should ever happen that a rector in that place does not live worthily before God, or is perhaps less dutiful toward the prince, we establish that, if he is deposed because of his negligence, their right of election shall remain inviolate.” See Charles the Bald’s *Capitularies*, title II, chapter 3, and the council at Saponaria, chapter 11.]

When I returned to the monastery, I conveyed this to the same abbot as gently as possible. I assigned men to escort him and granted him horses, clothing, and silver for his journey. When I was setting out, by order of our lord the king, on the second day before the Kalends of December, I decreed that he should leave the monastery by the third day before the Nones of that month, since I hoped to come before the king on that day.

After I had done this according to my judgment, following the solemn reception the king asked what I had done with the aforesaid abbot. Believing that this abbot had acted in accordance with what was suitable for us, I replied that I had fulfilled his command concerning him. Having received permission, when I approached the monastery on the day before the Ides of December, I discovered that the aforesaid abbot was still staying there.

I was therefore extremely anxious, because I had told our lord one thing but found another. I sent someone ahead that night to tell him courteously to leave at first light: it would not be honorable either for me to delay my entrance or for him to be found there against our lord’s command. When he sent word that he intended to leave the next day, I replied, so as not to leave my enemies any opportunity for slander, that I would not enter until he himself had departed.

Thus he left the monastery, retaining everything I had previously given him and receiving some additional things as well. I immediately informed my household officials of the matter, and at a suitable opportunity explained it myself to our lord, exposing the lies that were being spread as a result. Everyone unanimously agreed that I could not have acted otherwise. Let those who spread different stories judge whether they did wrong. For my part, since I have a single eye in this matter, I trust, on divine authority, that my whole body will be full of light.

I wish you happiness and abundance in every good thing.

## LETTER XXII. TO LOUIS

[Note: “To Louis.” This is how the manuscript commonly reads, or *Hludoguicus*, which is also the frequent spelling of this name in the *Chronicle of Centula*. This Louis was a relative of Charles the Bald and abbot of the monastery of Saint-Denis in the Paris region, as Charles himself teaches in a charter for the monastery of Saint-Denis: “Our venerable relative Louis, abbot of the monastery of the chief of the Apostles and of Christ’s most excellent martyrs, Denis, Rusticus, and Eleutherius.” Charles likewise calls him his relative in a charter for the monastery of Centula, preserved in Hariulf, Book III of the *Chronicle of Centula*, chapter 7. Sirmond inferred from Lupus’s Letter 27 that Louis was also the same King Charles’s chancellor; speaking of this Louis, Lupus says that he held “the office of letter-writer at the palace.” He is named among the presidents of the Council of Ver. Several letters of Lupus to him survive, revealing his great dignity and authority.]

[Col. 0472D]

To Louis.

Even if I did not write, you could easily infer from our longstanding affection how greatly I rejoice in your more prosperous successes. Perhaps I may justly ask that your Excellency not disdain my insignificance, but deign to retain the acquaintance and condescension once granted to me. Know that I am faithfully prepared for your service.

I also ask your renowned generosity to order two of our servants to be instructed by your craftsmen, whom widespread fame proclaims to be exceptionally skilled in works of gold and silver. Through your kindness they would be of great benefit to us and to our neighbors. Therefore, lest our wishes be delayed too long, if we have deserved to obtain what we request, we have already arranged for one of those whom we wish to send to be trained in that art.

Also order that the gold which this brother of ours deposited with you be returned to him, so that, after inspecting the work, we may be able to assess what we should do.

I wish you happiness and daily growth in virtue.

## LETTER XXIII. ALSO TO THE SAME, ON BEHALF OF ODO

To Louis, deservedly adorned with the highest honors, Odo, last of the abbots, and the whole community of the monastery of Ferrières send abundant greetings.

[Note: “Odo.” Abbot of Ferrières, as we said in the note to Letter 21. The next three letters also belong to him. It is therefore very surprising that the keen-eyed Sammarthani did not notice this and omitted his name from their catalogue of the abbots of Ferrières.]

Whenever we are shaken by some storm of trouble or necessity, we flee in safety to the harbor of your goodwill. Open to everyone for acts of kindness, it rejects no one who presents himself seeking help.

But, not to delay you, you remember that this year we were entrusted with Abbot Zacharias, at a time when your prudence favored us so greatly that he was commended almost not to us but to others. [Note: “Zacharias the abbot entrusted.” This was the customary expression whenever they meant to say that a monastery had been given by the prince to someone so that he might be abbot there, as we shall say below. Here, however, it is not used in that sense. The matter concerns an exiled and wandering abbot whose necessities had become so extreme, including even the means of sustaining life, that King Charles sent him to Ferrières and ordered Abbot Odo and the monks of that monastery to support him and his companions. Since the monastery of Ferrières was not equal to bearing that burden, they ask that these men be sent elsewhere.]

Now this same abbot is going to our lord the king to ask what he should do above all. Let your distinguished diligence therefore take our smallness into consideration and deign to work so that he may now be sent either to the place from which he came to us or to some other place, because, to confess the matter to you plainly as it is, the expenses assigned to his men burden us considerably. We therefore ask to be relieved through you, so that we may have the means to extend the grace of hospitality to others who come flocking to us.

## LETTER XXIV. ALSO TO THE PERSON MENTIONED ABOVE

[Col. 0474A]

To Louis, most worthy of the highest honors, Odo, last of the abbots, sends abundant greetings in the Lord.

Seeing more clearly than daylight that your goodwill is favorably disposed toward my insignificance, I give many thanks and pray that God may reward your devotion. For my part, I am ready faithfully to obey whatever your Excellency may deign to command.

Necessity, however, compels me once again humbly to implore the protection of your aid. For after returning burdened by illness from the Aquitanian expedition, having obtained permission through your assistance, I have been almost continually worn down by the same illness and have not yet recovered. [Col. 0474B] This prevented me from attending the appointed assembly with the others. Nevertheless, I sent our men together with the count of the district to perform the duties of the expedition in the customary manner.

We therefore beseech your devotion to deign to relieve us from fear of offense. Although I had the strongest willingness to obey with the others, I could not overcome my physical weakness.

## LETTER XXV. ALSO TO THE PERSON MENTIONED ABOVE

To the most illustrious Louis, a man worthy of the highest summit of reverence, Odo, last of all the abbots, and the whole community of the monastery of Ferrières send greetings in the Lord. [Note: “O.” That is, Odo, the same man as in the two preceding letters. In Masson’s edition, however, Odo’s name is omitted here, and Lupus’s name is written instead in this form: “To Louis, Lupus, last of all the abbots,” and so forth.]

[Col. 0474C]

We are not unaware that you are oppressed by the weight of many great matters converging upon you from every side, and that even time itself scarcely suffices for arranging them. Yet we trust your devotion so far that we believe room for our affairs is always open with you. It can scarcely be expressed how ready we are to obey your will, if you deign to command anything, and to attend your Excellency with services worthy of you.

Meanwhile, as far as we are able, we continually offer our most devoted prayers to our Lord God for your health and prosperity, which we regard as our own. Receive once again our petition, and, we ask, deign to press for its fulfillment.

Our men have been wearied for almost the entire past two years, either with us or alone, by the hardships of the general expedition. Having spent the resources of their household property in this service, they are weighed down by poverty. Therefore, let your distinguished clemency assist them and, if possible, obtain permission for them to return home, so that they may breathe a little and once again prepare the expenses of future service.

Furthermore, a report is circulating among us that palace clerics are seeking and demanding control of various monasteries, having no other concern than to satisfy their avarice by oppressing the servants of God. Therefore, in this matter also we ask your vigilant prudence to watch over us, so that through you our poverty may be safe.

Since you were brought up not far from us and were also once among us, the character of our monastery is by no means unknown to you. Apart from its devotion to religion, by which it has established its name among other monasteries, there is nothing there that one who thinks highly of himself would desire—unless perhaps someone so sacrilegious should be found as to dare convert the provisions of those serving God to his own uses and make their poverty his luxury. [Note: “The provisions of those serving God.” That is, the possessions of the monks, who in those times were commonly called “servants of God.” A charter of Charles the Bald for the monastery of Saint Peter of Besalú in the diocese of Girona states: “Whatever the fiscus could hope to obtain from it, we grant entirely to that church for eternal recompense, so that it may contribute to the sustenance of the poor and to the provisions of the servants of God serving God there, for their increase.” Clarius the monk writes more clearly in the *Chronicle of Saint Peter of Sens*: “In the year 865 Archbishop Wenilo died. He was succeeded in the bishopric by Lord Eigil, a monk distinguished for every goodness, who, caring for the monastery of Blessed Peter, gave the estate of Alsonis to support the monks serving God there.” And there are hundreds of similar examples.]

Therefore let your diligence provide for us in this matter as well, so that, made secure through you, we may pray more freely to the Lord on your behalf.

## LETTER XXVI. TO MARCWARD AND SICHARD.

To the most reverend and illustrious Fathers Marcwardus and Sichardus, [Note: I think that the sixth letter of Bishop Frotharius of Toul was addressed to him.] Sichardus, [Note: O., that is, Odo. This letter too was headed in Lupus’s name in Masson’s edition. We have followed the authority of the manuscript codex. Thus Masson’s edition read: “To Marcwardus and Sichardus, Lupus, perpetual servant,” etc.] Odo, perpetual greetings.

[Col. 0475C] Since your men, who were setting out to join you, readily gave us the opportunity to write, we have by no means neglected the duty of correspondence; and we beg your holiness, in turn, to send us letters as quickly as you can, containing news of your health and the condition of your prosperity. We, however, placed as we are in a kind of middle position, are wavering uncertainly, since we cannot discover who, above all, ought to claim our region for himself. For, as the report of your men made clear, varying opinions are being spread here. Nevertheless, we earnestly ask your fatherhood that, if the general consensus is more favorable toward Lothair, and if, as we hope and believe, divine mercy has granted you a place with him for the benefit of God’s servants, you do not disdain to remember us; and may you not hesitate, insofar as you can, with the help of God’s grace, to drive away the perversity of evil men from our humble selves. We wish you good health and success that grows happier with each passing day.

## 51. LETTER XXVII. [Note: To Jonah, bishop of Orléans, as we said concerning Letter 21.] TO JONAH, BISHOP.

To the most reverend prelate Jonah, [Note: L. and Vv. Thus the manuscript codex expressly reads, whereas Masson printed “Lupus, perpetual.” The rest is similar.] Lupus and VV. send greetings in the Lord.

[Note: Your book. That is, a certain book recently published by Jonah, bishop of Orléans, and sent by him to Lupus and VV. so that it might be corrected through their scholarly efforts. Baronius thinks that this refers to Jonah’s books against Claudius of Turin, the only works of Jonah’s that had been published in Baronius’s time. Perhaps he would have thought otherwise had he lived into our own age.] We have read through your book, as you requested; but, to put it as mildly as possible, we wished to change nothing in it, so that you yourselves might be the correctors of a work of which you are the authors. For we had to take account of our own tenderness and insignificance, and consideration had to be given to your age and rank. Nor ought we to imitate a certain readiness—and pleasure in finding fault—that we regularly observe in some people. [Note: The pleasure of criticizing. He refers to those who, like Momus, always find something to criticize in the literary labors of those who devote their studies to public use. Such folly must be avoided. If a wise man ought to beware of disparaging anyone’s literary work, how much more must this be avoided in the books of a man who is both old and a bishop. For this reason Lupus and VV. refrain from censuring the book Jonah had sent them, adding prayers that Jonah should judge the work severely himself. Today no teacher is so insignificant that he does not think himself entitled to more. Such is the power of the long passage of time to change things. It often happens that those who criticize the labors of learned men most freely and arrogantly are the very men who publish nothing themselves, being secure, naturally, from the law of retaliation. For this reason Arnulf of Lisieux was reluctant to publish his letters. Writing in his first letter to Giles, archdeacon of Rouen—for this is how I correct the reading “archbishop” found in the editions—he says: “Indeed, I would rather condemn them to everlasting darkness than provide envy with material for ridicule; for envy mocks the works of others all the more securely because it does not expose its own to a similar danger.” John of Salisbury thinks that this audacity in attacking learned men arises from the ignorance of half-educated people. His are these words in Book VII, chapter 9, of *The Frivolities of Courtiers*: “Yet the man who contradicts most quickly and resists most stubbornly is the one who has spent his life learning only a few things and is so constrained by poverty of vocabulary that, if you take away one or two words, he becomes speechless and more silent than any statue.”]

## LETTER XXVIII. ALSO TO THE SAME.

[Col. 0477A]

To the most reverend Bishop Jonah, Odo, [Note: O., that is, Odo, as we have already noted many times. This passage was badly corrupted formerly, since Masson read *opto* instead of *Odo*; yet that error indicates that the correction we propose is genuine. It is surprising that Duchesne did not notice this.] perpetual greetings.

Yesterday—that is, on the fourth day before the Ides of August—after the ninth hour, our men returned from the Aquitanian expedition and reported that everything had gone well. For the defense of Aquitaine has been divided into three parts, with a large number of military men distributed according to the suitability of the locations. One of these divisions, which is stationed at Clermont, [Note: Clermont. At that time the chief city of the Arverni in Aquitania Prima.] is commanded by Modoinus, [Note: Modoinus. This bishop of Autun is mentioned by Theodulf of Orléans, where Sirmond notes that he was appointed judge by Ebbo, archbishop of Reims, in the year 835. There is also a letter of Florus of Lyon to him, formerly printed by Morel; and two other letters of the same Florus survive in the Petavian codex 791. One is a longer letter on behalf of the Church of Lyon, addressed “To the excellent man Modoinus,” etc.; the other is shorter and calls Modoinus bishop of Augustodunum, since *dun* in the ancient language of the Gauls means “mountain.” Florus addresses him as follows:

> Hail, holy father, venerable priest of Christ,  
> Powerful shepherd in the citadel of Mount Augustus.  
> The sacred order illuminates you with shining merits,  
> And devotion to holy doctrine raises you to the stars.]

bishop of the people of Autun, and Count Autbert of Avallon, [Note: Count of Avallon. That is, count of the county of Avallon on the borders of Burgundy, as is clear from Book I of the *History of Vézelay*. Vézelay belonged to the county of Avallon. Avallon, or Aballon, is also mentioned in the *Itinerary of Antoninus* and on the Peutinger Table, where it is noted that Aballon lies sixteen Gallic leagues from Sedelocus and twenty-two from Auxerre. Frodoard also mentions Avallon in his *Chronicle* under the year 931: “Gislebert, son of Manasses, defected from King Rodulf because of the fortress of Avallon, which Queen Emma had taken from him.” Charlemagne likewise mentions the county of Avallon in the charter dividing the Frankish Empire: “the county of Avallon and that of Als.” The capitularies of Charles the Bald, title XII, likewise mention “Hugh, Gozso, Nivilungus, envoys in the Nivernais, the Als region, and the Avallonnais.” Avallon is the name commonly used today.] together with certain others.

The second division, which is stationed at Limoges, [Note: At Limoges. That is, in the city of the Lemovices, whose ancient name was Ratiastum according to Claudius Ptolemy. Those who look for Ratiastum elsewhere are mistaken, misled by the similarity of the names.] is commanded by Gerard, [Note: Gerard. A son-in-law of Pippin, king of Aquitaine, as is established from the *Life of Louis the Pious* and from Ademar of Chabannes. His wife was therefore named Bertha, as Besly writes in the *History of the Counts of Poitiers*, and Justel in the *History of the Viscounts of Turenne*. I would gladly accept their view if it were supported by the authority of some ancient writer. Gerard was killed in the battle of Fontenoy in 841, as can be inferred from Ademar. It is therefore clear that he must not be confused with Gerard of Roussillon, who did not die until 867, as the author of the *Chronicle of Vézelay* teaches. Indeed, Volume IV of Dom Luc d’Achery’s *Spicilegium* contains a letter from that Gerard to Pope Nicholas. Moreover, our Gerard was not count of Limoges, as Duchesne and Justel thought, but count of the Auvergne, as can be inferred from Ademar. It is therefore surprising that he was not placed at Clermont rather than at the city of Limoges, especially since he was a man of such distinction. It is equally surprising that Justel did not include him among the ancient counts of the Auvergne. Count Gerard had a son, Ramnulf, who, while his father was still alive, was appointed count of Poitiers by the emperor Louis the Pious, as Ademar records.] formerly a prince and dear to King Pippin, with associates suitable for the same task.

The third division was placed under Count Reinoldus, [Note: Reinoldus. Masson’s edition and Duchesne’s likewise read *Reindardus*, incorrectly. The authority of the ancient codex therefore confirms the conjecture of the most learned Jean Besly, who judged that Lupus’s *Reindardus* should here be read *Rainaldus*, for *Reginardus*. The manuscript codex clearly has *Reinoldus*, which is also the form found in the *Chronicle of Vendôme*. In the *Annals of the Kings of the Franks* published by Justus Reuber, and in the *Chronicle of Saint Wandrille*, he is called *Reginoldus*, which amounts to the same thing. He was count of Arbatilica and later of Nantes. Besly rightly criticizes Fauchet for having inferred from this passage of Lupus that he was count of Angoulême. He was killed at Messac in Brittany Minor on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September in the year 843, while fighting bravely against the Bretons.] stationed at Engolism, [Note: Engolism. That is, Angoulême, as Masson’s edition has it. This is how the place was written in those times. Eginhard, among others, also calls it *Ecolisena*. In Hincmar it is written *Aequolesina*. See also our notes on the Council of Narbonne, held under Charlemagne.] [Note: Established. Thus the manuscript codex reads, whereas the editions have *constitutus*. The reading of the ancient codex is unquestionably preferable. The sense is: “Another cohort was established at Angoulême; and Count Reinoldus was placed over that cohort which had been established at Angoulême.” The word *constitutae* cannot refer to Reinoldus, whom he has just said was placed over the division of soldiers stationed at Angoulême.]

They reported that the lord king would come that same day—that is, on the fourth day before the Ides of August—to Saint Martin, [Note: At Saint Martin. In the suburb of the city of Tours.] and from there would pass through the city of Orléans. This seemed to me likely, since the highly gifted Louis, [Note: Louis. Chancellor of King Charles the Bald, as we said in Letter 22.] who held the office of correspondence in the palace, took care to instruct me to meet the lord king either at Tours or, at any rate, at Orléans, phrasing his encouragement conditionally, in case the king should travel through Orléans. Meanwhile Gunboldus and Hugh are returning as suppliants to the king and are believed likely to recover their former honors. The king himself has arranged to come, with his life preserved, to Quierzy on the ninth day before the Kalends of September. [Note: Quierzy. A famous place in those times, made distinguished by the palace of our kings. Sirmond thinks it was the place now called Crécy on the Oise, to distinguish it from other places of the same name; he considers this view wholly established by the authority of Fredegar. But Philippe Labbe thinks that the ancient *Annals of the Franks*, which place Quierzy on the Oise, should here be corrected, and that one should read *on the Serre*, making it Crécy on the Serre, Cressy-sur-Serre, in the diocese of Laon. Indeed, in Guibert of Nogent’s third book *On His Own Life*, chapter 5, there is mention of a certain nobleman of Laon named Gerard of Quierzy because he was lord of the castle of Quierzy; this indicates that Quierzy was situated in the county of Laon. See the fourth book of the most learned Mabillon’s *De re diplomatica*, p. 258.]

## LETTER XXIX. [Note: To Guenilo, bishop of Sens. He is commonly called Wenilo in the Gallican synods held during that period. Previously he had been a cleric of the royal chapel of Charles the Bald, from whom he received the bishopric of Sens after the death of Archbishop Aldric in 841. Charles himself testifies to this in his accusation against that same Wenilo at the general synod held at Savonnières in 859: “A portion of the kingdom was entrusted to me, by divine disposition, by the Lord and by my father, Louis Augustus of pious memory, among my brothers, the kings. In that portion of the kingdom the metropolitan see of Sens was then vacant: in accordance with the custom of my predecessors, the kings, with the consent of the holy bishops of that metropolis I entrusted it for governance to Wenilo, then my cleric serving me in my chapel, who had commended himself to me in the manner of a free cleric and had promised me fidelity by oath; and, insofar as it depended on me, I prevailed upon the bishops to ordain him archbishop there.” Later, when Louis, king of Germany, Charles’s brother and enemy, invaded Charles’s kingdom at the persuasion of certain men, Wenilo alone among the Gallican bishops defected to Louis’s side, setting a very bad example. Charles’s anger was aroused by this, to such an extent that at the council at Savonnières he presented a serious complaint against him to the bishops. They threatened Wenilo with the penalties established by the forefathers—that is, deposition—unless he cleared himself of the charges. Since we nowhere find that he was actually deposed, this should be attributed not to his innocence but to the clemency of the prince, as the author of the *Annals of Saint-Bertin* records under the year 859: “Wenilo, bishop of Sens, was reconciled to King Charles without a hearing before the bishops.” Yet the stain remained forever. For notorious traitors later came to be called *Ganelons*, from the name Wenilo or Guenilo, slightly altered. Matthew Paris, speaking of the count of Nevers under the year 1216, says that he belonged to the family of Guenilo, the traitor. Likewise, in the *Spanish March*, the name of Bera, count of Barcelona, became notorious because he violated the fidelity he owed to the emperor Louis the Pious. Hence in the *Usatici of Barcelona*, for some six hundred years or thereabouts, a traitor who violates a pledged faith has been called a *Bara*, as the illustrious archbishop of Paris notes in Book III of the *Spanish March*.] TO GUENILO, BISHOP.

[Col. 0479A]

While iniquity abounded and the charity of many had already grown cold, and while we see more and more people rejoicing when they have done evil and exulting in the worst deeds—when, with our sins having brought the commonwealth to ruin, the madness of the wicked runs rampant with impunity and fear of the laws is abolished—we ought to be filled with the greatest joy if at least someone is found who, mindful of the future, conceives in a devout spirit contempt for the fleeting world [Note: “The contempt of the fleeting age.” Thus Faustus of Riez praises Ruricius in Letter 6, who later became bishop of Limoges, because “after the storms of this life he turned toward the harbor of religion, the prow of salvation, with the hand of the Most High guiding him; after the shadows of deceiving vanities and the illusions of fleeting dreams, he desired what would endure and be solid; and at last, having scorned the unhappy world, he seized its great art and acquired happiness and profit for himself from the world that was perishing,” and so forth. Faustus seems to say that Ruricius adopted the monastic way of life, following the advice of Faustus himself, who had given such counsel in Letter 5.] and, through the working of God’s grace, grasps the summit of perfection.
