Because two of our priests seemed to me to be striving toward this—one called Ardegarius, the other Baldricus—I sent one of them [Col. 0480A] (for unavoidable necessity detained the other) to Your Reverence, together with a military man to protect him on the journey, so that you might learn from the priest the desire of both, and so that, through the report of our messenger, their earlier life and their present devotion might appear more certainly attested.

But your prudence denied them permission to leave [Note: “Their titles.” That is, the churches to which they had been ordained. Since in those ancient times no one was permitted to be ordained without a title—namely, by what was called an absolute ordination—bishops so bound clerics to the titles to which they ordained them that they were not permitted to leave them without grave cause, nor to do so without the permission of their own bishop. Thus Ardegarius and Baldricus, priests of Sens, having resolved to profess the Rule of Saint Benedict in the monastery of Ferrières, approached Wenilo, their metropolitan, asking that for this reason they might be allowed to leave their titles. Wenilo refused to do so until Lupus the abbot had demonstrated, by clear and authentic evidence, that it could be done without fault—that is, in accordance with the canons. For the very prudent pontiff undoubtedly knew that Pope Innocent, writing to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, described the clerical order as a higher rank in comparison with the monastic profession. When the man who had approached Wenilo returned to Lupus, it became clear that Wenilo did not wish to grant the priests permission to withdraw from the sacred ministry for the reason mentioned above. Lupus then wrote this letter to Wenilo, in which he attempts, by many arguments, to prove that priests are permitted to renounce their titles and abandon pastoral care in order to become monks. Yet he adduces no authority—although Wenilo had explicitly requested one—whether from the canons of councils or from the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, demonstrating that this was permitted. But, possessing a mind both agreeable and fertile, he handles his case wonderfully: that is, he tries by every means to persuade Wenilo to allow those priests to enter the monastery and profess the Rule of Saint Benedict. Whether Wenilo accepted Lupus’s advice is unclear. [Col. 0480D] The same thing later happened to Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, as had happened to Wenilo. “Two priests of our bishopric,” says Arnulf in Letter 63 to the Cistercian abbot, “namely Arnulf and Ricardus, intending to renounce the world, after frequent admonition and through the zeal of our brother William, now abbot of Pin, went to the venerable and religious man Ricardus, abbot of Valassia; having first relinquished into our hands the churches which they possessed, they devoted themselves and their possessions with the greatest readiness. Following their devotion with the favor it deserved, we committed them, free and absolved, with their possessions, into the abbot’s hands, to serve God perpetually in the aforesaid monastery.” Today, if any priest wished to become a monk, he would doubtless do so without the knowledge of his own priest, because of the privileges involved. At that time, however, this was not permitted.] and more strictly follow the institution of blessed Benedict, unless perhaps our lowliness could draw from you the authority that this may be done without fault. Although I have never heard this disputed, nor discovered it through authoritative reading, I shall nevertheless disclose simply what I think to your authority.

The Lord Jesus said to the rich man who arrogantly claimed to observe the legal commandments and asked too boldly what he still lacked: “Go, sell everything you possess,” and so forth (Matthew 19). There he made clear that voluntary poverty would be fruitful if what he teaches elsewhere were fulfilled: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart,” and the rest (Matthew 11). Nowhere can this be done either more securely or more effectively than in a monastery, where one’s freedom of will is cut away for the love of God—a most laborious undertaking—in such a way that every action of those subject to authority is formed according to the decision of the prior.

Although some among us, through the overflowing grace of God and with great strength of spirit, have avoided human society, fulfilled the aforesaid saying of the Lord, entered the wilderness, and steadfastly spent almost their entire lives in the work of God, let it not be that priests are removed from that perfection which God has also proposed to laymen.

But someone may say: “What are the congregations to do, whose pastoral care they had canonically undertaken?” [Note: “The care they had undertaken.” From this we learn that priests were then accustomed to be assigned to their churches in such a way that, because they had received the care of souls from our Lord Jesus Christ, they could not leave them except in a case of extreme necessity; indeed, at their ordination they promised stability in the place to which they were ordained. Book 5 of the Capitularies, chapter 108: “Let priests who are consecrated to titles, according to the canons, make a promise of stability in that place before they are ordained.” For at that time, as we understand from Lupus, the pastoral care of each priest was compared with carnal marriage. From this comparison it followed that a priest could not abandon his church without sacrilege, just as a husband may not dismiss his wife except on account of fornication. Thus Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, who flourished under King Pippin, decreed in chapter 63 of the Rule of the Canons: “Let a priest have no more than one church, just as a man has one wife.” The same was enacted in canon 7 of the Council of Nantes in these words: “For just as a bishop may have no more than one city and a man one wife, so a priest may have only one church.” And in chapter 49 of the Capitularies of Herard, archbishop of Tours: “Let a priest have no more than one church, just as a man has one wife.” [Col. 0481C] Likewise, Book 6 of the Capitularies, chapter 73: “It has pleased the entire synodal assembly that no priest presume to claim more than one church for himself. For just as every layman ought to have no more than one wife, so every priest ought to have no more than one church.” And just as a husband is bound to remain with his wife and protect her because of the frailty of her sex, as is written somewhere, so priests ought not to be absent from their churches without grave cause, nor on every occasion: “lest, because of their absence, both the dangers to souls and the duties of the churches in which they have been appointed be neglected,” as Chrodegang writes in chapter 76 of the same rule. If a priest, through the fault of human weakness, leaves the church to whose title he has been attached without the knowledge of his own bishop, he is to be brought back to it and, if obstinate, deposed, as is clear from Book 6 of the Capitularies, chapters 59 and 85. Moreover, the church to whose title a priest has been attached may become vacant only because of death, crime, or such bodily illness as prevents the priest from fulfilling his duties. Indeed, chapter 17 of the Capitularies issued by Hincmar of Reims to priests in the year 852 clearly shows that priests then ordinarily remained in their churches until death. When this right had become greatly relaxed, as commonly happens, because of its antiquity, Urban II restored it at the Council of Nîmes, where this law was enacted in canon 11: “When priests are appointed to govern churches, let them receive the care of souls from the bishop’s hand, and there let them serve God throughout their entire lives, unless they are degraded by canonical judgment.” Hence, in addition to the other arguments available, it follows that a priest cannot leave his church except for a grave cause and with the permission of his own bishop. This was why Gerohaldus, a priest of Sens, who because of a serious eye disease could not perform his duty, asked Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, to be given a successor, as we shall note in the annotation to Letter 73. For it is unlawful for a priest to abandon pastoral care so long as the salvation of the sheep can be provided for, as Lupus teaches in this Letter 29. Thus the ancients judged that priests, whom we today call parish priests, had been established by God and would render an account of the souls entrusted to them to Christ, the supreme shepherd, as Leo IV says in a homily to priests. It is therefore all the more surprising that some contend that, before four hundred years ago, no priest was so bound to his church that the bishop was not permitted to remove him from it at will. They think their opinion is supported by a custom that has arisen in certain dioceses, where priests are sent by bishops to govern parishes on the condition that they may be removed whenever the bishop of the place wishes. Such priests are called removable vicars. Let those, then, go their way who degrade the dignity of priests to such an extent, contrary to the canons and the institutions of the ancients—priests who, as is evident, were not distinct from bishops in the ancient Church. The authority of bishops must indeed be preserved, so that priests may receive the care of souls from them and, if they do anything contrary to the rule, may be corrected by them. Nevertheless, due honor must be maintained for the rectors of parish churches, whom we today call parish priests. I have said that priests were once so bound to their churches that they could not leave them without the permission of their own bishops. This was said on the occasion of the two priests of Sens who were considering abandoning their churches in order to become monks. Wenilo, bishop of Sens, refused to give his consent until he had learned whether this was permitted. For the common law made it clear that no priest could leave his church, just as a husband may not leave his wife. Later Urban II opened the door of the monasteries, as Stephen of Tournai teaches in Letter 1: “Parish priests,” he says, “owe to their bishops the obedience which they promise, and they are sacramentally bound to the churches which they govern as to their own wives. By the common law of the canons, without the permission of their bishops, whom they are bound to obey, neither may they depart nor may others receive them. But by a private law, which is written in the heart through the prompting of the Holy Spirit, if they pass to a monastery or a regular canonry, such men may be received even when their bishops object. For Pope Urban says: ‘If anyone retains a people in his church under a bishop, but, inspired by the Holy Spirit, wishes to save himself in some monastery or regular canonry, let him go freely by our authority even if his bishop objects. For the law is not laid down for the just. But where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. And if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.’ Behold: neither the obedience promised to the bishop nor the church entrusted to the priest could prevent one who wished to pass to a better way of life.” I remarked there, in passing, that priests in the ancient Church—that is, in the period close to the apostles—were not distinct from bishops. I did not say this merely from my own opinion, but on the authority of Jerome and certain others, from whose view Augustine was not far removed. I am not unaware, however, that there was always a great distinction between the authority of bishops and that of priests, even though it is clear that the name was once common to both. Bishops succeeded the apostles, whereas priests succeeded the disciples. Theodoret, commenting on chapter 3 of the First Epistle to Timothy, says: “Formerly they called the same men both presbyters and bishops; but those who are now called bishops they called apostles. As time went on, however, they left the name ‘apostles’ to those who truly were apostles, and assigned the name ‘bishops’ to those who had formerly been called apostles.” Jerome, however, being a man of impetuous temperament who sought to defend his own rank from contempt, went further; and while attacking the arrogance of the deacons of his time in favor of the priests, he ran even to the point of insulting bishops, as though heated by youthful zeal. “The presbyter and the bishop are therefore the same,” he says in his commentary on the Epistle to Titus. “Before factions arose in religion at the instigation of the devil and it was said among the peoples, ‘I am of Paul,’ ‘I of Apollo,’ and ‘I of Cephas,’ the churches were governed by the common council of the presbyters. But afterward, when each person considered those whom he had baptized to be his own and not Christ’s, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one of the presbyters should be elected and placed over the others, to whom the entire care of the church would belong and by whom the seeds of schisms would be removed.” These words of Jerome must certainly be softened and understood in the sense that Jerome meant to say that the terms “bishops” and “priests” were once used interchangeably, although the dignity and authority of both were different. For Jerome himself, in his letter to Fabiola concerning the forty-two encampments, says that bishops succeeded the apostles, whereas priests succeeded the seventy disciples. Nor should it be supposed that the saintly man approved the madness of Aerius, who taught that priests were entirely like bishops. Jerome always and everywhere attributes certain things to bishops which he says are denied to priests. Yet he could have been vehement in his own cause, especially since he understood that the dignity of priests was so great and sublime that it approached the episcopate. Possidius reports in chapter 4 of his Life of Augustine that Augustine held this view.] Surely the one who calls these men to fulfill what we sing in the psalm—“Be still and know that I am God” (Psalm 45)—will provide others to be placed over the governance of souls.

“But,” he says, “just as a carnal union may not be dissolved except on account of fornication,” [Note: “On account of fornication.” Lupus therefore says that a carnal union may be dissolved on account of fornication. Sirmondus observes, in his note on Avitus’s Letter 49, that even in the time of Avitus it was still believed in Gaul that, because of fornication, a husband could separate from his wife and, with Christ’s permission, marry another; he cites canon 2 of the Council of Vannes. See also the letter of Magingozus, bishop of Würzburg, to Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, which is the eighty-seventh among the Bonifatian letters. See also Ivo of Chartres, Letter 18, and Gratian’s Decree 32, question 7.] so, once pastoral care has been undertaken, it is unlawful to lay it down so long as the salvation of the sheep can be provided for. [Note: “The salvation of the sheep.” Thus the old manuscript is entirely correct. For the reading in Masson’s edition is a furious error, where it is printed “the salvation of all.” The same error also occurred in the Apologeticus of the priest Orosius, where, immediately at the beginning, the printed editions commonly read: “I am compelled to point out the wolves caught in the flock of all”; better is the manuscript of the exceptionally good copy belonging to the celebrated Sorbonne college, formerly owned by the eminent cardinal Armand-Jean Richelieu, which the distinguished Nicolas Petitpied, doctor and fellow of the Sorbonne, shared with me with his singular courtesy. In that manuscript it is written: “I am compelled to point out the wolves caught in the flock of sheep.” Likewise, in the letter of Richard of Pophis, it is written: “How much more gravely I would grieve in every offense against the Lord,” whereas it should read: “How much more gravely I would grieve in the offense against the Lord’s sheep,” and so forth. From this, too, the reader may recognize how prone the ancient scribes were to this error.] We concede the point—unless perhaps the one who established the marriage himself dissolves it, and the one who imposed the governance himself, by a hidden inspiration, commands that it be abandoned so that he may be more freely devoted to himself. For the one who commanded that what God has joined together man should not separate, since he is God, has separated marriages whenever he wished; indeed, we know of many worthy persons of both sexes who, after breaking off carnal relations, served the Lord separately in sacred places.

But what shall I say about priests, when scarcely any monastery can be found into which some of them have not withdrawn, fleeing the turmoil of the world? If we attempt to assert that they acted wrongly, we shall be overwhelmed by the authority of those who surpass us in holiness and perhaps precede us in wisdom. For it was not written without reason: “The fear of the Lord is wisdom itself, and to depart from evil is understanding” (Job 28).

Indeed, to say nothing of marriages separated for the love of God, of which we have a great abundance, there was once a noble abbot and priest of the monastery of Ferrières, which I, unworthy, serve, [Note: “Sigulfus.” Abbot of the Canons of the monastery of Ferrières. Thus this abbot escaped the diligence of the Sammarthani, for they made no mention of him in their catalogue of the abbots of Ferrières. He succeeded Alcuin, whose disciple he had been, as will be written in the Life of Saint Aldric, archbishop of Sens, and likewise in the Life of Alcuin. I believe that he became abbot of Ferrières when Alcuin, exhausted by age and bodily illness, divided the monasteries entrusted to him among his disciples and withdrew to Saint Martin of Tours; this occurred before the year 804. Later Sigulfus himself, worn out by old age, resigned the governance of the monastery of Ferrières and transferred its administration to his disciple Adalbertus, as stated in the Life of Saint Aldric. This occurred under Louis the Pious, when Sigulfus changed the canonical habit for the monastic habit and allowed himself to be placed under his own disciple, namely Adalbertus, as Lupus says. The ancient author of the Life of Alcuin reports that this Sigulfus came from a noble family. It is therefore clear that the manuscript reading is the best: where Masson’s edition has “for us,” it gives “noble” in this place. The Life of Saint Aldric states that he was English by nationality. The author of Alcuin’s Life says that he was a man of refined intellect, and Alcuin himself calls him exceptionally devoted to sacred learning; for that reason Alcuin dedicated to him his Questions and Answers on the Book of Genesis. Hincmar mentions this work in chapter 27 of the later treatise against Gottschalk and in chapter 4 of the Epilogue.] Sigulfus, who until old age [Note: “In the canonical habit.” The meaning of this passage is as follows: Sigulfus, who throughout his life had been a canon, voluntarily abandoned this institution in order to become a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict; and all the Canons of Ferrières became monks with him. From this we infer that at that time the monastery of Ferrières was inhabited by Canons, not monks. In those days the designation “monasteries” included establishments of both Canons and monks. The monks throughout Gaul were for the most part committed to the Rule of Saint Benedict. The Canons, however, were bound by no definite law until the emperor Louis the Pious ordered a rule to be written according to which Canons should live; it was read and approved at the Council of Aachen in 816. We owe this information to Ademar of Chabannes, whose words are: “The emperor Louis the Pious went to Aachen to spend the winter, where, having held a council—that is, in the tenth indiction, in the third year of his reign, from the Incarnation in 816—he ordered a Rule to be made for the Canons, excerpted from various writings of the Fathers, and decreed that it be observed by the Canons; so that, just as monks look to the book of the Rule of Saint Benedict, so the Canons might read among themselves the book of the Life of the Clergy. The deacon Amalarius, commanded by the emperor, compiled this book from the opinions of various teachers. The emperor gave him access to the books in his palace so that he might extract from them whatever seemed appropriate. Thus, together with the decrees of the bishops who were present, the life of the clergy was strengthened.” For Louis, as the author of his Life teaches, “sent that book throughout all the cities and monasteries of his empire belonging to the canonical order by the hands of wise envoys, who were to have it copied in all the places mentioned above.” One of these envoys was Notho, whom Louis the Pious sent for this purpose to Arno, archbishop of Salzburg, as is clear from the same emperor’s letter to Arno, preserved in Goldast, volume 1 of the Imperial Constitutions, page 150, where this book is called the “Form of Canonical Institution.” That care of Louis, however, achieved little. Thus, when the Canons abandoned the rule as vices gained strength, many monasteries of Canons turned to monks and adopted their institution. The abbot Sigulfus and the Canons of the monastery of Ferrières were seized by a desire to abandon the canonical life and put on the monastic habit; and this holy ambition proceeded so far that Sigulfus also renounced the governance and administration of the monastery. At that time the authority of princes was supreme in such matters. Without them, not only could the status of sacred places not be changed, but they themselves sometimes, on their own authority, expelled Canons from monasteries in order to substitute monks, and later, if circumstances required, expelled the monks in order to restore the Canons. This can be proved by many examples. Nor was this right effective only in the kingdom of the Franks, but also among the English. Thus their king Edgar, who was living in the year 966, decreed: “Fearing, therefore, that I might incur eternal misery if, having obtained power, I failed to do what he himself—who does all that he wills in heaven and on earth—has shown by his examples to be the act of a just judge, I, the vicar of Christ, expelled bands of corrupt Canons from various monasteries of our realm; since they could not help me through any intercessions, but rather, as blessed Gregory says, provoked the vengeance of the just judge: contaminated by various stains of vice, they did not do what God commanded, but rebelled against everything he did not desire. As an eager investigator, I observed the bands of monks pleasing to the Lord, who would intercede for us without hesitation, and with devoted joy placed them in the monasteries under our jurisdiction.” See Selden’s notes on Eadmer, page CLV. Thus Sigulfus approached the emperor Louis the Pious so that he might obtain the fulfillment of his wish. Louis granted permission for a change of habit and rule, made monks out of the Canons, and appointed over Sigulfus and the others an abbot who had previously been a canon in the monastery of Ferrières—namely Adalbertus, Sigulfus’s former disciple—as we shall say below. Perhaps the author of Louis’s Life refers to this change when he says that the monastery of Ferrières was restored by him. Finally, in the eighth year after Louis’s death, the same change was carried out in the monastery of Saint Martial of Limoges. Ademar narrates the event as follows: “In the eighth year after the death of Lord Louis the emperor, in the year 848 from the Lord’s Incarnation, Ainardus the prince of the basilica of Saint Martial, together with all the other Canons, inspired by God, cast off secular weapons and changed themselves in the same monastery from the canonical habit into the habit of monks. For Charles the Bald held his general assembly at Limoges at that time, during Lent, with the bishops of Aquitaine and its leading men. While Charles the Bald was seated on the royal throne, Ainardus and all the Canons of Saint Martial suddenly prostrated themselves at his feet and asked him to grant them permission to become monks in that same place. The king, giving thanks to God, fulfilled their request with great joy and inclined all their bishops and leading men to their will. But Stodilus, bishop of Limoges, took the matter very badly and alone remained inflexible; at last, compelled by the king, he consented, overcome by gifts. The Canons did not wish at that time to have an abbot from among themselves, but appointed Odo, abbot of Saint Savin, over them.” Long afterward, Odolricus, abbot of Saint Martial, discussed this change, which had been made by royal authority, at the Council of Limoges. He is mistaken, however, in saying that it was carried out by Pippin and Charles, the sons of Louis the Pious. Thus, in the time of Louis the Pious, the Canons of Saint Denis, one of whom was Hincmar, converted themselves to the regular life and habit; that is, after laying aside the canonical habit, they became monks. Hincmar is a clear witness to this in Letter 26 to Pope Nicholas: “In the monastery,” he says, “where from the earliest beginnings of childhood I had been raised in the canonical habit, and from which I had been taken out and had spent a considerable time in the palace of Lord Louis the emperor, when the brothers in the monastery of Saint Denis, where I had been brought up, had converted themselves to the regular life and habit, I returned to it as a fugitive, without hope or desire of the episcopate or of any other preeminence, and remained there for a long time.” So, not to mention individual cases, the monastery of Saint Albinus at Angers had Canons before monks of Saint Benedict were established there. This was carried out in the year 966 by Geoffrey Grisegonelle, count of Anjou—at the command, naturally, of King Lothair, as the author of the Chronicle of Saint Albinus edited by Labbe teaches—as he himself bears witness in volume 6 of Dacher’s Spicilegium, page 422: “In the aforesaid monastery of Saint Albinus,” he says, “the perfection of the monastic order, the canonical congregation having been removed—a congregation which until then had devoted itself there not to divine gains but to its own worldly gains.” Then Nefingus, bishop of Angers, at the request of Count Geoffrey and Abbot Albertus, granted privileges to the monks, which had previously been possessed by the Canons; Nefingus himself bears witness to this in the following charter, which now appears for the first time from the cartulary of Saint Albinus: “In the name of God. I, Nefingus, unworthy priest of the church of Angers, to all orthodox faithful, and so forth. Let our successors know, therefore, that the church of blessed Albinus, founded before the gate of the city of Angers toward the east by Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, through the will and command of King Childebert, had obtained from antiquity certain privileges above the other churches of Angers, namely, the status of a royal abbey. For it is one of the royal abbeys. Lord Geoffrey, a most powerful count, and Albertus, abbot of the same church, therefore came into the presence of our humility, humbly requesting that the privileges which had formerly been obtained by the Canons of that church might also be transferred and confirmed by our authority for the brothers now serving God there according to the rule. We, wishing to exalt the holy order, did this most willingly. These privileges are as follows: the Epistle and the Gospel in our ordinations, if brothers from that church are to be ordained; the Gospel on Palm Sunday; absolution on Good Friday; and our station on the second feria of Easter; immunity, so that for any matter or offense …” The rest is missing.] lived laudably in the canonical habit, voluntarily stripped himself of his authority, assumed our religion—that is, the monastic one—and, until the day of his death, [Note: “To his disciple.” Adalbertus. While Alcuin was alive, he had been Sigulfus’s disciple and afterward had remained attached to him. Without doubt he became a monk when Louis the Pious appointed him abbot of the monastery of Ferrières. When Adalbertus finally died, Aldricus—who, as is clear from the Life of Alcuin, had also been Sigulfus’s disciple with him—became abbot of Ferrières, having previously been a canon and a monk there.] allowed himself to be placed under his disciple, [Col. 0486A] whom the emperor Louis, at his own request and with the consent of the brothers, had appointed abbot of that place. [Note: “Had appointed abbot.” By common law, all monasteries at that time were under the power of kings. Concerning the monasteries of Septimania, Louis the Pious testifies in a charter for the monastery of Saint Grata in the diocese of Urgell, an authentic copy of which we saw brought from the archives of the church of Urgell: “The aforesaid bishop Possedonius, through our faithful Matfredus, suggested that we receive under our power, indeed under our protection and lordship, the monastery which the same bishop had rebuilt, called Saint Grata, situated on the river Bosegia and dedicated in honor of holy Mary, the ever-virgin Mother of God; and that the monks and the possessions belonging to that place should be our own in the same way as the other monasteries within Septimania are acknowledged to be ours.” Richerius, in Book 1, chapter 16 of his Chronicle of Sens, teaches that the monasteries of Germany were subject to the same right. Chapter 8 of Book 2 of the Capitularies, chapter 181 of Book 5, and the Second Council of Aachen, held in the year 836, provide ample evidence concerning all the monasteries of the kingdom. Its words in chapter 9, addressed to the same Louis the Pious, are: “Likewise we ask that, in appointing abbesses and rectors of monasteries, you take special care to avoid danger, as has often been said to you and repeatedly made clear through divine authority.” Likewise, the bishops of the provinces of Reims and Rouen, in a letter written in the year 858 to Louis, king of Germany, residing at the palace of Attigny: “Command firmly and earnestly also that the rectors to whom you entrust monasteries,” and so forth. Thus whenever the abbot of a monastery had died or withdrawn from administration, the king appointed another in his place by his own authority, without anyone objecting. There are almost innumerable examples of this right, supported by the testimony of councils and bishops, should anyone require them. Yet the testimony of Charlemagne must not be omitted; it reads: “Concerning monasteries and hospitals which appear to be located under various counts, let them be royal possessions; and whoever wishes to possess them shall hold them as a benefice granted by the king.” What is written here is “counts” for “counties.” A county in this passage is the same as a district. Hence “count of the district” occurs in Lupus’s Letter 24. Thus Charles decrees that the monasteries situated throughout the various counties of the Frankish kingdom should be royal possessions, so that no one could be abbot there except one to whom the king had given the abbey. In time, however, our kings transferred that right to the monks, but on the condition that they were not permitted to choose as abbot anyone other than one who had long demonstrated his character in the monastic profession. For only the prince possessed the authority to entrust monasteries to secular persons. The grant of the right of election was commonly expressed in these words: “And whenever divine piety shall have taken the aforesaid abbot from this light, so long as the monks themselves are able to choose from among themselves men capable of governing that congregation according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, let them have permission, with our consent and command, to elect abbots from among themselves.” You see, reader, that the law imposed upon the monks required that the abbot be chosen entirely from the monks of that same monastery, and indeed one who was equal to the burden. Everyone can see that this is a condition of the privilege: if the stipulated safeguard cannot be observed, the matter must return to its original author. Yet the prosperity of succeeding ages was such that it always produced distinguished men suited to carry out this ministry. Consequently, it was not necessary for our kings to draw the administration of monasteries back to themselves. Finally, because the reservations of the Roman Curia seemed intolerable, our kings once again, under the fortunate auspices of Francis I, assumed responsibility for monasteries. For the right our kings exercise in nominating abbots is not to be referred to a privilege granted by the Roman pontiff, even though it might appear on the surface that it ought to be sought from that source. Only the ancient authority of princes was restored—an authority they themselves had voluntarily surrendered in favor of the monks. But the injustice of the times required that what arose from ancient law be ascribed to a privilege. The testimony of Louis the Pious must nevertheless not be omitted; these are his words in Book 1 of the Capitularies, chapter 86: “How, with God’s help, we have in part arranged the affairs of the monks; how we have granted them permission to choose abbots for themselves from among themselves; and how, with God’s help, we have ordered that they be able to live in peace and preserve their purpose without weariness, we have caused to be carefully recorded in another document, and we have confirmed it so that it might be valid among our successors and preserved inviolate.” When he says that he provided for the peace of the monks, he means the freedom he granted to the monasteries, so that they might be free…
namely, that they were free from the authority of the bishops. For in those turbulent times, as we said above, the liberty of the monasteries depended upon the will of the princes. The authority of the Apostolic See was then invoked more rarely. Nevertheless, not long afterward exemptions granted to monasteries by the supreme pontiffs began to become frequent. Following the example of the kings, these pontiffs extended their protection and defense to the monasteries, so as to free them from the authority of the bishops, as has been said in the note to Epistle 13. This is to be understood with respect to observance of the Rule and the administration of the monastery’s property. For matters involving violation of the canons were reserved to episcopal judgment, as we said above. Moreover, monks could not leave the monastery or depart for a distant region without the bishop’s permission, as was stated in the note to Epistle 102.]

[He] had appointed the abbot. ^55^ Indeed, your predecessor, Aldricus, of blessed memory—

[Note: Aldricus. When he was abbot of Ferrières, he was made archbishop of Sens at the command of the Emperor Louis the Pious, as Lupus writes. This occurred in the year 829, when Jeremias, archbishop of Sens, died. The Chronicle of Saint Peter of Sens says: “When Archbishop Jeremias died on the seventh day before the Ides of December and was buried in the basilica of Saint Columba, Saint Aldricus, abbot of Saint Peter of Ferrières, by the divine will assumed the episcopal see, while Louis the Pious was still alive.”

Among the letters of Frotarius, bishop of Toul, there is also a letter—if I am not mistaken, by this same Aldricus—to Frotarius, in which he laments his lot. Although he had formerly embraced the monastic way of life in order to live for himself, he had nevertheless later become abbot because the monks compelled him, and now, although unequal to so great a burden and thinking of nothing less than such an office, he was a bishop. He therefore asks Frotarius to assist him with his prayers before God and to obtain from Him virtues worthy of a bishop.

Meanwhile, the words of Clarius the monk, author of the Chronicle of Saint Peter of Sens, deserve notice. What Lupus says was done at the emperor’s command, Clarius attributes to the divine will, saying that Aldricus assumed the episcopal see by divine will. This would lead us to understand that the authority then possessed by princes came from heaven. Hence, in canon 3 of the synod held at Thionville in the year 844, it is written that bishops are given by God, regularly designated by the princes then ruling—namely, the sons of Louis the Pious—and consecrated by the grace of the Holy Spirit. See the notes to Epistle 98.

But to return to Aldricus: he died in the year 841, on the sixth day before the Ides of October, and was succeeded by Wenilo. He had determined—as Lupus writes, and likewise the ancient author of Aldricus’s Life—to return to the monastery and lay aside his episcopal duties if he had lived longer. For the memory of the past returned to him, and in a man who loved monastic quiet above all, complaints and tears doubtless sometimes broke forth: although he could scarcely suffice for himself, he was nevertheless compelled to divide his mind among many cares. He considered those especially fortunate and blessed who, far from episcopal dignity and far from the dangers of the world, lived a tranquil and blameless life in monasteries, troubled about the salvation of no one except under the universal law of charity, and accountable to God for no soul other than their own.

For this reason he was considering abandoning pastoral care, if the canons had permitted it, so that he might serve God more freely and work out his salvation. But because the canons forbade this on account of the danger to souls, he wished to provide for the difficulty by seeking a successor who would be equal to the burden and could be ordained in his place. In the midst of these plans, the holy man was carried away by unavoidable necessity. Who can perish in such a way and be extinguished?]

Aldricus, who, at the command of the aforementioned emperor and through the remarkable efforts of good men, was taken from us while he was abbot and made bishop of the Church of Sens, had firmly resolved to return to us, setting aside the episcopal office; but instead—as we believe—he exchanged this life for a happier one. Who could say that these men were ignorant of the canons, unless he himself were first senseless? Indeed, they were recalling the beginnings of the Christian faith. The blessed Luke, commending them, shows that at that time everything was held in common: after each person had allowed the apostles to distribute the prices of their fields and of every kind of possession according to each person’s need, they devoted themselves to God alone, and they had one heart and one soul in the Lord.

Nor do I find that priests were excluded from this holy fellowship. The evangelist mentioned above, foreseeing that we too should be instructed by this example, says: “A great number of priests obeyed the faith” (Acts 6).

[Note: A great number of priests. Here Lupus uses rhetorical argument to show that the purpose of Ardegarius and Baldricus was holy, bringing forward Luke’s testimony in chapter 6 of the Acts of the Apostles, where it is written that many priests embraced the faith of Christ: “A great number of priests,” he says, “were obedient to the faith.” Those priests who, spurning their former religions, devoted themselves to the faith of Christ are certainly worthy of praise. This is the highest form of piety. Ardegarius and Baldricus, therefore, would have deserved praise if they had previously been priests of false gods and had then sought to be incorporated into the body of Christ, which is the Church.

In Jerome’s letter to Heliodorus there is a notable passage in which that great man teaches that anyone who wishes to follow Christ must proceed even by trampling upon his father: “Although,” he says, “a little nephew may hang upon your neck; although your mother may display the breasts that nourished you, with her hair disheveled and her garments torn; although your father may lie across the threshold—trample upon your father and proceed; with dry eyes fly to the banner of the cross. In this matter, the only kind of piety is to be cruel.”

Erasmus of Rotterdam applies this passage very aptly to our subject: “It seems to me that Jerome also somewhat twists this passage to serve his own purpose. For it applies when pagan parents forbid someone to become a Christian—not when one abandons parents who perhaps need one’s assistance and hides oneself in a desert or monastery, although one could live a Christian life among Christian parents, provided that one purifies the mind of worldly affections. Such a distortion is acceptable in exhortation or deterrence. But others everywhere and in earnest twist everything said about the world—that is, about worldly life—into an argument about the common life of Christians; and what is said about following Christ they apply to the monastic life.”

Thus Lupus, employing rhetorical license, diverted this passage from Luke, which speaks of priests who were not yet Christians, to Christian presbyters, so that by a pious deception he might extract Wenilo’s consent. I do not say this in order that anyone may suppose that I condemn those who become monks, but to show how much some of the ancients occasionally believed themselves permitted to do whenever an opportunity arose to draw people away from the errors of the world. For I myself believe that very many become both wiser and holier in monasteries, and I would not wish to turn anyone away from that purpose—especially if someone embraces the institution of Saint Benedict, as Ardegarius and Baldricus were contemplating doing. Benedict is the Father of monks, from whom the other monastic institutions in the West received their form of life, as I think is sufficiently well known.]

“As I have said, a great number of priests obeyed the faith” (Acts 6). Although we are as far as possible from the perfection of such holy men, nevertheless we retain their traces and, so to speak, certain outlines of the apostolic form of life: none of us claims anything for himself, nor is he permitted to dissipate his mind in worldly concerns; rather, we are constrained by the rigor of the Rule, to which we have freely subjected ourselves, to fulfill the prescribed order of prayer and abstinence.

[Note: Many monks. Even at that time, therefore, some monks were bringing monastic life into disrepute and, by their conduct, had made certain devout men conclude that the monastic life was no holier—or even worse—than the life of other Christians. Lupus rightly warns that the rest should not be judged by the lives of those wicked monks. The devil, after all, is always eager to sow weeds among the good seed.]

Nor should you be surprised; rather, as a bishop, you should sympathize if you have found many monks shamefully deviating from their profession, since human nature is inclined toward evil and our enemy is always eager to sow weeds over the good seed. Nevertheless, in my opinion and that of many others, there is no order within the holy Church in which a faithful soul can more surely merit God’s favor than by devoting itself to monastic discipline and observing its purpose with integrity.

But lest we seem to praise ourselves excessively, the blessed Gregory, whose authority shines so greatly in the Church, commends our father Benedict in these words (Gregory, *Dialogues*, book 3, chapter 36): “He wrote a Rule for monks, distinguished by its discretion and eloquent in expression.”

Saint Benedict shows that priests both can and ought to be received into a monastery. Although he does not make entry easy for them, he nevertheless permits it; and he grants them authority to retain their office at the abbot’s command. He would certainly not do this if only criminals were to be admitted.

[Note: Criminals to be admitted. He is speaking specifically of criminal presbyters, whom several synods had decreed should be confined to monasteries to perform penance. There is nothing, however, to prevent us from saying that other wicked people as well were received into monasteries, for monasteries were harbors of repentance.

This is confirmed by the authority of Pope Zacharias, whose words in his letter to Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, are as follows: “These ministers of Satan, therefore, and not of Christ, wherever you find them, dearest to us, having gathered the provincial and priestly assembly, avoid them entirely; and once they have been deprived of priestly honor and subjected to the monastic Rule and to penance, you shall arrange for them to end their lives.”

Among the Essenes, an ancient kind of monastic community in Judea, no one guilty of any offense, however slight, was admitted, as Solinus testifies in chapter 38: “For whoever is guilty even of a slight fault, although he may wish with all his might to obtain entry, is divinely excluded.”]

For we do sometimes receive even such men, but only with the greatest difficulty and when they are deeply contrite. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost (Matthew 18).

Since the blessed Gregory approves the Rule of our father Benedict, and since that same Rule judges that priests should be received together with their office, unless one is afflicted by a contentious spirit, he certainly does not doubt that priests of upright life have been received into our order from its very beginning. Therefore, may your fatherly dignity deign to consider these matters with particular care, and may you not hesitate to open an avenue of permission to priests who are striving for a better state from a good one—

[Note: Toward a better state from a good one. That is, from the clerical state to monasticism. Yet above we saw that Innocent I calls the clerical state a better rank in comparison with the monastic life. For this reason, the ancients used to choose for the clergy from among those who remained in the monastery “only the more proven and better men,” as Augustine teaches in his letter 76 to Aurelius. That supremely wise monk Jerome, writing to Heliodorus, says: “The case of monks is one thing, that of clerics another. Clerics feed the sheep; I am fed.”

This also greatly pleased Pope Urban II, who by a law prohibited “any canon who had regularly professed the canonical life from becoming a monk, unless—God forbid—he had publicly fallen,” and imposed a penalty upon those who resisted. This decree is found in Gratian, *Decretum* 19, question 3, and also in the first letter of Stephen of Tournai and in the *Collection of Canons* of Anselm of Lucca, a copy of which, transcribed from an old Vatican manuscript, Dom Lucas Dacherius, a Benedictine monk, recently showed me. It has not yet been published.

That canons are the same persons who are also called clerics is clear from chapter 73 of the first book of the *Capitularies*. Finally, we infer that the clerical state was considered the better rank from the fact that, at the Synod of Chalon, criminal presbyters were sent down to monasteries to perform penance. See the letter of Ivo of Chartres, number 36, and Francis Florens, book 2 of *Dissertations on Canon Law*, p. 198.]

—lest perhaps, which we emphatically do not wish, you should appear to diminish the divinely provided increase of our order, which the highest and best pontiffs not only have not brought into disrepute but, as was fitting, have adorned with their praises and heaped with their exhortations.

For, as far as we have been able to discern, the judgment of the sacred canons nowhere weakens our position. We have taken care to strengthen it both by divine authority and by distinguished examples. ^57^ We shall obtain this above all from your excellence: that you do not take offense at our admonition. It is evident enough, I think, both from the weight of the matter and from the gentleness of our style, that we have undertaken it not from a desire to display knowledge but in fulfillment of the duty of charity.

## LETTER XXX. [Note: [Col. 0492D] To Gotteschalcus. This man was famous in the age of Lupus and Hincmar and consequently provided much material for people’s conversations. His memory has been especially revived during the past twenty years because of the teaching of Jansenius, bishop of Ypres. R. P. Cellotius of the Society of Jesus set forth the history of Gotteschalcus in a substantial volume; he devoted very great effort to it and brought forward many new observations not unworthy of learned men’s curiosity. In this letter Lupus discusses the beatific vision and how it comes about. Hincmar of Rheims treated the same subject at length in Letter 3, chapter 8, where he also cites a passage from Augustine’s *City of God*, Book XXII, chapter 29. See Alcuin, *Confession of Faith*, Book III, if it is indeed Alcuin’s.] TO GOTTESCHALCUS THE MONK.

If I had not feared that, by thinking me turned away from the practice of charity and incapable of being moved by anyone’s prayers, you would offend that same charity, I would even now, while still sheltering in the hiding-place of silence [Col. 0491C], have answered nothing concerning the matters on which you consulted me, for two reasons.

The first was that I might not either lessen or take away from your leisure the material for exercising your intellect. The second was that, after considering those whom I once learned that you had troubled with this same question, I might show that my mediocrity did not prejudice the excellence of certain others, as established by their own estimation [Col. 0492A].

But now that I have obtained both their conversation and their written reply, you wish to discover what I think about the matter, since differing in one’s opinion about the same questions, so long as one does not oppose the faith, is either no fault or only a slight one.

I shall not hesitate to explain what the most blessed and most learned Augustine seemed to me to think in the passage that you proposed for interpretation.

Let the earlier question be entirely set aside. Since it could scarcely, or not at all, be settled by examples or testimonies from the divine Scriptures, he left it open: namely, whether, at that summit of resurrection so desired by all the faithful, the eyes of the flesh will possess anything resembling the mind. For if we could even imagine that we might apprehend, with some keenness of mind, future images of things that have surpassed the understanding of so great an author [Col. 0492B], that would be the height of madness.

Nor will anything be taken away from our happiness in that resurrection if the excellence of divinity is not visible to bodily eyes. For we do not now feel that we suffer any loss of understanding because we cannot touch with our hand the reason that we contemplate with the sharpness of the mind—something incorporeal.

Nor will our nature suffer anything unworthy if the spirit is endowed with a far higher excellence. From the very beginning of our birth, the spirit has so greatly excelled that the image of God has always remained in it, although for a time discolored because of sin, and the flesh, brought into one and the same person with it, has been governed by it [Col. 0492C].

[Note: [Col. 0492D] The image of God. Here Lupus places the image of God, which is said to exist in man, in the soul. See what we note below concerning the book *On Three Questions*.]

Let us instead carefully consider the words with which that same pre-eminent author prudently moderated the second question, and examine their meaning.

> “Or, to make it easier to understand, God will be known and conspicuous to us in such a way that he will be seen by the spirit of each of us in each of us, seen by one in another, seen in himself, seen in the new heaven and the new earth, and in every creature that will then exist” (*The City of God*, Book XXII, chapter 29) [Col. 0493A].

Thus far I do not see what obscurity these words produce. Indeed, the very lucid author, because he was most attentive to divine authority, explains more fully how God will be all in all: namely, that divine grace will raise the elect to equality with the angels, remove the cloud of their former ignorance, fully reveal God himself to them, and make them eternally blessed through his ineffable vision. He will gladden them with such manifest evidence of his presence that each spirit will be unable to doubt that God exists in us and in all the other saints, and also in every creature.

Thus God glorifies only the rational creature through knowledge of himself; but the irrational creature—that is, earth and heaven—he, wholly present everywhere, contains and governs [Col. 0493B]. Accordingly, he will be present to the rational creature through knowledge and presence, and to the irrational through presence alone. Yet this presence will be brought far more excellently than now within the knowledge of the elect, producing not only an increase of knowledge but also an increase of happiness.

Even now, by his presence, he governs heaven and earth, whose truthful word is: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah XXIII). But our mind’s vision grows dim when it tries to comprehend how he is wholly in heaven and wholly on earth, so long as “the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul” (Wisdom IX), preventing it from freely exercising the power of its nature.

When the body has been freed not only from the burden but even from the suspicion of all corruption—its nature glorified, not changed—for he who said, “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke XXIV), has not allowed us to err in this matter [Col. 0493C—Col. 0493D]—then it will possess such harmony with the spirit, which now resists it, that thereafter it will neither wish nor be able to sin with it.

Then the same spirit, truly cleaving to its God and becoming one with him, will deserve to behold its indweller and the ruler of creatures like itself, and the governor of all the rest.

This is the vision in which secure happiness and happy security will both be established. To behold it, Truth commands that the eyes be cleansed—not the eyes of the body, but those of the heart, that is, of the mind:

> “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew V).

Faith begins this purification here; charity completes it there.

For as long as our affection is able to say to God, “What have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Psalm LXXII)—that is, as long as we place the hope of our happiness in the power of some heavenly creature or in worldly excellence and allurements, rather than in God, by whom we were created—we suffer from a thick cataract drawn across our eyes.

But when those things begin, through God’s mercy, gradually to seem worthless which previously either deceived our mind perniciously through the falsity of opinions or delighted it with deceptive sweetness, and when the darkness has slowly faded, our sight is restored and is daily sharpened by the collyrium of the divine commandments, until, laying down the burden of mortality, it is led to see him toward whom all its attention had been transferred [Col. 0494A].

After speaking at some length about the foregoing words and their meaning—not as we wished, but as we were able, since the reality they signify is incomprehensible—the same wondrous author added (Augustine, same work):

> “And through bodies in every body, wherever the sight of the spiritual body’s eyes may be directed” [Col. 0494B].

Here no one even slightly instructed in secular literature doubts that something must be supplied from the common construction: “and that he may be seen by the spirit through bodies in every body.”

For Augustine himself most plainly excludes the opinion that God might be seen by bodily eyes unless they receive something belonging to the mind.

What he wished to be understood by the words “through bodies in every body” could be investigated with excessive precision, unless he had first prepared the matter by means of a certain comparison.

He had prefaced the statement as follows:

> “Each person knows his own life”—clearly meaning the spirit—“by which he now lives in the body, gives strength to these earthly limbs, and makes them living, through the inner sense, not through bodily eyes. But the lives of others, although they are invisible, he sees through the body. For how do we distinguish living bodies from nonliving ones unless we see both the bodies and the lives at the same time, although we cannot see those lives except through the body?” (Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XXII, chapter 29) [Col. 0494C].

From this very clear statement we gather that God will be seen “through bodies”—that is, through the eyes of the body—“in every body” that those eyes behold. He will not be seen in his substance, a privilege reserved for the spirit, but in the most evident presence of his governance.

For when, through our bodily senses, we observe the lives of others in their bodies, we do not see invisible lives; nevertheless, we cannot doubt that they are present through the power of giving life [Col. 0494D].

Nor will the eyes suffer any insult if, while the spirit comprehends God as present everywhere, they can behold him only in the bodies toward which they direct their gaze, as I have shown above. Just so, they do not suffer any dishonor now when the sense of hearing receives some sweetest sound and is itself confined within the limits of its proper function.

The understanding of the passage that I have presented will free you from all the difficulties of the questions you proposed. Among other things, it will make clear that God will not be conspicuous in any body to eyes that possess nothing resembling the mind—neither literally nor figuratively.

For the dignity of the spirit will claim for itself the literal knowledge of God. But anyone who thinks soberly will easily recognize that the statement signifies nothing except that the divine majesty will govern its creatures so evidently that it cannot even remain hidden from bodily eyes [Col. 0495A].

The surrounding circumstances, considered without superstitious obstinacy, lead the cautious and well-instructed reader to this conclusion. It is so clear to me that I believe even the most blessed Augustine, if he were to return to life, would be greatly astonished that anyone had thought otherwise.

Therefore, always paying and never fully discharging the debt of charity, I exhort you, most honored brother, not to wear out your intellect any further on such matters, lest, occupied with them beyond what is fitting, you become less capable of investigating or teaching things more useful.

Why should we seek so intensely what perhaps it is not yet expedient for us to know? Certainly, the mind enlightened by God speaks to God:

> “The eye has not seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who await you” (Isaiah LXIV).

And yet we desire, with a mind still weighed down by the accumulated filth of vices, to grasp the fullest account of that ineffable vision?

For the present, let us walk about in the broadest field of the holy Scriptures. Let us devote ourselves wholly and entirely to their meditation, and let us seek the face of the Lord humbly, devoutly, and continually, because those who seek the Lord “shall not lack any good thing” (Psalm XXXIII).

It will belong to his mercy, while we refrain from seeking things higher than us after considering our condition, and from investigating matters too difficult, to raise us to things more sublime and more powerful. When the sight of our mind has been purified—the sight to which he revealed that he could be seen—may he deign to show himself to us [Col. 0495B].

As for whether, after the resurrection, he will give the eyes anything resembling the mind, let us leave it to his judgment, whose decision permits us, while we live as mortals, to remain ignorant without penalty of this and countless other matters.

Somebody had slipped the quire that you found beneath my papers. As for the words whose explanation you requested, since the complete answer to all of them did not immediately occur to me, and since the great mass of affairs with which I am constantly overwhelmed prevented me from investigating them, I have postponed them to another time. I am not unaware, however, that the proper meanings of Greek words should rather be expected from Greeks.

Certainly, if you ever decide to write to my insignificance, I beg you not to burden me with excessive or false praises. Rather, pray to the Lord for me, that he may always make me desirous of his praise, and defer the fruit of praise from me until that time when praise will come to each person from him [Col. 0495C].

## LETTER XXXI. TO GUENILO, BISHOP.

To Guenilo, a distinguished prelate worthy of the highest reverence, Lupus sends his most cordial greetings.

When I was setting out for the king, I had first sent to inquire what he wished me to do. He had ordered me to meet him at the monastery of that illustrious confessor on the feast of blessed Martin. But since public business had drawn him elsewhere, I again sent messengers through friends and obtained, with his favor, permission to return.

As our messengers reported, the reason why our lord the king did not proceed to Saint Martin, as he had arranged, was that the Bretons, who had fallen into unusual disagreement among themselves, summoned our king toward Brittany, so that the party opposed to Nomenoius might safely defect to him [Col. 0496A].

[Note: [Col. 0495C] Nomenoius. The duke of the Bretons. After the death of Louis the Pious he had joined Charles the Bald, but later rebelled and dared to aspire to the kingdom in Brittany, persuaded by Lambert, count of Nantes. Charles bore this badly, unwilling to tolerate a rival in his kingdom. Accordingly, taking advantage of the dissensions that had broken out among the Bretons—one party favoring Nomenoius and the other rising against him—he set out for Brittany in order to join himself to Nomenoius’s enemies. The event is shown to have occurred in the year 846 by the chronicle of Ademar: “Charles,” he says, “proceeding again to Brittany, fought with the duke Nomenoius and emerged victorious. But Nomenoius escaped by flight.”] [Col. 0495D]

Nothing certain was being said at court about Pippin, concerning whom Your Paternity had inquired. Rumor merely suggested that those who had recently defected from him would return to an agreement with him.

Some who had come from Aquitaine reported that the Northmen had made an incursion in those days between Bordeaux and Saintes, and that our men—that is, the Christians—had engaged them in battle on foot and had been miserably slaughtered, except for those whom flight could save [Col. 0496B]. They also testified under oath that the duke of the Basques, Siguinus, had been captured in that battle and killed.

[Note: [Col. 0495D] Siguinus. From this too we learn that this letter was written in the year 846. For Ademar confirms that in that year Siguinus, count of Bordeaux, or duke of the Basques, as Lupus calls him, was killed by the Northmen, in these words: “In the following year, Siguinus, count of Bordeaux and Saintes, was captured and killed by the Northmen.” Siguinus, duke of the Basques, is also mentioned in Einhard’s *Annals* under the year 816.]

How true this report is, the Lord’s saying indicates: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated” (Luke XI); and it shows what reward awaits those who embrace discord.

We wish you good health.

## LETTER XXXII. TO LOUIS.

To his most desired Louis, supreme among abbots, Lupus sends present and future salvation.

It cannot be said how greatly I was recently afflicted when, amid the calamity of the state, treacherous rumor happily spread the report that you too had fallen among the others. To speak the truth, no day would ever have taken this grief from me except the day that took away my final breath [Col. 0496C].

But when I learned the truth, I exulted, as was fitting, with inexplicable joy that he was alive with whom, if I could and if it were necessary, I would gladly divide my years, in the words of Horace:

> “I would gladly divide my years with you.”

[Note: [Col. 0496C] “I would divide my years.” Lupus uses this Horatian mode of expression to show Louis the abundance of his affection for him. Muretus, the illustrious ornament of my homeland, observed in Book IX, chapter 1, of his *Various Readings* [Col. 0496D] that among all the forms of speech by which the ancients expressed an extraordinary force of love toward someone, this one appears to excel: they indicated that, if it could somehow be done, they wished to combine and share with the person they loved the years allotted to them for living, so that whatever remained of life for themselves might be added to that person’s life.]

Therefore, dearest of all, I give immense thanks to almighty God for preserving you for me; by preserving you, he preserved me as well.

Moreover, grieving over the adversity of our lord the king and rejoicing beyond measure at his deliverance, like that Gospel widow who put two small coins into the treasury, I have sent you whatever gift I was able to obtain, to be offered through you. Please deign to make it acceptable to him, as you see that it is expedient for me [Col. 0497A].

[Note: [Col. 0496D] The king’s adversity. In this letter, as also in the following one, Lupus discusses the defeat that had befallen Charles the Bald. It was so great that Charles was reported to have been struck down in battle, together with Abbot Louis, to whom this letter was written. It is therefore clear that the matter here is the victory won by the Bretons against Charles the Bald in the year 845. The *Annals of Fulda* report: “Charles engaged the Bretons, and, after great loss to his army, scarcely escaped with a few men.”]

[Note: [Col. 0497C] Whatever gift. In the kingdom of the Franks, during those times there were certain monasteries that owed gifts and military service to the king, as is clear from an old *Notice* published by Sirmond in Volume III of the *Councils of Gaul*, later reprinted by Duchesne. The same is taught by the anonymous author of the *Annals of Aniane*, who writes: “There were also certain monasteries among them that performed gifts and military service.” Ferrières was among these, as we learn from the same *Notice* and from Lupus’s letters. This meant, I think, that each year those monasteries were burdened with the necessity of offering gifts to the ruler, as well as with the expense of great emergencies.

Thus Charles’s distressed circumstances demanded the customary gifts from Lupus. Besides those monasteries that owed the king gifts and military service, there were others bound to gifts alone, without military service. Finally, some owed “neither gifts nor military service, but only prayers for the safety of the emperor or his sons and for the stability of the empire.”

Among these, in addition to those mentioned in the *Notice* cited above, was Tutela in the Limousin, as Ademar, viscount of the Stairs and lay abbot of the monastery of Tutela, confirms in his testament: “The monks,” he says, “are under the king’s protection for safeguarding the place, not for paying anything, except only prayers.”

Bernard, count of Périgord, confirms the same concerning Sarlat in Périgord, in these words. After stating that he wished to restore that monastery, he says: “Therefore I hand over the aforesaid place to Lords Odo and Adacius, abbots, and to the monks whom they have brought there or will gather there, so that they and their successors may hold both the monastery and the whole abbey without any contradiction, and, after their departure, may choose and appoint for themselves whatever abbot they wish according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. Let those monks also be subject to the king for safeguarding the place, and not for paying anything, except only prayers” [Col. 0498C].

As an incidental point, the abbots Odo and Adacius are to be understood as Odo and Adacius, who jointly governed the monastery of Tutela, as we noted in the addition to Book VIII of *On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire*, chapter 25. It follows that the monastery of Sarlat was then subject to the monastery of Tutela and was a colony of the monastery of Tutela.

Count Bernard distinguishes between the monastery and the abbey for the reason that the property of the old abbey belonged to him, while the monastery was then being newly built to receive monks. Thus Ademar, viscount of the Stairs, distinguished the monastery of Tutela into the old abbey and the monastery [Col. 0498D].

In England too there were certain monasteries free and exempt from all secular services, as Ingulph, abbot of Croyland, teaches. His monastery enjoyed that liberty.]

I said that I had faithfully sent everything I had been able to find because, owing to the frequent service imposed on us by him—something previously not demanded from my predecessors—together with the withdrawal of our cell and an unprecedented shortage of grain, everything has now been exhausted. The brothers have already been supported for a full month by purchased grain and must live on it until the new harvest; nor have the supplies prepared for common use been sufficient. Under the pressure of unavoidable necessity, a very few vessels and the other ornaments of our church are being sold, to everyone’s sorrow.

Your prudence sees, even without my warning, where this situation leads and how greatly it can impede the prosperity of the state [Col. 0497B].

Therefore I humbly implore your piety to disclose my needs and those of the brothers to the king—indeed, our genuine misery—and to suggest that he deign at last to alter what he did against Saint Peter and us, at the greatest peril to himself. Let him remember the vow by which he bound himself this year, so that he may have the prince of the apostles as a helper in his doubtful affairs and may be able to have all of us as intercessors from the heart.

[Note: [Col. 0498D] This year. That is, the year 845, as we have said. From this we learn that the vow which, at Hincmar’s urging, Charles the Bald conceived at Saint-Denis—as Lupus testifies in Letter 42—was made in the year 845.]

For he ought not to despise the prayers of the servants of the Lord, since it is said of any one just man: “The persistent prayer of a just man is very powerful” (James V); and the sacred psalm sings concerning several worshipers of the Lord: “He will do the will of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayer” (Psalm CXLIV).

You must also carefully admonish him not only concerning the restoration of our monastery but concerning the condition of the whole Church, lest, God forbid, he be compelled to leave to us, lamenting, and to its enemies, both hidden and manifest, mocking, the Church whole as he received it but divided [Col. 0497C—Col. 0498A].

Would that what God threatens his despisers might not befall him:

> “Affliction alone will give understanding to those who hear” (Isaiah XXVIII).

Nor should he experience what the Apostle says:

> “It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews X).

In the Aquitanian expedition, as you know, I once lost everything.

[Note: [Col. 0498D] In the preceding year. That is, the year 844. At that time Lupus served as an envoy in Burgundy at the command of King Charles.]

The preceding year, when I was sent to Burgundy, I lost ten. Now the poverty I mentioned weighs upon us.

I also wish, if it pleases God, to teach what I have learned and am always learning. If he wishes to summon me to the royal court, I ask you to bring these matters before the king—apart from the last, since he would judge that one useless to the state, although in my judgment it is the most important of all—because unless I strip an altar or burden the brothers with intolerable hunger, I have no means by which I can spend eight days in his service, until the new harvest brings the hoped-for resources [Col. 0498B].

Unless you can do so without danger, I do not wish you to ask for leave for our military men, although you yourselves readily know how necessary it is for them as well.

If you judge that the little letter of congratulation will be useful—namely, that it may in some way encourage him to act well—see that it is delivered in the name of my insignificance.

[Note: [Col. 0498D] The little letter of congratulation. That is, an exhortation to King Charles after the defeat he had suffered. Lupus therefore leaves it to Louis’s judgment whether the exhortation should be delivered to the king. It is found in the following letter.]

If not, it will be enough for you to know what I have in mind.

Send word through my messenger what I should do about the annual gifts that I still have in my possession.

I have sent Your Highness a token of a small gift, since in excessive embarrassment I had nothing else to send. Please do not disdain it, remembering our first friendship [Col. 0498C].

Kindly remember my insignificance and accept my wishes for your good health and for your continual increase through prosperous success, to the benefit of the good [Col. 0499A].

## LETTER XXXIII. AN EXHORTATION TO THE LORD KING.

Most excellent lord, and, if I may dare say so, most beloved: when I recently heard of the adversity that had befallen your condition, I was consumed with ineffable grief.

For I considered within myself the character of your nobility, which I desire to see perfected by the maturity of age and the gravity of wisdom, and I thought that it had been taken from us far too soon. Because this seemed irrecoverable, since treacherous rumor persistently spread the report, I devoted myself entirely, together with the brothers who strive to serve God with me, to obtaining the salvation of your soul. I greatly feared that the persuasions of certain men who did not fear God sufficiently might harm it [Col. 0499B].

But since we have been granted your safety, and have been filled with incredible joy, we admonish Your Highness’s majesty with sincere faith to give and offer the greatest thanks to almighty God together with us. He has shown us how much we ought to love him, since, as I may say with everyone’s agreement, when human assistance ceased, he himself powerfully and mercifully preserved you, and deigned to show how much you ought to rely upon him.

Therefore, do not grieve excessively over the contrary outcome. Rather, believe his truthful words:

> “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV).

And:

> “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans IX).

And:

> “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth” (Psalm CXIII).

And:

> “All my will shall be done” (Isaiah LVI).

And:

> “A king is not saved by great strength” (Psalm XXXII).

And:

> “It is not difficult for the Lord to save by many or by few” (1 Samuel XIV).

And:

> “He who glorifies me, I will glorify; but those who despise me shall be held of no account” (1 Samuel II).

Rejecting the counsel of those concerned with the flesh, of whom it is said:

> “The Lord destroys the counsels of the nations; he rejects the thoughts of the peoples, and he rejects the counsels of princes; but the counsel of the Lord remains forever” (Psalm XLIV),

submit to the counsel that he himself deigns, through the Prophet, to give mortals:

> “Cast your thought upon God, and he himself will nourish you” (Psalm LIV).

And:

> “Mercy will surround those who hope in the Lord” (Psalm XXXI).

And:

> “When you were little in your own eyes, you became head among the tribes of Israel” (1 Samuel XV).

And:

> “Offer to God the sacrifice of praise, and fulfill your vows to the Most High. And call upon me in the day of tribulation: I will deliver you, and you will honor me” (Psalm XLIX) [Col. 0499C—Col. 0499D].

Moreover, remember that Solomon, when he was to rule the people of Israel, over whom he presided for a long time in the greatest peace, asked above all for wisdom.

Do not disdain even the counsels of those who, although they did not know God, saw what was useful not so much for themselves as for us. Among their teachings is the principle that, before beginning anything, we ought prudently to inquire what should be done; and once we have found it, we ought to complete it with mature haste; and that a war should be prepared for a long time so that it may be won quickly (Sallust, *Catiline*) [Col. 0500A].

I have briefly set these matters before Your Highness so that, by divine and human authority, you may know without doubt what you ought to do.

May God himself grant that you may prosper spiritually and bodily as much as I desire.

## LETTER XXXIV. [Note: [Col. 0499D] To Altwinus. The title of the letter indicates that he was a monk, but it does not say which monastery was his. Papirius Masson’s edition has, “To Altwinus, a Senonese monk.” But it is clear from Letter 20 that, at least when that letter was written, he was staying in Germany, and therefore was a monk of Fulda. See *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, Volume VI, page 60.] TO ALTWINUS THE MONK.

To the venerable brother Altwinus, Lupus sends perpetual salvation.

If questions could be discussed by anyone with as much ease as they are raised, every diligent person would long ago have advanced to perfected wisdom.

But now that the study of letters has nearly grown obsolete, how few can be found who do not rightly complain about the incompetence of teachers, the scarcity of books, and finally the lack of leisure [Col. 0500B]?

You therefore ought not to be indignant with me if I judge that the very little leisure that scarcely falls to my lot should be spent in investigating what I do not know rather than in discussing what I have already attained.

Nor, I think, am I mistaken if I indicate that those for whom, by divine favor, I have either opened or made smoother the way of understanding must follow where I have gone before: that is, if, with reading as my teacher, whether I am using it or have used it, I impose the same thing on my hearers by speech when they are present, or by obstinate silence when they are absent.

Nevertheless, your persistence has prevailed upon me to clarify some of the matters you have diligently investigated.

Priscian approves the lengthening of the penultimate syllable of *locuples* in Book V, where he discusses nouns ending in a lengthened *-es*. He says:

> “Appellatives, if they concern human beings—what among the Greeks are called common or movable, and among us common—include *heres* and *locuples*” [Col. 0500C].

In Book VII, while showing with remarkable care when the penultimate syllable of the genitive of the third declension should be lengthened or shortened, he says:

> “It is lengthened in those words whose nominative ends long, whether by nature or by position, such as *sol, solis* and *infans, infantis*. Exceptions are Greek words ending in *-on*, and both Latin and foreign words ending in *-o*, which sometimes shorten and sometimes lengthen the penultimate syllable of the genitive. In addition, words ending in *-ms*, *-bs*, *-ps*, or *-x* always shorten the penultimate syllable of the genitive. Likewise *par, lar, vas, pes, Ceres, compos, bos; sus, grus*: although these lengthen their nominatives, they shorten the penultimate syllable of the genitive.”
