Since, therefore, words whose nominatives are lengthened either by nature or by position consequently lengthen the penultimate syllables of their genitives—with the exception of these six nouns, which long usage has identified and marked, since, as he himself testifies, *locuples* ends in a lengthened *-es*—the penultimate syllable of its genitive will likewise be pronounced long according to the same authority [Col. 0500D].

I could also confirm this by poetic testimony, unless the authority of so great a man could carry so little weight with contentious people.

We can establish that *locupleto*, with its penultimate syllable lengthened, must unquestionably be pronounced long—just as, because *robur, roboris* is shortened, *roboro* is pronounced with the same penultimate syllable shortened—as an active verb in Cicero (*On the Orator* and Book I of *On Duties*). We also sing it used in this sense in the Psalm:

> “You have greatly enriched it” (Psalm LXIV) [Col. 0501A].

From Priscian, in the aforementioned Book VII, we can discover what we ought to think about the pronunciation of *mulieris*. He says that nouns ending in shortened *-or* may be masculine, feminine, neuter, or common; but among nouns ending in lengthened *-er* there are Greek masculines and one Latin word, though a rather spurious one. He then continues:

> “Some words that shorten the nominative shorten the penultimate syllable of the genitive, while others lengthen it. They lengthen it in neuters ending in *-al* and *-el*, and in derivative neuters ending in *-ar*. Other words ending in *-or* likewise lengthen the penultimate syllable of the genitive, such as *cursor, cursoris*; others shorten it, such as *Hector, Hectoris*; but all the remaining words that shorten the ending of the nominative likewise shorten the penultimate syllable of the genitive. The exception is *inquies*, which preserved the simple declension in the compound, although it shortens the end of the nominative” [Col. 0501B].

Therefore, if *mulier* ends in a shortened *-er*—about which there is no doubt—and if Priscian did not include it among the exceptions, its genitive will, according to him, be pronounced with a shortened penultimate syllable.

I do not yet have any poetic testimony to strengthen this point. Since, as he himself says, “nothing in human inventions is perfect in every respect” (Priscian, Preface to Book I), perhaps this matter was omitted by him not through ignorance but through forgetfulness.

For this reason, I do not wish to risk my own authority by changing established usage until either my diligence or that of my friends succeeds in finding something here that is not necessarily more solid, but at least more evident [Col. 0501C].

The same distinguished author himself explains why he said that *ulciscor* and *vindico* are to be understood in both senses. He adds that they may be used both on behalf of one who has been injured and against the one who has inflicted the injury; hence *vindicta* may mean not only punishment but also deliverance.

The meaning is also readily apparent to those who consider Virgil’s verses correctly. In the line:

> “Having avenged my husband, I exacted punishment from his hostile brother,”

*ulta* is used on behalf of the injured person. Sicharbas—or, as Virgil writes with poetic license, Sichaeus—had been injured by Dido’s brother Pygmalion, who had put him to death. Dido later avenged her husband, not by inflicting any punishment upon him, since he was already dead [Col. 0501D], but by depriving Pygmalion of the money for which he had committed the crime. Thus she exacted punishment from the one who had inflicted the injury on behalf of the one who had been injured.

The same verb is therefore used on behalf of the injured person. It would have had the same meaning if the meter had permitted him to say, “I avenged the man” [Col. 0502A].

The following example:

> “Today we shall not all die unavenged,”

is used against the one who inflicted the injury.

For when Aeneas encouraged his companions to resist the Greeks, who had brought their city under their own power, he used the word—as Virgil represents him—as meaning that vengeance and retribution for his countrymen who had already died, and for himself before he died, were to be exacted bravely from those who had injured them.

I have not wished to discuss the next point until I could investigate it more carefully in Livy.

I have always heard *propitius* pronounced with a hiss from people who were not without learning, and in the most ancient manuscripts I have never found it written except with *t*.

It is not clear in Priscian whether the *u* of the past tense changes into the present tense’s *i*. In old manuscripts, however, you will find it written indifferently in both forms.

I rejoice exceedingly that our patron, the bishop, is safe and well.

[Note: [Col. 0501D] Probus. A presbyter of Mainz, as was noted in the commentary on Letter 20.]

As for Probus, I am less surprised that he has published something than that he has not already deprived everyone of material for writing [Col. 0502B].

Farewell; and, if you love me, please do not cease to pray to the Lord for me, for my father, and for my mother, both through you and through the other friends.

## LETTER XXXV. TO EBRARDUS THE MONK, HIS RELATIVE.

You press me continually, dearest friend, with requests that, by pursuing in a letter the antiquity of our kinship and exceptional friendship, I should write something that might be, if not useful to you, at least pleasing. I might perhaps have done this suitably if, when you asked for a work, you had provided the material. But since you promise that whatever it may be will be welcome to you while I write, I did not wish to torment myself with laborious diligence in searching out material, [Col. 0502C] much less with painstaking elegance of wording. I shall therefore explain extemporaneously whatever occurred to me while I was attempting nothing of this kind.

I am very pleased that some people cultivate with the greatest zeal the wisdom now coming back to life in these regions of ours; but I am by no means moderately disturbed by the fact that some among us, desiring a part of it, insolently reject another part. Yet by everyone’s agreement there is nothing in it that can or ought rightly to be excluded. It therefore appears that we ourselves are opposed to ourselves, while foolishly attempting to attain wisdom. Indeed, most of us seek from it the cultivation of language; and you will find very few who propose to learn from it moral integrity, which is much more beneficial.

[Note: [Col. 0501D] Cultum sermonis, “cultivation of language.” Salvianus, presbyter of Marseilles, was lamenting the same thing long before the age of Charles the Bald. These are his words in the preface to his books *On the Governance of God*: “For all of them,” he says, “in their writings pleaded only their own causes; and, caring more for their own praises than for the usefulness of others, they did not strive to be considered sound and beneficial, but learned and eloquent.” Dio, book XXXVIII: “Cicero made the bitterest enemies for himself by always striving to place himself before every man of distinction and by exercising his freedom of speech toward everyone without restraint, even to the point of satiety. For he was seeking the reputation of being more fluent and more eloquent than the rest, rather than that of being a good man.”]

Thus we fear the faults of the tongue and strive to purify it; but we make light of the faults of life and increase them. Yet since all wisdom is from the Lord God, as the divine Scriptures demonstrate, let us pursue it in the proper order, and without doubt we shall attain it. This is drawn for us from divine authority. “My son, if you desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and the Lord will provide it for you” (*Ecclesiasticus* I). There also what wisdom is is defined most fully and beautifully: “The fear of the Lord is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding” (Job XXVIII).

As for those who live wrongly but desire to speak correctly, and who reject corrupt speech more than corrupt morals, we are instructed as follows: “All the labor of man is in his mouth, and his soul shall not be filled” (*Ecclesiasticus* VI). For it is surely fitting that one who assigns the first place to learning rather than to holiness should be excluded from the nourishment of wisdom by a fatal hunger.

Therefore, if we apply ourselves diligently to polishing our speech, we ought to devote ourselves much more earnestly to attaining goodness and justice. But since there are various schools of philosophers, each perfect in its own kind, none of which prevents another from introducing its followers into the sanctuary of philosophy, and since all are united in a kind of concordant disagreement, it is clear that the diversity of their aims—which, so to speak, separates the most peaceful people of God inseparably—does not prevent right living, and that the temple of Mother Church is open to those who come devoutly by different paths, since each order possesses its own perfection. Nevertheless, the final point is all the more certain because divine things surpass human things.

Accordingly, I urge the disposition of your nobility that, whatever rank of the Christian religion may be most pleasing to your mind, you should, while preserving reverence for the others, advance in it day by day with God’s assistance and show yourself upright in it. But if you are able to rise from good to better and from the lowest to the highest, I would have you strive for this with the utmost determination, so that, serving your Author with greater labor, you may be crowned by him with greater glory.

“Cast your thought upon the Lord” (Psalm LIV), so that from him you may obtain enduringly blessed and blessedly enduring [Note: [Col. 0503D] *Nitorimenta*. Thus the manuscript expressly reads, whereas the editions had *inter incerta*, “among uncertain readings.” It is clearly a new word, but Lupus evidently means by it a splendor of the mind, that is, of the soul, which will endure forever. Otherwise the words *inter incerta* have no place here.] splendors.

Above all, always keep before your eyes that he himself made you, restored you when you were lost, and finally increased you through such frequent, such abundant, and such profitable benefits; so that, having here the material for praising him, while you both possess and return thanks to him for the gifts received, you may become more worthy of receiving greater ones, and, relying upon humility, may obtain perseverance in good works—which is an unlosable gift.

Certainly, while you are occupied with these studies, I would not have you pass over negligently the honorable arts suited to your intelligence. Rather, ask their knowledge from him who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach anyone; and they will undoubtedly be granted to you according to the measure of your faith.

Farewell, dearest and most longed-for friend; may you flourish through a long life, increase daily in health-bringing virtues, and always remember me kindly.

## LETTER XXXVI. TO ALWINUS

If you had brought us your sudden presence, you would certainly have returned with the cost of fruitless labor. For you would have found me so entangled in various and unavoidable affairs that I could scarcely have offered you an hour’s free attention within many days. Indeed, the absence of the abbot would have greatly hindered your purpose.

Therefore, since I too, as I have stated above, am occupied, and the abbot is scarcely expected to return before autumn, if you think you must come to us, you see that you must await a suitable opportunity. As for your brother, as you requested, I shall endeavor to assist him with my prayers as far as I can.

## LETTER XXXVII. [Note: [Col. 0503D] To Heribold, bishop of Auxerre, as we said in the note to Letter 19. Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, wrote a letter, as Flodoard reports (book III, chapter 21), “to Abbo of Auxerre on behalf of the deceased bishop Heribold, who, appearing to a certain brother, admonished him concerning almsgiving and prayers and offerings to be made for him.” For Abbo, Heribold’s brother, had succeeded him in the see of Auxerre in 854 by command of King Charles the Bald.] TO HERIBOLD, BISHOP.

The letter recently sent by Your Excellency seemed suspicious to me. For that reason I thought my reply ought to be restrained until I learned the truth of the matter. Now, since our mutual brother has disclosed both the reliability of that letter and the truth concerning your condition, I reply briefly in writing, wishing you the speediest recovery of good health.

If, mindful of nature, which has joined us by the closest bond of kinship, and of our former affection, which has bound us uniquely and singularly—for one of these is a matter of circumstance, the other of judgment [Note: [Col. 0504D] “One is a matter of circumstance.” Thus the emperor Galba addresses Piso, whom he was adopting, in Tacitus, book I of the *Histories*: “To be born and begotten by princes is accidental and is not valued beyond that; adoption belongs to sound judgment.”]—you have resolved to show me sincere goodwill, indeed because you have resolved to do so, the distances between places of which you complained to me will not be able to cause us harm.

For we frequently have the opportunity to see one another; and if some circumstance prevents this, we are by no means without written communication, through which we can familiarly disclose our thoughts to one another—if your sublimity stoops so far.

Moreover, I am sending you, to oblige you, a manuscript of Blessed Jerome’s annotations on the prophets, which I have not yet read. May your diligence quickly arrange either for it to be copied or for you to read it, and order it to be returned to us. I judged that I should warn you of this, lest, while you are occupied with many and constant affairs, delay in these matters, bringing you no benefit, should harm us.

And would that your lofty and divine intellect, insofar as possible, might be turned away from public affairs [Note: [Col. 0504D] “Public affairs.” This is evidently because he was *archicapellanus*, chief chaplain. “By virtue of his office,” as Marca writes in book VIII of *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*, “the chief chaplain administered ecclesiastical cases at the palace”—namely, those that were public, as Lupus says, that is, serious. “Besides the authority proper to the chief chaplain, the chaplain always took part in every consultation concerning public or private affairs held at the palace by the counselors, who were partly clerics and partly laymen,” as Marca explains in book IV of the same work. It should therefore not seem surprising that Lupus says Heribold was occupied with many and constant public affairs.] and transferred to the investigation of the secrets of human or divine wisdom. Your nobility [Note: [Col. 0505C] “The illustrious rank of your office.” That is, the archiepiscopal dignity.] would certainly have received a benefit worthy of its greatness.

I would not have you take this as though I were boastfully considering myself perfect in this respect, or imagining that I could in any way contribute to you, much less excel you. But just as I rejoice that you have been endowed with appropriate honors, so I desire to know you adorned also with intellectual gifts, especially those that excel in the arts.

Gaius Julius Caesar is no historian of the Romans. Only the *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, whose reputation has reached you, survive; and, as far as I know, there is nothing else of his relating to history. For after Julius himself had been overwhelmed by the burdens of almost the whole world’s affairs, his secretary Hirtius undertook to arrange in the *Commentaries* the sequence of his other achievements.

As soon as I can obtain Julius’s *Commentaries*, I shall arrange for them to be sent to you. I wish you prosperous health.

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO KING CHARLES

To the most excellent lord Charles, an illustrious king, worthy, in the judgment of the wise, of many and mighty kingdoms, whose name must be uttered with the highest reverence: Lupus, in every respect your most devoted servant.

Although unavoidable necessity temporarily removes me from your presence, my mind is nevertheless so attached to you that I always keep you and yours before my eyes; and, to confess the truth to you without the taint of flattery, I embrace you with a love scarcely capable of being comprehended.

For it is easily apparent in you why you ought to be loved by all good people. Therefore, insofar as I understand, am able, and comprehend, I am faithful to you.

I have endeavored, through the venerable Louis, who is faithful to you no less than he ought to be, to make my present needs known to Your Majesty. I ask that, according to the prudence divinely granted to you, in which we all rejoice, you kindly take care of them, so that at the beginning I may now be able to lay foundations for God’s service and yours that, with the grace of that same God and your favor assisting, may correspond to the devoted efforts of my future service.

Know that whenever I can, I earnestly implore God’s mercy in prayer to grant you prolonged health, bloodless victory, everlasting peace, hatred of vices, and possession of virtues; and so to make you reign on earth that you may not lose your kingdom in heaven.

## LETTER XXXIX. [Note: [Col. 0505C] To Ebroin, bishop of Poitiers. He too was chief chaplain of the sacred palace under Charles the Bald, as Charles himself testifies in the charter he granted to the monastery of Glanfeuil concerning the estate of Bidisciacus: “The venerable bishop Ebroin,” he says, “chief chaplain of our sacred palace, approaching the serenity of our eminence, made a request,” and so forth. He presided at the Council of Verneuil in 845 over Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, for this reason, as Sirmond observes in his notes to Charles the Bald’s *Capitula*: because he was chief chaplain, that is, the summit and head of all the palace dignities.] TO EBROIN, BISHOP.

[Col. 0506B] Lupus sends perpetual greetings to the most illustrious Ebroin.

I have made my affairs known to our Louis; I thought it superfluous to repeat them in this letter, since I both wish and know that you will read what was delivered to him. I ask only that you deign to assist me in every respect, as you will learn from those letters that you will also read.

I have sent you an ivory comb. Please keep it for your use, so that, while combing your hair, a more intimate remembrance of me may be impressed upon you.

I wish you good health.

## LETTER XL. [Note: [Col. 0505D] To Rabanus, at that time abbot of Fulda and later archbishop of Mainz. This letter was written after the death of Louis the Pious, at the time when discord prevailed among his sons. Hence Baronius is mistaken in thinking that Lupus became abbot of Ferrières in December 838. But we shall soon establish the date of Lupus’s promotion with, I believe, clear arguments.] TO RABANUS, HIS TEACHER.

Lupus sends greetings to his most reverend father and excellent teacher, Rabanus.

Until now I have been unable to thank you in deeds. Yet the one who knows hidden things has always seen how great my gratitude has been in feeling. Henceforth, however, if that same God prolongs your life and restores the desired peace, it will not be impossible for me to show by deeds what I bear in my heart.

For, with the consent of our brothers [Note: [Col. 0506D] “With the consent of the brothers.” Thus monks in those times had no right in the election of abbots except through their consent. The rest belonged to the king. Nevertheless, Lupus says in Letter 42 that he was elected by the monks of Ferrières. In Letter 45, written to King Charles, he says that Charles entrusted the monastery of Ferrières to him at the monks’ request and election. This must be understood as follows. When a monastery was vacant, the prince appointed an abbot, with an order that the monks receive him. Then, if nothing canonical stood in the way, the monks elected him, and in this way added their consent to the royal appointment. Sometimes, however, the monks assembled to make an election of the man whom they wished to be abbot and afterward approached the prince, asking that he be given to them as abbot; this comes to the same thing. It makes no difference whether the prince grants the abbey before or after the monks’ election, provided that he acts by royal right. As for Lupus, the benefice conferred upon him can refer to no one other than the prince. In Letter 6 he expressly writes that many people believed that, when he was being advanced through the queen’s favor, a position of dignity would soon be conferred upon him; and a palatine monk could expect such dignity from no one but the prince. Moreover, the right to elect their own abbots had not yet been granted to the monks of Ferrières. It was later granted by Charles the Bald at Lupus’s request.] our monastery of Ferrières was entrusted to me on 22 November [X Kal. Decemb.] [Col. 0506D] and our lord Charles, favoring me with remarkable condescension, bestowed his grace upon me.

I therefore ask that Your Benevolence deign to commend me and the congregation entrusted to me to your holy prayers, so that, just as you greatly aided my studies through learning, you may likewise temper the difficulty of my office by your constant prayers.

Moreover, I have heard that you have laid down the burden of your administration [Note: [Col. 0507D] “Have laid down.” From this passage learned men long ago inferred that Rabanus had resigned the governance of the monastery of Fulda before becoming bishop. But no one has yet made clear when this occurred, except that the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius says it happened in 838. The matter therefore requires more thorough investigation.

Rudolph, a priest and monk and a disciple of Rabanus, relates in his *Life* that Rabanus laid down the burden of pastoral care in the twentieth year after he had undertaken it. He had undertaken it in 822, according to the author of the *Annals of Fulda*. He then withdrew to the church of Saint Peter that he had built, which was about twelve stadia from the monastery of Fulda.

“For when that venerable man,” Rudolph says, “had nobly governed the monastery entrusted to him for twenty years, laying down the burden of pastoral care, he withdrew to the church that I mentioned above, built to the east of the monastery of Saint Peter on the mountain; and remaining there, serving God, he devoted himself to heavenly philosophy.”

It is therefore clear that Rabanus abandoned responsibility for the monastery of Fulda in 842, after presiding over it for twenty years. The *Chronicle of Hildesheim* says: “In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 842, Rabanus, abbot of the monastery of Fulda, was expelled from the monastery.” Finally, in the *Books of the Antiquities of Fulda*, published by Pistorius, there are many records of that period showing that Rabanus was still abbot of Fulda in the second year of Lothair’s reign, whereas Hatto was already abbot in the third year of the reign of King Louis of the East Franks, that is, Louis, king of Germany. We shall discuss Hatto, to whom Rabanus transferred the pastoral care, more fully in the notes to Letter 86.]

and are now concerned solely with divine matters, while you have left to our Hatto the care that is full of toil. I shall await in your blessedness’s letter an account of this matter, together with anything else that may seem relevant. I wish you good health and ask you graciously to remember me forever.

## LETTER XLI. [Note: [Col. 0508C] To Immo, undoubtedly bishop of Noyon, who took part in the Council of Beauvais in April 845 and perished in the destruction of the city of Noyon in 859, slain by the Normans, as Jacobus Meyerus relates.] TO IMMO.

[Col. 0507B]

Lupus sends eternal greetings to the venerable Immo, whom I sincerely honor for the merit of his holiness.

I read your letter, which gently delighted me and sweetly revived the memory of our friendship, with the greatest pleasure, as was fitting; and I entrusted the thoughts that had wholly entered my mind to a careful memory. For if, as you wrote, you truly count me among your dearest friends, it may perhaps be pardonable that, burdened by the discomforts of travel, you scorned to lighten me with the comfort of a letter, especially when so many opportunities that could easily have been found were neglected.

Yet the pain of so great a slight is greatly aggravated by the fact that you did not fulfill what was often agreed between us: that whenever you found an opportunity, you would disclose especially to me whatever I ought to know. But enough of this for another time.

Otherwise, by the favor of the Lord our God, I have returned safely. Apart from the death of my lord and foster father Aldricus—which, as far as I am concerned, was wholly unfortunate [Note: [Col. 0508D] “Death.” Aldricus died in 841, on 10 October [VI Idus Octobris], as stated in the note to Letter 29. This letter was therefore written not long afterward.]—and that of certain other friends, I do not think that anything very sad has happened to me from outside.

I was astonished that you asked to be told what books I had either written or read in Germany, and I could not sufficiently understand your reason, unless perhaps you wished cleverly to test me by putting two things to me, one of which, if I had assented to it, might seem boastful, the other childish imprudence.

I therefore frankly disclose to you that I devoted my principal effort there to reading, both as a remedy against forgetfulness and for the increase of learning, and that I acquired a few books. I did not, as certain people foolishly claimed, take up the burden of so great and prolonged a labor out of love for the German language. [Col. 0508B]

I am very grateful that you admonished me to devote myself to divine authorities in a spirit of humility. I would have you believe that I have so acted until now that I attribute entirely to God’s grace what God made me and what he granted me through his benefits; and I humbly beseech him to preserve and increase these things in me.

To what you proposed I add also that evangelical saying: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark IX); and what Paul, who knew the secrets of heaven, teaches: “What have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Corinthians IV).

Nor has this escaped me, although I do not consider myself great at all: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (*Ecclesiasticus* III).

From this I retain so many, so powerful, and finally so salutary lessons that I cannot even dream of claiming any of God’s benefits as my own. Yet plainly, whoever possesses some outstanding divine grace [Note: [Col. 0508D] “Some outstanding divine grace.” Lupus rightly warns that those whom God has made eminent in some matter are especially exposed to the attacks of envy. Eminence is never free from envy, as Velleius Paterculus says in book II. In Livy, book VIII, we read that envy, like fire, seeks the highest places. Plutarch also notes in the *Life of Publicola* that he could not avoid envy, to which great men are always subject. Thus Tacitus not unjustly praises his father-in-law for arranging his life so that he was “neither outside envy nor outside glory.” Sallustius gravely warns that one who has shone through illustrious deeds must take the greatest care not to expose himself to the blows of fortune, since envy follows glory. The example of Christ, cited by Lupus, presses the point more forcefully: although Christ was most holy and wise, he could not escape the teeth of malice. See Freinshemius on Curtius, book VIII, chapter 5.] cannot escape the various opinions of different people.

For concerning our Savior, upon whom no suspicion of reproach at all falls, some said, “He is good”; but others, “No, he deceives the crowds” (John VII).

Therefore, for the wise person there will be a firm and singular refuge in this saying: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Matthew VI; Luke II).

I ask that you remember me kindly and enjoy good health.

## LETTER XLII. [Note: [Col. 0509C] To Hincmar, bishop of Rheims. He is too well known for us to need to say anything about him here. I would not, however, omit the fact that he was first a canon at the monastery of Saint-Denis; afterward, when all the canons of that monastery became monks, Hincmar too became a monk.] TO HINCMAR, BISHOP.

I am not unaware that, since you abound in such great gifts of divine grace, you spontaneously consider that you have received from God the ability, at the prince’s court, to assist good men, so that they may possess in you what they do not have in themselves and provide material for rewarding your diligence. Therefore, with the confidence of friendship, I admonish you that, while you have the opportunity, you should take care to multiply the interest on your talent, so that, like the sun, the radiance of your benevolence may shine upon everyone and exclude no one except him who, in proud blindness, rejects the light of justice.

The nobility of your lineage is adorned by beneficial learning, and the height of your office is commended by the religion of your profession. I have written these things to Your Eminence not through the fault of arrogance but out of friendship, so that, since nobility and wisdom have come together in you, the power of this union may be evident even against the will of those who strive to obscure the very lights of the Church.

The loss of our estate is known to you: namely, that the king, through no fault of mine, has taken away from us the cell [Note: [Col. 0509D] “The cell.” That of Saint Judoc, frequently mentioned in these letters of Lupus.] which his father had also granted by an edict because he had learned that monastic religion could not endure among us unless it were supported by an increase of resources.

We have therefore been reduced to such poverty that this year we scarcely have enough grain to sustain us for two months; the servants, whose service we cannot do without, are almost naked, and we have nothing with which to help them. Most of the brothers are forced to avoid nakedness with worn-out and torn clothing; poverty compels us to reduce our hospitality; and in this turbulent time of the state, living on the resources that our predecessors gathered, we ask mercy from the king and patience from our common Lord.

Thus, distressed by the weariness of our needs, I repeatedly consider resigning the office to which I was elected by the brothers. Yet I am drawn back from this both by the destructive greed of secular people and by the charge of impatience, if I abandon those same brothers in such great turmoil.

For although I have served the king to the limits of my strength, indeed beyond my strength, and have always prayed earnestly for him, I have not deserved even that he contribute something to the modest resources of our monastery. On the contrary, I have incurred this reproach: that he handed over its best part to a secular man [Note: [Col. 0509D] “To a secular man.” He means Count Odulphus, to whom Charles had given the cell of Saint Judoc, from which many benefits flowed to the monastery of Ferrières.] not to be governed, but to be overthrown.

Perhaps my own worthlessness has caused this. But why has the holiness of so many men, who serve God with me, been despised?

At your admonition, he ought to know that there are among us some of whom Scripture rightly testifies: “He will do the will of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayer” (Psalm CXLIV); and: “He who touches you is like one who touches the pupil of my eye” (Zechariah II).

What has that secular man’s distinction contributed to him? Has he afterward subjugated some barbarous nation, or restored this kingdom, which is divided against itself?

But if he had fulfilled in full, without regard to any person, the vow by which, I believe at your urging, he bound himself in the church of blessed Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0509D] “In the church of blessed Dionysius.” That is, in the year 845, as stated in the note to Letter 32. Charles, seeing that the affairs of Gaul were being driven and thrown into confusion by hostile destiny, turned to God’s help as the sole remedy for his afflicted situation; and, at the urging of Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, he made a vow in the monastery of Saint-Denis. Lupus does not explain what the vow was. He nevertheless seems to imply that Charles promised that, if his affairs went well, he would restore to churches and monasteries the goods that had been taken from them. Lupus therefore attributes Charles’s misfortune to the violation of the vow, since the cell of Saint Judoc had not been restored to the monastery of Ferrières.], indeed if he had first followed the counsels that were sought and found at Verneuil [Note: [Col. 0510D] “At Verneuil.” This was added from an old manuscript; the edition of Masson lacked it. Lupus means the council held at the palace of Verneuil in December 845. Labbe says that palace was at a place now called Vernoni on the Seine, in the diocese of Évreux.], he would already have been made to reign in peace by the one of whom the sacred writings say: “There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs XXI).

I sent you the same canons—or, as you call them, chapters [Note: [Col. 0510D] “Chapters.” At that time the regulations issued at synods were called *capitula*, “chapters,” rather than canons, as had formerly been customary. Nothing is more common.]—which had then been composed in my style [Note: [Col. 0510D] “In my style.” From this it is inferred that Lupus wrote and composed the canons of the synod held at Verneuil. This is why we published that council together with Lupus’s works. Certainly many things in these canons bear the characteristic stamp of Lupus, as we shall note there. It was especially honorable that, although Hincmar was present at the synod, the task of composing the canons was entrusted to Lupus.]; I believe that a later age will judge their fairness, and the searcher of hearts and reins will not forget my devotion.

Meanwhile, I ask you to show me and all who suffer similar things the constancy of Mordecai and the piety of Esther, so that through your diligence—or rather, through divine power—the enemies of God’s servants may be conquered and crushed, not to their destruction at the time of which I speak, but for their perpetual salvation.

We wish you good health.

## LETTER XLIII. TO LOUIS, ABBOT

Lupus sends eternal greetings to the most excellent abbot Louis.

I have sent the gifts owed to the king, which he ordered to be sent through you. Your benevolence will not disdain to arrange that they be pleasing to him.

But because I have heard that Odulphus [Note: [Col. 0511C] “Odulphus.” Thus the old manuscript expressly reads, in place of *Edilulphus*, which the edition of Masson had, plainly incorrectly. This is the Odulphus to whom, as we said above, Charles the Bald had given the cell of Saint Judoc. I believe he is the same person called Count Haudulphus in Letter 6 of Frotharius of Toul.] will come to the king with the queen [Note: [Col. 0511C] “With the queen.” Irmintrude, Charles’s wife, through whose influence Odulphus was undoubtedly being advanced.], I ask you to deign to remember us, so that at last we may recover our cell, in which almost nothing besides bare ground now remains [Note: [Col. 0511D] “Almost nothing.” He means the disaster by which the monastery of Saint Judoc was devastated. The author of the *Chronicle of Fontenelle* says that this disaster occurred in 844. But the author of the *Annals of Saint-Bertin* assigns it to 842, in these words: “At that time the fleet of the Normans, arriving suddenly before dawn at the trading-port called Quentovicus, so raged through plundering, captivity, and the slaughter of people of both sexes that they left nothing there except buildings redeemed at a price.”

The date recorded in the *Chronicle of Fontenelle* is more accurate. For this letter mentions the queen, that is, Irmintrude, the wife of Charles the Bald. She had not yet married Charles and therefore was not yet queen. Charles married her only toward the end of the forty-second year of that century, as the author of the *Annals of Saint-Bertin* also reports. Nithard, at the end of book IV, further says that the marriage of Irmintrude and Charles was celebrated in that same year, on 14 December [XIX Kal. Januarii].

Moreover, this disaster occurred when Lupus was already abbot of Ferrières; he attained that dignity only toward the end of 842, as was said in the note to Letter 40. It is therefore clearly established that the disaster occurred after 842.] and since I lost it through no fault of mine. Nor does our establishment possess such resources that religious observance can survive there without the aforesaid cell.

For from it the church received wax, and the brothers and servants clothing, fish, cheese, and vegetables. Would that, through the loss of all these things, we were not suffering a double loss [Note: [Col. 0512D] “A double loss.” That is, a loss of soul and body. A loss of soul, because eternal punishment threatens one who removes or takes away things dedicated or donated to churches; and a loss of body, because, as Lupus repeats many times, there is fear that God may become angry with Charles because the cell was taken away and grant victory to his enemies. He supports this also by the visions of certain people shortly afterward and in Letter 53. Thus the Fathers of the Council of Meaux declare that the Normans were sent into Gaul by an avenging God because the canons of the Council of Verneuil and of other synods held in those times had not been observed.], to our lord, as we groan.

Therefore admonish him of his danger, so that he may take thought for himself, for us, and for others similarly afflicted by him; and let him not fear to appease God through our consolation, since he did not fear to offend him through cruel oppression.

For it is the general assertion of religious men that, apart from the final vengeance that awaits him, he will never attain the prosperity of his desired happiness until he restores the Church that he divided and submits to the grave and mature counsels of good men—that is, of those who fear God.

I wish you good health.

## LETTER XLIV. TO HINCMAR

Lupus sends every good wish to Hincmar, the bishop whom I honor with the highest reverence.

[End of supplied text]

The departure from you after your audience with the king recently prevented the fulfillment of my petition [Col. 0512A]. Since urgent necessity presses, I renew it in this letter, so that at least by my importunity—which excludes even his own natural sense of shame—I may drive you to help me and others suffering the same plight. For we do not grieve that the means of collecting gold and silver and other precious objects have been taken away from us, but rather the means by which we supported life modestly—that is, the means by which we obtained clothing and supplies of food at all times.

We are therefore compelled to wear worn-out and mended garments and to temper our hunger almost continually with nothing but vegetables and purchased legumes. Hence the sick complain. Guests seek among us the customary provisions, but do not find them. The present circumstances are bringing us into disrepute, and God is undoubtedly being provoked to vengeance.

But since, as I set out seriously rather than flatteringly in my previous letter, we believe that you have been adorned with dignity and endowed with the prince’s familiarity for the sake of the whole Church, and since we wish this to be demonstrated by deeds, please take pains, while Odulphus is said to be working on the matter, to bring it about that the king strip himself of so great a sin and free us from such enormous poverty. Otherwise our prayer may not so much lift him up as his unbearable affliction weigh him down.

Indeed, instructed by your exhortation, he can have a great opportunity to alter what he has done wrongly, especially if he recounts to the secular persons to whom he has distributed ecclesiastical property what disadvantages have subsequently befallen both himself and them, and tells them that God’s anger cannot be appeased unless they restore what belongs to Him; nor will they otherwise recover their strength and judgment unless, returning to God from the heart [Col. 0512C], they abstain from plunder and, conscious of their weakness, submit themselves to His omnipotence.

But unless our lord the king hastens to do this, and trembles where there is no cause for fear, I fear beyond anything that can be said that he will very quickly provide his enemies with their desired joy, while leaving disgrace to us, who love him uniquely. I wish you good health and daily progress toward better things.

Imitating the ancients in the art of learning, I would even now have attempted to recover our property [Col. 0513A], had I not discovered by personal experience that this effort is futile: even if Virgil were to rise again and expend all the strength of his threefold work on moving certain hearts, he would not obtain so much as a reading of this present letter.

> **Note:** “The strength of the threefold work” means the *Bucolics*, *Georgics*, and *Aeneid*. These are the works Virgil left behind.

## LETTER XLV. TO LORD KING CHARLES

Remember, I beg you, the omnipotent God, who freely gave you life, nobility, beauty, power, praiseworthy prudence, and—greater than all these things—the knowledge of Himself.

> **Note:** “Beauty.” Beauty too belongs to majesty. Hence certain peoples did not take their kings from the nobility, but chose the man who excelled in facial appearance and bodily form—that is, the most handsome. See the very learned Freinshemius in his notes on Quintus Curtius, Book VI, chapter 5.

And honor Him in His servants.

> **Note:** “In His servants,” that is, in monks. For we have noted in connection with Letter 25 that during those times they were commonly called “servants of God.”

For, since He possesses everything, you can contribute nothing to Him. He deigns to promise: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5). Show mercy to us, who are in extreme need, so that He Himself may repay you with the blessedness of the merciful on our behalf.

It is more or less four years since the seventy-two monks whom you entrusted to me, according to their vow and choice, and who, while we are occupied in various affairs, keep unceasing vigil for your safety and prosperity, have been suffering an incredible shortage of clothing, legumes, and fish because their resources were taken away.

> **Note:** “Fish.” It is probable that the monks of Ferrières at that time abstained from eating meat. Lupus never complains that he lacks meat, but rather legumes, fish, cheese, and similar things. Thus, following the institution of Saint Boniface and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, the monks of Fulda abstained from eating meat, as Boniface himself states in Letter 142, addressed to Zacharias, Roman pontiff. Even today the monks of the congregation of Saint Maur, who observe the Rule of Blessed Benedict more strictly, entirely abstain from meat except on account of illness.

Public hospitality, which according to the ordinances of earlier kings was to be offered to travelers, has also been discontinued; the monastery’s servants are tortured by squalor and cold. Nor can I help these miserable people, since the multitude gathered from elsewhere has been left to me, while the abundance from which they were supported has been taken away.

For when your glorious mother intervened, your most serene father, Louis Augustus, had bestowed this supplement upon our monastery for the remedy of his soul and the salvation of his posterity.

> **Note:** “Your mother.” Judith, the last wife of Emperor Louis the Pious.

Yet even when we possessed it, we were not overflowing with harmful abundance, so as to indulge ourselves intemperately in luxuries, because the provisions permitted by the Rule could scarcely be obtained even with the monastery’s full resources. Now, having received far less, we abstain unwillingly and shiver under compulsion; because of our poverty we cannot support the children, the old, or the sick.

In such calamity we offer daily prayers and an annual service for your father and mother, as though we possessed what they bestowed. For they did everything they could and secured their gift most firmly. Let affection for those through whom you came into being touch you. Restore their almsgiving, which has until now been suspended at enormous peril. Do not forget yourself either. Indeed, you now need almsgiving.

It is time for the fear and love of God to pierce your heart, since your body has now reached manhood. Do not delay any longer, I beg you, the good deed which you say you desire; for although you do not know what the coming day may bring, nevertheless, since you are advancing with us each day toward the judgment of Him to whom it is most truly said, “You will repay each person according to his works” (Matthew 16), you cannot possibly doubt this.

It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God (Hebrews 10). Nor should you deign to say that you cannot do it. For, as the Apostle says, “God is not mocked” (Galatians 6). He knows how much power He has bestowed, since He demands nothing except what is just.

Do not tremble with fear where there is no fear. Rather, dare to do good if you desire to reign prosperously in this life and happily in the future. Why should you not steadfastly dare to change what no one could show to be just? By the agreement of all good people, what we request is just, possible for royal power, necessary for us, and useful not so much to us as to you.

We shall obtain from this favor a temporal benefit, but you, with other good things added, an eternal reward. Let the most just petitions and the humblest prayers, which extreme poverty extorts, therefore bend your piety. Even now deign to complete what you once granted most firmly, when I set before you that saying of David to be observed: “What I have spoken is fixed” (2 Samuel 19).

> **Note:** “I set before you to be observed.” This refers to the exhortation Lupus delivered to Charles the Bald, which he also mentions in Letter 53. That exhortation does not now survive.

For neither is anything else fitting for your nobility and integrity, which ought to be an example to all; nor does anything else accord with your salvation and the peace of the commonwealth. We, for our part, shall not be found negligent in rendering the service we owe, and we shall strive with fervor, insofar as we can, to reconcile the divine power to you.

## LETTER XLVI. TO A CLOSE ASSOCIATE

Since abundant and legitimate material is available, do not hesitate—you and those whom you have judged faithful—to overturn the schemes of the traitor, who with extraordinary shamelessness exploits my benefits, by which he survives in our monastery, and never ceases to tear at the man by whom he is supported. Covered with disgrace and filled with envy, he tries to drive me away from the place from which he cannot extricate himself.

And because the victory he desired has escaped him, in astonishing madness he takes pleasure in sowing infamy—alas, like one who, knowing that he can never recover something for himself, nevertheless does not cease trying to remove it from others.

Why do you not crush him with the most steadfast, unconquerable, and irrefutable arguments, when, in accordance with the testimony of the divine oracle, his soul is detested by God because he mixes human and divine laws and sows discord among those whom either nature has produced as brothers or religion has made brothers?

But do not let any sort of wrongdoing tear you away from our place. With divine help, what you fear will not happen, and what you desire will quickly come about. Consequently, we shall work with confidence; everything is already clear to me.

Our Demosthenes sometimes needs even a stalk of cabbage, and now and then sustains himself moderately on household bread. Brought to this pass by the lack of wine, he takes pleasure in purchased beer; and even here he surpasses Tully, since what the latter suffered while asleep, this man suffers while awake. Thus he acquires no strength in his sides and takes no care to preserve his voice. Forgetful of rhetorical performance, he is content with the means of preserving life.

But in truth, the author of all good things will, as we believe, abolish our poverty and yours through abundant wealth.

## LETTER XLVII. TO THE SAME

There is nothing for you to fear. For both domestic and external enemies, although they claim much for themselves, will do me no harm, since He who commanded me and granted me the ability to trust in Him will deign to protect my insignificance. Therefore all their efforts are to be mocked—those who are either tormented by implacable envy or tortured by inexhaustible desire.

## LETTER XLVIII. TO SAR

Having laid aside the obstinacy of contention and the stubbornness of seeking victory, as a fair assessor of necessities, see that the abundant supply of grain which I entrusted to you benefits our needs. With due diligence applied to sowing, to the fodder of the animals, and to proper hospitality—which I wish you to take very seriously—I have no doubt that enough will remain to provide no small advantage.

## LETTER XLIX. TO HINCMAR, BISHOP

To the venerable H., bishop, Lupus sends complete good wishes.

A messenger whom I sent explained to you our distress, produced both by the length and by the severity of the season, and found in your fatherly care nothing other than what I had expected of it. Indeed, we previously competed in service, and we have not asked as much as we have provided—namely, the material for fulfilling charity.

Therefore, since we have long been suffering from a shortage of everything required for daily use, come to our aid with great haste, so that the desired effect of your benevolent promises may follow.

We are staying in a villa which, by antiphrasis, is called Viniacus, and it lies a little more or less one mile southwest of Attiniacum.

> **Note:** “From Attiniacum.” We have restored this place from an old manuscript, since Masson’s edition had *Hiniacum*. It was a royal palace in the diocese of Reims, on the river Aisne. There Charles the Simple, king of the Franks, established twelve men of the ecclesiastical order who would attend divine offices day and night at the appointed hours.

This is mentioned so that your distinguished prudence may also consider transportation, since we have no means for that either. Deign to make known by a letter returned through this bearer where, for how long, and when you intend to visit us, so that meanwhile we may be refreshed by hope and be able to foresee what we ought to do.

## LETTER L. TO A TRUSTED FRIEND

You are not unaware of the long labor which I have undertaken in pursuit of recovering the cell. Still burning with this purpose, by the king’s command, and with life as my companion, I shall set out for the conference which the kings will hold at Traiectum.

> **Note:** “At Traiectum.” That is, near the town of Traiectum, in the place called Marsna, as recorded in the capitularies of Charles the Bald. That meeting of the emperor Lothar, King Louis of Germany, and Charles the Bald took place in February 847. For it is clear that this very meeting is being discussed here. Lupus says in Letter 59: “You are not unaware, I believe, that our kings will hold a conference at Traiectum in the second week of Lent,” which refers to the same event. As Sirmond notes, in 847 Lent began on 16 February. Lupus also seems to mention this synod in Hincmar’s letter to the Annal of Lyon, preserved by Flodoard, Book III, chapter 21.

We now have no money, which could scarcely have sufficed for so long a journey. Therefore, since it did not seem wise to abandon unfinished efforts before it became clear what result they would produce, I did not consider it altogether dishonorable to seek help from friends whose loyalty in similar circumstances I have found unfailing.

Accordingly, I have directed my greatest hope toward Lady Rh. With our messenger—or, if you judge it more convenient, separately—I want you to explain to her the reason for my present need and bend her with the gentlest prayers, so that, as always, she may now come to my aid and, through this messenger of mine, generously help me with the silver I shall use on this journey.

In this way she may both participate in the restoration of our monastery, for which we are laboring, and, if possible, make me still more devoted to her. If you have also received anything from anyone, do not hesitate to send it to me, who am pressed by extreme necessity, since you will not be able to send anything so valuable or so small that we would not have to spend it on food.

> **Note:** “Pressed.” This is what the manuscript has, and entirely correctly. The reading in Masson’s edition is absurd: instead of *arctato* it has *Arentalo*.

## LETTER LI. TO THE BROTHERS OF FERRIÈRES

To the beloved brothers, greetings.

If any one of you is uncertain what joy I take in R., let him recall that divine authority declares that robbers will not possess the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6), and he will no longer be able to doubt.

But let R.’s teacher, lest he boast that he has found an irrefutable argument, understand that the administration and labor of all our estates belong to me—mine, I say—while the use of their produce, according to my arrangement, is common to the brothers. Thus religion neither diminishes secular authority, nor does authority confound religion.

Meanwhile, look after our horses, so that they are not taken away by either teacher or pupil. Without any consideration for me in this matter, strive to do whatever you can according to the law against the violent usurper, knowing that your diligence will be more pleasing to me the greater and more conspicuous it proves.

As for the more important matters I am attempting, it will be my concern to complete whatever opportunity—or rather, whatever God—allows from this point.

Since I am going to Traiectum with the king, God willing, where the brothers will meet him for a conference, and since I have good hope of recovering the cell, I cannot be present with you. Therefore let each of you deal with me as he usually does and ought to do. As we agreed last year, whoever can act should do so until I return and learn whether anything needs to be changed.

Let the sowing be attended to with the greatest care; and whatever our oxen have not been able to provide after the customary obligation, let frequent collections make up.

I wish you good health and that you pray for us most diligently.

## LETTER LII. TO THE PROVOST

> **Note:** “Our E.” Here we have faithfully reproduced the manuscript. Masson’s edition instead had: “Our brother, probably.” The reading of the old manuscript appears more authentic and therefore ought to be retained.

Our E. has made plausible everything that was being done by you, which pleased me; and I advise you to remain, as you began, in the service with sincere loyalty.

Know that I shall strongly refuse that madman about whom you wrote, since even when repentant he is suspect to me, and we are filled to nausea with genuine holiness. If he thrusts himself forward, persuade the others that he must not remain beyond three days; for there is no need for us to seek from outside what we can tolerate.

## LETTER LIII. TO LORD KING CHARLES

Most excellent king,

Although I have so far accomplished nothing by keeping silent, speaking, or writing, nevertheless, since the cause I am pursuing is God’s cause, I do not dare to rest. For your safety and prosperity I warn you and humbly beg you to free yourselves from danger and, in accordance with your frequent promises, to relieve your most devoted servant—myself—from this harshest labor.

What your father, of blessed memory, bestowed, with the intervention of your glorious mother, upon travelers and servants of God for the redemption of their souls, those now afflicted by various necessities and unable all to be present seek from you through me after four years.

To let you know their very words, they say that it is unjust for you to torment them with hunger and cold when they are compelled continually to pray for your temporal and eternal salvation; and that you will not obtain the happiness you desire until you return to friendship with our little Saint Peter.

> **Note:** “Our little Saint Peter.” The monastery of Ferrières is dedicated to Saint Peter. Lupus had no reason to fear that Peter would be angered by such familiar language as “our little Saint Peter.” Nevertheless, the emperor Tiberius may have disliked a similar familiarity in Cotta Messalinus, who, as Tacitus reports in Book VI of the *Annals*, complained about the power of Manius Lepidus and Lucius Arruntius and added: “The Senate will protect them, but my little Tiberius will protect me.” Matthew Paris, under the year 801, reports that a certain theologian, having publicly discussed the mystery of the Trinity and seeing his audience applauding him, rashly burst out with these words: “O little Jesus, little Jesus, how much I have confirmed your law and exalted it in this question!” In Bohuslaus Balbinus’s *History of Holy Mary of the Holy Mountain*, we read *Jesulus* for the child Jesus. Ripamonti, however, in Part II of his *History of the Church of Milan*, p. 57, writes that a demon inhabiting a woman’s body, after she had been brought first unsuccessfully to the relics of Saint Syrus and then to Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, who was at that time in the region, was pressed to depart and cried out: “Neither could little Syrus drive me out before, nor will little Bernard drive me out today.”

And lest you think they are joking, our old men seriously affirm, from their own experience, that whoever has inflicted some notable harm upon our monastery, unless he quickly repented, suffered great misfortune or endured loss of health and life; and say that this was handed down to them, when they were boys, by older men.

Therefore, do not obstruct your prosperity through such a deed or anything similar. Do not despise the poverty of God’s servants, nor make your own salvation uncertain. Rather, fulfill your vows to God while you can, as you advance each day with us toward His exceedingly fearsome judgment, at which, without regard to dignities or persons, each one will receive what he deserves.

This life is brief and uncertain, and those younger than you die each day. God Himself promises and threatens: “Those who honor me, I will honor; but those who despise me shall be dishonored” (1 Samuel 2).

You have reached manhood. Do not fear doing justice, so that through it your throne may be established. My lord king, consider that, as was wisely said recently in the exhortation, you are now a father and are still engaged in great labors. Show yourself to all as a man whom the good may desire and wish to see as a fortunate and happy grandfather, and, after the passage of this life, as a possessor of the heavenly homeland.

> **Note:** “In the exhortation.” See above in the notes to Letter 45.

## LETTER LIV. TO A CLOSE ASSOCIATE

I knew that you would act exactly as I wished and as was proper, and that with immense authority you would prevent the crimes of that utterly lost man. Therefore I congratulate you, and I offer and owe to almighty God, if not worthy thanks, then as much thanks as I can, because He deprived me in part of necessary support in such a way that its loss was nevertheless supplied by the devotion of a most faithful man.

But not only must that shameless enemy be guarded against and thwarted; those whom I recently placed in office while uncertain must also always be strengthened by your diligence, so that they strive to be obedient to orders and do not think it safe in any way to resist you.

When I return, my presence may perhaps remove your fear. Meanwhile, do not be afraid of the ungrateful.

## LETTER LV. TO MARCWARD, ABBOT

> **Note:** “To Marcward.” The abbot of Prüm, as we stated in the note to Letter 5.

To the most illustrious abbot Marcward, whom I regard with the greatest desire and veneration, Lupus sends present and future salvation.

The arrival of Nithard at Silvacum, where the needs of the monastery had drawn me, made me exceedingly happy. His presence caused this letter to be delivered to your fatherhood, since it showed that you and our common son Eigil were safe and that Eigil had recovered from a very serious illness with the help of divine favor.

> **Note:** “Nithard.” The very distinguished Paulus Petavius seems to doubt in his *Syntagma* on Nithard, the grandson of Charlemagne, whether this passage of Lupus should be understood of him. The fact that he had been a monk of the monastery of Centula in the diocese of Amiens seemed to support this: Angilbert, Nithard’s father, had enlarged that monastery and had been its abbot, and was buried there. Nithard himself was also abbot of Centula. Yet Petavius saw that from this letter of Lupus it could be inferred that this Nithard had instead been a monk of Prüm rather than of Centula. I would believe that Nithard first adopted the discipline of Blessed Benedict in the monastery of Centula, out of memory of his father, but later, because of Marcward’s great reputation, withdrew to the monastery of Prüm—not to become a monk there, but as a guest. Then, returning to his own community, he became abbot of Centula. He died in 855, as the same Petavius believes. He wrote four books on the dissensions among the sons of Louis the Pious, addressed to Charles the Bald, king of the Franks. He supported Charles against Lothar and Louis and was also advanced by him to positions of honor.

> **Note:** “Eigil.” He later became abbot of Prüm after Marcward in 853, as Regino relates. Then, in 855, Lothar, emperor and son of Louis the Pious, became a monk at the monastery of Prüm, then governed by this Eigil. Regino writes: “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 855, Lothar, having summoned the leading men of the realm, divided the empire among his sons. He gave Italy to Louis and caused him to be called emperor. To his namesake, that is Lothar, he granted the kingdom which is called by his name. To Charles, who was younger in age, he gave the kingdom of Provence. Having thus disposed and ordered the affairs of the realm, he bade farewell to his people, left the world, came to the monastery of Prüm, cut off his hair, received the habit of holy conduct, and ended his last day in the profession of religion on the third day before the Kalends of October.”
>
> But here is the old tale of the monk of Angoulême: “The emperor Lothar, falling ill, became a monk in the monastery of Prüm because he had expelled his father from the empire and kept him imprisoned. After his death, the brothers saw a dispute over his soul between evil and good angels. The holy angels said: ‘The Lord sent us not to the emperor, but to the monk. You take the emperor; we shall take the monk with us.’ The holy angels took his soul with them. The demons received the body and began violently to drag it from the house before everyone’s eyes; but, put to flight by the brothers’ prayers, they vanished.”
>
> Several years later Eigil resigned the government of the monastery of Prüm, as Regino attests in these words: “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 860, Abbot Egil voluntarily relinquished the abbey of Prüm.” Returning afterwards to Francia, he became archbishop of Sens after Wenilo. Odorannus writes in his *Chronicle*: “In 865 Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, died; he had anointed Louis, Charles’s brother, king in Burgundy. Abbot Egil succeeded him. In 870 Lord Egil, archbishop, died; he made a privilege for Saint Peter concerning the altar of the estate of Alson. With the consent of the younger Lothar and at the command of the bishop of Trier [the text reads ‘Trejectensium’], he was taken from that diocese and from the monastery called Prüm, and King Charles made him abbot in the monastery of Flavigny. Afterwards, for his merits, he was made archbishop of Sens; he rests in the monastery of Saint Peter.” See also Eigil’s charter on the foundation of the monastery of Corbiniacum in volume IV of *Gallia Christiana*. The *Chronicle of Saint Peter the Living at Sens* says: “In 865 Archbishop Wenilo died and was buried at Valliliae, on the fifth day before the Nones of May, in the crypt of the virgin Saint Anastasia. Lord Egil, a monk conspicuous for every goodness, succeeded him in the bishopric.” Letters 105 and 109 of Lupus, addressed to him while he was still a monk, survive.
>
> **Note:** “At Silvacum.” A royal villa in the county of Laon, as Sirmond gathered from Hincmar of Laon’s letter to the archbishop of Reims. Hence that same very learned man rightly concludes that those who confuse Silvacum, or Silvaticum—for the villa is found under both names—with Silvanectum are mistaken. Lupus mentions Silvacum again in Letter 57.

I have experienced your benevolence and generosity so greatly that I feel I owe a greater devotion to no one than to you. Although the malignity of the times has prevented me from showing through acts of service what I rightly desire, trusting in your goodness I dare to beg you not to hesitate to come to our king.

For you may perhaps be able to recover your own property and may also help us greatly in recovering the cell of Saint Judocus. Concerning this matter, he has already promised both you and me very frequently, and most recently Louis, with such seriousness that, if you deign to be present, he will be unable to find any excuse for delay.

Thus he will be frightened by the danger to the property which his father and mother left to travelers and to us monks and which he has taken away; and he will be constrained by the sequence of his promises at least then to do what he once pledged he would do.

> **Note:** “To Louis.” In the manuscript one reads *ad*, abbreviated *hal.*, instead of *Ludovico*, while Letter 88 has *Adalh.* Since I could not determine how this was to be explained, I thought it should be recorded. Otherwise the name Louis is not pointless here, since it is well established that he was a close friend of Lupus and was frequently urged by him to use the influence he enjoyed with Charles the Bald to help him and the monks recover the cell. For this reason we have altered nothing. For which Louis this was, see above in the notes to Letter 22. Lupus states here and in another letter that the cell of Saint Judocus was recovered chiefly through the efforts of this Adalh.

On the day before the Kalends of December I went to the royal court, and I am constantly with the king amid enormous expenses and labors, while he continually postpones my hopes on account of the absence, as he admits, of Odulphus.

He is said to be ill—not so dangerously that, if admonished, he might not be corrected, which we would desire; nor so gravely that he might die, which we would grieve on account of his most certain damnation.

> **Note:** “Most certain damnation.” The dream of the damnation of Charles Martel arose from beliefs of this kind. Some people at that time thought that the salvation of anyone who dared even to touch, so to speak, with the tip of a fingernail the property of monasteries was entirely lost. In Caesarius of Heisterbach, who lived four hundred years ago, one can read that many powerful men were condemned to eternal death for this reason. This is useful in deterring or exhorting. Thus Boniface of Mainz, writing with several bishops from some synod to Ethelbald, king of the Mercians, to turn him away from seizing churches and monasteries, cites the example of Ceolred, king of the Mercians, and Osred, king of the Deirans and Bernicians, who “were condemned by God’s just judgment for breaking up monasteries, cast down from the royal summit of this life, overtaken by premature and terrible death, excluded from perpetual light, and plunged into the depths of hell and the abyss of Tartarus.” See Boniface, Letter 19.

Hasten, therefore, so that, since we have come somewhat nearer to one another, I may be refreshed by the conversation I have desired after such long intervals and, through your efforts, by the grace of God, be freed from anxieties scarcely bearable.

I beg you to be toward our young men what you have been not only toward ours but also toward all people who have piously sought your fatherly care. In the name of my insignificance, deign to greet the most beloved Eigil and all the other brothers.

I would never have presumed to impose upon you a most laborious and extremely difficult task at such a difficult time, especially when I have deserved nothing from you, had I not learned that our king was inviting you to a conference. Indeed, at this time he instructed me that, if you happened to come to our monastery, I should arrange to escort you to him.

Having obtained permission, you could conveniently suggest to the emperor, among other matters, that I and our brothers, who always pray for him, are wearing you out with our pleas: since you belong to our community and only your body has been removed from it by ecclesiastical duty, and since it is being severely weakened by the diminution of its resources and poverty is obstructing religious observance, you should devote the help of your intercession with the greatest zeal to its restoration.

> **Note:** “You belong to our community.” Thus Marcward was first a monk in the monastery of Ferrières and later abbot of Prüm.

Farewell, my lord and most beloved father, and always remember your Lupus kindly.

## LETTER LVI. TO ABBOT RATBERT

> **Note:** “To Abbot Ratbert.” Of Old Corbie in the diocese of Amiens, who flourished under Charles the Bald and whose full name was Paschasius Ratbertus. In my old manuscript there is a *Life of Saint Richarius*, abbot of Centula, at the end of which these words are written:

> “Here ends the Life of the most holy confessor of Christ, Richarius, written in truthful style by the venerable men Ratbert and Alcuin Albin. Supplication of the said Albin:
>
> Whoever you are who read the deeds of the illustrious patron,
>
> O Christ, remember your poor Albin.”

To Ratbert, abbot:

To Ratbert, worthy of the affection of all good men, Lupus sends greetings in the Lord.

After carefully considering what was expedient, with our Vulfegis urging him on, I suggested to the lord king that he should ask you, concerning Ivo, to ensure that, since Ivo had not returned to the monastery and it was likely that he would repeat the behavior to which he had been accustomed whenever he attempted to return, he should not be fortified by the protection of his authority to the ruin of himself and others.

For it would be unworthy of his majesty to open access to the perverse except to those who repent, much less to grant them the security of impunity.

He, with the expression he usually wears when he appears gracious, replied, after some other remarks, that he would henceforth deny that monk access to the authority which he had until now scorned to use; and that it seemed better to him, lest the man perish, that he should first be restrained by suitable custody until he recovered communion with the community.

Although he offered what we could scarcely have hoped for at all, and we embraced it as was proper, we firmly maintained that we would neither stop short of the Rule’s decree nor wish to go beyond it.

I did not wish to proclaim my opinion of your generosity hastily, before testing whether the supply of fish that was expected—both very great and, as I thought, of the finest quality—would exceed the capacity of my little intellect.

## LETTER LVII. TO THE SAME

To the most beloved abbot Ratbert, Lupus sends complete good wishes.

What you requested, I undertook to carry out without delay. After working through many arguments, I brought this man to the position that it would not merely do no harm but would be of the greatest benefit if, toward his kinsman who had departed during the time of upheaval and would return once peace had been restored, you were to show yourselves gracious. I confidently promised that you would gladly do this and would obey in everything he might deign to command, so long as you enjoyed his favor; and I persisted until he most firmly promised that he would do nothing against you without first discussing the matter with me.

Thus I concluded the terms of my petition with this condition: if at any time rebels should demand that their complaints be supported by his favor, he should not comply indiscriminately, but reserve only matters worthy of your consideration. I have learned certain other things that must be disclosed so cautiously that I have not thought it safe to include them in a letter, yet they are so necessary to know that you ought to come to meet me as quickly as you can, setting aside every other advantage. Moreover, unless it is already burdensome, send a messenger to Silvacum to meet me when I depart with the king, if God wills; so that, when I begin to give thanks, a fuller abundance of words may not fail me as I vainly strive to say many things. To close this letter in earnest, I beg you not to regard me as a burden because, trusting in our excessive familiarity, I ask so much: for if God grants me life and prosperity, I shall not now be readier to receive than I shall one day be ready to give generously.

## LETTER LVIII. TO THE SAME.

What you asked, I have not yet suggested to the king, because the opportunity was lacking. Nevertheless, with God’s help, I shall hasten to satisfy you, while preserving our common dignity. Farewell.

## 101. LETTER LIX. TO MARCWARD, ABBOT.

You are not unaware, I believe, that our kings are to hold a conference at Traiectum in the second week of Lent [Note: At Traiectum. See the notes on Letter 15.]; ecclesiastical necessity is drawing me there. Because of that necessity, as I have already expressed to others in letters, I have now been with the king for the fourth month, so that I have not been away from his retinue even for a single day. Let your desirable fatherhood therefore make itself present to me there at least, so that we may be able to learn about our affairs familiarly, in person and by word of mouth. If, beyond this, you should have the opportunity to assist us—as you commonly do everyone—know that we shall gladly accept it. For parents ought to store up treasures for their children (2 Cor. 12), as the authority of the divine Spirit, which cannot deceive, confirms. I desire you to remember me kindly and to fare happily.

## LETTER LX. TO THE SAME.

To the most beloved Father Marcward [Note: Marcward, abbot of Prüm, as has already been stated. Lupus therefore thanks him for the gifts sent, which he had requested from him in the preceding letter. Meanwhile he complains about his own situation, namely that he is returning from Traiectum—the place from which this letter is written—to his monastery without seeing Marcward. Nevertheless, he says that this sorrow is relieved by Marcward’s promise: Marcward had written back that he would soon go to the monks of Ferrières. Lupus warns him not to come to him before the second week of May, since a great synod was to be held at Attiniacum on the fifteenth day after Easter, and he thought it impossible that he himself would not be compelled to attend.], Lupus sends greetings.

Your considerate kindness has surpassed my request, which only lightly touched upon what the urgency of the moment required. It was therefore more welcome than those free from troubles can appreciate. I am exceedingly distressed, however, that I am departing without seeing you. Yet my sadness is consoled by your promise to visit our humble community after Easter [Note: Easter. This year it fell on 10 April.]. I think you will do this conveniently, and while I am present, if you undertake the journey to us in the second week of May. For on the fifteenth day after Easter [Note: The great synod. At the assembly held at Marsna in 847, Lothair, Louis, and Charles had agreed that, in order to confirm what had been enacted there, a common decision, or general assembly, should be held in Paris on the following feast of Saint John. Charles therefore decided to convene a great synod at Attiniacum in the intervening period, so that he might arrange the civil and ecclesiastical affairs of his kingdom before the assembly and afterward deliberate jointly with his brothers. It was to be held on the fifteenth day after Easter, that is, 24 April. I do not, however, think that this synod was held, any more than the Parisian assembly. Although the kings seemed to have established peace at Marsna, discord afterward arose between Lothair and Charles, as the Annals of Fulda report under the year 847: “That year rested from wars, and Lothair and Louis spent it in mutual affection. Each, invited to the other’s home, was honored with banquets and royal gifts. Louis, however, could not reconcile Lothair and Charles as he wished, because Lothair refused on account of the wrong done to him by Gislebert, Charles’s vassal, in the abduction of his daughter.” At last harmony was restored again at Marsna in 851.] a great synod, as they say, will be celebrated at Attiniacum [Note: Attiniacum, a royal palace situated in the diocese of Reims, as stated in the note on Letter 49.]. I believe that our bishops will by no means allow me to be absent from it [Note: They will by no means permit it. The very holy bishops of Gaul valued our Lupus so highly that they regarded him almost as a framer of the canons and in some sense considered his presence at synods necessary. He had already demonstrated his sacred learning in the canons of the council of Verneuil, as stated in the note on Letter 42.].

Concerning our cell [Note: Our cell—that is, the cell of Saint Judoc. It had not yet been restored to Lupus, although he had good hope that it would be recovered at the assembly at Traiectum, as is clear from Letter 51.], I can tell your fatherhood nothing except that the abundance of promises produces almost daily various hopes for us, and that, as with everything except evil, the outcome of this matter too remains uncertain. The abbot of the monastery called in German Saligstat [Note: Saligstat. Today Seligenstatt. It is a monastery in the diocese of Mainz, situated on the River Main, which gave its name to the town. It was founded by Einhard, Charlemagne’s secretary, who was its first abbot.]—his name is Ratlegio [Note: Ratlegio. His name was omitted from Masson’s edition, but it appears in a manuscript. He succeeded Einhard, who calls him Ratleicus in the account of the translation of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter. I agree with the learned and diligent Christoph Brower that Ratlaicus, abbot of Seligenstadt, is precisely the man whom Einhard, in that account, calls his secretary, Book I, chapter 11.
