Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz, composed Ratlaicus’s epitaph, which reads:

> Behold the servant of Christ, called by the name RATLAICUS;  
> Here his body rests, while his spirit seeks the heights.  
> He was a priest and a devoted lover of wisdom;  
> He performed well the office and work of an abbot.  
> Skillful and vigorous, he learned the teachings of the divine law  
> By investigating them, and taught them to others.  
> Coming from Cologne, he was closely joined to King Louis  
> And was of great service to him.  
> For he taught many by his words and had them write  
> Many things suitable for various offices.  
> Leaving this life while still young, he departed to heaven,  
> And there he holds true joys with Christ.

You see here, reader, that Ratlaicus is commended for his study of Scripture, evidently because he carefully arranged for the writings of the best authors to be copied. This observation greatly illuminates this passage of Lupus, who says that Ratlegio undertook to have a portion of a certain book copied for Lupus. From the epitaph we also learn that he was taken away by an untimely death.]—promises that he will have a certain portion of a book copied for me and will hand it over to your messenger, so that it may be returned to me. I beg you to be so kind as to send him, in the second week after Easter, the panels that the painter Hilperic [Note: To the blessed martyrs. That is, to the holy Marcellinus and Peter, whose sacred relics are preserved in the basilica of the monastery at Seligenstadt. They were brought there through Einhard’s efforts in 827, as the author of the Annals of Fulda records in these words: “The bodies of the blessed martyrs of Christ Marcellinus and Peter were brought to Francia in the month of November.” Einhard began that basilica; Ratlaicus completed it. The painter Hilperic, as Lupus explains, had vowed panels for decorating the basilica. Rabanus, Hymn 24, on the saints Marcellinus and Peter:

> These witnesses of Christ, from the city of Rome,  
> The good man Einhard received and established here.  
> His successor Ratlaicus, having completed the church,  
> Founded this shrine for the saints.

] vowed to the blessed martyrs. I also wish you to expedite this as the purpose of my request, so that when you come to us you may take care to bring us the aforesaid portion of the book. You will do us a great service in the boys if you do not disdain to complete, with fatherly kindness, what you began. Perhaps sparing my nephew drink will relieve his headache, if he is found to be too eager for it. Otherwise, it will be reserved for our physician to cure—one who confidently believes that he can drive away every illness, since he is ignorant of none. I desire, with the greatest affection, that you fare most happily, and I earnestly beg you to deign always to assist me especially before God.

## 103. LETTER LXI. [Note: To Guigmund. Bishop of York in England. William of Malmesbury mentions him nowhere except by name alone, calling him Wimundus. Matthew of Westminster says that he died in 854. Francis Godwin, bishop of Hereford, writes that he succeeded Wulfsige in the see of York and occupied it for seventeen years. In an old catalogue of the archbishops of York, published through the efforts of R. P. Labbe, the following is written: “After Eanbald, Wulfsige governed the archbishopric, while Eanred was king. When Wulfsige died, Wimund succeeded him, while the aforesaid king was reigning. In the sixteenth year of his episcopate, when Wimund died, Wlfhere succeeded him in the archbishopric.”]

### TO GUIGMUND, BISHOP OF YORK.

To the most reverend and highly honored Guigmund, bishop of the Church of York, and to all those serving God under him [Note: Serving God. That is, the monks of the Church of York. At that time everything among the English was full of monks, according to the institution of Saint Augustine. There was a strong fellowship between the monks of York and those of Ferrières; Lupus asks that it be renewed because it had been interrupted. The abbot to whom the following letter is addressed was therefore abbot of the monks of the Church of York.], Lupus the abbot and the entire congregation of the monastery of Ferrières send greetings in the Lord.

A great span of time has passed during which, as various disturbances grew more frequent, the fellowship entered into by our predecessors, with the Lord as its author, has produced no signs of charity apart from prayers. Now, however, as the grace of peace opens before us and the cell of Saint Judoc has been restored—the place from which we are writing this—we have taken care, as was proper, to be the first to vie in dutiful service and to invite you either to renew or to declare our friendship. First of all, we humbly ask that you deign to remember us both in your private and in your public prayers. Next, we wish, in return, to endeavor to provide whatever letters sent between us show to be welcome, insofar as opportunity permits. Therefore hasten to reveal your will to us, so that we may immediately prepare ourselves to serve you obediently and so that our Lord God may be glorified and pleased by the fruit of affection. I desire you to fare happily, most beloved Fathers.

## 104. LETTER LXII. [Note: To Altsig. Masson’s edition reads, “To Altsig, abbot.” I have not wished to depart from the reading of the old manuscript. He was the abbot of the monks of the Church of York, as I have said.]

### TO ALTSIG, ABBOT.

To the venerable Altsig, abbot, Lupus of the Bethlehemite monastery, or Ferrières, sends greetings in the Lord.

By the great mercy of our God, the plague of discord that has so savagely afflicted all Gaul and Germany has been calmed. At the very beginning of peace, I have endeavored, by letters addressed to the most reverend Bishop Guigmund, to renew the bond that formerly existed between our Church and yours. Since I have learned that you burn with love of wisdom, of which I too am desirous—either, in Cicero’s words, “equals are easily joined with equals,” or, according to the accepted assertion of Scripture, “Every creature loves its like”—by this letter I offer you my friendship and seek yours, so that we may mutually strive to benefit one another both in sacred prayers and in every other useful matter.

And so that you may be the first to carry out what I promise, I earnestly beg you to send me, through thoroughly reliable messengers, to the cell of Saint Judoc, which has at last been returned to us [Note: Has been returned. It follows that this letter was not written before 847. Letter 51 establishes that the cell of Saint Judoc had not yet been returned to Lupus when the kings were about to assemble at Traiectum. That conference was held at the beginning of 847, as noted on Letter 50.], to be delivered to Lantram, whom you know well and who will have them copied there and returned to you as quickly as possible, the Questions of Blessed Jerome, which, as Cassiodorus testifies, he composed on the Old and New Testaments; likewise the Questions of your Bede [Note: Your Bede—that is, born in your England and originating there. He was a man of great renown, as I suppose even the bleary-eyed and the barbers know. He died in 735, approximately a hundred years before this letter of Lupus was written. See Labbe in his Historical Dissertation on Ecclesiastical Writers and our notes on Letter 76 of Lupus.] on both Testaments; and also the remaining books of the explanations of the aforementioned Jerome on Jeremiah, apart from the first six, which are found among us; in addition, the twelve books of Quintilian’s *Institutio oratoria*. If you cannot send all of them, please do not hesitate to send at least some, so that you may receive from God the reward of fulfilled charity, and from us merely whatever return for so great a labor we are able to make.

Farewell, and as soon as the opportunity presents itself, gladden us with the welcome reply we long for.

## LETTER LXIII. [Note: To Bishop Prudentius. Trecassinus, as the title in Masson’s edition stated, and as is sufficiently known from other evidence.]

### TO BISHOP PRUDENTIUS.

To his beloved Prudentius, Lupus sends greetings in the Lord.

On 7 April, Bishop Heribold [Note: Bishop Heribold. Of Auxerre, to whom several of Lupus’s letters are addressed.]—who had shortly before returned from the king—reported to me, by order of that same king, that since he himself had excused himself from the duties of an embassy [Note: The performance of the embassy. This embassy of Lupus and Prudentius took place in 844, as stated in Lupus’s Life. This is confirmed by Letter 32: “In the preceding year,” he says, “I was sent into Burgundy and lost ten horses.” That letter was written in 845, as we noted there.], we should in turn carry it out energetically and quickly [Note: Carry it out. That is: Since Bishop Heribold excused himself from undertaking the embassy that Charles had assigned to him, the prince ordered that you and I, Prudentius, should assume the responsibility that Heribold had declined. The embassy was of this kind: the envoys were to visit, in the king’s name, the monasteries established in Charles’s kingdom and report to the prince anything they considered worthy of attention, as we explained in the note on Letter 12.], so that the aforesaid king might be informed about each place at the general assembly.

Since the time is approaching, since we can confer only with difficulty—especially because of fodder for the horses—and since we must not begin what has been ordered before grass is plentiful, immediately inform me by letter both of your health and of your view on this matter. To disclose my own opinion, I consider it unnecessary to visit again those places whose condition we have already examined, since no improvement has followed. In the districts of Orléans and Sens, and in your own and ours, some monasteries remain in which we can spend the intervening time, so that the king may learn what needs correction in these places as he has in the others. And lest his command be disregarded by his envoys, let him impose a sanction if he wishes. For the esteem in which we are held—or rather, the honor lavished upon us by the very man who sent us—and the restoration of discipline in the monasteries have made this clear.

Before beginning the embassy, therefore, I have decided to suggest these matters to the king through my own agency and to receive our *tractoriae* [Note: *Tractoriae*. As Sirmond notes in his edition of Charles the Bald’s Capitularies, whenever envoys set out on their embassies they were given a *tractoria*, that is, a letter by which they were received and obtained their *congius*, namely the payment or tribute undoubtedly demanded from those on whose account the envoys were sent. In the *tractoriae* it was customary to record how much was to be supplied to each envoy according to his rank. Agobard therefore calls it a “stipendiary *tractoria*.” See Book IV of the Capitularies, chapter 73, and Marculf, Book I, chapter 11, with the notes of the learned Jerome Bignon; also Justellus’s notes on the Code of the Canons of the African Church, p. 93.], and then, with God’s favor, to depart. Express your view in writing in return, so that the best course may be discerned from the judgment of both of us.

But do not fail to understand this: however much we may labor on this embassy, neither we nor our men may relax in any respect; we must do what the others do, should disturbances like those that have afflicted these places until now arise again.

## LETTER LXIV. AN EXHORTATION TO KING CHARLES.

I have collected, with faithful devotion, the duties you must observe if you are to reign peacefully and successfully. Always give thanks and render thanks to your Creator, God and future Judge, who has hitherto freed you from many evils and adorned you with many blessings; and ask him in your daily prayers to grant you a beginning, progress, and perseverance in good works. When you were children, you spoke as children and understood as children. But now that you have reached manhood, in accordance with the same Apostle (1 Cor. 13), through whom the Spirit of God clearly spoke, put away the things that belonged to childhood. Avoid all that is foolish and empty, and pursue what is rational and beneficial to your present and future salvation.

Carefully foresee what must be done and examine it closely, taking counsel with those who are wholly faithful to God and to you; for, as the divine word instructs us, “If a man is evil to himself, to whom will he be good?” (Ecclus. 14). Do not subject yourselves to anyone in such a way that you do everything at his discretion. Why do you claim the royal name if you do not know how to rule?—let me say this with the goodwill of all—neither you nor the people benefit from your making anyone your equal, much less placing him above you. For God, who knows what is in man, warns: “Do not give power to your sons during your lifetime” (Ecclus. 33), because it is better for them to entreat you than for you to entreat them. If this is not to be granted even to sons, how much less to others?

Who does not know that you hold God’s place? Yet he himself says: “I will not give my glory to another” (Isa. 42). Therefore do not admit advisers whom the common people call *bajuli* [Note: *Bajuli*. That is, advisers, as Lupus interprets the word while using Sallustius’s terminology; or guardians and governors of an imperial youth, to use Tacitus’s term. The *Deeds of Dagobert I*, king of the Franks and son of Clotaire II, says: “He had a son named Dagobert, whom he had received from Queen Bertrude, destined to succeed his father and worthy in character and strength. While still a boy, he was entrusted by his venerable and most holy father to Arnulf, bishop of the city of Metz, so that he might raise him according to his wisdom, show him the path of Christian religion, and be his guardian and *bajulus*.” The Annals of Saint-Bertin under 861 say: “Charles, leaving his son Louis under the guardianship of Adalard, uncle of Queen Irmintrude,” and under 879: “Entrusting his son and namesake Louis especially to the guardianship of Bernard, count of Auvergne.” Hence guardianship is called *ballium* in the acts composed in the time of King Louis of France. Thus, while Louis the Pious was still in his cradle, Charlemagne appointed Arnold as his guardian, as the author of Louis’s Life writes. See Hincmar’s Letter 11 to Emperor Charles III, chapters 2, 6, and 7. Baronius appears to think that this letter was written in 850.], lest they divide your glory among themselves and estrange the better love of the people from you.

In imitation of God, do not judge personally [Note: To judge personally. That is, imitate God when issuing judgments, for with him there is no respect of persons. Before him rich and poor are equally secure. Cassiodorus speaks in the same way; these are his words in Letter 8 of Book II: “Who is more rightly loved according to the laws of equity than he who is adorned with the priesthood? He who, through love of justice, knows not how to judge according to persons, and, loving all in common, leaves no place for envy.”]; but in the same case let the rich, the middling, and the poor all find you the same, so that there may be something to terrify the powerful and something to soothe those who do not resist. Once something has been done well, never change it except for the better, so that all may marvel at your faithfulness and constancy. Flee fickleness; embrace maturity of conduct, so that your integrity may benefit all your subjects.

Avoid the company of the wicked, for, as you recall from Scripture, “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15). Embrace the fellowship of the good, for “with the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent you will be innocent; with the elect you will be elect, and with the perverse you will become perverse” (Ps. 17). And in the same king and prophet it is beautifully said: “He who walks in the spotless way, he served me. He who acts proudly shall not dwell in the midst of my house; he who speaks unjustly has not been straight in my sight” (Ps. 100).

Do not fear the powerful whom you yourselves have made powerful and whom, whenever you wish, you can reduce. Do not put your trust in princes, in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation (Ps. 145); but transfer your hope to God, who made heaven and earth and who keeps truth forever. Conceive an honorable standard of truth, so that no one may knowingly dare to ask of you what it is unworthy for you to grant. Think about many things, but do not say everything, whether according to divine Scripture—“He who guards his mouth guards his soul from troubles” (Prov. 21)—or according to secular literature [Note: Secular literature. Lupus was firmly convinced that the book on morals attributed to Seneca was genuinely Seneca’s. The following testimony is accordingly cited from secular literature, that is, from a non-Christian author. It remains to investigate whether it truly belongs to Seneca or to Martin of Braga, as some have thought. I would believe that Seneca wrote it first and that Martin later copied and abridged it, thereby making the book his own. Certainly the sentences that Lupus unquestionably cites from that work are expressed by Lupus in different and more elegant words than those found in Martin of Braga, who has them as follows: “What you wish to remain secret, tell no one. If you have not commanded yourself, how do you expect silence from another?” Thus we have a fragment of Seneca in this letter of Lupus.]: “Tell no one what you wish to keep hidden. For how can you demand from another the silence that you do not yourself maintain?” And: “A voice once sent forth cannot return” (Horace, *Art of Poetry*, line 390, in substance).

Let everyone recognize that the common welfare and advantage of all are most dear to you, so that all may compete with one another in seeking to put you first. Let no one be permitted to despise either divine or human laws, provided that they are just, because impunity for wrongdoing has always produced an increase of vices.

Let humility adorn all your works, for it is written: “Why is earth and ashes proud?” (Ecclus. 10). And: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Ecclus. 3). Our Redeemer himself also admonishes us: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11).

Appease God toward yourselves by continual almsgiving, according to the saying: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30), because, as the sacred writings state, almsgiving delivers from death and does not allow the soul to go into darkness (Tob. 4). The Savior also commends it in this way: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11).

Glorify God in all things, for Scripture itself testifies: “Those who glorify me, I will glorify; but those who despise me shall be without honor” (1 Sam. 2). The outstanding king and prophet likewise places God before himself: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. 113).

If you carefully observe these things, you will please God and all good people. You will suppress and overcome the rebels, since, as we believe, God will fight on your behalf; and after a temporal and arduous kingdom you will attain one that is eternal and truly peaceful.

## LETTER LXV. TO THE BROTHERS OVER WHOM HE PRESIDED.

To his beloved brothers, Lupus the abbot sends greetings in the Lord.

Our enemies, inflamed by desire, have attempted many things, but under the Lord’s protection and through the merits of the saints they have been cast down from their hope. With his aid they will never attain the outcome they desire. I have taken care to inform you of this so that worthy thanks may be rendered to God and his saints, and so that, security having been recovered, your minds may enjoy the peace that follows.

## LETTER LXVI. [Note: To Bishop Reginfrid. It is not clear of which see he was bishop. Nor do I accept the opinion of the Sammarthani, who identify him with the man who was bishop of Meaux and attended the synod of Pontigon in 876. Lupus died many years before Ragenfrid became bishop of Meaux. Perhaps this Reginfrid had previously been a notary of King Charles the Bald. In the charters of that period I find a Raginfrid subscribing as representative of Louis. Since the occasion has arisen, I shall also give the words of Charles the Simple, which settle the dispute over the location of Pontigon. He says this in the charter by which he established a dowry for his wife Frideruna: “Pontigon, moreover, in the district of Perthes, upon the rivers Saltus and Brustio.” It is called Pons Hugonis in the Annals of Aniane, doubtless through the error of copyists. See Book IV of *De re diplomatica*, p. 317.]

### TO BISHOP REGINFRID.

To the most reverend bishop Reginfrid, Lupus sends greetings in the Lord.

As we were preparing to depart for Rome, we learned that our route would pass not far from your city. There we desire to experience in practice the kindness that we anticipate in our hearts, especially by exchanging for the silver of Italian currency—which alone will be useful to us and of which we are completely destitute—something else; everyone whom we have questioned unanimously confirms this. With God’s favor, you will also grant us the sight of you, thereby increasing the benefit of your service with the kindness that is fitting. In truth, I cannot set a definite time for our arrival. Nevertheless, I suspect that it will be either in the height of summer or certainly at the beginning of autumn. I desire you to fare well.

## LETTER LXVII. TO W.

To the venerable V., Lupus sends greetings.

An opportunity to see you has presented itself to me unexpectedly, though it is something I desired, since I have learned that the road lies open to those traveling from the city that rests under your care and protection toward Rome, where I myself am heading. Therefore arrange matters so that, setting aside other occupations, we may enjoy the conversations of sincere charity and discuss both present advantage and future salvation.

It seems unnecessary to warn you in advance to strive to assist me in whatever necessity may demand, since I ought to trust fully in your prudence and generosity, from which I must not detract. Strive therefore to provide us with your knowledge of the region in which you live and with affection for the homeland in which we were born. If God wills, I shall pass through your territory, as I think, either at the end of summer or certainly at the beginning of autumn. I desire you to fare happily.

## 111. LETTER LXVIII. TO LORD MARCWARD, ABBOT.

To the most beloved and greatly longed-for Father Marcward, Lupus sends abundant greetings.

[Col. 0532A] For the sake of prayer and of certain ecclesiastical matters, which, God willing, I shall explain to your fatherhood when I return and see you, I am setting out for Rome. And since, in arranging the affairs of the [Note: [Col. 0531C] Apostolic. That is, of the Roman pontiff.] Apostolic See, I shall need the knowledge of that authority, and since this cannot conveniently be obtained without [Note: [Col. 0531C] The intervention of gifts. It had already become clear, evidently, that the Roman curia was exceedingly greedy for gifts, and that nothing could be obtained there for free, so that everything in Rome was for sale. Thus, setting out for Rome, Lupus was considering providing himself with travel funds, lest he suffer rejection by the Apostolic See. He therefore took care to solicit gifts with which he might win him over. The Reverend Father Cellotius praises this passage of Lupus in his *History of Gottschalk*, in order to refute the opinion of those who write that Gottschalk went to Rome to gain access to the pope. Cellotius denies this, for the obvious reason that it is not probable that the ears of the Roman pontiff would have been open to a poor little monk offering no gifts, when, at that same time, a man of very high standing with King Charles the Bald—namely, Lupus, abbot of Ferrières—did not think that the Roman bishop would be favorably disposed toward him unless he were won over by the offering of gifts. From Cellotius’s observation we learn that the interpretation of the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius is vain and futile: he interprets those gifts of Lupus as gifts given to the Roman pontiffs out of friendship, and therefore as expressing a token of charity in the giver, while in the recipient they would not signify avarice, as Baronius writes under the year 865. But if Lupus took care to solicit gifts because he thought that the Apostolic See would not be favorably disposed toward him unless it were appeased beforehand by gifts, as Cellotius observes, it is clear that Lupus’s gifts proceeded from necessity more than from charity, and therefore that they indicated avarice in the recipient. Let us nevertheless admit that the pontiff then presiding over the Roman [Col. 0532C] Church was afflicted by the vice of avarice. Nevertheless, the Roman Church is holy. For, as Saint Leo says, the rights of sees are one thing, and the vices of those presiding over them another.] the intervention of gifts, I flee to you as to a paternal—indeed, maternal—bosom, begging you, just as you have never failed me in any necessity, so now to deign to assist me, and, if you can in any way, to send me through the present messengers two blue cloaks and an equal number of linen cloths, which in German are called [Note: [Col. 0532C] *Glizza*. Hence *camisia glizzina* in the monk of Saint Gall’s *Life of Charlemagne*. Thus François Pithou read it, not *cilicina*, as Duchesne’s edition incorrectly has it in Book I, chapter 39. It is evident that *glizzina* cloth was of great value.] *glizza*, which I have discovered are especially precious and pleasing to him. If providing all these should prove difficult for you, the half itself will not seem to us something to be despised. For we have been so trained in secular learning that, while hoping for smaller things, we ask for greater ones. And lest you suppose that our ingenuity has lacked a broader subject, if you should ease our journey by providing a pacing horse, or any other very strong horse, we shall consider that a very great favor has been conferred upon us. Indeed, I shall not take it badly if I have obtained nothing, provided that, after sharing this letter with our common son Eigil, [Note: [Col. 0532C] May each of you have restrained his laughter. He refers to the witty remarks above, with which he has touched upon the Roman curia, and congratulates himself as though he had accomplished an outstanding deed worthy of triumph. The better minds have always delighted in exercising their ingenuity in such jokes, even at the risk of giving offense. Cicero testifies concerning himself that he could not escape this offense. Thus he writes in Letter 16 of Book IX of the *Letters to Friends*: “But if I wished to escape the offense caused by certain sharp or witty remarks, I would have to cast away my reputation for talent; and if I could do that, I would not refuse.” Here the offense would plainly have arisen if Marcward had sent this letter to Rome. But Lupus evidently thought that many jokes occur in letters which, when brought into the open, seem foolish; and many serious matters which nevertheless ought not to be divulged in any way, as Tullius writes in the second book of the *Antonian Orations*. He supposed that Marcward, too, a prudent man and his friend, would not be unaware of this. Therefore he believed that he could write to him freely.] each of you has restrained his laughter. I wish you good health and ask you kindly to keep me in your memory.

112 **LETTER LXIX. TO ANSBALD.** [Note: [Col. 0532D] To Ansbald, a monk of Prüm and indeed a companion of Eigil, who is mentioned below. This letter was written to him when he was abbot of Prüm; see Letter 117 below.]

To his beloved Ansbald, Lupus sends greetings.

I was displeased that, although you had discovered such a favorable opportunity, you—if I may put it very mildly—wanted neither to entrust me with anything nor to write to me. Yet, although you have so easily laid aside your concern for me—a fault I reproach in you—I shall by no means imitate you, but shall embrace you, even as you disdain me, in a pious conversation. I shall have the Ciceronian letters that you sent compared with ours, so that from both, if it can be done, the truth may be extracted. You, however, give Cicero *On Aratus* to this courier of ours, so that from it he may supply what our Eigil has revealed to me is lacking, which I believe I shall obtain from you. Fare well, and always protect me in your prayers.

**LETTER LXX. TO MARCWARD.**

To Marcward, most dearly loved and deservedly revered for the integrity of his life, abbot, Lupus sends perpetual greetings.

We are unable to repay you with worthy thanks, but that is no reason why we should not at least attempt it in words. Among the many other benefits you have already bestowed upon us, you have made our boys participants in your language, the use of which at this time no one except one who is exceedingly slow-witted fails to recognize as absolutely necessary. Thus you have conferred upon all of us not merely something pleasing, but something exceedingly useful as well. I gladly received our dearest brother Eigil and the others on the fourth day before the Nones of September. But so that they might devote an appropriate period to their treatment, we sent them away sooner than was proper, binding them by the condition that, when they return, they should depart through us. We are exceedingly anxious about their health, both for their sake and for yours. Moreover, we commend to your holiness this new courier of ours, who in every kind of conduct corresponds to his profession, except that, still, I believe because of nocturnal fears, he cannot sleep alone. I wish you good health and ask you always to remember me with paternal affection.

**LETTER LXXI. TO KING CHARLES, BEFORE THE RECOVERY OF THE CELL.**

[Col. 0533C]

Most excellent lord, my king, I humbly beg you to deign prudently to consider and mercifully to treat the petition of your most devoted servant. The most religious Emperor Louis, the founder of your nobility, at the request of your mother, the Empress Judith of glorious memory, bestowed the cell of Saint Judoc upon the monastery of Ferrières and confirmed his gift by a [Note: [Col. 0533D] *Precept*. That is, by a royal diploma. Such was then the name for a ruler’s diploma. Today we call it letters patent.] precept, so that the monks might serve God in the monastery without want, might provide hospitality in the aforesaid cell to pilgrims according to the fear of God, and might [Note: [Col. 0533D] Pray to the Lord with delight. Royal precepts granted to monasteries ended with these solemn words: “So that it may please them continually to implore the mercy of the Lord for us, for our wife and offspring, and for the stability of our entire kingdom.” Thus it was written in Louis the Pious’s precept concerning the cell of Saint Judoc.] pray to the Lord with delight for the welfare and prosperity of both. You first kindly granted their alms, and also confirmed them by a new precept; but afterward, at the persuasion of those who do not fear to grow rich at the cost of offending God, you were compelled, after the twofold alms had been annulled, to fulfill the desire of secular men concerning the aforesaid cell. For this reason the servants of God, who pray for you continually, have not received their customary clothing for these three years, and what they are compelled to wear is worn out and mostly patched; they are sustained on purchased legumes, and very rarely receive the comfort of fish and cheese; the servants do not receive the clothing owed to them. All these things were supplied to us from the aforesaid cell, where the care of foreigners and other poor people has been interrupted and care for its own cultivation neglected. May God not charge this to you.

I am burdened, beyond the common necessity and exceptional labor, by the deepest shame, because what other abbots have obtained through imperial generosity for the stability of religious life, I, as though the basest and most useless of all, have lost. Nevertheless, hoping to recover through my service what I lost through no fault of mine toward you, as God is my witness—and especially since I hold your promise concerning it, which it is impious to break—I implore you not to delay any longer what we justly demand, but to deign at once to provide for both you and us, so that you may make God favorable toward you and render us, your last servants, more ready at all times to intercede for you.

115 **LETTER LXXII.** [Note: [Col. 0533D] To Dido, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter at Vives in Sens. The *Chronicle of Saint Peter at Vives* says: “After Anastasius, abbot of Saint Peter, died, Dido succeeded him,” evidently in the year 847. He died in 869 and was succeeded by Aquila, a disciple of Eigil, archbishop of Sens, as is written in the same Chronicle.] **TO DIDO, IN THE PERSON OF MARCWARD.**

To the most reverend Dido, abbot, celebrated by the praises of many, Marcward sends abundant greetings.

The exceptional expertise of your art, made widely known by the reports of many, and especially by the account of our brother Nithard, has become known to us. Through him we have also learned that you freely open access to the needy [Note: [Col. 0534D] Open. After this word one leaf was missing from the old manuscript. Had it not been missing, it might have been useful for repairing the ruins in the following letters.] and secure perpetual benefit for the sick through a temporal remedy. Therefore, although we are still unknown to you, we have not hesitated, because of the unity of the same religious order [Note: [Col. 0534D] Of the same religious order. That is, of Saint Benedict. For both the monastery of Prüm and that of Sens professed this saint’s Rule, as did the other monasteries of Gaul and Germany ever since the time of Louis the Pious.], whose most observant adherence we congratulate you upon, to offer you voluntarily an opportunity to bestow a benefit upon us, prepared to respond to your widely renowned generosity in every way we can.

For our sons, whom we wish also to be your sons, were suffering from bodily illness, which several physicians summoned to us were unable to drive away. Trusting in the Lord and in your charity, we offer them to you for treatment, so that, through you, they may enjoy the consolations of the health they desire, and together with us return thanks to its author and to your labor. Let them, as monks, repay you with the devotion that alone they can offer; but let us render an entirely worthy service.

We did not wish to prolong our request with many words, lest perhaps we should seem to doubt the perfection of your charity, which strives to benefit not only strangers but even enemies. And therefore, as you know very well, the command of the oracle is confirmed by prophetic testimony. We wish you good health.

**LETTER LXXIII. TO GUENILO.**

To the most reverend bishop Guenilo . . . whose reading, overcome by your love, I almost . . . through our common kinsman from . . . send. How greatly he is loved . . . since I have never permitted anyone except you . . . but of our church [Col. 0535B] which the shrine appr . . . you have now decreed most fairly and . . . you will understand perfectly for yourself. Although I thanked you at the recent assembly, thinking that the dispute had been entirely settled, know that nothing has been decided, but that, according to the desire of those who are not ashamed—indeed, who seek—to be victorious even unjustly, the benefit sought by your priest has been prepared by the opportunity of delay, while our own hope, which he despises, has now been left empty.

Accordingly, your distinguished prudence, which has learned from the Gospel not to judge according to persons, is also instructed by that ancient command: “Judge your neighbor justly” (Leviticus XIX). Let it steadily and promptly complete the truth of the judgment, as it has begun, lest—God forbid—those who have undertaken the patronage of greed abuse your nobility. For greed itself has devised for them a new oratory [Col. 0535C] for the destruction of our church, and, lest they yield to the truth and dissolve the unanimity of charity, she still encourages them in this matter.

I also ask you, at the supplication of Gerohald the priest, to deign to ordain Lau., his kinsman, a deacon, as priest in his title, [Note: [Col. 0535C] Lau., a deacon. Here we lack the authority of the manuscript. We have therefore adopted what conjecture offered. From these two words Masson made a single name, *Laudiaconus*. We have judged that they should be distinguished. He asks that Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, ordain that deacon a priest in the title of Gerohald the priest, [Col. 0535D] who was so afflicted by an eye disease that he could not perform the priestly office, and therefore requested his own bishop to give him a successor—namely, Lau., his kinsman, the deacon. From this we infer that successions in ecclesiastical benefices had already been introduced, but that they nevertheless depended upon the discretion of the proper bishop, and that the authority of the Roman pontiff was not ordinarily invoked. That right continued until the time of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, who in Letter 36 mentions a certain canon of Angers who asked his bishop to remove him from the canonry and to give his prebend to his nephew, namely, the son of his brother or sister; the bishop of Angers refused to do this. If the authority of the Roman bishop had then been understood to extend to this matter, it could have provided a remedy against the refusal. But not a word is said of it. We also learn from this letter of Lupus that the bodily infirmity which prevented a priest from performing the duties of his office had to be absolutely necessary. Otherwise he was liable to rejection. For at that time they considered it wrong for a priest to lay aside pastoral care so long as the salvation of the sheep could be provided for, as our Lupus teaches in Letter 29. Finally, from this we also learn that Gerohald requested a successor entirely canonically. Otherwise Wenilo could not have given him a successor against his will. See what we note concerning infirm bishops in the commentary on Letter 130. These words, “at the supplication of Gerohald,” deserve notice. Even today we call *supplication*, or *supplica*, that part of a papal diploma in which a vacant benefice is requested from the supreme pontiff. Such a supplication is formulated in these words: “Most blessed Father, Since today the devout petitioner of Your Holiness, moved by certain causes affecting his mind, has resigned into the hands of Your Holiness a secular priory, etc., he humbly SUPPLICATES Your Holiness, the devout petitioner of that person, etc.” I do not, however, think that Gerohald’s supplication was committed to writing. At that time they acted more simply.] because, owing to impaired sight, he frequently cannot fulfill the priestly office. In all other respects . . . I ask to be informed immediately of the perfection . . . you may depart from me, however unworthy and small I am . . . I wish you good health . . .

**LETTER LXXIV. TO THE SAME.**

To the most reverend prelate Guenilo, Lupus sends greetings in the Lord.

Send Livy through this man . . . attend to it, because we need him very much. Fare . . . nevertheless you deign to fulfill what we requested . . . you will grant me a share in the holy orders along with . . . his illness prevents advancement . . . I am handing over what I have worked on and . . . the truth of the price by which we were redeemed [Note: [Col. 0536D] “I myself chose for you.” From these words begins the leaf that followed the one said above to be missing in the old manuscript.] I myself chose to show you how, and through whom, to send it, so that, in the leisure divinely granted to us, you may more easily examine with me the subtlety of such matters.

**LETTER LXXV. TO BERTOLD.**

To his beloved Bertold, Lupus sends greetings.

At the assembly we recently held, although I had wished—and had said so to your bishop—that we should see one another, I am astonished that this did not happen. Among the other matters that we would have discussed familiarly, I had decided to ask you for what I now earnestly request: that in the forest at your Matriniacum you grant us twenty trees, and lend us several skilled cutters, so that, together with our men, they may construct for us a little boat better than any we could find for sale. Through this messenger, then, send back word of whatever you are pleased to grant us.

**LETTER LXXVI. TO HINCMAR.**

To the most illustrious bishop Hincmar, Lupus sends perpetual greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0536D]

Bede’s *Collection*. I am astonished that this passage was not noticed by the most illustrious Cardinals Baronius and Bellarmine, nor by the Reverend Father Labbe. For it settles the dispute concerning Bede’s *Commentary on the Epistles of Paul*: Baronius denies that it belongs to Bede, whereas Bellarmine asserts that it does. Hincmar also attributes this book to Bede in his later work against Gottschalk, chapter 1: “If anyone nevertheless does not have these same books,” he says, “let him look in the collection of the venerable priest Bede from the works of Saint Augustine on the Apostle; there he will be able to learn what he previously did not know.” Henceforth, therefore, there will be no reason to doubt that this work is by the venerable Bede.

Nevertheless, Trithemius, in Book II, chapter 44, *On the Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, attributes that book to a certain monk named Florus, as he himself writes, of Saint-Trond in the diocese of Liège, whom he declares to have been an outstanding admirer of Saint Augustine’s books. Trithemius had therefore undoubtedly seen an old manuscript in which the work was attributed to Florus. The library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés at Paris preserves such a manuscript, divided into two volumes and brought from the monastery of Corbie. On its very first page are written these words: “This volume contains expositions of the Epistles of the blessed Apostle Paul, collected by a certain Florus from the books of the eminent teacher Saint Augustine.” Then the greatest care was taken to ensure that Florus’s name should not perish. At the end of each Epistle it is noted that the exposition of the following Epistle was collected by Florus. One example will suffice; the others are similar: “Here ends the exposition of the First Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians. Here begins the exposition of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, collected by Florus from the books of Saint Augustine.”

Thus it is written in an old manuscript of the famous Sorbonne College: “Here begins the first part of Florus’s book in the exposition of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians.” Here Florus the teacher is evidently meant, who flourished under Louis the Pious. He too wrote *Collections* on the Epistles of Paul from various writings of the ancient Fathers, as the learned Pierre-François Chifflet testifies in his *Pauline Illustrated* and in the preface to the *Excerpts of Fulgentius on the Incarnation of Christ*. This fact misled those who attributed Bede’s work to Florus.

At the end of the Corbie manuscript these words are written in an ancient hand: “This book was composed by Richer, subprior, and John, his scribe and one-eyed man, in the year in which the Church of Saint John at Corbie was restored and Tours was the second see of the city of Rome, in the year 1164, during the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, with Theodoric bishop of Amiens and John abbot of Corbie.” This is a notable passage and should not be lightly passed over. It refers to the Council of Tours celebrated by Alexander III; and because Alexander was then sitting there when this manuscript began to be written, John the scribe says that the city was the second see of the city of Rome. John also says that this book—which they nevertheless knew had been edited by Florus—was composed by himself and Richer. Thus the word *composed* means “written.” The sense is: “This book was written by me, John, at the command and under the direction of Richer, the subprior.”

Concerning Florus of Lyon, Sirmond testifies in his notes on Avitus that Florus drew his exposition of the Epistles of Saint Paul from exactly ten Fathers: Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, Pacian, Jerome, [Col. 0538C] Ephrem the deacon, Paulinus, Pope Leo, Fulgentius, and Avitus. Chifflet, however, in his notes on Ferrandus, page 322, thinks that the *Collection* on the Epistles of Paul was attributed to Florus from Augustine’s works because in certain manuscript codices the work was entitled as follows: “Bede’s book of Florus, from the books of the blessed Augustine, on the Epistles of the Apostle Paul.” Indeed, Chifflet denies the work both to Florus and to Bede. “For the Collection on the Epistles of Paul from Augustine that is found among Bede’s works,” he says, “is so enormous a work that scarcely any continuous commentary on the same Epistles could equal it in size.”]

I was afraid to send you Bede’s *Collection on the Apostle from the works of Augustine*, because the book is so large that it could neither be concealed in one’s bosom nor carried conveniently in a satchel. Even if either could be done, the rapacity of wicked men lying in wait would be a cause for fear; the beauty of the codex itself would certainly have aroused it, and thus it might have been lost both to you and to me. Therefore I shall lend the aforesaid volume to you safely in person, when, God willing, we happen to meet somewhere safe and sound.

I have arranged for as many pine nuts as the courier could carry—that is, ten—to be sent. Let this same courier of ours, who has been sent for this purpose, receive your reply, which, as you wrote, an impediment prevented the notaries from providing, so that by reading it I may either be instructed or delighted. I wish you good health and ask you kindly to remember me.

119 **LETTER LXXVII.** [Note: [Col. 0538C] To Pardul, who later became bishop of Laon; for I do not think he was yet bishop when this letter was written. Nevertheless, the heading of the letter reads in Masson’s edition: “To Pardul of Laon,” evidently, in my opinion, from a gloss. For the manuscript has only this: “TO PARD.”] **TO PARDUL.**

[Col. 0537B]

To his dearest Pardul, Lupus sends abundant greetings.

As you arranged, I have sent a messenger who would bring back in your own writing what you thought about my recent letters and whatever you judged necessary to know. I therefore ask you not to send him back empty-handed or too late. I wish you good health.

**LETTER LXXVIII. TO THE SAME.**

To Pardul, his uniquely and singularly beloved bishop, Lupus sends greetings in the Lord.

I was not summoned to the king’s assembly. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0538D] I did not come to the assembly. The following letter shows that this concerns an assembly held in the same year in which Hilmerad became bishop of Amiens. I think it sufficiently clear that Hilmerad’s ordination took place in the year 849. Accordingly, this passage must be understood of the assembly that King Charles held near the city of Chartres in June of that year, as is evident from the *Annals of Saint-Bertin*.] I did not come to the assembly. I arranged to send a copy of the letter itself, so that, if mention of me should happen to arise, you might be able to show that I had rightly remained behind.

Moreover, since you have admitted me within the enclosure of your intimacy, I ask you now, and whenever God grants the opportunity, to take care through your intercession that I may be secure. As you know, I have not learned how to strike or evade an enemy, nor to perform the other duties of infantry or cavalry service; and our king does not need only warriors. At your urging—and, if necessary, that of Hincmar—if an expedition should arise, I beg that he be taught, since he does not highly value my studies, [Col. 0539A] to consider my [Col. 0539B] purpose [Note: [Col. 0539B] “Purpose.” That is, monastic profession, which is incompatible with the art of warfare. In former times, however, the Emperor Valens ordered monks to be compelled into military service and commanded that those unwilling should be beaten with clubs, even to death, as Jerome, Orosius, and Gregory of Tours relate.] or to deign to impose upon me other tasks that are not entirely contrary to them.

If you sincerely love me, you can accomplish this in such a way that I incur not only no offense but even gain some favor. Your prudence is known and tested by me in this matter. Therefore, while you have the time and opportunity, I ask you to come to the aid both of me and of anyone whom you can help, confident that God will be a just rewarder and that we shall preserve a sincere memory of your benefits. Send back a letter that will gladden me; and, always kindly remembering me, fare well.

**LETTER LXXIX.** [Note: [Col. 0539B] To Rotrannus, a monk of Corbie in the diocese of Amiens. For this reason he writes to him, since he was nearby, to show Hilmerad, bishop of Amiens, a fragment of the letter written to Hincmar of Reims. He is commonly called Ratramnus, a man of great reputation.] **TO ROTRANNUS, A MONK.**

[Col. 0540A]

To his dearest R., Lupus sends greetings.

Source/review notes: The draft omitted the greater part of the editorial note beginning with Boniface’s continuation and ending with the Hincmar citation, as well as the note explaining *Breves*. It also mistranslated the description of Ammianus as author of the *Augustan History*.

Since I was not summoned to the assembly, I did not wish to thrust myself forward uninvited. I therefore sent a letter to the venerable Bishop Hincmar, in which, among other matters, I took care to commend our Hilmerad’s case to him. I have inserted here the words from that letter, so that you may show Hilmerad himself how much I wish to favor his interests.

Hilmerad, I say, whom the king ordered to be bishop of the Ambianensians, is connected with me by a certain relationship. I beg you to let the fact that I possess considerable influence with you benefit him. For although he may perhaps lack some learning,

> **[Note: “Some learning.” It is astonishing that Hilmerad, an uneducated and illiterate man, should be supported so enthusiastically by Lupus. Nor is it sufficient that he hints that Hilmerad’s morals are blameless. For an innocent bishop, as Saint Hilary says, benefits only himself unless he is learned. I shall cite Hilary’s own passage, which is exceptional on this subject. In Book VIII *On the Trinity*: “It is not immediately characteristic of a good and useful priest,” he says, “either merely to act innocently or merely to preach knowledgeably; for the innocent man benefits only himself unless he is learned, and the learned man is without the authority of teaching unless he is innocent.” Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, followed Hilary. I shall quote his words all the more willingly because they were written by an apostolic and most holy man; indeed, this letter of Boniface is entirely worthy, as Serarius says, “of being read very frequently by all shepherds of souls, especially by bishops and archbishops.” Thus Boniface writes in Letter 105, to Cudberth, archbishop of Canterbury, speaking of bishops whom he calls teachers: “For the Apostle calls the bishop a teacher, the prophet a watchman, the Savior of the world a shepherd of the Church, and a priest; and all agree that the teacher who remains silent about the sins of the people is guilty, through his silence, of the blood of lost souls.” Meanwhile I agree with Serarius, who thinks that here one should read *they prove him guilty by their silence*. Boniface continues: “For this reason a terrible and most pressing necessity compels us, in accordance with the saying of the Apostle, to present ourselves as an example to the faithful. That is, unless my judgment deceives me, a teacher must live so justly that he does not nullify his words by contrary deeds, and that, while he carefully lives rightly in his own conduct, he is not condemned through silence concerning another’s sin. For he is set over the Church of God in order not only to instruct others by the example of living well, but also, by preaching with confidence, to set each person’s sins before his eyes and show what punishment awaits the hardened and what glory the obedient. For, according to the Lord’s word to Ezekiel, he to whom the dispensation of the word has been entrusted, even if he lives holily, will perish with all who perish while he is silent, if he is ashamed or afraid to rebuke those living wickedly. And what will it profit him not to be punished for his own sin, when he is to be punished for another’s?” In speaking to Ezekiel, the Lord terribly forbids the silence of a priest. He calls the priest a watchman: just as it belongs to a watchman, from a higher place, to observe more than everyone else, so the priest ought to be higher through the sublimity of his merits and possess the grace of greater learning, by which he may instruct the rest.

This passage is copied almost word for word from Book I, chapter 20, of Julianus Pomerius’s *On the Contemplative Life*. After those times a third Cato fell from heaven—Arnulf, namely, bishop of Lisieux—who, in a sermon delivered at the Synod of Tours before Alexander III, said that learning is necessary for a preacher. “Perfection of learning is required,” he says, “so that the preacher may have from which to bring forth new things and old from the treasury of his heart; so that he may know how to expound learned discourse to those who await it, and temper what he says according to the qualities of persons; so that he may know to whom he ought to give milk to drink rather than food, and to whom he ought to minister more solid nourishment.”

Peter of Blois, a man of those times and indeed Arnulf’s friend, says in Letter 112 that the Lord will require from the hand of the mute—that is, unlearned—priest the blood of the one who perishes. That is, to use Boniface’s words, an unlearned bishop will be guilty through his silence of the blood of lost souls, and will therefore perish because of the people’s sins, even though he carefully lives rightly in his own conduct. Saint Gregory gravely warns prelates accordingly in Book III, chapter 5, of the *Pastoral Rule*, that they must take care “lest they be judged for the errors of those subject to them, even though they find themselves already secure as regards themselves.”

Atto, bishop of Vercelli, speaks admirably to this effect in Letter 9, addressed to priests and their ministers residing in the diocese of Vercelli. “Woe to us,” he says, “who have undertaken the work of this ministry, if we neglect to preach the truth. Woe to us if we suppress in silence what we are commanded to distribute to the bankers.” Bishops cannot avoid this miserable misfortune otherwise than by applying themselves to studies of letters that can be of use in instructing their peoples and shaping their morals. Thus it seems altogether necessary that a bishop be learned. For how will he teach others what he himself has not learned? It is the bishops’ office to teach the peoples subject to them, as is sufficiently clear and as Saint Gregory teaches in Book I, chapter 1, of the *Pastoral Rule*. Hence Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, complained that “I was snatched from tribunals and the insignia of administration to the priesthood, and compelled to teach what I had not learned.” For, as Innocent I writes to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, “it is a miserable thing for one to become a master who has never been a disciple.”

Gregory VII, Book IX, Letter 2: “Concerning that person who was to be chosen archbishop, we say that, although he seems sufficiently prudent and generous, he nevertheless lacks the foundation of discipline, namely the discipline of literary learning. You yourself understand sufficiently how necessary this virtue is not only to bishops but also to priests, since without it no one can either teach others or defend himself.” Finally, Ferrandus, deacon of Carthage, plainly declares in his letter to Severus, a scholar of Constantinople, that authority to teach is assigned to bishops: “Let those speak and preach,” he says, “to whom the honor of the priesthood has assigned the authority of teaching. We are ready to learn; we do not presume to teach others.”

Moreover—if I may mention this also in passing—the judgment of Agobard, archbishop of Lyon, is harsh indeed. In his book *On the Manner of Ecclesiastical Government*, he says that one who has undertaken the office of preaching and a position of governance but neglects it, and seeks comfort and distraction in riches, metal ornaments, hunting, fowling, fishing, and, what is worse, feasting, drunkenness, and musical sounds, is not a helper of God but a destroyer of God’s work and thereby a helper of Antichrist; and although he may seem to be a priest in human eyes, he is not one in the eyes of God.

But to return to Hilmerad: as I said, it is very surprising that he should be commended so warmly by Lupus, who knew the man’s ignorance. Yet here too we may observe that nature returns, though you drive it out with a pitchfork. Something must be conceded to human affections. Nor am I especially pleased by what some say: that Lupus’s prophecy was entirely true, because he foretold that Hilmerad, though unlearned, would nevertheless be very useful to the Church. They infer this from the fact that he is found to have attended several synods during those troubled times. It would indeed be remarkable if a man otherwise useless had not appeared at synods from which he was not permitted to be absent without a grave reason. Let them at last produce some illustrious deed performed by Hilmerad in synods, or even outside synods. Then we shall admit that their observation is entirely true. But, beyond doubt because of that ordination, Hincmar laid himself open to his detractors, by whom, as he himself relates in chapter 36 of his later work against Gottschalk, it was publicly alleged against him that “bishops were ordained in cities without examination or inquiry, almost ignorant of literary learning, and falling short of the apostolic precept; through this circumstance especially ecclesiastical vigor was lost.” See chapter *Et hoc diximus*, 16, 4, 7.]**

he will nevertheless be able to be useful, since he will also obey your instruction. And if he cannot fully teach the divine ordinances, he may nevertheless accomplish something by which both he himself and those who follow him may become capable of eternal salvation.

This is what I wrote to him. I ask you always to remain in the friendship you have begun, confident that I shall never withdraw from my duty. Farewell.

**121 EPISTLE LXXX. TO USUARD, ABBOT**

> **[Note: Usuard, Abbot. I do not know of which monastery this Usuard was abbot. I would almost venture to affirm that he was abbot in the diocese of Augustodunum.]**

To his beloved Usuard, abbot and archdeacon, Lupus sends greetings in the Lord.

You have not forgotten how, in the presence of the principal men of your church, I showed you the synodal decree and the decree of the metropolitan Amulo, issued concerning the priest Godelgar,

> **[Note: Amulo. Bishop of Lyon, whose two letters survive: one to Gotteschalk and another to Theobald, bishop of Langres. The former was published by R. P. Sirmond, the latter by the most distinguished Nicolaus Camuzatius.]**

and how I terrified you by warning that, unless you fulfilled the command of our lord the king,

> **[Note: “Confirming.” For what the synod had decreed was not valid unless the prince’s confirmation had been added.]**

who confirmed what the holy synod and the metropolitan had ordered, you would suffer the loss of a severe exile.

But since you have delayed this until now, and since the aforementioned priest,

> **[Note: Priest. It is clear from this that archdeacons possessed great authority in those times. For what purpose would this Usuard have been wearied with so many petitions unless it had been entirely clear that the priest Godelgar was completely subject to his authority? Priests were so subject to the archdeacon that even the archpriest himself was subject to him, as is evident from Isidore’s letter to Ludifred, Distinction XXV, chapter “Perlectis”; Innocent III took this material from there in chapter “Ad haec nos,” in the *Decretals*, on the office of an archdeacon. The Council of Toledo also states in canon 3 that the archdeacon ought deliberately to settle every complaint, case, or ecclesiastical matter concerning priests, deacons, or subdeacons. See Hincmar’s chapters addressed to archdeacons and priests, chapter 3, and Peter of Celle, Book VII, Letter 10.]**

wishes to escape such a long misfortune, I admonish you by the authority alike of the synod, the metropolitan, and the king to complete without delay what was imposed upon you through me, lest perhaps, for a threefold contempt, you be compelled to endure a multiplied vengeance.

Also see to it, without any excuse, that the inventories—which, as we said in the first letter, are inventories—you were required to send concerning the property of your monastery are delivered to me at Sedelocus.

> **[Note: Sedelocus. A village belonging to the bishop of Augustodunum, also mentioned by Charles the Bald in a charter issued at Attigny in 844 for the benefit of the Church of Augustodunum: “the parish of Saint Andochius at Sedelocus.” Amulo likewise mentions it in his letter to Theobald: “For we have also learned by reliable report that similar things are being done, or rather pretended to be done, in the territory of Augustodunum, at the place called Sedelocus, near the church in which the holy martyrs Andochius, Tyrsus, and Felix lie buried.” The earliest surviving record of this place is found in Ammianus Marcellinus, an ancient writer of history. In Book XVI he relates that Julian Caesar, appointed and sent into Gaul by Constantius, reached Augustodunum on the eighth day before the Kalends of July; after deliberating there about which route should be chosen as safe, some thought that the journey ought to be made through Sidoleucus. Thus the eminent Peter Pithoeus first corrected this place in Book II, chapter 1, of his *Miscellaneous Adversaria*, since Ammianus had previously read *per sedes Leucorum*. I shall not hesitate to reproduce the passage from the edition of the most learned Henri Valois:

> “On the eighth day before the Kalends of July Julian reached Augustodunum, as a long-serving commander, outstanding in strength and counsel, intending to attack the barbarians wandering about in various places wherever fortune should give him the opportunity. When, therefore, a deliberation had been held with men familiar with the region standing by, and the question was being discussed from many sides as to which route should be chosen as safe, some argued for going through Arbor . . . . . while others firmly maintained that they ought to proceed through Sedelaucum and Coram.”

> In his notes on this passage, the distinguished scholar observed that the correction was owed to a manuscript in the royal library. For those traveling from Augustodunum to Autissiodorum, the route led through Sedelaucum, as is evident from the *Itinerary of Antoninus* and the Peutinger Map; in both works Sedelocus, or Sidolocus, is mentioned. The name remains today, for the village is commonly called Saulieu, four hours’ journey from Augustodunum.]**

Farewell.

**EPISTLE LXXXI. TO AMULO, BISHOP**

> **[Note: To Amulo. Also called Amulo and Amolo by others. He was archbishop of Lyon and therefore metropolitan of the bishops of Augustodunum and Cabillonum. This letter was written at least in the year 844, since in that year a charter of Charles the Bald was issued for the benefit of the Church of Augustodunum, in which Altei, the bishop who succeeded Berno, is explicitly mentioned.]**

On behalf of Guenilo and Gherardus.

To the most reverend and distinguished prelate Amulo,

> **[Note: Guenilo. Archbishop of Sens.]**

Guenilo, bishop, and Gherardus, count,

> **[Note: Gherardus. Clearly the man who founded the monastery of Vézelay in the diocese of Augustodunum; for he governed those regions with the rank of count. For that reason the prince entrusted him with the task of ensuring that Berno should as soon as possible be ordained bishop of the Church of Augustodunum. For the same reason Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, wrote to him concerning the ordination of Isaac, bishop of Langres, as Flodoard relates in Book III, chapter 26.]**

send perpetual greetings.

We would have revealed many important matters, entrusted to us most confidentially by command of our lord the king and on his behalf, if it had been possible for you to meet our expectation at the city of Augustodunum, as he himself desired and also indicated to you in his own letter, and as we too very greatly wished. But since your messengers disclosed to us the most certain reasons for your inability—reasons which he commissioned us to set forth fully and in detail—we have endeavored to explain them to your wisdom in a concise letter, preserving the truth of their meaning. [Col. 0543B]

He therefore commanded us to tell you in his words that he faithfully holds to the belief that the King of kings, and likewise the Priest of priests, who alone was able to govern the Church which he redeemed [Note: [Col. 0543C] Whom he redeemed. King Lothair, son of Louis the Overseas, appears to have had this passage of Lupus in mind in a charter for the monastery of nuns at Poitiers: “How much more,” he says, “does it pertain to the due providence of kingship that we should endeavor to exercise pious and solicitous care in all things for the Catholic and apostolic Church, which Christ redeemed with his precious blood and entrusted to us, who exist by adoption as sons, to govern and protect.” See Besly, *Probationes Historiae Comitum Pictaviensium*, p. 251.], after raising his humanity into heaven, while remaining always with his own in divinity, divided his power for governing that same Church among priests and kings, so that what holy pontiffs teach, devout kings themselves might fulfill and cause to be fulfilled. [Col. 0544A]

For this reason he desires to offer due reverence to your holiness, as to one whom he knows to wish to preserve the worship of the Divinity intact; and in turn he asks that you enter with him into such a pact of harmony that, wherever he wishes, in matters of great importance, to consult ecclesiastical utility within the portion divinely allotted to him, through the disposition of your authority, he may immediately be assisted by the unanimity of your agreement. And lest we weary you longer with lengthy circumlocutions, the recent misfortune of the Church of Augustodunum and its prolonged disturbance moved his piety to ask that, by his generosity [Note: [Col. 0543C] By his generosity. That is, from his liberality, as is clear from Book II of the *Capitularies*, ch. 8, and from Lothair’s charter concerning Ebbo’s restoration. For the gift of a bishopric was made by the king; and thereafter it was necessary that the metropolitan ordain the man to whom the king had given the bishopric, provided that no canonical obstacle stood in the way. Thus Lupus says that a bishop is to be ordained for the Church of Augustodunum through royal generosity and through the promotion of Amulo, the metropolitan.

Charles the Bald explained this practice more openly at the Synod of Toul of the twelve provinces in 859: “A portion of the kingdom, among my brothers the kings, was entrusted to me by divine disposition from my lord and father Louis Augustus of pious memory. In that portion of the kingdom the metropolitan see of Sens was then vacant of a pastor. In accordance with the custom of my royal predecessors, I entrusted it for government to Wenilo, then my cleric serving me in my chapel, who, in the manner of a free cleric, had commended himself to me and promised fidelity on oath, with the consent of the holy bishops of that metropolis; and, so far as lay in me, I prevailed upon the bishops to ordain him archbishop there.”

Among examples from Charles’s royal predecessors may be counted King Dagobert’s memorandum to Sulpicius, bishop of Bourges, concerning the ordination of Desiderius, bishop of Cahors: “It befits royal highness to strive by every means to promote to the pontifical office those whom it knows to live in the fear of God, to preserve the Catholic faith intact, and to observe the evangelical precepts. Therefore, since we know that you hold the archmetropolitan office, we have taken care to send these present letters to your venerable eminence with the due office of greeting, asking that you hasten to bless him and send letters to your fellow provincial brethren, so that they too may be present, in order that, canonically and according to apostolic institution, he may be consecrated by pontifical blessing in your presence at the holy Paschal solemnity.” Other examples, if anyone seeks them, will not be difficult to produce.

There survives in Marculf, Book I, ch. 5, a “Charter concerning a bishopric.” From it, as the most illustrious Hieronymus Bignon observed there, it is apparent that in those times it was customary, when a king learned of a bishop’s death, to write to the metropolitan bishop directing him to ordain and bless the man whom the king himself had approved and chosen as bishop in the deceased’s place. Bignon proved by many examples that this was the most constant practice in Gaul. I use his authority the more willingly because, besides the universal agreement that he was a great man and that these studies with which we are now concerned owe him much, he was also a close friend of the most illustrious Pierre de Marca, archbishop of Paris, formerly my patron.

From Gaul we must pass over to England, a neighboring country living by almost the same customs. There kings anciently granted bishoprics by royal right, as is clear from what the most learned Selden noted on Eadmer, pp. 142–143, and especially from the letter of King Edward III to Pope Clement VI. Speaking of the cathedral churches of England, he says: “At each vacancy our said predecessors conferred those churches, by royal right, upon suitable persons; and afterwards, at the request and insistence of the said [apostolic] see, they granted, under certain modes and conditions, that elections should take place in the said churches through their chapters.” Our kings likewise granted churches elections of bishops, following the example of Emperor Charles the Fat, who was liberal in this respect toward the churches of Geneva and Chalon.

The prince of the islands called Orkney also exercised the same right. It consisted in this: the bishop whom the prince had granted the bishopric was to be ordained by the archbishop of York. Thomas, archbishop of York, judged this procedure canonical in writing to Lanfranc of Canterbury: “A certain cleric came to us, sent by Earl Paul from the parts of Orkney with sealed letters, signifying in them that he had granted the bishopric of his land to that cleric. The latter, observing the order of his predecessors, asks to be consecrated bishop by us; and we cannot unjustly deny what he justly asks. We therefore ask your fatherhood to send us two bishops, supported by whose prayers and assistance we may canonically complete the sacrament of so great a matter.” Lanfranc judged this equitable and ordered the requested bishops—Wulfstan of Worcester and Peter of Chester—to go “to assist Thomas, as he requested, at the consecration of the aforesaid cleric,” as is recorded in the *Life of Lanfranc*, ch. 13. See the letters of Thomas and Lanfranc in Selden’s notes on Eadmer, p. 201, and among Lanfranc’s works edited by Dom Luc d’Achery.] and through your advancement, he appoint over it a man capable of energetically repairing its ruins both spiritually and temporally.

There is one whom his kinship greatly commends to your kindness: Bernus [Note: [Col. 0545B] Bernus. Following the custom of his predecessors, Charles had appointed him over the Church of Augustodunum. Then, according to the ancient practice, he asked the metropolitan Amulo to ordain that man. I, for my part, believe that Amulo did not reject the prince’s request, and therefore that Bernus was ordained by him. I do not agree with those who say that Amulo rejected his nomination and consecrated Alteus in his place. They drew this opinion solely from the conjecture that Alteus was ordained bishop in the see of Augustodunum at nearly the same time. But it is probable that Bernus died not long after his ordination, and that Alteus was then ordained in his place. For how could they persuade themselves that Charles had suffered rejection in the person of his kinsman Bernus, an otherwise exceedingly suitable man, while consideration had been given to Godelsadus, a cleric of the palace? Finally, let them prove by legitimate testimony that Bernus was rejected by Amulo. I do not, moreover, agree with Roverius, who confuses this Bernus with Bernard, abbot of Réomé.], brought up from childhood by the glorious emperor Louis of blessed memory and adorned with distinguished honors. The king himself, at the present time, has found him suitable through many tests and, with the help of God’s grace, believes him exceptionally well suited to so great an undertaking.

In this matter he has the agreement of his most approved counselors [Col. 0546A] [Note: [Col. 0545C] The agreement of his counselors. From this passage the most illustrious Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, inferred that our kings at that time held that palace clerics could be designated for the episcopate by the prince alone, with the agreement of his counselors. He writes that Amulo had to be entreated at greater length in Charles’s name because Amulo was not situated within Charles’s kingdom; Lyon lay in the kingdom of Lothair. See Book VIII of *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*, ch. 16, § 11.

The *Annals of Fulda* provide another example of this royal right under the year 856: “In the month of February, on the fourth day of the month, Rabanus, archbishop of the Church of Mainz, died. Carlus succeeded him, more by the will of the king and his counselors than by the agreement and election of the clergy and people.” The practice had already become established in the age of Louis the Pious, as Thegan, chorepiscopus of Trier, relates—though with indignation—in chapter 20 of his work on the deeds of Louis the Pious. Thus Drogo was given as bishop to the people of Metz, as the author of the *Life of Louis the Pious* reports under the year 823. See the notes to the *Life of Saint Maximinus*, ch. 11.].

Our lord therefore commanded us to suggest to your prudence that it is neither novel nor rash for him to procure bishops from the palace, especially for the more distinguished Churches. For Pippin, from whom our king traces his origin through the great Charles and the most religious emperor Louis, having explained the necessity of this kingdom to Zacharias, the Roman pope [Note: [Col. 0546B] Zacharias. M. Antonius de Dominis thinks this passage should be understood to mean that Pippin was then granted permission “to choose by himself the persons to be promoted to bishoprics and to arrange for their consecration, without the consent of any ecclesiastics, except for the consecration itself”; he says this can be inferred from Lupus’s own words, “in which the pope, derogating from ecclesiastical right, increased the rights of princes in that kingdom.”

De Marca, however, thinks the passage refers to Zacharias’s ratification: he judged that Pippin and Carloman had acted rightly and regularly when they appointed bishops by their own right. Long before Zacharias’s time, our kings had appointed bishops by their own right over vacant Churches, as De Marca demonstrates with many examples. The opinion of the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius must therefore rightly be rejected: from this passage of Lupus he inferred that the right our kings exercised in those times when granting bishoprics did not proceed from their own authority but from a concession of the apostolic see, since kings supposedly possessed no right at all in ecclesiastical matters. Certainly, the peoples beyond the Alps must be admitted to hold this view with Baronius. We Gauls, however, do not entirely exclude our kings from sacred affairs, namely from those matters that concern ecclesiastical discipline and the execution of ecclesiastical rules.], obtained from him, in a synod [Note: [Col. 0546B] In a synod. “He referred,” says De Marca, “to the synod of Liptina, in which Boniface attended as the pope’s representative. There Carloman, in his own name and that of his brother Pippin, who was also duke and prince of the Franks, appointed bishops. This synod, according to Zacharias, was held through the efforts of Pippin and Carloman.

Moreover, what began at the council of Liptina concerning the appointment of bishops was completed by Pippin at the Council of Soissons. This too was acceptable to the supreme pontiff, who saw that, through the commendable work of princes, bishops were being placed over Churches for the benefit of the faithful, and not, as before, laymen enjoying their revenues to the ruin of religion.”

It is clear that the synod of Liptina must be understood as the one held by Carloman in 743 in the presence of Boniface, legate of the Roman pope. Otherwise Boniface attended no synod presided over by Zacharias. At the synod of Liptina, I may add incidentally, there were also present with Boniface George, a Roman bishop—that is, as I believe, the bishop of Porto, in the special province of the Roman pontiff—and John the *sacellarius*, as is evident from chapter 7 of the bishops’ letter to Louis, king of Germany, residing in the palace at Attigny, written in 858, and from Hincmarus’s letter 37 to the archbishops Rodulfus and Frotarius.

These are the bishops’ words to King Louis: “Pippin caused a synod to be assembled at Liptina, over which, together with Saint Boniface, George, by name, legate of the apostolic see, presided.”

Hincmarus, in the said letter, chapter 5, writes: “And in the synod held at Liptina, over which, under Prince Carloman, Bishop George, John the *sacellarius*, and Saint Boniface presided by command of Pope Zacharias, it is read: ‘If a man has been unable to render the marital debt to a woman betrothed to him, endowed, and taken in public marriage according to the Apostle, and this has been made evident either by the confession of both or by any certain proof, they are to separate; and if the woman is unable to remain continent, she may lawfully marry another man.’”

This clearly refers to chapter 55 of Book VI of the *Capitularies*.
