Thus the decrees made in Book V of the same *Capitularies*, chapters 4, 5, and 6—concerning one baptized by a priest who had not been baptized; one who has held a stepson or stepdaughter before a bishop; and those who flee to other countries because of a feud—belong to this synod of Liptina, where they were issued at the urging of George the bishop and John the *sacellarius*, legates of the supreme pontiff Zacharias.

In these chapters one must read “George,” not “Gregory,” as the old editions have it; this is clear from a very ancient manuscript codex of the monastery of Ripoll in Catalonia and also from my old manuscript codex. Finally, those three chapters were copied into the books of the *Capitularies* immediately after the decree of the synod of Liptina that is commonly circulated. Besides these, Hincmarus preserved another Liptine canon, as we saw above.], in which the martyr Boniface [Note: [Col. 0546D] The martyr Boniface. Archbishop of Mainz, called a martyr because he was killed by pagans in Frisia while announcing the Gospel of Christ to them, in the year 754.] participated, his approval that he might, through the skill of his most trusted men, remedy the severity of the times when bishops died, lest through the simplicity of pontiffs something like what happened in this city of the Haedui, whose care now occupies us, should occur.

Accordingly, he asks that the honor granted to the Roman pope by his forebears, kings and emperors, and never until now weakened by the metropolitans of the Church of Lyon, over which, by God’s authority, you preside, should not, through any injury to you, be denied by you. [Col. 0547A]

[Note: [Col. 0547C] The Roman pope. Such was the modesty and simplicity of the ancients that, although they gave the name “pope” to individual bishops, whenever they spoke of the Roman pontiff they did not say simply “pope,” as is customary today, but “pope of the City,” or “Roman pope,” as our Lupus does here. Gradually that title withdrew from the other bishops until it was thereafter conferred upon the Roman alone. Thus Odorannus, monk of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif at Sens, who flourished under King Robert, honored Ansegisus, archbishop of Sens, by calling him “the second pope,” because he was vicar of the apostolic see. “Moreover,” he says, “Lord Ansegisus, after obtaining the primacy of all Gaul and meriting, through heavenly governance, to be called the second pope, etc.”

There followed the decree of Gregory VII, who at a Roman synod ordered that the name “pope” should belong to one person alone in the Christian world. From this the custom already received was confirmed; and such was the reverence of Western peoples for the Roman bishop that thereafter they gave the name pope to him alone, as I have said. The Roman pontiffs themselves also encouraged that custom. Not long afterward this honor was bestowed upon Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury: since he held a position of particular favor with Urban II, the Roman pope, he was called by him “the pope of another world,” as Gervase of Canterbury testifies. “He,” Gervase says, “was consecrated in the city of Canterbury and received the pallium from Pope Urban; and he enjoyed such favor with him that he called him the pope of another world”—clearly because he was patriarch of the Britons, scattered throughout the world, as Eadmer calls him. Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, writing at nearly the same time to Gerard, bishop of Angoulême—who, because he was legate of the apostolic see in Aquitaine, usurped many things contrary to right and law, as Geoffrey thought—says, among other things, in Book I, Letter 21: “You have made yourselves another pope.”

In the Eastern Church, by contrast, shortly before the pontificate of Gregory VII, the designation “pope” had descended so far that even readers were called “popes,” as is clear from the constitution of Emperor Isaac Comnenus of Constantinople, issued around the year 1058 and preserved by Theodore Balsamon. Hence later, among the Greeks, the benefices of junior clerics came to be called *papatus*, just as *junioratus* was used in the Latin Church, as the most illustrious and learned François Bosquet, bishop of Montpellier, observed in his notes on the letters of Innocent III, Book III, Letter 60. Even under Gregory V, however, the dignity of the bishop of Milan was called *papatus*, as is clear from the diploma of Emperor Otto III published by Holstenius in the *Collectio Bipartita*, part II, p. 219. See also Rigaltius’s observations on Cyprian and Selden’s notes on Eadmer.]

If he is not rejected in this matter, [Note: [Col. 0548B] He will do so. Wenilo and Gerard promise Amulo the favor of King Charles if he complies with the prince’s wishes. Amulo understood how important this favor was. He therefore took care to secure it, as we learn from the *Chronicle of Hugh of Flavigny*, where it is written: “Amolo also took possession of the bishopric of Lyon; his authority and Charles’s affection for him were of great value to Saint Pope Leo, as he himself testifies in the letter sent to him.” This may itself provide a strong argument for confirming what was said above concerning the ordination of Bernus, bishop of Augustodunum.] he promises that he will ensure that your ministry always enjoys due veneration in his kingdom and achieves the desired outcome.

We humbly join our prayers to his request, so that what seems best to such great men may also please you; and so that, by obeying you, you may make not only us but also them, as we desire, your most eager and deeply indebted debtors. We wish to obtain from your most faithful familiarity that you show us by letter as quickly as possible what God inspires you to do. Thus, through us, our lord the king—learning that your will toward him is favorable, as he greatly desires—may render worthy thanks to God and, before the necessities of the kingdom carry him farther away, put an end to the harmful delay of the bishop’s appointment, while sending you a most faithful assistant [Col. 0548A] to be ordained.

[Note: [Col. 0548C] Assistant. A coworker and suffragan. Suffragans are so called because they possess the right of suffrage with the metropolitan in provincial synods and ought to be in agreement with him. Charles the Simple says in a charter for the Church of Narbonne: “The venerable Arnutius, archbishop of the holy Church of Narbonne, approached our serenity, making known to the ears of our clemency that in his diocese, or in all the bishoprics placed under his suffrage, a very serious custom contrary to the canons and the institutions of the laws had grown up, etc.” Arnulf of Lisieux, in a letter to Saint Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, then exiled in Gaul, writes: “Considering that those on whose aid you ought to rely, whose counsel should fortify you, and whose suffrage should support you, withdrew from you as if in battle array, at the very time when they ought most to acknowledge the account they owed to their own name and show themselves your suffragans, not your opponents.” Arnulf therefore thought they were called suffragans because they ought to support their metropolitan by their suffrage whenever occasion arises and to be his assistants, to use Lupus’s word. See Fulbert, Letters 30 and 51.]

We also ask that you ordain Godelsadus [Note: [Col. 0548D] Godelsadus. Charles the Bald placed Godelsadus over the Church of Cabillonum at least in 844; this letter must have been written in that year, as we have already noted. He later attended the synod of Verberie in 853.], whom he has appointed from his palace [Note: [Col. 0548D] According to the custom of his predecessors. At that time, as De Marca noted in the passage cited above, our kings maintained that palace clerics could be designated by the prince alone, following the practice of earlier rulers, who generally appointed clerics from their palace to episcopal sees without seeking the votes of the bishops of the province; yet they sent the clerics so designated to those bishops, evidently only for consecration.], according to the custom of his greater royal predecessors, as has been shown above, to the Church of Cabillonum, which the manuscript writes *Cabillonensi* [Note: [Col. 0549C] *Cabillonensi*. That is how that age wrote it, as may be gathered from the synod of Verberie mentioned shortly above and from innumerable other places. Since this was the spelling of the manuscript codex, I decided to retain it. Masson’s edition had *Cabiloniensi*.] [Col. 0549A]

[Note: [Col. 0549C] He appointed him over the Church. That is, he ordered him to be bishop of Cabillonum, just as Lupus above said of Hilmeradus, bishop of Amiens. This emendation is therefore of great importance. The king does not demand that Godelsadus be appointed over the Church of Cabillonum, as the edition of Masson incorrectly has it. Rather, he asks that Amulo promptly ordain the man whom he himself had appointed to that Church.

We therefore owe it to the manuscript codex that royal authority in the appointment of bishops has here been restored in Lupus. Masson’s edition had shamefully buried it, reading: “The same king demands that Godelsadus, whom he asks to be appointed over the Church of Cabillonum from his palace, according to the custom of his greater royal predecessors, as has been shown above, not be burdensome for you to ordain during this Lent.”]

The same king asks that you not be reluctant to ordain him during this Lent. If, because of the absence of Bishop Teotbaldus [Note: [Col. 0549D] Bishop Teotbaldus. Bishop of Langres, a suffragan of the Church of Lyon, commonly called Teutbaldus and Teodbaldus. There is also extant a serious letter of the same Amulo to him against certain impostors who were presenting alleged relics of holy martyrs without proving by any legitimate evidence that they were genuine. Teodbaldus attended the Council of Verberie in 853.], this should seem impossible, at whatever time you determine to be suitable, we shall arrange to provide a substitute from our bishops [Note: [Col. 0550C] From our bishops. That is, from bishops established in the kingdom of Charles the Bald.], so that God may graciously deign to accomplish through you, without delay, what benefits the Christian people.

## LETTER LXXXII. TO GUENILO

To the most reverend bishop Guenilo, Lupus sends greetings.

This priest, named Erlegaudus, of the church of Saint Peter and of our own community [Note: [Col. 0550C] Erlegaudus. He was a priest in a certain cell of the monastery of Ferrières, or perhaps in the monastery itself, as may be inferred from this letter. At that time he had been accused before Wenilo, metropolitan of Sens, and by Wenilo’s authority had been forbidden to exercise the functions of his office. Since the case concerned a priest, Lupus asks Wenilo to allow him to perform his ministry until his case could be judged in the synod that was soon to be held. The cases of priests were therefore treated in synods. In the meantime, however, a bishop was permitted, at his discretion, either to remit or to increase the penalty. See the Council of Sardica, canon 17; the capitulary of Charles the Bald at Compiègne, ch. 4; and Book V of the *Capitularies*, ch. 218.], complains, both in the name of the church of Saint Peter and in our own, that he is suffering a calumny and is in danger of losing his rank. We therefore ask your fatherly care to deign to assist him justly and reasonably, lest he be crushed by the plots of any persons who, perhaps forgetful of the fear of God, stubbornly seek to overcome an innocent man.

May your prudence therefore benefit both him and those others, so that, if he is innocent, he may be freed, while those who attempt to sin by injuring their neighbor may find no opportunity. Until, by God’s inspiration, you accomplish this and the time of the synod arrives, we ask that, if it can be done and seems suitable to your holiness, he be granted the freedom to exercise his office, lest, according to the desire of his enemies, he be unable to find an opportunity to clear himself by their testimony. We desire that you remain well.

## LETTER LXXXIII. TO LOUIS

[Before the recovery of the cell.]

To Louis, most excellent and most dear to all good men, Lupus sends his warmest greetings.

When, by the king’s command, I sent a messenger to the palace, I ordered him to approach you, so that through you I might learn accurately and quickly what I must do. Therefore, may your distinguished kindness set down in a letter whatever it is necessary for me to know; once informed by it, I shall attend to the matters requiring action.

There is one thing I earnestly ask: if the undertakings that are secretly being conducted, as is reported, with the Bretons are believed likely to succeed, do not disdain to let me know. Even the spirits of energetic men strongly shrink from labor that has been attempted in vain, is fruitless, and is dangerous; and it has been discovered and recorded in writing that unwilling men must by no means be compelled to go to war.

If an opportunity arises to recover our cell, strive to help us in this matter as in all others, so that through your diligence the king may be cleansed of a very serious sin and we may at last be freed from our excessive necessity. May you always remain well, as I desire.

## LETTER LXXXIV

[Note: [Col. 0550D] This is a synodal letter, given in the year 849. It may be inferred from the Chronicle of Fontenelle that the synod was held at a time other than autumn.]

### TO NOMENOE

Landramnus, metropolitan bishop of Tours; Dodo, of Angers; Aldricus, bishop of Le Mans; Guenilo, metropolitan bishop of Sens; Heriboldus, bishop of Auxerre; Prudentius, of Troyes; Agius, of Orléans; Ercanradus, of Paris; Hucbertus, of Meaux; Helias, of Chartres; Herimannus, of Nevers; Hincmarus, metropolitan bishop of Reims; [Note: [Col. 0550D] Rather, of Noyon. Perhaps Lupus’s Letter 41 was written to him, as we noted there.] Immo, of Noyon; Pardulus, of Laon [Col. 0550C] [Note: [Col. 0550D] At Laon. This is certainly what the manuscript codex has. Masson’s edition read *Lauduni*. It therefore seemed best to retain the reading of the old codex. The city’s ancient and correct name is *Lugdunum*, or, with the addition, *Lugdunum Clavatum*, as Sirmondus observes in his notes to the *Capitula* of Charles the Bald. In this form the bishops of Laon often subscribe in synods, as Pardulus does here in the synods of Soissons and Verberie in 853.]; Rhothadus, of Soissons; Hilmeradus, of Amiens; Erpoinus, of Senlis; Ermenfridus, of Beauvais; Paulus, metropolitan bishop of Rouen; [Col. 0551A] Saxbodus, bishop of Séez [Note: [Col. 0551A] Saxbodus. This is exactly how it is written in the old codex. In the privilege of the monastery of Corbie, however, he is called Saxobodus. Nevertheless, he is called Saxbodus in the council held at Sens in 852, at which the privilege of the monastery of Saint Remigius was confirmed; that privilege was published in volume II of the *Spicilegium*, p. 586.

In those subscriptions, however, “Raginarius, bishop of Amiens,” is written incorrectly. Hilmeradus was still alive: he attended the synod of Verberie in the following year and another synod of Verberie around the year 865. The question of the date of that synod must therefore be reconsidered, since it is clear that it was not held in 852, as we noted. The subscriptions of the bishops certainly show that it was held no later than 846. But why resort to conjecture in a manifest matter? It is clear from the *Capitula* of Charles the Bald, title VI, that Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, issued certain chapters in a synod of his province, attended by his suffragans. Thus we must correct what we said: that the name of Raginarius, bishop of Amiens, was incorrectly written in the subscriptions of that council. He held the see until 848 or 849.]; Freculfus, of Lisieux [Note: [Col. 0551B] Freculfus. The man who wrote the *Chronicle* from the creation of the world to approximately the year 600.]; Valfridus, of Bayeux; Nomenoe, leader of the Breton people [Note: [Col. 0551B] To Nomenoe. To the duke of the Bretons, who had held that position since the time of Louis the Pious. After Louis’s death, he joined the side of Charles the Bald against Lothair and Louis in 841, sending him gifts and binding his loyalty to him by oath. But two years later, with the same ease with which he had joined Charles’s party, he defected from him, driven by ambition for the kingdom, as we noted in Letter 31. Then, “with his customary treachery,” as it is written in the *Annals of Saint Bertin*, “he had overrun Angers and the surrounding regions.”], greetings in Christ Jesus our Lord.

It has long been the case that God, by a hidden yet just judgment, has permitted you to be ruler of your people. What kind of ruler you have shown yourself to be, however, is testified by your own conscience and by the bitter complaints of various churches, [Col. 0552A] as well as by the sufferings of nobles and commoners, rich and poor, widows and orphans, whom you have harassed with criminal greed and appalling cruelty. But because you have not entirely cast off the Christian name, and because we are indebted to everyone through [Note: [Col. 0551C] Apostolic succession. For bishops are the successors of the apostles, as all antiquity has consistently handed down. Indeed, Hilary, in the fragments, wishes each bishop to be a successor of Peter and Paul, when he says mockingly of the bishops who had condemned Athanasius: “O true disciples of Christ! O worthy successors of Peter and Paul!” This is indeed true. Nevertheless, by a particular right the Roman pontiff is the successor of those same apostles, because he sits in their chair, as Alexander III says in Letter 19, published in the Appendix to Peter of Celle. Hence, in the letter of Louis the Pious to the Roman pontiff—which survives among the acts of the Council of Paris held in 824—and in the letter sent by the Roman pontiff to Michael and Theophilus, the Greek emperors, as well as in the acts of the election of Charles the Bald as emperor in 876, the pope is called “the vicar of the apostles Peter and Paul.” For to these two our Lord gave primacy in the Church, as Geoffrey of Vendôme says in Book I, Letter 7. Alcuin must be understood as referring to these apostles when, in Letter 62, he calls Leo III “the vicar of the apostles.” Similarly, Lambert of Hersfeld calls Clement II “the vicar of the apostles.”] apostolic succession, so that we may exhort those who act well to perseverance and those who offend to repentance [Note: [Col. 0551D] By divine authority. Bishops have their authority from Christ, who alone and uniquely possesses the power to appoint bishops to govern his Church, as Cyprian says at the Council of Carthage. Stephen, therefore, bishop of Larissa in Thessaly, deserves censure. Writing to Boniface II, bishop of Rome, whose assistance he needed in retaining his see, he derives the authority of all the bishops throughout the world from the Roman pontiff: “Because,” he says, “when the Lord said a third time, ‘Do you love me? Feed my sheep,’ he first entrusted the command to YOU, and afterward, THROUGH you, bestowed it upon all the holy Churches throughout the world.” The judgment of this passage must therefore be brought back into conformity with the rule handed down by Saint Pope Leo, whose words are these, from his third sermon on the anniversary of the day of his accession: “For this reason it is said to blessed Peter, ‘To you I will give the keys,’ etc. The force of this power certainly passed also to the other apostles, and the institution of this decree reached all the leaders of the Church. But it is not without reason that what is communicated to all is entrusted to one alone.” The most holy pontiff held that this had indeed been said to Peter alone, but nevertheless to all the apostles and bishops in his person. It was especially honorable, however, that Christ publicly praised Peter’s confession and, in granting his authority to the Church, wished this to be done in Peter’s person. For this reason Augustine says that Peter represented the person of the whole Church in a figurative universality. Upon this confession, therefore—that is, upon Christ himself, whom Peter had confessed to be the Son of the living God—the Church was founded, and against it the gates of hell will not prevail. Although some refer this final part of Christ’s words to Peter and his Roman successors, [Col. 0552C] John XXI interpreted those final words of the Church in a letter written to James, king of Majorca. We now publish it for the first time, and both you, reader, and I owe it to the singular generosity of the distinguished man Antonius Vion of Herovall. “John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most dear son in Christ, the illustrious king of Majorca: greetings and apostolic blessing. He who rules all things by the command of the eternal law does not abandon even the least matters. Since he cares equally for all, ruling heaven and earth, he himself looks beneath all the heavens, and his light reaches over the ends of the earth. He has looked upon his own Jerusalem—that is, the most holy and catholic Church, which is built as a city not by masses of stone but by wondrous virtues—ascending singularly, wonderfully, and no less mercifully into the sublimity of those virtues from his prepared dwelling. Christ, the Rock, established this Church by an admirable and ineffable arrangement, and built it upon himself; he made himself the living cornerstone of its foundation, laying beneath it other foundations in the holy Fathers, the summits of catholic doctrine, for the sake of a more evident and secure strength. Thus, founded upon the holiest mountains, even if it should at times experience the assaults of those who shake it, it would fear no loss through ruin; rather, the gates of hell would not prevail against it. Raised to the heights of virtue, it would not remain hidden under a bushel, but its splendor would be evident to all as an example of salvation. In this Church, too, the same pious and merciful Lord looked upon and guided that same Church with a special gaze of kindness. Although he is present everywhere, so that his equal care of governance over all things rules and arranges everything, and so that what is bestowed upon great matters is not hindered by small ones, nevertheless, through the privilege of singular love, he appointed for that Church as his vicar the one to whom he entrusted the exercise of the keys and to whom he entrusted the feeding of the sheep—one who, standing on the watchtower, would continually show it the care of immediate direction. He would bear a burden made unbearable by human weakness but made light by divine omnipotence. The arrangement, or permission, of heavenly providence has imposed upon our weakness and upon the ministry of our brethren the immense weight of this burden in these days—a matter truly terrible and astonishing to us. For when our predecessor, Pope Adrian of blessed memory, had completed the short span of his life after his elevation to the summit of the highest apostolate, and after we had rendered him the customary offices of humanity at his solemn funeral, we and those same brethren assembled in the episcopal palace at Viterbo to devote ourselves, as necessity pressed and our ardent desire urged, to the election of a pontiff to replace him. Although, for several days, the obstruction of the citizens of Viterbo prevented us from even beginning the business of the impending election, once we were able to devote ourselves to it, the benevolent Spirit of wisdom stood by us, as devout faith supposes, having been humbly invoked according to custom by us and by those brethren themselves. On the first day, by the unanimous and concordant vote of those brethren, a canonical, common, and unanimous election of us—then bishop of Tusculum—proceeded, without prior deliberation or our knowledge, to the chair of Peter. In these circumstances, therefore, we are rightly astonished and equally terrified. Is it not astonishing, is it not terrifying, that we, who have always thought it safer to be securely cast aside in the house of the Lord than dangerously raised over the care and governance of others, have suddenly come into the depths of the sea? And while we reckon up the resources of virtue insufficient for the burden of the work imposed upon us, and gather forces unequal to it, we fear—and not unjustly—that we shall be overwhelmed by its storm. These considerations strongly urged us to remain in the vocation to which the Lord had called us, so that our weakness might reject the burden and our insufficiency avoid it. Yet because reward is measured out and granted in proportion to labors—for which reason the outstanding teacher and preacher, not boasting of his success but truthfully bearing witness to his labors, says, ‘I did not labor more successfully or profit more than all the others, but I labored more than all the others’—although the burden and labor frightened us, the reward of eternal recompense, unless the mercy of the one who repays should grant otherwise, invited each person to undertake the yoke of apostolic service and to labor in it according to his strength, in proportion to his labors. Trusting in him who gives strength to the weary, whose sufficiency alone is enough to make up for our deficiencies, we placed our weak shoulders beneath so great a burden and did not hesitate to expose our hands to the immensity of the labor. Nevertheless, because we see that the office we have undertaken exceeds our strength and that we cannot bear it alone—especially since we clearly perceive that the harvest is plentiful but the workers are few—we humbly implore the assistance of the faithful. We also judge that those who have assumed responsibility for secular power among the people of the Lord should be exhorted to work faithfully and diligently with us in that task, insofar as it pertains to them. Therefore we ask and earnestly beseech your royal highness in the Lord Jesus Christ that, prudently considering that a considerable part of the judgment of the world has been divinely entrusted to you, you love justice and diligently observe it toward all subject to your authority, without abandoning clemency. For empires are established by these firmest pillars, kingdoms are strengthened, princes are defended, and principalities rejoice in a secure and peaceful condition. Moreover, honor with careful attention that same Church, your mother, and those who preside over it, as well as ecclesiastical persons—indeed, the author of your salvation, through whom you reign and are governed, in the persons of his ministers. In these matters, dearest son, strive not only to imitate your predecessors of praiseworthy memory but to surpass them; indeed, surpass yourself through successive increases in virtue, advancing as though from virtue to virtue. You may have firm hope and confidence in us that, zealously concerned with affection like a father for your prosperity and that of your kingdom, we shall strive to preserve it, insofar as we can with God’s help, and, as our resources permit, to promote it favorably. Given at Viterbo, on the Nones of October, in the first year of our pontificate.” See Augustine, Treatises 118 and 124 on John, and likewise Jerome, at the beginning of Book III of his Commentaries on Matthew.] by divine authority call them to repentance; we feel the deepest sorrow for your offenses [Col. 0553A] and, with paternal and episcopal concern, wish to recall you from your destruction.

Through your greed the land of the Christians has been laid waste; the temples of God have been partly destroyed and partly burned, together with the bones of the saints and other relics; the possessions of the churches—which were [Note: [Col. 0554B] The offerings of the faithful. A celebrated passage, much praised during those troubled times in synods and in the capitularies of our kings. It is cited from a letter of Pope Urban I. In reality, however, it is taken from Julianus Pomerius, Book II, On the Active Life, chapter 9. For that letter of Urban is spurious.] the offerings of the faithful, the redemption of souls, and the patrimonies of the poor—have been unlawfully converted to your own uses; the inheritances of nobles have been seized; a very great multitude of people have either been killed or oppressed by slavery; the most savage acts of plunder have been committed; adulteries and violations of virgins have been perpetrated everywhere; legitimate bishops [Note: [Col. 0554B] Expelled from their sees. These were Subsannus of Vannes, Salaco of Alet, Felix of Quimper, and Liberalis of Oximus, as is clear from the account of the bishoprics instituted by Nomenoë, which was published by Sirmond after the Capitularies of Charles the Bald. Actard, bishop of Nantes, was also among them.] have been driven from their own sees; and, to speak more mildly—for we did not wish to call them [Note: [Col. 0554B] Thieves and robbers. Leo IV uses this designation of Gislard, who had been ordained in place of the expelled Actard, when writing to Nomenoë: “Not a thief or robber such as we perceive Gislard to be in the see of Nantes, who did not fear to usurp the place of a living man, although he had no right to it.” This chapter is found in Gratian, 7, q. 1. The Gallican bishops therefore expressed themselves more moderately. Instead of calling such invaders thieves and robbers, they called them merely hirelings, lest they should irritate the prince whom they were trying to draw back from these errors by using those atrocious terms against men whom he himself had made bishops. At such a time the man’s power was so great that, to use Sallust’s words, it had to be softened rather than provoked.] thieves and robbers—hirelings have been introduced; the diocese formerly belonging to our patron, blessed [Note: [Col. 0554C] In the diocese of Martin. That is, the metropolitan jurisdiction of the archbishop of Tours, who is the successor of blessed Martin. Before Nomenoë, Brittany had always been subject to the established metropolitan of Tours. In these times, however, the Breton bishops withdrew from his authority and thereafter became subject to the archbishop of Dol, against the will and opposition of the Roman bishops, until the time of Innocent III. The decree of Pope Urban II at the Council of Clermont did little to help. In an old manuscript of Aniane it is written: “Restitution was made to the metropolitan church of Tours of Lesser Brittany.” Hildebert of Le Mans also mentions the same decree in a letter published by the most learned Francis Florent, under title VIII, On the Use and Authority of the Pallium: “Thus,” says Hildebert, “to one who considers the matter carefully it is clear that all Brittany is contained within the limits of the Church of Tours. Yet I do not raise this complaint as though it were still to be debated, since religious persons know and testify that it was long ago decided in the Roman Church. The venerable privilege of Pope Urban, granted to the metropolitan church of Tours, also testifies to this; whoever reads it understands that all Brittany is subject to it as to its own metropolitan.” This did little good, as I said. For that province continued to have its own archbishop for a very long time after the Council of Clermont. In Besly, in the proofs to his History of the Counts of Poitiers, p. 414, there are also certain acts issued shortly after the Council of Clermont, namely in 1096, in the fourth indiction, on the sixth day before the Nones of March, to which Rolland, archbishop of Dol, subscribes. Even Gregory VII’s effort was unsuccessful: he had decreed “that both the bishop of Dol and the other bishops of Brittany should henceforth render perpetual subjection and obedience to the archbishop of Tours.” Finally, Innocent III brought that dispute to an end, and thereafter the Breton bishops were subject to the archbishop of Tours. —Diocese. That is, province. At that time the word diocese was chiefly used to signify an entire province. The parish of any individual bishop, however, was called his diocese, as we explain in our note on canon 3 of the Council of Verneuil.] Martin, from which you cannot deny that you come, has been violated; and, finally, every ecclesiastical order has been thrown into confusion. We say this with profound grief and compassion.

[Col. 0556A] These things alone were sufficient for your destruction. But, to complete the sum of evils, you increased your audacity and injured all Christendom when you [Note: [Col. 0555B] The vicar of blessed Peter. That is, Pope Leo, the fourth of that name, as he will say shortly. Thus, as a title of honor, the Roman bishop is commonly called in the books of ancient writers and even by the Roman pontiffs themselves, evidently because he occupies Peter’s place. But, remarkably, the other bishops too are often called vicars of blessed Peter, because Peter, when Christ said to him, “Feed my sheep”—words that also pertain to the other apostles—represented the whole Church in a figurative universality, as Augustine says. A notable passage occurs in Ambrose’s On the Dignity of the Priesthood, chapter 2, where we read of Peter: “And when he had been questioned three times and had followed with a threefold response, the Lord said for the third time, ‘Feed my sheep.’ These sheep and this flock were received not only by blessed Peter at that time, but he received them together with us, and with him we all received them.” In chapter 1 he had said that all priests received the keys of the kingdom of heaven in blessed Peter the apostle. Hence Mapinius, bishop of Reims, writing to Villicus, says not without reason: “Although we read that the Lord said this to Saint Peter, ‘Feed my sheep,’ the present sentence pertains to all who perform the priestly office.” Peter, abbot of Celle, was bolder—and indeed this was after the time of Gregory VII. He dared to write to Hugh, archbishop of Sens, that the same responsibility rested upon him as upon Christ and Peter. These are his words from Book I, Letter 8: “The wolves, those savage beasts, devour the grapes of Christ’s vineyard, or the sheep of his fold, all day long; they trample them underfoot and tear them apart with their hands, while your vigilance, most kindly Father, neglects to oppose them. Why do you not consider what the great shepherd owes the sheep in virtue of his office, his pledge, and his love? Certainly defense, certainly instruction, certainly care. But what kind and how great? Without doubt, as great as Christ’s and of the kind Peter’s.” He derives this authority from Christ’s words to Peter, believing, like Ambrose and Mapinius, that they were spoken to all the apostles in Peter’s person. For shortly afterward he says: “To you, indeed, it was said in Peter, ‘Feed my lambs’—that is, with sound doctrine. To you again it was said, ‘Strengthen your brethren’—that is, by a good example. Nevertheless, you hold the keys of the kingdom of heaven, so that you may exclude the goats and admit the lambs.” In the same century Saint Bernard wrote in Letter 41 to Henry, likewise archbishop of Sens: “Therefore, since by God’s authority you received the keys of the kingdom of heaven entrusted to you,” etc. Since those good men believed that Christ had spoken to all bishops in the person of blessed Peter, whom Peter of Celle therefore calls in Book VII, Letter 1, the best model of all prelates, they consequently called not only the Roman bishop but also the other bishops vicars of Peter. These are the words of Charlemagne in Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 163: “This can easily be understood from the words of the Lord, who said to blessed Peter, whose place the bishops occupy, ‘Whatever you bind,’” etc. Jonas of Orléans, in his short work On Royal Instruction, chapter 2: “What, then, is the power and authority of the priesthood can easily be perceived from the words of the Lord, who said to blessed Peter, whose place we unworthily occupy, ‘Whatever you bind on earth,’” etc. Hincmar of Reims, in the Capitula he gave to archdeacons and priests in 877: “Blessed Peter the apostle, whose place bishops occupy in the Church,” etc. Hence the words of the Gallican bishops at the assembly of Pîtres in 869: “According to the authority that we received in blessed Peter, when the Lord said, ‘Whatever you bind,’” etc. And in the acts of the coronation of Ermentrude, wife of Charles the Bald, the bishops interpret as referring to the entire college of bishops the passage in chapter 12 of the Acts of the Apostles where it is written that the Church prayed without ceasing to God for Peter. Peter of Blois, in Letter 23: “An unlearned bishop is a mute herald. It is the duty of a prelate to teach his subjects, to make the people acceptable to God by opening the mysteries of Scripture. For Peter and his successors are commanded to cast the net into the deep—that is, to open up the profound understanding of sacred Scripture for the capture of human beings.” He expresses his meaning more clearly in Letter 148 to the bishop of Bath: “Remember, Father, that you are Peter’s vicar. In him it was once said to you: ‘If you love me, feed my sheep.’” Peter of Celle, writing a congratulatory letter to William, archbishop of Sens, praises him highly because, in the election of John of Salisbury, bishop of Chartres, he had shown himself impartial and incorruptible. “Certainly,” he says in Book VII, Letter 8, “this will be written on your Rational and Superhumeral, most loving Father, with an iron stylus and a diamond claw: in choosing Peter’s vicars, no human favor moves you, no partiality, no carnal affection, no greed for money.” Finally, Gildas the Wise, who flourished under the emperor Justinian, plainly seems to hold that every bishop occupies Peter’s see. Thus he writes in his Letter on the Ruin and Complaint of Britain: “Britain has priests, but they are foolish … usurping the seat of the apostle Peter with unclean feet, yet deservedly falling from it, through their greed, into the pestilential chair of Judas the betrayer.” Peter of Blois also writes in Letter 150 that each bishop presides over Peter’s little ship. We may therefore establish the following. Christ the Lord, the true and only bridegroom of the holy Church, who alone could rule the Church he redeemed, ruled it with supreme authority as long as he dwelt among human beings, to use Lupus’s words. Having once assumed the helm of the Church, he did not abandon it, but is always with us in divinity; as the same Lupus says, “by his will, command, and presence he governs both the leaders themselves and the Church together with its leaders,” as Cyprian writes in Letter 69. Long after Cyprian’s age, Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, declared the same thing at the Council of Tours under Alexander III: “Moreover,” he says, “we have Christ himself assisting us. For he did not entrust the Church to us on the condition that he would abandon it. He is always present.” After Arnulf, John XXI expressed that very judgment in magnificent words worthy of the pontiff of the apostolic see, in a letter written to the king of Majorca, which has not yet been published and which we therefore give above. [Col. 0557A] Christ, therefore, having once assumed the helm of the Church, did not abandon it. For he promised the Church that he would be with us all days, even to the consummation of the age. Yet, because he understood that after his ascent into heaven it was necessary for some to fill his place on earth, preserving the true faith and commending holiness of life, he made some apostles, others prophets, others evangelists, and others pastors and teachers. Nevertheless, he willed the rest to be subject to the apostles, to whom he gave the highest authority in the Church, decreeing that whatever they should jointly establish should bind all Christians. Hence Cyprian, in Letter 55, calls the power of bishops, which they received for governing the Church, a lofty and divine power; for, as Cyprian himself writes in Letter 27, the Church has been established upon them. All the apostles, moreover, had equal honor and equal power. Yet to Peter, because of his manifest confession of Christ, was granted the prerogative of primacy, so that, when a head had been appointed, the occasion of schism might be removed. Hence, because bishops succeeded the apostles by a vicarious ordination—as Firmilian writes to Cyprian, and Cyprian himself in Letter 69 to Florentius Pupianus—and because Peter is the chief of the apostles, bishops in subsequent ages were called vicars of blessed Peter and successors of the apostles Peter and Paul. This was why Edgar, king of the English, who lived in the year 966, said that bishops possess Peter’s sword: “I have Constantine’s sword,” he says, “you have Peter’s sword.” Later, however, as Christians’ piety and reverence toward the Roman pontiff increased, and as his authority happily became more and more evident from day to day, this dignity of Petrine succession was reserved for him alone; and it seemed sufficient for the other bishops if their dignity were derived from succession to the remaining apostles. [Col. 0557C] Thus Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, endured a grave calumny in his own age because, as some said, he had dared to assert that the Roman pope was not of greater dignity than he himself. Since Hincmar was burdened by this accusation, he attempted to clear himself of it and declared his accuser liable under the Remmian law. To state the matter briefly, we must hold that Christ bestowed his authority upon the apostles, that is, upon bishops. For, as Cyprian writes in Letter 65, the Lord chose apostles, that is, bishops and prelates. All the apostles had equal honor and equal power, as the same Cyprian writes. Bishops succeeded the apostles, but in such a way that the bishop of Rome, who occupies the see of Peter and Paul, has the first and greatest judgment in matters of truth, as Facundus of Hermiane says. Therefore, if any matter of great importance arises which requires an assembly of the Lord’s priests, a synod must be held, in which the true faith may be established. But this remedy is to be applied only for a grave cause. For Augustine, writing against the two letters of the Pelagians, Book IV, chapter 12, vigorously attacks their pride because they sought the glory of demanding that a synod of East and West be convened on their account; he judges this unjust. In synods, however, all bishops possess the highest authority. And in governing their own Churches, of which they are the masters, to use the language of Salvian and Agobard, they are accountable to no one but Christ, unless there is a common cause, as Canon 9 of Antioch teaches. What was said a little above, in three words following Cyprian’s opinion, namely that all the apostles had equal honor and power, must be explained somewhat more fully because of the scandal of the weak. But at the very outset Cyprian’s own passage must be set forth according to Baronius’s edition: “And although after his resurrection he grants equal power to all the apostles and says: ‘As the Father sent me, I also send you; receive the Holy Spirit; if you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven him; if you retain anyone’s, they are retained’; nevertheless, in order to make unity manifest, he established one chair and by his authority arranged that the origin of that same unity should begin from one. Certainly the other apostles were what Peter was, endowed with an equal fellowship both of honor and of power; but the beginning proceeds from unity. Primacy is given to Peter, that the one Church of Christ and the one chair may be shown.” From this passage of Cyprian it is evident that primacy over even the other apostles was conferred upon Peter by Christ. Hence Pope Gelasius also said that the Roman Church, founded by Peter, had been set above the other Churches not by synodical decrees, but had obtained primacy by the evangelical utterance of our Lord and Savior. Baronius understood how important this passage of Cyprian was for asserting the primacy of the supreme pontiff, and therefore reproduced it in full under the year 34, § 199. Had his continuator Odoricus Raynaldus seen this passage of Baronius, he would have refrained from the censure which he issued far too imprudently and rashly against the cardinals assembled in Livorno, a town of the diocese of Pisa. For these cardinals, having sent circular letters in every direction, in which they expressed their grief over the division of the Church and the great desire urging them to procure the restoration of concord, began those letters with that most celebrated passage of Cyprian, without any mention of Cyprian, as though it belonged not to Cyprian but to the cardinals themselves. But Raynaldus, to whom this very common passage was still unknown, when he reached the words, ‘Certainly the other apostles were what Peter was,’ etc., interrupts the cardinals’ discourse and exclaims: “This heresy was fabricated, namely that the apostles were endowed with equal honor and power with Saint Peter, when the cardinals, stirred by the greatest indignation of mind, wished to subject the pontiff to themselves; nor did they observe that Saint Peter had been established by Christ as prince of the remaining apostles, although they had received the greatest authority from the same Christ; nor did they consider that, if the apostolic primacy fell, the cardinalitial dignity would altogether collapse, nor would cardinals be more worthy than the other parish priests.” See Raynaldus, volume XVII, under the year 1408, § 21. From this passage, meanwhile, we learn that Raynaldus held that the institution of cardinals should be referred altogether to the time when primacy was given to Peter, and yet that they are parish priests. He then laments the blindness and madness of those cardinals, who did not perceive how great a wound they inflicted on themselves if the things written concerning the equality of the apostles were true. For their dignity would collapse and would be reduced [Col. 0559C] below the episcopal. I said that bishops are accountable to no one but Christ for their administration, unless there is a common cause. This must be understood with respect to the administration of each diocese: namely, ordinations of clerics and the other practices customarily exercised in Churches, as Canon 9 of Antioch teaches. For by common causes here I do not mean major causes, namely those which by ancient law must be referred to the apostolic see. Moreover, if a bishop falls into a crime or does anything contrary to rule, he may be corrected by the metropolitan and the provincial synod, as is known to everyone. And if anything occurs in any diocese that deserves to be brought to the notice of the fellow-provincial bishops—for example, if a priest is accused of a crime, or some other common cause of the province arises—then the bishop must reserve that cause for the judgment of his colleagues, so that all may deliberate together about what ought to be done.] the vicar of blessed Peter [Col. 0557A]—Leo the apostolic, to whom God had given [Note: [Col. 0558C] Primacy throughout the whole world. Thus Arator the subdeacon calls Pope Vigilius “the first of all priests in the whole world.” This is the heading of Arator’s letter in the very ancient manuscript of the monastery of Corbie, now preserved in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris: “To the holy, most blessed, and apostolic lord, first of all priests in the whole world, Pope Vigilius, Arator the subdeacon: ‘With walls resounding with waves,’” etc. Similarly, Lucentius the bishop said during the sixteenth session of the Council of Chalcedon that Pope Leo was the chief bishop of the whole Church. The emperor Justinian also says in Book 7 of the Code, On the Holy Trinity, that the blessedness of the pope of Old Rome is the head of all God’s most holy priests. Likewise, Hincmar of Reims, in chapter 36 of his later work against Gottschalk, calls Pope Gregory “the pontiff of the first see throughout the entire world.”] primacy throughout the whole world—despised. When you had asked him to enter you in his book, to implore God’s clemency on your behalf, and he [Note: [Col. 0558D] By letters sent. Nicholas I mentions this letter of Leo IV to Nomenoë when writing to Solomon, king of the Bretons: “Finally,” he says, “the most holy Pope Leo, writing to Nomenoë, calls Actard, among other things, a distinguished man, and declares that he thinks soundly, teaches soundly, lives soundly, and perseveres soundly; but he marks Gislard as the zealous usurper of the aforesaid Actard.” A fragment of the same letter of Leo is found in Gratian, 7, q. 1, chapter “Not a thief.”] had promised in a letter sent to do so if you would obediently heed his admonition, you not only did none of what he had commanded, but did not even receive the letter itself. Because you were unwilling to desist from evil, you were afraid to listen to one who admonished you for your good. In this, therefore, you injured the apostles, whose prince is Peter. You injured the bishops who now reign with God in heaven and shine forth on earth through miracles. You injured us as well: for although we do not possess their merit, by divine grace we nevertheless possess the same office.

Recently also, receiving [Note: [Col. 0559C] Lantbert, formerly count of Nantes, who, so inflamed against Charles because he had appointed Reinold count over the people of Nantes—to his own disgrace—that he had turned to the Bretons and was helping them both with military forces and with extensive military expertise. See the Chronicle of Ademar of Chabannes and Adrevald, Book I, On the Miracles of Saint Benedict, chapter 33, as well as the charter of Angély edited by Besly. He later returned to Charles’s favor in 849 and received back from him his dignity, namely, the guardianship of the Breton frontier, as the author of the Chronicle of Fontenelle confirms: “The mark was restored to Count Lambert.” But since he was accustomed, through fickleness of mind, to change from peace to war, the following year he again joined Nomenoius’s party, as is written in the same Chronicle under the year 850: “Count Lambert and his brother Warnarius, plotting tyranny, defected from their allegiance and joined Nomenoius, the tyrant of the Bretons. But not long afterward Warnarius was captured by Count Gausbert [Col. 0560B] and presented to the king.” Lambert then died in 852, as is recorded by Ademar and in a fragment of the Chronicle of Limoges: “852: Count Lambert was killed by Gausbert, count of the people of Le Mans, on the Kalends of May.” The Chronicle of Fontenelle says: “At that time Lantbert was killed by the young Gausbert, and his brother Warnarius [Col. 0560C] suffered capital punishment by order of the king.”] Lantbert, whom the Church had received in part with maternal compassion, on the specific condition that he correct himself and entirely abandon his customary evils, you made yourself a participant in—indeed, the author of—the disturbance of the Christian people. For our lord the king, a lover of peace, had removed him from your territory at your urging [Note: [Col. 0560C] At your urging. From this it may be inferred that Charles granted this in response to Nomenoius’s urgent requests, so that he might remove Lantbert from the city of Nantes. The Bretons had doubtless come to detest him because of the tireless military vigor with which he frequently harassed them, as is clear both from this passage and from the Annals of Fulda under the year 825. And, as generally happens in such matters, they afterward willingly received into their own party a man famous for his many military exploits when he withdrew to them, hoping through his aid to cause the greatest possible harm to those peoples with whom they were waging war.] and had honored him with other dignities. Yet now, when he is attempting rebellion, you have received him as though into your embrace, and you do not cease to encourage him so that he may advance in evil. Have your books brought forth [Note: [Col. 0560C] Your books. That is, the divine books, as Baronius correctly observed when citing this passage of Lupus. Nomenoius was a Christian. And the divine books are the books of Christians, just as jurists call the books containing laws “our books.”]. In them you will hear the Lord threatening: “You give aid to the wicked, and you join yourself in friendship to those who hate the Lord” (2 Chronicles XIX); and you will find that not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are worthy of death.

[Col. 0560A] Nor are you unaware that [Note: [Col. 0560C] Definite boundaries. It is certain that there were almost continual wars between the Franks and the rulers of lesser Brittany. But when the boundaries of the Franks and the Bretons were established is not so well determined. It is nevertheless probable that this occurred during the reign of Clovis I, by whose valor the Bretons were subdued, as Gregory of Tours teaches in Book IV, chapter 4: “For,” he says, “the Bretons were always under Frankish authority after the death of King Clovis; and they were called counts, not kings.” Nantes, Rennes, and Vannes, however, were not subject to them; only the peoples extending from their territories as far as the Ocean were. Since it therefore seemed too narrow to be confined within such restricted boundaries, they sometimes crossed the Breton frontier and for a time held the cities of Nantes, Rennes, and Vannes under their authority. But the Franks again took these from the Bretons. Finally, Nomenoius also invaded them; and although he and his son Erispoe retained them by force, Charles the Bald transferred their control to Erispoe, as the author of the Annals of Saint Bertin teaches.] from the beginning of Frankish rule there have been definite boundaries, which the Franks claimed for themselves, and definite boundaries which, when the Bretons requested them, they granted to the Bretons. How, then, do you despise the law of God, which commands that you not move the boundaries established by your fathers (Proverbs XXII)? You attempt unjustly to defend Frankish territory for yourself, and you do not fear the words: “Cursed is he who moves his neighbor’s boundaries” (Deuteronomy XXVII)? O, what will you do on the day of the great judgment, when an account must be rendered to you for your years, months, hours, and moments? And this will happen quickly. For it is true that a young man may die soon, but that an old man cannot live long. Before you, the age was long; after you, God knows with certainty how long it will last. Do not, for the sake of this very brief life, acquire everlasting misery for yourself.

Unless you abandon the seizure of what belongs to others, the oppression of everyone, and alliances with the wicked, and accept the admonition of our apostolic see and our unity, your faith will not benefit you, nor any good works you may think you possess. For the Savior says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven—he will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew VII). [Col. 0561A] Consider what punishment is deserved by one who has scandalized one of the little ones; and thus you will be able to gather what an immense condemnation you will endure unless you repent, since you have gravely disturbed the greater part of the Christian people.

We warn you, we implore you, we adjure you, desiring your salvation: put an end to your evils; turn to the Lord, whose judgment none of us can escape. Produce fruits worthy of repentance. That is: because you have sinned greatly, practice good works greatly, so that you may not only avoid being tortured with the devil and the reprobate in hell, but also rejoice with God and his elect in heaven. We also promise you this: if you restore yourself to God, we wish to be intercessors with him for your sins; and with our devout prince we will try to obtain that he may kindly provide for you and your descendants.

We know that you have incurred the greatest guilt by rejecting the letter of the apostolic see, thinking that it contained something harmful to you [Note: [Col. 0561C] Harmful to you. Leo IV had sent Nomenoius a certain letter, which he refused to accept because, as Lupus says, he thought that it contained certain things contrary to his dignity. This is customary among our Gauls whenever Roman-curial rescripts are thought to conflict with the rights of our kings or the liberties of the Gallican Church. Since, however, the bishops recognized that Nomenoius’s objection was entirely justified, they offered themselves as guarantors that Leo’s letter contained nothing violating the rights of his majesty.]. But the copy of it which the venerable pope was gracious enough to send us makes it known to you that it contains nothing affecting you adversely; and therefore, if you wish, we are prepared to send a second legate of the aforesaid see with writings revered by the whole world [Note: [Col. 0561D] A legate. Leo had therefore sent a legate with the letter mentioned above. Nomenoius, however, prohibited this legate from reaching Brittany, since at that time rulers thought that the Roman pontiff was not permitted to send legates into provinces without the consent and will of those to whom God had entrusted the government of peoples.]. If you do not receive him, we who have warned you will be excusable. But if you receive him and listen to him, you will have both the Lord and blessed Peter favorably disposed toward you, and you will have us joined to you in faith and effective in intercession. If, however, you despise us when we kindly admonish you, let it be certain to you that you will never have a place in heaven and soon will have none on earth: because, separated through your fault from the apostolic and our fellowship, you will have a place under the vengeance of anathema in hell—may God avert it.

We also declare this through your ministry to Lantbert’s men and to all members of your people: if they associate themselves with him and consent to his rebellion, they will be condemned by anathema and, handed over to Satan, will perish without end. Those who turn back, however, we receive, and we desire that they remain in Christian peace; and for their sake we are prepared, as far as we can, to incline the clemency of our lord the king.

## LETTER LXXXV. TO MARCWARD

To the most reverend and distinguished Father Marcward, Lupus offers perpetual salvation.

Recently returning from magnificent feasts—that is, from the Breton expedition—and scarcely having regained my breath, I wish through this courier to learn the truth of your prosperity, so that, since I am burning with my own anxieties, I may at least find rest in your favorable successes. My lord the king, your foster-father, when he freed me from the pleasures with which he burdened me, ordered me to greet you in his name; how willingly I do so you can judge. Deign to greet in my name our dearest friend, that is, our mutual son Eigil, and after him Ansb. and the other brothers. When it is convenient for you, arrange to send me cups suitable for travel, extremely precious in form and quality, though made only of wood; for when I see the more valuable ones you have given to others, I almost contract the disease of envy. I wish you prosperous health.

## LETTER LXXXVI. [Note: [Col. 0561D] To Hatto. He later became abbot of Fulda, surnamed Bonosus and Gloriosus; through the fault of copyists, as Browerus notes, he is called Waldo in Lambert of Hersfeld. Hence, through a major error, the events at Regensburg concerning Abbot Waldo and his brothers, Counts Udo and Berengarius, which are recorded in the Frankish Annals under the year 861, are attributed in Lambert to Waldo, abbot of Fulda. He succeeded Rabanus, who later became archbishop of Mainz. In what year this occurred had until now been uncertain. Some report that he succeeded Rabanus in 847, when the latter became archbishop; Browerus considers this opinion untenable. Moreover, Lupus’s Letter 40 shows that Rabanus had resigned the governance of the monastery of Fulda before attaining the episcopate and had transferred this responsibility to Hatto, which occurred in 842, as we noted there. Hatto died in 856, as the author of the Annals of Fulda teaches: “Hatto, abbot of the monastery of Fulda, died on the day before the Ides of April; in his place, by the election of the brothers and royal authority, Thioto, one of the monks themselves, was appointed.” Hatto’s epitaph is found in Book IV of Christoph Browerus’s Antiquities of Fulda.] TO HATTO

To his dearest Hatto, Lupus sends greetings in the Lord.

Although unavoidable occupations prevent our conversation, which ought to be frequent, [Col. 0562C] nevertheless, once they have been set aside for a little while, we ought to look after one another, lest the salutary counsels with which, by God’s help, we can assist each other be neglected any longer to our detriment. Therefore arrange to meet me at your Arceiae this October, on the day you indicate, so that, meeting at a place midway between us, we may conveniently consult about necessary matters. You should also know that we have asked Abbot Odacer and our kinsman [Note: [Col. 0562D] Abbot Odacer. Of the monastery of Cormery in the diocese of Tours; he later became the first abbot of the monastery of Villeloin in the same diocese. He lived until 868 and died on the fifth day before the Nones of May.] to recover from Vivianus the pound of gold with which you are familiar, since his humanity must not be exasperated by any inhumanity [Note: [Col. 0562D] Vivianus. Rector or abbot of Saint Martin of Tours. Thus at that time rulers commonly entrusted monasteries to secular men. He is perhaps Vivianus, prince of the district of Le Mans, mentioned by Hericus in Book I, chapter 48, On the Miracles of Saint Germanus of Auxerre. I think that “prince” here means duke or count. For the author of the Chronicle of Fontenelle says this about Count Vivianus under the year 849: “That year, in the month of March, Count Vivianus captured Charles, the brother of Pippin, who had been sent to Aquitaine to aid his brother, together with several of his accomplices.” He died in 851, as is written in the Chronicles of Limoges and Angoulême: “When Charles, for the fourth time returning to Brittany, engaged Erispoe, Nomenoius’s son, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, he lost part of his army together with Duke Vivianus.”]. Send this courier back promptly, so that at the time you indicate I may be able to meet you at the place mentioned. After I had already sent out the courier, Rath. arrived and revealed your circumstances with complete truthfulness. Once I learned them, it seemed to me all the more necessary to hasten our meeting, so that, with God showing the way, we may prudently confront difficult matters through careful discussion. Meanwhile, work diligently to restore that same Rath. [Note: [Col. 0563D] Rath. We owe this man’s full name to Letter 91, where he is called Ratharius.]—who suffered the force of indignation without deserving it—for it is a grave injustice that, because of a matter having nothing to do with him, he should be deprived of the reward for such prolonged labor.

## LETTER LXXXVII. [Note: [Col. 0563D] To Hugh. Abbot of Saint Martin of Tours, born of royal lineage, as Pope John VIII attests in Letter 305. He died in 887, as is clear from the Chronicle of Angers and from Abbo, Book II, On the Siege of the City of Paris. See Sirmond on the Capitularies of Charles the Bald, p. 104. The following letter is also addressed to him.] TO HUGH

Our brothers who were sent to you reported to us your agitation, which arose on account of that man who, while pursuing robbery with other criminals, forced his own life to be taken; you know very well that we were not accomplices in this affair. Therefore, when your venerable son and our familiar friend Stephen reported the matter to us—not as it was, but as it had falsely been reported to him—we sent our provost, a man experienced in such matters and, as befits his age and nobility, deeply religious; according to the prudence he had acquired in the world, he was to investigate and settle the case with your messenger. But because the man who was seeking justice himself refused to carry it out, the matter could reach no conclusion. Thus we have arranged for these letters to be sent to your highness. Through them we wish to calm the agitation of your mind, which none of our negligence or obstinacy has provoked. For the power of your eminence ought to favor not persons but just causes, and to attend not to our lowliness but to the divine majesty—whose unworthy servants we are—and to the reverence due to blessed Peter. Nor should you threaten or inflict any harm upon us, since we seek justice in the same manner in which we are prepared to render it. We also remind the prudence of your highness not to reject the patronage of blessed Peter and our ancient familiarity for the sake of defending ruined men. Rather, remembering what is written, [Col. 0564A] “Mercy will surround the one who hopes in the Lord” (Psalm XXXI), and “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XVIII), deign so to quiet the controversy that has arisen that you neither permit us to be burdened nor allow your own people to act wrongly with impunity—lest, God forbid, divine vengeance on account of consent to the wicked rebound upon you. We wish you good health and that in all things you may act as befits your nobility and wisdom.

## LETTER LXXXVIII. TO HUGH, ABBOT

To Hugh, most worthy of reverence and chief of abbots, Lupus offers present and future salvation.

Ever since I began to know you, I confess that I long desired to come into your acquaintance. Having finally achieved this through your graciousness, I dare to place great confidence in you, since I frequently observe both your singular nobility and the wisdom appropriate to your nobility [Note: [Col. 0564D] Singular nobility. As we said in the preceding letter, he was born of royal lineage, as Pope John VIII attests in these words in Letter 305: “To Hugh, vigorous, noble, born of royal lineage, and most excellent abbot.” For this reason Charles the Bald and Louis the Stammerer call him their kinsman, as Sirmond notes.]. For this reason, when something happened to me which I had neither feared nor, as I believe, deserved—namely, that our lord the king gave Count Odulf the cell of our monastery, which had been taken from us and concerning which we possess an edict of both the king himself and his father, the lord Louis, most serene Augustus, and had restored it to us, as befitted him, by God’s inspiration and with the cooperation of the most distinguished man Adalh. [Note: [Col. 0564D] Adalh. On this man’s name, see what we note on Letters 55 and 92. From this letter we further learn that Odulf did not withdraw from possession of the cell of Saint Judoc, although Charles had ordered it restored to the monastery of Ferrières. Lupus therefore asks Hugh to use his authority to restrain Odulf’s audacity.], I believed that you above all should be sought—especially at the urging of Adalh. himself—so that you might prudently restrain Odulf’s dangerous greed and kindly restore to us the cell in question. Therefore, may your goodness, widely known far and wide, come to the aid of us who are in great need, for the love of God and in accordance with the royal letters, as quickly as possible; so that compassion for our misfortune may bring you an eternal reward, and so that both we and our descendants may faithfully celebrate the memory of your benefaction.

## LETTER LXXXIX. TO PARDULUS. On behalf of the queen

In the name of God alone and almighty. Irmindrudis [Note: [Col. 0564D] Irmindrudis. Or Hirmintrudis, the wife of King Charles the Bald. Since Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, was situated in Charles’s kingdom, he could have called no other woman “queen.” Massonus is therefore wrong when he expanded the abbreviation Irmind. (which occurs in the manuscript) as Irmingarde; he did the same in Letter 95.], by the grace of God’s providence queen, sends greetings to the venerable Bishop Pardulus.

We wish to receive and hear that the new matters concerning which you indicated that you could write nothing except what you had already ordered through Rhotbertus are, by the overflowing grace of God, turning out favorably. As for the day of your ordination, we shall strive to make it solemn, if only our prayers and those of our people may benefit you. Moreover, the gifts you sent were pleasing to us; and we shall gladly undertake to experience the labor of the stole you imposed, and, according to your suggestion, with the favor of God, who created us and has heaped upon us such blessings, we shall strive to avoid harmful idleness. Yet may we always be aided by your effective prayers, since you will never grant us anything which we have not presumed upon from your commendable fidelity. We wish to obtain this from your kindness: that you earnestly implore God’s clemency for those who laid down their lives in defense of their homeland, and that you assist their survivors as much as you are able.

## LETTER XC. [Note: [Col. 0565C] Abbot Odacer. Lupus’s kinsman, as Letter 86 established.] TO ODACER, ABBOT

On the third day before the Nones of July, by God’s favor, I returned to our monastery. As soon as I could, I made a point of sending these letters to your prudence, through which I express with all my affection my thanks for your kindness: you received our brothers and the other men, overtaken by the distress of such great calamity, with the open embrace of charity and fostered them with maternal compassion. Their release made me so happy that the narrowness of a letter can scarcely reveal the evidence of my affection for you, since you treat my brothers with singular love and extend to all our people, with the greatest generosity, what they could scarcely ever have hoped for. Therefore I pray that divine grace, by whose gift you are such men [Note: [Col. 0565C] Such men. I think this was imitated from Salvian, in his letter to Eucherius, bishop of Lyons: “It remains,” he says, “that the Lord our God, by whose gift such admirable young men are what they are, may make them equal to your books.”], may deign to grant my insignificance enough strength to repay even a small part in kind, while the full reward is restored to you by him who established the sum of his commandments in the fullness of charity.

## LETTER XCI. TO MARCWARD, ABBOT

[Note: [Col. 0565D] In Aquitaine. That is, in 845, when Pippin the younger, king of Aquitaine, attacked Charles the Bald, routed his army, and killed or captured many distinguished men. The author of the Annals of Saint-Bertin says: “Pippin, son of the former King Pippin, encountered in the district of Angoulême an army hastening from Francia to Charles, who was besieging Toulouse; he routed it so swiftly and without loss to his own men that, after the leaders had been killed, he either captured the rest—who had taken flight even before the engagement, with scarcely a few escaping—or allowed them, stripped of their possessions and bound by oath, to return home.” Below: “Those captured were Ebroin, bishop of Poitiers; Ragenarius, bishop of Sombrieu of Amiens; and Abbot Lupus.” This may also illuminate Letter 32 of Lupus himself, in which he writes to Abbot Louis: “In the Aquitanian expedition long ago, as you know, I lost everything.” I think it was of some importance to mention this.] In the Aquitanian battle, having been rescued from certain death and freed from the troubles of captivity, delivered from both dangers by the immense grace of God, in whom above all I placed my trust, and by the help also of a certain Turpio [Note: [Col. 0566C] “By the help of a certain Turpio.” These three words were added from a manuscript, since there was a lacuna here in Massonus’s edition. I think he means Turpio, count of Angoulême, whose fame was great in those times. He ended a distinguished life by a glorious death [Col. 0566D]. The Chronicle of Limoges records this about him under the year 863: “Turpio, count of Angoulême, engages the Normans; after killing their king, named Maurus, he himself is killed by him.” He had a brother, Emmeno, formerly count of Poitiers and later count of Angoulême, who was himself overcome by a memorable disaster. The Chronicle of Limoges under the year 866 says: “Emmeno, brother of Turpio and count of Angoulême, engages Landric, count of Saintes; after killing Landric, he is carried wounded to the castle of Rancon and dies on the eighth day.” See Ademar of Chabannes.] I returned in full health to the monastery on the third day before the Nones of July. There I learned with greater certainty what I already knew from my own knowledge: from the report of my brothers Hatto and Rath. [Note: [Col. 0566D] Hatto and Rath. See the notes on Letter 86.], and from reading your letters, namely, that you had been deeply distressed by my misfortune. I seem already to see you rejoicing with immense joy when you receive me, whom you had mourned as either captive or dead, alive and residing in the monastery. I, in turn, and all the brothers congratulate you with the greatest joy on your return so fruitful [Col. 0566B], and we give immense thanks to our Lord God, who not only restored your excellence to us but also, through your efforts, provided us with the double protection of the saints. We prayed to God daily for your safety and return; and, while we held back the conveyance of the saints’ relics in fulfillment of a vow, your beloved zeal for God easily led us to hope such things about you. For we praise God together, who has granted more than we would dare to ask. One thing alone remains to complete our joy: that you present yourself to us. Your letter declared that you could not do this at all; we shall take it as having promised this. If you do so, you will benefit both our insignificance greatly and yourself in some measure. For you will bring us consolation and an incentive to virtue, and you will gain a knowledge—and, if possible, a firmer affection—of the brothers who, after your departure, took the place of those who had died. I also ask you to send a diligent monk to Saint Boniface [Note: [Col. 0566D] To Saint Boniface. That is, to the monastery of Fulda, in which Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, was buried.], who on your behalf may ask Abbot Hatto [Note: [Col. 0566D] Hatto, abbot of the monastery of Fulda, as we said in Letter 86.] to send you, for copying, Suetonius Tranquillus’s *Life of the Caesars*, which among them is divided into two not very large volumes [Col. 0567A]; and may you bring it to me yourself—or, if this happiness is being postponed because of our sins, arrange for it to be sent through a completely trustworthy messenger. It is nowhere found in this region, and we believe that we shall obtain this benefit also through your generosity. I wish to send you my nephew, the son of Guago, and your kinsman, together with two other noble boys who, if God wills, will one day be useful to our monastery through their service, so that they may acquire knowledge of the Germanic language. The three of them are content with only two tutors. When the opportunity first arises, do not hesitate to let me know whether you would deign to grant this. Last year we suffered a shortage of wine. In other respects we are supplied according to the season, and by God’s gracious generosity we enjoy a little peace—except that certain laymen who wish to invade our monastery are plotting ambushes against us. Therefore, because of the obligation of charity, you must earnestly pray to God that he may bring about in the hearts of princes what is most advantageous to us.

## LETTER XCII. TO LOUIS

To the most excellent and distinguished chief of abbots, Lupus offers many greetings.

Having regard for your occupations, I disclose to you briefly that the great Adalh. [Note: [Col. 0567D] Adalh. See what we note about this man on Letters 55 and 88. He was evidently a man of great distinction, as is clear from Lupus’s words, in which he calls him a great and most distinguished man. Perhaps he is Adalardus, who was count of the palace under Charles the Bald.] solemnly promised me, when he was still departing, that now, with the opportunity presenting itself of its own accord, he would recover for us the cell of Saint Judoc and make every provision so that no one could harm us in anything before the king. But when I had returned from Aquitaine, preserved by God’s goodness and clemency, and wished to rest a little from the many calamities I had suffered for my loyalty to the king, rumor spread that our monastery had been given to Egilbert. Therefore, remembering our friendship, strive as usual to help me concerning both matters, especially since you know both my loyalty and service to the king and can easily understand that it is a great injustice for me to be compared with the aforesaid Egilbert, much less to have him preferred to me. I would briefly summarize what you ought to propose in such a matter, were it not that your natural prudence and abundance of learning would suggest it to you without prompting. I wish you good health and that, remembering my insignificance, you may increase day by day in happier successes.

## LETTER XCIII. TO LORD KING CHARLES

It cannot easily be explained how greatly I, your least servant in all things, glorious lord King Charles, desire both your spiritual and temporal prosperity [Col. 0568A]. For this reason I have several times come forward of my own accord, both in words and in writing, so that, with God’s grace assisting, my devotion might benefit your happiness. Now too I disclose briefly what, while meditating on many matters most useful to you and your kingdom, has occurred to me.

The observance of justice not only wins you merit before God but also strengthens earthly power. Association with good men brings you advancement and praise, after the example of blessed David, who, setting himself forth as an example for imitation, says: “He who walks in the blameless way—he will minister to me” (Psalm C). The exclusion of the wicked is equally praiseworthy, as that same David established: “He who acts proudly shall not dwell in the midst of my house; he who speaks unjustly shall not prosper in my sight” (ibid.). That every most faithful person ought to be among one’s most intimate associates, we are taught by this saying: “What plague can be more effective for causing harm than an intimate enemy?” [Note: [Col. 0568D] Boethius, Book III of *The Consolation of Philosophy*.]

By whose counsel the commonwealth, with the Lord bringing it about—of whom it is said, “Let there be peace within your strength” (Psalm CXXI)—may be safe and tranquil, Holy Scripture intimates in these words: “The multitude of the wise is the health of the world” (Wisdom VI). For they understand that “there is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs XXI), and in David’s counsels they do not depart from the path of equity. [Col. 0568C] Hence those same counsels are directed by the Lord himself toward useful results.
