Elsewhere too we are taught this clearly enough, where we read: “Always seek counsel from a wise man” (Tobit IV). By “wise” here we understand one whom experience has taught, reading has educated, or divine inspiration has preferred to others. When you are about to undertake something great, I ask you to recall that most prudent saying: “Before you begin, deliberate; and once you have deliberated, you need timely action” [Note: [Col. 0568D] Sallust, in *The Conspiracy of Catiline*.]. Thus both rashness and harmful delay will be avoided.

Deign, for your and our benefit, to consider in this single brief statement what counselors the Romans, masters of the world, used: “The Senate-house was the faithful and lofty heart of the commonwealth, fortified and enclosed on every side by the salutary protection of silence; those entering its threshold cast aside private affection and put on public affection” [Note: [Col. 0568D] Valerius Maximus, II, 2.]. Seek men of this kind—men who prefer public devotion, that is, devotion to the entire people, to private advantages—and, by God’s mercy, these most troublesome disturbances will subside.

I have taken care to offer to your majesty a very brief summary of the deeds of emperors, so that in them you may easily observe what ought either to be imitated or avoided. Above all, I recommend Trajan and Theodosius for your consideration, because from their deeds you will be able to adopt many things most usefully for imitation. May you reign for a very long time, so that God may always reign in you.

## LETTER XCIV. TO MARCWARD

To the most religious Father Marcward, Lupus sends greetings.

[Col. 0569A] If we prudently consider that, on account of original sin, we have been made exiles by God’s most just vengeance, we will not be surprised when adversity befalls us. For, driven away from our homeland of joy, we have been cast into the valley of tears. Rather, we ought piously to contemplate and praise God’s ineffable clemency, which does not abandon us even in anger and usually tempers sorrowful things with consolations, lest, overcome by grief, we fall into the abyss of despair.

Hence the rashness of certain people must be condemned: accustomed to the continual benefits of divine grace, when they are touched by some misfortune they increase their sins by complaining, although they ought to recognize, even without admonition, the debts of those sins. Yet it is credible that among the faithful there are some distinguished by the holiness they have received from God, whose merits rather than whose offenses are increased by adversity. For God did not bestow this gift upon blessed Job alone, whom he placed upon the citadel of patience for his servants to imitate. What conquered in him conquers in many, with whom he promises to remain until the end of the age.

If someone’s happiness were never disturbed by any upheaval, how dull he would be unless he feared that he might one day hear, together with the rich man clothed in purple: “You received your good things during your life” (Luke XVI). And how could that truthful sentence not terrify him: “They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld” (Job XXI)?

But whoever recalls with vigilant memory, “God scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII), if he is weighed down by illness, tested by the death of a relative, or struck by the diminution or loss of his possessions, how could he not be stirred to give thanks by affection toward a loving parent, whose care leads him to presume that he is deemed worthy of the privilege of correction? The sweetness of the future life would be sought less eagerly if the bitterness of the present were not felt more often.

Many are pleased with life as it is. Indeed, more people would be pleased if continual prosperity followed everyone’s desires. Therefore, who does not see that, through the incomprehensible piety of God, the troublesome instability of this life impels us by a certain movement to seize the unchanging life of the next? [The source repeats the phrase “impels us through the troublesome instability of this life”; the wording is uncertain.]

The Lord Jesus, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit will be our blessedness, instructs by his example those who adhered to his teaching to endure adversity: “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (John [Col. 0569D] XX), so that they would not despair of being loved by him when they were battered by various misfortunes, remembering that the Son, dearly beloved by the Father, had passed through the same things.

Nor did he conceal what awaited them: “In the world you will have tribulation; but take courage, I have overcome the world” (John XVI), so that they might know that they possessed in him the strength to overcome, since he was almighty.

The holy Apostle, in whom the Spirit of God evidently spoke, seeing his own times and foreseeing ours, says: “All who desire to live in Christ will suffer persecution” [Col. 0570A] (II Tim. III). By this persecution we understand that the devout suffer either from unclean spirits or from wicked people.

Yet whether God himself tests us or permits us to be tested, so that we may not succumb in womanly fear, he strengthens us elsewhere with these words:

“God is faithful, and he will not permit you to be tested beyond what you can bear; but with the testing he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure” (I Cor. X).

[143] Let us therefore not complain that anything unbearable has happened to us, since he who sets the contest before us, if we faithfully ask, supplies the opportunity to conquer. Let us therefore bless him at all times: he both invites us through prosperity and disciplines us through adversity. May his praise always be in our mouth, so that what, by his generosity, we shall do blessedly for ever and ever, we may already now practice with devotion.

I have endeavored to send these thoughts to your holiness, briefly gathered [Col. 0570B] for the sake of avoiding weariness and for your consolation. They will, I believe, be beneficial to you, since they were sought from the fountain of charity and flowed from that same fountain. I ask that you kindly remember me and that you prosper happily.

## EPISTLE XCV. TO HERIBOLD, On behalf of the queen

[Note: “To Heribold, bishop of Auxerre, who has been mentioned so often above.”]

In the name of the Lord alone and almighty. Irmindrudis, queen by the ordering of his grace, sends greetings to Heribold, venerable bishop.

Since prolonged illness denies us the welcome conversation of your holiness, we write to you in your absence what we would more gladly say in person. Your brother, deprived of his honors and especially distressed because of the men who served him, sought the aid of our compassion, trusting that, after God, through our efforts he would escape the distress of his calamity. We pity him with our customary gentleness and, with God providing the opportunity, wish to help him.

But so that he may await the fulfillment of our desire at court, we urge you not to be burdened by relieving his need with the things required. Since your generosity customarily supplies what outsiders request, you can likewise provide the same to a needy brother, not without hope of divine recompense. We would easily demonstrate this from the sacred writings, unless we believed that it readily occurred to you and that we had regard for both your person and ours.

Therefore, show the affection owed to religion and kinship, and, remembering us continually in your prayers, farewell.

## EPISTLE XCVI. TO KING CHARLES

To the glorious, most excellent lord, King Charles, Lupus, wholly faithful, sends greetings.

When I was departing from your majesty, you ordered me, as Lent was approaching, to send you something from which you might derive some fruit of edification. I therefore sent to your prudence a sermon of blessed Augustine in which he dissuades the habit of swearing and demonstrates how deadly perjury is [Note: “The habit of swearing.” He undoubtedly means Sermon 28, *On the Words of the Apostle*. Augustine nevertheless disputes in many places against those who swear on every occasion, and likewise against those who commit perjury. See Jonas of Orléans, Book II, *On the Instruction of Laymen*, chapter 25.], believing that it would greatly benefit you if, at your admonition, some people ceased swearing continually and did not despise an oath rightly sworn.

I do not say this to curry favor with you through flattery, but out of concern for the salvation of those who, together with us, invoke the Father in heaven. Whoever has confirmed his allegiance to you by oath, if he secretly withdraws from it, has already inflicted death upon his soul [Note: “The death of the soul.” He is speaking of those who had bound their allegiance by oath to King Charles the Bald but later changed it. Because of this crime Lupus says that they incurred the death of the soul—that is, were condemned to eternal death—unless they repent. Such is the gravity of violating an allegiance sworn to a prince! Our author is entirely in agreement with Atto, bishop of Vercelli, who flourished around the year 940. In his tenth letter, written to the bishops neighboring the diocese of Vercelli, he says: “I judge that the fidelity owed to our lords and kings must be fully observed in all things. For we cannot be found pure before the eyes of the divine majesty if we are in any respect unfaithful to them.” The distinguished Benedictine monk Lucas Dacherius, a man of great learning, shared this letter of Atto with me out of friendship; he will shortly publish it, along with many others by the same author. We discussed the punishment of bishops who violate the allegiance sworn to a prince in the letter to Agobard. See *Patrologia Latina*, volume CIV.]

and cannot be children of God, since they do not wish to be peacemakers. Let your diligence therefore warn them of their danger and invite them, through the most health-giving instruction of so great a teacher, to the remedy of correction.

I also sent your highness the gemstones that our craftsman had earlier received to carve and polish. If you approve their form and brilliance, I shall congratulate the craftsman. I wish and pray that you may always act well and, with God propitious, enjoy success and happiness for a very long time.

## EPISTLE XCVII. TO HILDUIN

To the most excellent abbot Hilduin [Note: Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis in the territory of Paris and archchaplain of the sacred palace], Lupus sends temporal and eternal salvation.

Remembering the custom of our companionship during your adolescence and the beginning of my youth, and considering that your nobility and integrity of character cannot in any way be changed by the flatteries of fortune, I write to you now as frankly as we spoke familiarly then.

Almighty God has preferred you above all others, as seems fitting to many people because of your purpose, in the distribution of wealth [Col. 0571C]; and without doubt, from the one to whom he has given so much, he will demand much in return. For he himself says: “Whoever glorifies me, I will glorify; but those who despise me will be held in low esteem” (I Kings II).

Therefore, do not regard what I am about to say as burdensome. Honor through fear and love the one who has so greatly honored you; and while good things abound for you in this world, take care to please continually the one who gave them to you. Do not let the transitory happiness of the world deceive you, while the perpetual blessedness of heaven is promised to you [Col. 0572A].

Practice justice wherever you can, and extend mercy to all whom you are able to help, because you do not know how long the one who granted you the ability to do good will permit you to possess it. His voice says: “Watch, because you do not know the day or the hour” (Matt. XXV).

We also, who love you uniquely and trust that through you we shall have some consolation, believe that you will possess the dignity for a considerable time [Note: “Duration.” From this we may infer that the office of archchaplain was customarily bestowed by the prince in such a way that it could be taken away at the prince’s pleasure. For this reason Lupus warns Hilduin that, since he cannot know how long this administration will last, he should use his time well, show himself just in rendering judgments, and nevertheless be merciful toward those who have deserved this favor. In this office he either personally handled all ecclesiastical and sacred affairs or discussed them with the king, to use Sirmond’s words. See also what we said about the office of archchaplain in the note to Epistle 37], if you devoutly submit yourself to the giver of all good things.

Until I may be worthy to see you, read or recall these words frequently, without weariness, so that just as we glory in your excellence, we may rejoice more certainly in your integrity.

I also ask that you receive honorably and treat kindly my kinsman, the abbot of your cell called Cor., who, as we believe, pleases God and, as is evident, all good people by his integrity. I trust that this will be sufficient, as befits your nobility, honorable learning, and increase of good reputation: deign always to advise him in every matter, and always as much as those who know what is good desire.

Farewell in the world and in the Lord.

## EPISTLE XCVIII. TO GUENILO AND HIS SUFFRAGANS

To the most reverend fathers and brothers: Guenilo, metropolitan bishop of the see of Sens; all his clergy; the prelates of the other churches counted within the diocese of the aforesaid see [Note: “Diocese,” that is, province, as we explained in the note to Epistle 84 and as is sufficiently well known. Of the countless testimonies that could be produced on this point, I shall give only one, from a charter of Charles the Bald for the monastery of Cuxa in the diocese of Elne, which we saw there in authentic form. The city of Elne, as I think no one can be unaware, was always a suffragan of the Church of Narbonne. Thus Charles the Bald says: “The aforesaid place is situated on the border of the march of Cerdanya, under the diocese of Fredaldus, archbishop of Narbonne, and the parish of Audesindus, bishop of Elne.”]; all who serve God in them; the clergy of the mother church of Paris [Note: “Mother church,” that is, the cathedral church of Paris, which is the mother of all the churches of Paris. Thus in ancient records the church of Elne is called the “Mother of all the Churches of Roussillon, Conflent, and Vallespir,” because the counties of Roussillon, Conflent, and Vallespir lie within the diocese of Elne]; and the community of the brothers of the monasteries of Saint-Denis, Saint-Germain, blessed Genevieve, and Fosses, and of various other monasteries—present and future salvation.

Although it has been widely reported that our venerable shepherd Ercanradus [Note: Ercanradus, bishop of Paris, who died in the year 853] has recently died, this could not have remained unknown to your holiness. Your wisdom understands both the grief that affects us at the calling away of our deceased father and the anxiety that moves us concerning the election of his successor.

Since the Lord Jesus promises principally to be with those who are leaders of religion [Note: “Leaders of religion,” that is, bishops. The Church consists in the bishops, as Cyprian says in Letter 69, adding that whoever is not with the bishop is not in the Church. Hence Jerome, Leo the Great, and others frequently call them “leaders of the Church,” which is equivalent to “leaders of religion”], we cannot long remain without a bishop whose teaching may instruct us for salvation [Note: “Whose teaching.” For it is the bishop’s duty to teach the people subject to him, as we said in the note to Epistle 79] and whose example may form us [Note: “By example.” A bishop owes the peoples entrusted to him not only sound teaching but also a good example of life, as was stated above in the notes to Epistle 79. As Arnulfus, bishop of Lisieux, said in a sermon delivered at the Council of Tours: “The holiness of one’s conduct is examined; for unless the preacher’s life is commendable, his preaching will not be gracious. When a person’s life is despised, his preaching too will necessarily be despised.” Hincmarus says that this was taken from blessed Gregory in chapter 36 of the later work against Gottschalk; Atto, bishop of Vercelli, likewise teaches it in his eighth letter, addressed to the priests and ministers residing in the diocese of Vercelli. Both things, therefore, are necessary. Would that it never happen—although we read that it has often happened—that bishops so unworthy of their dignity are established in the Church that they can benefit neither their peoples nor themselves: men so careless of their own affairs that they do not even know what account they will have to render to Christ, the supreme Shepherd, or what they owe to the sheep entrusted to their governance], fortified by blessings in the name of the Lord.

We firmly believe that, as the author of all good things, he will never leave us without his care, since he himself, in his mercy, has removed our anxieties and anticipated our wishes through his spontaneous kindness. For he, in whose hand is the heart of the king, has, as we fully trust, infused into the mind of our glorious lord Charles the desire to commit us to the governance of Aeneas [Note: “Commit us.” From this it may be inferred that princes at that time customarily appointed bishops to vacant churches on their own authority, as we said in the note to Epistle 81, even without awaiting the request of the clergy and people; afterward, however, an election was required, by which the clergy testified to their consent. We have noted that the same practice prevailed in the appointment of abbots, in the note to Epistle 40], a man whom he had proved through many experiences to be most faithful to him in divine and human affairs.

Therefore, embracing God’s ready mercy toward us and reverently considering the pious providence of our king, we all unanimously elect Aeneas, whose praises we have already proclaimed [Note: “Aeneas.” A man of great renown in those times, also distinguished by published scholarly works. An old manuscript codex exists in the Thuane Library containing a work by this Aeneas, bishop of Paris, against the Greeks. It was published through the efforts of Dom Lucas Dacherius, a Benedictine monk], and desire to have Aeneas as father and Aeneas as bishop.

Although our most excellent king possesses such wisdom and integrity that his judgment alone concerning this man could suffice, nevertheless, mindful of human nature and concerned about the future, we ourselves examined the character and conduct of the courtier long beforehand. Among serious and reputable men, fervent in holiness, all of us who were able to know him have, as is now evident, counted without error this man whom we desire to have as bishop.

Therefore, holy fathers, strive lest we be tormented by delay in the divine and royal benefaction [Note: “Divine and royal benefaction.” Here they join the divine benefit with the royal one in the election of Aeneas, which had been made by the prince. From this it may be inferred that the Franks of that time believed that the king, acting in God’s place, appointed bishops. See the notes to Epistle 29]. While we remain in suspense, while we desire and plead, let the lamp quickly be placed upon the lampstand [Col. 0573C], so that the people of God may see the light of truth and, following the bishop’s footsteps with rival devotion, prepare themselves for eternal blessedness.

With God’s consent, we have strengthened by our signatures the declaration of our agreement concerning Aeneas, who is to be our future bishop, through your ministry [Col. 0574A], each of us eagerly subscribing, so that, once you have learned of our unanimity, you may fulfill our wish with the greatest haste.

## EPISTLE XCIX. THE BISHOPS’ REPLY TO THEM

Guenilo, metropolitan bishop of the holy see of Sens; Heriboldus, bishop of Auxerre [Note: “Heriboldus.” It is clear that in those times there was no bishop of Auxerre named Heribertus. We have therefore removed that name here and substituted Heriboldus, who is frequently mentioned both in these letters and elsewhere. In this we follow the correction of the great and truthful Jacob Sirmond]; Agius of Orléans; Prudentius of Troyes; Herimannus of Nevers; Frotbaldus of Chartres; Hildegarius of Meaux—to the clergy of the mother church of Paris and to all who serve God under it in the various monasteries, greetings.

We are greatly distressed by the death of our most reverend fellow bishop Ercanradus and share in your grief. Yet, remembering God’s most just dispensation, we receive consolation when we learn from your letter that you, living under the good shepherd, who is supremely good [Note: “The good shepherd,” that is, Christ, who is called the good shepherd in the sacred books of Christians], seek without delay his visible vicar [Note: “His vicar,” that is, Christ’s. He therefore calls Aeneas, bishop of Paris, Christ’s visible vicar], the companion of our ministry, as your lines of reason make clear.

We believe that a good outcome has been prepared for him by God, through whose gift we see such an entrance lying open. Although our future colleague was formerly known to us and was made dear by the merit of his integrity, who has even lightly entered the palace [Note: “Touched the palace,” that is, “spent time at the prince’s court”] without becoming acquainted with Aeneas’s labor and observing his fervor in divine matters?

Therefore, with God’s favor, we gladly approve your election of him, unanimously decreeing that he be advanced to the dignity of the episcopate, since he will benefit God’s people. Let him therefore be your shepherd, one who has pleased God well through his merits. Following his true teaching and imitating his holy works, hasten happily toward the pastures of the heavenly kingdom.

We have all subscribed unanimously to his ordination, so that you may securely enjoy the ministry of his authority.

## EPISTLE C. AN ADMONITION

[Col. 0575A]

Afflicted by various evils, we ought to recognize the cause of those evils and, with the help of God’s mercy, avoid it once recognized. The Holy Spirit plainly reveals the cause of prosperity and adversity in these words: “Justice exalts a nation, but sin makes peoples miserable” (Prov. XIV).

The sin by which we are made miserable is, it is believable, this: although we are Christians by faith, we destroy our profession by our deeds [Note: “We destroy by our deeds.” Thus Salvianus says in Book IV of *The Government of God*: “From this one fact it can be understood what crime Christians are guilty of: they dishonor the name of God. Although it is written that we should do everything for the glory of God, we instead do everything to God’s injury.” A little later he says: “They read the Gospels and are immoral; they hear the Apostles and become drunk; they follow Christ and commit robbery; they live wickedly and claim to possess a righteous law.”].

And because we prefer temporal happiness to eternal blessedness, we lose the latter unless we repent, and we do not attain the former—which, however small it might be, we could possess if we wished to be upright. Since, therefore, God’s vengeance begins temporally in this life and extends, unless conversion comes to our aid, into the next life, which has no end; and since temporal goods often accompany the good here, while elsewhere eternal goods crown those same good people, whether rulers or subjects, let us all set aside our excuses.

Each of us is conscious of the ways in which he most seriously offends God. Let us therefore listen together and obediently to him who warns us: “Return, transgressors, to your heart” (Isa. XLVI). And again: “Wash yourselves, be clean; remove the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes; cease to act perversely; learn to do good” (Isa. I). Thus, through the saving course of repentance, we may reach the safest harbor of forgiveness.

In this way we shall be able not only to escape present evils but also to hope for future goods. Let us unlearn the practice of desiring only carnal things. Let us sometimes think about attaining spiritual things; and, so that our desires may be restrained and kept within some measure, let us remember how swiftly those whom we have seen in positions of dignity pass away, and let us not forget that we follow them daily. For we are hastening without interruption toward death.

Let us recall the customs by which this kingdom grew and flourished [Note: “This kingdom.” The kingdom of the Franks—not as it existed under Charles the Bald, but under Charles the Great. The latter greatly enlarged the Frankish kingdom by adding Italy, Tarraconian Spain, and the peoples whom he and his successors ruled in Germany. All this was called the Kingdom of the Franks. Yet it was not retained with the same virtues by which it had been acquired. Thus under Charles the Bald the single Frankish kingdom became three Frankish kingdoms, divided among the sons of Louis the Pious, each of whom was called king of the Franks. Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, bitterly laments this in his *Chronicle*, believing that it caused barbarian nations to invade the Frankish kingdom].

Let there be no factions, no conspiracies among us who invoke God as Father—among us to whom bishops say, “Peace be with you”; for whom all priests pray unanimously, “In your mercy, grant peace in our days,” and, “May the peace of the Lord be always with you”; and to whom he deigns to promise: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” [Col. 0576A] (Matt. V).

Let his threat not appear contemptible to us: “Woe to the one through whom scandal comes” (Matt. XVIII), lest perhaps—God avert it—“only affliction should eventually give understanding to those who hear” (Isa. XXVIII), so that, placed in torments, we may learn through unhappy experience what we now do not believe or pretend not to know.

Let us completely abandon plunder and robbery, which are utterly opposed to Christian conduct and most wretchedly exclude people from the kingdom of God. Against such people the apostolic word thunders: “Nor will the rapacious possess the kingdom” (I Cor. VI).

For fear and love of God, let us set aside our private profits and, eagerly and unanimously, care for the common and public good. Thus, while we strive to provide tranquility for the faithful and recover the strength to resist unbelievers, we may receive from him who is almighty the joys of both kinds of peace: the peace that is possible now and that consummate peace which will be granted only to the elect.

Let none of us fail to remember what the most learned people, down to our own age, have proved and believed: “Through concord small things grow; through discord even the greatest things fall apart” [Note: “Through concord.” This is taken from Sallust in his history of the Jugurthine War: “Through concord,” he says, “small things grow; through discord the greatest things fall apart.” The author of *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 18, says: “Thus senate and people, like one body, perish through discord and flourish through concord.” There is also the saying from the sacred writings: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste.” This passage properly applies to Lupus’s admonition, by which he urges Charles the Bald toward concord].

Otherwise, while we desire to hold our own possessions more securely or climb more successfully to greater things, the ruin of the kingdom—which we are preparing through our dissensions—may, by God’s just judgment, overwhelm us and drag us into the destruction of soul and body.

## EPISTLE CI. TO THE BISHOPS, On the reception of pilgrims, on behalf of Guenilo

To the most reverend prelates of Italy and Gaul and to the other faithful of God, Guenilo, metropolitan bishop of Sens, sends greetings in the Lord.

Whenever a just cause arises for addressing your holiness, the charity poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us, grants us the confidence to do so—especially when the matter concerns the advancement of a gratuitous work of piety.

Two monks of our province and diocese, from the monastery called Bethlehem or Ferrières, named Aldulphus and Acaricus and ordained to the priesthood, have determined, as we believe through divine inspiration, to travel to Rome out of a desire to pray. With the consent of ourselves and of their abbot, our most beloved Lupus, they are carrying out their purpose.

As is customary, we commend them to your fatherly care, asking that, since they have undertaken the labor of pilgrimage for eternal reward, they may find in you, both on their journey there and on their return, the consolation with which devout travelers are supported by religious men. You will share in their reward if you willingly assist their labor. We desire that you prosper happily.

## EPISTLE CII. ALSO ON BEHALF OF THE ABBOT

To the bishops of Italy and Gaul, worthy of the greatest veneration, and to all others who possess the Christian religion, Lupus, abbot of the monastery called Bethlehem or Ferrières, situated in the diocese of the city of Sens, over which the most reverend Guenilo presides, sends present and future salvation.

Although the world is declining toward its sunset, I do not doubt that charity burns in the hearts of the elect—a charity rightly called the “broad commandment” in the sacred writings (Ps. CXVIII). Therefore, I am not ashamed to ask something of those to whom I have rendered no service or whom I have never seen face to face.

Through that charity so customary among good people, God, who causes us to dwell together in unity, has established that changing transitory things into eternal goods is the greatest profit. Accordingly, I commend to your holy fatherhood two monks and priests, one named Aldulphus and the other Acaricus, who have decided to set out from our community to Rome to offer prayers, with the permission of the aforementioned bishop [Note: “The aforementioned bishop,” that is, Guenilo, archbishop of Sens].

They are fulfilling what they desired with the permission of the aforementioned bishop and of ourselves. Therefore, may your benevolence deign to provide assistance to them both on their outward journey and on their return. They were unable to carry sufficient provisions for so long a journey, and we believe that you will share in their reward if they experience you as fellow workers in their labor undertaken for God’s name.

[Note: “The aforementioned bishop,” that is, Guenilo, archbishop of Sens. From this letter and the preceding one we learn that monks were then not permitted—even to go to Rome—to travel to a distant region without their own bishop’s permission, as Canon 23 of Chalcedon had also forbidden. Book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 25, commands monks “not to leave their own monasteries, unless perhaps the bishop of the city orders them to do so for a necessary task.” For it is not beneficial to their souls for them to wander abroad, as is written in chapter 78 of the same book. Likewise, Book VI of the *Capitularies*, chapter 130: “Clerics or monks are not permitted to wander about without letters of recommendation and the permission of their bishop.” This law continued down to the time of Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux. In Letter 53 he reproves the abbot of Gristan because, “disregarding the authority of the episcopal command—indeed, setting aside your own salvation and that of the souls entrusted to you—you departed without our knowledge.” He therefore ordered him to return as quickly as possible from England, whither he had gone; compelled by the necessity of the episcopal edict, he was brought back, as Arnulf himself says in Letter 43. The abbot of Gristan was thus not permitted to leave his monastery without the knowledge of his own bishop, even if he wished to go to England in the king’s retinue.

A famous statement is that of Anselm, abbot of Bec in Normandy. As Eadmer relates in Book I of the *History of Recent Events*, when Anselm had been elected to the see of Canterbury, he denied that the election was valid until he himself had been released from the care of his monastery by authority of the archbishop of Rouen. “I am,” he said, “abbot of a monastery in another realm; I have an archbishop to whom I owe obedience, an earthly prince to whom I owe subjection, and monks to whom I owe the supply of counsel and assistance. I am bound to all these in such a way that I can neither abandon the monks without their consent, nor free myself from the dominion of my prince without his permission, nor evade obedience to my bishop, consistently with the salvation of my soul, without his release.” Likewise, when the Church of Rouen, vacant of a shepherd, elected Hugh, abbot of Reading, the election was not confirmed until the bishop of Salisbury, under whose authority Abbot Hugh stood, had granted him permission to leave his monastery. Thus the Church of Rouen writes to Pope Honorius II in volume III of the *Spicilegium*, p. 152: “We sought that he be rendered free and released to us by the bishop of Salisbury, under whose hand he discharged the office of abbot; and we received him with that freedom.”

Alcuin provided an earlier example. Although Charlemagne pressed him hard to remain in Gaul, even offering riches, he replied that this could not be done without the consent of his bishop, as is stated in his life written by a contemporary author. The same rule applied to nuns, as is clear from the letter of Lull, archbishop of Mainz, who succeeded Boniface, to the abbess Oswitha. In it he complains that she had “permitted two nuns to go freely into a distant region without the knowledge and counsel of Lull.” He therefore forbids these “wandering and disobedient women” to be received within the monastery. This letter of Lull survives among the letters of Boniface, no. 47. Thus Lupus does not repeatedly state without reason that his monks had been granted leave by Wenilo to go to the thresholds of the Apostles. For he saw that they would incur the disrepute of wandering monks if they set out without letters from their bishop. Indeed, at the Synod of Ver it had been decreed that those monks openly dishonor the profession of holy religion who wander about for the sake of gain.]

## EPISTLE CIII. TO THE APOSTOLIC LORD

[Note: “The apostolic lord.” Benedict III, according to Masson’s edition, as is clear from the context of the letter. The manuscript codex contained only the words “To the apostolic lord.” Benedict III occupied the see from the year 855. Masson published this letter in a more corrected form in his book on the bishops of Rome.]

To the most excellent lord and uniquely and singularly venerable among all Christians, the universal pope Benedict [Note: “Universal pope.” Thus at that time they called the Roman bishop, evidently because primacy had been granted to him throughout the whole world, as Lupus says in Epistle 84 to Nomenoius], Lupus, the least of the abbots, from the monastery of Gaul called Bethlehem or Ferrières, sends present prosperity and future blessedness.

[Col. 0578B] During the time of your predecessor, of blessed memory, Leo [Note: [Col. 0578D] Leo. Leo IV, of this name, whose homily to priests survives; concerning it, see our notes to Regino, pp. 531, 534, 602.], who had served as envoy at Rome, over which you preside by God’s will, and had been kindly received and treated by that same bishop—after reputation had declared that you were not inferior in religious devotion, and a careful consideration of your conduct had clearly shown that you were heirs not only of the most blessed Peter’s authority but also of his humility, which he made known in his address to Cornelius—I, so insignificant, dared to intrude myself by writing upon your exalted awareness, and to entrust my littleness and the unanimity of my fellow monks to your excellence [Col. 0579A], so that in your holy prayers we might deserve by God’s favor to obtain consolation in the present life and, in the future, a blessed share in salvation.

Moreover, we especially commend to your gentleness our brothers and fellow priests Aldulphus and Acaricus, who have undertaken a voluntary pilgrimage in the Lord’s name and, although with the greatest hardship, have at last reached the memorials of the most blessed apostles and the other saints. May you deign to support them with fitting kindness and carefully instruct them in the ecclesiastical customs that are observed differently in different places, so that through them Roman practice may reach us and all others who piously seek such things. For whenever variety creates uncertainty in matters pertaining to religion or morality [Col. 0579B], we believe that, if the best practices are to shine forth, one must return by diligent inquiry to the place from which the beginning of the faith spread everywhere [Note: [Col. 0579D] The beginning of the faith. Lupus was referring to Pope Innocent I’s letter to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio, in which the following is written: “Especially since it is clear that throughout Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, and Sicily, and the intervening islands, no one founded churches except those whom the venerable apostle Peter or his successors appointed as priests. Let them read whether in those provinces another of the apostles is found or is said to have taught. If they do not read it, because they find it nowhere, they ought to follow what the Roman Church observes, since there is no doubt that they received their beginning from it; lest, while they devote themselves to foreign assertions, they appear to omit the source of their institutions.”].

Furthermore, since parents ought to store up for their children (2 Cor. XII), as the apostle to the Gentiles makes clear, and we wish to be your most obedient sons, we ask that through the same brothers you send us, in a manuscript of venerable accuracy, Jerome’s commentaries on Jeremiah from the sixth book to the end of the prophet in question. If we obtain this, we shall without doubt return it to your holiness promptly, once it has been rapidly copied. For in our regions no copy of the commentary after the sixth book has anywhere been found; and we wish to recover in you whatever we feel is lacking to our small resources.

We also ask for Cicero’s *De Oratore* and Quintilian’s twelve books of the *Institutio Oratoria*, which are contained in a single, not very large volume. We possess parts of the works of both authors, but through you we desire to obtain their complete texts. With the same purpose we request Donatus’s commentary on Terence. If your generosity grants us these works of the authors, with God’s favor we shall take care to return them all faithfully together with the aforesaid manuscript of Saint Jerome.

May divine mercy deign to preserve your holiness for the enduring benefit of the whole Church [Col. 0579D] for many years [Note: [Col. 0579D] May he deign to preserve. Thus Rabanus, not yet archbishop, wrote to Archbishop Haistulfus, saying at the end of his letter: “May the grace of the heavenly protector deign to preserve your holy fatherhood as you pray for us, and always strengthen you for the defense of his holy Church.”].

## 156. LETTER CIV. TO REGINB.

Lupus to his dearest Reg., greetings in the Lord.

[Col. 0579D] We certainly desire your arrival, as is fitting, which your recent letter has already promised; but [Col. 0580A] we urge you, with the utmost vigilance, to choose a safe route, because, now that new disturbances have arisen in the kingdom of our king Charles, robberies are being committed with impunity, and nothing is practiced more safely or consistently than violent plunder. You must therefore seek the company of travelers whose numbers and courage will enable you to avoid the criminals’ faction or, if necessary, repel it.

Please bring us Sallust’s *Catiline* and *Jugurtha*, the books of the *Verrines*, and any other works that you discover we possess either in corrupt form or not at all, so that through your kindness defective texts may be corrected and works we do not possess—and could obtain only through you—may be acquired, all the more gratefully because they were unexpected. I wish you every happiness.

## LETTER CV. TO MARCWARDUS AND [Note: [Col. 0580D] And Eigil. This was added from an old manuscript. It is clear from the context of the letter, which was also written to Eigil, that it ought indeed to have been added. We stated above, in the note to Letter 55, that this Eigil was abbot of Prüm after Marcwardus.] EIGIL.

[Col. 0580B]

Lupus sends abundant greetings to his dearest Marcwardus and Eigil.

On the eighth day before the Ides of August I received your letter, while I was at the monastery of Farae [Note: [Col. 0580D] At Farae. Masson’s edition had *Fana*, very incorrectly. We have therefore followed the authority of the manuscript. We have spoken above in the notes to Letter 14 about the monastery of Farae.], setting out for the general assembly that our king had ordered to take place on the sixth day before the Ides of the aforesaid month [157]. Since, therefore, I had only four brothers with me, could not fully know the wishes of the others, and an extraordinary matter had occurred—namely, that G., who had been brought up in our monastery and had constantly heard divine admonition, had suffered no persecution and, at a mature age, had not sought the desert but, abandoning his proper habit, had departed to obtain secular dignity, something he had long contemplated and confessed to many, preparing a happy journey for others who would do likewise, and that now, at your urging, he was reported by you to wish to return to God after changing his purpose—I inform your holiness that, if his genuine conversion takes place, I shall rejoice greatly and shall wholeheartedly forgive him for whatever he has committed against me in repentance.

While I am returning from the assembly, earnestly strive to complete what you began for God’s sake: namely, that he return wholly to God and not attempt thereafter to transfer his guilt to another. Let him pursue moderation; let him not resume conspiracies; let him be neither the author nor a participant in murmuring; let him neither create nor encourage seditions, but let him himself possess peace and permit others to possess it. In general, according to God’s command, let him turn away from evil and do good [Col. 0580D] (1 Pet. III), and in our days let him suffer nothing in our community for which he may justly be reproached.

As soon as I return, with God’s favor I shall strive to persuade the brothers to obey your urging, and we shall communicate their agreement to your holiness by letter and take care to satisfy the emperor [Note: [Col. 0581D] The emperor. Lothair, son of Louis the Pious. The monastery of Prüm was situated in his kingdom and was then governed by Marcwardus.], to whom, because of his exceptional and universally renowned piety, we are most devoted, with a fitting reply. We wish your holiness to remember us kindly and to prosper exceedingly, our uniquely and singularly beloved fathers [158].

## LETTER CVI. ON THE RECEPTION OF PILGRIMS

Guenilo, metropolitan bishop of Sens, sends greetings to all the faithful of almighty God.

A certain monk of our diocese, named Dolivaldus, from the monastery called Ferrariae, has undertaken, by divine inspiration, as we believe—for he is exceedingly religious—the labor of pilgrimage, in order to implore God’s mercy for himself, for his fellow monks, and for us before the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul and the other saints of God, and to obtain through their prayers what he could not obtain by his own.

We commend him to your charity, entreating you, for the love of God, to receive, treat, and send him on his way as his servant, whether he is going or returning. For wherever he finds his religion—that is, Christianity—he ought to recognize his own homeland; and you should make this man, too, a friend among those who will receive you into the eternal dwellings.

## LETTER CVII. ALSO TO THE SAME PERSONS AS ABOVE

[Col. 0581C]

To the most reverend lords, distinguished by Christian religion, Lupus, abbot of the Gallic monastery called Bethlehem or Ferrariae [159], sends abundant greetings.

Our monk, whose name is Dolivaldus, a man of great simplicity and praiseworthy devotion, inflamed, as we firmly believe, by the Spirit of God, is setting out for Rome with the blessing of our venerable bishop Guenilo and myself, to pray to God and the holy apostles Peter and Paul for himself and for us. The greater the labor he has undertaken, the more confidently he trusts that he will be heard.

We commend him to your holiness, bearing witness to his goodness. Do not hesitate to provide him with whatever ought to be provided to any good person in need; for although he is unlearned, he demonstrates in his conduct the commandments of God that he has not read in a book, and he quickly deserves not only the love but also the reverence of all among whom he lives.

Therefore, we ask you to deign to treat him, whether going or returning, in such a way that from the one whose true worshiper he is you may confidently expect an everlasting reward.

## LETTER CVIII. [Col. 0582A] TO LORD LOTHAIR

To the most excellent lord Lothair, glorious Augustus, Lupus, the least of abbots, and the entire community of the monastery of Ferrariae send present prosperity and future blessedness.

Although the fact that, amid the administration of an earthly kingdom, you think about acquiring heavenly things gives those who sincerely love you great hope for your salvation—that you are winning an everlasting reward through good works—it nevertheless gives them the greatest joy that, without the pretense of flattery, we may simply say what we feel: you adorn the authority of your high office with a piety most pleasing to God and to human beings [160].

By persevering in this piety, you will be numbered among those to whom the Savior deigns to promise, “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V).

We, your most devoted servants, give special thanks to your majesty because you recalled our brother G. from the purpose he had abandoned—“brother” because we have heard that he has been converted—and brought him back to our community with remarkable condescension and even through an intercession that properly possesses the force of a command [Note: [Col. 0581D] Which properly possesses the force of a command. Ausonius writes in the *Parecbasis of the Cento Nuptialis*: “And what is the most powerful form of command? The emperor Valentinianus, who could command, was asking.” Tacitus writes in Book IV of the *Histories*: “They were petitions, but petitions that could not be refused.”].

Therefore, after God, we must attribute his correction to you, and he must attribute his salvation to you. For what your sacred documents [Note: [Col. 0582D] Your sacred documents. That is, your letters, your command, or your official diploma.] indicated—namely, that after resuming his habit he should continue in the office of composing letters—was neither appropriate for you nor possible for us to accept, because our purpose is scarcely maintained even moderately within the cloister of the monastery, much less can it be fulfilled amid the tumult of the world by anyone, especially one insufficiently cautious.

May our Lord and Savior preserve you in lasting health throughout this life, for the protection and peace of the Christian people whom he redeemed, and crown you with everlasting glory in the life to come.

## LETTER CIX. TO MARCWARDUS AND EIGIL

Lupus and the entire community of the monastery of Ferrariae send present and future salvation to their dearest Marcwardus and Eigil.

At last, after I had returned to the monastery from the assembly, and your diligent efforts concerning G.’s conversion had been explained to the brothers, all those capable of understanding such matters offered your holiness the thanks you deserved. They congratulated him because they heard that the recklessness leading to certain destruction had been laid aside and the pursuit of obtaining salvation resumed.

Let him therefore return confidently, if he is converted from the heart, as we hope; for if the angels, entirely free from sin, have joy at this, it would be cruel for us, who all offend in many ways, not to rejoice. Indeed, whatever the occasion by which someone returns to God, we are taught that we ought to rejoice by that extravagant son who was received through his father’s mercy; in the presence of that same father, poverty was not held as a reproach, since the dignity freely restored to him abolished it [Note: [Col. 0583B] Poverty as a reproach. Yet today, what person is there who remembers that a friend reduced from wealth to poverty was once among his closest companions? Even Agrippina, the mother of the emperor Nero, was abandoned by the crowd of visitors after Nero removed the military guards and German bodyguards and transferred her to a house that had belonged to Antonia. But if someone whose table had previously been meager becomes wealthy, then he first gradually avoids meetings with his old friend and finally grows disgusted with him. Our Muretus rightly notes in Book II, chapter IV of his *Various Readings*, that it is difficult and arduous to find a relative of a poor man. Arnulphus, bishop of Lisieux, therefore wisely warned Robert, bishop of Lincoln, to beware of setting an example in himself that could confirm the old saying, “Honors change character.” For he says in his second letter: “A new conscience of dignity creates a new heart and new affections; and those who have become rich grow disgusted with the friends of poverty together with poverty itself, lest anything of their former want appear to remain among them. They honor and love only those whom fortune recommends.” See our notes to Salvian’s second letter.

Yet I must bear witness to the truth, so that our age may know that it possessed a man whom it could compare with the ancients. Without doubt Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, was a great man and had reached such a degree of dignity that nothing more could be desired in the Gallican Church. Yet amid this glory of honors and riches he always retained modesty of spirit. I was with him for six full years, and through such long experience I learned how familiarly he received men of every rank and how courteously he dealt with everyone.

Athanasius, a rhetorician and priest from Constantinople, often visited him—a learned and educated man in other respects, but ragged and poor. Marca nevertheless did not consider him contemptible, since in addition to a good mind and extensive knowledge of sacred matters and of divine and human philosophy, he possessed a modesty truly worthy of a Christian and blameless conduct. Marca would seat this ragged man beside him in conversation; whenever he invited him to dinner, he had him sit at his side, even above certain others who were dressed in soft clothing and perhaps thought Athanasius inferior to them by many parasangs. See Freinshemius’s commentary on Curtius, Book IV, chapter 1, on the passage “The cause of poverty is integrity.”].

We have sent letters to the lord emperor for you to read and to present honorably to him, sealed with his majesty’s seal, so that you might see our purpose expressed correctly in them as well.

We wish Folchricus and Maur. to return with the brother mentioned above, so that they may enjoy with us the pear-drink [Note: [Col. 0584B] *Piractio*. I believe he means a drink made from pears, intended to take the place of wine, which was expected to be exceptionally scarce that year.] they especially enjoy—for there is fear of a shortage of wine this year. Yet the scarcity of fruit threatens that even this will be unavailable, to speak truthfully, while the poor harvest threatens beer.

We shall therefore all use the safe natural drink by which the health of soul and body is sometimes obtained—not drinking from a muddy cistern, but from the clarity of a well or the flow of a glasslike stream. We wish you every happiness and ask you kindly to remember our littleness in all things.

## 162. LETTER CX. [Note: [Col. 0584B] To Hilduin. Abbot of the monastery of Saint-Denis, who was also archchaplain of the sacred palace under Louis the Pious.] TO HILDUIN

Lupus sends present and future prosperity to the distinguished Hilduin, outstanding in the summit of nobility, dignity, and moderation [Note: [Col. 0584B] At the summit of dignity. Since he was archchaplain, the summit of all palatine dignities, and for that reason was everywhere preferred even to metropolitans, including at synods. Since the cases of all those in the clergy belonged to him, as to the official responsible for ecclesiastical affairs—for Hincmarus calls the archchaplain this—Lupus therefore calls Hilduin “master of ecclesiastical affairs.” For the same reason Hilduin is said to have been appointed by God over sacred matters in the letter of the Church of Sens written to him concerning the election of Jeremiah as archbishop. Frotarius, bishop of Toul, likewise calls him the father and teacher chosen by God. Thus in the empire of Constantinople the *chartophylax* of Constantinople, although only a deacon, sat before bishops or pontiffs, as Balsamon teaches in his commentary on canon 18 of Nicaea and canon 7 of the Council in Trullo.], master of ecclesiastical affairs.

It is not surprising that your greatness thought it safe to entrust us with the custody of your treasure, since the location of the monastery was unknown to you. If you had known it, you would have sent the treasure to us not merely with the expectation that it would be kept for a long time, but not even for the space of three days.

For although access here appears difficult for pirates [Note: [Col. 0584C] Pirates. That is, the Normans, who were then disastrously ravaging Gaul. He calls them pirates because they first reached Gaul by ship. Fearing them, Hilduin had ordered the treasure of his monastery—that is, the sacred relics of the saints and precious furnishings—to be transferred to the monastery of Ferrariae, which he considered a safe place against the Normans, since it lay inland and was therefore, as it were, inaccessible to pirates. Similarly, the inhabitants of the region of Coutances in Neustria, fearing the Normans, first transferred the relics of Saint Laud, once their bishop, to Rouen and then to the city of Angers. When the Normans reached there as well, the relics were finally taken to the monastery of Tulle in Limousin, where they are still preserved with the greatest veneration. We discussed this more fully long ago in our dissertation on Saints Clarus, Laudus, Ulfardus, and Baumadus, whose sacred relics are preserved in the cathedral church of Tulle.], for whom, because our sins deserve such things, nothing distant is not near and nothing difficult is inaccessible, nevertheless the weakness of our site and the small number of men capable of resisting inflame the greed of the plunderers. They can swoop down under cover of the woods, with no fortification and no concentration of people to stop them, and, sheltered by the nearby thickets, scatter in different directions in such a way that they themselves secure the money while leaving those who search for them with empty labor.

Your men recently inspected the situation and found it to be so [Col. 0584B]; and Ivo [Note: [Col. 0584D] Ivo. Perhaps a subdeacon and monk of Saint-Denis, mentioned in Volume IV of the *Spicilegium*, p. 231.], who lived among us for a long time, will be able to confirm it.

Therefore, let your prudence—rightly praised and deserving of praise—look to our fear and to your property, and arrange for the precious objects to be transferred elsewhere. Otherwise, if what we fear occurs, you will be tormented by late repentance, while we shall incur an offense we do not deserve. I wish your excellence every happiness.

## 163. LETTER CXI. [Note: [Col. 0585C] To Odo, abbot of Corbie, who attended the Council of Soissons with Lupus in 833 and later became bishop of Beauvais. Letter 127 of Lupus survives addressed to him when he was already bishop.] TO ODO, ABBOT

Lupus sends abundant greetings to his dearest Odo, distinguished among abbots.

Overwhelmed by the great and innumerable benefits of your generosity, if I attempted to express in words the thanks I hold in my heart, I would exceed not merely the limits of a letter but even those of a whole volume. Your greatness did not despise our littleness but relieved our poverty with extraordinary abundance; nor did it disdain to raise me, who hardly dared imagine such a thing and was utterly unequal to it, to equality through a most faithful friendship.

Enjoying the sweetest fruits of that friendship, although I lack the means to repay it, I do not cease anxiously to consider at least how I might reveal the feeling of my heart. Among all the friends whom divine kindness has granted me since my earliest years, I regard you most firmly as the foremost; I feel myself indebted to no one else as I do to your favor and most generous kindness.

Indeed, whenever I recall these things, I can scarcely avoid the distress of shame. Yet, exhausted, I find one singular consolation: that divine grace, which has raised me, deserving none of this, to so great a height of fellowship, will ensure that I do not remain ashamed forever.

Please do not think that I am deceiving you with flattering fictions, since matters that I touch upon lightly are so serious to me that my speech struggles to express them worthily.

Moreover, would that false rumor had reported that some of your men had been gravely wounded in the campaign against certain barbarians, among them G., greatly beloved by us, pierced with deadly wounds and scarcely likely to survive [164] [Col. 0585C]. Afflicted by this with intense grief, and continuing with my brothers to seek the help of intercession, I wish to be informed promptly by your letters of their condition.

I am also deeply anxious about you when I remember that you are accustomed, unarmed and incautiously, to rush into the midst of danger, into which the eagerness to conquer carries youthful agility. I therefore advise you with benevolent devotion to be content with the command alone, which is all that suits your purpose, and to allow armed men to carry out what they profess with the instruments of war.

Finally, a person makes great progress when he prudently looks after himself and others. Therefore preserve yourselves for your own place, preserve yourselves for your friends, preserve yourselves for all good people, and do not do anything that would cause many, including me, to mourn.

We postponed the purchase of iron, which was extremely difficult because of the harvest, and are ready to receive you on the ship we are building, unless you refuse to take away the freight charge. Send us, at the beginning of September—or earlier, if that is more convenient—brothers who will assign a portion of the woodland to us as we have agreed.

Let them also bring the unfortunate Faustus [Note: [Col. 0585D] The unfortunate Faustus. The bishop of Riez in the second Narbonnese province, as is clear from the following letter.], and faithfully report the answers to everything you will have commanded.

I sent the peaches I promised through the courier, whom you already know well. If, as I fear, he has devoured them, or complains that they were taken from him by force, use entreaties to extract from him at least the pits—unless he has consumed those too—so that you may at some time share in these most delightful peaches.

## 165. LETTER CXII. ALSO TO THE SAME PERSON

[Col. 0586B]

Lupus sends everlasting salvation to his dearest Odo.

If I could have divined that the letter recently delivered to me had been composed by you yourself rather than by another, I might perhaps have found an appropriate reply. Now, frightened by uncertainty, I anxiously search for the words and sentences I can use, lest I exceed the limits of moderation in addressing you, since I must constantly take special account of your person.

Who, after all, would judge me bearable if I accused you—though I owe you not merely thanks but almost everything—of a sinister suspicion? For if I knew another to be the author of the letter, I would, restraining my grief, demand to be taught by what manner the pursuit of fidelity could command its disclosure, since he had so shamelessly made suspect letters written, so to speak, with a pen dipped in truth.

I have never spoken to anyone about human affairs with greater truth; I have revealed nothing more purely to a friend; I have resolved to retain nothing more steadfastly. In other matters I readily admit amusing things, either for exercise or for pleasure. But in the profession of friendship, considering so great and so divine a gift, I embrace only serious matters.

For this reason I would have approved some witty invention concerning the number of peaches, if the exaltation of virginity [Note: [Col. 0585D] The exaltation of virginity. He is criticizing those who elevate virginity to such a height that they condemn marriage as well. Jerome was excessive on this subject and harsh even toward a single marriage. There were also people who condemned legitimate marital unions; against them the Council of Gangra issued a decree, later renewed in the synods of subsequent centuries. At the Council of Toulouse, held in 1119, Callistus II ordered those who condemned legitimate marital unions to be expelled from the Church as heretics. That decree was necessary against certain heretics who were then teaching that no one living in marriage could be saved; these were the seeds of the Albigensian heresy.

Helvidius, by contrast, made marriage equal to virginity. Jerome took this so badly that, because of his excessive favor toward virginity, he appears to have disparaged marriage almost to the point of sin, implying that a woman remains subject to a curse and to her husband’s authority so long as she desires intercourse. Erasmus nevertheless attempts to excuse Jerome on the ground that, at the beginning of his book against Helvidius, he testified that he was not disparaging marriage when praising virginity, so that whatever Jerome says more harshly in this matter must always be understood according to that rule.

I believe that Jerome, being a man of passionate intellect, could not endure Helvidius’s boldness and therefore, through his love of chastity, went somewhat farther than he ought. Great men have always been vehement in disputes of this kind.] were presented in such a way that conjugal humility was not despised.

Finally, the son of a virgin not only did not condemn marriage but also honored its beginning—namely, the wedding feast—by his first miracle [Note: [Col. 0587D] By his first miracle. For Christ the Lord performed his first sign at the wedding in Cana, as it is written in the second chapter of the Gospel according to John.].

Virgin integrity is therefore pleasing, and exceedingly so; but conjugal fellowship is not despised, not even by God himself.

How amusing, then, is your refusal to be taken aboard my ship because of the assessment of the fare to be imposed on you! But if the pressure of necessity, which I think will occur, compels you, take care lest you are forced shamelessly to beg the one whose offer you now reject so insolently, once he justly refuses you.

But, to return to a serious tone, I rejoice that the barbarians were vigorously routed and slaughtered to the point of annihilation by your strength—or rather by God’s—and I rejoice beyond measure that you and your men were freed from danger. I rejoice no less that some were at last warned and others taught by experience to believe that fortune must not be rashly trusted or frequently tested.

For G. and the others wounded in defense of their homeland, we shall not cease pouring out prayers until your report, informing our littleness that they have regained their health, makes us rejoice.

I requested that Faustus be sent to us—not the Faustus refuted by Augustine [Note: [Col. 0588D] Whom Augustine refutes. That is, Faustus the Manichaean, against whom Augustine wrote his notable work in thirty-three books.], but the one whom Gelasius censures in the *Decrees* [Note: [Col. 0588D] Gelasius. See the notes to Letter 128.].

I had entrusted you with the task of obtaining wine, because you despaired of being able to send any to us, discord among our people and the boldness of the barbarians standing in the way. But since you have now pressed me with a fresh reminder, although the harvest here has not yielded as much as had been reported, I shall strive through hard work to overcome the year’s barrenness, if you approve the plan my messenger will explain to you.

When I send what I promised, you will recognize how precisely I understand the Apostle’s indulgence toward those who defend their greater appetite for wine: “Use a little wine” (1 Tim. V). Surrounded as you are by the necessity of your circumstances, you will observe that, since you have been given no other drinking ration than what I sent, I understand “a little” in that sense [167].

Although I have ended the letter with threats, I wish you every happiness.

## LETTER CXIII. TO LOUIS, ABBOT

Lupus sends present and future salvation to the most distinguished of abbots, Louis.

I do not doubt that it was through the abundance of divine grace that your excellence deigned to condescend to my humility and count me among your friends in whatever order of rank. Through you, both often before and most recently, divine mercy freed me from an intolerable hardship, when an exceedingly troublesome and prolonged stay had been imposed upon me.

Therefore, believing and confessing that I am unequal to your innumerable and constant benefits, I implore the almighty God, by whose gift you have obtained such benevolence both toward me and toward all who need help.

Moreover, my men, exhausted by frequent expeditions, heard that our lord the king was setting out toward Brittany. Hoping for some postponement of the assembly announced long ago, they asked me to consult you about where and when I ought to join you.

Therefore, may your most indulgent moderation measure our difficulties and deign to indicate to us by letter how long after the appointed day of the assembly we may safely remain, so that we neither fail to attend the assembly nor lose some time while guided by your advice.

Please do not consider it tiresome also to add whether, without danger from the pirates [Note: [Col. 0588D] Pirates. That is, the Normans, as we said above. They had already begun sailing upstream on the Seine. This therefore occurred in the year 851, as is clear from the Chronicle of Fontenelle, in which it is written that the Normans were on the Seine that year from the third day before the Ides of October until the Nones of June—287 days. See Radbertus, Book IV of his Commentary on the Lamentations of Jeremiah.], our ship carrying supplies can keep its course along the Seine and proceed from there by way of the confluence of the Oise as far as [168] Creil [Note: [Col. 0588D] Creil. A town on the bank of the river Oise, commonly called *Oise*, not far from Chantilly; today it is called Creil.].

Above all, make my littleness rejoice at your desired good health; remember me kindly, and always prosper.

## LETTER CXIV. TO THE SAME PERSON

Lupus sends abundant greetings to the most distinguished of abbots, Louis.

Bound by your frequent—indeed constant—benefits, I grieve that I cannot repay you with corresponding thanks. For that reason I recently attempted to do so by letter, and your greatness did not disdain the narrowness of my shame. Thus, since it is the only thing I can do, I freely confess that your favor has bound my littleness with an even tighter bond of obligation.

I believe that such immense benevolence toward me and toward everyone comes from the one from whom it alone flows, and that he will repay it. We, who after God depend upon you, provide through our continual petitions an increase to that eternal recompense.

While on the road I learned that our lord the king had not returned to you even at the time he had appointed. Therefore, when my men demand a postponement, I take refuge, as usual, in the protection of your advice. Please regulate it by prescribing what I ought to do, so that I may remain safe from offense and, if an effective campaign against the barbarians [Note: [Col. 0589C] Barbarians. That is, the Britons; for the king was planning an expedition against them, as is clear from the preceding letter. See Letter 83.] is established with God’s inspiration, may assist it to the extent of my limited strength, whether in blunting or crushing them.

I wish you eternal prosperity.

## 169. LETTER CXV. TO ERCANR. From the persons of Gu. and the others.

Most Reverend Bishop Erc., G., H., and Ag., and the entire synod [Note: [Col. 0589C] Bishops. Those named here are Ercanrad of Paris, Wenilo of Sens, and Agius of Orléans. As for the one designated by the letter H., I do not dare pronounce an opinion. The editor who published the supplements to the Councils of Gaul was bolder.]

assembled at Murittum in the name of God, send perpetual greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0589C] At Murittum. The place where this synod was held was also reported by Duchesne’s edition; it is now confirmed by the authority of an ancient manuscript, since this passage was a lacuna in Masson’s edition. Labbe rightly thinks that the place was in the diocese of Sens and was the site now called Morettum. Nothing is more common in manuscript codices than the interchange of the letters *o* and *u*, as Peter Daniel noted concerning the *Querolus* falsely attributed to Plautus, and as we have observed elsewhere. Thus, instead of *Morittum*, *Murittum* could also have been written. Labbe further pointed out that this synod was held in the year 850.]

We thank Your Holiness because, although somewhat late, you nevertheless sent your vicar, who would share with us the burden of our deliberations and apply the necessary effort to settle the matters at issue. But your own person would have contributed that much more authority among all simple people by as much as you surpass him in the pinnacle of dignity.

[Note: [Col. 0589D] In the pinnacle of dignity. This was evidently because he was bishop of the royal city. Great cities bring their bishops extensive respect, especially those which have deserved to be the capitals of kingdoms.]

Therefore, since, by reason of our sins, this is a most turbulent time, and since, through so many successive years, the abundance of iniquity has deprived us of the opportunity to hold an assembly, while God softened the king’s heart so that he might grant us some opportunity for correction, and since the moments of our life allow no delay in their passing, we must attend to the cause of our Lord with no sluggishness. Nor ought we withdraw from carrying out the office which we have undertaken, unworthy though we are, for any reason except the necessity of impossibility.

[Note: [Col. 0589D] The necessity of impossibility. Both ancient and more recent regulations had established that no bishop summoned to a synod might neglect to attend except on account of the necessity arising from bodily weakness. The Synod of Agde even decreed that an excuse based on a royal command should be accepted. Accordingly, unless a serious illness prevented a bishop from traveling abroad, and unless the ruler denied him free access to the synod, he would incur the stigma of shamelessness and negligence if he did not attend. It must nevertheless be noted here that a bishop who asserts that he cannot attend is to be believed; this is indicated by the words, “Man looks at the face, but God at the heart,” that is, a bishop can lie when he says that he is constrained by an unavoidable necessity from attending the synod. He can impose upon men, who know only the man’s outward appearance; but not upon God, who searches hearts. Besides, it is not fitting that a priest’s lips be stained by falsehood, as Arnulf of Lisieux writes in Letter 11 to Alexander III.]

For, as it is written, “Man looks at the face, but God at the heart” (1 Kings XVI); and he will render to each person, as is stated most truthfully elsewhere, “according to his works” (Matthew XVI). [Col. 0589C] And would that we might do something beyond our obligation, so that he himself, on returning, might abundantly reward us with the desired recompense.

[Note: [Col. 0590C] “Of charity, therefore.” I think that after these words one folio is missing from the old manuscript. What follows does not cohere with them and certainly does not belong to this synodal letter. For afterward Lupus writes to one of his friends, as is clear. We have therefore separated this fragment of the synodal letter from the following fragment. We note meanwhile that this final fragment is written in a different and smaller hand in the old manuscript, although that manuscript too is extremely ancient and evidently from the same period. This was why earlier editors did not notice that something was missing here.]

Therefore, of charity . . . [lacuna]. The rest is missing.

[Col. 0590A] To compensate for the losses of our own community, where several well-instructed disciples have already died prematurely, through the education of those who are either advancing and desire further growth in their progress or who, by favorable signs, have already given us hope of their advancement—which we desire greatly—I should certainly believe that I could earn the author of every good a reward for such fruitful labor. Therefore, so that the aforementioned boy, for whom you rightly take thought, may become a participant in instruction, since he has permission and a letter from his bishop, let him be brought to us by our beloved Remigius on the fourth day before the Kalends of July; and, with the help of God’s grace, we shall endeavor to benefit him along with the others.

## LETTER CXVI. TO THE BROTHERS FROM THE MONASTERY OF SAINT GERMANUS

[Note: [Col. 0590D] Saint Germanus. Of Auxerre, as Masson’s edition had it.]

[Col. 0590B]

To the holy fathers excelling in the service of God in the monastery of blessed Germanus, Lupus, together with the community of Ferrières, sends abundant greetings in the Lord.

True charity has always flourished among the inhabitants of our monasteries, but never has it declared its greatness through such certain signs as in our own time. And if it had exercised anything extraordinary in us, it would seem that we ought to suppress it, lest someone think that we were reproaching you with forgetfulness of a benefit. In your case, however, we are especially free to recount the truth, for the increase of divine praise.

And since we assert what we have experienced with greater confidence than what we have merely heard,

[Note: [Col. 0590D] Experienced rather than heard. In accordance with the following line of Plautus:

“One eyewitness is worth more than ten who have heard.”

Those who hear know what they have heard. Those who see know clearly.]

I have decided to begin with myself, in order to establish the truth of my statement. When our illustrious king Charles came to Auxerre in the preceding autumn,

[Note: [Col. 0590D] Auxerre. Charles the Bald’s arrival in the city of Auxerre took place at the time when Louis, king of Germany, entered Charles’s kingdom—not as a guest but as an enemy—as is clear from Hericus the monk, *On the Miracles of Saint Germanus of Auxerre*, Book II, chapters 8–10. This occurred toward the end of the year 858, as the author of the *Annals of Fulda* teaches. See Sirmond’s notes on Charles the Bald’s *Capitula*, title 23.]

and his retinue occupied almost all the neighboring places, we thought that we should turn especially to you, since we were in need of lodging. We were not disappointed in our hope but were received with courtesy; and, although your public refectory entirely relieved us of royal service, whenever we were able to slip away, we never felt that our presence had become a burden to you.

After, through my very dear kinsman Remigius and my most valued student Fridilo, we had explained ourselves to Your Holiness, showing our intention—that we were unable to resist the king’s orders, although they diverted us in a direction other than the one we wished—we were about to depart. We did not even have the opportunity to offer thanks before the assembled community, because the impossibility of postponing the embassy was taking away every opportunity for delay.

[Note: [Col. 0591C] Of the embassy. Since, as we have said, in the year 858 Louis, king of Germany, invaded Charles’s kingdom, Charles’s affairs were so severely distressed that he was compelled to flee and withdraw into Burgundy. In this calamity, having almost become an exile from his own realm, he sent Lupus as an envoy somewhere, perhaps to Germany, so that Lupus—who had lived there for many years and was also well acquainted with the German language—might complain to Louis about the wrong done to Charles. Since those circumstances required prompt remedies, he ordered Lupus to depart immediately, without even granting him leave to embrace the monks of Saint Germanus. Charles’s affairs were so desperate that they seem to have been restored by no other means than Louis’s imprudence, as is clear from the *Annals of Fulda*. Nor do I agree with Cellot, who thinks that Louis withdrew his hand from the unjust war because of the bishops’ admonitions—a conclusion he believes he can draw from the *Annals of Saint-Bertin*. If I assert that the author of those annals shared the view of the writer of the *Annals of Fulda*, I do not think I shall have departed from the truth.]

For this reason we begged the beloved brothers mentioned above to fulfill our duty in our place until God should grant us the opportunity to carry it out ourselves.

In addition to the matters related above, when the violence of the brigands frightened us,

[Note: [Col. 0592C] Of the brigands. Clearly the Normans, who had by then reached the diocese of Sens. Lupus had therefore sent the ornaments of the monastery of Ferrières to the monks of Auxerre, as to a safer place, to be concealed there.]

you took care to hide the ornaments of our church, and you were not found reluctant to undertake this service.

Our dearest brother S., reflecting on these things and reviewing both what had been generously granted to him and what had been granted to many others, chose you, when the ruin of our place was threatening—as we feared, threatened both by our sins and by the proximity of the pirates—not as persons with whom he might live as a stranger, but as a community into whose fellowship he might be admitted and possess a lodging as the representative of our house.

Others too made the same request, wishing, though separate from one another, to remain in monasteries rather than live on an estate with the greater part of their people.
