Although, therefore, it is uncertain whether God in his mercy has removed the overthrow of our monastery forever or has postponed it for a time for some hidden reason, the aforementioned brother nevertheless persisted in demanding what he had conceived he ought to obtain. Would that he may attain it with your consent, lest, compelled by a similar circumstance, he be forced to seek farther afield!

We beg you to care for him piously while he remains with you, because he was long a partner in my labors and, on account of his uprightness and energy, has always been judged agreeable to all and universally useful.

Moreover, placing the greatest confidence in Your Holiness, we have dared to send you Brother Bernegaud, still an inexperienced monk, at the request of your paternal affection. He will obey your will and, through the examples and instruction of more perfect men, will be strengthened more diligently in his purpose.

Remember our smallness kindly. We wish you every happiness.

## LETTER CXVII. TO ANSBOLD

[Note: [Col. 0592C] To Ansbold. The old manuscript had only *To Ansb.* Masson’s edition, however, read *To Ansbold*. Since in Letter 69 he is called Ansbaldus, and in Masson he is easily misprinted as Ausbaldus; since in Letter 10 he is again called Ansboldus, and finally Masson has Ausboldus; and since it is established from these passages that he was a monk under Marcward, abbot of Prüm, I am readily led to believe that he is the man who became abbot of Prüm after Marcward and Eigil. Regino writes: “In the year 860 of the Lord’s Incarnation, Eigil voluntarily resigned the abbacy of Prüm, and Auspaldus”—to be read as Ansbaldus, according to Trithemius in the *Chronicle of Hirsau* under the year 860—“succeeded him in its government, a man distinguished by every holiness and goodness.” Thus from this passage also we learn that Lupus was not yet dead in the year 860, since he writes to Ansbold when the latter was already abbot. From what follows, moreover, it appears that Ansbold was expelled from the monastery and eventually restored, which indicates that this letter was written some time after Ansbald had assumed governance of the monastery of Prüm.]

## TO ANSBOLD

To the most reverend abbot A. and all his brothers, Lupus and the entire community of the monastery of Ferrières send greetings in the Lord.

Having overcome the harshest difficulties, we rejoice that you have at last, through divine grace, been restored to your proper place. Nor do we fail to receive gladly the fact that you pursue our goodwill toward you with pious affection and pleasant conversation, although we would wish that far more and greater things had been done for you.

You heard some of our tribulations with sorrow and witnessed others with anxiety; but, with our Lord God moderating them or removing them altogether, we desire that they may be useful and sincerely pleasing to you and to yours who have come to us.

Therefore, so that the familiarity once begun may advance toward a richer increase, when our recovered resources in the western region have become an aid, our journeys there and back will disclose to us what is being done on both sides.

We wish you always to remember us kindly and to enjoy every happiness.

## LETTER CXVIII. TO HERARD, BISHOP

[Col. 0592C]

To Herard, most reverend bishop of the Church of Tours, Lupus and the united community of the monastery of Bethlehem send abundant greetings in the Lord.

As you graciously wrote, you have, by divine providence, joined the bonds of friendship with our smallness. For charity, as the Apostle writes, is from God (1 John VII), and it shines most brightly in those who are bound together by sincere friendship.

Would that we could contribute something to you either spiritually through prayer or in worldly matters through service! Certainly, we would faithfully reveal our goodwill toward you in the case of our very dear brother T., whom, in accordance with your request, we are granting permission to govern the monks in the cell of Roclena. How important he is in our eyes can easily be assessed from the office he discharged with the greatest labor.

We ask Your Holiness to cherish him with continual kindness, so that he may experience in you a fatherly affection whose sweetness may always refresh him amid the bitterest troubles of the world.

## LETTER CXIX. TO AENEAS, BISHOP

[Note: [Col. 0593C] To Aeneas. Bishop of Paris. See Letters 98 and 99.]

[Col. 0593A]

To his dearest Aeneas, Lupus sends eternal greetings.

As I explained to you after other matters, I had disclosed my intention to our king, most devoted to learning: namely, that I wished, with the favor of God, the author of every good, to resume the labor of the liberal disciplines by reviewing them and instructing others, if he himself were to have leisure and, in his indulgence, to grant me a share in the reward. He embraced my wish with a serene expression and flattering words and promised that he would see to it that I could bring it to completion. I therefore thought it necessary to inform you immediately, so that, when the opportunity was offered, you would know by what words he should be encouraged to undertake so great a matter.

But as I entered the monastery, I was met by a sorrowful message announcing that your Hildegarius, who had my niece as his wife, had died. Therefore, moved by my own affection and by the urging of the relatives of both lines, who asserted that I possessed considerable influence with you, I have sent this letter to Your Holiness, asking you to deign to grant to his son, for whom he made a request, a benefice,

[Note: [Col. 0593C] Benefice. Not an ecclesiastical benefice, but a feudal one. When a vassal died, the benefice returned to the lord of the fief. The fief itself was later simply called a benefice, whereas at that time it was called a benefice.]

and to appoint as guardian a man who both accords with your character and can perform the required military service,

[Note: [Col. 0593C] Military service. That is, by reason of the fief. For the lord did not grant the benefice without reason. Since the person for whom the benefice was being requested was a boy, the Lord is asked to appoint him such a guardian as could discharge the obligations attached to the benefice. The guardian therefore also performs here the duties of his ward.]

with commendable prudence.

[Note: [Col. 0593D] The widow. That is, the widow of the aforementioned man.]

If I obtain this, the widow of the aforementioned man and his relatives will strive to honor you appropriately; and God, with other good merits also lending support, will gather you into the company of those to whom he promises: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew V).

I wish you every happiness.

## LETTER CXX. TO ARDUIC, BISHOP

[Note: [Col. 0593D] To Arduic, bishop. Of Besançon, who is frequently mentioned here and there by Hincmar and who took part in the Council of Toul at Saponaria in 859, and likewise in the Council of Toul at Tusiacum in the following year, and finally in the Council of Douzy in 871. He is mentioned by Flodoard, Book III, chapter 20. It should meanwhile be noted that the name of this bishop has here been restored for the first time in Lupus’s letter. The other editions had *To Arbricen, bishop*, which is utterly nonsensical. We owe this correction, like many others, to the manuscript.]

## TO ARDUIC, BISHOP

To the desirable bishop A., Lupus and his brother monks send everlasting greetings.

We grieve that, while we remain suspended in expectation of your most gracious promises, time is flowing uselessly, since we cannot help but regard the attacks of the brigands with suspicion.

[Note: [Col. 0593D] Of the brigands. The Normans, as we said concerning Letter 116.]

Therefore, so that your desire may be hastened and our danger removed, we earnestly implore you to deign, for the sake of heavenly reward, to trouble yourself by coming to some place that is not inaccessible to me and certain brothers. Thus, when you explain our need to us and we disclose your intention to you, we may be fully able to understand one another.

Specify also the day of the month and the place, lest we be confused by any uncertainty.

We wish you every happiness.

## LETTER CXXI. TO WULFAD, ABBOT

To his united friend Wulfad, Lupus sends every blessing.

[Note: [Col. 0593D] Wulfad. Abbot of the monastery of Rebais in the diocese of Meaux, who took part in the Council of Pîtres in 862 together with our Lupus. From this too we may conclude that Lupus was not yet dead in the year 862.]

Rumor has made known that the king’s arrival will take place differently from what he had arranged. Therefore, explain to me in a friendly letter the reasons for this change, when he will finally come, or where he will remain in the meantime, so that, with the favor of God inspiring me, I may judge from your letter what I ought to do.

For a messenger’s report does not win credence, since it is frequently stained by obvious falsehood.

Farewell.

## LETTER CXXII. TO GERHARD

To the most excellent duke G. and his most illustrious wife B., Lupus sends present and future greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0594C] To Duke G. That is, Gerard, the same man who is called a count in Letter 81. It was customary in those times for men of rank sometimes to be called counts and at other times dukes. Thus Bernard, count and governor of Septimania and the Spanish March under Louis the Pious, is called a count in some places and a duke in others, for example by Nithard and the continuator of Aimoinus. Likewise, in the charters of King Lothar for the monastery of Saint Peter of Rodes in the diocese of Girona and for the monastery of Saint Genesius in the diocese of Elne, Guifred—who is commonly called a count elsewhere—is called duke, specifically duke of the county of Roussillon. Vivianus, who flourished under Charles the Bald, is likewise sometimes called a count and sometimes a duke, as we observed concerning Letter 86. In fact, Gerard, who is called a duke here by Lupus, was a count in the region of Burgundy.]

[Note: [Col. 0594D] His wife B. This was the reading of the old manuscript, and it is entirely sound, whereas Masson’s edition had gone enormously astray, reading *his wife Bil.* The wife of Gerard the count, to whom this letter was written, was unquestionably named Bertha. She is mentioned by Flodoard, Book III, chapter 27, where, in listing letters written by Hincmar of Rheims to various persons, he also mentions the letter written to this Bertha: “To Bertha, wife of Count Gerard, concerning the affairs of the Church entrusted to him in Provence, which he had entrusted to Gerard to protect and administer, asking her to be an energetic intermediary with her husband concerning those same affairs.”]

The distinguished reputation of your uprightness has always gladdened all good people; but now it has blossomed more abundantly into everyone’s knowledge, since divine providence has confirmed that same uprightness of yours through a result beneficial to all Christians.

Praise, thanks, and exquisite acclaim belong to him by whose authority you have partly destroyed and partly driven away the most troublesome enemies. When you have granted what you first deigned to promise and later to confirm, we shall endeavor to multiply our thanks.

As for what you carefully investigate, know that my monk and disciple Ad. never fled from our monastery. Rather, at the request of Abbot Marcward, he was honorably sent by us to Prüm—or Pronea—and, after living there for some time, avoided the traps of certain envious men.

[Note: [Col. 0595D] Or Pronea. I think that these words should be deleted, since I believe they were added through a copyist’s error. The copyist did not understand what Prüm was and wondered whether one should read *Prüm or Pronea*, so he included both, leaving the learned reader to prefer the reading judged more correct. We have noted that this frequently happened among ancient copyists in our comments on Book IV of Salvian’s *On the Government of God*. In Masson’s edition, instead of *or Pronea*, we find *or wrongly*, in a most disgraceful error. See above in the Notes to Letter 3.]

From there, out of a desire for learning and love of peace, he settled in the city of Lyon.

[Note: [Col. 0595D] From a desire for learning. Note the reputation of the city of Lyon for the study of letters. Hence Juvenal’s line:

“May he grow pale, like one who has trodden on a snake with bare feet,

or like the rhetor of Lyon about to speak at the altar.”

See the most illustrious Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, *On Primacies*, § 105.]

When the most reverend men Remigius, metropolitan of that city, and H., bishop of Grenoble, earnestly requested this and praised the aforementioned brother’s conduct, he also received regular letters,

[Note: [Col. 0596D] Ecclesiastical letters. This is what he calls the letter by which Wenilo had granted that monk permission to travel into another diocese, since otherwise such travel was not permitted. See the Notes to Letter 102.]

although long ago I had given him permission orally. These letters, once produced, will testify in good faith to what I think of him.

I know with complete certainty that he also has ecclesiastical letters from our venerable bishop Guenilo; nor is there anything that could rightly invalidate his election, if God calls him.

He conducted himself well among us. He is capable of teaching what the Church most greatly needs; he is supported by regular and episcopal letters; he is distinguished by the nobility of his ancestors. In his holy vocation he continues devoutly, according to the judgment of the aforementioned bishops among whom he lives.

What remains except that what God inspires in the holy bishops may be done? And what wonder if I once spoke somewhat harshly about him? That was the fault of his enemies, who shamelessly spread falsehoods.

What I now commit to writing is my own judgment: the account of one who consistently reports what he first saw and later learned.

I wish you every happiness.

## LETTER CXXIII. TO ANSBOLD

To his dearest Ansb., Lupus sends unfailing greetings.

[Col. 0596A]

As you learned, a pressing and general necessity had taken me away; and for that reason, when you returned, we were unable, as both of us desired, to refresh ourselves through a faithful conversation. At some time, however, divine grace will compensate for this loss.

Meanwhile, let us reasonably take pleasure in the sincerity of our affection.

Some time ago we received letters announcing the day of your entry into the monastery. After they had been read aloud at the assembly and deservedly praised by all, we replied with what seemed to us to follow from them. But upon examining your recent letters, we understood that those letters had not yet been delivered to you.

Now, however—that is, on the Nones of March—we suppose that you have those same letters, and therefore it would be pointless to repeat what they contain.

Greet all the brothers courteously, and earnestly obtain from them that they deign to pray for us, who are devoted to them.

We wish you the greatest happiness.

## LETTER CXXIV. TO GUENILO, BISHOP

To the most reverend bishop Guenilo, Lupus sends present and future greetings.

It is no wonder if the metropolitan bishop deceived you for so long by a lie, just as the wicked servant David deceived for a time by a plausible fabrication. That servant was punished by the loss of half the estates with which he had been endowed.

But the bishop must fear that he will be deprived of the fullness of the heavenly promises, since, as the most wise Solomon testifies, God’s soul detests one who sows discord among brothers (Proverbs VI).

[Note: [Col. 0596D] The metropolitan bishop. Herard of Tours, as I said. He had been assigned the task of visiting Wenilo and conveying the synod’s instructions to him. But when Herard fell ill, he sent Robert, bishop of Le Mans, in his place to carry out the embassy on his behalf before Wenilo, as is clear from Herard’s own memorandum to Wenilo. Herard evidently conveyed orally through Robert that it had not been through Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, that Wenilo had failed to be deposed. Wenilo therefore wrote to Lupus, complaining that he had just cause to protest against this deed and treachery, if the accusations were true. As we said earlier, Lupus endeavored to clear himself before Wenilo.]

This and everything else that the imprudent dismiss as matters to be despised because of weariness or impossibility will easily receive its judicial outcome, when all things are recalled to memory with such clarity that neither will the authors of evil attempt to clear themselves of the charges—or rather, the facts revealed—nor will any rational creature be able to doubt what the Creator’s justice will set before all to know.

There, unless he has made satisfaction, you will see him trembling in vain—the man whom, as a human being, you trusted to report the truth, though he was false.

For how could I become so depraved as to desire the deposition of one whose consecration I had received from God?

I confidently make him my witness, whose judgment we shall both experience: ever since you began to preside and deigned to admit me into your friendship, I have always desired that you should advance both in holiness and in dignity. And if, while my own affairs remained intact, some misfortune—which God avert—had befallen you, I was prepared to assist you to the best of my ability and to prove in every possible way, with the utmost clarity, that I was your closest friend.

But if I remembered that I had incurred treachery, I would not conceal so great a crime by denial; rather, I would try to obtain pardon through a simple confession.

For who, even if he has looked only slightly into the sacred writings, does not encounter, freely and very often, the words: “Whoever digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it” (Proverbs XXVI; Ecclesiastes X; Ecclesiasticus XXVII)?

Would that he who will reveal these things in the future, removing every ambiguity, might make clear in the present how true they are, and grant me, entirely innocent in this matter, the ability to retain your unbreakable friendship for the benefit of us both!

What I had learned elsewhere, and what you deigned to communicate, is that, if God permits, the lord king will become our neighbor. After his departure, if it pleases you, I desire, as soon as it can be done, to visit you at a place suitable for both of us and, with the mediation of the Holy Spirit’s grace, to recover the friendship that the malice of an evil spirit has disturbed somewhat.

Then I shall also be able to report what they have decided concerning Brother Bernegaud, the monk of Saint Germanus, and what alone we can grant, without harm to ourselves, to our fugitive, who recently troubled Your Clemency with his entreaties.

Remember our smallness always. I wish you every happiness.

## LETTER CXXV. TO FOLCRIC

[Col. 0598A]

To the most reverend bishop Folcric, Lupus sends temporal and eternal greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0597C] Folcric. Bishop of Troyes, who took part in various Gallican councils during that period. He became bishop after Prudentius, who, as recorded in the *Annals of Saint-Bertin*, died in the year 861. From this too we learn that Lupus was not dead before the year 861, since he writes to Folcric.]

It has pleased me to set down in writing the abundance of grace bestowed upon you by God’s gift, both as praise of Him who gave it and as a condemnation of greed and commendation of unconquerable charity. For when the most cruel pagan pirates [Note: That is, the Danes, who were then waging war against the Northmen within Gaul, and later joined them, as will shortly be said.] had put in at an island of the Seine [Note: This was doubtless an island situated near Oscellus, as is clear from Aimoinus, Book II of *The Miracles of Saint Germanus, Bishop of Paris*, chapter 10: “The Northmen, however, residing in an island of the Seine near that same place called Oscellus, often came by a naval expedition to Paris whenever it suited them perfectly well.” Charles the Bald also mentions it in his *Proclamation against Wenilo*.], which lies below the town of Melledunum [Note: Melledunum is a town in the diocese of Sens, on the river Seine, commonly called Melun. Hence we learn that this town had been burned by the Northmen in an earlier attack; for this incursion, which is discussed here, was only the second. The first occurred in 851, as was said in the note to Letter 113; the latter in the following year, as is clear from the Chronicle of Fontenelle: “In the year 852, the fleet of Sidroc and Godfrid, leaders of the Danes, enters the Seine on 7 October and advances as far as Autun.” This letter was written to Folcric, bishop of Troyes, who attained that see in 861. Therefore this arrival of the pagans at Melledunum cannot be understood as the second incursion of the Northmen, which we have shown occurred in October 852. But the true date of this letter may be gathered from the Annals of St-Bertin, where the following is read under the year 861: “The Danes, who had previously burned the city of Thérouanne, returning from England under the leadership of Weland, ascend the Seine with two hundred and more ships, and besiege the fortress built by the Northmen on the island called Oscellus, together with the Northmen themselves.” Below: “Meanwhile another part of the Danes, with sixty ships, ascends from the Seine into the river Oise; from there they come to those besieging the fortress and join their company. But the besieged, compelled by hunger, want, and every squalor of misery, give the besiegers six thousand pounds of gold and silver and join them; thus they descend the Seine as far as the sea, which the approaching winter prevented them from entering. Therefore they divide themselves by their respective companies among the individual ports, from Paris itself as far as [the sea]. Weland, however, ascends the Seine with his companions as far as the fortress of Melun. The garrison, together with Weland’s son, occupies the monastery of Fosses.”], recently burned by others [Note: That is, by the Northmen. This burning must have occurred shortly before this letter was written.], and, unless God’s mercy had come to our aid, we regarded their neighborhood as it actually was—most dangerous [Note: That is, the neighborhood of the Danes and Northmen. Why would they not dare the same things at the monastery of Ferrières that they had done at Fosses? For Weland’s son occupied the monastery of Fosses at that time, as has been said.], we neither dared remain in the monastery nor, crushed beneath the burden of so great a calamity, could find anywhere to which we might move.

[Col. 0598B] In the midst of these circumstances, when you had come to visit me in my serious illness and found us stricken with immense fear, you immediately, without any weariness of deliberation, relieved us of our shame; and, anticipating our petition, you offered the estate of Aix [Note: The estate of Aix—that is, the Villa of Aix, sixteen miles from Augusta Tricassium. It is commonly called Aix-en-Othe, because it lies in that part of the province called *le pays d’Othe*.], the chief property of your lordship, where we might more safely avoid the wickedness of the times without being wholly deprived of the opportunity to maintain our profession.

Moreover, you showed, with scarcely credible goodwill, that you would offer the most generous kindness. Therefore, in return for the incomparable consolation divinely offered to us through you of your own accord, especially in so monstrous a danger, we have tried, as was fitting, at least to give thanks to God and to you. But, our understanding failing us, we were unable properly to conceive them in our minds, much less express them with our mouths.

181 [Col. 0598C] Thus, astounded by iniquity abounding everywhere and by the charity of many growing cold, we have wondered that in our days someone was found who, at such great loss and diminution of his household property, would assist those in need. Indeed, this was not to close one’s heart to brothers suffering want; this was to show episcopal compassion; finally, this was to fulfill charity.

But since the overflowing mercy of our God, whose indulgence conceals our countless and enormous sins, has overthrown the threats of the brigands, who, after devastating celebrated places far and wide, were boasting that they would also seek the seat of the merchants and their cloaks [Note: *Minas praedonum* (“the threats of the brigands”). Goldastus, vol. I of *Rerum Alamannicarum*, p. 197, considers this passage, which he says is extremely corrupt, to require emendation as follows: “He overthrew the threats of the brigands, who, after laying waste celebrated places far and wide, were boasting that they would also seek the seat of the merchants and the cloaks of the leisure-loving,” etc.], and has turned them away from us—as I wish He would do from all Christians—we all hope, as though we had made use of a benefit granted to us, that so abundant a good may have a reward safely reserved for you to be presented by God when He begins to glorify His elect and to repay grace with grace [Note: Compare Tacitus, *Annals* IV: “Benefits are pleasing so long as they seem capable of being repaid; when they have come too far in advance, hatred is returned instead of gratitude.” On this passage, see the most learned Curtius Pichenus. An ancient epitaph found in Rome in the cemetery of Callistus and published in the latest edition of *Roma Subterranea*, Book III, chapter 22, reads: “ALEXANDER. IS. NOT. DEAD. BUT. LIVES. ABOVE. THE. STARS. AND. HIS. BODY. RESTS. IN. THIS. TOMB. HE COMPLETED HIS LIFE UNDER THE EMPEROR ANTONINUS, WHO, FORESEEING THAT A GREAT BENEFIT WOULD COME TOO FAR IN ADVANCE, RETURNED HATRED INSTEAD OF GRATITUDE.”]

But our smallness, almost … bound by the report of your generosity, will never be ungrateful to you … and will show itself most ready to serve you in whatever ways it is able, whenever occasion is given. Yet let the estate of Aix, throughout the period of your episcopate—which may God grant to be long—be assigned as our refuge, should a similar misfortune occur. Let the buildings be maintained, and let the garden also be cultivated with greater care, as you have rightly planned. Let the fields suitable for this purpose be planted with vines, and let the grain stores be increased through the industry of proper labor, so that you may have enough both to distribute each year, as is customary, to your household dependents and to give mercifully to those seeking aid; and, if the final necessity should draw us there—as we fear it may, if our sins demand it—the harshness of our hiding place may be softened by the aforesaid resources.

Why, however, do you ask what we want concerning those things which you have deigned to receive from us? Why do you not consider how small a portion of our service it would be if it were offered in exchange for your very great benefit? And lest, by this sort of dissimulation—which we cannot endure—you cunningly suppose that we are planning to choose something greater, we plainly express what we have in mind.

You have learned that although our place is called Bethlehem, that is, “house of bread,” we shall soon suffer a scarcity of bread unless the kindness of you and our other friends comes to our aid. Then, remembering your true promise, you can feed your dependents for half a month free of charge, and support us, as though from a debt, with interest besides. And lest you accuse us of shamelessness—or rather of folly—recall that we do not reject rhetorical skill, which teaches that when we intend to obtain lesser things, we should ask for greater ones [Note: That is, he says this practice derives from secular learning; see Letter 68.].

I desire that you may prosper happily and continually adorn the eminence of your dignity with honorable conduct and holy deeds.

## LETTER CXXVI. TO GUENILO

To the most reverend bishop Guenilo, Lupus sends present and future salvation.

I would gladly have obeyed the letters of Your Holiness, had my wish not been hindered by bodily distress. [Col. 0600B] For when, after the long and harsh illnesses of this year, I was beginning to recover well, I suddenly developed a cough which, obstructing my passages, almost deprived me entirely of the power to breathe [Note: “Was depriving me.” So the old manuscript reads. Masson’s edition had *adjuvabat* (“was assisting”); a similar error also occurred in Letter 116, where *adjuvante* was printed instead of *adimente* (“depriving”). The same correction is needed in Arnulf of Lisieux, Letter 52 to Alexander III, where it is printed: “For ecclesiastical dignity advances royal dignity rather than assists it.” The reading should be *adimit* (“deprives”), as Juretus correctly noted in his annotation to Letter 190 of Ivo of Chartres.].

For this reason I lost a great deal of blood and contracted the greatest weakness. Accordingly, I dare go nowhere until, through rest and medicines—or rather through the help of the Divinity—some small measure of health is restored to me.

I shall therefore petition you unanimously in all things, and I shall urge my brothers to do the same: may God inspire you with a plan by which you may be of general benefit to all Christians, lest the sin of injustice, which has already made us wretched, drag us into everlasting condemnation.

During the days of your episcopate, vices have burst forth into such great freedom [Note: Namely, on account of the wars—more than civil wars—that have miserably afflicted this kingdom. At that time bishops sometimes neglected many things among themselves and many things among the people, and were compelled to neglect many others; thus religion suffered great damage in every order, namely among clerics, monks, and laypeople. Some were heading toward destruction through ignorance, while others, accustomed to long license, trusted that they could sin with impunity, as is written in canon 2 of the Council of Verneuil. Worldly license had advanced so far that impunity seemed to have been promised to every purpose by an announced decree, and no one feared either God, the king, or the bishops. Those times therefore required neither slow remedies nor sluggish physicians. For this reason Lupus urges Wenilo to apply his hand diligently to the work.], that, with impunity having been vindicated, no one fears God, the king, or the bishop in any open matter.

Why do you delay? What more are you waiting for? Either God, through your diligence and authority, will restore human affairs to justice, or these growing evils, after unheard-of outrages, will overwhelm almost all the innocent who remain—few though they are.

You see that, according to blessed Isaiah, “the one who departs from evil becomes a prey” (Isaiah LIX); and no one is safe from the violence of robbers except one who prevails by strength or has entered their company.

I desire that you may prosper happily and that you may kindly and continually remember my insignificance.

## LETTER CXXVII. TO ODO, BISHOP

184 [Note: To Odo, bishop of Beauvais in Belgica Secunda. He is frequently mentioned in the synods and writers of that age. He had previously been abbot of Corbie, as was said in the note to Letter 111.]

To Odo, the uniquely and singularly beloved bishop, Lupus sends abundant greetings.

Assisted by your many and great benefits, I hasten confidently to you, intending also to make use of what you have instructed my messengers that you will provide. But since you did not send a horse, and I had no suitable animal that could carry me comfortably [Note: “Carry me easily.” The manuscript read *mexolutim ferret*, which I judged should be read *me exolutim ferret*, that is, “carry me in such a way that there could be no doubt that the horse could carry me easily.” *Exolutim* is used for *exolute*, that is, “without doubt.”], I shall, if God wills, make my way to you by ship.

Therefore, may your most indulgent piety, which has received me freely and willingly to be cared for, not allow me, once I have disembarked, to be troubled by the jolting of a rougher horse. I do not doubt that you will arrange, as you have deigned to instruct, for us to pitch our tent in a place near you and for suitable fodder for the horses to be provided with your people.

Our courier, until we arrive—which I think will happen, with God’s mercy supporting us, on the Kalends of June—has occupied the place of a poor man in your household; and, if he is permitted, he will collect the fragments so that they do not perish, and will also dry the cups so that they do not lose their sweetness through moisture.

## LETTER CXXVIII

[Note: James Sirmond, that distinguished light of the Society of Jesus, published this letter, as well as the following one, at the end of his book *On Three Questions*, where he judges them to be letters of Lupus of Ferrières. They had previously been published in Belgium by Donatus Candidus, after being copied from an old manuscript through the work of Antonius Grimbert, a monk of Elnon. In Sirmond’s edition the title of this letter reads: “Of Lupus Servatus to King Charles.” In the Belgian edition it reads: “Of the same Lupus Servatus to the Lord King.” Since we understood that the Belgian edition more closely followed the writing practices of that age and therefore of Lupus, we gave this letter the title “To the Lord King.” We wished to add these letters at the end of the collection, as belonging properly there. For there can be no doubt that they are Lupus’s, the abbot of Ferrières.]

### TO THE LORD KING

To the glorious lord King Charles, Lupus, sincerely faithful.

Long ago, in the city of Bourges [Note: I agree with the distinguished president Mauguin, who thinks that these events occurred when Charles the Bald, after taking Toulouse, came to the city of Bourges in December 849, as the author of the Chronicle of Fontenelle relates. Lupus was only one or two days’ journey from that city. Therefore, since access to the king was easy, he went there. After the formal reception, Charles no doubt asked him, in Lupus’s words, what news he brought. Lupus related that a synod had been held concerning the Bretons; then he reported that serious controversies had been raised concerning free will, predestination, and Christ’s blood. For some said that free will had been restored to man by Christ in such a way that man could nevertheless do nothing by the power of free will without Christ’s grace; that some were predestined from eternity to glory, others to punishment, so that what God had foreknown that He would do in judging would undoubtedly come to pass; third, that Christ’s blood was shed only for believers, not for unbelievers; fourth, that no one is saved except through Christ, but that all whom He wills are saved, and consequently that whoever are not saved are altogether not His will to save. Lupus no doubt added that, on this occasion, the minds of learned men were being divided into parties. Charles was curious about such matters. He therefore asked Lupus what his own opinion was on these questions. Lupus took advantage of Charles’s accessibility and wrote the book on that subject at that time, namely in 849, as he himself testifies at the beginning of the book. But that book aroused against him the hatred of many, who inferred from it and spread abroad that Lupus did not think piously and faithfully concerning God, and that, from a desire to display learning, he was departing from received opinions. For this reason he wrote this letter, which is apologetic and as it were a summary of the book *On Three Questions*, to Charles in the following year.], you asked me what I thought about predestination, free will, and the redemption by Christ’s blood; and I briefly disclosed to Your Majesty what I had learned in the divine writings and found in the greatest authorities. Since some people think otherwise [Note: Namely Hincmar of Rheims, Pardulus of Laon, and perhaps others, as the same Mauguin rightly judges.] and suppose that I do not hold pious and faithful thoughts about God, with God Himself—whom I have trusted greatly from the age at which I could understand—guiding my mind and my style, I shall briefly, truthfully, and clearly resolve the aforementioned questions, which many rashly discuss but few understand intelligently.

Nor ought I keep you occupied with a lengthy disputation, deceive you in any matter, or delay you with obscurities, since I am not unaware of your occupations in ordering the affairs of the state, and since, after God, I owe you singular loyalty [Note: This passage rightly led the same distinguished scholar to conclude that this letter was written by Lupus of Ferrières. For that reason he owed Charles special loyalty: the monastery of Ferrières was situated in Charles’s kingdom and owed him both gifts and military service.].

God created Adam upright, as Holy Scripture teaches, and originally created us all upright in him. This parent of the human race, abandoning his natural uprightness, sinned without compulsion so greatly that he both destroyed himself and condemned in himself all those born from him, of either sex.

God therefore made human nature exceedingly good, but the human being himself miserably corrupted it through voluntary guilt. In short, Adam existed, as blessed Ambrose says, and in him we all existed. Adam perished, and in him all perished.

Let us therefore praise God’s workmanship and recognize that nothing is owed to our guilt except punishment. But God, to whom past, present, and future are equally present—for He is the One who is, and nothing is added to or subtracted from His knowledge—knew that in Adam the whole mass of the human race would be corrupted by sin. Yet He did not withhold from it the good of His creation, intending to use even evils for good; and before the foundation of the world He chose from it those whom He would free by grace from the punishment they deserved, as the Apostle says: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians I).

The others, to whom mercy did not grant this grace, He left by a just judgment in the condemnation they themselves had deserved by sinning. Thus, as the Apostle teaches: “He has mercy on whom He wills, and He hardens whom He wills” (Romans IX). He has mercy on those whom He takes up by grace; He hardens those whom He does not soften by that same grace, but whom He leaves—although by a hidden, yet just, judgment.

Those, then, on whom He has mercy are predestined to glory, according to the Apostle’s words: “Those whom He foreknew, He also predestined” (Romans I), and they are called vessels for honor. They owe God everything they are and possess: they were made by His goodness when they did not exist, and by His kindness they were saved when they were lost.

Those whom He hardens—that is, does not soften—and who are left in the condemnation they deserved either originally or through actual sin, are called vessels for dishonor, perfected or prepared for destruction. That they are created is God’s gift; that they are punished is their own evil.

Blessed Augustine, in many books and in the last work he composed, does not hesitate to say that these were predestined to punishment—not understanding this as a fatal necessity imposed on the lost, but as the unchangeable abandonment of those who were left behind. For he read concerning God: “If He shuts a man in, there is no one who can open” (Job XII); likewise: “Consider the works of God, that no one can correct him whom He has rejected” (Ecclesiasticus II); and also: “I gave them over to the desires of their hearts; they shall walk in their own inventions” (Psalm LXXX).

And, as I think, the following testimony especially directed him toward this understanding: God is the One who made the things that are to come. To Him it is also said: “You will repay each according to his works” (Psalm LXI). He will indeed do this for all, except those whom He makes blessed by forgiving their iniquities and covering their sins.

Those who exalt God’s grace with the highest praises can say: “He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities.” Jerome and Gregory agree with Augustine in different words; Bede and Isidore agree in the same words. If it pleases Your Highness, I shall easily be able to demonstrate this from the authorities themselves.

Certainly, the first human being, by sinning, lost free will in the good that he despised, but retained it in the evil that he chose. Just as someone may kill himself, if he wishes, by depriving himself of food, but, once dead, cannot bring himself back to life, so a human being, by sinning through his will, was able to lose the use of free will in the good, but cannot, even if he wishes, recover it by his own strength.

He will therefore not possess free will in the good unless divine grace has liberated him. The Lord Jesus knew, as it is written, what was in man (John II), and, beneficially disclosing this, said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV)—nothing, that is, of the good. For He cannot be the author and accomplice of evil, since, as John the Baptist says, He is “the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world” (John I), both those that have been committed and those that they may not commit.

Likewise the Lord says elsewhere: “If the Son makes you free, then you will truly be free” (John VIII). Saint Cyprian, a most glorious martyr and most gracious teacher, carefully weighing the Apostle’s words, “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians IV), concluded that no one should boast, since nothing is ours [Note: Cyprian, Book III of *Testimonies to Quirinus*, chapter 4].

Hence good will also is prepared by the Lord, as the Apostle mentioned above teaches: “It is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish the work of good will”; for which reason he adds, “and to accomplish,” according to good will (Philippians II).

The teacher of the nations also shows that good thought itself comes to us from God: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians III).

God’s grace precedes us, as it is written: “My God, His mercy will come before me” (Psalm LVIII), so that we may will and begin what is good. God’s grace follows us, as it is written: “And Your mercy will follow me” (Psalm XXII), so that we may not will and begin in vain.

These things are principally God’s, as the preceding testimonies have made clear, and consequently ours also, because they are done by us willingly. It is written: “Lord, give us peace, for You have accomplished all our works for us” (Isaiah XXVI).

The guilt of sin is removed in baptism, but the struggle against it is preserved for the exercise of faith, so that we always need God’s help both to restrain vices and to obtain virtues. Every person who devoutly serves God feels this in himself, and the Apostle, having already received the sacrament of Christ, humbly confesses it as follows: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner man. But I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members” (Romans VII).

Thus all who have understood the mind of the divine utterances with credible judgment have unanimously held this view concerning free will.

Finally, whom the Lord redeemed by His blood can be gathered from the Gospel reading in Matthew. The Lord says: “Drink from this, all of you; for this is my blood of the new covenant, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew XXVI). In Mark: “This is my blood of the New Covenant, which will be poured out for many” (Mark XIV). In Luke, however: “This cup is the New Covenant in my blood, which will be poured out for you” (Luke XXII).

Thus two evangelists say “for many,” one says “for you,” since the disciples too are numbered among the many; none says “for all.”

And lest I be thought to have examined this rashly, Saint Jerome, explaining the Gospel passage, “The Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many” (Matthew VII), says: “When He took the form of a servant in order to pour out His blood for the world, He did not say that He would give His life as a ransom for all, but for many—that is, for those who would wish to believe.”

By this explanation, in accordance with the Catholic faith, he taught that only the faithful are to be understood, whether they are to remain in grace or to depart from it through their own fault.

Likewise, blessed Augustine, explaining to the people the meaning of the Gospel: “You do not believe because you are not of my sheep” (John I), says: “How did He say to these people, ‘You are not of my sheep’? Because He saw that they were predestined to everlasting destruction, not to eternal life purchased by the price of His blood.”

Who would dare contradict such clear lights, strengthening their teaching with the sense of the Gospel, except those who are ashamed to appear without lights?

Yet, speaking with the peace and reverence due to so great a man, John, bishop of Constantinople, did not perceive this understanding flowing from the fountain of the Gospel when he was explaining the Apostle’s statement about how, by the grace of God, Christ tasted death for all. He says: “Not for the faithful only, but for the whole world; indeed, He died for all. But what if not all believe? He fulfilled what belonged to Him.”

He did not, however, support his view with any divine testimony.

If anyone has shown or should show Your Excellency a certain Faustus who writes something very different about these matters [Note: See the notes to Letter 112], do not assent to the erring man. For Gelasius, together with seventy bishops, highly learned men, teaching which writers should or should not be received, first commended Augustine and bestowed singular praise on Jerome, but declared the writings of the aforementioned Faustus disqualified in these words: “The little works of Faustus of Riez, a Gaul, are apocryphal” [Note: Gelasius with seventy bishops. Our Lupus cites the same authority in nearly the same words at the end of his *Collection on Three Questions*. This decree concerning canonical and apocryphal books is commonly attributed to Pope Gelasius. In an old manuscript of the cathedral church of Urgell, however, containing the genuine collection of Isidore, the same decree is attributed to Hormisdas, the Roman pontiff who flourished not long after Gelasius. Moreover, long ago, through the kindness of the distinguished Dom Luke Dacherius, a Benedictine monk, I saw an extremely ancient manuscript of the Dionysian Collection in which this decree was said to have been issued by Pope Damasus, long before the time of Gelasius. Perhaps it may therefore be inferred that Damasus was the first of all to make a public ruling concerning books of this kind, and that Gelasius later renewed Damasus’s decree and enlarged it by adding the names of authors who lived after Damasus. The same may also be said of Hormisdas. See the distinguished John Pearson, Bishop of Chester, in his *Vindications of the Letters of Saint Ignatius*.].

This faith, which I expressed in the questions mentioned above, was held by the unconquerable defenders of the Catholic Church. I, the least of all, preserve it; I display it to those who wish to see it, without envy; to those who do not, conscious of my mediocrity, I do not force it upon them.

Nor, as some pretend to suspect, do I wish to become known frivolously—that is, from a desire for empty glory—since I am greatly frightened by the Lord’s statement concerning the scribes and Pharisees: “They do all their works in order to be seen by men” (Matthew XXIII); and concerning hypocrites: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matthew VI).

But, with a view to asserting the truth, I openly disclose without contention what, by God’s inspiration, I have discovered in the divine authorities and in the pre-eminent authors who follow their meaning, to those who seek it.

If Your renowned prudence has now been satisfied, I rejoice. If not, either now or when our God has granted you the rest you desire, because of other ecclesiastical business as well, if you summon to an assembly the more learned men, a subtler discussion by many may discover whether I think rightly or wrongly.

May God, I hope and pray, make you reign happily for a long time, so that He may grant you to reign with Him eternally.

## LETTER CXXIX. TO HINCMAR

191 [Note: The distinguished president Mauguin believes that this letter was written by Lupus in 849 in response to an inquiry from Hincmar, who, after subjecting Ratramnus, a monk of Corbie, to examination, sought Lupus’s opinion.]

To the most reverend bishop Hincmar, Lupus sends perpetual salvation in the Lord.

As I had long and earnestly examined predestination—the matter about which, in the peace to which we have been called by God, we inquire and deliberate—to determine what should reasonably be believed, lest the Apostle’s words, “Those whom He foreknew, He also predestined” (Romans VIII), remain unexplained; and lest the phrase “vessels of wrath perfected,” or “prepared,” or “made ready for destruction” (Romans IX); and the statement divinely written elsewhere, “A person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred” (Ecclesiastes IX); and also, “Consider the works of God, that no one can correct him whom He has rejected” (Ecclesiasticus VII), along with similar passages found throughout the divine utterances, should lack a fitting interpretation, this seems the truest position: predestination in the good is, according to the understanding of the most learned Augustine, the preparation of grace; predestination in the evil is, according to our capacity, the withdrawal of grace.

Concerning these matters the same most authoritative writer says: “He does not help those whom He does not wish to help, concerning whom He decided something else in His predestination; yet in both groups the Creator is found to be wholly just, since He grants the grace of mercy to the former, while to the latter He does not grant the same grace, although by a hidden yet just judgment.”

While we were all created upright in Adam and received freedom of will without the impediment or interruption of any difficulty, Adam sinned voluntarily; and in him, as the Apostle bears witness, all sinned (Romans V). Thus all who were subsequently born from him, of either sex, lost the dignity of their condition, and by our own merit incurred the punishment of sin—that is, concupiscence and death, not only of the soul but also of the body.

This is why we are not born as Adam was created by God, but as sinners originally, condemned to the punishment of sin. The first of these states was brought about by the voluntary guilt of our first parent; the second is the dreadful severity of the most just Judge punishing that guilt.

Since, then, we are all condemned together, God has mercy on whichever of us He wills, and hardens whichever He wills—that is, leaves him in his own hardness. He has mercy through great goodness; He hardens without any injustice.

Thus He predestines those whom He hardens, not by driving them toward punishment, but by not withdrawing them from the sin that deserves punishment—just as He hardened Pharaoh’s heart, not by forcing him into guilt, but by not recalling him from guilt after it had been softened by grace.

In this way we may rightly say that those who pray, “Do not lead us into temptation,” are led by God into temptation—not because He Himself leads them into the temptation of evil, since elsewhere it is taught that He is “untempted by evils” (James I), but because, by a certain manner of speaking, He is said to lead them into temptation when He permits those whom He has abandoned in judgment to be led into temptation, and grace does not lead them out of temptation.

Yet no one should suppose that the truth of predestination imposes a fatal necessity upon either the just or the unjust reprobate, since in both groups the suspicion of necessity is excluded by the freedom of the will. The elect, receiving from God both the will and the power to accomplish, willingly do what earns eternal reward; the wicked, abandoned by that same God, act not unwillingly but willingly, and thereby do what justly merits eternal punishment.

Who, then—if I may speak mildly, who but a dull person—would assert necessity where he sees will reigning, either aided by mercy or abandoned by divine judgment?

The divine utterances thus commend the will of the good: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly desire His commandments” (Psalm III). On the other hand, they reveal the will of the wicked as follows: “He did not wish to understand, so as to act well; he meditated iniquity in his heart; he stood in every way that was not good, and he did not hate wickedness” (Psalm XXXV).

The unjust person is therefore permitted to do what he chose, so that God’s good work amid evil might make clear the difference between one who serves Him and one who does not, and so that those who have been saved might recognize how great their thanks to God ought to be, when, having the same cause of condemnation, they see in the other what they themselves escaped through the grace of their Deliverer.

This assertion of the will has a place even in the case of the recently born. For either, if they die after receiving the grace of baptism, they are saved by God’s will; or, deprived of that same grace by the judgment of the same God, they are condemned for the inherited sin committed through the will of their father.

I have simply disclosed to you what I think. You, in turn, if you differ from me in anything, do not hesitate to disclose it. I sent a similar letter to our Pardulus [Note: Bishop of Laon.].

I desire that you may prosper happily.

194. LETTER 130

[Note: This letter was written by Lupus in the name of Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, and his suffragans. That it is not complete is evident from the letter which Pope Nicholas wrote to them, first published by the most distinguished man John Cordesius, canon of Limoges, in an appendix to the letters of Hincmar, and later by R. P. Sirmond in volume III of the Councils of Gaul. The reason for writing this Lupine letter was as follows. Herimannus, bishop of Nevers, was, as Wenilo complained at the synod held at Soissons in April 853, of such doubtful health and suffered from so severe a headache that he seemed somehow to have fallen into insanity, and thereby dishonored the episcopal college by his conduct. “It was enjoined upon the metropolitan”—namely, Wenilo—“that, taking several bishops with him, he should proceed to the town of Nevers and prudently settle all ecclesiastical affairs there. He was also to keep his fellow bishop Herimannus with him at the city of Sens until the summer season had passed, which was reported to be very harmful to his illness; and then, with the Lord’s favor, once he had become accustomed to suitable abstinence, been instructed in episcopal gravity, and formed according to apostolic conduct, the clergy and people should recall him usefully to his own see, with God’s grace favoring them.” After the summer had almost passed, Herimannus, who was undoubtedly being advanced by the favor of King Charles, appeared to have returned to a better way of life. For this reason the bishops assembled at the palace of Vermeria in the following month of August restored Herimannus “to his jurisdiction and authority, to his episcopal guardianship, and to the governance of his own Church.” Some years afterward Nicholas became pope and was seated on Peter’s throne. Meanwhile Herimannus returned to his former errors and aroused Wenilo’s anger against him. Since Herimannus was favored by Charles, and it was therefore not easy for the bishops to remove him from the see of Nevers, Wenilo, wishing to crush him more forcefully, invoked the authority of the Roman pontiff in his own name and that of his suffragans, being well aware of the temper of his times. Pope Nicholas eagerly seized this opportunity. Having praised at length Wenilo’s and his suffragans’ piety and reverence toward the apostolic see, he perceived that the occasion could establish an example for the future. Acting more cautiously, he drew the case to himself under the pretext that no one should be condemned in his absence and unheard, especially by a judge who is wholly ignorant of the crime. Wenilo had not reported any specific offenses of Herimannus, but only in general terms that, although he had often been admonished and long awaited so that he might recover, he had nevertheless not been reformed and therefore could not fulfill the episcopal office. Accordingly, Nicholas declared that the accused’s faults had to be investigated. What happened afterward is unknown to me. Perhaps Wenilo was rebuked by the Gallican bishops—whom Nicholas, in writing to Wenilo, not obscurely reproaches as showing too little deference to the authority of the Roman bishop and presuming to decide episcopal cases in their own provinces by their own right. Perhaps Wenilo was also rebuked by the king, because without his knowledge he had appealed to the Roman pope against a Gallican bishop, and therefore abandoned the accusation.]

TO POPE NICHOLAS. [Col. 0608B] In the name of Guenilo and his suffragans.

We bring to the attention of your most gentle fatherhood that in our diocese [Note: That is, province, as we noted in the letter 84. For the bishop of Nevers is a suffragan of the archbishop of Sens. Thus Ivo of Chartres, writing to Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, says in letter 61: “But concerning the fact that you have decided to perform at Autun the consecration of the elected bishop of Nevers, which belongs to our diocese…”] in a town called Nevers there is someone endowed with episcopal office, named H., who, although frequently admonished and long awaited so that he might recover, is not capable of fulfilling that office with a sound mind.

Pope Melchiades is said [Note: This decree of Pope Melchiades appears in his letter to the Spanish bishops: “Do not judge bishops; do not condemn them without the authority of this see. If you do so, your judgments will be void, and you will be condemned. For this privilege was established for this holy see from the time of the apostles, and it remains inviolate to the present day.” It would undoubtedly have been established that bishops’ judgments were reserved to the Roman pontiff if the authority of this letter had prevailed. But because it had first emerged in those times—having long been hidden in Spain until Bishop Riculfus of Mainz, who flourished under Charlemagne, brought the Isidorian Collection from there into Gaul—it seemed altogether exposed to suspicion on account of its novelty. This was especially so because the Gallican bishops, who refused to admit that Collection, publicly declared that the letters of the ancient Roman prelates brought forth by Isidore possessed no authority, because they did not appear in the Code of Canons. Accordingly, Wenilo, who understood that his own authority needed the support of external power, undoubtedly desired above all that some means should at last be found by which the Gallican bishops would not be free to reject the authority of Melchiades’ letter. Since, however, the matter had to be handled with a certain skill, lest causes of anger be supplied to his colleagues, he judged that his action should be so moderated that, although he might seem to doubt greatly the letter’s authenticity, he would nevertheless provide the Roman bishop with an opportunity to draw episcopal judgments to himself. Therefore, to remove every occasion for criticism from his fellow bishops, he decided that the archives of the Roman see should be consulted, and that Pope Nicholas, who then presided over that see, should be asked to send him an authentic copy of that Melchiadian letter, taken from those archives. “Therefore,” he says, “we beseech you to deign to send us its statutes intact, just as they are held among you.” Wenilo’s request was certainly most reasonable: if anyone suspects a letter attributed to some Roman pontiff of being forged, he ought to seek it in the archive of the Roman Church, as Jerome advised in his Apology against Rufinus. This was also done by Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, as is clear from his letter 15, written to Nothelm, archbishop of Canterbury. Nevertheless, this untimely and inappropriate request struck Nicholas’ suspicious mind, since he was eager to preserve his authority. For he saw that the question was probing the treasury of his dominion and that much was being demanded in the public interest: perhaps the Gallican bishops wished to know what the new pontiff Nicholas thought about those new letters of ancient pontiffs, and whether he would send the Melchiadian letter from the archive of the Roman Church, where it was plainly not found, after laying aside all shame. Therefore, that this suspicion or fear might not become evident, and that through imprudence he might not write something by which he would disgrace his own reputation if he were understood to be false, the most prudent man left the bishops of Sens without an answer in this matter. He evaded their request by praising them profusely and repeatedly insisting that the absent and unheard Herimannus ought not to be condemned. Later, however, this most religious pontiff became bolder. For, writing some years afterward to the Gallican bishops concerning the case of Rothad, bishop of Soissons, he did not hesitate to assert that the holy Roman Church kept in its archives these decretal constitutions of the ancient pontiffs. Later, the age of Gregory VII showed that Tertullian’s observation was entirely true: in his book On the Veiling of Virgins he says that, while the rule of faith remains unalterable and immutable, other matters of conduct and discipline admit the novelty of correction. For Nicholas had argued, and indeed with great force, that an absent bishop could not be condemned. Gregory VII, however, established this rule: “That the pope can depose an absent man.” In any event, I think it will be neither unpleasant nor useless, after these observations, to present to readers this letter of Nicholas to Wenilo, which displays great skill and industry. I have therefore thought that it ought to be added at the end of the notes. (See among the Works of Pope Nicholas, in Migne, Patrologia, volume CXIX.)]

Pope Melchiades decreed [Col. 0609A] that no pontiff should ever be deposed without the consent of the Roman pope. Therefore we beseech you to deign to send us his statutes intact, just as they are held among you, so that, strengthened by his words, we may either follow them, or, as blessed Gregory the teacher did with the bishop of Ariminum [Note: This decree of Gregory appears in book VII, letter 49, to Marianus, bishop of Ravenna. He decrees that, since the bishop of Ariminum was afflicted by such a severe headache that, even by his own confession, he could not rise to govern that Church, and had therefore asked Pope Gregory of Rome to provide him with a successor, Marianus should examine the man who had been elected; and, if he were found suitable, should send him to Gregory with the written decree: “So that, with the Lord of the Church disposing, he may be consecrated bishop by us.” Thus, if the bishop of Ariminum had been so obstinate that he refused to acknowledge his illness and had not sought permission to withdraw from the sacred ministry, Gregory would by no means have attempted to place a bishop over him, however mentally incapacitated he might be. In that case, however, Gregory teaches in book XI, letter 8, that an assistant should be given to a mentally incapacitated and ineffective bishop, to perform the episcopal office—namely, those duties which concern jurisdiction, as we say today—and that, if he outlives the sick bishop, he may succeed him in his place. Thus the example of the bishop of Ariminum had no force in the case of Herimannus, bishop of Nevers, who plainly resisted Wenilo’s desire to ordain another in his place. A later age did not hesitate to hold that one who is unequal to the burden should be removed from episcopal office. For Matthew Paris relates that Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, while presiding at the synod of Westminster in 1075, thought it a just cause for deposing a bishop if he were so ignorant and unfamiliar with secular affairs that he could neither speak French nor give advice to his king in emerging matters; and for this reason he decreed that Ulstan, bishop of Worcester, should be deposed. Paris, however, relates that God judged otherwise. Nor can I refrain here from recalling the wisdom of my fellow countryman, Pope Innocent VI. In 1358 he ordered that Salviannus, bishop of Worms, who was burdened both by old age and by serious bodily illness, be given an assistant by Gerlach, archbishop of Mainz, but without future succession, in accordance with the rule prescribed by Gregory the Great. By this single act, even if the other arguments were lacking, I would prove that Innocent was a man of the ancient custom. Innocent III had been bolder; Matthew Paris calls him “the bold jurist.” For in 1209 he ordered the bishop of Périgueux in Aquitaine Secunda to be compelled to resign, because he appeared ineffective and was wasting the Church’s goods.] who was suffering from a similar infirmity, or, as Saint Gelasius teaches, let the mentally incapacitated man be removed [Note: Gelasius’ authority should be sought in his letter to the bishops Rusticus and Fortunatus, which appears in Gratian, 7, question 2, chapter “Nuper.” In it Gelasius says that he had previously decreed that in the Church of one suffering from epilepsy the neighboring bishops should make a suitable visitation—that is, should exercise episcopal office there because of the illness of its own bishop. This is the same as saying that a mentally stricken man should be removed from episcopal duty, to use Lupus’ words; and the statement agrees with the view of Gregory the Great. Following this form, the bishops assembled at the synod of Soissons, mindful of the letter of Saint Gregory, which they cite, decreed that, during Herimannus’ illness, Wenilo, the metropolitan, should “provide and arrange for the Church of Nevers whatever it required through a visitation.” For these most prudent men knew that the boundaries established by our fathers must not be transgressed, nor the ancient rules abandoned unless overwhelming necessity compelled it.]

So that we may know the truth beyond doubt, we seek and await your judgment, lest we incur in any way the charge of rashness, but, guided by your direction, may in no respect depart from the path of truth and righteousness.

[Col. 0611]

THE COUNCIL OF VERNUM

[Note: Lupus declares himself to be the author of the canons of this council in letter 42, where, speaking of Charles the Bald, he writes to Hincmar, archbishop of Reims: “If he had accepted the counsels that were sought and discovered at Vernum, the one of whom the sacred writings say, ‘There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord,’ would already have established him reigning in peace. I sent you, in my own hand, those same canons—or, as you call them, chapters—which I then committed to writing. I believe that a later age will judge their equity, and that the searcher of hearts and kidneys will not forget my devotion.” Certainly many things in these canons breathe the spirit of Lupus so strongly that it is entirely necessary to acknowledge them as the work of the same author as the Lupine letters, as we shall note shortly. From this it seems to me that Charles, whom Lupus reproaches for not observing the canons of Vernum, can be excused because they had not yet become known to him, as the bishops of the synod of Meaux complain. For this reason they believe that the Normans were sent by God as avengers: “The fourth matter,” they say, “was begun by agreement at the aforesaid assembly [at Thionville] and completed at the palace of Vernum; but through the envy and wickedness of the devil or his ministers it had not yet been disclosed to the ears of the prince and people. Since, therefore, as was necessary, obedience did not follow the divine commands, the Lord gave from the North—from which, according to the prophet, every evil is spread forth—apostles worthy of our merits, namely the cruelest and most savage persecutors of Christendom, the Northmen,” and so forth.]

HELD IN THE YEAR 844

195. The canons of the council held at the palace of Vernum, where Ebroinus, bishop of Poitiers, presided; together with Wenilo, archbishop of Sens; and Louis, abbot of Saint-Denis; and Hincmar, later bishop of Reims, in the fifth year of the reign of our lord Charles, son of the emperor Louis, in the month of December, in the seventh indiction.

196. PREFACE

[Col. 0611A] We, the bishops and other faithful who have been summoned to Vernum from various regions, give thanks to almighty God, illustrious King Charles, because, having laid aside the discord from which so many evils have arisen—evils which it would take too long to enumerate and which we still cannot avoid—you have returned to peace with your brothers, to whom you are bound both by nature and by religion [Note: You returned to peace. Namely, at the synod at Thionville, in the place called the Judgment, where the three brothers—namely, the emperor Lothair, Louis king of Germany, and Charles the Bald king of the Franks—met in October 844 and became friends.] We beseech you through Christ, who is our peace, that you may always remain in it, so that you, who see your greatest affairs almost ruined by discord, may soon see them restored by harmony and faithful assistance.

For we must yield to God, of whom the most truthful Scriptures say: “The Most High has power over the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he wishes” (Daniel 4); and who, with wondrous condescension, promises: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5).

Since, moreover, under the inspiration of that same God you have deigned to command us to deliberate about the condition of the Church, which has been grievously disordered by the magnitude and multitude of our sins—in his name and with his help we humbly disclose to your Highness and to the devotion of the faithful people what we have discovered through common deliberation.

We do not claim to approve ourselves as righteous. Considering our conscience, let us humbly say with Jeremiah: “It is through the Lord’s mercy that we have not been consumed, because his compassions have not failed” (Lamentations 3). But as we meditate on returning to God and bringing you back with us, we perform our duty, which will benefit all who consent to it. For we speak to you not by our authority but by that of the one who says: “Whoever is of God hears God’s words” (John 8). But may what follows not be fulfilled in you: “Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God.”

197. CANONS

I. That the king should place the worship of God above all things and preserve mercy together with judgment and justice.

Accordingly, we first address you because your integrity can benefit all your subjects: place the worship of God above all things. For he himself says: “Those who honor me I will honor; but those who despise me shall be held of no account” (1 Samuel 2).

Moreover, preserve mercy, judgment, and justice: let mercy temper the severity of power; let judgment restrain those who persist in sin; and let justice restore what is fitting to those who deserve it. For it is written: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5); and: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and practice justice at all times” (Psalm CV); and: “The honor of a king loves judgment” (Psalm XCVIII); and: “Justice strengthens the king’s throne” (Proverbs XXV), as the authority of the wisest Solomon—or rather of God speaking through him—declares.

If you act in this way, divine grace will, as we believe, provide you either with a bloodless victory [Note: A bloodless victory. Lupus, letter 38, to Charles the Bald: “May he grant you long health, a bloodless victory, and perpetual peace.”] or with a just victory over your enemies.

David and Hezekiah can serve as examples to you. By the merit of their holiness they overcame the enemies of God’s people with wondrous speed, whether by fighting or by prayer. So too can your own household’s light, Emperor Charles, who adorned the name that he bestowed upon your family through his most illustrious deeds.

God’s same grace will grant you not merely the greatness and stability of your kingdom, but, if you govern well, eternal glory after the course of this life. To that glory the king and prophet sighed when he said: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Psalm 17).

We do not bring these matters rashly before your Majesty, since you too have been entrusted to our care. Through our ministry, by faith and baptism, you have been cleansed and await with all the faithful the day of the dreadful judgment.

II. That legates from the king’s side should be sent to restrain perpetrators of crimes and despisers of apostolic discipline.

But, to return to us bishops: during this civil discord we have sometimes neglected many things in ourselves and in those entrusted to us, and at other times have been forced to neglect them. Thus religion has suffered great damage in every order. Some, through ignorance, are heading toward destruction; others, having grown accustomed to prolonged license, trust that they may sin with impunity.

Accordingly, now turning to the correction of ourselves and of others, we ask that perpetrators of crimes and despisers of apostolic discipline be restrained by trusted legates sent from your side [Note: From your side. The bishops ask King Charles to send legates from his side into the provinces to restrain the bishops’ offenses and order the canons to be observed; and they ask that these legates be instructed, in performing their duty, to show themselves impartial, without regard to persons or being blinded by gifts—that is, chaste, abstinent, and upright. Bishop Jonas of Orléans presses this argument forcefully in book II, chapter 24, of On the Instruction of the Laity. In earlier times, princes sent certain men into the provinces whom they honored with the dignity of legates from their side, as Jerome Bignonius observed in his notes on Marculf, and Christophorus Justellus in his notes on the Code of the Canons of the African Church. Legates from the emperor’s side are also mentioned in the Life of the Emperor Louis the Pious under the years 824 and 827.] without regard to persons or blindness caused by gifts. Then, with leisure granted to us as far as possible, the word of God may bear fruit through preaching, and the venerable authority of the canons may everywhere possess its due force.

III. That religious and suitable men should be sent to investigate monasteries in which discipline has collapsed and afterward report to the synod.

In holy places—that is, monasteries—we have found that some, through zeal, others through laziness, and many overcome by necessity and want of clothing, have deviated from their profession. We ask that religious and suitable men be sent throughout all the parishes [Note: Parishes. That is, dioceses, as he said. At that time, and for a long while previously, the word was used to signify an entire bishop’s diocese. But since R. P. Cellotius interpreted a passage from Sulpicius Severus differently, it will not be useless to pause here briefly and restore light to this passage of Severus. In the age of Sulpicius Severus there were no churches except episcopal and parish churches. Other sacred buildings were called oratories, as is well known. For even in the time of the emperor Justinian monks did not possess a church, as Cujacius noted on the fifth novella of that emperor. Yet Cellotius thinks that all monks are insulted if they are denied churches in their monasteries in those ancient times; and therefore he criticizes the most illustrious Francis Hallier, later bishop of Cabellicum, because Hallier noted that wherever the word “Church” is found among the ancients, a parish church must be understood. To prove that Hallier was mistaken, Cellotius cites the authority of Sulpicius Severus, whose words in chapter 3 of the first Dialogue are: “After departing from there, I went to the town of Bethlehem, which is six miles from Jerusalem and sixteen stages from Alexandria. The priest Jerome governs the church of that place. For it is in the parish of the bishop who holds Jerusalem.” From this passage Cellotius concludes that Jerome did not possess the church—that is, in the language of our age, the parish church—of the city of Bethlehem, since the parish belonged to the bishop, and therefore not every church is a parish. “Thus,” he says, “the monastery has its own church, indeed in the city, distinct from the city’s parish. Jerome, who does not agree with the bishop, does not possess the monastery’s church.” Cellotius plainly failed to notice that Severus does not use the word “parish” here in the sense in which we use it today. Severus meant that the Bethlehem church, the parish church, was in the parish—that is, the diocese—of the bishop of Jerusalem. It follows that Jerome held the parish church of the town of Bethlehem from the bishop of Jerusalem, contrary to Cellotius’ view. For it is firmly and consistently established, beyond all controversy, that Jerome governed the church of the town of Bethlehem. This was why the author of the book On Heresies, to which Sirmond gave the title Predestinatus, calls Jerome “the Bethlehemite presbyter.”] by your gentleness, with knowledge of the bishops, so that they may investigate and correct them, and at a time appointed by you report the condition of each place to your Highness and to our humble selves.

IV. That wandering monks should return to their own places and that fugitives or expelled monks should be corrected; likewise concerning clerics who desert their churches.

We order that monks who wander about for the sake of greed and shamelessly disgrace the purpose of holy religion return to their own places and be received through the prudent care of their abbots.

For those who, after an evident monastic profession, have also abandoned the habit, or who are expelled through their own fault, we believe that a remedy can be provided if, unless they consent to return and fulfill what they promised to God, they are confined in prisons [Note: In prisons. This canon was imitated from chapter 6 of Pope Siricius’ letter to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, where it is written: “So that, shut up in their prisons, they may lament such a great crime with continual mourning,” and so forth.] and kept away from human society for as long as necessary, and subjected, for the sake of mercy, to suitable works until they accept the health of correction.
