Those who were once monks but afterward, having abandoned the profession of solitude, descend to military service or marriage must be cleansed by satisfaction in public penance, according to Pope Leo’s decree (letter to Rusticus).

Concerning clerics who desert their churches, the ancient rule of the Council of Chalcedon must be observed [can. XXI]. It prescribes that, if a bishop receives a cleric belonging to another bishop, both the cleric received and the bishop receiving him are to be deprived of communion until the cleric who migrated returns to his own Church.

V. Concerning those who unlawfully associate with nuns.

Those who unlawfully associate with nuns and enter into sacrilegious unions with them are, by the judgment of Pope Innocent [Note: Of Pope Innocent. Either Lupus was deceived by his memory here, or the scribe made an error. For that decree is not Innocent’s but Gelasius’, among whose decrees it appears as chapter 20: “We have learned that certain men rashly associate themselves with consecrated virgins and, after their dedication to God, enter into incestuous and sacrilegious unions with them. It is right that such men should immediately be expelled from sacred communion and not received at all except through public and approved penance. Nevertheless, if they have repented, the viaticum should not be denied them when they depart from this world.” This decree is cited from Gelasius in Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 106.] ordered to be suspended from communion and not to be received at all except through public and approved penance; yet, if they have repented, the viaticum is not to be denied them when they depart from this world.

VI. Concerning a betrothed woman carried off by another man and the punishment of the abductor.

A girl betrothed to one man but carried off by another is to be restored to the man to whom she had been betrothed, according to the statutes of the Council of Ancyra (can. X), even if she suffered violence from the abductor.

Concerning abductors, we think the best course is that, since they make little of ecclesiastical excommunication, they should be terrified by the severity of secular laws.

VII. Concerning nuns who, for religious reasons, assume men’s clothing or cut their hair.

If any nuns, for the sake of religion—as they falsely suppose—either assume men’s clothing or cut their hair [Note: Cut their hair. The reason for this prohibition is explained by canon 17 of Gangra in these words: “If any woman, because of divine worship, as she supposes, cuts the hair which God gave her as a reminder of subjection, let her be anathema as dissolving the commandment of obedience.” In my opinion this concerns married women, who ought to be subject to their husbands. For this type of nun had not yet been devised, a type which arose later, among whom the hair of those who undertake the holy institute is immediately cut.] we judge that, since they err more through ignorance than zeal, they should be admonished and corrected, lest, as transgressors of the Old and New Scriptures, they be cut off from the body of the Church by the severity of an anathema, according to the Synod of Gangra (can. XIII).

VIII. That bishops who do not go to war should entrust their men to one of the king’s faithful.

Since bodily weakness protects some bishops from the labor of military expedition, while your indulgence grants others the rest desired by all, precautions must be taken for both groups lest military affairs suffer loss through their absence.

Therefore, if your Highness approves, let them entrust their men, who can benefit the commonwealth, to whichever of your faithful they judge suitable for the purpose; and let them be kept under observation by his diligence, so that they may not be able to withdraw themselves from their duty.

IX. That a bishop should as soon as possible be appointed to the Church of Reims, long deprived of a shepherd.

201. [Note: The Church of Reims. Its last bishop, Ebbo, had been deposed on the charge of treason because he had joined the party of Lothair, son of Louis the Pious, who had dared to oppress his father to such an extent that he even confined him in prison and arranged that Ebbo be subjected to public penance. From that time the Church of Reims had been without an archbishop. The bishops assembled at the synod of Vernum grieve over this and ask Charles to appoint to that see a bishop capable of restoring the many ruins that Church had suffered. This was done in 845 at the synod of Beauvais, where Hincmar, with the support of King Charles, was ordained archbishop of Reims, as Flodoard relates in book III, chapter 1, of his History of Reims. Hincmar himself, in chapter 36 of his later work against Gottschalk, moderates his wording so that he seems to say that he was requested by the bishops assembled at the synod of Beauvais, and that, in response to their prayers, King Charles allowed Hincmar, although from another province, to become archbishop of Reims.]

We cannot acknowledge without profound grief that the Church of Reims, long and greatly deprived of a shepherd, recently stripped of its possessions and burdened with injuries, remains without one. Since we desire to rescue both your Highness and our lowliness from danger, we beseech you to restore that Church, so shamefully torn apart, and, in accordance with the constitution of the venerable canons, promptly seek out and appoint to it a worthy bishop. Thus the clergy and people, worn down by such great spiritual and bodily afflictions, may, having received consolation with their bishop, strive to supplicate the common Lord for your salvation and prosperity.

X. That the king should permit the ordination of Agius as bishop of the Church of Orléans to stand.

The Church of Orléans is also known to be suffering from the greatest confusion. Nevertheless, since last year Archbishop Wenilo, with the support of his suffragans, ordained Agius, a priest of your palace, from that same place to the aforesaid Church [Note: Agius the priest. A relative of Jonas, bishop of Orléans, who had recently died, as Lupus teaches in letter 21.]—having been supported by the testimony and urged by the petition of reputable canons and laymen—and since that Church is exposed to danger for both us and you, we see no other outcome in this matter than that your piety should permit what was done by so many men [Note: Permit it to stand. The Gallican bishops therefore recognized at that time that an ordination lacking royal consent was not valid. Why would they have asked Charles to permit Agius’ ordination to stand if the prince had possessed no right in the matter? Moreover, to draw him more easily toward consent, they flatter him by saying that Agius was a priest of the royal palace.] to stand.

XI. Concerning the advancement of Drogo: it should appear necessary to await the assembly and consent of the bishops of Gaul and Germany.

Concerning the advancement of the most reverend Drogo [Note: Drogo. Archbishop of Metz, to whom Pope Sergius II had delegated the functions of the apostolic see. Drogo was a son of Charlemagne by a concubine, and therefore, as Hincmar says, “raised up by the arrogance of royal lineage, he obtained from Pope Sergius the advancement in the regions beyond the Alps during the time of the emperor Lothair. But what he sought through affection he did not obtain in reality; and what he could not obtain by force, since those concerned did not consent, he bore with the greatest patience, as was fitting for him, lest by causing scandal to his brother priests he introduce schism into the Church.” Thus, although Drogo presided at the council at Thionville, in the place called the Judgment, it should not immediately be supposed that this honor was granted to him because he represented the apostolic see. It was granted to his nobility, not to his legation. For it is expressly written in the heading of the synod at Thionville that Drogo presided there with the consent of those same kings, namely Lothair, Louis, and Charles. See the most illustrious Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, book VI, chapter 29, of On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire.]

We dare define nothing except that the greatest assembly that can be convened from Gaul and Germany should be awaited, and that at it the consent of the other metropolitans and bishops should be sought—a consent which we neither wish nor are able to resist.

For our part, if such a matter can be entrusted to anyone, and if no other reason lies hidden beneath the one being alleged, it seems especially suited to him who is joined to us by the communion of the priesthood and to your Highness by the privilege of kinship.

## XII. That the ecclesiastical places and estates possessed by laymen be restored to churches and monasteries

We now come to the final part of our admonition. May God grant that you, the nobles, and all the other faithful receive with equal devotion this admonition which we pour forth with such purpose. For we see that God’s anger hangs over us and over you—not only on account of robberies and other monstrous crimes [Col. 0617C], but especially because the resources of the Church, which kings and other Christians have vowed to God for the support of God’s servants and the poor, for the reception of guests, the redemption of captives, and the restoration of God’s temples, are now [Note: [Col. 0618C] In secular use. Who does not see that this was written for the recovery of the cell of Saint Judoc? Louis the Pious, as Lupus repeatedly emphasizes, had given it to the monastery of Ferrières, but Charles had taken it away in order to hand it over to Count Odulph, plainly a secular man. But here are Lupus’s words from Letter 44, to Hincmar of Reims, concerning the recovery of the cell—so similar to the words of this canon that an egg is scarcely more like an egg:

“We are therefore compelled to wear garments that are worn out and patched, and to temper our hunger almost always with vegetables and purchased legumes. Hence the sick complain: guests seek the customary provisions among us but do not find them. The present times are disgraced, and God is undoubtedly provoked to vengeance.”

Likewise, in Letter 71, to King Charles, before the recovery of the cell:

“For this reason the servants of God, who constantly pray for you, have not received their customary clothing during these three years; what they are forced to wear is worn out and mostly patched, and they are sustained by purchased legumes, while they very rarely receive the consolation of fish and cheese.”] being kept for secular use. Consequently, many servants of God suffer want of food, drink, and clothing; the poor do not receive their customary alms; guests are neglected; captives are defrauded; and the reputation of all is deservedly torn apart.

Indeed, if the Church suffered these things at the hands of pagans, she would demand patience. But now, oppressed by our own sons—that is, by those whom we or our predecessors have begotten in Christ, making them Christians through our ministry—we receive no consolation of patience, because we fear their destruction [Note: [Col. 0618D] “We fear.” Lupus, Letter 44, in the same matter: “I fear beyond what can be said lest he very soon provide his enemies with the joy they desire.”].

Certainly, no one, however shameless, will dare deny that the possession of the Church is the vow of the faithful, the patrimony of the poor, and the redemption of souls. How, then, does anyone dare to take away from God another person’s vow? With what audacity does anyone presume to invade the inheritance of the poor? [Col. 0618B] From the place where some redeemed their souls, why do others lose theirs?

Therefore, certain venerable places [Note: [Col. 0618D] “Venerable places,” that is, monasteries. Above, canon 3: “in holy places,” that is, monasteries], something never before heard of, are wholly possessed by laymen; in some they claim a share for themselves; and the estates of others, divided in many ways, they have caused to be handed over to them as an inheritance.

The Egyptian priests, when hunger compelled everyone else to sell everything, retained their possessions (Genesis 47); and false gods earned reverence from their worshipers, which in this respect the one true God alone does not receive. Uzzah was struck down because he presumed to support the tottering ark, which it was unlawful to touch (2 Samuel 6). Let someone laugh at this—unless, as we say with the deepest grief, certain oppressors of the Church in our own time have also found an end worthy of their conduct.

The prophet cries out:

> “Those who said, ‘Let us possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance’: O my God, make them like a wheel and like stubble before the face of the wind” (Psalm 82).

Finally, the Lord Jesus himself, its founder and redeemer, says:

> “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but loses himself and brings ruin upon himself?” [Col. 0619A] (Matthew 16).

And is anyone so audacious and desperate as to seize and invade God’s possessions to his own certain destruction? [Note: [Col. 0619B] “Certain destruction.” Lupus, Letter 55, speaking of Count Adulph, who possessed the cell of Judoc: “He is said, he says, to be languishing—not so dangerously that, once admonished, he might be corrected, which we would wish; nor so gravely that he might die, which we would grieve on account of his certain damnation.”]

O you who are faithful to God and to yourselves, do not, for the sake of temporal abundance of riches, earn an everlasting accumulation of miseries; and do not any longer defile the honor of your souls with so destructive, so unheard-of, and finally so certain a sacrilege. Return to God what is his, so that you may possess what is yours in peace, escape eternal torments, and afterward be admitted, as faithful servants, to the joy of our Lord.

Let secular persons possess secular honors; let ecclesiastical persons receive ecclesiastical honors. Nor should you accuse us of insatiable greed, since, whatever we may be, you yourselves know that we speak the truth. And although we are few, there are nevertheless some among us [Note: [Col. 0619B] “Some among us.” Lupus, Letter 42, to Hincmar, concerning the recovery of that same cell:

“Let my own advantage have done this. Why has the holiness of so many men who serve God with me been despised? At your reminder, we ought to know that there are among us some of whom Scripture rightly testifies: ‘He will fulfill the desire of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayer.’”] who fear God and who, in accordance with that prophetic saying [Col. 0619B], will be heard:

> “He will fulfill the desire of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayer” (Psalm 145).

For the end of all things approaches daily; and the things that are seen are temporal, while the things that are not seen are eternal. If we wish to escape present calamities and avoid future miseries, let us all together turn from our wickedness to the Lord; and, turning away from evil, let us do good, so that we may deserve to see the Lord’s goodness in the land of the living (Psalm 36; 1 Peter 3; Psalm 27).

But you, most illustrious king, since it is written most truly, “Bad company corrupts good character” (1 Corinthians 15), flee the companionship and counsels of the wicked [Note: [Col. 0619C] “The companionship of the wicked.” Lupus, Letter 64, which is an exhortation to King Charles: “Avoid the society of evil men, since, as you recall from Scripture, bad company corrupts good character”], and let no one dare to ask you for what it would not befit your majesty to grant [Note: [Col. 0619C] “Dare to ask.” Lupus, in the same Letter 64: “Embrace honorable truth, so that no one who knows better may dare to ask from you what does not befit you to grant.”].

Nor fear angry men [Note: [Col. 0619C] “Nor fear the angry.” Lupus, in the same Letter 64: “Do not fear the powerful, whom you yourselves have made and whom, whenever you wish, you can reduce. Do not place your confidence in princes, in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. Rather, transfer your hope to God, who made heaven and earth and who keeps faith forever”], that is, earth and ashes, more than God, who created you and who will judge you in truth. If you follow his will perfectly, we believe that he will free you from the defiance of any men [Note: [Col. 0620B] “Will free you from defiance.” Lupus, in the same Letter 64:

“By diligently observing these things, you will please God and all good people; and you will crush and overcome the rebels, with God—as we believe—fighting on your behalf. Then, after a temporal and laborious reign, you will attain an eternal and truly peaceful one.”], mercifully rescue you from every distress, and after this temporal kingdom lead you, with happiness heaped upon happiness, to the everlasting kingdom.

In conclusion, we address everyone: if you accept our salutary counsels, we shall rejoice greatly in your advancement. But if you despise us—or rather, God speaking through us—we shall be compelled by the necessity of fulfilling our ministry to pronounce a sentence against you, something we would be unwilling to do [Note: [Col. 0620B] “Necessity of fulfilling the ministry.” Thus the Fathers of the universal synod held at Saponaria in 859, writing to the bishops of Brittany concerning the reverence owed by those bishops to Herard, metropolitan of Tours, say at the end:

“But if, which we do not wish, you should henceforth withdraw from the care of that same metropolitan, and it should become clear that you are resisting our exhortations flowing from charity, we shall be compelled by the necessity of our ministry to pronounce a canonical sentence against you.”

For wounds that do not respond to the medicine of soothing applications must necessarily be cut out with a knife, as Pope Siricius writes to Himerius—that is, with the knife of excommunication, as Julianus Pomerius interprets it. But elsewhere we shall discuss more fully, in our notes on the letters of Ruricius, bishop of Limoges, the moderation and wisdom of the ancient bishops in applying the knife of excommunication. It will not then be useless to investigate more deeply whether, during those turbulent times, the authority of the Roman bishop was developed in this matter.]

[Col. 0619]

# B. THE BOOK OF SERVATUS LUPUS, ABBOT OF FERRIÈRES, ON THE THREE QUESTIONS

[Note: [Col. 0619D] For the past fifteen years there has been a great dispute among scholars: whether the *Book* and the *Collectaneum on the Three Questions* belonged to Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, or to Servatus Lupus the priest, who was supposedly different from the abbot of Ferrières. But when I consider the matter, it is perfectly clear to me that learned men sometimes become stuck even on matters of no importance—as I believe happened in this case. For if anyone were to compare those little books with Lupus’s letters, he could not reject the truth that forces itself upon his eyes, nor would he unwillingly admit that the little books were written in the same style as the letters. I think this will be still clearer if, in the following notes, I transcribe from the letters phrases similar to and familiar in Lupus of Ferrières, which the author of the little books used.

As for the fact that some are influenced by the authority of Trithemius, who writes that Servatus Lupus the priest died in 851 and thus seems to distinguish him from Lupus of Ferrières, that authority is not weighty enough to hold anyone back—especially if the matter is examined more deeply and Trithemius’s own words are carefully considered. For if the Lupus to whom Rabanus wrote eight books on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans is himself the author of the book *On the Three Questions*, it cannot be denied that this work must be restored to Lupus, abbot of Ferrières. For while still a monk and deacon, Lupus had been sent by Abbot Aldric to Rabanus for the sake of study, so that he might be instructed in the doctrine of Sacred Scripture; and he encouraged Rabanus to publish a commentary on Paul’s Epistles, as can be gathered from Rabanus himself in his letter to Bishop Samuel. That this Lupus was at a considerable distance from Rabanus when the commentary was written is clear from Rabanus’s letter to Lupus.

Since, moreover, the letter to Samuel mentioned above shows that the monk and deacon Lupus had been advanced from the diaconate to a higher rank when that letter was written, I believe it is clear that the Lupus in question was once a monk and deacon and afterward a priest and abbot of Ferrières. That he was a priest is attested by the Acts of the Council of Soissons, held in 853.

It is therefore false what Trithemius says: that Gottschalk was defeated and refuted at the Council of Mainz by Servatus Lupus. For these little books contain almost no doctrine other than that defended by Gottschalk. From this one may judge how reliable Trithemius’s reports of events are. His statement that Lupus departed to the Lord in 851 was undoubtedly his own conjecture.

Yet if someone obstinately insists that a certain Lupus the priest attended the Council of Mainz in 848, what prevents us from saying that Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, went there at that time to visit Rabanus, once his teacher? It is also possible that he was an envoy of Charles the Bald to Louis, king of Germany. For we learn from the *Annals of Fulda* that at that council or assembly there were envoys of Louis’s brothers—namely, Charles and Lothair—and that they were heard by him and dismissed.

Finally, lest the unusual name “Servatus Lupus” trouble anyone, we have from Letter 130, as Sirmond observed, that this was the true name of Lupus, abbot of Ferrières. For it cannot be denied that this letter, like many others, was written by Lupus the abbot of Ferrières in the name of Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, and his suffragans. Yet the old Floriacensian codex from which it was copied has this in the title of the letter:

“Written by Servatus Lupus to Pope Nicholas.”

Thus, after the conjecture of so great a man has been confirmed by the authority of an ancient codex, there should henceforth be no doubt about Lupus’s name.

Moreover, the most illustrious president Mauguin was pleased to maintain that the *Collectaneum* was indeed the work of Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, but that the book was by Lupus the priest of Mainz. Yet apart from the fact that Trithemius himself does not say where this Lupus was a priest, so that even if we granted that he was different from Lupus of Ferrières it would still not be established that he was a priest of Mainz, the two works seem so alike to me that I consider an egg scarcely more like an egg, and believe that one was composed from the other.]

## THE BOOK OF SERVATUS LUPUS, ABBOT OF FERRIÈRES, ON THE THREE QUESTIONS

[Col. 0619]

## 205. PREFACE OF JACQUES SIRMOND: On the two following little works and on the author’s name

[Col. 0619D] First, Reader, this must be established concerning the author’s name: he ought to be called not “Lupus Servatus,” as most people today call him with Sigebert and Trithemius, but “Servatus Lupus,” as the ancient books and copies of others show [Col. 0620D]. Just as no one doubts, in the cases of Caecilius Cyprian, Eusebius Jerome, Aurelius Augustine, Sulpicius Severus, and similar names, that the true and proper name of each is the one placed second, so in this case the name “Lupus” must be placed second because it is the proper name. We once discussed this matter in the notes to Sidonius, and there is no need to repeat it.

Of the book *On the Three Questions*, which occupies the first place here, three ancient copies came into our hands: one from Verdun, which belongs to us; another from Saint Arnulf at Metz; and a third from Saint Victor in Paris. We saw only a copy of a fourth, from the Cluniac monastery of Silviniacum. But, surprisingly, the Metz copy attributed it not to Lupus but to Bishop Hincmar; in the Silviniacum copy the name of Amalarius was attached to it, as I suppose because it followed Amalarius’s works in the same codex. In the Verdun and Victor copies, however, the true title was present: *The Book of Servatus Lupus on the Three Questions* [Col. 0621B].

Since we possessed only one copy of the *Collectaneum* on the same Questions—an anonymous and mutilated one from the library of Corbie, in which everything else was missing—the distinguished and most courteous J. Bouhier, senator of Dijon, conveniently sent us another complete copy from his own collection, bearing this title [Col. 0622A]: *The Collectaneum of Servatus Lupus on the Three Questions*. Relying on this evidence, when we prepared this edition three years ago, we allowed both works to be attributed to the same Lupus, although the matter had not been fully established.

As for the two remaining letters [Note: [Col. 0622D] They were published above as numbers 12 and 129], the one written to Hincmar occupies the first place in the Verdun and Elnon copies; the other, written to King Charles, precedes the *Collectaneum* in the Corbie copy and follows it in the Dijon copy. Since in both letters the author calls himself simply Lupus, anyone who argues that they should rather be attributed to Lupus of Ferrières—whose other letters to the same men survive and whose opening and closing forms of address are not dissimilar—will be free to do so.

Indeed, to state my own view, it was long my conjecture that the preceding little works also belonged to the same Lupus. This is now confirmed above all by the fact that the letter of Wenilo, apparently bishop of Sens, to Pope Nicholas concerning Herimann of Nevers shows that this Lupus’s first name was Servatus [Col. 0622B]. The letter was evidently written in the name of Wenilo, bishop of Sens, and reads as follows in the Floriacensian codex:

> “Written by Servatus Lupus to Pope Nicholas.”

“We submit to your most gentle fatherhood,” etc. It appears among the letters as number 130.

## 207. THE BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0621]

[Col. 0621D] When we share with others what we judge useful to us, we win God’s favor without opposition, since we respond to his command with devoted obedience; and if, with sincere goodwill, we impart what we have already received, we shall obtain through his gift what we have not yet received [Col. 0622D].

Reflecting on these matters with myself, after the persecutions and false opinions that had arisen from the beginning of the Lord’s incarnation had been overcome, and after I had discovered that, in the 849th year from that same incarnation, the Church was in the peace which the Savior left to her, promising that he himself would be with her, in accordance with his pledge, until the consummation of the age—I found that first in Italy and then in Gaul, although the faith was not being shaken, the understanding of certain people was certainly being disturbed, because various unheard-of claims were being publicly circulated concerning free will, the predestination of the good and the wicked, and the taxation of the Lord’s blood. I wished that those who could not investigate these matters for themselves might become better informed through me [Note: [Col. 0623C] “First in Italy.” I think it can be inferred from this passage that Lupus went to Italy in 849 to undertake the embassy which, on the order of King Charles, he had assumed to Pope Leo IV; he mentions it himself in his letter to Pope Benedict, which is number 103].

Having invoked the aid of God, from whom we have received not only existence but also knowledge [Col. 0623B], I first turned to those authorities to which the consensus of all the faithful assents. Then I anxiously and for a long time investigated what the most illustrious interpreters and most unconquered defenders of those authorities had thought about the questions mentioned above. Their works, brighter than the sun and illuminated by divine utterances, would rightly make me liable to the charge of superfluity or arrogance if everyone either understood or possessed them, and if I were merely to impose the same things upon them in different words, or presume that I could accomplish what they themselves had been unable to accomplish.

But since both gifts have been granted to many, one or the other to some, and perhaps neither to certain others, I shall strive to be of assistance to those who possess one or neither, without offending those who possess both—provided, that is, that they judge these writings of mine, whatever their worth, worthy of their consideration. Thus, I shall endeavor to carry out what I have undertaken, attributing little to myself and very much to God [Col. 0623C].

God, maker of all things, is free from place and time and therefore from all mutability. For he is not enclosed by a place that contains all things, nor is he increased by the passage of time, since no temporal beginning confines him. While preserving within himself, in eternal immutability, the principles of every creature, he made spiritual creation subject to time alone, but bodily creation subject not only to time but also to place.

Indeed, spiritual nature shows itself subject to time: created good, as is fitting for something created by a good God, it partly corrupted itself through its own fault and did not remain in the truth, and therefore fell; but partly, cleaving to its Creator in pious submission, it both revealed that it was capable of falling and received the gift of being so firmly established in such great happiness that it would fall no further.

For when the Redeemer had removed the notion of conjugal intercourse in the resurrection, he would certainly not have promised us equality with the angels if any suspicion of their sinning, and consequently falling, had remained in them [Note: [Col. 0623C] “The notion of conjugal intercourse.” He refers to the subtle question of the Sadducees. Since they were enemies of the resurrection, which Christ frequently proclaimed while living among human beings, they asked him about a woman who had had seven husbands: whose wife would she be after the resurrection? Jesus gave them a divine answer: there would be no marriage after the resurrection. “They neither marry,” he says, “nor are given in marriage.” By these words he removed the notion of conjugal intercourse in the resurrection, as Lupus says. The story is found in Matthew, Mark, and Luke].

For how would we be granted a happier condition than the one we now possess, unless, after passing through the danger of mortal life, we were placed in such security of blessedness that we could neither sin nor wish to sin any longer? The nature of the body, moreover, both began in time and acknowledges, through growth and decline, without the capacity to be transformed into another thing, the successive changes of mutability—all of which take place in time.

That it is subject to place is not doubted by anyone who considers that every body, consisting of length, breadth, and height, and called solid, is always contained only in a place. Preserving the properties of both natures—spiritual and bodily—God the Creator formed the human being from soul and body, as we learn from the same one who revealed this, namely, the one who made him.

Yet he made the soul in his own image [Note: [Col. 0623D] “In his own image.” Most of the ancients believed that the image of God said to exist in human beings was located in the soul, not in the body; for the image of something incorporeal cannot be a body, as Claudianus Mamertus says in Book III, chapter 16, of *On the Status of the Soul*. Hence Cassiodorus concludes, in chapter 8 of his book *On the Soul*, that the human soul is immortal because it was made in the likeness of God. “For,” he says, “how could it be the image or likeness of God if human souls were enclosed by the limit of death?”

Augustine too, in his book *On Heresies* addressed to Quodvultdeus [Col. 0624C], counts among the heresies the opinion of those who say that the human body, not the soul, is the image of God. These were the Homuncionites, as the author of the book to which Sirmond gave the title *Praedestinatus* teaches, Book I, chapter 76.

Let the most learned masters of theology consider, moreover, whether this opinion agrees with the principles of the philosophers, who say that the human being is constituted from soul and body—that is, that the soul alone is not the human being, nor the body alone. Yet God made the HUMAN BEING in his own image.

Nevertheless, Tertullian, a man undoubtedly imbued with the principles of human and divine philosophy, believes that the soul even by itself constitutes the whole human being. These are his words from chapter 1 of *On the Testimony of the Soul*:

> “I call upon a new witness—indeed, one more widely known than all literature, more active than all teaching, more common than every publication, greater than the whole human being: that is, the whole of what is human. Stand forth in the midst, O soul,” etc.

See a little farther below what is brought forward from Maximus of Tyre.]

because, although it began in time as a creature, it will remain eternal in its own manner, as God is eternal; or because he bestowed upon it, as he did upon the holy angels, a share in reason and understanding. But he did not form the body wholly unlike that of the other animals, except that those animals [Note: [Col. 0624D] “Prone upon the belly.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book I:

> “And while the other animals look down upon the earth, prone…”]

He gave man an uplifted face. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book II, chapter 1: “For whereas all other living creatures look toward the ground with bodies bent forward, because they have not received reason and wisdom, we have instead been given by God the artificer an upright posture and a lofty countenance,” and so forth. Maximus of Tyre, in dissertation 38:

“It does not seem that the view of those who attach the human form to images of the gods ought to be condemned. For the human soul is near to God and most like God. Nor does it seem just that God should have wished to enclose what is most like himself in a deformed body; rather, he gave it a body that could most easily carry the immortal soul, light, suited to movement, and—alone among all earthly bodies—capable of raising its head toward heaven, beautiful, lively, and well formed.”

Ruricius, bishop of my fellow Lemovices, book II, letter 42: “Of all animals, man alone was created and made sublime.”] upright, whereas the others were bent forward upon their bellies; and he fashioned it so that the soul, obedient to the commands of its Maker, might employ its faithful service in reaching higher things.

A pagan author attempts to express how much the soul surpasses the body when, speaking of both, he says: “The one is common to us with the gods, the other with beasts.”

[Note: A pagan author. That is, Sallust, whose words occur at the beginning of his book *On the Conspiracy of Catiline*: “But all our power lies in soul and body. We use the one more under command, the other more in service. The one is common to us with the gods, the other with beasts.” Lactantius also cites this passage of Sallust in book II of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 12, and in the first chapter of *On the Workmanship of God*; so too does Ennodius, book VI, letter 3. Faustus of Riez imitated Sallust in letter 6, written to Ruricius, bishop of Limoges.]

Thus he established the first man, Adam, together with his wife Eve—whom, wondrous to say, God brought forth from a rib removed from him while he slept—in the paradise of delight, as the sacred Scriptures testify. Since everything necessary for use was available, God did not condemn him to burdensome labor; rather, by taking away from him the possibility of working, he removed the weariness of idleness.

But lest man fail to know that he owed a return of submission and obedience to the one from whom he had received existence and from whom he happily received well-being, with no contrary movements of soul or body resisting his desire, God granted him all kinds of the garden’s fruits for food, but forbade one tree, which he called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

And because the hope of escaping punishment is a great inducement to sin, he added to the command a threat of punishment, assuring them that they would die on the day they ate from the tree he had forbidden.

[Note: An inducement to sin. I recognize here the characteristic insight of Lupus of Ferrières, who says that hope of impunity is a great enticement to sin. Thus, in letter 126, he said that in his own age vices had burst forth into such great freedom that, with impunity having been secured, no one feared God, the king, or the bishops openly, so that—as the same Lupus says in the second canon of the Council of Verneuil—mortals, accustomed by long license, confidently believed that they could sin with impunity. In letter 64 he likewise says that impunity for evils has always produced an increase of vices. Tacitus similarly says in book XV of the *Annals* that the desire for impunity has always opposed great efforts. Cicero, book II of *On Ends*: “What appetite will not rush forth and throw itself forward when concealment, impunity, or license is held out?” Hugo Falcandus, in his *History of Sicily*, page 122, attacking Gaito Peter, whom he says had offended and disturbed the queen and the entire court with impunity and exposed them to great dangers, adds: “Nor is it surprising, since the very impunity of crimes gives him confidence to dare whatever he pleases.” Matthew Paris, describing in the year 1265 how a certain friar of the Order of Friars Minor, named Mansuetus, sent to England by the pope, abused the authority granted him by absolving whomever he wished—including excommunicated persons, forgers, and perjurers—says: “Hence many acquired boldness to offend. For ease of pardon produces an opportunity for sinning.”]

The ease of observing the command was complete, since neither necessity invited them to violate it nor could an enemy—who was the devil alone—drive them to do so by force. He himself had already fallen through pride; he envied human beings the possibility of attaining what he himself had deservedly lost.

What could one do who could neither lay aside the malice once conceived nor overthrow man unless he were acquiescent, consenting, and willing? The author of his own evil and discoverer of another’s, he clothed himself in the serpent. Since the divine command was not to be investigated for its cause but promptly carried out, he incited the inexperienced to ask what he himself pretended to be seeking: namely, why God had not permitted them unrestricted use of all the fruits.

When the woman answered—she whom the crafty investigator had discovered to be easier to deceive—he led the unwary woman away from the true judgment, and immediately brought her into the false belief that they would not die. He added that he knew that, if they ate what had been forbidden them, their eyes would at once be opened and they would become like gods.

[Note: “To know God.” I think we should read “to know that,” namely, that the devil knew it. *Eum* is used for “himself.” The sense requires this. It is as though he said: “The devil added that he knew that, if Adam and Eve ate the forbidden fruit, their eyes would immediately be opened and they would become like gods.”]

Thus he might at least corrupt their faith through the plurality of gods, if, tempted to disobedience through the vice of gluttony, they had not desisted.

The woman was taken captive, both by the enemy’s falsely sweet words and by the excessive beauty of the forbidden fruit. She ate first and persuaded her husband to eat. Immediately both died, not in soul alone but also in body, when they incurred the unavoidable necessity of dying.

And because man did not shrink from the death of sin, from which he had been free to abstain, he eventually arrived unwillingly at the payment of bodily death.

No one will wonder that man was immediately dead when he presumed upon what had been forbidden, provided he recalls that a man wounded by a deadly blow, or already corrupted irreparably by the contagion of poison, is rightly called dead because death so certain hangs over one in such a condition that no hope of escape can be found. The Apostle too is the author of this judgment, saying: “The body is dead because of sin” (Romans 8).

It possesses the necessity of dying, which it did not have before sin. Adam had indeed been so created that he could refrain from sinning if he wished, and could avoid dying unless he sinned. But when goodness alone did not suffice for him unless he also acquired experience of evil, and he turned his will toward sinning, he lost the ability not to die and incurred the inability not to die. Thus, too late, he experienced the knowledge of the good of obedience, which he had voluntarily abandoned, and found the knowledge of evil, which he had sought through impious curiosity.

For what he had never feared, he now felt: desire, the avenging companion of sin—namely, the appetite of the genital members. He shrank from it so greatly that he sought a covering of leaves as a remedy for shame; yet he loved it so greatly that, for the just judgment of condemnation, he was not even able to avoid its importunate enticement.

[Note: “Was sufficient to avoid.” Valerius Maximus, book IX, chapter 1: “Luxury is also a seductive evil: it is somewhat easier to accuse it than to avoid it.” Ruricius, book II, letter 12: “And therefore see, dearest brother, what an evil it is which, while detested, is admitted; while shunned, is scarcely avoided.” For this reason Pseudo-Plautus said in the *Querolus* that adultery is not a crime. He then adds: “This is what can neither be permitted nor prohibited.”]

That he could sin if he wished, he demonstrated by sinning; but that he could also refrain from sinning if he wished, the Creator made clear by threatening punishment and warning him not to sin. Adam therefore possessed free choice of the will both toward good and toward evil: toward good, to be aided by divine grace; toward evil, to be abandoned by divine judgment.

For how could he not be aided in the good by the one who was the life of his soul, as the soul was the life of his body? Finally, if “the soul that sins shall itself die,” as prophetic authority declares (Ezekiel 18), it follows that the soul that has acted well lives, with God giving it life.

Human free choice had therefore to be abandoned to divine judgment in evil, because, although he possessed equal ability toward good and evil, no need and no violence bent his will toward evil. He contemptuously regarded as suspect, through sacrilegious impiety, the command of his God—which was exceedingly easy to observe and from whom he saw that he had received such great blessings—and he not only failed to refer the prompting of an unknown enemy, of whom he had absolutely no need, to God for examination, but received it with bold recklessness as though it would benefit him.

It was therefore most just that what he had freely chosen should cling to him. And because, as the Apostle asserts, “all sinned in him” (Romans 5), nature was corrupted in all those born from both sexes, so that, insofar as we are nevertheless permitted to advance, free choice is ours for doing evil as it was his, but for doing good it is not free unless it has been liberated by God’s grace.

In our first parent—would that he had stood firm!—we all fell by sinning, and all together were condemned, by our common desert, to a punishment indeed most terrible but entirely just. Man would not have been ungrateful to the one who had made him; he would have obeyed his Creator, not his seducer; he would have wished to be only what the one who had made him by power and governed him by mercy willed him to be.

We have learned, with sacred Scripture revealing it, the words of the enemy that sounded outwardly through the serpent. But what machinations of suggestion he brought inwardly against the human mind, although we cannot grasp with certainty, we can nevertheless estimate by a plausible conjecture.

For “the devil put it into the heart of Judas to betray the Lord,” not by making a public din with words, but by secretly kindling the wretched man with the torches of avarice. In his pride the devil had desired the loftiness of likeness to God; and, already eager for what belonged to another, he had fallen from the dignity of his own rank. Since he neither wished nor was able to recover it, he envied the one who would possess it, and perhaps, before he uttered his words, corrupted the unwary man with the very plague by which he himself had perished.

For how would Adam so quickly have consented outwardly to take the food unless he had first swollen inwardly in order to obtain his own liberty? However it happened, the author of our race plainly fell through his own fault. And because we all sinned in him, his ruin unquestionably dragged us all down with it.

Just as anyone, whenever he wishes, can throw himself into a pit that is spacious and has no rough ledge, but, when he wishes to climb out, cannot do so unless aided by efforts from outside, so the first man fell voluntarily, and in him we fell originally; but we cannot, even if we wish, free ourselves from the mire of sin and rise again unless the grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord, draws us out and raises us up.

[Note: “By external efforts.” Thus he says in a letter: “He called enemies *extrarii*.” *Extrarius* is the same as *extraneus*, “external” or “outside.”]

The evil of a voluntary crime bound not only the first man but also all his descendants, proceeding through the union of both sexes, to the deservedness of condemnation. Since the cause was the same for all, all would have suffered it together, for all had listened not to God but to the devil.

Nor could a just complaint arise from this, with equity preserved, except that they deserved it, unless there were a God who, just beyond comparison, was also ineffably compassionate—or, to use the word of our Scriptures, by which we are gathered and saved, merciful.

Since all would have had to perish by their own desert, many are saved by divine goodness. In them let us recognize and embrace his mercy; and, that we may deserve to be counted among them, let us bend his indulgence through humble observance of his commandments and constant prayers.

When, on the other hand, many are condemned, let us not criticize him, because they are justly condemned according to their desert. Rather, let us fear the judgment of him who is “terrible in his counsels over the sons of men,” and marvel that we, who deserved the same things, have been able to be saved. By considering this, we should be kindled more fervently to love, praise, and proclaim his mercy.

Once these points have been established and retained with faithful assent, no sober-minded person will be unaware that God is not the author and cause of man’s destruction: he created man upright and showed, by warning him, that he could remain in his condition if he wished.

For his nature had not yet been corrupted, so that he would either be unable to know what ought to be known or be unable to carry out what he had understood because of an impediment of difficulty. Clearly, man conceived and brought forth evil either from himself or from the devil, when, removing divine reverence from himself, he believed the deceiver and, by taking the forbidden food, committed a capital crime.

This—this plainly—was the cause of all evils for the human race.

[Note: Punishment follows sin. Salvian, in book I of *The Government of God*: “What greater and clearer judgment could God have pronounced upon sinners than that punishment should immediately follow those who sin?” See what we have noted there.]

Sin is indeed followed by punishment; and whatever present mercy does not consume by forgiveness, justice eventually repays by vengeance.

[Note: “By vengeance eventually.” That is: although God does not presently punish the guilty and those stained by crimes, they will nevertheless not escape with impunity, but will at last feel the power of the divine hand. “And therefore we must understand,” says Salvianus in book VII of *The Government of God*, “that it was an act of divine mercy that he postponed punishment long owed, but that it was because of expiatory offenses and crimes that the sinful people eventually suffered what they deserved.” Hence that saying of Valerius Maximus, which we wrongly attributed to Caesar in our notes on Salvianus: “For the divine anger advances slowly toward its own vengeance and compensates for the slowness of punishment by its severity.” In Caesar’s book I of the *Gallic War*, however, Caesar himself is said to have replied to the ambassadors of the Helvetii, whose leader was Divico: “The immortal gods are accustomed, in order that men may feel more severely the change of circumstances, to grant those whom they wish to punish for their crime more favorable circumstances for a time and a longer period of impunity.”]

But let someone from the number of the bitterly complaining say: “God should not have made man, since he knew that man would sin.” How much more rightly would he say: “Man should not have committed the sin which he could avoid with the greatest ease and by which, if he believed God’s words, he knew that he would die”—although it would not have accorded with divine goodness not to create a man whom he could make good after his fall, or even from whom he could produce some good.

Or let him add: “He should have made man such that he could not sin.” Why not ask instead: “Why, when man had been made such that he could refrain from sinning if he wished, did he not wish to remain in that condition, so that by obeying he might eventually merit so much from God that he would not wish, or would not be able, to sin?”

But why should that will have been denied to man by which, if he used it well, he could await a reward, or, if he transgressed wickedly, be compelled to suffer the punishment that had been foretold?

I would confidently say that God would not have made any creature that would become evil through sinning unless he had decided either to make it good again or to make some good come from it. For he preferred to make good persons or good things from evil rather than permit there to be no evils at all.

Indeed, he reforms many human beings, evil either through original sin or through their own fault, into good persons, without imputing to them any iniquity—by his own gratuitous goodness, which must be held with the greatest firmness.

But he grants no unclean spirit this grace; he has determined to provide no remedy of pardon for their stubborn pride. Nevertheless, he makes good use of the service of these spirits and of the ruined human beings who share in them, even against their will, when, whether they rage openly or plot secretly, he exercises the patience of the saints, which is one day to be crowned with an everlasting reward.

Nor does he produce good from evil any less when he repays each of them with punishment according to its merit. For it is good that the unconverted wicked should be punished, so that the arrogance of the proud may be restrained, the devotion of the humble increased, and divine praise augmented through both.

By the reasoning given above, as I think, it is irresistibly established that man was condemned both in soul and in body, and that the misfortune of his condemnation can in no respect be attributed to anyone other than himself and his seducer.

It has also become clear that man could fall into sin by his own powers, but could never rise again by his own strength. Therefore the merciful Creator, in order to accomplish what man could not accomplish, made his co-eternal Son, like himself in equality of will and power, man by a new privilege of birth—not from male and female, but from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary—without sin.

Through him, who was not conceived by the heat of lust because the Holy Spirit overshadowed him, he might abolish all sin from those who had been conceived in sins.

Born from a virgin and born of a virgin, he lived without fault from the time of his conception and birth, and without any stain of offense. After he had sufficiently carried out the dispensation of our salvation through teaching—

[Note: “The dispensation of our salvation.” That is, the incarnation of Christ the Lord. Among the Greeks, the mystery of the incarnation is commonly called οἰκονομία, “dispensation” or “administration,” as Marca noted in book III, chapter 13, section 1, of *On the Harmony*. Thus the anonymous author published by Sirmond, who composed the *Brief Statement of Faith against the Arians*, says at the very beginning: “The Lord speaks of himself according to the dispensation of the assumed flesh.”]

—true God and true man, one in both, that is, one in and from both, through wondrous condescension he voluntarily endured the death owed to sin, while entirely free from its contagion, and liberated us sinners from eternal death.

Then, rising within three days, he lifted our hope to heaven and gradually explained the truth of the original fall and the completeness of our restoration, not only in his own words but also through the words and writings of his disciples.

The sacred writings called the Old Testament also expressed the one with marvelous precision and signified the other through mystical prefiguration. For they both recorded the sin of our first parent and foretold that the human race would be restored through the Lord Jesus—among many other passages, most fully and clearly in this one:

“He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 71).

Let the faithful and devout examiner therefore carefully consider how great man’s iniquity was, since no human being and no angel could atone for it, but only the blood of God himself. Let man believe that he deserves nothing but punishment. Even after the cleansing of baptism—which opens the gate of the heavenly kingdom also to infants—although he suspects that he has done certain things worthy of pardon more than he knows that he has done them, there are nevertheless far more matters for which he must fear the severity of divine judgment.

Even good deeds are to be feared, since so great a man says: “All our righteousnesses are like a menstruous cloth” (Isaiah 64). For our righteousness, although it sometimes shines before human beings in deed and speech, becomes filthy in God’s sight through wicked thought.

As stated above, we have free choice from Adam, but not toward good and evil in the condition that he received from the Creator. Rather, we have it in the condition that he voluntarily chose by turning downward and earned through sinning: free choice toward evil; but toward good, if indeed that should come to us by divine gift, it must be liberated by God’s grace, as we have already said.

Unless I am mistaken, the first book of divine authority shows this in these words: “The sense and thought of the human heart are inclined toward evil from his youth” (Genesis 8).

Paul, too, the faithful interpreter of heavenly secrets, already baptized and perhaps already raised to the third heaven, says:

[Note: “Fellow-delighting.” I prefer to read *condelector*. In letter 128, page 188, he cites this entire passage of Paul from the Epistle to the Romans, and from the same version.]

“I delight in the law of God according to the inner man,” namely, in that law which he established: “You shall not covet.” But I see another law in my members opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members (Romans 7).

He calls the law in the members “coveting.” After sin, the first parents experienced it in their genital members. Even those who practice continence repel it by relying on divine help, but while they live here in mortality they can never exclude it so completely that it will not return.

The Lord Jesus too, who, as Creator, uniquely knew what was in man, reminded us of our weakness:

[Note: “Without me, nothing.” He cites this passage from John in the same version in letter 33, page 67; in letter 128, page 187; and in the *Collectaneum*, page 762, section 270.]

“Without me,” he says, “you can do nothing” (John 15)—nothing, that is, that is good or conducive to salvation.

Nor should the person who has been saved and is being saved be indignant that he can do nothing without the Savior, since he promises: “If the Son makes you free, you will be truly free” (John 8).

And someone may say: Why is something commanded as possible that is later shown to be impossible?

“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Matthew 22); and: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (ibid.); and: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you” (Matthew 5); and: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9); and many other commands, which at one time prohibit sins, at another instruct faith, and at another shape our strength.

Plainly, this is so that, when a person strives but is not sufficient to fulfill what is commanded, he may be humbled by his weariness and return to the place from which, by asking, seeking, and knocking, he may receive what he desires, and may glory in all God’s benefits not in himself but in the Lord.

A person devoted to God should not think that the sinews of his strength are being removed when he is instructed by such evident testimonies that he can do no good by himself. Nor should he think that his merit is diminished. For to suppose, or even dream, that a human being can accomplish anything more through himself than with God cooperating is not merely the mark of a proud man but of a madman.

[Note: “But of a madman.” Lupus, letter 30, page 58: “For if we could even suppose that, by some sharpness of mind, we were able to grasp beforehand the images of those things which have surpassed the genius of so great an author, that would be the height of madness.”]

And from his fullness we have all received grace upon grace: for the grace he bestows through laborious goodness, he repays with the grace of blessed recompense.

The prophet Jeremiah too does not hesitate to affirm that man has no free choice in the good:

“I know, Lord,” he says, “that man’s way is not his own, nor is it in man to walk and direct his steps” (Jeremiah 10).

Therefore he immediately asks for help:

“Correct me, Lord, but in judgment and not in your anger” (ibid.).

That is: “Since it is not within my power to correct my perversity and to grasp and hold fast the rightness of your justice, apply the correction of judgment, by whose terror you heal the weak to their salvation, not the correction of anger, by whose severity you horribly condemn the proud. Thus, with my will changed and strengthened, I may do, with your cooperation, what I cannot accomplish by my own powers.”

The most renowned prophet Isaiah, affirming that everything is to be attributed to God and absolutely nothing to us, says:

“Lord, grant us peace, for you have accomplished all our works for us” (Isaiah 26).

For if we rashly claim for ourselves the health of free choice, after striving long and vainly we are confounded by impossibility as by a most hostile enemy and wearied by an arduous struggle, until, exhausted, we turn back to divine assistance.

Once that assistance has been obtained, we attain the peace of which it is said: “Great peace have those who love your law” (Psalm 118). Our mind, through a good disposition, rests in God as in a most secure fortress, and now confidently performs the commands that bring salvation, since the one who commands them is himself carrying them out.

Someone might wonder whether even the smallest works are not done by us from ourselves but by God himself, unless he understands that good thoughts themselves, and both the beginning and the perfection of faith, do not proceed from us but are inspired and strengthened by God in those who possess them.

The teacher of the nations makes this public—or rather, the Spirit of God through him.

[Note: “Rather, the Spirit of God through him.” Lupus, letter 64: “According to the same Apostle, in whom the Spirit of God evidently spoke: ‘Put away the things that belonged to childhood.’” Likewise in letter 94: “The holy Apostle, in whom the Spirit of God evidently spoke.”]

“We are not sufficient,” he says, “to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3).

That is: insofar as it pertains to the holiness of religion, we indeed cannot think anything sufficient; but in order that we may be sufficient, we receive good thoughts themselves from God.

Likewise, concerning the beginning of faith: “But I obtained mercy,” he says, “so that I might be faithful” (1 Corinthians 7). For he does not say, “Because I was faithful, I obtained mercy,” but, “I obtained mercy so that I might be faithful.”

Concerning the perfection of faith: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from you; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2).

And not only concerning faith but also concerning the good will itself he says: “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish” (Philippians 2).

That perseverance in good works is likewise God’s gift, and therefore God’s grace, is easily demonstrated by a sufficiently authoritative testimony:

“We trust in the Lord Jesus that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Christ Jesus” (Philippians 1).

That is: God, who began to work in you what he commanded, will continue working until, as each departs from life, he begins to render what he promised.

By all these teachings we are instructed not to place our hope in ourselves, committing a more serious offense through that opinion. Rather, let us fortify our condition and transfer the fullness of all our hope to him who calls us to himself for the purpose of supporting us, invites us to ask for what will benefit us in order to grant it, and terrifies us lest we trust in ourselves, so that he may not abandon us.

For “cursed is the man who places his hope in man.” Whoever places it in himself places it in man. Therefore he is cursed.

The goodness of God is splendidly commended when the man who trusts in the Lord is declared blessed, and sometimes the very disposition of the one who trusts already receives the reward of blessing.

The unclean spirits, however, delight, through the cunning of deception, in transferring human hope to themselves. They have brought this about in their worshipers, or, through a kind of collusion, have inserted false opinions into their minds, as though, because of the dignity and excellence of their nature, it were safest for them to place some hope in themselves.

This can be demonstrated from the writings of those who, empty of divine knowledge, nevertheless became distinguished in worldly wisdom.

Cicero has Marcus Porcius Cato the Elder express the view—not Laelius or Scipio, which might have been uncertain—as his own definite opinion:

“Those who possess no resources in themselves for living well and happily find every period of life burdensome. But for those who seek all good things from themselves, nothing that the necessity of nature brings can seem evil.”

“You should have said, Marcus Tullius, that they seek all good things from the true God, not from themselves; then you would have pleased us not so much by the splendor of your words as by the truth of your judgment.”

Virgil too, as befitted a man handling poetic fictions, suggested rather than explicitly stated something of this kind while occupied with another subject:

“Each person has hope for himself.”

Would that he had said, “God, the true God, is the hope of each person,” and believed it; and would that, instead of speaking flatteringly of Maecenas, he had proclaimed this about the same true and only God, singing it properly and supremely:

“Without you, the mind begins nothing lofty.”

Our own authors, easily superior in wisdom and equal in divine eloquence—when they wish, they bring it forth; when they wish, they conceal it—I mean Cyprian, Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, and certain others—have deeply examined the meaning of the divine utterances and expressed it for our salvation.

They teach, plainly, that for the good we need our free choice to be liberated, and that God’s grace is not given according to our merits.

Thus the most glorious martyr Cyprian and most gracious teacher, taking everything away from our powers and assigning it to God, briefly embracing every kind of merit, says that no one should glory in anything, since nothing belongs to us (Cyprian, book III of the *Testimonies to Quirinus*, chapter 4).

[Note: “Most glorious martyr Cyprian.” Lupus, letter 3: “the glorious martyr Cyprian,” that is, “the most glorious martyr Cyprian.” In letter 128: “Saint Cyprian, most glorious martyr and most gracious teacher.”]

Ambrose, writing that our heart and our thoughts are not in our power, also included the very deeds and words that plainly proceed from the heart and thought.

Jerome, eminent in divine and secular learning—

[Note: “Secular learning.” That is, secular literature or education, as Lupus says in letters 30 and 68.]

—and, together with Augustine, a kind of father of ecclesiastical philosophy, which neither pursues human philosophy very much nor rejects it in every respect, powerfully crushed the recently arisen Pelagian heresy. He says:

“If God’s grace consists only in this, that he created us with our own will, and if we are content with free choice and no longer need him—lest, if we need him, free choice be broken—then we ought no longer to pray or bend his mercy through prayers, so as to receive each day what, once received, lies within our own power.”

[Col. 0634B] Again, a little later:

“Let us always give thanks to the giver, and let us know that we are nothing except insofar as he himself has preserved in us what he bestowed.”

Elsewhere, in Deuteronomy, it is clearly demonstrated that we are preserved not by our works and righteousness, but by God’s mercy: “The Lord your God will not give you this excellent land to possess because of your righteousness, for you are a stiff-necked people” (Deut. IX).

Again, a little later: “You will save them for nothing” (Ps. LV)—without doubt, the righteous—“because they are saved not by their own merit, but by God’s clemency.”

[Note: [Col. 0633D] “Without doubt, the righteous.” This is a very familiar phrase with our Lupus. In Epistle 4, while praising this passage from the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, “The sorrow of the world produces death,” he adds, “without doubt, spiritual death.” And in Epistle 30, p. 60, citing that passage of Augustine, “his life, indeed,” etc., he adds, “without doubt, of the spirit.” Likewise, at the end of this book, p. 241, when adducing that passage from chapter VIII of the Epistle to the Romans, “He did not spare his own Son,” he adds, “without doubt, God.” So also in the Life of Saint Maximinus, chapter 4, p. 279: “without doubt, Maximinus.”]

Again, elsewhere, in explaining the saying, “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, and let not the strong man glory in his strength, and let not the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this: that he knows, understands, and recognizes me, that I am the Lord, who practice mercy, judgment, and righteousness on the earth” (Jer. IX):

“Where are,” he says, “those who claim that man is governed by his own will, and that the power of free choice was given in such a way that God’s mercy and justice would be removed?”

Augustine himself—whether one should admire him more for his discovery of things or for the felicity of his expression you cannot easily determine—discussed free choice and the grace of God so extensively that his works can scarcely be read by anyone in their entirety. Yet, in my opinion, although they are exceptionally clear and useful, no one can retain them all in memory.

[Note: [Col. 0634D] “Although they are exceptionally clear.” He writes that Augustine’s words are exceptionally clear. Thus, in Epistle 30, speaking of the same Augustine, he says: “So far I do not see what obscurity these words produce. For he is an exceptionally clear author,” etc.]

For just as no one investigated what should be thought about free choice and the grace of God with such laborious inquiry as he did, so no one treated both subjects for so long; and, if I may say so with the permission of all, no one discovered both with such exact conformity to the truth, no one asserted them with such abundance of eloquence, and no one defended them with such a wealth of unconquerable arguments.

Therefore, since all his works were excellent and almost innumerable, and since I was hesitating about what should chiefly be selected, I resolved to invite the diligent to read those works which, with what they already know, they will be able to penetrate more easily, rather than deprive them by setting down only a few passages, whether similar, better, or otherwise.

Yet I could not conceal this one point which, among his other observations concerning free choice, he detected with the greatest acuity. “If,” he says, “we seek free choice that is innate and wholly incapable of being lost, it is that by which even those wish to be blessed who do not wish for the things that lead to blessedness.”

Nor should anyone suppose that either those great men or we assert the good things that we receive as God’s gifts in such a way that they are not also ours. They are certainly God’s, and principally so, because they are given by him. Consequently, they are also our good things, because they are believed to exist in us through his gift. And when we conceive or perform some good action, free choice exists in us, because it has been liberated from the inclination toward sin by God’s grace.

The same work is both God’s, since he is at work in us, and ours, because we do by our will what has been commanded us. Good thoughts are God’s, because they are given to us by him, as was established above by apostolic testimony: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (II Cor. III). Yet those same thoughts are also ours, because the Spirit of God admonishes us: “Cast your thought upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you” (Ps. LIV).

Our conversion belongs to God, to whom the prayer is addressed: “Convert us, O God our Savior” (Ps. LXXXII). Yet that same conversion is also ours, because we are divinely commanded: “Turn to me with all your heart” (Joel II).

The inclination of our heart toward God’s commandments belongs also to God, whom we appease by prayers taught by him: “Incline my heart toward your testimonies” (Ps. CXVIII). Yet that same inclination is ours, because it exists in us when we will. Hence we rightly glory in saying: “I have inclined my heart to perform your righteous ordinances forever” (Ps. CXII).

Finally, all our good works are also God’s, for he says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV). Yet they are also ours, because it is said to him prophetically: “Lord, grant us peace, for you have performed all our works for us” (Isa. XXVI).

God’s grace is therefore the author and cause of all our good things. For after Adam’s sin, in which we all sinned and were justly condemned—for the Lord our God is righteous, and there is no iniquity in him—what does the corrupted succession of the whole human race deserve, being condemned on account of original sin and, if it reaches the age of moral action, destined to be condemned also on account of additional personal sins, except everlasting punishments?

The whole human stock, corrupted by sin, would plainly have been compelled to suffer these punishments, as was stated above, unless, from that same stock, subject to the same cause of condemnation, some were left by God’s hidden judgment—though entirely righteous—in the condemnation they deserved through his justice, while others were saved through his mercy by manifest grace.

[Note: [Col. 0635D] “By God’s hidden judgment.” This too is a phrase very familiar to Lupus. Epistle 4, p. 11: “Although hidden, it is by no means an unjust judgment.” Epistle 84, p. 126: “It is long since God, by a hidden yet just judgment.” Epistle 128, p. 186: “Although by a hidden yet just judgment.” Epistle 129, p. 191: “Although by a hidden yet just judgment.” Likewise below, p. 239: “Although his judgment may at times be hidden, it is never unjust.”]

There is no basis for the liberated to puff themselves up, because they received what they had not deserved. There is no basis for the condemned to complain, because they were compelled to endure nothing except what they had deserved.

But why God saves these rather than those, or why he saves these instead of those, is beyond humanity; no explanation of God’s secret, especially of so great a secret, should be demanded by man. “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. IX).

Therefore, as the same author says, “He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Rom. IX). He has mercy through overflowing goodness; he hardens without any intervening injustice.

He hardens, however, not by driving anyone into sin—for God is not a tempter to evil (Jas. I)—but by abandoning the person in sin, since he alone is the liberator of those whom he wills to liberate. And certainly, just as he is the liberator of some, he could have been the liberator of all if he had willed it. “For the Lord has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth.”

But he willed to exercise mercy in such a way that he would weaken justice in no one. For when the venerable Paul says, “who wills all people to be saved” (I Tim. II), this should not be understood as though, when God generally wills all to be saved, he were unable—because of certain exceedingly powerful obstacles—to accomplish what he wills, despite being omnipotent. Rather, it should be understood in this way: all those whom he wills to save are saved, whether they will it or not. Indeed, many baptized in infancy, having no ability to distinguish these matters, are transferred to glory immediately after departing this life.

Thus God wills all people to be saved, but no others than those who are saved.

The evangelist John used the same manner of expression when he said: “He enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I). This does not mean that he enlightens by the light of faith everyone who comes into this world—for it is utterly absurd to think so, since many are obscured by the darkness of unbelief—but rather those who are enlightened, since they are enlightened by no one other than him.

That “all” does not always embrace the whole universally, but can sometimes include a particular exception, is also authoritatively shown by the Apostle himself, whose meaning is under discussion, when he says: “I please all people in all things” (I Cor. VI). To say nothing of the still greater portion of the faithful, whom he certainly could not please, he did not please those by whom he was beaten, those by whom he was buried under stones, or, finally, those by whom he was driven from the city as though dead. He pleased only the faithful, who were so numerous that they could rightly be called “all,” and who glorified God in him because he had changed persecution into preaching.

We can also understand “who wills all people to be saved” (I Tim. II) in a sound sense as meaning that he gathers people of every kind to salvation: some Jews and some Gentiles; some of either sex; some magistrates and some private citizens; some masters and some servants; some intelligent and some dull; and people of whatever other distinctions can be discerned by careful observers—people who may rightly be counted under the name “all.”

Luke used the same word in the same sense in the Gospel: “Woe to you, Pharisees, who tithe mint and rue and every herb” (Luke XI). The Pharisees were not tithing every kind of herb throughout the entire expanse of the earth. Rather, “every herb” must plainly be understood as every kind of herb that they possessed.

Nor is this interpretation contrary to the truth: that when he says he wills people to be saved, he who makes us willing may have intended to signify that all people are to be saved. Thus, although we know that many are called but few are chosen, we may without distinction wish all to be saved.

In the same way we find in the Apostle: “The Spirit himself pleads for us with indescribable groanings” (Rom. II)—that is, he makes us plead.

Commending this grace, by which all of us who are saved are freely rescued, while many others are left in the condemnation that we too deserved, the chosen vessel says: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless in his presence in love; he predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, for himself” (Eph. I).

What an effective remedy was provided against our being puffed up by God’s gift, before the disease of pride arose! God chose us before the foundation of the world, not because we were holy and blameless, nor because we were going to become holy and blameless—for otherwise he would not be bestowing the gift of his grace so much as repaying, as though by debt, a reward for our present or future merit—but he chose us before the foundation of the world so that we might be holy and blameless. Unless he willed it, we could not be so much as one of these.

Moreover, whenever the Apostle speaks of election, foreknowledge, or predestination, those who claim that God chose, foreknew, or predestined certain people because he foresaw that they would be devoted to him and would remain in that devotion—although they may possess great authority in other matters—must not be heeded at all in this matter, lest the gift of divine grace be emptied of its force if it is distributed according to some human, even future, merit.

Nor should those who do not know that Christ himself is speaking here be indignant that the Apostle is preferred to them—Christ, who testifies that he is, as he is, the truth. All these were predestined solely by grace, of whom the Savior says: “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned will come to me” (John VI).

This teaching of salvation, by which one comes to the grace of the Savior, is very far removed from the senses of the body. It is not apprehended by ears through sounding words, but by minds, through the prompting of the Creator, who works even silently in them whatever pleases him—mercy, so that those who are called may be liberated, or judgment, so that those who are left may be condemned.

It plainly works in the minds of the devout, helping them to will what is salutary and to advance in it. It works in the minds of the impious by abandoning them, so that they will nothing except what is harmful and fall into worse things.

Understanding this, the Prophet prays: “Help me, and I shall be saved” (Ps. CXVIII).
