Of the reprobate, who sin willingly and, when God’s judgment abandons them, rush into worse things, the Apostle says: “Because they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is improper” (Rom. I).

Will distinguishes the two groups: in one, aided by God’s mercy; in the other, unaided by his judgment.

No one is so ungrateful as not to believe and confess that God, who helps the will to be good, is the author both of that will and of all the good things that proceed from it, as well as of the rewards that undoubtedly follow them.

But no one except a mad and ruined person will dare to suppose that God is the author of the evil will of the lost. For one whose will is supremely good does not make another’s will evil. Thus, just as he is not the author of the evil will of the impious, neither is he the author of any sins of others that proceed from such a will. Yet although he is the author of no guilt whatsoever, he is certainly its examiner and judge.

Just as a person condemned for treason rightly attributes his punishment only to himself or to his accomplices in crime, so a person condemned by God’s judgment cannot rightly turn the blame for his punishment against one whom he cannot accuse of the sin he freely committed.

Let man, then—or, if he prefers, the Devil, whom he rashly believed—attribute to himself both sin and the punishment of sin: that is, both the cause of condemnation and condemnation itself. But let him attribute to God the good work and the reward of the good work.

No evil person approaches this good except one who is about to depart from evil; no good person reaches it except one who has been drawn. For just as it is true that “they went out from us, but they were not of us” (I John II), so it is true that “no one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John VI).

Here the perversity of our nature is shown—a nature which, using a transferred and improper term, we nevertheless call “nature,” following the Apostle, who says: “We were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. II). He calls “nature” that which already possesses sin contrary to nature, whereas nature is properly and truly called that uncorrupted state in which Adam was created.

The perversity, I say, of our nature is shown; elsewhere it is described as being inclined by the sense and thought of the heart toward evil from youth—that is, from the time when it can possess the judgment of discernment—and as being dragged reluctantly and against its will toward virtue.

But to return to the subject: no one is admitted to the good or to the reward of the good unless he was chosen by grace, foreknown by grace, and predestined by grace before the foundation of the world, as we learn when the divine Spirit opens this truth to us.

Election confesses the salvation not of everyone, but of some. The foreknowledge of future things—only from our perspective, since all things are simultaneously present to God—suggests prior knowledge. Predestination, understood positively, is said in the sacred writings to indicate the preparation of grace; grace itself expresses the gift.

God foreknows whatever he will either do or permit, neither by necessity, and the latter without any participation in injustice. He predestines whatever he has decided immutably to do. Indeed, he predestined all that he was going to do at the time when he made all things that were going to be.

Therefore predestination is never without foreknowledge. God does not predestine anything that he does not know he will do. Foreknowledge, however, often exists without predestination: God foreknows the crimes of the wicked, but just as he did not predestine himself to commit them, so he did not commit them.

Nevertheless, he fixed the number of the elect, to which no one can be added and from which no one can be subtracted, lest God should appear—an impious thing to suppose—to have erred in the truth of his predestination.

If someone wishes to be strengthened by this point, he may be instructed by that saying of John the Baptist reported in the Gospel: “Produce fruit worthy of repentance, and do not say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father’; for God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones” (Luke III).

By this he sufficiently shows that these people are to be cut off unless they produce fruit, and that others are to be substituted for them, either by physical descent or merely by imitation as children of Abraham, so that, while God’s promise remains secure, no one may be lacking from the fixed total.

And still more openly in the Apocalypse, where it is commanded: “Hold fast what you have, so that no one else may take your crown” (Rev. III). For if no one else will receive it unless this person, by losing his place, has made room for a successor, the number of the elect is fixed.

But the reason why these words are likewise addressed to those who will persevere, as though it were uncertain whether they will persevere, is that fear is necessary for those from whom the disease of pride may still steal away perseverance. Such weakness still exists in them that it must not be nurtured by security, but subdued by another form of weakness.

Let us recall the Apostle, who was suffering from an uncertain bodily or mental affliction and asking for a remedy. The heavenly physician, knowing better than the Apostle himself what was appropriate for him, showed that the antidote suited to his weakness was this predestination: God makes saints; he does not find them; and after the course of the present life he perfects and crowns them.

[Note: [Col. 0639D] “He makes saints; he does not find them.” This seems to have been modeled on Tacitus, in the Life of Agricola: “With exceedingly rare moderation, he preferred to seem to have found good men rather than to have made them.”]

This predestination, I say, which is supported by illustrious testimonies of divine revelation and unconquerable arguments, all the faithful everywhere accept and steadfastly defend; in it, as is fitting, they place the hope of their salvation with devout agreement, and not without reason. For no path of human salvation can be found except the one that divine grace has provided and revealed. Once this is excluded, no return to salvation is open at all.

Many shrink from saying that God’s predestination applies to the lost; among them are certain distinguished lights among the bishops, plainly lest God be believed to have created some out of a desire to punish them and to condemn unjustly those who were unable to avoid sin and therefore unable to avoid punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0639D] “Distinguished lights among the bishops.” He undoubtedly means Hincmar of Reims, Rabanus of Mainz, Pardulus of Laon, and perhaps several others.]

If they would consider that, just as all sinned in Adam when he sinned by his own will, so all previously existed without fault when he himself was without fault; that God did not impose the necessity of falling upon man, although he permitted the power to fall; and that he, as the one who made what was to come and who calls things that are not as though they were, both foreknew the fall and determined what would follow it—namely, that the human race, corrupted by its own will, should neither be wholly condemned because of mercy nor wholly saved because of justice—they would suffer no obscurity.

God created those who were upright in their origin; their own will corrupted them. Those whom mercy does not liberate, he punishes by judgment in such a way that they, not God, are proved to be the authors of their own condemnation.

Here someone may perhaps become more irritated and say, instead of being appeased:

“And if I must perish once and for all, why do I waste the brief span of this life? Why, since I am destined always to fare badly elsewhere, may I not fare well here for a while? Why do I not let loose all the reins of pleasure and complete whatever delights me?”

May God turn this madness away from every Christian, lest anyone believe himself to belong to the number of the lost, suppose that he cannot return from evil, or distrust that he can be saved by God’s immeasurable clemency.

This belongs to those who pass over into the inclination of the heart—that is, those who love evil with insatiable affection, have resolved with the most obstinate determination to remain in it, and have plunged themselves into the abyss of despair through an irrevocable impiety.

[Note: [Col. 0640D] “The abyss of despair.” Epistle 3: “They could even have cast them into the abyss of despair.” Epistle 94: “Let us fall into the abyss of despair.”]

But whoever remembers that he was redeemed by Christ’s blood at so great a price, and knows that he was initiated through baptism into so great and sacred a sacrament, does not doubt that the way of repentance lies open as an indication of his salvation. Why, I ask, after obtaining such great benefits without any merit of his own except evil, does he not unweariedly implore God to grant him good merit as well, and the things that follow good merit?

Why does he despair of being restored while he is alive, when he ought rather to rely on God’s goodness, since he lives for the very reason that he may at last correct himself? Who has ever hoped wholly in the Lord and been unable to attain forgiveness?

Rather, let each person, condemned by his own judgment, flee from God to God: from the angry God while he sins, to the appeased God while he repents. Let him reveal his way to the Lord, hope in him, and he himself will act—namely, so that the person abandons his evil ways, full of evil as they are, and now eagerly and joyfully embraces the good.

No one can obtain God’s mercy who cannot hope in him. For, as he himself reveals, mercy will surround the one who hopes in the Lord.

O how secure a refuge for us is God’s compassion! God is ready to spare those who submit and to conquer the proud. For those who abandon guilt and tearfully ask forgiveness, he is ready to grant pardon.

Who would not greatly love this God, so as to obtain the forgiveness of many sins?

Let everyone therefore hasten to the harbor of repentance and confidently seize and hold it. Let everyone set before himself, with emulous devotion, King David and the Apostle Peter. One of them, rebuked for adultery and murder, said, as was fitting, in profound grief, “I have sinned against the Lord” (II Sam. XII).

[Note: [Col. 0641D] “The sin was transferred.” That is, David’s sin: his crime was first punished in his son, and afterward in David himself. Salvianus should certainly be consulted in Book II of On the Government of God, pp. 38 ff.]

Immediately afterward he deserved to hear that his sin had been transferred and that he would not die. The other, after being looked upon by the one who had briefly turned his face away from him, became troubled and—being looked upon, I say, that is, roused to an attitude of repentance—swiftly washed away and erased with bitter tears the stain of denying God, so great a crime.

But if someone, by contemplating such great men, has conceived despair rather than imitation, because they overcame and crushed the greatest crimes by an abundance of virtues, while he laments that he is covered only with vices, let him at least look upon the thief who unquestionably deserved the punishment of the cross through his criminal acts, yet by faith alone—which immediately produced confession and hope—found life in the midst of death.

Finally, if someone knew that he was so unhappily enslaved to sin that he would certainly be condemned without any doubt, why would he not restrain himself from vices? Why would he not also strive to pursue whatever good he could, so that at least a lighter punishment might later chastise him?

Who, if given the choice, would not choose lesser punishments and avoid greater ones, when he must be tortured by the punishments of this life? Divine Scripture, consulted on this point, answers that lesser punishments are repaid for lesser sins, and greater punishments for greater sins.

“You will repay,” says the Prophet, “each person according to his works” (Ps. LXI)—that is, according to the quality of the good or evil, you will restore to each the rewards he deserves.

But if, with divine favor, we have already advanced somewhat in persuading people to a good hope, let us disclose, after the reasoning set forth above, whether the predestination of the wicked should be affirmed, through the assertion of blessed Augustine.

[Note: [Col. 0641D] “This most reliable authority.” He is speaking of Augustine, whom he also calls “the most reliable authority” in Epistle 129. Likewise, in Epistle 30, speaking of the same Augustine, he says: “Certainly a most distinguished author, because he was most observant of divine authority.”]

This most reliable authority, because he was exceptionally attentive to the divine Scriptures, made progress by writing. Hence, in his book On the Predestination of the Saints, he criticizes certain people because, though they had been eager to read his books, they had not likewise striven to make progress with him. He wrote while making progress, yet did not attain perfection in his own judgment.

For he held what Priscian also understands in his remarkable work on grammar: that nothing perfect in every respect can be found in human expressions.

[Note: [Col. 0641D] “Priscian.” Lupus also praises this passage of Priscian in Epistle 34. But the reading here is *locutionibus*, “expressions,” instead of *inventionibus*, “discoveries,” as it appears in Priscian and in the edition of Donatus Candidus. This resulted from our attempt to follow Sirmond’s edition, although Sirmond himself noted that *inventionibus* is read elsewhere.]

Indeed, as our Apostle says: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (I Cor. XIII).

He deigned frankly to confess this in his most exacting book On the Gift of Perseverance, which he published after, or among, the books of his Retractations.

In the books of the Retractations, he was not ashamed to make public whatever errors he discovered in himself, condemn them with censorial severity, and, wherever he could, correct them by applying the standard of divine authority and the sharpness of the most cautious reasoning. He advanced so far that every diligent reader should confidently draw from his singular teaching, while no malicious reader can find anything in it that he can justly criticize.

Who cut away vices more incisively than he? Who urged, or rather—to speak more accurately—drove people toward virtues more powerfully? Who persuaded those whom he wished to persuade more successfully?

Although, as Tully says, “the least part of an art is to speak about it, and the greatest to speak from it,” whenever he wished to speak perfectly from the art of rhetoric, he fulfilled the role of an orator. In Book IV of On Christian Teaching, he provided capable readers with splendid aids concerning the art itself, revealing its power.

Who was holier than he, more cautious, or keener?

Thus, adorned with so many divine gifts, this man, not hesitating, not investigating, and not arguing, but plainly teaching as though this were an established doctrine, indicates that there is a predestination of the wicked.

I have set down his words from the book he called the Enchiridion. When, in his Retractations, he wished to place upon it, as they say, the finishing hand, he found nothing to add, nothing to remove, and nothing to change.

“These are the great works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Ps. CX), and sought out so wisely that, when the angelic and human creature had sinned—that is, when the creature had done not what God willed but what it itself willed—God nevertheless fulfilled what he willed through that same will of the creature by which what the Creator did not will had come to pass. He uses evil things well, as supremely good, for the condemnation of those whom he justly predestined to punishment and for the salvation of those whom he mercifully predestined to glory.

And do not suppose that this escaped him, or that it was not established and confirmed as a known and certain truth. It can be confirmed both from many passages of his books and from that work I mentioned shortly before, entitled On the Gift of Perseverance, which he published at a mature age, having been thoroughly practiced and possessing a firm judgment.

[Col. 0642C] “Those whom he does not wish to assist,” he says, “he does not assist; concerning them, in his predestination, he secretly but justly judged otherwise. For there is no injustice with God.”

Saint Gregory the pope, Fulgentius, and Isidore held views similar to these. I have refrained from setting down their testimonies, lest our labor become less welcome by being prolonged at length through the writings of others.

Let us learn how weighty Augustine’s authority is from Pope Celestine’s teaching.

[Note: [Col. 0642D] “Pope Celestine.” In chapter 2 of the epistle to the bishops of Gaul. Lupus also reports this passage of Celestine in the same words in his Collectanea, p. 246.]

“We have always held Augustine, a man of holy memory, in our communion, on account of both his life and his merits. Never has a rumor of sinister suspicion stained him, whom we remember to have once possessed such great learning that even among teachers he was always counted so by my predecessors. Therefore everyone unanimously formed a good opinion of him, since everywhere he was both loved and honored by all.”

But lest, as we learned while being instructed in secular literature, we be judged to embrace the errors of teachers out of love for them—Augustine himself properly warns us away from this in the aforementioned book On the Gift of Perseverance, in these words:

[Col. 0643A] “Although I would not wish anyone to embrace all my writings in such a way as to follow me, except in those matters in which he has recognized that I do not err…”

Let Paul therefore come forward, so that he may at last disclose this secret in his own words, and so that truth may be sought from the place where it should chiefly be sought:

“Wishing,” he says, “to show his wrath and make known his power, God endured with much patience the vessels of wrath that are perfected for perdition, in order to make known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy that he prepared for glory.”

[Note: [Col. 0643D] “They are perfected for perdition.” See Epistles 128 and 129.]

Behold, the teacher of the Gentiles confirms that the vessels of wrath are perfected for perdition.

Certainly, insofar as human opinion is concerned, it is more fitting to say that something is “perfected” than that it is “predestined.” For, given the variability of human circumstances, what has been perfected cannot become unperfected, whereas what is predestined can at times be changed.

But insofar as God’s majesty, which contains all things, is concerned, the same thing is both perfected—for he made what was to come—and predestined, because it is to be fulfilled by immutable truth.

He calls that wrath the punishment inflicted on the reprobate. It is concluded in these words of the Gospel: “Whoever does not believe in the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John III).

To avoid this wrath the Prophet prayed: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your wrath” (Ps. XXXVII).

But perhaps the intention of those who think differently will not be quieted by this passage either, because many copies read not “the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction,” but “the vessels of wrath suited for destruction.”

As though, for this reason, the vessels of wrath could not be predestined for destruction because they are suited for destruction. Let the Lord Jesus therefore approach and himself untie the knot of the question.

Finally, he himself says in the Gospel: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given” (Matt. XIII).

He is speaking to the disciples: “To you it has been given”; “but to them it has not been given”—that is, to the crowds flowing together from every direction.

If I understand the teacher correctly, mercy gathers those to whom it has been given, while judgment repels those to whom it has not been given—that is, it leaves them by not assisting them.

The elect to whom it has been given have been predestined, and their number is fixed. For God would not predestine those whose total number he did not know.

Since the reprobate cannot aspire to that number, because it has not been given to them to be saved, who could demonstrate or dare to affirm that their condemnation has not been predestined?

Again, the Gospel prescribes an immutable sentence: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John III). To what purpose, do you suppose, except for punishment?

Why, I ask, unless he sinned in Adam, who sinned of his own will, and God’s grace did not liberate him? Or did he also heap up condemnation upon himself by choosing to remain in unbelief? Indeed, that is so.

But why did he refuse to believe? Because, as it is written, “faith is not possessed by all.”

But why is faith not possessed by all? There is a fixed limit, which no one except an impious person dares to exceed: because it has not been given to them.

Why it has not been given to them belongs solely to the counsel of that one whose judgment, although at times hidden, is never unjust.

This severity probably also resounds in the saying:

[Note: [Col. 0643D] “Consider the works of God.” Lupus praises this passage from Ecclesiasticus in exactly the same words in Epistle 129.]

“Consider the works of God: no one can correct the one whom he has despised” (Ecclus. VII).

That is, the vessel of wrath suited for destruction, or prepared for perdition, being evil, remains obstinately fixed in evil forever. Even if it seems temporarily to feign correction, it returns to sin and brings death upon itself, as a dog returns to its vomit.

Let students who take great pleasure in the adornment of speech recognize in this same sentence not only the brilliance of its eloquence, but also its rhythmically falling cadence.

[Note: [Col. 0643D] “The adornment of speech.” Lupus writes in Epistle 35: “For most of us seek elegance of expression from it.”]

Now, since the matter is secure, let us put aside disputes about words, lest, quarreling with one another in childish contentiousness for the empty display of victory, we be rebuked by the Apostle, who says: “Do not contend with words. For it is useful for nothing except the subversion of the hearers” (I Tim. II).

Since we have one heavenly teacher, who is the true one and the truth itself—from whom all truth is received and to whom all truth must be referred—why should we fight for our own discoveries, so that we may all say the same thing: that it is not our invention but his teaching? Let us peacefully and humbly discover what is most correct.

But if some are moved by such great authorities and understand that they have been overcome not by our assertion but by manifest truth, let them not disdain to change their opinion, because a person should not be so ashamed of having erred as of refusing to avoid a recognized error.

[Note: [Col. 0643D] “Refusing to avoid it.” Lactantius, Book III of the Divine Institutes, chapter 23: “What shall I say about those—I do not know what to call them—who, once they have gone astray, persist steadfastly in folly and defend empty things with empty arguments, except that I sometimes think they do it either for the sake of a joke…”]

“...to philosophize, or for prudent and knowledgeable people to undertake the defence of lies, as though in evil matters they were to exercise or display their talents.” Claudianus Mamertus, *On the State of the Soul*, book I, chapter 1: “And since they have fallen through human imprudence, they choose to defend the audacity of their fault through obstinate persistence, lest they appear to have been capable of sinning.” Tully [Cicero] eloquently attacks men of this kind in the passage that Lupus immediately appends.]

not to wish to avoid it. The most eminent orator Tully [Cicero] subtly and usefully demonstrates this by an example suited to his purpose. “If,” he says, “we should appear rashly to have overlooked something of someone’s, or not to have followed it with sufficient elegance, once instructed by someone else we shall readily and willingly change our opinion.” [Col. 0644D] For it is not shameful to have learned too little, but to have persisted foolishly and for a long time in what one has learned too little; the former is attributable to the common weakness of human beings, the latter to the particular fault of each individual.”

Having dealt with the two questions—that is, concerning free will [Col. 0645A] and predestination [Note: [Col. 0645D] Not as we wished. Epistle 30: “Having set forth the preceding words, whose meaning we discussed at length, not as we wished but as we were able.”—] not as we wished but as we were able, let us proceed to the third, namely, concerning redemption: how great Christ’s blood is, which is the final question. And from whom could we better take the beginning of our consideration than from the one whose words he fulfilled afterward as a man, but foretold beforehand as God? These are his words: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John XII).

In this lifting-up, which he endured by humbling himself so that we might be exalted, that blood was poured out for many for the remission of sins. For thus the same Jesus—that is, “Saviour” in our language—saved his people from their sins. Finally, he did not choose one particular nation alone to save in its entirety by a singular privilege; but, as Caiaphas prophesied, perhaps not on his own merit but through the dignity of the priestly office that he was to commend, Jesus died not only for the Jewish nation from which he derived his human lineage, but also “to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad.” Not because they were still children of God, but because, in the course of being gathered, they became children of God when they joined the unity of faith.

Therefore, not inappropriately, he drew all things to himself, as he had foretold, since from every human race he chose all whom he had determined to save. They are called “many” because certainly many are saved; yet they are called “all” because they are gathered from every human race. Scripture signifies that the blood of God was poured out for these people because the Word became flesh—that is, God became man—using a part to signify the whole, as elsewhere: “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke III) [Col. 0645C], that is, every human being. And because, when God assumed our complete nature, he certainly retained his own incorrupt nature, the universal Church, spread throughout the whole world, confesses this. It is bound by the necessity of remaining in the sanctification it has received, as the Apostle explains: “You were bought with a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (I Corinthians VI).

Likewise, counting himself among all, the same Apostle says: “He did not spare his own Son”—without doubt, God’s Son—“but handed him over for us all” (Romans VIII). Again, concerning all these people, in the Epistle entitled to the Hebrews: “We see Jesus, who for the suffering of death was crowned with glory and honour, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for all” (Hebrews II). And immediately, explaining who these people are, he added: “For it was fitting that he, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, having brought many sons into glory, should perfect the author of their salvation through suffering.”

It was fitting, indeed, that God the Father—for whom are all things, that is, whose goodness is the cause of all things, and through whom are all things, because from him the Son, co-eternal with him, was begotten, through whom all things were made (for the holy Psalm says, “You made all things in wisdom” [Psalm CI])—it was fitting that he should perfect through suffering the author of their salvation, that is, the author of those who are saved. The Father had brought many sons into glory, since no one had come to the Son unless the Father himself had drawn him. Thus he perfected the author of their salvation through suffering so that he might fulfil what is said of him: “The things that Jesus began both to do and to teach.” What he himself had first taught as something to be done in the world, namely, “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends,” he fulfilled, and the Father perfected him through suffering—that is, displayed him as consummate and perfect. What he had taught well, he not only did not refuse to fulfil, although the task was difficult, but also stirred up others by his example.

It should be observed that those whom he calls “all” in what he stated shortly before—namely, that “by the grace of God he tasted death for all”—he now shortly afterward calls “many,” saying that he had brought “many sons into glory.” Carefully weighing this authority of the divine utterances [Col. 0646B] suggests that the Son of God can be understood to have tasted death for all in the same way that God wills all to be saved. For just as he wills all who are saved to be saved, so he redeems all who are redeemed. But not all are saved, nor are all redeemed. Therefore he does not will all others to be saved or redeemed except those who are redeemed and saved.

Blessed Augustine is found expressing this sense in the book mentioned above, called the *Enchiridion*. The passage is as follows:

> “The Church spoken of among the holy angels and powers will become known to us as it truly is when we have been joined to it at the end, in order to possess eternal blessedness together with it. But this Church, which is a pilgrim on earth, is better known to us to the extent that we are in it, and because it consists of human beings, as we too do. This Church has been redeemed from every sin by the blood of the Mediator, who had no sin. Its voice is: ‘If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all’ (Romans VIII). In the Church, then, which has been redeemed from every sin by the blood of the sinless Mediator, he understands all those included by the apostolic testimony: ‘He handed him over for us all.’
>
> “Nevertheless, let those who investigate the divine utterances not be troubled by the fact that it can plausibly be said that Christ died for all who receive the sacraments of his faith, whether they will preserve them or not. That he died for those who will preserve them can be doubted by no one. For those who will not preserve them, the Apostle is a sufficient authority in the testimony: ‘Through knowledge the brother for whom Christ died will perish’ (I Corinthians VIII). Nor is it surprising, since faith without works is idle, and many are called but few are taught to be chosen.
>
> “Yet some vehemently abominate and condemn this as though it were blasphemous, because, unless he redeemed all human beings universally, they think that great injury is done to the Redeemer. We, however, while preserving the faith [Note: [Col. 0645D] Preserving the faith. “Since to hold different opinions concerning the same questions,” Lupus says in Epistle 30, “so long as this is not contrary to the faith, is either no fault or only a small one.”—], namely, that God redeemed by his blood all whom he wished to redeem, and that none have been redeemed except those whom he himself redeemed, leave the matter open. If anyone can demonstrate that the same blood of the Redeemer benefits even the lost in some way [Col. 0647A], we will not merely offer no resistance; we will gladly adopt their opinion.
>
> “For if the sun warms the blind, although it does not illuminate them, why should the more powerful sun—although it does not save those blinded and condemned through their own merit—not lessen their punishment by the merit of so great a price? This is so, provided that the benevolence of his counsel permits it; of him it is sung: ‘The Lord is sweet to all, and his mercies are over all his works’ (Psalm CXLIV).”

Yet the Apostle seems to oppose this opinion when he says: “I, Paul, tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will benefit you nothing” (Galatians III). For if Christ will benefit those who have been baptised and have also received the Holy Spirit nothing, as the same Apostle declares in these words, “Did you receive the Spirit from works of the law or from hearing with faith?” (Galatians V), if, I say, Christ will benefit such baptised people nothing when they fall away from the faith [Col. 0647B], how will he benefit those who have been baptised, have afterward fallen back into crimes without reforming, or have died in unbelief?

But lest those who are pleased to say that all, whether good or evil, have been redeemed indiscriminately by Christ pronounce me worthy of ridicule and rejection, I shall offer one testimony that agrees with them and, as I think, restore all of them to goodwill. John of Constantinople, a bishop distinguished equally for doctrine and holiness, explained the statement already cited—“that by the grace of God he tasted death for all”—as follows: “that by the grace of God he tasted death for all, not only for the faithful, but for the whole world. And indeed he died for all. But what if not all believe? He fulfilled what belonged to him.”

Let each person, then, after carefully considering the points above, choose whatever God has suggested to him as best by hidden inspiration, or whatever his teacher, Scripture, has set forth with evident reason.

245. These are the things I had to say concerning the three questions that should not be despised—and may they have been as useful as they were lengthy. If diligent readers do not disdain learning them, although they may be unable to approve my blunt and unpolished discussion, still, I believe, they will not condemn it, since I have willingly and benevolently set forth for those who wished to learn what I thought useful.

[Col. 0647]

## B. COLLECTION OF SERVATUS LUPUS, ABBOT OF FERRIÈRES, ON THE THREE QUESTIONS

246. Since many commendably diligent people desired to learn, in the authors’ own words, what outcome the questions concerning predestination and free will, as well as concerning the redemption through Christ’s blood, have, I faithfully fulfilled their wish. In this way, through God’s grace, may the instruction of those who piously inquire receive increase, and may the contradiction among those who hold different opinions be softened.

Nor will a benevolent and prudent reader take offence if I identify the teachers through whom I have advanced and continue to advance, or if, after presenting their more obscure statements, I shed some light upon them. He should consider with me the honour due to them, and can readily perceive [Col. 0648C] that I reveal what I have discovered not from the vanity of display, but from the desire to make the truth evident [Note: [Col. 0647D] “He does not display.” Vanity. In Epistle 128: “Nor, as some pretend to suspect, do I desire to become known pointlessly—that is, from a desire for empty glory … but with a view to asserting the truth,” and so forth.—]. Let the narrative now carry out its purpose.

[Col. 0647D] [Note: [Col. 0648D] Pope Celestine. He cites the same passage in the *Book on the Three Questions*, p. 237.—]

Pope Celestine commends blessed Augustine in these words (Epistle 8, to the bishops of Gaul):

> “We have always held Augustine, a man of holy memory, in our communion on account of his life and merits, and never did even a rumour of sinister suspicion stain him. We remember that he was once a man of such great learning that he was counted even among the teachers by my predecessors. Therefore everyone unanimously formed a good opinion of him, since everywhere he was an object both of love and of honour.”

This most distinguished teacher [Note: [Col. 0648D] “Most distinguished teacher.” He is speaking of Augustine, whom Lupus calls “a most distinguished author” in Epistle 30.—], praised by so great an encomium from the Apostolic See, in the book addressed to Laurence on Faith, Hope, and Charity, which he published when already a bishop and an old man, indicates that the good and the evil are predestined (chapter 100 of the *Enchiridion*):

> “These are the great works of the Lord, sought out according to all his purposes, and sought out with such wisdom that, when the angelic and human creature had sinned—that is, had done not what he, but what it itself willed—even through that same will of the creature, by which what the Creator did not will came to pass, he fulfilled what he willed. He makes good use even of evil things, as supremely good, both for the condemnation of those whom he justly predestined to punishment and for the salvation of those whom he kindly predestined to glory.”

[Col. 0648D] In the final book of the same work, *The City of God*, which he composed when already a bishop, he had expressed the same point (Book XXII, chapter 24, near the end):

> “All these things are consolations for the miserable and the condemned, not rewards for the blessed. What, then, are those rewards, if these things are so numerous, so excellent, and so great? What will he give to those whom he predestined to life, who gave these things even to those whom he predestined to death?”

But in the penultimate book of that carefully composed and wondrous work he had taught as follows:

> “The reason why the Church does not now pray for the evil angels, whom it knows to be its enemies, is the very reason why at that future judgment it will not pray even for human beings who are to be tormented in eternal fire [Note: [Col. 0649D] “Eternal fire.” See what we said concerning eternal fire in the notes on Salvian, and likewise on Vincent of Lérins.], although it will then possess perfect holiness.
>
> “For now it prays for those whom, within the human race, it regards as enemies because this is the time of fruitful repentance. What does it pray for them above all except that God may grant them, as the Apostle said, repentance, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive according to his will?
>
> “Finally, if the Church were so certain about some people that it knew who they were—people who, although still living in this life, had nevertheless been predestined to go into eternal fire with the devil—it would pray for them no more than it prays for the devil himself. But because it is certain about no one, it prays for all its human enemies who are living in this body, although it is not heard on behalf of all.
>
> “For it is heard only on behalf of those who, although they oppose the Church, have nevertheless been predestined in such a way that the Church’s prayer for them is heard and they become children of the Church. But if some retain an unrepentant heart until death and are not converted from enemies into children, does the Church now pray for them—that is, for the spirits of such dead people? No. Why is this so, except because one who, while in the body, was not transferred to Christ is now counted among the devil’s portion?
>
> “The reason why prayer will not then be offered for human beings destined for eternal fire is therefore the same reason why prayer is offered neither now nor then for the evil angels. And this is likewise the reason why, although prayer is now offered even for evil human beings who are alive, it is no longer offered now for unbelieving and ungodly people who have died.
>
> “For the dead, whether of the Church itself or of certain pious people, prayer is heard on behalf of some; but on behalf of those whose regeneration in Christ was not so compromised by a badly conducted life in the body that they should be judged unworthy of such mercy, nor so upright that they should be found not to need such mercy.”

Likewise, in the second book addressed to Marcellinus (chapter 17), Augustine, already a bishop, writes of the predestined evil:

> “That what was hidden may become known, and what was not pleasing may become sweet, is the work of God’s grace, which helps human wills. The reason why they are not helped is likewise found in those wills themselves, not in God—whether they have been predestined for condemnation on account of the wickedness of pride, or are judged against that very pride of theirs so that, having been instructed, they may become children of mercy.”

Likewise, in the book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, which he published either among or after the books of the *Retractations*, he holds this view concerning the predestined evil (chapter 11) [Note: [Col. 0649D] “Among or after the books of the *Retractations*.” So it is stated in the *Book on the Three Questions*, p. 235.—]:

> “He does not help those whom he does not wish to help; concerning them, in his predestination, he secretly but justly formed another judgment. For there is no injustice with God.”

In the same book (chapter 17), he confirmed by apostolic testimony that predestination is signified by the term “foreknowledge.” “God did not reject his people whom he foreknew.” What he says—“foreknew”—is not correctly understood unless it means “predestined.”

As for what “to predestine” means, he had defined it earlier in the same book as follows (chapter 17), a statement that must be retained in faithful memory:

> “The gifts and calling of God are without repentance. For to arrange in his foreknowledge—which cannot be deceived or changed—the future works of his own hands is precisely, and nothing else than, to predestine.”

He did not hesitate to preach publicly concerning the predestination of both groups, that is, of the good and the evil:

> “Because you loved me before the foundation of the world” (John XVII). For in him he loved us too before the foundation of the world, and he has already predestined what he will do at the world’s end. “Righteous Father, the world has not known you” (ibid.), because you are righteous, therefore the world has not known you. For that world, predestined to condemnation, did not know him deservedly; but the world whom he reconciled to himself through Christ knew him not by merit but by grace.

250. In the work which Prosper bears witness that he composed last, during the assault of the Vandals, at the very end of his days, persevering gloriously in defence of Christian grace [Note: [Col. 0649D] Prosper. Specifically, in the *Chronicle*. This is that celebrated Prosper, the most energetic and learned defender of Augustine’s works. Gennadius composed a brief account of his life in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*. But since the oldest manuscript of the monastery of Corbie has a somewhat different version of what Gennadius says about Prosper from the printed editions, I shall quote the passage itself from that manuscript: “Prosper, a man from the region of Aquitaine, counsellor of Pope Leo, scholastic in speech and vigorous in his assertions,” and so forth.—], he speaks as follows:

> “What does it help you that you have thrown before me those whom God’s patience awaits, to be corrected through repentance, and for whose sake he makes his sun rise and sends rain, when I have thrown before you the goats of the left-hand side? The one who knows all future things cannot be unaware that they will live without repentance to the end in their impiety and crimes and therefore be punished with eternal torment.
>
> “He does not refrain from granting the good of his creation even to those for whom it would have been better neither to be born nor to receive, for as long as it pleases him, the good of nourishment and continued life, although it would be better for them to die as quickly as possible. Among them are certainly many who, if they were snatched from this life as infants, would, according to your false heresy, be completely removed from every punishment, and according to the Catholic faith would be removed from the gravest condemnation.
>
> “Moreover, what of the fact that among these goats of the left-hand side, destined in God’s infallible foreknowledge to everlasting fire, there are many who, after being washed in the bath of regeneration, later perish either through apostasy or by living so criminally and shamefully that they are undoubtedly assigned to that left-hand side? They are not snatched away, as some are, lest wickedness change their understanding; nor is God prevented by a fatal necessity from granting them so great a benefit; nor does he change because he grants it to some rather than others through partiality toward persons.”

This is what Saint Augustine says concerning predestination. But lest anyone who hears of the predestined evil suppose that God is the author of their destruction, just as he is the author of the salvation of those whom he predestined to glory, let him consider that the same God created Adam upright [Note: [Col. 0651D] “God made Adam upright.” Epistle 128: “God created Adam upright, as Holy Scripture teaches, and in him created us all upright in our original condition.”—] and originally created us all upright in him. Adam existed, as blessed Ambrose says, and we all existed in him; Adam perished, and we all perished in him [Note: [Col. 0651D] “Adam existed.” The same statements are reported exactly in Epistle 128.—].

Since, then, we were all upright in Adam, when he sinned without any necessity, we were undoubtedly corrupted by sin and condemned by divine judgment. From this mass of the entire human race, rightly condemned, when vessels are made for honour—that is, when the elect are formed—God’s mercy overflows, and corrupted nature is saved by his grace alone. Therefore both their creation and their salvation belong to God: the one is attributed to his workmanship, the other to his beneficence.

But when vessels are made from the same mass for dishonour—that is, when those who will not be saved are brought forth—there should be no surprise, because the mass from which they are created was condemned justly on account of voluntary sin. Therefore, the fact that they are created is God’s; the fact that they are condemned is theirs [Note: [Col. 0651D] “Therefore, the fact that they are created is God’s.” Epistle 128: “That they are created is God’s gift; that they are punished is their own.”—]. And who does not know that the creation of anything at all, much less of a human being, is good, while punishment for a fault voluntarily committed is just?

When, therefore, we hear of the good as predestined, let us contemplate God creating them and liberating them by his grace from the mass condemned on account of its merit. When we hear of the evil as predestined, let us likewise consider God creating them and, in accordance with the merit of the condemned mass, leaving them to judgment. Thus in both groups the goodness of creation will always be evident to us, while either mercy in those who are taken up or justice in those who are left behind will shine forth.

For God does not drive those whom he created into destruction; rather, those whom he does not liberate from destruction by grace he leaves in the destruction that they deserved either by being born or by living afterward, through a hidden yet not reprehensible justice [Note: [Col. 0652D] “Hidden, yet not reprehensible.” This is among Lupus’s more familiar and customary ways of speaking, as stated above in the note to p. 225.—]. Thus God, in accordance with blessed Paul, “has mercy on whomever he wills, and hardens whomever he wills” (Romans IX), and he does everything that he wills in heaven and on earth. Yet the Lord our God is upright, and there is no injustice in him.

Concerning those who are liberated it was said: “Do not fear, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke XII). Concerning those who are left behind: “He gave them over to the desires of their hearts; they shall walk in their own inventions” (Psalm LXXX).

Blessed Augustine made this meaning sufficiently clear in the book mentioned above, which, as I have shown, he composed last (Book I, chapter 126):

> “When all are said to come from one person into condemnation, the mass itself is signified from which the potter makes some vessels for honour—that is, those who are taken up into grace—and others for dishonour—that is, those who are left to pay what is owed. In this way the children of grace may know that what has been given to them would not have been unjust if it had been demanded of them, and thus may glory not in themselves but in the Lord.”

A little later, refuting what Julian had written—“Piety and reason have explained that my God forms no one for dishonour”—he says:

> “If your god forms no one for dishonour, he is not the God of the Apostle Paul. For he was speaking of the true God when he said: ‘O man, who are you to answer back to God? Will the thing formed say to the one who formed it, “Why did you make me like this?” Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same mass to make one vessel for honour and another for dishonour?’ (Romans IX.) But you, evidently a great craftsman, bring forth from the Pelagian workshop a better god, one who made no vessel for dishonour.”

Again, somewhat later (chapter 182):

> “God does not withhold the good of his formation even from a condemned stock. But if you dislike God’s creating those whom he condemns [Col. 0652B], then oppose him, if you can, so that he may not create those whom he foreknew would become evil, persevere in wickedness to the end, and therefore undoubtedly be condemned. Or, if you think it right, suggest to him that he forbid the snatching from this life of so many thousands of unbaptised infants whom he knows will live destructively and whom he himself will condemn to eternal fire with the devil, while they are still innocent and good.”

After a brief interruption he continues:

> “For when you suppose that you are making an envious accusation by saying that God creates those whom he condemns, consider how much more enviously another person could similarly and foolishly say that God regenerates those whom he condemns, since it lies within his omnipotent power to remove them from the temptations of this mortal life before they become condemnable.
>
> “But if you cannot say these things, cannot contradict God, and cannot offer your counsel to that wisdom—for ‘who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?’ (Isaiah XL)—stop introducing to us another potter who makes no vessels for dishonour, and stop reproving the one who makes them. Recognise that, so that you may not involve yourself in this sacrilege, the Apostle says to you: ‘O man, who are you to answer back to God?’ (Romans IX).”

Let us return from controversy to the Apostle Paul, and, with so great an authority illuminating his obscure passage, understand it to our benefit:

> “What if God, wishing to show his wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory toward the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory?” (ibid.).

254. Concerning these vessels of wrath and vessels of mercy, both here and often elsewhere, as well as in the Epistle to Bishop Optatus (Epistle 157), the same author clearly expressed what should be understood:

> “Why, then, are those also created whom the Creator knows to belong to condemnation rather than to grace? The blessed Apostle recalls this with brevity as concise as his authority is great. For he says that God, wishing to show his wrath and demonstrate his power, brought forth with much patience vessels of wrath that have been completed for destruction [Col. 0653A], in order to make known the riches of his glory toward the vessels of mercy. Earlier he had described him as a potter who, from the same mass, makes one vessel for honour and another for dishonour.
>
> “It would rightly seem unjust that vessels of wrath should be made from it for destruction if the whole mass had not been condemned in Adam. Therefore, that they are made from it by being born belongs to the punishment that is owed; but that they are made vessels of mercy by being reborn belongs to grace that is not owed.
>
> “God therefore shows his wrath—not, certainly, a disturbance of mind such as the anger of human beings, but a just and fixed vengeance—because from the stock of disobedience there descends a succession of sin and punishment. ‘A human being born of woman,’ as it is written in the Book of Job (Job XIV), ‘is short-lived and full of wrath’; for he is a vessel of that with which he is full, and therefore they are called vessels of wrath.
>
> “He also demonstrates his power, by which he makes good use even of evil people, granting them many natural and temporal goods and employing their wickedness to exercise the good and admonish them by comparison, so that in them the good may learn to give thanks to God: they have been distinguished from the evil not by their own merits, which were equal in the same mass, but by God’s mercy.
>
> “This is seen especially in infants. When they are reborn through Christ’s grace and, ending this life at that tender age, pass into eternal and blessed life, it cannot be said that they are distinguished by free choice from other infants who die without this grace under the condemnation of the same mass.
>
> “But if only those people were created from Adam who would be recreated by grace, and if no others were born besides those adopted as God’s children, the benefit granted to the undeserving would remain hidden, because no deserved punishment would be inflicted on anyone coming from the same condemnable stock.
>
> “But when he brought forth with much patience vessels of wrath completed for destruction, he not only showed his wrath and demonstrated his power by exacting vengeance and making good use of those who are not good; he also made known the riches of his glory toward the vessels of mercy.
>
> “For the one justified freely learns what has been granted to him when, not by his own merit but by the glory of God’s most generous mercy, he is distinguished from the condemned person with whom he himself would have been condemned by the same justice. He therefore wished so many whom he foreknew did not belong to his grace to be born through creation that, by an immeasurable comparison, they would greatly outnumber those whom he deigned to predestine as children of promise for the glory of his kingdom. Thus, even by the multitude of the rejected, it might be shown how insignificant in the sight of the just God is any number, however great, of those most justly condemned.
>
> “And so those who are redeemed from that condemnation may also understand from this that what was owed to the whole mass was returned to so great a part of it. This is evident not only in those who add many evils by the choice of an evil will to original sin, but also in so many infants [Col. 0654A] who, bound only by the chain of original sin, are snatched from this light without the Mediator’s grace.
>
> “For the entire mass would receive the due of just condemnation unless the potter, who is not only just but also merciful, made from it other vessels for honour according to grace, not according to what was owed—helping infants, whose merits cannot be mentioned, and anticipating adults so that they might possess some merits.”

The distinguished author Jerome, a disciple of the same Hieronymus [i.e. Jerome], read about the predestined evil in Augustine’s work addressed to Marcellinus (*Against the Pelagians*, Book III, at the end) [Note: [Col. 0653D] “Holy man.” This is the passage in which Jerome praises Augustine. It is established that Augustine outlived Jerome. Thus, following the custom of his age, he calls Augustine a holy man even while he was living; we have discussed that custom at greater length in the notes on Salvian, and need not repeat it. Yet it seemed worth adding the notable passage from Book I, chapter 11, of Saint Gregory’s *Pastoral Care*. Speaking mournfully of bad bishops, the holy man cries: “For no one harms the Church more than one who, acting perversely, bears the name or rank of holiness. No one presumes to rebuke such an offender; and the fault spreads vehemently as an example when, out of reverence for his rank, the sinner is honoured.” Salvian said similarly of religious persons—that is, of the clergy generally—in Book V, p. 117: “After the disgrace and crimes of their former shameful acts, they inscribed upon themselves the title of holiness and changed only their name, not their life: not by conduct, but by profession.”]. He not only did not criticise that work but also praised it highly. His words are these:

> “Some time ago the holy and eloquent bishop Augustine wrote to Marcellinus—who was later killed by heretics, though innocent, amid the odium surrounding the tyranny of Heraclian—two books against your heresy concerning the baptism of infants, through which you wish to assert that infants are baptised not for the remission of sins but for the kingdom of heaven. He also wrote a third book to the same Marcellinus against those who say, as you do, that a human being can be without sin if he wishes, without God’s grace.
>
> “Therefore I think this labour should be set aside, lest Horace’s words be said to me: ‘Do not carry wood into the forest.’ For either we shall say the same things unnecessarily, or, if we wish to say something new, the better arguments have already been taken up by that most distinguished intellect.”

The same teacher expressed the meaning of predestination in another passage, in his exposition of the First Psalm:

> “But whoever does not believe,” he says, “has already been judged; for he has already been prejudged for punishment.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The ungodly do not rise in judgment; they do not rise to be judged, because they have already been judged. For ‘whoever does not believe in me has already been judged.’”

Likewise, in the *Dialogue*:

> “It is one thing to strike with the affection of a teacher and parent, and another to rage against adversaries with a cruel spirit. For this reason he also sings in the First Psalm: ‘The ungodly do not rise for judgment’; they have already been prejudged for judgment.”

[Col. 0654D] Likewise, in his exposition of the prophet Isaiah (chapter XXIV):

> “For ‘the devastated earth,’ the Seventy interpreted ‘the corrupted world’; and for ‘its afflicted face’—that is, the face of the earth—the same translators rendered, ‘and he will reveal its face,’ so that the dead may come forth from their graves; or, ‘he will uncover it,’ so that all its works may be brought into public view, and the inhabitants may be scattered to different places, destined either for rewards or for punishments.”

Philip, a not-unworthy hearer of the same Jerome, says in his exposition of blessed Job’s statement, “Before his days are fulfilled he will perish” (Job XV):

> “A person’s days are said to be fulfilled when the recompense of good and evil people arrives. Therefore this person, whether human or the devil, will perish before the day of manifest judgment that the Lord will assign to him in the future judgment. He has been foreknown in predestination, just as the Prophet also says of the cruel [the printed reading is uncertain, *incrudelis*]: ‘The ungodly shall not rise in judgment’ (Psalm I), or as the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Whoever does not believe has already been judged’ (John III).”

Saint Pope Gregory indicates the predestined evil in still more compressed language (Book XXXIII, chapter 11):

> “Leviathan, who with his members has been assigned to eternal torments, and deceit is directed in his hand, while strength dwells in his neck, accomplishes with more perverse power what he desires temporarily through a perverse will against the good, so that the more nothing hinders him from adversity in the present, the less anything remains for him of prosperity in the future.”

Explaining, nevertheless, how this same predestination or assignment is to be understood, he says in the *Moralia*:

> “‘I will not raise him as though I were cruel. For who can resist my face, and who has given to me beforehand that I should repay him?’ This openly indicates the meaning. I do not raise him as though I were cruel, because by his strength I powerfully rescue my elect; and, in turn, I condemn the reprobate not unjustly but reasonably. That is, I can wondrously rescue those whom I kindly choose, and I do not unjustly abandon those whom I reject.”

And somewhat later:

> “In a wondrous manner the equitable Creator both chooses some before others and justly leaves some in their own reprobate ways.”

Likewise, in the *Moralia*, while explaining the statement (Book II, chapter 5), “If he destroys, no one can build; if he imprisons a person, no one can open” (Job XII), he says:

> “Almighty God destroys the human heart when he abandons it, and builds it when he fills it. For he does not destroy the human mind by attacking it, but by withdrawing from it, since the mind, when left to itself, is sufficient for its own destruction.”

Again, somewhat later in the same chapter:

> “‘If he imprisons a person, there is no one who can open.’ For just as no one resists the generosity of the one who calls, so no one opposes the justice of the one who abandons. To imprison, therefore, belongs to God: to those who are shut in, he does not open. Hence it is also said to Moses concerning Pharaoh: ‘I will harden his heart.’ He is said to harden it through justice when he does not soften the reprobate heart by grace.”

The same author, in his exposition of the Gospel sentence (Homily IV, on the Gospels), says:

> “Do not go along the road of the Gentiles” (Matthew 10): “By a subtle and hidden judgment,” he says, “the holy preaching is withdrawn from the ears of certain people, because they do not deserve to be awakened through grace. [Col. 0656A] Hence, dearest brothers, it is necessary that in everything we do we fear the hidden counsels of the omnipotent Lord concerning us, lest, while our mind, poured outward, does not recall itself from its own will, the judge within should terribly arrange adversities against it. The Psalmist, observing this well, says: ‘Come and see the works of the Lord, how terrible he is in his counsels concerning the sons of men’ (Psalm 65). For he saw that one person is called mercifully, while another is rejected as justice requires. And because the Lord arranges some things by sparing and others by anger, he was terrified by what he could not penetrate; and because he saw him not only as inscrutable in certain of his judgments but also as unbending, he declared him terrible in his counsels.”

Bede, deeply learned in the divine Scriptures, unequivocally asserted that the good and the wicked are predestined when explaining the passage in Genesis: “Rise up, leave this place, because the Lord is going to destroy this city”; and “he seemed to them to be speaking as one who was jesting” (Genesis 19). [Col. 0656B]

> “The fact that the angels shut the door on Lot,” he says, “so that the Sodomites could not seize either him or anyone from his household and carry them away to destruction, plainly signifies that the impiety and persecution of the reprobate will destroy none of God’s elect, since the Lord says of his sheep: ‘And I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them from my hand’ (John 10). Likewise, the fact that Lot, although he tried very hard, was unable, by the opportunity granted him by the angels, to recall any of the treacherous citizens to salvation—not even his own relatives or friends—signifies that no human labor can add even one soul to the number of the predestined, who were chosen by the Lord before the foundation of the world. [Col. 0656C] God knows those who are his. Yet although, in our frailty, who belong to the company of the elect is hidden from us, we must not cease to care for our salvation, nor must our tongue be restrained from instructing our neighbors. Rather, after the example of the blessed Lot, we must live chastely and also offer the service of charity for the correction of those who err. For it is certain that, although we cannot save those predestined to destruction, we do not lose the reward of our kindness, which we extend for their salvation.”

[Note: [Col. 0655D] *Tameneisi.* In place of *tametsi*. This word, which had already become so obsolete that scarcely anyone recognized it, was brought back from oblivion by the great J. C. Jacobus Cujacius, who should be compared with those ancients, as our Muretus says in Book XI of the *Various Readings*, chapter 17. There he cites numerous testimonies proving that the word should be retained. Lupus likewise uses it on page 258.]

Saint Fulgentius, bishop of the African province of Ruspe, as John, deacon of the Roman Church, writes, discussed the predestined in this manner in his book to Peter, *On the Rule of True Faith* (*On the Faith to Peter*, chapter 35):

> “Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in any way, that all those whom God makes vessels of mercy by gratuitous goodness were predestined by God before the foundation of the world for adoption as sons of God; that none of those whom God predestined for the kingdom can perish; and that none of those whom God did not predestine for life can be saved by any means. For that predestination is the preparation of a gratuitous gift, by which the Apostle says that we were predestined for adoption as sons of God through Jesus Christ and in him.” [Col. 0657A]

Likewise, in his book to Monimus (chapter 5), Fulgentius expressed the blessed Augustine’s view concerning those predestined to destruction in these words:

> “I think that nothing else should be understood in that statement of Saint Augustine which affirms that certain people were predestined to destruction, except destruction by punishment, not by sin; not to the evil that they unjustly commit, but to the torment that they will most justly suffer; not to the sin by which they either do not receive or lose the benefit of the first resurrection, but to the punishment that their own iniquity wickedly produces for them and divine justice rightly repays; not to the first death of the soul, in which infants are born, or into which criminals fall when, as blessed James says (James 1), they are drawn away and enticed by their own desire; but to the second death, which they must suffer when the most just Judge repays them—whether they depart from this world before receiving the grace of baptism, or, having received the grace of God in vain, prefer to remain servants of sin until the end of the present life after baptism, and refuse, while the time is favorable and the day of salvation has come, to turn from their evil way and live. They do not know that God’s kindness leads them to repentance; instead, according to their hardness and impenitent heart, they store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment.” [Col. 0657B]

Likewise, John, deacon of the Roman Church,

[Note: [Col. 0657C] *John the Deacon.* Thus this is his exposition on the *Heptateuch*. Whether he was also the author of the *Life of Saint Gregory the Pope* is not so firmly established.]

expressed the predestined wicked in the words of blessed Augustine, wishing to show what is signified by the passage in Genesis (chapter 1): “Let the waters that are under heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear”:

> “What is the dry land?” he says. “In the Church, every soul thirsting for the Lord is called dry land. For the waters were separated, and the dry land appeared. This sea is the world, and the waters, which are bitter, were separated and gathered into one gathering—that is, predestined toward one end, to which the omnipotent God directs those whom he separates from the saints.”

Bishop Isidore says in Book II of the *Sentences* (chapter 6):

> “Predestination is twofold: either of the elect to rest, or of the reprobate to death.”

Nevertheless, some think that he should be censured because he alone introduced a twofold—that is, a doubled—predestination [Col. 0658A], since, according to them, the simple nature of God embraces the good and the wicked in a single, simple predestination. If they observe that some are established on the right by grace, while others are left on the left by justice, then—even if predestination is simple, as they wish—they will not deny that its effect is twofold, since one thing is to receive the punishment that is owed and another to receive gratuitous glory. Nor will they, except with the most shameless contentiousness, bring any further charge of verbal quibbling against the learned man.

[Note: [Col. 0657D] *Against the learned man.* Isidore.]

But so that they may finally cease from this, and so that those who intend to teach may first approach teachers—

[Note: [Col. 0657D] *To teachers.* That is, for the purpose of learning, as Lupus immediately says. For everyone ought to learn before teaching, as Pope Hormisdas of Rome writes in Letter 25. Accordingly, Pope Celestine wrote to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne: “Let all who teach badly know that it is more fitting for them to learn, ever more and more, than to teach.” Julianus Pomerius, not long after Celestine, likewise complained bitterly in Book III of *The Contemplative Life*, chapter 10, that there are certain people who eagerly teach what they do not know. Saint Gregory also laments this in the prologue to Book I of *Pastoral Care*. Jerome, in his customary manner, raises the same complaint more sharply in his letter to the presbyter Paulinus: [Col. 0658C]

> “The art of the Scriptures,” he says, “is the only one that everyone everywhere claims for himself. Learned and unlearned alike write poems indiscriminately. An old chatterbox presumes upon it, a senile old man presumes upon it, a verbose sophist presumes upon it; everyone presumes upon it, tears it apart, and teaches it before learning.”

Bernard too seems forceful on this point when he writes in chapter 2 of *The Life of Saint Malachy*: “Let those who attempt to teach what they have not learned read this.” Antiquity has instructed us by these examples and lessons, so that we might understand that arrogance must be avoided above all and that we ought to learn before presuming to teach others. See Saint Gregory, Book I of *Pastoral Care*, chapter 1.]

not as judges but as pupils—let them review God’s statement to blessed Job: “Do you know the order of heaven,” he says, “and can you set out its reason on earth?” (Job 38). And they will find that blessed Gregory, both supremely learned and wonderfully eloquent in his exposition of this passage, used the plural “predestinations” (Morals, Book XXX, chapter 18).

> “To know the order of heaven,” he says, “is to behold the hidden predestinations of the heavenly dispositions; but to set out its reason on earth is to disclose the causes of such mysteries before human hearts.” [Col. 0658B]

Concerning free will, blessed Augustine shows in his book to Laurence what should be thought in these words:

> “By using free will badly, man both destroyed himself and destroyed free will itself. For just as one who kills himself certainly kills himself by living, but, by killing himself, does not live and cannot raise himself again once he has killed himself, so, when he sinned by free will, free will too was lost, overcome by sin. For by whatever someone has been overcome, to that he has been assigned as a slave.” [Col. 0658C]

This is certainly the statement of the apostle Peter. Since it is true, what sort of freedom, I ask, can a person assigned as a slave possess, except when he takes pleasure in sinning? For he serves freely who willingly does the will of his master; and therefore the one who is a slave of sin is free to sin. Hence he will not be free to do what is just unless, having been freed from sin, he begins to be a servant of righteousness. This is true freedom, because it permits right action, and at the same time it is pious servitude, because it obeys the commandment.

But from where will this freedom to do good come to a person who has been assigned and sold, unless the one whose voice says, “If the Son makes you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8), redeems him? Before this begins to happen in a person, how can someone glory in free will through a good work when he is not yet free to work well? (chapter 31.) Unless, swollen with empty pride, he exalts himself—a pride restrained by the Apostle when he says: “You have been saved by grace through faith” (Ephesians 2). And lest they arrogate even faith to themselves in such a way that they would not understand it to have been divinely given, just as the same Apostle says elsewhere that he obtained mercy so that he might be faithful, here too he added: “And this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, lest anyone should boast.” And lest it be thought that good works would be lacking in believers, he added again: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them” (Ephesians 2).

We therefore become truly free when God forms us—that is, fashions and creates us—not as human beings, which he has already done, but so that we may be good human beings, which he now accomplishes by his grace, so that we may be a new creation in Christ Jesus, according to what is said: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 50). For, insofar as the nature of a human heart is concerned, God had certainly already created his heart (chapter 22). [Col. 0659B]

Likewise, lest anyone should glory in free choice of the will itself, even if not in works, as though merit began from that choice and the freedom of doing well were something to which a reward was owed, let him hear the same herald of grace saying: “For God is the one who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure” (Philippians 2); and elsewhere: “Therefore it is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans 9). Yet, without doubt, if a human being is of an age already capable of reason, he cannot believe, hope, or love unless he wills, nor can he reach the prize of God’s heavenly calling unless he runs willingly. How, then, is it “not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs,” except because the will itself, as it is written, is prepared by God? [Col. 0659C]

Likewise, in his book *On Rebuke and Grace* (chapter 1), he says:

> “We must confess that we possess free will both for doing evil and for doing good. But in doing evil everyone is free from righteousness and a slave of sin; in doing good no one can be free unless he has been freed by the one who said: ‘If the Son makes you free, then you will truly be free’ (John 8). Nor is it the case that, once someone has been freed from the condemnation of sin, he no longer needs the help of his liberator. Rather, hearing him say, ‘Without me you can do nothing’ (John 15), he should himself say to him: ‘You are my helper; do not abandon me’ (Psalm 26).” [Col. 0659D]

A little later he says:

> “Free will is sufficient for evil, but for good it is weak unless it is helped by the omnipotent Good.”

Likewise, in his book *On the Gift of Perseverance* (chapter 7):

> “The one who is not led into temptation does not depart from God. It is not at all within the power of free will, such as it now is, to resist sin; yet this power had existed in human beings before the fall.”

The same author, in the work mentioned above against Julianus, says:

> “The innate and wholly indestructible free will of human beings is that by which everyone wishes to be blessed, even those who do not want the things that lead to blessedness.”

A little later:

> “What does nature [Col. 0660A] flee so much as misery? What does it desire so much as blessedness? In the end, the free will that we possess concerning this matter is naturally implanted in us in such a way that no misery can take from us the fact that we do not wish to be miserable and wish to be blessed. So much so that even those who are miserable because they live badly do indeed wish to live badly, but nevertheless do not wish to be miserable; rather, they wish to be blessed. This is that will fixed immovably in our minds—not the will by which we wish to act well, for through human iniquity we were able to lose that, and through divine grace we can receive it—but the free will by which we wish to be blessed and do not wish to be miserable. Neither can the miserable nor the blessed lose it.”

A little later:

> “This free will is helped by God’s grace, so that we may possess through good living what we naturally desire—that is, to live happily.”

That the guilt of sin is removed by regeneration, that is, by baptism, while its conflict nevertheless remains, the same author expressed in the work mentioned above:

> “Why do you quarrel about concupiscence as it quarrels—that is, about the law in the members resisting the law of the mind? It is called the law of sin because it persuades us to sin and, so to speak, commands us; and if the mind serves it, one sins without excuse. Concupiscence itself is called sin because it was made through sin and desires to sin. Its guilt has been dissolved by regeneration; its conflict has been left for the contest. Its evil is clear. We resist it not by the strength of our will, as you think, unless we are helped by God. This evil must be fought, not denied; it must be conquered, not postponed.” [Col. 0660B]

After an extensive discussion of other matters, he says:

> “This world is so wicked that, unless we depart from it, the promised rest cannot come to us. Although, through the transgression of the first human being, toil came upon his descendants, nevertheless, even after the guilt of that transgression—which we have inherited—has been dissolved, toil remains for the testing of faith and for the struggle. We must contend with vices and labor in the very contest until it is granted to us to have no adversary. Therefore, so that good soldiers may be led to their rewards, punishments are turned into battles. The guilt inherited by little children having also been dissolved, their labors nevertheless remain, although they are taught to have arisen from that very guilt, because it also pleased God in this way to test the faith of adults. For those by whom children are brought to be regenerated—what would be the nature and extent [Col. 0660D] of their faith in invisible realities if visible reward immediately followed, rather than the promised rest being deferred and the business of faith being conducted with the heart, not with the eyes? In this way the future age, where there will be no labors, which is not yet seen, would be believed more sincerely and sought more desirably. Thus God, by wondrous kindness, turns our labors—that is, our punishments—to our advantage.” [Col. 0660C]

Likewise, in the same work:
