> “Since, after the former fall, so grave that we fell into the misery of this mortality, God first wished us to contend, granting us that we should be led by his Spirit and put to death the works of the flesh, and that, with him granting the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ, we should afterward reign with him in eternal peace, it is clear that, unless God is present, no one is fit to contend with vices—either to avoid being dragged away by them without a contest, or, once already contending, to avoid being defeated in the very struggle against them. Therefore in this contest God wished us to contend more by prayers than by strength, because he himself supplies to those who fight the very strength, in whatever measure it is appropriate for us to possess here, which we ask of him. If, then, those whose spirit already desires against the flesh in every action need God’s grace so that they may not be overcome, what freedom of will can those possess who have not yet been snatched from the power of darkness, who have not begun to contend because iniquity rules them, or who, if they have wished to contend, are overcome because the servitude of their will has not yet been freed?” [Col. 0661A]

Likewise, in the first book of his *Revisions*:

> “The perfection of good is that there should not even be the concupiscence of sin in a human being. When one lives well, the will does not consent to it; nevertheless, it does not perfect the good, because concupiscence is still present and the will resists it. The guilt of this concupiscence is dissolved in baptism, but its weakness remains; until it is healed, every believer who makes good progress struggles against it with the greatest diligence.” [Col. 0661B]

The other light of the interpreters, Jerome, says in his *Dialogue*:

[Note: [Col. 0661D] *The other light of the interpreters.* Claudianus Mamertus calls this same Jerome “the foremost of interpreters” in Book II of *On the State of the Soul*, chapter 9. “Interpreters” (*tractatores*) were called the interpreters and teachers of sacred literature, such as Jerome, as Lupus also explains in his third letter. Sirmondus thinks that this term originated in the age of Vincent of Lérins, because of this passage from the *Commonitorium* of Peregrinus: “The teachers, whom they now call interpreters.” Nevertheless, before Vincent, Tertullian and Cyprian had used the verb *tractare* for what we call “to teach.” For in chapter 2 of Tertullian’s book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, complaining about the cunning of heretics, who always wrap falsehoods in obscurity so that they may not be understood or expose their flank to the defenders of the true faith, he says: “Heretics, from awareness of their weakness, never interpret systematically.” Cyprian, in Letter 52 to Antonianus, plainly used *tractare* for what is commonly called teaching. For he says: “I learned from the bishop’s teaching that sacrifice must not be offered to idols.” And again, in Letter 56: “Nor should anyone, dearest brothers, be disturbed when he sees our people driven into exile and scattered through fear of persecution, because he does not see the gathered brotherhood or hear the bishops teaching.” See Juretus’s notes on the seventh letter of Ivo of Chartres.]

> “Adam did not sin,” he says, “because God knew that this would happen; rather, God, as God, foreknew what Adam was going to do by his own will.”

A little later:

> “The Lord says to the disciples: ‘I am the vine, you are the branches; whoever remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit, because without me you can do nothing’ (John 15). Just as the branches and leaves of vines immediately wither when they have been cut off from the trunk, so all human strength withers and perishes if it is abandoned by God’s help. ‘No one,’ he says, ‘can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him’ (John 6). When he says, ‘No one can come to me,’ he breaks the pride of free will: even if someone wishes to go to Christ, unless what follows occurs—‘my heavenly Father draws him’—his desire is futile and his effort fruitless. At the same time, we must observe that the one who is drawn does not run of his own accord, but is led either resisting, slowly, or unwillingly. If no one can come to Jesus by his own powers and labor, how can he avoid all sins at once and avoid them forever?” [Col. 0661C]

[Note: [Col. 0662D] *Pope Celestine.* From this it is clear that Lupus thought those excerpts *On the Grace of God and Free Will* were Celestine’s. I can also affirm that the great man Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, held the same view.]

Pope Celestine too, who must be numbered among the great teachers, instructed everyone concerning free will, as was fitting for so great a pontiff. These words are taken from his decrees (chapter 3):

> “It is clear that, in Adam’s transgression, all human beings lost their natural capacity and innocence, and that no one can rise from the depth of that ruin unless the grace of the merciful God raises him.”

Likewise (chapter 6):

> “No one renewed by the grace of baptism is capable of overcoming the devil’s snares and conquering the desires of the flesh unless, through God’s daily help, he receives perseverance in a good way of life.”

Likewise (chapter 7), concerning the fact that no one uses free will well except through Christ, he also calls Pope Innocent as a witness, setting out his statement (Innocent, in his letter to the Council of Milevis):

> “Understand at last, O perverse doctrine of the most depraved minds, that the freedom itself of the first human being deceived him, so that, while he used its reins too indulgently, he fell through presumption into transgression. He could not be rescued from this until the coming of Christ the Lord restored him, through the providence of regeneration, to the condition of his original freedom.” [Col. 0662B]

Likewise Celestine (after Celestine’s third letter, chapter 8) says that all the efforts, works, and merits of the saints must be referred to the glory and praise of God, because no one pleases him for any reason other than what he himself has granted (chapter 9).

Likewise:

> “God works in such a way in human hearts and in free will itself that holy thought, pious counsel, and every movement of a good will are from God, because we can do no good except through him, without whom we can do nothing.”

Likewise (chapter 10):

> “Whoever says that the grace of justification is given to us so that, through grace, we may more easily accomplish what we are commanded to do by free will—as though, even if grace were not given, we could indeed fulfill the divine commandments without it, though not easily—let him be anathema. For the Lord was speaking about the fruits of the commandments when he did not say, ‘Without me you can do so with greater difficulty,’ but, ‘Without me you can do nothing.’” [Col. 0662C]

Saint Pope Gregory too, who contributed greatly to all those capable of understanding the Latin tongue and piously devoted to his teaching, expressed the nature of human will with his customary subtlety and sweetness in Homily IX on Ezekiel:

> “I heard the voice of one who followed, and he said to me: ‘Son of man, stand upon your feet, and I will speak with you’ (Ezekiel 2). Then it is added: ‘And the Spirit entered into me after he spoke to me, and set me upon my feet.’ [Col. 0662D] Behold, the divine voice commanded the fallen prophet to rise. Yet he could not rise at all unless the spirit of the omnipotent God had entered him, because through the grace of the omnipotent God we can indeed strive toward good works, but we cannot accomplish them if he who commands does not help. Thus Paul, when he admonished the disciples, saying, ‘Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling’ (Philippians 2), immediately added who it was that worked these very good things in them: ‘For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure.’

> “This is why Truth itself says to the disciples: ‘Without me you can do nothing’ (John 15). But in this we must consider that, if our good works are so much the gifts of the omnipotent God that nothing of our own is in them, why do we seek eternal reward as though it were for our merits? If, however, they are ours in such a way that they are not gifts of the omnipotent God, why do we give thanks to the omnipotent God for them? But we must know that our evil deeds are ours alone, while our good deeds belong both to the omnipotent God and to us: for by inspiring us he goes before us so that we may will, and by helping us he follows after us so that we may not will in vain but may be able to accomplish what we have willed. Thus, when grace goes before and good will follows, what is the gift of the omnipotent God becomes our merit. Paul explains this well in a brief statement when he says: ‘I labored more than all of them’ (1 Corinthians 15). And lest he appear to attribute this to his own strength, he added: ‘Yet not I, but the grace of God with me.’

> “Because he had been preceded by a heavenly gift, he recognized himself as alien to his good work, saying, ‘Yet not I.’ But because prevenient grace had made free will within him good, and by that free will he had followed the same grace in his work, he added: ‘But the grace of God with me.’ It was as though he said: ‘I labored in a good work—not I, but also I.’ Insofar as I was preceded by the Lord’s gift alone, it was not I; insofar as I followed the gift by my will, it was also I.” [Col. 0663C]

[Note: [Col. 0663D] *He goes before us.* Letter 4: “Indeed, God both goes before us and follows after us by his grace, so that we may be able to will and accomplish some good.”]

For whom and for what people the holy blood of the Lord was poured out and whom it redeemed, blessed Augustine declares in his book to Laurence (*In the Enchiridion*, chapter 61):

> “This Church, which exists in the holy angels and the powers of God, will become known to us as it is when we have been joined to it at the end, to possess eternal blessedness together with it. But this Church, which now journeys on earth far from that one, is more familiar to us because we are in it, and because it consists of human beings, as we do. This Church has been redeemed from every sin by the blood of the Mediator, who had no sin. Its voice is: ‘If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all’ (Romans 8).” [Col. 0663D]

For in the Church, which has been redeemed from every sin by the blood of the Mediator, who had no sin, he understands all those included in the apostolic testimony: “He handed him over for us all.”

Likewise, the same author, in the work mentioned above against Julianus, says:

> “All who are redeemed are redeemed by the one who came to seek what had perished. Even before he came in the flesh, he redeemed them through the faith by which it was believed that he would come. They are redeemed into the freedom of eternal blessedness, where they can no longer serve sin.”

And, explaining most plainly to the people the passage of the Holy Gospel according to John—“You do not believe because you are not of my sheep” (John 10)—he says:

> “Why did he say to these people, ‘You are not of my sheep’? Because he saw that they were predestined for eternal destruction, not for eternal life purchased at the price of his blood.” [Col. 0664B]

Likewise, in the first book addressed to Pollentius:

> “Just as every human being redeemed by Christ’s blood is a human being, although not every human being is also redeemed by Christ’s blood, so everything that is permitted is not expedient, although not everything that is not expedient is also forbidden.”

Blessed Jerome likewise makes clear in his Commentary on Matthew that he holds the same view, in these words:

> “Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve” (Matthew 20).

Observe that we have often said that he who serves is called the Son of Man, and that he gives his life as a redemption for many, when

[Note: [Col. 0663D] *The form of a servant.* These words, says Rigaltius in his book *On the Beauty of Christ’s Body*, almost signify that Christ did not possess a form worthy of command. But Peter of Clairvaux applied this passage elsewhere in the year 1353. For, writing a very long letter in the name of Jesus Christ to Pope Innocent VI and the Roman Curia, he introduces Christ as speaking in chapter 18:

> “We do not readily wish to accept the execution of temporal affairs, giving you an example so that you may follow our footsteps: although we were in the form of God, we did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied ourselves, taking the form of a servant.” Why, then, do you seek immediate authority in temporal kingdoms? This desire proceeds from ambition. Rather, following our example, you ought cordially to reject it through the virtue of humility. For these honors and riches pass away like a shadow.”

From our oldest manuscript, from which perhaps that letter will shortly emerge into the light. It is now held in the former Royal Library.]

he took the form of a servant in order to pour out his blood for the world. And he did not say, “to give his life as a redemption for all,” but “for many,” that is, for those who would wish to believe. The most celebrated teacher cautiously understood this to refer to believers of every kind, because of the passage: “The brother for whom Christ died will perish through your knowledge,” and also because of this: “All of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death” (1 Corinthians 3). And also because of this: “How much worse punishment do you think will be deserved by one who has trampled upon the Son of God and regarded as profane the blood of the Testament by which he was sanctified?” (Hebrews 10). As well as all similar passages that devout investigators can find in the divine utterances.

Bede, in his exposition of Mark, sets out Jerome’s meaning in Jerome’s own words:

> “For the Son of Man also did not come to be served, but to serve. Observe,” he says, “that we have often said that he who serves is called the Son of Man, and that he gives his life as a redemption for many, when he took the form of a servant in order to pour out his blood for the world. And he did not say, ‘to give his life as a redemption for all,’ but ‘for many,’ that is, for those who would wish to believe.” [Col. 0665A]

Likewise, Jerome, explaining the passage of the Psalm (43), “You have sold your people for no price,” says:

> “Until now the martyrs have spoken about themselves; now they speak about the Jewish people, to whom it was said: ‘You were sold because of your sins.’ And therefore ‘for no price,’ because the blood of the Lamb was not poured out for them.” [Col. 0664D]

Saint Pope Gregory, in the *Morals* (Book IV, chapter 11), explaining the passage “Let him not be counted among the days of the year” (Job 13), asserts the same meaning in these words:

> “We may appropriately understand the year as the preaching of heavenly grace: for just as time is completed in a year by the accumulation of days, so in heavenly grace the manifold life of the virtues is brought to completion. The year may also be understood as the multitude of the redeemed: for just as a year is formed from a multitude of days, so from the gathering of all good people that innumerable community of the elect is completed.” [Col. 0665B]

It is not surprising that two most illustrious lights among the doctors, blessed Augustine and Jerome, and after them Gregory and Bede, are found to hold this view, since their teaching depends upon evangelical authority. In Matthew this is indeed found as follows: “Drink from this, all of you. For this is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many for the remission of sins” (Matthew 26).

[Note: “In Matthew.” These three Gospel passages are also cited in Letter 127.]

In Mark, however: “This is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many” (Mark 14). But in Luke: “This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which will be poured out for you.” Hence, agreeing with Luke, when we perform the divine rite we say in the prayer, “This is the cup, the mystery of the blood of my New and eternal Testament, of faith, which will be poured out for you”; but, harmonizing with Matthew and Mark, we add, “for many, for the remission of sins.”

[Note: “John, bishop of Constantinople, surnamed Chrysostom.” Lupus also cites the same passage in Letter 128 and in *On Three Questions*, p. 244.]

Yet John, bishop of Constantinople, explaining that passage of the Epistle to the Hebrews—“so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone” (Hebrews 2)—says: “Not for the faithful alone, but for the whole world; indeed, he died for everyone. But what if not everyone believes? He fulfilled what was his to do.”

This interpretation, however, he did not support with divine utterances.

[Note: “Faustus.” See the notes on Letter 112.]

A certain Faustus as well, formerly abbot of Lérins and later bishop of Riez in Gaul, wrote on these matters—that is, on predestination, free will, and the redemption effected by Christ’s blood—quite differently from the outstanding authors mentioned above. But a more intelligent examination of the integrity of the divine utterances entirely removed the opportunity for error; and the most reverend Pope Gelasius, together with seventy highly learned bishops, while determining which writers were and were not to be received, after approving Augustine and bestowing the highest praises upon Jerome, removed the aforementioned Faustus from authoritative standing in these words: “The little works of Faustus of Riez, a Gaul, are apocryphal.”

Therefore, following the uncorrupted meaning of the Holy Scriptures and respecting the authority of the Apostolic See,

[Note: “Of the Apostolic See.” That is, of the Roman See. Although in former times all episcopal sees were called apostolic, the Roman See was nevertheless called apostolic in a special sense, because Peter and Paul—the foremost of the apostles—established it, and were consecrated there through the martyrdom of Christ, as we said in our note to Vincent of Lérins. With God’s help, we shall discuss at greater length the dignity and authority once possessed by the apostolic sees in our note to Agobard. See *Patrologia*, vol. 104.]

what else can we say but this: “Let Faustus and those who think like him be silent; let Jerome and Augustine speak with their companions.” We recall, of course, that proverb: “Let the frogs fall silent while heaven thunders.”

And, so that we may leave this labor of ours fruitful for others, we always warn that the following must be kept in mind concerning the reprobate: “Those who distance themselves from you will perish”; but concerning the elect: “In every nation, whoever fears God and does what is right is acceptable to him.” And so that, separated from the former by God’s grace, we may be joined to the latter by that same grace, we must together implore this through constant prayers. For he who, with ineffable compassion, bestows blessedness upon little ones who have been regenerated and then soon depart this life has also graciously provided for the salvation of those to whom he has granted the ability to hope perfectly in him.

[Col. 0665]

275

[Note: This *Life of Saint Maximinus, Bishop of Trier*, was first published by Surius. I agree with the most learned Johannes Gerardus Vossius, who thinks that Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, was the author of this Life. I believe that Waldon, to whom Lupus dedicates it, was none other than Waldon, the abbot in Germany mentioned in the Fulda Annals under the year 861. It is indeed probable that he was known to Lupus when Lupus was living in Germany for the sake of his studies.]

# LIFE OF SAINT MAXIMINUS, BISHOP OF TRIER

## By Saint Lupus

[Col. 0665]

Lupus sends greetings to his Waldon.

That friends should vie with one another in honorable services and wish mutually to anticipate one another with sincere acts of devotion is rightly counted among the chief concerns of human life. For our weakness, relying upon reciprocal assistance and cooperating with divine grace, is neither vainly exalted in prosperity nor, when made equal to adversity, easily overcome by it.

Careful consideration of so great a matter persuaded me, dearest Waldo, to oblige you, and compelled me not to refuse what you have earnestly requested ever since the beginning of our acquaintance: namely, that I should work out the Life of blessed Maximinus in my own style, and restore to a dignity suited to their subject the events that have come down to us in whatever sort of writing.

Added to this was my firm confidence that the man just mentioned would be of great benefit to me with God through his merciful intercession, if, celebrating his deeds with as much diligence as I could, I placed them before those who did not know them for their imitation.

But in this work I am greatly constrained by the fact that, although it is clear that many things he did while still alive have been suppressed in silence, scarcely a few memorials of his deeds remain; and even among these some are found to resemble fables.

[Note: “Fabulous.” Thus it was already recognized at that time that the Acts of the saints had been polluted by many prodigious fables, and that there had always been in this world certain people who could be pleased by nothing without the portents of fables. This happened because foolish men thought that the single mark of sanctity was for someone to be shown to have performed miracles surpassing all belief. By contrast, Agobard notes the opinion of the ignorant populace, which judges the lives of priests solely by miracles and does not believe a man to be just if his prayers, poured out for the public good, have not been heard by God, although this ought rather to be attributed to the people’s own depraved morals and grave offenses against God.

For if we attend to miracles, Agobard likewise notes that “even Judas, a false disciple and a true betrayer, had been granted great grace for performing mighty deeds,” and that offerings made to God by priests of blameworthy life were accepted in such a way that they even healed bodily illnesses. Such men, perhaps together with other reprobates, will say to God: “Lord, Lord, in your name we cast out demons and performed many mighty deeds.”

Prodigies are likewise reported of Croesus the king, and of the emperors Vespasian and Hadrian, and of many others who were by no means Christians, as though such things had happened to them. Their histories also testify—if the account is reliable—that the gift of miracles was not denied even to heretics. Thus, from the fact that some people healed bodily illnesses in the Lord’s name and became renowned for miracles, it does not immediately follow that they were holy men, unless their other qualities were equal.

Certainly, miracles were once granted for a time to unbelievers. But afterward, once faith in Christ had been confirmed among all nations everywhere, there was no need for miracles to be performed indiscriminately on every occasion, especially those prodigious and old-womanish tales with which the books of certain later writers are filled.

Lupus considered such fabricated narratives to be avoided by a sound historian; nevertheless, he did not avoid them. He added so many remarkable fables to this book that it is extremely surprising that a learned man stumbled over such obvious obstacles. Unless, just as he believed that seeking out fables and entertaining the minds of readers with invented stories was far removed from the dignity of history, he did not dare to deprive widely circulated traditions of their credibility, following the example of Tacitus.

This is my own view: the saints are in heaven and reign there with God. But certainly many things have been written in some histories whose credibility is rightly regarded by learned people as highly doubtful. Therefore, those who publish genuine Acts of the saints, untainted by the ravings of fabulists, seem to me deserving of the greatest praise. In these there breathes an ancient Christianity—pure, holy, innocent, and drawing nearer to God. From them we are more strongly stirred to true piety than from those fabricated narratives.

Would that the Acts of the martyrs existed which Eusebius says he collected in Book IV, chapter 15, of his *Ecclesiastical History*! Yet I would not have what has been said above understood as though I were disparaging miracles—those, namely, reported by thoroughly reliable authors. Far from it. I intended to criticize the foolishness of certain people who prefer those prodigious portents to the evident and simple proofs of holiness.

Nor would I deny that miracles are performed even at the end of time through the prayers of the saints. For Christ still lives and is among us, although he has withdrawn his face from human eyes. Indeed, he promised that he would be with us until the consummation of the age.]

This makes the subject matter of writing seem scarcely adequate to the highly esteemed majesty of so great a man. Therefore, omitting those matters that could diminish the credibility of the rest, I shall now undertake to narrate only what is worthy of remembrance, relying not on my own talent but on divine grace.

# CHAPTER ONE

Maximinus, a native of the city of the Pictavians in Aquitaine,

[Note: “A native of the Pictavians.” Lupus seems to say that Maximinus was born in the city of the Pictavians itself. Nevertheless, the most illustrious Henri-Louis Castanea de la Rocheposay, bishop of Poitiers, points out that he was born not in the city itself but in the village of Sigiliacum. These are his words in his notes on the Pictavian Litany: “Nevertheless, an old-standing tradition among our countrymen maintains that Maximinus was born at Sigiliacum, opposite the city of Lodun; a fact unknown to Lupus, perhaps a foreigner, who therefore assigned the cradle of this holy bishop to the chief city of the region. Sigiliacum is commonly called Sillé or Montersillé; there the parish church is honored under the title of Saint Maximinus.”]

was born of the most illustrious ancestry.

[Note: “Of distinguished birth.” This is a common affectation among writers, who always assign the noblest origins to the saints whose lives they describe, evidently thinking that a virtue joined to noble birth is more beautiful. Yet, as Paulinus says in his letter to Sclantia: “Religion does not know how to accept our persons or the conditions of human beings, but examines the spirit of each individual. It judges slave and noble by their conduct. The highest nobility before God is to be illustrious in virtues.”

I am surprised that no one has yet been found to report Saint Peter as descended from a noble and ancient family. It might indeed have seemed magnificent if great nobility had been displayed in the man who had established his seat in the city that ruled the nations.]

His parents, having inherited an ancient lineage descended from ancestors of the senatorial order,

[Note: “Of senatorial rank.” In Gaul, and especially in Aquitaine, there were certain very noble families which, since they undoubtedly traced their origin to Roman senators, were called senatorial. In general, one may affirm that illustrious families are meant by these terms.]

happily brought forth Maxentius and this Maximinus. Nobly reared, they were also instructed in sacred letters, destined in time to become outstanding defenders of Christian doctrine.

But as time passed, the Church of the Pictavians claimed Maxentius for its bishop, and he later governed it with the greatest distinction. Maximinus, however, leaving his native land at the prompting of God and migrating to Belgic Gaul, stopped in the city of Trier and submitted himself to be instructed under the teaching of the distinguished bishop Agritius,

[Note: “Agritius.” Bishop of Trier, who took part in the Council of Arles in the year 814.]

in whom such an abundance of spiritual grace shone forth that it adorned the summit of episcopal dignity with the title of sanctity.

[Note: “The summit of dignity.” Since the episcopate is the summit of the highest dignity, as was said in the note to Letter 125. Moreover, Agritius was a metropolitan and therefore possessed the summit of the episcopate by a special title.

Thus, in the letter of Florianus to Nicetius, archbishop of Trier, Nicetius is said to have been placed “at the summit of the pontificate.” Fortunatus, in Book III, chapter 11, for this very reason calls the same Nicetius “the summit of the faith and head of bishops”; calling him the supreme shepherd, he says that he surpassed the apostolic fold. In chapter 13 he calls Magnericus, Nicetius’s successor, “father of fathers.”

When we said here and on page 453 that the summit of the episcopate is established in each individual bishop, we made no prejudice against the primacy of the Supreme Pontiff, divinely instituted. For he holds the summit of the pontificate in a particular manner.]

The fame of this achievement had summoned others from various regions, and Maximinus as well. Thus, having been brought to the notice of so great a man and diligently trained for some time in ecclesiastical conduct, he was bestowed with the honor of the clergy.

And while increases in virtue were preparing for him the advancement of subsequent dignities, a certain Quiriacus, endowed with remarkable holiness, entered the church of blessed Eucharius at night, as was his custom, to pray. There he was privileged to see an angel confronting him—not in sleep but while awake—and with his bodily ears he heard the angel’s voice commanding him, by divine order, to inform Maximinus that, once Bishop Agritius had been admitted to the joys above, Maximinus himself would soon undertake the pastoral ministry.

When Quiriacus had promptly fulfilled this command, blessed Maximinus confessed in every way that he was unequal to the burden. Thus, although the inspector of hidden things had already approved him, he, a strict judge of his own weakness, thought poorly of himself.

[Note: “Would that this were so.” This is an exhortation addressed to those who in Lupus’s time sought the episcopate. He sets before them the example of Maximinus, who declared himself unequal to so great a burden.

A notable passage occurs in Sulpicius Severus, who likewise laments the morals of his own age: “At that time,” Severus says in Book II of his *Sacred History*, “almost the whole world was stained with the blood of holy martyrs. For people rushed eagerly into glorious struggles, and martyrdoms were then sought with much greater eagerness through glorious deaths than episcopates are now pursued through depraved ambitions.”

Saint Pope Gregory, in Book I of *Pastoral Care*, chapter 8, says: “At that time it was praiseworthy to seek the episcopate, when there was no doubt that through it one would reach more severe punishments.” And below: “He is therefore his own witness that he does not seek the episcopate who seeks through it not the ministry of good works but the glory of honor.”

Lupus’s age had added greed to ambition. Such was the calamity of Lupus’s times that priestly offices were everywhere obtained for a price, and the one who had more money in hand was commonly preferred to the rest—not the one who was assisted by greater devotion and merit. See Alcuin, *Confession of Faith*, Book III, chapter 36, and John of Salisbury, *Policraticus*, Book VII, chapter 20.]

Would that people now wished both to behold and to imitate this example! Certainly, they would never go to purchase ecclesiastical honors—which belong only to holy and learned men—

[Note: “Holy and learned.” Those who have undertaken to feed the Christian people ought to be holy and learned, so that they may instruct them by their example and preaching. See the notes to Letter 97.]

if they were subject to the corruptions of vice, ignorant of heavenly revelations; nor would they ever, unwilling and protesting, impose upon their shoulders a burden that would weigh heavily upon and crush them.

But, to bring our discourse back from the slight digression it has made, once the immutable divine plan had decreed that blessed Maximinus should be placed over his people, this was revealed to Agritius through angelic ministry, so that he might appoint Maximinus as his successor.

[Note: “Appoint him as his successor.” This account is false, and I am surprised that Lupus wished to retain it from a fable. Unless, although he was thoroughly familiar with the morals of his own age, he was insufficiently acquainted with ancient history.

In former times no one was permitted to choose a successor for himself. Canon 23 of the Council of Antioch says: “A bishop may not appoint another successor for himself, even if he has reached the end of his life. But if anything of this sort has been done, such an appointment is to be invalid.”

There is nevertheless a contrary example in Eusebius, Book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 22, concerning Anatolius. Theotecnus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, had designated Anatolius, once he had been ordained bishop, as successor to his Church, and for some time both governed the same Church together.

The most learned Henri Valesius, who recently restored Eusebius’s long chronology, correctly notes that this is one of the earliest examples of what are now called coadjutor bishops: “They were first established to relieve the old age of bishops; later, once the practice had become customary, they began to be created through favor and ambition even when no necessity demanded it. To prevent this evil from spreading further, the Fathers of the Council of Serdica provided a remedy.”

But Marca, in his book *On the Singular Primacy of Peter*, while noting that Peter and Paul governed the Roman Church together, although not on equal terms, says that before the Council of Nicaea it had been the discipline of the Church that two bishops could preside over one Church.

This is very different from Lupus’s account. For he does not say that Maximinus was ordered to be ordained in order to relieve Agritius’s old age, but that he was to succeed him after his death—something contrary to the customs of ancient times.

“As the institution of the holy Fathers provides,” says Peter of Blois in Letter 44, “a coadjutor is to be added to bishops who are infirm and old. Thus Augustine was also joined to Valerius, bishop of Hippo.”]

Without hesitation, obeying the divine command, Agritius designated him as the pontiff who would follow him, confirming him by his blessings. Not long afterward Agritius exchanged temporal death for the happiness of eternal life and entered the most glorious company of confessors, on the Ides of January.

# CHAPTER II

Saint Maximinus, with the consent of the sacred orders and the support of the entire people, was elevated by the neighboring bishops to the excellence of the episcopal office.

How vigorously he carried out that office may be recognized from the testimony of the great author Jerome, who was either his contemporary, though still a child, or lived very near his time. In his celebrated *Chronicle*, after recounting how, beginning in the second year of the emperors Constantine, Constantius, and Constans, Arian impiety—supported by the protection of the aforementioned emperor Constantius—had persecuted first Athanasius and then all bishops not of its own party through exile, imprisonment, and various forms of affliction, Jerome, having inserted only a few intervening words and intending to record whatever memorable events there might have been in the sixth year, says: “Maximinus, bishop of Trier, was held in high esteem.”

# CHAPTER III

Anyone who examines what has preceded will easily understand that the madness of the Arian ruler was then raging with the greatest fury through the persecutions inflicted generally upon true bishops. Saint Maximinus too willingly took his share in those sufferings; he not only avoided the contagion of corrupted faith but also opposed the perverse and violent efforts of its defenders.

It would not have been difficult to overthrow those efforts swiftly and completely, had not the inventors or defenders of that abominable crime—miserably blinded, as they deserved to be, by their detestable impiety—refused entirely to admit the light of reason.

For who, I ask, would ever have dared even in sleep to doubt the consubstantiality of the Father and the Son, except one who had passed over with deaf ears that most evident declaration of God: “I and the Father are one” (John 10)? By saying “one,” he plainly wished himself to be understood as being as great as the Father is known to be.

Indeed, he would not have commanded the mystery of baptism to be handed down to believers in the name of the Father, of himself, and of the Holy Spirit unless he had likewise wished honor to be rendered to himself as to the Father and the Holy Spirit.

But who could endure men who were no less foolish than impious? Finally, when the Son himself says, “that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (John 5), the most ignorant men had advanced to such audacity that they maintained that the Son was less than the Father.

They strove to establish their position through cunning inventions of argument. Against them, through Athanasius, Maximinus, and the other distinguished champions and leaders of apostolic doctrine, authority always prevailed. Falsehood was laboriously adorned with carefully contrived arguments. Truth, intrinsically beautiful and simple, shone forth. At last human power had forged a turbulent and threatening war against the strongest warriors; divine majesty supplied the courage, strength, and weapons by which they would conquer.

# CHAPTER IV

From the words of blessed Jerome quoted above, although they are few, the holiness of Maximinus can nevertheless be sufficiently estimated. But Jerome was not content with them; he introduced a matter that, in my judgment, deserved to be pursued with the highest praise.

“By him,” he says—there is no doubt that he means Maximinus—“Athanasius, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, was honorably received when he was being sought by Constantius for punishment.”

[Note: “There is no doubt that he means Maximinus.” This is a familiar manner of expression in Lupus, as we noted on page 223.]

O most blessed man, deservedly to be ranked with the Church’s highest leaders, who spurned the unjust assault of royal power and, at the risk, if not of his life, certainly of his dignity, embraced the guardianship of the charity divinely entrusted to him!

Suppose that an emperor, driven mad, was offering rewards for betrayal. If he could have imagined that there would be someone who, when able, would not merely refuse to betray Athanasius but would also carefully conceal him, what proscriptions, exiles, and tortures would he have threatened, and what punishment would he afterward have inflicted upon the man once he had been discovered? It will then become perfectly clear how much weight ought to be assigned to the justice of this Saint Maximinus’s steadfastness.

Certainly, confidence drawn from divine utterances taught him to what extent secular powers ought to be obeyed. For God himself has not given human beings the power either to despise rulers who issue just commands or to obey rulers who command injustice.

Although he prescribed that we should render to Caesar what is Caesar’s and to God what is God’s (Matthew 22), the Apostle made clear that he wished this to be done without violating God’s commandments. For when he was about to say, “Honor the king; fear God” (1 Peter 2), he took care to place the latter command first.

But oh, the degenerate morals of our age! Almost all the sinews of our former strength have now collapsed. Steadfastness, broken by slight terrors, has yielded. Money is valued more highly than justice. Who now would not fear to reveal to emperors the salutary severity of the divine commands? Who, inflamed by zeal for the fear of God and without the disguise of flattery, would disclose to them the dangers they face?

I am entirely certain that there is now either no one or scarcely anyone who, if he saw someone fleeing the unjust hostility of emperors—as the great Athanasius once did—would, like Maximinus, relying upon God, open to him the embrace of charity; indeed, everyone would shrink from providing even the remotest hiding place, lest, while attempting to shelter another, he expose himself to the snares of calamity.

[Note: “Provide a hiding place.” Here the illustrious Cardinal Baronius criticizes Lupus for thinking that Athanasius came to Trier at the time when, having fled from Constantius, the son of the emperor Constantine, he was being sought for punishment. Whether Baronius rebukes him justly or unjustly is not for one like me to decide. I would merely point out that the passage from Jerome quoted shortly before seems to support Lupus’s view.

For the rest, Hilary takes a powerful weapon from this against Athanasius’s enemies: Maximinus restored communion to him, and did so as one who, in addition to his own virtues, was bishop in the most distinguished city of Trier. Thus he says in the fragments: “But you will deny that you were ignorant that communion had been restored to Athanasius by Hosius, Maximinus, and Julius, while Valens, Ursacius, and Saturninus demand his condemnation from you.”

On the other hand, Sulpicius Severus says that Priscillian and his associates were also at fault because they had as opponents Damasus, bishop of Rome, and Ambrose of Milan, “whose authority at that time was supreme.”]

But Maximinus, receiving the strongest Confessor in that most celebrated and at that time also royal city,

[Note: “Royal city.” That is, the city of Trier, whose dignity was then considerable because Constantine the Great had established there the seat of the prefect of the Gauls. Lupus therefore had in mind not so much the period of Maximinus as the later period. The emperor Maximus subsequently made Trier a royal city around the year 383, as Gregory of Tours writes in Book I, chapter 38, of his *History*.]

and openly sharing in his danger, gained a share in his eternal glory.

# CHAPTER V

He also demonstrated elsewhere with what zeal he watched over the preservation of the integrity of the faith, when, after convening a synodal assembly at Agrippina,

[Note: “At Agrippina.” He means the Council of Agrippina, which is said to have been held in the year 346 against Euphratas, bishop of Cologne, who denied the divinity of Christ. We would know nothing of this synod without Surius.

Cardinal Baronius appears to have doubted the council’s authority because Euphratas, whom the Acts report to have been deposed at that synod, is found to have taken part in the Council of Sardica the following year.]

using ecclesiastical censure, he removed from episcopal rank Euphratas, a bishop corrupted by heretical depravity, with the many bishops who had assembled.

For, joining himself to deranged heretics, Euphratas preached that Jesus Christ was not the true Son of God.

Nor was the gift of miracles lacking to Saint Maximinus. By performing them, he made the truth of his preaching credible to those who were slow to believe. He poured the desired light into the eyes of the blind, restored the loosened limbs of paralytics to their former strength, and freed from a thoroughly foul domination those whom demonic possession had deprived of the human mind.

If this should seem incredible to anyone, it may be confirmed by the many things that are still done in his memory to the present day.

# CHAPTER VI

It was his established custom to visit the memorials of the saints and to implore their aid with humble prayers. For this purpose, when he was traveling to Rome, he met the highly renowned Confessor Martin. The two supreme bishops,

[Note: “The supreme bishops.” Namely, Maximinus of Trier and Martin of Tours. What are you saying, Lupus? Martin, a bishop, traveled to Rome with Maximinus of Trier? Yet Maximinus had vacated his see many years before Martin attained the episcopate, and long before Martin became associated with Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, which was the beginning of his renown.

Nevertheless, this fable is also found in the *Life of Saint Mansuetus, Apostle of the Leuci*, published by the illustrious François Bosquet, bishop of Montpellier, in Part II of his *Histories of the Gallican Church*, p. 35.]

intent upon divine matters, were joined together, and they did not regard the hardship of the journey as others did.

As they proceeded farther, a bear happened to encounter the little donkey that carried the blessed men’s baggage and immediately devoured it.

[Note: “Perhaps a little donkey.” Peace, most learned man! This has been taken from those poetic fictions by which, as you say, the history of Saint Maximinus was polluted.]

At this point Maximinus is said to have commanded the beast in the name of the Lord that, since it had not driven away the animal but had consumed it, it should itself take up the animal’s burden.

It is a very remarkable thing that the bear immediately succeeded to the burden, served most tamely as a pack animal until they returned to the place called Ursaria, and there at last received from the holy man permission to resume its former freedom of wandering—though first deprived of the license to harm anyone.

But just as the wicked are burdensome to themselves, while the good always take delight in one another’s company, Saint Maximinus compelled blessed Martin to visit the city of Trier with him, and brought back to his people a doubled exchange of blessing.

There Martin entrusted to Maximinus for instruction a spiritual son of his own, Lubentius. Obedient to Martin’s wishes, Maximinus instructed him in sacred letters, ordained him to the priesthood, and placed him in charge of the village called Cubrinus.

Lubentius himself, mindful of his family, returned to his homeland; after living among his own people, he departed this life there not long afterward and received from the Lord, with accumulated reward, the full fruit of his holy labors.

# CHAPTER VII
Paulinus succeeding in the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0673D] Paulinus. This is that famous Paulinus, bishop of Trier, who, as Hilary says in the *Fragments*, “was judged unworthy of the Church by the bishops, but worthy of exile by the king.” This took place at the Council of Arles in the year 353, as is clear from this passage of Hilary and likewise from Sulpicius Severus, in Book II of the *Sacred History*. This synod had been convened so that peace might be restored between the opposing parties—namely, the Arians and the Catholics—or, if that could not be achieved, so that those who refused to subscribe to Athanasius’s condemnation might be expelled as a kind of contagion to the Catholic faith. Athanasius had already been condemned at the Synod of Antioch, which was regarded as legitimate. The bishops of the Catholic Church demanded “that, before we were compelled to subscribe against Athanasius, they should rather debate the faith; and that the matter should not finally be investigated only after judgment concerning the person had been settled,” as Severus writes. Otherwise, there was reason to fear that the defense against malicious deception would be brought against Athanasius’s enemies, if they pressed his condemnation so obstinately that the case appeared to concern Athanasius alone and not his doctrine. Lest anyone think that I have invented this defense, the Easterners later brought precisely this charge against our men in a letter written to the delegates of the Council of Rimini, published among Hilary’s *Fragments*. There they speak as follows concerning the heretic Aetius: “This deception is being prepared: that Aetius, the author of this heresy, should himself be condemned rather than these impious statements, and that the sentence should appear to have been passed against the man rather than against the doctrine.” Severus adds: “Valens and his associates wished first to extort Athanasius’s condemnation, not daring to contend about the faith. As a result of this conflict between the parties, Paulinus was sent into exile.” This should not be understood [Col. 0674D] as though Paulinus had been driven into exile by the judgment of the synod. These words of Sulpicius Severus must be referred back to the meaning of Hilary’s words, so that we understand Paulinus to have been expelled by the emperor Constantius only after he had been condemned by the judgment of the bishops. Expulsion from a city, which is a secular punishment, belongs to rulers, not to bishops. Yet execution of the synodal sentence would not have been so readily accomplished unless imperial authority had added force to the ecclesiastical decree. That the ruler’s consent was sometimes thought necessary for a bishop’s deposition to be valid is shown by the example of the bishop of Augsburg. The Gothic king Theodoric restored him to his former dignity, so that he possessed all the rights of the episcopate that he had previously held, as Cassiodorus records in Book I, Letter 9 of the *Variae*. Likewise, the emperor Lothar acted in the case of Ebbo of Reims, as recorded by Flodoard.]

Paulinus, who confirmed the truth of his faith by enduring exile, decided, after taking counsel with the clergy and people of Trier, that Saint Maximin should be brought back from Aquitania, where he had been buried. Accordingly, the clergy and people formed a procession and proceeded toward Aquitania. After covering long stretches of road, they finally halted, extremely weary, not far from the place where that treasured relic was concealed. While the others were caring for their bodies, one of the elders prostrated himself on the ground and entreated the Lord that they might deserve some indication of that desired place, which he and his companions entirely failed to identify. He had scarcely finished his prayer when a boy, following a flock of sheep and bearing the name of the blessed Maximin in an oath [Note: [Col. 0675D] *Jurative*. That is, swearing by Maximin. Moreover, this account is so extraordinarily elaborate that I do not think a more charming fable could be found.], threatened to drive away a sheep with a blow if it approached where he did not want it to go.

The elder, astonished, asked where Maximin, whom the boy had named, was resting. In turn, the boy marveled and asked who could be so ignorant of the memory of so illustrious a man. When he learned that they had come from elsewhere, he led them all the way to the place they sought. Thus, praising God and the blessed Maximin, and made still more certain by an angelic revelation, they came to understand that what they were seeking would be found where they had been shown.

But the church’s custodian, suspecting what came to pass, ordered those who had arrived to leave that same church; and they concealed the outcome of the affair. Soon, however, swift rumor spread the news, and a huge force of Aquitanians was stirred up to prevent the people of Trier from taking the relic away. A most wicked crime might have been committed [Note: [Col. 0675D] *A most wicked crime*. This seems to have been modeled on Sallust in the *Catiline*: “On that day, after the city of Rome had been founded, the most wicked crime would have been perpetrated.” Likewise in Tacitus, Book I of the *Annals*: “When Caesar the dictator had been killed, the deed seemed to some the worst of crimes, to others the finest.”], had not the people of Trier, setting Christian brotherhood against them, affirmed that they had gathered solely for the purpose of prayer.

The Aquitanians, supposing the people of Trier to have been terrified by fear of them, relaxed into rejoicing, indulged in wine, and—as naturally followed—were overcome by deeper sleep.

## CHAPTER VIII

Meanwhile, an angel commanded the blessed Lubentius, mentioned above, to take the key of the church from the custodian’s head and, entering the church without disturbance, carry away the desired treasure. He made ready with a gathering of other priests [Note: [Col. 0675D] *A gathering of others*. What do you say? Were there so many priests that they constituted a gathering? Evidently bishops were easygoing in those days and ordained many priests without a specified assignment. You see, reader, how shamefully this history has been corrupted.], and hastened with all possible speed. With success accompanying the undertaking, the key was quickly returned to the place from which it had been taken, and what the waiting crowds desired so greatly was brought to them.

As the people of Trier hastened their departure, the Aquitanians first declared that they had withdrawn out of fear. But when they learned the truth of what had happened, they assembled a large army and pursued them for three days. When the two peoples had come within sight of one another, the Aquitanians were driven back by repeated flashes of lightning, peals of thunder, and frequent bolts, none of which touched the people of Trier. They returned home, not without shame.

As the people of Trier resumed their journey, a certain man blind from birth begged to be taken to the bier in hopes of recovering his sight. When its shadow touched him, the darkness of his long-standing blindness immediately departed. Thus many rejoiced in the restoration of one man.

## CHAPTER IX

When they had reached the fortress of Mosomagum [Note: [Col. 0676D] *Mosomagum*. A village in the diocese of Reims on the River Meuse, mentioned by Saint Remigius in his letter to Fulco, bishop: “It was therefore right, he says, that you should have believed that the Church of Mosomagus, which the metropolitans of the city of Reims have always governed by their own appointment with Christ’s help, was to be occupied by you through your unlawful ordinations.” Hincmar mentions the district of Mosomagus, in which Duziacum is situated, in his *Life of Remigius*. Later, what had once been called Mosomagum was called Mosomum, as in Flodoard, Gerbert, and elsewhere. Commonly, Mouzon.], a certain paralytic was brought to the blessed Maximin to be healed. The prayers of the faithful were not in vain. For, restored without delay to the health they desired, he offered a most beautiful spectacle to those who watched.

And so that the inhabitants of the place might appear to give thanks, they built a church to God in honor of the blessed Maximin, where his sacred relics had been deposited.

The fortress is called Evogium and now belongs to the territory of Trier. When the bearers of the relics entered it, a woman possessed by an evil spirit asked why the people of Trier had brought the blessed Maximin there, when the saints of God Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus, as well as Agritius, ought to have been sufficient for them—saints whom the demons were made to endure as violent torturers. The dreadful enemy did not long rejoice in the misery of the wretched woman. For, after uttering the foregoing words, he was compelled by the merits of the blessed Maximin to depart and was deprived of the power to mock her.

From there, when the holy relics had been brought to the fortress called Ardo, two lepers approached. They had already learned from favorable report how powerful Maximin was and implored his aid with believing minds. Their hope did not deceive them. Having soon experienced divine healing, they attained complete health.

## CHAPTER X

After so many and such great divine miracles had been celebrated, Maximin—formerly bishop of Trier, but now a most certain patron with God—approached the city that he had once governed. It would scarcely be credible how great a multitude then flocked to him. The entire city poured out to meet the bishop; a dense crowd of peasants gathered from the fields; and many also hurried from neighboring cities.

Veneration for Maximin had brought these crowds together, and Paulinus, the standard-bearer of all devotion, adorned them with his glorious presence. Frankincense of precious fragrance was burned, an abundance of candles shone brightly, the ranks of the sacred orders stood in array, and festive songs resounded.

Thus the illustrious confessor Paulinus received the most sacred Maximin, conducted him in procession, and committed him to a magnificent burial in the church of the most blessed John the Evangelist.

Later, a man blind from birth, brought from the territory of Beneventum, named Creton, declared that while he was staying in Rome in hope of recovering his sight and praying at the memorial of the apostle Peter, he had been instructed by the prince of the apostles to go to Belgic Gaul, where Saint Maximin rested, because through Maximin’s merits he could obtain the joys of the health he desired.

He set out and came to the place. After he had told the story to the church’s custodian, named Gosbert, he was admitted to the inner part of the tomb and there, to his astonishment, immediately found the restoration of light.

The most blessed Peter could have granted the blind man’s request with the greatest ease, but he preferred to transfer the glory of the miracle to Maximin, so that he might clearly reveal to everyone the quality of Maximin’s merits.

## CHAPTER XI

Moreover, in the crypt where the bones of the venerable bishop had been buried, water gradually rose until it covered an area one cubit wide. It is marvelous to relate that it surrounded the entire tomb within its circuit, yet stood back from its base and caused no small astonishment to those who saw it.

Accordingly, the venerable bishops Hildulphus [Note: [Col. 0677D] *Hildulphus*. Or Hildolfus, bishop of Trier, who flourished under King Pippin. His *Life* appears in Surius, Volume IV, from which it is evident that he was a most holy man; this is also attested by Richerius the monk in Book I of the *Chronicle of Senones*. Stephen III “entrusted to him and several other bishops of those regions his responsibilities for investigating the acts, virtues, deeds, and miracles of Saint Swibert, in order to canonize that saint,” as Saint Ludger, bishop of Münster, writes to Rixfrid, bishop of Utrecht. Hildulphus was made archbishop of Trier at the command of King Pippin, as the author of his *Life* expressly reports: “Soon, he says, his fame spread through the court of King Pippin, father of Charlemagne; and by his decision Hildulphus was declared worthy of the archiepiscopate and determined to be raised to that dignity.”], Clement, and Gosbertus assembled together and carefully examined what had occurred. They judged that the bones of the blessed man should be transferred from the crypt just mentioned and placed where they now lie [Note: [Col. 0678D] *To be transferred*. The author of Saint Hildulphus’s *Life* also mentions this translation in these words: “Among the other magnificent works that he carried out, he transferred the body of Saint Maximin, bishop of Trier, from the place where Saint Paulinus of Aquitania had buried him to the place where he is now venerated.”].

The outcome that followed showed that they had made this decision in accordance with the divine will.

To this, I think, may appropriately be added the case of a certain woman, Frankish by nation and noble by birth, named Rodoara. A harmful humor had withered her shin and foot. She came to the memorial of the blessed man and continued her prayers there with great persistence, even though her family urged her to leave, despairing of her obtaining health. After a long time, she recovered the health she had desired, to the astonishment of everyone.

## CHAPTER XII

How marvelous, moreover, is what happened to the prince Charles [Note: [Col. 0678D] *To Prince Charles*. His surname was Martel; he was the father of King Pippin, whom we mentioned shortly before.]

When he was afflicted by a prolonged fever and, through disgust with food and drink, had come into danger of death, the blessed Maximin appeared to him as he slept and showed him that he should follow him as he departed to his memorial.

When he awoke, Charles asked a guardsman who happened to be sitting beside him whether he had seen the blessed Maximin, who had spoken with him shortly before. When the man denied it, Charles said: “He has just gone outside and commanded me to follow him at once; I shall receive health at his tomb.”

Thus, when Charles had been carried there in a litter and had fallen asleep, Saint Maximin spoke to him again and showed that he had entreated the Lord’s mercy on his behalf. He warned Charles not to give himself over to vices any longer.

As soon as Charles awoke, therefore, he rose. In fulfillment of his vows and promises, he withdrew into the sacristy and asked that food be brought to him. For the previous thirty days he had scarcely kept himself alive by drinking water alone, since he had lost the ability to take nourishment.

After eating, he sensed his lost strength returning. Not forgetful of this favor, he enlarged Saint Maximin’s monastery with estates, one of which is called Patriosala, another the church of Witmari, and a third Comiciacus. To Saint Peter he offered the estate of Andacla.

## CHAPTER XIII

At the aforementioned memorial, two women—one called Weltrudis and the other Elithildis—had formerly been incapacitated by weakness of their hands and feet. Through the intervention of the most glorious confessor, they recovered the ordinary use of their limbs.

A man of Frisian origin, named Albo, gave himself and his property to the blessed Maximin. After doing so, while laboring for the benefit of the brothers, he was obliged to travel overseas for the sake of trade. He therefore joined a fleet of six ships and put out to sea.

When they had proceeded into the open sea, a storm suddenly arose, battered the six ships, and immediately engulfed them in the surging waves. Caught in this moment of danger, Albo encouraged the sailors to implore Saint Maximin’s aid with him.

As they humbly did so, Albo suddenly saw a man shining like the sun and walking upon the sea without his feet being submerged. He ordered Albo, who was confessing his faith, to recover his confidence; by his voice he drove away fear, and by his presence he restored calm.

Thus, brought safely back, they poured forth praises with the greatest rejoicing to God and Saint Maximin, the author of such evident salvation.

There are many great miracles worthy of God, who works through his servants, and worthy of being transmitted to posterity in celebrated proclamation. Yet this deserves more careful consideration: in addition to such an abundance of powers, the blessed Maximin was granted, as if by a special grace, the power to drive away demons. This will easily become clear from what follows.

Others may speak of this matter more effectively—those whose purity of life has made them acquainted with heavenly mysteries. For my part, in my weakness, it seems that this man deserved that privilege for the following reason: while living the common life, he was especially free from those vices to which apostate spirits chose to enslave themselves irrevocably—namely, pride and envy. It therefore seemed just to the divine plan that the man who had cast down pride through humility and crushed envy through charity should possess dominion over those who, corrupted by their own perverse will, refuse ever to aspire to those virtues.

## CHAPTER XIV

Accordingly, King Pippin, father of the great Charles, sent one of his clerics, named Bruncho and possessed by impure spirits, to the tomb of the blessed Maximin by the hand of the archdeacon Hellarius.

This man had been led around to the memorials of various saints, but had not deserved to be freed from that dreadful affliction. As soon as he touched the threshold of the holy man, he was immediately cleansed and began to glorify God’s mercy toward him and proclaim the power of Saint Maximin.

The same Pippin later sent Herricus, an Alamannian by birth, suffering from the same affliction as the man mentioned above. They had bound him with a chain, but he had broken it with extraordinary ease by supernatural strength. They scarcely managed to restrain him with another chain before presenting him to the illustrious confessor to be cured.

After the brothers had long struggled for the wretched man’s deliverance, one day, while they were celebrating the divine rites, he burst through his broken chain and rushed to the tomb of the sacred bishop, saying: “Do you not see the adversaries who had claimed me for themselves? The blessed Maximin is pursuing them as they flee.”

This brought his madness to an end.

Cunibertus, grandson through a daughter of that same King Pippin, was cruelly tormented by a demon. After he had been taken around to many places, he was finally brought to the holy man and cleansed of that plague.

## CHAPTER XV

And, moving from individual cases to the multitude of those delivered, we are told that once, at the festival of the blessed bishop—for on that occasion he displays greater power than usual—thirty-seven people oppressed by demons came together, and all were cured on the same day.

Among them, we learn, was the woman who had reportedly been subjected to an unclean spirit for forty-seven years. At last expelled from possession of such long duration, the spirit itself, destined for torment by fire, presented to the eyes of those standing by an imaginary blaze, so that it seemed the entire house was burning; and it covered the church with a fitting odor—that is, a sulfurous one.

That illustrious angel left behind these splendid tokens of his presence and power. The following year, at the same solemnity, twenty-two were cleansed. In the third year, thirteen returned from Saint Maximin’s monastery with the joy of restored health.

With this, I think, we have adequately and more than adequately instructed those who wish to read how effective and how outstanding the grace and power of expelling lost spirits are in this most sacred man.

But if we wished to record by the work of our pen how often he flourished up to this year in the many and varied forms of his other virtues—namely, the year in which we write, 839 from the incarnation of the Lord—we would exceed the limits of a book and become less pleasing to the learned reader by frequently recounting similar matters.

At the end of our little work, therefore, let us together implore the mercy of the blessed Maximin, so that he who has repeatedly driven bodily illnesses from others may deign all the more to free us from the diseases of our souls, showing in this respect also how greatly his power prevails. Thus, having now obtained forgiveness of our sins, may we one day deserve to behold his glory and rejoice in our own portion. Amen.

[Col. 0679]

[Note: [Col. 0679D] We owe this *Life of Saint Wigbert* to the learned man John Busaeus, a priest of the Society of Jesus, who published it at Mainz in 1602 together with the letters of Hincmar.]

# LIFE OF SAINT WIGBERT, ABBOT OF FRITZLAR  
## BY SAINT LUPUS

[Col. 0679C]

To the most reverend Abbot Buno [Note: [Col. 0679D] *To Abbot Buno*. Or Bruno, who governed the monastery of Hersfeld at that time and died in 846, as Lambert of Hersfeld writes, himself formerly a monk of Hersfeld: “Brun, he says, abbot of Hersfeld, died, and Brunwart succeeded him.” Earlier, together with Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, he had begun the church of Saint Wigbert at Hersfeld, as the same Lambert records under the year 831: “The abbots Brun and Rabanus dug the foundation of the church of Saint Wigbert on the sixth day before the Ides of July, a Monday.” Buno left it unfinished; Rabanus, later archbishop of Mainz after having been abbot, completed and dedicated it in 850, as the same author testifies: “The church of Saint Wigbert was dedicated on the sixth day before the Kalends of November by Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz.” Buno, moreover, to mention this as well, was born of a distinguished family in Swabia. He had first become a monk under Abbot Bangolfus in the monastery of Fulda and attended the dedication of the monastery of Hirsau in 838, as Trithemius records. Lupus therefore rightly dedicated this *Life* to Abbot Buno and the monks of Hersfeld.], and to all his brothers, Lupus sends the fullest good health.

While I hesitated, distrustful of my own strength, to attempt to treat the life of Saint Wigbert in writing, your insistence, beloved fathers, compelled me. Indeed, it would have been reasonable for me to persist in my most obstinate refusal, since my inadequate talent was unequal to so great a subject, and you requested this work precisely at a time when I was most occupied. I would have done so had charity not compelled me, setting aside my gravest necessities, to comply with your wishes. For one who obeys this principle sometimes looks after the interests of his brothers while neglecting his own.

I have therefore yielded to your command.

It will belong to divine mercy and to the intercession of the blessed man—whose deeds I have decided to touch upon in part—to ensure that they are written in language worthy of a worthy memory, and that what is most distinguished in character will not be disfigured by the coarseness of my unpolished expression.

Nor should anyone judge this work weak merely because, composing this little book in the year 836 from the incarnation of the Lord, in the fourteenth indiction, I appear to be recounting events from ninety years earlier. Anyone even slightly educated surely knows that Sallustius Crispus and Titus Livy narrated many events that long preceded their own age, learning them partly by hearsay and partly through reading. Among Christian writers, Jerome likewise illuminated in writing the life of his Paul, which had certainly occurred in a very remote period, and Ambrose, the bishop, left us a published account of the passion of the virgin Agnes, who was certainly not his contemporary.

Nor is the negligence of our ancestors a new matter requiring only an apology: the deeds of so great a man were not committed to memory, even though we know that some very important events have been suppressed not only by those who lived shortly before us but also by those who lived much earlier.

Accordingly, I do not see why my credibility should be diminished. If it was previously a fault that the virtues of this exceptional man were not recorded in writing, I now remove that fault from myself. I offer readers nothing except what you have most firmly learned and, in a certain sense, entrusted to me.

I ask this, moreover, of the knowledgeable and kindly reader: wherever the smoothness of the Latin language is roughened by the vernacular names of people or places in the German language, let him bear it patiently. Let him remember that I am not writing a poem, in which poetic license sometimes mutilates names and bends them toward the sound of Roman speech, or changes them completely [Note: [Col. 0681B] *But a history*. “For history, however written, gives pleasure. Human beings are naturally curious, and they are captivated by knowledge of things even when presented without embellishment.” (*Pliny*, Book V, Letter 8.)], but a history, which refuses to be obscured by the obliquities of stylistic coloring.

But let us now begin the work we have undertaken.

## CHAPTER I  
### How the Saxons became inhabitants of the island of Britain

[Note: [Col. 0681C] *Indigenous*. This is said with reference to the circumstances of the present time and because, in Lupus’s age, the purity of the Latin language had greatly declined. Strictly speaking, indigenous people are those who have inhabited particular lands from before all human memory and have not been mixed with the arrivals and settlements of other peoples, as Tacitus explains in his treatise on the customs of the Germans. In the *Agricola*, when speaking of Britain, he contrasts indigenous inhabitants with immigrants. Thus, if we proceed according to strict legal usage, the Anglo-Saxons were not indigenous but immigrants, since they had arrived by ship, as is clear from Bede and the other English writers.]

It is demonstrated by documentary evidence that the indigenous inhabitants of Britain, who are called Anglo-Saxons, trace their origin to the Saxons who inhabit the northern region of Germany.

For once the British king Wrtigernus [Note: [Col. 0681C] *Wrtigernus*. Since the Britons were afflicted by the gravest evils from every direction—from the sky, from the ocean, and even from the land, namely from pirates and plunderers—“it pleased everyone,” says Bede in Book I, Chapter 14 of his *History of the English*, “together with their king Vortigern, to summon the Saxon people from overseas for assistance. It is clear that this had been arranged by the Lord’s will, so that evil might come against the wicked, as the outcome of events more clearly proved.”], having nearly lost his forces in the repeated fires of war, arranged, with the consent of his people, to obtain aid from Germany.

The Saxon armies summoned by him crossed the sea that stretches along the shores of Gaul and Britain. Having received from the aforementioned king a place to settle in the eastern part of the island [Note: [Col. 0681D] *A place to settle*. Here Lupus transcribed Bede, whose words in Chapter 15 of the same book are as follows: “In the year 449 from the incarnation of the Lord, Martianus, who was the forty-sixth after Augustus to hold the imperial power together with Valentinian, held the throne for seven years. At that time the race of the Angles or Saxons, invited by the aforesaid king, came to Britain in three longships and, at the command of that same king, received a place to remain in the eastern part of the island, as though they were going to fight for their country, but in reality to conquer it. They therefore engaged in battle with the enemies who had come from the north to fight, and the Saxons won the victory. When this was reported at home, together with the fertility of the island and the sloth of the Britons, a longer fleet of armed men was immediately sent there, bringing a stronger force, which, added to the contingent already sent, made an invincible army. Those who had arrived therefore received from the Britons a place of habitation among them, on the condition that the newcomers would fight for the peace and safety of the country against its adversaries, while the Britons would provide the soldiers with the pay owed to them. They came from the three strongest peoples of Germany: the Saxons, the Angles, and the Jutes.” Thus far Bede. Prosper, however, a man of that age, does not say that the Saxons were summoned, but merely that “Britain, torn apart by various disasters and reversals down to that time, was reduced under the power of the Saxons,” in the eighteenth year of the reign of the emperor Theodosius Augustus. These words seem to say that the Saxons gained possession of Britain by force, and they confirm the account of Geoffrey of Monmouth, who recorded that the Saxons landed in Kent, approached Vortigern, and, after being invited to fight against the Picts, won a victory for Vortigern.]

they soon engaged in battle with their adversaries [Note: [Col. 0682C] *Adversaries*. That is, the Picts, who on this occasion had brought war against Vortigern, as Geoffrey of Monmouth explains in Book VI. Vortigern, a noble Briton, had taken Constans from a monastery and placed him on the throne, then arranged his murder by secret means. The deed was carried out by the Picts, whom Vortigern had summoned to guard the prince. After Constans had been removed, Vortigern made himself king; and, as though he had not participated in Constans’s murder, ordered the Pictish guards to be killed—security for the present and an example for the future. The Picts took this grievously and with resentment, and on that account raised a very serious war against Vortigern while avenging the slaughter of their people. Fortune indeed favored the Picts, until the Saxons arrived, as we have said, and restored Vortigern’s shattered fortunes.], routing them in flight without suffering loss.

When they reported this to their people, along with the island’s fertility, a stronger force of armed men was sent there once more [Note: [Col. 0682D] *A stronger force*. Geoffrey says in Book VI, Chapter 12, that eighteen ships filled with chosen soldiers were then hired.]. They received settlements from the Britons on the condition that the newcomers would diligently guard the country, while the indigenous inhabitants would pay wages to those serving as soldiers.

Taking advantage of this opportunity, Saxon power subdued a large part of the island under its own rule within a short time.

## CHAPTER II  
### On the origin of Saint Wigbert and how he was loved by everyone in those regions because of his devotion to virtue

[Col. 0683A]

From the descendants of these people, after they had submitted themselves to the Christian religion, came the blessed Wigbertus, who traced his noble origin to the Anglo-Saxon people. By the merit of his virtues he far surpassed the worldly nobility of his birth.

From his earliest years he shone so brightly in uprightness of conduct that it was already openly apparent that such a disposition would, by divine providence, attain something great and wholly beyond the ordinary measure, as indeed happened. Carefully instructed in sacred letters, he won far and wide, through his exceptional dignity, an ardent love and no less ardent veneration.

## CHAPTER III  
### On his reputation and honor, and a brief account of the sanctity and martyrdom of Saint Boniface [Note: [Col. 0683C] *Boniface, archbishop of Mainz*, frequently mentioned by the writers of that age.]

As his excellent reputation spread abundantly, it reached, by divine will, the ears of the illustrious Boniface.

Boniface displayed such great sanctity that, by universal agreement, everyone firmly believes and freely confesses that in every respect he should be deemed equal to the glory of our forebears—not only in Germany, where he labored in the Lord’s field, it is uncertain whether more zealously or more successfully, but also in Gaul and in other parts of the world.

He was both a most ardent defender of the Christian faith and its most watchful propagator. He did not seek the favor of princes through shameful flattery, nor did he weaken ecclesiastical honor or rigor through deadly shortcuts and falsely sweetened relaxations [Note: [Col. 0683C] *To weaken*. Lupus praises Boniface here because he nowhere permitted ecclesiastical authority to be broken, and did not consent to its violation by the princes among whom he spent much time. From this we infer that Lupus regarded as legitimate the acts of those princes mentioned in the letters of Boniface. In his third letter, Boniface acknowledges that he could not exercise any part of his office—he was a legate of the apostolic see—without the authority of Charles, ruler of the Franks. In Letter 42 he says that the authority to convene synods belonged to each ruler within his own kingdom; for this reason he calls a certain synod convened by Pippin the synod of the duke of the western provinces. In Letter 132 he says that he wished to appoint a successor for himself, but that this could not be done without the ruler’s will: “For this, he says, does not seem possible if the ruler is opposed.”].
