After he had devoted himself wholly to God, labored intensely, and brought the new people of the Frisians into the embrace of the Church, the fury of the barbarians did not hesitate to strike the invincible soldier of Christ with the sword. It caused him to return from battle bearing the crown of martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0683D] *The crown of martyrdom*. This happened in Frisia, where he was preaching the word of God, in the year 754.].

But, to return from this brief digression to the subject at hand—

## CHAPTER IV  
### How he was summoned by that same Boniface to assist in preaching

When Boniface had resolved to open the way of salvation to unbelievers and, with God’s help, to lead back those who had gone astray, he carefully arranged, not long after coming to Germany, for the blessed Wigbertus to be summoned as a future support in preaching [Note: [Col. 0683D] *To be summoned*. Evidently from England, where he held the dignity of abbot. For I think this Wigbertus was none other than the abbot of the monastery of Nursling in England, under whom Boniface began the monastic life, as the priest Willibald teaches in Chapter II of his *Life of Boniface*. “When, he says, with both vow and mind he continually sought, with great insistence in prayer, that the Almighty’s assistance might be present to him, at last, by divine grace inspiring him from heaven, he came to the monastery still called Nursling. There, moved by the spiritual diligence in letters of Wibertus of blessed memory, who honorably governed that monastery under regular discipline, he chose him as his teacher,” and so forth. [Col. 0684C] Boniface derived such joy from Wigbert’s arrival from England in Germany that, when he learned Wigbert was approaching, he went out many thousands of paces to meet him, as Wigbert himself writes in a letter to the monks of Glastonbury, which is Letter 53 among the Bonifacian letters. From that letter we also learn that Wigbert’s mother was named Tetta.].

Wigbertus obeyed the holy Boniface—indeed, God—who was calling him. At the time when Charles, duke of the Franks, held power, he entered into partnership in the holy undertaking. The blessed Boniface received him, as was fitting, with the greatest gratitude and regarded him with the highest veneration, bound to him by genuine brotherly love, since, as the elder, Wigbert had earlier burned with zeal for divine studies.

## CHAPTER V  
### How he was appointed abbot of the monks at Fritzlar
Not long afterward, having himself by divine grace been raised at Mainz to the most eminent dignity of the pontifical rank, he appointed the priest Wigbercht [Note: [Col. 0684C] Of the second order, that is, a presbyter. For I do not agree with Christopher Brower, who noted in his scholia on the poems of Rabanus that the administration of the bishopric of Buriburg had been entrusted to Wigbert by Boniface. He infers this from the passage of Lupus in which Wigbert is called a priest of the second order, taking a priest of the second order to be one who elsewhere is called a suffragan or vicar of a bishop and an archdeacon. Brower’s error here is so obvious that I do not think it necessary to dwell on it further. [Col. 0684D] One should consult only the most illustrious Petrus de Marca, *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*, book II, chapter 14, § 5. Lupus’s meaning, however, is this: Wigbert, who was already a priest of the second order, that is, a presbyter, was appointed abbot by Boniface in the monastery at Fritzlar. Unless Lupus calls an abbot a priest of the second order, and says that one who was already an abbot was appointed by Saint Boniface as superior of this monastery—a possibility I could readily believe.] of his own community, whose name in the German vernacular [Col. 0684C] is Friteslar [Note: [Col. 0684D] Fritzlar. A famous monastery in the Saxon March, on the river Eder, five German miles from Erfurt, as Georg Bucelinus noted in his *Topography of Germany*. It was founded by Saint Boniface as a bulwark against the Saxons, the implacable enemies of the Hessians and adversaries of the cross of Christ. “At Fritzlar,” as Brower notes in his scholia on the poems of Rabanus, “the first fruits were gathered of the Church of the Hessians. These people, who before the Saxons had been converted to the Christian faith together with the Thuringians and stationed on the frontier of the kingdom against the Saxons, foreign enemies, were cultivated assiduously by Saint Boniface and his disciples, and so rendered vigorous military service to the Frankish empire.”], and placed him in charge as master, so that he might establish there the rule and order of monastic life. While he lived there for a long time with his Megingo [Note: [Col. 0685D] Megingo. At that time a monk of Fritzlar, but afterward bishop of Würzburg, or Herbipolis, succeeding Burchard. Before becoming a bishop, he had been abbot of the monastery of Neustadt on the Main, as Nicolaus Serarius observes in his notes on the letters of Boniface of Mainz. I agree with Serarius that Magingaoz, or Megingum, is the person elsewhere called Megingozus, Mengozus, and Megingaudus. The presbyter Wilibald dedicated his *Life of Boniface* to him and to Lullus of Mainz. Three letters of this bishop of Würzburg to Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, are extant and published among the *Bonifaciana*, nos. 80, 87, and 94.], who afterward attained the episcopal dignity, he corrected the brothers’ previously lax and undisciplined manner of life according to the pattern of his own conduct; and this conduct was unquestionably governed by the authority of the sacred Scriptures.

## CHAPTER VI. That he went to Ordorff at the command of Saint Boniface

When the disciples had imbibed there, through long practice, a zeal for the sacred profession, and many of them, emulating their master, had undertaken the responsibility of teaching, blessed Boniface would by no means allow the light of so great a man, through Christ’s preceding grace, to have dispelled the darkness of only one place. At his fatherly urging he compelled him to migrate to another monastery, which is called Ortdorff [Note: [Col. 0686D] Ortdorff. A notable monastery in Thuringia, on the river Or, five German miles from Erfurt, as Georg Bucelinus noted in his *Topography of Germany*. It was founded by Saint Boniface, as Wilibald writes in chapter 8 of his *Life*, in these words: “Then too churches were suddenly restored, and the teaching of his preaching flowed forth in many forms; and a monastery was built at the place called Ortorff, where a community of servants of God and the holiness of monks had been gathered. In apostolic fashion, by laboring diligently with their own hands, they obtained for themselves food and clothing.”].

There, laboring with similar success, he corrected what was being done wrongly; and himself taking without deviation the narrow way that leads all who are tireless to life, he successfully drew a band of brothers after him. For, instructed by the example of the Savior, he first fulfilled what he was to teach (Acts I); and wherever he urged others to go, he was accustomed to go before them.

## CHAPTER VII. That, having returned again to Fritzlar, he devoted himself to a stricter life

And so, after several years had been spent there—not only was he weighed down by old age, but he also suffered from an intermittent and dangerous illness—he was unwilling to undertake anything without the authority of Saint Boniface. By his most earnest prayers, nevertheless clothed in profound humility, he obtained [Note: [Col. 0686D] He obtained. For it was not permitted to leave a monastery without the bishop’s permission, especially to one who was an abbot. Therefore Wigbert, intending to relinquish his office, asked Boniface for permission to retire.] that, returning to his former monastery, he might spend whatever remained of his life there as though released from active service.

There, welcomed by a throng of rejoicing brothers, as though becoming a boy and young man again, he diligently undertook anew the rudiments of holiness and the struggles of the strictest way of life. He was unwilling to measure either his age, which had earned its rest, or so many labors already completed; rather, forgetting the past according to the Apostle (Phil. III), he devoted himself to the joys of eternal blessedness, whose attainment is worth every expenditure that can be made in this life. And although, as we have said, illness oppressed his body, his spirit did not permit him, out of indulgence toward himself, to loosen the restraints of a more generous abstinence. This was not because he thought those blameworthy who, when ill, take more lenient care of themselves; but because the Vessel of Election confirmed by his own example that anyone may make considerable progress toward winning God’s favor by voluntarily abstaining from what is permitted. Thus, most observant of charity, he adapted himself to the fellowship of the brothers; yet he obstinately refrained from idle words and never laid aside meditation on the sacred law.

## CHAPTER VIII. That, when asked, he visited the sick without waiting for companions

Wigbert always had this established custom: when asked by some faithful person to go and hear a confession, and unable to avoid meeting travelers, he would not rashly begin a conversation with anyone or waste time on greetings—greetings which, as a certain elegant writer rightly observes, are sometimes poured forth because of an opportunity afforded by a journey, not from a desire to obtain some kind of salvation—but, retaining the Lord’s special commandment and intending to offer serious counsels for salvation, he hurried on, impatient of delay.

And wherever he encountered a gathering of people in need of salutary advice, he immediately set aside temporal matters and brought forward what contributed to the soul’s perpetual salvation. Attracting his listeners by various meanings of the divine law, he healed the hidden illnesses of their souls like an exceedingly skilled physician.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the vine of extraordinary size that he planted from a grape

I must not pass over in silence the following event, which the most steadfast report of the faithful presents without any need of invention. Once, while he was performing the divine service as usual, wine was lacking—wine without which the Lord’s blood is not consecrated. He promptly left the church and, happening to see a cluster hanging on a vine, plucked it and immediately pressed its juice with pure hands into the chalice.

When these rites had been completed, he found one grape-seed that had remained unharmed by the crushing. He at once planted it before the church and immediately returned to carry out the service he had begun. When it was finished, a more inquisitive brother, who had observed what he had done shortly before, humbly asked him the reason for the act.

Then, realizing that he had been discovered, he said: “If my works are a concern to the Lord, within the space of nine years he will surely deign to make this known.” Nor did the event believed to follow fail to reach such an outcome. For so many shoots of vines sprang from that single seed that, in a short time, they occupied an immense area of ground and, leaning upon supports that had been placed beneath them, provided delightful covered walks beneath their natural descent.

## CHAPTER X. In what manner he left the world

Blessed Wigbercht continued in the aforementioned monastery, ministering according to the divine commandments and always shunning crooked conduct, until the divine summons freed him from the bonds of the flesh. As a more serious illness preceded his arrival at the limits of the present life, he died [Note: [Col. 0687D] He died. In the year 747, according to Laubertus of Schafnaburg. After his death Boniface wrote a letter to Tatwin, the abbot, and the principal monks of the monastery at Fritzlar. It is the seventeenth among the *Bonifaciana*, and in it he prescribes how the monastery should be governed. Among those to whom he writes, a presbyter named Wigberthus is mentioned; in my opinion, three letters to Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, among the *Bonifaciana*, nos. 83, 102, and 110, are his. Serarius is mistaken in thinking that those letters were written by Wigbert, abbot of Fritzlar. He had died many years before Lullus succeeded Boniface.] and became a companion of the saints.

## CHAPTER XI. That a most beautiful bird appeared above his body

At the hour of his death a marvelous event occurred. While the brothers stood around him, a certain bird of extraordinarily beautiful appearance was seen to fly three times over his little body and never to appear afterward. Everyone undoubtedly recognized this as a sign of his most pure life.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the many signs performed at his tomb

His body was laid before the church in a tomb of no pretension [Note: [Col. 0688D] Of no pretension. That is, modest; Tacitus reports that the tomb of the emperor Otto was of this kind. Pliny writes admirably, *Letters* IX.19: “The expense of a monument is superfluous. Our memory will endure if we have deserved it by our life.”], and rested there for several years. It would scarcely be credible how many and how great signs divine piety used to bestow there in honor of this man. Although neglect has prevented them from being preserved in writing, they are nevertheless widely reported and have not yet fallen into disuse. Therefore, aiming at brevity, I shall relate a few of them.

My own opinion is plainly this: the miracles that God deigns to grant to the needy for the remembrance of the saints are always much more worthy than those which truthful writings report him often to have performed through them while they were still burdened by the weight of the body, although living sincerely. In the latter case they could still be tested and could fear even the smallest fall. But in the case of those who have already experienced every kind of fall, the miracles are more happily and more solidly affirmed. In the former, human favor is tolerated, but not without danger; in the latter, when the miracles are performed, the title of their holiness cannot be darkened even by suspicion of empty glory.

## CHAPTER XIII. That, through fear of the Saxons, the Hessians dug up his body

To carry out at last what we promised: the savage nation of the Saxons, having crossed its own boundary, had poured into the fields of its neighbors and had driven the natives, insufficiently confident in their own strength, by fear of them into the town called Buriburch [Note: [Col. 0688D] Buriburch. A town on the borders of the Hessians and Saxons, beyond the river Eder and opposite Fritzlar, on a high mountain ridge, as Brower noted in his scholia on the poems of Rabanus.].

Those shut inside, judging that they could still preserve their safety behind the town’s weak wall-work, arranged for the bones of the blessed man to be transferred into the town as their protection, especially because they feared that Saxon madness might seize the opportunity to violate his tomb. Yet even this transfer was not easily accomplished by those who wished to make it.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the difficulty of that same transfer

For, accompanied by an immense crowd, when they had reached a valley not very deep that lies opposite the town, and had set down the sacred ashes there for a brief rest and were preparing to continue toward the destination they had begun to seek, marvelous to relate, the relics they had carried became heavy, and it was impossible to move them from the place.

Struck with terror and thinking it better to face the final danger there than to leave their patron in uncertainty, they finally turned the Lord’s decision by their most persistent prayers and obtained their request. Once the bier had been lightened with the greatest ease, they attained their goal.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the candle plunged into the river

This too was a remarkable miracle. While they were crossing the river Eder, showing the relics of the blessed man the greatest reverence with crosses and banners, as well as with candles and fitting praises, a matron, astonished by the novelty of the event, let a candle fall from her hands, and it sank completely into the river.

Several people then strove together to recover it. Although this seems to exceed belief because it runs contrary to the nature of the elements, it was found emitting a ball of flame no less brightly than before. Yet we, who unhesitatingly confess that whatever occurs by God’s will occurs according to nature, consider it credible that fire did not yield to water any more than human nature yielded to fire in the case of the three youths (Dan. III).

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the sortie of the townspeople and the slaughter of the enemy

After the precious relics of the blessed man had been carried into the town, the Saxons followed in a hostile column and began to harass the townspeople and to drive them from the fortification with all their strength. But the townspeople made a sortie and, aided by the merits of Saint Wigbercht, engaged them with the greatest success. They proved superior, struck down and routed many of their opponents with their weapons, disabled many who were lagging behind from their wounds, and finally forced them all to seek safety by flight.

## CHAPTER XVII. That the Saxons, terrified by the majesty of a heavenly vision [Note: [Col. 0688D] Were terrified. I do not accept Brower’s opinion that this story should be distinguished from the one found in Regino. I believe that the subject here is the church of the monastery at Fritzlar, which the Saxons attempted to consume by fire; this is clear from chapter 23 and from other passages in the same *Life*. Regino relates the event in these words:

“In the year 874 of the Lord’s incarnation, while the king was delayed in those regions—that is, in Italy—for this business, the Saxons, taking advantage of the opportunity and setting aside their oaths, made an attack on the borders of the Franks and came as far as the fortress called Buriaburg. When the inhabitants perceived their arrival, they withdrew into the aforementioned fortification. Then, when the raging nation had begun to burn the buildings of the villages outside, they came to a certain basilica at the place called Friedislar, which the martyr Boniface of holy memory had consecrated and had foretold through the prophetic spirit would never be destroyed by fire.

“The aforementioned Saxons began with every effort to attack that basilica, seeking by every device to burn it with fire. While they were doing this, two young men in white garments appeared to certain Christians who were in the fortress and likewise to certain pagans who were in the same army; they were protecting the basilica itself from the fire. For that reason the Saxons could light no fire against it, either inside or outside.

“Meanwhile, terrified by the divine sign and overcome by dread of the majesty of God, they turned to flight, with no one pursuing them. Later one of those Saxons was found dead beside the basilica, on his knees, leaning forward over his feet, holding fire and wood in his hands and, as though blowing with his mouth, trying to burn the basilica.” The author of the *Life of Charlemagne*, the author of the *Annals of Fulda*, Einhard in his *Annals*, Marianus Scotus, and others relate the same story. Lambert of Schafnaburg mentions it briefly.]

took thought for their lives by fleeing

After this repulse the Saxons became more enraged. Wishing, by renewing the contest, to recover their disgrace through flight and to destroy to the last man those whom they had previously defeated but who had now proved victorious, they saw on that very night, whose dawn was expected to bring the day of so cruel an undertaking, a church—the one already mentioned—suddenly surrounded by an incredibly brilliant light sent down from heaven. On its roof they perceived a remarkable figure, outlined in the features of a human body but far surpassing mortal beings in power and dignity, and clothed in white garments, walking back and forth.

Terrified, therefore, by divine command and by the majesty of this vision, they abandoned their baggage and all other necessities and, hastening to preserve only their lives, once again took to flight.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the division of the spoils

The next morning, those who had been shut inside the town and had delayed the enemy’s attack by presenting the walls went out. When they discovered that the enemy had departed—or rather, that they had escaped as though stripped bare, abandoning everything indiscriminately—they gave thanks for the divine munificence, divided the spoils of their adversaries among themselves man by man, and brought back an unexpected joy.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the man afflicted with perpetual paralysis

Not long afterward, when the same Saxons returned to renew their repeatedly unsuccessful attacks, one of them took fire, placed fuel beneath it, and attempted to set fire to the church mentioned above. But his effort was futile and fruitless. Repelled by divine power through the intercession of Saint Wigbercht, he received a reward worthy of his truly sacrilegious attempts: he was afflicted with perpetual paralysis.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning the robber deprived of reason and sight

One of them also attempted to plunder the same building. Having broken down the door, he burst inside, seized a silver plate from the cross, skillfully gilded, and did not hesitate to carry it away in his profane hands.

But divine vengeance immediately followed and so rendered him incapable of controlling himself that you would have taken him for a brute animal rather than a human being. Wandering about the church with the plate, he returned—though now unknowingly—the object he had knowingly stolen. The relics of the saints, which those same men had carried away, were also found intact at the village of Gesmari, which is not far away.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the ineffective power of fire

Nor should I pass over the fact that the aforementioned Saxons, having applied fire and abundant fuel—indeed, material highly suitable for fire—and repeatedly piling it against the church building, attempted to burn it. But through the intervention of blessed Wigbercht their madness was frustrated.

The outcome was so far removed from their undertaking that the fire, applied by the raging hands of the barbarians, accomplished nothing beyond consuming the fuel placed beneath it. One could see the simple wood, not even smeared with alum, as if removing the power of fire from itself and, astonishing to those who witnessed it, displaying that by God’s will it had been endowed with the power to resist the force to which it had previously been subject.

## CHAPTER XXII. That the church itself could not be stained by any filth

After the Saxons’ departure, a considerable number of Hessians—for those who inhabit that district are called Hessians—came to cleanse the church, greatly distressed that it was filthy because the Saxons had made horse-stalls in it and had shown no respect for religion.

But when they entered, they found absolutely nothing that ought to cause fear. Divine power had so wiped away the filth and squalor. Nowhere did any trace of the entire defilement remain.

## CHAPTER XXIII

These events occurred around the church before which, as we have shown, his tomb remained for a long time. But after his bones had been transferred into the town, just as precious ointment spreads the most agreeable odors far and wide when it is stirred, so the relics of this man, when moved, abundantly breathed forth the fragrance of miracles.

The true and intimate Judge plainly revealed, once the structure of human limbs had already been weakened, to what spirit those limbs had once obeyed while blessed Wigbercht governed them, granting him frequently, within two or three days, the fellowship of nine signs.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That, following a heavenly admonition, his body was brought to the monastery of Herolfesfeld

[Col. 0691A]

After several years had intervened, someone appeared in a dream to Albuin, bishop of Fritzlar and of that same town [Note: [Col. 0691D] To Bishop Albuin. He is also called Witta by another name, and Wittana in the letter of Pope Zachary addressed to him, in which he is called bishop of the Church of Barbarana. Serarius explains this expression as referring to Buriburg, whose bishop he says Albuin was; I do not disagree. He was therefore bishop of the town of Fritzlar because Fritzlar lay within the diocese of Buriburg and was, as it were, a suburb of Buriburg. Thus the archbishop of Narbonne was formerly called the archbishop of Redès because the district of Redès lay within the diocese of Narbonne. Similarly, the bishop of Ausona was called the bishop of Manresa because Minorissa, or Manresa, lay within the diocese of Ausona; and the bishop of Elne was called the bishop of Roussillon because the town of Roussillon, or Ruscino, was situated in that diocese, and because the county of Roussillon constituted the greater part of the diocese of Elne. The same applies in other cases.], saying that he had been divinely sent to the monastery called Herolfesfeld [Note: [Col. 0692D] Herolfesfeld. It later began to be called Herveldia. Lambert of Schafnaburg, under the year 844, writes: “Louis came to Herolfesfeld on the second day before the Kalends of November; he gave privileges to the monks and secured them with his seal. The monks of the same monastery of Herveld were also reconciled with Otgar, the archbishop.”], and commanding that the bones of the blessed man be transferred there.

The bishop mentioned this revelation to Lullus, prelate of the Church of Mainz. Lullus brought the matter before Charles the Great and immediately obtained his consent. Thus, at Lullus’s command, his suffragan Albuin secretly entrusted the sacred ashes of blessed Wigbercht to three monks of the aforesaid monastery—Ernust, Baturich, and Wolff—to carry them by night to the monastery.

He feared to do this during the day, lest the people, bound by affection for so great a man, should assail the aforementioned brothers in a blind uprising or attack them with various injuries, and, being superior in strength, claim for themselves the possession of so remarkable a treasure.

This was not because the venerable bishop distrusted Saint Wigbercht, who could surely protect those carrying his relics through his intercession; rather, he had very wisely judged that, although God was plainly favorable, consideration of human prudence—as something just—should in no way be set aside. For it is full of Christian devotion, so long as a person has something he can do, not to put the Lord his God to the test.

If anyone should think that this assertion can be invalidated, we shall turn his attention to the following point for explanation: when the Lord had dismissed the Israelite people from Pharaoh, he did not lead them by the road through the land of the Philistines, lest perhaps the people should repent when they saw wars rising against them.

No one can pass over that passage with sound understanding unless, agreeing with our view—or rather with that of our predecessors—he admits that it shows that everything which can be done by sound counsel to avoid adversity ought to be done, even when God is most openly our helper. (From Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 41.)

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning the chest placed upon his tomb

The aforementioned brothers therefore swiftly carried to the monastery of Herolfesfeld the very great gift entrusted to them by the bishop [Note: [Col. 0692D] They carried it in. Lupus does not record the date of this translation. Brower nevertheless thinks it occurred not long after the Saxon incursions, that is, around the year 780.]. There it was received by the other servants of God and magnificently placed in the church in the first position.

With the approval of Charles the Great, Lullus then arranged for his monument to be adorned with gold and silver, as well as with the other appropriate metals, in the manner in which the tombs of other saints are seen throughout Gaul and Germany. He completed the work on the Ides of August. Afterward, through the overflowing grace of God, great and marvelous signs shone forth there. Since they are almost innumerable, I shall append here only a few, so that anyone who wishes may measure the others by considering these.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning the healing of Hunther

A certain sick man was brought to the aforementioned monastery in a cart fitted out like a litter. There, with the merits of the blessed Confessor aiding him, he did not merely recover somewhat but attained complete health with certainty. Afterward he gladly assumed the monastic habit and found himself in no way unequal to performing the duties of the monastery. His name was Hunther.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning Burgwart, the paralytic

Another man, named Burckwart, almost entirely deprived of the strength of his body, lay for a considerable time before the threshold of Saint Wigbercht. At length, through the assistance of the saint’s most effective prayers, he was granted full health. Having long since forgotten the use of walking, once he recovered it he even journeyed to Rome to pray.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning Sigebert, the demoniac

Nor did the Lord deny this most proven servant of his the grace of driving out wicked spirits. For, in recent memory, a certain man seized by an exceedingly cruel demon, named Sigebraht, was dragged there miserably in iron handcuffs and, through the intervention of Saint Wigbercht, was freed from the violence of his enemy.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning Bertger, the demoniac

Likewise, another man named Beratgar, whom an evil spirit had transformed from a human being into a bestial madness, was cured of the same horrible affliction at the memorial of this saint.

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the threefold healing of Ramnulf

Moreover, a man born in Aquitaine named Ramnulphus, mute from infancy, deaf, and almost bent forward on his belly like an animal, was brought here. By a very great and exceedingly rare miracle, he suddenly received speech and the opening of his obstructed ears; and, in accordance with the privilege of human beings, he was also raised upright to look toward heaven.

Thus, although he had been afflicted by these three weaknesses, he marveled that he had suddenly gained an equal number of benefits belonging to ordinary human use.

## CONCLUSION OF THE WORK

I have set forth these matters, as you wished, in completed discourse. I have added nothing fictitious from outside, and I have expressed, following the course of truth, what your diligence ordered to be inserted. May blessed Wigbercht, Confessor of Christ, pursue it with kindly favor; and may he deign to repay with intercession you who supplied the material, together with me, who reduced it to some sort of form.

[Col. 0693]

## B. TWO HOMILIES OF SERVATUS LUPUS, ABBOT OF FERRIÈRES, ON THE SOLEMNITY OF SAINT WIGBERT

### FIRST HOMILY

[Note: [Col. 0693D] We owe these homilies to Johannes Busaeus, a priest of the Society of Jesus, who published them at Mainz in 1604 in his book *Paralipomenon*. Their authorship by Lupus is established by nothing more than the conjecture of Busaeus himself, who assigned them to Lupus for the reason that they were attached to the *Life of Saint Wigbert* in a manuscript belonging to the Dominican fathers of Mainz. Although we could determine nothing certain, we nevertheless did not wish them to be missing here, any more than two hymns for the feast of the same saint. Here are Busaeus’s own words:

“Since two years ago the *Life of Saint Wigbert*, formerly the companion of Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, was published together with the letters of Hincmar, and its author was Servatus Lupus, it has now seemed fitting to add two hymns and likewise two homilies in praise of the same saint, apparently composed by the same author. We found them attached to the *Life of Saint Wigbert* in a very old manuscript codex belonging to the Dominican fathers residing in this city of Mainz.”]

[Col. 0693B]

Rejoice and exult in the Lord, dearly beloved brothers, who have gathered with devoted minds for the solemnity of Saint Wigbert; and praise the Lord Jesus Christ most devoutly in manifold ways, for he never abandons those who hope in him, but mercifully provides us, established in this most wretched prison-house of the world, with admirable patrons to intercede for us. Thus, instructed through them in the Christian religion and nourished by heavenly provisions, we may now possess hope of heavenly rewards, if we follow there with heart and deed. Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, the holy Creator of all, established all the saints; and no one ever becomes holy by himself, without God’s generous providence. Therefore, as we read in the sacred Scriptures [Col. 0693C] (Luke II), from Abel the protomartyr until now he glorifies his saints and chosen ones through saving miracles in this world—those who were not ensnared by worldly allurements, but who, with every effort of mind and body, thinking rightly and restraining themselves from all iniquity, resisted the devil’s suggestions with the greatest effectiveness.

Therefore, through the overflowing grace of God, they are companions and heirs of the angelic seats in heaven, where they can desire nothing further, but enjoy without satiety the vision of the Lord Jesus Christ and the companionship of the heavenly citizens. And so, dearest brothers, let us take up, with divine assistance, their weapons and examples: through faith, with God’s aid, they conquered transient kingdoms, practiced righteousness, and obtained the promises. [Col. 0693D] And, just as the Lord Jesus Christ foretold in a truthful word in the Gospel: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew V).

Indeed, the outstanding preacher Paul gave this warning, saying: “We do not have here a lasting city in this muddy world, but we seek one to come through good works” (Hebrews XIII). Therefore, you who hold the apostles’ most sincere faith ought to strive to imitate them in all things, with a keen and tireless mind, insofar as you are able. For, as we read in the sacred pages, the apostles were so inflamed with love for Christ that in no way could tortures, threats from kings, or even the persecutions of unbelievers tear them away from him; rather, with firm faith and deed and with an unbreakable charity, they persevered unanimously until, summoned by God from this world, they were deemed worthy to ascend to heaven.

What shall we say about the virgins? Human ingenuity is not sufficient to write or imitate anything worthy of them, given the frailty of the flesh. They possessed one faith, unchanging love, and one charity; they had virginity of the flesh, an untouched body, and virginity of the soul, an incorrupt faith. And because they were adorned with devout endeavors in the Lord Christ, they received in heaven the palms and crowns of virtues as fitting rewards.

What, moreover, should be said about the martyrs? They handed over their earthly bodies to torments in despised and threadbare garments, so that they might be worthy to possess God, the ruler of all, and to reign eternally with him. They rejected the flower-filled blossoms of this world, together with its deceptive cares by which men delude themselves through their inventions; with all their strength they loved the Lord Christ, and for this reason they reign in the heavenly chambers.

Concerning the confessors, from whose fellowship this servant of God comes, and concerning all the saints as well, we read in the divine histories that all of them ascended to heaven through various tribulations, departing from the path of this world. From the most holy life of all these, therefore, we must imitate something insofar as human frailty permits, because we too were made in the image of God, [Col. 0695A] as they were. Thus we ought to return our undefiled images to God enthroned on high, as he says elsewhere: “Let Caesar’s image be returned to Caesar, and God’s image to God” (Matthew XXXII; Mark XII; Luke XX).

Even if, in comparison with them, our life appears filthy in relation to holiness, we nevertheless must not, with the Lord’s help, fall into despair, which is dangerous, because “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm XXIV), distinguished by their end. For the benign and ineffable will of the almighty discerns nothing except what is most justly fitting. None of the saints mentioned above was so learned [read: holy] that he did not need the greatest mercy. For the increase of divine goods is never sufficient for anyone in such a way that nothing further remains for a mind armed with divine assistance both to desire to understand and to undertake.

Therefore, let no one despair because of the magnitude of his sins, as he says elsewhere: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live” (Ezekiel XXXIII). Nevertheless, the medicine of conversion to God must be hastened, lest the time for correction and amendment be lost through delay and negligence, since the final day is known to none of us.

Let us therefore attend with the ears of our hearts to Paul’s truthful statements, where he says: “Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day” (Romans XIII). None of the works of our Lord Jesus Christ is without mercy, since he provides for human beings both through forgiveness and through chastisement; and in his mercy he provides temporal severity, lest he justly inflict eternal punishment.

Therefore, let no one grow sluggish on the journey of this life, lest he lose the most delightful place in his homeland. Whoever seeks God with a good will seeks nothing other than everlasting joy in heaven, for God contains within himself the highest of all goods and every good that is perfect. Let us therefore seek the Lord, as this blessed servant of God did, and for this reason he is crowned before God and human beings.

Let us seek him with the weapons by which we can find him: by loving God and loving our neighbor, by giving alms, by frequenting the church in constant prayer, and, with the Lord’s gift, always resisting the devil’s weapons, because mortal life runs through various accidents like the orbit of the world. No one possesses heavenly joys in this life. But from the beginning of the world until now many have gone astray through ignorance, because amid so many turbulent and deceptive things it is difficult to know and love God.

For this reason, let us do as the prophet says: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near. Let the wicked abandon his way, and the unjust man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him” (Isaiah LV). Seek, therefore, the good without end, and persist in what you have found; for it is necessary that true blessedness be situated in the supreme God, and this cannot in any way be denied. It is not permissible for a human being either to comprehend by intelligence or to explain in speech all the mechanisms of divine activity. A time will come when we shall grasp in the reality of things what we now enact in appearance.

We have touched on these matters briefly and concisely. What, moreover, is happier or more salutary than to serve God, who governs the world with such great mechanisms and wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy II)? Thus, when the universal day arrives, may we all, rejoicing over our good works and protected by God’s assistance, be deemed worthy to receive eternal blessedness together with his saints.

## HOMILY II

It remains, then, to say something briefly about Saint Wigbert, who shone in this world through such great benefits and among all Christians that the entire Christian people rightly rejoices in his solemnity with the highest veneration—especially we who place our confidence in his patronage with God, both here and in the future.

For we believe that, in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ, he is able to obtain everything for which one asks him with devout and pious prayers, since he has made so many miracles renowned in the presence of the people, as you have often heard, for his praise.

You see, therefore, dearest brothers, how great a glory it is for the human race to follow God with a devout mind. He never abandons those who hope in him; rather, he honorably exalts in the eternal joys of heaven all who, for love of him, despise the flourishing world, as the Truth himself bears witness, saying: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John XIV).

The apostle Paul likewise said of those who love God: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians II).

This holy man Wigbert was, as sacred report relates, distinguished by every dignity, joyful in heart because of God’s love, always composed in conduct, and energetic in every work of God. His private manner of life in vigils and prayers, as well as in fasts, in holiness of life, and in the display of signs, gives this to be understood. His constant labor, which he endured daily for Christ’s name, demonstrated his charity.

He was always advancing in the divine work throughout all the days of his life; because of his outstanding works he was pleasing to the almighty and agreeable to all the people. From childhood he gave with generous hands everything he was able to possess for works of mercy, so that he might himself, in poverty, follow Christ, who became poor for us.

For who could be so eloquent in speech as to explain one by one, in continual words, all the wonders or benefits that God works through him? He did not worry about tomorrow, but, always trusting according to the Gospel in God’s clemency, he fed all who came to him with eternal provisions. He despised no one in his distress, but, supported by brotherly love, always refreshed the sorrowful with divine consolation; and for God’s sake he strove to benefit everyone.

Raised in mind and body toward lofty things, he was a stranger and a poor man to the world. Although he was nourished by earthly uses, he nevertheless always devoted all his strength to heavenly matters. Therefore he is crowned eternally with the most just Lord and with all the inhabitants of heaven, where the one for whom Christ is joy can never be deprived of joys.

Let us therefore, insofar as we can with the support of divine grace, strive with all our strength to imitate him, so that, even if we cannot acquire such rewards in heaven, at least we may not be deprived of some refreshment there.

We possess the weapons of righteousness, as this servant of God held them: loving God, loving our neighbor without pretense, maintaining charity and peace with everyone—for it is Christian perfection to be at peace with one’s enemies, in hope of correction, not in agreement with wickedness—and showing humility and patience in heart and deed. For the evil and proud spirit led the first man, in his pride, to death; Christ, being humble, brought the obedient man back to life.

Let us be lovers of mercy and the Christian religion, compassionate, united in good works, and firmly guarding concord, which is the guardian of virtues, as he says elsewhere. Therefore beware, men, lest there be a discordant judgment in your minds: let one love join together what we understand; let what we live and comprehend stand firm in one and the same devotion. Nothing firm is separable, and nothing among human beings pleases God without peace—not even the greatest gift upon the altar.

Likewise, armed with divine assistance, let us flee the devil’s weapons, that is, pride. All vices have power only in evil works; pride alone must be guarded against in perfect and righteous deeds, because without doubt God breaks every proud person and always resists the proud.

Afterward, with every effort and inclination, drunkenness must be avoided, for it is the root of all mortal offenses. Let us flee anger, which very often, through rage, falls into its own death. Let us drive luxury and [Note: [Col. 0697D] Avarice. Namely, avarice concerning money, as is evident. Yet some ancient writers, when employing rhetorical language, transfer avarice to other things as well, namely glory and lust. Quintus Curtius, Book IX: “Again, avarice for glory and an insatiable desire for fame allowed nothing to appear inaccessible or remote.” Bachiarius, in his letter to Januarius on receiving the lapsed: “For you cannot reckon avarice only in money, because avarice is especially perceived in lust, to which no end is ever imposed.” Thus Horace, in his *Art of Poetry*, line 329, had said: “Greedy for praise.”] avarice from us like poison, with God’s help.

Luxury, with its evil counsel and honeyed flavor, condemns people to irreparable punishments. Nothing in the present age so miserably devastates the whole human race as avarice. Let us therefore reject hatred and envy from our hearts, because it is wholly unfitting for a Christian to hate the image of God. Nevertheless, among evil things we utterly hate wickedness and love the creature. With the help of divine generosity, let us also flee discord and fraud. Nothing good can exist where fraud and discord reign.

It is shameful to discuss these matters at greater length. With the Lord’s help, let us leave aside the evil sirens that accustom human minds to disease rather than freeing them. Let us also hold fast to those virtues in which alone there is health and eternal happiness.

Therefore, dearest brothers, know that the rich of this world are in the greatest poverty, since they do not possess the riches of righteousness and truth. But those who faithfully serve the Lord enthroned on high discover goods that can in no way perish. The goods of the present age are small. Eternal goods are never lost except through negligence and carelessness.

Therefore, you who have been marked with Christ’s triumphant sign and who, with the Lord’s help, wish to overcome this perilous life, in which there is nothing but seductions and assaults, always love in conduct and works what Christ, the true lover, now possesses. Lovers of the world burn with concern over losses and pestilential profits.

Since the world is wholly filled with bitterness and ruin, and false joys flow away, draw near to God through good deeds, and he will draw near to you. Seek him not falsely but truly, and you will find him. Let no one, I beg you, doubt in faith, hesitate about the abundance of forgiveness, or waver concerning the effect of a pious petition; for the more confidently and kindly we beseech God, the more quickly we shall be deemed worthy to be heard.

Faith abounds in every good, as the Savior himself says in the Gospel (Matthew VII): “Everyone who asks with faith receives; whoever seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it will be opened.” And again: “To everyone who has, it will be given, and he will abound. But from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away” (Matthew XIII).

We have many examples of our fathers in the divine pages. We also have before our eyes the most certain example of this holy man, whose festive day we celebrate today: in fervent faith, for love of God, he abandoned his homeland, family, and worldly friends; he despised earthly things and their showy praises in order to seek heavenly things.

With the Lord’s support, let us also despise the world and love our Creator together with his commandments, so that through the present good works we perform we may be able to reach the joys of eternal blessedness, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who by his paternal power is threefold and one, and lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HYMNS FOR THE SOLEMNITY OF SAINT WIGBERT

### I

The wonderful natal day  
Of Wigbert has now arrived,  
Already illuminating us with light,  
May Christ preserve us, gathering us together.

This confessor of the Lord,  
A brother humble in mind,  
Whom Christ had already foretold  
As one who would receive his kingdom.

Through his prayer we believe  
That we shall all journey to the stars,  
If we perform the worship  
Of him who sits above the angels,  
Who sits above the cherubim,  
And likewise above the seraphim,  
And governs the starry hosts  
By his power.

May he himself rescue us  
From Tartarean torment,  
And defend us from the devil’s snare  
With his standard.

Saint Wigbert, we ask you:  
Pray for all of us,  
That the King and Lord of angels  
May wash us from our crimes.

O gracious shepherd, intervene now  
For the devout clergy.  
Your worthy prayers  
Take away our sins.

Our Savior, release  
And erase our crimes  
Through the illustrious merits  
Of the confessor Saint Wigbert.

### II

Behold, Wigbert’s feasts shine forth,  
Returned with devout vows,  
To be honored by us with annual worship.  
O Christ, favor your numerous people.

Here, like a bright, gleaming lamp,  
He scattered throughout the world  
The shining rays of his excellent character,  
Walking along the steep paths  
Of the righteous way.

And, so that nothing of sacred merit might be lacking,  
He bowed his pious neck  
To the highest command,  
So that he might be  
A poor minister of Christ’s cross.

The Godhead itself so blessed him  
That, for the age in which he dwelt,  
He might be an example in this way  
To posterity that stumbles along.

May his example gather into one  
A not-small crowd of those who serve him,  
So that the praises of Christ  
May always resound in their faithful hearts.

God will redeem that crowd from every hardship  
When he shakes his powerful, flashing right hand,  
Granting, after their final labor, rest  
To behold himself.

May the offspring of the Father, and the Father himself,  
And the Holy Spirit, equal to both, grant this;  
For the one name of the Godhead  
Belongs to them throughout every age.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 866: RODULF, BISHOP OF BOURGES

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON RODULF

*(From* Gallia Christiana, *volume III.)*

Rodulf was born of a noble and ancient family, namely of Rodulf, count of the Cadurci, and Aiga, parents equal in both nobility and piety, [Note: [Col. 0699C] From Mabillon, *Benedictine Century IV*, part II, p. 156. These were the children of Count Rodulf and Aigua: Rodulphus the cleric—he is our archbishop—Count Godefridus, Rotbertus, and Landricus; their daughter Emenana was abbess of Saint Generius at Sarrasiacum. Concerning John, who had been abbot of Bellilocum, there is complete silence. Nevertheless, mention of this John will be made below. Robert’s wife, Retrudis, was buried in the monastery of Bellilocum. You will find much concerning them in the appendix to the history of Tulle.] By them he is said first to have been handed over for clerical formation to Bertranno, a religious man, with a certain estate outside the association of his brothers assigned to him as a patrimony. In the same way, his noble parents granted a certain church to Emenana, Rodulf’s sister, when she was to be given the habit of a nun.

“Clerical formation” may here mean monastic life, which ancient writers not infrequently designate by the term *clericatus*, especially since we see that Rodulf had been an abbot before becoming a bishop. Nor does the title assigned to him—or the estate assigned as a kind of title for his clerical life—present an obstacle; for this was also customary with monks, as is proved by a charter of a certain Rotardus in the archive of Bellilocum among the Lemovices. From there an instrument has been recovered concerning an estate given to Rodulf as patrimony. For there Rotardus grants to Rodulf, abbot of Bellilocum—he was our Rodulf—and to the monastery of Bellilocum, “for the clerical service” of a certain relative named Gumbertus, that Gumbertus might hold these possessions until the abbot and monks of the aforesaid place, or the church, granted him another dignity by which he could live according to the office of his clerical service.

In the same way, when our Rodulf, still a young man, [Col. 0701A] was handed over by his parents to monastic life, his parents simultaneously gave the demesne estate of Bellomons in the district of Limoges, as is proved by the monastery of Saint Peter of Bellolocum’s charter of donation of this estate, which Mabillon presents in *Benedictine Century IV*, part II, p. 157.

Rodulf was afterward abbot of an uncertain place. Mabillon proves that in the year 840, when he obtained the see of Bourges, he was indeed an abbot, but not yet abbot of Fleury, Veterina, or Bellilocum, since those two monasteries had not yet been founded.

Rodulf began to preside over the metropolitan church of Bourges around the year 840 or 841. Indeed, in 840 he is still called merely an abbot in the sale of the estate of Beliacum made by Boso and his wife Talasia to Abbot Rodulf—our Rodulf—in the first year after Lothair, the most excellent emperor, assumed imperial power, namely after his father Louis had died in June of the year 840.

A little later, however, Rodulf became archbishop of Bourges, as he himself teaches in a charter that he calls his testament. [Col. 0701B] At its end one reads: “Rodulf, bishop of the first see, subscribed this document of the testament … Given in the month of March, in the first year of King Charles.” This was the first year of Charles, surnamed the Bald, as king, after the death of his father Louis. Perhaps this was still reckoned as the year 840 of Christ, up to Easter.

To speak now of the deeds of Saint Rodulf during his episcopate: in the same year in which he ascended the episcopal chair, he built the monastery of Veterina among the Lemovices. Mabillon published an instrument concerning its foundation in the eulogy of the holy bishop, volume IV of the *Acts of the Saints of Benedict*, part II. In it Rodulf offers to the Lord Savior certain properties of his own: Suraziacum, namely, with the estate of Saint Genesius, situated in the district of Cahors, in the vicariate of Casiliacum, as well as a lordly residence at Veterina on the river Sordarien (the Sordoire), in the territory of Limoges. He had received these from his mother Aiga.

He placed over this monastery Silvius as abbot, without doubt the same man whom we see at this time as abbot of Solemniacum. The patrons of the new monastery were, besides the Savior of the world, the apostles Peter and Paul, all the apostles, and the martyrs Saints Laurence, Sebastian, Dionysius, Maurice, and others; among the confessors, Hilary, Martin, and others.

In the same year, 840, the monastery of Bellilocum was founded through Rodulf’s generosity on the river Dordonia. We read that Veterina was later made its priory; the two places, moreover, are not far apart. For this abbey Rodulf wished to appoint the venerable Abbot Gairulf, although he himself, as abbot, retained responsibility for both the monasteries of Bellilocum and Veterina.

In the year 843 the pious archbishop turned his attention to founding another monastery [Note: [Col. 0701D] That Rodulf was not the first builder or founder of this monastery seems to be suggested by a charter of the same place, which begins: “In the name, etc. Charles, by the grace of God king, etc. We decree and confirm that the aforesaid monks shall perpetually hold, with complete integrity, the aforesaid properties assigned to them for their support by the venerable Bishop Rodolphus or his predecessors, etc.” Perhaps the scribe’s error introduced *predecessors* in place of *successors*. For we do not possess the autograph of this Carolingian diploma.] within the boundaries of his diocese. To endow it, he contributed certain estates belonging to his church.

It was built at Dover [Devre], but afterward, because of the harshness and attacks of the inhabitants, it was transferred to a nearby fortress called Virzio. The first abbot after Rodulf—who presided over all these monasteries—of the monastery of Dover and of the new congregation serving God there was Aimericus. Charles the Bald mentions him in a privilege issued to confirm this monastery [Note: [Col. 0702D] See Mabillon, *Benedictine Century IV*, part II, p. 158.]

In the same year, with the assistance of his mother Aigua, Rodulf founded near the fortress of Caziliacum, in the district of Cahors and at the estate of Sarasiacum, a monastery for women, as we have already noted. Its abbess was Emenana, Rodulf’s sister. So great was the generosity of Countess Aigua in founding this convent that she is regarded as its foundress. She was also buried there after her death, near Count Rodulf, her husband, who had been buried there.

In Aigua’s documents this sanctuary is said to have been founded with the consent of Archbishop Rodulf, Count Godafred, Robert, Landricus, and John, Aigua’s children. The time when the place was founded is made known in this clause of the document: “This session was held in the month of February, in the first year after the death of the good-memory Rodulf just mentioned”—Aigua’s husband, the count—and “in the third year since the lord Lothair assumed imperial power.”

Leaving aside monastic affairs, let us perhaps turn to matters of greater importance. In the year 845 he attended the council of Meaux; the council of Mainz in 848, if Trithemius is to be trusted; and the council of Toul, at a place called Saponaria, in June 859. At the latter he was chosen as a judge, together with Remigius of Lyon and other bishops, in the case of Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, against whom King Charles the Bald had submitted a written complaint at this synod.

He subscribed the letter of all the bishops present to the same Wenilo, and another letter to the Breton bishops who had defected from their metropolitan, Herard, archbishop of Tours. [Col. 0702B] His subscription is also read in the second council of Toul, held at Tusiacum in 860. There Archbishop Hincmar of Rheims, by order of the synod, wrote to our Rodulf and to Frotarius, archbishop of Bordeaux, saying that the assembly of bishops had entrusted to them, who were the bishops of the principal sees of the kingdom of Aquitaine, the determination of the case concerning the marriage of Stephen and the daughter of Count Regimund, with the counsel of their fellow bishops and the leading men of the land, as is read in volume VIII of the Councils and volume III of the Councils of Gaul.

His name occurs among the subscriptions to the privilege granted to Saint-Denis in 862, at the first synod of Pîtres, and to the constitution for the monastery of Saint-Germain of Auxerre, made at the second synod of Pîtres in 864.

Moreover, Pope Nicholas I recognized Rodulf as primate of the Aquitanias and honored him with the title of patriarch in a letter found in volume VIII of Labbe’s *Councils*, nineteenth letter of the first appendix, column 504. In this letter Nicholas’s response to the questions of our Rodulf is especially noteworthy: he determined that ordinations performed by chorepiscopi were by no means to be repeated: “For they were made according to the pattern of the seventy [disciples],” he says; “who would doubt that they possessed the offices of bishops?”

The same pope (letter 40) warned Rodulf to abstain entirely from communion with the bishops Theutgaud and Guntarius, whom the apostolic see had condemned. Flodoard, Book III, chapter 21, mentions the letters that Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, had written to the same man, asking him to undertake the guardianship and defense of the goods of the abbey of Saint Remigius in the district of Limoges.

Rodulf composed fifteen chapters concerning ecclesiastical matters for the clerics and priests of his diocese. The distinguished Stephanus Baluzius recently published his chapters, dealing with nearly the same subject, in volume VI of the *Miscellanea*, p. 139.

After administering the church of Bourges for a long time with piety and vigor, and extending the monastic order in many places, he died, deservedly receiving the title of saint, in the year of Christ 868, according to Ado, on 11 July. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Ursinus at Bourges, where he is honored with great veneration.

The only blemish found in the life of this holy archbishop is that he held so many abbeys. Yet in those he had founded he retained no profit for himself; rather, he took care to return everything for the benefit of the monasteries. He appointed abbots to them, retaining for himself almost only the bare title of abbot—that is, of father—which suited a generous founder very well. Nevertheless, in this he seemed worthy of criticism to the fathers of the council of Toul held at Saponaria in 859, because he had possessed the abbey of Fleury together with the archbishopric.

[Col. 0703A] Charles the Bald had granted it to him while Abbot Bernard was still alive, hoping to win Rodulf’s support through this favor and use him during the disturbances among the Aquitanians. On account of his noble birth, his relationships with nearly all the nobles of Aquitaine, the dignity of his see, and above all his reputation for holiness, this archbishop’s power was extremely great.

But at the First Council of Toul the fathers took offense at this, and in chapter 11 one reads: “The general synod humbly requested, prostrating itself to the ground before King Charles, and beseeching and adjuring him and Rodulf, archbishop of Bourges, by the cross and blood of Christ, that they should strive to preserve valid and inviolate the privilege of the monastery of Saint Benedict, which they had confirmed with the aforesaid king’s agreement, and which the same Rodulf had subscribed, although he irregularly held the aforesaid abbey.”

Mabillon supposes that Rodulf relinquished the abbey because Bernard did not cease to perform the office of abbot for several years; but perhaps he exercised a delegated rather than supreme authority.

Among the other qualities of his character, this bishop excelled in the highest prudence, by which he won for himself the favor of princes who disagreed with one another and contended for the kingdom. We have already spoken of Charles the Bald’s goodwill toward him, when we related that this prince had granted him the church of Fleury even against ecclesiastical laws.

Pippin the Younger, king of Aquitaine, son of another Pippin, likewise king of Aquitaine, also proved generous toward him; he granted several estates, concerning which that prince’s diploma speaks, recorded as issued in the eleventh indiction, in the tenth year of the reign of the renowned King Pippin.

## THE CHAPTERS OF RODULF

*(In Baluzius, Sacred Miscellanies, volume II.)*

### THE PROLOGUE BEGINS

[Col. 0703B]

Rodulphus, the humble servant of the servants of God, sends greetings to his brothers and fellow priests of our Church of Bourges.

We believe that your Blessedness’s diligence is not unaware of how much concern for ecclesiastical discipline constrains us, and by how many daily anxieties—together with the burdens of our subjects and of temporal affairs—we are incessantly hemmed in on every side.

Therefore, as I have discussed with you, I was long unable to extract from the writings of the ancients, and also from the beginnings of Scripture and the canons, a little work concerning the life of priests and concerning penitence and satisfaction, because a mind divided among diverse matters is slower in dealing with each one.

I did not resist your request through a harsh aversion to leisure, [Col. 0703C] but was bound by the force of the impossibility described above. Now, however, unwilling to resist so many complaints, I judge it worthy and useful to comply with worthy desires and satisfy laudable requests.

Therefore, brothers, I do not wish to deny myself to you. With an ardent spirit, without any word of excuse, I do not refuse to take up this burden brought to me by you and also to be lifted by the Lord, casting my thought upon Christ, at whose urging I shall give growth to this work. For he himself says: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it.”

Indeed, I am greatly troubled because I have found in the booklets of our priests, which are commonly called penitentials (Council of Chalon II, chapter 38), errors whose authors are uncertain, and judgments concerning penitents so confused and diverse, and supported by the authority of no one, that a prudent mind can scarcely endure the damage caused by such grave discord.

Setting these aside, and applying my study to certain and catholic writings, I have taken care to gather, in one volume, a small work from the judgments of the holy Fathers and the canons concerning what priests ought to do, how they ought to conduct themselves, and how, as pastors endowed with intelligence and with speech softened only by a medicinal remedy, they ought to lead Christ’s flock back to the folds of perpetual pasture. [Col. 0704B]

And so that I might cause no weariness to fastidious and less learned readers, I have compressed the substance of this modest work into forty-five chapters.

But if anyone, filled with paschal and manifold dishes, should despise this product of our labor, I ask that, while preserving charity, he may avail himself of Attic resources, omitting to oppose our efforts of pure devotion without any display of arrogance.

I do not cease to implore, with all the efforts of my inmost heart, the diligence of readers, so that, refreshed by the gift of love, they may carefully undertake to amend and correct charitably whatever, with a discerning eye, they perceive in these pages to be corrigible or less suitable—not as mad detractors, but as benevolent embracers—without the obstacle of tearing them apart. Thus the perfection of love may be preserved in the mind, and the effect of excellent study exercised in the work.

Therefore I ask you, dearest brothers: pour forth prayers to the Lord with humble vows for my sins, that he, merciful and very compassionate, may loosen the bonds of my depravity and grant eternal joys. May almighty and eternal God, the shepherd, protect you everywhere and free you from every disturbance.

## CHAPTER ONE  
### On the Faith of the Holy Trinity: How It Is to Be Held and Preached by Priests

*(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 76.)*

First of all, it must be believed and universally preached to everyone that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, almighty, eternal, and invisible, who created heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them; and that there is one divinity, substance, and majesty in the three persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Likewise, because the Son of God was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary for the salvation and restoration of the human race, became human, suffered, was buried, rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven, he sits at the right hand of the Father. He will come to judge all human beings according to their own merits. All the dead will rise again in true flesh: the wicked, because of their crimes, are to be cast with the devil into eternal fire, while the righteous are to be joined with Christ and his angels in eternal life.

## CHAPTER TWO  
### On the Honor and Restoration of Churches
(Lib. I Capitular., chap. 67, and lib. VI, chap. 377.) We have thought it appropriate to admonish our brothers and fellow priests that the church of God, throughout their parishes, should receive its due honor; that the altars should be venerated and adorned according to their dignity; and that the houses of God and consecrated altars should not be accessible to birds and dogs. Secular business and idle talk must not be conducted in churches, [Col. 0705B] because the house of God ought to be a house of prayer, not a den of thieves (Matthew 21), and no one ought to assemble in church for any other reason than to praise God and perform his service.

(Capitularies of Theodulf, chap. 10.) Disputes, disturbances, idle talk, buffoonery, and other shameful activities must be altogether prohibited from that holy place. For where God’s name is invoked, sacrifice is offered to God, and the presence of angels is certainly believed to be found, it is dangerous to say or do anything unsuitable to the place. If the Lord drove from the temple those who bought and sold the victims they offered there (Matthew 21), how much more angrily will he cast out those who defile a place devoted to divine worship with lies, idle talk, laughter, and such trifles? [Col. 0705C] We also admonish them to build and repair the aforesaid churches well, according to their means, and to provide them with lights as is fitting, so that God may be honored in all things and the holy Church, purchased with Christ’s blood, may be venerated, magnified, and exalted (Lib. II Capitular., chap. 5).

## CHAPTER III. That Mass must in no way be celebrated anywhere except in a church, and that storerooms must not be made in churches.

(Capitularies of Theodulf, chap. 11.) The solemn celebration of Mass must in no way take place anywhere except in a church—not in just any houses or humble places, but in the place chosen by the Lord, according to what is written: “See that you do not offer your burnt offerings in every [Col. 0705D] place that you see, but in the place that the Lord will choose, so that his name may be placed there.” The exception is those who, going out on military service, have tents and dedicated altars for this purpose, in which they may complete the solemn celebration of Mass.

We also frequently see harvests, wine, hay, and kinds of other produce being gathered in churches. (Capitularies of Theodulf, chap. 8.) Thus they prove to be storehouses or storerooms rather than churches. And because of this—which is sacrilegious—we have often learned that homicides, adulteries, thefts, feasts, drunkenness, obscene speech, and similar unlawful acts, shameful to see and hear, are committed there by many people. Therefore we wish this to be strictly observed: nothing other than ecclesiastical vestments, sacred vessels, books, and things appropriate to the church’s honor or not detrimental to it may be stored in a church, [Col. 0706A] lest, if other business than what is proper is conducted there, we should hear from the Lord: “My house shall be called a house of prayer. But you have made it a den of thieves.” And again: “Take these things away from here, and do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce.”

## CHAPTER IV. That henceforth the dead must not be buried in churches.

(Capitularies of Theodulf, chap. 9.) In these regions there was formerly a custom of burying the dead in churches, and places consecrated to divine worship and prepared for offering sacrifices to God were often made into cemeteries or burial grounds. [Note: [Col. 0705D] See the Notes on Regino, p. 557.] Therefore we wish this practice henceforth to cease, and no one is to be buried in a church, unless perhaps the person is a priest or some other just man who, by the merit of his life, acquired such a place for his dead body through the way he lived.

The bodies buried in churches in former times must not be cast out. Rather, the visible tombs should be sunk more deeply into the ground; and, after a pavement has been laid over them so that no trace of the tombs remains visible, reverence for the church should be preserved. But where there is such a multitude of corpses that this is difficult to do, let that place be treated as a cemetery. The altar should be removed from it, and another constructed in a place where sacrifice may be offered to God reverently and purely.

## CHAPTER V. [Col. 0706C] Concerning books and ecclesiastical or priestly vestments, and sacred vessels.

(Lib. I Capitular., chaps. 68 and 103, and lib. V, chap. 229.) Priests must also be admonished to take care that they possess a well-corrected missal, lectionary, psalter, and other booklets necessary for them, because often, while they wish to ask God for something properly, they ask wrongly by means of uncorrected books. They must not allow their boys to corrupt these books, whether by reading or writing in them. They must correct them, and sacred vessels consecrated to God must be held in great reverence. No one may turn a chalice, paten, or any sacred vessel consecrated and devoted to divine worship to other uses.

(Capitularies of Theodulf, chap. 18.) Whoever drinks anything other than Christ’s blood—which is received in the sacrament—from a consecrated chalice, or uses a paten for any purpose other than the ministry of the altar, must be deterred by the example of Belshazzar, who, when he took the Lord’s vessels for common uses, lost his life together with his kingdom. We also decree that they prepare clean linen cloths for the altars with the utmost care, and strive to have the priestly vestments in which the sacrifice is offered as fine and clean as their means permit; whether new or worn out with age, they must in no way allow them to pass into other uses.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the Eucharist.

(Lib. I Capitular., chap. 155; Capitularies of Theodulf, [Col. 0707A] chap. 5.) Priests must always have the Eucharist prepared, so that whenever someone falls ill, or a sick child is present, they may communicate them immediately, lest they die without Communion. The loaves that you offer in the sacrifice must be made, either by yourselves or by ministers of yours who are fit for this task, cleanly and carefully in your presence. It must be diligently observed that the bread, wine, and water—without which Mass cannot be celebrated—are handled with the greatest cleanliness and care, and that nothing base or blameworthy is found in them. The consecrated elements must be collected with great care by those who are worthy and preserved honorably.

(Lib. I Capitular., chap. 67.) We urgently admonish everyone to take care that they are not kept for too long, lest they appear rotten and unseemly, [Col. 0707B] but that they be kept in a thoroughly clean vessel only until they are replaced by other consecrated elements.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the life and conduct of priests.

(Capitularies of Theodulf, chap. 2.) Priests of God ought to devote themselves continually to reading and earnestly to prayer, because the life of a righteous man is instructed by reading, adorned by prayer, and fortified by constant reading, in accordance with the one who said: “I have hidden your words in my heart, so that I may not sin against you.” These are the weapons—namely, reading and prayer—by which the devil is defeated. These are the instruments by which blessedness is attained.

(Ibid., chap. 3.) By these weapons vices are restrained; by these forms of nourishment virtues are nurtured. And whenever reading or prayer ceases, [Col. 0707C] manual labor should follow, because idleness is hostile to the soul, and the ancient enemy, when he finds someone free from reading, prayer, and work, easily drags him down to the depths. Therefore Christ’s priest ought to shine before all through disciplined conduct, a cheerful countenance, profitable speech, a wholesome example, a peaceful spirit, and freedom from deceit and pretense, as well as through every virtue in common, so that he does not drag those entrusted to him to ruin through the zeal of envy and bitterness, but calls them to salvation through the care of charity and gentleness.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the teaching and observance required of priests.

(Lib. I Capitular., chap. 66.) Priests, who ought to be useful both to themselves and to others, must strive above all to hold correct doctrine; observe Catholic baptism; understand well the prayers of the Mass; keep the canonical hours, by day and by night; and chant the psalms properly according to the divisions of the verses. They must themselves know the Lord’s Prayer, the Creed, and their explanation, and preach them to everyone in an intelligible manner, so that each person may know what he is asking from God. In this way many may be drawn to God’s service by their teaching and example, as the Lord himself commanded in the Gospel: “Let your light so shine before human beings that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

## CHAPTER IX. [Col. 0708A] That lay elders of churches must not, on any pretext, have occasion to live with women and dogs in priests’ houses.

We admonish all lay elders of churches in common that they must not presume under any circumstances to live in priests’ houses—which ought to be clean, chaste, and religious—with their wives, other women, or dogs. For it is unlawful that a man commanded to serve God alone should become entangled in wanton speech and unnecessary disturbances, and should corrupt the boundaries fixed for the duties entrusted to him: psalm-singing, keeping vigils, prayer, and, when necessity arises, baptizing and assisting the sick and the dying.

We forbid this sacrilege henceforth, lest God’s ministers be harmed by secular oppression [Col. 0708B] and Christ’s flock, purchased at so precious a price, be condemned to eternal death through pastoral negligence. If anything of this kind should henceforth occur, let it quickly come to our attention, so that by divine authority the transgressors may be brought to correction, even against their will.

## CHAPTER X. The order in which priests are to celebrate Mass.

(Capitularies of Theodulf, chap. 7.) A priest must never celebrate Mass alone, because just as it cannot be celebrated without the priest’s greeting, the people’s response, the priest’s admonition, and likewise the people’s response, so it must certainly not be celebrated by one person alone. There must be two or three people standing around him, whom he can greet and who can answer him. [Col. 0708C]

No layman, nor any cleric who has not first received the office of subdeacon, may presume to read the Epistle. For just as priests are commanded to celebrate Mass and deacons to read the Gospel, so subdeacons are known to proclaim the Epistle during the sacred solemnities of Mass. If a subdeacon is absent, however, it should be read either by a deacon or by the priest himself, so that the sacred ministry is not disparaged but God is honored in all things.

(Ibid., chap. 6.) While a priest is celebrating Mass, women must in no way approach the altar or touch the sacred vessels, but must stand in their own places. Women ought to remember their weakness and the frailty of their sex. For this reason they should fear to touch anything sacred in the ministry of the church. Laymen too ought to fear doing so, lest they suffer the punishment of Uzzah, who, when he wished to support the Lord’s ark outside the proper [order—sic], died when the Lord struck him.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning hospitality.

(Ibid., chap. 15.) Priests must be admonished to love hospitality themselves and to encourage others to love it, and to refuse lodging to no one. If they happen to provide lodging for someone, they must accept no gift from him, unless the guest freely gives something of his own accord.
