They should also be told how many people pleased God through the practice of hospitality, as the Apostle says: “For by this some pleased God, receiving angels as guests.” And again: “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.” The Lord himself will say at the judgment: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me.” Let all who love hospitality know that they receive Christ in their guests.

The hungry must therefore be fed, the thirsty given drink, the naked clothed, the sick and those in prison visited, and guests welcomed, as the Lord says: “For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink,” and so forth. Each person ought to perform all these acts spiritually in himself and fulfill them bodily toward others.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the observance of councils.

According to the decrees of the ancient Fathers, all priests established throughout the parishes are commanded to come to the council, so that there the bishop may examine the affairs of every question, approve what is useful, and correct canonically whatever is useless or unlawful. Therefore we admonish everyone not to neglect observing these salutary instructions, but to make every effort to attend the synod without exception or excuse, so that, once unanimity has been preserved, the destructive dissensions of all disputes may be removed. If anyone attempts to oppose these regulations, and, despising synodal rights, delays hastening to our council and to that of our ministers, unless he produces a just reason for his excuse, he will experience the penalty of canonical excommunication.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the preaching of priests.

[Col. 0709C] (Capitularies of Theodulf, chap. 28.) We urge you to be ready to teach the people. Whoever knows the Scriptures should preach the Scriptures. Whoever does not know Scripture should at least say to the people what is most widely known: that they turn away from evil and do good, seek peace and pursue it, because “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are attentive to their prayers; but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to cut off their memory from the earth.” No one, therefore, will be able to excuse himself by saying that he has no tongue with which he can edify anyone. As soon as he sees anyone going astray, he should, according to his ability and strength, draw him away from error—by reproving, pleading, or rebuking—and urge him to carry out a good work.

The method of preaching is as follows.

(Ibid., chap. 21.) First, love the Lord God with all one’s heart, all one’s soul, and all one’s strength; then love one’s neighbor as oneself. Next: do not kill; do not commit adultery; do not steal; do not covet; do not bear false witness; honor all people; and whatever one does not want done to oneself, let one not do to another. Renounce oneself in order to follow Christ; discipline the body; do not love luxuries; love fasting; refresh the poor; clothe the naked; receive guests; visit the sick; bury the dead; assist those in tribulation; console the sorrowful; make oneself a stranger to the affairs of the world; put nothing before the love of Christ; do not give full effect to anger; do not reserve time for wrath; do not retain deceit in the heart; do not offer false peace; do not abandon charity; [Col. 0710A] do not swear, lest one commit perjury; speak the truth from heart and mouth; do not repay evil with evil; do not inflict injury, but patiently endure injury done to oneself; love enemies for God’s sake; do not curse back those who curse, but rather bless them; endure persecution for righteousness; do not be proud, drunk, excessively greedy, sleepy, lazy, given to murmuring, slanderous, or quarrelsome; place one’s hope in God.

When one sees something good in oneself, let one attribute it to God, not to oneself. But let one recognize the evil one has done and reckon it to oneself. Fear the day of judgment; dread hell; desire eternal life with every spiritual longing; regard death daily as standing before one’s eyes; guard the actions of one’s life at every hour; know for certain that God observes one in every place; cast away evil thoughts that arise in the heart; guard one’s mouth from evil or corrupt speech; do not love speaking much, because, according to Scripture, “In much speaking sin will not be absent”; do not speak empty words or words suited to laughter; do not love excessive laughter; willingly listen to holy readings; frequently devote oneself to prayer; confess past evils to God daily in prayer with tears and groaning; amend those evils thereafter; do not fulfill the desires of the flesh; hate one’s own will; obey the priest’s commands in all things, even if he himself—God forbid—acts otherwise than he ought, remembering the Lord’s command: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do.”

Fulfill God’s commandments daily through one’s actions; love chastity; do not harbor zeal or envy; do not love contention; venerate elders; love the younger; make peace with those who are at odds before sunset; and never despair of God’s mercy. These are the spiritual instruments. When they have been fulfilled by us ceaselessly, day and night, and presented again on the day of judgment, the reward that the Lord himself promised will be repaid: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him.”

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning priests who come on Maundy Thursday for chrism, so that each may carry three flasks.

(Lib. I Capitular., chaps. 93 and 156, and lib. V, chap. 145. [Col. 0710D] See the notes on the passages cited.) Concerning the priests who customarily come to the cities on Maundy Thursday to receive chrism, we decree that one be chosen from every ten to carry the chrism he has received carefully to his companions. Those who live no farther than six or seven miles from the city must come in person to receive the chrism.

All of them must carry three flasks with them: one for chrism, another for oil for catechumens, and a third for oil used to anoint the sick. In accordance with the teaching of blessed the Apostle James, to which the decrees of the Fathers also agree, the sick must be anointed by priests with oil blessed by bishops. For he says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing [Col. 0711A] him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him.”

This kind of medicine, which heals the ailments of body and soul, must not therefore be treated as insignificant. Priests must keep the chrism under seal, so that they do not presume to give it to anyone under the pretext of medicine or any kind of sorcery. If they do so, they must be deprived of their rank.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning parishioners, another priest’s parish, and another’s clergy.

(Capitularies of Theodulf, chap. 14; lib. VII Capitular., chap. 198, and lib. I, chaps. 147–148.) No priest may persuade another’s parishioner to attend his own church, abandoning his own church, nor receive him at Mass unless he is traveling, has a legal hearing there, or some other legitimate reason has intervened. No priest may presume to sing Mass in another’s church unless he is traveling or has been ordered to do so by the person to whom that church belongs.

He must not dare to receive tithes owed to another. Each priest should be content with his own church and people and should in no way do to another what he does not want done to himself, according to the Gospel saying: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them.”

We also prohibit in every way that any priest solicit or receive another’s cleric, because the sacred canons impose a severe judgment in this matter. Whoever violates these statutes or attempts to resist these admonitions of ours must know that he will either lose his rank or be held for a long time in the hardship of prison.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning women not to be received by priests.

(Capitularies of Theodulf, chap. 12.) No woman may live in a priest’s house. Although the canons permit a mother, sister, and similar persons, in whose case there is no suspicion, to live with him, we abolish this entirely for every reason, because other women not related to him come in their service or on their account and entice him into sin. Occasions of sin must be cut off, and all suspicions removed by which the devil’s cunning, under the pretext of charity and affection, is accustomed to ensnare unwary and uninstructed souls.

[Col. 0711D] Therefore, to safeguard their lives and reputation, we command by a special regulation that no priest associate himself with an unrelated woman through any conversation or familiarity. Not only must the woman not enter his house, but he himself must not have permission to frequent a woman’s house, nor may he admit a maidservant, freedwoman, or any woman whatsoever into a storeroom or private place.

If, after a first and second admonition, any priest suspected of the crime of fornication with a particular woman is found conversing with her or associating with her in any way, he must know that he is to be removed from the honor of the priesthood and from his office, with absolutely no hope of restoration left to him.

## CHAPTER XVII. [Col. 0712A] That no priest may dare to seize another’s church.

(Ibid., chap. 16; lib. VII Capitular., chap. 206, and lib. I, chap. 150.) If any priest is found to be giving or to have given gifts to a cleric or layman, or attempting openly or secretly by any sort of collusion, fraud, or deceit to seize another priest’s church, he must know that, because of this robbery and savage greed, he will either lose his rank or be detained for a long time in the misery of prison, doing penance.

We also decree that no priest may presume to give gifts in exchange for a church he has received. And in accordance with the decrees of the canons and of the most glorious Charles and Louis, we decree that each priest must leave to his own church the property he acquires after the day of his ordination.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That no fees may be demanded for baptizing or burying the faithful, for assigning penance, or for administering sacraments in the church.

(Lib. V Capitular., chap. 172, and lib. VI, chaps. 106 and 183; Capitula of Charles the Bald, title VII, chap. 2; St. Gregory, lib. VII, indiction 2, epistle 55.) We have heard that certain priests, moved by an evil impulse, have accepted unjust fees from some people for baptism or for a place of burial. We know that this most abominable crime is prohibited in all the institutions of our predecessors. For it is given freely, and it is commanded to be given freely.

Therefore, henceforth they must not presume to demand any fee for baptizing or burying people, since these things are given freely. Rather, at the appointed times they should freely baptize those whom bodily health permits to approach salvation. If people are at the point of death, they must admit them to the baptism of regeneration without any delay and without any payment.

When they have departed this life, the priests must carefully carry them to the grave with psalms and hymns, demanding no fee for this, unless the deceased, their relatives, or their almsgivers freely offer something. Likewise, concerning the assigning of penance and the administration of a sacrament in the church, ecclesiastical authority forbids absolutely the demanding of any gift.

Those seeking penance must be aided promptly. Those who swear must be admonished so that they do not fall into perjury. Sinners must be invited with every diligence to return to penance. [Col. 0712D] Those who swear must be persuaded by every means not to incur guilt.

For often some people, deterred by poverty, delay baptism and allow their children to die without the grace of baptism. Others, fearing the price of an oath illicitly demanded from them by priests, do not fear committing perjury. If any priest is found to have committed these prohibited acts, or, rather, does not promptly correct them of his own accord once committed, he will be subjected to the irreversible danger of losing his own honor.

## CHAPTER XIX. From which unlawful practices priests must chiefly abstain.

(Capitularies of Theodulf, chap. 13; lib. V Capitular., [Col. 0713A] chap. 325.) Priests must take care to abstain from drunkenness, because according to Scripture drunkenness excuses no vice. The Apostle also warns, saying: “Do not get drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery.”

They must not go about drinking or eating in taverns, nor wander through houses or estates out of any sort of curiosity, nor hold banquets with women or with any impure persons, nor devote themselves to feasting and the other plagues associated with gluttony. They must not go to the forum or marketplace under any circumstances, nor attend a secular court, unless perhaps to assist the poor or admonish judges from God’s word to judge justly. If their own case must be pursued, they should go with the bishop’s permission and with an advocate.

We prohibit in every way that priests become stewards or tenants of their lords, write documents, attend weddings, take up weapons, or act as guarantors. We admonish them to flee bodily pleasures, secular business, the empty delights of this world, immodest banquets, vain spectacles, the deadly pageantry of this age, obscene words of joking, useless laughter, hunting with birds or dogs, usury, illicit commerce, unjust weights, secular lawsuits, unjust gifts, every mortal sin, and anything similar.

For according to the Apostle, “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business, so that he may please the one to whom he has offered himself.” Therefore, as soldiers of Christ, they must piously and justly care for and govern the others who belong to the Church of Christ, by doing good and preaching according to the Lord’s saying: “Let your light so shine before human beings that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

## CHAPTER XX. That baptism is to be celebrated on appointed days and in the villages, and concerning the baptism of the sick.

The ancient Fathers decreed that baptism be celebrated at fixed times—namely, Easter and Pentecost. At other times canonical authority forbids anyone to be baptized, except one whom the greatest necessity compels because he is in danger of death.

At these two times, Easter and Pentecost, all priests must come from their cells to the villages. After completing the office there, they must baptize all who are to be baptized with the greatest care. They must then return to their own churches with those whom they have baptized and with their other dependents and celebrate the solemnities of Mass. All the baptized, and those who received them from the baptismal font, must all receive Communion. As long as they remain in white garments, their sponsors must lead them daily to the church with lights, and all must strive equally to receive the body and blood of Christ until the eighth day.

If a sick child is brought to any priest, at any time or hour, from any parish for the sake of baptism, the sacrament of baptism must in no way be denied to the child. If anyone refuses to grant this gift to one who requests it, and that child dies without the grace of baptism, [Col. 0714A] the one who did not baptize the child must know that he will have to render an account for the child’s soul.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning tithes to be given by the faithful.

We admonish that tithes from all possessions, according to the measure established by the blessed Fathers, are to be rendered with complete devotion by the entire people to the churches of God. Thus priests, who through their holy prayers and offerings implore the mercy of almighty God for peace, for the salvation of the entire Christian people, for the fruits of the earth, and also for the sick and the dead, may have food, clothing, and the other necessities they require, and may be able to provide help to guests and pilgrims, orphans and widows, the weak and the sick.

(Second Council of Chalon, chap. 19; Capitula excerpted from the Law of the Lombards, chap. 41.) Moreover, there are some who neglect to give their tithes to their own churches, where they themselves and their servants hear Mass. We have therefore decreed that everyone give tithes where their children are baptized, where they hear Mass, and where the possessions themselves appear to belong, according to the decree of their own bishop.

Priests must never accept pledges from those who do not give tithes. Those who, after repeated admonitions and sermons, neglect to give them must be excommunicated. We do not wish to compel them by oath, because of the danger of perjury.

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed, and spiritual fathers and children.

(Lib. II Capitular., chap. 46, and lib. VI, chap. 182.)

The faithful must be instructed so that everyone, from the least to the greatest, learns the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed. They must be told that the entire foundation of the Christian faith rests upon these two statements. Unless someone both retains these two statements by heart, believes them with all his heart, and repeats them very frequently in prayer, he cannot be Catholic.

It has been established that no one may be anointed with chrism, baptized, receive another from the baptismal font, or hold anyone before the bishop for confirmation unless he knows the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer by heart, except those whom age has not yet brought to the ability to speak.

[Col. 0714D] Sponsors must strive above all to instruct those whom they receive from the font of baptism, and teach them the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed, because they have given birth to them for the Lord and stand surety for them. Those who are undergoing public penance or are held liable for a criminal sin must not presume to receive anyone from the baptismal font or hold anyone before the bishop for confirmation until, having completed their penance, they have deserved to receive an appropriate satisfaction.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning the honor due to parents, and the admonition of masters regarding their subjects.

(Lib. I Capitular., chap. 65; lib. II, chaps. 41 and 44.) [Col. 0715A] The faithful of God’s holy Church must be admonished to teach their sons and daughters to show obedience to their parents, as the Lord says: “Son, honor your father and your mother.” Parents themselves must also act with restraint toward their sons and daughters, as the Apostle says: “And you, parents, do not provoke your children to anger.”

They must also be told that if, through such affection, they wish to spare their children’s offenses, the Lord does not allow them to do so with impunity, unless perhaps they offer themselves as worthy of penance. For it is lighter for children to endure whatever blows their parents inflict than to incur God’s anger.

Masters must also be admonished to act piously and mercifully toward their subjects: they must not condemn them on any unjust pretext, oppress them, or unjustly take away their small possessions; [Col. 0715B] nor must they impiously or cruelly exact the very dues that subjects are required to render.

Since it is evident that people of different conditions exist in the Church—nobles and non-nobles, slaves, tenants, dependents, and other such categories—it is necessary that all who rule over them, whether clerics or laymen, act toward them gently and treat them mercifully, whether in exacting labor from them or in receiving taxes or other dues. They must know that these people are their brothers, that they have one Father, God, with them, to whom they cry, “Our Father, who are in heaven,” and one holy mother, the Church, which gives them birth from the undefiled womb of the sacred font.

They must therefore be given the most merciful discipline and suitable governance: discipline, so that by living disorderly lives they do not offend their creator; governance, [Col. 0715C] so that, deprived of the assistance of their rulers in the daily necessities of life, they do not waste away.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That there is no partiality before God.

(Second Council of Chalon, chap. 34.) Since, as the Apostle testifies, there is no partiality before God, and partiality must be avoided in every judgment, it must be guarded against all the more in this judgment of penance, so that no priest ever judges differently out of favor toward or hatred of any person than what he finds in the sacred canons, or than what appears more correct to him according to the authority of the holy Scriptures and ecclesiastical custom.

If physicians who attempt to apply medicine to bodies do not, out of regard for any person, spare those whom they wish to heal the cautery, the knife, or any other harsh treatment, how much more must this be observed by those who are physicians not of bodies but of souls. Penance must not be assessed by the length of time, but by fervor of mind and mortification of the body. “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise.”

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning those who are at odds.

(Fourth Supplement to the Capitularies, chap. 50.) The offerings of brothers who are at odds must not be received either in the sacristy or in the treasury. It has also been decided that, as often happens, those who have separated from one another through hatred or a long-standing dispute and have refused for a prolonged period to return to peace must be expelled from the assembly of the Church by the most just excommunication until they hasten to return to charity, which covers a multitude of sins. [Note: [Col. 0715D] See the Notes on Regino, p. 550.]

## CHAPTER XXVI. How the Lord’s Day is to be observed.

(Lib. I Capitular., chap. 75; lib. VI, chap. 380, and lib. VII, chap. 276.) The apostles therefore sanctioned Sunday with religious solemnity because on that day our Redeemer rose from the dead. It is called “the Lord’s Day” so that on it, abstaining from earthly works and the enticements of the world, we may serve only divine worship. For just as the Lord Jesus Christ himself and our Savior rose from the dead on the third day, so we hope that we too shall rise at the end of the age. Hence, on Sunday we also pray standing, which is a sign of the future resurrection. The whole Church, which exists in the pilgrimage of mortality, does this, awaiting at the end of the age what was prefigured in the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the firstborn from the dead.

Sunday began to be celebrated by Christians after the Lord’s resurrection, and from that time it began to have its own festivity. The observance of this day must therefore be so strict that, apart from prayers, the solemn celebration of Mass, and what pertains to eating, nothing else should be done. That is, no servile work should be performed on it; men should neither engage in rural labor, cultivate vineyards, plow fields, reap the harvest, cut hay, erect fences, clear forests, cut down trees, work in stone quarries, build houses, make gardens, move earth, assemble for legal hearings, nor go hunting, except only because of the necessity of food or cold.

Likewise, women should not perform textile work, cut garments [the reading *capulent* is uncertain], sew, wash clothing, bleach it, beat flax, presume to card wool, or shear sheep, so that in every respect the rest of good people may be observed on Sunday.

For this is the first day of the age. On it the elements of the world were formed; on it the angels were created; on it manna was given from heaven; on it the Redeemer of the human race rose from the dead; on it the Holy Spirit descended upon the disciples.

On Saturday, people should assemble at the church with lights; they should assemble for vigils or for the morning office; and they should also come with offerings to the solemn celebration of Mass. When they assemble, there should be no quarrels; rather, the whole day should be devoted solely to God. They should not feast in gluttony and drunkenness, or in debauchery and joking speech, but should feast spiritually in the praises of God and in almsgiving with friends, neighbors, and strangers.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the feast days of the year

(Lib. II Capitular., chap. 35; Regino, lib. I, chap. 377.) We have decreed that the feast days of the year be celebrated: namely, that the Lord’s Day of Easter be venerated with all honor and sobriety; likewise, we have decreed that the whole of that week be observed; and that the day of the Lord’s Ascension be celebrated fully. Pentecost is to be observed in the same manner as Easter; likewise the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; the feast of Peter and Paul as one day; Saint Lawrence’s day; the Assumption of Saint Mary; the dedication of Saint Michael; and the feast days of Saint Martin, Saint Andrew, and all the apostles.

At the Nativity of the Lord, four days are to be observed; likewise the Lord’s octave, Epiphany, the Purification of Saint Mary, and the feast days of Saint Ursicinus, Saint Austregisilus, and Saint Sulpitius. We have also decreed that the feasts of those saints whose holy bodies rest in each parish, or whose relics are venerated there, be observed. On the days mentioned above, we have declared that people must rest from work. We judge that the other feasts of the holy apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins should be celebrated with appropriate honor.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How the faithful should offer and receive Communion at the solemn celebrations of Mass

Our Lord and Teacher, Christ, first instituted the sacrifice that Christians offer to God when, before he was handed over, he entrusted his body and blood to the apostles. Thus we read: “Jesus took bread and the cup and, blessing them, gave them to them.”

Some say that, unless some sin intervenes, the Eucharist should be received daily. (Regino, lib. I, chap. 194.) For we ask for this bread to be given to us daily, as the Lord commands, saying: “Give us this day our daily bread.” They speak rightly, provided that they receive it with religion, devotion, and humility, and do not do so through proud presumption, trusting in their own righteousness.

But if their sins are such that they should be removed from the altar as though dead, penance must first be performed. Thereafter, when this saving medicine is to be received, a person must, according to the Apostle, examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink from the cup. (Lib. II Capitular., chap. 40.)

If it is received indiscriminately, however, one must fear what the same Apostle says: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.” To receive it unworthily means to receive it at a time when one ought to be doing penance.

But if the sins are not so great that a person should be judged worthy of excommunication, he should not separate himself from the medicine of the Lord’s body, lest, while it is excessively delayed, it become harmful to the soul, the Lord saying: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves.”

Married people should abstain from sexual intercourse for several days and devote themselves to prayer, so that, purified, they may be able to approach so great a sacrament. Let them read the books of the kings, and they will find that the priest Abimelech was unwilling to give David and his men the bread of the Presence before asking whether the men were clean from women—not, of course, from foreign women, but from their own wives—and unless he had heard that they had abstained from marital relations from yesterday and the day before, he would never have allowed them to eat the holy loaves.

Therefore, certain days should be selected during which a person first lives with greater continence, so that he may be worthy to approach so great a sacrament. Likewise, those who offer bread and wine to the priests at the solemn celebration of Mass should abstain from their wives for some time. Afterwards, having washed with water and cleansed their clothing, they should offer offerings to God for their own errors and those of their families, and, if they wish, receive Communion. Those who are denied the cost of the sacrifice are not granted the opportunity to make an offering.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Lenten fast

[Col. 0718B] (Capitulare of Theodulf, chap. 37, 41, 43.) The days of Lent must be guarded with the utmost observance, so that the fast may in no way be broken during them, except on Sundays, which have been exempted from abstinence; for these days are the tenths of our year, and we must pass them with complete religious devotion and holiness.

There must be no occasion for relaxing the fast during these days, since at other times the fast is customarily relaxed for the sake of charity. During this period it must never be relaxed. To fast at another time is to gain a reward; during this period, however, anyone who does not fast, apart from the sick and children, acquires punishment for himself, because the Lord consecrated these same days by sacred fasting through Moses, Elijah, and himself.

During these most holy days one must abstain from one’s spouse, because a fast that is polluted by marital relations is almost worthless. Therefore, all the faithful should receive the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood on each Sunday of Lent, except those who have been excommunicated for a mortal crime. They must also receive Communion fully on Maundy Thursday, Good Friday, the vigil of Easter, and the day of the Lord’s Resurrection. All the days of Easter week must likewise be honored with equal religious devotion.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the other established fasts

(Lib. V Capitular., chap. 151.) Concerning the observance of fasting during the four seasons of the year, when twelve readings are read on Saturday, the holy Fathers established that in the first month it should take place in the first week; in June, in the second week; in September, in the third week; and in December, in the fourth week. For three days—namely, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday—everyone, except infants and the sick, should fast until the ninth hour and abstain from meat.

The same rule applies to the days of the Rogations: one must fast and abstain from meat for three days. Fasts imposed by priests are not to be broken without reasonable necessity. (Capitulare of Theodulf, chap. 38.) On days of fasting, almsgiving must therefore be practiced, and the food and drink that a person would have consumed, had he not been fasting, should be distributed to the poor. For to fast while reserving the foods of the midday meal for supper is an increase of food, not a reward.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the observances of the fasts

(Capitulare of Theodulf, chap. 40; Capitularies of Charles the Bald, title 38, chap. 8; Capitulare of Theodulf, chap. 42.) Abstinence during the days of fasting should extend to almost all delicacies, and one should live soberly and chastely, so that these holy days may be spent with heart and body sanctified.

The ministers of public affairs must also be warned that, from the Wednesday before the beginning of Lent—not even on that Wednesday—until after the octave of Easter, they must not presume to hold a public assembly or court, except for the reconciliation and pacification of those at odds.

Likewise, from the Wednesday before the Nativity of the Lord until after the consecrated days, and also during the fasts of the four seasons, the Rogations, and the other established fasts, they must strive in every way to honor those days of rest with the same observance.

On these days of fasting there should be no lawsuits and no quarrels; rather, one must persist in the praises of God and in necessary work. For through the prophet the Lord rebukes those who pursue quarrels and lawsuits during the time of fasting, and those who demand debts from debtors, saying: “Behold, on the day of your fast your own desires are found, and you pursue all your debtors. Behold, you fast for lawsuits and quarrels, and you strike wickedly with the fist.”

## CHAPTER XXXII. On penance to be given to the faithful

(Capitulare of Theodulf, chap. 36, 31.) One week before the beginning of Lent, confessions must be made to priests, penance must be undertaken, those at odds must be reconciled, and all quarrels must be settled. They must also forgive debts to one another from their hearts, so that they may say more freely: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

Thus, entering the season of blessed Lent with minds cleansed and purified, they may approach holy Easter and renew themselves through penance, which is a second baptism.

Confessions must be made of all sins committed either in deed or in thought. There are eight principal vices, without which scarcely anyone can be found. The first is *gastrimargia*, that is, gluttony of the belly; the second is fornication; the third *accidia*, or sadness; the fourth avarice; the fifth vainglory; the sixth envy; the seventh anger; and the eighth pride.

When someone therefore comes to confession, it must be carefully investigated how and on what occasion he committed the sin he confesses to have committed, and penance must be assigned to him according to the nature of the deed. He should be persuaded to confess his corrupt thoughts. He must also be instructed to confess the eight principal vices. The priest must name each vice to him individually and receive his confession concerning it.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the forms and remedies of penance

(Council of Chalon II, chap. 38.) The measure of penance imposed upon those confessing their sins must be determined either by the ordinances of the ancient canons, the authority of the holy Scriptures, or ecclesiastical custom, while the books called penitentials are rejected and entirely eliminated. They contain definite errors and uncertain authors, of which it may rightly be said: “They put to death souls that did not die, and they gave life to souls that did not live.”

For when, for grave sins, they impose certain light and unusual forms of penance, they sew cushions, according to the prophetic saying, “under every elbow of the hand,” and make pillows under the head of people of every age in order to capture souls.

For just as baptism cleanses sins, so does penance. Holy Scripture demonstrates that sins are forgiven in seven ways:

1. First, in baptism.
2. Second, through martyrdom.
3. Third, through almsgiving, according to the Gospel saying: “Nevertheless, give alms, and everything is clean for you.”
4. Fourth, when someone forgives the sins of one who has sinned against him, according to the saying: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven.”
5. Fifth, when someone converts others from their error through preaching and the practice of good works, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death.”
6. Sixth, through charity, according to the saying: “The charity of the Lord covers a multitude of sins.”
7. Seventh, through penance, according to what David says: “I turned in sorrow while the thorn was being fixed.”

Through these seven means, therefore, both forgiveness is granted and the reward of eternal recompense is acquired.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On public penance

(Council of Chalon II, chap. 25.) In many places, the practice of performing penance according to the ancient ordinance of the canons has fallen out of use, and the ancient order of excommunicating and reconciling is no longer observed. Therefore, whoever sins publicly must be punished with public penance and, according to the measure of his offense, excommunicated and reconciled in accordance with the canonical order.

For it is not lawful for priests to impose public penance. Those who sin publicly must, according to the decrees of the ancient canons, strive through the episcopal ministry to appease God with public satisfaction.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On interest and usury

Priests and all the faithful generally ought, whenever they gather and store up crops or certain revenues of the land, not to do so in order to sell them more dearly and accumulate treasures, but to assist the poor in a time of need. Nor should they lend anything at interest, since the Lord himself forbade everyone in the Law to lend anything at interest.

(Lib. I Capitular., chaps. 119, 124, 125.) Usury exists wherever more is demanded than is given. For example, if you give ten solidi and demand more, or if you give measures of grain or wine and later, on any pretext or in any manner, demand something additional.

Whoever, at harvest time or vintage time, buys grain or wine not out of necessity but from greed, and stores it until he can sell it more dearly, we call this shameful profit.

A person practices *fenus* when he lends something. A just lender, however, is one who demands no more than he lends.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On perjury and false testimony

(Capitulare of Theodulf, chaps. 26, 27.) It must be preached that the faithful beware of perjury and abstain from it with the utmost care, knowing that it is a great crime prohibited both in the Law and the Prophets and in the Gospel.

For we have heard that some regard this crime as trivial and impose on perjurers a light form of penance. They should know that penance for perjury must be imposed in the same manner as for adultery, fornication, homicide, and the other criminal vices. For in the Law, at the Lord’s command, we have this: “You shall not swear falsely by my name, nor profane the name of your God,” and, “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.”

They must also be told to abstain from false testimony, knowing that this too is a most serious crime and was prohibited by the Lord himself on Mount Sinai, when the same Lord said: “You shall not give false testimony,” or, “A false witness shall not go unpunished.”

Anyone who commits this must know that he is to be cleansed by such penance as was stated above concerning perjury. They must also be told that it is the height not merely of folly but of wickedness, for greed for gold and silver, clothing, or any other thing—or, as happens very frequently, because of drunkenness—to fall into so great a crime that one must either spend seven years in severe misery or be expelled from the Church. The Lord says: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” For while he may appear merciful toward others, he is cruel toward himself.

If anyone, after committing perjury, giving false testimony, or any other criminal sin, refuses to come to confession because he fears the long misery of penance, he must be expelled from the Church—that is, from Communion and the fellowship of the faithful—so that no one may eat or drink with him, pray with him, or receive him into his house.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On perjury, theft, and robbery

Whoever knowingly commits perjury must submit himself to seven years of penance and thereafter return to Communion.

Whoever, overcome by greed, commits theft must return what he has taken and perform penance for five years. Likewise, whoever unjustly takes another person’s property by robbery must restore what he has illicitly extorted by force and cleanse his guilt through the fasts of penance for the same number of years, namely five.

But if he does not know whom he has injured, or is unable to return what he has violently stolen, he must submit himself to more severe penance and, after seven years, attain full perfection once legitimate penance has been performed.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the observance of vanities

[Note: [Col. 0721D] See the notes on *Capitularia*, 1038.] Whoever among the faithful observes omens, auspices, dreams, or any sort of divination in the manner of the pagans, or the lots which they falsely claim to be those of the saints; and whoever, whether cleric or layman, is discovered either consulting or teaching such things; or whoever brings such people into his house to inquire into anything by magical art, or purifies his house by such means, shall be held outside the Church for five years, performing penance according to the ancient rules established.

For Christians are not permitted to observe or worship the traditions of the pagans, or the elements, or the moons, or the courses of the stars, or the empty deception of signs, whether for building a house, sowing a field, planting trees, or arranging marriages. For it is written: “Whatever you do, do everything in the name of the Lord.”

Nor is it permitted, when gathering herbs, to pay attention to any observances or incantations, except only together with the divine Creed and the Lord’s Prayer.

Likewise, Christian women are not permitted to observe vanity in their spinning and weaving, but should invoke God as their helper, who gave them the wisdom to weave, so that God may be honored in all things.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On homicides committed willingly and unwillingly

The holy Scriptures pronounce a severe judgment upon those who commit homicide voluntarily, the Apostle saying: “Whoever violates the temple of God, God will destroy him. For the temple of God is holy, and that is what you are.”

Whoever therefore voluntarily commits homicide must be expelled from the Church of God and separated from the fellowship of the faithful, in accordance with the canonical ordinances, where this is found written:

“Whoever voluntarily commits homicide must continually submit himself to penance, but he shall attain perfection toward the end of his life.”

And again:

“If anyone voluntarily commits homicide, let him always lie at the door of the Catholic Church, and let him receive Communion at the end of his life.”

But if homicide was committed not intentionally but by some accident, the earlier canon ordered seven years of penance, while the second commanded five years.

And elsewhere (Council of Ancyra, canons 22, 23): “Concerning homicides committed unintentionally, the first ruling indeed commanded that perfection be attained after seven years of penance. The second, however, ordered the completion of a five-year period.”

## CHAPTER XL. On homicides committed under various circumstances

If anyone kills his own slave, even one shown to be guilty of many crimes, without the knowledge of the judge, he shall atone for the guilt of bloodshed by excommunication or two years of penance.

But if a mistress, inflamed by the fury of jealousy, beats her maidservant with whips so that the maidservant gives up her life in torment within three days, and if it is uncertain whether she killed her intentionally or accidentally, it has been decreed that she abstain from Communion for seven years in the first case and for five years in the second.

If, however, she falls ill during the periods established, she shall receive Communion.

It has also been decreed that those who inflict death upon themselves, whether by sword, poison, throwing themselves from a height, hanging, or any other violent means, are not to be commemorated in the offering, nor are their bodies to be led to burial with psalms. The same has been decreed concerning those who are punished for their crimes.

## CHAPTER XLI. On women who kill their offspring and commit fornication with two brothers

(Council of Ancyra, chap. 21.) If a woman commits fornication and kills the infant born from it; or if she deliberately causes an abortion and kills what has been conceived; or if she strives not to conceive, whether from adultery or from a legitimate marriage, the earlier canons decreed that such women should not receive Communion even at death.

We, however, out of mercy, have judged that both such women and those who are aware of their actions should perform ten years of penance.

If a woman has relations with two brothers, or a man with two sisters, they must abstain from Communion until death; at the point of death, however, Communion is to be given to them out of mercy.

If they survive after receiving Communion and recover from their illness, they must perform full penance for the prescribed period, in accordance with the ancient ruling. We now define the matter more humanely, however, by granting them a period of ten years of penance, provided that throughout their entire lives they persist in weeping and humility.

## CHAPTER XLII. On adultery

(Council of Ancyra, chap. 20.) If someone’s wife has committed adultery, or if he himself has committed adultery, he must attain perfection through seven years of penance, according to the former stages.

If, while having a wife, he also keeps a concubine, he must not receive Communion until he abandons her and returns to penance.

But if a wife commits adultery with the knowledge of her husband, she must not receive Communion until the end of her life. If he leaves her, she shall receive Communion after ten years.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On those who commit unnatural fornication

(Council of Ancyra, chap. 16.) Concerning those who have acted, or do act, unnaturally—that is, those who have intercourse with animals or defile themselves with males—if anyone committed such a crime before the age of twenty, he may, after completing fifteen years of penance, merit Communion in prayer. After remaining in this communion for five years, he may finally receive the sacraments of the offering.

Their manner of life during the time of repentance must also be examined, and they are to obtain mercy accordingly.

Those who, after reaching the age of twenty, fall into this sin while having wives are to be received into the communion of prayer after performing twenty-five years of penance. After remaining in it for five years, they may finally receive the sacraments of the offering.

But if married men who have passed their fiftieth year commit such an offense, they shall receive the grace of Communion at the end of their lives.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the satisfaction and reconciliation of penitents

Satisfaction consists in excluding the causes and promptings of sins and not repeating the sin thereafter. Reconciliation is what is administered after the completion of penance.

For just as we are reconciled to God when we first turn from paganism through baptism, so we are reconciled when, after sinning, we return through penance.

When someone’s sins are public, the penance must likewise be public, for the periods which the bishop, according to his judgment, determines for penitents in proportion to the differences among their sins. Their reconciliation must be performed by the bishop, or by priests at the bishops’ command, as the canons of the African council testify. There it is written:

“Whenever a penitent’s crime is public and notorious and has disturbed the whole Church, hands are to be laid upon him before the apse.”

(Lib. V Capitular., chap. 137.) If a penitent falls into danger of death, he is to be reconciled by a priest with the bishop’s permission and strengthened by the grace of Communion, lest, bound by the rope of despair, he be dragged into eternal destruction.

Therefore, no member of the faithful is to be denied final penance, reconciliation, or reception of the body and blood of Christ.

But when sins are secret and have been revealed by spontaneous confession to the priest alone, the penance must also be secret, according to the judgment of the priest to whom the confession was made, lest the weak be scandalized in the Church when they see punishments whose causes they entirely do not know.

The decrees of Pope Innocent show at what time the reconciliation of penitents should take place. There it is written (letter to Decentius):

“Concerning penitents who perform penance either for more serious offenses or for lighter ones, if no illness intervenes, the custom of the Roman Church shows that they are to be released on the Thursday before Easter.”

For the rest, it belongs to the priest to judge the gravity of offenses, so that he may attend to the confession and to the penitent’s weeping and tears; he may then grant remission when he sees suitable satisfaction.

Certainly, if someone falls ill, he must be released before Easter, so that he does not depart from this world without Communion.

Above all, therefore, it must be guarded against that penance and reconciliation be denied to a penitent at the point of death, lest he perish in despair. The thief hanging on the right hand of Christ would have lost his reward if the penance of a single hour had not helped him.

True conversion to the Lord in those who are at the point of death must therefore be judged by the mind rather than by the length of time, as the prophet declares: “When you have turned and groaned, then you shall be saved.”

## CHAPTER XLV. On nocturnal emissions

(Saint Gregory, letter to Saint Augustine, chap. 11.) It must be asked whether, after the illusion that commonly occurs in a dream, anyone may receive the body and blood of the Lord, or whether a priest ought to celebrate the sacred mysteries.

The answer is that in the Old Testament a polluted person was not permitted to enter the church until he had first been washed with water, and then only after evening. The spiritual people understand this differently but within the same interpretation: a person is deceived as though in a dream when, tempted by vain images, he is defiled by impurity in thought.

He must therefore be washed with water, so that he may cleanse the sins of his thoughts with tears. Unless the fire of temptation has first departed, he must recognize himself as guilty until evening.

There must, however, be very careful discernment concerning this same illusion, which must subtly consider from what cause it arises in the mind of the sleeper. Sometimes it results from gluttony—that is, from excessive food or drink; sometimes from an excess or infirmity of nature; and sometimes from thought.

When it occurs from an excess or infirmity of nature, this illusion is in no way to be feared. The person who suffered it should cleanse himself and his clothing with water, then lawfully perform his ministry and approach the sacred mysteries with devotion.

But when the appetite of the palate is carried beyond measure in consuming food, and the receptacles of the humors are consequently burdened, the mind incurs some guilt from this—not, however, to the point of prohibition from receiving the sacred mystery or celebrating the solemnities of Mass, if perhaps a feast day requires it, or necessity compels the mystery to be offered because another priest is absent.

If others are present who can perform that office, the illusion caused by gluttony should not prohibit reception of the sacrament; nevertheless, in my judgment, the person should humbly abstain from offering the sacred mystery, provided that no shameful imagination has troubled the sleeper.

For there are people in whom such an illusion commonly arises without their minds, even while their bodies are asleep, being defiled by shameful imaginings.

But if the illusion arises from a shameful thought entertained while awake, the root of defilement pollutes the sleeping mind. For what he knowingly thought, he suffered unknowingly.

Such a person must not approach to receive or consecrate the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ until he has been cleansed through two or three days of penance and abstinence and washed with water; having received the Body in purity, he should hasten, free from defilement, to approach the service of so sacred a mystery.

## In the year of our Lord 867. Walter, Bishop of Orléans.

[Col. 0725]

## The Chapters of Walter

[Note: [Col. 0725C] The author of these chapters, Walter—also called Gualterus—Bishop of Orléans, sat as a judge with the others at our Council of Douzy and gave his judgment against Hincmar of Laon. He is subscribed there as “Walter, humble bishop of the people of Orléans,” and later at Pontigny as “Walter, humble bishop of the Church of Orléans.” From this we understand the excellent man’s modesty, and, proceeding from that modesty, the accumulation of his other virtues.

From this synod we possess material concerning pastoral concern and the observance of ecclesiastical discipline, material more substantial than anything transmitted to posterity by Hincmar himself or by Isaac of Langres, formerly a deacon of Pardulus, on the same subject. This is evident from these chapters, which, I hope, reader, you will not find unpleasant when joined or combined with the others.

We shall also add Theodulf, himself likewise of Orléans. His letter written to the clergy of his Church was transferred from Baronius’s edition into his *Ecclesiastical Annals* by Carolus Sausseius (*Ecclesiastical Annals of Orléans*, book VI), although Sirmond had not previously neglected it in its proper place (*vol. II of the Councils of Gaul*).

As for the date of the gathering of this diocesan synod and the promulgation of these chapters, we can state nothing certain, since the title lacks both the year of the Lord’s Incarnation and the indication of the indiction, which that age carefully recorded. “In the second year,” it says, “of his ordination.”

What shall we conjecture concerning the first? Agius, whom the very frequent councils of this period made famous, is not found subscribed beyond the Third Council of Soissons in the year 866. Anselm succeeded him on the see of Orléans. He is known only by name and is found in no council, not even that of Troyes in 867; how long he occupied the see is entirely obscure.

Those who assign him eight years in office and extend them to the year 876 of that century—and those who assign Walter to the year 885, if they intend this to refer to the beginning of his episcopate—go beyond the evidence. Both are plainly refuted by our Council of Douzy, at which Walter gave his judgment.

Therefore, if we wish to confine Anselm’s episcopate within proper limits in order to investigate the beginning of Walter’s, let us suppose that Anselm assumed the pontificate in the year 867 and must have ceased to hold it by at least 869, so that Walter could begin in 870 and sit in the Council of Douzy in the following year.

It is now easy to determine in what year of Christ these chapters were issued. The title says: “In the second year of his ordination.” Therefore, it was in the year 871, before the celebration of the Council of Douzy. Since that council was held in August, this allowed the Bishop of Orléans sufficient time, without difficulty, to convene a diocesan synod in May.

This is conjecture, until historical evidence gives us something more certain concerning the death of Anselm.]

Promulgated at the synod held at Bullense estate, in the second year of his ordination, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June.

[Col. 0725]

## CHAPTER I. How archdeacons should examine priests
(Hincmar, *Capitula issued to the deans*.) Let the archdeacons, throughout the parishes entrusted [Col. 0726C] to them, diligently [Note: [Col. 0726C] examine the faith of the presbyters. This chapter does not differ greatly from the first chapter likewise attributed to Hincmar; and, in general, what archdeacons ought to demand from presbyters and report to the bishop each year [Col. 0727C] when they go about visiting the parishes, Hincmar likewise covers in twenty articles (vol. III of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 623). He further wishes each person to commit to memory “the sermon of Athanasius on the faith, whose beginning is *Whoever wishes to be saved* [*Quicumque vult salvus esse*], and to understand its meaning and be able to state it in ordinary words.” Herard of Tours gives the same command in his capitula (Herard, chapter 16, vol. III of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 112), and wishes all these things to be kept in memory and sung publicly not only by presbyters but also by the people themselves. “Concerning the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed: let them know them by heart, as well as the *Glory be to the Father*, the *Holy*, and the *Credulity* [*Credulitas*], and let the *Kyrie eleison* be sung reverently by everyone. Likewise, let the psalms be sung distinctly by the clerics.” What that *Credulitas* is, if it is distinguished from the Apostles’ Creed, cannot, in my judgment, be anything other than the Athanasian Creed.]

Let them examine the faith, baptism, and celebration of Mass of the presbyters, to determine whether they hold the right faith; observe catholic baptism [Col. 0727A]; and understand the prayers of the Mass properly; let them sing the psalms worthily according to the divisions of the verses; [Note: [Col. 0727C] The Lord’s Prayer together with the Creed. That is, the Apostles’ Creed, not the one mentioned shortly afterward for recitation at Mass. Concerning this, the *Capitulary of Charlemagne* also commands (book VI, chapters 171–172) [Col. 0727D]: “Let presbyters announce the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer to all the faithful subject to them, so that, with the Holy Spirit illuminating them, they may be saved.” Soon afterward it adds that no one may receive infants from the sacred font unless he has “learned the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer by heart.” As for their explanation, which is to be handed on to the people, the same capitulary wishes “that there be no presbyter who does not publicly teach in church in a language.” See also the letter of Theodulf of Orléans, recommending all the same things.] and let them themselves understand the Lord’s Prayer together with the Creed and the catholic faith, and on weekdays let them explain them clearly to everyone for understanding [Col. 0728A], so that each person may know what he asks of the Lord. And let the *Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit*, [Note: [Col. 0727D] And let *I believe in one God* be sung by everyone at Mass. For it is fitting that, in order to celebrate and receive the mystery of faith, we prepare our minds by a public profession of faith. Thus Christ the Lord often summoned those asking for the benefit of healing to an exercise of faith, as can be seen in the Canaanite woman, the centurion, Lazarus’s sisters, and the father of the epileptic boy, who cried out, “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark IX). As for the recitation of the Creed, which the author of these capitula commands as something new and not yet established by universal custom, Walafrid Strabo nevertheless appears to recognize it as most ancient (*On Ecclesiastical Affairs*, chapter 22), and as having passed from the Greeks to the Romans and then to the Spaniards. Among the Gauls and Germans, however, in the time of Charlemagne, after the heresy of Felix of Urgel had been condemned throughout Spain, “the same Creed began to be repeated more fully and more frequently in the offices of the Mass.” It had therefore already been used earlier in at least some places, although more rarely.

Finally, the Constantinopolitan Greeks preferred the Creed of their own council to the Nicene Creed, both because it is more suitable for singing and “so that, against the poisons of heretics, the devotion of the faithful might celebrate even in the very celebration of the sacraments the remedies prepared at the see of the royal city.” Berno of Reichenau agrees with him concerning the singing of the Creed, but differs greatly concerning its date, when he relates (*On Certain Matters Pertaining to the Mass*, chapter 2)—without mentioning the Greeks—that in the time of Benedict III the Roman clergy were asked by the emperor Henry I why they refrained from reciting the Creed during the solemnities of Mass. They replied: “Because the Roman Church had never been infected with any filth of heresy, but, in accordance with the teaching of blessed Peter, had remained unshaken in the solidity of the catholic faith; and therefore it was more necessary for those who had at some time been stained by a heresy to repeat that Creed more frequently by singing it.” After hearing this, the emperor persisted and obtained from Pope Benedict that thereafter the Creed should be sung at the public Mass in Rome. This was done in the year of Christ 1014, when Henry was still recently crowned.

Thus, since from these authors we know the established reason for this custom—bringing immense glory to the Roman Church, the head and teacher of all the churches, which heretics try to obscure through Liberius and Honorius—the date of its institution, or rather of its most celebrated use in the Gallican Church, seems to be taken from the meeting of the legates with Pope Leo III, whom Charlemagne sent to Rome. Baronius reports this (*Annals*, under the year 809, vol. IX), the substance of whose account is as follows: Leo himself tolerated the authority to sing the Creed in Gaul, but not the addition in it of the word *Filioque*, which would create controversy. For this reason he advised: “Let the custom of singing that Creed gradually be discontinued in the palace, since it is not sung in our holy church; and thus what was done so that it might be sung—done not by any authority of the ruler, but rather because of the novelty of hearing it—if you abandon it, it will be abandoned by everyone.” The annals add that at that time the pope not only had not approved this recitation of the Creed, but had also shown by a public testimony engraved in bronze, in Greek and Latin, that he did not approve the addition of those four syllables. We may thus understand that even then the Roman Church was most tenacious of antiquity, whereas our nation was exceedingly fond of novelty.

For Leo persuaded our people so little to omit the Creed that, instead, the most illustrious bishops ordered it to be sung everywhere by everyone—a most fortunate and glorious outcome, since afterward both the Roman and universal Church followed both practices: the Creed was sung at Mass, and the phrase *Filioque* was added. Much was debated about this at the Council of Florence. Yet it must be admitted that novelty is always dangerous, and that introducing it is often an occasion of error.] and let *I believe in one God* be sung by everyone at Mass. And let the priest himself, together with the holy angels and the people of God, sing with one voice at Mass: “Holy, holy, [Col. 0729A] holy.” [Note: [Col. 0729A] Greek: Καὶ πᾶς ὁ λαὸς ἅμα εἰπέτω· Ἅγίος, ἁγίος, ἁγίος, Κύριος Σαβαώθ. “And let all the people say together: Holy, holy, holy, Lord Sabaoth.”] And the presbyters must be instructed in every way [Note: [Col. 0729B] That they are not to carry weapons. “For we who have abandoned the world,” as the Council of Mainz says (chapter 17), “wish by every means to observe this: that we possess spiritual weapons and lay aside worldly ones.” Thus the bishops necessarily had to break the military spirit that had burst into the clergy amid the wars continually raging on every side, and to wrench weapons from the hands of all clerics. This was done by the Council of Meaux (canon 37), which Hincmar attended soon after being raised to the episcopate, and which decreed: “Let those who appear to belong to the clergy neither take up military weapons nor walk about armed; rather, let them display the name of their profession through religious conduct and religious dress. If they disdain this, let them be punished by loss of their own rank, as despisers of the sacred canons and profaners of ecclesiastical holiness, since they cannot serve both God and the world as soldiers.” Therefore it was strictly forbidden for them to take up weapons during a revolt (*Capitulary of Charlemagne*, book VI, chapters 248 and 285): “Let clerics who, during any revolt, presumptuously dare to take up weapons be found and, having lost their clerical rank, be handed over to penance in a monastery.”

Since in those times bishops and presbyters were not initially forbidden to take part in battle, it is noteworthy that laymen and soldiers themselves petitioned the emperor Louis “that bishops henceforth, as until now, should not be harassed by the enemy, but, when you and we go against the enemy, should remain in their own parishes and strive to serve God faithfully. For we have seen some of them wounded among the enemy and in battles, and we have learned that some have died. The Lord knows that when we see them in such circumstances, terror seizes us, and some of our men, terrified by fear because of this, are accustomed to flee and turn their backs to the enemy,” and so forth. “We wish the same arrangement to be observed concerning priests: namely, that they too should not go against the enemy [the words *go forth* are absent], unless they have been blessed, and only by the choice and permission of their own bishops—bishops, nevertheless, such that we can all be confident in their knowledge, life, and conduct.” Walter therefore forbids any cleric, under pretext of his protection, to carry weapons [Col. 0729D] with which he could harm another.] not to carry weapons, but rather to place their confidence in God’s protection than in weapons.

## Chapter II. How the life and teaching of the cardinal presbyters are to be investigated by the archdeacons

(Capitulary of Charlemagne, book V, chapter 112.) Let the life, understanding, and teaching of the cardinal presbyters be investigated by the archdeacons. [Note: [Col. 0729D] The life, understanding, and teaching of the cardinal presbyters are to be investigated. Cardinal presbyters are assigned and incardinated to churches in which they are indeed appointed to provide for everyone, but in such a way that they themselves are not transferred from them. Since the *cardo*—the “hinge”—is said to be the principal part of every matter, they are the chief and primary presbyters of those churches, whom we call parish priests or curates. The bishop wishes their life or conduct, understanding, and teaching to be diligently investigated.

I do not see how the author properly distinguishes these two matters. For it might be said that understanding concerns one’s own knowledge: how learned he is and how catholicly he comprehends the mysteries of faith in his mind; while teaching concerns the instruction of the people: how readily, clearly, and openly he explains the thoughts of his mind while preaching. Yet this is disproved by the fact that in both headings he requires instruction directed toward the people.

If, however, we attend carefully to the words of the chapter, we shall assign understanding to contemplation and the mysteries of faith, and teaching to the practice of the virtues. Both parts are necessary for teaching the people, so that by believing rightly [Col. 0730A] and acting rightly he may fulfill the Christian name he bears. Although this is an improper meaning of the words, in a corrupted Latin there is no reason to demand a better one.

The archdeacon will therefore investigate three things in the parish priest’s understanding: whether he is learned, something he acquires from books and study; whether he thinks correctly about catholic mysteries, something he receives from true theology; and whether he can express intelligently and eloquently what he thinks correctly—a capacity whose principal mother we recognize as nature.

That this was found in few presbyters is explained by what we may call, if such a way of speaking is permissible, the barbarism of religion in those times: the scarcity of books, the continual disasters of war, and the tumult of clashing weapons. Everyone can see how hostile all these things are to literary studies.

In the second matter, Colluthus and Arius grievously failed at Alexandria. As heads of private churches, they abused the authority of their office and first divided their parishioners from one another by schism, then divided them from the Church by heresies [Col. 0730C]. The faction of Colluthus, suppressed almost at its birth, did little harm. Arius, however, more stubborn and more frenzied, under an outward appearance of modesty, with deceptive affability and feigned kindness, first drove a great number of holy virgins mad with his errors, then twelve priests; finally, penetrating even to the bishops themselves, he utterly ruined the whole Church. Epiphanius recounts all this at greater length (*Against Heresies* 69).

Without doubt the third quality was lacking in those of whom the *Capitulary of Charlemagne* decrees as follows (book VI, chapter 182): “Let there be no presbyter who does not publicly teach in church, in a language his hearers understand, to believe simply in the faith of almighty God in unity and Trinity. If he himself cannot clearly explain it in words, let him ask someone more learned to write it out for him in such a way that he can read it plainly and his hearers understand it; and if he can do no more, let him at least admonish them with these words: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.’”

O astonishing ignorance of the age! If monks had not then preserved the study of the disciplines in monasteries and supplied cities and provinces with bishops distinguished for their learning, what kind of church would our ancestors have had?

The teaching that this author requires has its principal foundation in conduct and life. No one will ever teach others virtue well who does not first practice it himself. Even slow-witted plowmen and stablemen, into whose minds words entrusted to their ears do not penetrate, readily perceive with their eyes that they must do what they see their prelates doing. They are therefore bound to imitate the shepherd and bishop of our souls, who first began to do and then to teach.

Herard of Tours saw this clearly (chapter 107). Omitting the learning that others require in presbyters, he grounds the matter in true holiness of life: “Let presbyters, as they are holier in rank, so also be more reverent in word, bearing, and action, because the loftiness of rank makes the accumulation of sin heavier.”]

Let the life, understanding, and teaching of the cardinal presbyters be investigated. The life, specifically, of modesty and sobriety, together with devotion to religious conduct in all their actions. (Capitulary of Charlemagne, book VI, chapters 155 and 173.)

As for understanding, let it be determined how capable each one is of instructing his brethren in faith in the holy Trinity: that they should believe the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be one almighty, eternal, invisible God, who created heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them; and that there is one deity, substance, and majesty in the three persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

And let it be determined how the Son of God was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and Mary ever-Virgin for the salvation and restoration of the human [Col. 0731A] race; suffered, was buried, rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven; and how he will come again in divine majesty to judge the living and the dead according to their own merits.

And because there will be one resurrection of the dead; and because the wicked, on account of their crimes, will be sent with the devil into eternal fire, while the righteous will enter eternal life with Christ and the holy angels.

As for teaching, let it be determined how he can instruct those who are slower to understand, by word and credible example, in faith, hope, charity, and the other virtues, according to evangelical, apostolic, and canonical instruction: how they must live without deviation and from which vices they ought to abstain, lest they be condemned with the devil to eternal damnation.

## Chapter III. On the conduct with women that presbyters must avoid

(Council of Nicaea, canon 3; letter of Theodulf to the clergy, chapter 12.) [Note: [Col. 0731B] In accordance with the prohibitions of the holy Fathers. It would be a mark of very painstaking diligence to seek out those prohibitions and gather them into a single bundle, since they are innumerable and, wherever one turns in the councils, one encounters canons forbidding presbyters improper access to women. I do not revisit the *ἐπεισάκτοι*—the “introduced women”—so strongly condemned in the earliest times by the Council of Nicaea, Augustine, Jerome, Gregory, and countless others.

I say nothing of the dangerous association with wives whom men had left after receiving orders. Genebaud of Laon provided a striking example. He was “a man noble in the flesh and learned in both sacred and secular literature,” who, as Flodoard excellently relates (*History*, book I, chapter 17), “trusting too much in his former life and the loftiness of his rank, carelessly allowed himself to be visited by the wife whom he had left, supposedly in order to instruct her. But it happened that the woman’s frequent visits and flattering conversations softened the bishop’s hard and vigorous heart against lust, and, as though moving a rock from the place of holiness, transferred it to the mire of licentiousness.”

I remain with matters among us. The *Capitulary of Charlemagne* warns (book I, chapter 98): “It has been established by the bishops concerning presbyters who indiscreetly permit women to live with them that, if they do not correct themselves after being admonished, they are to be struck with canonical censure as despisers of the sacred canons.” Concerning the access, association, and cohabitation of clerics with women, our Hincmar says (*Capitulary of the year 852*, chapter 21): “Accordingly, in accordance with the sacred canons, we have expressly, firmly, and carefully forbidden this in all synods, and it must be diligently investigated by us and our fellow ministers.” He adds quite a few things on this subject in his usual manner.

In another capitulary (*Capitulary of the year 874*, chapter 3), he later complains that these warnings were treated as worthless by parish priests: “I have already given you a chapter from the holy Scriptures and the sayings of Catholics concerning improper access to women and undue familiarity with them. But I see that some of you make little of it; therefore I wish it to be read again at your assembly.” And what follows.

Herard of Tours is briefer (chapter 19): “Let them abhor association with women, as well as their access and their service. Otherwise, let them be removed from office as despisers of the canons. For those whom they decree should be provided with necessities, let them arrange houses far away, where assistance is supplied not by themselves but through ministers.”

See more in the collection of Antonius Augustinus (book VI, title 30 and following), and everything in the special work of Theophilus Raynaudus, a man learned in every field, who recently exhausted this subject completely, as necessary for religious and secular presbyters alike (*On the Sober Association of the Other Sex*, etc.). It is entitled *Dissertation on Sober Association with the Other Sex by Sacred and Religious Men*.]

In accordance with the prohibitions of the holy Fathers, let no priest permit any woman whatsoever to live with him in his house; nor let him presume to speak alone with any woman without suitable observers or witnesses, lest suspicion of dishonor arise against him or one of his servants.

## Chapter IV. Let the presbyter keep everything clean

(The same, chapter 4.) Just as every presbyter is salutarily admonished to maintain cleanliness of soul and body, [Note: [Col. 0731D] Thus, the vestments of those who are to minister to God. Hincmar attaches such importance to the adornments of the house of God (*Visitation Capitula*, chapters 4 and 6) that, in the interrogation of parish priests by the deans, he formulates two questions on this subject: “What are the altar furnishings like? How many are new and how many old? How clean are they?” And immediately afterward: “What and how many priestly vestments does he have, how clean are they, and are they kept in a clean place?” The *Capitulary of Charlemagne*, moved by the same love of divine honor, commands (book I, chapter 152): “Let presbyters in their parishes preach to women that they prepare linen cloths for the altars.”]

so let them ensure that the vestments used for ministering to God and the altar furnishings, [Note: [Col. 0732B] And the apse around the altar. He wishes the *apsis* or *apsida*—what we now call the choir of the church, where the altar is contained and enclosed—to be kept as clean as possible, both because the sacraments are chiefly handled there and because angels are always present there with the sacraments. We can add a third reason: the relics of the saints are customarily placed there.

Thus, in Gregory of Tours (book X, chapter 31), Tetricus, bishop of Langres, laid the foundations of a tomb for his predecessor, Saint Gregory, “before the altar of the basilica, and constructed and vaulted the raised apse as a single work. After it had been vaulted and the wall broken through, he built an arch. When this work had been completed and adorned, he dug a place in the middle of the apse where he wished to transfer the body of the blessed Father,” and so forth.

An *apsis* or *apsida* is so called from a vault and arch, either because the place is rounded in the form of an arch or because it is customarily covered and vaulted above with a vault. Nor have I believed that the place called the *Trullus* at Constantinople was always something else—the place where the famous council was celebrated in the Trullo.

There is no doubt that the bishop’s seat was erected in the apse, as it still commonly projects today in cathedral churches. Nor should it be denied that one ascended to that apse by steps, so that Augustine aptly calls it a “stepped apse.” But I cannot approve the way most people use that passage of Augustine, as though they believe the apse itself to be the episcopal chair, since he clearly distinguishes the two. Writing to the Donatist bishop Maximinus to diminish the schismatic’s pride arising from rank and worldly pomp, he says (letter 203): “The honor of this world passes away; ambition passes away. At Christ’s future judgment, neither stepped apses, nor veiled chairs, nor troops of nuns coming forward and singing will be brought forward in defense when conscience begins to accuse and the judge of consciences begins to judge.”

Elsewhere, writing to the religious woman Albina concerning a disturbance raised in the church itself, he says: “I returned to our benches after leaving the crowd.” And shortly afterward (letter 225): “I was saying to those whom I could, who had ascended to us in the apse, men of greater honor and dignity.” Certainly they had not ascended into the bishop’s chair, but into the place where it had been set. Thus the apse contains the chair and is taken figuratively for the chair only.

The canon of the Third Council of Carthage (canon 32) must be explained in this way: “Let the hands of any penitent whose public and notorious crime is known to the whole Church be imposed before the apse.” The public offense should receive a public satisfaction. The bishop should not descend to the place of the penitents, as though he were to reconcile the guilty person in embarrassment; rather, the guilty person should ascend to the elevated apse to the bishop, and there, with everyone watching, the bishop should impose the reconciling hand from his chair.]
