the apse around the [Col. 0733A] altar—or rather, indeed, the entire building where the sacraments are handled and where the presence of the holy angels is always found—be foreseen and kept most cleanly and reverently, lest, when my envoys come there with the archdeacon, they find something blameworthy that would compel me to rebuke more severely the brotherhood of someone.

## Chapter V. Let sacred vessels not be given as pledges

(*Capitulary of Charlemagne*, book I, chapter 94; Herard, chapter 20.) [Note: [Col. 0733B] That no one is to give a sacred vessel. Thus Herard of Tours says (chapter 20): “Concerning ecclesiastical vessels and vestments: they are not to be given as pledges without the bishop’s permission, and those already given are to be recovered.” Hincmar forbids the same thing in other words (*Capitulary of the year 852*, chapter 11): “Concerning sacred implements not being given as security. Let no presbyter presume to give a chalice, paten, altar cloth, priestly vestment, or book as a pledge to an innkeeper, merchant, any layman, or a woman.”

He proves that this is unlawful by parity of reasoning. A priest is forbidden to go forth in sacred vestments to the people’s profane gatherings; by the canons he may not enter taverns to drink; consecrated vessels are forbidden to be handed over to unclean persons to touch. How much less may they be given as security? All these rules are drawn from the *Capitulary of Charlemagne* (book I, chapter 94, and book V, chapter 172), which corrected a wicked custom. “This transgression,” Louis the Pious says, “has been forbidden, both in the time of our father and in our own, at assemblies of bishops, in accordance with canonical authority, but has not yet been fully brought to correction.”

What, then, are we to make of certain historians who write that, when the most holy king of our people returned from Syria to Francia, he left the most sacred host as a pledge with the Saracen enemies? I know that Joinville is silent about this, while others categorically deny it. There are nevertheless some who assert that, in memory of this deed, the Eucharist is commonly depicted in taverns of ill repute throughout Palestine, and that, when people ask the reason for those images, the inhabitants tell the story of the Frankish king’s deed. We leave the matter undecided.]

Let no one presume to give a sacred vessel or anything consecrated to God as a pledge, except for the purpose of redeeming captives or repairing and restoring the church. And even this is not to be done except with the bishop’s permission. Let no one presume to sell or otherwise dispose of church property that has been offered by the faithful.

## Chapter VI. Let every presbyter have a cleric and a school

(Hincmar, *Capitularies of the year 874*, chapter 5.) [Note: [Col. 0733D] That every presbyter is to have his own cleric: a companion in life, a minister of sacred things, a teacher of the school, and a future successor. Hincmar wishes the parish priest to be asked this as well (*Capitula to the Deans*): “Whether he has a cleric who can keep the school, read the Epistle, or sing, as he sees necessary.” Elsewhere he calls such clerics “nurtured” (*nutriti*) (*Capitularies of the year 874*): “If you lived well and nurtured your own dependents in good life and good conscience, it would not be necessary for you both to lose what is yours and to send yourselves into damnation.”

Herard likewise wishes schools to be established by presbyters (chapter 17): “Let presbyters, as far as they can, maintain schools and corrected books.” Theodulf, however, wishes such schools to be free and joined with the greatest charity (letter to the clergy, chapter 20): “When they teach them, let them demand no payment from them for this, nor accept anything from them, except what their parents, out of charitable devotion, freely offer them.”]

Let every presbyter [Col. 0734A] have his own cleric, whom he should take care to educate religiously. And if he has the means, let him not neglect to maintain a school in his church; and let him carefully ensure that those whom he receives for instruction are nurtured chastely and sincerely.

## Chapter VII. On ecclesiastical books and on always having the Eucharist available

(*Capitulary of Charlemagne*, book VI, chapter 227; book I, chapter 161.) Let them have ecclesiastical books—namely, a Missal, Gospel book, Lectionary, Psalter, Antiphonary, Martyrology, and Homiliary—by means of which they may instruct themselves and others. Let them correct their books against well-corrected copies, lest they appear to perform the work of God negligently.

Let each one have chapters concerning major and minor vices, and also concerning virtues, by which he may learn or preach to his subjects so that they may beware of the devil’s snares.

[Note: [Col. 0734B] And let the presbyter always have the Eucharist. The great care taken that no Christian, however lawfully he may previously have abstained, should die without viaticum is taught by innumerable canons, and Hincmar solemnly represents it at our council.

The simplicity of the African faithful went so far that they even gave the Eucharist to the dead. This is forbidden by the Council of Carthage (canon 5): “It has also been decided that the Eucharist is not to be given to the bodies of the dead. For the Lord said: ‘Take and eat.’ But corpses can neither take nor eat.”

Since the Greek translation of that canon says, ἵνα τοῖς σώμασι τελευτώντων εὐχαριστία μὴ δοθῇ—“that the Eucharist not be given to the bodies of those who are dying”—and since the word signifies “those who are dying,” Balsamo warns, in his commentary on this fifth canon, that it ought to be understood as τοὺς ἤδη τελευτήσαντας, οὐχὶ τὰ ἔσχατα πνέοντας—“those who have already died, not those breathing their last.”

For this reason Hincmar commands (*Capitularies of the year 852*) that the parish priest be asked “whether he has a pyx in which the sacred offering reserved for the viaticum of the sick can suitably be kept.” In the same place he adds something worth noting: “Let the presbyter himself communicate the sick in person and not through just anyone; nor let him hand the communion to any layman to carry to his own house for the sake of some sick person.” There would be no need for this rule if people did not commonly violate it.

Nevertheless, this practice could not always have been used in the ancient custom of the Church. For that old man Serapion of Alexandria, mentioned by Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History* VI, 36), when death was approaching, did indeed ask that the sacred Eucharist be brought to him by one of the presbyters, but he received the offering from a boy.

The fact that he wishes the Eucharist to be given not only to the sick but also to sick infants seems to approach the opinion of Saint Augustine (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 24), who assigns to all the faithful no lesser necessity of the Eucharist than of baptism for attaining salvation, and believes that this necessity had been implanted in the churches by apostolic tradition.

Indeed, the *Capitulary of Charlemagne* shows that this was commonly accepted in Gaul at that time (book I, chapter 161), from which Walter took his command: “Let the presbyter always have the Eucharist ready, so that whenever anyone falls ill, or a sick infant is present, he may immediately give him communion, lest he die without communion.” The universal Church [Col. 0735C] never accepted this, although Saint Cyprian, in his book *On the Lapsed*, relates that an infant girl at Carthage participated in the body and blood of Christ, and Augustine reports the same without marking it as a novelty (letter 23).]

And let the presbyter always have the Eucharist ready, so that whenever anyone falls ill [Col. 0735A], or an infant becomes sick, he may immediately give him communion, lest he die without viaticum.

## Chapter VIII. On practicing hospitality

(The same, book V, chapter 221; Theodulf, letter to the clergy, chapter 25.) Let them eagerly practice hospitality toward one another and toward everyone, because the Lord himself will say at the recompense of the great day: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matthew XXV). The Apostle, praising hospitality, says: “Through it some pleased God, having received angels as guests” (Hebrews XIII).

If a presbyter says that, because of poverty, he cannot provide hospitality to travelers, let him at least gladly receive the traveler in his house, provide him with shelter, fire, water, and straw for a bed, and help him obtain what he needs to purchase. For Truth herself, speaking in person, says: “If anyone gives only a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple, truly I tell you, he will not lose his reward” (Matthew X).

## Chapter IX. Let presbyters have an endowment

Let the presbyters who have not yet obtained an endowment for their churches, according to what is contained in chapter eighty-five of the capitularies of our lord and master—namely, the most glorious King Charles—as well as of his grandfather and father, report this to us; and with our divine assistance and counsel let them obtain it from their lords. If they have anything more, let them render the service owed to their lords.

## Chapter X. On avoiding secular concerns and usury

(*Capitulary of Charlemagne*, book II, chapter 37; book V, chapters 107 and 112; [Col. 0735C] book I, chapters 125 and 130.) Let presbyters or deacons not engage in suretyships or hunting, nor act as contractors, nor practice or permit usury.

For usury exists wherever more is demanded than is given. For example, if you give ten solidi and demand more; or if you give a measure of wine or grain and then exact something further beyond it.

## Chapter XI. On forbidding oaths

[Note: [Col. 0735C] That they are to warn their congregations. Herard of Tours appears to prescribe the same thing (*Capitula*, chapter 22): “Let Christians guard themselves against idle speech and oaths. Let them not swear rashly, lest they swear falsely.” Chrysostom inculcates this so frequently in his homilies to the people of Antioch, and the *Capitulary of Charlemagne* does not omit it (book VI, chapter 2; book III, chapters 8 and 10), when, on the authority of sacred Scripture, it forbids taking the name of the Lord God in vain.

In the same capitulary other oaths are also forbidden, namely oaths made to men other than the king and, as they are called, one’s lords: “Concerning the oath: let loyalty not be promised by oath to anyone else except to us and to each person’s own lord, for our benefit and that of his lord, except for those oaths which, according to law, are rightly owed by one person to another.”

A little later other oaths are added, those made by witnesses in court. Isaac of Langres reports this chapter (title 8, chapter 2), in which it is altogether forbidden to admit anyone to an oath or testimony unless he is fasting. Herard commands the same (chapter 12): “Let witnesses swear fasting, and let them first be warned about perjury.” Indeed, the law commands judges themselves to be fasting: “Let the count hold no court,” the capitulary says (book III, chapter 38), “unless he is fasting.”

After Theodulf had strongly emphasized the crime of perjury (letter to the clergy, chapters 26–27), he rebukes presbyters who “regarded it as trivial and imposed on perjurers a light sort of penance”; he also warns that false testimony must be avoided, “knowing that this too is a very grave crime. For it is the height—not to say of folly, but of wickedness—to fall into so grave a crime out of desire for silver and gold, clothing, or any other thing, or, as happens most frequently, because of drunkenness, so that one must either spend seven years in harsh misery or be rejected from the Church.”]

Let them warn their congregations not to become accustomed to oaths.

## Chapter XII. On avoiding the excommunicated and criminals
(Ibid., bk. III, chs. 25, 42, etc.; Isaac, title 9; Council of Nicaea, canon 5.) Let no one associate with excommunicated persons or with notorious robbers—whether plunderers, murderers, or sacrilegious persons—nor sing Mass for them, nor say “Hail” to them on the road; let him not provide them burial, [Col. 0736B] nor speak with them in any manner except for the purpose of correcting them. On Sundays, moreover, let them proclaim at Mass to all residing in their parishes that they must not associate with such persons. If anyone acts otherwise, let him know that he stands condemned—unless repentance intervenes—by all the councils canonically established, and also by the 318 bishops assembled at the Council of Nicaea under the prior ordering of the Holy Spirit. For Paul, the chosen vessel, also testifies concerning these people, saying: “The rapacious shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6). The apostle John likewise speaks of this very matter: “Whoever says to him, ‘Hail,’ shares in his evil works” (3 John). For we know that Christ has no fellowship with Belial; each person is called the son of the one whose works he performs.

## CHAPTER XIII. — On the observance of fasts.

(Capitularies of Charlemagne, bk. VII, ch. 98, and bk. VI, chs. 183–184.) [Note: [Col. 0736C] That fasts imposed by pastors are to be observed. What fasts these are is explained by the capitulary (bk. VI, chs. 183–184): first, the lesser fasts, namely, “the Ember fasts, that is, in March, June, September, and December.” Then the greater fasts: “that the three customary fasts be held each year: forty days before the Nativity of the Lord, forty days before Easter, when we pay the tithes of the year, and forty days after Pentecost. Although some of these lack canonical authority, it is nevertheless fitting for all of us together, on account of the custom of the people and of our parents, to observe this practice, as stated above.” In addition, fixed weekly fasts are added: “Besides these customary periods of fasting, let there be a fast every Friday on account of the Lord’s Passion. Likewise, Saturday is regarded by many as consecrated to fasting, because on that day Christ lay in the tomb.” It is unnecessary to say what the Church has retained from all these practices in her usage. Yet it is altogether shameful, and exceedingly alien to the devotion of our ancestors, that the few practices remaining should be so greatly neglected by Christians and openly violated by pastors who see and know it. [Col. 0737B] Theodulf explains how these fasts were to be observed—or rather, how they were observed in those times—in the matter of food and the time of eating. He distinguishes the fasts we have seen imposed throughout the Church by tradition from those introduced by public custom, which depend more upon the will of individuals (Theodulf, Letter to the Clergy, ch. 37):

“Lent,” he says, “must be kept with the greatest observance, and the fast in it must in no way be relaxed, because those days themselves are the tenth part of our year. At another time the fast is customarily relaxed for the sake of charity; but during this period it must not be relaxed at all, because to fast at another time is to go beyond the commandment of God.”

He calls not fasting the breaking of the fast before the evening office. Thus he says below (ch. 39):

“Many who think that they are fasting eat as soon as they hear the signal for None. They must in no way be considered to be fasting if they have eaten before the evening office is celebrated.”

He places greater importance on the time of eating than on the foods themselves (chs. 38–40):

“He who can abstain from eggs, cheese, fish, [Col. 0737C] and wine possesses great virtue. But whoever cannot abstain from these because of illness or because of any kind of work may consume them; let him only solemnly keep the fast until evening, and take wine not for drunkenness but for the refreshment of his body.”

Accordingly, “one must hasten to the Masses, and, after hearing the solemn Masses or the evening offices and giving alms, approach one’s food.” Alms are to be given from the food and drink “that each person would have consumed had he not been fasting; for to fast and reserve the food of the midday meal for supper is an increase not of one’s reward but of one’s food.” This, in general, is what he says about fasting (ibid., chs. 36, 41–43).

Regarding Lent, which is the most sacred season of Christian abstinence, he prescribes the following. These instructions are useful not only for imitation but also for refuting the errors of certain innovators:

“One week before the beginning of Lent, confessions are to be made to the priests, penance is to be received, those at variance are to be reconciled, all quarrels are to be settled, and each must dismiss debts from his heart toward the others.”

But what sort of penance is this? Is it one that removes a person from the sacred altar and commands abstinence from Holy Communion?

“On every Sunday in Lent, except those who are excommunicated, the sacraments of the body and blood of Christ are to be received; and on the Lord’s Supper, Good Friday, the vigil of Easter, and the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, all must receive Communion without exception.”

At that time all lawsuits and disputes must cease.

“For through the prophet the Lord rebukes those who pursue disputes and lawsuits during Lent, and those who demand debts from their debtors, saying: ‘Behold, on the days of your fasting …’” (Isa. III), etc.

During those most sacred days, too, “one must abstain [Col. 0738B] from one’s spouses and live chastely and devoutly, so that these holy days may be spent with heart and body sanctified. For a fast that is polluted by conjugal intercourse, and not commended by prayers, vigils, and almsgiving, is scarcely of any value.”

We have transcribed these passages from a single work of Theodulf for our benefit; most of them are scattered throughout the capitulary.] Let them carefully observe the fasts imposed by pastors, lest—God forbid—they be found guilty on account of disobedience.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the practice of works of mercy.

(Theodulf, Letter to the Clergy, ch. 32.) Let them teach their subjects to become accustomed to works of mercy, that is, almsgiving and prayers, since through these two things the favor of God is obtained.

## CHAPTER XV. On prohibiting servile work on Sundays.

(Capitularies of Charlemagne, bk. I, ch. 15; bk. VI, ch. 186; Theodulf, cited above, ch. 24; Herard, ch. 2.) Let them not permit markets or the transport of goods to be conducted on Sundays; rather, from evening until evening, let the Resurrection of the Lord be honored.

## CHAPTER XVI. [Col. 0738A] On avoiding taverns and buffoonery.

(Capitularies of Charlemagne, bk. I, ch. 14, from the Council of Laodicea, canon 24, and the Third Council of Carthage, canon 27.)

Let priests and the rest of the ecclesiastical order not drink in taverns, nor become accustomed to buffoonery that provokes laughter. Let them know that they will give an account of every idle word—especially those whose speech ought at all times to be seasoned with salt—so that they may be examples in word and deed and offer a model to all who see them, while imparting grace to those who hear them.

## CHAPTER XVII. How they ought to conduct themselves in associations and banquets.

(Hincmar, Capitularies of the Year 852, ch. 14; Herard, ch. 108.) [Note: [Col. 0738B] That when they come to an assembly. A few matters must be touched on briefly here. What he decrees concerning not entering taverns is private, following innumerable canons and critics of that vice. What he requires here at assemblies and in priestly fraternities is public. They are called associations because they are fellowships of men, congregations of equals sharing the same condition of life and duty. Hincmar uses “guilds” for the same groups: “from the collections which they commonly call guilds and confraternities,” formed from money and contributions gathered from individuals.

The Council of Laodicea forbids such banquets to be held by both laymen and clergy (Council of Laodicea, canon 55): “that priests or clerics must not hold banquets from contributions, nor should laymen do so,” for fear of drunkenness, from which, says Balsamon, wantonness and insolence follow. The Latins prefer to allow those gatherings called agapes. But since, according to Cassiodorus (bk. VII, letter 3), “indiscipline is accustomed to arise among associates,” they must be governed and restrained by certain laws.

The Council of Nantes, inserted at the end of volume III of the Councils of Gaul, lays down such regulations (Council of Nantes, ch. 15), and Hincmar and our Walter undoubtedly drew from it. All these rules aim to commend temperance and the modesty worthy of consecrated persons. Hincmar strongly condemns “feasts, pastries, and revelries” at such gatherings (Capitularies of the Year 852, chs. 14–16), “because it is dishonorable and burdensome.” He forbids them to invite one another to drink, “and to urge one another, for the love of the saints or of one’s own soul, to drink, or to compel others to drink, because in such feasting and drinking, as irreligious people practice it, the devil always intrudes.”

[Col. 0738D] Walter orders rustic songs, shameful games, and female dancers to be absent from such banquets. He does so first on the basis of the discipline of the ancient Church, which removed clerics from the spectacles displayed at wedding banquets, according to the Council of Laodicea (canon 54): “before the theatrical performers enter, they must rise and withdraw.” The Synod in Trullo renewed this rule after forbidding clerics to watch all circus and theatrical games (Synod in Trullo, ch. 24; Balsamon there).

Balsamon writes that some explain this as requiring complete abstention from mimes and theatrical games, but not in every respect from equestrian performances, since some of these appear to take place with ecclesiastical permission. The patriarch, however, concludes his discussion with a memorable judgment. Many others, much more religious—and he himself agrees with them—do not admit distinctions of this kind, saying: “The canons ought to be interpreted according to what is more beneficial to the soul, not according to what is more dissolute and indifferent.” [Col. 0739A]

“Canons must be explained according to what is more conducive to the soul, and not according to what is more lax and indifferent” (Capitularies of the Year 852, ch. 14).

Then, because of the excessive license of those times, all these practices were prohibited by devout bishops, as Hincmar explains at greater length:

“Nor should anyone presume to bring forth disordered applause and laughter or empty stories there, or to sing; nor should he permit shameful jokes with a bear or with female acrobats to be performed before him; nor should he consent to have the demons’ masks, commonly called talamascas, displayed there, because this is diabolical and prohibited by the sacred canons.”

Those who, following their counsel, season their meals with sacred reading will remedy this evil. Hincmar recommends this to our Walter in the same passage:

“Let one of their clerics read some sacred reading.”

Herard also approves this:

“Let priests and clerics not permit shameful jokes to be performed before them, but let them have the poor and needy at table with them, and let a reading be given to them.”

Thus Augustine “preferred reading or discussion at table to eating and drinking, as a remedy against the plague of human custom” (Possidius, Life of Augustine, ch. 22)—whether that pestilential custom lay in the enjoyment of food and the immoderate desire to eat and drink, or in the depravity and wickedness of banquet conversation.

“For this reason he warned every guest that he ought to refrain from superfluous and harmful stories and from slander.”

That custom, like many others formerly practiced among ecclesiastical men, is now confined within the enclosures of religious monasteries and no longer dares to appear in public.

Theodulf does not even name these associations, but nevertheless demands modesty and temperance from priests (Letter to the Clergy, ch. 13):

“Nor should you hold banquets with women or with any impure persons, unless perhaps some head of a household invites you to his home and wishes, together with his wife and children, to rejoice with you in spiritual joy, to receive refreshment from your words, and to offer you bodily refreshment as an act of charity. For whenever any of the faithful refreshes you with bodily food, you ought to refresh him in turn with spiritual food.”]

When they come to an assembly, which they themselves call an association, [Col. 0739A] let them ride in a religious manner; let the younger offer the honor due to their elder brothers. Whenever priests are invited to a meal on someone’s anniversary, let them conduct themselves with complete modesty and sobriety, avoiding insolent talk and rustic songs. Nor should they permit female dancers, like the daughter of Herodias, to perform shameful games before them. Rather, when they assemble together, let them appoint a reader of sacred edification, just as they appoint the other servants of food and drink, so that they may display priestly reverence with commendable maturity, and so that God may be honored in their holy conduct through Jesus Christ.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On proclaiming and observing the feasts of the saints.

(Capitularies of Charlemagne, bk. I, ch. 164; bk. II, ch. 35; bk. VI, ch. 186.) [Note: [Col. 0739D] That the feasts of the saints are to be solemnly celebrated. He divides the feast days that must be publicly celebrated into two orders: public feasts, common to the whole Church or kingdom; and private feasts, peculiar to his diocese. He takes the former from the royal capitularies, and the latter from the usage of the Church of Orléans. I shall review both.

There is no proclamation concerning Sunday, but the greatest religious observance, because its identity is obvious: the people are not instructed when it returns, but how it is to be spent. This is admirably set forth in the capitulary of Charlemagne (bk. VI, ch. 202) and in Theodulf’s letter (Letter to the Clergy, ch. 24). Barnabas Brissonius, a most learned man, must also be consulted concerning the law of Sunday.] Let them celebrate the feasts of the saints with solemn worship and announce beforehand to their congregations that they are to be observed. That is, [Note: [Col. 0739D] They order the day of the Lord’s Nativity, together with the three following days, to be proclaimed to everyone; it is one of the three most celebrated feasts on which the bishop must admonish the public judges [Col. 0740A] (Capitulary of Charlemagne, bk. VI, ch. 106) “that all wretched persons held in chains must be released; and if the judge disregards the admonition of the pastor, he must be barred from the threshold of the church for as long as the bishop of that place sees fit.” The other two, equally well known, are Easter and Pentecost.

Christians celebrate the octave of the Lord, which the capitulary in one place calls by its own name “the Circumcision of the Lord” and the Kalends of January (ibid., ch. 186), with solemn worship. This has been the case since the religion of Christ, after idolatry was overthrown, took possession of the whole world. Previously the day had been spent in fasting and silence, as Baronius explains at greater length in the Martyrology (under the Kalends of January).] the Nativity of the Lord, Saint Stephen, Saint John the Evangelist, the Holy Innocents; the octave of the Lord, the Epiphany, [Note: [Col. 0740B] The Nativity of Saint Mary. Our Walter is the only one of all the authors to name it. From the silence of the Council of Mainz under Charlemagne and of the capitularies derived from it, Baronius judges that in the time of Charlemagne and the emperors Louis the feast was unknown in the Gallican Church (Martyrology, under September 8). If we trust this most diligent investigator of ecclesiastical affairs, we certainly owe to this author the first notice of its celebration among the Franks. The credit belongs to the Church of Orléans because, under Charles the Bald and through the institution of Bishop Walter, it began in Gaul, at first confined to a single diocese, when neither Herard of Tours, nor Hincmar of Rheims, nor Isaac of Langres, nor Theodulf himself of Orléans mentioned it. Ado of Vienne does name it in more than one place, but does not order that it be proclaimed as a celebration.] the Nativity of Saint Mary, the Purification of Saint Mary, the Assumption of Saint Mary; [Note: [Col. 0740C] Holy Saturday. I observe that it is absent from the catalogues of others as well, unless perhaps the capitulary’s order that the Paschal solemnity begin on Saturday evening refers to it (Capitulary of Charlemagne, bk. VI, ch. 187): “As holy Easter is celebrated when Saturday evening comes on.” Among ecclesiastical writers, the fast of that day is more celebrated—indeed, the fast of the entire three-day period preceding the Paschal feast—and it was especially customary among the Greeks. But I shall not dwell on these matters.] Holy Saturday, [Note: [Col. 0740C] The eighth day of Easter. I am especially surprised that this queen of Christian solemnities is omitted from Herard’s catalogue; this could have happened only through the carelessness of copyists. I note further that many authors add an eight-day holiday to the Great Sunday, which Walter expresses. This is stated most clearly in the capitulary of Charlemagne (bk. I, ch. 35), where we read: “We have decreed that the Lord’s Paschal Sunday be honored with all reverence and sobriety; in the same way, we have decreed that the whole of that week be observed.” Charlemagne wished this to be maintained according to ancient law and the law of Theodosius.

What, then, are we to make of the same capitulary (ibid., bk. VI, ch. 186): “At the Lord’s Easter, until the octave of Easter, after the Sunday, three days”? Does it order the entire week of Easter to be holidays, and in addition the following week’s three days of the Sunday in white garments? Certainly not. It means that those eight days, formerly festive by common law, as we have said, are by the present law reduced to the three days nearest Easter Sunday. This is still observed in certain places. In any event, we have at least two days of great solemnity. [Col. 0741A] Thus, according to the circumstances of the times and of piety, the ancient laws are either abolished or restricted. Yet this dispensation was not accepted everywhere at once, since in Herard of Tours we read (Capitularies, ch. 97): “Concerning how the eight days of Easter ought to be holidays.” In this matter he properly agrees with our author of Orléans.] the eighth day of Easter; [Note: [Col. 0740D] The Greater Litany. What our predecessors meant by the name “Greater Litany” is explained by the Council of Mainz under Charlemagne (ch. 32):

“Litanies are called by a Greek name what in Latin are called rogations. There is this difference between litanies and exomologeses: exomologeses are performed solely for the confession of sins, whereas litanies are proclaimed for entreating God and obtaining his mercy in some matter. But now both terms are included under a single designation,” since the litany was also composed for the performance of penance, as we shall soon see.

The designation “greater” presents somewhat more difficulty. For the Roman Ordo (bk. I) calls the litany celebrated by the authority of Gregory the Great on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, for the feast of Saint Mark, the Greater Litany. It calls the other one the Lesser Litany, instituted by Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, for the three days of rogations, which, “among us, is still most devoutly observed for various calamities,” as the same Ordo says.

Our writers do not agree. They simply call the former the Roman Litany and imply that it was retained with difficulty in Gallic usage, as can be seen in Herard (Capitularies, ch. 94): “Concerning the Roman Litany on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, so that it may be remembered.” That is, it is to be commemorated because, unless carefully commended, it would lapse. They call no other litany the Greater Litany than the three days of rogations. The capitulary of Charlemagne, plainly drawing on the Council of Mainz, names this one (ch. 33): “It has pleased us that the Greater Litany be observed by all Christians for three days” (Capitularies of Charlemagne, bk. V, ch. 85).

Walafrid Strabo, however, applies the name Greater to both—the Roman litany and this Gallican one (On Ecclesiastical Affairs, ch. 28). This is a minor and indifferent matter, provided it is observed with the proper religious devotion.

The cited Council of Mainz urges that it be celebrated “as we have found by reading and as our holy Fathers instituted it: not riding, nor dressed in costly garments, but barefoot and clothed in sackcloth, unless illness prevents it.” The council appears to refer to the Roman Ordo (bk. I), which prohibits every sign of secular joy during this period of penance:

“Let no one wear costly garments during these days, because we ought to mourn in sackcloth and ashes. Let drunkenness and banquets, as practiced among the common people, be prohibited. Let no one presume to ride, but let everyone walk barefoot. Let women by no means lead dances; for these are days of abstinence, not of rejoicing.”

Herard prescribes similar things (Capitularies, ch. 95).] the Greater Litany; [Col. 0741A] [Note: [Col. 0741D] The Ascension of the Lord. The capitulary says (Capitularies of Charlemagne, bk. II, ch. 33): “To celebrate the day of the Lord’s Ascension fully.” In former times some feast days were observed only during half the day and profaned by secular work after noon. The day of the Ascension appears to have been among them. The emperor Charlemagne strives to abolish this corrupt custom and wishes the day to be properly celebrated in its entirety.] the Ascension of the Lord; [Note: [Col. 0741D] Pentecost. Walter does not increase the celebration of Pentecost in any other special way, although others establish that it is to be made equal to Easter, in accordance with the capitulary of Charlemagne (Capitularies of Charlemagne, bk. VI, ch. 187):

“Let the priests proclaim it in the same manner as holy Easter is celebrated when Saturday evening comes, and let them likewise hold the day of Pentecost as most celebrated, like holy Easter, with its fast, Mass, and baptism.”

From this the antiquity of that fast is evident. In our youth it had fallen out of use among secular people; restored through renewed devotion, especially by the example of religious communities, it now commonly flourishes in the Church.

Nevertheless, in those times some objected to the interpretation of the Gospel saying, “The children of the bridegroom cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them” (Matt. 9). The Roman Ordo (bk. I) seems to have had this in mind when, in recommending the rogations, it expressly noted that abstinence from meat was to be observed, but not fasting.

Among the particular feasts of the saints, our author omits the dedication of Saint Michael and the Nativity of Saint Remigius, which are named in other catalogues, though not consistently. By contrast, Herard—indeed, the only one—adds the feast of All Saints. Pope Gregory IV introduced it into Gaul during the time of Louis the Pious, as Ado of Vienne reports (Martyrology, under the Kalends of November):

“At the urging of Gregory, the pope of holy memory, the most pious emperor Louis, with all the bishops of his kingdom and empire consenting, established that the feast of All Saints should be solemnly celebrated annually and perpetually on the aforesaid day.”] Pentecost, Saint John the Baptist, Saint Peter, Saint Paul, Saint Martin, Saint Andrew. [Note: [Col. 0742B] Our fathers besides. There follow the particular feasts of the Diocese of Orléans: those of bishops who distinguished that church by outstanding holiness and pastoral care. He wishes these to be established on the occasion of their departure, or death, not their translation; it does not seem necessary to examine the reasons for this.

I am surprised, however, that among those eminent bishops he omits the apostle of the people of Orléans and founder of that noble church, Altinus. He is not even named in his own church—although he was a martyr and a disciple of the apostolic men—and the list begins instead with Evurtius, or Evortius. Evortius was far inferior to Altinus and had several less distinguished predecessors.

To Evortius the illustrious city owes the construction of the Church of the Holy Cross. During his celebration of its dedication, the hand of Christ the Lord came forth from the clouds and three times distorted the figure of the cross, as the historians of Orléans report (Cardinal Saussay, Ecclesiastical Annals of Orléans, bk. II; Herard, capitulary 61; Capitularies of Charlemagne, bk. II, ch. 39).

This addition corresponds to the conclusion of Herard of Tours: “and those whose bodies and due veneration are celebrated in the individual places.” It is expressed more fully in the capitulary: “and we have decreed that the feasts of those martyrs or confessors whose holy bodies rest in each parish be observed.”

Since the piety of our kings has enriched all Gaul with many relics of the saints, they considered it right that the saints be venerated wherever they had deigned to pass. The feast of Saint Benedict is mentioned here for no other reason than that his body was buried, after its translation, in the monastery of Fleury in the Diocese of Orléans, as Charles Saussay recounts and proves in his Ecclesiastical Annals of Orléans (bk. IV; Marculf, Formulas, solemn formula 33).

This is why in Marculf’s formulas, the letter of safe conduct granted to traveling monks or clerics begins as follows: “I, in the name of God, bishop or abbot of that city or of that monastery where the precious martyr or confessor of Christ rests in the body.”] Besides, the feasts of our fathers, through whose pious patronage with the Lord we, their neighbors, are aided: the departure of Blessed Evurtius, the departure of Blessed Anianus, and likewise the departure of Blessed Benedict, Blessed Maximinus, and Blessed Lifardus; the Finding of the life-giving Cross and the Exaltation of that same vivifying Cross.

## CHAPTER XIX. [Col. 0743A] That those who come together for a synod must not litigate.

(Council of Nicaea, Arabic canon 7; Council of Antioch, canon 20.) When they are summoned to a synod twice a year, as the sacred canons teach inviolably, let them have their secular complaints and disputes over debts settled and reasonably resolved before their elder brothers or before their archdeacons, so that at that time no lawsuits or quasi-forensic complaints of accusers and defendants are brought forward, but only matters pertaining to the sacred ministry are discussed, so that we may either learn something or teach one another.

## CHAPTER XX. On learning by heart the rites of the sacraments and the ecclesiastical orders [Col. 0743B] and reciting them before the bishop.

Let each priest learn by heart the sacraments that must be administered for initiating a Christian through baptism, those involved in visiting and reconciling the sick, those required for the burial rites of the dead, and the canons [Note: [Col. 0743B] So that they may recite and explain them by heart before us. He requires two things of priests. First, they must learn by heart whatever is necessary for administering the sacraments properly and recite it before the bishop as evidence of their memory. Hincmar requires the same (Capitularies of the Year 852, chs. 3–4), but does not impose the necessity of reciting it before the bishop: “Let him commit it distinctly and reasonably to memory.” He adds shortly afterward: “Let him likewise learn by heart the prayers appropriate to the same requirement.”

Second, they must interpret and explain these ceremonies clearly and intelligibly, in a manner suited to the understanding of the people, and provide evidence of this before the bishop. Theodulf of Orléans, as though he considered all these matters already available to everyone, asks those who come together for something else, one especially fitting both their office and his own (Letter to the Clergy, ch. 28):

“When, with the Lord’s help, we have assembled together in synod, let each of us be able to say how much he has labored with the Lord’s assistance, or what fruit he has gained. And if anyone happens to need our help, let him admonish us with charity, and we likewise will not delay in offering him whatever assistance we can, with charity.”

Herard also established an excellent order for the synod: first examining matters common to the whole Church, and then private matters, which are ordinarily personal (Capitularies, ch. 1):

“Let general matters, which pertain to the rule of the whole Church, be settled first in the synod; afterward let particular matters be examined.”

Happy were the times when such discussions supplied the material of synods in charity.] so that they may recite and explain them by heart before us [Col. 0744A]. Let them likewise commit the ecclesiastical orders to memory. Let them know how each order originated in the Old Testament, how the New Testament corresponds to it, and how the Savior fulfilled these same orders in himself; and let them be able to explain all this with sound understanding.

## CHAPTER XXI. That they present only worthy students for the ecclesiastical orders.

Whenever priests offer any of their students for promotion to any order, they must, as fitting witnesses to the candidates’ approved life, present them instructed in the sacraments and orders specified above, so that they may both retain them by heart and know how to explain them intelligently.

## CHAPTER XXII. [Col. 0744B] On learning computation.

(Capitularies of Charlemagne, bk. VI, ch. 226.) [Note: [Col. 0743D] That all priests should possess skill in calculation. It can scarcely be said with what diligence people of those times worked to ensure that priests knew ecclesiastical computation almost as well as the Lord’s Prayer and the Apostles’ Creed. Hence the strict command of the capitulary (Capitularies of Charlemagne, bk. VI, ch. 226): “Concerning computation: let all truly learn it.” Herard states the same briefly (Capitularies, ch. 125): “Let priests learn computation.” Hincmar does not omit it either (Capitularies of the Year 852, ch. 8): “Let him also be fully instructed in the necessary computation and in singing throughout the cycle of the year.” Hence the celebrated expertise in computation found in Bede, Rabanus Maurus, and others, which in that age appears to have constituted a considerable part of learning.] Let all priests possess skill in calculation and diligently train their own people in it.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That they not be ignorant of the canons.

(Ibid., bk. I, ch. 55.) [Note: [Col. 0743D] The sacred canons besides. Parish priests are certainly not compelled to commit all the canons of the Church to memory, but only those necessary for governing the people entrusted to them well and properly, just as every craftsman must know the instruments of his trade. This is how the command in the capitulary is to be understood (Capitularies of Charlemagne, bk. I, ch. 55), where bishops and priests are instructed, from the decretal letters of Pope Innocent I, “that no priest may be permitted to be ignorant of the institutions of the holy canons.”

For this reason, learned bishops, to spare their people labor and expense, gathered from the infinite harvest of canons certain small sheaves sufficient to commit to memory. The capitulary is full of decrees of councils and Roman pontiffs, which the most Christian emperors chiefly wished to restore to practical use.

Thus Herard of Tours says in his preface: “Since the sacred authority of the canons permits no priest to be ignorant of the canons, we have decided,” he says, “and likewise enjoined, that each person henceforth possess these brief and concise chapters, selected through the diligence of our labor.”

Thus at Rheims, “among the other most salutary admonitions, while Bishop Hincmar was treating of laws and ecclesiastical affairs (Capitularies of the Year 852), these matters were brought forward at the end, to be committed to memory and observed with the utmost care.”

Isaac of Langres says that, following the example of Boniface of Mainz, he was moved to prepare an abridgment of his canons. Theodulf also had his own collection prepared (Letter to the Clergy, preface; Hincmar, cited above, ch. 8): “Let them read these chapters, which he briefly arranged for the correction of life, continually and commit them to memory.”

Hincmar further orders every priest “to read and understand carefully the forty homilies of Gregory, so that he may recognize that he has been advanced in ecclesiastical ministry according to the model of the seventy-two disciples, and may thoroughly learn and commit to memory the doctor’s sermon on the seventy-two disciples whom the Lord sent to preach.”

Nor are bishops exempt from this care, if they heed the salutary counsel of the Third Council of Tours under Charlemagne (ch. 3):

“No bishop may be permitted, if it can be avoided, to be ignorant of the canons or of the Pastoral Book edited by Blessed Pope Gregory, in which each person ought continually to examine himself as in a kind of mirror.”

O what a time! O what customs, when such sacred things were sought in the assemblies of priests!] No priest is permitted to be ignorant of the sacred canons [Col. 0745A], nor to do anything that could be contrary to the rules of the Fathers.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That nothing be done against the canons.

Let no one be permitted to act in any way contrary to the statutes of the canons, since, as is stated in the second chapter of the decretal letter of Pope Zosimus (letter 1): “If anyone disregards the prohibitions, he shall be subject to the danger of his order.”

Therefore, most blessed Fathers and dearest sons, remain vigilant in all things, with the help of divine grace, lest through this series of chapters you incur any blameworthy fault by which—God forbid—you may be hindered by the snare of prohibition.

**In the year of the Lord 867. Rothadus II, Bishop of Soissons.**

[Col. 0745]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE ON ROTHADUS

(From *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX.)

[Col. 0745B] ROTHADUS II was ordained bishop in the year of Christ 822 or the following year, that is, thirty years before his deposition, as is clear from Letter 27 of Pope Nicholas the Great. He therefore succeeded Rothadus I of that name, not Absalon or Bertharius, who are not even listed in their proper place, but rather in catalogues of better standing. He governed the Church of Soissons when the relics of Saint Sebastian the martyr were brought from Rome in 815 by Abbot Hilduin and placed in the church of Saint Medard.

There were, moreover, serious hostilities between Rothadus and Hincmar, metropolitan of Reims; more about Hincmar’s actions may be found in Sirmond, volume III of the Councils. Rothadus attended the Council of Beauvais in 845, the Council of Paris in 846, the Council of Quierzy in 848, the Fourth Council of Tours in 849, the Second Council of Soissons in 853, and the Second Council of Verberie in the same year. He subscribed at Saponaria in 859 and, finally, at the Council of Tusey in 860.

When the Council of Senlis was assembled in 863, before a large number of bishops and under the presidency of Hincmar, who was hostile to Rothadus because of an old hatred—since Rothadus had, as Hincmar argued, unjustly deposed a certain priest caught in fornication—Rothadus himself was condemned and expelled from the episcopate. After he had immediately appealed to the Roman See, another was appointed in his place contrary to the canonical rules, and he was thrust into a monastery, while Hincmar prevented him by various stratagems from going to Rome.

This same prelate, a man of venerable old age, had always exercised his episcopal office commendably. Pope Nicholas testifies to this in the following words, in Letter 29 to Hincmar:

> “From the truthful report of many who grieve, we have learned that Rothadus, our brother and fellow bishop of the Church of Soissons, was attacked by Your Holiness on account of a certain priest who, because of the nature of his offense, had been deprived of his own office of honor three years earlier; and that, even after appealing—as is clearly permitted to him by the Fathers—to the Apostolic See, he has, what is a sacrilege, been stripped of the honor of the episcopate even in his absence and deported into exile, and remains to this day confined in a monastery. For this we groan and grieve exceedingly. For although, on account of his age, he ought to have been advanced with many honors, and although, for all the labors and services he had faithfully and usefully expended in the Church of God and likewise before the rulers of the world, he ought to have enjoyed greater dignity and at last remained at peace without anyone’s compulsion, now, on the contrary, he exists dishonored, and—to the injury of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose See he had appealed to—worn down by hunger and thirst and countless miseries, deposed and at the same time rejected. [Col. 0746B] We therefore expressly decree that, thirty days after this letter of ours has been delivered to you, you restore the aforesaid Rothadus completely to his former dignity.”

Nicholas also wrote back to the bishops of the Council of Senlis, rescinding its acts against Rothadus by apostolic authority. Concerning Rothadus’s misfortune he wrote as follows in Letter 33:

> “Let your experience know, dearest brother, that our apostolate has grieved deeply—indeed, continues to grieve—over your tribulations. But we trust that God’s mercy will soon come to your aid, and that it will lead you out of the lions’ den as it led Daniel. Meanwhile, the metropolitan and the other bishops who pronounced judgment concerning you have reported to us many things, in a lengthy account of their proceedings, about you and against you. But we ordered them to lead you out of the monastery and to present you honorably, coming with you. Therefore, dearest brother, strive as much as you can so that, once the king and the bishops have granted you permission, as we have decreed, to hasten to Rome, you do not delay coming immediately, in whatever way you can.”

Hincmar, therefore, together with the other bishops who had attended the Council of Senlis and had removed Rothadus from his episcopate by an unjust judgment and thrust him into a monastery, was moved by the admonitions and command of Pope Nicholas. At last they obeyed and released Rothadus from his bonds. For this reason Nicholas is read to have written various letters to King Charles, to Hincmar, to the Church of Soissons, and to others. He himself writes as follows in Letter 34 to the most holy Rothadus:

> “Let Your Holiness know that we sent a letter of reprimand on your behalf to Hincmar, venerable archbishop of the holy Church of Reims, because, after your appeal to the Apostolic See, he pronounced a sentence of deposition against you. But now the religious deacon Liudo has arrived, bringing with him letters from the king, Charles, and from Hincmar, which acknowledged that, by the king’s command, you had been brought out of monastic custody and entrusted to a certain bishop who was your friend.”

Rothadus, therefore, proceeding to Rome, was restored by the pope at the Roman Council on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, in the year 865. Anastasius the Librarian continues the account in his Life of Nicholas; it is worthwhile to quote his words:

> “Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, deposed Rothadus, bishop of the city of Soissons, who had appealed to the judgment of the Apostolic See, contrary to the regulations of the Council of Sardica, and ordered him to be kept in strict custody. When the most blessed pope had received three petitions from this deposed man pleading his innocence, he wrote to the archbishop, admonishing and commanding him by letter to send the deposed Rothadus to Rome, where he could be heard together with his representatives. But when he came to the city of Rome according to the command of the blessed pope, and remained there for about nine months, no one at all from the side of the accusers ever appeared to contend with Rothadus before the most holy prelate. Then, on the day of the vigil of the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ—the bishop of this Apostolic See customarily celebrated the offices of the Mass on that day, according to the usual custom, with the clergy and people in the basilica of the Mother of God at the Manger—the kindly pope, assembling everyone, publicly spoke about Rothadus in the ambo, explaining how he had been deposed after appealing to the Apostolic See and how, for so many months, none of his accusers had appeared in his presence. Finally, with the assent of the entire assembly of bishops, priests, and deacons, he decreed that Rothadus, who had been accused by no one for so many months and had appealed to the judgment of the Apostolic See lest he be deprived of his honor, was worthy to be clothed in priestly vestments. Once clothed in episcopal attire, Rothadus promised that he would answer his persecutors for all time.

> “Again, after waiting several days—specifically until the feast of the holy virgin Agnes, which falls on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February—no one appeared against Rothadus to dispute anything, although he had already been restored as bishop. The most blessed prelate therefore assembled with everyone in the basilica of that virgin outside the walls of the City, on the Nomentan Way. There Rothadus, in accordance with his plea and his promise—by which he had promised that he would answer his accusers at all times—handed a written petition to the supreme pontiff. By order of the distinguished prelate it was read aloud before many listeners, and the form of his restoration was also read out. After the consent of all had been given, the aforesaid Rothadus, now restored as bishop, solemnly celebrated the offices of the Mass in the church of blessed Constantia, beside the same basilica of the holy virgin, by decree of the most blessed prelate mentioned above.”

Rothadus himself clearly set forth the entire course of his controversy with Hincmar in the written petition of protest which, while residing in Rome, he presented to the supreme pontiff. It contains an account of his life and is preserved in volume III of Sirmond’s Councils. Then, furnished with apostolic letters, he returned to his own See. Nicholas wrote to Charles the Bald on his behalf, asking him to support the man lawfully restored and to order that his Church’s possessions be returned. Rothadus is praised as a bishop “pure in conscience, innocent in conduct, distinguished by the simplicity of a dove and the prudence of a serpent.” After his restoration he attended the Third Council of Soissons in 866 and likewise the Council of Troyes in 867. He died, renowned for his achievements in the episcopate, around the year 868.

[Col. 0747]

ROTHADUS, BISHOP: PETITION OF PROTEST WHICH HE PRESENTED TO POPE NICHOLAS AFTER HE HAD ALREADY WAITED SIX MONTHS IN ROME.

*(General Council, volume VIII, column 785.)*

[Col. 0747C] I, Rothadus, a sinner, of the Church of Soissons, having appealed to the Apostolic See and irregularly deprived of the episcopate, submit the mournful history of my calamities—not recounting everything I have suffered, which was perhaps impossible, and lest an excessively tedious narrative seem burdensome and unwelcome to your ears, most devout prelate.

The venerable metropolitan Hincmar, bishop of the holy Church of Reims, when certain occasions had arisen, contending against me with bitter hostility, had long harassed my insignificance with many and various troubles. I, for my part, endured him as far as I could, but I was entirely unwilling to comply with his wishes in matters which I judged contrary to the authority of the sacred writers.

When we bishops had assembled at the synod convened by order of the glorious King Charles for the benefit of the holy Church of God, and he, presiding as though he were lord and master of everyone and holding the upper hand, was hastening violently and rashly to hurl a sentence of condemnation against me, I hastened to appeal to this Apostolic See and to its apostolic prelate, the supreme guardian of the universal Church. Since he did not dare deny me this, although the holy synod had decreed it, he reluctantly gave his consent to my departure, fixing a specified number of days beyond which I was absolutely not to delay my journey.

[Col. 0748C] From there I returned at a hurried pace to our city and would not tolerate delay in the journey that was at hand. How glad I would have been if I had deserved to hasten to the threshold of the apostles, so that I might reach the sacred presence of my lord, so great a pontiff and most devoted father, the safest defender and protector of all who flee to him.

When the departure for the journey already prepared was imminent, almost at hand, I took care to send letters to my lord the king and to my archbishop, entrusting our Church to them and earnestly asking both of them, each according to his office, to take care of its governance until the most excellent prelate of the city of Rome should determine a lawful conclusion in my case.

I also sent letters to that former priest, for whose canonical deposition—because he had been caught in fornication—I was judged by my metropolitan to be cut off, asking that he too might come with me here before your hearing, lord pope, to be examined. I have copies of these letters in my possession and, if it pleases you, I shall offer them to Your Apostolate.

I also wrote certain chapters and sent them to one of our brothers and fellow bishops, conveying at the same time by the same bearer the letters which, as stated above, I had addressed to the aforementioned king and prelate. These chapters contained the following petition of mine, which was to be communicated to the other bishops who did not wish to participate in my condemnation: that they should be ready, as lovers and followers of brotherhood and charity, to defend and protect my welfare in accordance with the apostle’s commandment (1 Timothy 6).

But that like-minded brother of mine, to whom I had entrusted this responsibility for me, was absent at that time. Hincmar, nevertheless, immediately perceived what was happening. The lord king and that same prelate of mine were still staying in the same place, where, during one and the same delay, the letters of my insignificance and those chapters were presented, as has been reported.

Then Hincmar himself, the archbishop, carefully ordered the bearer of the writings to be investigated as to why he did not show them the documents which he had carried separately. Compelled to confess, he added in his reply: “Because the man to whom I was entrusted with delivering them,” he said, “is not present here at this moment.”

He did not stop until, after persuading the king, he suddenly had the priest—the very bearer of the letters—brought in against his will, as though a synod had been assembled from the bishops who were present. They began to question, strike, and press him from either side, standing in their midst, just as this had been cunningly devised by an ambush, so that he would quickly present the letters which Rothadus had sent through him to his metropolitan at the synod.

“I was not sent to the synod,” he said, “nor did I receive from Rothadus the bishop—whose cleric I am not—any letters to be returned to Hincmar.” When the priest was unwilling by any means to disclose the chapters, he nevertheless handed them over under the king’s orders and compulsion.

Immediately Hincmar asked the king to send Abbot Transulf to me. He reached our city with great speed and found me already prepared to undertake our journey.

[Col. 0749C] Then the abbot, standing in the church courtyard, publicly declared, in the king’s words and by the authority of Hincmar the archbishop, that no one whatsoever was to leave that city with me or accompany me on my intended journey to Rome.

“I shall certainly not do that,” I replied. “Rather, since I first appealed to the Roman pontiff, I shall not, with God’s help, delay the journey I have arranged.”

I was therefore amazed and astonished, wondering what such a change could mean and why they were delaying me on my journey. But for several days rumor was spreading that Hincmar the archbishop intended to say that, by writing certain chapters, I had requested that my judgment be reopened.

This is completely false. I neither sent those chapters to him, nor mentioned any such judgment in them, nor stated the names or even the number of the judges chosen according to the sacred canons.

I call God, the creator of all things, as witness that it never entered my thoughts to divert the appeal to this most exalted See toward any other course. Alas! The opportunity to depart was taken away, and I was held in the same city, surrounded by guards.

They therefore hastened to convene a synod. When it had assembled in the suburb of our city, the illustrious king was invited by the council. Hincmar the archbishop then sent three bishops to me, ordering me to come to the synod without delay.

I replied to them that I was not permitted to do so, and that I would not dare in any way to give assent to anyone situated nearby in prejudice to the holy Roman Church, the mother of all Churches, and to its most excellent ruler. I continually appeal to that supreme authority, which no one can contradict and which received such preeminence from the Lord Jesus Christ through the blessed apostle Peter.

I therefore seek the judgment of the See to which I have appealed, and I consent to be judged nowhere but at Rome, because it is an inverted order to place an inferior before a superior.

After hearing this, the men who had been sent reported back to the synod. They invited me again, a second and a third time in succession, but found me persisting in the same position.

Finally, they tried skillfully to persuade me, pledging their good faith that I would suffer no harm, or at least that I might meet and speak with the lord king at the nearby site of the synod. The brothers of our Church, the sons of our Church, also began urging me to present myself to the pious prince in my insignificance.

I consented and went to the place to which they were leading me, clothed in priestly vestments and carrying the holy Gospel and a piece of the holy Cross upon my breast. When they had brought me into a certain lodging outside the doors of the synod, separated from all our people, I earnestly requested through the deacon Leudo that the lord king grant me the opportunity to speak with him.

Out of his piety he immediately deigned to come to me, unworthy as I was, and listened to me graciously, but he was not permitted to heed me. For when I pleaded with him very earnestly and anxiously not to take away the freedom to go to Rome which he himself had granted me, and to honor the holy Apostolic See in its privileges, he replied that this specifically concerned my metropolitan and the holy assembly; he professed that he would humbly obey only the sacred admonitions and dispositions of the bishops. Then he immediately withdrew, went into the synod, and took his seat there.

Again they sent three bishops to me in succession. They strongly urged me to enter the synod and pressed me, now flattering, now threatening, in an attempt to turn me aside. But I strove with all my strength to persevere in accordance with the original intention of my wishes.

When they saw that I was unwilling to comply with their efforts, they barred the doors and shut me inside the same cell. I could not leave at all until they had reached a decision about me, a sinner, as some of them then wished.

My archbishop, for his part, tried as far as he could to carry out the purpose of his will. He became, without cause, my accuser, my witness, and my judge. Just as he blamed me in my absence as he wished, so he neither feared nor reconsidered judging me rashly.

Among the other false charges he brought against me, he especially insisted that I had unjustly deposed the priest whom I mentioned above. This is unquestionably false, as many competent witnesses—bishops, other clerics, and laymen—have known and continue to know.

Nevertheless, three years ago, without my consent or consultation, Hincmar had received that priest into his communion and ordered him to exercise the priestly office, contrary to the statutes of the canons, although he had been legally deprived of it by the judgment of thirty-three bishops. The priest whom I had kept substituted in the condemned man’s place for approximately three years, however, Hincmar had brought to himself by force, without my knowledge.

For when that priest was prepared on the Lord’s Day to celebrate the solemn offices of the Mass for the people in the church, men suddenly appeared there by order of the archbishop. By deceit they led the priest outside the basilica, seized him suddenly, and dragged him at an unremitting pace into Hincmar’s presence. Hincmar immediately ordered him to be excommunicated and thrust into prison; he then restored to a church in my diocese that deposed priest, mutilated in his genitals.

[Col. 0751B] Hincmar also charged me with the offense of defiance and obstinacy because I was disobedient to him in such matters. He wanted me to serve his wishes not as a brother and fellow bishop, but as his personal cleric.

Likewise, he accused me of scorning his requests because of my allegedly unwarranted appeal to the Apostolic See—or rather, something I did not believe, of acting against canonical institutions.

He attributed these and other charges to me in an equally false manner. But, with divine grace favoring me and mercy coming to my aid, they will be reduced to nothing like a spark of ash and will vanish like smoke, with you, most merciful lord and fellow angelic pope, cooperating and assisting through the merits of the apostles.

I do not excuse myself from my many sins, nor do I justify myself by my good deeds, since I know that countless things not good can be said about me. Nevertheless, those accusations which I see were maliciously devised for my condemnation I declare, with God as witness and judge—God who will judge the living and the dead—not to be true.

Finally, my aforementioned archbishop, as though triumphing like an emperor and issuing decrees like the supreme pontiff of the Church, after subjecting the humility of his brothers to his power and crushing it, fearlessly—and, as I believe, impiously—pronounced a judgment of deposition against me. He cared little that he might later have to render an account of it to anyone; trusting in himself, he acted as though he owed an account to no one.

This became sufficiently clear when, because I had offended him alone, he tried to demonstrate that I could be rescued by no one else’s help, and that it was wholly harmful to me that I hoped for and sought another source of protection.

And behold, three bishops whom Hincmar knew to possess this sort of simplicity, having received from my condemner himself a sentence of excommunication—or rather, of conspiracy—hurried violently to me, who was shut in. As they had been ordered, they brought me their message with tearful sighs.

[Col. 0752A] I immediately fell prostrate on the ground and prayed and adjured them by the name of the eternal God to desist from this judgment and not deprive me, as I continually requested, of permission to depart for Rome.

Then, at once, like attendants dealing with a robber, men laid hands on me and violently dragged me away to prison custody. How many injuries I suffered afterward, and how I was dragged from place to place, how greatly I was wearied by hardship—it is tedious and shameful for me to recount.

They were trying to force me into this, sometimes promising and guaranteeing certain honors—namely, one abbey—provided only that I subscribe to my own condemnation.

Meanwhile, a bishop was appointed to the chair of one who was still alive, although the sacred canons are clearly known to forbid this from ever being done after an appeal to the Roman pontiff.

Nor, holy father, were your commands conveyed in apostolic letters observed with due reverence, in the customary manner, or with proper attention. Indeed, let Your Holy Pastoral Care and Diligence deign to inquire what kind of testimony our Church gave on my behalf, undeservedly, when a crowd from our city and the surrounding region went out to meet your venerable legates, Radoaldus and John, and what they sought from them, with great shouting and many petitions, concerning their pastor.

They were strongly prevented from doing so by Bishop Erchanraus, my fellow diocesan, through severe threats and beatings, after the king’s and my archbishop’s prohibition had been announced forbidding them to presume to shout anything of this kind.

And now I, the least of all bishops—although in the Lord I am called by some not a bishop, but, in accordance with the blessedness of Your Paternity, a bishop—trusting greatly in the Lord, have chosen to flee to the excellence of your episcopate, most devout lord. Hoping for help from your magnificent goodness, I have fittingly come to the most sacred threshold of the holy apostles to obtain the assistance of your support.

Behold, for half a year now I have stood knocking at the door of apostolic mercy, prepared to give an account of everything falsely and unjustly charged against me; yet no one is present to raise any accusation against me.

And because I know that before Your Dignity I am neither able to present myself as a false man nor explain the causes of my case, nor plead my petitions as I ought, it remains for you, according to the wisdom granted to you from heaven, mercifully to complete what you have begun. Thus the rash may not boast that, on account of my lowliness and unworthiness, they have succeeded in weakening the rights of the Apostolic See and the force of the canonical statutes.

ANNO DOMINI DCCCLXVII. NICOLAS I, ROMAN PONTIFF.

[Col. 0753]

LIFE OF POPE NICHOLAS I.

*(In Mansi, Councils, volume XV, p. 144.)*

[Col. 0753A] Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0753B] Nicholas. In the year 858 of the Redemption of Our Lord, during the reigns of Louis II and the emperor Michael, Nicholas was raised to the Apostolic See. After the emperor Louis had greatly harassed Pope Benedict and his See through the schismatic antipope Anastasius, he venerated Nicholas with the greatest devotion, to the great astonishment of everyone and through God’s singular providence.

He sent legates to the Bulgarians, who had recently been converted to the faith of Christ, so that, as their king had requested, they might instruct them in Catholic teachings.

When Ignatius, patriarch of Constantinople, threatened Barda, the uncle of the emperor Michael, with excommunication because of incest committed with his daughter-in-law, Barda, through the authority of the emperor Michael, had Ignatius removed from his See. In his place Photius was installed. Photius had previously sought the honor of the patriarchate and had joined himself to the schismatic bishops against Ignatius. He was brought from the civil forum and secular military service and installed as patriarch, then consecrated by Gregory, bishop of Syracuse, who had previously been deposed by Ignatius.

For this reason a schism arose at Constantinople and in the neighboring cities: some defended the promotion of Photius, while others opposed it. Accordingly, the emperor took steps to have the pontiff send legates to settle the schism and confirm the deposition of Ignatius.

The pontiff did indeed send legates, both to investigate the case of Ignatius and report back to him and also to oppose the Iconoclasts, who at that time were powerful in Constantinople. Contrary to the pontiff’s command, the legates assented to the election of Photius. When they had returned to Rome, the pontiff, after examining the case and convening a synod, deposed them; he decreed that the deposition of Ignatius was unjust and that the ordination of Photius was null.

He also restrained the emperor’s audacity. The emperor, angered that Nicholas had condemned Photius and that the king of the Bulgarians had requested that legates be sent from the Roman Church to instruct him in the faith, had written insulting letters to the pontiff and, with Photius’s support, convened a conciliabulum against him.

We shall discuss the distinguished deeds performed under Nicholas concerning Photius and other matters below, in the notes on the councils held under Nicholas and Hadrian, so that we do not repeat the same things twice, to the reader’s annoyance. SEV. BIN.] was a Roman by nationality, the son of Theodore, a regionary, and he sat for nine years, two months, and twenty days.

From the beginning of his childhood, the distinguished deeds of this most blessed man shone forth for all to see, and he was renowned for his blameless conduct. He was so adorned by the beauty of sacred works that no game, nor anything dishonorable—as is customary for boys—gave him pleasure. He devoted himself to patience and sobriety, burning with humility and exceptional purity.

His father, who was a lover of the liberal arts and possessed a most noble lineage, imbued him with [pure—perhaps “all”—] elementary studies and life-giving religious practices, adorning him with literary studies and the finest arts. Thus no branch of sacred learning remained which he had not embraced inwardly and assimilated into his knowledge.

As he grew in bodily stature, so too he grew in wisdom. Renowned for modesty and adorned with spirit and knowledge, whenever he saw men of approved character, he immediately hastened to attach himself to them and rejoiced with them in what was good.

[Col. 0753B] Whenever he frequently visited, together with his prudent father, a certain most blessed man who preached many things to the faithful through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, that man declared that Nicholas would rise to a lofty position. Seeing the greatness of his inner beauty and the radiance of his mind’s sweetness, he brought him into the clerical order by this appointment, so that what he had perceived through divine prompting might be fulfilled in the future.

When Bishop Sergius heard that Nicholas had risen to the heights of distinguished service, he led him from his parents’ home, placed him in the patriarchium, and, through the grace of blessing, established him in the rank of subdeacon. Living there with marvelous discipline, Nicholas enjoyed a heavenly fervor.

After Pope Sergius had been taken from this corruptible life, Leo assumed the governance of the Roman Church.

[Col. 0754A] Seeing in Nicholas again and again the fruit of perseverance, Leo consecrated him deacon with immense affection. While Nicholas served in this order, such grace had been granted him from above that everyone could see him shining with the full perfection of his ministry. He was loved by the clergy, praised by the nobles, and magnificently loved by the common people.

When Pope Leo had died, Benedict, a man of wondrous blessedness and a most sacred pontiff, protected by heavenly aid, was placed over the Roman See. He joined Nicholas to his administration because he loved him more than his own relatives, so that he took pleasure in being without him for not even an hour.

Whatever he perceived to be suitable for the usefulness of ecclesiastical affairs, he promulgated with Nicholas and committed to a decision, observing the resources of his most prudent judgment and the clarity of his understanding. Through the diligence of both, he always made matters more useful by his efforts.

[Col. 0754B] At last Benedict was brought to the end of his life and drank the cup of precious death. While Nicholas was still a deacon, he carried Benedict on his own shoulders, together with the other deacons, all the way to the basilica of the most blessed apostle Peter, and with his own hands placed him in the tomb, revealing the reward of the affection he held for him and the integrity of his love.

At that time the unconquered Caesar Louis had departed from Rome. When he learned of Benedict’s death, he returned there in sorrow with all speed. The Romans, having lost so great a pastor, poured forth tears with the most mournful lamentation.

When the clergy, the nobles, and the class of the leading men had assembled, they devoted themselves to fasts, prayers, and vigils, beseeching the Lord with unceasing effort to deign to show them a man like the one they had lost, whom they might raise to the summit of the pontificate.

While these things were taking place, they assembled with the entire people in the basilica of the blessed confessor and pontiff Dionysius.

There, after conversing for some time, inflamed by a starry radiance, they unanimously decreed that Nicholas should be pontiff of the Apostolic See. They immediately hastened with swift steps to the hall of the prince of the apostles, Peter, where Nicholas had taken refuge and was hiding. For he said that he was unworthy to assume the governance of so great a regime.

Those present, however, making a rush and pulling him by force from the same basilica, brought him into the Lateran patriarchium amid sacred acclamations and placed him upon the apostolic throne. Later, he was led by groups of the most noble men and by the entire people into the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter and was consecrated in the presence of the Caesar. Raised to the Apostolic See, he became pontiff and blessedly celebrated the solemn offices of the Mass over the most blessed body of the apostle.

With dense ranks of nobles and people, accompanied by hymns and spiritual songs, he was led back again to the Lateran patriarchium. Finally, he was crowned. The City rejoiced, the clergy were glad, and the senate and the full body of the people celebrated magnificently, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

On the third day after his consecration, dining with Augustus, he shone in *ophistic* [perhaps *sophistic*] speech and, full of charity, feasted in Christ. When the arrangements for the banquet had ended, he rose and, kissing the Caesar as a special and exceedingly dear son, embraced him with immense affection.

After these events, the most serene emperor departed and established his residence at a place called Quintus. When the most blessed prelate heard this, compelled by the fullness of his affection and love, he hurried with the nobles and leading men of the Roman name to the same place.

When the most excellent Augustus saw him, he came forward to meet him. Caesar took in his own hands the bridle of the pontiff’s horse and, on foot, led it along for as far as an arrow’s flight extends.

Entering the imperial tent with him, they enjoyed wholesome conversation with one another, and, with the tables splendidly furnished with food, they took their meal together with particular cheerfulness.
