When they were satisfied and the tables had been cleared away, the most serene Caesar presented many gifts to the blessed prelate. After receiving them, Nicholas mounted his horse and tried to return to the place from which he had departed.

Trusting in his love for Nicholas, Augustus mounted upon the saddle of the imperial horse and proceeded with him, rejoicing in spirit. When they reached a certain spacious stretch of the road, the emperor dismounted and again, as we recalled above, drew the pontiff’s horse along. Drawing near to each other with the sweetest kisses, they congratulated one another with abundant [perhaps “radiant”] joy.

The Caesar, returning to his tent, resumed the journey he had begun. The prelate, surrounded by the most noble groups by whom he had been escorted, entered Rome and was magnificently honored by this loving company.

He was handsome in appearance, comely in form, learned in speech, humble in conversation, distinguished in conduct, devoted to fasting and divine worship, generous to the poor, a protector of orphans, a supporter of widows, and the defender of all the people.

But since we cannot commit to writing all that he accomplished in sacred works, let us return to the things he offered to holy places.

This most blessed prelate, filled with divine inspiration, made in the deaconry of Holy Mary, Mother of God and Our Lady, which is called *in Cosmedin*, one wholly silken textile, *stauraci* (cross-patterned), bearing a figured scene with two large lions.

There he himself made one white, rose-colored veil, decorated all around with Tyrian purple of remarkable size. In the aforesaid deaconry he offered one gilded *gabatha saxisc(a)* [a shallow basin or dish] of the purest silver, weighing two pounds and four ounces.

[Col. 0756A] In the basilica of the Savior, which took the name Constantiniana from Constantine’s name, he made crosses of the purest silver, which hang before the representation of the substance of the flesh of the same Lord Jesus Christ. In them, for the adornment of that church on feast days, the customary candles were set up, weighing four and a half pounds.

Likewise, in the basilica of the ever-virgin Mary, Our Lady, which is called *at the Manger*, he made one pair of low-set silver *canthari* [vessels], weighing eight pounds and four ounces.

The God-protected and most blessed pontiff, filled with heavenly favor, offered in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, his fosterer, one *gabatha* of the purest gold, weighing three pounds and eight ounces and adorned with precious gems.

He also made in the confession of that most sacred basilica one *jugulum* [ornamental furnishing or neck-shaped vessel] of the purest gold, weighing two pounds.

Likewise, in the aforesaid church he made six crosses of the purest silver, weighing together thirteen pounds and five ounces. In the same manner, in the basilica of the blessed Apostle, teacher of the nations, he made two crosses of the purest silver, weighing together four pounds. For in the basilica of Saint Lawrence the martyr, which stands outside the walls, he also made two crosses of the purest silver, weighing together four pounds.

In the first year of his pontificate, a certain golden crown, adorned with the most precious gems and weighing eight pounds and four ounces, was brought for the blessed pope himself; with great devotion he raised it above the most sacred altar of his basilica on golden chains. Moreover, in the aforesaid church of the apostle Saint Peter, his spiritual father, he made nine vessels of the purest silver, weighing altogether twelve and a half pounds.

This venerable and illustrious pontiff, protected by God, made in the principal church of the monastery of Saints Stephen and Silvester—which the late lord Paul, of blessed memory, had newly founded—called the church of Saint Dionysius, four curtains of *stauracium* [a precious textile], for the honor and glory of the sacred altar.

In the time of this illustrious pontiff, on October 30, in the eighth indiction, the river called the Tiber left its bed and spread across the lowlands. It swelled with an inundation of many waters and entered through the postern called Saint Agatha’s Gate in the city of Rome, at an hour of the day that had passed [the wording is uncertain]. Meanwhile, in some places it entered the church of Saint Lawrence called Lucina’s. From there it extended itself and entered the monastery of Saint Silvester, so that, because of the quantity of water, not one of the steps ascending to the basilica of Saint Dionysius could be seen, except the one at the top. From there it spread over the street called the Via Lata and entered the basilica of holy Mary, Mother of God, which stands there. The water rose so high that even the doors of that church could not be seen because of its depth. From there it rose through the streets and lanes as far as the Clivus Argentarius. Then, overflowing, it entered through the portico situated before the church of Saint Mark. From there, gathering force, it began to run down into the sewer beside the monastery of Saint Lawrence the martyr, called Pallacini. From that day onward the water gradually began to subside, and, after causing great damage, the river returned to its bed.

For it overturned houses and walls, laid fields waste, tore up crops, and uprooted trees. In the same way, in December, on the twenty-seventh day, the feast of Saint John the Evangelist, in the indiction already mentioned, the same river called the Tiber once again left its bed and entered the Roman city as above; everything occurred as described above.

In the same way, the illustrious and most blessed pontiff made in the monastery of Saint Valentine, situated in the territory of Narnia near Interamna, one *fundatum* vestment bearing a scene of lions and bordered with *myzinum* [a textile or ornamental edging].

Likewise, the venerable and illustrious pontiff prepared from its foundations for construction and restoration the aqueduct called the Tocia, which, having become exceedingly damaged over the course of many years, conveyed water by the *centenarium* [a conduit or measured channel] into the city of Rome.

Moreover, in the church of the same Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, called Cosmedin, he built a spacious and ample guesthouse, sufficiently distinguished, for the assistance and benefit of pontiffs, so that whenever it was appropriate, they might be most generously lodged there with all who serve them.

In the same way, in the church of the apostle Saint Peter, prince of the apostles and his spiritual father, he offered curtains for the presbytery arches, with a *chrysoclavus* [golden-purple ornamental band], bearing a scene with forty figures of lions. In the same place he presented a chain made by skilled workmanship of the purest silver, weighing four pounds.

Likewise, in the oratory of the holy Cross, situated within the basilica of the apostle Saint Peter, he made one silver vessel weighing two pounds. This most sacred pontiff also made in the basilica of the apostle Saint Paul, teacher of the nations, one silver candelabrum weighing two pounds and six ounces. Moreover, in the titular church of Saint Eusebius, confessor of Christ, he made above the ciborium a cross with a curtain of the purest silver, weighing four pounds.

During his pontificate, Michael, son of the emperor Theophilus and emperor of the city of Constantinople, sent gifts to the blessed apostle Peter out of love for the apostles, through bishops whose names are these: Methodius, metropolitan; Samuel, bishop; and two others who had been deposed from the episcopal dignity, named Zacharias and another Theophilus; together with another imperial layman named Arsavir [Lasavir], a *protospatharius*. The gifts included a paten of the purest gold with various precious stones—white, green, and hyacinth-colored. Likewise, a golden chalice surrounded with stones, with hyacinths hanging around it on golden thread, and two *repidia* [liturgical fans], in the form of peacocks, with shields and various precious stones, hyacinth-colored and white; these weighed altogether […] pounds.

Likewise, they sent a *chrysoclavus* vestment with white gems, bearing scenes of the Savior, the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and the other apostles, as well as trees and roses. On either side of the altar it displayed, in letters of the emperor’s name, inscriptions of marvelous size and beauty. After presenting many other gifts to the pontiff, the envoys immediately delivered the words of the embassy entrusted to them.

The emperor of the Greeks, having found a pretext on behalf of the removers of the sacred images, requested that envoys of the Apostolic See be sent to Constantinople through the aforesaid legates. He was ostensibly bringing forward the case of Ignatius, the patriarch, and of Photius, the usurper of the Church of Constantinople; for, as later became clear, he cunningly desired to condemn that same holy man Ignatius through the judgment of the Apostolic See, out of envy, and to install the neophyte Photius in that Church.

Then the supreme pontiff, still unaware of the emperor’s most evil intention, sent two bishops there, namely Radoald and Zacharias. He ordered them to settle synodically whatever question might be brought forward concerning the sacred images, and only to investigate formally the case of the patriarch Ignatius and the neophyte Photius, and to report back to him.

How, and with what amount of insane money, they were corrupted there and acted in the manner of Vitalis and Mesinus [Misenius], despite disregarding the statutes of the holy pontiff, I shall briefly recount below.

Meanwhile, many people of Ravenna, who were suffering disadvantages in their affairs and in the property rights belonging to them from John, the archbishop of that city, came to this most blessed pope so that they might be rescued from such great oppressions. Hearing their cries with compassion, he repeatedly admonished the archbishop through his legates and letters to abandon such actions. But that man, in confusion of mind and despising the warnings of the pious Father, did not fear to add worse things to his former deeds. The more the supreme prelate’s kindly attention urged him to come to his senses, the more he turned toward the world’s worse ways. He did not cease adding iniquity to iniquity.

For he rashly excommunicated some, while turning others away from visiting the Apostolic See. He seized the property of certain persons without legal judgment. He also took away many estates belonging to the holy Roman Church. He scorned the pope’s envoys and, as far as lay in him, emptied the glory of the blessed apostle Peter. Whenever he found the privileges of Saint Peter, even in the possession of others, he broke them and transferred them to the jurisdiction of Saint Apollinaris. He deposed not only priests and deacons subject to himself but also those established throughout Emilia and belonging to the Apostolic See, without canonical judgment; some he caused to be thrust into prison and others into foul dungeons.

He compelled others to confess in writing crimes they had not committed. He also suppressed ecclesiastical institutions without the consent of the Apostolic See. When summoned by the supreme pontiff to Rome, he boasted that he ought not to appear at the synod.

Nor is it surprising that he later did these things, since at the beginning of his consecration, following the example of his predecessor Felix, he falsified the securities and little documents customarily kept in the chest by the archbishops of Ravenna, composing some barbarous writings and others that were outright false.

At that same time the aforesaid pope summoned him three times to the synod by his letters. When he contemptuously refused to come, he was deprived of communion by the holy synod. He then went to Pavia and brought his grievance to the ears of the emperor, Louis Caesar, seeking worldly aid. When the Augustus granted him distinguished envoys, he returned to Rome with them, filled with the swelling of pride.

But the kindly pontiff, because those envoys had communicated with the excommunicated man contrary to the rules of the sacred canons, gently rebuked them. When they lamented what they had done, the pope, preserved by God, sent word to the same archbishop that he should appear on the Kalends of November before the synod from which he had been excommunicated, demonstrate full satisfaction, and put an end to such great transgressions. But he refused and withdrew by turning back.

And behold, the people of Emilia and the senators of the city of Ravenna, together with an innumerable crowd, hastened with tears to the feet of this blessed Roman prelate. They begged him, in imitation of our Lord Jesus Christ, not to disdain going to Ravenna for their recovery, so that, after examining everything, he might lead them to complete freedom.

Accordingly, the most blessed pope himself proceeded to Ravenna. When the archbishop John learned of his arrival, he immediately set out for Pavia again, to trouble the emperor’s ears.

Then the excellent prelate mercifully restored to all the people of Ravenna, Emilia, and the Pentapolis the properties they had lost when the archbishop John and his brother Gregory seized them, by a decree of his own command, which he delivered and confirmed.

When the aforesaid archbishop arrived at Pavia, his fellow citizens there, together with their bishop Luithard, consecrated by the Roman pontiff, heard that this archbishop had been excommunicated by the supreme pontiff. They then placed themselves under such strict vigilance that they would neither receive him into their houses nor allow anything to be sold to his people, lest through such commerce they should even appear to share in their conversation and thereby incur the mark of excommunication.

Rather, whenever they saw some of the archbishop’s attendants walking through the streets, they shouted: “These men are among those who have been excommunicated; it is not lawful to associate with them.”

When the archbishop saw that he could not thereby accomplish the schemes of his will, he repeatedly asked to be assisted by the emperor. Through an intermediary the Augustus sent him this message: “Let him go, and, laying aside the arrogance of his pride, humble himself before the pontiff to whom we and the whole Church submit; let him bow his neck to obedience and subjection, because he will be unable to obtain what he desires in any other way.”

When the archbishop heard this, he began to be anxious. Again, after urgently requesting imperial envoys, he came to Rome. But the most blessed pope, learning what had happened, despised all his arrogance as a spider’s web and remained steadfast in the sentence previously pronounced; he was immovable.

Nevertheless, when the most holy pope was dealing with the imperial envoys, he spoke to them with great gentleness as follows:

“If our beloved son, the lord emperor, knew well the actions and character of this archbishop John, he would not merely refrain from asking us on his behalf; he would even send him to us, against his will, so that he might correct himself.”

Then, as that distinguished pope had decreed, many bishops of the provinces assembled together, and he sent word to the same archbishop that he should appear before him, make the fullest satisfaction for himself, and correct more suitably the matters in which he had transgressed.

When the archbishop heard this repeated three times and saw that no one could help him, he withdrew inwardly into the lamentation of anguish and extreme distress. He appealed with tears to everyone he could, saying: “Have pity on me, I beg you; have pity on me. Ask the supreme prelate’s mercy, that he may have compassion on me; for behold, I am ready to do everything he commands.”

Some people, seeing and hearing this, reported it to the supreme bishop and fully explained the appeals he made in a voice of lamentation. Then the most compassionate pope, imitating the Lord who does not desire the death of a sinner, moved by mercy, resolved at last to receive the aforesaid archbishop, who had turned toward the path of humility.

Immediately, taking up the parchment containing his promises and oaths—the writings that he had filled, at the time of his consecration, with incomplete and confused expressions, as they appeared in them—he composed them with his own hand according to the custom of his predecessors.

He climbed to the house called Leoniana, where the most blessed prelate sat surrounded by bishops, priests, nobles, and many distinguished men. He placed the writings he had prepared upon the life-giving cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, upon his sandals, and upon the sacred book of the four holy Gospels. Holding them in his hand, he freely swore aloud, before the countless people who had assembled, that throughout all the days of his life he would faithfully observe and fulfill everything contained and written in those writings of his response.

He also read them aloud himself before everyone and handed them to the supreme prelate.

When this had been done, the eminent and distinguished pontiff descended the following day with all the bishops and the entire clergy into the basilica of the Savior, called the Constantiniana. There, at the command of the supreme pontiff, the aforementioned archbishop appeared and cleared himself of the charge of heresy brought against him.

The pope restored him to communion and kindly granted him permission to celebrate the solemn rites of the sacred Mass. On the following day, while the same supreme and universal pope presided in that same Leoniana house and the most holy college of priests and fellow bishops sat according to custom, the archbishop appeared and, at the command of the supreme prelate, took his seat.

Then the bishops of Emilia came forward, submitting written complaints against the same archbishop John and stating that they suffered many prejudicial acts and exactions imposed by him. Some people of Ravenna and Emilia also testified to the same things. Anyone who investigates can find them in the records lying in the library.

Hearing this, the pontiff protected by God, together with the holy synod, declared that such acts were contrary to ecclesiastical rule. He decreed, with the holy synod acclaiming that it must be done, that all these transgressions should be corrected by gentle speech, lest the Lord’s flock entrusted principally to him be abandoned through negligence to be torn by wolves’ bites.

“Nevertheless, O archbishop John,” said the distinguished prelate, “so that everything now being reported may more easily be corrected by specific remedies, we command you, removing every excuse except serious bodily illness that entirely prevents you from coming, to make the effort to hasten to the Apostolic See once in every year, unless perhaps you receive permission from the Apostolic See to delay.

“Likewise, we decree that you shall not consecrate bishops throughout Emilia unless, after the election of the duke, clergy, and people, you have received by letter from the prelate of the Apostolic See permission to consecrate them. You shall in no way prevent those bishops whenever they wish to come to the Apostolic See. Nor shall you ever demand from them any payment that the sacred canons do not prescribe.

“We further command that you shall in no way compel those bishops to present or pay to the church of Ravenna the bad custom that some call the *tricesimalis*, nor shall you in any way attempt to exact from them any practice contrary to the privileges of bishops.

“Nevertheless, we command you never again to seize the property of any person, however it may have been acquired and possessed in the past, by whatever device or document, nor to impose a title upon it, until you have legally convicted the persons in the presence of the Apostolic See, or of its envoy, or of your own representatives at Ravenna.”

When the blessed pope had imposed and commanded these things for the archbishop John to observe, the holy synod rose and acclaimed three times:

“Right is the judgment of the supreme prelate; just is the decision of the universal shepherd of the Church; the wholesome instruction of Christ’s disciple pleases everyone. We all say the same; we all understand the same; we all judge the same.”

Then, after both the archbishop and the entire holy synod had been nourished by the food of the sacred word and satisfied by the sweetest nectar of the blessed prelate’s teaching, each person, having received the pontiff’s permission, departed for his own place.

At the same time, this distinguished pope, preserved by God, made in the church of blessed Mary, Mother of God, called Cosmedin, a *scalpi* […] of the purest silver, weighing five pounds and two ounces. Moreover, in the titular church of Vestina, he made an icon of the represented figure of the blessed martyr Vitalis, weighing four and a half pounds.

He also made in the basilica of the blessed martyr of Christ, Anastasius, four curtains of *blattinum* [purple cloth], surrounding the sacred altar with a *periclysis* [ornamental border].

In the basilica of the apostle Saint Peter, in the oratory of Pope Saint Gregory, he offered three *fundatum* vestments, ornamented around the edges with *oloverum* [a fine textile].

This most blessed and distinguished pontiff offered, with a pure heart, in the church of the apostle Saint Paul, teacher of the nations, a vestment of marvelous beauty woven with gold and bordered with hyacinth-colored, white, and green gems, together with carbuncle stones. There also he made and offered two curtains woven with gold in the same manner, with gems.

The church of Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin, which had first been called the Old Church and was then called the New, had been built from its foundations by Pope Leo IV, but he had not decorated it with paintings. This most blessed prelate had it painted in beautiful and varied colors, increasing its splendor, and adorned it with many objects from a pure heart.

As I mentioned a little earlier, a certain schism had grown in the holy Church of Constantinople. After the most reverend patriarch Ignatius had been expelled from the see of that Church, they suddenly installed in his place Photius, a layman tonsured from military service, as a neophyte bishop, contrary to the statutes of the venerable canons.

Because Michael, emperor of the Greeks, was attempting through denunciation of Ignatius, the patriarch of Constantinople—whom they had praised with encomiums during the time of Pope Leo IV—and through lavish praise of Photius the usurper, to persuade the Roman See to send its envoys there to investigate the allegations, he humbly consulted this blessed and illustrious pope through Arsavir the *spatharius*, his envoy, and by his letters.

Since the supreme prelate desired that ecclesiastical rigor should remain unimpaired, he did not refuse to have this done, wishing to tear out the heaps of weeds by the roots, lest through negligence any blemish should grow in the holy Church of God.

Then he sent from his own side two bishops, Radoald, bishop of Porto, as stated above, and Zacharias of Anagni, whom he judged suitable for this work. He ordered and instructed them to investigate only the reason for Ignatius’s expulsion and Photius’s installation, and to report back to him. Meanwhile, they were to avoid communion with Photius the neophyte until they had returned and taken care to give a definite answer about everything.

But after departing, they disregarded what they had been commanded. Not only did they communicate with Photius the neophyte, contrary to the sentence forbidding them to do so; corrupted by gifts, they also supported him and his consecration and, having convened a general synod, deposed that same man Ignatius the patriarch again. This can readily be found in the records compiled by them at Constantinople; it also remained reliably established through the envoys—namely Leo the *a secretis* and others—and through the aforesaid emperor’s letter.

When the envoys returned, they extolled with many praises what they had done in the case of Photius and condemned with many objections those who had wickedly acted against the patriarch Ignatius.

The rector and prince of the whole Church, the eminent and discerning prelate of the Apostolic See, considered these matters at Rome with holy attention. But when he heard what had been perpetrated contrary to his decision, he did not believe it until he had scrutinized everything according to the mystical meaning of his wisdom.

Meanwhile, he composed letters of his sacred authority both to Michael, the emperor of the Greeks, and to Photius himself—letters kept in the archive of this see—and gave them to Leo the *a secretis*, instructing him that he would consent neither to the deposition of the patriarch Ignatius nor to the installation of Photius until, after the truth had been ascertained, the legitimate case received its conclusion before him.

While some said that this had been the prelate’s decision and others acclaimed that Ignatius had been unjustly deposed, that same supreme pontiff continually prayed for heavenly judgment, asking that, through God’s mercy, it might be revealed to God’s Church that he had not consented to such actions, for nothing hidden is concealed from God.

Then, relying on divine zeal, he summoned a council of bishops. In it it was made abundantly clear that he had not consented to Ignatius’s deposition and that the envoys of the Apostolic See had gone astray in these matters.

Finally, by the decree of that same most pious prelate together with the holy synod, the aforesaid bishop Zacharias, who was then present, was deprived of priestly rank—indeed, of ecclesiastical communion—just as the blessed pope Felix had deprived the bishops Vitalis and Misenus, who, though compelled, had assented to Peter of Alexandria, defiled with heretical filth; for Zacharias was found to have exceeded the apostolic prohibitions in many respects.

The case of Bishop Radoald was suspended. Later, together with the holy synod, the pious pope condemned him as well, because he had violated the pope’s commands even in Gaul, broken excommunication, and evaded canonical judgment.

Thus that distinguished man and pontiff of holy zeal ordered that a certain deacon named Pompon, whom Bishop Pandulf had unjustly deposed while appealing to the Apostolic See, be restored to his office. Since he had been judged without a fixed number of bishops, indeed without proof of a crime, and the deacon himself without an oral profession, he annulled the entire sentence of judgment and, through apostolic piety, brought the case back to the path of justice.

While this outstanding prelate was governing the apostolic summit, Louis Augustus presented these gifts to the apostle Saint Peter, namely [Note: [Col. 0761D] Something appears to be missing here.].

The same most merciful pontiff was so diligent in keeping watch over the Lord’s flock that whenever some scandal arose in the holy Church, he granted neither rest to his body nor sleep to his limbs until peace had been restored through his envoys or letters and the people had recovered the benefit of tranquility.

For King Lothair, having abandoned Queen Theutberga and carnally taken his concubine Waldrada in marriage, although he had consulted the Roman See and that same pious pontiff about these matters, was wallowing in the rottenness of lust and the wantonness of the flesh.

As the supreme pontiff considered within himself how he might drive this evil from the Church of God, lest that king infect others with the plague of this disease, he began to suffer for a very long time. Grieving in his inmost heart, he lamented these errors greatly.

This was especially so when he heard that Theutgaud, archbishop of Trier, and Gunther, archbishop of Cologne, together with Hagano of Bergamo and the other bishops, had granted that king such authority that he could more freely reject Theutberga and lawfully take his concubine Waldrada as his wife.

The most blessed prelate discovered that those whom he ought to have had before God as helpers and guides were themselves, by granting this supposed authority to perpetual fire, traitors. Therefore, without delay, he sent his envoys to Francia, instructing and warning them that, once a synodal assembly had been gathered in the city of Metz, they should inquire why that king rejected Theutberga [alternate: Thietberga] or joined Waldrada to himself in marriage. After investigating and discovering the facts, they were to bring the matter to a legitimate conclusion.

When the envoys of the Apostolic See arrived there, they began to examine the case and heard Lothair say, among other things: “Whatever I have done, I have done on the advice of these bishops.”

The principal men present were the aforementioned archbishops Theutgaud and Gunther. The holy pope had already discovered that they were the authors of so great a crime. They asserted and declared that the union which King Lothair had contracted with the concubine Waldrada was a lawful marriage, and they promised that they could defend what they had said when they came before the distinguished lord pope.

Although the envoys of the Apostolic See had been deceived in many respects, they turned back toward Rome and reported to the supreme pontiff what they had heard and learned from the king and from the archbishops Theutgaud and Gunther.

While the most pious prelate awaited the arrival of the archbishops, behold, by the direction of heavenly mercy, Theutgaud and Gunther came to the city of Rome and requested to be presented at the sacred feet of this prelate.

The outstanding prelate received them kindly. They offered him a written statement, saying that they had done neither more nor less than the statement itself declared. When he examined it most carefully, he found in it not a few matters containing the obscenity of profane and unheard-of language. Since these exceeded the episcopal order, they bound the archbishops as though they were madmen.

Finally, when a synod had been convened afterward in the Lateran palace beneath the apostles, those same archbishops were found, as stated above, to have incurred the mark of condemnation, especially because they openly proclaimed themselves to have been the authors of so great a divorce.

They also did not deny, but loudly declared, that they had dissolved the sentence which the pope had pronounced against Ingiltrude, the wife of Boso, who had abandoned her husband Boso for seven years. She had been excommunicated, bound, and anathematized by the pious pope of the supreme see, yet had taken care to return to him; nevertheless, they had communicated and associated with her, indeed even spoken with her. Furthermore, as is shown by the badly composed records kept in the archive of this see, they had falsified the pious pontiff’s letter at their pleasure.

Then, when that holy prelate judged and decreed together with the synod, they were deprived of their priestly honor and deservedly incurred the penalty of deposition.

At this synod the kindly prelate immediately annulled the synod of Metz, where those records had been drawn up against the will of God and against his own will, and promulgated certain necessary chapters for the holy Church.

After these things had been completed, the already mentioned Bishop Hagano was involved as well. As certain bishops wrote to that prelate, his fellow servant, he was called “Heliu” because of the inept speeches that sounded in the profane records presented by Theutgaud and Gunther; Hagano himself had been the author of those records and had composed such things together with the same archbishops in unsuitable and lying language.

John, whose memory the preceding text mentions, was also summoned—the archbishop together with his full brother Gregory—and they were held liable for many transgressions, having forgotten the oath which they had sworn.

Those who had been deposed did not seek penitential lamentation and still did not grieve for the great offense they had committed against the wife of King Lothair. Together with the same Hagano, John the archbishop of Ravenna, and his brother Gregory, they began openly and secretly, fraudulently and arrogantly, to commit many abominable, many hostile, and many sacrilegious acts against the Roman See—indeed, especially against the supreme pontiff—and against the people subject to him, entrusted by the Lord Jesus Christ through the blessed apostle Peter, the keeper of the kingdom of heaven.

Their wickedness crossed mountains and seas. Setting their mouths against heaven, they cruelly tore apart the Lord’s people and deceived innocent souls through a viperous conspiracy. The evils of the past were not enough for them: at the devil’s urging, they did not refuse to commit other new and unheard-of acts, worse than those before. For they dared boldly to touch what had been expressly forbidden to each of them and synodically prohibited according to the nature of their crimes; and, despising God, alas, to their shame, they carried out what no one ought to attempt.

This friend of Christ kept written by him the names of all the lame, blind, and completely disabled people living in the city of Rome, and diligently provided them with their daily food.

For the other poor who had the ability to walk or possessed bodily strength, he wisely devised a way to feed them in turn. Specifically, he ordered tokens bearing his name to be made and commanded that they be given to them. By the sign of these tokens it could more easily be known how many were to dine on the first day of the week, how many on the second, how many on the third, and on the remaining weekdays.

On the tokens given to those who were to be fed on the first day of the week, he had two knots made on each one, and so on through Saturday, so that the number of knots on each token equaled the number of the weekday. He enclosed walnuts within the places where the knots were made, so that no poor person in the City would go even one day in the week without being fed from his alms.

Meanwhile, King Charles offered the holy apostle Peter a vestment made of the purest gold and gems, bearing green, hyacinth-colored, and white gems.

The most holy and radiant pontiff, grieving that the people were oppressed by so many calamities, invoked God alone with countless prayers and praised him with endless acclamations. Yet he did not abandon care for God’s churches; rather, amid tribulation and temporal trial, he increased it appropriately.

For he renewed the sacristy in the basilica of Mary, Mother of God, called Cosmedin, and there built a dining hall of beautiful design with fireplaces, for its honor and adornment.

In the same way, renewing the portico beside that sacristy, he constructed and built there an oratory in honor of Saint Nicholas, and the kindly pontiff bestowed many gifts there.

He also renewed the cemetery of the martyr Saint Felix and the shrine at the Via Portuensis. Likewise, at the cemetery on the same road, at Ursus Pileatus, where the bodies of the holy martyrs of Christ, Abdon and Sennen, rested, he restored the place, which had already fallen into ruins, with beautiful and wondrous dignity.

On the Appian Way, in the cemetery of the holy martyr of Christ, Sebastian, at the Catacomb, where the bodies of the apostles had lain and which had fallen into ruin over many years, he renewed it with better construction, established a monastery, gathered monks from wherever he could under the rule of an abbot, and ordered that the necessities of their sustenance and other stipends be provided.

Therefore, during his time, when many people hastened to the renown of his holiness, certain men from the English nation came to Rome. In the oratory of Pope Saint Gregory and confessor of Christ, constructed within the sacred building of the prince of the apostles at Frascati, they placed a silver panel weighing […] pounds.

The aforementioned most merciful pontiff had five hangings made of *fundatum* cloth in the church of the most blessed apostle Peter, keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom. These hangings, suspended above on the beams within the vestibule of so great a building for the adornment of the basilica, he caused to be decorated all around with the finest *oloverum*, and he bestowed them for the palm of eternal life.

In the time of this most blessed prelate, consultations from so many and such great provinces were directed to the Apostolic See—once the doctrine of his distinguished teaching had become known, clearer than daylight—that no one at all can recall such a number having reached it from ancient times. As an inspired prelate, he abundantly refreshed each person with the nourishment of the sacred word; he imparted mystical precepts and laws, satisfied them with blessed instruction, taught them, and sent them back to their own places blessed and instructed. Whatever he learned or heard was being done wrongly in any way, he preferred to correct solely out of regard for God. He devoted himself to profound laments and unending prayers, so that almighty God, through his mercy, might alter such conduct by good and excellent examples as though it had never existed.

Thus, when a report arrived from the island of Sardinia—he also recognized it through his household servants, who were Sardinians by origin—it was reported to him in these words: the judges of that island, together with the people subject to their government, were contracting incestuous and unlawful unions with their nearest and blood relatives, just as they had been accustomed to do in the time of Lord Pope Gregory IV.

Then, taught by the Holy Spirit, he composed honey-sweet yet terrifying letters of his preaching, which shone throughout the whole world, against the transgressors. He summoned and sent there two capable envoys, Paul, bishop of Populonia, and Saxo, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saints John and Paul, so that they might recall that Sardinian people from so great an error. When they went there, they found some of them strongly opposed and unwilling to accept the admonitions of discipline. Nevertheless, by the authority of the supreme prelate’s command, they excommunicated and anathematized the Sardinians who heard them, until they fled from the evil of these incestuous unions and sought the remedies of penance, as is contained in the letters that those same envoys had carried to Sardinia and that are included in the register of that prelate. Thus, after delivering abundant preaching, they returned to Rome.

[Col. 0764B–D]

Furthermore, a certain Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, deposed Rothad, bishop of the city of Soissons, although he had appealed to the judgment of the Apostolic See, contrary to the canons of the Council of Sardica, and ordered him to be held in close custody. When the thrice-blessed pope had received petitions from the said deposed man pleading his innocence, he admonished that archbishop by letter and ordered him to send the deposed Rothad to Rome with his envoys, so that the case might be heard.

When Rothad came to this Roman city in accordance with the blessed pope’s command and remained there for approximately nine months, no one at all from the accusers’ side appeared to contest the matter with Rothad before the most holy prelate or to accuse him. Therefore, on the day of the vigil of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, when—according to the customary practice of this Apostolic See—the prelate ordinarily celebrated the offices of the Mass with clergy and people in the basilica of the Mother of God at the manger, the kindly pope, having assembled everyone, publicly delivered a discourse about Rothad in the ambo. He explained how Rothad had been deposed after appealing to the Apostolic See and how, for so many months, none of his accusers had appeared in the pope’s presence.

Finally, with the consent of the bishops, priests, deacons, and the entire assembly, he decreed that Rothad—who had been accused by no one for so many months, had appealed to the judgment of the Apostolic See, and therefore should not be deprived of his honor—was worthy to be clothed in priestly vestments. Once Rothad had been clothed in episcopal attire, he promised that he would answer his adversaries at all times. Several more days were then awaited, namely until the feast day of the holy virgin Agnes, which falls on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February. But even then no one appeared to dispute anything against Rothad, who had now been restored as bishop.

When the most blessed prelate therefore assembled with everyone in the basilica of that Virgin outside the city walls on the Nomentan Way, Bishop Rothad handed the supreme pontiff a petition of defense and promise, in which he had promised that he would answer his accusers at all times. By order of the distinguished prelate, it was read aloud before all who were listening; the form of his restoration was also read out there. After the consent of everyone had been obtained, the aforementioned Rothad, now restored as bishop, solemnly celebrated the offices of the Mass in the church of Saint Constance beside the basilica of the same holy virgin, by decree of this most blessed prelate.

On the following day, a synod was again assembled in the house called the Leoniana. After Rothad had made his defense—as is recorded in the petitions acknowledged by him, inserted in two quires, sent and presented at different times, and preserved in the archive of this See—he was restored to his former rank, so that priests, and especially those appealing to the Apostolic See, would not thereafter suffer such dangers. As stated above, he was restored to his former rank and sent back to his own see with apostolic sanctions, so that, clothed in episcopal insignia, if challenged, he might henceforth answer his accusers before the prelate of the Apostolic See.

Together with him, the most holy prelate, preserved by God, immediately sent Arsenius, bishop, apocrisiarius and envoy of this gracious Apostolic See, both for Rothad’s restoration and for the dissolution of King Lothair’s union, as well as for preserving peace and concord among the kings of Gaul. He was to join them without resistance to the bosom of holy Church once peace had been restored, and to carry out with greater care and abundance certain necessary measures established in the Church of Gaul according to apostolic tradition.

[Col. 0765A–C]

Likewise, through his envoys, the same pope restored to his see Seufred, prelate of the See of Piacenza, who had been driven from his own see through the treachery of a certain deacon named Paul. He rebuked and disciplined that same deacon, who had dared to invade the see while its proper ruler was still alive, together with his followers, by an appropriate reprimand.

To eradicate completely this ill-omened and criminal presumption, he ordered—with the zeal of holiness and for the peace of God’s Church—that the aforesaid deacon should neither ever again attempt such an act nor presume to reclaim or accept the see of Piacenza, whether Seufred lived or died as bishop.

For this distinguished and illustrious pontiff, with piety as his guide, foresaw the sufferings and needs of all. Compassionating everyone mercifully, he swiftly came to the aid of the needy, and, in imitation of our Lord Jesus Christ, who descended from the heights to the depths in order to redeem the human race, he endured immense labors for the people.

Accordingly, when he saw the lame and blind, as well as those afflicted by various sufferings, lying in the portico of the blessed apostle Peter along the bank of the Tiber, unable to make their way to obtain relief from thirst, and when he divinely considered the welfare of the various peoples who came from every direction to seek the Apostolic threshold on account of their sins, he did not spare his own body. He ordered the aqueduct, which had collapsed many years earlier and consequently no longer brought water to the blessed apostle Peter, to be restored through the greatest possible effort to a better condition than before. Thus it benefited not only the physically disabled but also became a distinguished work for all who visited the church of the blessed prince of the apostles. Even to this day it is plainly visible and maintained as an adornment of the Leonine city.

[Col. 0765D–0766A]

Moreover, the most holy prelate, moved by heavenly inspiration, ordered the city of Ostia to be rebuilt with stronger and firmer construction. The blessed Pope Gregory of revered memory had built it for the salvation of many, so that the wicked Saracen people might not surround or kill the Lord’s people; but it was now lying in ruins. He restored it to a better state, fortifying its gates in very strong towers and stationing in it men ready for battle, so that no invasion by a foreign people could thereafter dominate it or inflict any harm upon its inhabitants—unless, God forbid, through negligence.

[Col. 0766B]

Meanwhile, as the merits of this most blessed man were everywhere overflowing, almighty God’s power at work—for he daily performs great signs and wonders through his servants—Michael, king of the Bulgarians, recognizing the teaching of Christianity and the holy faith, deserved to be baptized. He had previously raged with cruelty in servitude to creation; but in this pontiff’s time, submitting his neck to the Creator, he began to command with expansive religious devotion and displayed great piety.

Then, in the month of August, in the fourteenth indiction, he sent his envoys to this Catholic and truly orthodox prelate. He bestowed no small gifts both upon the holy places and upon the supreme pontiff himself, asking his apostolate what it would be more beneficial for him to do and what should be done concerning the remaining Bulgarian people, still deprived of holy baptism, so that they might receive the sacraments of the faith.

When the most blessed pope heard this, he was filled with great joy and rendered abundant praise to Christ. Rejoicing with the entire Church divinely entrusted to him, he offered infinite praises to our God, who in these last times had performed so great a miracle, with a devoted mind and also with a supplicating voice [or: vow].

After receiving the envoys of the Bulgarian king, whose name was Michael, the holy pope honorably kept them with him. Meanwhile, appointing as envoys of the Apostolic See Paul of Populonia and Formosus of Porto, bishops of great holiness, and instructing them with honeyed admonitions and teachings, he decided to send them to preach to that people.

Because the overland route through the Bulgarian kingdom extended as far as Constantinople, he also sent suitable envoys—Donatus, bishop of Ostia; Leo, priest of the holy Roman Church; and Marinus, deacon of the holy Apostolic See—so that they might make known to that Church through his representatives whatever had been decreed concerning the holy Church of Constantinople, although this same pope had already made it known throughout the East once and twice by apostolic letters. Paul and Formosus were to convert the Bulgarian people to the faith, while Donatus, Leo, and Marinus were to announce in every respect what the Apostolic See had determined concerning the Church of Constantinople.

This was accomplished in the name of the Lord, with the assistance of Saint Peter. But while the venerable bishops Paul and Formosus mentioned above were staying in Bulgaria, Donatus, the revered bishop, Leo the priest, and Marinus, minister of the Apostolic See, wished to proceed to Constantinople. They encountered a certain Theodore guarding that frontier between Bulgaria and the Constantinopolitan territories. He did not allow them to go any farther; rather, he heaped countless insults upon them and abused envoys of so great a See to such an extent that he even struck the heads of the horses on which they were riding, saying: “Our emperor has no real need of you.”

[Col. 0766C–0767A]

Yet that same emperor is said to have said to the envoys of the king of the Bulgarians: “Unless envoys of the Apostolic See had come through Bulgaria, they would neither see my face nor see Rome during their lifetime.” After remaining there for forty days, they learned that the Greek emperor had ordered this to be done. They turned back and, compelled to return to Rome, reported the same matters.

The apostolic envoys were then received by the aforementioned king of the Bulgarians with eager spirits and great devotion. They began to instruct the people with salutary admonitions and, from the least to the greatest, washed them by God’s grace in the sacred font. They introduced among the Bulgarians the entire rite of the Christian faith, just as they had been instructed by the most holy pope.

The glorious king of the Bulgarians, kindled by such great zeal for the faith and attracted by the constancy of this pious father’s admonitions, began to act with such determination that, expelling all foreigners from his kingdom and relying solely upon the preaching of the aforementioned apostolic envoys, he resolved that he himself should continually be refreshed by the pastures of eternal life. He also requested that Formosus, one of these bishops, a man of episcopal life and conduct, be given to him as archbishop.

Then he again sent his envoys to Rome. Among other matters, he reported this to the most blessed pope and asked his holiness for priests to instruct that people. When the pope learned these things, he rejoiced greatly. Rendering infinite praises to God, he examined a considerable number of priests in his presence and sent those whom he found worthy, by the grace of preaching, to Bulgaria. With them he sent the bishops Dominic of Trivento and Grimoald of Polimartium.

Since Formosus, as bishop, ought not to abandon the people entrusted to him, one of these priests who might be found worthy was eventually to be chosen in the name of the Lord for the archbishopric and sent to the Apostolic See for consecration.

[Col. 0767B–C]

Meanwhile, the most blessed pope, most diligent corrector of vices and worshiper of God, determined that when the bishops themselves entered Bulgaria, Paul of Populonia—whose memory we mentioned above—and Bishop Grimoald should carry out in Bulgaria whatever pertained to the divine ministry and the instruction of that people. The often-mentioned Formosus and the venerable Bishop Dominic, however, were to proceed again to Constantinople because of the schism that had arisen there, about which I have already spoken at length.

But while these things were being done, by God’s judgment a deserved vengeance struck Michael, the emperor of the Greeks, and killed him by a wicked murder. When Basil was emperor in Constantinople, God willed that the constant labors of that holy pontiff, which he had endured for the holy Church of Constantinople, should be brought to completion with the consummation of a good work. As the report had it, the neophyte and usurper Photius was expelled as an adulterer, and, according to the decree of the Apostolic See, Ignatius was restored to the patriarchal throne of Constantinople.

For this most pious and Catholic pope, executor of divine works, placed and sought first not his own interests but those of God. With the assistance of Saint Peter, he took care to wage the Lord’s battles spiritually, with the supreme balance of stewardship. He carefully moderated all prelates so that they would not injure their subjects; like a father, he admonished them. He also decreed pastorally that subjects should obey their prelates, in accordance with the privileges of each person.

Whoever wishes to recognize his holy zeal will be able to find it, clearer than daylight, in his letters, which he sent throughout the regions of the world with sound judgment. He placed his soul in his hands; he thought of nothing except heavenly things; occupied night and day with fasts, vigils, and prayers, he gave neither rest to his body nor sleep to his limbs. For if we wished to insert in writing all the works of holiness that he performed, filled with Christ’s grace and rich in virtues and faith, and all that he taught and fulfilled by his conduct and life, perhaps parchment would run out before speech.

Nevertheless, before turning our pen to the end of his life, let us return first to the things he bestowed upon the holy places.

[Col. 0767D–0768A]

This distinguished pope, out of love for the prince of the apostles, the apostle Peter, his nourisher, made four hangings for his basilica, some of *stauracium*, some of *fundatum*, and others of beautiful and varied colors. He completely covered all the major beams facing the presbytery around its circumference; they brightly adorn it, increase its splendor, and, through their marvelous size, confer still greater honor.

There also, something that no one had attempted after the devastation by the Saracens, he made a silver arch and placed it in the middle, better than it had formerly been, above the lofty beam situated before the ciborium. It weighed [lacuna] pounds. He sculpted three silver images: one representing the Lord Savior and two depicting angels. He overlaid them with nine pounds of gold, one of them weighing eighty pounds, another seventy pounds, and the third likewise seventy pounds.

He also made one golden cross adorned with precious gems, weighing [lacuna] pounds, and placed it at the top of the same arch. There, for the breadth of its adornment and display, he hung one golden crown, two silver crosses, two silver chalices, and two silver *staupos* [cups]. Moreover, upon the purple marbles that retain silver folds before the body of the blessed apostle Peter, he placed, as offerings, two silver crosses, one on the right and one on the left, weighing [lacuna] pounds.

[Col. 0768A–B]

In the Lateran patriarchal residence he ordered a most beautiful and exceedingly splendid house to be built. Constructing there an oratory of the holy Mother of God, the most blessed pontiff himself offered garments and appropriate ornaments with radiant vows, for the love of eternal life.

The same man, protected by God and surrounded by heavenly grace, renovated many sites of the saints that threatened to collapse. He bestowed various gifts upon various churches and greatly increased their advantages. In the ciborium of the Constantinian basilica he hung four excellent hangings, made of *siforium* and *fundatum*. Then, in the ciborium, he offered an equal number of excellent hangings to the keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom.

He did the same in the church of the Teacher of the Nations. In the church of the holy Mother of God at the Manger he acted likewise, for the rewards of eternal recompense. In the church of Saint Lawrence, martyr of Christ, outside the city walls, he also gave four excellent hangings for the ciborium.

In the days of this blessed prelate there was such abundance and supply of food that this prosperity consigned every memory of the famine that had occurred during the days of his predecessor to oblivion.

He held one ordination in the month of March: seven priests, four deacons, and sixty-five bishops for various places. After he had ruled the Apostolic See most victoriously, and as a true athlete of God, in a Catholic and principled manner, he departed from this light to the Lord on the Ides of November, in the first indiction.

What more should I say? Not only did the various nations of humanity, endowed with full understanding, mourn his departure, but even the elements of the world themselves, insofar as the air’s disorder was concerned, wept for a long time and remained in sorrow over the death of so great a man. After his death, his body was buried before the doors of the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter.

[Col. 0768C–D]

# The Letters and Decrees of Pope Nicholas I Arranged in Chronological Order

## (Year 858.) I. Nicholas’s Letter to Wenilo, Archbishop of Sens, and His Co-Bishops

Concerning the illness of Herimann, bishop of Nevers.

[In Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XV.]

[Col. 0769A]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy brothers Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, and his co-bishops.

We have received the letter of Your Holiness, by which you rightly sought from our apostolate an answer concerning the case of Herimann the bishop, and by which, following the practice of the universal Church, you took care to demand instruction from our authority. But before turning the eyes of our mind to your questions, we considered it worthwhile to linger briefly over your praises. You foresaw, with the vision of your serenity, toward whom you ought to go and where you ought to hasten in doubtful matters and in great ecclesiastical affairs; and you ran there with the humble steps of your devotion.

You acted against those who despise the most radiant teaching and See of the most blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, and of his successors—him whom the Son of God established in his holy Church as the greater luminary in heaven. Like scorpions wandering about, they move in the noonday, and while it is still day, the sun sets for them.

Indeed, through knowledge of God, like Balaam, they have their eyes open; yet they fall because, blinded like Balaam himself by avarice, they do not see where they can direct their steps toward justice. Walking along precipitous and trackless paths, they refuse to follow the head and are plunged into vast abysses.

But you, dearest brothers, who, with the Holy Spirit revealing it, have laudably begun to understand the authority of the Apostolic See and to walk already in the splendor of its light, strive to think with it to the end and always to walk with it. Judge it impious to depart from it, and do not consent for even a moment to differ from its judgment. Receive those whom it receives, and remember to drive away those whom it rejects, just as it does.

For it rejects only members that do not adhere to it, and cuts away from itself only those whom it finds placed as a scandal to many. I say, it neither cuts off nor tears away from itself anything except a member known to have become an offense and ruin to the healthy members.

But let us return to the matter at hand. Your Holiness reports that Bishop Herimann contracted an illness by which he was long prevented from properly fulfilling his episcopal office. For, to use your own words, having at times been deprived of sound judgment, he committed certain acts very like those of a madman. You add that, when summoned to provincial synods, he delayed coming.

Here it must be carefully considered that coming to a synod is itself a priestly duty. Since you said that he could not properly fulfill his priestly office and had lost sound judgment, we are astonished that Your Reverence compelled him to come to the synod—especially since you yourselves testify that he resembled a madman and remained in the same illness. If he was so burdened, it would have been more fitting for your holiness to lighten his burden than to add weight to it, and to strengthen charity in him rather than close against him the entrails of compassion.

You indicate that he was frequently accused of certain offenses. Since the person of the accused himself is absent, we certainly cannot believe one party to the detriment of the other. Moreover, you have not yet explained what those offenses were, nor clearly shown whether this prelate was of sound mind when he committed them. We consider it preferable, at least for the present, to regard any illness as the punishment of sin rather than as the sin itself, since he should be helped and pitied more than punished or struck in any way.

The admonition, or formal remonstrance, of Your Beatitude, which you say you addressed to him, is also very pleasing—provided that what sounded gentle and sweet in our ears proceeded not from feigned charity but from the simple eye of the mind; or provided that it pleased the eyes of the supreme Judge in the same way that it appeared before human eyes. That it did so appear is sufficiently and abundantly evident.

We wish Your Holiness good health in Christ.

## (Year 859.) II. Nicholas’s Bull for the Monastery of Fulda

He orders that an account of the condition of this monastery be rendered to him from time to time.

[In Schannat, *History of Fulda*, p. 139.]

[Col. 0769D]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Theoto, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of the Lord Savior, and through you to your successors in that venerable monastery forever.

Since whatever accords with reasonable desires must always be granted, authority ought by no means to be denied, in the granting of privileges, to the devotion of a founder's pious construction. Therefore, because you requested that the monastery of the Savior, built by Archbishop Saint Boniface in the place called Boconia, beside the bank of the river Fulda, should be adorned with the support of a privilege of the Apostolic See, and that, established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, in which by God’s authority we serve, it should not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other church, we, favoring these pious desires, commit to effect by this authority of ours what has been requested.

Accordingly, we prohibit any priest of any church from exercising any jurisdiction or authority in the aforesaid monastery apart from the Apostolic See. No one may presume to celebrate the solemnity of the Mass there unless invited by the monastery’s abbot. Thus, in accordance with the privilege established under apostolic protection, the monastery shall remain endowed without disturbance. Its places and possessions—both those it holds or possesses at the present time and those that divine mercy may grant it to acquire through the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful—shall enjoy perpetual security without contradiction from any person.

Moreover, after deliberation, we establish that at suitable times it be reported to our ecclesiastical concern how monastic observance is being directed according to the regular habit and how it is being devoted with appropriate ecclesiastical diligence to concord. Otherwise, God forbid, under the pretext of this privilege, the mind and steps of your rectitude might in some way be diverted from the norm of justice.

We also establish by the text of this decree that whoever—whether a prelate of any church or a person invested with any dignity—attempts to violate this charter of our privilege, which we confirm by the authority of the prince of the apostles, shall be anathema. Incurring the wrath of God, let such a person remain excluded from the assembly of all the saints. Nevertheless, by apostolic authority, the dignity of the aforesaid monastery, granted by us and supported by us, shall remain perpetually inviolate.

Written by the hand of Peter, notary and scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of June, indiction VII. Farewell.

Given on the eleventh day before the Ides of June, by the hand of Tiberius, primicerius of the holy Apostolic See, while the most pious lord Augustus Louis, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in the seventh indiction. Amen.

## (Year 860.) III. To Adelwin, Archbishop of Salzburg

He grants the use of the pallium.

[In Kleinmayern, *Reports on the Condition of the Regions and City of Juvavia*—Appendix 92.]

[Col. 0771D]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy brother Adelwin, bishop of the holy Church of Juvavia.

If shepherds of sheep are content to endure only the sun and frost, day and night, for the protection of their flock, so that with ever-watchful eyes they may ensure that none of the sheep perish by wandering or is carried away, torn apart by the bites of wild beasts, let us consider with what exertion and care we ought to remain vigilant, we who are called shepherds of souls. Let us not cease to discharge the office we have undertaken in guarding the Lord’s sheep,

[Note: Something is missing. Letter 87, to Rembert: “If shepherds of sheep are content to endure the sun and frost, day and night, for the protection of their flock, so that …,” etc.]

[Col. 0772A]

lest, on the day of divine judgment, the guilt of negligence on account of our sloth torment us before the supreme Shepherd—although for this very reason we are now judged higher than others in the reverence of honor.

We grant your fraternity the pallium for celebrating the solemn offices of the Mass. Yet we grant you its use, while the privileges of your Church remain in their status, only on the following occasions: on the day of the holy and revered Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ; on the feasts of the holy apostles; on the feast of the blessed John the Baptist; on the Assumption of the blessed Mother of God, Mary; on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, the day of our Lord God; on the day of your church’s solemnity; and also on the anniversary of your ordination, just as was decreed by our blessed predecessor, Lord Gregory, prelate of this gracious See.

Your fraternity should put on the pallium in the secretarium and then proceed to the solemn offices of the Mass. You should arrogate nothing more to yourself through rash presumption, lest, while something is improperly seized in outward dress, even those things that might properly be permitted should be lost.

Since the honor of this garment must be preserved by modest vigor in one’s actions, we exhort you to ensure that all the ornaments correspond, so that, with God as author, you may everywhere be conspicuous as a ruler.

Therefore, let your life be a rule for your sons. Let whatever strength has been imparted to them be directed in it; let them see in it what they should imitate; by constantly considering themselves in it, let them advance, so that, after God, their good life may be seen to be yours.

Let neither prosperity, which temporally flatters, exalt the heart, nor adversity cast it down. Whatever it may be, let it be overcome by the virtue of patience. Let hatred find no place with you, nor indiscriminate favor. Let the wicked know you as strict; let an evil suggestion not make the innocent person guilty before you; let favor not excuse the guilty. Do not show yourself lenient toward offenders, lest you permit the commission of what you have failed to avenge.

Let there be in you both the sweetness of a good shepherd and the severe strictness of a judge: the one to cherish those who live innocently, the other to restrain the restless from wickedness by striking them when they must be struck.

But because at times the zeal of superiors, wishing to act as the strict avenger of the wicked, turns correction into cruelty, restrain anger by judgment. Use the censure of discipline in such a way that you strike at faults while not withdrawing affection from the persons whom you correct.

Show yourself merciful to the poor, as far as virtue permits. Let your defense assist the oppressed; let your measured reason oppose the oppressors. Do not regard anyone’s face contrary to justice [or: “do not look upon anyone’s face”]; do not disregard anyone who makes a just complaint.

Let the guardianship of equity excel in you, so that neither the rich person’s power may persuade him to dare anything against reason in your presence [or: “out of frenzy”], nor the poor person’s humility cause him to despair of himself. Thus, by God’s mercy, you may be useful, as the sacred reading commands when it says: “A bishop must be blameless.”

But you will be able to use all these qualities beneficially if you have charity as your teacher. Whoever follows it never departs from the right path.

Behold, dearest brother, among many other things, these are the duties of the priesthood; these are the duties of the pallium. If you preserve them diligently, you will possess inwardly what you have shown that you received outwardly.

May the Holy Trinity surround your fraternity with the protection of its grace and so direct you in the way of its fear that, after the bitterness of this life, we may deserve to arrive together at eternal sweetness. Amen.

Written by the hand of Soronius, regional notary and scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, indiction VIII.

## (Year 860.) IV. To Michael the Emperor

[Note: This letter is preserved complete in Latin in the Eighth Ecumenical Synod, session 4, in Anastasius’s translation.]

[Col. 0773B]

He complains that the synod at Constantinople dared, without the authorization of the Apostolic See, to deprive Ignatius of his honor and substitute Photius in his place. He demonstrates by many arguments that a layman cannot ascend to the rank of pontifical dignity. He refuses to approve Photius’s promotion unless the case is first examined by envoys and brought before him in its entirety. He adds some points concerning the veneration of images. This is the first letter sent by the Apostolic See to the emperor Michael through the bishops Rodoald and Zacharias.

[In Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XV, cols. 162–167.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Michael, glorious emperor of the Greeks.

The primacy of divine authority, therefore, which the Creator of all things bestowed upon his chosen apostles, establishing it upon the solid firmness of the faith of the prince of the apostles—namely Peter—he determined to be his distinguished, indeed first, see. For the Lord’s voice had said to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16).

Peter, then, from the firmness of the rock—which is Christ—never ceases to fortify by his prayers the unshaken structure of the universal Church, made solid by the strength of faith, so that he may hasten to restore the madness of those who err by the rule of right faith, and may likewise strive fearlessly to reward those who consolidate it. Thus the gates of hell—that is, the suggestions of evil spirits and the assaults of heretics—may not prevail in breaking the unity of that same Church.

Therefore we render manifold thanks to almighty God, who has deigned to pour this into your heart: that, having become defenders of the Church of God, you desire to promote its concord, lest the beauty of faith be consumed by any rust of error and the understanding of apostolic tradition be shattered. For, as you yourselves know, the holy Fathers have often assembled for the preservation of its integrity; and by them it was both determined and observed that, without the consent of the Roman see and of the Roman pontiff, no conclusion should be given to any deliberation that had arisen.

Accordingly, the council assembled by you at Constantinople—as your letters have made known to our ears—disregarding the substance of this rule, did not hesitate to withdraw its consideration from the institutions mentioned above, to such an extent that the assembly convened there deprived Ignatius, patriarch of the aforementioned city, of his honor without consulting the Roman pontiff.

How deserving of reproof this was is made clear by those who had been set against him, because the canonical institution prohibits persons of the kind whom we read of in your letter from acting as such; and it is plainly evident that they were brought forward through envy, since he himself did not openly acknowledge with his own mouth the charges brought against him—as your letters of instruction assert—nor did his accusers prove them according to the provisions of the sacred canons.

Moreover, after these matters had thus been unjustly carried out, the assembly directed its ill-considered purpose toward things still more detestable: from the ranks of the laity it chose a shepherd to preside over it. O what presumptuous rashness! He is placed over the divine fold who does not yet know how to rule his own spirit. For one who has not learned to order his own life, having not been led through the degrees of the Church, how will he be able to correct another’s life when suddenly elected?

We do not believe that you are unaware of what the company of the apostles did after receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit. Although they had been enlightened by the Lord’s vision, by his continual speech, and by the joy of his resurrection, and had been strengthened by the descent of spiritual grace, they did not presume so boldly to choose the twelfth from among the chosen seventy-two to take the place of Judas the transgressor. Rather, through certain stages, so to speak, they selected two from the number of the seventy-two: Joseph, who was called Justus, and Matthias (Acts 1). Not yet knowing which of the two they should place above the other, they sought a divine judgment; and when the choice had been made, the one who appeared more righteous to human eyes was found inferior in the sight of the Godhead.

The undertaking of that assembly, therefore, since it appeared to make no effort to carry out any of these things, seems to have departed from the straight path, inasmuch as it did not take care to place over the guardianship of the Lord’s flock a shepherd in the manner that was proper.

Indeed, in the sphere of secular learning no one is rightly considered worthy of the title “master” unless, proceeding through the stages of the disciplines, he has first been instructed. But this Photius, previously a teacher, burst forth before he had become learned; he wishes to appear a master before being heard as a disciple. He ought first to have been a hearer and afterward an instructor. But choosing, contrary to this order, the chair of a teacher, he chose first to teach and afterward began to be taught; first he took care to sanctify and finally to be sanctified; first he wished to illuminate and afterward to be illuminated.

This, then, the catholic order forbids; and our holy Roman Church has always forbidden such an election through our predecessors, the teachers of the catholic faith. Observing their rule, we judge their institutions to be inviolable.

The Council of Sardica, finally, completely prohibited the election of a bishop from among the laity in its thirteenth canon, saying:

“If by chance either a rich man, or a scholar from the laity, or someone formerly an administrator is sought as bishop, he is not to be ordained beforehand unless he has first performed the office of lector and fulfilled the ministry of deacon or presbyter, so that, if he is worthy, he may ascend through each degree to the summit of the episcopate.”

And so forth.

Coelestine likewise, that most holy teacher and distinguished prelate of our Roman see, asserting this in the decree of his sanction (Letter 2, chapter 21), says:

“We have heard that certain cities, deprived of their own rulers, wish to seek bishops from among the laity, and to consider so great an eminence so worthless that they think we can confer it upon those who have served not God but the world—not merely judging badly of their own clergy, whom they do this to despise, but judging most badly of us, whom they believe to think that we have the power to do this. They would never dare to do so if the opinion of certain persons there, agreeing with them, did not restrain them. Thus nothing that has been decreed so frequently is of any effect, since this is ignored as though nothing had ever been written on the subject. What benefit is there in having served through the various clerical ranks and spent one’s entire life in the Lord’s camp, if those who are to preside over these men are sought from among the laity? Such persons, occupied with the world and ignorant of the whole ecclesiastical order, seek in reckless haste to overstep another’s honor through immoderate desire and, trampling upon the reverence due to ecclesiastical discipline, to pass into another kind of life?”

Therefore, dearest brothers, since we guard the helm of our jurisdiction—that is, of the canons—we must oppose such persons. By our letters we admonish your fraternity that no one admit or allow a layman to be ordained into the clerical order, lest he deceive that man and generate for himself causes by which he may be condemned under the established decrees.

Finally, Leo, that most holy teacher and distinguished pontiff of the apostolic and Roman see, whose praise is magnified in the Fourth Synod, prohibited this very thing in his Decretals, chapter 33 (Letter 88 to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica):

“In cities whose rulers have died, the following procedure is to be observed regarding the appointment of bishops: the person who is to be ordained, even if supported by the testimony of a good life, must not be a layman, a neophyte, or the husband of a second wife,”

and so forth.

Gelasius, moreover, that most holy prelate of the Roman Church, not inferior in merit to the aforementioned teacher, Leo, prohibited not only the making of bishops from among the laity but also forbade presbyters to presume such things in his Decretals, chapter 3 (Letter 6), saying:

“But if someone from among the laity is to be added to ecclesiastical offices, it is appropriate to examine such a person in each of the matters set forth above with proportionately greater care, inasmuch as the difference between worldly and religious life is known to be considerable. For ecclesiastical ministries that are suitable must be restored, not imposed upon those whose merits are unsuitable. The more one must seek in their training whatever may be fit for sacred service, the more the time from which these attainments ought to have been acquired is cut short, so that one may be shown to possess in character the integrity which a longer habit has not bestowed. Otherwise, under the pretext of supplying the shortage of clergy, we may be judged to have introduced vices into divine worship rather than secured the advantages of a legitimate household, when in their promotions we substitute six months even beyond the limits of a year.”

For, as has been said, there ought to be a distinction between a person devoted to divine worship and one coming from the way of life of the laity. Nevertheless, we have believed that this may be granted to the extent that, in those churches where, through the devastation of wars, either no ministries at all or only a few have remained, they may be renewed. Once these have been restored, by God’s favor, through the appointment of persons to the ecclesiastical degrees, the ancient form of the fathers’ canons must be preserved, so that what is provided as a remedy for the deficiency of the churches of the West may not in any way prevail against them. No new law is being proposed against the decrees of our predecessors; other churches, which have not been devastated by a similar calamity, must continue to observe the former judgment in making ordinations and must withdraw from this pretext.

The more, therefore, we have been admonished by this opportunity, the more earnestly we entrust to you the observance of the venerable canons, admonishing the consciences of those in each degree not to attempt to rush into unlawful excesses.
