Let no bishop presume that it is lawful, at his pleasure, to attach to divine ministries bigamists, men who have contracted second marriages, or those whose spouses have been abandoned by others; nor persons after penance; nor those without letters of commendation; nor those physically impaired; nor persons bound by servile status; nor those entangled in the obligations of the court or of public affairs; nor persons examined indiscriminately, without waiting for an appropriate period of time. Nor should they endeavor, at their own discretion, to invade the rights of others without a mandate of just disposition from the apostolic see.

Our predecessor, therefore, of this nurturing see, namely Adrian, that most holy prelate, established in the letter that he had sent to Constantinople concerning the venerable images (Letter 5, near the end) that henceforth no bishop whatsoever was to be ordained from among the laity in that same Church of Constantinople. If you wish to know the text of this provision, you can find it in the council held in that city during his time.

With these matters briefly stated beforehand, we cannot give the assent of our apostolate to the consecration of the aforementioned man until everything that has been done, or will be done, in that city so frequently named concerning ecclesiastical matters or orders has been reported to our ears by our envoys whom we have sent to you.

And so that the right order may be preserved in all things, we wish, O merciful Augustus, that Ignatius—whom, as you have taken care to inform us by your imperial letters, you say voluntarily and of his own accord abandoned the governance of the aforementioned see and was deposed by a council assembled from the whole people—appear before our envoys and the entire council, under your imperial authority, so that it may be investigated why he rejected the people entrusted to him and, disregarding and despising the institutions of our predecessors and of the holy pontiffs, namely Pope Leo and Benedict, held them in contempt. His deposition must be subjected to careful examination by the legates acting under our command, so that it may become clear whether or not the canonical rule was observed in his case. Then, once it has been reported to our pontificate what ought to be done concerning him, we shall define the matter by apostolic sanction, so that your Church, which is shaken daily by such great anxieties, may thereafter remain inviolable and unshaken.

Regarding the images and their observance, although there would have been no need to write, since the holy concern of our venerable predecessors, the pontiffs, kindled by catholic zeal, established many things highly useful and beneficial to the Church of God, nevertheless, because frequent repetition of instruction commonly makes an intention more venerable to the hearer, we have therefore taken care to explain something about these matters to the people of God for the preservation of unity.

This holy catholic and apostolic Church therefore holds and defends the ancient tradition of the holy Fathers, which we received for observance from our most blessed and orthodox predecessors, the pontiffs who sat after blessed Peter in his apostolic see, and which we have preserved hitherto unimpaired.

It is therefore necessary, with the full intention of the mind and the utmost effort of desire, to venerate and honor the venerable images both of our Lord Jesus Christ and of his most holy Mother, and of the blessed apostles and of all the saints, so that we may strive with all the strength we possess to resist the madness of the heretics who forbid the people to venerate them.

For, once the Church has been established in peace, there can be nothing contrary to this if images depicting the saints themselves increase in the faithful the growth of love. Indeed, when their faces are viewed and the activity of their works is recalled, God—whose dwelling is recognized to be in them—is perfectly praised.

Certainly, if God, who is invisible and incorporeal, appeared to the eyes of mortals and believers not through the substance of his own divinity but through an assumed created form, and this was the highest object of honor, why should the souls of the saints, who are known to have possessed the face of each person while remaining in the body, and who, according to God’s ordering, are said to have done what pleased him, not be venerated by us with great honor? Why should we execrate the images of those through whom we have recognized the truth of faith?

God indeed appeared to Abraham, our father, not in flesh or in soul, but in the form of three men. Seeing one thing in them and understanding them to be something else, he bowed to the ground in worship and said: “Lord, if I have found favor in your sight, let me bring water, so that your feet may be washed” (Gen. 15). Abraham immediately believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, and he was called the friend of God.

Jacob likewise saw God through the form of an assumed created being, and therefore said: “I have seen the Lord face to face, and my soul has been saved” (Gen. 32). Behold: incorporeal and invisible God wished to make himself visible to mortal eyes through the form of an assumed created being, so that for believers it might be a means of grace. Why, then, should the icons of the saints, whom we believe to have been corporeal and visible, be capable of bringing guilt upon us if we venerate them as true friends of Christ?

For if their images were believed to be detestable, surely their relics also—whose flesh experienced corruption in the tomb—ought not, God forbid, to be held in any regard. But if we desire to come into their company, then here we ought certainly to venerate with the most solemn honor everything connected with the saints: not only the relics of their bodies but also of their garments, and likewise images of their faces painted in any place. We should recall what Isaiah testifies that he saw in the form of an assumed created being, saying: “I saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting upon a lofty throne, and the things beneath him filled the temple” (Isa. 6), and so forth.

Moses and Aaron also approached to see the throne where God had stood, and beneath his feet there was something like a work of sapphire stone, and like the firmament of heaven in the brilliance of splendor; and cherubim stood there made of pure gold. All these things, according to what Solomon later fashioned in the temple, he saw imagined and prefigured on the mountain while speaking with the Lord.

Knowing these and similar things, the Fathers who preceded us painted images of our Savior Jesus Christ, of his most holy Mother and ever-Virgin, and of all the saints on the walls of churches, as the present age itself confirms; and they have not to this day forbidden such images to be painted with all devotion in suitable places.

What harm does it do to the truest Christian if he paints on a wall or on wood what he loves and cherishes—not deifying it for worship, but depicting it for solemn reverence?

What harm, indeed, is there if we look upon images of Christ in the temple of the Church and, in the secret place of the heart, meditate beforehand upon the fact that he whose image we see will come swiftly as judge of the living and the dead?

What contradicts our faith in the fact that, in the center of the chamber, above the altar, our souls desire his figure—of him who is the Word made flesh and dwelt among us—and that his image retains the inscription of his name? And since by nature we worship the Son, why should we not also worship, by adoption, the new name written upon a tablet or upon gems?

The holy altar, then, upon which we offer vows of sacrifice to almighty God, is by nature an ordinary stone, differing in no way from the other slabs that adorn our walls and floors. But because it has been consecrated through God’s assistance and has received a blessing, it thereby becomes a holy table.

The bread that is offered upon it is likewise ordinary bread; but once it has been consecrated by the sacrament, it truly becomes and is called the body of Christ. So too a small quantity of wine, possessing its ordinary nature before the blessing, after the sanctification of the Spirit becomes the blood of Christ.

The image of the cross itself, before it receives the likeness of that form, is wood common to everyone. But once it has received the altogether venerable likeness, it is sacred and terrifying to demons, because Christ has been represented upon it.

**[Note: The passage is corrupt.]**

Having passed rapidly over these matters in a brief style, although we could have said much, we have transcribed them for your serenity because Adrian, our most holy predecessor, wrote and transmitted much concerning them in letters that are still held by the Church of Constantinople. In those letters you will be able to find whatever the necessity of this matter may require.

For we have heard that your imperial dignity flourishes in all ecclesiastical benefits. It is necessary, therefore, that you deign in your time to restore the ancient custom which our Church maintained, so that no one may presume to gainsay blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, with respect to the authority which our see exercised through bishops established in your regions—namely the bishop of Thessalonica, who acted in the place of the Roman see throughout Old Epirus, New Epirus, Illyricum, Macedonia, Thessaly, Achaea, Ripuarian Dacia, Inland Dacia, Moesia, Dardania, and Praevalis. [The printed Latin is syntactically defective at this point.]

This authority was enlarged by the sacred dispositions of our predecessors, the holy pontiffs Damasus, Siricius, Innocent, Boniface, Coelestine, Sixtus, Leo, Hilary, Simplicius, Felix, and Hormisdas. We have taken care to send to your Augustan power, through our envoys, the institutions that they sent to those regions, so that you may learn the truth of the matter.

Moreover, let the Calabrian and Sicilian patrimonies, and whatever possessions were granted to our Church and which it obtained to hold and endeavored to govern through its own officials, be restored through your concessions. For it is unreasonable that ecclesiastical property—from which the lights and adornments of the Church of God ought to be provided—should be taken away by any earthly power. Once restored to the house of God, let it multiply the merit of the one who returns it, and let the vow of the one who receives it be exercised in the gains of spiritual desire.

Amid these matters and those stated above, we wish the consecration of the archbishop of Syracuse to be granted by our see, so that the tradition established by the apostles may in no way be violated in our [printed Roman edition: your] times.

We have sent to your serenity the most reverend and holy bishops Rhadoald, of the holy Church of Porto, and Zacharias, of the holy Church of Anagni, acting as envoys of our apostolate. We beg your greatness to receive them honorably and to grant them frequent audience. Do not hesitate to believe what they say irreproachably concerning the state of the Church.

When they sit in the assembly of the Church for ecclesiastical definitions, let them feel no hostile opposition from you or from anyone else. When it is lawful for them to return, grant them your own envoys—men who, in suitable dromons, may strive, with God’s favor and through the prayers of the apostles, to bring them safely to Rome—so that for all your good devotions we may more devotedly give thanks to almighty God the Father, to his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the Holy Spirit, to whom are honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

Given on September 25, in the ninth indiction.

**[Column 0780A] End of the letter sent by the apostolic see to the emperor Michael through the bishops Rhadoald and Zacharias.**

### (Year 860.) V. TO PHOTIUS

He reserves the whole case of Photius until the arrival of the envoys. This is the first letter sent to Photius through the bishops Rhadoald and Zacharias, who traveled to Constantinople.

**[At Mansi, same volume, column 168.]**

All usefulness and progress of souls are fortified by the catholic faith and protected by love of the Gospel. It saves all those enclosed within it and does not regard those outside it as its own.

Therefore, after receiving the written communication from you, we rejoiced, because we recognized in it that you are catholic. In it we perceived the usefulness of your prudence, and for this reason we rendered many thanks to almighty God, since we discovered that your knowledge flows from the catholic source.

But we grieved that you had not maintained the right order, since, without having been led through the degrees of the Church, you leapt from the condition of a layman [Roman edition: lay status] to so great an honor. Your prudence ought to have lived canonically within the clerical order, so that, doing nothing outside the canonical institutions, you might in due time and by legitimate advancement be established as pastor of the Church.

Your permitting this [printed alternative: your anticipating this] clearly shows that you acted against the statutes of the Fathers. For the Council of Sardica completely prohibited the presumption of so great a rashness (canon 13); likewise, the institutions of the holy pontiffs of the Roman see—Coelestine, the distinguished teacher; Leo, the most holy, whose praise is celebrated in the Fourth Synod; and Gelasius, equally most blessed in doctrine and merit—forbade such an ordination to be presumed.

Therefore we cannot at present consent to your consecration until our representatives, who have been sent by us to Constantinople, return and we learn through them the character of your observance, your constancy in ecclesiastical usefulness, and the zeal with which you devote yourself to the defense of the catholic faith.

Then, if you are found worthy, we shall honor you as the prelate of so great a see, as is proper, and embrace you with brotherly affection.

Given on September 25, in the ninth indiction.

### (Year 860.) VI. TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN KING CHARLES’S KINGDOM

Concerning Ingeltrude, the fugitive wife of Count Boso: that they are to excommunicate her if she refuses to return to her husband.

**[At Mansi, same place, column 326.]**

NICOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy HINCMAR, our fellow-brother and archbishop, and to all archbishops and bishops established in King Charles’s kingdom.

Canonical authority does not cease to proclaim everywhere that the people devoted to divine worship ought to be blameless. For by what means could this better be brought about than through the care of those who have undertaken the charge of the Lord’s flock in the place of shepherds? Therefore we admonish your brotherhood—indeed, your holiness—not to permit your diocese to be defiled by fornicators.

Behold, we formerly sent you instructions concerning the wife of Count Boso, who fled after leaving her husband, that you should have caused her to be recalled to her husband; but we see that this has not been done because of intervening circumstances. Hence perhaps we may judge you negligent. Therefore, supported by apostolic authority, we command you to make her return to her own husband, granting her forgiveness for the offence which she committed against him. And if, disobeying you, she scorns to return, hasten to excommunicate both her and all others who appear to support her wrongdoing from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and from the fellowship of all the faithful, so that the house of God may be governed by such rulers as the catholic order is known to have chosen. We desire your holiness to be well in Christ.

### (Year 860.) VII. TO KING CHARLES

He admonishes him diligently to ensure that King Lothair expels from his kingdom Ingeltrude, the adulterous wife of Count Boso, and compels her to return to her husband.

**[At Mansi, same place.]**

NICOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to CHARLES, glorious king, our spiritual son.

May your royal dignity draw the discernment of justice from the fountain of piety. No one, therefore, ought to act more justly than he to whom the ordering of laws seems to have been entrusted. For, behold, kings are accustomed to counsel [variant: favour] kings. But it is fitting that they should reciprocally exchange those things which the reasoning of justice teaches, and should not cease, in a corresponding manner, to remove whatever wickedness [Note: [Col. 0781D] The passage is somewhat obscure.] commands.

Accordingly, we exhort your royal greatness to correct King Lothair, your nephew, lest he permit so great a crime to remain in his kingdom; that is, that he not consent to the fugitive wife of Count Boso remaining there so long that she is not restored to her husband, forgiveness having been granted for the offence which she committed against him. Moreover, we wish also to admonish you that, if she happens to come into your kingdom, you act similarly. For we have commanded all the archbishops and bishops of your kingdom that, if, her fault having been forgiven, she refuses to return to her aforesaid husband, they excommunicate her from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and from the fellowship of all the faithful; for it is fitting that so great an evil should not arise in your kingdom, and, if it has arisen, that it be quickly extinguished. Thus we bind with the aforesaid excommunication all who consent to her evil. We desire your excellence to be well in Christ.

### VIII. ACTS OF THE ROMAN COUNCIL OF THE YEAR 861

Concerning John, archbishop of Ravenna.

(See *Patrology*, vol. 106, column 787, in the appendix to the pontifical of Agnellus.)

### (Year 861.) IX. TO HUNTFRID, BISHOP OF MORIENSE. Fragment

A bishop is not to abandon his Church in persecutions.

**[Mansi, same place.]**

You inquire through the priest Guldagarius whether, when you are driven from your bishopric by the Northmen, you ought thereafter to live in a monastery. In this matter, dearest brother, know that if it is ruinous for a helmsman to abandon a ship in calm weather, how much more so amid the waves.

By this we do not say that we should not flee the snares of persecutors, especially pagans, when they rage for a time and, on account of the multitude of our sins, divinely obtain the power to do harm; particularly since we ought not voluntarily to go out to meet them, and since it is clearer than light that many prophets and apostles, and the Lord himself, fled pursuers of this kind. But it is certainly fitting above all that we, who as rams lead the flocks—indeed, who are also their shepherds—by God’s help should remain with them in dangers according to our strength. And when, by divine mercy, calm has come and the assault of those raging has been stilled, we must at once seek out the flock, gather it into one, and raise its spirits upward, chiefly by preaching the peace and security of the heavenly country. We must remain solicitous for their protection until, if by God’s judgment they perhaps lose the advantages of the present time, they may hope without doubt to receive the everlasting joys of the life to come.

### (Year 861.) X. TO THIETGAUD, ARCHBISHOP OF TREVES

He absolves him and his clergy from their oath.

**[At Hontheim, *History of the Church of Trier*, vol. I.]**

Following the authority of our venerable predecessors, and specifically of the most blessed Pope and martyr Alexander, fifth from blessed Peter, we absolve from all oaths and obligations of whatever kind those who, compelled by the violence of the ungodly, bound themselves thereby; and we have forbidden their observance. This applies both to the aforesaid archbishop of Trier and to his provost, and to all who, having then been captured, bound themselves to those men in any manner. Nor do we permit them ever, by the authority of God and the holy apostles and our predecessors, to suffer on that account any infamy, calumny, or sequestration from their goods; as the Lord says through the prophet: “Loose the bonds of wickedness.”

Furthermore, we command our aforesaid brother and the sons of the Church of Trier and its defenders to pursue those evil men and their supporters with both spiritual and material sword until the possessions, or whatever ecclesiastical things were alienated or plundered by this deed or by any compact, are restored intact.

**[Note: [Col. 0781D] Thietgaud, together with his clergy, had been compelled by the disturbances of civil wars and the wrong inflicted by plunderers, under grave fear, to bind himself to his enemies by an oath of fealty. [Col. 0783D] BROWER, *Annals of Trier*, book VIII, no. 124. Nicolas the pontiff released them from the bond of this oath by the present decretal addressed to the bishops of Gaul, which Gratian inserted in his *Decree*, Cause 15, Question 6, Canon 2. How great at that time were the tumults of robbery and plundering in these regions may readily be gathered from the fact that at the assembly held at Koblenz in 860 by the brothers King Charles the Bald and Louis the German, and their nephew Lothair, the following, among other things, was decreed: “We will that the churches and houses of God, bishops and God’s people, clerics and monks, and nuns, have such protection and honour as they had in the time of our predecessors . . . But concerning these robberies and plunderings, which many now maintain by custom almost as law, from this day forward we forbid them under God’s ban and our own, so that no one may presume this any longer; but let each person remain within his country in peace and without oppression of the poor and of those dwelling round about, and when coming against an enemy, to an assembly, or to the court, let him set out from his own resources and from his own house, so that he may be able to come in peace, remain with us, and return to his own house.”]**

### (Year 862.) XI. TO ALL THE FAITHFUL

That Ignatius was deposed from the Eastern Church without any consent of his own by the legates of the apostolic see, and Photius substituted.

**[At Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XV.]**

NICOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of the holy Church of God.

What, therefore, has become known and publicly proclaimed to the entire people of God is by no means unknown to Your Holiness: namely, how some time ago the holy Church of the city of Constantinople—indeed, the illustrious Greek emperor together with the Christian people subject to his rule—sent their own envoys to this holy Church, the mother of all churches, concerning certain transgressions that had arisen in that Church [Col. 0783B] and various dissensions that had wickedly broken out among that people over the usurper Photius and the patriarch Ignatius. They consulted us with the utmost discretion, asking what judgment ought to be imposed, according to our decision, upon such transgressions.

Led, that is, by a holy and salutary discretion, they sought judgments from this principal Church, which they rightly understand to have received from Christ the Savior the privileges of its primacy, asking—not undeservedly—for the edification of religion and the recovery of peace and concord to be granted to them under a canonical determination. Yielding to their most salutary petition, we took care, as is clear to all, to send thither envoys from the side of our pontificate [Col. 0783C]. Furnished with our apostolic authority, they were to correct errors, bring whatever had been corrupted back to the path of rectitude, and carefully investigate the truth of what had occurred concerning Photius and the patriarch Ignatius. With God as their guide, they were to report fully to our apostolate what should legitimately be determined, so that our envoys' role would be inquiry and true examination only, while the decision whether the accusation brought against the patriarch Ignatius was true or false would remain reserved to us.

But when our envoys, who had been sent for this work, were returning, we nevertheless received from those same regions an imperial letter addressed to our apostolate through the emperor’s own envoy. From its contents and from the actions of the envoys we learned that, as the evils of dissension and envy [Col. 0783D] multiplied among them, they had, without any consent of ours or indeed any knowledge on our part, indiscreetly installed Photius in the place of Ignatius and deposed the patriarch Ignatius. This most indiscreet act is wholly contrary to us and to our entire Church [Col. 0784A], because, contrary to the sacred canons—which prescribe that no one be condemned without the most genuine proof, nor another be installed in his place beforehand—they condemned the patriarch Ignatius.

Moreover, when the Lord says, “Let the disciple not be above his teacher, nor the servant above his master” (Matthew 10), the aforesaid bishop Ignatius suffered the prejudice of his own rank at the hands of his subjects and of ministers of his own order. And contrary to the command of the outstanding teacher Paul to his beloved disciple Timothy, that he should “lay hands hastily on no one,” and, “Do not appoint a novice,” he says, “lest, being puffed up, he fall into the judgment of the devil” (1 Timothy 3), they rashly presumed to ordain Photius bishop, suddenly drawing him from secular lay service. This action, wickedly carried out against [Col. 0784B] the divine order, remains wholly contrary to our apostolate and to our entire Church, as has been said.

Let the whole Church of the saints therefore know in general that it was neither with our knowledge, nor by our command, nor by our will that Photius was installed or the patriarch Ignatius deposed. And, in satisfaction of the holiness of all of you, we most truthfully declare concerning such transgressions that, after the most genuine deliberation of our examination, we neither receive Photius nor condemn the patriarch Ignatius; we neither ordered nor consented to these things; nor do we judge that such an ordination or indiscreet deposition should remain ratified or secure without the balance of a just determination. We shall in no way consent to its being upheld. We do not count, and shall not count, the patriarch Ignatius among the deposed [Col. 0784C]; nor do we count, and shall not count, Photius among the episcopal order.

Therefore, beloved brothers, and all you who govern the Catholic Churches of Alexandria, Antioch, or Jerusalem, as well as all the eastern metropolitans and bishops, we make it clearer than light and more explicitly known that the apostolic see in no way permits the venerable patriarch Ignatius to be so rashly stripped of the privilege of his own dignity. Rather, after expelling from the sacred bosom of the holy Catholic and apostolic Church the most wicked Photius, the usurper—as we may put it, the adulterous intruder into the place of a living man—it judges and decrees once again, by canonical and legal examination, that the most holy patriarch Ignatius remain in the dignity of his priesthood [Col. 0784D], as it formerly decreed.

And so, in order that you, properly preserving the privilege of this see, may, as Catholics united in the same religion, also share with us the same judgment concerning the restoration of the priesthood of the venerable patriarch Ignatius [Col. 0785A] and the expulsion of the usurper Photius, we impose and command this upon you by apostolic authority. We also command you, in the manner of a father, to ensure that this document of our pontificate reaches the knowledge of all in your dioceses, and that you take care to preach to others concerning this matter according to the decision of the apostolic see, and that you yourselves likewise hold it immutably.

Furthermore, dearest brothers and beloved sons, what the authority of our apostolate [Col. 0785B] sends back in reply to the Greek emperor and to the whole holy Church of Constantinople concerning such transgressions, and concerning the matters for which we recently sent our envoys to those regions with apostolic letters—as is manifest to all of you—we command to be read below, in satisfaction of the holiness of all of you.

Given in the month of March, on the eighteenth day, in the tenth indiction.

---

### (Year 862.) XII. TO PHOTIUS

He refutes the arguments of Photius, who claimed that he had rightly advanced from the rank of the laity to episcopal dignity by the example of Ambrose, Nectarius, and Tarasius; and he demonstrates that Photius had ascended to that rank unjustly, both because he was a layman and because Ignatius was still alive.

[In Mansi, in the same volume.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most prudent man Photius.

After the Lord and our Redeemer Jesus Christ—who, for our redemption, deigned to appear from the womb of the Virgin as true God before the ages and true man at the end of the ages—had granted to blessed Peter, chief of the apostles [Col. 0785C], the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth, and had given him the keys with which the gates of the heavenly kingdom were to be opened, He deigned to establish His holy Church upon the solidity of Peter’s faith, according to His truthful saying:

> “Amen, I say to you: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16).

Upon the cement of this promise and holy apostolic institution, the foundations of this Church began to grow from precious stones [Col. 0785D], and, by divine mercy, through the labor of its builders and the vigilance of apostolic authority, they were brought indissolubly to the summit, there to remain forever, standing firm without being shaken by any adverse wind. Its primacy—as is manifest to all orthodox men, and as was briefly declared above—was deservedly obtained by blessed Peter, chief of the apostles and gatekeeper of the heavenly kingdom.

After him, his vicars, sincerely serving God and free from the dense clouds that customarily obstruct the straight path, received this dignity more worthily and remained diligent in the care of the governance they had undertaken for the Lord’s sheep. Among them the mercy of almighty God has deigned to number our lowliness [Col. 0786A]. We therefore stand as fearful as we consider that at the eternal judgment we shall render an account for all and before all who are reckoned under the name of Christ.

Since the whole company of believers seeks doctrine from this holy Roman Church, which is the head of all churches, requests the integrity of the faith, and entreats the forgiveness of sins for those who are worthy and redeemed by God’s grace, it is necessary that we, to whom this charge has been entrusted, be vigilant and hasten to watch over the Lord’s flock with a fervor proportionate to the eagerness with which greedy wolves [the Roman edition: “greedy wolves”] seek from every side to tear it apart with open jaws [variant: “open mouths”]—which we know by hearing and confirm by experience.

Those whom, because of the great distances of the earth or the swelling waves of the sea, we cannot visit in person [Col. 0786B], let the sequence of written letters address as though with a living voice, so that neither the guilt of silence may be demanded of us nor those who hear be given the opportunity to excuse themselves on the ground of ignorance. For we must also beware of what is said through the Prophet: “Mute dogs that are unable to bark” (Isaiah 56). The Apostle likewise says: “Be urgent in season and out of season” (2 Timothy 4).

It is established that the holy Roman Church, through blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, who by the Lord’s own mouth deserved to receive the primacy of the churches, is the head of all churches; and that all churches should seek from it and follow its rectitude and order in every useful matter and ecclesiastical institution, which it preserves inviolably and irrevocably according to the canonical and synodical decrees and the sanctions of the holy Fathers [Col. 0786C].

It follows, therefore, that what is decreed with full authority by the rulers of this see must not be removed because of any impediment of custom, merely by following one’s own desires, but must be held more firmly and immovably.

In this matter our apostolate has admonished your prudence: you did not refuse to cross suddenly from the lay order to the dignity of the patriarchate without canonical approval, contrary to the promulgations of the Fathers; rather, you rashly and shamelessly presumed to approach the summit of so great an honor. You take as though an occasion for yourselves from the most holy man Nectarius, whom the Second Holy Synod wished to elect and ordain to priestly dignity from the lay order [Col. 0786D] for no other reason than that it was distressed by the hardship of a great necessity: in the holy Church of Constantinople no cleric could be found who had not been obstructed by the cloudy darkness of the worst heresy.

For this reason, lest that Church, already mentioned, should remain too long deprived of a shepherd, as though widowed, the aforesaid Second Synod elected Nectarius, the conqueror of heretics, their defender and governor, to ecclesiastical care and priestly dignity. But it did not confirm, decree, or establish that this should happen again. And therefore, although what necessity is shown to produce contrary to the Fathers and to canonical institutions is not to be maintained as authoritative [Col. 0787A], it is nevertheless necessary to take ever greater care that such a necessity should not arise again. For whatever can be censured by others appears more fitting and becoming if the care of correction follows before the source of reproach grows stronger [for “succedat,” II has “succidat”].

As for the advancement of Tarasius, who was likewise promoted immediately from the lay community to the summit of the patriarchate, and whom you also wish to take as an authority for your defense: if you examine more carefully the holy synod celebrated among you in the time of the most holy lord [variant: *domni*] Adrian, pope, and attend to it more closely, you will find what that same most holy man decreed when consulted, and how, while censuring the act of his consecration, he declared that he was enduring profound grief over so presumptuous an undertaking [Col. 0787B] [“nimirum,” II has “nimium”].

For he says:

> “Unless, in restoring the images, you had resisted more fervently, like a true soldier of Christ, against those who deposed and trampled upon them, we would in no way have given our assent to your consecration or received your devotion into the patriarchal order. Your advancement is shown to have been as disorderly as it is proved to have been outrageously presumed upon contrary to the apostolic decrees.”

Why do you set the most blessed Ambrose [Paul on Saint Ambrose, in his Life], the most renowned and brilliant lamp of the Church, who was advanced from the catechumenate to episcopal dignity through successive stages by divine foreknowledge, against us as a defense for you and place him before your unlawful promotion? He was chosen not by human instigation, but [Col. 0787C] by divine calling, through miraculous signs.

While he was sleeping in the cradle of infancy under the care of his nurse, and was being carefully turned, suddenly a swarm of bees came to his open mouth and covered his face and lips, repeatedly entering and departing [variant: “entering and departing”]. His father, walking with the child’s mother or daughter, prevented the maidservant who had undertaken responsibility for nourishing the infant from driving them away. She was anxious that they might harm the child; nevertheless, they awaited with paternal affection the outcome with which the miracle would end. After flying about for some time, they were lifted to such a height in the air that they could no longer be seen by human eyes. At this, the terrified father said: “If this little child lives, he will become someone great.”

[Col. 0787D] Afterward, when the boy had grown and been instructed in the liberal arts, he went to Milan, where Auxentius, the Arian bishop, held the episcopal chair—not to govern it, but to tear it apart. When Auxentius died and the people gathered in the Church to elect a bishop, behold, a certain child cried out, saying, “Ambrose, bishop!” At this cry the whole assembly likewise acclaimed, “Ambrose, bishop!”

This must not be believed to have happened through human wishes, but through divine inspirations, for the salvation and rescue of the faithful from the jaws of our adversary, who, “as a roaring lion, seeks whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5). Although Ambrose sought to hide himself by many and various devices and to conceal himself from so great an honor [Col. 0788A], he was finally overcome and divinely elected by the whole people and clergy to priestly dignity. Proceeding from the catechumenate through each ecclesiastical grade [better, “progressing,” II], he was consecrated bishop on the eighth day by the consent of all Catholics, with divine mercy approving.

Let your devotion therefore attend carefully and consider with the eye of your innermost heart whether those things that come to the faithful through miraculous signs ought to be equated with things undertaken solely by one’s own inclination in order to obtain the glory of dignity; and whether you should take the aforesaid men as precedents in defense of your authority.

Here is Nectarius, appointed because of necessity and the shortage of clerics; here is Tarasius, appointed because of ecclesiastical doctrine and the defeat of the heretics who had presumed to depose the venerable images; here is Ambrose, advanced to govern the Churches through miraculous signs [Col. 0788B]. But what else is to be thought about you, against whom so many authorities of councils and decrees of the most holy pontiffs stand in opposition, except that an unprecedented custom has arisen among you?

According to the judgment of the holy Fathers, you must be considered blameworthy not only because you suddenly leapt from the lay order, contrary to canonical authorities, to govern the Church of Constantinople, but also because, while the man was alive and remained unharmed—namely, the most religious patriarch Ignatius—you seized his chair, that is, the Church of Constantinople, like an adulterer, and presumed to invade it, setting aside what is written: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Matthew 7).

Therefore, because your consecration was carried out outrageously and contrary to the institutions of the holy Fathers, we do not presume to give it our assent while holding the scales of equity. As for your statement that you neither possess nor accept the Council of Sardica or the decretal letters of the holy pontiffs, we are not readily granted the ability to believe this—especially since the Council of Sardica was held in your own regions and is accepted by the whole Church. On what grounds, then, would it be fitting for the holy Church of Constantinople to reject it and, as it deserves, not retain it?

As for the decretal letters established by the holy pontiffs of the first see, the Roman Church, by whose authority and sanction all synods and holy councils are strengthened and receive stability: why do you say that you neither possess nor observe them [Col. 0788D]? Is it because they contradict your ordination and resist your sudden leap from the laity to the summit of the patriarchate? They stand against the apostolic injunction: “Lay hands hastily on no one” (1 Timothy 5).

If you do not possess them, you are to be accused of neglect and carelessness; if you possess them and do not observe them, you are to be corrected and rebuked for rashness.

You assert and protest that you were forcibly promoted to priestly dignity, but the circumstances of your consecration show that this was not so. After you had been established upon the patriarchal throne, you showed yourself not gentle like a father among his sons, but harsh in the deposition of archbishops and bishops, and you burned with excessive fury in the condemnation of the innocent Ignatius [Col. 0789A], whom you regard as deposed.

In his deposition, unless we first learn with complete truth of his transgression or guilt, we do not count him among the deposed, nor do we condemn him, for it is extremely necessary to beware lest an innocent man be condemned without cause. Just as the holy Roman Church retains him in his former honor if the charges deserving condemnation are not proved against him, so it does not receive you, who were promoted carelessly and contrary to the traditions of the Fathers, into the patriarchal order; nor does it consent that you remain in the priestly order before the patriarch Ignatius has been justly condemned [possibly “you,” H.].

Let your devotion not suppose that this is done against you out of envy, or because we hate you, or that we are improperly inflamed against your ordination [Col. 0789B]. Rather, we are guided by zeal for the tradition of the Fathers, wishing the holy Church of Constantinople—which, for its stability and firmness, customarily turns in the usual manner to this holy Roman Church under the judgment of the holy Fathers—to remain free from stain, reproach, or any transgression, and wishing to cut away whatever conflicts with ecclesiastical rules.

Above all, we wish utterly to remove what is refuted canonically by every authority [variant: *canonica*] and is opposed to such a consecration, but which you defend as though it had been performed regularly through long-standing custom. Since we love you as we love ourselves, we undoubtedly wish to call you back from this by the rebuke of paternal affection, imitating the Apostle, who says: “The father chastises and corrects by scourging the son whom he loves” (Hebrews 12) [Col. 0789C].

As for the customs that you seem to have set against us, writing that different churches have different customs: if no canonical authority opposes them, we neither judge them nor resist them for that reason. Nevertheless, we wish to take care that this custom of yours—which is refuted by the promulgations of all the holy Fathers, namely, that a bishop should not suddenly be ordained from the laity—does not gain strength or flourish further in your Church. We do not cease to oppose it with our apostolic censure, in proportion as we recognize that it has been rashly presumed upon.

Nor must we remain silent concerning our envoys, whom, at your request, we sent to those regions in the service of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, for the benefit of the holy Church of Constantinople, against the deposing of the images or other pressing needs, and also solely to investigate the cause of the deposition of the aforesaid Ignatius [Col. 0789D].

For, as they say, they were denied the opportunity for one hundred days of speaking with anyone except their own people; they were not received as envoys of the apostolic see with the dignity due to them, nor retained as was proper. We think this was done for no other reason than to prevent them from finding an opportunity to investigate the deposition of the aforesaid man. For, as was included in our apostolic letter—though we do not know through whose deception it was falsified, as we found when we examined the synodical document sent by you—we did not wish our envoys to hear or learn about his promotion or his entry into office, but only about the outcome of his deposition [Col. 0790A], as we now desire.

According to their report, they were threatened with prolonged exile and enduring consumption by lice if they persisted in such an intention. Some informants said that what had been entrusted to them by us they could not complete secretly, because you and your followers resisted them; nor were they able to discover whether the deposition of the aforesaid Ignatius had been just or unjust. Once this was known, canonical and apostolic censure would have been applied to him according to its proper measure.

Given in the month of March, on the eighteenth day, in the tenth indiction.

---

### (Year 862.) XIII. TO THE EMPEROR MICHAEL [Col. 0790B]

This letter was sent to the emperor Michael by Leo, the imperial secretary—namely, the imperial envoy—after the return of the apostolic envoys, together with the letter to Photius [the Roman edition has “we sent”]. It disapproves the deposition of Ignatius and the promotion of Photius, rashly approved by the envoys. It brings forward many arguments on behalf of Ignatius and against Photius, and demonstrates that Photius’s election is not to be compared with the promotion of Nectarius and Ambrose, nor is the council at which Ignatius was condemned to be compared with the Council of Nicaea. It urges the emperor to restrain the disturbers of the Church. It complains that its letter was corrupted.

[In Mansi, in the same volume.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most pious and glorious son, Michael, great emperor.

The glory of Your Most Serene Empire, which appears to stand firmly established upon the integrity of the orthodox faith, has determined, when certain improper things have occurred in the holy Church of Constantinople [Col. 0790C], which seems to exist under the protection of your defense, to consult this holy Catholic and Apostolic Church—namely, the Roman Church, the head of all churches, which always follows the most sincere authorities of the holy Fathers in all its actions.

If, following its counsel, it takes care to act in matters appropriate to ecclesiastical affairs, it will undoubtedly be able to arrange, order, and define irrevocably everything that ought to be done or removed. We remember that you did this in letters recently sent to this see. For this reason, and at your request, we also sent our envoys to those regions to investigate carefully and report to us concerning certain presumptions by which you asserted that your Church was being troubled, as well as concerning the dissensions that had arisen on account of the religious man Ignatius, patriarch, and Photius [Col. 0790D].

But when they had returned to us, they reported nothing in writing about the most reverend man Ignatius, although we had instructed them to do so, both through them and in our letters. They reported only orally what had been done concerning him contrary to our wishes.

After several days [a space is missing, H.], a prudent and faithful envoy from your side, named Leo, the imperial secretary, brought to our apostolate an imperial letter together with the records of what had been done among you. When we ordered it to be read, we learned that, concerning the case of the aforementioned patriarch Ignatius, a sentence had been rashly introduced contrary to our command [Col. 0791A], and that nothing had been carried out that even remotely resembled our orders, but rather that everything had been done contrary to them [more correctly, “similar,” singular, and “carried out,” H.].

For, since in your letters—which we hold before us—you had previously declared that he was burdened with many accusations, and on that account had been expelled and Photius elected [instead of “had been elected,” H.], we necessarily sent envoys of our see, supported by apostolic authority, to investigate the numerous crimes alleged against the aforesaid patriarch Ignatius and report them to us. We suspended the sentence expelling the most reverend man Ignatius or receiving Photius, reserving the matter not to the judgment of our envoys but specifically to our own examination.

But since you have now retained Photius and expelled the most prudent man, the patriarch Ignatius, without the judgment of our apostolate [Col. 0791B], we wish you to know in every respect that we absolutely neither receive Photius nor condemn the patriarch Ignatius.

Finally, it is worth considering what is meant by this: you had repeatedly acknowledged in letters that we possess that Ignatius had innocently exercised the priesthood of your royal city for almost twelve years and flourished in the holy virtues of modesty and chastity. Not only did you make this known to us in your letters, but your letters also confess that you continually praised and exalted him with great honors, as did the synodical statements issued in his time. Yet now, without having marked him before the apostolic see as an invader or as guilty of any crime, you have condemned him out of envy.

This most indiscreet act is wholly inconsistent with our entire holy Church, with our apostolate, and with the ancient definition of the holy Fathers [Col. 0791C].

Concerning the most noble man, the patriarch Ignatius, we have learned not only these things but also that he was distinguished not merely by birth. From the earliest period of his life he ascended through each ecclesiastical grade from the monastic life, with the consent of the entire ecclesiastical body, and attained the summit of the episcopate—as we learned from the letters (*apicibus*) that you had sent to the most holy bishop Leo, our predecessor.

But we know that Photius did not ascend through any ecclesiastical grades; rather, he was obstinately ordained bishop directly from secular lay service. Therefore we necessarily persist in the judgment on which we have stood, and we in no way receive the venerable patriarch Ignatius as condemned, nor do we receive Photius in any manner [Col. 0791D].

But because, after setting aside all the accusations by which you asserted that the vigorous man, the patriarch Ignatius, was liable before the apostolic see, you opposed only one charge—namely, that he had seized the see by secular power—and by your own special decision deposed, condemned, and expelled him, while rashly installing Photius, taken from the ranks of the laity, as bishop in his place [“and Photius,” H.], we cannot tolerate this with equanimity, especially since we had ordered that the case of these two men be investigated and reported to us, not decided.

For this reason, as we have said, we give no assent whatsoever to the deposition of the prudent man, the patriarch Ignatius, or to the installation of Photius, until the truth, stripped of every disguise of falsehood, shines forth in our presence. We know your custom in the royal city: no one can hold the office of archieratic authority there without the consent of the ecclesiastical people and the imperial suffrage. For that reason we neither wish nor ought to condemn the patriarch Ignatius [Col. 0792A].

Moreover, you decree that the ordination of Photius, whom you consecrated suddenly from secular service to the summit of so great a government, should be ratified, because Nectarius supposedly deserved to be made bishop not only from lay dress but even from paganism, by the ordination of the Second Holy Synod [“to be made bishop,” added].

Yet Nectarius, a Catholic of the true religion, conscious of no deposition of a Catholic, assumed the governance of the see without scandal, without force, and without any schism. You yourselves recall that, with the help of the Holy Spirit and the talent entrusted to him, he resisted the treacheries of the heretics and destroyed their doctrine, which had been flourishing for a long time and had infected many with its contagion [Col. 0792B]. We therefore testify that the Second Holy Synod, supported by the authority of the apostolic see, rightly and most properly approved Nectarius (concerning Nectarius, Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 5, chapter 8).

Likewise, you assert that the blessed and most brilliant teacher Ambrose [Paul on Saint Ambrose, in his Life] was made bishop from secular service and from the catechumenate, although he had been called by divine signs of miracles from his very cradle until the time of his consecration, and although he was compelled to undertake ecclesiastical governance when peoples who had been in disagreement were suddenly summoned into unity.

He did not pursue sedition or schism. Rather, when he offered himself to the people not voluntarily but under compulsion [Col. 0792C], he rejected and removed the alternatives he encountered. Nor did he seek the condemnation of anyone, which he would never have consented to for the sake of increasing his own dignity. Instead, compelled and forced, he yielded to their wishes, while observing the norm of ecclesiastical rules throughout his life, conquering all heresies, girded with the weapon of the word of God. For this reason, the holy Roman Church properly received him as well.

Thus necessity rightly received this exception, because he knew that nothing had rashly been done against the privilege granted by the canons.

You, however, have not weighed the comparison with these illustrious men correctly. You expelled the frequently mentioned patriarch Ignatius, who had been rightly ordained by you, unjustly from the patriarchate, and elevated Photius suddenly from secular service to episcopal dignity [Col. 0792D]. For that reason we do not permit this to have any validity, because it has never been the custom of the holy Roman Church to expel one person rashly or unjustly and install another in his place. Rather, it has taken pains to weigh the affairs of all with an even balance and define them justly.

Since you say that the number of those who attended your venerable Council of Nicaea at the deposition of the patriarch Ignatius was nearly equal to the number of those who attended the Council of Nicaea, we are astonished. What benefit, we ask, is there in a college of equal number presiding when its members violate the judgment of the very council whose number they imitate [more correctly, “the number,” H.]? We regard this as worthy not of praise but of condemnation, because the accumulation of sins is greater wherever the band of transgressors has been multiplied.

We do not merely follow the synodical constitutions of the numerous bishops of the holy Councils of Nicaea and Chalcedon and of the other holy Fathers [Col. 0793A]; we venerate their generous and just judgments, inspired by God. They are not observed by us merely because there were many of them in person; rather, we judge them to be more numerous because of the strength of their judgments.

As for your claim that our envoys said that, after the condemnation of the most religious man, the patriarch Ignatius, his entire consecration ought to be annulled, condemned, and uprooted [for “omnis ejus consecratio,” H.], far be it from us to permit this. Since we neither condemn the patriarch Ignatius nor receive the adulterer Photius, who rashly presumed to usurp for himself the see of a living man who guarded and preserved it chastely [possibly “preserving,” H.], and since—if we may put it so [possibly the word “since” is to be deleted, H.]—he was not ashamed to occupy it contrary to order, we shall not consent to the multiplication of scandals in your Church [Col. 0793B].

Rather, most serene son Augustus, we admonish, persuade, and announce to Your Devotion by apostolic authority that at last you resist those who, raising themselves by the pleasure of their own will as prelates over the Church of Constantinople, repeatedly depose men without canonical examination, without our knowledge, and attempt unexpectedly to consecrate another in his place.

For this reason, alas, this dispute is being greatly stirred up throughout your eastern Churches. Take greater care, whenever anything arises from which schism might emerge, to conduct the matter with the counsel of our Church, so that—as we already know was done in the case of the holy images—what has been justly deliberated may remain confirmed by the authority of the apostolic see [Col. 0793C].

But whatever is attempted solely out of rivalry or willfulness, contrary to canonical or synodical censures and without consulting the Roman Church, must be restrained by the arm of your religion, lest, in the course of your reign, the holy Church of God and the glory of the royal city should, God forbid, be diminished in any respect.

Let it therefore be permitted for the holy Church, which Christ redeemed from slavery to corruption with His sacred blood, to remain, while preserving the orthodox faith through your effort, tranquil and at peace, free from every disturbance by its assailants.

Finally, we exhort the Church of Constantinople concerning its condition, so that it may strive with every religious care to nourish men learned in such matters, who may be capable of being installed to the honor of the see [Col. 0793D] itself when its bishops die or depart for any reason in the future. This must be observed not only in so great a patriarchate, but also, according to canonical custom, must be maintained and guarded with great caution in every individual city.

We have also taken care to inform Your Clemency of this: as is found inserted in the records sent to the apostolic see and to our pontificate, our letter addressed to you was falsified through fraud or deceit—we do not know whose. Not only was it not reread in your presence according to its text or order, but we do not know what reckless person presumed, when reading or interpreting it before your imperial presence, to pass over several excerpts containing the sense of the letter itself and to substitute one thing for another [Col. 0794A]. If you order it to be examined in the presence of Your Majesty, you will find that it has been altered and falsified in certain places.

We, however, most merciful triumphant emperor, wishing that Your Excellency may stand untouched by every charge of instability, and that the sublime tranquillity of your empire may remain most sincerely in God’s service throughout long ages, admonish you as a spiritual father admonishing a spiritual son, urging you to fulfill through apostolic exhortations those things that are pleasing to God. And just as your predecessors who occupied the imperial summit were accustomed to venerate this holy Roman Church with the fullest devotion, so we beseech you also to carry out the apostolic instructions. For the measures that in the present matter we have taken care to establish through ecclesiastical ordinances were not undertaken out of envy or any deceit, but because we wished to preserve your imperial dignity and the holy Church of Constantinople unharmed, and, moved by the most fervent zeal of charity, to guard it from every reproach. As is found in the text of the letter sent to you, fearing God, we resolved to order these things and desire that they all be observed.

Almighty God, who has deigned to choose you to restrain the savagery of many peoples upon the imperial throne, preserve your most devout empire for many generations in the stability and defense of his holy Church; and, while granting you life and health, always allow you to desire those things that please him. Thus, just as he has graciously granted you the power to rule happily in the present age, may he permit you in the age to come to possess the rewards of eternal happiness for your good deeds and observance of justice, which ought to be weighed under your governance.

Given on 19 March, in the ninth indiction.

## XIV. SUPPLEMENT TO THE ROMAN COUNCIL OF THE YEAR 862

[In Mansi, at the same place.]

### I. On John, archbishop of Ravenna

John, archbishop of Ravenna, whom we summoned to the synod on account of certain ecclesiastical necessities and various acts of presumption, and who, because our bishop Nandecisus of Pola is said to have brought against him a written accusation to our episcopal court, allegedly entangled in the worst error of heresy—and this has also been stated orally—delayed coming and despised the summons, and refused to clear himself of the charge: in accordance with the ruling of the nineteenth chapter of the Council of Carthage, we separate him from the solemn celebration of the sacred Mass and from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and in the present synod we excommunicate him, until he comes into our presence here at Rome and we see the integrity of his purification.

[Note: This bishop was unknown to Ughelli and should therefore be added to the catalogue of the bishops of Pola in *Italia sacra*.]

If anyone should presume to communicate with him, let them likewise be subject to the bonds of excommunication.

### II. That the Lord Jesus Christ suffered only in the flesh

It must truly be believed and confessed in every respect that our Lord Jesus Christ, God and Son of God, endured the suffering of the cross only according to the flesh, while in his divinity he remained incapable of suffering, as apostolic authority teaches and the lucid doctrine of the holy Fathers most clearly demonstrates.

### III. On those who say that the divinity was passible

But those who say that our Redeemer Jesus Christ and Son of God endured the suffering of the cross according to his divinity—because this is impious and execrable to Catholic minds—let them be anathema.

### IV. On those who say that original sin is not forgiven to everyone in baptism

Let there be anathema upon all who say that those who are reborn from the most holy font of baptism, believing in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, are not equally cleansed from original sin.

### V. The decrees of the council of the most blessed Pope Leo IV shall remain inviolate

Anyone who attempts to violate the sacred statutes of the venerable council of our predecessor, the most blessed bishop Leo IV, established by the present council—as we recall was done after the passing of our predecessor, the most holy pontiff Benedict of blessed memory—we bind with the bond of anathema.

[Note: Labbe subsequently included in his *Collection*, volume IV, the council edited by Holstenius.]

### VI. No one shall presume to oppose the election of the Roman pontiff

If anyone should presume to oppose the election of the Roman pontiff by the priests or primates, nobles, or the entire clergy of that holy Roman Church, let him be anathema, as was established in the council of the most blessed Pope Stephen.

[Note: Observe who at that time would have had responsibility for the election of the Roman pontiff.]

[Note: Gratian, *Decretum*, distinction 33, chapter 8, reports the decree of Pope Stephen IV, whom others call Stephen V. There it is established what procedure was henceforth to be followed in the election of the Roman pontiff. Baronius, Binius, Papebrochius, Natalis Alexander, and other Catholic writers, however, considered this an invention and imposture of men strongly favoring imperial authority, at the time when the wars between the priesthood and the empire were raging. Pagi, by contrast, in his *Criticism of Baronius* under the year 897, maintains that this decree was a genuine work—not of Stephen IV, who ceased to live in 817, but of Stephen V, called by some Stephen VI, who was elected pope in 896.

Yet the Acts of the Roman council that I am now publishing seem capable of resolving this famous controversy. When Nicholas I, discussing the election of the Roman pontiff and wishing to eliminate the disturbances that regularly arose in it, confirms and decrees that whatever had been established in the council of the most blessed Pope Stephen must be observed, the decree of Stephen—without doubt Stephen IV—must have preceded it for this purpose. This could scarcely have been anything other than the decree praised by Gratian; nevertheless, if one wishes to add something to it that was supplied by subsequent pontiffs, I will not object.

At the Roman council held under the Emperor Lambert, and therefore in the year 904, as Baronius and, after him, Labbeus in volume IX of the *Councils* believed—but in fact in the year 898—the ancient custom observed in the election of the pontiff was confirmed. If there was already an ancient custom at that time, its beginnings may reasonably be traced back as far as the time of Pope Stephen IV.]

### VII. On those who presume to strike a bishop

Concerning those who presume to strike, beat, or assault a bishop, we decree and establish by irrevocable promulgation that they shall be exposed to the danger of anathema.

*(Year 862.)*

## XV. LETTER OF NICHOLAS TO ADON, ARCHBISHOP OF VIENNA

He sends the pallium to the new archbishop and transmits to him the Acts of the synod celebrated by him at Rome.

[In Mansi, at the same place.]

### Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy fellow bishop Adon, archbishop of Vienna

You have taken care to send letters to us in obedience to canonical sanction and institution. Through them you have brought joy to the apostolic heart, although, after reading them, we were also afflicted with sorrow because, while observing four synods, you omitted the fifth and the sixth. For in your petition for the pallium we granted your request. Nevertheless, having obtained such an occasion, your petition ought not to have been fulfilled unless, after examining the stated intention of the letter sent, we had learned that you wished in every respect to hold what the holy Church teaches as dogma.

Therefore we wish—and at the same time ask Your Holiness—that you send us as quickly as possible an account of what you think concerning those fifth and sixth synods.

With the grace of the Holy Spirit exhorting and assisting us, we celebrated a synod at Rome in the month of March for various benefits of the Church. There also we established certain chapters, and we sent them to Your Holiness for safekeeping and for transmission through you to your fellow archbishops, and we exhort you to instruct your suffragans to observe them.

*(Year 862.)*

## XVI. TO THE SAME

Concerning the divorce between King Lothar and his wife Theutberga, answering Adon’s inquiries.

[In Mansi, at the same place.]

### Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy fellow bishop Adon, archbishop

Because we see the steadfastness with which Your Holiness watches most fervently over the condition of the holy Church of God, and because we observe that, through zeal for righteousness, you are aroused against the conduct and actions of wrongdoers—indeed, of transgressors and violators of the holy laws—we give thanks to almighty God. We admonish Your Holiness by every means, with the authority granted to us through blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, so that, with his help, you may advance in such matters.

To the extent that, as you have informed us in your letters, you see them acting wickedly and recklessly, to that same extent we exhort you, relying on the help of divine law, to resist them through priestly and pontifical authority, showing no partiality toward any person and setting forth new and old things in the word of preaching, lest their blood be required from your hands.

Perhaps the most gracious and generous mercy of almighty God will deign to recall them from their own willfulness. If, through your zeal and labor, they are received again within the fold of the Lord’s flock, may you deserve to receive the reward of fraternal gain from their recovery. For behold, the time is at hand when you must rise up against them, set yourself as a wall for the house of Israel, and stand in battle on the day of the Lord.

And after other matters:

Regarding the chapters on which Your Beatitude wished to consult us, our apostolic concern has taken care to reply as follows, according to the sanctions of the Fathers.

1. You ask whether, if a man dismisses a woman whom he has lawfully betrothed and married because he later imposed a bad name upon her, he may, without a decree of a general synod, take another wife contrary to evangelical authority, or, while the first woman is still alive, keep a concubine in place of a wife.

Supported by apostolic authority and in accordance with evangelical sanction, we altogether resist this. We neither allow those who do such things to have the union of another wife while the dismissed wife remains alive, nor grant them permission to keep a concubine.

2. Concerning a betrothed woman who is violated without the bridegroom’s knowledge, and afterward, once the dowry has been given, the same bridegroom lies with her in the manner of a husband: whether, after an interval has elapsed [Roman edition: “after an interval has intervened on both sides”], he may dismiss her as though she had first been violated by another and then take another woman, as though the first had not been his wife, or keep a concubine in her place.

We do not consent to this either: those who are joined by a lawful bond of marriage and become one body for some period of time must not divorce. What they voluntarily concealed at the beginning of their union, when they learned that she had been violated, they must afterward continue to endure; and, if they did not conceal it voluntarily, they must nevertheless preserve the union unwillingly. They must also abstain altogether from concubines.

3. Whether those who seize, devastate, plunder, or presume to retain sacred objects given to churches and offered by the faithful, on the pretext that princes have granted them to themselves [the Roman edition adds: “and plundered”], are to be excommunicated and anathematized by episcopal authority.

Concerning these goods, which, once contributed and dedicated to God, are afterward seized by certain persons under the pretext of a grant from princes, we decree that the matter first be brought before the prince, so that such a presumptuous act may be cut off and it may be determined whether the grant is truly his or merely the presumption of the invader.

If it was the prince’s disordered generosity, the prince himself must be rebuked for correction. But if the presumption of the invader is established, he must be restrained by the penalty of excommunication until he makes amends.

And after other matters:

Know that John, archbishop of Ravenna, has been received paternally by the apostolic see, purified by an oath from the error of which he was accused, and that both he and his successors have sworn to us over the bodies of the saints that they will show the Roman see the reverence due to it.

When you next send us the written petitions to us, we shall send them to Your Holiness.

And after other matters:

We exhort you to labor most earnestly, both through yourself and through our other fellow bishops, so that the evils occurring in the kingdom of Gaul may be corrected by the zeal of piety, and that you may resist with the greatest strength, prepared for so many evils.

*(Year 852.)*

## XVII. TO KING LOTHAR

He sends legates to convene a synod, to which he orders two bishops from Charles’s kingdom to come, just as he had ordered two others to assemble from the kingdom of Louis, his uncle, and Charles, his brother.

[In Mansi, at the same place.]

### Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to King Lothar *(concerning the synod)*

[Note: I have restored this salutation from the Roman edition.]

Your royal Excellency recently sent word to our apostolate asking that we deign to send legates from our side for the completion of the synod. Even before receiving your letter, and afterward as well, we were impelled by an ardent desire to do this. But because until now we have been occupied with many matters concerning the interests and benefits of God’s holy churches, we could not send them as quickly as we wished.

Now, however, with the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, we are sending legates of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve: two most reverend bishops, Rhadoald of the holy Church of Porto and John of the holy Church of Ficulensis [Roman edition: Fundensis], our beloved men, through whose arrival and presence the synod of God’s priests may be assembled.

As we already informed you in our letters, your greatness was told that two bishops from the kingdom of King Louis, your uncle, and two from the kingdom of King Charles, your brother, ought to come to that synod. Now we wish, and by our letters we command, that two from the kingdom of the glorious King Charles, your uncle, likewise be present there without any ambiguity.

As we send these letters to your nobility, we ask you to transmit them at once to King Charles through one of your faithful men, so that, as we have said, two bishops of his kingdom may be able to come to the aforesaid synod, which is to be assembled with the Lord’s assistance, together with our legates.

Let Your Excellency receive these legates of our apostolate with fitting honor and grant them a place in your familiarity, so that, with the Lord’s help, when they have returned to us and report to us worthy things concerning your side, we may give the greatest thanks to God and enrich you with the gift of apostolic blessing, rejoicing in the faithful devotion of your humility.

May the right hand of the heavenly Majesty deign to preserve you unharmed for many years.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, in the eleventh indiction.

*(Year 862.)*

## XVIII. TO CHARLES THE BALD, KING

That two bishops from his kingdom should depart for the synod to be convened at Metz.

[In Mansi, at the same place.]

### Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Charles, glorious king *(concerning the synod)*

This holy and pre-eminent see, entrusted with the anxious care and oversight of the Lord’s flock, strives, relying on divine assistance, to order and complete all things throughout every part of the world by the salutary arrangement of its righteousness. What it can accomplish by its singular authority, it often determines by the agreement of many priests, and by the judgment of justice it deliberates over correcting those things that have been committed somewhere wrongly and beyond measure.

Therefore we wish Your Royal and God-beloved Excellency to know that for the future synod to be assembled at Metz, the city of Lothar, your nephew, on account of Theutberga, sister of the cleric Hucbert, and Waldrada, we order two bishops from your kingdom—whom you know to be prudent and truthful—to come there. Together with the legates of our holy see, whom we are now sending there with the Lord’s help, and with the assembly of other venerable bishops who are to gather for the same synod, they are to strive to examine and decide all matters by careful investigation and thoroughly correct inquiry, according to God and the venerable institutions of the holy Fathers.

[Note: Concerning Theutberga and Waldrada, see the *Life of Saint Deicolus*, volume II of the *Acts of the Order of Saint Benedict*, p. 114. HARD.]

We have likewise sent letters to your brother, the glorious King Louis, summoning two bishops from his kingdom to that synod, so that in all matters to be established there righteousness may prevail, justice may have strength, and, falsehood having been driven away, truth may shine forth, so that the Church of Christ may stand unshaken against every adversity through the venerable contest of God’s priests.

Let your nobility not delay these bishops as they come and, in obedience to our command, wish to hasten to the aforesaid synod. Rather, for the love of God, allow them to proceed to that synod without delay.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, in the eleventh indiction.

## XIX. TO THE EMPEROR LOUIS II

He commends the legates sent to Francia concerning the cause of his brother Lothar.

[In Mansi, at the same place.]

### Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the Emperor Louis *(concerning the synod)*

Through these letters of our apostolate we inform Your August Serenity, resplendent in imperial majesty, that, hindered by the many daily concerns and interests of God’s churches—matters to which it is fitting that we devote ourselves vigilantly—we cannot send our legates to Francia for the completion of the synod that, by our apostolic authority, we have decided to hold concerning the cause of the glorious King Lothar, your brother, as quickly as was agreed among us.

Because we are inflamed by zeal for ecclesiastical righteousness and benefit, with which we must always burn, we have now sent there, as we have said, two of our venerable bishops as legates: Rhadoald, bishop of the holy Church of Porto, and John, bishop of the holy Church of Ficulensis [Roman edition: Fundensis], our beloved men, to settle canonically the matter in question, which you know.

May Your Clemency receive them kindly and provide them with a faithful and prudent man who will conduct them safely and peacefully, with every courtesy, to the place where they may be received by men whose escort will enable them to reach the aforesaid King Lothar, your brother, unharmed.

[Roman edition adds: “Let Your Clemency also know.”]

For the common peace and concord of the Church, we have ordered two bishops from the kingdom of King Charles, your uncle, to come to the same synod, which, with the Lord’s help, is to be assembled at Metz, summoned by a letter of the apostolic see. Together with our legates and the assembly of other priests of God, they are to decide justly and canonically whatever must be determined.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, in the eleventh indiction.

*(Year 862.)*

## XX. TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL AND GERMANY

That they should come with the legates to the synod at Metz, hear Lothar there, and investigate and decide his divorce case canonically.

[In Mansi, at the same place.]

### Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all archbishops established throughout Gaul and Germany *(concerning the synod)*

We do not believe that it is unknown to you how, on account of the two women connected with King Lothar, the face of the Church of God has been stained by the blemish of an illicit marriage, or how, after rejecting one of them, that king most wickedly joined another to himself.

The first of them, named Theutberga, grieving bitterly over her repudiation, sought the judgment of our see concerning this matter through a legation that she sent. For this reason we considered it wholly uncanonical to judge the cause of one party without the other.

Therefore we have decreed that your fraternity, assembled at Metz together with our legates, hear Lothar’s case and decide it by a common canonical judgment.

Accordingly, while we were preparing to send two other bishops to different regions, it came to our attention that Lothar, after rejecting his lawful and first wife, had taken a second woman as his spouse, neither awaiting the judgment requested and promised by our see nor submitting anywhere to a canonical judgment. What else does this make clear except that, where he anticipated the judgment of many, he showed himself a transgressor by his own judgment?

For this reason we have sent this letter of apostolic authority universally to your fraternity, so that, inflamed by zeal for the Christian religion, you may travel to Metz together with our legates, summon Lothar there, hear him, and pronounce a canonical judgment against him.
