But if he delays coming, withdraws from the synodal presence of our legates who will be there, and takes no care to return to penitence and satisfaction—so that he does not appear personally before the synod and our legates to give satisfaction and abandon his crime—we shall henceforth render him excommunicated and, for as long as he persists in this, exclude him from fellowship with the entire Church.

*(Year 862.)*

## XXI. TO THE BISHOPS SITTING IN THE COUNCIL OF METZ

That they should examine and decide Theutberga’s case and send the Acts of the council to him.

[In Mansi, at the same place.]

### Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all our most reverend fellow archbishops and to the bishops sitting in the council being held at Metz

[Note: I corrected this letter, which in the printed editions is riddled with errors here and there, according to the standard of the Roman edition of the *Pontifical Letters*, 1591. The same was done in the other cases as well. — Mansi.]

The honor due to priests is then properly shown when we see them, in all matters that must be weighed by them under the balance of equity, holding the scale of mercy together with the balance of righteousness and, while holding it, neither held back by anyone’s favor nor moved by anyone’s threats, nor even turned in any way from the path of justice by abundant money or the grandeur of honors.

To the extent that they are granted care in examining the causes of their neighbors, an equal measure of fear, together with zeal for righteousness, must unquestionably be applied to their own protection, lest they appear forgetful of that apostolic saying: “Each will receive his own reward according to his labor” (1 Corinthians 3).

While our apostolic mind was extending itself among the many ecclesiastical matters that seem to pertain to the salvation and firmness of the faith of God’s people, a report concerning a dispute between certain women—namely Theutberga and Waldrada—made us especially attentive, as some persons reported it. Pastoral care moved us to hear the matter, and, lest the Lord’s flock be wearied by any illness of violence through negligence, the fervor of charity urged us more passionately toward the restoration of health.

The aforesaid Theutberga repeatedly endeavored to appeal to the apostolic see through tearful letters. In them, speaking in a plaintive voice, she says that she is pure and innocent of the crime of which she is accused.

Concerning this matter and the discernment of judgment, just as we recently decided to admonish your fraternity through apostolic letters, we wish you to be present at our apostolic exhortation. When legates come from our side, you are to assemble there, supported by apostolic authority, a synodal gathering at which they preside together with your fraternity, and together with them you must act with the greatest vigilance, without the stain of deceit, the stimulus of envy, or the nourishment of hatred—things that can turn people from the way of truth and, alas, make them deviate from the path of righteousness.

Always keeping God before your eyes, despising the persons of princes and the threats that rise for a time and end in time, strive, with the said legates, to discover what is more just and what is truer in these matters, and by their agreement to decide and establish it without doubt.

Take care to avoid what is said through the prophet: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness, who call bitter sweet and sweet bitter” (Isaiah 5).

Among other things, the evangelical saying that instructs us to live well also admonishes us: “Do not judge according to appearance, but judge a just judgment” (John 7:24).

The Psalmist likewise says: “If indeed you speak justice, judge rightly, sons of men” (Psalm 57).

There are many things with which we could admonish your fraternity—not judging you out of forgetfulness or ignorance, but embracing the labor of charity. We believe, however, that these reminders are sufficient, since we do not doubt that, in such matters, you remember the many teachings of evangelical, apostolic, and prophetic reading.

The essential point is that, in the present examination, you should define the causes of your neighbors together with the aforementioned legates, with the justice of equity and without any deceit or stain of envy, as we have said, since you stand in the presence of God. Strive to do so justly and irreproachably, with the fear of God, so that your agreement and judgment, and that of the legates, may appear to all to shine with equity.

For if we perceive that either you or they have turned in any direction, out of favor toward anyone, from the canonical institutions and those of the holy Fathers—which we do not wish—we shall not hesitate to rebuke you.

If matters concerning other ecclesiastical interests arise in the same council, examine them with worthy scrutiny and strive to decide them with the fear of God. But if any dispute arises there in which you are perhaps unable to impose the authority of a decision, we decree that you reserve it for our judgment.

We establish, moreover, that you promptly report to our pontificate, in a written account of the proceedings, everything that has been done and decided in that council. If we see that these matters have been decided with the beauty of justice and a credible ordinance, we shall give thanks to almighty God. But if, which we do not wish, the proceedings have been marked by injustice and a contrary intention, we shall order them to be renewed with the utmost urgency.

As we informed Your Affection in our first letter, we were unable to send the legates of our pontificate because we were occupied with certain ecclesiastical interests. But now, with Christ’s help, we have decided to send most reverend legates distinguished by knowledge and learning: namely, the bishops Rhadoald and John, our beloved men and counselors. They are to strive to celebrate the aforesaid council together with Your Holiness, as we have stated.

May almighty God, who has adorned you with the summit of sacred government, fill and adorn the hearts of Your Beatitude with the brightness of righteousness and justice, so that in all your actions you may be seen to shine with the fullness of equity.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, in the eleventh indiction.

*(Year 862.)*

## XXII. TO CHARLES THE BALD, KING

He asks him to spare Baldwin, who had abducted his daughter and taken her as his wife.

[In Mansi, at the same place.]

### Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Charles, glorious and foremost king *(concerning Baldwin)*

The holy Church, redeemed by the blessed and precious blood of Christ our God and founded by the sacred word of that Lord himself upon the solid rock of true faith, opens the bowels of her compassion to all—not only to those whom she has regenerated from water and the Spirit when they have sinned, but also to all those whom the sacred water of baptism has not yet washed—and rejoices to cherish them in her healing bosom.

Therefore, from the beginning of her institution, all who recognize that they lie in some crime of wickedness should hasten to flee to her with worthy devotion, as to the loving bosom of a most dear mother, so that through spiritual grace, which rightly forgives the penitent, they may be released from the bonds of sins.

And because many people oppressed by the burden of crime flee daily from various parts of the world to this holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, the mother of all lands, which by the primacy of her privilege divinely excels the other Churches of God spread throughout the whole world, begging with humble and profound sorrow of heart that remission and pardoning grace be granted them, from her all who seek it with faithful intention receive and are granted the assistance of a just balance, through the distinguished merit of love and the grace of due compassion.

For this reason Baldwin, your vassal, endeavored with ardent spirit to flee to the thresholds of the most blessed princes of the holy apostles, Peter and Paul, and to approach our pontificate. He stated with his own mouth that he had incurred your indignation because, without the consent of your will, he had chosen in marriage Judith, your daughter, who loved him above all others, and that he had taken her willingly.

For this reason he poured out many prayers before our pontificate, earnestly asking that, through our intervention, he might deserve to obtain the favor of Your Greatness.

Moved by his repeated petitions and by the abundance of mercy, we earnestly implore Your Royal Excellency through these letters of our apostolate and through the presence of our legates—namely, the most reverend and holy bishops Rhadoald and John, our beloved men—that, for the love of Jesus Christ our Lord and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, whose help Baldwin himself sought with devout faith more than that of the kings of the earth, and out of the affection that we clearly recognize you have for us, you grant the aforesaid Baldwin both pardon and complete grace, since it is known that something of this kind formerly happened to other kings as well.

Thus, relying on the benevolence of Your Greatness, he may remain safe among your other faithful subjects.

We ask you to grant him the favor of Your Sublimity not only because, out of pious love, we ought to assist all who have been stained by the contagion of some crime and who ask and seek with humble devotion the aid, mercy, and protection of this apostolic see, according to the nature of the deed, but also because we fear that, on account of your anger and indignation, Baldwin himself may join the impious Northmen, enemies of the holy Church, and introduce some danger into the people of God whom you ought, with prudent counsel and an attentive mind, to rule and govern safely and unharmed, or cast among them the fuel of scandal that might ravage the assemblies of the faithful. As a result, may danger not—God forbid—befall your soul.

May the right hand of the heavenly Majesty protect you and deign always to keep you unharmed from every adversity.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, in the eleventh indiction.

*(Year 862.)*

## XXIII. TO QUEEN HERMENTRUD

He intercedes for Baldwin, who had come to Rome to implore assistance.

[In Mansi, at the same place.]

### Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hermentrud, queen *(concerning Baldwin)*

The whole community of the faithful, from peoples of various parts of the world, whatever their rank or age, if they are perhaps held back by some guilt of crime or by fear of their lords, hasten to this holy Roman Church, the mother of all lands, in order to receive a saving remedy. As is evident to all, they humbly beg to receive from her salvation not only of the soul but also of the body.

Supported by many divine authorities and strengthened by the teachings of the holy Fathers, she supplies them with consolation in motherly love and does not refuse, in compassion, to offer the breasts of consolation for them to suck.

And because this Baldwin, who abducted your dearest daughter contrary to the sanctions of the divine laws, acknowledged that he was guilty of this, he presented himself sorrowfully at the thresholds of the holy apostles with tearful and mournful prayers. He also sought, weeping, to present himself before our apostolate in order to receive apostolic help for so great a crime.

When we learned of his lamentable petition, filled with so great a crime, the Lord’s saying through the prophet came to mind: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6). We took pity on him and decided that these letters of apostolic concern should be sent to your diligence, beloved in Christ. We also sent to Your Majesty our most reverend and most holy bishops Rhadoald and John, our beloved men, as legates on his behalf.

Through them we earnestly beseech you that the aforesaid Baldwin may receive, for the love of God, the favor that he desires to obtain from Your Magnificence through the intercession of the apostles, and that, through the pronouncements of our pontificate, he may receive consolation in his distress. Thus, since he does not deny that through an unhappy fault he has deviated from the standard of equity, may he recognize the apostles’ remedy and, with your help, obtain favor from your lord.

May the right hand of the heavenly Majesty protect you and deign always to guard you from every adversity and stain.

*(Year 862.)*

## XXIV. TO STEPHEN, COUNT OF THE AUVERGNE

He orders him to restore Sigon, bishop of Auvergne, to his church after removing the usurper, and to present himself before the synod of the legates to give satisfaction concerning the charges brought against him.

[In Mansi, at the same place.]

### Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Count Stephen
What and how much you have obstinately done against the canonical and ecclesiastical rules—indeed, against natural rights—does not at all escape the knowledge of the apostolic see, which is spiritually present everywhere through the ministry entrusted to it. And although such things ought to be driven away from our minds with such hatred that we are rightly compelled to bring their authority upon you with a rod, nevertheless, while still hoping that you may repent of such great evils, we are sending you this letter of our apostolate, so that, with the neck of your obstinacy bowed, you may obey the commands of the holy priests, repent of the past, and carefully and diligently guard yourself against the future, lest by persevering in such conduct you fall into the everlasting snares of the devil.

Moreover, since what is more wicked than these things is that, contrary to everything consistent with the Christian religion, after casting out the most holy Sigon, bishop of Arverne, you substituted in his place the usurper Adon, a cleric, we command you by the authority of almighty God and of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul that, without allowing any delay, you restore the most holy bishop Sigon to his church after removing the usurper, and henceforth allow him to remain in the full dignity of his priesthood.

Since, moreover, certain shameless and most criminal charges are repeatedly brought against you, we decree by apostolic authority that, in order to give the fullest satisfaction concerning them, you make every effort to appear at the appointed place in the presence of our legates, who will preside over the synod established by us. If you neglect this, and attempt to evade your presence at the synodical examination, know that by the authority of our episcopate you are entirely excommunicated from participation in wine and meat until you appear at Rome in our special presence to render a strict account.

But if the usurper of the holy church of Arverne attempts, after this our decision, to remain there, and presumes by any device to cause any impediment to the most holy bishop Sigon, let him know that he likewise is to be completely excluded not only from participation in wine and meat, but also from participation in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, for as long as he obstinately delays coming into the apostolic presence in obedience to our commands.

Farewell.

## XXV. TO SALOMON, KING OF THE BRITTONES

Concerning the renewal of the examination of expelled bishops before the archbishop of Tours or before the apostolic see, and concerning the right of the metropolitan among the Brittones.

[In Mansi, same place.]

**[Column 0806B]**

**NICHOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to SALOMON, king of the Brittones.**

**[Note: Column 0805D]** Hardouin compared this letter with a manuscript of the archives of Tours, from which he noted various readings that are included in the text.

**[Note: Column 0805D]** “To Salomon, king of the Brittones.” Third and last, as it appears in Gratian, 3, question 6, *Haec quippe*. But the letter is wrongly attributed there to Pope John, since it is Nicholas’s. Hincmar of Laon also quotes the passage in his first defense, from another unpublished letter of Pope Adrian to the same Salomon on the same subject: “But the present lord Pope Adrian, mindful of this duty and that of his predecessors, recently commanded the following from a letter sent to Salomon, duke of the Brittones: ‘The priests of the neighboring dioceses lament that other priests have been placed over them—British priests, if indeed they should be called priests, and not rather usurpers and sacrilegious men. Moreover, when they have certain business, they are not permitted to attend the councils of bishops, but, contrary to the sacred canons and venerable laws, are dragged before the tribunals of secular persons. They do not receive an episcopal judgment, but incur a popular judgment imposed contrary to the rules; and when they are overtaken by death, whatever support remained is seized. Bishops are also judged by readers and laymen, whom it was proper to examine only according to the canonical laws and in the presence of the metropolitans or of us, as the Lord says through the prophet: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets” (Psalm 104); and again: “Whoever touches you is like one who touches the pupil of my eye” (Zechariah 2).’” SIRM.

Blessed be the God and Father of my Lord [manuscript: “our”] Jesus Christ, who, through the grace of his great mercy, has deigned so to illumine your heart with exalted understanding that, on account of the brilliance of your wisdom, the place where you dwell is rightly regarded no longer as the West but as the East. For the sun of righteousness, which is Christ himself, has risen among you, and the darkness of unbelief has vanished.

But we ask the same almighty God that, just as he has graciously granted you recognition of the true faith, so he may also kindly grant the effect of good works.

For the rest, let your prudence know that we diligently searched in the archives of the holy Roman Church, which by the great mercy of almighty God we serve, concerning the bishops who were expelled and others substituted in their places. In the exemplars of the letters given by my predecessors—namely, the pontiffs of blessed memory Leo and Benedict—as well as by me, to Nomenoius and to you, and also to the archbishop of Tours, we found the matter very differently from what you claim in your letters.

**[Manuscript of Tours:]** “and sent to the bishops of your kingdom,” rather than “we found Pope Leo …,” although in your documents you do not even read that Pope Leo, of holy memory, granted Nomenoius counsel or authority to depose bishops, since it is clear that he commanded in many ways and by many means that this should not be done by anyone other than a fixed number of bishops.

For when Nomenoius consulted him about what should be done with those who sell the grace of the Holy Spirit, he replied that nothing should be done except what the holy canons prescribe concerning such matters, inserting the rules themselves into his letter. When he wrote concerning how, by how many, and by whom he decreed that bishops should be condemned, he made this clear, among other things, in writing at that same time to the bishops of the region of Britain, equally enjoining that all matters be conducted in councils of bishops. Let us set down his very words:

“We decree that there is never to be any condemnation of bishops unless it occurs either before the legitimate number of bishops, which is constituted by twelve bishops, or at least by a proven judgment of seventy suitable witnesses—such as are able to bring an accusation and who first give an oath upon the four sacred Gospels of Christ that they will state nothing false—as the blessed Silvester and the holy Roman Church appear to hold.”

Following this, my predecessor Benedict, of holy memory, because he had learned that bishops in your region had been expelled contrary to the decree of his predecessor—not by bishops but by laymen—wrote, filled with deep sorrow and indignation, that no reason permitted bishops to be driven from their sees whom the number of twelve bishops had not expelled.

I too followed their footsteps and held—and still hold—the same view. Bishops cannot suffer any loss of their honor unless it is established that they were expelled by twelve bishops, with the metropolitan bishop present and holding the first judgment, when they examined the accused.

Even if they are said to have confessed some crime, it may be believed that they admitted it only under force or fear, rather than truly confessing a deed which they had not done, since they saw laymen and all manner of secular persons conspiring against them together with the king—something that they had not even heard.

For whoever utters with the mouth alone, and not with the heart, what he says does not confess but merely speaks. Nor does a confession appear just when it has not been elicited through a legitimate examination.

Concerning the bishops Gislard and Actard [manuscript: Aitard, and so throughout], of Nantes, about whom you wrote, we found in our archive something very different from what your letter reported. Actard is indeed not acting properly, because he is consecrating again those whom Gislard is known to have ordained to that rank. Nevertheless, Actard is found to have undertaken the office of bishop before Gislard.

Finally, when the most holy Pope Leo wrote to Nomenoius, he called Actard, among other things, an outstanding man, and declared that he thought rightly, taught rightly, lived rightly, and continued rightly; but he marked out Gislard as a persistent usurper of the aforesaid Actard.

Having listed and investigated these and similar disputes and difficulties, and having found, established, and ascertained matters in this way, we cannot improperly depart from the rule of the holy Fathers or from the institutions of this see.

But if you wish to receive the blessing of almighty God, or if you truly desire to carry out our commands, accept my counsel and willingly heed what I indicate to you in this letter. For we exhort Your Glory, and with your namesake, the most wise Solomon, we admonish your affection, as it is said:

“Hear, my son, the discipline of your father, and do not abandon the law of your mother” (Proverbs 1).

**[Gratian 3, question 6, *Haec quippe*: where this letter is attributed to Pope John.]**

These are indeed the commands of God your Father, and this is the law of the Church your mother: namely, that you do not hesitate to send all the bishops of your kingdom to the archbishop of Tours, and do not disdain to request his judgment. For he is the metropolitan, and all the bishops of your kingdom are his suffragans, as the documents of my predecessors clearly demonstrate. Those predecessors took pains to rebuke your predecessors with forceful denunciation because they had withdrawn them from his care, although our letters sent concerning this matter also appear not to be lacking.

When the expelled bishops have been regularly examined before the aforementioned prelate of the Church of Tours and an entire number of his colleagues—that is, twelve bishops—at a duly convened assembly, and it has become clear that they were canonically expelled, those who have been consecrated in their places may certainly possess the honor of the episcopate while the expelled bishops remain in their deposition.

But if the expelled bishops are declared innocent, those who have been substituted for them must be removed, and the expelled bishops themselves are to receive their churches.

For when my predecessors, the Roman prelates, neither admitted nor approved the expulsion of those bishops who had been driven from their churches, they did not call those who had been substituted for them legitimate bishops while the expelled bishops were alive.

If, however, you disdain to send them to the archbishop of Tours, make every effort to send two bishops from among the expelled and two from among those substituted, together with a representative of Your Glory, to the apostolic see of blessed Peter. There, after a worthy examination has been conducted, it may become clear who the legitimate bishops are, and they may not irregularly lose their churches.

For nothing else can be definitively settled in the present matter.

Since there is a great dispute concerning who is metropolitan among the Brittones, although there is no record that you ever had a metropolitan church in your region [manuscript: metropolis], nevertheless, if you wish, after God establishes peace among you and our beloved son, the glorious Charles, you will easily be able to determine this.

But if you believe that the matter must be pursued with such great contention, hasten to send it to our apostolate, so that, by our judgment, it may become clearer than daylight which church was anciently the archiepiscopal church among you, and thereafter, with every ambiguity removed, your bishops may know without hesitation which one they ought to follow.

Nor is it necessary that the churches of the Lord suffer divisions or losses through the discord of kings, since they should strive, as far as depends on them, to preserve among themselves and toward all people the peace that they preach.

Having thus laid these matters before you, we wish Your Excellence to know through us that, if you obey our paternal admonitions and are willing to heed us both concerning the right of the metropolitan and concerning the renewal of the examination of the expelled bishops, there will be peace, concord, and every legitimate order in your kingdom.

But if you decide merely to question us and not to obey, scandals, discord, and every kind of confusion will not be absent from your life.

Moreover, we gladly commend to your affection the legates whom you sent to our pontificate. Considering their prudence and faith toward you, we have greatly rejoiced in the Lord.

May almighty God piously surround Your Glory, your illustrious wife, your noble children, and all who are under your rule with every joy and blessing.

---

## XXVI. TO CAROLUS, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, AND HIS SUFFRAGAN BISHOPS OF GERMANY [Note: Column 0809D]

This letter was not written before the year 858, when Nicholas I was made pope, nor after the year 863, when Carolus, archbishop of Mainz, died. It declares that he had issued no judgment against the bishop Salomon; that Abbo’s marriage, contracted within the fourth degree of consanguinity, must be dissolved; and it assigns penances for various sins.

[In Mansi, same place.]

**[Column 0809B]**

**NICHOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother in Christ, Carolus, archbishop, and to his suffragans Altfrid, Salomon, Hiltigrim, Theodoric, Gunton, Gebehard, Arn. Wingarius, Egibert, most reverend bishops, and to Grimald, Egilberht Thiotoniamal, and Adalgar, religious and venerable abbots.**

The shining definitions of divine teachings proceed from the sacred womb of knowledge of our see, and continually descend from it, because it knows how to give birth to the appearance of uprightness and justice and to administer established institutions according to an arrangement of love. It is recognized as a lover of peace and justice and a friend of kindness.

Supported by its custom and diligence, we have sent a letter to Your Beatitude, pouring out the sweetness of uprightness and adorned with an approved decree. Since we had determined to examine in your presence, through the careful investigation of the bishops, the case of Abbo, concerning whom you have reported, we preferred to learn the truth of the matter through you.

Concerning Bishop Salomon, we certainly issued no sentence either of crime or of wrongdoing, except that he should not bind with oaths the people entrusted to him by the Lord, as we had heard.

The letter which the abbot Grimold presented to you as though it had been sent by us was never written by our hand, nor issued by us, nor sent from our see. Rather, its wording is shown to be entirely full of falsity and constructed from lies.

Since you have endeavored, according to the deliberation of our institution, to investigate the case and intention of the aforementioned Abbo through synodical examination, and have informed us of the truth of the matter in your records, we give great thanks to Your Beatitude. Because you possess such great devotion toward the see of the key-bearer of heaven, we joyfully embrace your holiness with spiritual arms.

Since, as you report, it was established before your council by truthful witnesses that Abbo had presumed to take a wife contrary to the decrees of the holy canons and had joined himself to her even in the fourth generation, we decree and promulgate by apostolic decision that the bond of this unfortunate marriage be dissolved in every respect, because it is shown and recognized to be within his own consanguinity and kinship.

In answer to your question, we establish this also: no Christian may take a wife from his own consanguinity or kinship for as long as the degree of relationship is known or retained in memory.

We rejoice and praise your diligent observance because, in this matter, you have hitherto continued to observe in your parishes the decrees of our most blessed predecessors, the pontiffs Gregory and Zachary, as you have stated in your letters.

You said in which degree the faithful may be joined to one another. We, however, do not define the number of degrees in this matter; rather, as we have stated above, we admonish you to observe it without hesitation.

If priests fall into the snare of fornication and crime, and the act is manifest or demonstrated, they cannot retain the honor of the priesthood, according to the authority of canonical institution.

But if priests are accused of the crime of fornication and the crime is not proven against them, or they themselves have not disclosed it, what else is to be done except what is read and demonstrated in the chapter of the holy Council of Neocaesarea? Nevertheless, if they wish to purify themselves by oath, they shall have permission to do so. Deacons who are similarly accused shall proceed in the same manner.

Women who have been consecrated with the sacred veil, if—which God forbid—they have committed fornication, must not presume to lay aside the veil. Rather, subjected to the yoke of penance, they must strive with all their strength to reach the grace of pardon and remission.

Concerning parricides and fratricides, we command that they persevere for the cycle of one year in prayer before the doors of the basilica, imploring the Lord’s mercy. When the year has been completed, they are to be admitted into the church, but only among the hearers, until the period of one year has ended. Whenever they come to hear the solemn celebrations of the Mass or other sacred offices, they must stand.

When these things have been carried out, if the fruit of penance is seen in them, let them become participants in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, lest they be hardened in the darkness of despair.

They are not to eat meat on any day of their lives, nor presume to consume wine or cooked food except on three days of the week. They are to fast every day until the ninth hour, except on feast days and Sundays.

They must not dare to carry or take up arms except against pagans. Wherever they wish to go, they are not to be transported in any vehicle, but must make every effort to proceed on foot.

We place the duration of this penance in the judgment of Your Beatitude, so that, according to their conversion, you may extend or shorten it.

They must not be separated from their wives, if they have wives. If they do not have wives and are unable to remain continent, let them take legitimate women in marriage, lest they appear to fall into the abyss of fornication.

If the end of their lives should come before the completion of the cycles of the two aforementioned years, the viaticum is not to be denied them.

If anyone has committed fornication with two women, or with those persons whom sacred Scripture forbids, and has performed worthy penance but does not wish to maintain continence, he may take a legitimate wife in marriage. A woman who has fallen into such a crime may likewise do so, lest she be carried into the chaos of fornication. But we establish this only concerning laymen and laywomen.

If anyone has committed fornication with a spiritual mother, he is struck, as you know, by the blows of anathema. We likewise promulgate that the same punishment is to be inflicted upon one who commits the crime of fornication with a woman whom he has received from the sacred baptismal font, or with one whom he has held before the bishop and who has been anointed with sacred chrism.

If he has a legitimate wife, however, he is not to dismiss her.

Among these matters, Your Holiness also took care to ask whether, if a man’s wife has committed adultery, it is lawful for her husband to kill her according to worldly law.

The holy Church of God is never bound by worldly laws. It has no sword except the spiritual and divine one; it does not kill but gives life.

Concerning those who have committed homicide unintentionally, you have the definition of how they ought to act in the twenty-second chapter of the Council of Ancyra. Homicides may enter the church after the passage of one year.

A widow who has placed the sacred veil upon her head, prayed in the church among the other women mentioned, and offered an oblation with them, if she has professed that she will remain in the same habit and promised never to remove the veil of religious observance, must not presume to depart from that observance.

We wish Your Holiness well in Christ.

---

## XXVII. TO THE SAME

[Wasserschleben first published this letter in *Beiträge zur Geschichte der vorgratianischen Kirchenrechtsquellen*, Leipzig, 1839, p. 165, from the Darmstadt manuscript. Dr. Ploss of Bonn revised it against the same Darmstadt manuscript 2117, formerly Cologne 118 fol., where it appears on pp. 49ff., and corrected Wasserschleben’s errors.]

**Here begins the letter of Pope Nicholas to Carolus, archbishop of the holy Church of Mainz.**  
**[Note: Column 0811D]** The words of the title are illuminated in the manuscript.

**[Column 0811D]**

**NICHOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother in Christ, CAROLUS, archbishop of the holy Church of Mainz.**

Those who, untouched in the radiance of sacred teachings, are seen to shine in the contest are undoubtedly perceived to glitter with the favor of heavenly light [Note: Column 0812D: manuscript reading: “Lumilis”], because they seek the actions of a perfect norm and the increase of blessed ordinance.

Compelled, as we believe, by these considerations, you preferred to question us through the nectar of your letters concerning certain salutary matters, so that you might adorn the integrity of the flock entrusted to us with a saving governance and might correct the rashness of delinquents and the snares of criminal acts with diligent discipline, committing them to the effect of an approved decree. In such matters we rejoice most, and, enriched by eagerness, we establish them through apostolic speech.

Whoever delivers a priest to death by his will, or commits parricide, must not eat meat on any day of his life, nor presume to drink wine. He must fast until evening, except on feast days and Sundays. He must not take up arms, and wherever he wishes to go, he must not be transported in any vehicle, but must proceed on his own feet.

For the period of five years he must not enter a church. When the offices of sacred prayers or the solemn celebrations of Mass are being held, he must remain outside the doors of the basilica, praying and beseeching the Lord that he may be cleansed from so great a crime.

When the five-year period has been completed, he may enter the church, but he must not yet receive communion. He must stand among the hearers alone, or, when permission is granted, sit.

When the course of twelve years has ended [thus the manuscript], permission to receive communion is to be granted to him, and the remedy of riding is to be allowed. In the remaining observances, however, he is to continue for three days each week, so that he may more perfectly attain the summit of purification.

Those who have been subjected to the yoke of penance for various errors or any offenses are in no way to be separated from a lawful marriage, lest they be overwhelmed in the abyss of fornication and, while they are hoped to be raised to the heights, fall into the mire.

After completing their penance, homicides must not take up arms except against pagans.

Concerning those who have committed homicide unintentionally, we promulgate the following: for a period of three years they are not to receive communion, but must devote themselves with every diligence to fasts and continual prayers. They must not eat meat for three days each week, nor presume to drink wine until they have completed the period of ten years.

Women who, before the completion of the proper term, voluntarily expel infants conceived in the womb are undoubtedly to be judged as homicides.

But women who appear to suffocate their children while sleeping ought to be judged leniently, because they have fallen into this situation unwillingly and without awareness.

If a man marries a widow who has a daughter by her former husband and later has intercourse with that same daughter, the marriage must be dissolved in every respect, and the man must submit to the sanctions of penance, so that he is suspended from the sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ for a period of three years.

He must not eat meat; he must abstain from wine and cooked food; and each day he must hasten to observe a fast, except on feast days and Sundays. He must devote himself with every diligence to prayers.

When the end of the three years has arrived, he is to become a participant in the sacred communion. For the course of another three years he must take the greatest care to observe and complete fully the remaining practices, as we have stated.

The same observance is to be maintained concerning women who have secretly submitted themselves to intercourse with their father and with their son.

We decree something different concerning those who acknowledge that they have secretly polluted themselves with two sisters [thus the manuscript; uncertain reading].

**[Column 0813A]**

We have briefly set these matters out for the sake of the urgent necessity of your letter-bearer, who wished to return quickly to your territories, and because we were occupied with certain ecclesiastical duties.

At a suitable time, take care to send to our episcopate a fitting legate of Your Beatitude together with letters; then, with the help of heavenly grace, we shall strive to set forth more fully and completely all these matters and arrange to send them to Your Holiness.

We wish Your Holiness well in Christ, now and always.

---

## XXVIII. PRIVILEGE OF NICHOLAS I FOR THE CHURCH OF BEAUVAIS

**[In the year 863.]** He confirms to the Church of Beauvais the monasteries of Oratory and Flaviac, granted by King Charles the Bald.

[From *Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, among the instruments.]

**[Column 0813B]**

**NICHOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy ODO, bishop, and through you to the beloved Church of Beauvais, perpetual greeting.**

Whoever in this fleeting age is held in some danger, lest he be unhappily overwhelmed by weakness as though in the open sea of a tossing ocean, can find no better saving harbor for his infirmity than the see of him to whom it was said by divine utterance: “Once you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.”

Therefore, since by the abundance of heavenly grace we exercise his office throughout the universal Church of Christ, we ought to assist the weaknesses of all who are infirm and willingly extend to them the hand of our confirmation.

But since Your Holiness has reported and represented to our apostolate that the Church of Beauvais in the province of Rheims, over which, by the favor of divine grace, your venerable self is known to preside, has remained deprived, through earthly power, of the resources it enjoyed in earlier times, and in recent days has also been greatly weakened by the incursion and plundering of pagans, Your Holiness, solicitous with pastoral care, approached the clemency of the pious ruler, asking that the flock entrusted to you should not perish from want of resources, whether through what violent hands had inflicted or what hostile devastation had brought about.

And if no other support of consolation could be provided, you asked at least that the piety of the glorious King Charles not deny some aid of restoration from the goods taken from that church.

Moved by your petitions, the religious king said that he could not restore the goods that had been taken in their entirety, lest he appear to deprive his state of military service; nevertheless, he kindly promised to provide assistance to the holy Church of Beauvais.

For this reason he granted it two monasteries established within the same Church of Beauvais: namely, Oratory, which was once a convent for girls, and Flaviac, in which canons had lived, as compensation for the monastery of Fontenay. That monastery is proved in every respect, by the testimony of truthful witnesses and the assertion of Scriptures of irrefragable authority, to have belonged by right to the aforesaid mother Church of Beauvais.

These monasteries, however, even before they had been granted to secular persons, had been considerably destroyed through the uprising of civil discord. Now, because of barbarian invasion, they have been utterly overthrown, so that they have been deprived not only of their own goods, but also of the choir of canons and sacred virgins who had previously lived there; that community has been removed almost entirely, and the church and all the buildings have likewise been destroyed.

No hope of their restoration remains if they are again placed in the hands of secular persons or if they remain without an ecclesiastical pastor, as they have done until now.

Therefore Your Venerability requested that a privilege of our authority be made for your church concerning these same monasteries, so that they could not be taken away from the Church of Beauvais either during your time or during that of your successors.

The most glorious and beloved son, our king Charles, also made known to us his petitions concerning the same matter, similarly asking for this.

Consequently, considering that the petition was just and pious, so that the Church of Beauvais would not lack assistance after its devastation and the aforementioned monasteries would not remain entirely stripped of their religious order, we have decreed that what was requested be done.

By apostolic authority we establish that the aforesaid monasteries—namely, Flaviac and Oratory—granted to the Church of Beauvais by the kindness of the glorious King Charles, together with everything they possess, shall remain perpetually subject to that church for all time to come.

They are not thereafter to be taken away in any manner by royal or judicial power, whether from you, who are presently recognized as bishop of that church, or from your successor bishops.

This is to be done, however, in such an order that the goods granted or to be granted to these monasteries may be used to assist the needs of the Church of Beauvais, according to the will and judgment of the bishop who presides over that church; and that the monasteries themselves not be deprived of support either for the buildings of their houses, for the restoration of their churches, or for the needs of those serving God there.

Rather, the bishop of the Church of Beauvais is to arrange the goods in such a way that the monasteries themselves may be restored and preserved according to the measure of the resources granted to them, and that those who serve God there—whether women or men—may be assisted with the necessary provisions.

Thus, places dedicated to God and the goods granted to those churches may serve above all where the offerings of the faithful to God are known to have been bestowed. For it is neither pious nor just that the aforesaid churches should be stripped of their own goods so that they may serve the needs of another church, while no care appears to be given to their own needs.

Therefore let the bishop of Beauvais diligently see to it that he undertake such care both for the women serving God there, for men of whatever order, and for the restoration and preservation of the monasteries, that the house dedicated to God may rejoice in having a worthy administrator and that the rector who presides over it may not incur the judgment of heavenly censure because of negligence.

The monasteries themselves must henceforth never come into the hands or power of secular persons for any reason or under any pretext. For it is no light danger before the eyes of the supreme Judge to place secular authority over religious places and monasteries dedicated to God, and to entrust the concern of pastoral care to one who does not know what a shepherd is and seeks not the profit of souls but a monetary revenue—not that service may be rendered to divine worship, but that it may serve his own uses according to his desire for domination.

Therefore no king, no judge, and no person supported by the dignity of secular power shall have authority over the goods of the aforesaid monasteries, their estates and waters, their servants, or anything else granted to those monasteries, whether to rule, receive, or remove it, except the bishop of the Church of Beauvais.

Whatever has now been assigned to those monasteries, whether in gold or silver, in any kind of equipment, or in the whole substance of their resources, and whatever may be granted to them in future, is to be subject to the distribution and arrangement of the bishop of Beauvais. No right or domination of any other power is to exercise authority over them except insofar as divine authority, law, and justice permit.

But if any person, great or small, presumes with reckless daring to act against this apostolic decree of ours, let that person know that he is bound by the bond of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and condemned with all the impious to the fire of eternal punishment.

But whoever proves to be an observer of this command shall merit to obtain grace, mercy, and eternal life from the most merciful Lord our God.

Written by the hand of Peter, regional notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of April, in the eleventh indiction. Farewell. Amen.

On the fourth day before the Kalends of May, by the hand of Tiberius, first secretary of the holy apostolic see, during the reign of our most pious lord Augustus Louis, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, in the fourteenth year.

---

## XXIX. TO TRASULF, ABBOT OF CORVEY

**[In the year 863.]** Privilege of the monastery of Corvey.

[In Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XV.]

**[Column 0815D]**

**NICHOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to TRASULF, religious abbot, and through you to the venerable monastery of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul, which is called Corvey, perpetual greeting.**
It is fitting to apostolic governance that blessed Peter, the foremost of the apostles, through the grace divinely attributed and revealed to him—although our merits are far unequal to his—has conferred upon us, by a singular prerogative, the distinction of excelling principally throughout the whole community of the Christian religion; so that, just as by his singular privilege we surpass all others in dignity and authority, so also we may have responsibility for all the Churches of God and provide suitable assistance to each of the faithful and to pious places where the divinity is continually appeased by the devotion of those who serve God. [Col. 0816A]

Accordingly, since not many years ago the venerable Odo, who was then abbot of the monastery of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul called Corbie, and our glorious and beloved son Charles, king of the Franks, had petitioned our predecessor, Benedict, the bishop of holy memory, by letters and messengers sent to him, asking that he grant the aforesaid monastery free disposition of its property and regular and canonical permission to choose an abbot from among themselves, and since he received their petition graciously, granted what they requested, and issued a privilege to the said monastery so that the permanence of his grant might be preserved, now the venerable Odo, bishop of Beauvais, who had previously been abbot of the monastery of Corbie, came and made known to us both the petition of that benevolent prince and your request—you who are recognized as abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Corbie—in which you asked that we not refuse to confirm, by the promulgation of our authority, what had previously been granted to that monastery by our predecessor, Pope Benedict of blessed memory.

We therefore, considering your petition religious, and that we would establish nothing new if we followed the decrees of our predecessors, and recognizing that it is likewise part of pastoral duty continually to look after the advantage and welfare of God’s servants, decree that the monastery of Corbie, which is recognized as having been built to the praise of God and in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and founded at the beginning by Balthild, queen of the Franks, and her son Chlothar, and enriched with gifts and the necessities of life, situated in the county of Amiens on the river Somme, shall in every respect possess free and regular authority to dispose of its property. Thus, whatever shall have been offered to that monastery in gold or silver, in lands or servants, or in any other goods, or whatever is known to have been granted on the present day, shall remain under the disposition of you, your successors in the abbacy, and the brothers, so that whatever you shall have decided to do regularly and canonically, according to the fear of God and for the benefit of that Church, you may have free authority in every respect to carry out. [Col. 0816C]

The bishop of Amiens, however, shall neither receive nor demand any portion of these goods; nor shall he possess authority over the abbot, the brothers, or the monastery itself; nor shall he hold any jurisdiction by designation over its cells, or over its clerics or servants, or over anything whatsoever that appears to belong to the property of that monastery, just as we know was formerly granted to that monastery by the bishop of Amiens [Bertefrid] and by other bishops of Gaul, and confirmed by a privilege of cession, both in the time of our beloved son Charles, who now reigns, and in former times, when Balthild and Chlothar ruled the Franks—except insofar as canonical order permits.

Neither the bishop himself, nor his steward, archpresbyter, archdeacon, or any person acting on his behalf shall have authority to enter the monastery or its cells, unless perhaps he comes after being summoned by the abbot of the monastery or by the brothers, either because of necessity or out of affection; this is so that the brothers or abbots may not suffer any disturbance through his importunity or the harassment of his ministers. Nor shall he attempt to cause any disturbance in the churches subject to the aforesaid monastery, or among the priests ordained in those churches, whether against the abbot or the brothers, by establishing something new and violating an ancient custom. Rather, just as these matters have been arranged regularly and canonically and have remained so for a long time, so also shall they remain undisturbed in future times. Nor, abusing the power of episcopal arrogance, shall he wish to arrange anything by force against the established ordinances of our predecessors and against the will of the abbot and the brothers serving God in that monastery at any time. [Col. 0817B]

He shall not delay carrying out whatever ordinations are necessary in the monastery, whether of monks or of canons, and which the abbot and brothers request. He shall also willingly grant the blessings or consecrations of altars and basilicas, as necessity requires, either in the monastery itself or on the lands of the monastery. He shall not delay providing chrism and consecrated oil each year. For all these services he shall accept no gift, lest, in attempting to sell the grace of the Holy Spirit, he suffer—God forbid—the condemnation of Simon.

We decree that not only the bishop of Amiens but all bishops throughout the provinces of Gaul and Germany, wherever the aforesaid monastery is recognized as possessing churches, lands, or servants, shall observe this constitution without hesitation or contradiction, so that no one may abuse any right of authority over the property of the aforesaid monastery without the will of its abbot and the brothers of that monastery. Rather, everything that has been or shall be granted shall remain under the authority and regular disposition of the monastery’s rector. No one, whether king or any person supported by a position of power or dignity, shall violently or forcefully invade or seize anything from the property of the aforesaid monastery. [Col. 0817C]

The brothers of that monastery shall always have the power to choose their abbot from among themselves, and they shall choose a person who professes the monastic way of life in habit and conduct—not a canon, a layman, or a monk of another monastery. For to place over a monastic order either a layman or a canon is not to preserve the profession of the order but to overthrow it. Each superior will be a propagator of the order to which he belongs; nor will anyone ever govern the life of any kind of service well if he himself has not been an adherent of the way of life he governs. [Col. 0817D]

Nor shall the king or any power place over the monastery of Corbie a person whom the brothers of that monastery have not chosen. For worldly princes ought to render to God the honor that they wish God to render to them: namely, just as they desire the honor of kingship conferred upon them by God to be preserved, so they should not disdain to preserve the law of Christ’s Church. It is neither fitting nor could it appear just that they should repay those serving them with compensation from the possessions of Christ’s Church, and wish to render from what has been offered to God what they ought to give from their own public treasury. [Col. 0818A]

Therefore, we command absolutely that no person be placed over the monastery of the blessed Peter and Paul called Corbie—whether one of those serving the king, or one taken from another monastery—unless that person is chosen by a credible election, whether he be a layman, a canon, or belong to any other order.

Since, however, importunate people seek many opportunities for malicious action, and it is always necessary to repel the adversary’s darts with the shield of protection, we decree that, after the abbot has been elected and ordained, he shall not be removed by any prevailing power unless he is found guilty of a crime such that, on account of it, he ought not to administer the office of rector. If he is attacked with stains of infamy or accused of some crime, he shall not be deposed except after canonical and regular examination. [Col. 0818B]

If anyone violates this constitution, the bishop of Amiens, whoever he may be, shall summon him by our authority, confront the one who has disrupted the ordinances of this see, admonish him concerning his guilt, and make known to him the danger to which he will be subjected. If the bishop himself should neglect, despise, or fear to carry this out, the metropolitan bishop, summoned by the brothers of that monastery, shall not delay confronting the person who has violated this sanction. He shall make known to him the testimony of this decree and, by his own authority and ours, solemnly warn him not to delay withdrawing from what he has done wickedly. [Col. 0818C]

But if that man should obstinately decide to persist in the continuation of his act and prefer not to correct what he has done unjustly, the brothers of the aforesaid monastery shall have permission to approach the Roman apostolic see, lay the causes of their necessity before the pope who shall then be in office at Rome, and make known the provisions of the present decree. Thus, after investigating the case, the Roman pontiff shall not hesitate to punish the guilty man with the sentence of just condemnation.

If any priest or cleric, recognizing this page of our constitution, attempts to act against it, let him lose the dignity of his order. But if a layman, whatever his power or dignity, violates in any respect the decrees of this privilege, let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed. Unless he either restores what evils have been taken away by him [Col. 0818D] or mourns his unlawful actions with worthy [Roman edition: or legitimate] penance, let him, by the authority of God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and by our sentence, remain bound by the chain of anathema, excluded from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and subject to strict vengeance at the eternal judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve what is just toward that venerable monastery, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and with the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal rest.

Written by the hand of Leo, regional notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of April, in the eleventh indiction. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, by the hand of Tiberius, primicerius of the holy apostolic see, while our lord, the most pious Augustus Louis, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in the fourteenth year of his reign and after his fourteenth year [perhaps: “in the fourteenth year after his consulship,” Hardouin], in the eleventh indiction. [Col. 0819A]

## (In the year 863.) XXX. PRIVILEGE OF NICHOLAS FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT-DENIS

[In Felibien, *History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis*, among the proofs.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our beloved brothers and sons living now and in future times in the venerable monastery of Saint Dionysius, martyr of Christ, in religious observance under the rule of Saint Benedict.

When hearts of Catholic kings are to be stirred by episcopal admonitions toward those things that ought to be stirred, and when, through the divine grace at work, they follow these admonitions with such ardent desire that they voluntarily ask for them, those requests should be granted with a spirit as much more ready and joyful as the very things they desire ought to have been requested if they were unwilling to carry them out.

Therefore, in accordance with the written petition of our son, the most excellent King Charles, by this decree of our present authority we grant, concede, and confirm this privilege to the same monastery, for your time and for future generations, so that, just as our most glorious son, led by divine love, established and confirmed by a command of his authority the arrangement that had previously been made in the time of his father, Louis Augustus of pious memory, of Dagobert, formerly king, and of the other kings, as well as of his great-grandfather, the illustrious King Pepin, and his grandfather, the emperor Charles of divine memory—an arrangement by which the estates, resources, and stipends specially assigned to the monks and to the uses of the church’s ornaments, lights, matricularies (persons supported from the church roll), guests, and poor were preserved, improved, or increased—and just as he had caused a privilege to be made and confirmed for our venerable brothers and sons, the bishops of those regions, so, as it is contained in that privilege and in the royal commands of our son Charles, all these provisions shall remain perpetually undisturbed. [Col. 0819C]

We also establish, by the authority of blessed Peter, that no king, bishop, abbot, or anyone endowed with any dignity whatsoever may, under any pretext or appearance of a case, presume to diminish or take away anything from what is contained in the aforesaid privilege or in the commands of our son Charles concerning the arrangements mentioned above, or from what he or anyone else may in future lawfully grant from his own resources for these specific uses; nor may anyone presume to appropriate such things for his own uses or grant them to others—under the guise of “pious causes”—as an excuse for his greed.

Rather, everything that has been offered or may be offered for the aforesaid uses of the monks, the church’s ornaments and lights, the matricularies (persons supported from the church roll), guests, and poor shall remain, for all time, unimpaired and undisturbed, and shall in every way continue to benefit the uses of those for whose support and administration they were granted, without any disturbance.

We therefore decree that all the provisions contained in this page of our command and decree shall be preserved forever both by you and by all who succeed you in the order and place in which you now are, and by those whose concern they may be, with the authority and honor of the holy Roman Church and the privilege of the apostolic see preserved in all respects in accordance with everything contained in this decree.

But if anyone, great or small, should presume with reckless daring to act against this apostolic decree of ours, let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema, excluded from the kingdom of God, and condemned with all the impious to the punishment of eternal fire. But may the one who proves an observer of this command deserve to obtain grace, mercy, and eternal life from our most merciful Lord God.

Written by the hand of Sophronius, regional notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of April, in the eleventh indiction. + Farewell. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, by the hand of Tiberius, primicerius of the holy apostolic see, while the lord, the most pious Augustus Louis, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in the fourteenth year of his reign, in the eleventh indiction. [Col. 0820B]

## (In the year 863.) XXXI. LETTER OF NICHOLAS TO CHARLES THE BALD

[In Dublet, *History of Saint-Denis*, p. 456.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the excellent Charles, king of the Franks.

In consideration of heavenly mercy, we have undertaken the care of this governance so that we may favor the vows of those who pray devoutly and lend an ear toward establishing the stability of the saints, in whom divine praise is offered to God day and night throughout the whole world of God’s Church. For we believe that we shall receive a most pious reward from the merciful Lord if venerable places, suitably organized and brought to a better condition, are strengthened by our privileges. [Col. 0820C]

Therefore, because you informed us in the letters of your highness, dearest son, about the monastery of Saint Dionysius, martyr of Christ, your special patron, which, as you wrote, had formerly been taken from the authority of the bishop of the see of Paris by Louis, son of Dagobert, king of the Franks, with the counsel of the bishops of that country, and had thereafter always been administered under the governance of kings or most distinguished abbots, you asked us to strengthen by the authority of our privilege—or rather, by that of the prince of the apostles—the privilege made by the bishops concerning that monastery. In accordance with your benevolence, we most willingly support this petition.

Therefore, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, who received from the Lord the power of binding and loosing (Matthew 16), and whose vicars we are, we establish that this holy place, just as it is supported by royal commands and apostolic privileges, shall remain sound in every respect for all time, without any bishop of the see of Paris, any judicial authority, or any powerful person making any further claim upon it, just as your benevolence earnestly desires and requests. [Col. 0821A]

Thus the venerable abbot and brothers of that place may delight in offering thanks and vows to God for the condition of your kingdom and the cleansing of your sins and those of your sons.

But if anyone, great or small, should presume with reckless daring, out of greed or desire for power, to violate this decree of ours, let him know—unless he repents—that he is bound by the chain of anathema, utterly excluded from the kingdom of God, and condemned with Judas the traitor and all the impious to the punishments of eternal fire. Let the cause of the violation of our privilege be transmitted to our successors.

But may the observer of this confirmation deserve to obtain grace, mercy, and eternal life from our most merciful Lord God.

Written by the hand of Sophronius, notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of April, in the eleventh indiction. Farewell. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, by the hand of Tiberius, primicerius of the holy apostolic see, while the lord, the most pious and perpetual Augustus Louis, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in the fourteenth year of his reign. [Col. 0821B]

## (In the year 863.) XXXII. TO HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

Confirmation of the Synod of Soissons of the year 853, together with the privilege of Hincmar, archbishop, and of the Church of Rheims.

[In Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XV.]

Nicholas, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims.

We are constrained by the care of pastoral solicitude and prompted by the sublimity of the position in which heavenly providence has placed us over the universal community of its entire household, so that the summit of our apostolate, like a cornerstone set in place, may, in imitation of that stone, present itself to the faithful and humble as the safest and strongest refuge against which all the swelling waves of enemies may be shattered; but to those who take offense at the word and do not believe in the one in whom they have been placed, may it be a stone of offense and a rock of stumbling. [Col. 0821C]

Therefore, because your affection, following the institutions of our predecessors, has taken care, in an episcopal manner [specifically], to refer to us, as to the head and summit of the episcopate, those matters that could receive some question—which we gladly accepted, since by this we recognize your affection as mindful of the canons—we decree by apostolic authority that the synod which was celebrated by you and the other venerable archbishops and bishops in the city of Soissons [Soissons?], in the year 863 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first indiction, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, and which was confirmed by our predecessor, Pope Benedict of blessed memory, shall remain forever confirmed and irrefragable, just as that pontiff of holy memory confirmed it, and shall endure perpetually, although the command and judgment of the Roman see in all matters remain reserved.

Moreover, we decree that no one regularly subject to the Church in the province of Rheims—Durocortorum—in the region of Belgica, disregarding or setting aside you and the provincial synod of the co-bishops of that diocese, may with impunity dare or be able to seek or await foreign judgments, receive irregular ordinations contrary to the canons, or flee irregularly to other provinces. Rather, as has been promulgated by the canonical definitions of Nicaea and the other councils, and decreed by the constitutions of the blessed pontiffs of the Roman see—Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Boniface, Leo, Hilary, Gelasius, Gregory, and the others—all, whether in a position of pre-eminence or in due subjection, observing the order handed down by ecclesiastical regulations, shall obey the authority of your metropolitan, provided that he commands honorably and canonically, and shall strive with the greatest diligence to comply. [Col. 0822A]

We also promulgate and establish by apostolic authority that you, whom the holy bishops who preceded us in that province confirmed as its primate—Leo, namely, in the granting of the use of the pallium, and Benedict by the privilege of his confirmation, just as their predecessors confirmed your predecessors by canonical authority and ancient custom, in accordance with the distinction of the metropolitan Church [of Rheims]—are likewise confirmed by us, who, by God’s voice, have received the primacy of blessed Peter.

Let no attack ever oppress you in opposition to canonical and apostolic decrees or judgments, strip you by force or power of the Church entrusted to you, or presume to judge or condemn you before the hearing of the Roman pontiff, since the ecclesiastical regulations do not permit this. Even if some reckless person should perhaps presume to do so, you shall not be held bound by any sentence of excommunication, obligation, or condemnation without a decree of the Roman pontiff. But if you are summoned by anyone or from anywhere so that you are to be judged, we decree, by our authority—or rather, by that of the apostle Peter—that you are reserved for the judgment of the apostolic pope. We command that you be subjected to no other person’s jurisdiction or judgment except the authority of the see of the Roman pontiff, nor may you be summoned to the synod of another primate’s province except by common agreement—provided, however, that you are found obedient to the commands of the apostolic Roman see in no matter whatsoever. [Col. 0822C]

We also establish that no one from the metropolitan province subject to you may in any way, through contempt, tear away the right due according to ecclesiastical constitutions to the primacy of your Church and to you, and handed down and established according to the sacred canons, the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, and ancient custom; nor may anyone presume to divide the province or persistently inflict any violence upon you or your Church contrary to those canonical constitutions and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs.

We prohibit anyone from violating all the foregoing, under threat of anathema, by the authority of the prince of the apostles and by our apostolic sentence.

We grant you all these provisions through the page of this command and decree, to be held throughout all the days of your life, and we intend them to contribute to the security, tranquility, and honor of your position, on this sole condition: that both now and always, so long as you remain alive in this life, you deviate in no respect from the commands of the apostolic see. [Col. 0823A]

But if at any time you are found to have separated yourself from the constitutions of the holy Roman Church or from the commands of its bishops, and have neglected to obey their instructions, whether sent by letter or spoken by word, the substance of this privilege and command shall be judged entirely without force, and everything contained in it shall forever be wholly null and void.

But if anyone, great or small, should presume with reckless daring to act against this apostolic decree of ours, let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema, excluded from the kingdom of God, and condemned with all the impious to the punishment of eternal fire. But may the one who proves an observer of this command deserve to obtain grace, mercy, and eternal life from our most merciful Lord God.

Written by the hand of Zacharias, regional notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of April, in the eleventh indiction. Farewell. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, by the hand of Tiberius, primicerius of the holy apostolic see, while the most pious lord Emperor Augustus Louis, crowned by God, great and peaceful, was reigning, in the fourteenth year of the empire, in the eleventh indiction. [Col. 0823B]

## (In the year 863.) XXXIII. TO THE SAME

Concerning Rothad: he again commands that Rothad be sent to Rome, in accordance with the letter sent in reply to the synod; and concerning the privileges that Hincmar had requested to be confirmed for his Church, he postpones his consent.

[In Mansi, same work.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hincmar, archbishop.

After reading the letters of your Beatitude, in which we found your fraternity displaying toward the holy Roman see, over which we preside by the authority of the Most High, and toward our pontificate, the same devotion in which it was accustomed [Roman edition: “to persist”], we were filled with great joy and rendered the due offices of thanksgiving to almighty God. We praised your holiness for coming to the apostolic see to report what seemed necessary to you and to seek our apostolate’s aid for the needs and advantages of the Church entrusted to you. Judging entirely that there was nothing we ought to deny your fraternity, we immediately conceived the intention and resolved in our mind to grant your requests.

When, moreover, we read the records of the proceedings to which your venerability appeared to have subscribed together with your other co-bishops, we discovered that our most holy brother Rothad, appealing to the apostolic see, had been deposed from the episcopal rank by your judgment. We were deeply grieved; and the joy in our heart that had been produced by the arrival of our brother and co-bishop Odo was driven away by continual sorrow when we learned that such an act had been committed by your veneration contrary to expectation. [Col. 0824A]

For such longstanding confidence in your reverence had existed among the bishops of the apostolic see that, if your affection were present there, we could never have believed in any way that anyone appealing to the apostolic see would suffer any disadvantage—even if we found absolutely nothing in the sacred canons about what ought to be observed in such a matter. This was especially so because we knew you to be a man of such wisdom and had found your holiness to possess such confidence of intimacy with our beloved son, King Charles, that we had resolved, through the diligence of your solicitude, to cut out at the root any evils that might spring up in those regions in the Church of the Lord.

Your Beatitude certainly ought, when you had examined Rothad so many times, to have written in honor of the memory of Saint Peter and to await his judgment in every way, even if Rothad himself had never appealed. And if you had not wished to do this, at least after his appeal you ought not to have ordained another to the very see from which he appeared to have been expelled before his case had been concluded in our judgment according to the sacred canons.

But concerning Rothad, a venerable man, it is recognized that we have decreed and determined what was required of us by the authority granted to us by the holy regulations, which prescribe that what appears appropriate to our judgment, whatever its quality, must be observed. We did this in the letter that we sent to our common brothers and co-bishops established in the kingdom of our glorious king Charles, our dearest son, among whom your holiness is numbered. [Col. 0824C]

By referring to that letter, your fraternity will easily be able to learn what we have judged concerning you. You will do well to pay attention to our decision, lest, if you should presume to act against the prohibitions for any longer time, you be constrained by canonical laws.

Furthermore, you ask that privileges be confirmed by the apostolic see for your Church, although, as far as lies within you, you labor to weaken our privileges. You call the holy Roman Church a saving harbor, yet you do your utmost to ensure that no one be saved in it. How, I ask, can your privileges stand if those privileges through which yours are known to have begun are thus annulled? Or of what importance will yours be if ours are treated as worthless? For if the salt has lost its savor, with what shall it be salted? (Matthew 5.)

Nevertheless, we charge and command your holiness and affection that, after reading the page of our sanction which we sent through Odo, our common brother and co-bishop, to your Beatitude and your other fellow ministers, you strive together with them to bring to completion what we have decreed concerning the frequently mentioned Rothad. Thus you may always be found a participant in our charity, friendship, and favor, and we may henceforth regard your holiness as joined with us in cutting away the harmful shoots of the enemies of God’s holy Church and planting what is salutary. [Col. 0824D]

Then, finally, we shall strive all the more vigorously—even without being asked—to fight against all your ill-wishers and the adversaries of your Church by promulgating privileges for you and adhering to you more closely, the more we perceive that your fraternity does not strive by any argument or contrivance whatsoever against the privileges of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of his see, but wishes to persist with all its strength and all its purpose in honoring, defending, and excusing them.

For the rest, dearest brother, we exhort you always to instruct and kindle our most beloved son Charles, the excellent king, toward the divine commands, and to strive with watchful zeal and prudent diligence always to ensure that he remain in the devotion and affection toward the holy Roman Church and apostolic see with which he began.

Our common brother and co-bishop Odo, who greatly gladdened our mind by recounting the virtues of your holiness, will be able to relate orally the other matters not included in the wording of this page.

Finally, we wish to bring to your memory that we have now sent word to your holiness for the second time that you should send the venerable man Rothad to the apostolic see. You must take care that, if we are compelled to direct this same request to your affection for a third time, we do not pronounce—as we do not wish to do—a definitive and final sentence against one who despises the sacred canons.

May the right hand of the heavenly Majesty always protect you and deign to keep you unharmed from every adversity.

## (In the year 863.) XXXIV. TO THE SAME

That he restore Rothad, bishop of Soissons, who had been deposed, to his see within thirty days, or come with him to Rome to answer the case.

[In Mansi, same work.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims.

We had learned through widespread report that your holiness, whom we have always found engaged in the exercise of the virtues and advancing in ecclesiastical teachings, held apostolic reverence before your eyes in a manner different from what common opinion frequently declares.
