Finally, we learned through the reliable testimony of many grieving faithful that our brother and co-bishop Rothad, of the Church of Soissons, was prosecuted by your holiness on account of a certain priest who, three years ago, had been deprived of his own office of honor because of the nature of his deed. Although Rothad appealed to the apostolic see, as it is established that the Fathers permitted him to do, he was nevertheless deprived of the honor of the episcopate in his absence and carried into exile; and to this day he remains confined in a monastery. [Col. 0825D]

For this we groan and grieve deeply. For whereas, on account of his old age, he ought to have been increased in many honors; whereas, for all the labors and services he had faithfully and usefully rendered in the Church of God and likewise to worldly princes, he ought to enjoy greater dignity and at last remain in peace without anyone’s instigation, now, on the contrary, he exists dishonored and, to the injury of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose see he had appealed to, worn down by hunger, thirst, and countless hardships, and at once deposed and rejected. [Col. 0826A]

We are therefore greatly astonished and exceedingly amazed at how so sudden a darkness could have obscured the brightness of your eyes, so that you disdained to regard the privileges of the apostolic see, which the whole Church of Christ preserves inviolate, and somehow—God knows by what authority—violated the very canons of the Fathers.

We shall certainly not allow this to remain unpunished, so that one who has presumed to do what was prohibited may not learn what canonical censure is. We shall make it clear to all that we will in no way permit our brothers to suffer any loss, nor will we allow the statutes of the holy Fathers to be debased.

Meanwhile, therefore, by the authority of almighty God, of the holy princes of the apostles Peter and Paul, and of our authority through them, we charge your fraternity that, if you wish—as until now you have wished to appear—to remain participants in our charity and communion, you restore our aforesaid brother Rothad both to his episcopate and to his former office of honor. He must in every respect be adorned with such honor and restored whole in all his offices as he is known to have been at the time when, about to be expelled, he made appeal to the apostolic see. [Col. 0826B]

Then, if there appear to be any accusers of his, let them come without delay and without continual excuse to Rome together with that priest who was the cause of his deposition and with the frequently mentioned Rothad, so that they may appear together.

We expressly decree that, after thirty days have passed from the time this letter of ours is delivered to you, you must either restore the aforesaid man Rothad completely to his former dignity or, if you believe that you acted justly toward him, you yourself—or your legate, carrying your authority in all matters—must come with him to Rome, so that we may know clearly the case of both parties. [Col. 0826C]

But if, after the appointed thirty days, you do not strive to obey and carry out what is fully contained in this letter of apostolic authority, we decree and promulgate that you shall not have permission to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass for as long as what we have determined has not been brought to completion.

We decree that this sentence shall bind not only you but also all the bishops who are known to have consented with you to the deposition of the aforesaid man Rothad. We command that you make the same matter known to them.

### (Year 863.) XXXV. TO THE BISHOPS OF THE SYNOD OF SILVANECTUM

He rescinds the acts of the synod against Rothadus; orders that he be recalled from exile and sent to Rome with representatives of the synod to have the judgment reconsidered. He also replies near the end concerning Baldwin and the case of Lothair and Theutberga.

[In Mansi, same volume.]

[Col. 0826D]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend brothers, the metropolitans, bishops, and other prelates of the various provinces and cities who have assembled at the public estate of Convicinum, near the city of Silvanectum, for the synod. [It seems it should read: “for the purpose of the council,” from Gratian, Distinction X, chapter 1.]

[Col. 0827A]

Having received the writings of your beloved fraternity and examined attentively in them all the streams of knowledge, wisdom, and holiness that flow from you—streams which could have poured into your hearts from no other source than the very fountain of life—and having recognized the devotion and profound affection that you have shown yourselves to retain toward this holy Roman Church and the apostolic see; and since, out of love, according to the constitution of our predecessors—to repeat those very words—you recognize that not only concerning all matters that may admit some doubt or incur any question, but also concerning other and more important ecclesiastical affairs, you ought to refer matters to the summit of the episcopate, that is, to the see of blessed Peter, we have offered manifold expressions of thanks to God, the author and giver of every good thing.

He wished to place you, shining in the holy Church like splendid stars containing the word of life and illuminating those near you far and wide by the light of your conduct and virtues, so that, in accordance with the teaching of that same Master, we might rightly call that same holy Church “heaven,” where such luminaries plainly shine.

But, beloved brothers, when we learned that you are laboring in your provinces under frequent attacks by pagans, and, in addition, that the churches of Christ established in those regions are suffering many hardships from internal enemies—that is, from their own people—we lamented greatly, sympathize with you most deeply, and grieve with you. Yet, beloved ones, you ought not to grieve and be afflicted over these matters to such an extent, knowing that “tribulation produces perseverance, perseverance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope, while hope does not disappoint” (Romans 5).

For this is the place of affliction; this is the valley of tears, until we see the God of gods in Zion. Here we sow in tears, so that afterward we may reap in joy. This is, I say, Egypt; this is the iron furnace, where spiritual Israel must be wearied by harsh brickmaking until we enter the promised land—that is, until the Lord, when we have perfectly pleased him, reveals himself to us as the one promised in the land of the living.

Here it is necessary that whatever pertains to the construction of the holy temple be fitted together by the hand and providence of the supreme craftsman, so that when the shavings, crashes, pressures, and persecutions of the present age have passed, we may be found approved in every respect, like suitable living stones, in the heavenly structure, without any crookedness or unevenness.

Therefore, knowing these things, beloved ones, fasten the anchor of your hope in the heavenly harbor and disdain the storms of this world, because our omnipotent protector no longer sleeps. He commands, and the sea and the winds obey him, and a great calm arises.

For this reason, since you rightly endeavored to report Rothadus’s condemnation to the apostolic see, you asked that what you claimed had been done concerning him in your council should also be confirmed as valid by our authority. We utterly refuse to do this, because—as we may put the same words that Saint Leo addressed to Flavianus—since we desire the judgments of the Lord’s priests to be mature, we cannot decide anything prejudicial to either party in matters unknown to us, before we have truthfully heard everything that was done.

But perhaps you will say that you truthfully reported to us everything that had been done concerning him in the written account, and that our brother and fellow bishop Odo, who was almost always present at your councils, fully disclosed everything to us. Know that we would have been able to give these statements sufficient credence and to lend our support for the preservation of ecclesiastical discipline, had not the explanations and defenses of that man, together with a series of submissions demonstrating his innocence and your wrongdoing, been presented to the apostolic see by a number of your neighbors; and had not our brother and fellow bishop Odo, when questioned by us, refused to bring any public accusation against him.

Even if he had brought one, it would have contributed nothing to the condemnation of the aforesaid Rothadus, since it is clear that no one from his side who might either acknowledge or reject the charges had come into our presence. For accusers say whatever they wish, and we know that one is not a just mediator who listens to one party in such a way that he reserves nothing for the other party.

Especially since, speaking through Moses on behalf of one who is absent and unheard, the Lord commands: “You shall not curse the deaf, nor place a stumbling block before the blind” (Leviticus 19).

We do not permit your fraternity to remain unaware that our spirit has been wounded to no small degree because, according to the tenor of the acts and of the submissions that you directed to the apostolic see, you deposed the same Rothadus after he had appealed to the apostolic see, and shut him away in a monastery. There is no doubt that this was presumed and rashly undertaken in contempt of blessed Peter, whose judgment he had sought, and in insult to the sacred canons and ecclesiastical traditions.

Moreover, to diminish the privileges of the apostolic and supreme see—privileges by which you also ask that the privileges of your churches be confirmed—you bring forward imperial laws, by which, as though they prohibited it, you attempt to establish that Rothadus did not possess the right of appeal. Yet it is clear from the constitutions of worldly laws and emperors that not all ecclesiastical controversies are to be governed by them [perhaps: “that they are not to be used in all ecclesiastical controversies,” Harduin], especially since they are sometimes found to oppose ecclesiastical [Roman edition: evangelical] and canonical sanction.

The testimonies of two great heroes, namely Innocent and Gregory, are sufficient to demonstrate this.

Saint Innocent, in his decretal letter to Alexander, bishop of Antioch, says:

“For concerning what you ask,” he says, “whether, when provinces have been divided by imperial judgment so that two metropolitan cities are formed, two metropolitan bishops ought likewise to be appointed: it has not therefore seemed right that the Church of God should be changed according to the shifting needs of worldly affairs, or that it should endure the honors and divisions which the emperor has judged should be made for his own purposes.”

Blessed Gregory, writing to the patrician Theoctista, says among other things:

“For if they say that marriages ought to be dissolved for the sake of religion, it must be understood that, although human law has permitted this, divine law nevertheless forbids it.”

Behold how ecclesiastical rights cannot be dissolved by imperial judgment; behold how what human law has permitted is forbidden by divine law.

We do not mean that the laws of the emperors—which the Church often uses concerning heretics, often concerning tyrants, and by which she is often defended against the wicked—are to be wholly rejected. Rather, we assert that they can bring no prejudice against the evangelical, apostolic, and canonical decrees, to which they must be subordinate.

Although you have written that his appeals were frivolous, and that his explanations and delays were merely complaints, it is not readily apparent by what arguments you establish this, especially since he appears to have solemnly appealed to the apostolic see with the canons supporting him. For, according to the testimony of truth, no one knows what is in a person except that person’s spirit which is in him (1 Corinthians 2).

Who, moreover, is unaware of the decrees of the Council of Sardica? After several chapters, in chapter four, they prescribe:

“If any bishop has been judged in some case and thinks that he has a good case, so that the judgment may be renewed by another council, if it pleases you, let us honor the memory of the holy apostle Peter, so that those who examined the case may write to Julius, the Roman bishop. And if he judges that the judgment ought to be renewed, let it be renewed, and let him appoint judges. But if he determines that the case is such that it should not be reopened, especially if he decrees that the proceedings already conducted should stand, they shall be confirmed.”

Likewise, in chapter eight, Bishop Hosius said:

“It was also decided that if one of the bishops is accused, and the bishops assembled from that region judge him and depose him from his rank; if the deposed man appeals and takes refuge with the bishop of the Roman Church and wishes to be heard, and if he considers it just that the examination be renewed, let him write to the churches that are in the neighboring and nearest province, so that they themselves may carefully investigate everything and decide according to the faith of charity.

“But if the one who asks that his case be heard again moves the Roman bishop by his petition to send a presbyter from his side, it shall be in the power of the bishop to determine what he wishes and considers appropriate. And if he decides that those who are to judge together with the bishops while present should be sent, possessing the authority of the one by whom they were appointed, it shall be at his discretion. But if he believes that the bishops are sufficient to bring the matter to an end, he shall do what he judges by the wisest counsel.”

Yet, as we find in your written submissions, you attempt to assert that Rothadus did not possess the right of appeal because he did not have a good case. It is nevertheless clear that the aforesaid Rothadus still considers himself to have a good case, and that the venerable council permitted not only the man who had a case, but also the man who at least thought that he had a good case, to appeal to the apostolic see; it decreed that his judgment should be renewed by that see.

This is especially so because, according to the constitution of this holy synod, even if he had never protested and had never mentioned the apostolic see, you, who examined his case, ought to have honored the memory of Saint Peter and written to him that, if he judged the judgment should be renewed, it should be renewed and he should appoint judges. Certainly, as we recalled above, the sanction of that same council said that he should decide if the proceedings appeared proven [perhaps “or certainly,” Harduin].

But why should it be surprising that you have despised this in contempt of the prince of the apostles, when you are found to have committed something even worse, in violation of the sacred canons and the decrees of the venerable Roman pontiffs? Namely, after Rothadus’s appeal and protest, you consecrated another man in his own chair [Roman edition: “you have consecrated”], although it is most clearly contrary to the sacred rules that anyone be ordained in the place of one who has been deposed until his case has been determined in the judgment of the Roman bishop.

But you say that after his appeal to the apostolic see he changed his position and sought a council of bishops. With your permission, we acknowledge that, although we give credence to your assertions and hold as true that he did so—for there is no reason not to believe a man of such integrity—we nevertheless do not fail to recognize what his intention was in doing this, or what he might answer if questioned by us, so that, as in other matters, uncertainty concerning an uncertain matter may undoubtedly be removed only after an examination of both parties. [Note: [Col. 0829D] The passage is obscure.]

Furthermore, we do not believe that your fraternity is unaware that we previously sent letters from our apostolate to our brother, the bishop of Rheims, instructing him either to restore the aforesaid venerable Rothadus to his former rank within thirty days after our letter had been delivered to him, or, if he himself could not come, to send him with a suitable legate, together with the accusers of that man, if indeed there were any, and with the presbyter who had been the cause of his deposition.

If he had been unwilling to do either of these things, then after the appointed thirty days neither he nor any bishop who had consented to the deposition of the aforesaid bishop would have had any permission at all to celebrate the solemnities of Mass until they had obediently and fully brought to completion what had been salutarily decreed by us.

But, turning to your writings, which you have now sent to the apostolic see through our brother and fellow bishop Odo, we find that the most holy man has, by your judgment and consent, been deprived of his bishopric and confined in a monastery up to the present time; moreover, another bishop has been ordained in his chair.

The enormity of this abomination, and the fact that we cannot tolerate it in any way, cannot be adequately expressed, even if every limb of the body were turned into a tongue.

Certainly, when the submissions, reports, prayers, and consultations of your holiness had been pressed upon our ears in your writings and in our conversations, we immediately formed our intention and had almost resolved to grant and concede nearly everything. But when we perceived the injury done to Saint Peter, the diminution of the privileges of the apostolic see, and the trampling underfoot of the sacred canons, we could offer you no sweetness, for we were entirely filled with bitterness.

Indeed, on the contrary, considering the magnitude of such contempt, we would rightly punish you with the severity of canonical correction, were not apostolic moderation to incline us somewhat toward magnanimity, and your affection to move us.

As for how we might appropriately and regularly exercise this against you, you yourselves have taught us abundantly and most clearly in your letters, which, if the opportunity arises, can easily be collected and exhibited.

In the meantime, by apostolic and canonical authority, we command you bishops alone—those who either gave judgment or offered their consent in the deposition and exile of the aforesaid Rothadus—to recall him immediately from exile.

And because he is said, in accordance with the permission granted to him by the written rules, to have continued to appeal to the apostolic see, do not in any way delay sending—indeed, directing—him to Rome, so that his case may be conducted and determined in our apostolic presence.

For it is fitting that the man who was assigned to exile by the judgment of all of you should, conversely, through the common zeal of all of you, be honorably presented to the memory of blessed Peter and to his see.

We command that two or three of you be sent, or more if you wish, who should so represent the presence of all of you that, whatever must be done or investigated, they may inquire into everything that has been discussed before us entirely in the place of all of you.

If you cannot come yourselves, send your representatives, and let them come together with your aforesaid religious brother Rothadus, bearing your place and person in every respect, as we said above, for carrying out or investigating everything that may have been brought before us.

But if, setting aside our judgment—which we have promulgated and decreed by apostolic authority—you disdain to come, then, by the authority of almighty God, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, through whose glorious martyrdom this holy Roman Church, over which by divine disposition we preside, has been consecrated to the Lord, and of the holy canons, whose contemptors you show yourselves to be in your own writings, as well as by the authority of our unworthiness, you shall be wholly barred from celebrating the solemnities of Mass until you obey our decisions.

This shall apply if, after the tenor of this page has been read, within the space of thirty days you have not taken care to complete what we have decreed must be done concerning the venerable man Rothadus.

Know assuredly that if thereafter you continue for a long time in contempt of the sacred rules and [perhaps: “of our rules,” Harduin], Rothadus himself will be released by us, in the manner of the apostolic see, from the bond of condemnation; and, once an assembly of bishops has been convened, the pit that you dug for him will undoubtedly be prepared for you.

But, beloved ones, do not take our decrees amiss. For, as blessed Innocent writes to the Macedonians, it ought not to seem burdensome to your most devout minds that anyone’s judgment should be reconsidered: truth, when repeatedly tested, shines more brightly in the light, while destruction, when recalled for judgment, is condemned more severely and without repentance.

For, beloved brothers, the divine fruit of justice will then be fresh, especially since we have no more to do with Rothadus than with all Christians.

Nevertheless, with God’s grace granting our request, we shall defend the privileges of our see until death, following the footsteps of our fathers. You too must work and urge others with all your strength and every desire that these privileges be preserved inviolate, since they are remedies for the entire Church of the Lord.

For the privileges of the apostolic see are, so to speak, the shields of the whole Catholic Church; the privileges of this Church, I say, are defenses against every assault of wickedness.

What has happened to Rothadus today—how do you know that the same thing will not happen tomorrow to one of you? Thus the Apostle warns, saying: “Let the one who thinks he stands take care lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10).

And if that should happen, to use prophetic words, to whose help, I ask, will you flee?

Let this suffice concerning Rothadus.

As for Baldwin, about whom you have already written much, let your beatitude know that we do not wish to corrupt the rules and sacred decrees. But because he came to the threshold of the apostles and asked us to help him, although we knew that our son Charles, the glorious king, could legally, if he wished, give him his daughter in marriage and extend to him his mercy, nevertheless we did not send commands; we offered prayers.

The text of our letters, which we sent to the aforesaid most excellent king and to our daughter the queen to obtain this, will sufficiently indicate this to you.

Indeed, in view of that man’s exceedingly presumptuous rashness, and especially as we consider the contrition of the heart and the natural affection of the breast of our beloved son Charles, the exalted king, we have grieved deeply and to this day sympathize with him with all the affection of our mind.

But let your fraternity take heed, as the Apostle says: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Ephesians 5). And now, as you yourselves testify in your letter, dangerous times are at hand.

Therefore, lest something worse should arise, intercede with that same glorious king, our dearest son, so that you may both dispel the sorrow of his heart and ensure that he does not remain altogether inflexible toward Baldwin—especially since Baldwin has implored the assistance of the apostles and sought divine aid.

No king ought to consider it burdensome to forgive his fellow servant a debt of one hundred denarii when perhaps he desires that ten thousand talents be forgiven him by the supreme King and Lord of lords.

As for what we have judged concerning Lothair’s wives, since you also wrote to our episcopate about this matter, you will be able to find it in copies of our letters, which we sent to Gaul through our brothers and fellow bishops Rhadoaldus and John.

We have transmitted those copies, together with the memorandum that we gave to the aforesaid brothers when sending them to King Lothair for this same case, to your holiness through our brother and fellow bishop Odo.

In those documents you can plainly observe and know that we have absolutely no need—as I judge—to change for the better the position that you wished to urge us to adopt. For, with divine grace favoring us, we desire only to cut this kind of crime out by the roots from the face of the Church, in accordance with the heavenly ministry entrusted to us.

Thus, if on this occasion Lothair is unwilling to obey our salutary admonitions, our stated decisions, and our letters regularly sent to him, and if he does not return as quickly as possible to repentance after making suitable satisfaction, he will be made entirely alien, by canonical and apostolic sentence, from us and from the body of the whole Church, together with all his supporters and accomplices.

This applies especially to the man whom you report to have pronounced a blessing over adulterers on the day of the Lord’s Nativity—a pronouncement that ought rather to be considered a curse [Roman edition: “to have requested”].

Lest anyone simple-minded should falsely think that we have in any way yielded to adulterers, fittingly communicating our mind on this matter to all our brothers and fellow bishops, explain it fully to everyone by preaching publicly in your churches.

As for summoning bishops from each province to assemble a synod, concerning which you wrote, let your holiness know that we sent two brothers and fellow bishops from our side to Gaul, whom we mentioned above, to convene a synod for examining the case of the women Theutberga and Waldrada. We also ordered two prelates from among you, as from the other kingdoms, to be present there.

Unless they have returned beforehand and we have learned what they have done, we cannot hastily deliberate about holding a council.

Although, after they had departed from us, we heard that Lothair did not wait for the consultation requested from the apostolic see—no doubt because he had foreseen that he would not obey his detestable crime.

But after our aforesaid brothers have returned and have told us what they accomplished, we shall take care, with God’s assistance, to send suitable legates to the designated place to convene the council that you request.

May almighty God, for the advancement and protection of his flock over which he has wished to set you as rulers, deign to preserve your holiness unharmed here and grant you a glorious reception of the crown after the struggle in the heavenly homeland.

---

### (Year 863.) XXXVI. TO CHARLES THE BALD, KING

[Col. 0833D]

He intercedes for Baldwin and reports what he has written to Hincmarus and the other bishops concerning Rothadus; he also urges the king to send him to Rome. Then he explains his sharper letters, by which Charles had been offended.

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Charles, the glorious king.

[Col. 0834A]

How true, dearest son, is that saying which Wisdom, as Solomon testifies, declares about herself when she says: “Through me kings reign, and lawgivers decree what is just!” (Proverbs 8.)

If this were not true, your sublimity could never have been clothed with the beauty of such humility. If this were not true, you could never have grasped the decrees of the apostolic see concerning private laws with so ready an understanding.

For when it is said of one who raises himself against God, “He is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41), and when, by contrast, we see you endowed with the greatest humility, what else can we perceive but that your royal excellence is the son, by imitation, of him who says: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11)?

Kings therefore reign through wisdom, because the Wisdom of the Father, according to the Apostle, is Christ (1 Corinthians 1), who is the King of kings—that is, of those who know how to govern all the movements of the body and all unlawful desires of the mind with suitable restraint.

By divine grace, we perceive and rejoice that you are among their number, and we offer manifold thanks to almighty God, from whom you reign.

Meanwhile, let your belovedness know that Baldwin, as you informed us, who joined your daughter to himself in marriage by theft and against law, and whom the venerable prelates governing the Church of God in your kingdom therefore bound with the bonds of anathema, came to the threshold of the apostles and approached the apostolic see so that he might be released from those bonds and find grace through us.

[Note: [Col. 0833D] Baldwin, who took your daughter. A clandestine marriage was first contracted between Baldwin and Judith, and afterward a lawful one. Hincmarus, in the same letter, in Flodoardus: “Moreover, our lord the king, your son, did not wish to be present at this betrothal and union; but, having sent ministers of public affairs, as he promised you, he promised to join them to one another in marital union according to the laws of the world, and he granted honors to Baldwin solely at your request.” JAC. SIRM.]

But we not only did not release him from the bonds or receive him into our communion; rather, we detested such presumptuous rashness, and, considering the natural affection of your heart, we grieved, became participants in your sorrow, and continue to sympathize with you to this day.

Yet because he had recourse to divine aid and sought the assistance of your beloved apostles Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, we could not fail to intercede with your devout excellence so that he might receive your grace.

Nevertheless, keeping your affection before our eyes in every respect, although we know that you could legally, if you wished, give your daughter to him in marriage and mercifully extend your kindness to him, we did not send commands; we offered prayers.

But because the Apostle says, “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Ephesians 5), and because the dangerous final times foretold by him are now evidently upon us, let your prudent sublimity take care lest something still worse arise from this.

Thus regulate yourself everywhere with cautious foresight, so that the sorrow of your heart may be driven far away and so that you do not remain, to the very end, wholly unyielding or inflexible toward the aforesaid Baldwin [variant: “inexorably or inflexibly,” Harduin].

We do not say this because we wish you to transgress the boundaries established by our fathers, which, by God’s grace, we always desire to remain unmoved; rather, because we love your glory beyond what can be expressed, we do not want to give any opportunity to one seeking an occasion [perhaps “to one complaining,” or “for complaint,” Harduin].

Especially since Baldwin has sought divine assistance and, as we have stated, the help of Saints Peter and Paul, your intercessors, and has requested an embassy and intervention so that he might obtain full grace from your clemency.

He was plainly not forgetful of the fact that, some years ago, a man who had fallen into a similar offense had approached the memory and see of the heavenly key-bearer and, through the intervention of his vicar, had received from the emperor Lothair, of pious memory, complete pardon and grace without losing his wife.

Moreover, no king ought to consider it burdensome—as we say with your permission—to forgive his fellow servant a debt of one hundred denarii when perhaps he desires that ten thousand talents be remitted to him by the supreme King and Lord of lords.

Your belovedness should also know that we have written to our brother Hincmarus, bishop of Rheims, and to the other metropolitans and bishops of your kingdom, instructing them to recall the venerable Rothadus from exile and send him to Rome so that his case might be examined in our presence.

For it is fitting that the man who was sent into exile by their judgment should, through their common zeal, be honorably presented to the memory of blessed Peter and to his see.

We ordered two or three of them to come, or as many as they wished, so that they might represent in every matter the presence of all the others who could not come, and, once the proceedings had been reopened, act entirely in the place of all of them in whatever had to be done or investigated.

But if, setting aside our judgment, they wickedly despise what we have promulgated and decreed by apostolic authority, then, by the authority of almighty God and of the blessed princes of the apostles, through whose glorious martyrdom this holy Roman Church, over which by divine dispensation we preside, has been consecrated to the Lord, and by the authority of the holy canons, whose contemptors they have plainly shown themselves to be in their own writings, as well as by the authority of our unworthiness, they shall be wholly barred from celebrating the solemnities of Mass until they obey our decisions.

This shall apply if, after the tenor of the page sent to them by us has been read, they do not within thirty days take care to complete what we have decreed must be done concerning the venerable man Rothadus.

Know assuredly that if thereafter they continue for a long time in contempt of the sacred rules and of us [perhaps: “henceforth,” Harduin], Rothadus himself will be released by us, in the manner of the apostolic see, from the bonds of condemnation; and, once an assembly of bishops has been convened, they themselves will fall completely into the pit that they dug.

For this reason, we nevertheless admonish your most gracious piety, and with all the strength we possess earnestly beseech—or even, as a devoted son, confidently command—you to send the aforesaid Rothadus to us, mercifully supported by your assistance, so that, in accordance with the decrees of the holy pontiffs of the Roman Church and the statutes of the sacred canons, his case may be concluded by our judgment.

For believe me: in the condemnation of the aforesaid man, not only is our spirit wounded beyond measure, but the entire body of the Church’s sons who have learned of it is deeply offended.

This is especially so because, both before and after his condemnation, that same venerable man appealed to the judgment of the apostolic see, but did not obtain it; and by such presumption the privileges of the supreme see appear to have been rashly violated.

We shall not, however, with God’s help, following in the footsteps of our predecessors, tolerate until death that these privileges be annulled in such a manner.

And you, beloved son, we strongly urge to venerate them with whatever observances you can.

For how do you think that, if the occasion should demand it, we could offer some assistance to your kingdom and to your efforts [Roman edition: “commands”], or provide a shield of protection against your adversaries, if, insofar as it lies within the territories of your kingdom—for these things cannot be wholly separated—you allow those privileges to be diminished by which your fathers obtained every increase of their dignity and all their glory?

For the privileges of the Roman Church are, so to speak, remedies belonging to the whole Church of Christ and the Catholic Church. The privileges of Peter, I say, are weapons against every assault of wickedness, as well as defenses and instructions for the Lord’s priests and for all who occupy positions of eminence, indeed for all who suffer various hardships from those same powers.

You are disturbed and afflicted with great sorrow, as we have learned from the writings of your belovedness, because we addressed you with a forceful attack and burdened your majesty with harsh rebukes.

Your sublimity should not have been altogether saddened by this. For even if there were no fault, as you humbly strive to maintain, on account of which your piety ought to have been corrected more severely, a discerning father sometimes endeavors to instruct a beloved son through various terrors or even suitable blows when he sees nothing at all in him that deserves reproach.

Thus the Lord is said to have struck blessed Job without cause (Job 2), when he found nothing at all in him that deserved punishment by such blows. Yet he did not strike without cause, because he acted as a discerning father, so that Job’s merits might be increased through patience.

So it is, so it is indeed, dearest son: perhaps in silent thought you complain that your sublimity has been injured by us without cause.

Yet we know from what root this rod against your belovedness has grown. It was certainly not intended to destroy you utterly—God forbid—but to instruct you more happily for the glory of the eternal kingdom. To speak more openly, it came from the branch of inward affection as paternal discipline, not from the root of hatred as malice.

You are therefore struck—or rather, admonished—even when your heart does not reproach you, so that, through God’s guidance, you may be found more cautious, more solicitous, and safer in those matters in which you were about to offend.

Therefore, dearest son, when harsher letters have sometimes been sent from the apostolic see to your royal power, do not take them amiss, nor suppose that you are hated by us. Either the arrows of our correction are plainly just, or else they are hidden and have some reason behind them.

For this reason, in either case, do not lose confidence that you will always find in them an antidote for your salvation.

We have always held you close in the depths of our affection and have implored the mercy of almighty God for you.

But after our brother and fellow bishop Odo, together with our most faithful Primus, whom we had sent to your glory, reported to us so many praises concerning your devotion—and that of your most exalted and beloved wife—toward the apostolic see, and concerning the love that you have for the Lord’s priests, we love you all the more closely.

We pray to the Lord Jesus Christ all the more earnestly for the well-being of your kingdom and for your salvation and that of your people; and we offer exultant thanks to the author of all things for the fury of the Northmen having been subdued by you.

For we confidently believe that these achievements will serve not the swelling of pride or the heat of human desire, but the exaltation of the churches of God, the freedom of Christ’s people, and his praise.

We wish your excellence good health in Christ, now and always.

---

### (Year 863.) XXXVII. TO CHARLES THE BALD, KING

That he should restore Rothadus to his former honor and then permit him to come to the apostolic see, to which he appealed. He also indicates what he wrote to Hincmarus concerning this matter.

[Mansi, same volume.]

[Col. 0837C]

NICOLAUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our beloved son CHARLES, the glorious king.

The frequent intercourse and constant diligence that you maintain with ecclesiastical and wise men are now worthy of praise. We have learned with joyful approval that you exercise this diligence for the benefit of the Churches of God—provided that your Eminence has not injured any of the pastors of that same holy Church, with whom you beneficially undertake this humility and solicitude, under some appearance of justice, as we have now learned from the report of many that you have done in the case of a certain man named Rothad [Col. 0837D]. This is especially serious since he is said to have appealed to the apostolic see, as canonically granted him permission to do.

Therefore, dearest son, we earnestly beseech your glory to have the aforesaid man restored to his episcopate and to all his former honor, and thereafter to deign to grant him a safe and prompt means of proceeding, for love of us, to the apostolic see, to which it is established that he appealed. We make this known with this proviso: we believe that you then love our apostolate, as you often seem to profess, if we clearly learn that you likewise fear and love God, our Lord. Moreover, preserve inviolate the privileges of the holy apostolic see and the statutes of the Fathers, [Col. 0838A] and do not permit anyone to cheapen or destroy them.

Furthermore, let your Eminence know that we have sent word to our brother Hincmar, the archbishop, that either within thirty days after reading the letter we sent him he must restore the same bishop to his former rank, or, if he himself could not do so, come to Rome with a suitable legate of his, together with the accusers of that man, if indeed there were any, and with the priest who was responsible for his deposition. But if, after the thirty days appointed, he did neither of these things, neither he nor any of the bishops who consented to the deposition of the aforesaid bishop would have any permission whatsoever to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass until they obeyed us in those matters which it would be beneficial for them to carry out, and had brought them fully to completion.

(Year 863.) XXXVIII. TO ROTHAD, BISHOP OF SOISSONS. That he should come to Rome as soon as permission is granted him; and, if it is denied, should not cease appealing to the apostolic see.

[Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 0838B]

NICOLAUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverent and holy bishop ROTHAD.

Let your experience know, dearest brother, that our apostolate has deeply grieved—and indeed continues to grieve—over your tribulations. But we believe that God’s mercy will soon come to you, bringing you out of the lions’ den like Daniel (Dan. VI), and clothing you in the first robe like the prodigal son (Luke XV). We believe that you know what we first sent concerning you to Charles the glorious king and to Hincmar.

Now, however, the metropolitan and the other bishops who pronounced judgment concerning you [alternative reading: “against you,” HARD., Roman edition] have reported to us, in a detailed account of the proceedings, many things concerning you or against you, and have requested that what they had promulgated against you be confirmed by our consent.

But we have deferred doing this. Rather, we ordered them to bring you out of the monastery and, coming together either themselves or through their representatives, to present you honorably at the memorial of Saint Peter, so that the council might be renewed and we might conclude your case in our judgment according to the rule of the canons. If, after reading the letter we sent them, they did not take care to carry out our constitution within thirty days, then after thirty days they were to cease entirely from celebrating the solemnities of the Mass—something we had firmly forbidden them to do—until they demonstrated perfect obedience to our decisions.

Therefore, dearest brother, since we cannot dismiss your case without examination, lest we seem to prejudice ecclesiastical discipline, and since, in your absence, we hesitate to have your case examined and decided by the judgment of others, lest you be unjustly harmed, strive with all your strength, as soon as the king and the bishops have granted you permission to hasten to Rome, in accordance with our decree, not to delay coming, by whatever means may be available. But if they do not grant you the opportunity to come here, nevertheless take care to inform us of this [Col. 0839A].

Yet do not cease, as boldly as you dare, by whatever means and in whatever manner you can, to appeal to the apostolic see and to make known your desire to approach it—provided that you know yourself to have been unjustly harmed and believe by God’s grace that your case is just. For, with divine clemency giving us strength, we will in no way allow you to be consigned to oblivion for as long as life remains.

We wish your holiness well-being in Christ. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh indiction.

(Year 863.) XXXIX. TO LOUIS AND CHARLES, SONS OF CHARLES THE BALD, KING. He rejoices that they have returned to favor with their father; urges them not to separate from him in future; and commands them to appear before the synod to make satisfaction.

[Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 0839B]

NICOLAUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to LOUIS and CHARLES, sons of Charles the glorious king.

[Note: [Col. 0839D] Louis and Charles. According to our annals, Charles the Bald had four sons by Queen Ermentrude: Louis, Charles, Carloman, and Lothair. Lothair, a child and abbot, and Charles, a young man and king of Aquitaine, died in the year 866. Carloman, who was also a cleric, died before his father; thus only Louis survived and succeeded his father. JAC. SIRM.]

It has come to the knowledge of our apostolate that, deceived by the cunning suggestions of wicked men, you withdrew from your father’s favor and fellowship. Overcome by excessive sorrow on this account, we had resolved to send you an appropriate correction from the apostolic authority, one that would restrain you from disgraceful and foolish impulses and, once corrected, restore you to your father’s favor.

But now, because our most holy brother and fellow bishop Odo has come and informed us that your devotion has been fully restored to your father’s favor, we have given thanks to the Lord God. Therefore, exhorting your devotion, we decree that henceforth you take care never to separate yourselves from the unity of so great a father. Like an evangelical father, after your transgressions he kindly received you when you turned back to him, clothed you in the first robe, and placed a ring on your hand and sandals on your feet. Thus, just as that erring son at last returned, obtained favor, and became an heir of his father’s inheritance without limit, so you should strive to persevere in the good condition to which you have returned, so that you may always enjoy your paternal inheritance and may not, through any negligence whatsoever, fall away from the blessing, favor, and communion of the holy Roman Church, which desires you to become more glorious [Col. 0839D].

Indeed, we order you to present yourselves humbly at the synod that is to be assembled at the place appointed by us, at which we believe legates of apostolic authority will be present. There you are to answer truthfully concerning the matters of which you have been accused and submit yourselves fully to the canonical rules, ready to give satisfaction.

We wish you well-being in Christ.

XL. TO HUCBERT, ABBOT, BROTHER OF QUEEN THEUTBERGA. (Year 863.) He replies to his letter and states that he ordered his and his sister’s case to be examined at the synod by legates.

[Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 0840A]

NICOLAUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the religious abbot HUCBERT.

We willingly received the written statement of your defense, sent through Odo, our brother and fellow bishop, to the apostolic see. Considering its contents more attentively, we found that you complained of having been addressed by us with harsh reproach and that, contrary to your expectation—while you hoped to receive letters of consolation from us as you continually protested, together with your brother and sister—you instead found us harshly accusing and correcting you [Col. 0840B].

Your devotion ought not to have taken this amiss. For a father’s discipline is sometimes applied to a beloved son even when he has scarcely sinned—not so that he may be needlessly subjected to the severity of blows, but so that, lest he fall into suspected crimes, he may be frightened by benevolent reproach. Although a son may endure dreadful lashes with the greatest distress because he is struck without fault, the father nevertheless knows that he has kept the discipline measured within a gentle heart, so as to guard him from impending dangers.

Since no discerning person at all doubts that this is so [variant: “no one at all,” HARD.], it must be observed, and guarded against with the utmost care, that when harsh words are sometimes sent to you from the apostolic authority, you should not take offense at them in any way. For either the blows of our correction are open and true, or they are hidden and just, and have some reasonable basis.

Moreover, because you appear to commend your innocence by seeking examination before the priests and by protesting it daily, we are pleased and pray God that the truth may indeed be so. Nevertheless, because you still appear to be standing in the battle line, apply perseverance to your innocence, so that, although some now mark you with blame, once the truth has been recognized you may later be praised [Col. 0840C].

Furthermore, in accordance with the ministry divinely entrusted to us, we believe that none of the sons of God’s holy Church is unaware of how vigorously we have persevered from the day on which your case and that of your sister were brought before our apostolate. Your brother himself will be able to relate what we have done concerning him. For we can neither be considered idle and negligent nor suspected of this, since we have ordered a synod to be assembled to resolve and examine other matters as well and to bring them finally to a legal conclusion, and have sent legates of apostolic authority there. Through their judgment, in the assembly of the brethren, you will either be canonically punished for guilt or justly cleared of the charge on account of innocence.

We wish your religious devotion happy well-being in Christ.

(Year 863.) XLI. TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF LOTHAIR. That they should urge King Lothair to remove Hilduin, to whom he gave the church of Cambrai, and grant free permission to elect a bishop.

[Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 0841A]

NICOLAUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverent and holy brothers, the archbishops and other bishops established in the kingdom of Lothair.

[Note: [Col. 0841D] Bishops in the kingdom of Lothair. Hincmar, writing to Nicholas about this letter, says in Flodoard, book III, chapter 12: “In the letter of your holiness, addressed through Bishop Odo to the bishops in the kingdom of Lothair on behalf of the rights of the Church of Cambrai, I read that your authority was asking through whose neglect that same Church had remained vacant for more than ten months.” It was vacant after the death of Bishop Theodoric and at this time was held by Hilduin, whom Lothair had installed, until Hilduin was finally expelled and John was appointed by legitimate votes in the year 866. JAC. SIRM.]

Whenever we hear from reliable reports concerning the holiness of your devotion things believed to be pleasing, welcome, and acceptable to God, we rejoice in the Lord and, exulting with immense gladness, render manifold thanks to him [Col. 0841B]. But when we hear that you languish in the sluggish idleness of torpor, consigning the heavenly commands to oblivion as though you had taken some Lethean poppies; not suppressing sins but fostering them; not uprooting vices but planting them; not cutting them down with the hoe of the sacred word but, as we might say, pouring out the waters of flattering tongues so that they may grow; and, what is more wicked, supporting and defending the perversities of others—we are saddened and fail under an abundance of grief proportionate to the degree that we see those with whom we thought we could ascend in opposition to every power and resist with a free voice on behalf of the house of the Lord, or even extend the rod of correction and the rigor of justice, instead leading those who follow them into the abyss and pit of iniquities [Col. 0841C], and, alas, going before them with blind eyes. But we judge that this should be passed over in silence for a little while, until the time for speaking arrives.

Furthermore, we have learned from the certain report of the faithful that Lothair, our glorious son and king, gave the Church of Cambrai to a certain cleric named Hilduin. This church is said to lie within his kingdom, but is reported to belong to the diocese of our brother Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims. Since he judges that the aforesaid cleric has been censured in many respects by the sacred canons, the king is deprived of the opportunity to consecrate another man who might be found worthy—an opportunity that you, as the authorities in this matter, ought to provide, since you do not correct Hilduin.

Thus the Church of Cambrai, occupied by the aforementioned Hilduin, has now remained deprived of its bishop for more than ten months, contrary to the rule of the sacred canons [Col. 0841D]. It is continually stripped of its possessions, and the divine ministries that ought to be celebrated there are not performed, because it lacks episcopal ministry.

Therefore we command you to advise our son, Lothair the glorious king, and to take the greatest care to persuade him not to inflict any prejudice upon the Church of Cambrai. Let him remove the aforementioned Hilduin and grant the clergy and people of that Church [Col. 0842A] permission to elect from among themselves a bishop according to the sacred canons.

For if you disregard this apostolic command of ours, know that, on account of your disobedience and the poison of your pestilential counsel by which you have already infected the aforementioned king so often, you are to be completely removed from our communion. Moreover, we command you to deliver to the aforementioned cleric Hilduin the letter that we are sending him. Unless you excommunicate him by the authority of God, blessed Peter, and ourselves, so that he claims nothing for himself from the Church of Cambrai and never attempts or requests to be advanced to the episcopate in that same Church, you are to remain separated with him from communion in the Lord’s body and blood, by the judgment of God and of our humble office.

Indeed, we wish you to know without any doubt that we shall diligently investigate why, and through whose negligence, you permitted the Church of Cambrai to remain deprived for more than ten months of a ruling bishop elected from its own clergy, contrary to the definition of the holy regulations. With God’s help, we shall discover through careful examination who is deserving of what punishment of vengeance, without tolerating any further delay.

We wish your fraternity well-being in Christ, now and always.

(Year 863.) XLII. TO LOTHAIR, KING. That he should reject Hilduin, the usurper of the Church of Cambrai, and permit Hincmar to exercise his privilege in arranging matters there.

[Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 0842C] NICOLAUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to LOTHAIR, the glorious king.

Among the countless exceedingly sinister and detestable things reported about you, which cause us no little grief because we desire your salvation in soul and body, we have also learned from a truthful report that you have added this to your transgressions: you plunder the possessions and estates of the holy Church of Rheims, over which our venerable brother Hincmar presides as archbishop by divine dispensation, even though they are situated within the borders of your kingdom; and you so violently restrain him from his diocese [for “with a violent arm,” HARD.] that you do not permit him to have any power whatsoever to consecrate a bishop in the Church of Cambrai—which has now been deprived of its pastor for ten months—or to arrange anything there according to his ministry, while it remains vacant, contrary to the ordinances of the venerable canons [Col. 0842D].

We do not wish this presumption, detestable to all Christian laws, to be committed by your glory against ecclesiastical institutions, nor will we tolerate it in any way. For if it is proper to kings to restrain and govern rebellious bodily impulses by the command of reason, your Excellence ought certainly to have been present for the defense of all the Churches in your kingdom, and you ought by no means, after setting aside the right of the metropolitan of Rheims in the parishes of your kingdom, to have established Hilduin from elsewhere as usurper over the bereft Church [Col. 0843A].

For this reason we exhort and admonish your devotion and, by apostolic authority, forbid and restrain you: do not extend unlawful designs to matters belonging to the holy Church of Rheims, do not subject them to your dominion, and do not permit the usurper to remain any longer in the Church of Cambrai. Unless you do this and restore everything to the metropolitan of Rheims, so that he may arrange matters there according to his privilege—for we can no longer bear with equanimity such great horrors and detestable acts committed by you for so long against the body of God’s holy Church—know that, so that you may at least be compelled to come to your senses, you are to be struck very swiftly with the ecclesiastical sword, so that thereafter you will fear to perpetrate such things [Col. 0843B] in God’s holy Church.

As for the usurper of the Church of Cambrai, named Hilduin, know that he is to be entirely separated from communion in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and from all fellowship with Christians if, after this prohibition by our apostolate, he attempts to remain there, until he comes into our presence to give canonical satisfaction concerning these matters.

We wish your glory well-being in Christ.

(Year 863.) XLIII. TO HILDUIN, THE CLERIC. That henceforth he should abstain from the Church of Cambrai, which he had usurped.

NICOLAUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HILDUIN [Col. 0843C], the cleric.

Although the desire of our will always wishes to learn good things about everyone, we have been greatly saddened by what certain truthful men have reported with reliable testimony to our ears concerning your perversities. For you are said to have invaded the Church of Cambrai contrary to the statutes of the holy canons; to oppress and dishonor the clerics of its holy people; to plunder its possessions; to render no due submission or obedience to its metropolitan, our brother Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims; and, without his consent, to hold that same Church, which has now been vacant for ten months, in your occupation. Other detestable matters concerning your rashness have also been reported to our apostolic concern, but for now we are silent about them [Col. 0843D].

We command you only this: do not delay returning to the aforesaid Church everything that you removed from it and are known to possess. And although some human power may permit it, divine and canonical judgment by no means allows you to be consecrated bishop in that Church; indeed, it keeps all who share your character and presumption far from so great a dignity. Especially since no prejudice ought to be inflicted upon the metropolitan of the province of Rheims, to whom the Church of Cambrai is subject, we command you to depart from that Church of Cambrai as quickly as possible, taking nothing from it [Col. 0844A], so that a man who is in no respect censured by the holy canons may be elected by the clergy and people of that Church and consecrated by the archbishop of Rheims.

But if you delay returning to the aforesaid Church what you took, apart from the things belonging to food and drink, or if you remove anything further from it and do not withdraw yourself entirely from its authority and administration, then, by the sentence of our God, of the holy apostles, and of our authority, you shall be bound by the chains of anathema for as long as you persist with obstinate mind in resisting this letter of our decision.

(Year 863.) XLIV. TO KING CHARLES. [Col. 0844B] A decree sent in the year 863 by Saint Nicholas and the holy Roman see to Charles, the most glorious king of the Franks, to be confirmed and strengthened by queens and Churches under the anathema of all the bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0843D] These first decrees are not Nicholas’s, but Saint Gregory’s, who issued them at the Lateran Council. Nicholas, however, adopted them as his own and sent them to Charles, king of the Franks. MARTENE.]

Our previous office, which we exercised in governing a monastery, teaches us how necessary it is to provide for the peace of monasteries and to consider their perpetual security. Therefore, since we know that many monasteries have suffered numerous prejudices and burdens from bishops, it is fitting that the provision of our fraternity should beneficially arrange their future peace, so that those living in them in God’s service may, with his grace assisting them, persevere with free minds.

But lest, through a custom that more properly ought to be corrected, anyone presume to inflict any trouble upon monks, it is necessary that the matters we have taken care to enumerate below be guarded by the diligence of the bishops’ fraternity in such a way that no opportunity for further disturbance may arise from them.

Therefore, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the authority of Peter and Paul, the chief apostles, in whose place, by God’s appointment, we preside over this Roman Church, we prohibit and forbid any bishop henceforth to presume to diminish, by any method or investigation whatsoever, the revenues, possessions, documents, cells, or estates of monasteries, or anything belonging to them. We entirely forbid the bishop to make ecclesiastical inventories of the monastery’s possessions or documents.

We also completely prohibit him from celebrating public Masses in the monastery, lest any opportunity for crowds be given in the retreats of God’s servants [Col. 0844D]. When an abbot dies, while inventories are being made, acquisitions provided for, or things given being sought out, he must not involve himself in the monastery’s affairs on any pretext; he must not dare to set up a chair there, exercise any authority of command, or make any arrangement, however slight, unless he has been asked by the abbot of the place. Thus the monks may always remain under the authority of their abbots, every monastery may possess its own protection of liberty, and the pontifical decree, the immunities of kings, and the constitution of the Roman pontiff may retain unviolated and perpetual force throughout the ages.

So be it.

Also, in the decrees of the same Pope Nicholas:

By the authority of our apostolate, we decree that every monastery situated in Gaul shall have free disposition of all its possessions in every respect, according to the benefit of that Church, the advantageous administration of God’s servants, and the election of its abbot from among themselves.

No other person, whether secular or ecclesiastical, shall possess dominion over any property in any monastery, nor shall anyone possess or claim for himself any share. Everything shall remain under the administration of the abbot and of the brothers serving God there, so that whatever they wish to do regularly or canonically for the benefit of the monastery may lie within their power [Col. 0845B].

Nor shall the bishop of that region approach the monastery as though abusing a right of personal authority, unless summoned by the abbot or brothers. His arrival must not disturb the brothers’ peace through the pressure of his presence, nor may he ever presume to devise any deceit or scheme against either the abbot or the brothers, whether personally or through his agents.

Rather, whatever he can usefully, modestly, and kindly contribute to the servants of God residing in the monastery for the preservation of their order, let it advance for the love of God and in hope of eternal reward. Let him not violently or cunningly contrive any evil or disturbance against them, as we have heard certain men wish to do.

No regional bishop shall claim anything for himself within the monastery, whether personally or through his ministers, whether from the clergy, the monks, the canons, or the laity, by right of authority or episcopal arrogance, without the consent of the abbot of that place and of the brothers living there; nor shall he presume to arrange anything.

As for ordinations requested by the abbot or by the brothers themselves, the consecration of churches, the blessing of an altar, or the sanctification of chrism and oil, he shall not delay providing them as requested by the abbot and the inhabitants of that place. For a bishop ought to perform the duty of his common office not for the sake of profit, but as the ministry of the administration entrusted to him. It is the mark of pastoral care that he seek to provide for the sheep committed to him out of love rather than authority.

The brothers shall always have the power to elect their abbot from among themselves, and in his election they shall not look to any constitution or arrangement made by the bishop. And since many plots are often fabricated against God’s servants through the snares of wicked men, we decree that one who has been ordained cannot be deposed unless a criminal case proves him guilty.

If he has been marked by infamy, no fewer than ten assemblies of archbishops or bishops are to be held by royal provision. For it is not just that a pastor elected and ordained for the Church should be expelled by chance and without judgment, without the accusation of any manifest crime. No one is condemned before an earthly king unless he has been found guilty in a criminal case and this has been shown by the testimony of truth. Thus an abbot, elected by many and ordained with priestly blessing, must in no way be deprived of the honor of his order [Col. 0846A].

But if anyone, treating this decree of our constitution as of little account, inflicts violence upon any holy monastery, abbot, or brothers, or appears as an invader against them, their servants, or all the possessions of that monastery, let him have no doubt that he will appear guilty in the divine judgment and will be condemned to punishment by divine censure.

All the bishops replied: “We rejoice with the liberty of the monks, and we confirm what your Beatitude has decreed concerning them.”

(Year 863.) XLV. LETTER OF NICHOLAS TO ALL THE BISHOPS AND PRINCES OF GAUL. The privilege of liberty is confirmed for the monastery of Saint Karilefus.

[Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 0846B]

NICOLAUS, bishop of the Roman see, to all the bishops and princes [Roman edition: pontiffs] of Gaul, eternal salvation in God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ.

[End of supplied source.]

When the hearts of kings are divinely inspired to show concern for religious places, thanks ought to be given to God, and in everything they piously and religiously undertake, their will must be obeyed with every eager devotion. Indeed, prayers ought to be offered that they might take up an affectionate concern and solicitous care for the holy places. But now that they voluntarily offer themselves for these tasks, they too should be congratulated, [Col. 0846C] and whatever they command must be carried out without hesitation.

Thus the glorious king of the Franks, Charles, inspired from heaven, among the other works of devotion that he has always undertaken with ready zeal for the Church of God, has also deigned to assume responsibility for the monastery of Saint Karilefus the Confessor, built in the district of Le Mans above the river Anisola. From the first day of its foundation, ever since the blessed confessor of Christ, Karilefus, came to rest there in body, a religious community of monks has lived there; and the monastery has possessed the privilege of freedom both in the administration of its property and in the election of its abbot from among its own members [Roman edition: “was in body, a religious…”].

But because the enemy of the human race never ceases to attack the Church of Christ, he shook and attempted to tear away the security of the freedom that the monastery had possessed for many years, although he did not completely sever it—both a few years ago and also in the present period, that is, during the reign of King Charles himself. Since divine mercy never abandons those who trust in it, it moved the prince’s mind so that not only would the enemy’s persuasion not prevail, but he also wished to ensure that, in times to come, the privilege of freedom once granted to that monastery could thereafter be overturned or violated by no one.

Therefore the aforesaid pious prince deigned to send us his representative, namely the venerable Odo, bishop of Beauvais, and to send letters expressing his favor. In them he requested that we confirm by our authority the freedom granted to that monastery by the bishops and by the kings of the Franks, and strengthen it so that it might endure in future times.

Accordingly, considering that this was a pious request, absolutely necessary for the peace of God’s servants, and something that the pastors of the Churches ought to request and secure if the princes of this world failed to secure it, we decree by the authority of our apostolate that the monastery of Saint Karilefus the Confessor, situated in Gaul in the district of Le Mans above the river Anisola, shall have complete freedom in every respect to administer its property according to the good of that Church and the benefit of God’s servants. The bishop of the city of Le Mans—whether Rotbert, who now presides over that see, or his successors—shall have no right of possession or domination over that monastery, nor shall they attempt to bring the aforesaid monastery under the subjection of their city. Rather, the abbot who is now there, Engilharius, and the brothers of that monastery shall always possess the right of governance, according to ecclesiastical statutes, both now and in future times.

Specifically, whatever has been or shall thereafter be offered to that monastery, whether in gold or silver, in lands and servants, or in any other kind of property, neither the bishop of Le Mans—whether Rotbert, who now presides over that city, or those who govern the Church of Le Mans after him—nor any other person, whether secular or ecclesiastical, shall possess or claim any share for himself. Everything shall remain under the administration of the abbot himself and the brothers serving God there, so that whatever they may regularly and canonically wish to do for the benefit of the monastery itself shall lie within their power.

Nor shall the bishop approach the aforesaid monastery as though abusing a right of personal authority, unless he has been summoned by the abbot and the brothers, lest the pressure of his arrival disturb the brothers’ peace. Nor shall he ever presume to devise any deceit or scheme against the abbot or the brothers, either personally or through his agents. Rather, whatever he can usefully, modestly, and kindly contribute to the preservation of the order for the servants of God residing in the aforesaid monastery, let him carry it out for the love of God and in hope of eternal reward.

Nor shall he violently or craftily contrive any evil or disturbance against them, as we have heard that certain people wished to do, displaying certain documents by which they attempted to make the monastery subject to their city by right of possession. These documents are plainly shown to have been entirely false, since the privileges of the kings, granted to that monastery long ago from the time of the ancient Frankish kings, disprove them, as do the very documents still preserved in the monastery’s archives as testimony to the freedom granted to it.

Even if it had perhaps happened that the monastery had at some time been under the power of the bishop of Le Mans—which the facts themselves and the evidence produced for the monastery prove never to have happened—nevertheless, according to the laws of the world, after so many centuries and such a span of years it could in no way lawfully have been reclaimed. What had once received freedom could never again have been enslaved under another’s authority.

For in the laws we find that all claims must be settled within a period of thirty years. In ecclesiastical cases, no complaint can be brought after the fortieth year if it was not brought within that span of years. And behold: since this monastery possessed freedom under the first Christian king of the Franks, namely Clovis, and his son Childebert, and thereafter remained free under all the kings, both in the administration of its property and in the election of its abbot, it is now being reclaimed as though under the domination of proprietary right. Yet even if it had been a secular possession, and had lacked the domination of its possessor for so many years, the ancient possessor could in no way have claimed it for himself according to either the laws of the world or ecclesiastical law.

But what is wicked even to say is that episcopal ambition attempts to claim as a right of servitude the possession of Christ and the fellowship of God’s servants, which secular power granted to be free. It is therefore apparent that whoever perversely contrives these things is not seeking the profit of souls, but rather yearning for the arrogance of domination and the gains of greed.

Accordingly, suppressing this pernicious ambition by every means, we command that Rotbert, bishop of Le Mans, and whoever becomes his successor, claim no power of jurisdiction over the aforesaid monastery. Rather, it shall remain, according to the freedom granted to it for many years, removed from all episcopal pressure and domination. Let no bishop of the aforesaid city presume to claim anything there, either personally or through his ministers, whether from the clergy, the monks, the canons, or the laity, by right of authority or episcopal arrogance, without the will of the abbot of that place and the brothers residing there—whether for ordaining, arranging, or ruling anything.

As for ordinations requested by the abbot or the brothers themselves, consecrations of churches, the blessing of an altar, and the sanctification of chrism and oil, let him not delay in providing them as the abbot and the inhabitants of that place request. For the bishop ought to perform the duty of his office not for profit, but as the ministry of the stewardship entrusted to him. It belongs to pastoral care that he seek to aid the sheep entrusted to him out of love rather than authority, although both are necessary toward subjects according to the circumstances. Love ought to generate diligence, while authority must be tempered by love, so that the charity of Christ may burn more strongly than the rigor of power grows arrogant.

The brothers of the monastery of Saint Karilefus shall always have the power to elect their own abbot. In his election, the bishops of Le Mans shall neither be consulted nor allowed to impose any constitution or arrangement. Instead, the brothers shall choose whomever they judge worthy in life, character, and teaching, and useful and suitable to them as a steward in pastoral office; and they shall report him to the king, so that he may receive the power of governance with the king’s grant and consent. No payment shall be received or given for his ordination or appointment, because the gift of the Holy Spirit must be obtained not by a price but by grace.

And because many deceptions are often contrived against God’s servants through the plots of wicked men, we decree that an abbot who has been ordained may not be deposed unless a criminal charge proves him guilty. If he has been marked by accusations of infamy, then, through royal provision, no fewer than six bishops shall be convened, and the bishop of Le Mans shall be one of their number. After his case has been examined according to the canons by their judgment, he may not otherwise be deposed unless he has been shown guilty by clear and certain evidence.

For it is not just that a pastor of the Church, elected and ordained, should be expelled by chance and without judgment, without any clear accusation of a crime. No one is condemned under the laws of the world unless he has been detected in a criminal matter and proved by the testimony of truth; no one consecrated to the orders of the Church ought rightly to be deposed unless he has been shown to have been convicted of certain crimes.

Thus the abbot, elected by many and ordained with priestly blessing, must in no way be deprived of the honor of his order unless he has been accused and convicted of manifest crimes. Therefore, under this authority, we command that once the abbot of the monastery of Saint Karilefus has been regularly and canonically elected and ordained [Roman edition: “and ordained”], he may be deposed by no one—neither by bishops, kings, nor any other person—unless a criminal charge has arisen for which he ought rightly to be deposed according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and the provisions of the canons.

We wish these constitutions to remain wholly inviolable in every respect in the present and future times, and not to be violated by anyone, whether king, bishop, or person of any order. If anyone, treating the decree of our constitution lightly, does violence to the monastery of Saint Karilefus, its abbot, or its brothers, and appears as an invader either against them, their servants, or the entire property of the monastery, let him not doubt that he will appear guilty at the divine judgment and be condemned to punishment by divine censure.

We therefore establish that, first, whoever attempts such a thing shall be deprived of the dignity of his honor, whether he is a secular or ecclesiastical person. Then he shall be excluded from the fellowship of ecclesiastical communion and shall not share in the body and blood of Christ until he either corrects what he has unjustly done or makes satisfaction through worthy penitence.

If the brothers of that monastery learn that any of these provisions has been violated—that someone has attempted to prevent them from electing an abbot, or has decided to enslave the monastery’s possessions or offerings made there to his own right, or that the bishop of Le Mans has attempted to subject the monastery itself to the subjection of his city—they shall have permission to approach the metropolitan bishop of Tours and make their oppression known. After investigating the case, the metropolitan shall summon the person through whom they are being harassed, declare to him, on the basis of this present authority, what danger has been assigned to him, and admonish him that he should amend what he has done wickedly.

If he prefers not to listen willingly and to correct his guilt, then, according to the decree of this constitution, the metropolitan shall exclude him from the communion of Christians and from participation in the body and blood of Christ, whatever his person or dignity may be. If the metropolitan bishop refuses to provide assistance in response to their petitions and appeals, the brothers of the monastery of Saint Karilefus shall have permission to approach the apostolic, that is, Roman, see; to lay the cause of their need before the bishop who at that time presides over the city of Rome; and to make known the constitution of this present edict. Thus, once the case has been learned, the Roman pontiff shall not delay in exercising a just condemnation of anathema against the guilty person, so that the aforesaid monastery may possess its own protection of freedom, and so that the pontifical decree, the immunities of the kings, and the constitution of the Roman pontiff may possess perpetual and inviolable firmness.

(Year 863.) XLVI. TO THE EMPEROR MICHAEL. The sequence of the account concerning the expulsion of Photius and the installation [Vatican Codex: restoration] of Patriarch Ignatius; likewise concerning the deposition and excommunication of the bishops Zacharias and Rhadoaldus, formerly legates, with intervening chapters.
