With matters standing thus, and with the letters of our apostolate sent to Constantinople and to other parts of the world to make clear the purpose of our will—as you can gather and understand from the preceding writings recited up to this point—we now briefly indicate to your fraternity in Christ and your pious community what was done after our satisfaction had been obtained and our resolve concerning the restoration of our brother and bishop Ignatius and the expulsion of the adulterer Photius had been publicly displayed before the entire Church that is with us, with Leo, the secretary, and the imperial legate whom we mentioned above physically present, as well as what was done after the latter’s departure.

At the time these things were taking place, the bishops Rhadoaldus and Zacharias, whom we had sent from the apostolic see to Constantinople, had not yet been detected or exposed as having deposed Patriarch Ignatius or communicated with the intruder, adulterer, and layman Photius. But as time passed, rumors brought to Rome by many who came from those regions—and, indeed, by those fleeing persecutions stirred up by Photius’s supporters—gradually began to spread that the same bishops had been corrupted by gifts, and to publicize that they had communicated with Photius and deposed Ignatius.

When we heard this, we were filled with profound sorrow and began to consider and ponder how we might remove every unfavorable suspicion from the Church of Christ over which, by divine favor, we preside, so that it might have no “spot or wrinkle” or anything of that kind—not even providing the slightest opportunity for mockery.

Then we summoned a gathering of the most holy bishops from the western regions of many provinces and assembled a holy synod in the Church of God where the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, shines in body and, [text uncertain: “and shines with manly virtues”] several times manifests his power. Later, because the place was colder, we assembled in the Church of the Savior called Constantiniana by its founder, which was the first church built in the entire world. There all the documents translated from Greek into Latin were read aloud: both the wicked synod whose proceedings had been brought to the apostolic see by the aforementioned Leo, and the imperial letters, in all of which the deposition of Ignatius was contained.

The bishop Zacharias was then brought forward, since Rhadoaldus could not at that time be produced because of his absence. After he had been examined and carefully investigated, he was found wholly culpable in the deposition of Ignatius and in communion with Photius. Zacharias, then a bishop but now deprived of honor and communion, recognizing himself as liable, confessed with his own mouth and in his own writing that he had been sent to Constantinople from the apostolic see; that he had neglected the tasks entrusted to him by us; and that he had carried out what had been forbidden to him—namely, deposing Ignatius without the command of the apostolic see and communicating with Photius against the instructions of our apostolate.

Then, when the holy synod had decided together with us, the aforesaid Zacharias received the sentence of his deposition and excommunication and fell into the pit that he had prepared for others. The examination of the other man, Rhadoaldus, was postponed until another synod because of his absence.

What we unanimously and harmoniously established and promulgated in that venerable and holy synod concerning our brother and fellow priest Ignatius, the patriarch, or concerning Photius, the intruder and usurper of that Church, and his supporters, as well as concerning the sacred images, is set out below in chapters. In addition, what we once decreed in another synod previously assembled by us against those who, together with Valentinus, Manes [Mani], Apollinaris, and Eutyches and their followers, are said in certain regions of your lands to preach, against the first pastor and apostle, that the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ was passible—although that apostle says that Christ suffered only in the flesh—is also declared in the appended chapters.

I. Photius, who is known to belong to the party of schismatics and of those who have withdrawn themselves from participation in holy communion, and who, from secular administration, military service, and the law-court, was suddenly tonsured by Gregory of Syracuse, a former bishop condemned in synod, and was ordained bishop though convicted by the apostolic see; who, while our fellow priest Ignatius, patriarch of the holy Church of Constantinople, was living and survived, invaded his see; who entered the Lord’s sheepfold not through the door, which is Christ, but from elsewhere and on the opposite side, like a thief and robber, and burst in as a violent, rapacious, and wicked adulterer upon the bride whom, as friend of the bridegroom, he had received from Christ the bridegroom to keep undefiled; who, daily and without distinction, communicated and associated with condemned and anathematized persons, and with those whom my predecessor Pope Benedict of blessed memory had bound so that they might not presume, before a hearing, to exercise even priestly office; who, contrary to his pledged faith and his own profession—by which he promised that he would hold no hostile council against the aforesaid patriarch—assembled a council and, together with his followers, persons deposed, condemned, excommunicated, and anathematized, others without sees, and those by whom he himself had been irregularly and unlawfully promoted or whom he himself had rashly and improperly promoted, dared to pronounce deposition and anathema against the same Ignatius, our brother and fellow minister; who presumed, by whatever devices he could, to turn away from our commands, in the manner of Acacius, the former heretical patriarch of Constantinople, the envoys of the apostolic see whom we had sent concerning sacred images, to investigate and report to us the aforesaid patriarch’s expulsion, and to discover the manner of this neophyte’s promotion; who drew them, as their profession has disclosed, into the procession held for him with his peers, and—as the Holy Spirit revealed to the venerable synod assembled by us—despite the embassy, which ought to have been respected even according to the custom of the gentiles, drew them into communion with condemned persons and schismatics, and made them return not merely ineffective, in mockery of the blessed apostle Peter from whose see they had departed, but opponents of all that had been commanded them;

who finally banished into exile the bishops unwilling to communicate with him as an adulterer and invader, and did not fear to substitute accomplices in his wickedness in their places; and who to this day does not cease to assail the Church of God with various persecutions, so that he does not cease to afflict our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius, the most holy patriarch, with unheard-of punishments and dreadful tortures, and to strive without omission, by whatever means he can, to destroy all whom he discovers persisting with him for truth and faith: since he has committed these and similar acts contrary to evangelical, apostolic, prophetic, and canonical ordinances, let him, by the authority of God Almighty, of the blessed chiefs of the apostles Peter and Paul, of all the saints, and of the venerable six universal councils, and by the judgment of the Holy Spirit through us, be deprived of every priestly honor and title and wholly stripped of every clerical office. Thus, if, after learning of this sanction—which we believe to have been drawn forth by divine inspiration and to have been promulgated beyond doubt with the unanimity and concord of the holy synod—he attempts to sit on the throne of Constantinople, or prevents the oft-mentioned venerable Ignatius, our fellow bishop, from governing without any disturbance the Church entrusted to him; or if he further dares, according to his former practice, to touch anything of the sacred ministry in the manner of a priest: he shall by no means have hope of communion or opportunity for satisfaction. Bound in the chains of anathema together with his communicants and supporters, by God’s judgment and sentence through our lowliness, he shall receive the sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ only when death is near.

Let every person learn from this not henceforth to dare, by rash presumption, suddenly to rush from the laity into the Lord’s camp by a kind of unexpected assault, preferring to exercise command out of love of primacy before completing the service of a recruit, and attempting to teach before learning—as we have learned has often been presumed in that Church of Constantinople. Nor, when the clergy are despised—though in so great a city they are a plentiful multitude, laboring unremittingly in Christ’s Church from, so to speak, their very cradles, and offering the Lord unceasing offices of service—shall one who comes from outside, from another fold, suddenly seize Christ’s leadership and endeavor to tear apart those whom he does not recognize as his own; nor shall the Lord’s flock begin wholly to despise him as an outsider and unexpected intruder, especially when it sees that the wages of its own merits have availed it nothing and sees another consuming the fruits of its labors.

II. As for Gregory, who irregularly and in contempt of God presides over the Church of Syracuse, since he too belongs to the party of schismatics, and after having been deprived of episcopal office by a synod and bound by my predecessor Pope Benedict of holy memory, did not fear suddenly to consecrate the layman Photius as bishop and dared to meddle much with the sacred ministry: according to the preceding rule we decree, and by canonical deliberation define and establish through apostolic authority, that he shall lack every priestly ministry and be deprived of it. He shall by no means have, in any synod, hope of restoration or an opportunity for satisfaction. If henceforth at any time he presumes to minister in sacred office in the manner of a priest, let him be anathema. And if he stirs up tumults against Ignatius, our brother and fellow bishop, or turns the faithful away from his communion, let him be anathema. Let all who communicate with him be cast out from the Church, and let them too be anathema.

III. Those whom Photius, the neophyte and invader of the see of Constantinople, promoted in any ecclesiastical order—since it is manifest that they assented to all the wickednesses of their consecrator and communicated with him after the invasion—we deprive of every clerical office and wholly exclude by apostolic and canonical authority and synodal decree.

IV. We proclaim, sanction, and decree by the authority of the supreme Judge, our Lord Jesus Christ, that our most reverend and holy brother and fellow bishop Ignatius, patriarch of the holy Church of Constantinople—who was first deprived of his own throne by imperial violence and terror; was afterward anathematized by Photius, the adulterer, transgressor, and invader of the see of Constantinople, and by his accomplices (that is, by men excommunicated, anathematized, condemned, without episcopal sees, and bound by my predecessor Pope Benedict of holy memory); and was finally stripped of priestly insignia by an envoy of the apostolic see contrary to our command, as the Holy Spirit revealed to the holy synod and as Bishop Zacharias, formerly one of those two legates, made known in his own confession—has never been and is not deposed or anathematized. He was driven from the Church by imperial power without any canonical authority; he could not be bound by any bond imposed by persons who were themselves bound, who possessed neither authority from the apostolic see nor power to judge him, and he ought not to have suffered any loss of his rank.

Therefore, with every bond of anathema removed from him, through the power conferred by the divine voice upon most blessed Peter, and through the authorities of the sacred canons and decretal constitutions issued after the manner of the holy Fathers, we restore, establish, and confirm him—that is, the same Ignatius, our brother and fellow priest and patriarch—to his former honor, dignity, see, rank, patriarchate, pontifical insignia, and offices. Whoever, after learning of this apostolic and synodal sanction, prevents him from receiving all the insignia of the pontificate stated above, does not obey this decree in every respect, separates himself from his communion, or further attempts to pronounce any judgment against him without the prior consent of the apostolic see alone: if he is a cleric, let him be excluded from every clerical office before God and men, be bound to everlasting punishment as one who has betrayed his master with Judas the traitor, and, unless he withdraws from his wicked purpose, remain condemned by perpetual anathema. But if a layman—whoever he may be—attempts to oppose this constitution of ours and does not permit him to receive his see and all his former dignity, or, after he has recovered his former see, again attempts to drive him out and expel him from the patriarchate, or inflicts any molestation upon his person or priestly honor without the consent of this first see, let him be deprived of every paternal blessing, punished with the curse of Canaan son of Ham, who saw his father’s nakedness and did not cover it but mocked it, struck by the Lord’s judgment with eternal punishment together with parricides, and not wholly freed from the bonds of anathema unless he repents.

V. We establish that those bishops and clerics of every order who, after the unjust expulsion of Ignatius, our brother and fellow bishop, were banished into exile or maliciously deprived of ministry or rank, shall have their exile lifted and receive their own sees and ranks. If anyone presumes to oppose this decree of ours and prevents them from recovering their sees or ranks, let him be anathema until he obeys. If any of them are accused by others, we decree that they shall first receive their sees and proper ranks; but we do not permit them to be judged except by the Roman see. If they are said perhaps to have acted contrary to the rule, we establish that they are to be reserved for judgment by our decree, as the sacred canons also command.

VI. We decree that we must preserve the ordinances of our elders with unwavering regard of mind and always venerate in every respect the doctrines of the holy Fathers. Accordingly, concerning the sacred and venerable images of our Lord Jesus Christ, of Mary his ever-Virgin Mother, and of all the saints believed to have pleased God from righteous Abel onward, which the holy Church spread throughout the world received of old, and concerning what the bishops of the apostolic see decreed and established regarding them, we decree that these shall remain unimpaired and undefiled. Therefore we sanction that John, formerly bishop of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0855D] Either the John placed after Antony by Constantine Porphyrogenitus, Book III, no. 26, in the year 844. HARD.], and his followers, who with polluted mouth assert that these images ought to be broken and trampled underfoot, shall be anathema from Christ and from the Catholic and apostolic Church as long as they do not agree with us concerning these matters and do not think in accordance with the decrees of the holy Roman pontiffs and the ordinances of the other Catholic Fathers.

(The chapters which follow were first promulgated in another synod assembled by us.)

I. That the Lord Jesus Christ suffered only in the flesh.

It must truly be believed and professed in every way that our Lord Jesus Christ, God and Son of God, endured the passion of the cross only according to the flesh; but according to his divinity he remained incapable of suffering, as apostolic authority teaches and the clearest doctrine of the holy Fathers demonstrates.

II. Concerning those who say that the divinity was passible.

But those who say that our Redeemer and Lord Jesus Christ, God and Son of God, endured the passion of the cross according to his divinity—which is impious and abhorrent to Catholic minds—let them be anathema.

When Rhadoaldus therefore returned from Gaul, where he had acted no less wrongly than in the city of Constantinople, and learned that his colleague had suffered such a fate, he became afraid—indeed, provoked by his own conscience. Seeing this, we strongly urged him not to fear, adding only that we would take no action against him apart from the synod’s examination, nor would we bring any adversity upon him without a charge having been presented against him.

But “the impious flees when no one pursues him.” While he enjoyed our sufficient kindness and had done no evil, before the time of the synod and before his own vindication, he abandoned his church and his own diocese and went off to other dioceses, thereby evading the examination. While he remained there for some time, relying on apostolic restraint, we delayed inflicting upon him the canonical punishment he deserved, lest we appear too ready for vengeance or too hasty.

Accordingly, after sending our representatives—namely, most holy bishops—to various places, with letters indicating where rumor alone reported that he was hiding, we judged that he should be summoned. But he penetrated various hiding places, like a son of night and darkness who always flees the works of light and day and fears having his case brought into the light of the sun for the manifestation of justice. As long as he was able, he scorned to obey us. When he found no safe hiding place for his evasion, he finally dared to return to Rome.

While we were staying with the blessed apostle Peter amid the tongues and hands of raging adversaries, he, an unexpected enemy, burst in upon us among those enemies. As is now clear, he came deceitfully, intending to depart again. Although his body had returned, not his mind, and although the time of the synod had been postponed because of the imminent oppression of enemies, a rumor increasingly spread that Rhadoaldus was again planning to flee.

When we heard this, we could not abandon the Church, which had no “spot or wrinkle” [Roman edition adds: “or anything of this kind,”] without also freeing it from false suspicion. Nor could we admit into our communion, without satisfaction, a man defamed by such great acts of treachery and stained in the mouths of men by so many crimes [perhaps: “stained by the filth of so many crimes”]. In the presence of many brothers and bishops, and of very many sons of this holy Church, we therefore admonished him that, as before, he should not leave the city of Rome in any direction without our permission. Instead, residing there, using his property freely and without fear, and freely retaining his friends and dependents, he should await without alarm the time of the synod at which he would be required to clear himself, knowing for certain that he would suffer no injustice either before or after the examination of the synod, but would remain secure in whatever justice he possessed.

Moreover, let him know that if he should depart from the city of Rome without our permission, from that moment he would be deposed and excommunicated. But, scorning our satisfactions and the judgments pronounced against him—or rather, scorning the constitutions of the holy Fathers—he despoiled his own Church without our permission, abandoned the sheep entrusted to him to the wolves’ teeth, departed for other dioceses, and fled the approaching synod. And because [Col. 0856D] he did not refute these and many other charges brought against him, by evading examination in every way he confirmed that what was being said about him was true.

Therefore, after a numerous and venerable synod of most holy bishops had been convened in the Church of the Saviour mentioned above, which is called Constantiniana, by the authority of almighty God, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, the princes of the apostles, and of all the saints alike—whose rules and decrees he had violated in many ways—and also by the judgment of our apostolate, we deposed him and excommunicated him from the body and blood of Christ. In this we followed the statutes of the holy Fathers, and especially the example of Saint [Col. 0857A] Felix, who deposed and excommunicated the bishops Vitalis and Misenus because they had once perpetrated in the city of Constantinople an offense wholly equal to this apostasy (Felix III, *Epistola* 5).

If the aforesaid Rhadoaldus, formerly a bishop but now deposed and excommunicated, should henceforth at any time associate with Photius, the anathematized usurper of the Church of Constantinople, oppose Ignatius, our brother and fellow bishop, and further disturb the Church of God; or if he should complain about his condemnation, he would be anathematized. Consequently, he would be separated and alienated from all Christians until he should voluntarily submit himself to our judgment and to the college [collegio, “fellowship/college”; the construction is uncertain]. Rhadoaldus, therefore, is now deposed and excommunicated; and if he should communicate with Photius, he is anathematized. [Col. 0857B] We inform you of this, dearest brothers, so that you may know with whom we communicate and whom we exclude from our apostolic and catholic communion, in order that, according to the sacred canons, and especially in accordance with the Council of Nicaea (canon 5), those rejected by some may not be received by others.

Therefore, extending our hands to the Church of God, reject from yourselves those whom we reject; and receive those whom we receive, so that God and the Father may be glorified with one mind and one voice through Jesus Christ in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

Moreover, after we had taken care, through our other letters, to make known to your holy fraternity and pious devotion the matters that have been read thus far in this volume, [Col. 0857C] a certain protospatharius named Michael came to the apostolic see, sent by the emperor of the Greeks with a letter. In it we found that the same emperor was asserting that he regarded you—most blessed patriarchs and our dearest brothers—as led astray and deceived, inasmuch as you had become supporters of that execrable apostasy: namely, that you consented both to the irregular deposition of our brother and fellow priest Ignatius and to the consecration of Photius, the adulterer and invader of the Church; and that, contrary to our statutes and also against the see of the prince of the apostles, Peter, you were joining with them in rebellion.

Although we certainly do not believe this about you—for we have nowhere read that anything of this kind was ever done by your Catholic predecessors, the bishops—[Col. 0857D] we do not want you to be unaware that we have received these accusations against you in the emperor’s own written communication, since we are more concerned for you than for ourselves. We inform you of this in writing and admonish your united charity to look upon yourselves as in a mirror and recall that we have taken pains to make these things known to you for this reason: as we said above, the decrees of the holy and great Council of Nicaea command that in every province a canonical letter be observed, so that those who are rejected may not be received by others.

Furthermore, always be cautious and vigilant, lest, deceived by anyone’s persuasion or by human threats or by any kind of falsehood, you dissent from the head—that is, from the first see—or be divided from the charity and unity of that Church [Col. 0858A] over which he presided whom the voice of Christ placed above all.

Indeed, if you recall former days according to the wisdom divinely given to you, and bring to mind the ancient bishops of your sees, you will surely discover with what veneration your predecessors honored the see of blessed Peter, and with what love of charity they always embraced its decrees. In short, in the universal councils nothing is held valid or wholly accepted except what the see of blessed Peter has approved—as you yourselves know. Conversely, whatever that see alone has rejected remains rejected to this day.

Therefore, let the charity of your unity grieve with us over the deposition of our most holy brother and fellow minister, Ignatius, the patriarch, [Col. 0858B] and with us offer him whatever consolations can prevail. For if, according to the Apostle, when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it (I Cor. 12), how much more must one sympathize with him who is known to have held the foremost place among the other members? Thus, whether on account of the rejection of that one and particular person, our aforesaid brother, or certainly on account of the trampling underfoot of the supreme priesthood, you ought to grieve, groan, weep, hasten, and contend.

For if secular power were permitted to judge the bishops of the Church of the Lord in this manner, or if it should again be lawful for inferiors to perpetrate such things so recklessly against their superiors, consider whether such presumption might prevail to your destruction—or rather, to that of the whole Church—now and in future times. If you attend to this, [Col. 0858C] you can already see it. For impiety has raised its head so high that, with the bishops of the Churches set aside and canonical order trampled underfoot, laymen now hold ecclesiastical governance: at their own pleasure they remove some and promote others in their places; and again, those whom they now approve they reject shortly afterward, overcome by their own fickleness of mind.

For, so that these same secular and laymen may freely commit any crimes and may not be openly reproved for them by any bishop—although one promoted from the clergy could restrain them with the highest authority—they do not permit men from the clerical register to be advanced to holy orders, men who, having served under Christ the leader in arduous warfare both more boldly and for a longer time and more familiarly, could restrain them more forcefully. [Col. 0858D] Instead, they choose from among themselves those who are less likely to presume to criticize their deeds, since they remember that shortly before they had been promoted from their own circle by the favor of those same men.

This presumption is practiced all the more familiarly in those regions—namely, that laymen are suddenly tonsured and consecrated as bishops—in proportion as they testify that it has grown through custom. We, on the contrary, desire all the more earnestly to eradicate it from the Church of God, in proportion as we have already shown it to be exceedingly harmful to the clergy and to the entire religious people. And we know from the sacred canons that a bad custom must be avoided no less than a pernicious corruption. We know also that, gradually increasing, it has already invaded many people with the burden of its pestilential wickedness, to such an extent that this recklessness has grown so far [Col. 0859A] that they now have no need of clergy at all: contrary to the sacred canons, they suddenly choose from among themselves anyone they wish after tonsuring him; they do not turn the eyes of their minds toward the labors of the clergy; and thus it happens that an outsider consumes the fruit of their labors, and an unexpected foreign enemy seizes the rewards of their merits.

In this way it profits clergy nothing to have served in the Lord’s camp or to have risen step by step through each of the ecclesiastical orders, while another leaps over all these ranks at a bound and suddenly rules over them—one who, while among them, neither took up arms against spiritual enemies nor ever stood firm by fighting for the truth against the Church’s various adversaries.

But that no one may be rashly chosen from among the laity for the episcopate, the sacred canons forbid this, as the Sardican canons show, with Bishop Hosius saying in the thirteenth chapter [Col. 0859B] (canon XIII):

> I consider this necessary: that you examine with the greatest care whether perhaps a rich man, a scholar from the marketplace, or someone from a civil administration has been sought for the episcopate, so that he may not be ordained before he has first fulfilled the ministry of lector and the office of deacon or presbyter; and so, if he is worthy, let him ascend through each rank to the summit of the episcopate. For through these promotions, which will necessarily extend over a considerable period, it can be proved with what faith, modesty, gravity, and propriety he is endowed. And if he has been found worthy, let him be honored with the divine priesthood. For it is neither fitting nor permitted by reason or discipline that anyone who is a neophyte should be ordained rashly and lightly, whether as bishop, presbyter, or deacon—especially since the blessed [Col. 0859C] Apostle, teacher of the nations, appears both to have warned and forbidden that this be done (I Tim. 3). Let those be chosen whose life has been examined over a long period and whose merits have been proven.

Look, therefore, also toward future evils—or rather, behold the evils already pressing upon you. You are physicians: foresee the diseases that threaten by means of their preceding signs. You are bishops: discern the dreadful destruction arising against the Church of Christ. You are watchmen: climb to the high citadel of the mind and observe from afar the savage beast eager to rush upon the Lord’s flock. Raise your voice like a trumpet and announce their crimes to the people of God. Ascend a high mountain—that is, to the height of virtues—you who evangelize Zion (Isa. 40). Stand firm in strength; rise in opposition to the powers of this age; set up a wall [Col. 0859D] for the house of God and resist every power that acts unjustly. Thus it will come about that you can neither be accused, like mute dogs, on account of your silence, nor be compelled to render a strict account to the Lord for hiding your talent. May you, at his command, commendably rescue yourselves, our fellow priests, and indeed the Church of Christ established in those regions from immense destruction and harmful defilement, and govern them wondrously.

We previously did not send this letter, which we addressed through the aforesaid protospatharius Michael [Col. 0860A] to the glorious Augustus Michael, along with our other writings to your holiness, or to your united affection, because the brothers through whom those writings were sent were urgently requesting permission to depart, and because, being occupied with many ecclesiastical affairs, we could not have this letter, solemnly arranged as hastily as we wished, ready at hand when they departed.

---

### (Year 863.) XLVII. TO ROTHADUS, BISHOP OF SOISSONS

He recalls how many letters he has so far written to Gaul on his behalf and promises that he will not fail him if he comes to Rome.

[Mansi, in the same place.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most holy and most reverend Rothadus, bishop of the city of Soissons.

[Col. 0860B] Let your holiness know that we sent a letter of rebuke on your behalf to Hincmar, venerable archbishop of the holy Church of Reims, because after your appeal to the apostolic see he pronounced a sentence of deposition against you. A certain man who had come to Rome with Count Boso was supposed to carry that letter to you; but the revered Archbishop Hincmar himself wrote back to us that he had by no means seen it.

Moreover, both Hincmar and the other bishops who had assembled for the same synod, where they issued the sentence of deposition concerning you, gave us a fuller account, in the record of their proceedings, of what they had done against you. They put forward numerous accusations against you by way of self-defense and [Col. 0860C] reported them orally to our apostolate through Odo, the venerable bishop. Through him we wrote back both to those archbishops and bishops collectively and specifically to our beloved son, Charles, the glorious king, rebuking, admonishing, and at the same time ordering them to bring you out in person from the monastic cloisters and present you before our presence.

[Col. 0860D] Now the devout deacon Liudo has arrived, carrying with him letters from the aforementioned king and from Hincmar. They acknowledged that, by the king’s order, you had been brought out of monastic custody and entrusted to a certain bishop who was your friend. Through him we again wrote both to Charles, the glorious king, and to the aforesaid Hincmar, your metropolitan archbishop, that since we cannot hear one party without the other, they should send to Rome, for the renewal of the judgment in our presence, both you honorably and some of those who judged you—or their representatives.

Now let your fraternity carefully reflect upon what we are saying to you as though into your very ears: if your conscience reproaches you, or if perhaps you acknowledge the judgment pronounced concerning you by the bishops, do not wish either to weary yourself or to trouble others. But if, relying on our advice, they restore your episcopal dignity to you, as we have written to them, all is well. If, however, disregarding our advice, they delay doing this, and you choose to come to us while persisting in your original course, come without fear and trusting in God’s mercy, knowing for certain that, with God’s help, we will not abandon you until justice is turned into judgment and the Lord deigns to reveal what is now hidden. [Col. 0861A]

You will undoubtedly be granted access to come to us. We have established this both by apostolic authority and by firm decree; and our beloved son Charles, the most Christian king and most devoted to us, together with Hincmar, our brother and fellow bishop, have most firmly and in every way promised in their letters at the present time that they will send you to us.

---

### (Year 863.) XLVIII. TO CHARLES THE BALD, KING

He urges him to provide travel assistance for Rothadus when he comes to Rome.

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Charles, the glorious king.

[Col. 0861B] When we see you bowing beneath the powerful hand of God with such humility and devotion, bending in reverence to his chief apostles, we see fulfilled what holy Job says concerning the Lord: “Under him those who bear up the world are bent” (Job 9). For unless you, placed in royal eminence like the foundations of some immense structure, bore the world in a certain sense through your own sweat, you would never receive in Greek the name βασιλέων—“of kings.” Again, unless you had bowed before the supreme God with so great a humility, you would never so readily submit the neck of your obedience to us, although we are unworthy servants of his.

The same God works this in you; he is also [Col. 0861C] to be praised for it, since he foresaw you and appointed you to govern the kingdom. Under his authority, as we see, happy times smile upon you, and, as we have heard, prosperity follows prosperity. Therefore we glorify his mercy, and because we do not know by what divine judgment these things are accomplished in you, we earnestly exhort your affection: remembering human frailty, do not let prosperity lift you up or favorable circumstances dissolve you. Always return to yourselves and carefully consider that there is nothing in a human being by which one ought to be exalted.

If anything is granted from heaven according to your wishes, do not let your prudence fail to bring the giver before your eyes. Do not suppose that the end consists in those good things granted temporally; and, delighted by swiftly vanishing [Col. 0861D] happiness, do not cease to seek the joys of everlasting blessedness. Let the prosperity of the world be for you an occasion for seeking heavenly rewards, not fuel for tending toward the depths. Hence the distinguished Apostle admonishes us: “Those who use this world, as though they did not use it” (I Cor. 7).

We confidently believe that you can reach eternal glory if we perceive that, although placed in the glory of this life, you truly pursue humility. For it is written: “Humility precedes glory” (Prov. 15); and conversely: “The heart is exalted before destruction” (Prov. 16). But your tranquil mind should willingly know that we have touched upon these matters briefly, with the paternal affection with which we unhesitatingly love your eminence, for your edification; and your kindly spirit should gratefully receive them with the same disposition of mind with which [Col. 0862A] they are sent by us.

As for the venerable Bishop Rothadus, concerning whom it is not permissible for our apostolate to remain silent, we again and again urge you to put aside all bitterness which your Highness retains against him, and, for love of the prince of the apostles, at whose see he cried out when his heart was troubled, grant him your favor. Let your piety toward him show itself entirely conciliatory and gracious in every respect, so that, when he sets out for Rome, he may not lack sufficient assistance from you on the journey. Rather, enriched at least by your benefits bestowed for our sake and supported by your aid, may he be able to reach his intended destination without any difficulty.

Concerning the matters on which you rightly decided to consult our apostolate, [Col. 0862B] we have instructed our brother and fellow bishop Hincmar to guard and determine what seems tolerable to us. Moreover, we do not want your sagacity to be unaware that, although we have always loved you, those presently bearing these letters have inserted a very great measure of love into our heart, for by their repeated reports they have impressed upon our ears such admirable things about you. Therefore we rightly praise almighty God and, accordingly, kindle our heart more and more toward the ardor of affection for you. We wish your glory good health in Christ.

---

### (Year 863.) XLIX. TO HERMINTRUDE, QUEEN

He replies that he cannot leave Rothadus’s case, which she had urged in favor of King Charles, unexamined.

[Mansi, in the same place.]

[Col. 0862C]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hermintrude, the glorious queen.

Dearest daughter, behold, we have now received for the second time a letter from your affection urging us to hear Charles our king, your husband and our beloved son, in the case of Bishop Rothadus. Believe me, this causes us great anxiety and presses us hard on every side, since we cannot persuade you to agree with us concerning him and to desire the same thing; nor, on the other hand, is this a case in which we can set both matters aside without offending God.

But, daughter, to speak to you with charity, judge for yourself whether it is necessary [Col. 0862D] to obey God rather than human beings. For our part, by the power of God, while life remains to us, we will not allow Rothadus’s case to remain unexamined—unless that venerable man is first restored to his former honor and dignity, before his case is brought before our personal presence for judgment.

Who, I ask, throughout the whole world of your kingdom, if injured or about to be injured, would ever cry out to your Highness, whose voice you would disregard, rather than avenge his injuries with strict punishment? How, then, do you seem to urge us not to hear the voice of our brother’s blood? Or how shall we stop our ears to his cries, when [Col. 0863A] we greatly fear that because of this our prayer may become accursed, and that we may cry out, as it is written, yet not be heard?

Certainly, because of the concern we maintain for the whole Church of God and the special care which, above all, we have for all our brothers, even if he had never called out, we ought to seek him with the utmost diligence and assist him with fitting zeal.

As for what you wrote—that if we hear our son, not harm but an increase of privilege will be generated for our Church—we are absolutely convinced that the privileges of the holy Roman Church can suffer no harm; that the planting which our heavenly Father planted cannot be uprooted; and that the foundations laid by the supreme architect cannot be displaced by any fluctuations, however great. [Col. 0863B]

Nevertheless, dearest daughter, great danger awaits both those who through their negligence allow these privileges to be diminished in any way and those who through their presumption strive to violate them.

Concerning whether our son Charles, your husband, should be heard or not heard, we have sent you through the venerable Liudo what we believe to be a sufficient explanation. Whatever we send him by admonishing, exhorting, or even rebuking him, we do not doubt—indeed, with God as our author, we are entirely confident—that it will contribute to his salvation and that of those dear to him, and to the security of his kingdom. May divine majesty preserve your serenity unharmed, dearest daughter.

---

### (Year 863.) L. TO CHARLES THE BALD, KING

On behalf of Rotbert, bishop of Le Mans, against the monks of Saint Calais.

[Mansi, in the same place.]

[Col. 0863C]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Charles, the glorious king.

We make known to your Excellency that Rotbert, bishop of the holy Church of Le Mans, earnestly petitioned us in a letter with exceptional devotion of heart, informing us that the monastery of Saint Calais, situated in the county of Le Mans, in the place anciently called Casa Gaiani, on the river Anisola, had been withdrawn from his jurisdiction and power, and that what had previously been arranged by the decree and will of his predecessors had now been placed under the governance [Col. 0863D] of an abbot without his consent.

For this reason, through these apostolic letters, we admonish and exhort your God-loving magnificence not to neglect, in accordance with the judgment of truth, to preserve justice for the aforesaid Church of Le Mans in this matter and to grant the pious assistance of your devotion. For God’s sake and out of love for our paternal office, willingly permit the aforesaid Bishop Rotbert to continue to possess the monastery, as it lawfully remained with him and his predecessors, and to order its affairs beneficially for the needs of that venerable place. Let no force of your power be brought to bear upon this in any way; rather, let him securely possess what he declares his predecessors always held justly, as is also acknowledged by the [Col. 0864A] privilege he showed us.

If any of the monks of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Calais continue to resist, so that it may not remain under the authority of the Church of Le Mans, and if they persist in this obstinacy, let Bishop Rotbert choose as judges from among the neighboring bishops whom he wishes. Let them be summoned together by our authority, along with the other bishops who appear to be present in the dioceses of the holy Church of Tours, so that such disturbances and dissensions, which have arisen through cunning design, may be cut off by the just judgment of the holy Fathers, and every ambiguity in this dispute may be removed by peaceful truth. In this way, with God’s help, the monastery, founded in ancient times, together with all the property rightfully belonging to it, shall remain intact under the authority of the Church of Le Mans, [Col. 0864B] if that is just.

For this reason we admonish your greatness not to neglect, as stated above, to preserve justice and equity in this and in all other matters, for the sake of future recompense, because of any worldly prosperity.

If, however, in that same judgment the aforesaid bishop of Le Mans, compelled by some necessity, should appeal and declare that he wishes to conduct judgment on this matter in our presence, we wish and command that both the bishop himself, or his legate, and three of the monks of the aforesaid monastery come to us at the appropriate time, without making any excuse, so that such a dispute between the two parties may be cut off by the examination and judgment of the apostolic see, and the just party may reach the right of due equity without delay and with an unquestionable conclusion. [Col. 0864C] If those monks, summoned by our command, should perhaps disdain to come, deign to compel them by the command of your power to hasten here; and send with them one of your faithful men to ascertain both the beginning and the end of that case and dispute.

---

### (Year 863.) LI. TO ROTBERT, BISHOP OF LE MANS

He relates what he has decreed concerning the dispute over the monastery of Saint Calais.

[Mansi, in the same place.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Rotbert, bishop of the city of Le Mans.

[Col. 0864D] Since it is clear that your holiness sent letters filled with devotion to the apostolic see, we give many thanks to almighty God—and to you as well—for, observing the reverence that is due, you sought us as helpers in your interests and humbly preferred the holy Roman Church, mother of all lands, as your advocate. It is clearer than daylight that you did this in order to obtain advice from us.

Concerning the ill-considered intention of those monks of Saint Calais, we have decreed that, if they come and ask that such concessions be made, then, moved by our love for you, we will neither assent to their uncouth petitions nor grant them the judgment of our authority in such matters. If they should perhaps produce some false assertion, as though decrees issued by our institution, we do not wish [Col. 0865A] them to be believed until the matter has become known to our pontificate. For, as we have said, we will give them no assent in such matters, nor grant apostolic permission to those wishing to do anything else—unless there should be a reason so evident [perhaps: “unless a reason should be evident to us,” HARD.] that it compels the matter to be settled in that way.

We have also admonished the glorious king Charles and the bishops of his kingdom through our exhortations not to bring forward, discuss, or permit to be heard any judgment against the privileges of your church, supported as they are by our authority. Rather, with divine clemency assisting, let them judge justly. We have decreed that the monastery be restored to the men of the city of Le Mans and to its bishops as it was, and that it be placed under your pastoral care.

We have expressly established for them that, if judges are chosen [Col. 0865B] from among yourselves by you to determine the case canonically, they must obey your will, so that judges may be appointed and the issue of this matter may be fairly debated. If, however, because of some impediment the matter cannot be settled there, we command that both parties—you or your legate, and three of those monks—come into our personal presence, so that in our presence they may receive a lawful conclusion.

We have also informed our confrere, Archbishop Herard, of these matters by apostolic letters and have communicated what we have established. Therefore we have judged it fitting to rebuke and admonish those same monks, so that they may begin to resist their own arbitrary will, not raise their minds beyond measure, and not presume to seize anything unlawful. Rather, restraining the audacity of such great presumption, let them not delay [Col. 0865C] obeying you and submit their necks to your church.

---

### (Year 863.) LII. TO THE MONKS OF SAINT CALAIS

He orders them not to refuse subjection to the bishop of Le Mans and to appear for the case before the bishops or before the apostolic see.

[At Mansi, in the same place.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the entire congregation of the monastery of Saint Calais.

[Col. 0865D] We have learned through the report of the faithful that, desiring to transgress your proper bounds, you are attempting to withdraw yourselves from the jurisdiction of the city of Le Mans, in whose diocese you reside. And, as we understand by the judgment of our apostolate, you appear to be raising your spirits toward your own destruction and perdition by living according to your own will.

Because we desire the salvation of your souls, we have endeavored by apostolic authority to recall you from such conduct. We expressly command that you not be led by your own pleasure into a course by which your mind may become arrogant. Rather, return according to your usual custom to your principal church, namely, the Church of Le Mans; obey its bishop; strive to fulfill the life to which you are called by name; and prudently undertake the ministry of your order with holiness.

If these hidden matters of your minds have not penetrated you, then take care to state your case before the most holy bishops who shall be summoned by Rotbert, the bishop of Le Mans, so that the matter may be more fully settled according to the course it has taken. [Col. 0866A] For if a canonical judgment is not rendered there between the aforesaid bishop of Le Mans and you, then we unhesitatingly command that three be chosen from among you to come, together with the aforementioned bishop or his legate, into our apostolic presence. Thus, with every excuse set aside, the matter may appear before our examination and receive its conclusion by canonical decision.

We wish you good health in Christ.

---

### (Year 863.) LIII. TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF CHARLES THE BALD

That they should examine the case between the bishop of Le Mans and the monks of Saint Calais.

[At Mansi, in the same place.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the most reverend and holy fellow archbishops and bishops dwelling in the kingdom of Charles, the glorious king.

[Col. 0866B] It is fitting that those adorned with priestly reverence should, according to the judgment of the holy Fathers, weigh everything on the scales of equitable moderation in such a way that they do not cease to fortify the enclosures of the flocks entrusted to them by the Lord, nor postpone providing them with the care that is due. Otherwise, when negligence begins to arise, an entrance may be left open for the instigator, through which he may enter the Lord’s sheepfold in a pestilential manner and begin to tear apart the Lord’s sheep and lacerate them with a savage bite.

We certainly do not wish this to be said of you, brothers. Rather, we admonish you to undertake [Col. 0866C] such diligent care for the advancement of all your subjects as you desire to hear the promise that the Lord mercifully made to those who confess him: “Well done,” he says, “good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25).

For this reason we wish your holiness to know that, from the beginning of its construction, the monastery of Saint Calais, situated in the region of Le Mans, was subject to the jurisdiction of that same city of Le Mans and to its bishop; and, in accordance with canonical institutions, the congregation of that monastery lived under the governance of the person who presided over the care of that diocese.

But now, as has sounded in our ears, its monks, disregarding regular authority, do not follow the zeal of paternal tradition and do not wish to preserve the proper measure. Since they seek to live according to their own pleasure, doing what is not permitted, they declare that they have not been under the jurisdiction of the parish in whose diocese they reside.

Therefore, through letters of apostolic authority, [Col. 0866D] we have decided to admonish all your reverences that, with the balance of rectitude and justice intervening and with the Lord before your eyes, you do not permit this to be done contrary to the institution of the holy Fathers. Rather, after considering the case in every respect, preserve and uphold whatever you find to be more right and more useful. Do not allow the people of Le Mans to suffer prejudice, nor decide and investigate what belongs to them by an inappropriate judgment, so that neither the order of your fraternity is violated nor the bishop of that church is compelled to lose what is his. [Col. 0867A]

Therefore, if judges are chosen from among you by that bishop of Le Mans to examine a question of this kind, and another election has also been agreed upon, then, if the dispute cannot be brought to an end there because of some difficulty that arises, we command that both parties come into our personal presence, so that the issue of the litigation may be debated and declared by a lawful judgment before our pontificate and brought to a conclusion clearer than daylight.

May almighty God always incline your minds and hearts toward good action, so that, by clinging to good works, you may appear exalted to the summit of equity and justice.

---

### (Year 863.) LIV. TO HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

He censures him because, favoring the monks of Saint Calais, he has stirred the mind of King Charles against the bishop of Le Mans.

[At Mansi, in the same place.]

[Col. 0867B]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy brother, Hincmar, archbishop of Reims.

From the report of certain persons we have learned that your fraternity has been greatly angered against Rotbert, bishop of the city of Le Mans, because he wishes to claim the monastery of Saint Calais as belonging to the jurisdiction of the church entrusted to him. So much so that he has stirred up the mind of our beloved son Charles, the glorious king, against him; and it is said that, in the synod which your holiness is now said to be convening, you are attempting to prepare some sort of ambush for him under another pretext, being most eager to harm him—something which we have judged unworthy to believe of so great a man. In short, if Bishop Rotbert is asking for what he ought to ask, let him obtain it; but if he is seeking what he ought not to seek, let him never obtain it. Nevertheless, on that account he must not suffer injury of any kind. Your holiness, dearest brother, must take the greatest care to prevent this, lest—something we do not believe—the same bishop be unjustly harmed in any respect by your reverence, even under the pretext of equity.

But if a charge is brought against him, let an examination of it precede the judgment, so that a decision against him may then follow according to the measure of our authority. For since he appears to regard you as suspect, it is unbecoming, indeed reckless, that he should suffer any danger at the hands of your holiness. Moreover, let your beatitude, acting in our place, endeavor to make the mind of our most devoted son Charles, the pious king, toward the aforesaid bishop peaceful and gentle. Let it be made clear to all that, having laid aside his anger, while—by God’s help—he strives to direct his mind toward continuing to obey us and to govern kindly toward the often-mentioned bishop, he is truly a king; and let his piety become manifestly known to everyone.

We wish your fraternity well in Christ.

## (Year 863.) LV. TO VITALIS, PATRIARCH OF GRADO

He invites him to attend a synod to be held at Rome.

NICOLAUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy fellow-bishop VITALIS, patriarch.

We have judged it necessary to make known to your religious conscience that, for various needs of the holy Church of God, we have arranged to celebrate our synod or council together with our other most holy fellow-bishops on the third day before the Kalends of November at the Roman see. Therefore, by apostolic authority and pastoral exhortation, we admonish your fraternity that your holiness should make every effort to be present at the appointed synod, so that, with your diligence together with that of the other holy bishops, and with God’s clemency assisting us, we may be able canonically and lawfully to resolve according to God—indeed, according to his will—matters that greatly concern the holy Church of God and are held to be sufficiently useful and necessary.

If, however, as we very much do not wish, your presence cannot in any way be given in person, let your holiness by all means determine that among your suffragan bishops there be sent capable men, together with a presbyter and a deacon, who, furnished with your authority, may vigilantly fulfill the duty of your fraternity. With them, by God’s providence, we may most beneficially and canonically instruct or decide matters belonging to our ministry and yours.

We wish your fraternity well in Christ.

## (Year 863.) LVI. TO THE BISHOPS OF GERMANY

Against Thietgaud of Trier and Gunthar of Cologne in the matter of King Lothair’s divorce.

[In Hontheim, *History of Trier*, vol. I, p. 200.]

NICOLAUS, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brothers, the archbishops established in the kingdom of Louis, king of Germany.

The crime committed by King Lothair—if indeed he can truthfully be called a king who has restrained none of the appetites of his body by any wholesome discipline, but rather yields to their unlawful impulses through slippery weakness—namely, with Theutberga and Waldrada, is manifest to all. [Note: Some material is missing here.] Almost the whole world, moreover, flowing from every direction to the threshold or see of the Apostle, reported to us that he had long had Bishops Theutgaud and Gunthar as protectors and supporters in such an act; those who were absent also wrote this to the apostolate. We were all the more unwilling to believe it because we could not at all expect to hear such a thing about bishops, until they themselves came to Rome at the time of the council and were found before us and the holy synod to be such as many had often described them. Thus they were caught by the writing which they had confirmed with their own hands and which they wished us to strengthen with our signature: while they sought to set a trap for the innocent, they themselves were ensnared by their own plots.

And so, by God’s agency, what is written in Proverbs was fulfilled: “In vain is the net spread before the eyes of the winged.” For they themselves were bound and fell; but we, who were said falsely to have fallen into this disgrace, rose up and stood upright, with the Lord’s favor, together with the defenders of justice.

Therefore, by the decision of the holy synod with us, they were deposed in their presence, excommunicated from priestly office, and unquestionably deprived of the administration of their bishoprics. Hence our fatherly authority, observing the rule of the canons and keeping the sanctions of the decrees, takes care that no one presume to receive into the catalogue of priests those whom we have rejected. The sentence of deposition which we pronounced against the aforesaid Theutgaud and Gunthar, together with the other chapters which we promulgated with the holy council’s approval, is appended below.

[Note: See the Acts of the Council of Metz, in Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XV, col. 651.]

## (Year 863.) LVII. TO KING LOTHair

Fragment.

[In Jaffé, *Regesta Pontificum Romanorum*.]

[Col. 0869B]

You consented to yield to the impulses of your body, and, loosening the reins of pleasure, cast yourself at will [variant: “forbiddenly”] into the pit of misery and the mire of filth; and you, who had been placed in charge of governing peoples, became a ruin to many.

The lawful downfall of Thieguald of Trier and Gunthar of Cologne, formerly bishops, proves this: because they did not properly instruct you, they have been deposed by the authority of our apostolate and regularly separated from every administration of a bishopric.

Are you not to be struck with strict vengeance, since you are recognized as having imitated the adultery of Lamech and his crime in taking two wives?

## (In the same year.) LVIII. ALSO TO THE SAME LOTHair

Fragment.

By apostolic authority, and not through royal favor, a bishop is to be chosen.

[In Gratian, *Decretum* I, Distinction 63, chapter 4.]

Furthermore, know that it has been reported to us that whoever is to be advanced to the episcopate in your kingdom is permitted by you to be elected only if he is favorable to you. Therefore, by apostolic authority, under the solemn appeal of divine judgment, we charge you that you permit no one to be elected in the city of Trier or in the colony of Agrippina until a report concerning this matter has been made to our apostolate.

## (Year 864.) LIX. TO ADо, ARCHBISHOP OF VIENNE

He responds to various questions of his: concerning King Lothair’s divorce and the cleric Alvicus.

[In Mansi, same work.]

[Col. 0869D]

NICOLAUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy fellow-bishop ADO, archbishop of the holy Church of Vienne.

[Col. 0870A] We have received the letters of your consultation brought to the apostolic see. They contained questions on various matters and asked that your fraternity receive from us a written response concerning them, and they earnestly desired that apostolic authority should decide whether certain practices ought prudently to be maintained in the Church of God. [Note: Perhaps read “that apostolic …”; Hardouin.]

We certainly praise your concern in such matters, and, rejoicing over you, we raise your holiness to great rewards, because we wish to make you increasingly diligent in ecclesiastical disciplines, so that we may be made most joyful by true and certain reports of the very things in which we now rejoice.

But since the bearers of your letters, as was necessary, were unable to remain behind their companions without being exposed to the ambushes of wicked men in unknown places, we could not therefore reply to you so suddenly. This was especially so because, as canonical custom requires, this holy Roman Church bears concern for the others, and at the same time, because of the days of the Paschal feast, a greater ecclesiastical burden of administration than usual fell upon us.

Nevertheless, let your fraternity arrange to send another message at a suitable time, so that what it now requests may then receive a more tolerable response concerning the matters sought.

Furthermore, since you are cultivators of the Lord’s field and hold the place of shepherds, we admonish you, with pastoral foresight, to entreat the glorious King Lothair, concerning the dismissal of the former woman and the taking of another, with sacred admonitions and divine rebukes [Note: The passage is corrupt], so that what he commands in word may be truly approved by his conduct as an example to his subjects. Let there not persist in him the incontinence of youthful pleasure, on account of which he may forever lose the kingdom of flowering glory.

Let him cease—yes, let him cease—to tread the path of iniquity, and, walking along the way of justice, let him reach the Lord’s camp safely and without the violence of storms, through your intercessions. We pass over these matters briefly because we trust you to declare what is appropriate for his salvation.

(Distinction 32, concerning that cleric.) Meanwhile, concerning that cleric named Alvicus, whom you say lived chastely through the ecclesiastical orders up to the diaconate, we are surprised that he married by our authority, since we have never granted anyone permission to marry except those whom ecclesiastical regulation permits to have a wife. For we neither recognize the copy of the letter which you sent nor remember that its style was directed by us.

Therefore, let your fraternity seek through careful investigation to discover who was the author of that letter, so that, when apostolic authority is sent, it may not be obscured. And if you have sent your legates, we wish you to send the letter itself to us through them, so that, after examining it, we may make you fully certain concerning this matter.

We wish your holiness well in Christ. Given on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## (Year 864.) LX. TO HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

He is indignant that Rothad was prevented from traveling to Rome. He orders that Rothad be sent as soon as possible and forbids another bishop to be ordained in his place in the meantime. Finally, he warns Hincmar and his suffragans to avoid communion with Gunthar.

[In Mansi, same work.]

[Col. 0869D]

NICOLAUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HINCMAR, archbishop of Rheims.

We are sending to your fraternity a letter addressed to our beloved son Charles, the glorious king, which is titled in his name and is to be sent by you. Therefore, by a writing of our apostolate, we exhort you to ensure that it is sent more urgently to the aforesaid king, and to have it presented without delay for love of us.

Moreover, we are astonished and cannot bear with equanimity why, having so often despised our apostolic admonitions concerning our fellow-bishop Rothad, you do not refuse to disregard them. We have sent them to your charity not merely three but four times, so that he might be recovered; and finally we determined that, in order that he might be restored to his former honor, he should either be presented to our apostolate on the Kalends of May of this twelfth indiction with your legates, or be restored.

Not only did you refuse to do this, but when he himself wished to come and had already begun the journey, he was not permitted to proceed; rather, he was compelled to turn back. This makes it clear that your fraternity might be ready to bring about his downfall, since the apostolic command is not observed in those regions—to the injury of the blessed Apostle Peter—and is despised and violated by you.

If you had goodwill toward our apostolic charity, you would at least have informed us why Rothad was prevented from coming. Recognize and consider, then, that you are not at all proved to be acting well, since it is established that, with the Lord’s assent, we will by no means leave the case of the aforesaid Rothad unexamined to the end. Rather, because he appealed to the apostolic see, we intend to bring it, as far as we can, to the equity of a true examination.

But you, dearest brother, lay aside all disobedience and, both through yourself and through our son Charles, the glorious king, make every effort to send the same bishop—with your messengers, as quickly as possible—to the apostolic see of the blessed Peter, to which you are proved to belong as members. We have ordered him to come to us for a hearing, and we order it again, if you desire to place your charity firmly in integrity upon that strongest rock where Christ founded his house.

Moreover, do not consecrate another bishop who has received the see after Rothad’s deposition until, after a preliminary examination before us, we have investigated his case with a true intention, as clearly as daylight. For, as we have often said, repeated, and maintain, we will not dismiss him without an examination.

We must also necessarily inform you of what your fraternity ought to guard against: namely, Gunthar, one of the condemned, who, contrary to the statutes of the holy Fathers and to the decree of our apostolate and the holy synod, is said to presume—following his former custom—to lay hands upon the sacred ministry from which he had been prohibited, and irreverently seeks to defend what was canonically done against him.

But since we have determined this together with the holy synod, if the report is true, we do not communicate with him in any way. Rather, we judge him entirely excluded from all communion of the faithful, together with his followers, associates, and supporters.

Nevertheless, lest you or your suffragan bishops be defiled merely by his filth, as we have already commanded you, we exhort, admonish, and order you with the greatest urgency. We also command that everyone be informed publicly, by word of mouth, what this same Gunthar is like and how greatly he has transgressed the rules of the holy Fathers, and that provision be made to proclaim openly that his presumption must be avoided under canonical censure.

May almighty God preserve the fraternity of your holiness unharmed for the exaltation of his holy Church.

## LXI. CHAPTERS OF THE RESPONSES OF POPE NICOLAUS

To the embassy of Bishop Salomon, sent in the year 864 by King Louis the German.

[In Mansi, same work.]

I truthfully confess that our apostolate was angered against him, not because he consented to an unlawful union, but because, just as he did not consent, so he did not prohibit it. It is not sufficient for salvation merely not to do evil if we do not do good. It would not have been enough for holy Job to be innocent through simplicity unless he were also upright through equity.

The two sons of Judah—one wicked, and the other spilling his seed upon the ground—signify two kinds of people: one harming through wickedness, and the other unwilling through benevolence to provide what is good. But the Lord in anger killed both.

Again, he who wishes us to be simple as doves admonished us to be prudent as serpents. The Holy Spirit, too, was shown in the dove and in fire, because he makes all whom he fills both simple and burning: simple in purity, burning in zeal. See, therefore, how simplicity cannot please God without zeal.

He ought accordingly to have shown himself, through zeal for uprightness, against injustice in such a way that it would be clear to all that a just king and upright ruler did not approve so monstrous a crime, especially when it concerned his own blood and his own flesh.

But when those simple men saw him so lukewarm and observed that outwardly he was moved by no zeal for the truth, they supposed that, unless the matter pleased him, he could not possibly have maintained such silence. Thus deceived, they followed wickedness as wickedness.

Eleazar, whose story is read in the books of the Maccabees, guarded against this. When he was compelled to perform what had been forbidden by command, he did not even wish to be thought to have yielded to such persuasions. Although, out of respect for him, his executioners wished to please him, and although he could both escape death and avoid sinning against the Lord’s ordinances, he preferred to choose death rather than cherish life for the weakening of the feeble.

For what good would it do not to deny God secretly, yet not to glorify him openly? Since Christ is the truth, whoever does not openly contend for the truth undoubtedly denies Christ before human beings.

### I

If his will neither was, is, nor will be in that unjust union, we give thanks to God, because we love him greatly. For that reason we would grieve exceedingly if, God forbid, the matter were otherwise.

But because, thanks be to God, he is a king and stands in lofty power, let it be openly known to all that he does not will such a union, so that, when people see his good works, they may glorify our Father who is in heaven. For, as the Truth says, “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house” (Matthew 5).

Therefore, let him abandon concealment and seize the free boldness which he ought not to have feared to take up for God’s name—not only since he is a king, but even if he were utterly poor.

Since, however, when they held their synodal assembly, neither he nor the bishops of his kingdom were present, this is not greatly to be praised, because, had they been present, perhaps they would have objected, perhaps they would have risen in opposition and set up a wall for the house of the Lord. Yet we judge it better that they were not there than that, had they been present, they should have consented even by silence.

But since, at our request and for love of his brother, he maintained familiarity with him, established his kingdom, and still wishes to establish it, he does well if he obeys our command. But, alas, what does an earthly kingdom profit him who loses the heavenly one? Or what fellowship of familiarity can be maintained with one who is separated from God, hates his own flesh, takes Christ’s members away, and makes them members of a prostitute?

### II

If that Lothair has departed from the way of truth and has not obeyed the rule of justice, and if Lord King Louis seeks our apostolate—as we believe, because he asks from a sincere heart, and as we trust, because, after seeking our counsel, he will not treat it lightly but will obediently carry it out—we meanwhile intend to admonish the same Lothair, and let this uncle likewise do so.

But if, after being summoned so many times, he delays obeying us, we do not wish any Christian to have any familiarity with him. Rather, from then on, let him and his associates be to everyone as a heathen and a publican.

You, most holy bishop, know well that many people, when compelled, return to the way of salvation. Therefore, if, just as he could find no refuge for his iniquity among us, he had found no place of escape among his uncles and brothers, he would already have returned, even under compulsion. But because he has found rest and protection among them, he scorns to return.

Since, moreover, together with the holy synod and according to the canons, we deposed Theutgaud and Gunthar on the condition that, if they dared to lay hands upon anything belonging to the sacred ministry according to their former custom, they would in no way be permitted either to have hope of restoration in another synod or to find a place for satisfaction, and that all who communicated with them would likewise be excluded from the Church—especially if, after learning that a sentence had been pronounced against the aforesaid men, they should attempt to communicate with them—and since we now hear that Gunthar has usurped the ministry forbidden to him, we therefore give this counsel and, by the authority of God, of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, the chief apostles, and of all the holy Fathers together, enjoin upon Lord King Louis that he withdraw himself and all his people, especially his bishops, from communion with that Gunthar and also with Theutgaud; and that he keep himself and as many of his people as he can from the familiarity of those who communicate with or in any way favor them.

This applies, however, only if it is true that they are carrying out the episcopal office forbidden to them, or if they have attempted to gather assemblies against the decision pronounced against them by us.

Likewise, let him entirely suspend himself from communion with Lothair, provided that Lothair, disregarding our admonitions, has chosen to remain in the union with Waldrada, or has presumed to communicate with or favor any of the aforesaid condemned men who resist our decrees.

Otherwise, he will certainly be unable to have communion with God, with the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, or with the holy catholic and apostolic Church.

### III

We highly praise the devotion of the Emperor Louis, of blessed memory, and we are prepared to follow the footsteps of our predecessor Gregory, of holy memory.

### IV

Concerning the bishop of Bremen: although Gunthar could not have granted this permission and ought not to have been asked for anything of the kind, nevertheless, for love of Lord King Louis, since his request is pious, let the bishop, by our authority, possess at the aforesaid place of Bremen the power and honor of an archbishopric over the Danes and the Swedes, and in like manner let his successors perpetually hold and possess them throughout future times.

### V

Concerning the bishop of the city of Radasben: if he is so weakened, as you say, that he cannot exercise any care for the sheep entrusted to him, let him declare in writing, with his own signature, to his metropolitan that, because of his serious illness, he is unable to confer any benefit upon the people entrusted to him.

Let him likewise promise that he will never again reclaim the episcopal office, provided that this is wholly his will and that all hope of his recovery has in every way been abandoned.

After these things have been done, let not someone whom he himself chooses be consecrated as his successor, lest he appear to have chosen his own successor contrary to the canons. Rather, let the person whom the clergy and people choose, with the consent of the metropolitan, be consecrated in every way as bishop in his place. From that same Church, sufficient support for the surviving bishop throughout his life is to be assigned through his successor, the bishop.

### VI

Concerning Hartuvig, bishop of the city of Pazzou, whom you assert was struck by paralysis four years ago, so that he is unable to speak and the Church entrusted to him is scattered and reduced to nothing, while it remains deprived of all pastoral care and enclosed by no episcopal oversight: if this is so, the same bishop ought at least to declare in writing that he is unable to perform that office.

But if he cannot do this, how can we take his own Church away from a living bishop, when no one can comprehend the riches of God’s mercy, and when circumstances which we consider unlikely may arise through God’s administration?

Let the care of the ecclesiastical property be entrusted to a chosen steward from his own clergy, in accordance with the sacred canons; and let the matters belonging to the bishop be administered meanwhile by the bishop whom the metropolitan prelate chooses for this work.

We have spoken differently about this man than about the former, because we can learn the former’s will from his speech, whereas we cannot know this man’s will.

### VII

Concerning the young bishop [variant: “the young man”], we do what he piously wished to request from us.

### VIII

Likewise, concerning Liudbert, the archbishop, we do what he requested.

### IX

The angelic hymn—that is, “Glory to God in the highest”—is not to be said by presbyters except at the Paschal feast. This is demonstrated by the *Book of Sacraments*, and is clearly shown by the custom observed from ancient times in the Roman Church. Blessed Innocent lucidly explains at the beginning of his decrees that everyone in the ecclesiastical orders ought to follow this custom.

### X

Concerning the king of the Danes, who vowed a vow to God and to Saint Peter, we give thanks to that same God, praying at the same time that, just as what is reported to us concerning Cornelius the centurion, so also in the case of this man he may mercifully allow us soon to hear good news.

Although the prayers and alms of Cornelius did not benefit him before baptism for the cleansing of his impiety, they did benefit him in coming to know the truest piety.

### XI

Since you announce that the faithful king has arranged to come to Tulln and thereafter to confirm peace with the king of the Bulgars and to make Rastiz obedient to him, whether willingly or unwillingly, we pray almighty God that the angel who was with the patriarch Jacob may also be with him and all his people, that he may direct his journey well, and that he may return to his own land in peace and joy.

### XII

Since you also say that the most Christian king hopes that the king of the Bulgars himself wishes to convert to the faith and that many of them have already become Christians, we give thanks to God, praying that he may make the increase of fruits abound in his granary.

As for fasting and prayers on their behalf, as you exhort us through your message, we shall perform them with God’s favor.

### XIII
