Furthermore, you acknowledge that the most devoted prince begs us not to believe anyone who reports anything unfavorable about him to us through a messenger or letter before he himself can come in person or send suitable legates to us.

To him we reply that we retain the pledge of his promised love and devotion. Remembering this, if we should happen to hear anything harsh about him, we shall strive to avoid it as though it were the croaking of frogs. Let him, however, always act in such a way that we may rejoice in triumph and offer due thanks to God for it.

### XIV

Moreover, you have assured us that Lord King Louis wishes henceforth to become obedient to us in all things, for our mutual exaltation and that of the holy Church of God, as a son to his father and a junior to his teacher, if he may have firm hope in us, as he did after God established us in this holy see.

We tell him to place such hope in us, after God, that there may be no one to whom he could believe that we do not wish every joy and every happiness to come to him and his people. We wish—and constantly implore almighty God—that he may not only reign prosperously in the present age and flourish through many cycles of time, but also live blessedly with Christ without end in the future, contemplating God as he is.

## LXII. LETTER OF NICOLAUS TO ANSGAR, ARCHBISHOP OF HAMBURG, OR BULLA FOR THE UNION OF THE BISHOPRICS OF HAMBURG AND BREMEN, GIVEN IN THE YEAR 864

NICOLAUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whoever does not doubt that the Lord and our Redeemer Jesus Christ descended from the bosom of the Father to earth in order to demonstrate true and certain faith to human hearts certainly does not fail to understand that all who, through his grace, have become participants in that same faith—and especially we, who hold the foremost place through the first minister of such great power—ought to devote themselves to winning human beings, sowing the seeds of the word among all nations, and ministering to those who bring comfort. [Col. 0876C]

Now, because the most exalted King Louis, through Solomon, the venerable bishop of Constance, took care to inform our apostolate that his father, the piously remembered Louis, [Note: Bollandists’ edition lacks “pious.”] the pious emperor, [Note: The Bollandists read “his father” instead of “his progenitor.”] had taken a certain monk named Ansgar from the monastery of Corbie and placed him beside the River Elbe, on the borders of the Danes and Saxons, [Note: The Bollandists read “and Slavs.”] in a fortress called Hamburg, between the two bishoprics, namely Bremen and Verden. From these places he took churches and tithes and granted them at the aforesaid place, with the approval of our predecessor, Pope Gregory of blessed memory, who provided the solemn privileges of the apostolic see, for the support and advancement of the aforesaid bishop and his clergy.

By his authority also an archiepiscopal see was established among the aforesaid people of Nordalbingia, in the aforementioned fortress of Hamburg; and after receiving the pallium from the apostolic see at that same see, Ansgar was ordained its first archbishop. To him the aforesaid supreme pontiff entrusted the care of sowing the word of God and winning souls for God. [Note: The Bollandists do not read “supreme.”] [Note: Here the Bollandists’ text ends. What follows begins an excerpt given by Rembert in the *Life of Saint Ansgar*.]

A document concerning this delegation and authority, and concerning the reception of the pallium, was sent to us by our aforesaid son, King Louis, through the aforementioned most holy bishop Solomon; it had been formally issued according to the custom of the holy Roman Church. [Col. 0877A] From the wording of this document we have learned that these things were done just as the piety of the aforementioned king had informed us through the faithful man, Bishop Solomon.

Therefore, following the footsteps of so great a pontiff and our predecessor Gregory, and recognizing there the entire providence established in a manner worthy of God, we have resolved to strengthen the wish of the great princes—namely Louis, the Augustus of blessed memory, and his namesake, his most excellent son the king—both by the command of this apostolic authority and by the granting of the pallium, according to the custom of our predecessors. Thus, established upon so great an authority, the aforementioned Ansgar, the first archbishop of Nordalbingia, and his successors after him, devoting themselves to winning peoples, may be stronger against the assaults of the devil. [Col. 0877B]

To our aforesaid son Ansgar we grant public authority to preach the Gospel in all the surrounding peoples of the Swedes, Danes, and Slavs, and in all the other places situated in those regions wherever divine mercy may open a door for them.

We further decree that the very see of Nordalbingia, called Hamburg, consecrated in honor of the holy Savior and of his holy, undefiled Mother, the ever-virgin Mary, shall henceforth be archiepiscopal. And, so that after the death of the aforesaid Archbishop Ansgar a person suitable for so great an office may frequently be chosen, we establish under the invocation of divine judgment that there shall always be a succession of worthy successors.

But because King Charles, the brother of the aforesaid King Louis, after the death of his father, the Emperor Louis of pious memory, removed from the aforementioned place called Hamburg the monastery called Torhout, situated in western Francia, which his father had given there for the provision and sustenance of the bishops and their clergy, the ministers of the altar began, as is reported, to withdraw. For when the necessary resources failed, they withdrew from those peoples, and the same mission to those peoples was brought to an end by this action. The metropolitan church of Hamburg itself was also left almost deserted. [Col. 0877C]

While these things were taking place, the diocesan bishop of Bremen died; that see is said to be contiguous with this one. When the aforementioned king saw both that this diocese was vacant and that the new foundation was failing, and moreover that both Churches had been greatly weakened by the savagery of the barbarians through the hidden judgment of God, he began to seek how the aforementioned Church of Bremen might be united to and placed under the aforesaid new archiepiscopal see, with our decree strengthening this wish.

Accordingly, through the aforementioned venerable envoy, Solomon, Bishop of Constance, this matter was reported to us for confirmation, and it was requested that it be strengthened by our authority. We therefore weighed it with careful examination and observed that, because of the pressing need and the gains of souls evident among the peoples, everything proved beneficial to the Church and not contrary to the divine commandments ought to be permitted and carried out. We have no doubt that this is especially so in the planting of so new a Christianity, in which various circumstances commonly arise. [Col. 0878A]

Therefore, by the authority of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we decree by this document, in accordance with the wish of the most reverent King Louis, that the two aforementioned dioceses, namely Hamburg and Bremen, shall henceforth not be two but one, and shall be called and placed under the see which, by the decree of our predecessor, has been elevated to archiepiscopal dignity. The portion taken from the possessions of the Church of Bremen is to be restored to the bishopric of Verden.

No archbishop of Cologne, however, shall henceforth claim any authority for himself in that same diocese. Rather, we urge both him and all worshipers of true religion to provide assistance and support to those carrying out this sacred mission, so that they may deserve to receive the full reward of this benefit from him who said: “Go, teach all nations”; and, “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matthew 10 and 28). [Col. 0878B]

Accordingly, we also confirm by our authority everything assigned by our beloved son Louis to this service worthy of God, together with his pious wishes. And because past events make us cautious for the future, we strike with the sword of anathema anyone who opposes or contradicts this, or in any way plots against these efforts of ours; and we condemn such a person, as guilty of perpetual vengeance, to the lot of the devil. Thus, by zealously defending the apostolic summit and the cause of God with pious devotion, according to the custom of our predecessors, we may be more securely protected from adversaries on every side. [Col. 0878C] [Note: Here Rembert’s text ends.]

And because divine mercy has appointed you, dearest son Ansgar, to be the first archbishop in a new see, and because we grant you the pallium for celebrating the solemnities of the Mass—and grant that you may use it throughout your lifetime and that your Church may enjoy its privileges in perpetuity—the honor of this garment must be preserved by you through the vigor of your conduct.

If shepherds of sheep watch over their flock with ever-vigilant eyes, in sun and frost, lest any of them perish by wandering or be torn apart by the bites of wild beasts, with how much exertion and care ought we to remain watchful, who are called shepherds of souls? We admonish you not to entangle the office you have undertaken in earthly affairs to any degree. Let your life be a road for your sons. If there is any strength in them, let them direct it in that life; let them see in it what they should imitate. Let them always advance by contemplating it, so that what they live may appear, after God, to be your good work. [Col. 0878D]

Therefore, let neither prosperity, which temporally flatters, raise your heart, nor adversity cast it down. Let the wicked know you to be stern; let the well-disposed find you compassionate. Let another’s wickedness not stain an innocent person in your judgment, and let favor not excuse the guilty. Let your defense assist widows and orphans who are unjustly oppressed.

Behold, dearest brother: among many other things, these are the duties of the priesthood; these are the duties of the pallium. If you carefully observe them, you will possess inwardly what you have shown yourself to have received outwardly. Nevertheless, understand that all the things set out above have been granted to your blessedness by the apostolic see, provided that you deviate in nothing from the faith and decrees of the holy Catholic Roman Church. But if you presume to depart from the faith and institutions of the apostolic see, you will lose the benefits conferred upon you by us. [Col. 0879A]

Moreover, we permit you to use the pallium only according to the custom of the apostolic see: namely, that your successors, personally or through their legates, shall profess in writing and by oath that they will maintain the faith with us; receive the six holy synods; and reverently observe and carry out, throughout all the days of their lives, the decrees of all the prelates of the Roman see and the letters delivered to them.

Written by the hand of Zachariah, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the twelfth indiction, during the reign of the Emperor Louis, in his fifth year. [Note: In Lunig, *Spicilegium*, p. 73, where this bull is likewise found, “in his fifteenth year” is correctly read.]

## LXIII. To Horic, King of Denmark

*(In the year 864.)*

[From the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. I, p. 407.]

[Col. 0879B]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Horic, king of the Danes.

[Note: This is the younger Horic, who received the kingdom as a child in 854 and is believed to have reigned beyond the year 888, when Saint Rembert died. Adam, chapter 28, and Albert, under the year 858, write that Saint Ansgar pacified him, that he accepted Christianity, and that he ordered all his subjects by edict to become Christians. [Col. 0880D] Indeed, it is reported in an old writing of the Church of Bremen, published together with a history of the archbishops of Bremen after Adam, that the king of Denmark—that is, of the Danes—was baptized by Saint Rembert. We are surprised that this is mentioned nowhere in the *Lives of Saints Ansgar or Rembert*. From this letter it is clear that he favored the Christians; and from the *Acts of Saint Ansgar* it is clear that he permitted his subjects, if they wished, to embrace the faith of Christ.]

We have given many thanks to almighty God at the arrival of our brother and fellow bishop Solomon, who, sent by our son, the glorious King Louis, both presented your gifts and greatly gladdened us concerning your faith—which, even before the grace of baptism, you are recognized to have already possessed through God’s prevenient mercy.

Therefore, lifting our eyes to him who alone is true, unique, and almighty, we continually and humbly implore his mercy for your salvation. He who said that light should shine out of darkness, and who, by the illumination of his holy Spirit, dispelled the darkness of ignorance or unbelief from the hearts of those who were to believe in his name through his prevenient grace, has now, in his accustomed goodness, seen fit to display in you the work of his mercy. May he also open your eyes to know the truth, drive the darkness of ignorance from your breast, remove the hardness and veil of your heart, show you the light of true faith and religion, draw you to knowledge of himself, and lead you to the saving font, to the everlasting kingdom, and to eternal life. There is joy without sorrow, satiety without weariness, continual salvation, unfailing life, peace without end, supreme security, and everlasting glory. [Col. 0879D]

There God will be seen as he is; all the righteous will reign with him; and their kingdom is neither confined by boundaries, shaken by wars, enclosed by an end, nor terminated by completion. Recognizing this, we who hold the faith of Christ and are called Christians believe in him who promised us such life and kingdom, and we serve and worship him far more for that life than for this one, which is wholly miserable and wholly full of dangers: here there is continual sorrow, satiety accompanied by pain, brief health, mortal life, quarrels, insecure security, and glory that soon fades. Here it is written: “The life of man upon earth is warfare, and his days are like the days of a hired laborer” (Job 7:1). Here, I say, the kingdom is brief, shaken by constant wars, and after a short while taken from the hand of its possessor—if not by human strength, then nevertheless by the condition of death.

Therefore, cease to worship idols, and stop serving demons. For, as the Psalmist says, “All the gods of the nations are demons; but the Lord made the heavens.” [Note: The manuscript or edition adds “not made” after “who made”; the sense is that the Creator, not the creature, is to be worshiped.] Accordingly, the one who made, and was not made, the Creator and not the creature, must be worshiped.

For behold, your idols, made by hand, are deaf, mute, and blind. Consider, I beg you, what salvation they can confer upon you when, being without sense, they are wholly unable to provide any help even for themselves. [Col. 0880B]

Worship God, therefore; adore him; render singular service to him alone. He is almighty, all-sustaining, indescribable, immeasurable, infinite, simple, unchangeable, uncircumscribed, immortal, wholly good, wholly merciful, and wholly holy. He can help you in this age and make you blessed in the future; after death he will give you life that does not end and grant you a kingdom, if you worship him perfectly and love him—a kingdom that knows no setting and experiences no decline of its condition.

May almighty God, the illuminator of all, illuminate your heart and deign to lead you to knowledge of himself.

## LXIV. To Queen Hermentrud

*(In the year 864.)* Gratitude for the gifts she sent.

[In Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XV.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hermentrud, the glorious queen.

Recognizing your devotion and faith, which we perceive your Highness to possess toward the veneration of the blessed apostles, we have rendered worthy thanks to the Lord Jesus Christ. In the various kinds of gifts you offered, we considered not so much their value as your pious affection, and we preferred your diligence to that of the Queen of Austria. [Col. 0880D]

Indeed, your gifts were received before us with as much greater gratitude than those of the aforementioned queen as she offered gifts to a mortal king, whereas you, dearest daughter, offered to the immortal King and to the princes of his Church—who reign happily with him and bring you comfort through their intercessions—not gifts so much perishable as everlasting and continually flourishing before God.

And truly, if the gift of that woman who put only two small coins into the treasury was so acceptable before God, how pleasing do you think yours will be, since you have contributed so much? Indeed, what is greater, you present yourself with complete devotion and faith to the Lord and to his servants. May almighty God keep you safe, most beloved daughter. [Col. 0881A]

## LXV. To Rodulf, Archbishop of Bourges, and His Fellow Bishops

*(In the year 864.)* He writes again concerning Theutgaud and Guntharius, condemned by the apostolic see, and urges them to abstain completely from their communion.

[In Mansi, same volume.]

[Col. 0881B]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverent and holy brother Rodulf, archbishop of Bourges, and to all our venerable brother bishops of your diocese.

Recently, dearest brothers, we sent you a letter in which we made known to your holiness the condemnation of Theutgaud and Guntharius, formerly archbishops of your region. But we are entirely unaware whether it has reached you. Therefore we have decided to send you what follows, so that you may not be ignorant of what the apostolic judgment is, and how justly our authority has been aroused against the supporters of adulterers. Thus you may share with the apostolic see a zeal for these matters on behalf of the house of the Lord, since even before our sentence you had in no way doubted that these men were worthy of condemnation.

For, like the false prophets of whom it is written that they saw and prophesied falsehoods, they sought to favor an earthly king who was following his own desires; they despised the heavenly King, before whose eyes every device of trickery lies open and every cunning is scattered like a spider’s web. Moreover, to increase the measure of their condemnation, they not only failed to make Ingeltrude, the wife of Boso, return to her husband—she had abandoned her own husband and was living as an adulterous woman with an adulterer in their dioceses—nor did they separate her from every Christian fellowship by binding her with the bonds of anathema, as our predecessor, Pope Benedict of holy memory, and we had repeatedly warned and threatened them to do; [Col. 0881D] but even after she had been anathematized by us, together with her accomplices and supporters, and after the sentence we had pronounced against her had been communicated to them, they agreed to favor her to such an extent that they permitted her to live in their dioceses, enter churches, and share conversation, food, and drink with the faithful. Indeed, as they themselves professed before us and the holy synod, they granted her permission and opportunity to conduct herself in this manner, and, contrary to the Nicene canons, accepted the very woman whom we had rejected.

All these things, clearly, had been forbidden to them, as our command sent concerning this matter to the aforementioned persons indicates. Should so monstrous a crime, then, have gone unpunished, brothers? Should the apostolic see, which has responsibility for all the Churches of God, have left the authors of so great a sacrilege free to the subversion of the faithful? And where would be the command that the first occupant of that see heard three times from the supreme Lawgiver: “Feed my sheep” (John 21), if, with no zeal kindled in us and using no rod, we allowed those sheep to be torn apart by such ravenous wolves? For although we are unworthy sons born in the place of our fathers, we have nevertheless been appointed by God’s grace as rulers in his house over all the earth, acting in his stead.

Now, because growing rumor reports that one of the condemned men, namely Guntharius, is troubling the emperor and the kingdom by his words against the canonical statutes, and deceiving the hearts of certain brothers with false and persuasive speech, while shamelessly wishing to rise up against what has been done against him, we have not communicated with him in any way, since this has been defined by our apostolate and by the holy see. Rather, by God’s authority we have judged him to be wholly excluded from the communion of the faithful, together with his associates and supporters. [Col. 0882B]

Therefore your fraternity must take the greatest care and be especially vigilant, lest—God forbid—by clinging to a perverse man you fall from that rock upon which the true architect wished to establish the foundations of his whole house; and lest, by following the author of wickedness, you lose communion with him from whom both the episcopate and the apostolate took their beginning, and through whom, by God’s grace, you have become not only bishops but also Christians.

Cling, therefore, to the head of religion, that is, to the holy apostolic see. But crush the head of the serpent—namely, the evil suggestion—before it penetrates the heart, at the very outset. For we have begun to catch foxes for you, beloved ones, as one of our fathers urged us to do, the foxes that were destroying the vineyards (Song of Songs 2). See to it that he who appointed you as its guardians does not find you sleeping and, angered by your negligence, strike you for the vineyard that has been devoured.

What validity can your judgments have if ours are in any way weakened, although they may not be retracted? What strength can your councils possess if the apostolic see loses its authority, without whose agreement no councils are read to have been either valid or accepted? Read the sacred canons, turn over the acts of the synods, and see that it has always been customary for the apostolic see to condemn or absolve not only any metropolitans—whose causes must always be reserved to that see—but also patriarchs, according to the circumstances that arise; and that it has always possessed the right and authority to judge all priests. For it is the see to which the power has been granted, by a special prerogative throughout the whole Church of Christ, to establish laws, enact decrees, and promulgate sentences. [Col. 0882D]

Let not your reverence think that, because we are speaking of our own matters, we are saying anything contrary to the truth. These things belong to God rather than to us, having been conferred upon the Roman see through the merits of blessed Peter. We believe that you too are by no means ignorant of what we assert here, and that you possess in abundance, stored in your archives, the matters we write in this present document.

Having said this, we turn the course of our letter toward your fraternity. If we did not love you with such great devotion, we would never urge you with such affection to turn away from evil and pursue equity. Therefore, under the gaze of the divine Majesty, and before his holy angels and blessed apostles, we rightly forbid and adjure you not to pollute the sincerity of your communion with any contamination from the aforementioned men, namely Theutgaud and Guntharius, or from those who favor them; nor to corrupt your innocence through association with them or with those who communicate with them—if indeed, by God’s grace, you wish to be found, as until now, participants in our communion and charity, should they presume to resist or refuse to submit to what we have promulgated against them.

Otherwise, know that by the perpetual sentence of our authority you are to be separated from the communion, grace, and peace of the apostolic see. Indeed, you too will undergo completely—something we do not desire—what they have experienced, as we formerly decreed. [Col. 0883B]

But, so that you may show more clearly that you share our judgment and will, we urge you to take care to send around the Kalends of November two legates from the college of priests of your holiness, acting on behalf of all of you, to the apostolic see. In this way, once the recurring presumption of the transgressors, who have already been condemned and are the authors of every evil, has been cut out at the root, goodness may arise from within the holy Church, and due praise and the everlasting glory of thanksgiving may be rendered to the divine Trinity.

Amen.

[Note: At the end of this letter the following was noted in an old book: “This was read at the synod of Soissons.”]

## LXVI. To Rodulf, Archbishop of Bourges

*(In the year 864.)* He responds to his letters and inquiries.

[In Mansi, same volume.]

[Col. 0883C]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverent brother Rodulf, archbishop of the holy Church of Bourges.

Having received the letters of your blessedness [variant: holiness], filled with the gift of humility and crowned with the flowers of every virtue, we render manifold expressions of gratitude to the author of all good things. We greatly praise your devotion toward the apostolic see, recognized over many past years, and we earnestly exhort your fraternity to persevere in this salutary purpose.

For in this way, with the Lord revealing it, you will be able more clearly to foresee in what direction the foot of holy conduct ought to proceed, and more freely to anticipate and avoid the darts of the wicked, if, following the example of your ancestors, you place your protection upon the rock of the apostolic see and strive to cling more closely to its faith, teaching, and decrees. Upon that rock he consecrated his seat whom the Lord Jesus Christ chose to retain as the first and special summit of his Church and appointed as the supreme gatekeeper of the heavenly court. [Col. 0883D]

Therefore, although we are now more narrowly occupied than usual with ecclesiastical affairs, and consequently cannot respond at length to your inquiries, nevertheless, wishing to satisfy your holy desire concerning the blessed Peter of whom we speak, we do not fail to set out briefly some points as God inspires us.

### I

You state that many ordinations of presbyters and deacons have been performed in your regions by chorepiscopi, whom some bishops depose while others consecrate again. We say that the innocent ought not to be struck down, and that no reordinations or repeated consecrations should be performed.

For chorepiscopi were established according to the pattern of the Seventy; who could doubt that they possessed the offices of bishops? But because the sacred canons forbid everyone to claim everything for himself, and thereby the dignity of bishops might appear to be transferred to their chorepiscopi, making the honor of a bishop less valuable, we decree that nothing further is to be done in this matter contrary to the rules. [Col. 0884B]

### II. [9, question 3, “Conquestus”]

Our brother Sigebod, archbishop of Narbonne, complained to our apostolate that you compel his clerics, against his will, to come to your judgment, and that, without consulting him, you dispose of matters belonging to his Church as though by virtue of your patriarchal right. Antiquity, to which the holy Fathers ordained that reverence be shown, contains no such practice, and the authority of the holy canons entirely forbids it—unless perhaps, in cases that cannot be settled among themselves, they appeal to you as to their patriarch, or, if their bishop has died, they wish you to administer the affairs of their Church by your judgment.

We define that primates and patriarchs possess no privilege over other bishops except what the sacred canons grant and ancient custom conferred upon them from of old. Thus their privileges are to be preserved according to the Nicene rules, except where the apostolic see has decided to honor a Church or its ruler by some special privilege. [Col. 0884C]

### III. [Distinctio 23, “Praeterea”]

You further ask whether, when they are ordained, the hands of presbyters alone, or also those of deacons, ought to be anointed with chrism. In this holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, this is done for neither. Nor, unless memory deceives us, have we read anywhere that it was done by ministers of the New Law.

Therefore we send your holiness the canonical decrees of Pope Innocent of blessed memory. The opening of the letter sent to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio, will fully instruct you concerning what is to be observed by you in consecrations and ordinations. [Col. 0884D]

### IV

Concerning those who perform penance for crimes and return to military service, it is clear that they act contrary to the sacred rules. But because crimes are not equal, and you report that some of these men, because of excessive dullness, are in despair, while others have fled to the pagans for this reason, we entrust the decision to you. You are present there and are able to examine the place and circumstances of that region, the nature of the offense, the penance, and the groans of those who come to confession. [Col. 0885A]

### V [30, question 1, “De his qui”]

Concerning those who hold their stepchildren before bishops for confirmation—that is, those who support upon themselves, while the bishops chrism them, the children of their wife by a former husband—if, as you state, this happens through ignorance, it is indeed a sin, but it is not to be punished to the point of separation from the marriage. Nevertheless, let them mourn and wipe away this offense through worthy penance, saying to the Lord: “Do not remember the sins of my ignorance.”

### VI [33, question 2, “Interfectores”]

Those who kill their own wives—since you do not add “adulterous wives,” or anything of that sort—what else are they to be considered but homicides? Accordingly, they must be brought to penance, and marriage is entirely denied to them, except in the case of adolescents, concerning whom the twenty-fifth decretal rule of blessed Leo—or rather the indulgence contained in it—is to be observed. [Col. 0885B]

### VII

The *Gloria in excelsis Deo* is to be sung by bishops at the solemn celebration of Mass on the Lord’s Supper, according to our custom. But on that same day they may use the apostolic pallium only if the apostolic see has specifically permitted them to do so.

These matters, although we are placed amid so many ecclesiastical affairs, we have scarcely been able to select even in summary for sending to your fraternity. If your incomparable love had not pressed us so strongly concerning the matters mentioned, we would now, hindered by innumerable necessities, have postponed responding to your inquiries for a while.

But we necessarily request one thing from your charity: whenever you happen to send someone to the apostolic see, let your fraternity take care to advise him not to appear excessively hurried on his return. As you yourself know, we are constrained by responsibility for all God’s sheep; and when many come from every direction to the apostolic see seeking different things, we become slow in responding to individuals because we wish to spread our kindness and generosity among many. [Col. 0885C]

Certainly, the matters that we communicate to your blessedness in another apostolic letter must be followed with vigilant care and carried out with particular diligence by you alone. For toward us and toward the see of blessed Peter, there is no other sign of the devotion you profess than obedience and the completion of our decrees and definitions. Although unworthy, we are nevertheless, through the abundance of the grace of Christ himself, his vicars.

Moreover, let your blessedness without delay send the other letter delivered to your holiness to Hincmar and the rest of our fellow archbishops who govern the Church of the Lord in the kingdom of our son, the glorious King Charles. [Col. 0885D]

We wish your holiness good health now and always.

## LXVII. To Franco, Bishop of Tongeren

*(In the year 864.)* Having accepted his profession, he grants him pardon because he had taken part in the synod of Metz, and urges him to strive to care for King Lothair through his admonitions.

[In Mansi, same volume.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverent and holy Franco, bishop of Tongeren.

Having received, through Richard, your venerable deacon, the letter of your excuse, the profession of your holiness—in which you make clear that you dissent in nothing from the apostolic see, and which we had expected from you less than from anyone else—greatly gladdened us. Yet your confession also caused us to rejoice in the Lord. For by asking for pardon you unquestionably show that you have sinned.

And indeed, how could you have escaped without sin, when you are shown to have consented to the profane proceedings by sitting in a council of vanity and, if not by favoring, at least by remaining silent; if not by writing, certainly by failing to resist? Behold, the Lord says through the prophet: “Raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce their crimes to my people” (Isaiah 58). Therefore, because you did not announce them, you sinned; and because you saw and remained silent, you unquestionably consented.

Nevertheless, now that, through the grace that gives life, we see you emerge alive through confession—though we had thought you inwardly dead through corruption—we rejoice incomparably and give immense thanks to the Author of all good things. We hope that this will no longer be counted against you by divine judgment; whatever your offense may have been, we ask the Lord to forgive it, and, insofar as lies within us, we forgive you from the heart. We know that blessed Leo spared all who had sinned by consenting to error in the Ephesian Robber Council, after removing the sole author of the entire scandal, namely Dioscorus of Alexandria.

What wonder, then, if Guntharius, whom you say is making use of an office forbidden to him, did not fear to treat the apostolic sentence with contempt, when he is shown to have so often disregarded the divine commandments? It is clear, and manifest to all, even if he had furnished no other indications of his wickedness, what kind of man he was before his punishment, since he displayed himself as such after his punishment; and how deservedly he earned his blow, since even afterward he did not refuse to commit what should have caused him to be struck still more severely. [Col. 0886C]

Thus, at the urging of that same man, he now wanders in disobedience to the apostolic institutions, just as he is said recently to have continually opposed the heavenly oracles—namely, at the prompting of the ancient adversary, who, as the first apostle says, “like a roaring lion, prowls around seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8).

But let us return to the matter at hand and, with God’s help, mercifully grant your wishes insofar as we can. Therefore, if you have not received Bishop Theutgaud into the catalog of bishops, as you profess, until we deal with him more humanely; and if you have not only refused to receive Guntharius, who is usurping an office forbidden to him, among the bishops, but have also refused communion to him and his supporters; and if you have opposed him episcopally while he persists in his crime; and if, according to your ability, you have deviated in nothing from the constitutions and judgments issued by the prelate of the apostolic see; and if henceforth you agree with us and strive with us, according to your strength, for the Catholic faith, the correction of the faithful, and the preservation of the privileges of the apostolic see; and if you urge your brothers and neighbors to share our judgment—then may almighty God, through the intercession of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, loose the bonds of all your sins, and in his mercy forgive you whatever, in human weakness, you have done that displeased the eyes of his Majesty, and, filling you with the grace of his blessing, lead you to the blessedness of seeing him. [Col. 0887A]

Furthermore, we admonish you: if you are truly a bishop, truly govern yourself, preserve yourself [Roman edition: save yourself], and seek the glory of King Lothair in yourself. Thus, since your unity clings more closely to us, you should strive to heal his wound by admonishing, soothing, and persuading him; and, in the remaining time, by setting before his eyes the brevity of the present life, the punishments of hell [Roman edition: by explaining the punishments of hell], and the heavenly kingdoms.

You cannot do this unless he receives back his own flesh, which, hating it, he casts away from himself in accordance with the Apostle [Roman edition: unless the Apostle himself casts it away from him], after the member of the prostitute has been cut off, according to our judgment and yours—whether willingly or, at least, unwillingly [Roman edition: rejects it]. [Col. 0887B]

We wish your holiness good health in Christ.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the thirteenth indiction [variant: fourteenth; Harduin; Roman edition: fourteenth].

(Year 864.) LXVIII. TO ADVENTIUS, BISHOP OF METZ. He approves Adventius’s profession and grants him the pardon and peace he desired.

[In Mansi, in the same place.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy Adventius, bishop of Metz.

When we received your letter of apology through Theuderic, your religious presbyter, in which you indicated that you were placed at the end of your life, a great grief immediately took hold of us. But your profession, by which you make clear that you dissent in nothing from the Apostolic See—and which we had expected you to offer us less readily than others—mingled fitting joy with our sorrow. For although we grieve over the outward man when we are deprived of his fraternal companionship, we rejoice incomparably over the inward man, whom we had thought extinguished but now hear has been brought to life again by the grace of God.

Although your apology seems to have a plausible basis and you are shown to be innocent, satisfaction would nevertheless suffice even if you were held by some guilt for past offenses: a satisfaction which, placed—as you yourself acknowledge—at the point of death, you displayed in the letter sent to our apostolate, as we had determined. The thief bears witness to this: hanging upon the cross and already standing at the very moment of death, he confessed and deserved to hear from Jesus, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23). The prophet likewise demonstrates the sudden salvation of one who groans: “When you have turned back and groaned,” he says, “then you will be saved” (Isaiah 30, according to the Septuagint).

Nevertheless, God is powerful enough to act mercifully, so that we who have accepted your apologies and promises of obedience, and have thereby gained confidence in your immortal life, may also receive from this temporal course of life, through the longevity divinely granted to you, the opportunity to enjoy abundantly the fruits of God’s word and thus to glory in the Lord.

What wonder, however, if Guntharius, formerly archbishop, did not fear to treat the apostolic sentence as worthless, when he is convicted of having so often disregarded the divine commandments? It is clear, and manifest to all, that even if no indications of his depravity had preceded, such as he was before his punishment is shown by the sort of man he displayed himself to be after his punishment; and how deservedly he earned his blow is shown by the fact that even afterward he did not refuse to admit what should have caused him to be struck still more.

Therefore, at the urging of that same ancient adversary, he has now become disobedient to apostolic institutions—the adversary at whose prompting he was recently found always to have opposed the heavenly oracles, and who, according to the first apostle, “like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5).

As for what you say, that you are subject to kings and princes because the Apostle says, “Whether to the king as supreme” (1 Peter 3), that is acceptable. Nevertheless, consider whether these kings and princes to whom you say you are subject are truly kings and princes. Consider whether they first rule themselves well, and then their subject people; for “he who is wicked to himself, to whom will he be good?” Consider whether they rule lawfully; otherwise they should be regarded as tyrants rather than held to be kings. We ought to resist such men and rise up against them rather than submit to them. Otherwise, if we are subject rather than superior to such men, we must necessarily favor their vices.

Therefore be subject to the king as supreme—but to virtues, not to vices—yet, as the Apostle says, “for God’s sake,” and not against God.

I judge it superfluous that, as you assert, certain men read in the assembly of bishops the chapters of Saint Pope Leo and of the Council of Antioch. For although the holy man decreed that the metropolitan bishops of each province should possess unimpaired the right of the dignity anciently entrusted to them, he did not remove the privileges of this See, nor diminish the rights divinely granted to it.

For, as he himself writes to Anastasius of Thessalonica, and through him to all (letter 88):

“Among the most blessed apostles, although there was a certain distinction of authority amid the likeness of honor, and although the election of all was equal, nevertheless one was given precedence over the others. From this pattern also arose the distinction among bishops, and provision was made by a great ordering that they should not all claim everything for themselves, but that in each province there should be individual bishops whose judgment would hold first place among their brethren. Again, certain men established in the greater cities should undertake a more extensive care, through whom the care of the universal Church would flow toward the one See of Peter, and nothing anywhere would differ from its head.”

Elsewhere, likewise, he orders that a full report be sent to him concerning matters to be settled and those that have been settled.

Again, if the Council of Antioch acknowledges (chapter 9): “Throughout the various regions, it is fitting to know that the metropolitan bishop exercises care over the whole province,” what prejudice does this cause to the Apostolic See, which exercises care not only over one province but over the whole Church? The same council rather restrains, curbs, and confines metropolitans, since it says that they are to exercise care over no more than their own provinces.

For whoever exercises care over others must necessarily also claim judgment over them, as blessed Pope Innocent writes to Alexander of Antioch (letter 20): “Those for whom the greatest care is expected from you ought especially to merit your judgment.”

Therefore, since the greatest care of the whole Church awaits us, the whole Church must undoubtedly especially merit our judgment.

But let us at last return to the matter at hand and, with God’s assistance, mercifully assent as far as we can to your requests.

Accordingly, if you do not receive Theutguald, formerly a bishop, into the catalogue of bishops, as you profess, until we deal with him more humanely; and if you not only refuse to receive Guntharius, who usurps a ministry forbidden to him, among the bishops, but also refuse communion to him and to his supporters; and if you episcopally oppose the king who persists in crime; and if, according to your strength, you deviate in nothing from the constitutions and judgments issued by the bishop of the Apostolic See; but henceforth think with us concerning the Catholic faith, the correction of the faithful, and the preservation of the privileges of the pontifical Apostolic See; fight with us according to your strength; and exhort your brothers and relatives to share our judgment—may almighty God, through the intercession of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, release the bonds of all your sins, and mercifully forgive you whatever you have done humanly that displeased the eyes of his majesty, and, filling you with the grace of his blessing, lead you to the blessedness of beholding him.

(Year 864.) LXIX. TO ADO, ARCHBISHOP OF VIENNE. On the authority of Pope Innocent I, he teaches that the subordinate Churches ought not to depart from Roman customs.

[In Mansi, in the same place.]

[Col. 0889C]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother Ado, archbishop of the holy Church of Vienne.

We have often received letters from Your Holiness which admonished and earnestly begged us to instruct you how your Church ought to act concerning ecclesiastical matters. Therefore nothing seemed better to us than to teach Your Holiness from the decrees and institutions of our predecessors, who have left us written instructions, most clearly to be observed, concerning the order in which the Church over which, by God’s authority, we are recognized as presiding ought to act, as well as the other Churches founded far and wide from it.

The most blessed Pope Innocent instructed Decentius, bishop of Gubbio, as follows—something we always wish to be remembered by Your Holiness:

“If the Lord’s priests wished to observe intact the ecclesiastical institutions as they were handed down by the blessed apostles, there would be no variation or diversity in those orders and consecrations. But while each person considers not what has been handed down, but what seems right to him, they appear to hold or celebrate different things in different Churches. Thus scandal arises among the peoples, who, not knowing that the ancient traditions have been corrupted by human presumption, think either that the Churches do not agree with one another or that the apostles themselves implanted this contradiction.

“For who does not know, or who fails to observe, that what was handed down to the Roman Church by Peter, the prince of the apostles, and is preserved to this day, ought to be observed by all, so that nothing may be imposed or introduced that either lacks authority or appears to take its example from elsewhere?”

After other matters:

“They ought to follow what the Roman Church observes, from which there is no doubt that they received their beginning, lest, while they pursue foreign preferences, they appear to lose the source of their institutions.”

Again, after other matters:

“If your predecessors held something less or differently, we answer this now not because we believe you ignorant of it, but so that with greater authority you may instruct your own people, or, if any depart from the institutions of the Roman Church, that you may either admonish them or not delay judging them. Thus we may know who are introducing innovations, or who think that the custom of another Church rather than that of the Roman Church ought to be observed.”

Given on the third day before the Ides of December, in the thirteenth indiction.

(Year 864.) LXX. TO GALLIO, ARCHBISHOP OF SIENA. Fragment.—Since the other party is absent, no definitive sentence is to be issued.

[Gratian, Part II, question 3, canon 9, chapter 12.]

In truth, he is not a just mediator who, while one party is litigating and the other is absent, does not fear to decide the disputes arising between both parties.

With these matters thus prefaced, we wish and admonish by apostolic authority that, if the presbyter in question wishes, after his excommunication, to approach the Apostolic See, no one should presume to impede his journey.

(Year 864.) LXXI. SERMON OF POPE NICHOLAS I, which he delivered from the pulpit during Mass in the basilica of Saint Mary at the Crib concerning the case of Rothad, on the day of the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity.

[In Mansi, Councils, volume XV.]

Because of those brothers who have not always been present with us, it is necessary, brothers, for us to disclose to Your Holiness, as far as the Lord grants us ability, the case of our brother and fellow bishop Rothad in due order. Thus, once your fraternity and unanimity have come to know his affair thoroughly with us, you may also grieve with us over the privileges of the Apostolic See, or of the holy Roman Church, which certain men have wickedly diminished and annulled; and, kindled with more fervent zeal, may be solicitous and attentive to recovering them, and may strive to reconsider and reflect upon such a great man, namely Rothad, our fellow priest.

He is the man who, from the ends of the earth, so to speak, first cried out to us while absent, and who, amid raging tongues, did not consign the memory of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to oblivion. From strict monastic custody he cried out to the Lord and to his apostles, described as dilectores vel dilectos (“loving” or “beloved”), like Jonah from the belly of the whale and Daniel from the lions’ den. Then, after being dragged out, although abandoned, stripped, and weakened on every side, at last, with God as his guide, he sought his protection—that is, the See of Peter—upon which he had set the feet of his hope and confidence as though upon a firm rock. When God’s power had destroyed the many difficulties and troubles and the barriers of impediments, he obtained what he had eagerly and anxiously desired, and may now depart with consolation, assistance, and the recovery of all his former status, as an example and encouragement to many. May the privileges of the holy Roman Church and of the Apostolic See, always inviolate, remain and endure, and may no one thereafter dare to violate them.

Finally, brothers, for many previous years the present Rothad had been continually watched by his metropolitan and by certain of his followers, and even by a person of high secular rank, so that he might somehow be caught in their snares; but, protected by God’s grace, he could never be caught at all.

At last, concerning a certain presbyter who had been caught in a shameful crime and had been mutilated in his genitals, his enemies found grounds for attacking him because he had removed that criminal presbyter from office and, after three years—a period the canons do not allow—had wished to restore him, although he had made no formal complaint.

For this reason, when a general council had been summoned—although no one has the right to convene one without the command of the Apostolic See—they summoned this bishop, whom the king’s order, at the suggestion of Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, had caused the bishops to assemble, so that he might give an account before the synod concerning that presbyter.

At first he willingly went. But afterward, when he saw that some of them were held captive by fear of King Charles, who was present, while others had been won over by favor toward Hincmar, his enemy, he reasonably avoided their judgment. He had already found some hostile to him and suspected others because of their previous judgments. He therefore requested the judgment of the Apostolic See and declared that his case ought to be dealt with in the city of Rome, supported by the authority of the canons.

When Hincmar heard this, he granted him permission to come to Rome for a short time, but shortly afterward completely obstructed him. Indeed, after summoning certain bishops again, he ordered Rothad to appear before a synod for examination.

When Rothad heard this, he replied that he had appealed to the Apostolic See and requested its judgment, and that for this reason he could not appear before that judgment, since it was wholly unlawful to appeal from a greater to a lesser authority.

It is therefore utterly absurd that Hincmar pretends Rothad said that, after appealing to the judgment of the Apostolic See, he again requested the judgments of others, changing his position. Even if this had happened, as Your Fraternity knows, it should have been corrected by him, so that he would not appeal from an examination by a greater authority to a judgment of lesser force.

Yet no evidence at all reveals that he ran from our judgment to that of another. It is clear that at the very moment when a sentence was about to be pronounced against him, he appealed to the Apostolic See.

But if he had asked to be judged by that See and had cried out before everyone, it would not have been just for him to turn to their judgments—even if he had not appealed to the Apostolic See at all. Nevertheless, they ought not, as you know well, to set themselves against so many and such great decretal statutes and rashly depose a bishop.

How, moreover, did Rothad choose other judges, when in that document by which they pretend that he appealed from our judgment to theirs, he is judged neither to have rejected our judgment nor to have requested theirs? Especially since, if he had chosen judges besides us, he would have named a definite number of judges to be chosen, and would not merely have requested fraternal assistance, as he requested in that document.

Whether that document was sent by Rothad or not, however, is certainly unknown, since the man who is known to have carried it is proved to have belonged to someone else, not to Rothad.

Even if he had never appealed, he should never have been deposed without our knowledge, because the sacred statutes and venerable decrees have entrusted the cases of bishops—as greater matters—to be decided by our judgment.

(Year 865.) LXXII. LETTER OF NICHOLAS TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF THE ROMAN CHURCH. The absolution and restoration of Bishop Rothad.

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the bishops, presbyters, and deacons of the holy Roman Catholic Church, and to the entire community of the Roman people in Christ.

Let it be known to your charity, my brothers and most beloved sons, that certain bishops of Gaul, kindled by the torches of the devil’s jealousy and envy—for, as it is written, “death entered the world through the envy” (Wisdom 2)—laying snares for this brother of ours, the venerable Rothad, deliberated for approximately eight years how they might deprive him of his own episcopate.

But after laboring for a very long time without being able to bring any danger upon him, at last they used worldly powers and most brutally issued a sentence of deposition against him, although he had appealed to the Apostolic See. In contempt and abhorrence of the privileges of the holy Roman Church, indeed of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, they drove him from his own rank and committed him to imprisonment.

We therefore repeatedly ordered and urged those bishops, through many letters, to bring him, as he cried out for this, and to send him to our judgment, to which he had appealed without interruption before his deposition and afterward, together with their representatives who, if they could, might pursue him with a legitimate accusation.

But behold, beloved ones, as you yourselves know, although Rothad has now been present and staying with us in Rome for six months, and although we have been awaiting his accusers or their representatives, no one who might accuse him appears to be present.

What else, brothers, does this make clear except what the holy Pope Boniface says: just as the innocent seeks to be acquitted, so the guilty evades judgment?

But we, with God’s authority and supported by the assistance of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, following also in the footsteps of our predecessors and striving to recover the privileges of the Apostolic See—which they are proved to have wickedly violated—have now restored the aforementioned man, namely the present Rothad, to his former rank, former offices, and former episcopate. In every respect we have made him again what he is known to have been before the sentence of excommunication and deposition was issued against him, or when he appealed to the Apostolic See and made his canonical appeal.

(Year 865.) LXXIII. TO CHARLES THE BALD, KING. He urges him to support the restored Rothad and orders that the property of his Church which was taken away be returned.

[In Mansi, in the same place.]

[Col. 0893B]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Charles, glorious king.

Although the priests of the Lord who govern the Churches entrusted to them in your kingdom ought never to have deprived the venerable bishop Rothad, who had appealed to the Apostolic See, in contempt of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, through whom the apostolate and episcopate began in Christ and whose episcopate we exercise, though unworthy; nevertheless, because they presumed—or rather attempted—to do this, we bore it with sufficient equanimity for the sake of your request. We repeatedly employed exhortations and commands rather than blows, so that they might correct such great temerity.

But the sole author of this—or rather of this contumacy—is Hincmar, bishop of Reims. He ought not to have deposed the aforementioned Rothad even if Rothad had never appealed to our judgments. But, disregarding us, he deposed him insofar as it lay within his power and treated the multitude of our commands as refuse.

Finally, when the deposition of Rothad himself had been reported to our ears, we immediately sent a letter of our apostolate in which we ordered that the aforementioned Rothad either be restored to his honor and his own Church, or be sent to Rome into our presence with some of the bishops or their representatives who appeared to have condemned him. Otherwise, after the lapse of thirty days, we ordered that those who had deposed him abstain from the solemn celebration of Mass until they had taken care to obey us concerning these matters.

We also then informed Your Excellency of that letter. But what shall I say of brother Hincmar, who, veiled in the manner of Dioscorus, neglected not merely to hear it but even to look at it?

So that no one may be disturbed about why we ordered Bishop Rothad to come to Rome, or to be heard and judged before us, let him know that we acted out of zeal for the canonical tradition of our fathers and the special prerogative of the Apostolic See, and followed them.

To mention only a few matters among many: if a cleric has a complaint against the metropolitan bishop of a province, the Council of Chalcedon orders him to seek the primate of the diocese or the See of the royal city of Constantinople, and to be judged before him. Yet no one doubts that this must be observed much more fully with regard to the city of Rome than with regard to Constantinople.

Rothad himself, according to the Council of Sardica (canon 4), cried out that his case ought to be dealt with in the city of Rome. Blessed Pope Innocent, without prejudice to the Roman Church, also commands in his letter to Victricius that, when cases or disputes arise among clerics, whether of higher or lower rank, no one may abandon those priests who, in the same province, govern the Church of God by divine will and flee to other provinces.

Pope Julius, writing to the Easterners (letter 1), likewise ordered both parties—namely Athanasius and his adversaries—to hasten their presence, so that the accused might be heard with both parties present and, once condemned by all, might thereafter be restrained from the priesthood. “This,” I say, “ought first to have been done, and then another should have been appointed to the vacant place.”

Yet, although we were repeatedly and in many ways despised in all these matters, afterward through Odo, the venerable bishop, we sent further instructions amid many admonitions: namely, that Rothad, brought out of monastic custody, should either be restored to the honor of his former Church or sent to Rome, with the representatives of the bishops who had consented to his deposition, to be examined in our presence; otherwise, after thirty days, neither Hincmar himself nor the other bishops who had condemned him would have permission to celebrate Mass.

But once again our brother Hincmar, acting in contempt of us, chose not only not to obey us but also retained for four months the letter we had sent to him and to the bishops who had consented to Rothad’s deposition. Thus he refused to carry out what we had decreed concerning Rothad, even though our other letters had repeatedly been sent to various persons concerning the same matter and had been repeatedly disregarded.

Furthermore, he ordered that Rothad, brought out of monastic custody, be transferred to civil custody.

At last he wrote to us, saying that he had sent, together with the other bishops, his representatives, who would come with Rothad into our presence. But he said that they had been told that, because of the guards, they would have no access to enter Italy, and that for this reason they had returned from where they had come.

After this, what could be judged more empty or foolish than to abandon so great a task and turn back without any benefit merely because of an empty verbal statement, when no person opposed them and no definite adversary contradicted them?

Especially if we had certainly found them prevented from completing the responsibilities or ecclesiastical business entrusted to them, we would have been inflamed with appropriate zeal and inveighed against such reckless men all the more fervently, the more certainly we appeared to know that this impiety had been perpetrated by them.

But they either say or do these things toward us as a jest. Behold, two years have passed since, laboring in various ways for the aforementioned man and proposing now this, now that to them, we have accomplished absolutely nothing. Yet we still dissemble; we still cover the matter. And, to speak with blessed Pope Simplicius, “we do not wish to exaggerate what has been done, lest we be compelled to judge what is deserved” (letter to John of Ravenna).

For, as the equally holy Pope Zosimus teaches (letter to Hesychius), “whatever is repeatedly usurped after being forbidden is done in a spirit of insult.”

Meanwhile, setting these matters aside, it is worth considering that Odo, the venerable bishop, who was previously present in person, and afterward our other legates, testified that they had brought no accusation against Bishop Rothad. The representatives of the bishops, who were said to have been sent by those very prelates to give an account of Rothad’s deposition, wrote to us and professed that they had not been sent by their bishops to accuse Rothad.

This is especially clear since the aforementioned Rothad has now remained for approximately eight months in the Apostolic See which he requested, and we have been entirely unable to see anyone who might accuse him.

Therefore, since this is so, it remains that he who suffers no accuser should in no way suffer the loss of his integrity on any grounds.

It is clear, finally, that an accuser evades examination when he despairs of being able to bring forward just complaints.

Thus the Jews thought that the adulterous woman should be buried under stones. But when they brought her to the true judgment, they did not see what they had expected to see, and they heard what they had not expected to hear; ashamed and awestruck, they departed.

So, precisely so, the depositors of Rothad, when they came to the examination of the judgment in which they themselves had been both his enemies, accusers, and judges, stood motionless before the face of the man whom they had tried to overthrow.

But when an appeal was made to our judgment, in which, by God’s revelation, the truth would shine into the light if the matter were examined, all the arguments of falsehood were destroyed, and the makers of lies suddenly turned their backs.

Bishop Rothad, however, pure in conscience and innocent in conduct, distinguished by the simplicity of doves and the prudence of the serpent, recognized that the examination of the Roman Church had been reached. There he had no suspected person and suffered no enemy. There, as holy Pope Celestine says (letter 4), assistance is always given to Catholics. He did not fear the judgment; he requested that his examination be renewed; and he resolved willingly to accept whatever he saw us decide, because, as blessed Pope Boniface says (letter to Patroclus and others), no one doubts that the guilty person evades judgment in the same way that the innocent seeks to be acquitted.

Let the accusers or condemners of Rothad therefore see with what intention they refused to undergo judgment with him. For Rothad, who is innocent by God’s authority, not only did not evade the council of the saints but earnestly requested it.

Therefore let Your Sublimity know that, with God as author, we have restored the aforementioned bishop to his former dignity and to his Church.

Whether what some report concerning your affection is supported by truth will now become clear. If you were to give blessed Peter thousands of gems and precious objects, these would neither be as acceptable to him nor as beneficial to us as your obedience to us in this matter would be; for his concern is to seek the salvation of human beings, not to heap up piles of treasure.

We ask you, then, favor us as we repeatedly approach you on behalf of the often-mentioned man, so that he may find through you not an impediment but complete assistance in recovering the Church entrusted to him.

Do not let it be said of us in the course of time, we ask, what is now stated about Theodoric in a written document (Roman synod IV). Before recovering the patrimony or Churches that he had lost, he—being an Arian and a most wicked king—ordered Pope Symmachus to enter into dispute with his opponents. Although a council of the honorable bishops of Italy had ordered, by his authority, that everything he had lost through the accusations of his enemies be restored to him, he was first to be restored legally to his former status; then he would come to the case and, if it seemed right, respond to the proposals of his accusers.

Instructed by this example and by several other decrees and precedents, we too have decreed the same concerning Bishop Rothad.

We therefore solemnly implore and beseech you to obey our pious admonitions, not the persuasion of wicked men. Know that, if you equate yourselves—as God forbid—with the worst of kings and refuse to obey us in this matter, despite agreeing with us concerning it, you will undoubtedly be erased from our charity and remembrance.

For by the authority of God and the apostles we have decreed and established that whoever in any way obstructs the aforementioned Bishop Rothad from recovering the Church once entrusted to him or from carrying out his episcopal ministry, until he yields and abandons his attempts to resist him, shall be removed from the sacred mysteries and from entry into the Church, and separated from all communion with the faithful.

Moreover, we wish Your Excellency to know that many informants have reported to our ears that various possessions and certain endowments belonging by right to the holy Church of Soissons had been distributed according to the will of the usurper consecrated there and granted as benefits; or that, after he had died by the just judgment of God, they had likewise been granted as benefits by Your Excellency to certain men.

For this reason, we also exhort and beseech Your Affection in this matter to order, through your pious authority, that those endowments and possessions themselves, whatever and wherever they may be, be restored to the aforementioned Church, and that Your Excellency take care that everything be returned to its rightful ownership.

Thus, in accordance with the sanction of the sacred canons, all the possessions of the Church are to remain in the power of the bishop, and he is to distribute them, according to the fear of God, to whomever he wishes and in whatever manner he wishes. Your pious diligence should strive to accomplish this for the love of God, of the chief apostles, and of us.

Know for certain that whoever wishes to enjoy these possessions and perhaps delays returning them to the aforementioned Church will be expelled by us from the company of the faithful, entangled in the bonds of anathema, separated from the sacred mysteries, and cast out as profane, as a rapacious and impious man.

(Year 865.) LXXIV. TO HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS. He demonstrates that Rothad was legitimately restored; orders that his Church and the possessions taken from it be returned; then, once Rothad has recovered his strength, allows Hincmar to dispute with him at Rome, if he wishes.

[In Mansi, in the same place.]

[Col. 0897A]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother Hincmar, archbishop of Reims.

If any regard for the canons of the Fathers or for the Apostolic See existed before the eyes of your prudence, you would never have attempted to depose Rothad, bishop of the city of Soissons, without our knowledge. Especially since, when you were examining and repeatedly investigating a matter that rightly ranks among the [Col. 0897B] more important—namely, judging a person whose rank in the Church is higher than that of the others—it presented you with such difficult outcomes that you worked for nearly eight years to have him deposed, and amid such a tangle of causes and such an interval of time, you had absolutely no remembrance of blessed Peter. Yet when mention was made of the one being deposed, he is recognized, by the decision of your religious authority, as having been deprived of his own rank.

And although Your Blessedness has written to the Apostolic See on your own occasions, requested that it extend a hand to you against false brothers, and asked that certain privileges be granted to you, in the case of Rothad you alone failed to remember the Apostolic See—as though it did not need his assistance—and certainly did not visit it. Indeed, against this same appellant, the venerable man, you did not hesitate to prepare and contrive such great efforts and machinations [Col. 0897C] that, after he had been granted permission to come to Rome, and before he had taken leave of you and the king, you afterward dragged him from our tribunal to yours, so to speak (for it cannot be called a synod where our consent is not supplied), and subjected him, unwilling to enter the court, to deposition in tyrannical fashion. You took your opportunity from a certain letter, as though Rothad, after appealing to our judgment, had again, with a changed expression, summoned an examination before yours. This is entirely false.

That letter, through which you attempt to derive this advantage—as the truth makes clear, and as we discovered through very careful investigation—was being sent by Rothad to brothers [Col. 0897D] whom he did not know to have conspired with you against him, and whom therefore he did not regard as suspect. In that letter he neither rejects our judgment nor despises the Apostolic See; he does not request alien judgments, nor does he specify the number of chosen judges—indeed, he does not even mention their names. Rather, he merely assures the brothers and fellow bishops of his innocence and makes them attentive, so that, if it should perhaps please our apostolate, in accordance with the indulgence of the sacred canons, to write to those situated nearby for the purpose of renewing the examination—as he himself at that time intended to bring a petition to us and thought that we too would act—it might provide for his innocence and, with a just balance, pursue his case according to our arrangement and without respect of persons [Col. 0898A] (2, q. 6, “Arguta sapientia”).

But your “subtle wisdom”—would that it had been accepted for good—took this as fuel for judgment and material for a decision against Rothad, turned him back from the journey to the Apostolic See, condemned him repeatedly while he was appealing to the Apostolic See, and committed him to imprisonment. Yet even if no one had appealed from your judgment, you ought in no way to have consigned the privileges of the Apostolic See to oblivion. By those privileges, the venerable canons command that the judgments of the whole Church be brought to this See, and, as Gelasius recalls, decree that no appeal be made from it. Consequently, it alone is to judge concerning everything, and no one is permitted to appeal from it. But even if he had appealed from our judgment to yours, he would have stood before you as one to be corrected as erroneous [Col. 0898B]; indeed, he ought not even previously to have been corrected in a special manner, because he ought to have been wholly embraced by you with particular affection.

But when we sorrowfully learned that, with a hardened disposition, you had set all these matters aside contrary to expectation, we sent you our letters and ordered you to bring him out of the confinement of the prison and either immediately restore him to his former rank or send him into our presence with your representatives and the bishops who had consented to his deposition. If you did neither, then, thirty days after that letter of ours had been read, neither you nor any of those who had given you their consent in this matter was to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass until you had fulfilled what we had commanded concerning Rothad.

You regarded that letter as unworthy even of your touch and, imitating Dioscorus [Col. 0898C], at least consented in no way to read it. Therefore, while Rothad still remained in custody, through the venerable bishop Odo we again imposed the same command by letters upon Your Holiness and your other accomplices. We added also that, if you continued thereafter to be disobedient to us, we would restore Rothad to his former dignity and Church and render to you a fitting recompense.

Your Fraternity, having received these letters on the ninth day before the Kalends of July, as is reported, allowed no one to look at them for approximately four months. After this, when Rothad had finally been brought out of custody, you scarcely granted him permission to come to Rome. But the representatives whom you ought to have sent with him departed as far as they wished and informed us by letter during the journey that they had been told that [Col. 0898D] no passage to Italy lay open to them because of its enemies, and especially that they would be frustrated in meeting those whose assistance ought to have supported them. They added that, even if they somehow managed to reach Rome, they would bring no accusation whatsoever against Rothad.

After these events had taken place—since first we experienced your presumptions and transgressions, then discovered your disobedience and evasion, and finally, while Rothad had already been retained among us for approximately eight months, had been examined at length and with great care, and you and your representatives were loudly declaring that you had no accusation at all against him—what remained except that, in accordance with the promise mentioned above, he should at last be restored to his former episcopate [Col. 0899A]? This has now been done through our humble agency, as your diligence will be able fully to know. We warn you not to neglect to display every kind of patience in this matter, insofar as your prudence can do so, lest our authority be compelled to render you the retaliation that we promised long ago (2, q. 6, “Arguta,” § “Haec quippe nos”).

You should know that we carried out these actions concerning Rothad for this reason: so that the privileges of the Apostolic See, which appeared to have been wrongly violated by you and could not, despite all the labors we undertook, be recovered because of your stubborn resistance, might at last be adorned with their former and proper honor by apostolic authority and the canonical deliberation of the Fathers.

Moreover, if anyone has accusations against Rothad, or if he himself has until now endured from Your Holiness [Col. 0899B] complaints that are justly brought against him, we wish and decree that, when both parties are present, whatever the matter may be, it be brought before our special presence. But if no one wishes to attack the aforementioned man with accusations before our apostolate, let what we have decreed concerning him remain unimpaired and undiminished.

At last, let Your Fraternity choose one of the two alternatives that we place before you by our own option, whichever you wish, because both are canonical and both belong to the privilege of the Apostolic See. Either fulfill what we have arranged concerning the aforementioned brother and fellow bishop, our brother Rothad, and be found in no respect resisting but rather carrying it out; or else hasten without delay to Rome, to appear before us—that is, before the holy Roman Church—in order to engage in litigation with him and dispute the matter.

[Col. 0899C] This is to be done only after Rothad himself, with everything taken from him recovered as we have decreed, and with his honors restored, has regained his strength after returning to his former health following the long period of weakness, so that he may possess his office longer and enjoy all that belongs to him. But if you should perhaps do neither of these things without deliberately causing delay, and if you continue, in your customary manner, to resist what we have decreed concerning him, then from this point forward you are to be separated from every priestly dignity by God’s judgment through us and by the authority of the Apostolic See, so that you may never hope for a place of satisfaction or restoration to your order.

## (Year 865.) LXXV. TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF GAUL

That they should receive Rothad, restored by him, kindly; here he discusses at length many matters concerning the privileges of the Apostolic See and the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs.

[In Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 0899D]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brothers, the archbishops and bishops established throughout Gaul.

Although there are said to be many individual Churches because of the diversity of lands, there is nevertheless one Church, the one Church of her Bridegroom, just as he himself says in the Song of Songs: “My dove is one” (Song of Songs 6); and as the Psalmist says: “Deliver my one from the hand of the dog” (Psalm 21). Our Lord Jesus Christ, who created and redeemed her, is pastor, bishop, and high priest [Col. 0900A], so that he is truly and principally all these things, in accordance with what is said to the faithful through the first Apostle: “You have now turned to the shepherd and bishop of your souls” (1 Peter 2); and in accordance with the statement of the distinguished preacher concerning him: “Such a one,” he says, “was fitting for us as high priest” (Hebrews 7).

Yet, when he was about to ascend into heaven, he entrusted her to the apostles and, through them—as though by hereditary right—to their successors, namely, to us, whom he established as pastors, bishops, and pontiffs over her.
