He entrusted her care to our oversight, so that, born as sons in place of fathers and appointed as rulers over the whole earth in their place, we might be their imitators, as also of Christ himself.

But among the most blessed apostles there was, as that great Leo also writes (letter 88, to Anastasius), a certain distinction of power despite the likeness of honor [Col. 0900B]; and, although the election of all was equal, one was nevertheless given precedence over the others. From this pattern too arose the distinction among bishops. By a great arrangement it was provided that not everyone should claim everything for himself, but that in each province there should be individual bishops whose judgment would hold first place among their brothers. Again, certain bishops established in the greater cities were to undertake a more extensive care, through whom the care of the universal Church would converge upon the one See of Peter, and nothing would ever dissent from its head.

If some of you had understood these matters with any inward perception, you would never have deposed Rothad, bishop of the city of Soissons, without our consent [Col. 0900C], plundered him, and, after driving him into exile, committed him to monastic custody. For how can you claim everything for yourselves, when you have entrusted the judgments of bishops—which rightly rank among the more important affairs—to your own deliberation? Does it seem a small matter to you to subject your brothers and fellow bishops to deposition without the consent of the Apostolic See? If you do not count the condemnations of bishops among the more important affairs, whose cases do you count among those affairs?

What, I ask, is done concerning priests or clerics of lower rank, whose cases, when reason requires it, are commanded to be heard even before us according to the regulations of the Council of Chalcedon (canon 9)? If you depose bishops with such ease, how, I ask, does the care of the universal Church converge through you—whether you hold first place in individual provinces or, established in the greater cities, undertake a more extensive care—upon the one See of Peter, when you take no care to bring anything to its knowledge concerning the deposition of major bishops [Col. 0900D]? Are bishops not of the universal Church, so that nothing concerning their condemnation need be brought by you to the one See of Peter? Or how does nothing dissent from its head, when you dissent from the head—that is, from the Apostolic See—concerning the judgment of the Church’s principal members, namely, bishops? Is the Apostolic See not the head?

Therefore, to pass over many matters, the Council of Sardica rightly said to Bishop Julius, among other things, in its letter to Julius: “[Col. 0901A] It seems most excellent and entirely fitting that the priests of the Lord from each province should report concerning every matter to the head, that is, to the See of the Apostle Peter.” Behold, it calls the See of Peter the head, to which the priests of the Lord ought to report from each province.

In contrast, you despise it to such a degree that you take no care to report anything concerning the Church’s more important affairs to it, and presume to depose a bishop without consulting or respecting it—and especially one who was appealing to the Apostolic See. It is exceedingly absurd that you say Rothad, who appealed to the judgment of the Apostolic See, afterward requested your judgments with a changed expression. Even if this had been so, your Fraternity ought to have corrected him, because he had appealed from a greater to a judgment of lesser authority and therefore ought to have been set right.

Although it may not be apparent from any definite evidence that he fled from our judgments to yours, it is nevertheless established that, at the very moment when sentence was about to be pronounced against him, he appealed to the Apostolic See and cried out before everyone that he asked to be judged by it [Col. 0901B]. It would not have been equitable if he had turned to your judgments; yet even if he had in no way appealed to the Apostolic See, you still ought not to have proceeded against so many and such weighty decretal statutes, nor in any way to have deposed a bishop without consulting us.

Nevertheless, to speak while preserving the charity we hold toward you in our innermost being, we grieve that you set this aside, and we rightly rebuke you for having despised in this matter the decrees of various pontiffs of the Apostolic See.

Far be it from us to say that the writings of anyone who has persevered in the Catholic faith until the final day of his life, [Col. 0901C] whether decretal constitutions or any explanations concerning ecclesiastical discipline, should not be embraced with due reverence and the greatest discernment. The holy Roman Church has preserved these writings from ancient times and has entrusted them to us also for safekeeping; it venerates them, properly stored in its archives and venerable ancient records.

Far be it from us to say that their writings should in any way be treated as insignificant, when by God’s authority we see the holy Church adorned by them—either flowering with rosy blood or beautified by dew-laden labors and salutary words (Distinction, “Si Romanorum”).

For if the writings of other interpreters are approved or rejected by the decrees of these men, so that what the Apostolic See approves is now held as accepted, while what it has rejected is considered ineffective to this day, how much more ought those things that it has written at different times concerning the Catholic faith, the rejection of profane doctrines, and the Church’s various and manifold needs and the conduct [or: movements] of the faithful to be preferred with every honor and reverently received by everyone, whenever circumstances require, with discernment or dispensation as guide [Col. 0901D]?

Yet some of you have written that the decretal letters of the ancient pontiffs are not transcribed in their entirety in the whole body of the canonical code, although you yourselves use them without distinction whenever you see them supporting your purpose, and now claim that they are less acceptable only to diminish the power of the Apostolic See and to increase your own privileges. For some of their writings are held among us, and they are known to give precedence in their own cases not only to the decrees of various Roman pontiffs but also to those of earlier authorities [Col. 0902A].

But now, when these writings conflict with your minds, and when we do not cease to labor so greatly to preserve the privileges by which your status may remain secure—privileges that are demonstrably beneficial, have been beneficial, and will always be beneficial to the universal Church—you resist them. It is therefore right that where the entire weight of the structure rests, there the foundation should be held firm and strong in every respect (Distinction 19, “Si Romanorum,” § “Si ideo”).

Moreover, if they say that the decretal letters of the ancient Roman pontiffs should not be admitted because they are not written into the canonical code, then neither the holy Gregory’s nor any institution or writing of anyone else who lived before or after him should be received [Col. 0902B], because it is not written into the canonical code. Let them therefore erase their teaching and decrees from their own books; why do they occupy parchment if they are not accepted?

But why should we delay over this, when, if we decide to listen to these men, we would no longer even accept the divine Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments? Neither of these is inserted into the code of ecclesiastical canons.

But those men, who are always more ready to resist than to obey, will reply that among the canons there is a chapter of Saint Pope Innocent (Decretal, chapter 27), by whose authority it is taught that we must accept both Testaments, although neither of them is contained in its entirety within the canonical texts [Col. 0902C].

To this it must be asserted that, if the Old and New Testaments are to be received not because they are attached in their entirety to the canonical code but because the judgment of Saint Pope Innocent concerning their reception appears to have been set forth, then it plainly follows that the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs are to be received even if they have not been joined to the canonical code. For among the canons there is known to be mixed one chapter of Blessed Leo, in which all the decretal constitutions of the Apostolic See are commanded to be guarded in such a way that, if anyone violates them, he should know that forgiveness will thereafter be denied him.

For he says in chapter 5 of his Decretals (letter to the bishops throughout Campania): “But lest anything be thought to have been omitted by us, we command that all the decretal constitutions—both those of blessed memory, Innocent, and those of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the discipline of the canons—be so guarded by your love that, if anyone violates them, he should know that forgiveness will thereafter be denied him” [Col. 0902D].

By saying “all the decretal constitutions,” he omitted none of the decretal constitutions that he did not command to be guarded. And again, by saying “of all our predecessors,” he excluded none of the Roman pontiffs who had preceded him; rather, he commanded that their decretal constitutions be guarded by everyone in such a way that, if anyone violated them, he should know that forgiveness would thereafter be denied him.

[Col. 0903A] Therefore, it makes no difference whether all the constitutions of the Apostolic See are mixed among the canons of the councils, since everything cannot be joined together in a single body, and those constitutions are included that give firmness and their own force to what is absent. This is especially so since the acts of synods, among which the canons themselves were established, are not contained in the canonical code, but are nevertheless venerated by us with every due honor.

Saint Pope Gelasius, most blessed and eloquent, agrees with this Blessed Pope Leo in his Decrees, saying as follows (in the Roman synod, concerning canonical writings): “We decree that the decretal letters which the most blessed popes, at different times, issued from the city of Rome in response to consultations from various Fathers are to be received with reverence.”

Here it must be noted that he did not say “the decretal letters that are contained among the canons,” nor merely “those which modern pontiffs have issued,” but “those which the most blessed popes issued from the city of Rome at different times.” By saying “at different times,” the holy man also included those periods when, as pagan persecutions multiplied, it was exceedingly difficult for the cases of bishops to be brought to the Apostolic See [Col. 0903B].

Having thus laid these matters out, with divine grace favoring us, we have shown that there is no difference between the decrees of the prelates of the Apostolic See that are contained in the canonical code and those that, because of their abundance, are found only individually throughout separate volumes. We have proved that the outstanding prelates Leo and Gelasius commanded that all the decretal constitutions of their predecessors, and the decretal letters that the most blessed popes issued from the city of Rome at different times, be received and guarded with reverence [Col. 0903C].

Although this too is often recalled: Blessed Leo, bishop of the Apostolic See, wrote to Anastasius, archbishop of Thessalonica (letter 82), and most powerfully struck at the presumption of certain among you, plainly declaring that you ought not to decide such matters without consulting us. He says:

“For since it was open to you to suspend greater affairs and more difficult outcomes of cases while awaiting our judgment, neither reason nor necessity required you to turn aside into something that exceeded your measure.”

And again, a little later:

“Especially since, even if such a matter deserved such treatment, you ought to have awaited what I would write in response to your consultations” [Col. 0903D].

And shortly afterward:

“But even if he had committed something grave and intolerable, our decision ought to have been awaited, so that you would determine nothing to come before you had learned what pleased us.”

We too can say this concerning Rothad to you, with no less reason: while you were examining the matter for nearly eight years, neither reason nor necessity required you to turn aside into something that exceeded your measure. But even if he had committed something grave and intolerable, our decision ought to have been awaited, so that you would determine nothing before learning what pleased us.

But you say that the judgments of bishops are not greater affairs and that their cases do not have more difficult outcomes. We, however, rightly call their judgments greater affairs and judge their cases to have more difficult [Col. 0904A] outcomes because, the more eminent their rank and the higher they stand in the Church of Christ, the greater the affairs and the more difficult the outcomes are believed to be when their condition or their fall is at issue.

They are, in fact, first in the Church; they hold the measuring rod and measure holy Jerusalem; they preside over God’s building; they are the watchmen of the city of God; they are the rams; they are the shepherds of the Lord’s flock; they are the pillars of the house of the supreme King. Do you suppose that the cases of lower clerics are greater affairs, so that you assign their cases to us and the affairs of bishops to yourselves?

Although we also conclude, without a doubt, that the cases of clerics of lower rank are to be settled by us when time or circumstances demand it, as blessed Pope Innocent says to Victricius (letter to Victricius): “If any cases or disputes should arise among clerics, whether of higher or lower order, they are to be settled, in accordance with the Council of Nicaea, when the bishops of the same province have assembled; nor may anyone, without prejudice to the Roman Church, abandon those priests who govern the Church of God in that province by divine will and hasten to other provinces” [Col. 0904B].

Do you admit that the affairs of metropolitans alone are greater affairs? Then hear again what the holy Leo asserts concerning bishops:

“Although their dignity is common, their order is nevertheless general; and in truth, one of the seven orders of the Church is the order of metropolitans and the remaining bishops. And when the Apostle says that a bishop must be blameless, [Col. 0904C] I do not see that this applies any less to metropolitans than to the other bishops. Unless, perhaps, anyone among the metropolitans deprives himself of the episcopate by judging that this statement of the Apostle does not concern him.”

Therefore, in the affairs of bishops we seek no smaller number or men of a different reputation as accusers, witnesses, or judges than we require in the cases of metropolitans. For this reason, we rightly wish and have decreed that the outcomes of both their affairs and those of metropolitans be reserved for us.

By God’s authority we bear general responsibility for the whole Church, and we are bound by the care of all who constitute the Church. All those whose care is especially entrusted to us ought principally to obtain our judgment, as Innocent writes to Alexander of Antioch (letter 20)—not only concerning metropolitans, but concerning all priests without exception, indeed concerning all who recognize that they belong to the sheep divinely entrusted in the first place to Peter: that is, not only all those who belong to the number of those concerning whom the Lord said to the chief of the apostles, “Once you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22), but also those who belong to the fish that recognize themselves as being within the net which he himself specially commanded to be dragged ashore.

Yet, for the sake of contentious people, it is still worth asking: what judgments, or whose, do you proclaim to be greater affairs, if you do not count the cases of bishops among the principal affairs? Do you place the judgments of laymen and ordinary people among the greater affairs, when almost every day we receive them, with or without your representatives and letters, to be examined and judged, and then dismiss them after they have been examined, judged, or acquitted [Col. 0905A]?

In the end, either you will place the judgments of secular persons among the greater affairs and those of bishops among the lesser, reserving the judgments of bishops to yourselves and those of laymen to us; or, if the judgments of bishops are greater affairs, then, according to Leo, you ought to have been free to suspend these matters while awaiting our judgment. Or, if the person being judged deserved such treatment, you ought to have awaited what I would write in response to your consultations.

For it is absurd that you should send any laymen, even the least important people in your churches, to us to be judged, thereby adding them to our daily labor, while subjecting bishops, who are the Church’s principal members, to the discretion of your own deliberation.

[Col. 0905B] Finally, leaving these matters aside, know that we, with God as our guide, have wholly annulled and rendered void what was wrongly committed by you under the instruction of rashness, and what you hastily perpetrated without consulting us against our brother and fellow bishop Rothad—even if he had never appealed to the apostolic see—by the authority of God, of the most blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul, and of all my predecessors, as well as of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea under the pious emperor Constantine. We have restored the aforesaid Rothad completely to his former rank, former dignity, and former honor, so that, having recovered his former faculty of celebrating the divine mysteries and having been restored to every priestly office, he may, without anyone’s opposition, freely preside over his own Church, from which he was expelled without our knowledge.

Indeed, when for two years we had earnestly urged by letters and words that Rothad either be restored to his own Church or, at least, that you send him to Rome, together with your representatives and his accusers, so that we might examine and judge him, and when we could obtain nothing from you because you continually raised one pretext after another as excuses for sins, at last, with God inspiring us and the decree of the Council of Nicaea supporting us—a decree which, among other things, commands that the privileges of Churches be preserved—we judged that Rothad, mindful of the privileges of the apostolic see, ought to be released from the bonds with which you had bound him so that he could neither exercise his office nor preside over his Church, since we had not judged him deserving of such confinement.

For no one so foolish, or so far astray from the path of tradition, can be found as to assert that privileges should be preserved for all other Churches but taken away from the Roman Church alone, which is the teacher, mother, and head of all the Churches. If anyone perhaps secretly mutters—because he does not dare to admit it openly—that privileges of this kind did not belong to the Roman Church, privileges by which the apostolic see had the power to release what had been bound by other bishops, then, apart from the proof supplied by ancient precedents and by the citation of certain passages of Scripture, blessed Gelasius is a witness. We have brought him forward as a witness on these matters because he is commended not only exceedingly by his life and teaching, [Col. 0906A] but also sets forth and demonstrates the matter in question in a few words, offering us, as it were, in a brief statement what he drew from the sources of many volumes.

For, writing to the bishops established throughout Dardania, he says, among other things (Epistle 11):

> “Nor do we remain silent about what the whole Church throughout the world knows: that the see of blessed Peter the apostle possesses the power of releasing those bound by the judgments of any bishops, since it is rightly entitled to judge concerning every Church.”

Again, writing to the Eastern bishops, he says:

> “They wish to overturn the decrees of Christ after five hundred years, although the law of human beings cannot be broken after thirty years. Thus holy Athanasius was not condemned by the synod of the East because this see did not consent; nor was holy John of Constantinople, nor holy Flavian.”

If, therefore, with this one see not consenting, those men could not be condemned by the synod of the East, it follows that anyone condemned with this one see alone consenting has indeed been condemned.

Here it should be noted, among other things, that if this holy man rebuked so severely those who were attempting to overturn the decrees of Christ after five hundred years, when the law of human beings cannot be broken after thirty years, how much more must those be reproached who strive to tear them out even after eight hundred years and more?

What “decrees of Christ” he meant he explained below, when he stated that no one could be condemned without the consent of the apostolic see alone, and that one who had been condemned with its consent alone was to be regarded as condemned. He therefore said that the decrees of Christ were being overturned after five hundred years because approximately five hundred years had already passed when the venerable pope declared that the apostolic see had received these decrees of Christ.

For the Roman Church obtained its privileges from Christ through Peter, and these are the decrees of Christ—decrees which certain people then, after five hundred years, and now, after eight hundred years, are attempting to nullify. The privileges of the Roman Church, I say, are so ancient and venerable that the Council of Nicaea, as the apostolic bishop Boniface says in writing to the bishops established throughout Thessaly, did not dare to establish anything concerning it, since it appeared able to acknowledge nothing above its merit. In the end, it knew that everything had been granted to this Church by the Lord’s word. If everything, then the judgments of bishops as well.

Since blessed Boniface testifies that the Council of Nicaea did not dare to establish anything concerning it—clearly meaning the Roman Church—because it saw that nothing beyond its merit could be acknowledged, and since he says that it knew that everything had been granted to this Church by the Lord’s word; and since Saint Gelasius reproves those who wished to overturn the decrees of Christ while they were seeking to violate the privileges of the Roman see, it is plainly understood that the decrees of Christ are the same as all those things which the Council of Nicaea knew had been granted to this Church by the Lord’s word.

For from the time when the Council of Nicaea had been completed, fewer than five hundred years had passed up to Gelasius, so that this great man seems to have said of the statutes of the Council of Nicaea that they wished to overturn the decrees of Christ after five hundred years. [Col. 0907A] It remains, therefore, that he referred to that period from which approximately five-hundred-year cycles could be reckoned as having elapsed up to his own time.

Christ conferred upon the Roman Church the privileges established in Peter, ordained or confirmed, over which no council has rightly dared to establish anything, since it knows that everything was granted to her by the Lord’s word. The almighty Lord, preserving with himself the dispensation of the redemption of the human race, ordained before the ages of the world and manifested it in the time of his flesh. As he was about to ascend into heaven, he placed it especially in the confession and care of the apostle Peter, through whom both the apostolate and the episcopate received their beginning. He did not cease then through himself, and thereafter through the heirs of his care, to provide for the human race the things that the Lord entrusted to him. [Col. 0907B] These things he and his successors have continued to perform from that time onward, sometimes by words, sometimes by letters of their decrees issued from the city of Rome at different times, exercising above all their care for the sheep entrusted to them.

Therefore receive kindly Bishop Rothad, concerning whom up to now you have scorned to obey our commands, now restored by us—or rather by God—to his former rank. For that evangelical son, on returning, not only deserved to be received but was also found worthy of his father’s embraces; he receives the ring of faith and is clothed with the robe. What else does this signify but the insignia of the priesthood? Nor did the elder son prove acceptable to his father because he begrudged the one who had been received; nor did he possess as much merit with his father by remaining as guilt by refusing to receive his brother.

Therefore receive him as a brother; receive him, I say, as my own inward being. I gladly hear that you are concerned for his salvation; but I do not gladly permit anything to be done against his head. With you I extend my hand to the one to whom it must be extended; to the one to whom I extend it, extend yours together with mine. If you have forgiven anyone anything, so have I. For even if I have forgiven anything on your account, I have done so in the person of Christ, so that we may not be possessed by Satan. For we are not ignorant of his schemes, since he rejoices over separation.

The Apostles, moreover, speak words of declared kindness, as those words were most wisely repeated by the most blessed bishops of the apostolic see, Innocent and Boniface. Moreover, whoever, after learning of this decree of our apostolate, arrogantly acts against it and openly or secretly prepares any obstacle for the aforesaid Bishop Rothad when he seeks to recover and govern the Church of the city of Soissons—or in any way lays a snare for his person; indeed, if any one of you fails to offer him assistance in recovering his Church, like a brother to a brother, although he sees that his brother is in need and closes his heart against him, let him be regarded in every respect as alienated from that very charity, which is God, and from the body and blood of Christ, and from us, who are his members, like one in whom the charity of God does not remain.

Moreover, lest we seem to govern justice solely according to our own will and thereby be judged to oppose the canonical laws, we decree and determine that the aforesaid venerable bishop Rothad shall be ready to give an account of himself before the bishop of the apostolic see to everyone who regularly demands it, since, by God’s favor, we do not wish to favor either party against justice.

This provision is made, however, on the condition that, according to the definitions of our predecessors, he first recover with full right everything he formerly possessed, so that in every respect he may be what he is known to have been before the sentence pronounced against him. Then, once he has recovered his Church and possesses his episcopate in secure freedom, after resuming his relatives and friends, his property, and his restored strength, and after being clothed and protected with spiritual arms, let him answer his accusers and strive to satisfy completely those within and those outside concerning the matters of which he is accused.

(Year 865.) LXXVI. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF SOISSONS. That they should receive Bishop Rothad, restored to them, with every expression of affection.

[In Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 0908B]

To the clergy and people residing at Soissons.

Just as it is characteristic of parents of former generations to mourn the loss of their children with very bitter lamentation, so it is proper for devoted children to be affected by the loss of their father with intense grief and to be tormented by ardent sorrow. In this respect, it is somewhat contrary to nature if one part is anxious and grieves without the fellowship of the other part.

But in this matter, dearest sons, as frequent report concerning you relates, you were by no means cold, and—thanks be to God—you were by no means ungrateful. Indeed, no one doubts what varied and manifold calamities your devotion endured when, deprived of its proper protector and, so far as human affairs are concerned, remaining itself orphaned. But he who said to his faithful disciples, “I will not leave you orphans” (John 14), not only protected you by his present majesty, but also, in his merciful favor, gave back to you a ruler in the place where you had been desolate and deprived. He inwardly commanded and appropriately instructed us—“in him we live and move and have our being”—to return that ruler to you by the prompting of his compassion.

For behold, we have sent back to your eager devotion and pious affection the venerable man Rothad, our brother and fellow bishop, but your father, shepherd, and teacher. You were instructed by his long teaching; you were once nourished by the bread of his sacred word; you were surrounded by his prolonged labors and vigils; and through his instruction and teaching, by God’s authority, you were nourished. He has been restored to the insignia of his former priesthood, to his former honors, and to all the offices of the episcopate. [Col. 0908D]

You also have in this the example of Athanasius, of blessed memory, that most wise priest. Whom could his endurance fail to console? For whom could his unexpected return fail to inspire hope? He was expelled while Arius pursued him, but was recalled while the Lord advanced his cause. He suffered imprisonment and hardships; nor is it surprising that an apostolic man suffered those things in which the Apostle boasts that he had been exercised (2 Corinthians 11). Yet in all these things he followed the one who testifies that he is pleasing to himself in tribulations. Driven from there, he was strengthened in our regions. Finally, his status was restored here; in this see he found the rest of communion, from which the Catholics are always aided.

These are the words of holy Pope Celestine (Epistle 4, to Constantius), which we may suitably apply to Rothad, except that he mentioned the revered Athanasius and the blasphemous Arius; at present, however, Hincmarus is the pursuer and innocent Rothad is the accused.

“Rejoice, therefore, brothers, in the Lord; and again I say, rejoice: let your moderation be known to all people.” Rejoice, dearest sons, and give immense thanks to God for the return of your father. Be glad, O sheep of the Lord, and for your restored shepherd sing hymns of praise to the supreme Shepherd. Gather together, exalted sons; go out to meet him, rejoicing [Col. 0909B] with hymns, psalms, and spiritual songs, singing high-sounding praises to the Lord. Receive him with honor; approach him with joy; obey him as your most revered father and as your teacher; and in all things show yourselves toward him as devoted and peaceful sons. Know that divine protection will surely not be lacking to him, and that, so long as the breath of the Almighty remains and the breath of life breathes in my nostrils, our consolation will be present in his necessities.

For this reason, by another command of our apostolate, we order your unanimity to act with such diligence that you may not be found in any respect lacking affection toward the aforesaid man and your bishop. Rather, obey our admonitions concerning him in such a way that, with the Lord’s permission, the punishment that might have arisen from contempt of us may be transformed into the repayment of a just reward.

(Year 865.) LXXVII. TO ROTHAD, BISHOP OF SOISSONS. That he restores him in such a way that thereafter he should be ready to answer his adversaries if they attempt to bring any charge against him.

[In Mansi, same place.]

NICOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy Rothad, bishop of the holy Church of Soissons.

Imitating the examples of my predecessors and following the ardor of their wondrous virtues, I ought to prepare for everyone the abundant breasts of this Church’s compassion—this Church which is the mother of all God’s Churches—and to display an open lap of her mercy to all who flock to her from every direction, like a faithful and prudent servant of the great father of a household.

Therefore, since it is established that, when your metropolitan and certain of his followers brought charges against you, you suffered the loss of your rank and were deprived of your own Church without our knowledge, and thereafter, even when we had decreed it, had not yet received it; and since, in accordance with what we had ordered, you had received no restoration: we deliberate that this deposition, since it was irregularly effected without any judgment of ours, neither was nor is a deposition. For there was never a day on which we did not count you, whether absent or present, among the bishops, nor did we fail to write and associate with you. [Col. 0910A]

Therefore, by the authority of almighty God, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of all my predecessors, the bishops of the apostolic see, we restore you to your former rank and to your former Church. Whoever in any way prevents you from recovering the Church once entrusted to you or from carrying out the episcopal ministry shall, until he yields and abandons his attempt to oppose you, be removed from the sacred mysteries and from entry into the Church, and be separated from all communion with the faithful.

For we neither can nor ought to count among the condemned one whom no one has accused in person. This is especially so since we have summoned your condemnatory parties, or their representatives, by repeated letters of our apostolate, and have been wholly unable to see any of them accusing you. Instead, one person who was present and others in their letters informed us that they had no wish to bring any accusation against you, and that, even if they had been able to come in accordance with our command, they would have brought no accusations against your holiness.

Therefore, since throughout such long periods of time, despite sufficient delays being granted, no one came forward to accuse you—and especially since you have always been ready to give an account—we can neither condemn you nor leave you among the condemned.

Let your reverence therefore resume the office once entrusted to you. Enjoy the benefit divinely granted to you; exercise your episcopal ministry; having resumed your former dignity, recover the Church that the Lord entrusted to you, which you also received under good beginnings and adorned with worthy successions, with true and widespread reputation bearing witness on your behalf. Thus, without any opposition or impediment from anyone whatsoever, you shall be regarded in all respects as having been what you are acknowledged to have been before the sentence of excommunication and deposition was pronounced against you.

Yet, lest we seem to govern justice solely according to our own will and thereby be judged to oppose the ecclesiastical laws, we decree that your holiness, after first recovering everything which is known to have belonged to you previously, and after enjoying the authority of the Church and governing it without offense for some period, when your strength has been restored and everything taken from you has been restored, shall then, if there are any who attempt to bring something against you, engage them boldly and vigorously in the struggle of disputation.

In accordance with what reason dictates and the sacred decrees command, “clothed” against the clothed and “armed” against the armed, in ecclesiastical fashion and at a time to be appointed by us, you shall enter into conflict with your adversaries before the bishop of the apostolic see, ready without doubt to accept whatever shall have been regularly determined.

Since many are said to have taken away many things belonging to the holy Church of Soissons, or to various places belonging to it, and to have enjoyed them up to now in different ways, we decree and determine that, after your holiness has summoned and admonished them a second and a third time, whoever attempts to retain any of the property of the aforesaid Church which you are known at some time to have enjoyed for the use or support of those serving there or obeying you, and to claim it further for himself without your consent, and does not leave such property—whatever it may be, wherever it may be, and however great it may be—to the aforesaid Church of Soissons for its possession, shall, as a sacrilegious person bound by the guilt of anathema, be regarded in every way as alienated from the bosom of the Church, from the sacred body and precious blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, until he has yielded to this present decree of ours. As a violent invader and tyrant, he shall be deprived of the communion of Christians. Whoever receives such a person into communion shall likewise be held bound by the same punishment.

Written by the hand of Peter, regional notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of January, in the thirteenth indiction. Farewell in the name of the Lord.

(Year 865.) LXXVIII. TO CHARLES THE BALD, KING. He urges peace [Note: [Col. 0911D] with Emperor Louis. There seems to have been a dispute over the kingdom of Burgundy, as I suppose, after the death of King Charles. For that it was seized by Charles the Bald seems to be indicated by the capitularies sent by him into Burgundy under title 32. But Emperor Louis maintained that Burgundy, as his brother’s kingdom, belonged by right to him. Hence this passage in the present letter: “May it be permitted to your nephew to possess his empire peacefully together with the kingdom of his own brother,” and a similar passage in the following letter. JAC. SIRM.]—which he should preserve with his nephew, Emperor Louis, and that he should trust Arsenius, whom he is sending as legate to Gaul.

[In Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 0911B]

NICOLAS, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Charles, the glorious king.

The beginning of my address to you now, dearest son, takes its origin from the Apostle Paul, and my voice is his voice, saying: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4).

How, then, could Christ be formed more fully in your hearts than if, having torn out from your inmost hearts the thorns of hatred and hostility, you conceive peace in your inward parts—for Christ is peace, as the same Apostle says of him: “He is your peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 1)—and observe charity toward one another, which is God, as John describes it: “God is charity” (1 John 4)?

No one, therefore, doubts that whoever does not possess charity and peace within himself has cast out from his heart Christ the Lord our God, who is designated by these names, and has expelled him, as though he had been formed in the deepest recesses of his womb.

Therefore, just as the holy mother Church, over whom my humility presides through the abundance of divine mercy, once gave birth to you through the Gospel so that Christ might dwell in your hearts through faith, so now also, through the ministry of my apostolate, she is again giving birth to you so that the same Christ may be formed in your innermost hearts through peace and love, and may shape you so that you attain mature manhood.

But how can Christ be formed in you, when he does not dwell in divided minds, he who is entirely peace, entirely justice, and entirely truth? Or how is he formed in you when, although he dwells in your breast through his faith solid and whole [edit. Rom., “sound”], yet through discord he is regarded as less perfect in you, almost formless?

Conceive peace, therefore, sons; bring forth justice; embrace mutual charity. Hear what the Apostle says: “Pursue peace with all” (Hebrews 12). And again: “If it is possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Romans 12).

Hence it must be weighed with the deepest attention of the mind and the utmost diligence: if so great an Apostle urged that peace be pursued with all people and maintained with all, how much more necessary and salutary is it to pursue and maintain peace with those to whom you are nearer by blood relationship, closer by the kinship of the flesh, and more tightly bound by an oath to preserve reciprocal peace?

This is the matter on which I now speak, and my address is directed to your royal highness: directing you toward those things by which you may not only possess earthly kingdoms by rightful law and pass your days in the greatest tranquility, but also attain the inheritance of blessedness and receive the name of sons of God. For it is written: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5).

Remember, therefore, beloved sons; remember the name of the Lord our God. In the presence of several witnesses you invoked it and solemnly promised one another peace by oath. Fearing to take so dreadful a name in vain, fulfill your vows to the Lord. Let the covenant which you made with one another remain with you, preserved in inviolable truth, and let your unstained highness flourish, displaying to all the surrounding nations the insignia of faith.

Spare the sword, and dread with the greatest fear the shedding of human blood. Let anger cease; let hatred be appeased; let quarrels be put to rest; let every hostility be uprooted from you completely. Let each of you be content with his own portion and peacefully enjoy the inheritance allotted to him by God, neither invading, taking away, nor disturbing the rights of another.

May it be permitted to our most beloved son, and your nephew, whose empire God preserve, to possess his empire peacefully together with the kingdom of his own brother, to provide for his position with complete security, and to exercise its government with the authority that belongs to him, for the salvation and defense of the Christian people and for the liberty and exaltation of his holy mother, the distinguished Roman Church.

Let there not reign in you the fever of glory, the arrogance of the brow, or the ambition to usurp another’s boundaries, but justice, charity, and harmony; and above all, let peace hold the highest place among you.

When we write about harmony and preach peace, do not suppose that we are speaking of the harmony or peace which the world is accustomed to love and which the wicked observe among themselves. Indeed, in order that they may more freely and boldly perpetrate the evils they desire and find more numerous and stronger allies for what they pursue, they strive to maintain unanimity and to hold peace among themselves without resistance or interruption.

The Lord knew this and distinguished it from his own peace. He said to his beloved: “Peace I leave you; my peace I give you” (John 14)—“my peace,” he says, not that of the lovers of the world. Therefore he suitably added: “Not as the world gives do I give to you.” Saint Augustine explains salutarily and lucidly how this should be understood.

As for the remaining matters, which we did not think should be inserted into this page lest we exceed the limits of a letter, we have entrusted them to the most reverend and holy bishop Arsenius, legate and envoy of the apostolic see and our counselor, to set forth in writing and speech, as we believe, appropriately and with polished clarity.

Your glory will do well to attend to him in all things, and, regarding what he reports to you by the authority of our apostolate concerning the peace of the holy Church, to give him certain and unquestioning faith, not without good reason. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed, dearest son.

(Year 865.) LXXIX. TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF CHARLES. That, for the sake of peace, he is sending Arsenius as legate; accordingly, they should urge the king to preserve peace with his nephew, Emperor Louis.

NICOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all our most reverend and most holy fellow bishops, the archbishops and bishops established in the kingdom of Charles, the glorious king.

[Col. 0913C] It has always been, and remains, our earnest desire, dearest brothers, to extend continually and diligently the service of our office for the good of building mutual charity and peace—not only to those who are near but also to those who are far away. We have been especially encouraged to this by your urging us repeatedly, among the other matters which you have more frequently requested that we arrange among you.

But, hindered by the countless labors pressing upon the Church of Christ our Lord throughout the world, whose care we principally bear, we have so far been unable to do this as we wished.

Now, however, after that Macedonian man who once appeared to Paul has so often cried out to us through the pious [edit. Rom., “your own”] voices of your holiness, “Cross over and help us” (Acts 16), and after a door has at last been opened to our apostolate through your prayers, pleasing to God, just as it was then to that outstanding Apostle, we do not wish to bring either negligence or delay to so great a work.

Rather, setting aside for a little while our other ecclesiastical and highly necessary business, we shall seek the things that belong to the peace of Jerusalem—that Jerusalem which partly already reigns with her Bridegroom in heaven and partly still dwells and suffers on earth—so that, once the foundations of harmony and love have been laid in her building, there may consequently be peace in her strength and abundance in her towers.

For this purpose we have sent the present letter to your fraternity. Admonished by it, like good fellow soldiers and cultivators of the Lord’s vineyard, fight with us against vices [perhaps, “purge them”], proclaim the gifts of virtues, destroy discord, build unanimity, uproot hatred, plant charity, disperse quarrels, and preach peace.

Not, God forbid, the kind of unanimity or peace which the seditious crowd of the Jews employed when it conspired in the death of the Lord and Savior, or which Herod and Pilate, formerly enemies, made with one another at that time. Rather, the kind which the shepherds heard the heavenly host sing at the birth of our Savior, saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2).

In proclaiming “peace to people,” it added “of good will,” so as to separate people of evil will from peace of this kind. For all the perverse, the more peaceful they are among themselves, the stronger they undoubtedly become for doing wrong.

Therefore the Apostle not only admires the beautiful feet of those who proclaim good things (Romans 10), but also adds those who proclaim peace (Hebrews 12), indicating that no good exists without peace, and that peace, in turn, is not to be pursued without the other good things. Elsewhere he commands that peace with all and holiness be pursued, without which no one shall see God. By joining these together, he shows that either one without the other is less effective.

Having charity among yourselves, therefore, dearest brothers, pursue peace with all and holiness—not the peace which even ravens possess with one another, but that wondrous harmony which belongs to the simple doves, wholly free from tearing one another apart.

May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, not only preserve you, but also through you unite and bind together all who are governed under your rule.

Above all, hasten to instruct your king as we have written to him and in accordance with what we have taught him. Exhort him to remember the memory of the strict judgment. He invoked its name before many hearers and promised by oath that inviolable peace would be preserved for his brothers and their children. Fearing to take so dreadful a name in vain, let him fulfill his vows to the Lord, to whom alone it is wicked not to render vows freely promised to the Lord.

Remind him, therefore, to preserve in perpetual unity the covenant which he made with his brothers, and, guarding it unstained, to present to everyone an example worthy of imitation in himself. Let him spare war and greatly dread shedding the blood purchased by the blood of Christ. For it is written: “The Lord will abhor the bloody and deceitful man” (Psalm 5).

Therefore let him be content with his own portion and peacefully enjoy the inheritance granted to him from heaven, not attempting or desiring to usurp the rights of another. Let presumptuous recklessness cease, and let greedy longings be restrained from the depths of the heart—especially those directed against the borders of our beloved son, the most excellent Emperor, or against the boundaries of his kingdom, which lie far away.

Let the devout emperor [edit. Rom., “illustrious emperor”] therefore be permitted to lead a quiet and peaceful life; and, when his uncles show no presumption, let him not be compelled to turn against the faithful of Christ the use of the sword which he first received from the vicar of Peter, chief of the apostles, against unbelievers.

Let him, I say, govern with his faithful people, piously and most justly, the kingdoms that have passed to him by hereditary right, that have been confirmed by the authority of the apostolic see, and that have been most augustly adorned by the hand of the supreme pontiff placing a diadem upon his head. Let his empire, protected by God, which he received with blessing and with the anointing of the most sacred oil administered by the bishop of the apostolic see, be permitted to be governed freely and most rightly for the exaltation and peace of its mother, this holy catholic and apostolic Church.

Otherwise, whoever should presume to act against the page of this salutary admonition of ours, and should attempt to bring charges against the aforesaid son of ours, the Emperor, let him know that almighty God, whose empire knows no boundary, will undoubtedly oppose him, and that our apostolate, in accordance with the ministry proper to it, will certainly resist him.

Moreover, know that we have sent to your glorious king and to you the venerable man Arsenius, bishop of Hortense [edit. Rom., “archbishop”], legate and envoy of the apostolic see and our beloved counselor. His faith has been approved by us and his devotion ascertained; and his person, or at least his prudence, may perhaps not be unknown to all of you.

You and our son the king should receive him kindly all the more because you know that he labors for everyone, since he has not refused to undertake such great toil for the common affairs of the Church, which is the mother of all. Indeed, you should receive him all the more because, by carrying peace, he is recognized as bearing Christ, who is true peace, far and wide within himself.

Let your holiness also consent to join him and, as soon as his arrival becomes known to you, not refuse to hasten to him, so that, enjoying mutual sight and conversation, you may recognize more clearly the things that concern true peace. Thus you may understand more evidently the tenor of his legation, and he may understand what you have long desired.

Then, if there are matters which he can correct himself, let him correct them by our authority; but let the remaining matters, which may perhaps be more difficult, be reserved for definition by our apostolate.

We wish your fraternity and holiness well in Christ.

(Year 865.) LXXX. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF LOTHAR. That they should freely rebuke Lothar and compel him to cast off the adulterous woman whom he has.

[In Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 0915D]

NICOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy fellow bishops, the archbishops governing the Church of God in the kingdom of King Lothar.

Often, dearest brothers, you have learned of the concern of our apostolate for the cause of King Lothair—if indeed it is to be called a cause, though would that he were a king! For you have seen our frequent letters concerning this matter, and you know very clearly that we have already condemned so great a scandal in those who support him. But, alas! While we labor and toil without respite, although you profess in writing that you share and uphold our position, you have given us no indication at all whether you yourselves are laboring or not with the aforementioned man, whether your labor is accomplishing anything with him, or whose fault prevents it from succeeding, if it does not succeed. [Col. 0916A] Hence it may be understood that you have kept silent in this way because you have absolutely nothing useful that you can report.

Therefore I beseech you by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, before whose presence you will receive either a crown for lawful struggles or—God forbid—a punishment for sloth, that at last you reflect upon the ministry you have received, cast off your sluggishness, drive servile fear away from you, recover episcopal freedom, and take up the office of watchmen and shepherds. By praying, entreating, persuading, sometimes explaining the fleeting prosperity of this world, sometimes proclaiming joys that endure forever, visit the king just named more frequently. Both by God’s authority and by the command imposed upon you by our apostolate, take care, casting off every torpor and fear, to exhort and admonish him until, if he does not obey by casting off the adulterous woman whom he now has, we pronounce a final and permanent sentence upon her.

Cast off all torpor and fear; lay aside the sluggishness and weariness by which you have hitherto been weighed down; strive steadfastly and fittingly to rebuke and correct him, announcing at the same time what is going to come upon him—indeed, what is already threatening him: namely, that after the manifest sentence of ourselves and of the holy Church pronounced against him, you will have no further communion with him. For, as may be gathered from the opposite position, he himself has long since been deprived of our communion, together with the adulteress joined to him and his supporters. This can clearly be found in the letter and admonition that we gave to Rhadoald, then bishop, and to John, bishop, when they were serving as legates against that same Lothair.

Therefore, brothers, be like the strongest soldiers and the most vigilant shepherds. Watch from afar for the approaching wolf and announce the sword hanging over the man who is destined to perish. Do not cease to rescue and deliver this man who is being led to death and dragged toward destruction. Cry out; raise your voices like a trumpet; announce to him his crimes, by which he sins and causes Israel to sin. If he does not listen, he himself will die in his iniquity, and his blood will be upon his own head; but you will save your own souls. [Col. 0916D]

Only be mindful always of that sentence which our apostolate now sets down for your remembrance, drawn from the Apostle: “If anyone does not obey our word conveyed by letter, take note of that man and do not associate with him” (II Thess. III).

Moreover, these matters and the others that we have inserted in this letter we have entrusted to the most holy Bishop Arsenius, apocrisarius and legate of the apostolic see, our adviser, to carry out with you according to God’s will. Strive to show him your kindness and to offer him fitting reverence for love of the blessed Apostle Peter, from whose see he has departed. We wish your brotherhood, or your holiness, good health in Christ.

---

**(In the year 865.) LXXXI. TO ADО, ARCHBISHOP OF VIENNE. Why the synod was not held. Concerning Arsenius, sent as legate to Gaul and Germany. That Gunthar and Theutgaud were not restored to their former rank. That a priest should not rightly be called the priest of Count Gerard or of any other layman.**

*[In Mansi, same place.]*

**[Col. 0917A]**

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend and most holy brother Ado, archbishop of Vienne.

You wonder, brother, why we did not hold the synod that had been arranged, since we had intended there, among the other matters that now press upon us [perhaps, “threaten”] [Col. 0917B]—and it would take too long to recount the affairs being conducted among you—to examine especially, with God as our guide, the matters occurring there and to decide them together with you, that is, with you and our other brothers. We had hoped that through you—since the affairs of those regions are more clearly and adequately known to you by reason of your proximity than to us—we would gain a fuller understanding, and, in turn, that whatever had to be established by God’s revelation would become known in those regions. Yet you have been absent, although we had repeatedly summoned you and nearly all the bishops of God’s churches existing beyond the Alps to be called to the synod to be held at Rome, and although we have been especially and beneficially stirred by the unlawful and wrongful things being done there.

On another occasion we sent the venerable Bishop Arsenius, apocrisarius and legate of the apostolic see and our adviser, to the regions of Gaul and Germany, to investigate and discover with you certain matters concerning the affairs of the present time. For this reason we did not think that you ought to be absent from those regions for as long as it was known that he would remain there. Therefore your blessedness will do well to attach yourself to him and to share fraternally in his labors in the matters that must be undertaken at our delegation.

Your holiness asserts, however, that it is being reported everywhere that the former bishops Theutgaud and Gunthar have been restored by us to their previous rank. How could this have been done while the crime still continues—both the crime committed by King Lothair in rejecting Queen Theutberga and admitting a harlot, and that perpetrated by Ingeltrude, apostate and adulteress? We do not know whether you take any notice of the fact that he was one of their supporters, especially in the case of Gunthar, who, disregarding our decrees contrary to the sacred canons, dared, following his former custom, to undertake a ministry forbidden to him.

Although, therefore, we have so far kept nothing of this matter fixed in our heart, nevertheless, if we had done anything concerning the restoration of either of them, we would consequently have taken care to write to all of you about their restoration just as we wrote about their fall.

But, dearest brother, it sounded ridiculous that, when commending to us the bearer of your letter, you declared him to be the priest of the illustrious Count Gerard. Truly, I confess that I do not know what your prudence intended by writing this—or, according to Hardouin’s variant, why—or what you understood by such a statement. Did Count Gerard consecrate that priest? Is he of Gerard’s diocese? Where did you read this? Where did you learn it? Unless it is because priests are not ordained specifically for a city church, or a church belonging to an estate, or a martyr’s shrine, or a monastery according to the sacred rules, but are installed in the houses of laymen and associate so closely with secular people that they are now said to belong not to God and to some church, but to this count or that duke—so that what is said through the prophet has been fulfilled: “And it shall be: like people, like priest” (Hos. IV).

Perhaps this is one of the matters that, when we come together unanimously in the name of the Lord, will have to be more suitably corrected and cut away like poisonous hellebore. We wish your brotherhood [Col. 0918B] good health in Christ.

---

**(In the year 865.) LXXXII. TO ARDUIC, ARCHBISHOP OF BESANÇON. He replies to his inquiries.**

*[In Mansi, same place.]*

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother Arduic, archbishop of Besançon.

Among the other distinguished marks of your virtues, which deserve to be increased by abundant thanksgivings, we perceive that you possess the highest obedience together with the summit of humility. And since we see in you such great eagerness of spirit toward us, we do not doubt that your mind has been touched by the spirit of the apostles. When their primate merely said to them, “I am going fishing,” they immediately replied, saying, “We also are coming with you” (John XXI, 3). In the same way, when the brotherhood of your unanimity perceived that we wished, by words alone, to set out upon the path of zeal for winning and rescuing the souls of the faithful from the false and bitter whirlpools of this world, it promptly suggested that it desired to follow us and gladly walk in our footsteps, without allowing any delay; and by sending frequent legations it promised that it would fight with us against our enemies even unto death.

But we pray almighty God that, just as you have become like him in this promise, under his protection you may prove unlike him in denial. Yet even if such a thing had occurred, the same man would have been wholly worthy of imitation in his recovery: namely, the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, who, cutting off Malchus’s bodily ear with a sword, struck disobedience, and who, in Ananias and Sapphira, struck falsehood and greed with the spiritual blade of the word. Since you venerate his see and follow his commands, we believe that you will also obtain his protection and receive before God the shelter of his intercessions.

Now, concerning the inquiries of your brotherhood, to which you wished us to respond through the bearer of your letter, directing the eye of our mind as the Lord grants—“from whom is every good gift and every perfect gift” (James I, 17)—we will not withhold our attention from your charity; rather, we will bestow it as a gift freely received from heaven. [Col. 0919A]

### CHAPTER I

The Council of Neocaesarea commands that those women who have married two brothers, or those men who have taken two sisters as wives, be rejected until death and obtain the remedy of penance only at their end, once the bonds of this union have been dissolved. But blessed Pope Siricius separates those men or women who, after penance, have sought new marriages and forbidden intercourse from the communion of the Lord’s table, and he willed that such persons be assisted by the grace of communion only with viaticum when they begin to depart to the Lord.

How, then, can they enter into any marriage, when they are permitted neither to resume forbidden intercourse nor to contract new marriages, since even after the bonds of such a union have been dissolved, people of this kind can obtain the remedy only at the end of their penance? For, as we said above at the indication of the holy bishop Siricius, those who are striving to preserve their penance ought not to seek either new marriages or forbidden intercourse again.

Furthermore, how could any man be joined to two sisters, or any woman to two brothers, and then pass to another marriage while those persons were still alive, when—although not lawfully—a marriage had already been contracted with two persons, and, according to the Gospel, while one spouse from the marriage is alive, the other commits adultery if he takes another spouse?

But if those two sisters or brothers to whom the man or woman had been joined have already died, and for that reason it is thought that he or she may contract a third marriage, it must be understood that we have received no such permission from our Savior, from the apostles, or from apostolic men; nor shall we command that it be accepted.

### CHAPTER II

Who would not rebuke and condemn those who take wives from their own blood relationship or kinship, or women who marry within such relationships? For even our holy predecessors, the bishops of the apostolic see—Gregory and Zacharias—strike such persons with the sword of anathema and have altogether wished that such a union, contracted in the manner of beasts, be dissolved.

But after the union has been dissolved and the parties separated from one another, if they can, as you ask, move to a better marriage, no reason appears. Since they must be subjected to penance, they ought to seek neither the intercourse forbidden to them nor other new marriages.

Finally, if Tamar is reported to have contracted no marriage after being violently violated by her brother, and David’s concubines after being violated by his son, on account of incestuous intercourse; and if Adonijah was punished with death by Solomon because he asked that the girl who had merely slept chastely with his father be given to him as a wife—how much more must those who freely join themselves and irrationally mingle, once they have been separated and subjected to fitting penance, seek no marriage thereafter but rather chastity of mind and body?

Certainly, if someone from this unhappy union should die after the dissolution of the bond, and the survivor is still held in the years of youth, then, if some danger should arise, he has done penance and complains that he cannot remain continent, he may be assisted by the remedy of marriage. We wish the form of this indulgence to be observed also with regard to women. In this, however, we do not establish a rule; rather, together with the outstanding pillar of the Church, blessed Pope Leo, we judge what is more tolerable.

### CHAPTER III

*(Council of Ancyra, canon 17.)*

As for those who mate with animals, the holy synod commands that they not contract matrimonial unions, but that prayer be offered among those who are tormented by an unclean spirit. Nevertheless, if there are young men who, bound by so great a sin, have done penance when threatened by the approach of death or the exile of captivity, and who afterward, fearing a fall into incontinence, have fled to the remedies of married companionship lest they perhaps fall into the crime of fornication, they are recognized as having accepted a pardonable counsel—provided only that thereafter they avoid not merely the companionship of an irrational creature (horrible crime!), but absolutely every woman’s companionship except that of their own wife.

They have thereby imitated the righteous Lot, who, in order to escape the vast fires of Sodom, chose the small city of Segor so that he might at least be saved in it. Certainly, as we said above, we do not promulgate a rule in this matter; but, lest a worse sin be committed, we have judged that what we consider the lesser should in some way be granted indulgence.

Finally, according to full satisfaction, nothing is more suitable for those who do penance for so destructive a crime, one deserving every punishment, than persevering chastity not only of body but also of mind.

### CHAPTER IV. Concerning a bishop once elected

After the death of a bishop, whoever has once been elected in his place, if he deviates in no respect from the sacred canons, and if his election has been arranged not by any secular persons but by the clergy of the church with the consent of the principal men of that city, and if the promulgations of the holy Fathers agree in his regard, and if he accords both with the doctrines of the faith and with good morals, ought not thereafter to be removed for any reason. Otherwise, those who attempt this will be condemned by the sacred rules as transgressors and evaders. In particular, those who act against their own profession or subscription will be restrained by canonical laws.

### CHAPTER V

Concerning chorepiscopes, about whom you ask whether they are able to consecrate priests and deacons, the sacred canons will be able to instruct you sufficiently. But how can we say that chorepiscopes are able to consecrate churches which no bishop is permitted, according to the holy rules, to dedicate without our command? Therefore we shall not grant this to chorepiscopes. Hence we rightly rebuke you bishops for transferring the boundaries established by the Fathers.

Moreover, who ought to consign infants is shown by Saint Innocent, who says: “Concerning the consigning of infants, it is clear that it may be done by no one other than a bishop.” And again: “This,” he says, “belongs only to pontiffs: that they either consign or confer the Spirit, the Paraclete. Not only does ecclesiastical custom demonstrate this, but also that passage from the Acts of the Apostles which says that Peter and John were sent to confer the Holy Spirit upon those who had already been baptized.”

### CHAPTER VI

*(St. Gregory, Book XII, indiction 1, letter 25.)*

Concerning the priest who cannot receive restoration after a fall, to pass over many matters, blessed Pope Gregory declares this when writing, among other things, to Sabinianus, bishop of Jadera: “As for the priest,” he says, “about whom your brotherhood consults us through the report of the bearer of this letter, know that after his fall he can in no way either remain in the sacred order or be recalled to it.”

These matters, dearest brother, we have scarcely managed to answer concerning your inquiries, being occupied with many affairs. But the other matters that concern the common good you will be able to discuss fully and abundantly with the venerable Bishop Arsenius, apocrisarius and legate of the apostolic see, whom we have sent to those regions, when he arrives there with God as his guide. You may entrust our matters to him and, when he returns, you may commit to him whatever you wish him to explain to us, without any hesitation. We wish your brotherhood good health in Christ, now and always.

### CHAPTER VII

If anyone from his own kin has shed blood in murder, the sacred canons have decreed that he be rejected until death and counted among the rebellious.

---

**(In the year 865.) LXXXIII. TO LOUIS, KING OF GERMANY, AND CHARLES THE BALD, KINGS. He rebukes them because they did not send bishops to Rome for the synod. He urges them to continue admonishing Lothair concerning the divorce. Concerning bishops to be consecrated for the churches of Cologne and Cambrai, and concerning Rothad of Soissons.**

*[In Mansi, same place.]*

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest sons, the most glorious kings Louis and Charles.

We believe that it has proceeded from God’s gift, dearest sons, that you have become united, with pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith. Hence, with one mind and one mouth, God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is glorified through you, and your union advances toward the salvation and honor of the holy catholic and apostolic Church and of your kingdom.

Concerning our letters, which you received and delivered according to their tenor to the archbishops and bishops of your kingdoms, and also to the archbishops and bishops of Lothair’s kingdom, we have offered thanks to your Excellence. But because you said that they could not come to our synod, both because of the shortness of time and because of the difficulty of the journey, we took this rightly and severely, since the time was not so short that you could not at least have sent two from among those living with you—especially you, my son King Charles, who acknowledge that your kingdom is spread over a much greater distance than that of your brother, our dearest son, the glorious King Louis, from this holy see in the western regions beside the Ocean Sea.

It cannot be believed that your kingdom is so much farther away that, as we mentioned above [the Roman edition inserts: “at least from among those living with you,” etc.], you were unable to send even two legates representing one or two metropolitan sees. It is certainly very reprehensible that you added that most of the bishops were keeping watch day and night with your other faithful men against maritime pirates, and that for this reason the bishops were prevented from coming. The soldiers of Christ must serve Christ, while the soldiers of the world must serve the world, just as it is written: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs” (II Tim. II).

If soldiers of the world devote themselves to secular warfare, what is required of bishops and soldiers of Christ except that they devote themselves to prayer? We had not expected you, dearest son, who by God’s grace are renowned in all things, to break out into such statements.

Access to come for so great a matter ought not to have been denied to those bishops. And if they had wished to deny it, somehow, if they had chosen to obey our warnings, access and passage would have been opened to them. If they had come with their workers gathered together, we would certainly have taken better measures to prevent this from happening. For God had granted that, with them on one side and us on the other, he should stand in the midst of our assembly, so that thereafter access could not be denied either to our men or to yours.

We cannot speak better of our own men, nor worse of yours, because it would take too long to explain what impedes us. If they had endured something for God at Cluses during the intervening period, they would receive a great reward from the Lord for their trials and labors. But because they evade us under the pretext of the journey, we shall continue to bear these burdens, though compelled to do so; you, however, will see to it.

It is apparent that they do not wish to obey our warnings because of what is added in your letters. For after a certain amount they say that there is no necessity for sending bishops from your kingdoms to the synod at Rome. If you perhaps speak otherwise, we say what is divinely revealed: since we see the evils of innovations multiplying, if brothers from various provinces had come together with one another according to ancient custom, and if we, with their agreement and with the Lord’s revelation, had decreed what needed to be decreed, while they reported their needs and we explained ours, they would have made whatever had been decided reach everyone’s knowledge more effectively. They had always asked that a synodal assembly be convened by us.

Thus medicine would have been prepared according to the nature of the disease and spread far and wide for the healing of wounds. Solomon agrees with our words when he says: “There is salvation where there are many counsels” (Prov. XI).

Do you not know that certain prelates from certain provinces have acted in this way? You can learn this more easily if you wish, although, if you wish, it is by no means unknown to you.

Finally, we do not wish to rebuke men so prudent, so distinguished and renowned, whom God has united in true charity. Rather, we cherish you as our dearest sons with paternal love, and we beseech the mercy of almighty God that you may remain in the unity of the faith.

If some of our fellow bishops had sent us such letters, we would have known how to rebuke and reprimand them—except that, if they had said that your royal greatness had hindered them, the matter would appear to rest with you and to require correction.

Behold, an impediment is prepared for the bishops of your kingdoms, so that they will not come. But what prevents the bishops of Lothair, who is this man’s brother, except that they take an occasion from your example and, like your bishops, appear negligent in his regard? Among the other reasons, their coming would now have helped greatly in the case of Lothair, about whom we shall speak below, because after hearing the decrees and statutes they would report everything more clearly, so that nothing obscure would remain.

Perhaps, indeed, their delay and absence have harmed his correction more than his obstinacy has. For if there had been no absence and delay, his obstinacy would at least by now have ceased under compulsion.

But leaving these matters aside, let us turn our writing to your inquiries. You say that you admonished the aforementioned Lothair, as we were able to read in the admonition sent to us by you. You also affirm that you repeatedly instructed him that he wished to go to Rome and settle the matter of his marriage according to our arrangement.

But alas! You did not match your deeds to your words, because, although you repeatedly mentioned the sending of the admonition, the admonition itself was absent and never appeared before us, leaving us deceived. If we had possessed it, we would have learned of your struggle concerning these matters. But since it was lacking, we do not know whether your labor was fruitful.

Lothair himself, through imperial legates at various times, sent us word, as he did you, that he wished to come to Rome. We forbade him, and we altogether forbid him to undertake a journey in the condition in which he now is, because the holy Roman Church rejects and despises such a man and persists in this judgment, which has been spread throughout the world.

For, after long turning our eyes over your writings, we eagerly awaited reaching a point that would somehow grant us, even by a single word, a source of assistance by which we might anticipate some joy. But after examining everything and rereading it to the very end, once the reading was complete, the joy that had been present withdrew, and continual sorrow immediately took possession of us, because we were frustrated in every respect and, contrary to our wishes, abandoned.

Nevertheless, since you have arranged to admonish Lothair again around the feast of Saint John, concerning which we spoke, we did not take this amiss. Perhaps almighty God will deign to incline his heart toward what pleases him and, by converting him, finally make the transgressor beloved.

But if it is said that he secretly wishes to reclaim Theutberga in order to destroy her, then, if she chooses people through whom the most certain security for her can be guaranteed, let this be done. Otherwise, let Lothair provide an oath by which he promises to receive her in a worthy marriage, to honor and cherish her properly as his legitimate wife, and thereafter to keep her safe.

As for his penance, reserving the matter to our judgment, we have determined that if he wishes craftily to bring some other charges against the aforesaid Theutberga after he rejected her, this shall be cleared up by an oath, if necessity so requires.

But if she decides to remain unmarried and refuses to be reconciled with her husband, we decree that she be compelled to return to the embraces of marriage, because it was not the will of both parties to separate. If, however, both had consented to the divorce and Lothair had altogether ceased to resume intercourse, we do not prohibit this from being done, because the Lord made only the cause of fornication an exception regarding the dismissal of a wife.

Therefore, if Lothair—whose conversion we have hitherto awaited, and against whom we delayed making our vengeance known lest blood be shed and wars be stirred up—raises his horn and neglects to obey our warnings and yours, he must henceforth be regarded as the man whom you already know we treated as such in our letter sent to Rhadoald, formerly bishop, and to Bishop John.

But, dearest sons, singularly beloved by us, behold, we have sent the venerable Bishop Arsenius there with apostolic letters to discuss this matter with you and to correct him by admonitions.
