We have transmitted copies of these letters to your greatness through this bearer, so that, if the authentic letters had been intercepted, or defaced by those who perhaps handled them, or lost, or even treated otherwise according to their own pleasure in a way that might generate doubt in you about believing them, you would have these copies.

If you find that the authentic letters agree with these, give your assent to Arsenius. Otherwise, except concerning Rothad and Albuin, you ought not to believe him. Whatever is done in those regions, do not fail to send us a well-secured report under the form of official acts before we learn of it through others, so that we may be able to labor more effectively.

There are also many other matters that we ought to have commanded you, but since a few things are sufficient for men so illustrious and prudent, and since this bearer was unknown to us and unaware of these matters, we have ceased writing beyond them.

Concerning the Church of Cologne, about which you consulted us, we decree that a bishop be consecrated there. Concerning Cambrai, we wish the arrangement we have established to be observed: namely, that if there has been a canonical election, a bishop should be consecrated there.

Finally, there is something about which we cannot remain silent; indeed, we are astonished at your statements: namely, concerning the Church of Soissons. For, my son Charles, in what you say you speak through another’s mouth. You say that for approximately thirty years it has been uselessly occupied by Rothad, an unfruitful fig tree, and, apart from the name alone, has been deprived of pastoral care. We wonder why so great a king yields to persuasive words and does not instead strive to make us rejoice that Rothad obeys.

Therefore, cease, my son, and drive entreating words from your heart. Begin to obey our warnings, so that your most excellent glory may bear fruit with exultation and gather sheaves with joy. Nevertheless, how your Highness ought to act concerning him you will be able to learn more clearly from another letter of ours.

Once you know this, we believe that we shall obtain what we ask and that what we have decreed will be regarded as settled before the eyes of God and before you. For in our judgment the same Rothad remains a fruitful fig tree; but after his judgment has been renewed, it will be plainly shown whether he is fruitful or unfruitful, with all matters handled according to what we have decided concerning him.

We did not have this letter written in the customary manner because your legate could not wait, and, because of the Easter festivities, we were unable to have our scribes available as we should have, since they were occupied with their proper duties.

Furthermore, we ask and expressly adjure you to consider with the inner eye, not merely the outer, that what has been written above has proceeded not from simplicity of expression but from how great a sorrow and compunction; and consider in these matters all our needs, moved with compassion by the grief of a father, as our dearest sons. May the divine majesty preserve you unharmed for the exaltation of his holy Church.

---

**(In the year 865.) LXXXIV. TO EMPEROR LOUIS II. Fragment.—Everyone should submit to the judgment of his own primate, not to that of others.**

*[In Mansi, same place.]*

Finally, if Suffredus knew of a crime in himself for which he could rightly be deprived of the episcopate, or if he perhaps felt himself weighed down by an illness that prevented him from benefiting those nearby in his office, he ought to have awaited the judgment of his own primate, and not that of bishops of another diocese.

But if any ambiguity had arisen, or some dispute had perhaps emerged concerning his examination or his renunciation of the episcopate, it ought by custom to have been referred to the apostolic see, and everyone ought to have awaited our decrees in all these matters.

Because we grieve that this has so far been omitted, I earnestly implore your beloved greatness that the aforementioned Bishop Suffredus be restored to his own episcopate, and that, if he has done anything deserving of blame, it thereafter be determined either by correction or by fitting disciplinary judgment.

---

**(In the year 865.) LXXXV. TO SOLOMON, KING OF THE BRITONS, AND HIS WIFE. He refuses to send the pallium to Festinian, bishop of Dol, until he is convinced by authentic documents of his right to it.**

*[In Mansi, same place.]*

**[Col. 0925D]**

To Solomon, king of the Britons, and to his wife Gyembret.

Our apostolate had indeed proposed to respond individually to the suggestions of your Majesty. But whether the writings brought to us by a certain priest and other men of the British people were truly suggestions is made uncertain to us by the opening of the writing itself and by the impression of the seal, which was missing from the page.

Therefore your prudence must now take care to send us your writings impressed with your own sign and secured by [lacuna], so that nothing may craftily be added, removed, or changed except what you have ordered to be inserted in them.

Since the matters you are believed to have requested are pious, we shall therefore take care to disclose to your affection, in a brief style and as God inspires, what concerns them.

You ask us, then, to send the pallium to our brother and fellow bishop Festinian, who is recognized as presiding over the church of Saint Samson. We do not do this for the present because, as we remember writing to you formerly, no solemn petition appears to have been submitted for so great a dignity, nor was the request made in the proper legitimate order that should follow.

Therefore, leaving many matters aside, now that the time has passed, take care that he who greatly desires to be considered worthy of such merit among us and wishes, with the Lord’s help, to obtain such a gift, transmit those writings that his predecessors received from the apostolic see when they accepted the pallium. Thus, after carefully examining those same writings given by my predecessors, we may proceed in their footsteps, and in yours, with unhindered steps.

Let him also send other writings together with a suitable legate from his own clergy: the writings, namely, bearing the promised documents of the catholic faith and of the decretal sanctions that must be observed from the chair of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; and the legate, who, with his hands placed upon the sacred book of the Gospels, shall affirm by oath that his bishop believes and will henceforth observe what those writings sent to us by him are known to testify or contain.

For such is the authority of the apostolic see and the unshakable observance of the holy Roman Church, over which, by God’s appointment, we preside.

Whoever he may be, let him hurry here fully equipped in every respect, so that, if necessary, he may be able to remain here at least thirty days, lest the desire to depart deprive him of whatever ecclesiastical usefulness and custom require.

Finally, we admonish you that whenever you send us a letter, you should send as its bearer a man who is not driven by any disturbance, but who will remain with us until we are able to reply to what you consult us about with prudent consideration and sufficient time.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, in the thirteenth indiction.

---

**(In the year 865.) LXXXVI. TO EMPEROR MICHAEL. He rebukes the emperor, who, puffed up with pride and arrogance, had written many insolent things. He then demonstrates that the deposition of Ignatius has no validity, since he had been condemned by suspect and excommunicated bishops of inferior rank. He further recalls many privileges of the Roman Church and orders Ignatius and Photius to come to him, or their legates if they themselves cannot. He admonishes the emperor to obey his commands and rebukes him because he arranged for Ignatius to be deposed in a council and was the first to subscribe to his deposition.**

*[In Mansi, same place.]*

**[Col. 0926D]**

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most pious and dearest son, the emperor of the nations [Roman edition: “the conqueror”], and to the most tranquil emperor, Michael, ever Augustus, protected by God.

[Col. 0927A] Indeed, before the glorious Michael, your protospatharius and envoy, came to Rome bearing us a letter from Your Brightness, we had proposed sending you through our messengers writings of such a kind as the most weighty [perhaps: “most welcome”] son was accustomed to receive from a devoted father and worshiper of God—namely, as emperors were accustomed to receive from the pontiffs of the apostolic see. But when the aforesaid man arrived and presented us with your letter, which was wholly full of blasphemies and wholly full of insults, our harp was changed into mourning (Lam. V), and our organ into the voice of those who weep (Isa. V). For we expected grapes from a good vine, but received wild grapes; therefore we changed our style and, having displayed the wound, foresaw the application of appropriate medicines.

[Col. 0927B] Accordingly, as we are about to write to Your Power, with the Lord inspiring us, and to disclose to our mind the disposition of your diligence, as well as to intercede with you on behalf of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church—whose care in particular, and whose daily anxiety according to the Apostle, binds us—and to answer the assertions of your letter as the Lord grants us the ability and knowledge, we judge that nothing is more opportune, nothing more suitable, and certainly nothing more salutary—even though you began with insults—than humbly to beseech above all the One through whom kings reign, lawgivers decree what is just, and in whose hand are the hearts of kings; from whom every person who reigns piously derives his rule, and every person rules who does not resist that King of kings and Lord of lords: namely, our Lord Jesus [Col. 0927C] Christ, whom every rational creature serves.

He is the One whom even the insensible winds obey, and whom the sea obeys when he commands. May he open our lips to proclaim his praise, and may he also fill our open mouth with the nourishment of saving doctrine; may he himself, by the prompting of his inspiration, breathe inwardly upon your minds what we say outwardly to your ears through the office of our apostolate. For in vain is the soil of the heart ploughed by the ploughshare of our tongue unless it is inwardly watered by the sprinkling of heavenly dew. For God is the one who gives the increase (I Cor. III) and who teaches human beings knowledge (Ps. XCIII).

Do you suppose, Emperor, that we are not acting rightly: that you began your writing with insults, while we begin with prayers; that you began by reviling us—indeed, by speaking against the first [Col. 0927D] and chief teacher of all the churches—while we are about to address Your Power in praise and in the name of the Lord, and have opened our mouth? For we see a foreign giant, filled with fury and spewing forth blasphemies, opposing the holy boy and our harpist David, and at his first assault bringing no little terror upon the people of God (I Reg. XVII). But wait a little, and behold, you will see him struck down in the name of the Lord and, by the very hymn-singer who humbly pours forth praises, psalms, and prayers before the majesty of the Lord, felled by his own sword.

Indeed, we gladly endure insults directed specifically against us, especially when they are hurled at those laboring for justice by the opponents of justice. For we are disciples of the one of whom the chief of the apostles says: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten” (I Pet. II). Concerning such matters Truth says: “If they have called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more his domestics?” (Matt. X.) And again, he declares blessed those who would endure persecution and curses for his name, saying: “Blessed are you when they curse you, persecute you, and speak every evil against you falsely because of me” (Matt. V).

Wherever, then, God is in the cause, as conscience bears witness, blessedness is wholly to be hoped for; and where falsehood rages, no insults are to be feared. Therefore, just as for God’s sake we endure with equanimity the insults inflicted upon us even by those who speak what is untrue, so too it is fitting for Your Piety, for his sake whom they serve, to show priests—whatever they may be—reverence rather than insults.

But on these matters let us now speak with you through holy Pope Gregory (Epistles, Book IV, Letter 31): For in the divine utterances priests are sometimes called gods and sometimes angels. Thus through Moses it is said concerning the man who is to be brought for an oath: “Bring him to the gods” (Exod. XXII), that is, to the priests. And again it is written: “You shall not disparage the gods” (ibid.), namely, the priests. And the prophet says: “The lips of the priest shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II).

[Col. 0928C] What wonder, then, if imperial piety honors those whom God himself, granting them honor in his own utterance, calls either angels or gods? Ecclesiastical history also bears witness (Rufinus, Ecclesiastical History, Book I, chapter 2) that when written accusations against bishops had been presented to the emperor Constantine of pious memory, he indeed accepted the documents and, summoning the bishops who had been accused, burned before them the documents he had received, saying: “You are gods, appointed by the true God. Go and settle your cases among yourselves, for it is not fitting that we should judge gods.” In this statement he conferred more upon himself through humility than he bestowed upon them through the reverence shown to them.

Before him, pagan rulers had been leaders in the commonwealth who, not knowing the true God, worshiped wooden and stone gods, yet nevertheless granted their priests the greatest honor. [Col. 0928D] What wonder, then, if a Christian emperor honors the priests of the true God, when pagan rulers, as we have said, knew how to bestow honor upon priests who served wooden and stone gods?

We therefore assert these things not so much specifically as generally on behalf of all priests, since we still do not know what sort of person each one will prove to be at God’s terrible judgment. For the outstanding preacher Paul says: “Do not judge before the appointed time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the things hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts” (I Cor. II). Yet we say this briefly: although we are sinners and unworthy, we place greater confidence in the mercy of the Lord who is to come than in your piety.

[Col. 0929A] For there are many things concerning his judgment that human beings do not know: perhaps what you praise he will condemn, and what you condemn he will praise. You must therefore carefully consider not what sort of men the priests of the Lord are, but what they say concerning the Lord. Nor should you attend to who the vicars of the blessed Apostle Peter are, but what they undertake for the correction of the churches and for your salvation.

For you will not say that they are inferior to the scribes and Pharisees who sat upon Moses’ seat, concerning whom the Lord commanded, saying: “Whatever they tell you, do and observe; but do not act according to their works” (Matt. XXIII). Consider, then, Emperor: if he said that those who sat upon Moses’ seat were to be heard, how much more do you think obedience ought to be given to those who sit upon Peter’s seat? And if he commands that their words, not their works, be done and observed, how much more must the words and admonitions of these men, whoever they may be, be kept and embraced?

What evil, then, do we desire [perhaps: “Do we desire? Why are you angry in vain ...,” HARD.] that you are angry without cause? Why do you suppose that we should be assailed with the charge of frivolity, contrary to the Gospel, which says: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. V), when we strive to offer you nothing except what is salutary, nothing except what is acceptable to God?

[Col. 0929C] Yet we know that we endure both spittle and blows from the madmen whom we carry [as in the commentary, Galas. to Faustus: “Thus madmen are accustomed [to act], etc.,” HARD.], while nevertheless presenting them with what pertains to their salvation. By the abundance of God’s grace we also occupy the place of those who, laboring for the truth, often suffered such things from the Constantinopolitans as we are now recognized to be suffering—things that we shall sufficiently demonstrate below whenever the occasion requires. For we do not judge it lawful to allow ourselves to be thought, in imitation of inferiors [ed. Rom. adds: “and weaklings”], to be such as we see ourselves proclaimed by you to be.

Following the example of the Savior, who, when he heard from the Jews, “You have a demon,” rejected the charge by humbly saying, “I do not have a demon” (John VIII), we too, when we hear things about ourselves that are untrue, strive to remove them from ourselves by a truthful and reasonable reply.

Nevertheless, whatever you have written to the injury of the Roman Church, to the diminution of its privileges, and to the disparagement of the pontiffs of the apostolic see, we shall repel with as much firmness as we can; and, restrained by no terrors or calumnies of yours, we shall strive with all the strength we can to destroy them as hostile to the truth.

You said that none of our predecessors had deserved from you, since the Sixth Synod, what we are recognized to have deserved. Yet you gave no clear indication whatsoever of what we had deserved, unless perhaps by this statement you intended us to understand that we had deserved only now to receive commendatory letters from you, since the Sixth Synod, on account of some doctrine or ecclesiastical discipline.

You say this as though it were our disgrace that your predecessors had not deigned to seek the apostolic see in any matter, when their conduct was rather a dishonor to them: throughout so many years they did not seek medicinal aid while languishing from the diseases of various heresies; instead, like desperate men or those possessing an impenitent heart, they threw away the medicine voluntarily offered to them by us from their very jaws, while they destroyed in two ways the ministers who had offered them so great a salvation.

They either killed them spiritually by making them participants in their error, as happened in the time of Pope Conon of revered memory, who existed after the Sixth Synod; or else they killed them bodily when they refused to agree with them, as happened under the venerable Pope Gregory, who was after the Sixth Synod, when religious men and servants of God were sent into exile for their zeal for the faith and their reverence for the holy images [Col. 0930B], and ended their lives with a good confession.

Finally, since the Sixth Synod, emperors have been either heretics or, although very few, Catholics. If the heretics disdained to send to us, this is not surprising: for they knew that by God’s grace we would never become wholly allied with them. There was a time, however, when they repeatedly attempted to ally themselves with us but were rejected with great disgrace and shame, and were repeatedly repulsed by us with worthy firmness—not by the Church of Constantinople.

When they were Catholics and wished to defend a pious doctrine or ecclesiastical correction, they sought our support, as the synod held under Constantine and Irene indicates (Seventh Synod, Act [Col. 0930C] 2). At its beginning, that is, in the letter of Adrian, the pontiff of blessed memory, if you investigate carefully you will certainly find how strongly that same pontiff condemned the presumption by which certain laymen are suddenly tonsured and then rush headlong into the ranks of the bishops—provided, however, that the letter has not been falsified in the Greek manner, but remains with the Church of Constantinople as it was sent from the apostolic see. The various letters sent to the most holy pontiffs, namely our predecessors Leo and Benedict, bear witness to this.

Since these things are so, then, and we have recalled only some matters from among many, it is no longer true that what we have now deserved to receive from you was not deserved by us from the time of the Sixth Synod [perhaps “that we did not deserve,” HARD.].

[Col. 0930D] Furthermore, you wrote that you had ordered certain persons who are under our authority to be sent to you. This is far removed from the disposition of pious emperors, whose place you occupy; would that you also followed their piety. It is far removed, I say, from the practice of rulers who observe reverence for the pontiffs of the apostolic see.

Honorius certainly did not say this when he wrote to the reverend pontiff Boniface, saying (Honorius, in his letter to Boniface I): “We ask that Your Apostolate deign, in your daily prayers, to offer its zeal and prayer for the welfare and rule of us.”

Nor did the pious pair, Valentinian and Marcian, say this when writing to blessed Pope Leo: “We have thought it just,” he says, “to address your holiness, who possesses primacy in the episcopate of the divine faith, by a sacred letter at the beginning, inviting and asking that your holiness beseech the eternal Divinity on behalf of the stability and standing of our empire.”

Justinian likewise did not say this when he spoke to holy Pope John, inserting the matter even into laws he promulgated (law “Nos reddentes,” Code, On the Holy Trinity): “We ask your paternal affection that, in letters sent by you to us, your holiness make clear to us that you receive all who rightly confess the aforesaid faith, and condemn those who have dared, in Jewish fashion, to deny the true faith.” And again: “We ask,” he says, “that Your Blessedness pray for us and obtain for us the providence of God.”

Constantine did not say this when, writing to Pope Donus, he displayed goodwill and honor toward the apostolic see, even invoking an oath, in these words: “By God Almighty,” he says, “there is with us no partial favor, but we shall preserve equality for both parties. We shall in no way impose any compulsion upon those who are sent by you, in any matter whatever; rather, we shall treat them as worthy of every honor, with appropriate generosity and reception. If the two sides indeed reach agreement, good; but if they do not agree, we shall send them back to you again with every mark of humanity.”

And shortly afterward: “For we can invite and ask for every correction and for the unity of all Christians, but we in no way wish to impose compulsion.”

The other Constantine and Irene Augusta did not say this either. Writing to Pope Adrian, they say: “We ask Your Paternal Blessedness—or rather, the Lord God asks, who wishes all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (I Tim. II)—to give yourself and make no delay, and to come up here.” And a little later: “If he cannot come up here,” they say, “let him choose men of the highest worth and send them together with written instructions, and so forth.”

[Col. 0931D] O Emperor, do you not recognize, at least now, how much you differ in this matter from the piety of the earlier emperors, and how your conduct differs from the divinely inspired modesty of those men? They repeatedly say, scattered throughout their writings to the pontiffs of the apostolic see, “We ask,” “we invite,” and “we entreat,” yet they speak with equal piety.

You, however, as though you had become heirs not of their gentleness and reverence but of their imperial power alone, and as though you were unwilling to imitate them in matters of piety, assert that you commanded, ordered, and imposed upon us that we send certain of our subjects to you. We do not know whether you really did this; you say so while fascinated by whose instigations and given over to forgetfulness. We do not recall any such action on your part; nor, if we are not mistaken, do we remember that you have ever commanded such a thing to us. We have never known you to have descended to such irreverence toward the see of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

For when we review the letter that you then sent through the venerable bishops and Arsa, the glorious spatharius, we find that you did not command us anything at all, but rather earnestly entreated and asked us. From this it becomes clear that, since you now claim otherwise, either you have forgotten what you previously sent, or else you have repented of what you had humbly asked.

[Col. 0932A] You have burst forth into such an excess of fury that you inflicted an insult upon the Latin language, calling it barbarian and Scythian in your letter, to the injury of its maker; for every disparagement of a work rebounds upon the injury of its maker.

O fury, which does not even know how to spare the language that God made, and which, among the other languages, in the name of the Lord, at the Apostle’s exhortation, “confesses that our Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II)! This language, distinguished from the others together with Hebrew and Greek in the title of the Lord, holds an eminent primacy and proclaims to all nations “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews”—the title that many Jews tried to corrupt (John XIX), just as you now attempt to destroy the distinction of this most celebrated language, but have been utterly unable to do so.

For it had been divinely written in the Book of Psalms: “Do not corrupt the inscription of the title” (Pss. LVI, LVII, and LVIII). Or rather, since Christians, whose language you call barbarian or Scythian, are your glory, we are astonished that you are not ashamed. For since all barbarians and Scythians live like senseless animals, do not know the true God, and worship wood and stone, it is recognized by the very fact that the Latin language worships the true God how greatly it surpasses a barbarian or Scythian language.

But if you call the language barbarian because you do not understand it, consider that it is ridiculous for you to be called emperors of the Romans and yet not know the Roman language.

[Col. 0932C] Finally, if you now call the language so often mentioned barbarian because, when it is changed by translators into Greek expression, it produces barbarisms, the fault, as we think, lies not with the Latin language but with the interpreters, who, when necessary, strive to render not sense from sense but, forcibly, word from word.

For behold, at the beginning of your letter you called yourselves emperors of the Romans, and yet you do not hesitate to call the Roman language barbarian. Behold, every day—or rather, on the principal festivals—you mingle this language, which you call barbarian and Scythian, with the Greek language as though it were something precious; it would apparently diminish your dignity if you did not use it, even imperfectly and without full understanding, in your services and offices.

[Col. 0932D] Cease, then, to call yourselves Roman emperors, since, according to your own judgment, those whose emperors you claim to be are barbarians.

For the Romans use this language that you call barbarian and Scythian. Cease now to mention in your palace an expression that you hold in such detestation; and if you utterly execrate it, strive also to remove it from your churches.

For it is said that the Church of Constantinople first recites the apostolic and evangelical readings in the usage of this language at its stations, and only afterward pronounces those same readings in the Greek tongue, for the Greeks, of course. But since it is thought that this impiety alone has until now been lacking to the Church of Constantinople, so that every wickedness there might be complete, this is the one thing left for you to accomplish.

For the present, however, let it suffice that we have answered concerning this matter: our purpose is not so much to defend the language against insult as to emphasize the inconsistency of your changed mind.

Moreover, you say that you did not send to us so that Ignatius might undergo judgment according to your decision. To this we answer truthfully that you certainly sent for that purpose, since the subsequent outcome proves it. For if you had not wished it, you would not have allowed it to happen.

Rather, to speak more accurately, we did not send so that our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius might undergo just any judgment in the meantime, but so that his case, carefully investigated and fully ascertained, might be disclosed to us in a complete and unhesitating report, in accordance with the words of blessed Job: “I investigated most diligently the case that I did not know” (Job XXIX).

[Col. 0933B] Then, once we had been informed by the reports of our envoys in accordance with the sacred canons, if we decided that persons should be sent who, present with the bishops and possessing our authority, would judge the case, it would be within our discretion to determine who should be sent. If, however, we believed that the bishops were sufficient to bring the matter to an end, we would do what we judged by the wisest decision.

But if Ignatius, as you claim, had already been judged, why did you wish him to undergo a second judgment [perhaps “to be judged a second time,” HARD.], contrary to what is written: “He shall not judge the same matter twice” (Nahum I)? In this it is plainly shown that, when you dragged him again before the tribunals of the council, you did not possess a good conscience. Rather, as though he had not been perfectly or lawfully deposed, you attempted to subject him to condemnation in the presence of our envoys, who possessed greater authority [perhaps “to the condemnation of our envoys,” and shortly afterward “to the damnation,” HARD.].

When you say that he was condemned synodally, perhaps because you did not add “canonically,” what was done was divinely ordained. For an assembly of evildoers, not a canonically judging assembly, had subjected him to condemnation—or rather, had subjected him to affliction and tribulation.

Indeed, those who then assembled against the aforesaid venerable man were either suspect and his enemies of yesterday and the day before, or excommunicated, or deposed, or his subjects, or else of inferior rank. Without any doubt, none of them could possess the standing of legitimate judges—or of accusers, at least in all matters [Col. 0933D]. With God’s instruction, we shall attempt to demonstrate each point separately and all of them together.

Since suspect and hostile persons ought not to be judges, both reason itself dictates this and numerous examples confirm it. For what more agreeable and welcome gift can anyone give an enemy than to entrust to him, for prosecution, the person whom he may wish to injure? The Constantinopolitan synod is known to prohibit this in the sixth chapter of its canons, a chapter said not to have been found among us but to be preserved among you.

Nevertheless, instructed by apostolic teachings, we know that even the sayings of pagans may be used—how much more those of Christians and Catholics—even against the very people whose life we do not follow and whose erroneous mind we do not imitate.

The Apostle Paul, for example, included certain statements from pagan books in his writings, as in his letter to Titus: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies, and greedy” (Titus I). And again, in the Acts of the Apostles he says of God: “In him we live, and move, and are” (Acts XVII). Does that mean that everything else uttered along with these statements must also be accepted?

The aforesaid canon says: “Since many, wishing to confuse and overthrow the ecclesiastical order, fabricate certain charges against the orthodox bishops who administer the churches, out of hatred and through calumny, attempting nothing other than to defile the reputation of priests and to produce disturbances among sinful peoples, therefore it has pleased the holy synod of bishops who gathered at Constantinople that accusers not be admitted without examination, nor should everyone be directed to bring accusations against those who administer the churches.””

[Col. 0934B] Let us therefore come also to the holy Council of Chalcedon and hear what it reports to us concerning Athanasius, bishop of Perrha (Act XIV). When that bishop, summoned for the third time to the synod, did not appear, he had been canonically condemned by his patriarch. But solely because, when he was summoned to the synod, he cried out that the man judging him was his enemy, the holy Council of Chalcedon reserved the examination of the charges brought against him and decreed that he should recover his own church unless he were convicted anew.

If Athanasius, deposed by his patriarch because he complained of the patriarch’s hostility, was sent to have the judgment reopened, and if he was ordered to be restored to his own church unless manifest crimes stood in his way, how much more ought Ignatius—who was not merely a patriarch’s subject but himself the patriarch—under no circumstances to have been stripped of his own church by the decision of hostile and suspect judges?

Although this was done, he ought even more than Athanasius, whose enemies’ judgment was dissolved, to have been restored to his church.

Let our most eloquent Pope Gelasius also appear (in the Commonitorium to Faustus), that most powerful vanquisher of heretics, and let him explain to us what he said, in his customary manner, about the Constantinopolitans who were then suffering from this disease:

“I nevertheless ask them,” he says, “where the judgment they allege can be conducted: whether among themselves, so that the same persons may be both hostile witnesses and judges? Yet even human affairs ought not to be entrusted to such a judgment. If, in a judgment where the same persons are enemies and judges, even human matters ought not to be entrusted to it, how much less divine matters—that is, ecclesiastical matters? Let the wise person understand.”

Indeed, the pious emperor Justinian is known to have promulgated this principle in his laws (law “Apertissime,” Code, On Judgments), saying: “The person who considers a judge suspect may reject him before the suit begins, so that recourse may be had to another. For it is in a certain sense natural to avoid the snares of suspect judges and always to seek refuge from the judgment of enemies.”

For this reason holy Athanasius often avoided the snares of his enemies; for this reason holy John Chrysostom refused to enter the council assembled against him. Indeed, for this reason the psalmist David and Elijah, that outstanding prophet, wholly avoided the madness of Saul and Ahab (I Reg. XXII; III Reg. XIX).

[Col. 0935A] That those who had been deposed, excommunicated, or anathematized by the aforementioned brother and fellow minister of ours, Ignatius, could not bring any condemnation against him is made clear by the chapter of the Second Ecumenical Council, which says (chapter 6):

“If the crime brought against a bishop is ecclesiastical, then the persons of the accusers must first be examined, so that, in the first place, heretics may not be permitted to bring accusations against orthodox bishops in ecclesiastical matters.”

But lest you deny that these men were heretics, hear what follows: “We call heretics those who were formerly cast out by the Church, as well as those who afterward were anathematized by us.”

If you still do not believe this, hear what is added: “Besides these, we also include those who pretend to confess the sound faith; schismatics too, and those who, separated from the bishops who are in communion with us, hold private assemblies.”

Furthermore, “if certain persons have been reproved by the Church on particular charges and have been cast out or excommunicated, whether from the clergy or from the lay order, neither are these permitted to accuse a bishop until they have first cleared themselves of their own crime.”

Likewise, those who are themselves subject to a prior accusation are not to be admitted to accuse a bishop or other clerics until they have shown themselves innocent of the crimes charged against them.

[Col. 0935C] You are not unaware of the danger that threatens those who despise this rule. Moreover, who among those sitting there was not one of the aforesaid heretics and schismatics? Was not Gregory of Syracuse condemned a thousand times? Were not Eulampius, Peter, and another Peter—who, for their unspeakable acts, confessed with their own mouths, incurred deposition and then anathema—among them? And there were others whom it would take too long to enumerate.

Behold the sort of men who, among the rest, were not ashamed to open their mouths against their venerable father, contrary to the rule of the one hundred and fifty Fathers. Though bound, they attempted to bind; though dead and already foul-smelling in their inner chambers, they attempted to kill a man fragrant throughout the whole world and to bespatter him with the stenches of an evil reputation.

But observe again what the pontiff of the Roman see—derided by you, yet venerated by the unanimity of all Christianity—Coelestine, president of the great Synod of Ephesus, decrees concerning those who had been deposed and excommunicated by Nestorius, after Nestorius himself was believed already to have been deposed before the eyes of the supreme Judge.

You should consider this judgment to apply all the more to our brother and fellow priest Ignatius, who suffered such things not from some ordinary prelate, as those men did, but from persons whom he himself had deposed. For writing to the eastern bishops he says (Letter 6):

“If anyone, whether by Bishop Nestorius or by others who follow him, from the time they began to preach such things, has been either excommunicated or stripped of the dignity of bishop or cleric, it is evident that he both has remained and remains in our communion. Nor do we judge him to have been removed, because no one could remove anyone by a sentence who had already made himself liable to removal.”

Again, the same man says plainly to the clergy of Constantinople (Letter 4):

“The authority of our see has decreed that no one—whether bishop, cleric, or Christian by any profession—who, from the time Nestorius or his associates began to preach such things, was cast out either from his position or from communion, is to be regarded as deposed or excommunicated. Rather, all these persons both were and remain until now in our communion, because no one could either depose or remove a person who, while preaching such things, was himself wavering.”

[Col. 0936A] Do you understand, Emperor, from what has been said above, that those who had themselves formerly been removed could not remove anyone, much less their own prelate, nor could those already cast down depose anyone?

We also believe that the following is useful for weakening the sentence of the condemned. The holy synod, reporting to the aforementioned pope what had taken place among them (Council of Ephesus, letter to Coelestine), in order to cut short the exaggerated presumption of John, bishop of Antioch, stated that some of those who barked against holy Cyril and Memnon were without cities, vacant, and without churches; others had been deposed many years earlier by their metropolitans for serious causes, among many others.

In large part, your own men, so to speak, who deposed Ignatius may rightly be compared with them. For there too bishops were found without sees, wandering, and deprived of their episcopates by their own metropolitans for their grievous crimes. There too they are proved to have been excluded from communion and partners in the condemnation of anathema.

We therefore marvel how excommunicated men were admitted to judge, since according to the apostolic canons persons are forbidden to be received into communion without letters of recommendation (Council of Carthage III, canon 21). For it is absurd that someone who, according to the sacred rules, may not communicate even with the least persons should be permitted among you to judge even the greatest.

[Col. 0936C] But let us now speak fully on this matter, with God’s help, and demonstrate that a prelate ought not to suffer loss at the hands of his subjects or be attacked by their calumnies.

Because our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius endured this unjustly, it must be lamented with every expression of grief. Certainly, fathers are commanded to be honored by their children not only by divine laws (Exod. XX) but also by human laws. If this is required of carnal fathers, how much more ought spiritual fathers to receive complete and fitting veneration from their children? For as much as the spirit surpasses the flesh, so much more ought spiritual things to be preferred to all carnal things.

But if the subjects of Ignatius disdained to heed this, at least they should have shuddered to commit the crime that the Jews perpetrated against Christ. They should not, like serpents, have sharpened their tongues against their father and teacher; their lips should not have been a sword, nor their teeth weapons and arrows, nor their tongue a sharp sword. They should have feared that the wisest Solomon might seem to have spoken of them: “A generation that curses its father” (Prov. XXX). And again: “A generation whose teeth are swords, and which gnashes with its molars” (ibid.). And again: “The eye that mocks its father—may the ravens of the torrents pluck it out, and the sons of the eagle devour it” (Gen. IX).

Finally, if Ham, seeing his father’s nakedness, laughed rather than covering it, as the others did, and is read to have received a curse in his son, how much more should those have been cursed who not only failed to cover their father’s shame—if there was any—but also laughed at it, falsely incited others to mock his manner of life, and, what is worse, openly drew the arrow of judgment from the quiver of their iniquity against him?

Not so the sober sons; not so. They turned away and covered him. The outstanding teacher, Pope Gregory, interpreted this morally, saying (Moralia, Book XV, chapter 22): “We say that we turn away from what we reject.”

What, then, does it mean that the sons cover their father’s nakedness by coming with their backs turned and with a cloak thrown over them, except that good subjects so dislike the evils of their prelates that they nevertheless conceal them from others? They carry the covering behind them because, while judging the deed and venerating the office of teaching, they do not wish it to be seen what they cover.

But in saying these things, do not suppose that we wish to defend anything among our neighbors that deserves condemnation. Rather, we wish children to be so devoted and sober toward their spiritual father, and disciples toward their teacher, that they do not, with any rashness whatsoever, rush forward to judge their lives—or, to put it more mildly, even to criticize them slightly.

For, as the aforesaid pope teaches in the book of the Pastoral Rule (Book III, chapter 5):

“Subjects must be admonished not rashly to judge the life of their prelates if they perhaps see them acting reprehensibly, lest, in the very matter by which they rightly rebuke evils, they be plunged into deeper things through the impulse of pride. They must be admonished that, when they consider the faults of their prelates, they should not become more daring against them; rather, they should judge within themselves whatever in their prelates is seriously perverse, yet, constrained by the fear of God, should not refuse to bear the yoke of reverence under them.”

We demonstrate this more clearly if we bring David’s deed into the discussion. For when Saul the persecutor had entered a cave to relieve his bowels, David was there with his men, having by then endured the evils of Saul’s persecution for so long; and when his men incited him to strike Saul, he restrained them with rebukes, because he ought not to lay a hand upon the Lord’s anointed. Yet he rose secretly and cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak (1 Samuel 21).

For what is signified by Saul if not evil rulers? And by David if not good subjects? Saul’s relieving his bowels therefore signifies wicked superiors extending the malice conceived in their hearts into deeds of miserable stench, and displaying through external actions the harmful thoughts they have entertained within themselves. David, however, feared to strike him: for the devout minds of subjects, abstaining from every plague of detraction, strike the lives of their superiors with no sword of the tongue, even when they criticize some imperfection. Yet if at times, because of weakness, they can scarcely restrain themselves and speak humbly of certain extreme and outward faults of their superiors, they cut silently, as it were, the edge of the cloak: that is, while they harmlessly and secretly diminish the dignity placed over them, they are like those who soil the garment of a king set above them. Nevertheless, they return to themselves and rebuke themselves most severely even for the slightest tearing of a word. Hence it is rightly written there also: “After this David’s heart struck him, because he had cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak” (1 Samuel 24).

The deeds of superiors are not to be struck with the sword of the mouth, even when they are judged rightly deserving of criticism. If the tongue at any time slips against them, even in the smallest matter, the heart must necessarily be weighed down through the affliction of repentance, so that it may return to itself and, having offended against the authority placed over it, dread the judgment against itself of the one by whom that authority was set over it.

For when we offend against superiors, we oppose the ordering of the one who placed them over us. Thus Moses too, when he learned that the people were complaining against himself and Aaron, said: “What indeed are we? Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord” (Exodus 16). Likewise the apostle Paul, preacher of the truth, says to his subjects and to those to whom he preached Christ’s Gospel: “But to me it is a very small matter that I should be judged by you” (1 Corinthians 4).

For this reason Sixtus, bishop of the apostolic see, is described as having condemned Bishop Euphemius (*On the Purification of Pope Sixtus III*, chapter 8), alleging nothing else in his deposition except that he had accused Polychronius, bishop of Jerusalem, his pontiff.

Indeed, Polychronius was deprived of the governance of the Church and expelled from the city by legates of the apostolic see because he had falsely asserted that the see of Jerusalem was the first and had been proved to have performed ordinations through the heresy of simony. Yet Euphemius likewise, because he had presumptuously—although truthfully—accused him, was subjected to condemnation by a synod.

And because he had raised his tongue against the one placed over him, he received an anathema, so much so that Leo, a deacon of the Roman Church, said to him: “For you will be condemned by yourself, because you were condemning and accusing the pontiff who consecrated you as a co-bishop.” Falling to the ground before the entire council of bishops assembled there, he confessed that he had sinned, while Bishop Abundius, sent from the city of Rome, said: “No one is permitted to accuse his own pontiff, because a judge will not be judged.” When he heard this, Augustus Valentinian—as it is written among us, and as you ought in this matter to imitate him—rejoiced at the condemnation of Bishop Euphemius, who had become the accuser of Polychronius, his pontiff.

Saint Silvester too, and the baptizer of the great Constantine Augustus, agrees with this necessary judgment, saying: “He will be judged by neither Augustus, nor the entire clergy, nor kings, nor the people.”

There is no doubt that the ecclesiastical Pelagius, also an apostolic prelate, writing to a certain king of the Franks, says the same. [Note: To Childebert. This is the eleventh letter of Pope Pelagius:] “Although divine mercy has bestowed many gifts upon Your Highness, nevertheless, because of the love that you sincerely show toward his Church, it has made you more illustrious than many rulers. For it is certain that, among the other concerns of your kingdom, you display a special solicitude for the peace of the holy Church.”

Since these things are so, we are astonished that, as the report of the bearers presently before us has disclosed, you allowed both Sabandus, our brother and fellow bishop, the bishop of the city of Arles—whose Church in the Gallic regions is honored with the privilege of primacy and with the authority of the apostolic see—to be seized and ordered to appear for judgment before the bishop of a neighboring city, at the request of a bishop ordained by Sabandus himself. No ecclesiastical law or principle permits this. Thus, since he complains of the prejudice inflicted upon the dignity of his see, the one who usurped this authority must necessarily be censured for his unlawful presumption.

Therefore, relying confidently upon your Christian character, we ask with paternal concern that, if anything of this kind has occurred, it be swiftly removed through appropriate satisfaction, and that you not permit any such example to remain as a source of disturbance to the Churches that God has entrusted to you. In the future, you ought to exercise vigilant caution in cases of this kind, lest you grant anything contrary to ecclesiastical regulations to those who request it. For, as your religious mind knows well, royal devotion cannot rightly serve our God in any other way than by preserving the integrity of the ecclesiastical orders established by his providence.

Furthermore, our most gracious father and pope, Gregory, whom we mentioned above, giving instructions in a letter to the clergy of the Church of Milan concerning the election of their bishop, says (*Book II, Indiction XI, Letter 29*): “Therefore, weighing what is beneficial to all, and considering whom divine grace has placed over you, always render the most complete obedience in everything. For one who has once been placed over you ought no longer to be judged by you; rather, he must now be judged with the utmost care precisely because afterward he is not to be judged. Once, with God as its author, a pastor has been consecrated for you, commit yourselves to him with your whole mind, and serve in him the almighty God who has placed him over you.”

When all these points have been properly gathered, it has been shown, as we think, sufficiently clearly that subjects cannot lawfully judge the life of their superior, nor rashly criticize him—whatever his merit may be—except in the case of heresy.

But if you still wish to know something about this that may be pleasing, order the words of the ancient Father and venerable teacher Dionysius the Areopagite to Demophilus to be read to you. He even solemnly declares that, in a matter of piety, a priest who has committed an offense may not be judged by those who are lesser or inferior, lest something disordered occur in the Church of God and its condition be confused in any respect.

Thus far we have briefly proved that our brother and fellow minister Ignatius ought not to have been judged by his suffragans and subjects, nor easily criticized by them. Now, however, by divine inspiration, we shall not shrink from showing you—and it will not be impossible for us—if only you are willing to listen, that no one can rightly be subjected to judicial decisions by those who are inferior in dignity or order.

In the time of the Augusti Diocletian and Maximian, Marcellinus, bishop of the city of Rome, who afterward became a distinguished martyr, was so compelled by pagans that he entered their temple and placed grains of incense upon burning coals. For this reason a large council of bishops was assembled and an inquiry was conducted, and that same pontiff confessed that he had done this. [Note: At the Council of Sinuessa.]

Yet none of them dared to pronounce a sentence against him, although they all repeatedly said to him: “Judge your case with your own mouth, not by our judgment”; and again: “Do not,” they said, “let yourself be heard in our judgment, but gather your case into your own bosom”; and again: “For,” they said, “from yourself you will be justified, or from your own mouth you will be condemned”; and again they said: “The first see shall be judged by no one.”

[Column 0940B] For this reason too the confessor of Christ, Silvester, mentioned above, established degrees within the bosom of the synod (*Roman Synod*, chapter 3), so that no presbyter might bring any accusation against a bishop, no deacon against a presbyter, no subdeacon against a deacon, no acolyte against a subdeacon, no exorcist against an acolyte, no lector against an exorcist, and no doorkeeper against a lector; nor would the highest prelate be judged by anyone, because it is written: “The disciple is not above his teacher” (Matthew 10).

Likewise, when at a certain time some people attempted to bring accusations of ill repute against Pope Sixtus, and it was stated in the council at which Augustus Valentinian was also present (*On the Purification of Pope Sixtus III*, [Column 0940C] chapter 5) that it was not permitted to pronounce a sentence against a pontiff, the emperor immediately rose and granted the aforesaid pontiff the authority to judge his own case. For no pontiff is found to have been subjected to the judgments of lesser or inferior cities.

Thus John of Antioch, bishop of the third see, is read, among other things, as having been condemned in the synod of Ephesus until correction was made (*Letter to Celestine I*), because he presumptuously and irregularly condemned Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, that is, of the second see. The same venerable synod therefore petitioned Celestine, the prelate of the highest see, in writing as follows: “Let Your Religiousness therefore be duly indignant at these deeds. For if permission is granted to those who wish to afflict the greater sees with injuries and to pronounce sentences against them—against sees over which they have no authority—in violation alike of laws and canons, matters will proceed to the utter confusion of the Church.”

Then, in the holy Council of Chalcedon, when the judges charged Basil, bishop of Seleucia, with having subscribed to the condemnation of Flavian, and he replied, “Since I had been handed over for judgment to one hundred and twenty, or thirty, bishops, I was obliged to obey what they decreed,” and Dioscorus said to him in response, “Through shame before men you have transgressed what is good and have despised the faith. You did not heed what is written: ‘Do not be ashamed to your ruin,’” the aforementioned Bishop Basil replied: “If I had had martyrdom before the judges, I would have endured it. Indeed, at Constantinople I demonstrated my confidence; but he does not avail himself of a father who is judged righteous [HARD. reads: *qui judicatur, justis non utitur*, “one who is judged does not deal with the righteous”]; for a son, even when saying what is just to his father, must die.”

Finally, we read in the Epistle to the Hebrews that the lesser is blessed by the greater; it follows plainly, by the demand of reason, that he may also be cursed by him. For those who came before us, foreseeing these dangerous times, handed down a prudent custom in the Churches. Even today it is observed without interruption in the Roman Church, which is the teacher of all Churches, so that no priest attempts to bless anything without the indication of his greater fellow priest. Likewise, one who stands before the others to proclaim a reading requests a blessing, but no inferior person at all dares to bless him. Why is this? Is blessing a sin? Certainly not. For the Apostle speaks of those who curse, not those who bless: “They will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6). But by this it is indicated by what a strict bridle of discipline all inferiors must be restrained from judging their superiors, if they have no right even to bless them.

And truly, as we already said above from the Gospel, with blessed Silvester recalling it: “The disciple is not above his teacher” (Matthew 10). If he has no right to bless, how much less to curse?

The holy Fathers at Chalcedon detested this presumption to such an extent that, among other reasons, they condemned Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, without any possibility of restoration, chiefly because, persisting in contumacy toward the privilege of the first see, he refused to repent of his superstitions so that he might be preserved by the first apostolic see. “He set his mouth against heaven, and his tongue traversed the earth” (Psalm 72), and he pronounced excommunication against holy Pope Leo. Thus, in the sentence issued against him, they appear especially to have recalled this, saying that “by his second offenses he greatly surpassed his former iniquity. For he presumed to pronounce an excommunication against the most holy and blessed archbishop Leo of great Rome.”

Is it read there—in Action 1 of the Council of Chalcedon—that an inquiry was made into whether the aforesaid Dioscorus had pronounced that excommunication justly or unjustly? [HARD. reads, for the preceding wording: *jam fatus Dioscorus . . . dictasset*.] Not at all. Rather, without any controversy, they took vengeance upon him for this: although he was inferior, he had attempted to assail one superior with every kind of insult. Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, bears witness to this when he says: “Dioscorus was not condemned on account of the faith, but because he excommunicated Lord Archbishop Leo.”

For they wanted nothing rash, nothing confused, nothing disordered to occur in the house of God. Hence it was also suitably defined in the African council, chapter 53, as follows: “Let each one of us recognize the order appointed for him by God, and let those who come later defer to those who come before them; let them presume to do nothing without consulting them.”

The aforementioned Pope Gelasius, destroyer of many heresies, says in a decretal letter to all the bishops established throughout Dardania (*Letter 11*): “Certainly, if the dignity of cities is under discussion—of the second and third sees—the dignity of the priests is greater than that of a city which is not only scarcely counted among the sees, but is not even reckoned among metropolitan rights.”

And again, in the treatise addressed to the Eastern bishops, the same man says: “Especially when the matter concerns the prelate of the second see, he can be absolved by right not by any inferior, but by the first see. For an inferior cannot absolve a superior; therefore only a superior fittingly absolves an inferior.” From this it is clearly understood that an inferior cannot bind by judgment one whom he cannot absolve.

Moreover, when Theodoric, polluted by the dregs of the Arian heresy, wished to prosecute Pope Symmachus—even to condemnation, with many accusing him (*Roman Synod under Symmachus*)—and ordered as many bishops as he could gather from Liguria, Emilia, Valeria, various regions, and the island of Sicily to assemble at Rome for this purpose, he said to them upon their arrival that many horrifying reports concerning the deeds of Pope Symmachus had been brought to him and that, if the accusations of his enemies were true, this ought to be established by an inquiry in the synod.

The aforesaid pontiffs, who were about to undertake the defense, replied: “The one who was said to have been accused ought himself to have convened the synod.” They knew that to his see had been given, first through the merit or primacy of the apostle Peter, then through the command of the Lord and the authority of venerable councils that followed, a unique power in the Churches; and that no prelate of that see had previously been subjected to the judgment of inferiors.

And again they said: “Cases must be entrusted to the judgment of God himself, who can kill the body and cast the soul into Gehenna” (Luke 12), who says: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deuteronomy 32), before whom conscience is naked and from whom hidden things are not concealed.

Again, those same men said: “We reserved for the greater Judge what was being alleged, instructing them that, because Christ had become known to them through us, it was not for the sheep to foresee the ambushes of the wolf, but for the shepherd.”

At last, when these same venerable prelates saw that they could not raise their hands in opposition to the head without endangering themselves, they reserved entirely to God’s judgment whatever had been reported concerning the deeds of the aforementioned most holy Pope Symmachus. Thus each of them plainly indicated this in his subscription, saying: “Laurence, bishop of the Church of Milan, have subscribed to this decree of ours, in which we have entrusted the entire case to God’s judgment.” Likewise Bishop Peter of the Church of Ravenna and the other bishops subscribed.

This was plainly because, as Ennodius, the great confessor of Christ and bishop of Ticinum, who was sent by Hormisdas of apostolic memory to Constantinople and endured innumerable sufferings from the madness of the Greeks for the faith of Christ and the integrity of the Church—not merely once—recalls from the prophet: “Will the axe boast against the one who cuts with it, or will the saw exalt itself against the one who draws it?” (Isaiah 10).

Having recalled these matters from divine Scripture and the trustworthy teaching of the Fathers, we have shown more clearly than the sun that no one who possesses lesser authority can hand over one who possesses greater power to his judgments or subject him to his own decisions. On this general point, let what we have said thus far suffice.

But, to direct our pen specifically toward the prelates of Constantinople, almost none of them—or certainly scarcely any—can be found to have been expelled without the consent of the Roman pontiff, although they are nevertheless counted among the deposed to this day and are not remembered as having been driven out or killed by heretics or tyrants.

Finally, to mention a few of them: was not Maximus expelled from Constantinople after Pope Damasus had labored greatly in the matter, as his letters sent to various persons indicate? Were not Nestorius, Acacius, Anthimus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter expelled through the deliberations and decrees issued by the apostolic see?

Why, then, since this is so, have you sought to despise and consign to oblivion the memory of Peter in the case of Ignatius alone? Was it not because you wished to do everything according to your own desire, establishing a synod comparable in cruelty to the Second Council of Ephesus? In that council, however, there was an Alexandrian who, together with the fellow patriarchs associated with him, acted against the holy Flavian.

Here, however, leaving the patriarchs aside, no bishop of even a small city, nor any person of unknown standing, appeared as the promulgator of a sentence against so great a pontiff, except one who was among his suffragans and subjects.

But perhaps you will say that, in Ignatius’s case, it was not necessary to convene the apostolic see, because no error of heresy had entangled him. O spectacle of piety from one who worships God so rightly and avenges his own injury more than that of his God and Lord!

Was it not more fitting to show magnanimity toward him and to observe the regular discipline? For he had departed from God neither through heresy nor through schism at all. Would it have been preferable had he, endowed with every virtue, failed to adhere completely to the almighty Lord through orthodox faith?

You assembled a council against him, and all the lesser men served at the command of your imperial power. At the desire of secular persons, if we may say so with your permission, you descended from the imperial throne and ascended, so to speak, the episcopal chair. At the request of his imperial enemies, you forgot the scepters and imitated a certain king of Israel, taking upon yourselves the office of priestly ministry against him—especially since your imperial authority ought to be content with its daily administration of public affairs and ought not to usurp what belongs solely to the priests of the Lord (2 Chronicles 26).

Tell us, we beg you, where have you read that your imperial predecessors attended synodal assemblies? Unless perhaps it was in those councils where faith was discussed—the universal faith, common to all—which concerns not only clerics but also laypeople and all Christians without exception.

You not only attended the synod assembled in the case of a priest, but also gathered many thousands of secular people to witness his disgrace. In this you ought rather to have imitated the pious Augustus Constantine, of whom it is written that he said: “If I had seen one of those men clothed in religious attire committing some disgraceful act, I would have spread out my cloak and covered him, so that no one would see him.”

But in the case of this man, all these things are consigned to oblivion: applause is made over the Lord’s priest by clowns and actors. Alas, how the gold has been darkened! Let us cry out with Jeremiah: “The finest color has been changed; the stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” (Lamentations 4).

Then, contrary to ecclesiastical custom and venerable laws, an accuser is brought forward from the imperial palace, and one who can be commanded is employed to give false testimony. Judges become suspect and mercenary, and wolves become guardians who had appeared to be shepherds. They do not stand against the powers of the world on the opposite side, according to Ezekiel: “Nor do they set up a wall for the house of the Lord” (Ezekiel 13); rather, they descend alive into the underworld (Psalm 54), that is, knowingly.

He is subjected to the deliberations of lesser, inferior, and subordinate men, although the sacred canons command, and the examples of the holy Fathers demonstrate, that wherever greater authority exists, one must go there, and that in every controversy appeal must be directed to the judgment of the more powerful see. This is known to have been observed not only by Catholics but even by the heretics themselves.

Otherwise, it is obvious that a council is acephalous—headless—when it deals with so important a person and does not await the judgment of the greater authorities, since not even in the case of clerics of an inferior rank is only the judgment of their own bishop sufficient.

But lest we seem to pursue anything without canonical authority, let us now recall the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon, which determine as follows: “If a cleric has a case against his own bishop or against another bishop, let him be judged before the synod of the province. But if a bishop or cleric has a complaint against the metropolitan of that same province, let him seek the primate of the diocese, or the see of the royal city of Constantinople.”

In this, the following order must be observed: if a cleric or bishop has a complaint against a metropolitan and is pressed by such necessity—or if he cannot bear the matter as a serious burden—let him seek the primate of the diocese, wherever he may be situated. But if any of them is established near the city of Constantinople and wishes to be satisfied with the judgment of that prelate alone, let him seek the same royal city.

For when the holy synod had said, “Let him seek the primate of the diocese,” it issued a command and established a rule. But when it added, with a disjunctive conjunction, “or the see of the royal city of Constantinople,” it is entirely clear that it granted this as a permission.

Do you not therefore see, at least now, that one must always hasten toward greater authorities? And the more a complaint tends toward the judgment of a more authoritative power, the more it must seek an even higher summit, until it gradually reaches that see by whose decision the case is either changed for the better, when the merits of the matter require it, or reserved without question to God alone.

The primate of the diocese named by the holy synod is understood to be no one other than the vicar of the chief apostle. For he is the primate who is regarded both as first and as supreme. We shall demonstrate these points individually below, if the occasion requires.

Nor should it disturb anyone that the phrase uses the singular number, “of the diocese.” It must be understood that “the primate of the diocese” means exactly the same as if it had said “of the dioceses,” for the holy Scriptures are full of this form of expression.

Thus it is written: “A fountain went up from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth” (Genesis 2). For it does not say, “One fountain went up from the earth,” but says, “A fountain went up from the earth,” using the singular instead of the plural, so that we understand many fountains watering their own places or regions throughout the whole earth. Likewise, “a soldier” is said while many are understood; and “the locust” and “the frog” are spoken of in the plagues with which the Egyptians were struck (Exodus 10), although the number of locusts and frogs was countless.

So here too he used the singular “diocese,” but wished it to be understood in the plural because of the unity of peace and faith.

It was amusing that you claimed, as though for greater security, that the council assembled against our brother and fellow minister Ignatius had been equal in number to the holy synod once celebrated at Nicaea by the holy Fathers. If this is to be accepted because it had the same number as the holy Council of Nicaea, you must call this either the Seventh or the Eighth Council. You must also, amid its instability, assemble as many synods as there are known to have been councils gathered in order to follow the decrees of the Council of Nicaea.

But what benefit is it that you followed the holy synod merely in the number of persons assembled, while cruelly persecuting it in conduct? Would that they had not been so numerous, but that they had nevertheless possessed merits like those of the men to whom Christ said: “Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased my Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12).

It is not therefore an equal number of prelates, but merits no less worthy, that can make one synod the equal of the Council of Nicaea. More importantly, one must note that there, against the madness of a single designated presbyter, not only bishops of many regions but also patriarchs are reported to have presided.

Here, however, in the matter of a patriarch, not one of the patriarchs, nor even a single bishop from another diocese, was found to be present, as we have already indicated.

A small number therefore does not harm where piety abounds, nor does a large number help where impiety reigns. Indeed, the more numerous an assembly of wicked men is, the more powerful it becomes in pursuing the evil desires of its members. Nor should one glory in a multitude when warfare is not undertaken against the rulers of the darkness of this world and against spiritual wickedness, but the whole burden of war is brought against flesh and blood—that is, against human beings.

For unless the Psalmist had known of a certain multitude that was not good, he would never have prayed to God: “Scatter them in your strength” (Psalm 58). Scattering causes diminution, and diminution produces abolition.

Do not therefore glory in your multitude, because it is not the multitude but the cause that brings condemnation or justification. We would not call Ignatius more righteous than the aforementioned King David, the prophet of the Lord, who said: “Those who hate me without cause are more numerous than the hairs of my head” (Psalm 39).

But why speak of a human being, when we recognize nothing less of God himself—in whose person the Psalmist spoke these words—as having experienced something of the same in his passion, as the Gospel bears witness?

As for what you wrote, that some of our men wished to be present because we were said to be contending with the destroyers of the sacred images, this is plainly a new invention. Our envoys are present among you on behalf of the sacred images; yet neither has the matter been contested with due seriousness, nor have their attackers ceased to err up to the present. Just as uproar and blasphemies over this question did not cease among you until that time, so even now profane things are preached there and sacrilegious statements continue to be uttered.

It is therefore evident that you sought our legates not out of concern for piety but as an instrument of cruelty. The reason they were requested is made clear by the matter itself: namely, as has already been said, so that the judgment concerning Ignatius might remain accepted by all and permanently fixed, since it would appear to have been made by vicars of such great authority.

No rumor, however slight, has ever touched us suggesting that we share the opinions of those who think perversely—much less that we contend with them. For nowhere has the labor of the holy prelates of the apostolic see concerning the proper reverence and fitting veneration of the sacred images appeared cold or lukewarm.

Nor have the struggles of our predecessors against the attackers of those images been lacking. They addressed this error in writing, through various labors, and through their rebukes before the princes of this world, so that such an error might be driven far away.

Although you say that you did not need our assistance in combating the heretics because this heresy had already been summoned before the Second Council of Nicaea and afterward overturned by the great Methodius, it is as though the apostolic see of Rome itself had not presided over the Second Council assembled at Nicaea and had not first sent its spiritual arrow against those who held evil opinions.

And again, it is as though Methodius of venerable memory, while persecution was raging in Greece, had not obtained rest here with blessed Peter and among us—where Athanasius once found refuge, where Paul did, where many others found it with them and besides them, and where Catholics have always been aided—until, having been nourished by the milk of this holy Roman Church, the mother of all, he was instructed and became sufficiently strong to enter the field of combat and defend the catholic doctrine.

It is as though he had not received from this place the authority to preach, nor been enriched here with priestly insignia; as though, finally, he had not carried from here the steadfastness of Peter and all the weapons of Paul for defeating the Iconoclasts—that is, the breastplate of righteousness, feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

Do not therefore say that you had no need of the Roman Church in this matter of piety. It confirms the councils it has assembled by its authority and guards them by its moderation. Some of them, because they did not have the consent of the Roman pontiff, lost their validity.

How could any synod not need the Roman see, when in the Ephesian Robber Council all the prelates, and even the patriarchs themselves, were falling away, and the Catholic religion would have utterly collapsed unless the great Leo—an imitator, of course, of that lion of whom it is written, “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Revelation 5)—had been divinely roused, opened his mouth, shaken the whole world and even the Augusti themselves, and moved them toward piety?

For in the matter of the sacred images, even before the most holy Methodius, indeed even before the synod assembled at Nicaea under Irene, when this schism had only recently arisen and had invaded nearly all the people of Constantinople like a plague, the Roman prelates, Gregory and Stephen among them, are found to have fought valiantly after summoning bishops from the regions of the West, and to have condemned it completely.

We have answered these matters at the beginning of your imperial letter—not as much as we could have answered, but as much as we believed sufficient to refute the stupidity of those who think such things as seemed to resound in the letter marked with your sign and sent to us. For we did not believe that such profane and perverse words had proceeded from your pious heart or mouth.

As for the many remaining matters from that same letter, we omitted replying to them for the following reasons. First, our heavenly Father chastised us as his sons with such a serious illness, according to his good pleasure, that we were unable not only to set forth what we had seen to be suitable for answering your propositions, but even to dictate how those very answers should be composed, being weighed down by excessive sickness.

Second, your legate acted with such impatience that, before he had learned that we had recovered even slightly from our most severe illness, he would tolerate no delay and departed immediately from the City—though you call it ancient, while the pious Emperor Honorius calls it eternal—without consulting us. He did so for no other reason than that winter was already approaching and he greatly feared for his own safety and that of your soldiers who were with him. We could scarcely prevail upon him to remain at Ostia and wait at least while these things were being written, since he absolutely refused to return to the City.

Third, since the matters that remained in the letter, to which we gave no answer but rather dismissed them philosophically, were full of every kind of perversity and blasphemy, and spread their poisons against God’s own ordering, by which his ineffable providence placed the privileges of the Roman Church and see above the privileges of all the Churches, we believed—as we said earlier—that these words, which sounded so wrongly, were not yours. For this reason we could not send responses or defensive writings concerning matters that had become doubtful as though they were certain.

Nevertheless, if these were your words—those written and sent in contempt of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, indeed of God himself, whose ordering you resist—I confess that you have not diligently read the sacred rules, the acts of the venerable councils, the laws of pious emperors, or the truthful histories of trustworthy men, which you have attempted to recall so uselessly, improperly, and incongruously in disparagement of so great a Church. [Note: Perhaps more correctly, *tamen* (“nevertheless”).]

But we ask almighty God that he who has disclosed to you the mystery of his knowledge may also grant you a full understanding of his arrangements, by which the holy Church governs its mystery [variant: “the mystery of the holy Church”], and may mercifully reveal to you what the privileges of the Roman Church are, how great they are, and of what kind; from where they took their beginning; and who is the author of its supreme authority.
