But if you seek to learn from us, as ministers of Christ and stewards of his mysteries, we shall show it to you more clearly. But if you care little to know, and merely raise your efforts against the privileges of the Roman Church, beware lest they turn back upon you. For it is hard for you—[Note: [Col. 0947D] The words enclosed in parentheses are supplied from the Roman edition.]—to struggle against the force of the river, and hard to kick against the goad.

Moreover, if you will not listen to us, it remains that, in our judgment, you must necessarily be regarded as those whom our Lord Jesus Christ commanded to be so regarded: those who have despised listening to the Church of God. Especially since the privileges of the Roman Church, established by Christ’s own mouth in blessed Peter, arranged within that Church, observed from ancient times, celebrated by the holy universal synods, and continually venerated by the whole Church, can in no way be diminished, in no way violated, in no way altered. For human effort cannot remove the foundation that God has laid; and what God has established remains firm and strong. The person who attempts to resist God’s ordinance sins above all.

The privileges, I say, of this see, or Church, are perpetual. They are divinely rooted and planted. They can be struck, but they cannot be transferred; they can be dragged, but they cannot be uprooted. They existed before your empire and, thanks be to God, have remained hitherto undefiled; they will remain after you, and for as long as the Christian name is preached, they will not cease to endure unimpaired. [Col. 0948C–D]

These privileges, therefore, bestowed upon this holy Church by Christ—not bestowed by the synods, but merely celebrated and venerated by them—through which not so much honor as responsibility falls upon us, although we have obtained that honor not through our own merits but through the ordinance of God’s grace, through blessed Peter and in blessed Peter: these privileges compel and constrain us to be solicitous for all the Churches of God. For to that holy Peter has been added the fellowship of the most blessed Paul, the vessel of election and teacher of truth, upon whom the care of all the Churches continually rested (2 Corinthians XV).

These two men, therefore, divinely established in the Roman Church like the two great lights of heaven, wondrously illumined the whole world with the splendor of their radiance. Through their presence the West became, as it were, the East: like the shining sun, giving brightness of itself and flashing through their disciples as through rays of light. They were not brought to Rome by rulers after their deaths in order to confer greater honor of privileges upon the Roman Church, as has been done among you—not reasonably, but by force—namely, so that the other Churches might be deprived of their patrons and Constantinople alone enriched by the spoils and wealth it violently seized. Rather, they came to Rome in the flesh, proclaiming the word of life, removing the darkness of error from it, illuminating human minds with the light of truth, and completing their martyrdom there on one and the same day. By their rosy blood they consecrated the holy Roman Church and dedicated it to the Lord God, presenting it as having no stain or wrinkle or anything of that kind. Thus, finally, through blessed Mark, the son and disciple of one of these men, they made the Church of Alexandria their own. For a son’s inheritance lies in the power of his parent, and a disciple’s glory is without hesitation referred back to his teacher. [Col. 0949A–B]

Blessed Peter had also made the Church of Antioch his own by his bodily presence; as blessed Pope Innocent says (Letter 21), it would not yield to the see of the city of Rome except that Rome earned what it received in passing, whereas Antioch rejoiced because it had received blessed Peter among itself and witnessed his completion. Through these three principal Churches, therefore, the care of all the Churches undoubtedly awaits the direction of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, the foremost of the apostles.

For the sake of these fathers, by a divinely granted increase of grace, we have been born and established as sons, although—[Note: “Although unworthy, although, etc.”]—far unequal to them in merit, as princes over all the earth, that is, over the whole Church. For “earth” means the Church, as it is written: “Not so the wicked, not so; but like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth” (Psalm I). As Saint Augustine explains, the Church is understood here. Having therefore become heirs of these men, we must undertake both the authority they received from the Lord and, no less, the burden of their care. [Col. 0949C–D]

Accordingly, it must be observed that neither the Council of Nicaea nor any other synod conferred any privilege upon the Roman Church. It knew that in Peter she had fully earned the rights of all authority and had received the governance of all Christ’s sheep, as blessed Bishop Boniface attests [Note: [Col. 0949D] In the letter read at the Roman council, which Holstenius published under Boniface II. HARD.], writing to all the bishops established throughout Thessaly:

“The institution of the universal Church at its birth took the beginning of its honor from blessed Peter, in whom its governance and supreme authority consist. From his ecclesiastical discipline, as the cultivation of religion grew, a fountain flowed forth through all the Churches. The decrees of the Council of Nicaea bear witness to nothing else, to such an extent that it did not dare establish anything over her, seeing that nothing could be conferred above her merit. Finally, it knew that everything had been granted to this Church by the Lord’s word. If everything was granted, then nothing was lacking that he had not granted to her.” [Col. 0949D–0950A]

Finally, if the decrees of the Council of Nicaea are examined carefully, it will certainly be found that that synod conferred no increase upon the Roman Church. Rather, it took from her example the model for what it granted specifically to the Church of Alexandria.

These considerations, and others like them, make us solicitous for all the Churches. They also strongly urge us to undertake diligent care of the Church of Constantinople. They compel us, I say, to assist Ignatius the patriarch, who was deposed without any rule or ecclesiastical procedure prescribing it, as a brother. For among the rest, the one through whom these privileges were principally conferred upon us said: “And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke XXII).

Indeed, he fell into fault for this very reason, so that he might learn how he ought to have compassion on the weakness of others. These privileges, divinely inspired, commanded us to remove Photius, while Ignatius was alive, from the honor he had irregularly usurped: he had entered the Lord’s folds not through the door but by another way, thrusting aside the shepherd and scattering the sheep, and he was to be removed from the communion of Christians.

But concerning what your Excellency asserts—that you did not wish Ignatius to be judged by our legates because he had already been judged and condemned—we truthfully acknowledge that neither that proceeding appears in any respect canonical, nor did we order that their judgment be made, nor did we accept what was done. Nevertheless, it is plainly understood whom it pleased more, since you had confirmed what had been done in writing, something nowhere remembered as having been done by an emperor, and had ordered everyone to write concerning it.

We not only entirely refused to accept the deed, but also grieved over it and removed it far from our consent; indeed, by the authority and example of our predecessors, we declared it null. If time allowed, we could easily prove what we say from ecclesiastical records.

The perpetrators of the supposed judgment, however, were themselves judged by the judgment with which they judged, according to the Gospel; and “with the measure with which they measured, it shall be measured to them” (Luke VI). We did not send them to investigate or judge Ignatius’s promotion to, or entry into, the patriarchal see. We sent them to learn the circumstances of his deposition and to return and report to us the truth they had discovered. [Col. 0950B–D]

Our letters clearly testify to this, thanks be to God. We ordered three copies to be written in one continuous text by Zacharias, Peter, and Leo, beloved of God, the record-keepers of the holy Roman Church, and we distributed them in the presence of the holy Church that is with us. We retained one copy with us, for future security and because a question might arise later. This is precisely what, alas, we now see happening. We sent another to your beloved Sublimity. The third we gave to our legates, so that, keeping it before their eyes as a mirror, they might reflect upon what they ought to do and remember what we had established as having been commanded to them.

And if your Greatness should perhaps disdain to display the letter sent to you in the assembly of bishops, we ordered them to read without omission in that gathering in which we had commanded them to investigate and carefully examine the cause of Ignatius’s deposition the letter that we had given especially to them and that they knew to be identical in form with the other two; they were to recite it in the hearing of everyone, although they themselves acted contrary to everything that had been commanded to them.

For this reason, now also, since it is said that certain writings are among you as though sent in our name—although we did not send them at all—we ordered this letter, which we are directing to your gentleness, to be written in a second volume. Peter, who wrote one of the three aforementioned copies, is known to have written this one; the copy we retain was written, as is known, by the aforementioned Leo, beloved of God, the record-keeper of the holy Roman Church, whose fidelity has been proved to us. [Col. 0951A–B]

Moreover, your empire wrote to us asking that we send you Theognostus, who is known to have received from our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius the responsibility of an exarchate over certain provinces, and also other monks whom you regard as offenders against your imperial Excellency.

Yet, since they were not in fact your offenders, what else can this mean except that we should learn more clearly how great a punishment [variant: “how great punishments,” HARD.] and to what tortures those who are on Ignatius’s side and are under your dominion are to be subjected? These men are certainly not being sought for banquets or to receive the insignia of any honor, but rather for punishment—men whom you perhaps have never seen and whose character you have not at all recognized.

Finally, some of them have served the divine worship at Rome from their earliest years, and we do not believe that it would be just to subject such men to tortures. As for Theognostus, we testify that he proclaims nothing unfavorable about you, but rather what is pleasing. Why, then, you seek him, we do not know, unless perhaps, having been driven away from there, he has found here, as countless Christians have, a little rest. [Col. 0951C–D]

For many thousands of people, hastening from every region of the earth, place themselves daily under the protection and intercession of blessed Peter, foremost of the apostles, and intend to remain at his threshold until the end of their lives. Apart from the fact that the vessel lowered from heaven, in which every kind of animal was shown to blessed Peter, the ruler of them all, signifies the catholic Church, the city of Rome itself, where the bodily presence of that apostle is diligently venerated, is recognized as containing within itself the nations of all animals [cunctae; perhaps cunctas, HARD.]—that is, spiritually understood, of all human beings.

The Roman Church, therefore, has received and contains within itself what God commanded the universal Church to receive and contain. For it is most fitting and entirely appropriate that Peter should display among his own what was specially shown and commanded to him, and thus indicate what is more readily to be believed in the universal Church.

It must certainly be observed that this vessel, in which were all kinds of animals, was specially shown to Peter, and that he alone was commanded to kill and eat them. After the resurrection, too, the Lord specifically commanded him alone to draw to shore a net full of various fish (John XXI). We believe that your wisdom already perceives, even without our saying so, that he himself—whose place we have assumed, although unworthy—received from God, principally and specially, the care of the universal Church. [Col. 0952A–B]

Do you think, then, emperor, that it is just for us to hand over to rulers some of those whom we have now mentioned—rulers whose courts, dignities, honors, and benefices they have despised, or whose indignation and persecutions they have perhaps endured? Far be it from us. With God as our guide, we do not wish to be found like Judas the betrayer, nor to surpass the wickedness of the pagans. They themselves do not permit us to do anything of the kind that you urge us to perpetrate.

Finally, when one of your predecessors requested that a certain venerable man be sent to him by the ruler of the Hagarenes, offering many gifts, he not only failed entirely to obtain him but, as reported, received from the one he sought a rebuke in a corresponding letter.

Thanks be to God, through the authority and right of the foremost blessed apostles Peter and Paul, which we have partly explained above, we have the power not only to summon monks but also to call to us any clerics from any diocese whenever necessary and to invite them when ecclesiastical circumstances require it.

This is our responsibility. But it is not the responsibility of you or of pious emperors to seek monks for any purpose whatever, except to show them mercy and humbly request their prayers.

If you perhaps think that Theognostus disparages Photius among us and continually commends Ignatius, know truly that he says nothing about either of them except what is openly known, what the world says, what the whole Church proclaims, and what we ourselves have learned from the countless people who have come to Rome from Alexandria, Jerusalem, Constantinople and its surrounding regions, Mount Olympus, and the other parts of the world. Finally, he says what we have plainly understood through your legates and various writings.

What fault, then, does anyone commit if he says what you are known to have said? For here are your writings sent to our predecessor, preserved in our possession, which testify that you anathematized certain supporters of Gregory of Syracuse, with the bishops assembled, even in the absence of our brother Ignatius. What offense, then, does anyone commit? Or in what respect, we ask, have we offended—although, in reverse, you now censure those whom you then praised, and now extol with astonishing proclamations those whom you then pronounced guilty and condemned—if we believed what you wrote and now say what you said?

Finally, unless we change our policy—namely, so as to direct it according to your counsel—or unless, by becoming like you, we hand over the members just as you hand over the head, you seem to seek to frighten us with repeated threats and to menace us, as though you intended to bring the ultimate destruction upon our country and city.

With Christ’s favor and protection, however, we have not feared this until now, nor do we fear it now, believing that his angels guard its walls. Indeed, we know that the Savior has been placed in it as wall and bulwark (Isaiah XXVI), that is, the apostles as the fortress of their intercessions.

We have not failed to read, nor have we forgotten, the threats of Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, and of his servants against the city of Jerusalem and its people—threats no less great or fewer than yours. Again, we remember the Lord’s mercies: how one hundred and eighty-five thousand men of the Assyrian camp perished (2 Kings XIX), while the city and its inhabitants escaped. We recall it, give thanks, and take hope; and, if he grants strength, we have confidently endeavored to remove the worship of Baal from the house of the Lord. For he is now the same as he was then and will be forever; his mercy is not less, nor his omnipotence weaker.

Therefore, let dust and worm not presume to threaten. It is written: “Why does earth and ashes boast?” (Ecclesiasticus X). Let the flask not swell up in the waters, for shortly—behold—it is no more. “Why does he glory in wickedness who is powerful in iniquity?” (Psalm XXI). What is he going to do? Is he going to kill a man, for example? For he has nothing more that he can do (Luke XII). A single poisonous mushroom can do that as well.

O emperor, has the wickedness of a man powerful in iniquity been reduced to this, that he should be compared with a poisonous mushroom? Alas for the powerless powerful man! Alas for the man boasting in vain! [Col. 0952C–0953C]

Rather, let your powerful strength glory in the Lord, be praised in goodness, and exalted in justice; let it not seek to inflict threats and terrors upon us. For, according to Solomon, you do not know what the coming day may bring forth (Proverbs XXVII). And according to the psalmist: “The Lord brings the counsels of the nations to nothing; he rejects the thoughts of the peoples, and he rejects the counsels of princes” (Psalm XXXII).

Especially since there is no small distance between us and you, a distance that daily produces peoples who inflict no slight injuries upon you—indeed, dangers—and you ought rather to avenge yourselves upon them than upon us. We have inflicted no loss, no insult, and absolutely no injury—God forbid—upon the summit of your glory.

Nevertheless, as long as we endure, we shall honor our ministry, exercise the stewardship entrusted to us, follow the footsteps of our predecessors, and bear the care of all the Churches, in him who will strengthen us, our Lord Jesus Christ.

Why are men enraged? What evil have we done? Certainly we have not invaded Crete, devastated Sicily, or seized the countless provinces subject to the Greeks. Finally, we have not burned the churches of the saints, after killing numerous people, nor the suburbs of Constantinople, which lie almost adjacent to its walls.

And indeed no vengeance is exacted for these things from those who are pagans, who belong to another faith, who are enemies of Christ, and who continually oppose the ministers of truth. Yet against us, who by God’s grace are Christians, who come from Christian and Catholic parents, who believe the doctrines of one and the same faith, who are called servants of Christ, and who desire, insofar as we can, to be worshipers of truth—against us threats are displayed, terrors promised, and even certain hardships inflicted.

This is not a praiseworthy order; it is not an exchange worthy of imitation: that those who inflict innumerable evils should escape unpunished, while those who have done no evil receive such treatment for their sake; that those who blaspheme Christ should be released, while those who celebrate Christ should be subjected to threats of this kind. But we have one to whom we may look, and one in whom we may find consolation.

The Jews did the same: releasing the robber and holding the Savior; justifying the murderer and condemning the giver of life; freeing Barabbas and handing Christ over to death (Matthew XVII). [Col. 0953D–0954B]

But, setting these matters aside at last, we shall now direct our pen to the matters that we have prudently considered with the whole holy Church that is with us, and, together with blessed Gelasius, bishop of our see, we shall say advisedly:

“We are constrained by the necessary ordering of affairs, and summoned by the governance of the apostolic see, to weigh the decrees of the fathers’ canons and measure the commands of former bishops and our predecessors in such a way that, after careful consideration, we temper as far as possible whatever the necessity of the present times demands should be relaxed for the restoration of the Churches” (Letter 6, to the bishops throughout Lucania and Bruttium).

And since we judge that nothing more judicious, mild, or beneficial can be done concerning Ignatius and Photius than for both to come to Rome for a renewed examination, this is what we strongly desire, and we beneficially admonish you to consent to it. But we grant this by way of indulgence; we do not give anyone permission to carry it out according to his own pleasure. [Col. 0954C–D]

For, according to the canons, when there is greater authority, the judgment of inferiors must be submitted to it, whether for dissolution or confirmation. It is therefore clear that no one may review the judgment of the apostolic see, whose authority has no superior, nor is anyone permitted to judge its judgment.

The canons wished appeals from every part of the world to be made to that see, while no one was permitted to appeal from it. Accordingly, the most holy bishops Boniface and Gelasius, not through inventions of their own but because they knew the custom of the Roman Church, say the following.

Boniface, writing to Rufus and the other bishops established throughout Thessaly and the other provinces, says:

“No one has ever boldly raised hostile hands against the apostolic dignity, whose judgment may not be reviewed. No one became rebellious in this matter except one who wished to be judged concerning himself.”

Gelasius, in a memorandum given to Faustus, the master serving as envoy to Constantinople, says:

“They oppose us with the canons, although they do not know what they are saying. Against the canons themselves they reveal that they act by refusing to obey the first see when it gives sound and upright counsel. The canons themselves wished the appeals of the whole Church to be brought before the examination of this see. But they decreed that no appeal whatsoever should be made from it; consequently, that it should judge the whole Church, while it should itself come under the judgment of no one. They never commanded that its judgment be judged, and they established that the sentence of the see whose decrees they rather commanded to be followed should not be dissolved.” [Col. 0954D–0955B]

Therefore, concerning the judgment of the Roman bishop, which is not to be reviewed—for custom does not require the contrary, as we have established—we do not deny that the sentence of that see can be changed for the better when something has been misrepresented to it, or when it has decided, as a matter of prudent administration, to arrange something in consideration of ages, times, or serious necessities.

For we read that the distinguished apostle Paul also acted administratively in certain matters that he is known later to have rejected. This is so, however, when that Roman Church chooses to act with the most discerning consideration, not when it wishes to review matters that it has nearly defined—or [variant: “well defined”] defined well. [Col. 0955B–C]

Furthermore, lest you say that we have ordered Ignatius or Photius to come to Rome contrary to the law of the Church, know that in this we have followed the example of our ancient father and predecessor Julius. According to what is found in his letter (Letter 1), he is known to have given this command to those who had assembled at Antioch. The historian Theodoret also presents this very matter in these words (Book II, chapter 4):

“Eusebius and his associates sent the accusations brought against Athanasius to Julius, the Roman pontiff. Following ecclesiastical law, he also ordered them themselves to come to Rome and regularly summoned the venerable Athanasius to judgment; upon receiving the summons, he immediately came.” [Col. 0955C–D]

And if you say this as well: “He did indeed summon them, but they refused to come,” hear what follows, and you will see whether their refusal was counted to their praise or to their condemnation. For the same historian continued:

“But the bearers of the accusations did not go to Rome, knowing that their lie could easily be exposed.”

Therefore, do not say that we ordered the aforementioned men to come to Rome contrary to the law of the Church. For, as you have just heard from the historian, blessed Julius ordered both the accused and the accusers to come to Rome and regularly summoned the venerable Athanasius to judgment.

Athanasius, who possessed a good conscience, came without any resistance. But those who possessed a bad one refused, knowing, as it is written there, that their lie could easily be exposed.

We shall now prove the same regarding Ignatius and Photius, because the one whose conscience reproaches him will refuse to obey us out of fear—unless Ignatius, who is deprived of every human support, has not suffered your obstruction but has rather been mercifully assisted by your aid so that he may be able to come. [Col. 0955D–0956A]

But if they cannot come in person, first let them themselves inform us by letters of explanation why they cannot come. Then let as many as wish come from the party of Gregory of Syracuse, representing the others who belong to his side.

From the party of Archbishop Ignatius, let these also be sent: Antony of Cyzicus, Basil of Thessalonica, Constantine of Larissa, Theodore of Syracuse, Metrophanes of Smyrna, and Paul, bishop of Heraclea in Pontus. From among the abbots, let Nicetas of Chrysopolis, Nicholas of Studion, Dositheus of Ossidion, Lazarus the presbyter, and the monk called Cazaris be sent.

If these men are not sent, you will make yourselves suspect, because you are deliberately taking away from our sight those through whom we could become certain. For this reason, we shall admit no one from the other parties, except perhaps those whom we can truly recognize as having been sent from your side.

When representatives from both sides have assembled, and when we have heard in our presence, and in the presence of our brothers and fellow bishops, what question has arisen between the two parties, we shall more easily recognize it and bring it to a canonical conclusion.

Let Photius also send from his side whom he decides upon, to explain, if they can, that the manner of his promotion was irreproachable and canonical.

Let your imperial Highness, if you wish, also send courtiers from your side, so that, being present, they may plainly learn what conclusion justice and uprightness have given to both parties and report it to your piety. Those who are to be sent from your side, however, should be men who fear God, are not inexperienced in ecclesiastical traditions, and readily and obediently yield to the truth. [Col. 0956A–C]

But since some of those whom we have ordered to come to Rome have no means of support of their own and, relying only on the assistance of others, are entirely unable to undertake so long a journey, we earnestly beseech your clemency, as though we were present before you, to provide mercifully, out of love for God, what they need for such a difficult and lengthy journey.

We believe that this proposal will be acceptable to you, and that your royal honor will not take offense at what we have decided should be carried out in this manner, since justice, repeatedly sifted, shines more clearly into the light.

Accordingly, we trust that your piety will gladly assist in providing the means by which truth may be made manifest.

When your legates come, we ask that you also send the authentic letters that we previously sent through Rhadoald and Zacharias, formerly bishops, to your Eminence and to the synod that was then thought to be convened concerning the sacred images. If those letters remain among you as they are known to have been transmitted by us, let them be examined in our presence. Thus the lips of those who falsely say that we wrote something other than what we sent may thereafter be silenced.

But if certain passages have been inserted in them that we did not order written and did not wish sent, let us examine them carefully and discover whose fault produced this. For we have with us the companion of those two letters, which, as we have already said above, we retained for future testimony: it was set down in one continuous form with those two and composed throughout in the same words and syllables. [Col. 0956C–0957A]

We also ask your Belovedness to be so kind as to send us the authentic records of the proceedings in which it is contained how Ignatius was first considered to have been deposed. We ask you to send us the very authentic records of the acts that you sent through Leo, the secretary: both those in which the tyrannical stripping of Ignatius is reported and those in which the matter of the images was debated, although almost nothing was done and fewer bishops were found there than had been present at the supposed deposition of Ignatius.

This gives it to be understood that greater zeal was undertaken for injuring a man than for praising God. [Col. 0957A–B]

But if you obey our admonitions and strive to fulfill what we have communicated, then, with the Lord’s favor and having received authority from the holy foremost apostles, we shall grant your most Christian and gentle Sublimity permission to participate in the grace of communion with the holy catholic and apostolic Church—especially with us, with our fellow priest Ignatius, and with his party—except for communion with Gregory of Syracuse, his party, and those who share his views.

But if your Excellency is perhaps displeased by what we wrote above concerning sending legates from both parties, know that we have found nothing more suitable or convenient than that this should be done. [Col. 0957B–C]

Nevertheless, out of imperial love for you, lest we seem unwilling in any respect to satisfy you, we shall yield even on this point, and lest you think that we wish to pursue peace for the Church less than we have always wished.

For, as we have stated, no rule or custom shows that a sentence once issued by the apostolic see can be changed further without its own consent. Moreover, there is nothing that ought to turn you away, if you are willing; believe us, from sending the aforementioned men into our presence to seek justice and truth.

Almighty God is our witness that there is no intention or desire in our mind except carefully to investigate and discover what equity assigns to each party and what is fitting for the Church’s present and future condition.

Therefore, do not think that we wish to favor Ignatius against justice, or oppose Photius where the canons do not resist him. Certainly, it belongs to perfect Christians not only to wish to harm no one, but also not to repay evil with evil when they themselves have been injured (Matthew V; Romans XII).

In what position before God, then, or among whom would we be reckoned, if we sought to bring hostility upon those who have inflicted no opposition upon us? [Col. 0957C–0958A]

Let your piety therefore deign to believe that we do not wish to oppose these men in their justice, nor to assist Ignatius when the canons and ecclesiastical traditions do not support him.

But we believe in the Lord, who said that light should shine out of darkness and who gives knowledge to human beings, that if the parties we have mentioned reach the threshold of him who struck down the lying Ananias and Sapphira with the sword of the Holy Spirit (Acts V), whatever is uncertain and hidden will be revealed and made manifest.

For this is always our intention and our ardent desire: while preserving equality for both parties, to establish, with the Lord’s assistance, nothing except what the sacred canons and equity dictate. We wish harm to no one, and still less do we desire anyone’s peril. [Col. 0958A–B]

Why, then, have we been moved against the party of Gregory of Syracuse and proceeded against it with a scourge? If you wish to know, listen graciously.

We were not deaf hearers of the holy Evangelist, who tells us that our Redeemer made a scourge of cords and, entering the temple, drove from it all who were working evil there in various ways (John XXI). When the apostles saw this, being less perfect at that time, they could certainly have wondered—as perhaps you do now—how he had driven priests and all evil workers from the temple with such ease.

But afterward they remembered that it was written: “The zeal of your house has consumed me” (Psalm LXVIII).

Thus it was not hostility, not human hatred, and not any evil desire—thanks be to God—that impelled us against the men of the aforementioned party. Rather, it was zeal for the house of God, zeal for the traditions of the fathers, ecclesiastical order, ancient custom, and the care of all the Churches of God that we carry about with us.

The privileges, moreover, of our own see—received divinely in blessed Peter and passed on into the Roman Church, privileges that the universal Church celebrates and venerates, as we said above—set us ablaze and do not permit us in any way to remain silent or inactive. [Col. 0958B–C]

Therefore, since this is so—and, to speak the truth, it is so in every respect—and if time allowed we could demonstrate a thousand things that we say by testimonies and show them to you through the judgments of many credible writers: do not be indignant, do not bring a futile charge against us, and do not willingly listen to the words of perverse men. Rather, listen to us.

Do not threaten us, for, with the Lord protecting us, we fear no such threats, nor shall we carry out your commands through them unless they are clothed with divine commands. We are prepared, for the sake of truth, to shed our blood. Indeed, with Christ favoring us, we shall not hand over to you, or to any of your people, the people divinely entrusted to us. [Col. 0958C–D]

Your task is to consider whether you can accomplish what you are contemplating. Therefore, call to mind the days of old, and keep the eternal years in mind (Ps. 76). Carefully consider what the emperors who persecuted the Church of God, and especially the Roman Church—namely Nero, Diocletian, Constantine, Anastasius, and the others of their kind—endured, where they are now, and how execrable their reputation and detestable their name are throughout the Church of God.

Recall more attentively and diligently how great is the praise in the universal Church of those pious emperors, worshipers of God, who exalted the Church of God and especially the Roman Church—Constantine, of course, and Constans, as well as the elder Theodosius and Valentinian, and the others; how their praises resound everywhere, and how their names are continually commemorated amid the sacred mysteries. Thus strive to listen to us, imitating them. For we are your fathers through the grace of Christ, and we love you as our dearest sons. We can do nothing for you except point out the way of truth; we earnestly desire that your earthly glory be divinely increased. But what wrong do we do if, at the same time, we beg you to attain heavenly and eternal glory?

Therefore let your clemency consider how great was the love and zeal of your pious predecessors, the emperors, toward reverence for the apostolic see—especially those whom we mentioned above: how they elevated it with various privileges, enriched it with gifts, and enlarged its benefits; how they honored it in their letters, complied with its wishes, and ordered that its institutions be carried out; how they sought its prayers and decreed that its faith should be followed; how, moreover, they promulgated laws for churches to be united to it, yet did not command it concerning the gathering of councils and the issuing of judgments, but merely prayed and exhorted; and how they themselves consented to what it decreed and rejected what it condemned.

So, dearest son, so also let your sublimity—God forbid that it should belong to the faction of ungrateful and disobedient sons—imitate these other pious emperors, worshipers of God, and obediently heed what we have decreed concerning the Church of Constantinople. We ask that your piety not despise us, who have so often urged you, keeping before your eyes the words of the Lord: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me, and whoever despises me” (Luke 10), and so forth. Finally, the Apostle agrees with our Lord: “Therefore,” he says, “whoever despises these things does not despise man but God, who has given his Holy Spirit in us” (1 Thess. 4).

But if you judge that we ought to be despised, nevertheless we cannot despise or neglect the things that belong to God. We must both provide for your salvation and avoid endangering ourselves over the acceptance of the talent entrusted to us, since the administration of the heavenly seed has been imposed upon us: “Woe to us if we have not sown! Woe to us if we have kept silent!” (1 Cor. 9.)

Since the chosen vessel feared and cried out thus, how much more ought anyone of little account to fear? Accordingly, just as a serious danger rests upon pontiffs if they remain silent about what is proper for the worship of God and the correction of the Church, so—God forbid—there is no small danger for those who, although they ought to obey, despise. And if the hearts of the faithful ought generally to submit to all priests handling divine matters, how much more ought consent to be given to the pontiff of that see, whom the universal piety of all the Churches has continually honored?

Here your clemency clearly perceives that no one can ever, by any merely human counsel, raise himself against the privilege or confession of him whom the voice of Christ placed above all, whom the venerable Church has always confessed and devoutly holds as primate. What has been established by divine judgment cannot be driven from its place by human presumption. Therefore, we ask, let certain persons cease in your time rashly to seek the disturbance of the Church and to aspire to what they are not permitted to seek. Otherwise, they will neither enjoy what they have wickedly desired nor, unless they repent, retain Christianity itself.

But we ask you not to inflict prejudice upon the Church of God. It inflicts no prejudice upon your authority; rather, it prays to the eternal God for the stability of that authority and continually entreats him, with constant devotion, for your safety and perpetual salvation. Do not usurp what belongs to it; do not seek to seize what has been entrusted to it alone. Know that every administrator of worldly affairs ought to be as far removed from sacred matters as anyone from the catalogue of the clergy, or anyone serving God, ought to be kept from involvement in secular business. Finally, we utterly fail to understand how those who have been permitted to preside only over human affairs and not divine ones dare to judge those through whom divine things are administered.

[Col. 0960C] Before Christ’s coming, there were cases in which certain persons typologically existed as both kings and priests; sacred history records that holy Melchizedek was such a one. The devil imitated this in his members, since he always strives, in a tyrannical spirit, to claim for himself whatever belongs to divine worship; thus pagan emperors were called both emperors and supreme pontiffs. But when the true one—namely, Christ—came, although he was both king and pontiff, thereafter neither did an emperor seize for himself the rights of the pontificate, nor did a pontiff usurp the imperial title.

For Christ Jesus, the God-man, mediator of God and human beings, distinguished the offices of the two powers by his own actions and by distinct dignities. He willed that what was proper should be raised up through medicinal humility, rather than be plunged again into the depths through human pride. Thus Christian emperors would need pontiffs for eternal life, while pontiffs would use imperial laws only for the orderly conduct of temporal affairs, so that spiritual action might remain separate from carnal interference.

And for this reason the person serving God should not involve himself in secular business (2 Tim. 2), while, conversely, no one involved in secular business should appear to preside over divine matters. In this way the moderation of both orders would be preserved, so that no one might be exalted by being supported by both, and each particular office might be suitably adapted to the nature of its functions.

When all these points have been properly gathered, it is made sufficiently clear that a pontiff cannot be either bound or released entirely by secular power. It is established that the pious emperor Constantine, as we mentioned much earlier, called him “God”; and it is manifest that God cannot be judged by human beings.

Theodosius the Younger, writing to the holy First Synod of Ephesus, likewise says: “Accordingly, Candidianus, the most magnificent count of the vigorous household troops, has been appointed to proceed to your most holy synod and in no way to participate in the questions—or rather, the explanations—that must be addressed concerning pious doctrines. For it is unlawful for one who is not of the order of the most holy bishops to become involved in ecclesiastical discussions.”

What the Roman prelates think about this, what the Latin and Greek teachers explain about it, and finally what Maximus, the venerable monk—and at that time almost the only Catholic among you—asserted in his disputation, ask the elders, who are elders also in character, since it would take too long to write it all down; they will tell you.

Once these matters have been clearly established, it is evident that our fellow minister Ignatius could not in any way have been entirely expelled solely by an imperial sentence. Since the assent of the prelates also followed in his condemnation, it is apparent that the deed was carried out from flattery, not by legitimate sanction. Indeed, your sentence preceded that of the prelates to such an extent that not only was the same bishop expelled from the church by your command, before any inquiry had been made, from the office entrusted to him, but afterward, in his condemnation—as the acts of that robber synod indicate, which you sent us through Leo the illustrious secretary [Col. 0961C]—you wrote the bishop first and before all others, something that, unless we are mistaken, had never previously been done.

With these matters first set forth beneath God’s gaze, we purely and sincerely implore, beseech, and exhort your piety not to receive our petition with indignation.

Finally, we ask you to hear us in this life as we entreat you, rather than—God forbid—encounter us as accusers at the divine judgment. Therefore, we beg you not to be angry if we love you so greatly that we wish you to possess eternally the kingdom you have attained temporally, and that you, who command the world, may be able to reign with Christ. For with what confidence, we ask, will you seek God’s rewards there if here you do not prevent harm to his Church? Please do not regard as burdensome the things said for the sake of your eternal salvation. You read in Scripture: “The wounds of a friend are better than the deceitful kisses of an enemy” (Prov. 27). May almighty God mercifully open the heart of your empire to understand what we say, and may he deign, by the prompting of his inward inspiration, to grant that you obey us in the matters about which we write, most Christian and most beloved son.

Whoever in Constantinople reads this letter of ours and conceals anything written in it from our most august son, the emperor Michael—if he is able to find sufficient standing with him—let him be anathema (Epistle 10). Whoever interprets it and changes, removes, or adds anything to it, except what the idiom of the Greek language requires, or what the interpreter’s knowledge does not allow him to understand [read, as in Epistle 10: “the interpreter’s understanding,” etc. HARD.], let him be anathema.

The material written thus far in nine sections was previously enacted and sent by us through certain persons to be reported to your fraternal community, apart from that letter of our apostolate which we transmitted to Michael, the most excellent emperor, through one of his envoys, a man named Michael who called himself a protospatharius.

Later, when we learned that we were accomplishing nothing merely by writing to those who refuse to heed sound admonitions, we judged it appropriate to send our envoys and repeated letters to Constantinople, once again entrusting them with those measures that seemed beneficial to the Church. For this purpose we sent Donatus, the most holy bishop, Leo, the venerable presbyter, and our son Marinus, the deacon, so that those who, admonished by letters, refuse to obey might at last learn, when addressed with saving words, not to resist divine instructions.

In these writings we gave them the material contained below, which we decided should be divided into three sections. The first is the one that is also the tenth section of this volume. It contains the letter sent to the Augustus already mentioned, and another to the bishops and the other orders subject to Constantinople. The second section is the one that occupies the eleventh place in this collection; it contains two letters, one written to Photius and the other to Barda, his supporter. The third is the section that is also the twelfth of this codex; it contains separate letters sent to our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius, to the emperor’s mother, and to his wife, as well as a uniform letter that we judged should be written and sent separately to certain distinguished senators of the city of Constantinople.

## (865.) LXXXVII. TO REMBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF HAMMABURG. He grants the use of the pallium.

[In Lappenberg, *Hamburgisches Urkundenbuch*, Hamburg, 1842, p. 29 ff.]

[Col. 0962D] Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother RIMBERT, archbishop of Hammaburg.

If shepherds of sheep are willing to endure sun and frost day and night in guarding their flock, and with ever-watchful eyes keep careful lookout lest any of the sheep perish by straying or be carried off, torn apart by the bites of wild beasts, let us consider with what toil and care we ought to remain vigilant, we who are called shepherds of souls, and never cease to perform the duty we have undertaken toward guarding the Lord’s sheep, lest on the day of divine examination we be tortured before the supreme Shepherd by the guilt of negligence on account of our indolence.

Therefore, since we are now judged to possess a higher dignity of honor than others, we grant to your fraternity the pallium for celebrating the solemnities of Mass. We permit you to use it, while the privileges of your Church remain in their proper condition, only on the day of the holy and venerable Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ; on the feasts of the holy apostles and of blessed John the Baptist; on the Assumption of blessed Mary, Mother of God; on the day of the Nativity of the Lord God; on the solemnity of your Church; and also on the anniversary of your ordination, just as this was decreed by our most blessed predecessor, Lord Gregory, prelate of this nourishing see.

Your fraternity should put on the pallium in the sacristy and then proceed to the solemn celebration of Mass. You must arrogate nothing more to yourself through rash presumption, lest, when something is seized improperly in outward dress, what might properly have been permitted should also be lost.

Since the honor of this garment must be preserved by the modest vitality of your conduct, we exhort you to make all your adornments correspond to it, so that, with God as author, you may rightly be distinguished in both respects. Let your life be a rule for your children; let them direct themselves by whatever strength has been instilled into them through it; let them look to it for what they should imitate; let them always advance by examining themselves in it, so that whatever good they live may appear, after the Lord, to be yours [read: “so that the good in which they have lived may appear to be yours”].

Therefore, let neither prosperity, which temporally flatters, lift up your heart, nor adversity weaken it. Whatever happens, let it be conquered by the virtue of patience. Let hatred find no place with you, nor indiscriminate favor. Let the wicked recognize strictness; let evil insinuation not make an innocent person culpable before you, and let favor not excuse the guilty. Do not show yourself lenient toward offenders, lest you permit what you have failed to punish to be committed.

Let there be in you the gentleness of a good shepherd and also the severe strictness of a judge: the one to cherish those who live innocently, the other to restrain restless people, who must be struck, from wickedness. But since sometimes the zeal of superiors, when it wishes to act as the strict avenger of the wicked, causes correction to pass into cruelty, restrain anger by judgment and use disciplinary severity in such a way that you strike at faults without withdrawing your affection from the persons whom you correct.

Show yourself merciful to the poor insofar as virtue permits; let your defense assist the oppressed, and let modest correction oppose their oppressors. Look upon no one’s face against justice, and despise no one who brings a just complaint. Let the guardianship of equity excel in you, so that neither a rich person’s power may persuade him to dare anything contrary to reason before you, nor a poor person’s humility cause him to despair of his own possession.

Thus, by God’s mercy, you may become the kind of person whom sacred reading commands when it says: “It is necessary for a bishop to be irreproachable.” You will be able to use all these qualities beneficially if you have charity as your teacher; whoever follows it never departs from the right path.

Behold, dearest brother, among many other things, these are the duties of the priesthood; these are the duties of the pallium. If you diligently preserve them, you will possess inwardly what you have shown that you received outwardly.

As for your faith, which you briefly set out within your letter, although you ought to have explained it more fully, we nevertheless give thanks to our Redeemer that we have recognized it to be sound even in its very brevity. May the Holy Trinity surround your fraternity with the protection of its grace, and direct us in the way of its fear, so that after the bitterness of this life we may together deserve to reach eternal sweetness.

Written by the hand of Zacharias, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of December, in the fourteenth indiction.

## (865.) LXXXVIII. TO BERNARD, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, SON OF THE LATE BERNARD, COUNT OF BARCELONA. Fragment. He rebukes him for his many depredations.

[In Mansi, cited above.]

[Col. 0964B]

The duty of the care that we carry on behalf of all the Churches of God compels us to be concerned for the salvation of all Christians. Therefore, while also exercising providence concerning you, we hear what we did not wish to hear: that you are so lifted up against God that, plundering the Christian people, you commit numerous wrongs in the kingdom of our son, the glorious King Charles, to such an extent that . . .

## (866.) LXXXIX. TO HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS. He orders that a synod be convened at Soissons concerning Wulfad and his associates.

[Col. 0964C]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother HINCMAR, archbishop of Rheims.

From the report of many people coming from the regions of Gaul to the threshold or see of the apostolic Church, we have learned that your holiness has expelled from their proper ranks certain clerics who had been ordained by Ebo, formerly bishop of Rheims. When we heard of their deposition, although no special privilege primarily compelled us to undertake their case, we nevertheless judged it our duty to assist the oppressed, to raise up the crushed after the example of the Lord, and to free those in chains (Ps. 145).

We therefore considered it worthwhile to search more carefully through the archives of the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, and diligently investigate whether any written record concerning either those men or the one who ordained them might be preserved among us. We did so. For, after finding certain records there by God’s revelation, we also reread the acts of the council that you yourself sent us, namely the council in which the aforesaid clerics were degraded.

But after all these materials had been properly gathered and carefully examined—that is, both the records held by us and those which your holiness sent us—it is not yet plainly evident that these clerics were deprived of their proper rank according to the rule. Nevertheless, we do not meanwhile justify them, nor do we condemn anyone on this account; we do not readily reject their statement, nor do we rashly criticize your reverence. We do the former lest we be seen to close our ears to the cries of the poor, that is, the humble; we do the latter lest we appear prematurely to judge anything concerning matters unknown to us.

Accordingly, through the salutary language of this present letter, we necessarily exhort your fraternity to endeavor, with a merciful spirit and tranquil magnanimity, to summon to yourself the men mentioned—namely Wulfad and his associates—and, laying aside all hostility entirely, to discuss their restoration fraternally with them and strive to complete it mercifully.

We judged, and believed before God, that it would be more praiseworthy and more acceptable if, with his conscience questioned in the sight of God, you alone should graciously admit their restoration without any resistance, than if you first resisted and later, once justice had been demonstrated, embraced it together with many others.

But if a clear conscience does not permit you to be moved to this, we command our brothers Remigius of Lyons, Ado of Vienne, and Wenilo of Rouen, together with the other archbishops and bishops of Gaul and Neustria who are able to attend, to assemble for this very purpose with your blessedness and your suffragans at the city of Soissons in your diocese. We unquestionably wish you to summon Wulfad, together with his aforementioned companions, to that venerable assembly.

We have sent letters commanding this to everyone concerned—namely, to the archbishops and bishops as well as to Wulfad and his associates. There, examining in canonical order and investigating more closely everything done in their case, if you judge that anything just or pious should be done for their restoration, carry it out without opposition and restore them to their ranks.

Moreover, if, while you are disputing or perhaps reaching differing decisions, the aforesaid deposed men appeal to the apostolic see and ask to be condemned or absolved by its special judgment, we command that, if your holiness or Wulfad and his associates cannot come to us in person, immediately after the council—which has been convened by our authority for the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September of the present fourteenth indiction—has been completed, both parties must send vicars to the see of blessed Peter to examine and conclude this affair, with instructions to present your persons and without offering any excuse.

Lest an evil thought perhaps insinuate itself, saying that these removed clerics no longer have the right to make a formal complaint because the period of their deposition has exceeded the limit of a year, it must be known that nothing of this sort is found at all in the canons where appeals to the Roman prelate are discussed. Moreover, it may perhaps become clear that these men appealed within the year. Finally, as a letter of Pope Leo IV, of holy memory, found among us indicates, we have now learned without hesitation that they appealed to the apostolic see.

The complete deposition at issue here is, however, entirely different from suspended excommunication, concerning which a certain rule establishes that its voice—shouting arrogantly rather than making a humble request—is not to be heard after a year.

Since some people, imitating Pharaoh and his ministers, often oppress and afflict with devised burdens those whom they find oppressed and cast down, when they raise a cry about their needs, like the children of Israel of old, we therefore admonish your holiness before God that, when the frequently mentioned men perhaps obtain an examination of the cause of their deposition, encouraged by our letters, none of them should suffer your indignation, nor should any of them experience inconvenience through your reverence’s influence in carrying out what they have begun.

But you will say that you possess the privileges of the apostolic see confirming the decisions made concerning these men. Good—cleverly put. But if, as the copies preserved faithfully with us show, you have them in your possession and reread them carefully, you will certainly find that their ultimate force and validity have been reserved to the discretion of the authority of the apostolic see.

That see guards the rights of others in such a way as not to diminish its own; gives due honor in such a way as not to grant its own to outsiders; and so protects your affection from the enemy that it cannot itself be shown to be the enemy of those who demand its aid.

Therefore, just as, with God’s help, we are ready to set the shield of our protection against all who oppose you, so let your fraternity always hasten with kindly favor to assist those who seek the intercession of the apostles. Let the weapons we have bestowed be so effective on your behalf that, where necessary, they may possess the full strength of power for us, not against us.

Let your fraternity act in these matters so that, beyond the reverence due to obedience, the extent of your love for us—more precious than gold and precious stones—may become as clear as daylight in your mind, and by this display give a distinctive sign of your charity. Let what sometimes burns only inwardly now send outward the rays of its own brightness through these actions.

Know, moreover, that we have instructed our brother and fellow bishop Remigius, bishop of Lyons, first to visit you and present our letter to your affection. Then, if you fear to consent to the restoration of the aforesaid men solely because of the exercise of your own authority, let him endeavor to send you the letters entrusted to him by us for convening the council already designated by our decision.

Whatever you examine and discover in the council, send to our judgment in a record of the proceedings, as the venerable decrees prescribe, and report fully and faithfully to our authority whatever seems beneficial and worthy of confirmation.

Finally, take care not to regard as negligible in any way what we have decreed concerning the aforesaid removed clerics. You will be able to know without hesitation from us that, if it is despised, it will be avenged in every respect, since neither fraternal charity nor the administration of the place over which, by God’s authority, we preside permits us to abandon them until, with his assistance, the matter reaches a regular conclusion.

We desire that your holiness, or rather your fraternity, may prosper in Christ.

Given on the third day before the Nones of April, in the fourteenth indiction.

## (866.) XC. TO HERARD, ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS. He commands that, unless Hincmar voluntarily restores Wulfad and his associates to their ranks, a council be convened at Soissons for the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, and that they be restored there.

[In Mansi, cited above.]

[Col. 0967A]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother HERARD, archbishop of Tours, and to all the venerable bishops of your diocese.

From the report of many people coming from the regions of Gaul to the threshold or see of the apostolic Church, we have learned that our brother Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, expelled from their proper ranks certain clerics who had been ordained by Ebo, his predecessor. When we heard of their deposition, although no special privilege primarily compelled us to undertake their case, we nevertheless judged it our duty to assist the oppressed, raise up the crushed after the example of the Lord, and free those in chains (Ps. 145).

We therefore considered it worthwhile to search more carefully through the archives of the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, and diligently investigate whether any written record concerning either those men or the one who ordained them [or their ordination] might be preserved among us. We did so. For, after finding certain records there by God’s revelation, we also reread the acts of the council that our brother and fellow bishop Hincmar himself sent us, namely the council in which the aforesaid clerics were degraded.

But after all these materials had been properly gathered and carefully examined—that is, both the records held by us and those which the same bishop sent us—it is not yet plainly evident that these clerics were deprived of their proper rank according to the rule. Nevertheless, we do not meanwhile justify them, nor do we condemn anyone on this account; we do not readily reject their statement, nor do we rashly criticize the reverence of the brother mentioned. We do the former lest we be seen to close our ears to the cries of the poor, that is, the humble; we do the latter lest we appear prematurely to judge anything concerning matters unknown to us.

Accordingly, in the salutary language of our letter, we exhorted that same common brother of ours to endeavor, with a merciful spirit and tranquil magnanimity, to summon to himself the men mentioned—namely Wulfad and his associates—and, laying aside all hostility entirely, to discuss their restoration fraternally with them and strive to complete it mercifully.

We judged, and believed before God, that it would be more praiseworthy and more acceptable if, with his conscience questioned in the sight of God, he alone should graciously admit their restoration without any resistance, than if he first resisted and later, once justice had been demonstrated, pursued it together with many others.

But if a clear conscience does not permit him to be moved to this, we commanded you, together with the other archbishops and bishops of Gaul and Neustria who are able to attend, to assemble for this very purpose with the aforementioned brother and fellow bishop Hincmar and his suffragans at the city of Soissons. We unquestionably wish you to bring Wulfad, together with his aforementioned companions, to that venerable assembly.

We have sent letters commanding this to everyone concerned—namely, to the frequently mentioned bishop himself, to the other archbishops and bishops, and to Wulfad and his associates. There, examining in canonical order and investigating more closely everything done in their case, if you judge that anything just or pious should be done for their restoration, carry it out without opposition and restore them to their ranks.

Moreover, if, while you are disputing or perhaps reaching differing decisions, the aforesaid deposed men appeal to the apostolic see and ask to be condemned or absolved by its special judgment, we command that, if our aforementioned brother and fellow bishop Hincmar or Wulfad and his associates cannot come to us in person, immediately after the council—which has been convened by our authority for the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September of the present fourteenth indiction—has been completed, both parties must send their vicars to the see of blessed Peter to examine and conclude this affair, with instructions to present their persons to us and without offering any excuse.

Lest an evil thought perhaps insinuate itself, saying that these removed clerics no longer have the right to make a formal complaint because the period of their deposition has exceeded the limit of a year, it must be known that nothing of this sort is found at all in the canons where appeals to the Roman prelate are discussed. Moreover, it may perhaps become clear that these men appealed before the year had passed. Finally, as a letter of Pope Leo IV, of holy memory, found among us indicates, we have now learned without hesitation that they appealed to the apostolic see.

The complete deposition at issue here is, however, entirely different from suspended excommunication, concerning which a certain rule establishes that its voice—shouting arrogantly rather than making a humble request—is not to be heard after a year.

But the frequently mentioned bishop will say that he possesses the privileges of the apostolic see confirming the decisions made concerning these men. Good—and cleverly put. But if, as he claims, the copies preserved faithfully with us are in his possession and he rereads them carefully, he will certainly find that their ultimate force and validity have been reserved to the discretion of the authority of the apostolic see.

That see guards the rights of others in such a way as not to diminish its own; gives due honor in such a way as not to grant its own to outsiders; and so protects his affection from the enemy that it cannot itself be shown to be the enemy of those who demand its aid. For we also wish the weapons bestowed upon him by us to be so effective on his behalf that, where necessary, they may possess strength for us rather than against us.

Even without a decree of the apostolic see concerning privileges, we do not regard the provisions established by his holiness as something to be violated, unless perhaps they are found to conflict with the sacred laws.

Know, moreover, that we instructed our brother and fellow bishop Remigius, bishop of Lyons, that if our brother and fellow bishop Hincmar fears to consent to the restoration of the aforesaid men solely because of the exercise of his own authority, he should endeavor to send you the letters entrusted to him by us for convening the council already designated by our decision.

Whatever you examine and discover in the council, send to our judgment in a record of the proceedings, as the venerable decrees prescribe, and report fully and faithfully to our authority whatever seems beneficial and worthy of confirmation.

We desire that your fraternity may prosper in Christ now and always.

Given on the third day before the Nones of April, in the fourteenth indiction.

Letters of this same tenor were also sent to other bishops of various provinces.

## (866.) XCI. TO FESTINIAN, BISHOP OF DOL. He rebukes him for not writing to him with due reverence and commands him to recognize the Church of Tours as metropolitan, unless he proves the contrary by authentic documents.

[In Mansi, cited above.]

[Col. 0969B]

Although we received the letters of Your Love without the impression of any identifying seal, we have learned that you wrote—and indeed acted—in them quite otherwise than our apostolate had instructed you in writing. For on the front of your page you did not hesitate to place your own name before the apostolic name, using sheer presumption rather than simplicity. But since we have already reproved you for this very act, we are greatly surprised that you do not repent, remaining within your own proper bounds and directing your steps where they are not fitting. For this you will no longer escape without a fitting rebuke, unless the fact that we are uncertain whether the same letters that appeared to lack your seal were actually sent by you makes us hesitate, and apostolic gentleness, as is customary, prolongs the time for correction; this itself clearly shows how greatly you fear being subjected to ecclesiastical correction for so presumptuous an action. [Col. 0969C]

We had indeed instructed you, since you seek that the use of the pallium be assigned to the Church of Dol, to send us the documents which your predecessors had received from our apostolic see when they received the pallium, so that, after carefully examining them, we might rejoice to follow in the footsteps of our predecessors. We added that, to make us more readily believe you, the letters should be sealed with an episcopal and royal bulla, and that a suitable messenger of yours should accompany the documents; but you have delayed doing this. [Col. 0969D]

Finally, when a dispute arose among the Britons as to who was metropolitan, we decreed that you should have recourse to the see of Tours—which the judgments of many demonstrate to be your metropolitan see—or should endeavor to refer the matter to our apostolate, so that it might become clear which Church among you was metropolitan. But you were unwilling to accomplish either of these things.

Therefore, since, as far as we have learned, the Church of Tours is your metropolitan church, it remains necessary that your bishops follow it, approach it in their affairs, and not refuse to seek its judgment, as the records of our predecessor pontiffs and the examples of earlier times plainly show. [Col. 0970A] We do not know what reason of ecclesiastical tradition permits you, who have only seven bishops, to have a metropolitan see—especially since it is prescribed that a bishop be heard not by seven but by twelve. When a matter arises among you that must be heard by a body of twelve bishops, and the bishops cannot be summoned because of the division of the neighboring kingdom, the result is that losses are inflicted upon the Church in such circumstances, as we remember happened in those regions in the case of the deposition of bishops.

Yet you are not to be called metropolitan until you send us the writings of your predecessor bishops, which your predecessors received when they accepted your pallium. For if your Church earned the gift of the pallium from this holy see, that gift of such dignity was certainly not granted to you without some written document, which you ought to have preserved in your archives. [Col. 0970B]

You also wrote to us that Severinus, bishop of this holy Roman Church, had consecrated your predecessor Restoaldus archbishop, as is read in our records, and that Adrian had given the pallium to a certain Juthinaleus. But after reviewing the records of both men, we were entirely unable to find anything concerning these matters. Nevertheless, so that this uncertainty may be removed, if you wish to act so contentiously as to say that the see of Tours is not your metropolitan see, we decree—as we have said—and command our brother and fellow bishop Heraldo, who presides over it, to send his legate to our pontificate. Send with him your vigorous legates, and send at the same time the writings we have mentioned, so that, after the claims of both parties have been heard before us and the case has been weighed in an impartial balance, it may become clearer than daylight which Church among you is metropolitan. [Col. 0970C]

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the fourteenth indiction.

### (In the year 866.) XCII. To Salomon, King of the Britons

He refuses to send the pallium to Festinian, bishop of Dol, until he is convinced by authentic documents of the latter’s right.

[In Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 0970D] Having read the letters of Your Glory, which you appeared to have sent to our episcopate without the impression of any seal, we found that you had commanded us to do what you had often commanded before: namely, to send the pallium to Festinian, the venerable bishop of Dol, from the apostolic see over which we preside by divine authority.

But before writing any reply to this request, we had thought to correct you with a moderate rebuke because you had placed your name before the apostolic name when writing it. Nevertheless, because apostolic gentleness has never rebuked anyone with sudden harshness, and because it recognized that this may have happened somehow through the negligence of a scribe, it postponed restraining you according to your deserts. We wish only that you amend the matter to the extent that you fear being subjected to ecclesiastical correction for so presumptuous an act. [Col. 0971A]

As for the sending of the pallium, and likewise concerning the metropolitan see of Tours, we have often written to you what reason requires. But, as we read again in your letters, you have inclined your ears to our writings, yet not your hearts to their meaning.

It remains, then, that you finally consider which see has anciently been your metropolitan see. Your metropolitan see is the Church of Tours, as we informed you long ago, as the records of our predecessors and the examples of earlier times show. The bishops of your region ought to have recourse to it and, while reserving the authority of the apostolic see, seek the sentence of its judgment in every way rather than refuse it. For it seems reprehensible that, because of the division of the kingdom, anyone should attempt to claim for himself such rights as are said to be claimed among you. [Col. 0971B]

Therefore, my son, do not give your assent to those who wish this, but kindle others also, by the example of your obedience, to heed your words. As the Apostle says: “Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you in the time of tribulation” (1 Peter V, 6). For if you prove obedient to our admonitions, you will be filled with every good thing, and after the end of this age you will receive, through the prayers of the holy apostles, the kingdom that lives forever.

Moreover, if you have any authorities that declare that there was a metropolitan see among the Britons, or if you possess any writings of our predecessor pontiffs that demonstrate this, send them to us. Let the Church of Tours likewise send us, if it has any, authorities testifying that it was once your suffragan church, so that, after hearing both parties, we may determine which of the two is metropolitan. [Col. 0971C] For just as you proclaim, so does that Church proclaim that it held and still holds the rights of metropolitan authority in the British kingdom.

Or, if perhaps the aforesaid Church has lost its authorities, or yours has lost those it once possessed, disclose to us the manner of that loss; or send us from both sides suitable and distinguished legates who know how to render us a full and complete account of everything. Thus, as we said above, with the Lord’s help, we may put an end to the dispute among you.

### (In the year 866.) XCIII. To All Bishops

He again admonishes them concerning the sentence of excommunication which he had pronounced against Waldrada and her accomplices.

[In Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 0971D]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend brothers, the archbishops and bishops established throughout Italy, Germany, Neustria, and Gaul.

We had indeed resolved to temper the measure of punishment against Waldrada, the adulteress who stubbornly remained impenitent, less strictly than mercifully, and not to pronounce against her a sentence of just punishment proportionate to so great a crime, unless she had resolved to remain forever with an obstinate mind in the mire of adultery and had shown herself ready to heed neither sacred admonitions nor our own or your frequent exhortations. [Col. 0972A]

[Note: The passage is corrupt.]

Nevertheless, it remains entirely certain to God, who examines the heart, and to his faithful, that this was not done by her own will—for she would have remained of her own accord, if she could, indeed forever, in so great a crime—unless our unceasing diligence, together with the power of the supreme Maker, had been directed toward abolishing it; and unless her companion—shame upon the deed!—who admitted her in some manner as his associate, had shown himself somewhat more inclined to obedience.

It is plainly evident that what we say is true, since she has not yet recognized or confessed her fault, in accordance with what is written: “Declare your iniquities first, that you may be justified” (Isaiah XLVIII, according to the Septuagint). Nor has she sent us, who undertook to pursue her case, an embassy of lamentation asking pardon, and by first offering the remedy of repentance earned a fitting indulgence, as Solomon says: “He who conceals his sins shall not prosper; but he who confesses and abandons them shall obtain mercy” (Proverbs XVII). [Col. 0972B]

Finally, when she ought to have come to us by the right road and sought the assistance of the see of blessed Peter, so that, according to what had been established, we might decide her case with a consideration pleasing to God, she afterward turned back after Satan and redirected her journey to the province in order to rule it. This happened even though our legate’s diligence had recalled her again to Italy, and although she had accomplished almost nothing there. Thus a considerable scandal has been generated in the Church of Christ: she pursues worldly glory, rules the commonwealth, and, what is more grievous, is recognized as presiding even over holy places and religious persons. [Col. 0972C]

Moreover, she does not cease, as some testify, from the plot against Queen Theutberga that she began, while she seeks to revisit those places where access by her to King Lothar, and by that king to her, might easily be arranged. In short, to summarize everything, day after day she seeks by various devices a way to return to her former pleasures.

Nevertheless, to say briefly with the eminent Apostle what must often be repeated against her and those like her: “According to her hardness and impenitent heart she treasures up wrath for herself on the day of wrath” (Romans II). Therefore, until she has made satisfaction for her deeds to the Church of Christ, and especially to us, who principally have charge of her and who undertook to pursue and investigate her case; until, by accepting our counsel, she has also removed every unfavorable suspicion concerning herself—we have, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and by the authority of our humble person, expelled her, together with all her accomplices, communicants, and supporters, from participation in the reception of the Lord’s precious body and blood and from every fellowship of the holy Church. [Col. 0972D]

We remember that this sentence was promulgated by us on the fourth day before the Nones of February, and that we sent it to you in writing. But because we do not know whether it reached your knowledge, we have taken care to disclose it again to Your Reverence. For while the matter is still pending and the good work begun has not reached completion—indeed, while various indications make it understood that the breath of the wicked is always directed toward its former evils—it is urgently necessary to ensure that, while we remain sluggish, a final error does not follow, worse than the first.

For we are called watchmen in vain if we do not see the approaching wolf from afar. We are called bishops, that is, overseers, in vain if we do not contemplate the future outcome through the signs that precede it—especially since we have already experienced what we now see, and the manifestation of past events gives birth to certainty about those that are to come. [Col. 0973A]
