Therefore, at least, let your charity grieve over the daily attacks brought against Queen Theutberga and sympathize with the distinguished member of the Lord’s body with all the affection of your heart. And, so that our labor may not prove fruitless, let Your Fraternity raise spiritual weapons with us against the aforesaid adulteress and her communicants. In his diocese, where he governs the Lord’s people, or wherever she may happen to be, let him publicly and boldly declare in a living voice that she and her supporters are excommunicated, until she submits herself to worthy repentance by our special judgment. [Col. 0973B]

If, perhaps, someone should say that not only that woman but also King Lothar had sinned in this matter, and that he therefore ought to be bound by a similar penance, whether he speaks such things in order to instruct himself or to reproach us—although it is not necessary for us to answer anyone who makes such claims boastfully—it is nevertheless fitting that, from the authority from which this sanction proceeds, whoever he may be should seek the solution to this matter in the abundance of its prerogative. For the apostolic authority, to which the care of all the churches converges, possesses sufficient means of governance by which it may provide suitably for them all: through these it instructs the ignorant in the discipline of salvation and, by a stewardly dispensation, imposes upon those who reproach it the measure of fitting discretion.

Meanwhile, whoever among you receives this letter of sanction should take the greatest care to send it to the metropolitan bishops and distribute copies of it throughout the neighboring regions. In all these matters, let him show himself such that everyone may see him burning with the zeal of Phinehas, who appeased the Lord’s anger—not in defense of a harlot, but in avenging fornication. [Col. 0973C]

We wish Your Fraternity good health in Christ, now and always.

Given on the Ides of June, in the fourteenth indiction. [Col. 0973D]

### (In the year 866.) XCIV. To Egilo, Archbishop of Sens

He grants the pallium to the new archbishop, although he says that he does not approve of his having been taken from another church and monastery.

[In Mansi, same place.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Egilo, bishop of Sens.

We praise you for having humbly wished to evade the burdens of pastoral care; but we likewise approve that you afterward obediently bent the shoulders of your mind to bear them. For in you the action of two illustrious prophets, Jeremiah and Isaiah, has been fulfilled. [Col. 0974A]

One of them, when the Lord wished to send him to preach to the people, withdrew in fear because of his weakness, saying: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, I do not know how to speak, for I am a child” (Jeremiah I). The other, relying upon God’s mercy, replied when asked whom he would send: “Here am I; send me” (Isaiah VI).

Your resistance to coming to the burden of so great a dignity was therefore solely an indication of humility; but because you consented to arrive at it, this was the fullness both of that same humility and of its companion, obedience. This, together with the praise of your holiness, moved our pontificate, although with difficulty, to send you the pallium as a confirmation of your office. [Col. 0974B]

You state that you did not belong to the Church of Sens, but came to the episcopate of that church from a certain monastery. Wherever and whenever this occurs, we regard it as evil and consider it altogether grievous, namely because it tramples upon the sacred canons and scorns the clerics who, growing up in their own church, are shown, with the advancement of each successive age, to have devoted themselves to virtue, to the dignity of good morals, and to the pursuit of wisdom.

What does the consent of bishops avail when they assemble not according to the paternal rules but against the rules? Only then is one to be chosen from another church when no worthy person can be found among the clergy of the city itself in which the bishop is to be ordained. [Col. 0974C] We neither believe that this could happen in so large a diocese nor find that our predecessors, the bishops of the apostolic see, believed it could happen.

Whatever holiness anyone may possess, therefore, he ought not to seize the labors of others. He is commanded, after all, not to covet in any way what belongs to his neighbor. For precisely by appropriating the rights belonging to another, a person loses the grace of holiness. What holiness claims for itself a reward owed to another? What holiness usurps for itself the fruits of another?

Since, therefore, insufficient attention has been paid in this matter to the sacred regulations of the Fathers, at least recourse should have been made to the Gospel pages, in which it is read that, when the soldiers asked John the Baptist what they should do (Luke V), they immediately heard among his other instructions the command that they should be content with their pay. [Col. 0974D]

Here it must be considered: if the soldiers of this world are ordered by John, who was more than a prophet, to be content with their own pay, with what punishment must the soldiers of Christ be punished when they in any way intrude upon the pay of others?

But why should we labor to enlarge upon these matters, which your holiness compels us for the present to overlook? Since we shall, with God as our guide, send letters from our apostolate to you, to your compatriots, and to your fellow priests established in those regions where this presumption is especially common—letters recalling to you the ancestral canons—it will certainly be necessary that from now on nothing of this kind be done by you or by anyone else. Otherwise, by the force of those same decrees, the presumptuous and obstinate violator of the sacred regulations will be subject to their sentences. [Col. 0975A]

Moreover, dearest brother, observe your purpose. You who remained for a long time in a monastery must not depart from your former vow. For what you guarded for so long in humble dress, it is certainly unbecoming to abandon now that you have been placed in a higher order. Holy Scripture and the venerable decrees teach this fully.

We wish Your Holiness good health in Christ.

### (In the year 866.) XCV. To Charles the Bald, King

He disapproves of the abuse that had become prevalent, whereby bishops were taken from other churches; nevertheless, at Charles’s request, he sends the pallium to Egilo for the Church of Sens.

[In Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 0975B]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son Charles, king.

When we read the text of the letter we received from Your Love and learned from it that you commended the bishop appointed over the metropolitan Church of Sens with extraordinary praises, we were filled with great rejoicing not only because of him but also because of you.

We rejoiced because of him, since report proclaims him to be such as the Apostle indicates a bishop ought [perhaps, “ought to be,” Hardouin] to be—he writes that a bishop must have a good reputation and be commended by those who are outside the Church (1 Timothy III). We rejoiced because of you, since, thanks be to God, you always love what is better and always desire that what is more precious be offered to the Lord God by all. [Col. 0975C]

Yet although these things greatly gladden us, they also deeply distress us, because the same venerable man is said to have come not from that church itself but from a certain monastery.

[Note: From a certain monastery: Flavigny, in the diocese of Autun. A manuscript chronicle states: “In the year 864 the body of Saint Regina, virgin and martyr, was transferred to Flavigny, with Egilo, abbot, presiding over the place; he was afterward archbishop of Sens.” J. Sirmond.] [Col. 0975D; Col. 0976D]

Since the same rule must certainly be observed concerning monks as concerning clerics who are to be promoted, it is nevertheless unbecoming, or rather unlawful, for anyone to intrude upon the pay of others and, coming from elsewhere, seize command in a camp in which he has not served. The most blessed Caelestine, bishop of the apostolic see, commanded this, saying (Decree 18):

> “Then let one be chosen from another church if no worthy person can be found among the clergy of the city itself in which the bishop is to be ordained—something which we do not believe can happen. First, therefore, those men must be rejected, so that someone from another church may rightly be preferred. Let each person enjoy the fruits of his service in the church in which he has spent his entire life; let no one intrude upon another’s pay, nor dare to claim for himself the reward owed to another.” [Col. 0975D]

In these words, Your Love should wisely observe that either no worthy person was found among the clergy of the Church of Sens to be ordained—which we do not believe happened, especially since it is a metropolitan church and is not lacking in numerous clergy—or else, without these men having been lawfully rejected, someone from elsewhere was irregularly chosen to be placed over them, and someone was found to eat the fruits of other men’s labors. [Col. 0976A]

Indeed, since the predecessor of this man, whose memory is reverently held and whom you extol with such great praises, is said to have presided over that same church for no short time, it is utterly incredible that he left no one there who could canonically be appointed in his place.

Since this presumption and violation of the sacred canons have become especially widespread in your regions, it is necessary for us to devote particular diligence and concern to cutting them off. Therefore, we earnestly beg Your Love—whose works we desire to please the supreme Judge not in part but entirely—to possess zeal for justice while keeping it according to knowledge; to open your eyes vigilantly on one side while nevertheless seeing what is on the other. [Col. 0976B]

Let those who are promoted into the sanctuary give thanks to Heaven for the gifts bestowed upon them in such a way that they do not, like the Pharisee, rashly sharpen their tongues in disparagement of another. For it is dangerous to despise all the ministers of the Church in this manner and to place over them someone unexpected and unwanted.

Since we have learned from several complaints, uttered by those who grieve over this, that such a thing has often been presumed, we ask you, whom we rightly love, not to drive anyone toward so great a transgression. Otherwise, mindful of the sacred regulations and not sluggish in carrying them out, we shall strive, with girded loins, to defend them against the presumptuous. With Christ’s help, and providing for his Church, we shall no longer tolerate their violators with equanimity. [Col. 0976C]

Until, however, we begin to uproot this same transgression from your regions by the mattock of our general decree, we have judged that this brother and fellow bishop of ours should be spared. Therefore, according to the custom of his predecessors and at your request, we have sent him the pallium for his use.

But we ask that, just as we granted it to him because we listened to you, so Your Piety may graciously grant him what we request with generous bounty: namely, the property and everything else known to have been taken in any way from the Church of Sens, so that, just as he is outwardly adorned by the great gift granted to him by us, he may likewise rejoice inwardly through your clemency over the goods restored to the church entrusted to him. [Col. 0976D]

We wish also to urge you to exercise this work of piety concerning the other churches of your kingdom, so that it may not be recognized that this good work is lacking, by any arrangement, among your countless and splendid deeds.

How detestable it is that things given to God by pious kings and devout people should, with your permission, be taken away and assigned to worldly uses—we leave your wisdom to consider carefully, since our epistolary language has already exceeded its proper measure.

### (In the year 866.) XCVI. To King Charles

That nothing should be altered concerning Wulfad and his associates before the synod’s decision.

[In Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 0977A]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Charles, glorious king.

When we read through Your Excellency’s letters, which poured forth honey in their words, we plainly recognized anew the distinguished marks of the faith with which you burn toward the holy Roman Church. Once again we found in them the heights of your humility and most ready devotion toward the apostolic see—virtues difficult to describe adequately. [Col. 0977B]

Yet in those words Your Love asserts nothing except what your diligent experience learned long ago from us; it endeavors to demonstrate in writing nothing except what we see almost daily in your deeds. What could be a clearer indication of your supreme devotion and praiseworthy affection than the kindness your good will strives to show in the case of the venerable abbot Wulfad and his associates?

At first, indeed, we ourselves urged you to assist them. But now your piety is driven by such concern for them, while preserving reverence toward the princes of the apostles whose protection they seek, that it appears to be breathing from this pious activity of yours more than we seemed to have requested. [Col. 0977C]

For we invited you, as a most merciful ruler endowed with a twofold charity, to seek just redress for those who had been deposed; we did not incautiously urge you to restore them prematurely. How we encouraged you in this matter is made abundantly clear by the first letter sent to you concerning it.

Therefore, let your providence act for them as that letter indicates we requested, and your Excellency will remain, as we believe, entirely blameless before God. [Col. 0977D]

Moreover, remembering your eager obedience, formerly known to us and proved by countless experiences, and desiring that you should show it in this case also with regard to reverence for the princes of the apostles, we wrote to you, as to our dearest son, so that, kindly assisting those whose cry had reached their see in their just cause, you might likewise strive to obtain their assistance for yourself through their intercessions—not so that you might introduce into the Church of God a seedbed of blame.

For we, who preside over the Church of God through the abundance of heavenly grace, ought to present it in the form in which its founder presented it, cleansing it by his own blood: namely, as having neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of that kind.

But how can one act irreproachably now, when documents concerning their ordination lie before us in such diversity—some accusing these men and others defending them? To examine and distinguish these documents, we have ordered a synod of most reverend bishops to be held at this time in your kingdom, as you know. [Col. 0978A]

We wish their report to disclose to us, in the sequence of the proceedings, what was found there concerning the rejection of the men in question, just as the decretal constitutions prescribe. Only then shall we arrange what pleases God, once we have made our decision.

For we, who desire a mature judgment concerning all people, but especially concerning priests, do not know at all how to issue a definitive judgment about matters insufficiently known before we have fully learned, through the aforesaid bishops, everything that we decreed should be examined by them in due order.

Now, if, before the bishops inform us what they have found concerning these men, we restore any of the deposed clerics and anticipate by our judgment the synodal examination they must carry out, why do we wish them to be troubled in vain? Why do we wish them to be wearied by so long a journey without purpose? Or why was it necessary to inflict upon them so great an injury or humiliation? [Col. 0978B]

Therefore, if you wish us, with Christ as our guide, to bring the cause of justice and piety that we have begun to its proper conclusion, act so that whatever is found in the aforesaid synod concerning the previously mentioned deposed clerics may be disclosed to us through the report of all the bishops who assemble. Then, without doubt, await what the Lord reveals for us to determine. For if wisdom is a treasure to be dug out, it follows that whatever is wisely to be done must be sought out by every investigation, like refined gold.

We wish Your Glory good health in Christ, now and always, dearest son.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, in the fourteenth indiction. [Col. 0978C]

### (In the year 866.) XCVII. Nicholas’s Responses to the Questions of the Bulgarians

[In Mansi, same place.]

There is not much to answer to your questions, nor have we thought it necessary to linger longer over each one separately. By God’s authority we have sent to your country and to your glorious king, our beloved son, not only books of divine law but also suitable envoys who will instruct you concerning each matter as time and circumstances dictate. We have entrusted to them books that we judged necessary for you at present. [Possibly *illic*, “there,” rather than *illis*, “to them.”] [Col. 0978D]

#### I

At the beginning of your questions, you rightly and commendably state that your king seeks the Christian law. If one attempts to explain this at greater length, innumerable books would have to be written. But to show briefly what it chiefly consists in, one must know that the law of Christians rests upon faith and good works.

Faith is the first of all virtues in the conduct of believers. Hence, on the first day, light is said to have come into being, when God is described as saying, “Let there be light” (Genesis I)—that is, when the illumination of belief appeared.

Indeed, Christ descended to earth for the sake of this faith; but the Christian is likewise required to perform good works, as it is written in our law: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews XI). It is also written: “Just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead” (James II). This is the Christian law; whoever lawfully keeps it will certainly be saved. [Col. 0979A]

#### II

A person ought to love the one who receives him from the sacred font as a father; indeed, since spirit is superior to flesh, because this is a spiritual patronage and adoption according to God, the spiritual father must be loved in every respect more greatly by his spiritual son.

The evangelist Mark was Peter’s disciple and became his son through Peter’s sacred baptism. If he had not loved Peter as a father, he would not have obeyed him in all things as a son. There is no blood relationship between them or between their children, since the spirit does not know the things that belong to blood. For, according to the Apostle, “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to one another” (Galatians V). [Col. 0979B]

There is, nevertheless, another free and holy communion between them, which should not be called blood relationship but rather should be regarded as spiritual kinship. We therefore do not think that any kind of marriage union can exist between them, since even the venerable Roman laws do not permit marriage to be contracted between those who are sons by nature and those who are sons by adoption.

Indeed, the first book of the *Institutes*, when speaking of marriage, says among other things (*Institutes, On Marriage*, section “Therefore not”):

> “Marriage cannot be contracted between persons who occupy toward one another the place of parents or children, as between a father and daughter, a grandfather and granddaughter, a mother and son, or a grandmother and grandson, and so on without limit. If such persons unite with one another, they are said to have contracted an impious and incestuous marriage; and these relationships have such force that, even if persons have begun to stand toward one another in the place of parents or children through adoption, they cannot be joined in marriage. Thus, a woman who has become my daughter or granddaughter through adoption I cannot take as a wife.” And below: “If someone has become my sister through adoption, then, so long as the adoption remains in force, marriage between her and me certainly cannot exist.” [Col. 0979C]

If, therefore, marriage is not contracted between those whom adoption joins, how much more ought those to abstain from carnal intercourse with one another whom the regeneration of the Holy Spirit binds together through a heavenly sacrament?

It is therefore far more fitting to call my father’s son or my brother the man whom divine grace, rather than human will, has chosen to be his son or my brother. We are more wisely kept apart from mutual bodily intercourse because the Holy Spirit has united us by his love than if either carnal relationship or the mutual decision of some changeable mortal had joined us. [Col. 0979D]

### III.

We shall endeavor to show you, avoiding the prolixity of a lengthy style, in brief the custom which holy Rome adopted in ancient times and which the Church has maintained to this day in such unions, concerning the practice that you say the Greeks have in marital cohabitation.

Our people, both men and women, do not wear on their heads a band of gold, silver, or any other metal when they contract matrimonial bonds [Col. 0980A]. Rather, after the betrothal—which is the promised agreement of the future marriage and is celebrated with the consent of those who make it and of those under whose authority they are—and after the bridegroom has betrothed his bride with a pledge, marking her with the ring of faith upon her finger, and has handed over to her, before invited guests from both sides, the dowry agreed upon by both parties, together with a written document containing this agreement—either immediately or at a suitable time, lest such a thing be presumed before the period fixed by law—both are led to the marriage bond.

First, they are presented in the church of the Lord with the offerings that they ought to offer to God by the hand of the priest. Then at last they receive the blessing and the heavenly veil, after the example of the fact that the Lord, placing the first human beings in paradise, blessed them, saying: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. I), and so forth. Tobias too is described as having prayed to the Lord with his wife before he had intercourse with her (Tob. VIII).

Nevertheless, the one who enters a second marriage does not receive that veil. Afterward, when they have left the church, they wear crowns on their heads, which are always customarily kept in the church itself. Thus, after the nuptial celebrations have been completed, they are thereafter directed, by the Lord’s arrangement, toward leading an undivided life.

These are the laws of marriage; these are, besides others that do not now come to mind [perhaps, “come to our mind,” HARD.], the solemn agreements of wedlock. We do not say, however, that it is a sin if all these things do not take place in the matrimonial covenant, as you say the Greeks maintain, especially since some are often so constrained by poverty that no assistance supports them in preparing such things. Consequently, according to the laws, the consent alone of those whose union is at issue is sufficient.

If that consent alone should happen to be absent from the marriage, all the other arrangements, even when celebrated together with intercourse itself, are rendered void, as the great teacher John Chrysostom testifies when he says (Homily 32 on Matthew): “Intercourse does not make a marriage, but consent.”

You now ask whether, when a man’s wife has died, he may take another wife. Know that he certainly may in every respect, with the outstanding preacher Paul giving this counsel. He says (I Cor. VII): “But I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I do”; and again: “A woman,” he says, “is bound by the law for as long as her husband lives; but if her husband has died, she is free: let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord.”

For what he decreed concerning the woman must also be understood concerning the man, since Holy Scripture often speaks conversely about the man; but what is said about the woman is likewise implicitly meant. For example, we say: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked” (Ps. I), and so forth; and again: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord” (Ps. CXI). Here we rightly believe that not only the man, but also the woman who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked and who fears the Lord, is blessed.

### IV.

We consider it unnecessary at present to explain to you, who are inexperienced and in a manner children in the faith, during how many periods or days of the year one must abstain from meat [Col. 0981A]. For the time being, however, during the days of fasting, when the Lord must be entreated above all through abstinence and the mourning of repentance, one must abstain from meat in every way.

Although it is appropriate for everyone to pray and abstain, during the periods of fasting one ought to devote oneself more fully to abstinence—namely, so that one who knows that he has committed unlawful acts may, in accordance with the sacred decrees, abstain during those times even from certain lawful things. This applies to the forty-day period before Easter; to the fast after Pentecost; to the fast before the solemnity of the Assumption of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin, our Lady Mary; and also to the fast before the feast of the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ. These are the fasts which the holy Roman Church adopted in ancient times and still observes.

On the sixth day, Friday, of every week, and on all vigils of distinguished feasts, one must abstain from eating meat and devote oneself to fasting, so that one may truly say with the psalmist: “At evening weeping will remain, and in the morning joy” (Ps. XXIX).

If any of you should wish to abstain from meat on other days, they are not to be forbidden, for the more a person sows here in tears, the more abundantly he will reap in joy in eternal life. We, however, could not impose a burdensome yoke upon you, who, as we have said, are still inexperienced and must be nourished with milk like children, until you come to solid food. But just as for the present we avoid this, so too we admonish you in every way not to touch what is forbidden. For the first-formed human beings were driven from the delights of paradise merely by tasting the forbidden fruit [Col. 0981C].

### V.

Although on Wednesday, more than on the other days apart from Friday, one ought to devote oneself to sorrow, because on that very day the Lord was, in a certain sense, already buried in the heart of the earth—that is, in the heart of Judas the betrayer—while Judas was contemplating delivering him to death, nevertheless, if anyone among you wishes to do so, he may certainly eat meat on that day.

This is permitted unless it has been forbidden to him by himself or by a priest, since it is written: “Obedience is better than sacrifice” (I Sam. XV); or unless that Wednesday happens to fall among the days of fasting, since Jonathan, violating the fast imposed by his father by tasting a little honey, was sought by his father to be put to death; or unless he himself has bound himself by a vow not to eat meat on that day, since it is written: “Vow and repay to the Lord your God” (Ps. LXXV).

On Friday, however, in remembrance of the Lord’s Passion and of the apostles’ sorrow, our taste must be kept from every feast of meat and from rich foods, except if the Nativity of the Lord and his Epiphany, or the feast of the blessed Mother of the Lord and undefiled Virgin Mary, or that of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, or of Saint John the Baptist, or of blessed John the Evangelist, or also of the heavenly key-bearer’s brother—namely, the apostle Andrew—or even of blessed Stephen the first martyr, should happen to fall on that day.

For the fact that the holy Church, like a faithful soul, ought on their feast days to release fasts or abstinences that have not been undertaken by perpetual vow is attested by the Lord in the Gospel, where he says: “When a woman gives birth, she has sorrow; but when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers her distress, because a human being has been born into the world” (John XVI). By “woman” he means the holy Church.

For just as a woman rejoices when a human being has been born into this world, so the Church is filled with worthy exultation when the faithful people pass into the future life. For this birth, she labors and groans greatly in the present and suffers as though in childbirth. No one should therefore find it strange if one who has departed this life is said to have been born. For just as, in ordinary usage, someone is said to be born when he comes forth from his mother’s womb and enters this light, so anyone who reaches the light of the living from the darkness of this age may rightly be called born.

For this reason, then, ecclesiastical custom appropriately maintains that the solemn days of blessed martyrs or confessors of Christ—on which they departed from this world for the dwelling of the living—are called their birthdays; and their solemn observances are called not funeral rites, as for those who are dying, but birthdays, as for those being born into true life.

Therefore, if they were then born to God, to whom all things live, in whose hand are the souls of the righteous, when they appeared to the eyes of the foolish to be dying, the holy woman no longer remembers her distress because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world—that is, into eternal light. If she rejoices over this birth, then on that day she ought not to be occupied with fasting, abstinence, or, finally, any sorrow.

Although in this valley of tears one must always mourn, and until one reaches that festival of the angels one must always devote oneself to sorrow—for even if a solemnity is celebrated here, it is not continuous but momentary, and is scarcely ever completed without pain [Col. 0982C].

### VI.

You say that the Greeks assert that you ought in no way to bathe on Wednesday or Friday. To those consulting us about this, we reply that the blessed Pope Gregory, apostle of the nation of the English, is recorded to have preached the following to the Romans in a sermon concerning the Lord’s Day (Epistles, Book II, Letter 3):

“For it has come to my attention that perverse men have preached among you that no one ought to bathe on the Lord’s Day. Certainly, if someone wishes to bathe for the sake of luxury or pleasure of spirit, we do not permit this even on any other day. But if it is for bodily necessity, we do not forbid it even on the Lord’s Day. For it is written: ‘No one has hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it’ (Eph. V); and again it is written: ‘Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires’ (Rom. XIII). Therefore, whoever forbids care of the flesh in its desires plainly permits it in necessities.

“For if it is a sin to wash the body on the Lord’s Day, then the face ought not to be washed on that same day either. But if this is permitted for one part of the body, why should it be denied to the whole body when necessity demands it?”

Therefore, what this distinguished prelate and most gracious teacher permitted on the Lord’s Day, which is more venerable than the other days, we likewise do not forbid on Wednesday or Friday. We maintain this distinction: if someone wishes to bathe for the sake of luxury or pleasure of spirit, we do not permit it even on any other day; but if it is for bodily necessity, we do not forbid it on either Wednesday or Friday.

### VII.

You also ask whether someone who is clean or unclean may kiss or carry the cross of the Lord together with relics. One who is clean may certainly do so. For what is signified by the kiss except the love with which each person burns toward such things? And in carrying it, what is expressed except the mortification of the flesh or compassion for one’s neighbors?

The Lord himself commanded that it be carried, though in the mind; but it is also carried bodily, so that one may more easily be reminded that it ought to be carried in the mind. The cross is so called from *cruciatus*, “torment”; and, as the aforesaid bishop explains, we carry the Lord’s cross in two ways: when we afflict the flesh through abstinence, or when, through compassion for our neighbor, we regard his need as our own.

Therefore, venerating the Lord’s cross and his Passion, kiss it; and, for love of him, if necessity requires, arm yourself with the same thought. Carry it, but with the greatest reverence and with body and heart most pure, so that it may never fall from your mind—that is, so that you may always afflict the flesh through abstinence and regard the needs of your neighbors as your own. For one who shows grief in another’s need carries the cross in the mind.

We absolutely do not permit an unclean person to carry it. For it is written: “Be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. LII) [Col. 0983C]. No vessel of the Lord is more sacred than the Lord’s cross, which was worthy to carry the Lord himself.

Nor is it permitted for an unclean person to kiss it, since by the very fact that he is unclean he bears witness that he does not love the mortification of the flesh. Therefore, let him not kiss what he does not love, lest what is said reproachfully by the Lord through the prophet concerning the rejected be said of him: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX; Matt. XV); and as the psalmist says: “They loved him with their mouth, and with their tongue they lied” (Ps. LXXVII).

We say the same concerning the relics of the saints, whose bodies were and are temples and vessels of God, and whom the Holy Spirit used as instruments for every good work whenever he willed.

### VIII.

Therefore, when due reverence has first been shown and purity of mind and body accompanies it, even during Lent—the matter about which you have made a special inquiry—it is permitted both to carry the Lord’s cross and, while observing the rule stated above, to kiss it whenever one wishes. This is especially so at those times and in those places where the attacks or ambushes of the ancient enemy are particularly feared.

### IX.

You ask whether during the greater Lent you ought to receive the body and blood of the Lord daily. We earnestly implore almighty God that this may be done, and we exhort all of you most vigorously, provided that the mind is not inclined toward sin; provided that an unrepentant or unreconciled conscience is not accusing you of mortal sins; and provided that none of you is found unreconciled, through his own fault, with a brother with whom he is at odds.

For we judge that one whose conscience is gnawed by any of these matters is burdened by so great a gift rather than obtaining a remedy. For, according to the Apostle, “he eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (I Cor. XI).

Concerning this matter, and concerning those who enter the church but do not receive communion after making an offering, the sacred canons perhaps speak sufficiently. They should be given to your bishop, whom, with God as your author, it is to be our modest task to ordain; and he should disclose them only to priests who hold the keys of knowledge, and nevertheless make them known to you insofar as this is necessary and not prohibited.

For the present, however, throughout Lent—which the custom of the Church calls the greater Lent—communion must be received every day in accordance with the rule given above [Col. 0984B]. For one must always devote oneself to prayer, attend upon the offerings of the faithful, and continually recall the prophetic saying: “On the day of your fast you find your own will” (Isa. LVIII).

If, even at another time when the body is clean, married people by mutual consent devote themselves to prayer, how much more must every pleasure be renounced during this period, when we also offer to God the tithes of our flesh, when we imitate the Lord in abstinence, and when we rightly cut away from ourselves not only unlawful things but also many lawful ones? And, in order that one may devote oneself freely to prayer, must one not apply oneself to purity of mind and body?

### X.

You wish to know whether anyone may perform some kind of labor on Saturday or Sunday. The holy Pope Gregory, whom we have often mentioned, addressing the Romans, says (Epistles, Book XI, Letter 3):

“It has come to me that certain men of perverse spirit have sown among you things that are wicked and contrary to the holy faith, so that they prohibited working on Saturday. What else should I call such men except preachers of Antichrist? For when he comes, he will cause Saturday and Sunday to be observed without any work. Because he pretends to die and rise again, he wishes Sunday to be held in veneration; and because he compels the people to Judaize, in order to restore the external observance of the law and subject them to the faithlessness of the Jews, he wishes Saturday to be honored.

“The statement made through the prophet, ‘Do not bring burdens through your gates on the Sabbath day’ (Jer. XVII), could be maintained only so long as it was permitted to observe the law according to the letter. But after the grace of almighty God, our Lord Jesus Christ, appeared (Tit. II), the precepts of the law, which were spoken figuratively, cannot be observed according to the letter.

“For if anyone says that this must be observed concerning the Sabbath, he must also say that carnal sacrifices are still to be offered; he must also say that the command concerning bodily circumcision is still to be retained. But let him hear the Apostle Paul speaking against him: ‘If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing’ (Gal. V).

“Thus we understand spiritually what was said concerning the Sabbath, and we hold it spiritually. For ‘Sabbath’ means rest; but we have our true Sabbath in the Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer. Anyone who knows the light of his faith and brings the sin of desire into his mind through his eyes introduces burdens through the gates on the Sabbath day [Col. 0985A].

“Therefore, we do not introduce burdens through the gates on the Sabbath day if, established in the grace of our Redeemer, we do not draw the weight of sin into the soul through the bodily senses. For the same Lord and Redeemer of ours is read to have done many things on the Sabbath day, so that he reproved the Jews, saying: ‘Which of you does not untie his ox or donkey on the Sabbath and lead it to drink?’ (Luke XIV.)

“If Truth itself did not command that the Sabbath be observed according to the letter, whoever observes Sabbath rest according to the letter of the law contradicts none other than Truth itself.”

On Sunday, however, one must abstain from earthly labor and devote oneself entirely to prayers, so that whatever is done negligently during the six days may be expiated through prayers on the day of the Lord’s resurrection.

### XI.

You inquire on which feast days of apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins you ought to withdraw from earthly labor. Certainly, on the solemnities of the blessed Virgin Mary; of the twelve holy apostles; of the evangelists; of the Lord’s Forerunner, John; and of Saint Stephen, the first martyr; and also on the birthdays of those other saints whose memory, by God’s favor, is celebrated among you and whose day is kept as a feast.

It must certainly be understood that one is to cease from worldly work on feast days for this reason: so that a Christian may more freely go to church, devote himself to psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, give himself to prayer, offer gifts, share in the memorials of the saints, rise to imitate them, attend to divine words, and provide alms to the needy.

If anyone, neglecting all these things, should wish to devote himself only to prayer [perhaps, “should not wish,” HARD.] and turn to the other vanities of the world and to permitted labors, it would have been better for him on the day of the blessed Apostle Paul to obey his command and work with his hands, so that he might have something from which to give to those suffering want. Paul himself, although he says that the Lord ordained that one who announces the Gospel should live from the Gospel, did not use this authority but worked with his own hands, so as not to burden any of those to whom he preached the Gospel (I Cor. IV).

### XII.

You ask whether judgment may be carried out on the festivals of the saints, and whether on such a day a person, if deserving, ought to be sentenced to death. It must be understood that on those festivals on which, as we have shown above, one must abstain from every worldly work, we decree that one must much more abstain from secular business and still more from executions.

Although both activities might perhaps be carried out without guilt, nevertheless, when a person ought to cling more closely to the things of God, it is fitting that he entirely cut away from himself the things of the world. Especially since on that day, when a person approaches divine service, he ought not to be entangled in secular affairs (II Tim. II); and out of reverence for so great a solemnity nothing ought to be brought forward except what generates joy, peace, and spiritual gladness for all [Col. 0986A].

After these preliminary remarks, the law will adequately teach you on which days other than these no secular judgments are to be carried out.

### XIII.

You say that amid your questions and consultations you request worldly laws. Concerning this matter, we would gladly send you whatever books we might judge necessary for you at present, if we knew of someone among you who could interpret them for you. But if we have sent books on worldly law with our messengers, when they return we do not want them left there, lest someone should interpret them perversely for you or corrupt them in any way by falsehood.

### XIV.

You further report that a certain Greek falsely claimed to be a presbyter, although he was not, and consequently baptized very many people in your country. When you came to know, through God’s inspiration, that he was not a presbyter, you judged that he should lose his ears and nose, be beaten with the harshest blows, and be expelled from your country [Col. 0986B].

Behold, what the Apostle cries out concerning certain people has been fulfilled in you; forgive us for saying so: “They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. X). For although that man acted wrongly if he lied, you nevertheless showed in this matter a zeal that was indeed pious but insufficiently cautious. Although he pretended to be a priest, his pretense nevertheless brought salvation to many.

There were various people who proclaimed Christ in various ways, though not for Christ’s sake. But whether by opportunity or in whatever manner they proclaimed him, the Apostle did not prohibit them [printed: “only these he did not prohibit”; perhaps, “these, however, he did not prohibit,” HARD.]; he strove only with the greatest concern that Christ should be proclaimed. Since Christ had ordained that the one who announced the Gospel should live from the Gospel, if many preached Christ in order to acquire earthly advantages, then Christ was not the cause but greed. Again, since many preachers of the Gospel were raised to great honors by the faithful, some preached Christ so that they too might receive similar honors; therefore, Christ was not their desire, but envy.

Yet none of these people was prohibited from having Christ proclaimed through them. Indeed, Judas, sent by the Lord among the other apostles, performed miracles, proclaimed Christ, and baptized many in his name [Col. 0986D].

Therefore, as Anastasius, the bishop of the apostolic see, writes, it is not asked who or what kind of person preaches, but whom he preaches (Anastasius II, Letter to the Emperor Anastasius).

### XV.

You ask whether those people who received baptism from him are Christians or ought to be baptized again. They were baptized in the name of the supreme and indivisible Trinity; they are certainly Christians, and it is not appropriate to baptize again those who were baptized by any Christian.

For, as the aforementioned Anastasius, the apostolic pontiff, writes to his namesake, the Emperor, even baptism given far from the Church, or by an adulterer or a thief, reaches the recipient as an undefiled gift. The voice that sounded through the dove excludes every stain of human pollution, by which it is declared and said: “This is he who baptizes” (John I).

If, therefore, although baptism has been given by an adulterer or a thief, the gift nevertheless reaches the recipient undefiled, why should that not remain undefiled and without any repetition which a clean man gives, even if we do not know with what intention he pretended to be a presbyter?

Indeed, Acacius, once bishop of Constantinople, pretended to be a priest, although he was condemned by Pope Felix of Rome. But let us hear what the aforementioned bishop Anastasius says about him. Among other things, he says (ibid.):

“When Acacius, although condemned, claimed for himself the name of priest, a swelling of pride was inflicted upon the crown of his head. It was not the people, who thirsted for the gift of his ministry, who were excluded; rather, the soul alone that had sinned was rightly subject to judgment.”

This is what the extensive teaching of Scripture testifies; and truly, according to the most famous Apostle, “neither he who plants,” that is, catechizes, “nor he who waters,” that is, baptizes, “is anything, but God who gives the growth” (I Cor. III).

Therefore, by administering good things, the wicked heap harm not upon others but upon themselves. Consequently, it is certain that those whom that Greek baptized were touched by no share of injury, because of the saying: “This is he who baptizes,” that is, Christ; and again: “God gives the growth,” meaning, not a human being.

### XVI.

You who judged that person in this way ask whether you ought thereafter to do penance. Certainly, every sin is washed away by penance, which makes progress only with the accompanying grace of God. For the Lord first looked upon Peter, and then Peter turned to tears.

It is clear that you committed sin against that man. First, because, so far as we can understand, it had not yet clearly been established that the man was not a presbyter, and it is written: “Do not judge before the time” (I Cor. IV).

Second, even if he pretended to be what he was not, he nevertheless did not do something that would displease God or his faithful people—especially since, among that nation, where until that time no sound faith and no true religion had been worshiped, he saw that a divinely opened door for gaining many had been granted to him. Perhaps he was striving to lead very many to so great a gift, in which he perceived that God was mercifully helping him.

Finally, if David pretended to be mad in order to secure only his own safety (I Sam. XXI), what offense did he incur when, by whatever means, he drew such a multitude of people away from the power of the devil and from eternal destruction? Especially since, by pretending to be a priest, he did nothing in baptizing that no one ought to do except a priest in such an obvious emergency. We think that he pretended to be a presbyter for this reason: he had already realized that you had been persuaded that the ministry of baptizing had been granted only to presbyters.

Third, although he was very blameworthy in this pretense, he proved sufficiently praiseworthy in the conversion of so many people.

Fourth, even if he deserved punishment, the measure of vengeance ought not to have been exceeded, nor so many and such cruel injuries heaped upon one man. Once his own nose and ears had been spared, expulsion from your country would have been sufficient punishment for him, which, together with the mutilation of his limbs, he experienced at your judgment.

### XVII.

You report how, through divine clemency, you received the Christian religion and caused your entire people to be baptized; how, after they had been baptized, they all rose up with great ferocity against you, saying that you had not handed down a good law to them, and even wishing to kill you and establish another king; and how, with divine power cooperating, you prepared yourselves against them, overcame them from the greatest to the least, and held them captive in your hands; and how all their chiefs and nobles, together with all their offspring, were killed by the sword, while the middle-ranking and lower people suffered no harm.

You wish to know whether you have sin concerning those who were deprived of life. Certainly, this did not occur without sin; nor could it have happened without your guilt that children who had not participated in their parents’ counsel and who are not shown to have taken up arms against you were slaughtered together with the guilty.

For this reason the psalmist, after saying, “I have not sat in the council of vanity, and with those who act unjustly I will not enter; I have hated the assemblies of the wicked, and with the impious I will not sit,” shortly afterward, entreating the Lord, says: “Do not destroy my soul with the impious, nor my life with men of blood” (Ps. XXV).

For this reason the Lord declares through the prophet Ezekiel (chap. XVIII): “As the soul of the father is mine, so also the soul of the son is mine; the soul that sins, it shall die.” And shortly afterward, concerning the father, he says:

“But if he begets a son who, seeing all the sins of his father which he committed, fears and does not do the same; who has not eaten upon the mountain, nor lifted his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel; who has not violated his neighbor’s wife, nor saddened a man; who has not retained a pledge, nor committed robbery; who has given his bread to the hungry and covered the naked with clothing; who has withdrawn his hand from injuring the poor; who has not taken interest or excess; who has carried out my judgments and walked in my commandments and done them—he shall not die in his father’s iniquity, but shall surely live.

“His father, because he has slandered and used violence against his brother and done evil in the midst of his people, behold, he has died in his iniquity. And you say: ‘Why has the son not borne the iniquity of the father?’ Certainly because the son has practiced judgment and righteousness, has kept all my commandments and done them; he shall surely live. The soul that sins shall itself die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, and the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son.”

Although you ought also to have dealt more gently with the parents who were captured—namely, by reserving their lives for the love of God, who had delivered them into your hands, so that you might readily be able to say to God in the Lord’s Prayer, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI)—nevertheless, since you could have spared those who perished in battle but did not permit them to live and did not wish to save them, you acted altogether unwisely.

For it is written: “There will be judgment without mercy for the one who has not shown mercy” (Jas. II). And through the prophet named above the Lord says: “Is the death of the wicked my desire, says the Lord God, and not rather that he should turn from his ways and live?” (Ezek. XVIII.)

Yet because you sinned out of zeal for the Christian religion and ignorance rather than from another vice, through Christ’s grace, after the completion of penance, you obtain forgiveness and mercy for these deeds.

### XVIII.

You indicate that you wish to know what you ought to do concerning those who reject the Christian law. In this matter it must be noted that, just as every human being contracted through another’s fault—that is, Adam’s—the condition that makes purification through the water of baptism necessary, so, when he approaches the water of regeneration in order to promise faith, he in a certain sense chooses another father, namely a spiritual one, by whom he is to be received, instructed, fortified with every protection, and presented to the reader of the Church as a kind of deposit.

Moreover, the one who rejects the faith he promised must be recalled by the person by whom he was received and who acted as sponsor for his faith. If he does not listen to the one whom he himself appointed as his guarantor, the matter must be reported to the Church. She should make every effort to bring back to her own fold the sheep that has gone astray, and recall it in every way to the way of truth, which is Christ.

He must be admonished by her as by a mother and as by a teacher, so that he may see that he has imitated the apostate spirit, of which it is written that it did not remain in the truth (John VIII). Let him also consider that Peter, prince of the apostles, cries out:

“For if, having escaped,” he says, “the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the latter state has become worse for them than the former. For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. The proverb has happened to them: ‘The dog has returned to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud’” (II Pet. II; Prov. XXVI; Matt. XVIII).

But if he does not listen even to the Church, he should truly be regarded by everyone as an ethnic—that is, a gentile—and consequently may justly be oppressed by foreign powers as an outsider.

It is certain that God often stirs up powers against those who deny Christ and against deserters from baptism. No one should therefore wonder that God stirs them up so that these people may bow their necks and, humbled, return to the Church. For when Hagar had departed from her mistress, an angel met her and said: “What is the matter, Hagar, Sarah’s maidservant? Return to your mistress” (Gen. XVI).

Such a person is therefore afflicted so that he may return—and would that he might return, for then he will receive the promised inheritance together with his brothers. For unless Christian powers were stirred up against such people, how would they render an account of their rule to God? It belongs to Christian kings of this world to wish that during their reign their mother, the Church, from whom they were spiritually born, be preserved peaceful and undiminished.

King Nebuchadnezzar, who had erected his statue and compelled everyone to worship it, is recorded to have been moved by the praises of the three youths delivered from the fire and to have said: “I establish a decree for all tribes and languages throughout the whole land: whoever speaks blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shall be destroyed, and his house shall be devoted to destruction” (Dan. III).

If a barbarian king rages in this way lest the God of Israel be blasphemed, because he was able to deliver three youths from temporal fire, how much more ought Christian kings to rage because Christ is denied and mocked—Christ by whom not merely three youths, but the whole world together with its kings, is delivered from eternal fires [Col. 0990B]?

Those who are convicted of lying to them or of being unfaithful are scarcely ever, or never, allowed by them to live. How then should they not be indignant and rage when they see Christ, who is King of kings and Lord of lords, denied and mocked by human beings, and the faith promised to him not kept?

Let them therefore be zealous with the zeal of God, since they remember that through Christ they themselves have been delivered from hell more than that king who considered the three youths rescued from the flame.

### XIX.

The venerable laws, which we shall send to you in writing, will adequately teach you what ought rightly to be done to those who have risen up to kill the king. Nevertheless, this remains within the king’s discretion: he ought to forgive sin not merely once, but also seventy-seven times, according to what the Lord commanded Saint Peter in the Gospel.

For “to whom more is forgiven, he loves more”; and, as the Gospel teaches, a king would not have forgiven his servant ten thousand talents—that is, many and immeasurable sins—if he himself had refused to forgive his fellow servant a hundred denarii, that is, lesser offenses (Matt. XVIII; Luke VII).

## XX

What judgment should be passed on a free man who has fled from his homeland, if he is apprehended? Certainly, nothing other than what the laws decree. Nevertheless, the sacred histories reveal that many saints departed from their homeland and were venerated more widely in another; but, when no other causes were present, I have found—unless I am mistaken—that they were never judged culpable merely for departing, especially since God’s voice says to our father Abraham: “Go forth from your land and from your kindred” (Gen. XII). Moreover, some of our fathers lived as exiles for many years in a land not their own. Otherwise, a man is not free if he does not dare to leave his homeland.

Indeed, if he is free and is bound by no legal ties of status, he does not flee but departs from his homeland, just as Abraham is told not “Flee,” but “Go forth from your land.” Because he did this in obedience, no one judging him brought any penalty upon him [perhaps *pertulit*, “endured,” rather than *protulit*, “brought upon,” HARD.].

## XXI

If a slave has departed by fleeing from his master, and is apprehended, he should be forgiven; otherwise, the provisions of the laws must not be transgressed in his case. Nevertheless, the apostle Paul’s salutary admonition should always be kept before one’s eyes: “Masters, grant your slaves what is just and fair, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven” (Col. IV). And elsewhere, when he had commanded slaves to obey their earthly masters, he added: “Knowing,” he says, “that each of you will receive from the Lord whatever good he has done, whether slave or free”; and, “You masters, do the same toward them, giving up threats, knowing that both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no partiality with the Lord” (Eph. VI).

## XXII

Concerning those who, whenever you advance to battle against enemies, take flight: if compassion does not mercifully intervene first, at least let the severity of the laws be tempered.

## XXIII

Concerning those who are ordered to advance against the enemy but disdain obeying the order, we advise the same.

## XXIV

What a parricide—that is, one who kills his father or mother—or one who kills a brother or sister ought to suffer, the laws indicate. But if he has taken refuge in a church, we decree that what the bishop of the place, or the priest appointed by him, has determined should be done.

## XXV

You report that it is the custom of your homeland always to keep guards on watch between your country and that of others, along the boundaries; and that if a slave or a free person escapes through that same guard-post by any means, the guards are immediately put to death on his account. You then ask what judgment we give concerning this. The matter must be investigated in the laws.

Nevertheless, far be it from your minds that you should now judge so impiously, since you have acknowledged such a pious God and Lord—especially when it is more fitting that, just as until now you have readily dragged people to death, so henceforth you should lead those whom you can, no less, not to death but to life.

Thus, just as the blessed apostle Paul, formerly a persecutor and insolent, breathing threats and slaughter against the Lord’s disciples (Acts IX), after obtaining mercy and being converted through divine revelation, not only inflicted the penalty of death on no one, but even wished to be accursed for his brothers (Rom. IX), and was most willingly prepared to spend and be spent for the souls of the faithful (II Cor. XII), so you too, after being called by God’s election and enlightened by his light, must no longer, as before, hunger for deaths. Rather, on every occasion that presents itself, you must without doubt recall everyone to life, both bodily and spiritual.

Just as Christ brought you from the perpetual death in which you were held to eternal life, so you yourselves should strive to rescue all people from the destruction of death—not only the innocent, but even the guilty—according to the saying of the most wise Solomon: “Rescue those who are being led away to death, and do not cease to deliver those who are being dragged to destruction” (Prov. XIV).

## XXVI

Concerning those who have slaughtered their neighbor, that is, a blood relative such as a brother, cousin, or nephew [*fratrer*, evidently an OCR or textual error for *frater*, “brother”], let the venerable laws retain their proper force. But if they have fled to a church, let them indeed be rescued from the penalties of death; nevertheless, without doubt, let them be subjected to the penance that the local bishop or priest has considered appropriate: “I do not desire the death of the sinner,” says the Lord, “but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XVIII).

## XXVII

Concerning those who have handed over their companion to death, we decree the same as above.

## XXVIII

What judgment should be passed on one who has been apprehended with another man’s wife, you will find by reading the laws. But if the adulterer has taken refuge in a church, we decree that he should be judged by the bishop, according to what the sacred canons are known to have defined and what the holy prelates of the Apostolic See are clearly known to have established.

## XXIX

Similarly, we give our judgment concerning the man who enters upon a female relative of his own blood; but we refer the leprosy of so great a transgression more suitably, and certainly, to the priest’s consideration and judgment.

## XXX

Concerning one who has killed a man unintentionally, we establish what the sacred rules establish. Your bishop, who has been placed among you, ought always to keep these rules at hand.

## XXXI

Concerning thieves of animals, let the decrees of the laws be observed, if not mercy.

## XXXII

Similarly, concerning those who have abducted a man or woman, we permit the same judgment.

## XXXIII

You state that, when you used to enter battle, you carried a horse’s tail on the military standard, and you ask what you should now carry in its place. What else, certainly, but the sign of the holy cross? It is the sign by which Moses divided the sea and destroyed Amalek (Exod. IV), by which Gideon overcame the Midianites (Judg. VII), and by which Christ our Lord not only overcame the devil, who held the power of death, but also struck him down. It is the sign that we carry on our foreheads. By it we are defended against all enemies and protected from every attack.

This is the sign of faith and the great terror of the devil. Christian rulers always use it in their necessities, and kings who follow the true religion, with Christ’s favor, often win celebrated triumphs over their enemies. But so that you may know more clearly what you ought suitably to carry in military service, in place of that horse’s tail, when you go forth equipped for war, we think it useful to recall a few things about Constantine’s deeds. He was the most devout of the Roman emperors and the most famous propagator of Christianity.

When he was leading an army against Maxentius, the tyrant of the city of Rome, he was already at that time a supporter of the Christian religion; nevertheless, he had not yet received the sign of the Lord’s Passion, as it is customary among us to be initiated. As he journeyed, turning many thoughts over in his mind concerning the necessity of the impending battle, and frequently raising his eyes toward heaven [perhaps “raising his eyes” is missing], praying there for divine assistance, he saw in sleep, in the eastern part of the sky, the sign of the cross glowing with fiery brilliance.

When he had been terrified by so great a vision and disturbed by the unprecedented sight, he saw angels standing before him, saying: “Constantine, conquer by this.” Then, restored to joy and already confident of victory, he marked on his forehead the sign of the cross that he had seen in heaven, transformed it into military standards, and fitted out the banner called the *labarum* in the form of the Lord’s cross. Thus equipped with the arms and standards of religion, he advanced against the arms of the impious and, without bloodshed among the Roman people, as he himself had prayed to God, magnificently triumphed over the tyrant when Maxentius was drowned in the river.

## XXXIV

You further ask whether, when a messenger has arrived announcing that you must go to battle, you should depart immediately, or whether there is any day on which it is not proper to go out to fight. We answer that no day whatsoever must be strictly observed as a prohibition against beginning or carrying out any undertaking, except—unless excessive necessity presses—the most celebrated days mentioned above and venerated by all Christians.

This is not because something of this kind is forbidden on those days, since our hope must not be placed in days, nor is all salvation to be expected from days, but solely from the living and true God. Rather, if unavoidable necessity is absent, one should devote oneself on those days more diligently than usual to prayer and attend the mysteries of so great a festival.

For when the Hebrews, once observing the Sabbath, were unwilling to take up arms against their enemies on the Sabbath day, and Almighty God wished to show that hope and strength should be placed in him alone, and not in the observance of days, a thousand of them were killed. The survivors, moved to repentance, said to one another: “If we all do as our brothers have done, and do not fight against the nations for our lives and our ordinances, they will soon destroy us from the earth” (I Macc. II).

## XXXV

You report that, when you used to advance into battle, you were accustomed to observe days and hours, practice incantations, jokes, and songs, and perform various auguries; and you desire instruction concerning what you should now do. We would necessarily instruct you about this, were we not observing that you have already been divinely instructed in the matter. We cannot build anything upon a divine foundation.

Therefore, when you are preparing to depart for battle, do not fail to do in God’s name what you yourselves have mentioned: go to the churches, offer prayers, forgive sinners, attend the solemn celebrations of Mass, present offerings, confess your offenses to priests, receive reconciliation and communion, open prisons, release bonds, grant freedom to slaves—especially the broken, the weak, and captives—and distribute alms to those in need.

In this way what the Apostle admonishes will be fulfilled: “Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus” (Col. III).

For the practices you mentioned—observations of days and hours, incantations, jokes, wicked songs, and auguries—are the pageantry and works of the devil. Thanks be to God, you renounced them already in baptism, and, when you put on the new person, you completely laid them aside together with the old person and his deeds.

## XXXVI

Whether, on Sunday or on other feast days, when necessity presses, it is permissible to travel or to go forth to battle: you can understand this from the thirty-fourth chapter of these responses of ours.

## XXXVII

The books that we judge presently necessary for you, as you request, we gladly grant, and, God granting it, we desire to provide still more.

## XXXVIII

You say that, when you are in camp, you cannot offer a complete and appropriate prayer, and therefore you wish to be told what you should do. We advise you to do the opposite: the more fiercely the enemies rage and the more necessity or tribulation weighs upon you, the more urgently you should devote yourselves to prayer.

For our fathers were victorious more by praying than by fighting, and achieved the fulfillment of their desire more through prayers than through battles. Moses prayed, while Joshua fought; but Moses conquered more by praying than Joshua by fighting. It is therefore more fitting to take time away from weapons than from prayer.

## XXXIX

You inquire about the degrees of blood relationship, so that you may know clearly which women you may properly marry. We have already recalled what the laws decree on this matter, but we consider it worthwhile to summarize it again. They say:

“Therefore, we are not permitted to marry every woman; for we must abstain from the marriages of certain persons. Marriage cannot be contracted between persons who occupy among one another the place of parents or children—for example, between a father and daughter, grandfather and granddaughter, mother and son, grandmother and grandson—and so on without limit. Among persons joined through a collateral degree of kinship there is also a similar rule of observance, though it is not so extensive.”

What the sacred canons, and especially the decrees of Zacharias, the supreme prelate, promulgate concerning this, we leave for you to investigate with your bishop.

## XL

You report that it is the custom of your homeland that, before you advance to battle, your authority sends a most faithful and prudent man to inspect all the weapons, horses, and whatever else is necessary for battle; and that whoever is found to have prepared these things inadequately is punished by death. You now wish to know what we decree should be done about this.

We advise you to turn all these practices toward the spiritual equipment of arms, and we urge you to bend the harshness of such severity toward the exercise of piety. Just as until now the preparation of weapons and horses was carefully examined to determine whether it was properly suited against visible enemies, so now let it be diligently investigated whether each person possesses spiritual arms—namely, good works—prepared against “the principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in heavenly places” (Eph. VI).

Moreover, the horse is understood as the mind, because just as a man is carried by a horse, so he is guided by the mind. Therefore, rightly, the man who does not have weapons prepared against his enemies perishes, because it is written: “Cursed is the man who performs God’s work negligently” (Jer. XLVIII).

Concerning the horse whose mind is unprepared, the Psalmist rightly says: “The horse is false for salvation; in the abundance of its strength it will not be saved” (Ps. XXXIII). For unless it were false, it would not be unprepared. Conversely, concerning a prepared horse it is said: “The horse is prepared for the day of battle, but the Lord grants salvation” (Prov. XXI).

Therefore, what you have hitherto observed carnally, and the weapons that you perhaps cruelly exacted from the poor, who were unable to prepare them, now venerate spiritually; and piously and continually encourage great and small alike to prepare these spiritual arms.

## XLI

Concerning those who refuse to accept the good of Christianity and sacrifice to idols or bend their knees before them, we can write nothing else to you except that you should lead them toward the right faith through admonitions, exhortations, and reasoning, convincing them rather than coercing them that their beliefs are foolish: they worship the works of their hands and insensible elements, although they are human beings capable of understanding; indeed, they bend their necks to demons and sacrifice to them.

For, as the Apostle teaches: “We know that an idol is nothing, but what the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons” (I Cor. VIII).

But if they do not listen to you, you must neither eat with them nor have any communion with them at all. You should withdraw your services and companionship from them, treating them as strangers and polluted persons, so that perhaps, struck by such shame, they may, by God’s inspiration, turn to him who is the true and not false God, the Creator and not the created, not made but the maker of all things.

For, as the Lord commands (Matt. X), from the house of one who does not believe, a Christian should take away not only food but not even the dust from his feet. Thus the disciples, unaware of what had happened, were distressed that Peter, their leader, had entered the house of Cornelius, whom he himself, at God’s command, had made the first Christian from among the Gentiles (Acts X). Therefore, no communion whatsoever is to be joined with those who do not believe and who worship idols.

Nevertheless, no violence whatsoever is to be inflicted upon them so that they may believe. For nothing that does not arise from free choice can be good. It is written: “I will sacrifice to you voluntarily” (Ps. LIII); and again: “Accept willingly the offerings of my mouth, O Lord” (Ps. CXVIII); and again: “I will confess to him of my own free will” (Ps. XXVII). God commands that service be offered freely and only by those who offer it freely. For if he had wished to use force, no one could have resisted his omnipotence.

But if you ask what judgment should be passed on such unbelievers, listen to the apostle Paul, who, writing to the Corinthians, says: “What have I to do with judging those who are outside? Is it not those who are within that you judge? God will judge those who are outside. Remove the evil person from among yourselves” (II Cor. V).

It is as though he were saying: “I make no judgment concerning those who are outside our religion, but reserve them for God’s judgment, since he will judge all flesh. Nevertheless, remove the evil person from among yourselves, lest, remaining among you, he spread like cancer; or else, when he sees himself being admitted to communion by the faithful, he may think that his own vanity is also being admitted to communion, and consequently judge his sect to be truer and holier than our religion.”

Therefore, for the sake of conscience, the communion of idol-worshipers must be avoided with the utmost care. For whoever communicates with idolaters appears to communicate with the idols themselves, indeed with demons: “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Ps. XCV). And the Apostle, saying, “What the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God,” added: “I do not want you to become partners with demons” (I Cor. X).

## XLII

You assert that, when your king has sat at table on a seat, as is customary, to eat, no one sits down to eat with him, not even his wife; instead, you sit at a distance on stools and eat on the ground. You therefore wish to know what we command concerning this.

Since what is done is not contrary to the faith, although it greatly conflicts with good manners, we do not so much command as advise and exhort you to look to rulers who cultivate the Christian religion. Considering the height of their humility, lay aside from yourselves every useless arrogance.

For they have read in the Gospel the Lord’s words: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI).

The ancient kings, many of whom were deemed worthy of the company of the saints—and were therefore truly called kings, because they were found to be holy—are said to have feasted with their friends, indeed with their slaves. Indeed, the King of kings and Lord of lords himself, our Redeemer, is described as having reclined and eaten not only with his slaves and friends, namely the apostles, but also with tax collectors and sinners.

## XLIII

Which animals or birds it is permissible to eat, the Lord has, in my judgment, clearly shown when, after the Flood, he gave all animals to Noah and his sons for food, saying: “All the fish of the sea have been delivered into your hand, and everything that moves and lives shall be food for you, like green plants” (Gen. IX).

And when all living creatures were shown divinely to blessed Peter on that sheet, he was told—although this must be understood in a higher sense—“Kill and eat” (Acts X).

Thus, no animal whose food is demonstrably in no way harmful to the body, and which human society admits as food, is prohibited from being eaten. For that reason, as the holy and eloquent teacher Augustine writes, human custom has not admitted carrion as food, because the flesh of animals that have died, rather than those that have been killed, is diseased and is not suitable for the health of the body, for whose sake we take nourishment.

The Lord himself refutes the opinion of those who claim that something in foods is unclean, saying: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what proceeds from the mouth defiles a person” (Matt. XV). And it is said divinely to the apostle Peter: “What God has sanctified, you must not call common or unclean” (Acts X). His fellow apostle Paul, writing, says: “All things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean” (Tit. I).

Nevertheless, lest some of you should wish to point out certain animals prohibited in the Old Testament and restrain you from eating them, it should be noted that the pig is also numbered among those that are prohibited. Concerning this matter, the aforementioned holy Augustine, while passing over the other animals for the moment, also mentions this animal, writing:

“In the Old Testament, where certain foods of flesh are prohibited, let them understand, if they can, how this sentence is not contrary to the Apostle’s statement, ‘All things are clean to the clean,’ and ‘Every creature of God is good’ (I Tim. IV). The Apostle spoke of the natures themselves; but those writings, because of certain prefigurations appropriate to that time, called certain animals unclean not by nature but by their symbolic meaning.

“Thus, for example, if the question concerns a pig and a lamb, both are clean by nature, because every creature of God is good (ibid.). But by a certain symbolic meaning the lamb is clean and the pig unclean—as if you were to speak of a foolish person and a wise person. Both words, in their nature as sounds, letters, and syllables of which they consist, are certainly clean; but by their meaning one of these words, namely ‘foolish,’ can be called unclean, not by its own nature, but because it signifies something unclean.

“And perhaps what the pig represents among the figures of things is what the fool represents among the kinds of things. Both that animal and those two syllables constituting the word ‘foolish’ signify one and the same thing. That animal was declared unclean in the Law because it does not ruminate; yet this is not a fault of the animal but its nature.

“There are, however, people signified by this animal who are unclean by their own fault, not by nature. They gladly hear words of wisdom, but afterward think about them not at all.
