To turn over in the sweetness of recollection what you have heard that is useful, as though through the intestine of memory toward the mouth of thought—what else is this than to ruminate spiritually, in a certain manner? Those who do not do this are represented by the kind of animals in question.

“Therefore, abstinence from those meats itself warned us to beware of such a fault. For elsewhere, concerning this purity of rumination, it is written: ‘A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise, but a foolish man swallows it’ (Prov. XXVII).

“Let rational minds recognize these likenesses of things in figurative expressions and observances, for the useful and agreeable exercise of seeking and comparing. But many such commands were given to the earlier people not merely to hear but also to observe. For it was a time when prophecy had to be expressed not only in words but also in deeds. What was to be revealed in a later time, when it was revealed through Christ and in Christ, did not impose the burden of observances upon the faith of the Gentiles, although the authority of the prophecy was commended.”

## XLIV

There is no reason to engage in hunting during Lent. Hunters capture nothing except flesh; therefore, so that you may not appear to pursue anything carnal, you should suitably abstain from capturing flesh, especially during Lent. The more strictly one must devote oneself to divine worship during a time of fasting, the farther one must withdraw from all the harmful pleasures of the world—especially since sacred history shows that no one except the reprobate practiced hunting.

## XLV

You wish to know from us whether judgments should be carried out during Lent and whether anyone should be condemned to death. Know that concerning Lent we answer the same thing on this consultation as we are known already to have answered concerning feast days in the twelfth chapter of these responses of ours.

## XLVI

Whether during Lent it is permissible to go to war when necessity requires it—or when no necessity requires it—you do not need to have explained to you, since from the solutions to the earlier questions you yourselves can already gather, even without our speaking, what is appropriate for you to do.

The conflicts of wars and battles, as well as the beginnings of every quarrel, were certainly devised by the devil’s deceitful craft. Anyone eager to enlarge his kingdom, or a lover of anger, envy, or any other vice, is shown to devote himself to these things or take pleasure in them.

Therefore, if no necessity presses, one must abstain from battles not only during Lent but at all times. But if unavoidable necessity presses, one must certainly not spare the preparation for war during Lent for the defense both of oneself and of one’s homeland or ancestral laws. Otherwise, a person would appear to be tempting God if, having something he can do, he does not take care for his own safety and that of others and does not prevent harm to the holy religion.

Moreover, the walls of Jericho were brought down for the children of Israel, who had already undertaken to observe the Sabbath, even when they circled the city and sounded the trumpets on the Sabbath (Josh. VI).

## XLVII

You ask whether it is permissible to devote yourselves to jokes during Lent. This is not permissible for Christians not only during Lent but at any time. Yet because you are like the weak who cannot climb the mountain so as to receive from there the sublime commandments of God, but are placed on the plains, like the children of Israel once were, so that at least there you may receive the plainest and lesser commandments, we cannot yet persuade you to abstain from jokes at all times.

But during Lent and the time of fasting, when—as we explained much earlier—you ought to devote yourselves more fully and urgently to prayer, abstinence, and every form of penance, you should abstain not only from jokes but also from all empty talk, from foolishness unrelated to the matter at hand, and even from idle words, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “For every word that people speak, they will give an account” (Matt. XII). If this is true of an idle word, how much more of a harmful and criminal one?

Therefore, let no vanity of pleasures or jokes, especially during times of fasting, deceive you. Lamentation is not compatible with jokes, and false and deceptive joy does not know how to produce genuine tears in the near future. Moreover, there is a judge who said: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep” (Luke VI). Hence Solomon says: “Laughter will be mingled with sorrow, and mourning takes possession of the end of joy” (Prov. XIV). Again he says: “I considered laughter an error, and concerning joy I said, ‘Why are you deceived in vain?’” (Eccl. II). And again: “The heart of the wise is where sadness is, and the heart of fools where joy is” (ibid.).

For affliction on account of sin is a sacrifice pleasing to God, as the Psalmist testifies: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit” (Ps. L).

## XLVIII

Therefore, we in no way consider it appropriate to marry or hold feasts during Lent. You will learn again what the sacred canons say about this from your bishop.

## XLIX

You further ask whether it is permissible to give your wives, as you formerly did, gold, silver, cattle, horses, and so forth as a dowry. Since this involves no sin and the laws permit it, we do not prohibit you from doing so. Indeed, not only this, but whatever you did before baptism, you are certainly also permitted to do now (St. Gregory, *Homily 24 on the Gospels*).

For we know that Peter was a fisherman and Matthew a tax collector. After his conversion Peter returned to fishing, whereas Matthew did not return to the business of tax collection, because seeking a livelihood through fishing is one thing, while increasing one’s wealth through the profits of tax collection is another.

There are many occupations that can scarcely, or not at all, be practiced without sin. After conversion, therefore, the mind must not return to those that involve sin. But whatever a person practiced before conversion without sin, it is not wrong for him to undertake again after conversion.

## L

What judgment should be made concerning one who has had intercourse with his wife during Lent, we entrust to the consideration and decision of your bishop and of the priest whom he appoints. They will be able to recognize the conduct of each individual and must distinguish or moderate the circumstances of each of you according to persons and times.

For it would have been entirely permissible to sleep with her at that time without any contamination if fire and straw could have had some association without harm, or if the cunning of the devil’s deceit were not known. For wherever a male and female are together, it is difficult for the snares of the ancient enemy to be absent. Indeed, they were not absent when the brother and sister Amnon and Tamar remained alone together for a very short time (I Reg. XIII).

## LI

You ask whether it is permissible to have two wives at the same time; and, if it is not, you wish to know what you should do with a man in whose possession this has been found.

Having two wives at one time is permitted neither by the very origin of the human condition nor by any law of Christians. For God, who made humanity, made from the beginning only one male and one female (Gen. I). If he had wished, he could certainly have given him two wives, but he did not. For it is written: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife” (Gen. II); it does not say “wives.” Again: “The two shall be one flesh” (ibid.)—a male and a female, namely, in one flesh, not three or more.

Therefore, when two wives are found with one man at the same time, he should retain the first for the moment but be compelled to dismiss the second. In addition, he should be compelled to undertake the penance that the priest of the place determines [*praeviderit* may be intended as *praeceperit*, “has prescribed.” [Col. 1000A] “As considered in chapter 78,” HARD.].

Indeed, this is so monstrous a crime that the sin of homicide, which Cain committed against his brother Abel (Gen. IV), was punished by the Flood in the seventh generation (Gen. VII); but the wickedness of adultery, which Lamech was the first of all to commit with two wives (Gen. IV), was abolished only by the blood of Christ, who, according to the Gospel, came into the world in the seventh and seventieth generation.

## LII

If you wish to know what judgment should be made concerning those who castrate anyone, turn over the pages of the laws.

## LIII

You ask whether, when no priest or deacon is present, it is permissible to impress the banner of the holy cross upon a table and eat. This is certainly permissible, for everyone has been given the duty of defending all our possessions from the devil’s snares by this sign and of triumphing over all his assaults in Christ’s name.

Only this remains: when a superior is present, an inferior must not presume to claim this for himself unless commanded to do so, since “the disciple is not above the master” (Matt. X), and the Apostle again commands: “Outdo one another in showing honor” (Rom. XII).

## LIV

You say that the Greeks maintain that anyone who stands in church without his hands clasped to his chest is guilty of a very serious sin. We find nowhere, if we are not mistaken, that this was commanded; consequently, failure to do it is not a sin. Some people do this, others do that; sometimes the former display this kind of humility, sometimes the latter.

Unless, perhaps, the person stubbornly refuses to do what he sees everyone doing. Yet this practice, and many other practices of humility in different places, are performed as signs of humility; and, when this practice is performed, it is performed only for the sake of humility. Indeed, it is written: “The prayer of one who humbles himself will pierce the clouds” (Eccl. XXXV).

Therefore, whether a person devises this or some other expression of humility, he is not to be reproved, because according to the Gospel, “the one who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XVIII).

If someone approaches a mortal prince and stands, speaks, and walks with complete reverence and fear, how much more fitting is it for one who approaches God—who is eternal, fearsome, and exalted—not only to stand before him with all fear and trembling, but also humbly to present himself before him as a servant?

And since the hands and feet of certain reprobates in the Gospel are commanded to be bound (Matt. XXII), what else are those doing who bind their hands before the Lord than saying to God, in a certain manner: “Lord, do not command that my hands be bound so that I may be sent into the outer darkness, because I have already bound them myself, and behold, I am ready for the scourges”?

For this reason also we strike our breast, signifying that we are displeased with the wicked things we have done, and that therefore, before God strikes, we should strike them within ourselves; before the final punishment comes, we should punish what we have committed with fitting repentance.

## LV

You further assert that the Greeks forbid you to receive communion without belts. By what testimonies of the sacred Scriptures they can rightly prove this prohibition, we are wholly unaware—unless perhaps by the Lord’s command: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke XXII).

But this testimony of the holy Gospel must be fulfilled not according to the letter but according to the spirit. For if this command was given so that it should be observed literally in this way, why are the things that follow not likewise carried out—for example, “with lamps burning” (Exod. XVIII), or, as those eating the lamb are commanded, holding a staff in their hands?

These things have their own mystery, and to those who understand them they are so clear that they should be observed rather in the appropriate symbolic sense. The girding of the loins signifies chastity; the staff, pastoral governance; and the burning lamps, the splendor of good works, concerning which it is said: “So let your works shine” (Matt. V).

Therefore, as the holy and outstanding defender of the Church, Pope Celestine, writes (*Epistle 1*)—from whose words we have borrowed this summary—we must not lead the inexperienced minds of the faithful toward such practices. They should be taught rather than mocked; and commandments should not be imposed upon their eyes but infused into their minds.

### LVI

You assert that you wish to know whether all your people may, especially in a time of drought, undertake fasting and prayer to ask for rain. You are certainly permitted to do this, since fasting and prayer are great virtues [perhaps, “a great virtue,” HARD.], and your exhortation is of considerable value in promoting their continual observance. Yet it is more appropriate that these things be done by arrangement of the bishops. For they are the ones who receive the power of binding and loosing; at their command the armies of God’s people move out and rest. Without them you appear to be like a body without a head, and you proceed like wandering sheep without a shepherd. Indeed, in such matters in ancient times—and the holy Church still maintains this practice—the priests’ direction came first, as did the entire ordering of the matter; then the consent of the rest of the people followed. Thus, when the proper order was observed and unanimity preserved, God granting it, the desired result was provided.

### LVII

You report that the Greeks forbid eunuchs to slaughter your animals, to such an extent that they affirm that anyone who eats from animals killed by them has committed a grave sin. But what is said seems to us highly unreasonable, indeed still frivolous. Since we have not heard the reasoning of those who say this, we cannot for the moment make a definitive ruling about their assertion, which we have not yet fully understood.

One thing, however, we know: if eunuchs have kept God’s commandments, the cutting off of their bodily members cannot hinder them from attaining the heavenly kingdom, since, according to the Apostle, at the resurrection we shall all come to the perfect man (Eph. IV), and through the prophet the Lord promises certain joys to eunuchs if they observe his commands (Isa. LVI). Indeed, that Ethiopian eunuch is called a man by Saint Luke the Evangelist because of his virtue and integrity, when he says: “And behold, a man of Ethiopia, a eunuch, a powerful official of Candace the queen” (Acts VIII).

### LVIII

Whether a woman ought to stand in church with her head covered or uncovered, the Apostle teaches (I Cor. XI): “A woman praying or prophesying with her head uncovered dishonors her head; for it is one and the same as if she were shaven. For if a woman is not veiled, let her also be shorn; but if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her cover her head.” And again he says: “Therefore a woman ought to have a veil over her head because of the angels,” that is, the priests. And again he says: “Judge among yourselves: is it fitting for a woman to pray to the Lord unveiled? Does not nature itself teach you that if a man grows his hair, it is a dishonor to him, but if a woman grows her hair, it is a glory to her? For her hair has been given to her in place of a veil.”

### LIX

As for the breeches about which you inquire, we think the matter unnecessary. For we desire to see changed in you not the outward appearance of your clothing, but the conduct of the inner person. Nor do we ask what you wear apart from Christ, since “all of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III); rather, we inquire how you are advancing in faith and good works.

Yet because you ask about these things simply, evidently fearing that it might be counted as sin against you if, even in the smallest matters, you do something contrary to the custom of other Christians, and so that we may not appear to withhold anything from your desire, we say that in our books the making of breeches is commanded, not for women to use them, but for men. Now, just as you have passed from the old person to the new, so pass in every respect from your former custom to our practice. If not, do as you please. For whether you and your women remove or put on breeches, it neither harms your salvation nor contributes to the increase of your virtues.

Since we have said that the making of breeches was commanded, it should be noted that we put on breeches spiritually when we restrain the lust of the flesh through abstinence. For those places are confined by breeches in which the seats of lust are known to be located. Therefore perhaps the first human beings, after sin, feeling unlawful movements in their members, ran to the leaves of the fig tree and made loincloths for themselves (Gen. III).

But these are spiritual matters, which until now you have not been able to bear—indeed, to use the Apostle’s words, you are not yet able to do so, “for you are still carnal” (I Cor. III). Therefore we have said very little about this, although, with God’s help, we could say more.

### LX

You consult us about whether, outside the time of fasts, it is permissible to eat even a very small amount very early in the morning. We reply that we do not recall, nor have we found in any records, that any of our fathers ate before the third hour of the day, or that the holy Church accepted the practice of taking food before that hour. On the contrary, we find that some of them fasted until evening, others until the ninth hour of the day, and still others until the sixth hour. We find no one, however, who took even a little food in the morning, since we have rather read that a woe was pronounced upon those who eat in the morning (Isa. V).

Therefore, desiring you to remain free from this curse, we exhort you not to take any bodily food at all before the third hour of the day, even on the most important solemnities. For what solemnity can be more exalted than Pentecost, on which the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles, and thus human beings were found worthy to receive the Lord within themselves?

On this feast the holy apostles, together with several others, are found to have been fasting at the third hour of the day. When they were filled with the Holy Spirit and speaking in the languages of all the nations, some unbelieving hearers were astonished, while others falsely said that those who were present had been filled with new wine. Peter, the chief of the apostles, answered them: “These men are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day” (Acts II).

Here it should be observed that not only the apostles, but also all who were with them—that is, the one hundred and twenty men upon whom the Holy Spirit fell—are found to have been fasting at the third hour of the day. It should likewise be observed that blessed Peter did not simply say, “These men are not drunk, as you suppose,” but added, “since it is the third hour of the day,” as though he were plainly saying: “You yourselves know clearly that it is not their custom to break their fast before the third hour of the day; therefore you suppose without reason that they are drunk.”

Imitate them, then, so that the Holy Spirit, finding you fasting at the third hour of the day, if not later, may fill you also, as it did them, with the inspiration of his grace.

### LXI

You further indicate that you wish to know how many times a layperson ought to pray each day. In this you should understand that no one is exempt from what the Lord says in the Gospel: “It is necessary always to pray and not to grow weary” (John XVIII); and what the Apostle says: “Pray without ceasing” (I Thess. V).

As the aforementioned holy Augustine teaches most soundly, this is understood to mean that fixed times for prayer are not to be omitted on any day. What these fixed times of prayer are, which ought to be observed every day, seek and you will find.

### LXII

You report that, before you embraced Christianity, a stone was found among you. If someone takes something from it because of an illness, it sometimes provides a remedy for his body, but at other times remains without effect. The same thing is certainly known to happen with that stone to those who take it daily: some receive from it a remedy of health for their illness, while others waste away in sickness.

Therefore, when you consult us as to whether you should continue to use it or reject it, we reply and decree [Note: [Col. 1003D] The word “erroris” is either corrupt or superfluous. HARD.] that every use of that stone must be altogether prohibited and rejected in every way. Your hope for the whole of human salvation must be placed solely in that stone, our Lord Jesus Christ, “whom the builders rejected; he has become the head of the corner” (Matt. XXI), and from him, as the strongest remedy for recovering our strength, you must expect healing.

The most blessed Peter, first of the apostles, urges you to approach him and place all your trust in him, saying: “Coming to him, a living stone rejected indeed by human beings, but chosen and honored by God, you yourselves also, as living stones, are built upon him into a spiritual house” (I Pet. II).

### LXIII

You further consult us whether a man may, on the Lord’s Day, during the day or at night, have intercourse with or sleep with his wife. We reply that if one must abstain from worldly work on the Lord’s Day, as we have taught above, how much more must one avoid carnal pleasure and every bodily pollution? This is especially clear because the name “Lord’s Day” plainly shows that on that day a Christian ought to do nothing except what belongs to the Lord.

The same judgment must be applied to the night of that day as to its daylight hours. For it is one day, consisting both of daytime and nighttime, and containing twenty-four hours. Unless both the absence and the presence of the sun constituted one day, Scripture would never say: “There was evening and there was morning, one day” (Gen. I).

But if you are asking simply whether one may sleep with his own wife at that time, we have already briefly explained our view in the fiftieth chapter of these responses. To use the Apostle’s words, I say this for your benefit, not to lay a snare for you, but for what is honorable and what enables you to entreat the Lord without hindrance (I Cor. VII).

### LXIV

How many days a man must abstain from his wife after she has given birth to a son is declared not by our own inventions but by the words of blessed Gregory, Roman pontiff and apostle of the English people. Writing to Bishop Augustine, whom he himself had sent to Saxony, he said among other things (Epistle, Book XII, Letter 31):

“With regard to intercourse with her, her husband ought not to approach her until the child who has been born has been weaned. But a wicked custom has arisen in the conduct of married people, so that women disdain to nurse the children whom they bear and hand them over to other women to be nursed. This appears to have been invented for the sole reason of incontinence: while they refuse to exercise self-control, they despise nursing the children whom they have borne.”

### LXV

No one may rightly receive Christ’s communion when, being devoted to gluttony, he is not found fasting—so much so that, despising the mystical table, he appears first to have broken his fast by taking ordinary food, and, failing to distinguish Christ’s venerable body and precious blood from other foods, is known not to have placed them before every human nourishment but after it.

The body of Christ is a saving remedy against sin, and whoever does not reverently receive it before every other food [lacuna; Note: [Col. 1004D] The second part of this passage is missing]. And indeed, every day we see physicians administer their potions to empty bowels. If this is done for the health of the body, how much more ought it to be done for the salvation of the soul?

But no rule teaches why someone from whose mouth or nostrils blood has flowed ought not to receive Christ’s body and blood. What a person suffers unwillingly ought not to be counted against him as guilt, and therefore he ought not to be prevented from sharing in so great a remedy.

For we know that the woman who suffered from a flow of blood came humbly behind the Lord, touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her illness departed from her. If this woman, while suffering from a flow of blood, was not judged unworthy to touch the Lord’s garment—indeed, the Lord himself, for he said, “Someone touched me” (Matt. IX)—why should someone who suffers from a discharge of blood from the mouth or nostrils not be permitted to receive Christ’s life-giving sacraments?

### LXVI

You assert that the Greeks forbid you to enter the church while wearing the linen band that you wear on your head. Perhaps we too reasonably forbid this in the same way [perhaps “which,” HARD.]. For the often-mentioned and always-to-be-remembered Apostle Paul says: “Every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonors his head.” And again: “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God” (I Cor. XI). We believe that what is said about a covering ought likewise to be observed with regard to a wrapped band.

### LXVII

You report that it was your custom, whenever you intended to bind someone by oath concerning any matter, to bring a sword into the midst, and that the oath was administered over it. Now you ask us to prescribe by whom you ought to swear.

But we judge that before all else it is unworthy to swear not only by a sword but by any other created object whatsoever. For by whatever someone swears, that person evidently loves and venerates it, and entrusts his confidence to it with firm reliance. Therefore one ought to swear by God, who must be loved and venerated by human beings, in whom all hope and confidence must be placed, and from whom help must always be expected above all creatures.

For when the Lord commands that one must not swear by heaven, earth, one’s head, or Jerusalem, nothing other than the prohibition of swearing by a creature is certainly intended. That we are commanded to swear by the name of God, we have learned from God himself, who gives the command.

We may indeed swear by those creatures alone that have been set apart for divine worship, such as a church and an altar. Whoever swears by these swears by what is in them and by him who dwells in them, and the same applies to anything of this kind.

Therefore one may rightly swear by the Gospel. Whatever is contained in it is recognized as belonging to none other than God, who is written and read about in it. For it is our law; it is our testament, which our Lawgiver and Testator, the Lord and Redeemer, established for his chosen ones. If we love it, we also swear by it. Indeed, everyone who swears truly swears by the one whom he loves. Therefore, if we swear by the Gospel, we prove that we love both the Testator and the testament itself, and we plainly signify that we do not wish to depart from its commands.

### LXVIII

You have asked after how many days a woman may enter the church after giving birth. Following the footsteps of our predecessor, blessed Pope Gregory, we decree the same things that he decreed. Writing to instruct a new people, just as we are now instructing you, he said among other things (Epistle, Book XII, Letter 31):

“If a woman enters the church to give thanks at the very hour in which she has given birth, she is not burdened by any weight of sin. For it is the pleasure of the flesh, not the pain, that is blameworthy; and there is pleasure in the intercourse of the flesh, whereas in the bringing forth of offspring there is groaning. Hence it is said even to the first mother of all: ‘In pain you shall give birth’ (Gen. III). If, therefore, we forbid a woman who has given birth to enter the church, we count the very punishment imposed on her as a sin.”

### LXIX

You ask how many times baptisms ought to be celebrated throughout the year, whether it is permitted to eat meat on the same day, and how long abstinence from it should continue afterward.

The two principal or solemn seasons of the year in which baptisms are celebrated according to the canons are Easter and Pentecost. Yet among you no particular seasons need be observed at all for baptism, just as no fixed season need be observed for those who, fearing the danger of imminent death, desire to be cleansed by so great a washing.

Those who have been baptized on Holy Saturday or on the Saturday of Pentecost should unquestionably abstain from meat on that very day. But during the following seven days, which the ancients called the Days of Unleavened Bread and which are rightly celebrated together with the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, if anyone desires to eat meat at any time, he ought all the more to eat meat.

### LXX

You ask whether you ought to support and honor a priest who has a wife, or drive him away from you. We reply that although such men are greatly blameworthy, you ought nevertheless to imitate the Lord, who, as the Gospel testifies, makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matt. V).

You ought not to expel him from you for this reason, since the Lord did not expel Judas from the number of the apostles even when he was a deceitful disciple. But whatever priests may be like, you who are laypeople must neither judge them nor investigate anything about their lives; everything must be reserved in all respects for the judgment of the bishops.

### LXXI

You ask whether you ought to receive communion from a priest who has either been caught in adultery or has merely been touched by such a reputation. We reply that no one, however polluted he may be, can pollute the divine sacraments, which are remedies for cleansing every contagion.

Nor can the sun’s ray, passing through sewers and latrines, draw any contamination from them. Therefore, whatever a priest may be like, he cannot defile holy things. For this reason communion must be received from him until he is rejected by the judgment of the bishops.

For by administering good things, evil priests harm only themselves. A wax torch, once lit, causes injury to itself but provides light to others in darkness; from the very act by which it benefits others, it suffers loss itself.

Receive, then, without fear, the mysteries of Christ from every priest, since all things are cleansed by faith. For faith is what conquers this world. And because, as Saint Jerome teaches, the matter depends not on the giver but on the recipient, believe that baptism is perfect in every soul and that Christ’s body is perfect in every priest.

He again says, in agreement with sacred Scripture: “Before you hear, do not judge anyone; and before the accusation brought against someone has been proven, do not suspend anyone from your communion, because the one who is accused is not immediately guilty, but the one who is convicted is criminal.”

### LXXII

You have asked whether a patriarch may be ordained among you. We cannot give a definitive answer about this before our legates, whom we are sending with you, have returned and reported to us what number and unanimity of Christians there is among you.

For the present, have a bishop. When Christianity has expanded there through the increase of divine grace and bishops have been ordained in each church, one of them must then be chosen who, if not called a patriarch, should certainly be called an archbishop. Let everyone resort to him and await his counsel in matters of greater importance.

The apostolic canons likewise prescribe this, saying (Apostolic Canon 34): “It is fitting for the bishops of each nation to know who among them is to be regarded as first, whom they should consider as a head, and to undertake nothing beyond his knowledge and consent,” and so forth.

### LXXIII

You ask by whom a patriarch ought to be ordained. Know therefore that in a place where no patriarch or archbishop has ever been established, he must first be instituted by a greater authority, because, according to the Apostle, “the lesser is blessed by the greater” (Hebr. VII). Then, having received permission and the use of the pallium, he himself may subsequently ordain bishops who will be able to ordain his successor.

Whether you ask that a patriarch, an archbishop, or a bishop be ordained for you, it is more fitting that you should now desire him to be ordained by no one other than the pontiff of the see of blessed Peter, from whom both the episcopate and the apostolate took their beginning.

The order to be followed here is that a bishop should now be consecrated for you by the prelate of the apostolic see. If, with Christ’s assistance, the Christian people increase, he may receive the privileges of an archbishopric from us. He may then appoint bishops for himself, who will choose a successor for him when he dies.

Because of the length of the journey, the one who has been elected should no longer come here to be consecrated. Instead, the bishops who were consecrated by the archbishop who has died should assemble together and appoint him.

Meanwhile, however, before he receives the pallium from the Roman see, he must not sit upon the throne or consecrate anything except the body of Christ, just as all the archbishops of Gaul, Germany, and other regions are known to do.

### LXXIV

You ask what you should do if, after beginning a prayer, news arrives that enemies are approaching, so that you cannot complete the prayer. What else, surely, but to complete the good work you began wherever it happens that you have gone?

For Christians have no single place of prayer, as the Jews had at Jerusalem and the Samaritans on Mount Garizim. Rather, they have prayer in every place, as the Apostle also says: “I desire, therefore, that men should pray in every place, lifting up pure hands” (I Tim. VIII).

Moreover, “the one who perseveres in a good work to the end will be saved.” This is especially so at a time when one is moving against an enemy attack. As we have already said above, victory over the enemy should be expected more through prayer than through arms.

### LXXV

The written judgment concerning penance that you request will certainly be brought with them by our bishops whom we have sent to your homeland. Alternatively, the bishop who will be ordained among you will provide it when necessary. Laypeople, however, ought not to possess such a document, since no ministry of judging anyone is granted to them by virtue of it.

### LXXVI

We make the same assertion concerning the book used for celebrating Masses.

### LXXVII

You explain that, when certain Greeks receive a closed book in their hands, one of them takes a very small piece of wood and places it inside the book. If uncertainty about anything arises from any direction, they claim that through this they can know what they desire.

You ask whether this practice should be retained or rejected. It should certainly be rejected, for it is written: “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not turned to vanities and false insanities” (Ps. XXXIX).

### LXXVIII

You relate that the people who rose up to kill you because of the Christian religion now wish to do penance, but that the priests who are resident foreigners among you have refused to receive it. You now ask what should be done about them.

If, as you assert, they wish voluntarily to do penance, they must not be prevented. Rather, they must be submitted in every respect to the penance that the bishop, or a priest ordained by him, judges appropriate. For refusing to receive penitents is not the practice of Catholics but of Novatians.

### LXXIX

You report that it is customary among you for the sick to wear a certain hanging band beneath the throat in order to obtain health, and you ask whether we command that this be done in the future.

We not only do not command it, but absolutely forbid it from being done. Such bands are phylacteries invented by demonic deceptions and are shown to be bonds of human souls. Therefore the apostolic decrees command that those who use them, struck by anathema, be expelled from the Church.

### LXXX

You ask how you should establish and preserve peace with a people that seeks to have peace with you.

Whatever people wishes to offer you peace, do not refuse it. For it is written: “Pursue peace with all” (Hebr. XII). And again: “Keeping peace with all people” (Rom. XII). Since it says “all,” no one at all is excluded from mutual peace.

How peace itself is to be established or preserved with such people, however, cannot easily be determined unless the customs and words of the people with whom peace is to be made are known beforehand.

Nevertheless, since there is a praiseworthy peace and there is also a destructive peace, care must be taken that Christ be placed first in every pact. Thus, while his law—and especially unbroken faith—continues to be observed, the covenant made between the parties must remain intact.

The peace you ought to pursue is revealed by the Lord when he says: “I give you my peace” (John XIV). Therefore, with one who does not possess the peace of Christ, we ought not to have the peace of communion; nor should we have it with one who seeks peace for the purpose of committing harmful acts more freely.

### LXXXI

You ask whether, if you have made a treaty with a Christian people by an oath sworn by both sides, and afterward they wish to break the agreement and rise up against you, you may also dare to go against them, or whether you ought to do something else.

Every necessity must be endured rather than any iniquity being committed by us. Therefore the treaty you make must not be violated for any reason, unless perhaps, at the very time the treaty was confirmed, it was stipulated that one party would observe it only if the other party did not violate it by any evasion.

For every form of falsehood must be avoided by a Christian with the utmost care, because God says: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Ps. V). And again: “The lying mouth kills the soul” (Wis. I). The Apostle likewise says: “Do not lie to one another” (Col. III).

But if they, disregarding their oath and breaking the treaty, rise up against you, your bishop should answer your inquiry about what you ought to do. Since he is nearby and clearly knows the circumstances of the matter, the character of the times, the customs of the persons involved, and the justice of the parties, he will then be better able to indicate what he sees to be more appropriate and more salutary. Knowing all the circumstances beforehand, he will be able to explain fully to you what ought to be done.

For the present, however, since we do not know the facts, we more suitably advise you always to ask for the things that belong to peace.

### LXXXII

What sort of pact a Christian may make with pagans is indicated by the Apostle, who makes clear that there should be no communion between light and darkness or between Christ and Belial, nor between the believer and the unbeliever (I Cor. VI).

But if a believer enters into a pact with an unbeliever with the intention of drawing him toward the worship of the true God, this is not to be prohibited. The Apostle does not even prohibit a marriage consisting of a believer and an unbeliever from continuing (I Cor. VII). And Moses, wishing to lead his kinsman to knowledge of the true God, did not reject his companionship but earnestly begged that he become the guide of his company.

Some saints and believers are also found to have entered into various pacts and bonds of friendship with foreigners and unbelievers. But they did not honor them as though approving their unbelief and superstition; rather, they pressed them into compulsory services for various purposes, and especially employed them in earthly business and servile tasks.

### LXXXIII

You ask whether you are permitted to judge someone concerning criminal sins. If no one had wished to sin, no one would have had to judge anyone. But once sin has been committed, judgment certainly follows.

For we know, to speak according to the Apostle, that “the law is not laid down for the righteous but for the unjust and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the wicked, murderers of fathers and mothers, killers, fornicators, men who lie with males, kidnappers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine, which accords with the Gospel of the glory of the blessed God” (I Tim. I).

You are not, however, permitted to judge clerics, since it is more appropriate for you to be judged by them.

### LXXXIV

You think that we should be asked what judgment ought to be made concerning someone who has falsely accused another and afterward appeared as a deceitful accuser.

Although the venerable laws sufficiently indicate what is just in this matter, we ought nevertheless, following the Apostle, to exhort you rather toward the depths of mercy, which God declares that he desires above sacrifice. When he taught the nations of which he was the teacher, he did not call them to legal severity but rather summoned them to the depths of mercy, saying:

“Put on, therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, the depths of mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience, bearing with one another and forgiving one another. If anyone has a complaint against another, just as the Lord forgave you, so also do you” (Col. III).

### LXXXV

Therefore, concerning the person about whom you ask, who gave someone a deadly substance to drink, we likewise exhort you to mercy, just as the Lord commands, saying: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke VI).

### LXXXVI

If a thief or robber is caught and denies what is charged against him, you assert that among you the judge beats his head with blows and pierces his sides with other iron instruments until he reveals the truth.

Neither divine law nor human law permits this in any way. A confession ought to be voluntary, not forced; it must be offered freely, not extracted by violence. Finally, if it should happen that, even after such punishments have been inflicted, you find nothing at all concerning the crimes charged against the person who endured them, are you not at least then ashamed and do you not recognize how wickedly you judge?

Likewise, if the accused person, unable to endure such suffering, says that he committed what he did not commit, upon whom, I ask, does the enormity of such wickedness fall, except upon the one who compels him to confess falsely? He is not truly confessing, but merely speaking, since he utters with his mouth what he does not hold in his heart.

Abandon such practices, then, and utterly condemn what you have hitherto foolishly practiced. For what benefit did you derive at that time from those things of which you are now ashamed?

When a free person is accused of a crime, unless he has already been found guilty of some offense, he is either convicted by three witnesses and submits to the penalty, or, if he cannot be convicted, acquitted by swearing on the holy Gospel that he has not committed the offense charged against him. Thereafter an end is put to the matter, as the frequently mentioned Apostle, teacher of the nations, attests: “The end of every dispute among them is an oath for confirmation” (Hebr. VI).

### LXXXVII

You ask whether someone commits a sin if he makes a widow who does not wish to embrace the monastic life into a nun.

In this matter it should be understood that some virtues are necessary for entering into life, while others are required only from one who makes a vow. Without humility, chastity, almsgiving, and prayers, no one can enter into life; these, and similar virtues, are required of every person.

But putting on the monastic habit and leading a secluded life are required by God only of one who makes such a vow. Therefore, whoever uses force against someone so that she assumes a monastic habit and a more secluded life which she has neither desired nor chosen cannot escape sin as a violent person.

And since what is done does not arise from the will of the person who receives the habit, the recipient gains no reward from wearing the religious habit, while the one who inflicts this cruelty will not escape judgment for it.

### LXXXVIII

You ask about your parents who died unbelievers. It is not permitted to pray for them because of the sin of unbelief, according to the saying of the Apostle John: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that one should pray for it” (I John V). A sin unto death is found in those who die in that same sin.

### LXXXIX

It was also customary among the ancients to offer new crops and the first fruits of things. We read that Abel and Cain did this almost at the beginning of the world.

### XC

You ask whether animals or birds may be eaten if they are slaughtered without iron and die from a single blow struck by a human being.

Saint Augustine wrote fully about this against the Manichaean Faustus. Because of the length of the work, we touch briefly on a few of his words:

“When the Church of the nations had become such that no carnal Israelite appeared in it, what Christian now observes this rule—that he does not touch thrushes or smaller birds unless their blood has been shed, or that he does not eat a hare if it has been killed by a blow of the hand to the neck without a bloody wound? And those few who still fear touching such things are mocked by the others. So firmly has that saying of the Truth held the minds of all: ‘It is not what enters your mouth that defiles you, but what comes out’” (Matt. XV).

### XCI

Neither the animal that a Christian pursues and that a pagan strikes and kills, nor the animal that a pagan pursues and a Christian kills, should be eaten by a Christian. Otherwise the believer might appear to have shared even slightly with the unbeliever.

“For what partnership is there between the believer and the unbeliever?” (II Cor. VI). This is also forbidden on account of the conscience—not, of course, the believer’s conscience, but that of the unbeliever, who might boast that something had been shared with him by a Christian and thus conclude that, because he had not been rejected by the believer, the vanity of his error had been approved by the Christian.

## XCII

You wish to know how many patriarchs there truly are. Those are truly to be regarded as patriarchs who occupy apostolic sees through the succession of pontiffs—that is, those who preside over churches which are proved to have been established by the apostles: namely, the Roman, Alexandrian, and Antiochene churches.

The Roman Church was established by the chief apostles, Saints Peter and Paul, through their preaching, and consecrated by them through the shedding of their own blood for the love of Christ. The Alexandrian Church was established by the evangelist Mark, Peter’s disciple and son through baptism, sent there by Peter, and dedicated to the Lord Christ with his blood. The Antiochene Church is the one in which, after a great gathering of the saints had taken place, the faithful were first called Christians, and which blessed Peter governed for several years before he came to Rome.

The bishops of Constantinople and Jerusalem, although they are called patriarchs, nevertheless do not possess as much authority as those mentioned above. For none of the apostles established the Church of Constantinople, nor did the Council of Nicaea—which is more celebrated and venerable than all councils—make any mention of it. Rather, simply because Constantinople was called “New Rome,” its bishop was called patriarch, more through imperial favor than through reason.

The bishop of Jerusalem, although he too is called a patriarch and, according to ancient custom and the Council of Nicaea, ought to be honored—while preserving the proper dignity of the metropolitan see—was nevertheless called not “of Jerusalem” but “bishop of Aelia” even in that same holy and great council. For the true Jerusalem is only in heaven, and it is our mother. That earthly Jerusalem, however, was so utterly destroyed by the Roman emperor Aelius Hadrian, as the Lord had foretold, that not one stone was left upon another. It was rebuilt by that same Aelius Hadrian in another place, so that the site of the Lord’s cross, which was formerly outside the gate, is now seen within it, and that city is called Aelia after the aforesaid Aelius Hadrian.

## XCIII

You ask which of the patriarchs is second after the Roman patriarch. But according to what the holy Roman Church maintains, what the canons of Nicaea indicate, what the holy bishops of Rome defend, and what reason itself teaches, the Alexandrian patriarch is second after the Roman pope.

## XCIV

You report that the Greeks say that chrism originates in their country and is distributed by them throughout the whole world; and therefore you wish to know whether this is true. But by now we believe that your discernment has noticed how untrue it is.

## XCV

You ask what we decide should be done with those who flee to the church because of whatever offenses. Although the sacred canons demand that the provisions sanctioned by secular laws be observed, and although the laws appear merciless toward certain people, nevertheless we, who have not received the spirit of this world, say that if anyone flees to the church, he is not to be led out of it unless he wishes to leave of his own accord.

Indeed, if formerly robbers guilty of various crimes obtained protection by fleeing to the temple of Romulus as an asylum, how much more ought those who take refuge in the temple of Christ to obtain remission of their offenses and, once a sworn assurance has been given by the accused person, to be restored to all their former security.

## XCVI

Whatever your wife may have thought or done against you, or even if she has accused you, she is not to be rejected—except in the case of fornication—nor is she to be hated altogether (Matt. 5). She is to be loved, as the Apostle commands, just as Christ loves the Church (Eph. 5). How much, however, is Christ accused and blasphemed among the nations by the mouths of heretics; yet for the time being he tolerates those who preach perversely and does not drive those who repent from the embrace of his mercy.

## XCVII

The same rule must also be observed concerning a slave who accuses his master before the authorities: according to the Apostle, even threats are to be forgiven him by his master (Eph. 6). But why speak of a slave, when the Lord gives a general command to everyone and concerning everyone: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6)? And the Apostle says: “See that no one repays evil for evil to anyone” (2 Thess. 5). When he inserted the words “to anyone,” he also included a slave. But if you say that he did not include everyone, hear what follows: “But always pursue what is good toward one another and toward all.”

## XCVIII

You ask whether one who kills himself should be buried, and whether a sacrifice should be offered for him. He should indeed be buried, lest he cause an annoyance to the sense of smell of the living. Yet he is not to be carried to the grave with the customary rites and ceremonies, so that fear may not be instilled in others. If there are people who, out of humane concern, attend to his burial, they appear to be doing this for themselves, not for him who was the murderer of himself.

But a sacrifice is not to be offered for one who not only sinned up to the point of death, but also inflicted death upon himself. For who commits a sin unto death more than one for whom the Apostle John says that prayer should not be offered (1 John 5)—namely, one who, imitating Judas, is shown to have been the murderer of himself under the instruction of the devil?

## XCIX

You ask whether a Christian should be buried inside a church. Holy Pope Gregory resolves this question, saying:

> When serious sins do not weigh them down, it benefits the dead if they are buried in churches, because their relatives, whenever they gather in those sacred places, remember those whose graves they see and pour out prayers to the Lord for them. But those whose bodies are weighed down by serious sins are placed in churches not so much for their absolution as for the greater accumulation of their condemnation.

*(Book IV of the Dialogues, chapter 50.)*

## C

Whether one who has died in battle should be brought back to his own people, if his parents or companions wish it, you can gather from the preceding chapter. He should indeed be brought back to his own people if his relatives wish it, so that, when they look upon his tomb, they may remember him and pour out prayers to the Lord for him. Sacred history also reports that holy Joseph commanded that something similar be done with his bones when he died (Exod. 13).

## CI

You ask to whom alms should be distributed. The Lord clearly demonstrates this in the Gospel, saying: “Give to everyone who asks you”; and again, referring to the Father, he says: “He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5). The Apostle likewise says: “While we have the opportunity, let us do good to all, but especially to those who belong to the household of faith” (Gal. 6)—that is, to Christians.

Nevertheless, a certain order of discretion must be observed in giving alms. For the sake of brevity, we now omit explaining it fully. But first let us indicate what this word signifies: *eleemosyna* is called *misericordia* in Latin—that is, “mercy”; and it is certainly written: “Have mercy on your own soul, pleasing God” (Sirach 30).

Therefore, before all others, a person ought to give alms to himself. A person ought to begin every rule of good conduct with himself, pleasing God through purity of mind and body, and thus granting himself that living bread which descended from heaven.

Next, alms should be given to relatives who are suffering want, as it is written: “You shall not despise your own flesh” (Isa. 58). Nature itself also teaches us this: if I do not provide for my relative, when will a stranger provide for him? Mercy should then be shown especially to those who are ashamed to ask.

It should certainly be noted that there are some to whom nothing ought to be given, as it is written: “Give to the good, and do not receive the sinner” (Sirach 12); and again: “Do not give to the wicked” (ibid.); and again: “Set out your bread and wine over the burial of the righteous, and do not eat and drink from it with sinners” (Tobit 4).

A person gives his bread and wine to sinners when he supplies assistance to the wicked because they are wicked. But one who gives his bread to a needy sinner not because he is a sinner but because he is a human being undoubtedly nourishes not a sinner but a righteous person: for in that person he loves not guilt but nature. Hence certain rich men of this world, while the poor of Christ are tormented by hunger, nourish actors with lavish generosity.

## CII

We have already taught that violence must not be inflicted upon a pagan in order to make him a Christian.

## CIII

You ask what should be done with the profane books which, as you report, you took from the Saracens and have kept among you. They certainly must not be preserved. For, as it is written, “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15). Since they are harmful and blasphemous, they are to be consigned to the fire.

## CIV

*(Distinction 4, chapter “A certain Jew.”)*

You state that many people in your country were baptized by a certain Jew, though you do not know whether he was a Christian or a pagan, and you ask what should be done with those people.

If they were baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, or merely in the name of Christ, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2 and 19)—for the two are one and the same, as Saint Ambrose explains (Book I, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 3)—it is clear that they must not be baptized again. But first it must be investigated whether that Jew himself was a Christian or a pagan, or whether he later became a Christian.

Nevertheless, we believe that what blessed Augustine says about baptism should not be passed over:

> We have already sufficiently shown that, with respect to baptism, which is consecrated by evangelical words, it does not matter what error belongs to either the giver or the recipient, whether he thinks differently about the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit from what heavenly doctrine teaches.

And again:

> There are also some among that number who still live wickedly, or who lie in heresies or in the superstitions of the pagans; yet even there the Lord knows who are his. For in that ineffable foreknowledge many who appear to be outside are within.

And elsewhere:

> By now, I think, even those who are slower of heart understand that Christ’s baptism cannot be violated by any perversity of the human being, whether of the giver or of the recipient.

And again:

> A person who is separated can nevertheless administer it, just as a person who is separated can possess it; but how disastrously he can administer it. The one to whom he administers it, however, can receive it beneficially, if he receives it while he himself is not separated.

## CV

You consult us and ask to be instructed about what should be done with one who, exalting himself above the apostolic commands, attempts to preach. One of them—that is, Paul—answers and instructs, saying: “But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1).

Nevertheless, when this occurs, it must not be judged indiscriminately or rashly by you, who are laymen; for “we all offend in many things” (James 3).

## CVI

Finally, you earnestly beg us to grant you, as to the other nations, a true and perfect Christianity without spot or wrinkle. You assert that many Christians have come to your country from different places—Greeks, Armenians, and people from other regions—who speak many different things according to their own wills. Therefore you ask whether you ought to obey all of them according to their various opinions, or what you ought to do.

We, however, are not sufficient for these matters; our sufficiency is from God. Blessed Peter, who lives and presides in his see, gives the truth of the faith to those who seek it. The holy Roman Church has always been without spot and without wrinkle, because he established it whose confession of faith was approved by God.

Although no one can fully understand the mysteries of this Christian faith, with God inspiring us we have sent our writings, envoys, and various books to your country in order to make this faith known to you. Until you attain firm roots of strength, we will by no means cease watering you; and until you reach the solid nourishment of perfection, we will never entirely omit giving you milk to drink (1 Cor. 3). For “you are my joy and my crown in the Lord” (Phil. 4).

Regarding those whom you say have come into your country from different places teaching various and diverse things, we have already written much to you, and now we endeavor to write something further, supported by the holy utterances of the teacher of the nations. Fearing that such people might exist among the Corinthians, he said:

> “For I fear that when I come, I may not find you such as I wish, and that I may be found by you such as you do not wish—lest perhaps there be among you quarrels, jealousies, animosities, dissensions, slanders, whisperings, conceits, and disturbances” (2 Cor. 12).

Nevertheless, as far as the right faith is concerned, we do not care who preaches, but whom they preach. For he himself wrote:

> “Some indeed preach Christ because of envy and contention, but some also because of good will. Some preach out of love, knowing that I have been appointed for the defense of the Gospel. Others announce Christ out of contention, not sincerely, supposing that they can stir up affliction for my bonds. But what does it matter to me? So long as, whether by pretext or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, I rejoice in this and shall rejoice” (Phil. 1).

But hear what the same man who said this says elsewhere:

> “Avoid profane and empty talk, for they advance greatly toward ungodliness, and their speech spreads like cancer” (2 Tim. 2).

Nevertheless, in all these matters the mercy of God will attend our envoys and your future bishop, so that they may instruct you and teach you abundantly what you ought to do. They, whether now or hereafter, will always consult, according to custom, the apostolic see—the see of the whole Church—in doubtful matters and greater affairs. Instructed by it in what is necessary, they will establish you and teach the things of God through diligent preaching.

We have answered these suggestions or questions of yours as the Lord has granted—not as much as we could, but as much as we foresaw might be sufficient. When, God willing, you have a bishop through the ministry of our episcopate, he will teach you everything that pertains to his office; and if there are matters he cannot understand, he will receive guidance from the authority of the apostolic see.

May God, who has wrought the greatest salvation in you, bring it to completion, strengthen it, establish it firmly to the end, and make it strong. Amen.

---

*(In the year 866.)*

## XCVIII. To the Emperor Michael

He urges the emperor to listen graciously to the legates; repeats what was said in the preceding letters about Ignatius, Photius, Rhadoald, and Zachary; explains that the letter sent by him had been corrupted and restores the passages that had been altered; demonstrates that Photius’s promotion ought to be rejected, among other reasons because he had been consecrated by Gregory of Syracuse after Gregory had been condemned; and rebukes the emperor, who was defending Photius.

He asks that the letter full of insults, which the emperor himself had sent, be ordered to be burned. If not, he threatens to excommunicate its writers, arrangers, and instructors, and to order that the letter be burned publicly in a council of bishops, to the emperor’s disgrace. Finally, he shows that the cause of both Ignatius and Photius would be greatly advanced if each of them came to Rome.

*[In Mansi, same place.]*

## Nicholas, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his most pious and glorious beloved son Michael, great emperor

The greater the benefits of God which, by his gratuitous mercy, have been bestowed upon your piety, the more abundantly, beyond all doubt, ought the marks of your virtues to flourish. And the more gloriously your empire is recognized as elevated by his gift and raised above all the summits of kingdoms, the more necessary it is, considering your own weakness, to humble yourself to the ground beneath his mighty hand and, with a submissive mind, carefully and humbly to reflect that everything you possess that is good, everything that pleases you, comes from him.

For it is written: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Sirach 3); and again: “They have appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Sirach 32). And it is said to Saul: “When you were little in your own eyes, did I not make you head over the tribes of Israel?” (1 Kings 15).

Nothing offered to God by exalted persons is more pleasing than humility. Nothing is more fitting for the humility of princes than willingly to hear the voices of those who make petitions, the exhortations of preachers, and to guard against the calamities announced by the Lord’s watchmen as impending or future.

Since we have not all received the spirit of prophecy, how can we know what is happening concerning our subjects, or concerning those who share the same faith with us, if we entirely exclude from our hearing or sight the words of those present or the writings of those absent? The style of a letter is like a doorkeeper for those who arrive or for matters that have taken place.

How, then, will your piety, which has responsibility for all its subjects and especially for religion, be able to know anything if, once the doorkeeper’s office has been removed, it is not permitted that what various people outside request to report to your clemency be announced within?

You ought therefore always to receive the petitions of all with pious hearing, without any hesitation whatsoever, and graciously to admit the voices of those reporting matters of honesty—or rather, of justice and equity—without any discrimination. Then, with reason as your teacher, which ought never to be placed after but before private will, you should separate truth from falsehood and what is wholesome from what is harmful; and, when false or harmful things have been discovered by the strictest judgment, rightly reject them, while consequently admitting what is proved to be true or beneficial.

For it is a sign of a lover of justice to wish to discover it completely in everyone and in every circumstance. Justice is indeed a precious pearl, which must be sought not only in royal treasuries but also in dung heaps. How much more, then, should it be hoped for and awaited without hesitation from the see of Peter, to whom God the Father revealed the most precious pearl, that is, his Son; and it should be received with the whole embrace of one’s heart and with the greatest ardor.

Do not therefore, dearest son, exclude our writings or our messengers from your presence. Do not turn your tranquil ears away from the embassy of blessed Peter. It belongs to unbelievers—or rather, to those who despair of their salvation—to close their ears to the voice of preachers, like the deaf asp that stops its ears and does not hear the voice of the charmers (Ps. 58), that is, of preachers.

You, however, who are pious and, thanks be to God, willing to be persuaded, ought to open your ears all the more to hear the cries of the poor—that is, of the humble—and of those who cry out on behalf of the Church of God. You ought to direct your attention toward hearing the law all the more as you desire your prayer to be accepted before God, and as you cry out in times of need and ardently wish to be heard.

Those foolish virgins who stood outside and cried out in vain, “Lord, Lord, open to us” (Matt. 25), did not find the door opened for this reason: they had not opened the door of their ears to saving voices. Just as those who show mercy will obtain mercy—a principle that should be understood concerning every virtue—so the one who hears voices uttered on behalf of God’s cause will make his own voices heard, whereas the one who does not hear will not be heard, as it is written: “The prayer of one who closes his ears so as not to hear the law will be accursed” (Prov. 28).

When a certain woman, bearing the figure of the Church, cried out to the Lord, “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked” (Luke 11), she immediately heard that those are more blessed who hear the word of God and keep it (ibid.). Therefore, most serene emperor, hear the voices of our legates; hear the voices of our letters. Hear them patiently; hear them calmly. We trust in the Lord that you will find them in no respect dissenting from the divine commands or deliberately differing from the definitions of the fathers.

For if, before hearing them, you reject them and exclude them from yourself—[perhaps better: “exclude yourselves from them”; HARD.]—before you have inquired about those matters that may perhaps be doubtful in them, you will undoubtedly be judged to act against the divine command: judging what is unknown and condemning what has not been tested.

It is therefore enough to preface this letter to you as to a most beloved son with the words of the wisest Solomon, who invites the son whom he instructs above all to listen to him (Prov. 4).

Even if not for your sake, then at least for our own counsel, we do not omit writing what we have judged worth sending. We confidently set forth the causes of that Church and our own, if not to your ears, then at least as in the presence of God.

Therefore, what has been done in the Church of Constantinople during your reign, most excellent emperor, is still being investigated, as your wisdom clearly knows. But how we have acted and what we have arranged concerning these matters, carrying about, in the manner of my predecessors, the concern for all the churches according to the Apostle—“the zeal for God’s house” (2 Cor. 11)—we indicate to your piety in a style that is not so brief as it is truthful.

And lest anyone attempt to persuade your sincere mind otherwise, or cause you to understand what we did in another way, we instruct you through these present words. This would not have been hidden from your prudence if either the enemies of Christ, who truly is the truth, had not turned truth into falsehood; or if they had been willing to affirm that we wished, as a father toward his most beloved son, to disclose this to you; or if they had not wished to conceal beneath the color of falsehood the ardor of our love with which we burn for your salvation.

After we heard that certain men, inflamed by the fires of envy and arrogantly lifted up by the pride of arrogance, had risen up, in the manner of the Jews, against their pastor and teacher—namely, our brother and fellow minister, Ignatius, most holy patriarch of the aforesaid church—and that others, like vipers and parricides, had attacked their own parent, that same most blessed man, with bestial teeth, and had entirely removed him from the church over which he rightly presided by the force of their tyranny, we began, oppressed by the sharpest pains and tormented by intense grief, carefully to consider how we might show him the entrails of our kindness, as a brother.

For it is written: “If anyone sees his brother in need and closes his heart against him, how does the love of God remain in him?” (1 John 3).

This was especially so since we heard that considerable scandal and schism had arisen in the aforesaid city and in the cities adjoining it because of a certain Photius, who had been taken from the marketplace, from secular military service and dress, and from the imperial palace, suddenly tonsured, and promoted in that same church contrary to the sacred canons.

Some defended Photius’s promotion, while others rightly detested it as having been carried out against Ignatius, who had not been convicted and was still alive. While we were continually and anxiously considering with ourselves what should be done by us and how we might cure so great a pestilence, suddenly the legates of your highness arrived at the apostolic see with a royal letter. They brought certain accusations against our aforementioned fellow priest Ignatius and urgently requested that we send messengers from the apostolic see to calm those scandals and disperse those schisms.

After they had been kindly received, and after the content of the mission entrusted to them and of the writings they had brought had been examined, the sorrow that mere rumor had previously produced in our heart was immediately multiplied by the more certain report of the events that had been clearly demonstrated.

Therefore, since your divinely inspired imperial wisdom knows that we are bound by responsibility for all Christ’s sheep, and that by the abundance of heavenly grace we exercise his office—he to whom God specifically says, “Feed my sheep” (John 21), and again, “And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22)—we could neither dissemble nor neglect to visit the scattered and dispersed sheep, nor fail to strengthen our brothers and neighbors in faith and good conduct.

Among the other matters reported by those who had been sent concerning the schism of the aforesaid Church of Constantinople, they especially asserted that the same Church was being disturbed by the renewed controversy stirred up by the Iconoclasts, and that Christ was being blasphemed in their individual gatherings.

For this reason we sent two bishops who were with us and who seemed suitable for carrying out this task—namely, Rhadoald and Zachary—together with letters from our side and with the Church that is with us, to Constantinople, denouncing that same abomination. [The word *quae* may be redundant here; HARD.] We imposed absolutely nothing upon them except that they carefully investigate the case of Ignatius, the patriarch who had been expelled from the church before being accused by anyone, and report it fully to the apostolic see with truthful evidence, as blessed Job teaches: “I investigated most diligently the case that I did not know” (Job 29).

As for Photius’s consecration, we believed that it was by no means to be admitted in the meantime [the Roman edition reads *credidimus*, “we believed”]; indeed, we repeatedly and expressly ordered our legates not to communicate with him otherwise than as with a layman [perhaps, “unless it were as with a layman”; HARD.] until we had been informed.

For, as the eloquent Pope Leo says in a letter to Saint Flavian, bishop (Letter 10):

> We, who wish the judgments of the Lord’s priests to be mature, can determine nothing concerning anyone’s case to the prejudice of either party while the matter is unknown, before we have truthfully heard everything that was done.

We granted them permission to determine justly and piously whatever the matter might involve concerning the venerable images of our Lord Jesus Christ, his mother, ever-virgin Mary, and his saints.

Our letters, which we had sent through those same messengers to your gentle Augustan Majesty and also to Photius, can clearly show that all these things were as we say—if they are with you as they were transmitted by us. But we shall speak at length about this below; let us return now to our subject.

When those same messengers of ours arrived at Constantinople, they were frightened by threats from your imperial power—as they themselves later sometimes admitted—and driven by terrifying fears. They disregarded our warnings, despised the letters given to them by us before our entire Church, and, indeed, set aside the fear of God—as later became clear—and turned everything that had been commanded to them in the opposite direction.

But concerning these matters, after we had twice convened a council of the holy bishops of the western regions, in accordance with the Lord’s saying, “In the judgment with which they judged, they shall be judged, and in the measure with which they measured, it shall be measured back to them” (Matt. 7), what happened to them was similar to what once happened to the bishops Vitalis and Misenus.

This happened to them as it had once happened to the bishops Vitalis and Misenus, who, like these men, had been sent to Constantinople and were found to be not executors but opponents, because they communicated with the adverse party in the matter for which they had been sent. Blessed Felix, bishop of the apostolic see and condemner of Peter of Alexandria and Acacius of Constantinople, writing to the emperor Zeno, says among other things that he deprived Vitalis and Misenus, by apostolic judgment, of both honor and communion, because they had consented to such acts, even if under compulsion (Letter 10).

It happened, as he writes to Cyril, abbot of Acrinitum [Acoemetum], that the Christian people were deceived through their transgression. Referring to them again, he says to the aforementioned ruler concerning their offense:

> The Christian people were persuaded that we had given our consent to such men, whom, as soon as they returned, transgression did not leave unpunished. For, while a holy council was sitting with me before blessed Peter the Apostle, it stripped them of rank and communion after they had been convicted of telling many lies, so that their uncorrected faithlessness might not provide security to the enemies.

But if you used force against our aforesaid legates—as they themselves admitted—although they ought to have been deterred by the example of the bishops mentioned above, and indeed ought to have been restrained by the Lord’s command, “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. 10), so that they would not be driven into such actions, nevertheless it is proved that you, O Catholic prince, admitted an act contrary to divine reverence: that the embassy sent by blessed Peter the Apostle—or rather, the embassy of Christ speaking through him, who says, “Whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10)—was held as though reduced to captivity (from Letter 9 of Felix III).

But because the circumstances and persons of both parties at this time agree with that earlier case in almost every respect, we have taken care to address you also, most mercifully, with the words of the memorable Felix, the aforementioned bishop of the apostolic see. Writing to the emperor mentioned above, he says, among other things:

> Since, even among barbarian nations and among those ignorant of the Divinity itself, the sacred freedom of every embassy has always been preserved by the law of nations for the execution of either public or private business, this is known to everyone. How much more ought it to have been preserved inviolate by a Roman emperor and a Christian prince, especially in divine affairs?

But since above we mentioned the text of the letter sent to you by the aforesaid bishops Rhadoald and Zachary, which had been falsified, it remains for us to disclose some of the passages in which it was falsified, insofar as we have been enabled to know this by examining the Greek copies that you sent us through Leo, your secretary.

First, we assert that the proper order, and the order customary among the holy Fathers, was not observed in reading that letter. For the same letter contained not only the judgment of the apostolic see concerning the sacred images, but also its judgment concerning hearing our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius.

As for the case of our fellow priest Ignatius, which had previously been debated, we do not know what counsel you followed when you suppressed the letter in silence and later displayed it only when a synod was convened concerning the veneration of the holy images. Yet in what was read from it there, some things are found to have been added, many changed, and more removed. In every respect you made it such that we might appear to have arranged nothing, or almost nothing, through it concerning the case of our frequently mentioned fellow minister Ignatius.

But the records of certain councils gathered in ancient times demonstrate that matters were not conducted in this way in synods, nor were they conducted in that way. In those councils, the writings of the apostolic see were not concealed under a bushel of secrecy; rather, they were placed openly so that they might shine for everyone who was in the house of God. If anyone attempted to introduce any disgrace or blemish into the beauty of the faith, it would easily become visible. They were regarded as mirrors for all and honored as a kind of model of uprightness by which the others might be formed.

To make this clearer, we have decided to insert a few examples into this letter.

First, when the holy council assembled at Ephesus, it read the letter of Pope Celestine, of holy memory, before proceeding to carry out anything else.
