Saint Cyril presided before all others at that council precisely because he also held there the place of the aforementioned pope, as the records of that council testify. The letter itself was first read in Latin with appropriate honor and afterward translated into Greek and read before the council without any disguise of falsification.

Indeed, the wicked Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, was expelled almost on the authority of that letter, when the same council, in the sentence pronounced against him, proceeded in these words:

> Necessarily compelled both by the canons and by the letter of our most holy father and fellow minister Celestine, bishop of the Roman Church, we came, often weeping, to this sentence against him, full of sorrow.

Writing afterward to the same pope, the council reasonably asserts that the aforesaid Nestorius had been condemned through the letter written by that most holy bishop.

The letter of holy Pope Leo was also so venerable among all the eastern bishops that they called it “the pillar of orthodoxy.” All the bishops of Constantinople, with Anatolius at their head, subscribed to it. Thus it is entirely clear that the great Council of Chalcedon defined nothing, rejected nothing, and accepted nothing except what either that letter or those preserving there the prerogatives of the apostolic see had defined, rejected, or admitted.

This is also found in the report that the council addressed to Marcian Augustus, of pious memory. It says that the first cause of the downfall of Dioscorus, who had prohibited the reading of the letter of Saint Leo, was this:

> Therefore, considering the storms that had arisen throughout the entire world and investigating the cause of this matter, we discovered that Dioscorus, formerly bishop of Alexandria, was its author—first of all because he prohibited the reading of the letter sent by Leo, most holy archbishop of senior Rome, to Flavian, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, of holy memory.

But why should we linger over the individual councils of the synods, when in all of them a writing from the apostolic see was always brought forward, placed first in due order, and surpassed the other writings in authority?

If this has not escaped the wisdom of your highness, O emperor, then you ought also, in your own time, to have followed the traces of such examples.

But at last let us proceed, with the Lord’s help, as we promised, to point out the places in our letter that were partly falsified. As for the rest, we say that, to avoid prolixity, we decline to recall each item individually, since even in what we said in that same letter concerning the venerable images, the tenor of our writing and intention was not observed.

For when, among other matters, we had recalled that assemblies of the holy Fathers had often been held, by whom it had been both deliberated and observed that, without the consent of the Roman See and the Roman pontiff, no conclusion could be given to any deliberation that arose—and when we were referring only to the greater affairs of the Church, as both truthful histories and the acts of synods often testify to have been defined and often carried out—you erased “without” and inserted “with,” [Col. 1023A] evidently attempting to convey this meaning: “The holy Fathers had deliberated that every matter should be brought entirely to a conclusion with the consent of the apostolic See and of your Church.” Yet this could never in any way always have been done, nor does any example at all show that it was carried out; especially since this apostolic See has always persevered in sound doctrine.

Your Church, however, insofar as the episcopate is concerned, often languished when its head was weak; and for that reason it could in no way obtain the consent of one whose most evil and execrable judgment it rightly abhorred.

Then, when we appeared to complain in a reproachful spirit that an assembly convened at Constantinople, without consulting the Roman pontiff, had deprived Ignatius of his rightful dignity—something which, as far as can be recalled, had never been done to a Constantinopolitan bishop except perhaps by heretics and without the Roman pope—you altered this, saying that we had not written that what you had first done against us ought not to have been done, as though we had judged that it should be done afterward.

Or you altered it as though we had sent our legates to Constantinople not merely to hear Ignatius’s case and report it to us, but to decide it; although in that same letter it can be found that we had decreed, in words inserted there, that the judgment concerning the deposition of our fellow priest was not to be concluded but only investigated and reported to us, so that we might decide it with apostolic authority [perhaps: “by apostolic authority,” HARD.], as clearly as daylight.

For if we had instructed our legates in any way to decide the dispute concerning our brother Ignatius, or had decreed that he should be subjected to condemnation, why then should they not [perhaps: “should they refuse to,” HARD.] accept a definitive sentence, although they had struggled neither worthily nor lawfully, yet are proved to have resisted contradiction in whatever manner and to whatever extent, and to have opposed his deposition?

Indeed, to omit for now the other matters, we learned from your own mouth in your letter how they not only refused to give their consent to his condemnation, but also how they forbade you to commit so great a sacrilege against him. They certainly would not have contradicted this if they remembered that we had given them a mandate to be present at his deposition, and you afterward knew clearly that they had acted against our command. In that case you would by no means have sought both to commend them to us and to excuse them before us for such a transgression.

But if you say that we deposed them, although we so clearly know that they were unwilling to consent to the condemnation of the aforesaid patriarch, we reply that it profited them nothing to have begun well and not to have persevered in goodness, since “whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X).

For what benefit is it to anyone first to make an attack on behalf of the truth and shortly afterward to turn aside from the path of truth, whether through persuasion, fear, or any other fault? Moreover, if Vitalis and Misenus, whom we mentioned above, were deprived by blessed Pope Felix both of their dignity and of communion because they were driven or led into such actions, how much more ought these men to fall under an equal punishment, since they committed an equal transgression but suffered no punishment—or at least none comparable to what those men once endured.

After this, whatever we had written concerning the tyrannical expulsion of our aforesaid brother and fellow minister Ignatius, whatever concerning the thoughtless and envious sentence pronounced against him, whatever concerning the violation of the decisions of the Fathers, whatever concerning the irregular promotion of Photius—you passed over all these matters by a certain leap of craftiness. You wove together even the institutions of the holy Fathers, issued under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, so that they might not come to the council’s notice; and, as though bound in a kind of shroud of silence, you hid them in the earth while the talents divinely entrusted to you remained concealed, even though you continually proceeded before the eyes of our envoys and investigated the case of Ignatius.

For this reason, you joined together with the preceding words what we had written after much discussion: that he had despised the people entrusted to him and the ordinances of my predecessors. Yet you did not permit what we immediately added to be brought to the knowledge of the Church of Constantinople or to the hearing of the synod.

For after those words we added the following, continuing immediately:

“And in this matter, by a careful examination, the judgment concerning his deposition is to be investigated by the legates of our command, so that, in conducting the inquiry, they may discover whether it is manifest that the canonical rule was observed in this matter or not. Then, when it has been reported to our episcopate what ought to be done concerning him, we shall define it by apostolic sanction, so that your Church, which is shaken daily by such great anxieties, may henceforth remain inviolate and unshaken.”

But you, concealing these words, as we have said, withdrew them from the knowledge of the pious men who perhaps were present there.

You were aiming at nothing else than that the works of darkness should not be exposed by the manifestation of light, and that we should be considered to have given our consent to the things irrationally done there while our writings were kept silent.

This is especially proved by the final passage of the same letter, after many useful things in it had been corrupted or suppressed. In that passage, while commending our legates, we had entreated Your Magnificence, saying among other things:

“And when they sit in the assembly of the Church for ecclesiastical decisions, let them feel no attack of opposition from you or from anyone else.”

But you immediately added, as though we had attached these words continuously, saying:

“For matters of this kind are both arranged and decided by us.”

By this statement, may your sagacity, if it pleases God, have intended to suggest that whatever our legates had arranged and decided, we should be understood to have arranged or decided in every respect. Yet this written sentence neither came from us, nor did we command them to conclude or decide anything, either in writing or orally, except what concerned the sacred images—and even that was done irreproachably.

That this is so, in accordance with the statements we made above, the copies of our letter testify, and they abundantly inform us where the text has been corrupted. For if we had sent our envoys for the purpose of having them act in our place as judges in Ignatius’s case, as you claim—when, in writing about that robber council in which Ignatius is said to have been deposed, you assert that it was our judgment—then, unquestionably, before the whole dispute had been stirred up and before the controversy had begun, we would have judged that his proper see ought to be restored to him.

Thus he would lawfully recover what he had lost without any law requiring its loss, and through the ecclesiastical canon would resume what secular power had taken from him. Then, restored and equipped with his own see, as well as with all that he had previously possessed and with his strength recovered, he could undertake the field of battle and the contest of litigation with his accusers.

Since you judge that this should be done in worldly affairs under your laws, O emperor, your piety ought much more carefully to have foreseen that it should be observed in ecclesiastical and divine matters.

But of the innumerable falsifications of the frequently mentioned letter, let it suffice that we have briefly touched upon these matters out of zeal for the truth. You can easily recognize the remaining matters through our envoys, whom we have now sent to your empire protected by God, after examining the unaltered copies which we entrusted to them to display to Your Serenity.

Therefore, greeting Your Dilection with paternal affection, we also beseech you—and with the strongest entreaty we implore you by God, in whose hand are the hearts of kings—to deign to show this same letter, which we sent to Your Glory through the aforementioned Rhadoald and Zachary, to these present envoys of ours, and to allow sufficient time for it to be compared with the copies we gave them.

By this means they may learn whether the same letter remains in your possession in its entirety, as it had been when sent by us to Your Sublimity, or whether it was afterward brought by someone into the corruptions noted above.

And if such a great crime was committed by one of your people—for among the Greeks, as certain writings from different periods testify, this rashness is familiar—we marvel and are utterly astonished that the royal dignity of Your Excellence, which loves justice, could have been bent to so great a disgrace, since it was ordained by God rather for this purpose: to correct what has been corrupted and restore what has been falsified to the honor of its original truth.

Either what we sent was just, and therefore ought to have been preserved accordingly; or, if it was not thought just, it ought at least to have been explained in another writing, or reported to us, in what respect it was not just, and this ought to have been openly demonstrated by the highest reason. In none of these circumstances, however, ought it to have been deprived of the knowledge of the Church that is among you, or defrauded by any corruption of falsity.

Moreover, if this monstrous sacrilege was committed without the knowledge of Your Mildness, we are nonetheless led to immense astonishment, and we rightly grieve that so great an empire could both permit so great a fraud and endure it.

Finally, he is not unjustly said to have committed sacrilege who either removes from the knowledge of the faithful and of a pious ruler writings concerning piety, or obscures them under a veil of his own deceits by withdrawing them from their truth.

Nevertheless, however this letter may have been subjected to falsification or corruption, we give innumerable thanks to God, by whose inspiration we retained its faithful copies with us, and by whose permission those who wrote these things—or the authentic letter itself—are known to have survived.

As for the deprivation of our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius, whatever the circumstances, until the matter has specially been brought before us for reconsideration, we have never consented to it; and, with God confirming us, we will in no way consent to it henceforth.

Yet we do not justify him in such a way as to say that he committed nothing worthy of reproach, for which, after a lawful investigation, he might perhaps justly have endured any canonical stroke of judgment. For we confess what is written in the apostolic letters, saying: “We all offend in many things” (James III); and again: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I).

But we wish, and thus decree, that a pontiff of this kind should receive a penalty worthy of his deeds in such a way that priestly dignity may not be utterly cheapened, and that the summit of the episcopate may not so easily be bent down to the earth.

Thus, I say, we wish and decree that he—or any pontiff—be subjected to a just judgment in such a way that he is not judged by secular persons, is not tyrannically expelled, is not deprived of his Church before a hearing, and receives a judgment based on a correct assessment not from inferiors but from persons of greater authority.

Thus, finally, we wish and decree that the cases of this man—or rather of all priests—be examined and their guilt punished in such a way that we do not transgress the boundaries established by the Fathers, trample upon the sacred canons, or in any way violate the decretal constitutions of the apostolic See, by which the whole Church is supported and defended.

Finally, we wish and decree that a pontiff, whatever his character, be judged in such a way that the rights of the Church over which he presides are broken by no rashness and no presumption.

For no right of the Church can be preserved as it ought if its bishop is attacked by anyone, at any time, or in any manner, and is expelled so easily at the whim of whoever wishes.

Since this is so, in the meantime we cannot fail to number our brother Ignatius, whatever his character, among the holiest and most blessed patriarchs. Although among you he is wearied by so many reproaches and so many persecutions, by us he is regarded, believed in, and venerated only as he is regarded, believed in, and venerated by my predecessors.

He has been found guilty of no crime by any examination of ours, nor has he been found liable to anything by any special judgment of ours. Therefore, since there is none, he is to be condemned by no sentence, separated from the communion and fellowship of our Church by no sentence, and addressed by no terms except honorable ones.

Nor shall we in any way incline, by granting favor, to acquiesce in the wishes for Photius’s advancement to the priesthood. [Note: Here there is a large lacuna from Letter 10 of the same Nicholas.]

Therefore let Your Serenity now at least learn from the wording of this letter that the See of the blessed Apostle Peter will never consent to communion with Photius—a neophyte, an adulterer, and an invader of the Church of Constantinople—who was formerly justly condemned and more recently struck down by a synodal judgment, unless he ceases from his transgression.

For, to omit the other matters for now, having been instituted—or rather destroyed—by Gregory of Syracuse and the other schismatics, he cannot lawfully preside over another Church.

He is rightly believed to have been destroyed who, hoping to be built up by one who himself had been destroyed, lost whatever other good things he perhaps possessed by sharing in the rashness of his excessive presumption.

For how could Gregory build anyone up, when he was already known to have been struck down in many ways? How could he establish anyone in any ecclesiastical order, when, by rending the unity of the Church, he himself already appeared to have been utterly cast down?

For just as one who is bound cannot bind, and one who has been cast down cannot cast down, so one who has been destroyed could not build, nor could one who had been struck down ordain anyone.

A person who attempts either to overthrow another or to establish him must stand at the full strength of his own condition and rest in every respect upon firm foundations.

Gregory, therefore, who had been canonically and synodally deposed and anathematized, could not, as no reasoning shows, promote or bless anyone.

Photius consequently received nothing from Gregory except insofar as Gregory possessed something. But he possessed nothing, and therefore gave nothing.

For, as we read, the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of hands and invocation of those who knew how to lift clean hands to the Lord. But Gregory, who had become a transgressor of the law, undoubtedly provoked the Holy Spirit by the laying on of his hands—not toward the consecration of anyone, but rather toward anger against himself—even if the man being ordained had no other regulations opposing him.

For it is written: “He who stops his ears so as not to hear the law—his prayer will be accursed” (Prov. XXVIII). If accursed, then certainly not heard; if not heard, then ineffective; if ineffective, then plainly conferring nothing on Photius—who is recognized, rather, as having acquired through that laying on of hands a wounded head.

Moreover, if he claims that he was unjustly deposed by Ignatius, what will he say about all those who assembled in that synod at that time and pronounced judgment against him? And if he presumes to say that they too acted unjustly, why does he now communicate with them, and why does he consider some of them worthy of the priesthood? Yet he criticizes them for not having judged rightly before, and he knows that, according to his own view, they ought to submit to the judgment they pronounced.

But let us see by whose judgment or authority Gregory, after his deposition and anathema, presumed to preside in the honor of the episcopate [perhaps: “presumed” for *praesit*, HARD.], or recovered his former office.

Everyone knows that he had been deposed, bound by the bonds of anathema, and consequently deprived of communion with the whole Church.

Now, if you say that Gregory himself recovered both his honor and his former office, hear what the Apostle says: “No one takes this honor upon himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was. So too Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest” (Heb. V).

The venerable canons of Antioch also prescribe:

“If any bishop condemned by a synod, or a presbyter or deacon by his own bishop, should dare to touch anything belonging to the sacred ministry according to the preceding custom—whether he be a bishop, presbyter, or deacon—it is in no way permitted to him either to have hope of restoration or a place for satisfaction in another synod. Moreover, all who communicate with him are to be expelled from the Church, especially if, after learning that a sentence had been pronounced against the persons mentioned, they have dared to communicate with them.”

The Carthaginian regulations likewise openly declare that an excommunicated person who attempts to communicate before a hearing has pronounced condemnation upon himself.

If, therefore, according to the Apostle no one takes honor upon himself, and Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest—he who, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, glorifies those who glorify him, and who himself is the high priest of whom the same Apostle says again, “Such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners,” and so forth (Heb. VII)—

and if a bishop condemned by a synod, according to the sacred canons, should dare to touch anything belonging to the sacred ministry according to the preceding custom and to communicate before a hearing, he has pronounced condemnation upon himself, so that he is in no way permitted either to have hope of restoration or a place for satisfaction in another synod, and all who communicate with him are to be expelled from the Church—

how great a punishment, do you think, should Gregory suffer, who after his condemnation and anathema is proved to have committed all these things? That is, he exalted himself above Christ; he recovered for himself the honor that Christ himself did not take; he arrogantly glorified himself to become a pontiff; though excommunicated, he presumed to communicate before a hearing and to usurp what was forbidden; and, though condemned, he touched not merely something but many things belonging to the sacred ministry according to his former custom.

Gregory certainly ought not to have done this, even if no offenses had been committed for which he could have been condemned. For the judgment of superiors must always be feared by inferiors, lest, if they do not obey it—even if they were perhaps unjustly bound by it—they should deserve, through another fault, namely disobedience, the sentence of their own binding.

Accordingly, one ought to shudder at condemning superiors indiscriminately. Let all who are of lesser authority carefully avoid condemning their superiors, lest they transgress the judgment of those above them.

Otherwise, even if they have sometimes been condemned unjustly, from that rash transgression there certainly follow both guilt—which perhaps had not yet been committed—and punishment, which the guilt had not yet deserved.

The forbidden tree itself contained nothing deadly. But the person who ate from it in disobedience brought death upon himself and his descendants—not because the tree was evil, since everything God made he made good, but because the transgression was evil, and condemnation rightly arose through it for the person unwilling to submit.

Moreover, if you say that Gregory was received by your imperial power and by the bishops, I should like to ask, O most wise emperor, by what evidence and under what canons directing that this be done could it rightly happen that those who are expelled should be received by others? The venerable and universal Council of Nicaea most clearly forbids this in both professions of faith.

For it is clear that a priest can be neither bound nor loosed by secular power. Therefore it is fully established that Gregory of Syracuse could in no way have been reconciled merely by an imperial sentence. [Note: You may read these very words in Gelasius’s book on the bond of anathema.]

If the consent of the bishops was also joined to this, we ask whether it preceded or followed.

If it followed, the matter nevertheless returns to this: that absolution by secular power cannot be valid by command, and that the consent of the bishops that followed was more a matter of flattery or fear than of legitimate sanction.

If it preceded, let it be shown by whom and where it was carried out; whether it was celebrated according to the rule of the Church; whether it proceeded from the tradition of the Fathers; whether it was issued according to the custom of the elders; whether it was drawn from a competent examination; whether, according to the rules of the Church, it was referred to a see of greater authority than the one by which Gregory was held bound under condemnation; and whether the bishop who bound him also absolved him.

If these things were not done, by what custom or rite does Gregory of Syracuse boast that he was absolved, when he was sought neither by the bishops in the proper order nor under ecclesiastical laws, and could not possibly be absolved by worldly power outside the path of the Church?

Now, if you say, “I did not absolve him, but I asked the bishops that he be absolved,” then, on the contrary, they ought much more to have asked you that, if you wanted him absolved, a lawful absolution in accordance with ecclesiastical procedure should precede, and that all the matters mentioned above should be observed according to the course of the Church.

This was especially necessary since, as we learn from the apostolic canons, absolution can be granted not by an inferior or an equal, but by a superior person, and only by the one who separated him—or certainly by the first See.

An inferior cannot absolve either a superior or an equal without the consent of the superior. Only a higher authority can appropriately absolve an inferior. Accordingly, bishops of a lower rank could not absolve those whom their superior had bound without the first See.

Nevertheless, although they received the aforesaid Gregory, who had been expelled, contrary to the sacred canons of Nicaea, they never stripped him of the bond of condemnation and anathema. Rather, by their transgressive absolution they bound him more tightly, and while striving to loose him, they delivered him into greater bonds.

Indeed, by despising and transgressing the sentence of the superior—or even by attempting, through evasive counsel and mild judgment, to destroy the sentence they themselves had issued, thereby making themselves contrary to themselves—they are held bound by an equal transgression and are constrained by a similar punishment according to the apostolic canons and certain others.

Thus they are ordered to expel from the Church those who communicate with them. Consequently, it is clear that the guilty could not in any way justify the guilty, nor could those who were bound in any manner loose one who was bound.

Behold by whom Photius was instituted, O most Christian prince. Behold what kind of man Gregory is—one who might more appropriately be called “Dormitantius.”

Therefore consider, dearest son; reflect and diligently inquire with yourself whether Photius can stand, even if he is endowed with remarkable virtues and shines with every kind of knowledge, when the one who attempted to establish him has already fallen long ago; and when, wishing to be raised up with those attempting to raise him, he fell again, never to recover.

Let your divinely inspired dignity therefore consider how Photius can remain in the priestly rank, even if nothing else could lawfully impede him, since his institutor, when he was ordained, lacked not only the priesthood but even the Christian name itself.

And, as we have already explained, one who is condemned cannot justify, one who is deposed cannot raise up, and one who is bound cannot promote anyone through the laying on of hands. None of these things can be done. [Note: Here again there is a large lacuna from Letter 10 of the same Nicholas.]

Judge, therefore, most merciful emperor, whether obedience is owed rather to God or to human beings. Judge to whom resistance is rather due: to the power that almighty God established in Peter and exalted over the whole Church, or to the ordination of Gregory of Syracuse, concerning whom it must be said: “Woe to that man through whom so many scandals have come into the Church of Christ” (Matt. XXV).

Gregory, as you yourselves know, was formerly deposed by our brother and fellow minister Ignatius and by the synod that was under him, and a request was made to our fellow priest that the apostolic See consent to his condemnation.

But my predecessors of blessed memory, Leo and Benedict, while preserving the governance of the apostolic See, refused to hear one party in such a way that nothing at all would be reserved for the other. For there is no mediator of one party alone.

Therefore, since his deposition was not accepted by the apostolic See at that time, it remained without force.

When that same Gregory, through the legate of his party named Zachary, learned that the apostolic See had in no way consented to his deposition, he did not give thanks, nor did he cease from the insults with which he had begun to rage against our aforesaid brother.

Rather, abusing the kindness of God and the patience of the apostolic See in his pride, he irreverently sharpened renewed arrows of impiety against Ignatius, his patriarch. While Ignatius was still alive, Gregory consecrated a neophyte to the Church of Constantinople.

Indeed, he did not cease to be contumacious toward the decrees of this See. Although the decrees that had previously been issued by it for his sake and not against him ought to have been remembered by him as a grateful man, he does not remember them; and, like an evasive opponent, he prepares weapons against weapons that had contributed greatly to his protection and salvation, striving to destroy the wall that had most firmly guarded him from destruction.

He now does everything in his power to have those statutes regarded as wholly invalid—statutes which, when he himself needed them, he begged for; which, as stronger than diamond, he humbly desired; and which he humbly implored to aid him. Against them, perhaps, he formerly judged tyrants and sacrilegious persons who resisted them.

For if the apostolic See had not spared him, how could he have destroyed the most reverend Ignatius? He would have had no arm with which to do so.

But he used the kindness of the apostolic See in wickedness and turned the benefit into the destruction of his father.

Tell me therefore, I beg you, O emperor: since this is so, how ought we not to help Ignatius, or how can we fail, as far as lies in our power, to preserve him entirely unharmed until his hearing? Or how can we fail rightly to condemn Gregory and those who belong to his party?

If Ignatius had not been restrained by us, he might perhaps have struck them down canonically in such a way that they could not have shaken him by any effort.

These men, who did not cling to us, whom they deserved to have most ready to assist them, and who had not received counsel from us by which they might have been judged canonically together with their patriarch, preserved their forces from being broken by us and immediately prepared them against him.

Consider from every side how greatly we are now indebted to Ignatius, since we have become an obstacle to him and a shadow of defense for his enemies.

We did not, however, delay the judgment of these men for the purpose of preparing arrows with which they might injure him, but so that the sentence pronounced against them might have force, with an examination preceding it by us; and so that the accusations brought by them against him might be fully admitted before us, with Ignatius’s party summoned or convicted and not absent from our presence.

Therefore, after the judgment had been postponed for a short time and the sentence weakened, a written decision was sent to both parties to be presented to the sight of the pontiff of the apostolic See and, as was proper, to be subjected to his decisions.

But while Ignatius’s party was preparing its journey in haste, his enemies recovered their strength. No longer seeking apostolic faith, no longer deigning to remember Peter, Ignatius was dragged away, driven out, afflicted with innumerable evils, and removed from the governance of the Church.

All this happened because the aforesaid pontiffs, preserving equity toward both parties and seeking a hearing for both sides, had in a certain sense extended a hand to Ignatius’s enemies by not confirming his sentence, or rather by weakening it for the time being, since they had decided to defer the sentence pronounced against them until the presence of the apostolic See.

Therefore, dearest son and praiseworthy Augustus, since the occasion for Ignatius’s overthrow seems to have been found through us, it is necessary not only because a brother ought to be helped by his brother, but also because the oracle of Christ speaks especially to Peter, whose place on earth we, though unworthy, occupy: “Strengthen your brethren” (Luke XXII).

It is therefore also especially said that we must not only help and strengthen him, but, as you yourselves can perceive, must dispute on his behalf with all our strength in every respect, so that everything in him that is shown to have suffered violence because his adversaries found through us material for injuring him may be completely abolished; and so that, with Christ’s favor, he may recover everything that, while we acted moderately and according to the rule, he is recognized to have lost prejudicially.

For if our aforesaid predecessors, the pontiffs Leo and Benedict of blessed memory, had lived to see Gregory or his accomplices perpetrate such a deed in their days—namely, if they had abused the great benefit of the apostolic See’s compassion and patience toward them and laid hands upon Ignatius, or sharpened their tongues against him in such a manner without consulting those holy bishops—they would certainly have condemned them without delay as ministers of unrest, since they would have shown themselves manifestly liable to that charge, and would have earnestly sought to destroy so great a sacrilege of their impiety.

But since they have been taken from this vale of tears by divine calling, and have not yet seen this tyranny, we must take up their labor, just as we have succeeded to their honor. In our time the cruelty that began to put down roots in theirs has become fully manifest.

Therefore, first, because we retain the governance of the apostolic See, which has the right to judge concerning the whole Church; second, because we ought to assist brothers who have suffered injury; and finally, because, as we have already said, we must succeed to the labor of those whose pontifical honor we have inherited—just as they followed the examples of their predecessors and proved themselves energetic cultivators of their work—we have diligently undertaken to complete what they would certainly have done with the Lord’s help, possessing, as they did, the same zeal for justice and the same privilege of dignity.

To omit this, as it is clearly granted to everyone to know, is beyond our power.

But you say, O emperor, that even without our consent you will retain Photius and the Church, and that he will have communion with the Church, while Ignatius will obtain absolutely no improvement through us.

We, on the contrary, believe that the Church of Christ will not consign the sacred canons, especially those of Nicaea, to oblivion—canons prescribing that those who are expelled are not to be received by others.

We also believe that a member cannot long remain sound if it is joined to members that are not joined to the head.

Finally, we believe that the remaining members, if they desire to live, will eventually follow the head.

Yet in all these matters, according to the Apostle, it is “not of him who wills or of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX). Therefore, with God strengthening us, we do not grow weary of delays in the labor of piety, because although running is ours, it belongs to divine power to bring us to the palm of victory whenever he pleases.

What it was fitting for the apostolic See to do, as we wrote to all the orthodox of the Catholic Church, it has energetically done. It belongs to God to bring what has been begun to completion.

For we plow the soil of minds with the plowshare of the tongue and scatter in it the seeds of words; but God is powerful both to pour upon it the dew of his Spirit, to make it fertile by the increase of grace, and to bring it, in whatever measure and manner he wills, to abundant and manifold fruit.

For although we are cultivators of the Lord’s field, “neither he who plants is anything nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. III).

Yet, these matters being thus unquestionably established, it is clear that those who have once been struck by the sentence of the apostolic see’s prelates remain bound by that sentence even today. Thus, although the weapons of judgment pronounced against some of them did not immediately wound them because they were protected by the shield of imperial power, they nevertheless eventually pierced them to the marrow; while others, even after they had died, they rendered altogether detestable to everyone. All those whom the apostolic see retained in its communion were either received by the universal Church while they lived, or were afterward retained by it with the highest distinction. Moreover, those whose condemnation it did not share, it absolved by its unique prerogative. So that your Prudence may recognize this more clearly, we shall endeavor to recall a few examples.

First, Peter, the bearer of the keys of heaven and the first occupant of this see, struck down Simon Magus not with iron but with the sword of his tongue. But Simon, using the power of princes, not only persisted in his wickedness; he also died wickedly and, because of his own cause, inflamed the princes against the death of the very one who had condemned him. Then, when all the Asians, among others, thought—on the authority of the evangelist John—that Easter should be celebrated with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon [Note: [Col. 1033D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 24], the bishop Victor, distinguished by his merits and by his name, separated them from the communion of the college. Yet they, together with certain bishops of the Churches, not only refused to lend him their hand in the matter but also reproved him for obstinacy. Pope Felix likewise not only deposed Acacius of Constantinople but also bound him with unbreakable bonds of anathema [Note: [Col. 1033D] Felix III, Letter 3; and Liberatus, *On the Case of Nestorius and Eutyches*, chapter 18]. But he was so despised that Acacius, protected by the support of lovers of the world, continued even while certain Roman pontiffs were dying to exercise the priestly office according to the preceding custom [Col. 1034A], and, except for a few, enjoyed the communion of all the Easterners.

Furthermore, Agapetus, bishop of the apostolic see, likewise condemned Anthimus, bishop of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 1033D] Agapetus, Letters 4 and 5; and Liberatus, chapter 21. *Pontifical Book* [Col. 1034D] on Silverius and Vigilius], and appointed Menas in his place. Because of this Anthimus, the Roman pontiffs Silverius and Vigilius endured many hardships and dangers from the empress Theodora, but they were in no way induced to restore him.

Having therefore recalled, in passing, these examples from among the many great and illustrious rulers of the apostolic see, what wonder is it if we are despised on Photius’s account, when we see the prince of the apostles undergo death while defending the truth against Simon? For although only late, although after many labors [Col. 1034B], the entire world eventually defends what Peter is known to have defended against Simon and condemns what he is described as having condemned.

And what wonder is it if, while we labor for ecclesiastical correction, you do not give us your hand but even reproach us for harshness? We see Pope Victor, a martyr, truly victorious because he was a martyr for ecclesiastical tradition, reproved for obstinacy by the bishops of the entire Church. For now the whole Church agrees with him and proclaims that what he did is worthy of praise. Here we must observe that, if he had not then exercised such severity for justice, as certain bishops urged him not to do, perhaps that error would have remained to this day—especially since we read that, even after he had been inflamed with such zeal, it persisted in some places until the earlier Council of Ephesus [Col. 1034C].

What further wonder is it if, in your days, the apostolic see is held in contempt and is not heard by your imperial authority or by those subject to you, when we see the holy Felix so despised by your imperial predecessors that they protected Acacius, whom he had anathematized, so thoroughly that Acacius both abused the see of Constantinople throughout his life and died wickedly in his perfidy? Nevertheless, with Christ propitious and the pontiffs of the apostolic see contending tirelessly, the whole Church was at last brought round, by the unremitting exertion of the Catholics, to the judgment of the often-mentioned blessed Felix—that is, the judgment of the Church [f., “the judgment is the Church,” HARD.]. And because the aforesaid Acacius was not found to be still alive, it was subsequently decreed that his name should be silenced in the Church [Note: [Col. 1034D] Gelasius, Letter 11: “The absolution which, while alive, he neither sought at all nor deserved, he cannot obtain now that he is dead.” HARD.]. But you too, orthodox emperor, now share the judgment of the apostolic see concerning him; if you had been found at that time, perhaps you would have been inflamed on his behalf against it and in this matter as well.

Finally, what wonder is it if you threaten us on account of Photius’s deposition, when the imperial predecessors of your predecessors drove my predecessors, because of the aforesaid Anthimus, as far as confession? Yet although they labored and raged for a very long time [Col. 1035A], and stirred up so many savage afflictions against them, they were entirely unable either to change their sentence or to restore Anthimus to his former position. Though late, they nevertheless eventually detested both Anthimus himself and his opinions, which agreed with those of the apostolic see; and they reverently embraced Menas, the holy man promoted by that see—not as your people falsely assert, but by receiving him worthily in agreement with it.

Who, on seeing Peter or his successors so vigorously battle Simon and the aforesaid transgressors, could not have been indignant and considered them altogether mad, especially when the whole world, except for a very few, fought against them together with its princes on behalf of those same perfidious men? But because truth cannot be completely concealed by human efforts, and because the aforesaid and other holy and supreme pontiffs, relying on the hope that does not disappoint, undertook so many labors, therefore the sun of justice, perhaps sending forth its rays, dispersed the cloud of error and gradually displayed the light of truth. Thus, at last, it became clear how rightly those defenders of the Church had judged and how wickedly these others had gone astray.

So too we, to speak in the words of the distinguished Apostle, “having the same spirit of faith that our fathers had, as it is written: ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke’” (II Cor. IV; Ps. CXXV), have also believed, and therefore we speak. And we trust that he who gave Abraham a son against hope is powerful enough to grant us, who labor for his Church, an increase of spiritual [Col. 1035C] fruits and to multiply the abundant fruit of those same fruits.

Therefore, we ask you to say, most devout emperor: what length of disobedience, what multitude of insolence, or what superiority of power ought—or is able—to turn us even briefly from this faith or hope? Especially since the blessed Apostle, already designated, cries out: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Heb. XI); and again: “Hope that is seen is not hope; for what does a person hope for if he sees it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. VIII).

Strengthened, therefore, by the hope of this faith, dearest son [Col. 1035D], we have no doubt that we shall receive the reward of our labors—even if you never obey us, even if you strive with all your strength to resist the apostolic see. But concerning you, as our most beloved son, we groan and grieve deeply, because, following not the footsteps of your predecessors but the examples of wicked princes, you have been enticed by the persuasions of perverse men, set aside the decrees of the apostolic and first see throughout the whole world, and despised the bonds of anathema by which it has regularly ensnared the persecutors of Ignatius, our fellow minister—namely, Photius, who after his deposition dared, contrary to preceding custom, to usurp very many matters concerning the sacred ministry—and his supporters [Col. 1036A], as though you were less of a Christian.

How far this must be removed from a pious understanding and execrated by the hearts of the faithful, the outstanding bishop of our see, Gregory in conduct and name, demonstrated when he wrote about this, saying (book IX, Letter 49): “If there are people who most certainly think or maintain such things, there is no doubt that they are not Christians, because they think and speak against what I and all Catholic bishops, and the whole Church, anathematize. And again: They themselves are witnesses that they are not Christians, because they foolishly consider that they can dissolve the bonds of the holy Church by their efforts; and therefore they do not regard as true the absolution of the holy Church, which it grants to the faithful, if they do not consider its bonds effective. We must not dispute at length against such people, because they must be despised in every respect and anathematized, so that, by the very means through which they think they deceive the truth, they may truly be bound in their sins.”

But if you should perhaps say that we ought not to have believed so hastily what we heard, nor been so ready to pronounce a sentence, know, emperor, that this could reasonably be said if the offense had not been accompanied by an outcry, as in the case of the Sodomites and Gomorrahites; if what we have related above concerning Gregory had not been so entirely evident; if your writings concerning what was done at Constantinople against our fellow priest Ignatius, or concerning Photius—indeed, through Photius—had not clearly indicated it [Col. 1036C]; or if your Piety had kindly received our envoys and letters; or if, once received, no one had corrupted them by reckless deceit and removed them from the tenor of their truth.

But when the sacrilege was committed not only with a voice but with an outcry, and the blood of an innocent brother cried out to God from the earth, as it has until now; and when your people, in accordance with what the prophet is said to attribute to the attitude of the reprobate, proclaimed their sin like Sodom and did not hide it (Isa. III); after your writings also clearly demonstrated—that is, demonstrated the completed sin [f., “the sin itself,” HARD.]—and after we learned that our envoys had been turned away from conversation with the faithful, that they had been turned away from our commands, and that our letters had been concealed and falsified [Col. 1036D], what could we have done more wisely or cautiously than to uproot the crime completely, lest it spread more and more like cancer? And lest we be judged idle and negligent, what could we have done other than display a swift and fervent zeal for the house of God? Furthermore, because it had been falsely circulated that we had consented either to Ignatius’s deposition or to Photius’s promotion, we rightly foresaw that we must hasten to give satisfaction and to assure the Church of Christ of the truth.

Yet, just as crimes heard of should not easily be believed but, once known, should be punished without delay, so the holy pope Gregory, already named, an outstanding teacher, wisely instructs us, saying (*Exposition on Psalm [of] Penitence*): “Sin accompanied by a voice is guilt in action; but sin accompanied even by an outcry is guilt committed openly.” [Col. 1037A]

But what are we taught by this example except that we should never be hasty in pronouncing a sentence; that we should not rashly judge matters not investigated; that any evils merely heard of should not move us; and that we should not believe statements made indiscriminately without proof? We fear committing such things if we examine more carefully the deeds of our Creator. For, wishing to restrain us from issuing a precipitous sentence, although everything is naked and open before his eyes, he nevertheless did not wish to judge the evils of Sodom merely on hearsay. He says: “I will go down and see whether they have done according to the cry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. XVIII). Why, then, does the omnipotent Lord, who knows everything, seemingly delay until after investigation, unless to set before us an example of seriousness, so that we do not presume to believe human evils before proving them? [Col. 1037B]

Behold, he descends through angels to learn the evils, and immediately strikes the criminals; and he who is patient, he who is gentle, he of whom it is written, “But you, Lord, judge with tranquility” (Wis. XII); he of whom it is again written, “The Lord is patient, but he repays” (Ecclus. V)—when he found them involved in so great a crime, he seems to have set aside patience and did not wish to await the day of the final judgment for vengeance, but anticipated the day of judgment with the fire of judgment. Behold: he seemed almost reluctant to believe the evil when he heard it, yet he struck without delay when he discovered its truth by investigation, so that he might give us an example: greater crimes must be believed only slowly when heard, but punished more quickly when truly known [Col. 1037C].

How, then, were we inclined or hasty to punish evils merely heard, when, as we said far above, before your envoys—namely, the illustrious man Arsa, the *spatharius*, and the others—came to Rome, we had already truly learned what had afterward been done at Constantinople, although we had heard of it and nevertheless had not believed it fully? After those same envoys of yours reached the apostolic see, what we had first learned by hearsay began to be openly disclosed before us and before the entire Church that is with us; yet even then it did not in any way draw us toward condemning them.

But after our envoys, whom we had sent there to investigate these matters in due order, carefully and fully, and to report the truth to your knowledge, returned together with Leo, the imperial secretary and envoy; after we received from him both your letter and the other writings concerning what had been done at Constantinople and carefully investigated them; after we examined our envoys according to canonical procedure together with the holy synod; after we learned clearly everything that had taken place; and after we drove every cloud of doubt from our hearts—then, taught by the loud-sounding trumpet of Christ, namely the aforesaid Pope Gregory (book VI, Letter 14), and acting according to what we recalled above, just as we had believed the evils heard of only slowly, so, once they had been established by so many proofs, we necessarily hastened to punish them more quickly [Col. 1038A].

And this was proper. For, in order to recognize and condemn the impiety of Nestorius, the holy Council of Ephesus considered it sufficient to have his letter to blessed Cyril read aloud. Moreover, the Fifth Council struck with anathema even Origen and Theodore, already dead, when their writings were found to contain unsound opinions worthy of condemnation. The holy Pope Gelasius likewise writes to the Dardanians concerning the condemnation of Acacius, formerly bishop of your city, saying (Letter 11): “If an examination is sought, there was no longer any need for judgment, after he himself had confessed by his letters.” Furthermore, Pope Martin, confessor of Christ, contradicted the Alexandrian Cyrus and the Constantinopolitan Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul by condemning them after reviewing only their writings in his holy synod (Lateran Council).

Following these examples, therefore, and so many examples of my predecessors, it is clear that we solemnly condemned Photius and his accomplices—especially since we heard from you in writing that Ignatius, who must rightly be called the Lord’s anointed, had been pierced by the sword of judgment by his own subjects and inferiors, and had suffered the loss of his own dignity. This is aptly represented, according to David, by Saul, whom he calls the anointed of God, although history records that Saul was already recognized as rejected by the Lord [Note: [Col. 1037D] The passage is obscure.]. When David heard from the mouth of the Amalekite boy—even though the boy spoke falsely—that he had killed Saul, he sought no other proof but immediately struck him, saying: “Your blood be upon your head, for your mouth has testified against you, saying: ‘I killed the Lord’s anointed’” (II Sam. I) [Col. 1038C].

Yet what need is there to pursue many more examples here, when that same impiety still prevails today in the Church of Constantinople, transgression reigns, and schisms multiply? If you shudder at our sentence and think that it is a matter of some power, do not fear it merely because it was pronounced against transgressors and contaminators; fear it rather because it binds the disobedient perpetually and never releases them unless they repent.

Therefore, dearest son and most Christian prince, whom we address together with all subject to your empire, remove the evil from your midst; take away the adulterer, take away the tyrant and usurper of the Church; restore to our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius the Church divinely entrusted to him, from which you expelled him before any canonical hearing; restore what you took, and correct before God what you did against God; abandon evil, turn back to us, and be corrected. Once freed from evil, you will in no way be separated from us. For we did not pronounce a sentence against Photius because he is a human being or because he is called Photius, but because he is a transgressing person and because he usurped the Church of a living bishop who was not lawfully deprived of it in any respect.

Thus the wrongdoing that exists in him and in his supporters is punished by the imposition of a sentence. If that transgression and wrongdoing depart, the person against whom the sentence was pronounced will no longer be the same. The human being and Photius will remain, but the sentence does not condemn him insofar as he is human and bears the name of a human being; it condemns him insofar as he is a transgressor and wrongdoer. Therefore, if he ceases to be a transgressor, our sentence will have no place in him at all. He will be other than the one against whom the sentence was brought, since he will begin to be what he was not, or cease to be the one against whom the sentence was pronounced. For as long as he remains what he was when the sentence was imposed, that sentence is truly unbreakable.

However much the person against whom it was imposed may flourish, however many honors may flow to him, and however greatly he may be exalted with marvelous praises, that sentence will be broken for ever [the text reads *confringetur*; perhaps corrupt]. And unless he repents, if not now, then certainly after a few years, or even after many years, or at some time at least—even if he does not lose the Church during his life, which he tyrannically possesses—after death he will certainly lose the name of Christianity, whose profession he shamelessly tramples underfoot [Col. 1039B].

Now, if he judges that he and his supporters are bound by our sentence, and that he can be absolved together with them—for this is what you seem to mean when, in the letter addressed to us, you repeatedly urge us to change our will, counsel, and sentence—then he certainly does not plead its injustice, and does not doubt that it has some force: for it was able to bind, and he can be absolved from it together with his supporters. For it could not bind them unless it were just. Since it is just, it can be justly undone only when the error has been condemned.

Therefore, let Photius and his supporters confess their error; let all whom the just sentence holds bound lay aside their transgression. But you, dearest son, all the more, since in justice and piety you ought to surpass everyone: once the transgression has been dissolved, let each person consequently be released from the censure of the sentence pronounced against him. The prophet Nathan, after all, openly and publicly declared David’s error in the king’s own face; he did not at all conceal that David himself had committed it, but, once David had corrected it by confession, he consequently absolved him.

Moreover, we have thought it necessary to recall that last year, in the thirteenth indiction, we received through Michael the *protospatharius* a letter written in your name. It was so thickly covered with insulting words, indeed with blasphemies [Col. 1039D], that one can only think that its writer dipped his pen in a serpent’s throat and that the dictator’s lips poured forth poisons instead of words. If such things penetrate the hearts of the simpler-minded—for the ears of the prudent do not receive them—they immediately kill them, and all the more miserably because through that poisonous draught the death of the soul is admitted more than the death of the body.

Although we remember having already written to you concerning the enormity of this sacrilege, it is nevertheless not burdensome for me, but necessary for you and for many, to write the same things now to your Wisdom.

Finally, we have thought—and still think—that your Piety will eventually repent and yield to our salutary counsels concerning the restoration of the condition of the Church of Constantinople. Then, in the presence of the whole multitude of your empire, let it decree that all the writings badly compiled not only against us and this holy Church, but also against our brother and fellow minister Ignatius, be handed over to the fire. Otherwise it would become clear to all the faithful of the Church what authority belongs to the apostolic see and what vengeance threatens the fabricators of falsehood and inventors of perverse doctrines.

For although we consider our own special injuries to be of no account, it is impossible for us to endure with equanimity the blasphemies directed against so many and such great holy Fathers and defenders of the Catholic Church [catholic Church], against those who destroyed various heresies and defended the orthodox faith; nor can we endure the insults directed against so great a see, or against the outstanding Roman Church, in whose service we are, by God’s authorization.

Yet although we think humbly of ourselves, we nevertheless affirm, with conscience as our guide, that what you say about us is not true. But, as we said, setting those things aside, we seek instead the things that belong to Jesus Christ. Even if privileges have been established—badly heaped up against his servants, against his ordinances, and against his dispositions [for “disposition,” HARD.]—we tolerate them with no patience. We not only pant with all our strength to destroy them, but also necessarily plan to repay the authors of such perversity with a fitting recompense. This is so that no one, seeing them go unpunished, may dare now or later to compose such spectacles of falsehood or to oppose them with fabricated inventions of this kind of blasphemy.

Therefore, most exalted emperor, if, carefully investigating and scrutinizing for the Lord’s sake, you find that this exceedingly filthy letter—or rather, this letter infected with poisonous syllables—was not composed at your command, then, while we say nothing for the moment about the punishment of those who weave so many deceptive contrivances [Note: [Col. 1039D] Something seems to be missing here], it is fitting that, after its companion has been received and publicly burned before all by your august officials, you should, by letters dispatched both to us and to all to whose knowledge it has come, make suitable satisfaction and show yourselves wholly free from so perverse a meaning and such profane inventions, since they were not fabricated by your own mind [Col. 1040D].

But if, occupied with the many concerns of this world, you were deceived into ordering such things to be written, let it not burden your Clemency humbly to confess this also, and to decree by your laws that writings of this kind are to have no force. Let no one with whom they are found escape unpunished. Let the letters—or copies of the frequently mentioned and always detestable letter—be handed over to the devouring flames, while the sacred words remain untouched out of reverence [Col. 1041A], so that you may also be able to free yourselves from the stain of an evil reputation incurred through blasphemous writings. And do not appear ungrateful sons toward your mother, from whom you and your fathers received the height of imperial power according to an order arranged in heaven.

But if not, know this: once we have discovered that you intend to persist in this obstinacy to the very end, first, after assembling the venerable priests of all the Western regions, we shall, relying on apostolic authority, bind the writers, arrangers, and authors of such great deceit—or of such cruel disparagement of the saints and of the traditions of the Fathers—with dreadful bonds of anathema, removing them from the entire Christian structure. Moreover, following the footsteps of the Fathers and my predecessors, who were accustomed even to annul councils of numerous bishops wickedly celebrated, we shall consign to perpetual condemnation any associated writings or perhaps copies of the frequently mentioned letter; indeed, not only these, but also all the writings that were either unjustly composed against our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius or madly produced against us as we canonically pursued his case.

Then, with those most holy brothers and fellow bishops deciding together with us and considering the matter jointly, we shall give the letter itself over to ultimate destruction as a reproach to you before all the nations found around the memory of Saint Peter. They shall see it suspended from a stake, with a great fire placed beneath it [Col. 1041C].

When these things have been properly carried out, let the pious learn what he should love and the cruel what he should fear. For to hear and remain silent about so many and such great inventions of blasphemy—or rather, distortions of truthful writings—and to suppress them is to connive [Note: [Col. 1041D] For *connivisse*, as in Letter 104. The older books often misuse *cohibere* for *connivere*. HARD.]. Therefore, venerable emperor, as you yourself will be able to understand, I must take great care lest, if we do not swiftly oppose the fabrications of these spectacles, foolish people should deceitfully think that we admitted them as things recognized or approved [for *aestimemur*, HARD.].

Nor can we, by dissembling, leave in the Church of God such foul shoots—shoots that, in the time of our most blessed pontifical predecessors, either never arose or, if they arose from somewhere or in some manner, were uprooted from the foundation by the mattock of their judgment before they could grow [Col. 1041D].

Therefore, destroy and scatter them yourselves; otherwise, know beforehand that they are to be destroyed or utterly scattered by us in the manner we have stated. Before writing these things to you, we had thought that you would willingly do what we now urge your Sublimity to do. But because what was expected has so far produced no result, and because we desire your salvation to remain unharmed, we now admonish you with paternal affection to do this at least.

Otherwise, as we have already said, with God’s favor we shall henceforth keep watch and devote ourselves to every effort within our power, so that those who have not experienced the authority of Peter—or rather, have not understood that this authority is God’s, who ordered it in Peter—may be counted among the dead. In this way no one will thereafter dare to defend these writings, perniciously compiled as they are, or anything similar—not to put it merely in writing, but even to turn it over in his mind.

For we cannot leave unscathed, without peril to ourselves, the fabrications that resist God’s ordinance, contradict the evangelical utterances, oppose the definitions of the holy Fathers, and run counter to synodal constitutions; if left thus, they can inflict countless losses on the faithful who seek Peter’s aid. Nor can we leave, to our reputation either now or after our death, so great a stain—God forbid—or rather [the text is corrupt: “not merely a stain … but destruction”], the destruction of the simpler faithful and the mutilation of the privileges of the apostolic see [f., “stain,” as in Letter 104; Col. 1042B].

Therefore, most desirable son and most merciful Augustus, as a wisest son, gladden your father; and at last, as a most welcome offspring, drive sorrow from the breast of your mother by removing the adulterer and restoring the legitimate one to her. Destroy, we ask, the work of the devil and overturn all his subversions. Believe me: it is the work of the devil, and it has been accomplished through his subversions, that Ignatius was expelled as patriarch and that the adulterer Photius invaded the Church entrusted to him.

For that cunning and ancient enemy, wishing to impose perpetual silence on priests of lesser rank, first judged that he should attack the one whom he saw to possess greater authority [Col. 1042C]. To bring him down, he armed all the forces he could, and inflamed even the princes of the world with the torches of total envy.

Why did he do this, except so that, when they saw the man above them struck down, those of lesser authority would not dare to speak for the truth at all, and, with persons of such high rank already acting wickedly, would oppose them less boldly? They would be all the less free to climb the wall for the house of the Lord, since they saw such deeds being perpetrated against their superior.

But you, emperor, who conquer the enemies of the Church more by religion than by the arm of the flesh, conquer his wiles and overturn all his machinations. Hear us, if you will; but if not, hear at least your protector, and recognize that the words spoken to Jeremiah have been conveyed to you. For he says: “Behold, I have appointed you this day over nations and kingdoms, to uproot, destroy, ruin, and scatter, to build and to plant” (Jer. I).

Uproot, destroy, ruin, and scatter, in accordance with the ministry appropriate to your imperial power, all the devil’s arguments and all the contrivances of his members, especially those shoots that arose through Photius and are growing wickedly. Build and plant the strongholds of every virtue and the fragrant spices of honorable conduct. Indeed, rebuild whatever has been destroyed through you concerning the dignity of our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius, and restore whatever has been irreverently torn away from the matters belonging to the patriarchal office [Col. 1043A].

But if, whether because of sins obstructing you or because wicked men are persuading you, you do not consider it necessary to fulfill what our impending envoys—whose counsel we strive to commend to you even for the prosperity of your empire—will urge you to do, and if you decide, alas, that only delay should be pursued, we wish your Excellence to know that, concerning the persons of Ignatius and Photius, whose controversy is at issue, we judge nothing more prudent, mild, or salutary than that both of them should come to Rome for a renewed examination, which nevertheless we promise to conduct according to clemency, in the manner and order which we already signified to you through Michael the *protospatharius*.

In this way, you should support Ignatius, who is deprived of every human aid, with whatever assistance you may provide for the love of Christ, so that he may be able to come. If you wish to know the tenor or order of the letter through that same envoy of yours, by whom the matter has not now been brought to you, concerning the coming of the aforesaid persons to Rome, ask our present envoys, and you will be able to know it fully.

For we gave them copies of the letters that we sent to your Greatness and to Photius through Rhadoaldus and Zacharias, then bishops, written out for comparison with the authentic copies. Together with these, we also gave them copies of the letters that we sent to you and to Photius through Leo, the imperial secretary, and of this letter [Col. 1043C], which, as we have said, we sent through Michael the *protospatharius*, so that they might likewise carry them with them for comparison.

Accordingly, your perceptive diligence will find more fully the tenor and order according to which we have decreed that the aforesaid persons come here for a renewed judgment. We refrain from repeating it, in order to avoid the tedium of excessive length.

Having thus, with God’s inspiration, made these matters known to the ears of your Serenity, let your empire, redeemed by the Lord, know that our envoys have been sent from our episcopate, by God’s authorization: namely, the most reverend and most holy Donatus, bishop of the holy Church of Ostia; and the religious and venerable Leo, presbyter of the holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Lawrence, the martyr of Christ, which is called that of Damasus; and Marinus, deacon of our apostolic see [Col. 1043D].

Your Clemency, as a cultivator of the Christian religion, should receive them kindly, treat them piously in every respect, and decree that they remain unharmed and entirely safe for as long as they stay with you. Indeed, may you deign to grant them a suitable and sufficient opportunity and place to explain freely what has been entrusted to them. Then, once those matters in which God gives assent and grants success to your heart have been arranged, let them return to us immediately, unharmed and without any obstructing trouble.

But since they are being sent in the service of almighty God, by that dread name itself, which is the inseparable Trinity, and by the terrible divine judgment, [Col. 1044A] before whose fearful tribunal—that of Christ our God—we shall all stand and render a strict account according to our merits, we adjure you and beseech you with all our heart not to inflict any injury upon these envoys of ours while they are staying with you, nor to place any obstacle in their way when they wish to return from there, nor to permit anyone else to do so. Rather, make them fearless and secure from every plot devised against them. Thus, when they return to us effective—though they may be able to urge upon you your own salvation—it may be clear to all nations how greatly you honor God, who crowns you, for the peace and correction of whose Church they have carried out their embassy, and how much reverence you hold before your eyes for the chief apostles, from whose see they have departed.

Indeed, most tranquil emperor, we did not send them to celebrate a synod, nor did we dispatch them to stir up disputes and quarrels. For we know that, as the Apostle teaches, “the servant of the Lord must not quarrel” (II Tim. II). This, rather, is the whole purpose for which we sent them: namely, that, with due reverence for the authority of the apostolic see preserved, the Church of Constantinople may recover the restoration of its proper condition, and that peace and concord may be restored to the holy Churches and to your empire, and, with God’s favor, preserved for all time; and that your name may increase through long-lasting and prosperous success. And just as the name of the pious Augusti who preceded you is here exalted with marvellous praises after their death, may you enjoy in heaven the blessedness of the eternal kingdom.

Otherwise, according to the Apostle, “the word of God is not bound” (II Tim. II). He says again: “For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Hebr. IV). By that word we shall in no way be able to leave unpunished those who are disobedient, who oppose the Church of God, or who inflict injury upon its servants. “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. XI).

We say and undertake all this, albeit briefly, and carry it out diligently, while omitting very many further points, for the following reasons. First, so that, if we are found negligent, we may not be compelled before the supreme Judge to render an account for the reception of the talent that has been entrusted to us in the abundance of privileges. Second, so that we may not be thought in any way to have consented either to the irregular deposition of our fellow priest and brother Ignatius or to the promotion of Photius. Third, so that the priestly order may not become so disgracefully degraded that those who handle the Lord and his sacred body, who enter within the veils of his Holy of Holies, and especially those who hold the highest place in their own diocese, may thereafter be so easily driven out and cast down by any common or inferior persons, even laymen, and deprived of their proper rank and their own Church without any examination or proven crime.

Fourth, because it is clear that, when the apostolic see did not consent to the condemnation of Gregory of Syracuse and his associates, they rose up in the manner we have described to carry out these abominable acts [Col. 1045A]; and now, unless we correct or punish these things, we fear that guilt may be charged against us. For we are the successors of those whose kindness they abused, and although without our knowledge, they nevertheless fell into these actions. Fifth, so that your empire itself, or that of your successors, may not be so lightly stirred up against the Churches of God or their bishops by the breath of perverse suggestion.

Therefore we beseech your piety, and call God and his holy angels to witness, that you obey us, and in this life take care to listen to us as we exhort and implore you, rather than in the future find blessed Peter, the keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, accusing and condemning you. For if you do not obey us, he himself is despised, whose representatives we are and by whose authority [Col. 1045B] we speak. But if you despise him, consider now what will become of you, and what account you will render at the terrible judgment of God, since, placed in such exalted position, you show by your example to all your subjects the precipice of ultimate ruin—not only in the present age but also in the future, to emperors and all the rulers of the world, and indeed to all the faithful.

Therefore shudder at destroying the piety of so many people by your example; fear bringing about the peril of so many souls; dread preparing such ruin for the faithful who perhaps are striving toward salvation, and for all these things rendering before the strict Judge a complete account of everything, without any evasive excuses. For as many as by your example are drawn into such actions, so many losses of souls will unquestionably be charged to you; and, beyond doubt—something we do not wish—you will suffer as many punishments as the pattern of your guilty action plunges into the chaos of disobedience.

May the Lord avert all these things, with your piety obeying us; for we pursue and demand these matters for your salvation.

(From a letter of Pope Gelasius to the emperor Anastasius.)

Therefore, do not be angry if we love you so greatly that we wish the temporal kingdom you have attained to become perpetual for you; that you who now rule human beings may reign with Christ; and that you who are to die tomorrow may receive life and eternal glory [Vatican manuscript: “everlasting”].

Given on the Ides of November, in the fifteenth indiction.

(Year 866.) XCIX. TO PHOTIUS. [Col. 1045D] He reproaches Photius for many crimes that he committed in seizing Ignatius’s see; proves that he violated both divine and human law; announces that he has been deposed; and, if he does not submit to the sentence, threatens him with perpetual excommunication until death.

NICOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to PHOTIUS.

You are found liable to innumerable transgressions and, in many ways, shamelessly puffed up by insults against the venerable canons, the decisions of the Fathers, and even the divine commandments. For you are recognized as having belonged to the faction of the schismatics who, while our venerable brother and fellow bishop Ignatius governed the Church of Constantinople, turned people away from participation in holy communion contrary to the regulations; and, after being suddenly tonsured from secular administration, military service, and the public forum, you allowed yourself to be ordained and called a bishop by Gregory of Syracuse, formerly a bishop, condemned by a synod and convicted by the apostolic see. Even while Ignatius the patriarch was alive and still present, you invaded his see.

You stole away the bride whom Christ the bridegroom had entrusted, as the friend of the bridegroom, to be kept immaculate—not entering through the door, which is Christ, but breaking in from elsewhere, from the opposite side, into the Lord’s sheepfold like a thief or robber, and carrying her off by violence as a rapacious and criminal adulterer. Moreover, contrary—indeed, in opposition—to the apostolic canons, you used secular authorities [Col. 1046B] to obtain the church.

Then, by communing and associating daily and indiscriminately with the condemned and anathematized, and with those who had been bound by my predecessor, Pope Benedict of holy memory, lest they presume to perform priestly office before a hearing, you acted against the faith you had promised and against your profession, in which you pledged that you would devise no evil counsel against the aforesaid patriarch. You convened a council and, together with your followers—who had been deposed, condemned, excommunicated, and anathematized, as well as others without churches, and those by whom either you yourself had been irregularly and unlawfully advanced or whom you had rashly and improperly promoted—you dared to carry out the deposition of that same brother and fellow minister of ours [Col. 1046C] and to pronounce an anathema against him.
