Then, by whatever arguments you could, you presumed to turn away from our commands the envoys of the apostolic see whom we had sent concerning the matter of the sacred images, to investigate and report to us the deposition of the aforesaid patriarch, and to discover the manner of your promotion—acting in the fashion of Acacius, once the heretical patriarch of Constantinople. At the procession held for you and your associates, as was revealed by their testimony and made clear by the Holy Spirit to the venerable synod assembled by us, you proceeded, to the confusion of the condemned and schismatics and of yourself, disregarding the embassy—which ought to have been respected even according to the custom of the pagans [the text reads *pertransisti*; HARD. proposes *pertraxisti*, “you dragged them along”]. In mockery of the blessed apostle Peter, from whose see they had departed, you not only made them return ineffectual but also showed them to be opponents of everything that had been commanded to them.

Finally, you banished into exile the bishops who refused to communicate with you as with an adulterer and usurper; and, at their command, you did not fear to install in their places, contrary to the canons, accomplices in your crime. To the present day you have not ceased to attack the Church of God with various persecutions. Thus you do not cease to afflict our brother and fellow bishop, the most holy patriarch Ignatius, with unheard-of punishments and horrible tortures; nor do you fail to seek relentlessly whatever means you can to destroy all whom you discover persisting honorably in truth and faith.

[Col. 1047A] Therefore, recognizing that in these and similar matters you are rising up against evangelical, apostolic, prophetic, and canonical institutions, we grieve; and, overcome by profound sorrow, we necessarily admonish, exhort, and beseech you by this present letter not to be deceived amid such glory, nor to lose eternal goods for the sake of these brief ones. Consider how few are all the things that bring pleasure here, however numerous they may appear. Reflect, I beg you, how manifold and how prolonged is the punishment of Gehenna, and fear falling into it; shudder from the depths of your being at acquiring it for yourself.

For, according to the Gospel, “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Mark VIII.)

We know that you are regarded as endowed with wisdom and enriched with knowledge. But hear what the prophet says about certain wise men: “They are wise,” he says, “to do evil, but they do not know how to do good” (Jer. IV). Concerning knowledge, the eminent Apostle says: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (I Cor. VIII). Therefore observe how little it benefits—and indeed how much it harms—those who possess wisdom not for doing good but for doing evil. Do not boast if you possess knowledge without love, for, as the Apostle testifies, the former puffs up, while the latter builds up (I Cor. IV). It is certainly absurd and improper for you to possess the virtue that puffs up while lacking that which builds up.

What love did you possess when you saw our brother and fellow minister Ignatius driven from his church, attacked, and subjected to conspiracies and plots? And not only did you fail to help him, although you could have done so as a man distinguished and honored in the secular world, but you also joined the factionalists, contended with those who were plotting against him, and took part with those who were devising various schemes of wickedness. Indeed, the whole sin of all these acts, which produces death, has been brought to completion particularly in you, since you became the author of all the transgressions committed against him.

For even if we call you a murderer, we do not lie, since the apostle John cries out and says: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (I John II). If, then, he who hates his brother is a murderer, how much more is he a murderer who not only hates his father but also, insofar as he is able, slaughters him? Moreover, if, like Ahab, he seizes and possesses what belongs to another, he must be called a murderer—and not merely some ordinary murderer, but also a parricide [Col. 1047D]. Ignatius was your father, and you were his son; and he ought to have been revered by you far more than a natural father, insofar as the spirit by which you mutually possess these relational names is to be preferred to the flesh.

Further, if we call you a viper, we are not mistaken, since you believed that you could prosper only after your parent had been destroyed. Now, if we assert that you are so like [read: Ham; the following confirms this excessively: HARD.], even in this we do not err. For you burst forth into such mockery and insult of your father that you cast him from the priestly chair and shamelessly exposed him to the mockery of mimes and theatrical performers.

Finally, if we compare you with the Jews, perhaps we do not depart very far from the truth [Col. 1048A]. For you not only set yourself above your teacher, contrary to the Gospel, but also, resisting God’s ordinance, turned your teeth, arms, and arrows against him, and made your tongue a sharp sword. You did not fear, like holy David, to lay your hand upon the Lord’s anointed; rather, like the leaders of robbers who possess no good and who slaughter their own king, you carefully contrived to rise up against your ruler by cunning plots.

Holy David laudably ordered such men to be handed over to death as wicked men and slayers of their prince, just as he did the man who announced that he had killed the Lord’s anointed—namely Saul (II Kings I).

Even if you had committed nothing blameworthy in these matters, nevertheless, since only the day before you had been a layman and had served in the secular world, you ought by no means to have reached so suddenly the summit of the highest priesthood. For neither could you have attained so quickly, according to the tradition of the approved Fathers, the perfection of monks, since Gelasius, Gregory, and Hadrian, great and truly holy prelates of the Roman see, repeatedly prohibited precisely what we have already written both to the most serene emperor and to you.

If you did not recognize the marks of holiness of these men as though they were unknown—for it would be enough to know from their writings what faith and zeal they possessed—you should at least have kept before your eyes the reverence due to Celestine and Leo, pontiffs of that same see. The whole Church spread throughout the world bows before their judgments, and Christian religion holds their teaching in the highest honor, as may be seen in the sacred third and fourth synods [Col. 1048C].

Indeed, not only faithful kings but also unbelievers, tyrants, and barbarian rulers, softened by no small measure of reverence or fear, eagerly embraced and followed the splendor of their virtues, the brilliance of their eloquence, the uprightness of their conduct, and the sweetness of their exhortations.

If you do not deny that they were great and holy—for you cannot deny it, since otherwise the whole world would fight on their behalf against the senseless—then you ought carefully to attend to them and reverently accept them in all the doctrines and disciplines of the Church. For if, in other matters of our religion, you yield to their assertions, but in those matters in which they oppose your promotion you disregard them, it is clear that you care less for the common salvation than for your private lot, and thus seek not the things of Jesus Christ but your own.

Either those trees were good and bore good fruit, or they were evil—which God forbid—and their fruit was evil. If they were good and their fruit was good, you ought to follow them as good men. For, as the Gospel testifies, “a good tree cannot bear evil fruit” (Matt. VII). But if you do not think rightly concerning them in agreement with the whole Church of Christ, you must prove and assert, with many witnesses drawn from the entire Church, how either they themselves or their fruits were evil. For you alone, persuading others to think contrary to this matter, will not be believed.

Now, if you say: “The things they preached or decreed are good, acceptable, and beneficial, but not all of them; some of these things were sweet, others bitter,” the apostle James answers you on their behalf, saying: “Does a spring pour forth sweet and bitter water from the same opening?” (James III). For, as he says again: “Nor can salt water make sweet water” (ibid.). The Holy Spirit, whose vessels these men were, cannot pour forth anything but sweetness through those whom he has filled.

Moreover, if you profess that all their decrees are indeed salutary, but that you have hitherto been ignorant of them, you will still certainly not be excusable. If the sins of ignorance did not exist, the Psalmist would never have prayed to the Lord concerning them, saying: “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance” (Ps. XXIV). He says again: “He did not wish to understand, so as to do good; he meditated iniquity upon his bed” [Col. 1049B] (Ps. XXXV). For by saying not “He did not understand,” but “He did not wish to understand, so as to do good,” he clearly showed that ignorance is often brought about by a purpose of the will.

Therefore, you will remove every excuse based on ignorance if you consider the fearful words of the Apostle, who says: “But if anyone is ignorant, he shall be ignored” (I Cor. XIV). For, as Pope Gregory the holy teaches, those who do not know the things that belong to the Lord are not known by the Lord.

But you say: “We did not receive these things in the law, and transgressors—who are more significantly called in Greek *παράνομοι* (*paranomoi*)—are only those who commit some wickedness against the law they have received, as the Apostle says: ‘Where there is no law, neither is there transgression’” (Rom. IV).

But hear and be afraid of what the same Apostle says again: “For as many as have sinned without the law shall also perish without the law” [Col. 1049C] (Rom. II). Otherwise you will have to admit that the nations, which did not receive the law, are excusable.

For my part, I would call all who act wickedly transgressors, relying on the authority of the Psalmist, who sings: “I have counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors” (Ps. CXVIII). By saying, “I have counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors,” he includes even the nations that did not receive the law. For although they did not receive the law given through Moses, they nevertheless received the law of nature; and if that law had not been corrupted, the Mosaic law would not have been given. It is precisely this natural law that we now appropriately demand from you, since you boast that you have in no way accepted the edicts of so many holy pontiffs.

Finally, if your conscience has searched the book of your heart, it will undoubtedly not deny that this law was given to you. There you will find written, in the voice of the law of nature, that no one wishes to be harmed by anyone and that no one wishes what belongs to him to be taken away entirely. Therefore the command is fittingly given: “What you do not want done to you, do not do to others” (Luke III); and the Lord says: “Whatever you want people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. VII).

Therefore you will not be able to deny that you received this law, since nature itself teaches it and each person’s own will continually makes it known. But if you deny that this law was given to you, you plainly demonstrate that you did receive the decrees of the prelates of the apostolic see. For what else do those decrees say than “What you do not want done to you, do not do to others,” when they command that someone who has only recently become a cleric not rule over clerics who have served through each successive term of service and spent their entire lives in the Lord’s camp?

What else, I ask, do they command than “Whatever you want people to do to you, do the same to them,” when they command that no one, by an excessively premature leap, seek to cross into another’s honor with immoderate ambition, or strive at his own pleasure to seize another’s rights?

Certainly, if you had served through each successive term of service in the Church of Constantinople, spent your whole life in the Lord’s camp, and someone from an earlier profession had, by an excessively premature leap, sought your honor, crossed over into it with immoderate ambition, and tried at his pleasure to seize what was yours, you would at once have burst into protest and brought accusations against him.

And because it is commanded: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property, nor anything that belongs to him” (Exod. X), and again, “What you do not want done to you, do not do to others” (Luke III), you would openly have demonstrated this to everyone by sufficient written evidence. Recalling most earnestly what John the Baptist commanded soldiers—not to extort anyone, not to bring false accusations, and to be content with their pay—you would have said:

“Do not extort me; do not bring false accusation against me. Rather, since you have hitherto been a soldier of the secular world, be content with your pay, for this is what the Lord’s forerunner says to you.” You would have cried out in a loud voice and perhaps wept with sobs:

“Do not covet the pay that belongs to them or the fruits of their labors; do not steal them away; do not think ill of me or of my fellow soldiers. Do not now seek, by a leap of ambition, to overtake all of us, already wearied by so many courses of time in the Lord’s various battles and already wasting away from so many sweats and vigils on behalf of his city. Do not, though you have not been chosen or advanced from our military service, seize command over us by such a leap.”

Since, therefore, you find in the sacred writings what the prelates of the apostolic see established—or rather, since you continually read it within yourself—do not continue to assert that you have not accepted their decrees. They establish nothing except what the law of nature, the Mosaic law, and the law of grace have commanded; and they have defined that whatever the holy Fathers established in the Council of Sardica must be observed in every respect.

Among those Fathers, that famous man Hosius was present, and Athanasius was found great, although we fear what you may say in dreaming: that the canons of that council are not found among you [Col. 1050D]. Many indications prove this to be far from the truth.

First, when Zacharias, who claimed to be a bishop, came to the apostolic see on behalf of Gregory of Syracuse and his colleagues, requesting that their judgment be renewed, he said that he and those who had sent him had followed these canons in their appeal.

Then, when we investigated the matter with the utmost care, we found these canons written in Greek—not only in new but also in old and authentic books, which are customarily regarded as more reliable—with the same meaning and number in which they are seen inserted among the other Latin canons. Indeed, they were defined by the prelates of nearly the whole world, and the same Greek copies show that all those prelates were fully satisfied with them.

How will you alone be able to assert that the Sardican canons are not found among you, when they were established and promulgated not only by men of the Latin language but also, together with others, by men of the Greek language? It is not credible that what was defined there was not translated by each of them into his own language.

Or how are the Sardican canons not found among you [Note: [Col. 1051D] The collection of canons is that of John of Antioch and consists of fifty titles. Justellus published it. HARD.], when they themselves are found among the fifty titles through which the harmony of the canons is arranged among you?

Now, if you have also thought that the customs and decrees of those distinguished Roman pontiffs concerning the prohibition against rashly advancing laymen to ecclesiastical grades should be despised [possibly: “if you have also thought that the canons, together with the customs ...”; HARD.], at least you should have consented to listen to Paul the Apostle, teacher of the nations, and should have observed how the holy Fathers assembled at the Council of Sardica agreed with him on this point.

For we say boldly and profess truthfully that whoever has not received the Council of Sardica has not received the Apostle Paul. What did the Council of Sardica establish—leaving other matters aside—when it says:

“If perhaps a rich man, a scholar from the forum, or someone from secular administration is requested as a bishop, he shall not be ordained beforehand unless he has first served in the ministry of lector and in the office of deacon or presbyter; and thus, through each grade, if he is worthy, let him ascend to the summit of the episcopate. For through these promotions, which will necessarily extend over a considerable period, it can be tested with what faith, moderation, gravity, and modesty he is endowed; and, if he has been proved worthy, let him be honored with the divine priesthood. For it is neither fitting nor permitted by reason or discipline that a neophyte be rashly and lightly ordained bishop, presbyter, or deacon, especially since the blessed Apostle, the teacher of the nations, appears to have proclaimed and prohibited that this should happen. Rather, let those whose life has been examined over a long period and whose merits have been proved be ordained—except that the Apostle commands his beloved disciple: ‘Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the sins of others’ (I Tim. V). And concerning deacons: ‘Let these also be tested, and then let them minister’ (I Tim. III).”

Who could find greater agreement than that between these words of the Apostle and those of the council mentioned above? What else is a “neophyte” than someone who is promoted before maturity of age, before the time of examination, before the merit of labor, before experience of discipline, indeed before the display of submission, and who seeks the height of authority instead?

Now, if the Apostle commanded that deacons be tested and then minister, with how great a fire must a learned bishop be tested over long periods of time through the practice of every virtue, and examined like gold in the furnace of various temptations? Only then, once purified and [possibly: “with all disgraceful conduct removed, and his morals and virtues made manifest”; HARD.] cleansed of all bad habits, should he be advanced to the summit of authority.

Know, then, that we have written these things to you in summary concerning your unlawful promotion.

But you, who are also a witness to your own thoughts, will be able more easily to know how unlawfully you were advanced. Therefore cease henceforth to hold a place seized from another; do not become a stumbling block of iniquity to the house of Israel, and do not continue to lead the blind into error.

Have you not, to omit many other points, become a stumbling block to the house of Israel, since by abandoning Ignatius you compelled so great a people of the Lord to act contrary to its own subscription or profession? Did you not provide it with leadership into error when you craftily persuaded it to abandon its shepherd faithlessly and follow you, to whom nothing belonging to the sheep pertained?

Indeed, you would already bear the weight of so great a crime if you carefully listened to the judgment of truth, which says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea” (Matt. XVIII).

The millstone expresses the circuit and labor of secular life, while the depth of the sea signifies final condemnation. It would therefore have been better for you to have been bound for death under an outward appearance by the deeds of secular life than, by seeking sacred offices and scandalizing not merely one but many who believe in the Lord, together with their teacher, father, and shepherd, to show yourself as one whom the others could imitate in guilt [Col. 1052C].

For plainly, if you alone had fallen, the punishment of hell would have afflicted you in some way more tolerably. Flee, therefore, the authority wickedly usurped; avoid ruling, since you are recognized as continually harming innumerable people.

You have read that Jesus—who is certainly the true king—when he realized that they were about to come and seize him and make him king, fled (John VI). For who could have ruled over all without guilt more than he who would rule those whom he himself had created? Yet because he appeared in the flesh for this purpose—not only to redeem us through his passion but also to teach us through his way of life, offering himself as an example to those who follow him—he refused to become king.

When he willingly came to the gibbet of the cross, he fled the glory of offered eminence and desired the punishment of a shameful death, so that his members might learn to flee the world’s favors, not to fear its terrors, to love adversity for the sake of truth, and to avoid prosperity by fearing it.

Therefore, at last, listen to us. If you listen to us, you will not find us wholly inflexible toward you or excessively hard in showing mercy. For, as Leo the Great, prelate of the apostolic see, writes to the blessed Flavian (Letter XII, at the end): “Our Lord, the true and good shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep and who came to save human souls, not to destroy them” (John X), “wishes us to be imitators of his compassion, so that justice may restrain sinners, but mercy may not reject those who have converted” [Col. 1053A].

Accordingly, for all the things that we have recalled throughout the text of this letter as having been perpetrated by you against all the divine commands, by the authority of almighty God, of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul, and of all the saints together, as well as of the venerable six universal councils, and also by the judgment of the Holy Spirit through us, you are alienated from every priestly honor and title—which we declare with groaning—and completely stripped of every clerical office.

Thus, if after learning of this decree—which we believe has been drawn from divine inspiration and has doubtless been promulgated with the unanimity and concord of the holy synod—you attempt to preside on the throne of Constantinople, and impede our aforesaid venerable fellow bishop Ignatius so that he cannot govern without disturbance the Church entrusted to him [Col. 1053B], or if you dare thereafter to touch anything belonging to the sacred ministry in the manner of a priest, then, in accordance with the preceding custom—which is contrary to the canons—you shall in no way be permitted to retain hope of communion or a place for satisfaction. Rather, bound by the chains of anathema, together with those who communicate with you and your supporters, and subject forever to the judgment and sentence of God through our mediation, you shall receive the sacred body and blood of the Lord Jesus Christ only when the danger of death is near.

Let everyone, on learning these things, understand that no one should henceforth dare, with reckless presumption, to rush unexpectedly from the ranks of the laity into the Lord’s camp, and, out of love of authority, wish to be a leader before completing the service of a recruit, or attempt to teach before learning, as we have often discovered was presumed in that same Church of Constantinople.

And again, let no one, despising the clerics—of whom there is a great multitude in so large a city—suddenly seize the rule of another sheepfold of Christ from outside, without the labor by which those clerics have, as it were, from their very cradles, toiled in Christ’s Church and continually offered the services of their devotion to the Lord. Let no outsider strive to tear apart those whom he does not recognize as his own, and let the Lord’s flock not begin to despise him as entirely foreign and unexpected—especially when it sees that its own accumulated services have gained him no merits and that he is consuming the fruits of labors belonging to others.

Given on the Ides of November, in the fifteenth indiction.

(Year 866.) C. TO BARDAS THE CAESAR. [Col. 1053D] He grieves that he has been driven from the hope he had placed in Bardas because of the many things he had heard from the beginning about his piety; he urges him to come to his senses, to plead Ignatius’s case before the emperor, and to support the envoys of the apostolic see.

[In Mansi, same place.]

NICOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, the illustrious Caesar BARDAS.

[Cols. 1054A–1057D.] After the gifts of almighty God began to abound in you with wondrous success, and the marks of those gifts began most gloriously to shine far and wide, while also their fragrant reputation increasingly and commendably reached the hearing of our ears, we too began thereafter to give immense thanks to the same Lord, the giver of all gifts. We earnestly implored him to make these gifts increase in you—he who, because of the greatness of his piety and the abundance of his ineffable mercy, raised your lofty eminence so much higher, wishing through you to raise up the oppressed, restrain the oppressors, exalt those who exalt his Church, and humble those who humble her.

For he placed you in his Church like a cedar, so that the afflicted might find refreshment beneath your shade, and the desolate, torn by various hardships, might find protection. After this, however, we heard that in the city of Constantinople there were dissensions, disputes, outcries, conspiracies, plots, factions, hostilities, enmities, and other troubles or dangers, so that we now believe those times to be approaching which the Apostle foretold would arise in the last days, and that all the signs which our Redeemer declared would precede the end of the world seem to be pressing upon us.

What, then, is more wicked—or rather, more dangerous—than for a prelate to be driven from his see by secular power alone, before a just and canonical hearing, and to be deprived of the church divinely entrusted to him, reinforced by the agreement and subscription of the provincial priests and by the communion of his fellow patriarchs? And what is more wicked or dangerous than for him who is an interpreter between God and humanity to be removed from the intercession of the peoples without any fault being demonstrated, merely at the whim of one person or another?

What, I ask, is more wicked or dangerous than for disciples to lay hands upon their teacher? For sons, imitating vipers, to kill their own parent—as far as lies within them? To curse him by whom they were blessed? To cast him out, by whom they were advanced to the honor of their several ranks?

What, moreover, is more presumptuous than for one who has been expelled to attempt to expel another, or for one who has been removed to attempt to remove another, or for one who has been bound to attempt to bind another? What could be done more improperly, disorderly, and confusedly than, after entirely despising and rejecting so great a multitude of Constantinopolitan clerics—as though the whole body had been stained by violation of the faith, weakened by ignorance and folly, or entangled in various crimes—to set a layman over it, introduce an outsider into it, and, contrary to the sacred canons—or rather, against the Apostle—to ordain a neophyte over it?

Now, if you say that a neophyte means one newly planted in the faith, we reply that this is not what the word signifies for us. For in the word *neophyte* nothing relating to faith is expressed.

But you say: “This is how our holy Fathers interpret it, namely, that a neophyte is to be understood as one newly planted in the faith.” We reply that, since it is known that nothing concerning faith is expressed in the formation of this word, a neophyte may be called not only one newly inserted into the faith, but also one newly entered into the clerical service. Thus Saint Pope Gregory, and your intercessor before God, the apostle of the English people—who clearly understood the force of this word and perhaps carefully investigated those Fathers whom you mention—writes, among other things:

“Just as at that time a neophyte was called one who had been planted at the beginning in the way of life of the holy faith, so now a neophyte must be regarded as one who, suddenly planted in the religious habit, has crept in to seek sacred honors.”

What, again, is more pernicious than to grant anyone from among the schismatics authority within the Lord’s enclosure; to confer consecration through those who have been condemned; to raise to the priesthood through the deposed; to steal the place of one who is alive; to violate the bride of Christ entrusted to another; to plunge many into apostasy; to drive them into unbelief; to turn not a few away from their profession or subscription; to obtain the Church through external powers; and thus to climb into the Lord’s fold not through the door, but from the opposite side and by another way, and to creep into it like a thief, robber, or ravening wolf—and first to kill the shepherd, then to slaughter some of the sheep, scatter others, crush them, strip them, tear them apart, and destroy them by various means and devices?

Finally, what, we ask, is more horrifying and detestable than to violate the writings of the Lord, of the holy Fathers, and of the apostolic see, sent for religion, discipline, and correction; to conceal some of them from the faithful, defraud them of others, and cunningly corrupt certain passages by omission, alteration, and addition?

And what is more detestable than to turn the envoys of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, away by various devices from those entrusted to them, and drag them to the *praecessio* (“precedence”) [variant: *processio* (“procession”)], which was being conducted by schismatics, excommunicates, and condemned persons; to subject them to various hardships, despite their embassy—which ought to have been treated even according to the custom of the Gentiles—and finally, as an insult to blessed Peter, from whose see they had departed, not only to make them return ineffective, but even to portray them as opponents of everything that had been commanded?

Hearing that these things, and others like them and even more numerous, were being perpetrated in the city of Constantinople or in the cities adjoining it, we were filled with immense grief and disturbed by extreme anxiety. But because rumor reports that you are the author of them all, we are afflicted by unbearable anguish of mind and hemmed in on every side by sorrows. Therefore, with Jeremiah, we are moved to break into lamentation, to devote ourselves sorrowfully to mourning, and to cry out tearfully:

“Who will give water to my head, or a fountain of tears to my eyes” (Jeremiah 9), “that I may mourn and lament such a great and such a terrible calamity, such a great and such a terrible loss?”

For our hope has been frustrated; our confidence has deceived us. O incomparable loss! O destruction that must somehow be destroyed only through you, Lord Jesus! The gifts of God, once bestowed upon you, have been turned into armor against his Church, and what he granted for the salvation of many has been changed into the evident ruin of many.

But return, my son; return, most pious Caesar; return. For our merciful Lord will mercifully embrace you, when you return, with the outstretched arms of his kindness. He will not be so indignant at the injury you have inflicted upon his Church as he will rejoice if you strive to help the person whom you have injured against the Church.

Let your piety, therefore, extend a hand to the Church of Constantinople, and do not allow her to remain any longer deprived of her own ruler, walking in mourning and lamentation. May our Lord Jesus Christ always find the gifts of virtue that he has bestowed upon you prepared not against him, but for him and for his holy Church. May he rejoice that you have been improved by his benefits, and find you giving thanks continually, at every hour and moment.

Moreover, receive and treat the envoys whom we have sent to Constantinople in the name of the Lord—namely, Donatus, the most reverend and holy bishop of the holy Church of Ostia; and Leo, a religious and venerable priest of the holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Lawrence, the martyr of Christ, which is called that of Damasus; and Marinus, deacon of our apostolic see—as willingly and kindly as orthodox rulers are often reported, in many writings, to have received and treated the envoys of blessed Peter the Apostle.

Indeed, all those who have thought that envoys of the churches may be attacked with any insults are shown to surpass even the impiety of pagans. Among them, even if an embassy itself is perhaps not accepted, the person of the envoy is always considered inviolable, especially since the embassy of those mentioned above is concerned with nothing except what belongs to peace and seeks modestly to recommend only what justice loves.

That is, once the adulterer has been removed from the Church of Constantinople, she should be restored to her own bishop. And if anything should perhaps be brought against him once he has been restored, let it be heard and judged according to due order: namely, let the inferior be judged by the superior, and let him not be subjected to the judgment of lesser persons, which is contrary to all right.

What courage, moreover, will you display if you direct the whole weight of your indignation against two or three persons, and deem the feet of those who proclaim peace and proclaim good things fit only to be trampled or crushed? But take care—for the feet of that Head are being trampled which once cried out from heaven on their behalf when persecution was being inflicted upon him—lest you bind the word or conceal our embassy. For, as the Apostle says:

“Neither is the word of God bound, nor can the truth be concealed in any way” (1 Timothy 2).

It also says:

“Nothing is covered that will not be revealed, and nothing hidden that will not be known” (Luke 12).

If hiding the talent received in the earth deserves the ultimate condemnation, with what punishment must one be punished who takes away and hides another person’s talent when that person wishes to multiply it for his Lord’s profit—or who is not afraid even to defraud him of it?

You certainly cannot claim any excuse concerning the reception of the talent. You received no small gift of talent even before you attained the imperial insignia: namely, access to the Augustus through familiarity, and the easiest favor in obtaining whatever you wished.

If, therefore, you have said nothing to him on behalf of the Church, desolate through the loss of her own ruler; if you have not piously taken care to plead for those who, on behalf of our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius the patriarch, have been rejected, exiled, or oppressed, you will certainly have to render an account for retaining the talent.

Since your magnificence possesses with the Augustus the talent of obtaining what calls for condemnation, let it fear for the retention of that talent—unless [or: if not; the manuscript reading is uncertain] it intervenes urgently, using its influence with him to restore the former prelate of the Church of Constantinople or to rescue those who have been grievously oppressed.

This is especially so because, by the gift of divine grace, your eminence has not only obtained from the Augustus the power to secure what you wish, but through the imperial excellence you have acquired, you can yourself grant what you request and bestow what will profit you unto eternal gain. For the coming Judge will demand from each of us as much as he has given.

Therefore, dearest one, we must greatly fear, and dread in every way, what Wisdom says when it solemnly warns the rulers of the world:

“Learn, judges of the ends of the earth; give ear, you who rule multitudes and take pride in crowds of nations. For power has been given to you by the Lord, and sovereignty by the Most High, who will examine your works and scrutinize your thoughts. For though you were ministers of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly, nor keep the law of justice, nor walk according to God’s will. Terribly and swiftly he will appear to you, for a strict judgment awaits those who rule. The lowly may be pardoned, but the powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wisdom 6).

Let your piety diligently consider and ponder these words, O Caesar, and tremble; for, according to the Apostle, “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10). Therefore listen to our counsel, and hasten to correct by prompt satisfaction whatever you recall having done against our brother and fellow minister Ignatius, or against his associates or communicants. Restore with impartial care to their former condition all that has been destroyed through you.

You will easily accomplish all these things, as we believe, with the Lord’s help, if your tranquillity shows the envoys of Saint Peter the honor due to them in receiving and hearing them.

God is my witness how I long for you in the heart of Christ (Philippians 1). For this reason above all I make this request: that I may fulfill my ministry; that the condition and order of the Church may be restored; and that, by the Lord’s favor, the glory of your magnificence may be led from corruptible prosperity to incorruption, from mortal life to immortality, from an earthly summit to a heavenly height, and from temporary and quickly fading splendor to everlasting and enduring blessedness, and may enjoy the divine vision with all the saints and chosen angels.

Given on the Ides of November, in the fifteenth indiction.

## (Year 866.) CI. TO IGNATIUS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE

[Cols. 1058B–1061C.]

He informs Ignatius of everything that was done in his case after the return of the envoys Zacharias and Rhadoaldus, and how Photius was deposed and anathematized in the council together with his followers, while Ignatius himself, along with his supporters, was restored.

[In Mansi, same place.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend and holy brother and fellow minister, Ignatius, patriarch of Constantinople.

My dearest brother, it cannot be said with what griefs, or with what anxieties, we are afflicted on account of the magnitude of the tribulations and persecutions inflicted upon you, nor with what labors and struggles, summoned by fraternal love, we continually and unceasingly involve ourselves. For we take your cause to heart, and we bear the burdens of the whole Church.

Indeed, when we consider the ministry that we have received—divinely transmitted to us through blessed Peter the Apostle—we have no freedom to remain silent concerning our brothers, whom we recognize as requiring greater concern than all others in Christian devotion and in the correction of the churches, both because of their honor and because of their burden. We bear the burdens of all who are oppressed; rather, the holy Apostle Peter bears these burdens in us, and, as we trust, protects and guards in every respect the heirs of his administration.

We make known to your affection, in these words, what we have decreed concerning you, possessing the authority of the apostolic see and vindicating its privileges. For in our eyes you have always been what you received from the gift of almighty God to be—not what you are thought not to be through human will.

Therefore, after our envoys—namely, Rhadoaldus and Zacharias, formerly bishops—returned, having been sent to Constantinople solely to investigate the cause of your removal from the see of Constantinople, among the matters that they were commanded by us to conduct concerning the sacred images, and after we learned both from their report and from the writings brought to us by Leo, the imperial secretary, that they themselves had also issued a sentence against you, we were crushed by grief and anguish of mind as great as the opposition between their actions and everything that had been commanded to them; as great as the extent to which they seemed to have established what we believed would be utterly annulled; and as great as the extent to which it had been stealthily obtained and everyone persuaded that we had given our consent to such proceedings.

Accordingly, while the imperial envoy—that is, Leo—was present before us, we convened the entire Church that is with us and declared before him, as we also declare now, that we had never sent anyone for your deposition and the confirmation of Photius, and that we had never consented, nor would ever consent, to your deposition or to the advancement of Photius.

Having said this repeatedly and proclaimed it openly, and having inserted it in this form into the letters of our apostolate, we delivered these letters to the aforesaid Leo, the imperial secretary, to be conveyed by decree to the most excellent Emperor Michael and to Photius.

Then we began to consider and ponder how we might remove far from the Church of Christ, over which we preside by divine appointment, this sinister suspicion—that at least in this matter some slight occasion for mockery might arise—and how we might make our position clear.

Accordingly, when a gathering of the most holy bishops of many western provinces had been convened and a holy synod assembled in the Church of God, in which blessed Peter rests, first, with the holy synod joining us in judgment, Zacharias received the sentence of deposition and excommunication. The judgment against Rhadoaldus, his associate, was postponed because of his absence. [Note: The passage is corrupt.] Nevertheless, he too was similarly deposed, deprived of communion, and did not escape to the end.

Furthermore, we deposed Photius—or rather, God deposed him—as a neophyte, an intruder, and an adulterer; and we completely stripped him of every priestly honor, of the clerical office, and of the name of patriarch. If, after learning of this sanction of ours, he presided on the throne of Constantinople, or prevented you from taking possession of the Church, or dared to touch anything belonging to the sacred ministry in the manner of a priest, we deprived him altogether of communion and of any place of satisfaction.

Together with his communicants and supporters, we likewise anathematized Gregory, who, in contempt of God, presides over the Church of Syracuse, because he had separated himself from your communion, irregularly ordained Photius, and touched the sacred ministry after his deposition. We decreed and established that he was to be deprived of every priestly rank, so that if thereafter he presumed to minister in the sacred office in the manner of a priest, let him be anathema.

And if he raised disturbances against you—or should raise them—or turned the faithful away from your communion, let him be anathema; and let all who communicate with him be cast out of the Church. Let them too be anathema.

As for those whom Photius ordained, since it is clear that in everything they shared communion with the one who consecrated them, we stripped them of every clerical office.

But you, by the authority of the supreme Judge, our Lord Jesus Christ, we have proclaimed never to have been, and not to be, deposed or anathematized, since you were driven from the Church by imperial power without any canonical authority, and since, as one who cannot be bound by those who were themselves bound, you could not have been held by any bond. Nor ought you to have suffered any diminution of your honor at the hands of those who possessed neither the power to judge you nor authority from the apostolic see.

Therefore, after removing every bond of anathema from you by the power divinely conferred by God’s voice upon blessed Peter, and by the authority of the sacred canons, we restore and confirm you in your former dignity, see, rank, patriarchate, former episcopal insignia, and offices.

Accordingly, whoever failed in every respect to obey this decree, or separated himself from your communion, or thereafter issued any judgment against you without the consent of the apostolic see—if he were a cleric, he would be alienated from every clerical office before God and humanity.

But if the person who attempted to oppose our constitution, whoever he might be, were a layman—if he did not permit you to recover your see and all your former dignity, or if, after your restoration, he again attempted to drive you out, or through his speech inflicted any trouble upon you [the text reads “through your speech”; read “upon you”]—let him be deprived of every paternal blessing, punished with the curse of Canaan, son of Ham, who did not cover his father’s shame but mocked him, and struck with eternal punishment, along with parricides, when the Lord judges. Let him be released from the bonds of anathema only after he has repented completely.

As for those bishops or clerics of any order who, after your deposition—which ought never to have been pronounced—were exiled, deprived of their ministry or rank, or stripped of their offices, we decree that, once the exile has been ended, they are to recover their own churches and ranks. If anyone presumes to oppose this decree of ours and prevents or should prevent them from recovering their churches or ranks, let him be anathema until he obeys.

Concerning those who, perhaps, were accused by others from among this list, we have decreed that they are first to recover their own churches and rank, but are then to be judged only by the Roman pontiff of the apostolic see. If they should be said to have done anything contrary to rule, we have established that their judgment is reserved to our decree, in accordance with what the sacred canons prescribe.

These, dearest brother, are the things that, together with our brothers and fellow priests of the various western provinces, we have done and established in the venerable synod mentioned above, following the authority of our predecessors. We have taken care to make them known to your blessedness so that you may know our intention concerning the affair of your fraternity, and so that no one may be able to advise you otherwise concerning what has been done.

Now we exhort you, raised up by the hope that is in God, not to fail in your tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope; and hope does not disappoint (Romans 5).

Although we are far away, when we recognized the wickedness of those persecuting you, we too, burning with no small fire of fraternal concern, are consumed by a great flame. Yet among the Churches of God, which everywhere are understood as belonging to the one bridal chamber of Christ, nothing is distant and nothing is regarded as foreign.

Therefore, dearest brother, may your consolation come from God, who always gives strength to those who trust in him. You have the examples of the saints, who once sowed in tears but will reap in joy in the future. Our Lord does not love a servant unless he has been tested by trials; he continually exercises Christian souls in the arena of circumstances.

Our own people have made war upon us—if indeed they are to be called our own—whom we perceive to have crossed over to the enemy after breaking their covenant. No temporal tribulation exists if the eternal reward is before one’s eyes, since nothing can rightly be preferred to it.

Our hymn-singer cries out: “Though armies encamp against him, he must have no fear, through hope in his illumination” (Psalm 26).

We therefore ask you to bear patiently whatever the enemy has inflicted. He has imposed injuries, insults, and exiles. He endured these things in his own person who is recognized to have endured spitting, scourging, and death for us. Let Stephen, the first martyr of Christ, be a model of patience and steadfastness for you.

It would be tedious to proceed through each of those who purchased life either by dying or by confessing. Yet you, who have been expelled from the Church, have the example of blessed Athanasius, of revered memory, the most prudent priest of the Church of Alexandria. Who could not be consoled by his endurance? Who could not be given hope by his *exspectata* (“awaited”) [variant: *inexspectata* (“unexpected”)] return? He was expelled while Arius persecuted him, but recalled while the Lord advanced his cause.

He suffered imprisonment and hardships. Nor is it surprising that an apostolic man suffered what the Apostle boasts of having endured. Driven away from there, he was strengthened in our regions and found the rest of communion in this see, from which aid is always given to Catholics. Nevertheless, he felt weariness amid tribulations—the man who became a confessor during persecution.

Therefore you ought not to grieve over the temporal expulsion inflicted upon you, because, as we believe, you have not fallen from God. Let us therefore not fear Photius, lest we be cast out of the land [possibly: kingdom] of the living. That is ours; that is eternal. What passes away is not ours; rather, those things are truly ours which the most certain hope promises.

These are the things, as the Apostle says, “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—things that God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2).

Given on the Ides of November, in the fifteenth indiction.

## (Year 866.) CII. TO THE AUGUSTA THEODORA

[Cols. 1061D–1063A.]

He exhorts the Augusta, whom he adorns with many praises, to patience and to placing her hope in God. He shows that he is devoting all his efforts to the restoration of Ignatius.

[In Mansi, same place.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved daughter Theodora, formerly joined to an earthly emperor but now spiritually joined to the heavenly one.

As we carefully and attentively recall your virtues—by which in these days you have appeared inferior to none of the Augustas who preceded you, and by which, especially in the cause of piety, you have been found inferior to none of them—we do not cease to give immense thanks to almighty God, by whose gift you received them, and to bless his holy name. We continually recount, in the conversations of the faithful, the praises of your pious endeavors, so that those who hear them may imitate you.

For even while your imperial husband, the ruler, was alive and held opinions contrary to the laws of the Church, you did not fear to think soundly and defend what was right. You, I say, persevering in the orthodox religion, taught your only son to set out upon the path not of an earthly father, but of the heavenly one.

Who would be sufficient to recount the marks of your character and the brave deeds of your corrections? When you alone ruled, with the Lord’s cooperation, you protected the Lord’s Church not only from the visible enemy, but also—nor were you at all weaker in this than a man—from the invisible enemy, that is, error. You drove the cloud of perverse doctrines from the face of the Church as a ray of the sun.

The heretics perceived in you a manly heart and, astonished by your unconquerable strength, were uncertain whether you were a woman. Why was this, except that you followed the teachings of the apostolic see and embraced the instructions of the bishop of Constantinople, with whom the Roman Church was in communion?

For devoted sons thus honor paternal affection and are found in no respect ungrateful toward their parents. But what do enemies do? They seize, expel, and—what more need be said?—subject them to every dishonor.

Examples of patience by which you may learn to despise such things and to seek those that belong to the eternal kingdom are abundant, O most Christian daughter. The lawgiver Moses and holy Aaron of the Lord endured murmuring, harsh insults, and rebellion from those whom they carried in their bosoms like sons and loved so greatly that, when the Lord wished to destroy them and make Moses into a great nation, he said:

“Either forgive them this guilt, or erase me from the book that you have written” (Exodus 32).

Thus blessed Samuel is driven from his rule by those to whom he had rendered many benefits. Thus the prophet Zechariah is attacked with stones by the man whose father had secured the kingdom for him and whom Zechariah himself was showing the way of salvation.

But why should we linger longer over the human race, when our Lord Jesus Christ himself, the mediator between God and humanity, endured insults, spitting, scourging, and the death of the cross at the hands of those for whom he had illuminated the blind, restored many sick people to their former health, and raised the dead?

Alas, we have arrived at those dangerous times which blessed Paul the Apostle foretold when he wrote:

“In the last times dangerous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves and greedy” (2 Timothy 3).

There he also added:

“Disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace.”

Indeed, we have arrived at those mournful and lamentable days in which, as the Lord also says in the Gospel:

“Brother will hand brother over to death, and children will rise against their parents” (Mark 13).

But what do the enemies who do these things and rage against others accomplish? While they wish to harm, they benefit; while they attempt to injure, they render the greatest service. They tyrannically deprive their victims of temporal rule, but—though unwillingly—they grant eternal dominion. They take away earthly glory, but confer heavenly blessedness.

For their weapon of iniquity is changed into an instrument of equity, and the arms of destruction or tyranny are turned into instruments of salvation and piety. However fiercely rivals rage and enemies go mad, nevertheless for those who love God all things work together for good (Romans 8), because “there is no wisdom, no knowledge, and no counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs 21).

Therefore, dearest daughter, be strong in the Lord and in the power of his might, and in adversity seek the Lord alone as your refuge. Set your feet upon the rock on which the Lord principally chose to build his Church, and from the firmness of communion with him—just as you have not been alienated until now—do not allow yourself to be alienated by any stormy winds until the end.

As for us, who are unworthy vicars of that same Lord, do not for a moment believe that we shall be found negligent or inactive, whether concerning the condition of the Church of Constantinople or concerning the recovery of our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius, in accordance with the ministry entrusted to us.

How matters stand with you and with your beloved daughters, or whether anything is troubling your heart, please inform us through our present envoys, whom we ask you to support when circumstances require, with a faithful mind and an unwavering conscience.

Given on the Ides of November, in the fifteenth indiction.

## (Year 886.) CIII. TO THE AUGUSTA EUDOXIA

[Col. 1063B.]

He asks her to act on behalf of Ignatius with the emperor.

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter Eudoxia, the glorious Augusta [in the Vatican manuscript, “glorious” is absent].

Nothing is more fitting in royal exaltation than the love of justice, nothing more honorable in feminine weakness than fortitude of mind. What, indeed, is more praiseworthy or stronger than for a woman to put on a manly breast and, moreover, to surpass the efforts of men in a cause of piety?

Therefore, at the beginning of our letter, now addressing Your Highness for the first time in writing, we exhort you and earnestly [Col. 1063C] beseech you to love almighty God with the affection that is fitting and with the worship that is appropriate; and to watch over the state of His Church with particular concern. Thus, with the utmost persistence, procure from our most beloved son, Michael, the most tranquil emperor, protected by God, your husband—and, forgetting feminine weakness, strive to act manfully—that he restore the same Church, with his permission and favor, to our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius, once the invader of the Church of Constantinople, an adulterer and a neophyte, Photius, has been removed. For that venerable prelate was despoiled and deprived contrary to every rule and beyond all proper order.

Let Your Empire know, moreover, that for this very matter we have sent envoys and letters of our apostolate to our most desirable son, the pious Augustus, [Col. 1063D] preserved by God. Joining your piety to theirs, we ask that you assist their embassy and support them in everything as much as you inwardly desire blessed Peter the Apostle, the keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, always to be favorably present to your highness.

For Christ our God did not make your nobility the partner of your husband’s imperial power without reason, nor did He appoint you for any purpose other than that you should assist His Church, watch over its condition, help its servants, console those who mourn, raise up the oppressed [Col. 1064A] and broken, recall the expelled and exiled, and restore everything corrupted, confused, disordered, and destroyed to its former vigor. He also appointed you so that, as a strong woman and distinguished helper, you might offer assistance to your husband, who attends to many matters and arranges innumerable affairs, and might extend, as it were, a hand of consolation to him, lest amid so many variations he fall from the summit of justice.

Thus, at the beginning of the creation of humankind, the Lord granted the first-formed man a woman as a helper corresponding to him (Gen. I), lest a solitary man, deprived perhaps of another’s counsel, should fall more easily to the depths and rise again with greater difficulty after his fall, according to what is written: “Woe to the solitary, because when he falls he has no one to lift him up” (Eccles. IV). Yet they themselves turned the divine dispensation to the contrary and insolently abused the dignity [Col. 1064B] of free will and its most abundant power.

Now, if you offer prosperous or Church-friendly counsel to your colleague who cooperates with you; if you persuade him to repel the adulterer and restore the legitimate bishop of the Church of Constantinople; if you obtain from him that he return to its former order those things which, occupied and intent upon so many matters, he has jointly carried out less rightly—what shall we call you except his salutary assistance, and how shall we proclaim your companionship except as praiseworthy?

Believe us: in these times, the rejection of the venerable Ignatius, or the advancement of the violator Photius, has harmed your empire no less than Eve’s suggestion harmed humanity. But if, through your salutary name [perhaps: undertaking] or struggle, those things which have been cunningly advised or suggested to our most beloved son [Col. 1064C] are dissolved, and those measures which we have decreed for the common salvation are fulfilled, then throughout the sphere of your empire, as if through another Eve—that is, an obedient one—all that has been destroyed will be restored.

For that ancient serpent and old adversary never ceases to trouble the Lord’s Church, which is composed of both sexes, with various devices. Hence the Apostle, mindful of Eve’s seduction, strongly feared lest the minds of some should be corrupted from the chastity of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1063D] That is, “lest they should fall.” But there is a suspicion that something is missing; this will become clear from the eleventh chapter of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians. See that passage.]

Therefore, whenever he attempts through his vessels—that is, through evil workers—to lie in wait for your heel, that is, for the perfection of your good work, you must immediately crush his head: that is, at the very beginning, reduce to nothing the serpent’s wicked suggestions, once detected, and the poisonous [Col. 1064D] counsels of his ministers, as though trampling them underfoot. The heel is the extremity of the body, and by it consummated virtue is not inappropriately expressed.

For God established these enmities between the serpent and the woman so that the snake would be crushed by the woman whom it had deceived, not after any interval of time but immediately, at the very moment of its poisonous suggestion, and would not be granted prolonged opportunity to scatter its poisons—poisons that might creep like cancer and penetrate as far as the heart.

Your most excellent wisdom, we believe, has already understood what we mean. We do not wish you to be deceived by anyone; [Col. 1065A] we do not wish you to be overthrown from the charity of Christ by any devices; we do not wish you to be stirred against the Church of God by the viperous counsels of anyone. Rather, we desire and hope, and with the greatest earnestness implore your pious highness, that, persevering in the integrity of faith and on the path of righteousness among God’s people, which is the Church, like that holy queen Esther, you kindle your husband toward the fear and love of God and prudently inflame him toward the recovery of the holy Church of Constantinople. Thus, by guarding himself from communion with Photius—the adulterer, neophyte, and invader, and therefore condemned and anathematized—he may correct whatever harm he has inflicted upon our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius, and, by allowing Ignatius to govern the Church entrusted to him, may correct it; may provide for his own salvation and [Col. 1065B] that of his empire; and may make the Lord favorable to himself and to all his people.

We have no doubt that, with the power of the supreme King, in whose hand are the hearts of kings, you can obtain this; and we judge in every respect that, if there is willingness, you can have no excuse based on impossibility. For, according to the Apostle, “through a faithful woman even an unbelieving husband will be saved” (I Cor. VII). When rather [read: “When rather, etc., is it recognized?”] can a husband be saved through a most faithful woman—a husband who, thanks be to God, is known not merely to be no unbeliever, far from it, but to be most Christian and most religious?

Lay aside, therefore, all feminine weakness, and strive to obtain from him those things which are pious and which accord with the holy Church. Do not fail [Col. 1065C] or delay to act through unceasing suggestions and supplications with him, so that he may obey our prayers and hear our petitions as those of his spiritual father; and, girded as though with manly courage, contend with continual steadfastness.

For, as we have stated above, the Lord did not make you the partner of your husband’s empire without reason. If you do not labor lawfully for his people, you will unquestionably have to render a strict account at the strict divine judgment. Approach, then, and clothe yourselves with strength; undertake the struggle for the condition and order of the Church of God and for the raising up of the afflicted and oppressed. Imitate the blessed queen Esther mentioned above, who gave her life even unto death for God’s people and granted no respite to her struggle until she had delivered him [perhaps: “delivered [him] [Col. 1065D] from ruin.” HARD.]. Her praiseworthy uncle Mordecai, as he once urged her—and as we now urge you—had said to her, among other things:

“Do not think that you alone will save your life because you are in the king’s house, above all the Jews. For if you are silent now, the Jews will be delivered by another opportunity, but you and your father’s house will perish. And who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for this reason, that you might be prepared for such a time?” (Esth. IV.)

You can learn how devoted the pious empresses, whom we wish you to imitate, were to the see of the blessed prince of the apostles, Peter; how they honored it above all other sees; and how they inspired the most exalted rulers with reverence for the Roman pontiff [Col. 1066A] from the letter of Galla Placidia, which she wrote to the Augustus Theodosius. We mention only this one because we wish to avoid exceeding the limits of epistolary expression. She says:

“It is no small injury, in view of what has been done, that the faith which has been regularly preserved for so many ages, under our most sacred father Constantine, who was the first Christian to shine in the imperial office [the text is apparently corrupt: perhaps ‘who recently shone as the first Christian in the empire,’ HARD.], should now have Christianity recently disturbed. You are under the will of one man who is said, in the synod of the city of Ephesus, to have pursued rather hatred and quarrels, attacking Flavian, bishop of the city of Constantinople, with the presence and intimidation of soldiers, because he had sent a written petition to the apostolic see and to all the bishops of these regions through those who had been sent [Col. 1066B] to the council by the most reverend bishop of Rome, who, according to the definitions of the Council of Nicaea, are accustomed to attend, most sacred lord, beloved and venerable son, emperor.

“Therefore, by this grace, let Your Clemency, resisting such great disturbances, order that the undefiled truth of the faith of the Catholic religion be preserved, so that, according to the form and definition of the apostolic see—which we likewise venerate as pre-eminent—he may be referred to the judgment of the council and of the apostolic see, while Flavian remains in every respect in the priestly office. There the first man who was worthy to receive the heavenly keys established the primacy of the episcopate. It is fitting, of course, that we preserve in every respect your reverence toward this greatest city, which is mistress of all.

“Take especially careful precautions also [Col. 1066C] that what our generation preserved in ancient times may not appear to be diminished under us, and that, by the present example, similar things may be done [or: schisms be generated] against bishops and holy churches.”

Observe, therefore, most beloved daughter, how this worshiper of God, the Augusta, labored to preserve the ancient faith; how she grieved that the bishop of Constantinople had been attacked through fear of secular powers; how she recalled that he had sent a written petition to the apostolic see; how she venerated the apostolic see as pre-eminent; how she urged that, according to its form and definition, Flavian be submitted to the judgment of that see, just as we have determined concerning Ignatius and Photius; how she remembered that, in the Roman see, the first man worthy to receive the heavenly keys had established the primacy [Col. 1066D] of the episcopate; and how she judged that careful provision must be made lest what had been preserved in ancient times appear to be diminished, and lest the present example lead to similar treatment of bishops and holy Churches.

Attending carefully to all these things, most beloved daughter, and walking in the footsteps of this pious Augusta, show such reverence and such devotion toward the see of blessed Peter, and earnestly urge your most Christian husband both to show and to maintain them. Thus may you receive, together with those empresses who worshiped God and showed honor to the see of Saint Peter, the eternal empire which you have attained temporally; and, through the intercession of that eminent apostle, to whom we urge you [Col. 1067A] to show reverence through obedience in his envoys and embassy, may you attain incorruptible and unfading glory in the heavenly palace, granted by the Lord, the King of kings.

Given on the Ides of November, in the fifteenth indiction.

(Year 866.) CIV. TO THE CLERGY OF CONSTANTINOPLE. He reviews everything that had been done from the day Rhadoaldus and Zacharias were sent to Constantinople. He also recalls the decrees of the Roman council, repeats everything said in the preceding letter concerning the advancement of Photius and concerning Gregory of Syracuse, who consecrated Photius, and concerning the emperor’s letter, which he orders to be burned.

[In Mansi, same place.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend [Col. 1067B] and holy fellow bishops, the archbishops and metropolitans, and the bishops subject to the see of Constantinople, and to the entire venerable clergy of the Church of Constantinople.

We do not believe that Your Holiness is unaware of what was recently done and is still being done at Constantinople. But how, inflamed with zeal for the house of the Lord, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of truth, and following the example of my predecessors in bearing concern for all the Churches of God, we have acted and made our decisions concerning these matters, we shall report to you not so briefly as truthfully.

After we heard that certain of you, kindled by the fires of envy and arrogantly puffed up by the arrogance of pride, had risen, like the Jews, against your shepherd and teacher, [Col. 1067C] namely our brother and fellow minister Ignatius, the most holy patriarch of the aforesaid Church; and that others, like vipers and parricides, had attacked their own parent, that same most blessed man, with savage teeth, and had entirely removed him by the horn of their tyranny from the very Church over which he rightly presided—we, stricken by the sharpest pains and tortured by overwhelming grief, began carefully to consider how we might show him the compassion of kindness, as toward a brother.

For it is written: “Whoever sees his brother in need and closes his compassion against him, how does the love of God remain in him?” (I John III.) This was especially so since we heard that a considerable schism had arisen in the aforesaid city and in the cities adjoining it on account of [Col. 1067D] a certain Photius, drawn from the marketplace and from secular military service and dress and from the imperial palace, suddenly tonsured, and promoted in that same Church contrary to the sacred canons. Some were defending Photius’s advancement, while others rightly detested it as having been carried out while Ignatius was alive and uncondemned.

But while we were continually and anxiously considering what should be done by us in this matter, or how we might learn the truth of such a great disturbance, behold, suddenly certain bishops arrived [Col. 1068A] at the apostolic see with an imperial letter. One of them was the metropolitan of Gangra. They came with Arsa, a distinguished man and imperial spatharius, bearing an imperial embassy. They brought written accusations against our aforementioned fellow priest Ignatius, together with verbal defenses of Photius, and earnestly requested that we send envoys from the apostolic see to settle those scandals and disperse the schisms.

When they had been properly received, and the substance of the embassy entrusted to them and of the imperial letter they had brought had been examined, the grief which rumor alone had previously produced in our heart was immediately multiplied by a more certain report of the events clearly demonstrated.

[Note: [Col. 1067D] Here is a lengthy excerpt (*lacinia*) from Nicholas’s first letter.]

Therefore, since, as your divinely inspired wisdom knows, we are bound by concern for all Christ’s sheep, because through the abundance of heavenly grace we hold the place of Him who is specially told by God, “Feed my sheep” (John XXI), and again, [Col. 1068B] “And you, when once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke XXII), we could neither pretend nor neglect to visit the scattered and dispersed sheep, nor fail to strengthen our brothers and neighbors in faith and good conduct.

And because, among the other things testified by those who had been sent concerning the schism of the aforesaid Church of Constantinople, they particularly asserted that the same Church was being harassed by the Iconoclasts, who were reviving contempt, and that Christ was being blasphemed in their individual gatherings, we therefore sent from our side two bishops who were with us and who seemed suitable for accomplishing this particular task—namely Rhadoaldus and Zacharias—acting together with the Church that is with us, and with letters written by us to both the Augustus and [Col. 1068C] Photius. [The supplied *Ecclesa* is read as *Ecclesia*, “Church,” in this construction.]

We expressly enjoined them to do nothing whatsoever except carefully investigate the causes of the patriarch Ignatius, who had been expelled from the Church before he had been accused by anyone, and report them to the apostolic see with full and truthful evidence, as the most blessed Job teaches: “I diligently investigated the cause that I did not know” (Job XXIX).

As for Photius’s consecration, we believed that it should not be admitted at all for the time being; we also repeatedly and in every possible way commanded our envoys not to communicate with him except in those matters in which they might communicate with a layman, until we had been informed. For, as the eloquent Pope Leo says in his letter to Saint Flavian, [Col. 1068D] bishop (Epistle 10): “We, who desire the judgments of the Lord’s priests to be mature, can determine nothing concerning anyone’s prejudice in matters unknown, before we have truthfully heard everything that was done.”

We granted them permission to decide justly and piously whatever question might arise concerning the venerable images of our Lord Jesus Christ, of His mother, the ever-virgin Mary, and of His saints. Our letters, which we sent through those same envoys to the emperor’s clemency and also to Photius—if they are among you as they were transmitted by us—can clearly show that all these matters stood as we say.

For if we [Col. 1069A] had then commanded our envoys anything concerning the definition of the controversy of our brother Ignatius, or had decreed that he be subjected to condemnation, why did they refuse even to accept the definitive sentence, although they are shown not to have contended worthily or lawfully, yet are proved to have contradicted it and resisted his deposition to whatever extent and in whatever manner? Indeed, to leave aside the other matters for now, we learned from the imperial letter how they not only refused to give their consent to his condemnation but also forbade that such a great sacrilege be committed. They themselves certainly would not have opposed it if they remembered that we had given them a mandate to participate in his deposition. And our most beloved son, the pious Augustus, would not have attempted either to commend them to us or to excuse them for such a transgression, unless it had become clear [Col. 1069B] that they had acted beyond our command.

But if you ask why we deposed them, since you clearly know that they refused to consent to the condemnation of the aforementioned patriarch, we answer that it did them no good to begin something good and not persist in goodness, since “whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X). What benefit is it for anyone first to make an attack for the sake of truth and shortly afterward to turn aside from the path of truth through persuasion, threats, or any other fault?

Moreover, if Vitalis and Misenus were deprived by blessed Pope Felix both of honor and of communion because they were once either compelled or led astray into such actions, as these men now have been, how much more ought these men [Col. 1069C] to suffer an equal punishment, since they committed an equal transgression but did not suffer equal penalties—indeed, they suffered no penalties at Constantinople, unlike those men in former times?

Further, if we had sent our envoys for the purpose of making them judges of Ignatius’s case in our place, as the imperial letter sent through Leo a secretis asserted—falsely claiming that the robber council at which Ignatius was thought to have been deposed had been our judgment—we would unquestionably have judged, before the entire suit was brought and before any controversy began, that his own see must be restored to him, so that he might lawfully recover what he had lost without any law prescribing it, and might resume through an ecclesiastical canon what secular power had taken from him.

Then, restored to his own see and to all [Col. 1069D] his former possessions, and having recovered his strength, clothed and armed, he could enter the field of contest and the conflict of litigation with his accusers. Since this is judged necessary by law in worldly affairs, it ought much more to have been foreseen that it be observed in ecclesiastical and divine matters.

Furthermore, when we sent the aforesaid envoys, we instructed them to deliver to the most clement emperor the letter mentioned above. We ordered that it be written in three copies, in one and the same wording and with the same syllables. We retained one copy here with us as future testimony, already suspecting that the letter would be falsified—a suspicion which we later proved correct.

We gave another copy to the [Col. 1070A] pious Augustus mentioned above for them to present. We supplied the third to our envoys, instructing them to keep it for their own guidance, continually before their eyes like a mirror. If, when a gathering of priests was held at Constantinople in which our fellow minister Ignatius was to be heard by our envoys, the aforesaid Augustus did not wish the copy of our letter to be read there, they were to read in that very assembly the copy which we had given them to retain, and which was identical in every respect with the other two copies already mentioned, and were to convey it by whatever means to the knowledge of all of you.

But when they reached Constantinople, frightened—as they themselves later admitted—by threats from imperial authority, they disregarded [Col. 1070B] our instructions and the letters which we had given them before our entire Church. Indeed, as later became clear, they put aside the fear of God and turned into the opposite everything that had been commanded them.

Finally, they communicated amid the sacred mysteries with Photius the adulterer, invader of the Church, and neophyte, although this had been forbidden to them in many ways. They also condemned Ignatius, an old and holy man who had governed the Church of God innocently for twelve years and who communicated with us, with you, and with the universal orthodox Church; and, most perniciously joining the faction of the Constantinopolitans, they expelled him from the government of the Church by every means after stripping him of his priestly insignia.

We do not justify him in such a way as to say that he committed nothing worthy of reproach, for [Col. 1070C] which, perhaps, after a lawful investigation, he might deservedly have suffered some canonical stroke of judgment, since we confess what is written in the apostolic letters: “We all offend in many things” (James III); and again: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I).
