But we wish and decree that such a bishop receive a penalty worthy of his deeds in such a way that priestly dignity does not become utterly cheapened, nor the episcopal crown so easily bent down to the ground. Thus, I say, we wish and decree that he—or any bishop—be subjected to a just sentence, but not judged by secular persons, not tyrannically driven out, not deprived of his own Church before a hearing, and not receive a properly weighed [Col. 1070D] judgment from inferiors but from a person of greater authority.

Thus, finally, we wish and decree that the causes of this man—or rather of all priests—be examined and their offenses punished in such a way that we do not transgress the boundaries established by the fathers, trample upon the sacred canons, or in any way violate the decretal constitutions of the apostolic see, by which the whole Church is supported and protected.

In the end, we wish and decree that a bishop, whatever his character, be judged in such a way that the rights of the Church over which he presides are broken neither by rashness nor by presumption. For no right of the Church can be preserved as it deserves if its bishop is attacked by anyone, at any time, and in any manner, and is expelled so easily at the whim of any individual.

Since this is [Col. 1071A] so, for the present we cannot but count our brother Ignatius, whatever his character, among the most holy and blessed patriarchs. Although among you he has been wearied by so many reproaches and persecutions, he is nevertheless regarded, believed in, and venerated as he was regarded, believed in, and venerated by my predecessors. He has been found guilty of no crime by any examination of ours, nor has he been proved liable to anything by any special judgment of ours. Therefore he is not to be condemned by any sentence of ours, separated from our communion or from the fellowship of our Church, or addressed by any terms except honorable ones.

But let us return to the order of the narrative. Our envoys, after finally returning, reported nothing other than that Ignatius had been deposed and Photius firmly established [Col. 1071B] in the see of Constantinople.

Two days later, Leo a secretis, an imperial envoy, was received by us and presented two volumes. One contained the proceedings concerning Ignatius’s deposition; the other contained the acts concerning the holy images. From these we learned that the emperor had neither displayed our letter, by which we had decreed that our brother and fellow bishop be summoned before our envoys solely for a hearing, at the deposition of our fellow priest—which, as is thought, had previously taken place—nor had our envoys taken care to present a copy identical in every respect with the one which we had ordered them to read in the assembly of bishops.

Nor, as far as can be found in those volumes translated from Greek into Latin, was the lawful order customarily used by the [Col. 1071C] holy Fathers in the reading of that letter observed. Moreover, in the later assembly convened concerning the holy images, some additions, many alterations, and numerous omissions are found in what was read from it. It was made so entirely different that we seemed to have arranged either nothing or very little concerning the case of our frequently mentioned fellow minister Ignatius.

Whatever we had written concerning his removal or prejudice against him; whatever we had written concerning a sentence pronounced against him not by the Roman pontiff according to custom; whatever we had written concerning the violation of the fathers’ definitions; whatever we had written concerning the irregular advancement of Photius—all these matters they cunningly passed over [read: they passed over], even transgressing the institutions of the holy Fathers, issued under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, so that they would not reach the knowledge of the council [Col. 1071D]. In their customary deceitfulness, although talents had been divinely entrusted to them, they bound them as though in a shroud of silence and hid them utterly beneath the earth.

When we discovered this, we were deeply distressed, and immediately understood what had been done without our envoys. We plainly recognized that things such as these had been perpetrated with our envoys [the text reads: “who [read: what things] ...”]. Either what we sent was just, and therefore ought consequently to have been preserved; or, if it was thought not to be just, the reasons why it was not just ought at least to have been explained in another written document, reported to us, and clearly demonstrated with the greatest rationality.

In no respect, however, ought it to have been deprived either of the knowledge of the Church that is among you or of its content corrupted by any falsification.

The same Leo, [Col. 1072A] the imperial envoy, also brought an imperial letter begging that we give and subscribe our consent both to Ignatius’s deposition and to Photius’s confirmation.

But while the same envoy was present, by the instruction of divine grace, we summoned the entire Church that is with us and decreed, established, and professed before him and before that same holy Church—as we now also profess through it and through you before the universal holy Church of Christ—that we had never sent, and would never send, anything in support of the removal of Ignatius or the consecration of Photius; and that we had never consented, and would never consent, to the deposition of Ignatius or the advancement of Photius.

On the basis of these matters, repeatedly declared and openly announced, and inserted in this form into our apostolic letters, which were given to Leo a secretis [Col. 1072B] to defend before both the emperor and Photius, we sent him back from us.

At the time these events were taking place, the bishops Rhadoaldus and Zacharias, whom, as stated above, we had sent to Constantinople, had not yet been convicted by their own confession or by synodal examination, nor had it been openly demonstrated that they had deposed Ignatius or communicated with the adulterer Photius. Yet both councils held at Constantinople in their presence—the one against the patriarch Ignatius and the one convened in favor of the holy images—had clearly indicated this, and the imperial letter had plainly declared it. The aforesaid Leo a secretis, the imperial envoy, had also repeatedly and steadfastly said it to our face before us and the leading men of our Church [Col. 1072C], while they denied it.

As time passed, however, the murmuring of many who came to Rome from other [variant: those] regions—or rather, of those fleeing the persecutions stirred up by Photius’s supporters—gradually began to spread the report that these same bishops had been corrupted by gifts, that they had communicated with Photius, and that they had deposed Ignatius.

When we heard this, filled with the greatest grief, we began to think and reflect on how we might remove from Christ’s Church, over which by divine favor we preside, any sinister suspicion, since it has neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of that kind, lest at least a slight opportunity for mockery should arise against it.

Then, having summoned an assembly of the most holy bishops of many provinces and regions of the West, and having gathered a holy synod in the Church of God in which blessed [Col. 1072D] Peter, prince of the apostles, is fragrant in his body and shines forth in his miracles—and thereafter, because the place was colder, in the church of the Savior which is called Constantiniana after its founder and which was the first church built in the whole world—we had all the documents translated from Greek into Latin read aloud.

These included both the proceedings of that abominable synod which had been brought to the apostolic see by the aforementioned Leo a secretis and the imperial letter. In all of them the supposed deposition of Ignatius was contained.

Zacharias, then a bishop, was brought forward, since Rhadoaldus, because of his absence, could not at that time be produced. After being questioned and carefully examined, Zacharias was found wholly culpable in Ignatius’s deposition and in his communion with Photius. [Col. 1073A] Recognizing himself to be liable in this matter, Zacharias confessed in his own voice and in his own writing that he had gone to Constantinople after being sent by the apostolic see; that he had neglected to do what we had instructed him to do; and that he had carried out what had been forbidden him—namely, deposing Ignatius without the command of the apostolic see and communicating with Photius contrary to the instructions of our apostolate.

Then, when the holy synod had decreed with us, the aforesaid Zacharias received the sentence of his deposition and excommunication and fell into the pit that he had prepared for others.

The examination of the other man, Rhadoaldus, was prolonged until another synod because of his absence. Although he was repeatedly invited canonically to attend, he did not escape the sentence of deposition and excommunication which his accomplice [Col. 1073B] had deserved; nor did he rightly evade the bond of anathema, should he henceforth communicate with Photius.

It was fitting that equal iniquity should produce equal judgment for both, and that there should be equality in retribution where there had been parity in transgression. For since Rhadoaldus did not refute the charges brought against him, he firmly established, even if there were no other evidence, that the reports concerning him were true, by evading the examination altogether.

For this reason, his absence did not benefit him by right. It has been proved that he himself procured it, not because of some accidental circumstance, but through his own will, just as Nestorius and Dioscorus once did. For, as holy Pope Boniface teaches in his decretal (Epistle 1, to the bishops of Gaul), “It is manifest that he confesses the charge who, when judgment has been granted and so often assigned [Col. 1073C], does not use the opportunity to clear himself.”

It makes no difference whether all that was said is confirmed in the present examination, since it is also established that he repeatedly procured the absence itself as a confession.

From this, too, Hormisdas, the distinguished prelate of the Apostolic See and great champion of the Church, writes (Epistle 2, to the bishops of Gaul):

“Those alone,” he says, “avoid examination of conscience who do not observe what has been commanded.”

But why pursue the matter at length, when, according to what the Lord says, “By the judgment with which they judged, they shall be judged, and by the measure with which they measured, it shall be measured back to them” (Matthew II)? For what happened to them happened once to the bishops Vitalis and Misenus. Like these men, they were sent to Constantinople, but by communicating with the opposing party on behalf of those for whom they had been dispatched, they were found to be not executors but opponents [Col. 1073D] of their commission.

Concerning them, blessed Felix, prelate of the Apostolic See and condemner of Peter of Alexandria and Acacius of Constantinople, wrote to the emperor Zeno, among other things (in Epistle 9, to the Emperor Zeno):

“Vitalis and Misenus—whether they were driven to consent to these actions or consented willingly—the apostolic censure deprived alike of honor and of communion, because it happened, as he himself writes to the abbot Cyril of Acymetus [another reading: Acrinetus, perhaps Acoemetus], that through their treachery the Christian people were deceived.”

Later, mentioning them again, he says to the aforementioned ruler concerning their transgression:

“The Christian people were persuaded that we had given our consent to such men. When they returned, their treachery did not go unpunished. For the holy synod sitting with me before blessed Peter the Apostle, after they had been convicted of telling many lies, stripped them of rank and communion, lest their uncorrected faithlessness provide security to the enemies.”

Moreover, what we unanimously and concordantly determined and promulgated in the venerable and holy synod mentioned above concerning Photius, the usurper and invader of the Church of Constantinople, and his supporters; concerning our brother and fellow priest Ignatius, the patriarch; concerning those who belong to his party; and also concerning the holy images, in accordance with the canons, reasonably and catholically, is declared below in the appended chapters.

## I. The Condemnation of Photius

[Col. 1074B] Photius is recognized as belonging to the party of the schismatics and of those who have turned themselves away from participation in holy communion. From secular administration and military service, and from the law courts, he was suddenly tonsured and ordained bishop by Gregory of Syracuse, formerly a bishop but condemned by a synod and convicted by the Apostolic See. While our fellow priest Ignatius was alive and still patriarch of the holy Church of Constantinople, Photius invaded his see. He had received that Church as a bride to be guarded immaculate for Christ the Bridegroom, as though he were the bridegroom’s friend; yet he entered the Lord’s fold not through the door, which is Christ, but from elsewhere, from the opposite side, like a thief and robber. He burst in like a violent, predatory, criminal adulterer.

Then, communicating and associating daily and indiscriminately with the condemned and anathematized, and with those whom my predecessor, Pope Benedict of holy memory, had bound lest they presume to exercise the priestly office before a hearing [Col. 1074C]—contrary to his pledged faith and to his own profession, by which he had promised that he would devise no evil counsel against the aforementioned patriarch—he convened a council. Together with his followers, who had been deposed, condemned, excommunicated, and anathematized, with others who had no sees, and with those by whom he himself had been irregularly and unlawfully advanced, or whom he had rashly and improperly advanced, he dared to pronounce deposition and anathema against that same brother and fellow minister of ours, Ignatius.

Then, by whatever arguments he could devise, he presumed to turn aside from our commands the envoys of the Apostolic See whom we had sent concerning the holy images, to investigate and report to us the deposition of the aforementioned patriarch, and to discover the manner in which this neophyte had been promoted—after the example of Acacius, formerly the heretical patriarch of Constantinople (as in Felix’s Epistle 6, to Acacius of Constantinople). At the procession held for him and his companions, as was disclosed by their profession and revealed by the Holy Spirit to the venerable synod convened by us, it became clear that, despising the embassy—which ought to have been respected even according to the custom of the gentiles—he dragged them into communion with the condemned and schismatics. He thus made them return, in mockery [in Felix’s Epistle: “to the injury”] of blessed Peter the Apostle, from whose see they had departed, not merely ineffective but even opponents [Col. 1075A] of everything that had been commanded.

Finally, the bishops who refused to communicate with him as an adulterer and invader he banished into exile, and he did not fear to substitute in their places an accomplice of his crime. To this day he has not ceased to attack the Church of God with various persecutions, so that he does not stop subjecting our brother and fellow bishop, the most holy patriarch Ignatius, to unheard-of punishments and terrible tortures. Indeed, everyone whom he has managed to seize for persisting with Ignatius in truth and faith, he ceaselessly endeavors to destroy by every means at his disposal.

For these acts and others like them, by which he has risen up against the evangelical, apostolic, prophetic, and canonical institutions, let him, by the authority of almighty God and of the blessed chief Apostles Peter and Paul, of all the saints together, and of the venerable six universal councils, and also by the judgment of the Holy Spirit through us, be alienated from every priestly honor and title and completely stripped of every clerical office. Thus, if after learning of this decree—which we believe to have been drawn from divine inspiration and which has certainly been promulgated with the unanimity and concord of the holy synod—he attempts to preside on the throne of Constantinople, or prevents the aforementioned venerable fellow bishop of ours, Ignatius, from governing without disturbance the Church entrusted to him, or if he subsequently dares, in the manner of a priest, to touch anything pertaining to the sacred ministry, then, in accordance with the preceding custom, he shall in no way be permitted to have hope of communion or opportunity for satisfaction [Col. 1075C]. Bound instead by the bonds of anathema, together with those who communicate with him and those who support him, he shall, by the perpetual judgment and sentence of God through our humble agency, receive the sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ only when in imminent danger of death.

Let everyone who learns this therefore beware lest, thereafter, anyone rashly presume to burst unexpectedly from the ranks of the laity into the Lord’s army, as though by a sudden attack, and, out of love of authority, wish to assume command before completing the duty of a recruit, or attempt to teach before learning, as we have found repeatedly presumed in that same Church of Constantinople.

And again, let no outsider, despising the clergy—whose multitude in so great a city is abundant, and who from their very beginnings, so to speak, have labored unceasingly in the Church of Christ and rendered the Lord uninterrupted services of devotion—suddenly seize the rule of another of Christ’s folds and attempt to tear apart those whom he does not recognize as his own. Let the Lord’s flock not begin to despise him completely as a stranger and an intruder, especially when it sees that its own meritorious service has gained it nothing and observes a stranger consuming the fruits of its labors.

## II. The Repeated Condemnation of Gregory, Bishop of Syracuse

As for Gregory, who irregularly and in contempt of God presides over the Church of Syracuse, because he too belongs to the party of the schismatics; because, after being deprived by a synod of the office of bishop and bound by my predecessor, Pope Benedict of holy memory, he did not fear to consecrate the layman Photius suddenly as bishop; and because he dared to touch many matters pertaining to the sacred ministry: in accordance with the preceding custom we decree, and by apostolic authority, according to canonical deliberation, we define and establish that he shall be deprived of all priestly status and shall remain excluded from the ministry, so that he may in no way be permitted in any synod to have hope of restoration or an opportunity for satisfaction. If thereafter he presumes at any time to minister in the sacred office in the manner of a priest, let him be anathema.

And if he raises disturbances against our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius, or turns the faithful away from communion with him, let him be anathema, and let all who communicate with him be expelled from the Church [Col. 1076B]; let they themselves also be anathema.

## III. The Deprivation of Those Whom Photius Ordained

Those whom the neophyte Photius, invader of the see of Constantinople, promoted to any ecclesiastical order, because it is manifest that they consented in every respect to the wickedness of their consecrator and communicated with him after his invasion, we deprive of every clerical office. By apostolic and canonical authority and by synodal decree, we completely exclude them.

## IV. The Restoration of Ignatius

Our most reverend and most holy brother and fellow bishop Ignatius, patriarch of the holy Church of Constantinople [Col. 1076C], was first deprived of his own throne by imperial violence and intimidation. Afterwards he was anathematized by the adulterer, traitor, and invader Photius, by his accomplices—namely, excommunicated, anathematized, and condemned men without episcopal sees—and by men bound by my predecessor, Pope Benedict of holy memory. Finally, contrary to our command, he was stripped of his priestly insignia by envoys of the Apostolic See, as the Holy Spirit revealed to the holy synod and as Zacharias, formerly a bishop and one of those two envoys, openly acknowledged in his own confession.

By the authority of the supreme Judge, our Lord Jesus Christ, we promulgate, decree, and establish that Ignatius has never been and is not deposed or anathematized. He was driven from the Church by imperial power without any canonical authority; he could not be held bound by any tie imposed by men who were themselves bound; and he ought to have suffered no diminution of his honor at the hands of those who possessed neither the power to judge him nor authority from the Apostolic See.

Therefore, removing from him every bond of anathema, by the power divinely conferred by the voice of Christ upon the most blessed Peter, and by the authority of the sacred canons and of decretal constitutions issued, after the manner of the holy Fathers, we restore, establish, and confirm that same brother and fellow priest of ours, Ignatius the patriarch, in his former honor, former dignity, and former see; in his rank and patriarchate; and in his former pontifical insignia and offices [Col. 1077A].

Thus, whoever, after learning of this apostolic and synodal decree, prevents him from receiving all the aforementioned marks of the pontificate, fails in every respect to obey this decree, separates himself from communion with him, or subsequently attempts to issue any judgment against him without the prior consent of the Apostolic See—if he is a cleric, let him be alienated from every clerical office before God and human beings, bound with Judas the betrayer by everlasting punishment as one who betrays his master, and, unless he withdraws from his evil intention, condemned to perpetual anathema.

But if he is a layman—whoever he may be—attempting to oppose this constitution and preventing Ignatius from recovering his see and all his former dignity, or, after he has recovered his former see, attempting again to drive him out and expel him from the patriarchate, or inflicting any injury upon his person or priestly honor without the consent of this first see, let him be deprived of every paternal blessing and punished with the curse of Canaan, the son of Ham, who, seeing his father’s shame, did not cover it but mocked him. Let him be struck with eternal punishment, when the Lord judges, together with parricides, and let him not be completely released from the bonds of anathema except by repentance.

## V. The Bishops Banished by Photius Are Restored

As for those bishops, or clerics of any order, who after the unjust deposition of our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius were either banished into exile or maliciously deprived of their ministry or rank, we establish that, once their exile has been ended, they shall recover their own sees and ranks.

If anyone presumes to oppose this decree of ours and prevents them from resuming their sees or ranks, let him be anathema until he obeys.

If any of them are accused by others, we decree that they must first recover their sees and proper ranks; but we do not allow them to be judged except by the Roman See. If they are said to have done anything contrary to the rule, we establish that they are reserved for judgment by our decree, in accordance with what the sacred canons also prescribe.

## VI. Concerning the Sacred Images

Since we ought to preserve the statutes of our ancestors with the mind’s gaze unwavering, and always to venerate in every respect the doctrines of the holy Fathers, we define concerning the sacred and venerable images of our Lord Jesus Christ, of his ever-virgin mother Mary, and of all the saints believed to have pleased God from righteous Abel onward, that those images which the holy Church spread throughout the world received from ancient times, and which the prelates of the Apostolic See decreed and established on their behalf, shall remain unimpaired and undefiled.

Accordingly, we decree that John, formerly bishop of Constantinople, and his followers—who with polluted mouths assert that these images ought to be broken and trampled—are anathema from Christ and from the catholic and apostolic Church, for as long as they do not agree with us concerning these matters and do not hold the doctrine prescribed by the decrees of the holy Roman pontiffs and the institutions of the other catholic Fathers.

These are the things which the Apostolic See has established concerning them; these are the things which it has decreed synodally and canonically; these are the things which you ought to embrace with all the greater zeal and observe with all the greater care, the better you know that what it has established has always been held by the universal Church. Thus, against each error that has arisen in the Church, this first see, in accordance with the authority of its primacy, has always set the limit of judgment.

And so at last the universal Church, although at times it resisted for a short while in certain matters, eventually approved what that see approved and rejected what it rejected.

But however you obey or fail to obey the divine institutions and the paternal canons, we nevertheless will not in any way consent to any danger threatening our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius before his case is specifically brought back to us for reconsideration—indeed, since we have not consented until now, we shall never consent, God strengthening us.

Nor shall we in any way bend the wishes of our favor toward advancing Photius in the priesthood. With all our strength and effort, as long as I live, we shall work for the advancement of constrained justice—that is, the restoration of the legitimate man and the expulsion of the adulterer—and, God as our agent, we shall never cease to do what belongs to us: now by pleading, now by exhorting, now by rebuking, and now also by canonical admonition. Moreover, by apostolic authority we shall strike those who are obstinate, sometimes with words and sometimes with letters, and day and night we shall strive, with the power of the supreme Maker, to complete what is right, just, and already begun.

[Note: [Col. 1077D] Here there is a large lacuna, of the kind found in a letter of the same Nicholas.]

Therefore let your fraternity at least now learn from the tenor of this letter that the see of blessed Peter the Apostle will never grant its consent to communion with Photius, the neophyte, adulterer, and invader of the Church of Constantinople, formerly and justly condemned and recently struck down by synodal presence, nor with his supporters, unless they cease from their treachery.

To omit the rest for now, instructed—or rather destroyed—by Gregory of Syracuse and the other schismatics, Photius cannot, contrary to all right, preside over any Church [Col. 1078D]. For one is rightly believed to have been destroyed who, hoping to be built up by one who has himself been destroyed, lost whatever other good qualities he may perhaps have possessed by communicating with the rashness of that man’s excessive presumption.

How could Gregory build up anyone, when it was already known that he had been struck down in so many ways? How could he establish anyone in any ecclesiastical order, when, by splitting the unity of the Church, he himself already appeared to have been completely overthrown? For just as one who is bound cannot bind another, and one who has been deposed cannot depose another, so one who has been destroyed could not build up, and one who has been struck down could not ordain anyone.

He who attempts either to overthrow another or to establish him must stand at the summit of his own status in full strength and rely in every respect upon firm foundations [Col. 1079A]. Gregory, therefore, who had been canonically and synodally deposed and anathematized: how could he advance or bless anyone? No reasoning demonstrates that he could.

Photius consequently received nothing from Gregory except insofar as Gregory possessed something. But he possessed nothing and gave nothing. For, as we read, through the imposition of their hands and invocation the Holy Spirit was given by those who knew how to lift clean hands to the Lord.

Gregory, however, having become a transgressor of the law, undoubtedly provoked the Holy Spirit by the imposition of his hand more toward anger against himself than toward the consecration of anyone—even if the man being ordained had no other canonical impediments. For it is written:

“Whoever closes his ears so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be accursed” (Proverbs XXI).

If accursed, then certainly not heard; if not heard, then ineffective; if ineffective, plainly providing nothing to Photius—who, by that imposition of hands, is recognized rather as having a wounded head [Col. 1079B].

Moreover, if Photius claims that he was unjustly deposed by Ignatius, what will he say about all those who assembled in that synod at that time and pronounced judgment against him? If he presumes to say that they too acted unjustly, why does he now communicate with them, and why does he consider some of them worthy of the priesthood? Yet he censures them for not having judged correctly before, and he knows that, according to his own position, they ought to submit to the judgment they pronounced.

But let us see by whose judgment or authority Gregory, after his deposition and anathema, recovered the honor of the episcopate or resumed his former office [Col. 1079C]. Everyone knows that he had been deposed, bound by the bonds of anathema, and therefore deprived of communion with the whole Church.

Now, if you say that Gregory himself recovered his honor and resumed his former office, hear what the Apostle says:

“No one takes the honor upon himself, but only he who is called by God, as Aaron was. So too Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest” (Hebrews V).

The venerable canons of Antioch likewise prescribe (chapter 4):

“If any bishop condemned by a synod, or any presbyter or deacon condemned by his bishop, dares to touch the sacred ministry—whether a bishop according to the preceding custom, or a presbyter or deacon—he shall in no way be permitted, either in another synod, to have hope of restoration or to have an opportunity for satisfaction. All who communicate with him shall also be expelled from the Church, especially if, after learning that a judgment has been pronounced against those mentioned, they attempt to communicate with them” [Col. 1079D].

The rules of Carthage likewise clearly declare that an excommunicated person who presumes to communicate before a hearing has pronounced condemnation upon himself.

If, then, according to the Apostle, no one takes honor upon himself, and Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest—he who, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, glorifies all who glorify him—and if he himself is the high priest of whom the same Apostle says again, “Such a one was fitting for us as high priest, holy, and so forth” (Hebrews VII) [Col. 1080A]—

and if, according to the sacred canons, a bishop condemned by a synod dares to touch anything pertaining to the sacred ministry according to the preceding custom and to communicate before a hearing, he has pronounced condemnation upon himself, so that he may in no way be permitted, even in another synod, to have hope of restoration or an opportunity for satisfaction, and all who communicate with him are to be expelled from the Church—

how great a punishment, do you suppose, should be imposed upon Gregory, who after his condemnation or anathema is proven to have committed all these acts? That is, he exalted himself against Christ; he did what Christ himself did not do, recovering honor for himself; he arrogantly glorified himself in order to become a high priest; he dared to communicate while excommunicated and before a hearing, and to usurp what was forbidden; and, although condemned and forbidden to exercise the sacred ministry, he touched not merely one thing but many things according to the former custom [Col. 1080B].

Gregory certainly ought not to have done this, even if there had been no offenses for which he could have been condemned. For the judgment of superiors must always be feared by inferiors: if they do not obey it, even if they have perhaps been bound unjustly by it, they may deserve the sentence of their own binding because of another fault, namely disobedience.

Therefore one must always dread condemning superiors indiscriminately. Those who are inferior must carefully beware of being condemned and must not transgress the judgment of their superiors. Otherwise, even if they have sometimes been condemned unjustly, guilt for a transgression that perhaps had not yet been committed, and punishment that the guilt had not yet deserved, will undoubtedly follow from their rash treachery.

The forbidden tree itself contained nothing deadly; but the one who ate from it disobediently brought death upon himself and his descendants—not because the tree was evil, since God made everything he created good, but because transgression is evil, and condemnation rightly arose through the refusal to submit.

Moreover, if you say that Gregory was received by the emperor and by the bishops, I wish to ask, O wisest brothers, by what evidence and under what canons it could rightly be done that those who had been expelled should be received by others. The venerable universal Council of Nicaea expressly forbade this in the clearest terms concerning both orders of profession (chapter 8).

For it is manifest that a priest cannot be bound or released by secular power. Accordingly, it is fully established that Gregory of Syracuse could in no way have been reconciled merely by an imperial sentence [Col. 1080D]. If the assent of bishops was also associated with it, we ask whether that assent preceded or followed.

If it followed, the matter nevertheless returns to this: release received from secular power cannot be valid, and the assent of the bishops that followed must have been an act of flattery or fear rather than a legitimate decree.

If it preceded, let it be shown by whom and where it was carried out; whether it was celebrated according to the rule of the Church; whether it proceeded from the tradition of the Fathers; whether it was issued according to the custom of the ancestors; whether it was obtained through an appropriate examination; whether it was referred, according to the rule of the Church, to a see of greater authority than the one by which Gregory was held bound under condemnation; and whether the very prelate who bound him released him [Col. 1081A].

If these things were not done, by what custom or rite does Gregory of Syracuse boast that he was released, when he was freed neither by the bishops in the proper order nor by ecclesiastical laws, and could by no means be released by worldly power apart from the path of the Church?

Now, if you say, “It was not the emperor who released him, but he asked the bishops to release him,” then, on the contrary, the bishops ought much more to have asked the Augustus that, if he wished Gregory to be released, a legitimate release in ecclesiastical form should take place and all the matters mentioned above should be observed according to the way of the Church. This was especially necessary since, as we learn from the apostolic canons, a person may lawfully be released not by an inferior or an equal but by a superior, and solely by the one who separated him or, certainly, by the first see.

An inferior cannot release a superior or an equal unless the superior consents; only the more powerful can fittingly release the inferior. Therefore bishops of an inferior rank could not release, without the first see, those whom their superior had bound [Col. 1081B].

Nevertheless, although they received the aforementioned Gregory, who had been expelled, contrary to the sacred canons of Nicaea, they never stripped him of the bond of condemnation and anathema. Rather, by their treacherous release they bound him more tightly, and while attempting to loosen him, they handed him over to greater knots.

Indeed, by despising and transgressing the sentence of their superior—or even by attempting, through a deceitful policy and mild-mindedness, to destroy it and thereby making themselves opposed to their own judgment—they are held bound by an equal treachery and, according to the apostolic canons and certain others, are subject to a similar punishment [Col. 1081C], so that those who communicate with him are ordered to be expelled from the Church.

Thus it is clear that the guilty could in no way justify the guilty, nor could those who were themselves bound release the bound.

Behold by whom Photius was installed, O most blessed ministers of Christ; behold what kind of man Gregory is—one who could more appropriately have been called “Dormitantius.”

Therefore, dearest brothers, consider, examine, and diligently inquire within yourselves whether Photius can stand—even if he possesses wondrous virtues, even if he shines with every kind of learning—when the man who attempted to establish him had already fallen long ago and, wishing to be raised up with those attempting to raise him, fell again, never to recover.

Let your divinely inspired prudence consider how Photius could remain in the priestly rank, even if nothing else could lawfully impede him, when his installer, at the time he ordained him, lacked not only the priesthood but even the Christian name itself [Col. 1081D]. As we have also explained, one who is condemned cannot justify, one who is deposed cannot raise up, and one who is bound cannot advance anyone through the imposition of hands. It is impossible for any of these things to occur.

Therefore, dearest brothers, consider carefully not only these matters but also the canons of the Fathers, especially those of the Apostles, Antioch, and Carthage. Examine and recall most diligently what they prescribe concerning the condemned and excommunicated, and concerning those who have rightly been expelled from the Church because of their crimes.

For we have taken care, canonically, to make known to your fraternity in Christ what we have decreed and established concerning those whom we have received and raised up, and concerning those whom we have expelled and driven from the priesthood or from communion. The rule of the great and venerable Council of Nicaea also gives this admonition (chapter 10): concerning those who are at some time deprived of communion, whether they belong to the clergy or the laity, the bishops of each province must maintain a regular judgment, so that those who have been expelled are not received by others.

We have therefore done what we ought to do. We wished you to know that, with God as our witness, we acted only from zeal for uprightness and carried out our duty from a desire to preserve the constitution of the Fathers. It is your responsibility to obey. Otherwise you will justly and deservedly undergo the same sentence as they, since the canons of Antioch prescribe in their second chapter:

“If anyone among the bishops, presbyters, deacons, or any other member of the clergy is found communicating with excommunicated persons, let him also be deprived of communion, as one who confounds the rule of the Church.”

And again, in chapter four—which we also mentioned above—carefully recall what that anciently received council says on the same matter.

Beware, therefore, beloved, lest you mingle with those who have been disobedient to the institutions of the holy Fathers, lest one and the same sentence envelop those whom one bond of communion is found to have entangled.

Moreover, observe that you can no longer claim ignorance as a refuge of excuse, since, with God’s inspiration, you remember the canons and have now been instructed by our letters [Col. 1082C].

Do not therefore share in the sins of others; do not be disobedient to us, because disobedience expelled the first-formed man from paradise. Disobedience is rightly called idolatry, as the holy Samuel says to Saul:

“To resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse to comply is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Samuel XV).

Consider, then, how detestable resistance is and how abhorrent refusal to comply must be, since it is compared with the sin of divination and the crime of idolatry.

The chief of the Apostles cries out:

“We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts IV).

And his fellow apostle Paul says:

“He who resists the authority resists God’s ordinance” (Romans XIII).

Judge, then, whom one ought rather to obey: God or human beings. Judge whom one ought rather to resist: the authority that almighty God established in Peter and exalted above the whole Church, or the ordinance of Gregory of Syracuse, to whom, because of the wickedness he deserves, it must be said:

“Woe to the man through whom so many scandals have come into the Church of Christ.”

As you yourselves know, and as we reported above, Gregory was formerly deposed by our brother and fellow minister Ignatius and by the synod that was under him; and Gregory himself requested that the Apostolic See consent to his condemnation.

But my predecessors, Leo and Benedict of blessed memory, preserving the moderation of the Apostolic See, refused to hear one party in such a way that nothing at all would be reserved for the other; for one cannot be the mediator of only one side [Col. 1082D].

Therefore his deposition remained, for the time being, unaccepted and without force by the Apostolic See. When Gregory, through a representative of his party named Zacharias, acknowledged that the Apostolic See had in no way consented to his deposition, he gave no thanks and did not cease the insults that raged against our aforementioned brother. Instead, abusing the kindness of God and the patience of the Apostolic See to fuel his pride, he irreverently sharpened anew against Ignatius, his patriarch, the darts of his impiety, and while Ignatius was still alive, consecrated a neophyte in the Church of Constantinople.

Indeed, Gregory did not cease to be defiant even against the decrees of this see. He does not remember, like an ingrate, that the decrees issued shortly before on his behalf—not against him—were issued for his protection; like a prevaricator, he prepares weapons against weapons that had contributed greatly to his salvation, and attempts to destroy the wall that had guarded him most firmly so that he himself would not be destroyed [Col. 1083B].

Now he acts, as far as lies within him, to render entirely invalid those decrees which, when he needed them, he begged for as a suppliant; he submissively wished them to be stronger than adamant and humbly implored them to aid him. He perhaps even judged those who resisted them to be tyrants and sacrilegious men. For if the Apostolic See had not spared him, how could he have exercised his power against the most reverend Ignatius? He would have had no means.

Yet he turned the goodness of the Apostolic See into wickedness [another reading: “into malignity”], and transformed the benefit into the destruction of his own father.

Tell me, then, I beg you, brothers: since this is so, how should we not assist Ignatius, or, insofar as it lies within us, preserve him wholly unharmed until the hearing [Col. 1083C]? How could we not rightly condemn Gregory and those who belong to his party, when, unless we had restrained them, Ignatius might perhaps have struck them down canonically in such a way that they could not have driven him out by any effort?

These men did not adhere to us, though they had deserved to have us most ready to help them, nor did they take counsel from us about how they might either be reconciled with their patriarch or be judged canonically. Instead, they immediately marshaled against him the forces which we had preserved from being broken.

Therefore, I ask you to consider how greatly we are now indebted to Ignatius, since we have become an obstacle to him and a shelter of defense for his enemies.

We did not, however, postpone the judgment of these men so that they might prepare darts with which to injure him, but so that the sentence pronounced against them might possess validity, with an examination by us preceding it. Again, we wished the charges brought by these men against him to be admitted fully before us in such a way that the person of Ignatius’s party would be summoned and would not be absent from our presence, whether or not he had been convicted [another reading: “even if he had been convicted”].

Therefore, with the judgment deferred for a short time and the sentence meanwhile weakened, a document was sent to be presented before the eyes of the prelate of the Apostolic See by both parties and, as was proper, to be submitted to his determinations.

But while Ignatius’s party was preparing to hasten its journey, his enemies recovered their strength. They no longer sought the Apostolic See and no longer deigned to remember Peter. Ignatius was dragged away, driven out, and afflicted with countless evils [Col. 1084A]; he was removed from the governance of the Church.

All this happened because the aforementioned pontiffs, preserving equity for both parties and awaiting a hearing from both, by not confirming Ignatius’s sentence—in fact, by weakening it for the time being—had in a certain sense extended a hand to his enemies. They had not meanwhile revoked, by the authority of the Apostolic See, the sentence pronounced against those men, but had decreed that it be deferred until the presence of that same Apostolic See.

Therefore, dearest ones, since material for Ignatius’s deposition was, as it were, found through us, for this reason—not only because brother ought to be helped by brother, and not only because Christ’s oracle especially says to Peter, whose place on earth we hold, unworthy though we are, “Strengthen your brothers”—we must for this very reason not merely help and strengthen him, but also, as you yourselves can perceive, contend for him in every way with all our strength. Thus everything by which his adversaries, finding through us an incentive to harm him, are shown to have inflicted violence upon him may be utterly abolished, and, with Christ propitious, he may recover everything which he is recognized to have lost prejudicially while we acted with moderation and according to the rule.

For if our aforementioned predecessors—namely, the pontiffs Leo and Benedict, of blessed memory—had lived to see Gregory or his accomplices perpetrate such a deed, that is, if they had laid hands upon Ignatius after abusing the great benefit of the apostolic see’s compassion and patience toward them, or if, without consulting those holy prelates, they had sharpened their tongues in such a manner against him, they would certainly have condemned them immediately and without reconsideration, as teachers of unrest and as men who had shown themselves, more clearly than the sun, to be liable to condemnation; and they would have striven with the greatest ardor to destroy so enormous a sacrilege of their impiety. But because those men have been taken away by divine summons from this valley of tears without yet witnessing this tyranny, we must take up their labor, just as we have succeeded to their honor; in whose time the cruelty that had begun to put forth roots in their days appeared fully consummated.

Accordingly, first, because we retain the governance of the apostolic see, which has the right to judge concerning the whole Church; second, because we ought to assist brothers who have suffered injury; and finally, because—as we have already said—we must take up the labor of those whose pontifical honor we have inherited, just as they followed the examples of their predecessors and proved themselves diligent cultivators of their work, we have earnestly endeavored, with the Lord’s help, to carry out the same zeal for justice—or the same privilege of dignity—that they would certainly have fulfilled.

Indeed, we unquestionably cannot omit this, as is plainly granted for all to know: since we have said that we consecrated Gregory as a neophyte, let them not deny that Photius too was a neophyte when he was, as it were, consecrated to the priesthood. Let us recall the words of the holy Pope Gregory, apostle of the most extensive and most faithful nation of the English—for they themselves, in the Lord, are the seal of his apostleship—who says:

“But just as at that time one was called a neophyte who had been planted at the beginning in the way of life of the holy faith, so now one must be regarded as a neophyte who, having suddenly been planted in the religious habit, has insinuated himself into the pursuit of sacred honors.”

Moreover, we believe that we must not fail to recall that in the past year, namely in the thirteenth indiction, we received through Michael, the imperial protospatharius, a letter written in the prince’s name. It was so covered with insulting words, indeed with blasphemies, that its writer seems to have dipped his pen only in the throat of a serpent, and the author’s lips appear to have poured forth poison instead of words. The effect was such that, if these things should penetrate the heart of any simple person—for the ears of the prudent do not receive them—they would kill him immediately; and all the more miserably because through that poisonous draught the death of the soul is suffered more gravely than that of the body.

Although we recall having already written to the Augustus, through the aforesaid legate, concerning the monstrous enormity of this sacrilege, we have nevertheless considered it proper to write the same things now to your blessedness. Finally, we have thought, and still think, that his piety may at last come to its senses and agree to our salutary efforts to restore the condition of the Church of Constantinople. Thus, at last, let him decree that all the writings that have been wrongly compiled—not only against us and this holy Church, but also against our brother and fellow minister Ignatius—be handed over to the fire before the entire multitude of his empire.

Otherwise, it would plainly become evident to all the faithful of the Church what authority belongs to the apostolic see, and what vengeance threatens the fabricators of lies and inventors of perverse doctrines. For it is impossible—although we consider our own personal injuries to be of no account—that we should calmly endure the blasphemies of so many and such great holy Fathers and defenders of the Catholic Church, destroyers of various heresies and defenders of the orthodox faith; or that we should suffer the insults directed against so great a see, or against the Roman Church, so eminent, in which we serve God by his authority.

Yet, although we think humbly of ourselves, we do not, with conscience as our guide, assert that the things he alleged about us are true. Rather, as we have said, setting those matters aside, we investigate instead the things that belong to Jesus Christ; and if anything badly compiled against his servants, against his ordinances, or against privileges established by his dispositions is found, we tolerate it with no patience. We eagerly strive with all our strength to destroy them, and necessarily plan to repay the makers of such great perversity with a fitting recompense.

This is so that no one, seeing such men go unpunished, may presume, now or in the future, to compose such displays of falsehood or to combine inventions of blasphemies in fabrications of this kind.

For this reason we sent the most exalted emperor a letter of our pontificate, exhorting him; and in it it is also especially fitting that you labor in support of our resolve: namely, that he should diligently inquire and investigate whether, when he discovers that such a filthy—or rather, poison-infected—letter was composed without his own command, he should at least, after accepting its companion, have it publicly burned by his Augustal officials and send letters to us and to all to whom it has come, thereby giving adequate satisfaction and showing himself wholly free from so perverse a meaning and such profane inventions, since it was not delivered from his own mind but handed over to fabrications. We say nothing for the moment about the punishment appropriate for those who wove so many such deceptions, although it is fitting that they should be caught up in the zeal for truth that they profess to feel.

But if, while he was occupied with many such concerns, he was induced to order that these things be written, let his clemency not hesitate humbly to confess this also, and let him decree by his laws that such writings are to be considered entirely without force. Thus, whoever is found to possess them will not escape unpunished, and the written text or copy of that often-mentioned and ever-execrable letter, while its sacred words remain untouched out of reverence, shall likewise be given over to the devouring flames.

In this way he may be able to rid himself of the stain of evil repute incurred through blasphemous writings and may in no respect appear an ungrateful son toward his mother, from whom he and his fathers received, through a heavenly disposition, the height of imperial rule in due succession.

But if not, know that, once we discover that he wishes to persist in this obstinacy to the very end, we shall first, with the venerable priests of all the western regions assembled, and relying on apostolic authority, bind with harsh anathemas the authors, arrangers, and promoters of so great a deception and so cruel a derogation from the holy or paternal traditions, removing them from the whole Christian framework. Following also the footsteps of the Fathers and of my predecessors, who were accustomed to annul even councils of numerous bishops that had been wickedly celebrated, we shall proceed against any associated copies or perhaps exemplars of the frequently mentioned letter; indeed, we shall consign to perpetual condemnation not only these writings, but all writings that have been unjustly composed against our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius, or furiously brought forth against those who did not pursue his cause canonically.

Then, when those same most holy brothers and fellow bishops have decided together with us and considered the matter, we shall, with all looking on, suspend the letter from a stake and, with a great fire placed beneath it, consign it to final destruction, to the disgrace of the imperial document, before all the nations found in great numbers near the memory of Saint Peter. Thus, when these measures have been properly carried out, let the pious man learn what he should love, and the cruel man what he should fear. For to have heard so many and such blasphemous inventions—or rather, distortions of truthful writings—and to have remained silent is to connive.

Therefore, venerable brothers, I must take great care—as you yourselves will be able to understand—that, if we do not promptly confront these fabrications of deceit, foolish people may falsely suppose that we have accepted them as genuine or approved. Nor can we, by dissimulation in the Church of God, leave behind such spurious shoots, which in the time of our most blessed pontifical predecessors either never arose or, if they arose somewhere or somehow, were rooted out by the mattock of their judgment before they could grow.

Let him himself destroy and scatter them, with you also exhorting him. Otherwise, know in advance that they will have to be destroyed or utterly scattered by us in the manner we have stated. Yet, before we wrote these things to you, for which we now exhort his exaltedness, we thought that he would do this of his own accord. But since what was expected has so far produced no result, and since we desire his salvation to remain unharmed, we have now admonished him with paternal affection so that at least he may do this. Otherwise, as we have already said, with God’s favor we shall henceforth keep watch and devote ourselves to every effort within our power, so that those who have not consented to Peter’s authority—or rather, who have not understood that this authority is ordered by God in Peter—may be counted among the dead.

Thus no one will thereafter dare either to defend these writings, so perniciously compiled, or even to commit similar things to writing—not to mention turning them over in his mind. For we cannot, without danger to ourselves, leave unharmed and without perilous consequences the fabrications that resist God’s ordinance, contradict the words of the Gospel, oppose the decisions of the holy Fathers, and run counter to synodal constitutions—fabrications that, if allowed to stand, can inflict innumerable losses upon the faithful who seek Peter’s assistance. Nor can we leave behind, either now or after our departure, such a stain upon our reputation—God forbid—as would lead to the destruction of the simple and the mutilation of the privileges of the apostolic see.

Furthermore, so that the charity of your unanimity may grieve with us over the deposition of our most holy brother and fellow minister, the patriarch Ignatius, may it also offer with us whatever consolations are able to strengthen him. For if, according to the Apostle, “when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (1 Cor. 12), how much more ought we to suffer with him who is known to have held the foremost place among the other members?

Therefore, if not for the rejection of our brother, a prelate who is one particular person, then certainly for the trampling down of the supreme priest, you ought to grieve, groan, weep, hasten, and contend. For if secular power is permitted to judge the prelates of the Lord’s Church in this way, or if it is again lawful for inferiors to perpetrate such acts rashly against their prelates, consider whether such presumption may prevail to your ruin—or rather, to the ruin of the whole Church—now and in future times. If you attend to this, you already see it plainly.

For impiety has raised its head so high that, with the prelates of the churches set aside and the canonical order trampled down, laymen now hold ecclesiastical offices; according to their own pleasure they remove some and promote others in their place, and then, overcome by the fickleness of their minds, reject after a short time those whom they now approve. Thus secular and laymen are able to commit every kind of crime with impunity, and no bishop—although one promoted from the clergy could restrain such conduct with the highest authority—is permitted freely to rebuke them for it.

Nor do they permit men from the clerical ranks to be advanced to sacred orders—men who, having fought courageously for a longer time and more familiarly under Christ their leader, could restrain their way of life all the more boldly. Instead, they choose from among themselves those who are less likely to presume to criticize their deeds, because they remember that shortly before, with their favor, they had promoted them from their own circle.

This practice is carried out all the more familiarly in those regions—the presumption, namely, that laymen are suddenly tonsured and consecrated bishops—as they testify that it has grown out of custom. We, on the contrary, wish to eradicate it from the Church of God with all the greater zeal, the more we have already shown that it is exceedingly harmful to the clergy and to the entire religious people; and the more we know from the sacred canons that not only a bad custom, but also a pernicious corruption, must be avoided.

We know that, gradually increasing, it has already invaded many with the grass of its pestilential wickedness, so that this rashness has grown to such an extent that they now have no need of clergy at all. Against the sacred canons, they suddenly choose for themselves anyone they wish who has been tonsured, and do not turn the eyes of their minds toward the labors of the clergy.

As a result, an outsider consumes the fruit of their labors, and an unexpected foreign enemy steals away the rewards of their merits. Thus it benefits clergy nothing to have served in the Lord’s armies or to have climbed step by step through each ecclesiastical order, while another, by a single leap, passes over all these stages and suddenly rules over those among whom he has neither taken up arms against spiritual enemies nor at any time stood firm in battle for the truth against the Church’s various adversaries.

As for the matter of preventing just anyone from the laity from being elected to the episcopate, the sacred canons show, among other prohibitions, what the Sardican canons teach, with Bishop Hosius speaking in chapter thirteen:

“And this I consider necessary: that you examine most carefully whether perhaps a rich man or a scholar from the administration of the courts has been sought as bishop, so that he may not be ordained before he has first discharged the office of lector and the ministry of deacon or presbyter; and so, if he is worthy, let him ascend through each grade to the summit of the episcopate. For through these promotions, which will necessarily extend over a long period, it can be tested with what faith, modesty, gravity, and reserve he is endowed; and, if he has been proved worthy, let him be honored with the divine priesthood. For it is neither fitting nor does reason or discipline permit that a neophyte should be rashly and lightly ordained either bishop, presbyter, or deacon, especially since the blessed Apostle, the teacher of the nations, appears to have warned and prohibited this from happening (1 Tim. 5). Rather, let those be chosen whose life has been examined over a long period and whose merits have been proved.”

Look, then, and perceive the future—or rather, the pressing—evils. You are physicians: foresee the diseases that threaten by means of the signs that precede them. You are bishops: behold the dreadful destruction arising in the Church of Christ. You are watchmen: climb to the lofty citadel of the mind and observe from afar the most savage beast seeking to rush upon the Lord’s flock.

Raise your voice like a trumpet and announce their crimes to the people of God. Ascend a high mountain, that is, the height of virtues. You who proclaim good news to Zion, stand firm in strength; rise up against the powers of this age, set a wall before the house of God, and oppose whatever powers act unjustly against it (Isa. 52). Thus it will come about that you cannot be accused, like mute dogs, of silence, nor be compelled to render a strict account to the Lord for hiding your talent. With his help, you will praiseworthily rescue your fellow bishops and priests—and indeed the Church of Christ established in those regions—from immense destruction and harmful corruption, and govern them wondrously.

For the present, let it suffice that we have written these things to you concerning them. May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding (Phil. 4), penetrate the inmost recesses of your hearts. May almighty God mercifully reveal to you how solicitous we are for the salvation of all of you, and how we desire to hold you within the heart of Christ and in the embrace of the Church—which, spread throughout the whole world, is as it were the bridal chamber of the one Christ—and to remain with you in holy communion, so that we may all be of one mind and there be no divisions among us (1 Cor. 1). May he deign to reveal this by the grace of his illumination, so that, rejoicing together and congratulating one another over the corruption of the faithful, we may with one mind and one voice glorify and praise God, namely the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

Whoever reads this letter of ours at Constantinople and conceals anything contained in it from the knowledge of those to whom he understands it was sent—if he can find a suitable place for it—let him be anathema. Whoever also interprets it and changes, removes, or adds anything from it beyond what the character of the Greek wording requires, or what the interpreter’s knowledge of understanding does not permit, let him be anathema.

(Year 866.) CV. [Note: It is cited in the Eighth Council, but it does not survive in Greek. There it is said to be addressed πρὸς τοὺς συγκλητικούς, “to the senators.” HARD.] TO THE SENATORS OF CONSTANTINOPLE. That they should support Ignatius’s cause and abstain from communion with Photius.

[In Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 1089D]

NICOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to certain senators of Constantinople, each according to his rank.

From the reports of the faithful who come to the thresholds of the holy apostles for the sake of prayer, we have learned that your Glory is always devoted both to the fear and love of God, and is diligently occupied in his service with the greatest and constant devotion. Therefore we give thanks to God, and we humbly implore his mercy to grant perseverance in the good purpose you have begun and to bestow upon you in the future a worthy recompense.

We are especially grateful because you are said to sympathize with the misery of the Church of Constantinople and to bear its disturbance and ruin with the greatest distress, so that you grieve and lament with our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius, patriarch of that same Church, over his deposition—although, as was necessary, you scarcely offer him any assistance openly.

It belongs to perfect men not only to confess before all the princes of the world the justice and truth that is Christ, but also, if necessary, to defend it with all their strength even unto death. For which of his children, unless ungrateful and impious, would not grieve and labor even unto death for his spiritual father, so furiously deposed and so rashly removed from the pastoral care divinely entrusted to him, with an adulterer substituted in his place?

Which of his children, I say, unless ungrateful and impious, would not grieve and labor even unto death for his holy mother, the Church, when he saw her daily shaken by such great disturbances, so irregularly deprived of her ruler, and subjected at the whim of anyone whatsoever to an invader and a neophyte?

Run, therefore, dearest one, and if the fear of the Lord is perfect in you, conceal the truth from no power, hearing the Redeemer say: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna” (Matt. 10).

But if such freedom of spirit is not in you, and the love of Christ does not inflame you so greatly that you freely oppose the powers of the world when they do not correct what they have wrongly done, at least restrain yourself from every injury against our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius and those who communicate with him—although we say this indulgently—and withdraw entirely from communion with the invader, neophyte, and adulterer Photius.

Know that we have justly deposed him apostolically, canonically, and also according to reasonable judgment, synodically and lawfully, in accordance with the authority of the privileges of the apostolic see; and, because of his many transgressions and acts of presumption, we have anathematized him unanimously together with the bishops of many western provinces and regions.

Therefore let your prudence take care and beware, dearest one, lest you communicate in the sins of others and thereby become entangled in another’s bonds. Rather, if you can assist the Church of God in driving out the adulterer and restoring the legitimate bishop, do so. But if not, at least save your own soul, and according to the prophetic saying: “Go out from their midst, and do not touch what is polluted” (Isa. 52).

Moreover, let your charity strive kindly to assist the legates whom we have sent to Constantinople, for love of him from whose see they have departed, whenever an opportunity arises: namely, so that, with Christ propitious, their embassy may prove effective and they themselves may return to us without suffering any injury.

May almighty God further and more perfectly increase in your heart the piety and love toward the condition of the holy Church which widespread report testifies that you possess. May he grant you to enjoy here for a long time the gift of present happiness as you diligently pursue what we have said, and may he bestow upon you without end the rewards of future blessedness.

(Year 866.) CVI. TO ALL CATHOLICS. Acts [Note: This letter, interrupted by the insertion of copies of other letters, is divided into three parts. The first is published here in our order as CVI; the second, incorrectly addressed to the emperor Michael, is numbered XLVII in our edition and begins with the words “These things being so”; the third is found at the end of LXXXVII, beginning with the words “These things indeed,” and continuing to “we foresaw that it would be.” These are the final words of this letter. EDIT. After Jaffé, in the *Regesta Pontificum Romanorum*.] demonstrates the proceedings concerning Ignatius and Photius and prescribes the chronological order of the letters.

[In Mansi, same place.]

NICOLAS, bishop of the holy Catholic and apostolic Roman Church, to all ministers of the true religion and to all orthodox worshipers of the faith—namely, the most holy and reverend patriarchs, metropolitans, and other bishops, and all the faithful throughout Asia and Libya who follow exclusively, with us, devotion to the Catholic see of blessed Peter and defend sound doctrine.

We do not believe that your Holiness—or your religious devotion—is unaware of what happened shortly before at the city of Constantinople or what is still happening there. But because, burning with zeal for the house of God and, according to the Apostle, carrying concern for all the Churches (2 Cor. 11), we had determined what should be done concerning these matters, we briefly make it known to your charity in this letter of our apostolate.

And lest anyone attempt to persuade your sincere mind otherwise, or report to you differently what we have done, we inform you by a truthful account and by this present letter. After certain men, inflamed by the torches of envy and arrogantly puffed up by the pride of arrogance, rose up like the Jews against their own shepherd and tyrannically cast out their patriarch—the most holy Ignatius, our fellow minister and bishop of that aforesaid city—from the very church over which he rightly presided, they brought a certain Photius out of the forum, secular military service, and secular dress, as well as from the imperial palace; suddenly tonsured him; and, contrary to the sacred canons, placed him over that Church.

Then scandal and schism began to arise to no small degree in that city and in the neighboring cities: some defending Photius’s promotion, while others rightly detested it as having been carried out while Ignatius remained alive and had not been convicted.

Then Emperor Michael, who himself, persuaded by the cunning of the patrician Bardas, favored Photius’s party, took counsel and sent legates to our apostolate with letters, bringing certain accusations against Ignatius. He requested that we send men from the apostolic see who would calm those scandals and disperse the schisms.

When we heard this, because—as your prudence, inspired by God, knows—we are bound by concern for all Christ’s sheep, since we hold the place of him to whom it is especially said by God, “Feed my sheep” (John 21), and again, “When you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22), we could neither dissemble nor neglect to visit the scattered and dispersed sheep, or to strengthen our brothers and neighbors in faith and good conduct.

Moreover, among the other things reported by those who had been sent concerning the schism already created in the Church of Constantinople, they particularly stated that the same Church was being harassed by the Iconoclasts, who were reviving the controversy, and that Christ was being blasphemed in each of their assemblies. Therefore, together with the Church here, we sent to Constantinople two bishops who were with us and whom we considered suitable for carrying out this task—namely, Rodoald and Zacharias—abhorring so great a sacrilege and sending them from our side by letters.

We imposed no duty upon them except that they should carefully investigate the case of Ignatius, who had been driven from the Church before being accused by anyone, and report it fully and truthfully to the apostolic see.

We decreed not only that Photius’s consecration was by no means to be admitted, but also expressly and under every form of command instructed our legates not to communicate with him, except as with a layman, until the matter came to our knowledge. We granted them permission only to decide justly and piously whatever question might arise concerning the venerable images of our Lord Jesus Christ, his ever-virgin mother Mary, and his saints.

But when they went, they disregarded our admonitions, ignored the letters given to them by us before our entire Church, and, as later became clear, set aside the fear of God and turned everything they had been ordered to do into its opposite. Finally, contrary to the repeated and complete prohibition given to them, they communicated in the sacred mysteries with the adulterer, invader of the Church, and neophyte Photius.

They also condemned Ignatius, an old and holy man who had governed the Church of God innocently for twelve years and had remained in communion with us, with you, and with the universal orthodox Church, aligning themselves with the most pernicious faction of the Greeks. They stripped him of his sacerdotal insignia and expelled him by every means from the governance of the Church.

We have already made known to your holy fraternity in Christ and to your devout assembly that these things were done contrary to our disposition. Our aforementioned legates eventually returned and reported nothing other than that Ignatius had been deposed and Photius established in the see of Constantinople.

Two days later an imperial legate, named Leo, a secretary, was received by us and presented two volumes. One contained the proceedings concerning Ignatius’s deposition; the other contained the acts concerning the holy images. The same Leo also brought imperial letters requesting that we give and subscribe our consent both to Ignatius’s deposition and to Photius’s confirmation.

But while that legate was present, by the grace of God our teacher, we summoned the entire Church here and decreed, established, and professed before him and before the Church of God—as we also profess—that we had never sent anyone for the deposition of Ignatius or the consecration of Photius, and that we had never consented and would never consent to Ignatius’s deposition or Photius’s promotion.

After repeatedly stating and publicly announcing these things, inserting them in this form into the letters of our apostolate, and giving them to Leo, the imperial secretary, to convey to the emperor Michael or to Photius, we dismissed him.

Having shown these matters to your sincere religious devotion, we demonstrate below, appended individually to this document, the writings that we sent at the various stages concerning this affair. First are the letters of our apostolate sent through Rodoald and Zacharias to Michael, the most devout emperor, and to Photius, the invader of the Church of Constantinople.

Second is our response, the text of which we sent some time ago to your general body preserved by God. But because we did not know whether it had reached you, we thought it should be sent to you again, so that you might know what our will was concerning this affair.

Third is placed the letter that, after the return of our legates, we sent to the aforementioned Augustus Michael through Leo, the imperial secretary and legate whom we mentioned above, together with another letter to Photius.

Moreover, the writings that follow have been inserted into this volume in the order in which they are known to have been produced or sent at the successive stages.

(Year 866.) CVII. TO THE BISHOPS OF THE SYNOD OF SOISSONS. He severely reproves Hincmar for having acted craftily and evasively in the case of the deposed clerics, and for having dared to produce mutilated and corrupted letters of Pope Benedict. He therefore orders the bishops to meet again and to set down the history of the clerics accurately, while the clerics are meanwhile to be restored to their respective ranks. He does not approve, however, of their having promoted Wlfad to the episcopate before his full restoration.

[In Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 1093C]

NICOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy fellow brothers, the archbishops and bishops who, by God’s grace and our decree, have assembled near the city of Soissons.

Most Reverend brother and our fellow bishop Egilo, from your sacred college, arriving at the apostolic see, we received with great rejoicing. Learning through him of the good health of all of you, we became all the happier and offered immense thanks to the Author. We considered this especially good and welcome: that we have discovered you, brothers, to have dwelt together as one not only in body but also in mind, and that, together with our spirit, you possessed one heart and one soul in the relief of the deposed brothers. [Col. 1093D]

The assembly of priests testifies to the presence of the Holy Spirit, and those who gather together in his name show that they have the Lord in their midst. For no consideration permitted us to disregard the outcry of those same deposed clerics, and paternal charity did not allow us to close our ears to their cries, repeatedly sent to the apostolic see even under my predecessors. We bear the burdens of all who are burdened; indeed, blessed Peter the Apostle bears them in us, for, as we trust, he protects and guards us as heirs of his administration in all things. [Col. 1094A]

When, however, we were carefully investigating certain documents delivered to the apostolic see at various times, or even issued by it, in order to discover the truth of this matter, it happened that, by God’s revelation, the acts of the council which is known to have separated the aforesaid men under the authority of our brother and fellow bishop Hincmar came into our hands together with the proceedings concerning the venerable Bishop Rothad, having long ago been sent to us by that same venerable bishop. If we wished to set out one by one the mass of criticisms found in them, paper would run out more readily than words.

There, indeed, falsehood is found immediately at the beginning of the proceedings themselves. [Col. 1094B] Is it not falsehood when those deposed are said to have come voluntarily to the church doors out of necessity, though they are proved to have come unwillingly? Especially since Wlfadus was not there, although his name was deceitfully recited among the names of the petitioners.
