There it is recognized that judgment had already been given before the time of examination and condemnation had occurred before a lawful trial. There, before a hearing and before a definite number of bishops had assembled, priests and deacons were subjected to deprivation of their ministries.

There the metropolitan bishop sometimes lays down his rights and sometimes resumes them; sometimes he is subject to the synod, sometimes he presides over it; sometimes he approaches as though accused, sometimes as accuser, sometimes as judge. Arranging everything at his pleasure through alternating roles, he appears like a certain living creature that is not always of one and the same color. [Col. 1094C]

There, I say, men unwilling to make a formal protest are compelled to protest, and are forced, as though they were accusers, to submit a written petition of protest. Our brother Hincmar, however, did not insert the text of the petition in the proceedings according to custom, although he is shown to have inserted in them certain matters that were even less necessary.

There, a man who was absent—and, as it is stated there, ill—is condemned, and pain is added to pain: the absent Wlfadus is entered in the petition as though present, and, while lying in bed and never making a protest, is falsely alleged to have joined the other protesters who were present. Here one must consider that, if the laws of the world do not compel a sick man to answer even concerning financial matters outside himself, how much less should any sick priest of the Lord have been compelled to make a complaint concerning a matter that was recognized as being contrived against that very man and that was evidently driving him toward deposition? Where, I ask, is there greater pain in this life? [Col. 1094D]

To encompass almost everything briefly: there, the sole obedience of subjects, which the Apostle commands them to show their superiors, is counted as guilt; and those who did not rashly resist the judgment of their prelate but humbly submitted their necks are punished with the utmost severity.

There, men who committed no personal offense suffered the condemnation of heretics as though they themselves were heretics, and those who sought mercy did not even merit receiving a just judgment.

But what wonder if the text and conclusion of that council were not accepted, when it was not begun in the name of the Lord according to custom? For since the Apostle commands that whatever we do in word or deed, everything must be done in the name of the Lord Jesus (Colossians 3), and since ecclesiastical custom observes this in convening councils—and only in this instance, by the hidden permission of divine judgment, was it omitted—it is beyond doubt that they were not gathered in the name of the Lord. Consequently, they had him in no way in their midst: contrary to the Psalmist, they assembled such a council—or rather, their own cabals—out of bloodshed (Psalm 13), and, imitating a certain animal, thought that they could survive only once their own offspring had been killed. [Col. 1095A]

Now, if the same council is claimed to have been approved by the apostolic see, we briefly inform your fraternity by what crafty sophistry this was obtained from the apostolic see. [Col. 1095B]

Our brother and fellow bishop Hincmar, concerning the aforementioned clerics—namely Wlfadus and his associates—sent more than once to my predecessor, the bishop Leo of blessed memory, letters of supplication, asking him to approve that council and strengthen it with apostolic authority, as he himself thought appropriate. Leo not only gave no assent whatsoever, but also took care to act cautiously. He said that he had therefore suspended Hincmar’s requests for confirmation of the synod in which the aforesaid men had been deposed: some of the bishops who had sat in the synod ought first to send him its statutes, so that every doubt might be eradicated at its root, especially since legates of the apostolic see had not been present there.

Finally, Leo suspended his assent because those whom Hincmar claimed had been deposed by the authority of the synod had appealed to the apostolic see in their own letters, wished to be heard in the apostolic presence, and, if they were found guilty, did not refuse to undergo canonical censure. [Col. 1095C]

Yet the venerable Hincmar, knowing that that council—as shown above—was stained with many criticisms, did not send its acts through any of the bishops who had taken part in it. Nevertheless, he did not cease to press his requests anew so that they might be confirmed. But as the repeated outcry of the deposed clerics grew louder, the praiseworthy bishop still did not grant what was sought.

He did, however, order by another letter of his decree that our brother Hincmar should come with them to the council to which he himself had sent his own legate, namely Peter, Bishop of Spoleto, from his side. The purpose was to renew the judgment in his place and, with the bishops assembled again, to weigh and, with the Lord’s help, settle the dispute concerning the deposed men who were protesting. [Col. 1095D]

Thus, if it should happen that those deposed clerics ought to remain in their deposition and refused to obey, but again sought the apostolic see, permission to come to it was not to be denied them, lest the privilege of the apostolic see be dissolved. Hincmar or his representative was ordered to come with them, so that he could confer a just judgment concerning them with his fellow bishops and, when both parties had been heard, that holy see could canonically settle their cases.

But he who had earlier withheld from the sight of the apostolic see the bishop who was the legate of his council also withdrew his own presence from the hearing appointed by the apostolic see. In doing so, he proved true of himself what has been said—namely, that he had established such a council as was briefly described above. [Col. 1096A]

Meanwhile, when this hope had been frustrated, Pope Leo of the apostolic see, who knew of Hincmar’s purpose, was taken from this light. When Benedict of holy memory, an apostolic man, succeeded him in the pontificate, the reverend Hincmar again prepared his weapons. He secretly took advantage of that supreme bishop as though he were inexperienced in Hincmar’s stratagems, and at the very beginning of his consecration persuaded him to confirm a council convened at the desire of one man.

Yet he could neither secretly induce nor persuade Benedict in any way to turn even slightly from the path of just definition and the most discerning moderation. Nevertheless, as you can see—and perhaps have now recognized yourselves—he strengthened the council’s enactment by granting it a certain privilege, reserving to the apostolic see the highest authority. As we have already written to you, he thereby granted honor to the other without diminishing what he granted to himself. [Col. 1096B]

Thus it came about that what had been wrongly requested was granted by the wise bishop, instructed by the Spirit of God, and human deception achieved nothing where divine inspiration filled the breast of so great a pontiff. Nor did the persuasion of one man prevail where the prudent and most provident moderation of the holy bishop intervened. For in the very privilege he prefaced the condition that the matters requested would remain unshaken only if everything concerning that synod was exactly as our brother Hincmar had reported to him.

He inserted in it an ambiguous sentence, saying:

“If it is so, and as you have conveyed it to our bishopric in your letters and demonstrated it in the sequence of the proceedings, we proclaim by apostolic authority that these matters—or rather, these definitions—are ratified.” [Col. 1096C]

He himself, however, extracted this qualification from the text of the privilege he had granted, withheld it from our sight, and concealed it from the knowledge of others. He also inserted statements that the same supreme pontiff had either never decreed or had decreed differently.

For concerning the aforesaid definitions he said:

“We proclaim by apostolic authority that these matters are ratified and establish that they shall always remain in force,”

and then followed the rest, which he himself set down differently, while our brother Hincmar added certain things, removed many others, and otherwise recounted the matter. [Col. 1096D]

But Hincmar’s remarkable craft again appears in another matter, joined to a prudence that serves only his private wish. When Pope Benedict, our predecessor of revered memory, had granted him the privilege of which we have just spoken, he confirmed its contents in such a way that he attached to them a suspended judgment and, in every respect, reserved his privileges to the apostolic see—as we have already said—and its own rights of authority, which in this we too have followed.

Moreover, he imposed the bonds of anathema upon those whom he judged should be prohibited from stubbornly resisting any of the same canonical constitutions and decrees of the Roman pontiffs—that is, from attempting to act against either what he had granted to our brother Hincmar or what he had reserved to his own see. [Col. 1097A]

But Hincmar made public everything in these provisions that he saw favored his own desire, while concealing from everyone’s knowledge what had been reserved to the right of the apostolic see. The copies of that same privilege that he sent to the apostolic see at different times bear witness to this.

You yourselves have already been able to notice how harmful such corruption and mutilation of documents is. For, when you saw certain provisions of his decree in the council but did not see others—as we have learned from your report—you would now be recognized as having abandoned, discouraged, an incomplete pious effort on behalf of the oppressed, unless you had been instructed by our admonitions and strengthened there by our letters. [Col. 1097B]

The aforementioned bishop had often indicated in his letters to my predecessor of distinguished memory that those same clerics had appealed to neighboring bishops, had submitted a petition of protest against him, had chosen judges for themselves, and other matters too lengthy to enumerate.

But Leo, inspired by God, wrote back to him:

“If it is so, and as you have conveyed it to our bishopric in your letters and demonstrated it in the sequence of the proceedings”—words that brother Hincmar entirely erased from the text—“we proclaim that these matters” (the definitions are understood) “are ratified by apostolic authority,” without the words “in all respects,” which Hincmar himself added, “and we establish that they shall always remain in force.”

Then it was added that the matter should be arranged “so that no dispute might at any time arise from it,” which he changed entirely and expressed in a very different manner. [Col. 1097C]

Now, since it has been proved by us and by your holy council that the matter was not so, what he had proposed was rightly nullified: he had not straightforwardly obtained what he sought against the deposed men.

But let us return to our subject. At last, since the clerics so often mentioned—who had always appealed to the apostolic see—also set out in their letters to us their complaint concerning their deposition, we had no freedom to dissemble or to remain silent, since a greater zeal for the whole Christian religion rests upon us than upon anyone else.

Therefore we first sent word to our brother and fellow bishop Hincmar, urging him to strive, with a merciful disposition, to call the aforementioned men—namely Wlfadus and his associates—back to himself; to lay aside every animosity completely; to discuss their restoration with them as a brother; and to bring the matter to a merciful conclusion. Otherwise, he was to come together with them to the council with you, to whom we also wrote for this very purpose. [Col. 1097D]

Then, all of you assembling together, you were to examine the cases of those clerics and settle them, with God before your eyes, without allowing any dispute to arise. But if any dispute arose between the parties, representatives of both sides, acting in the place of the persons concerned, were to come to the apostolic see to receive its special judgment.

With the help of God’s grace, this was done, and we have now received letters expressing the cherished devotion of all of you. They clearly indicate that the frequently mentioned clerics were declared worthy of being restored to their grades by the council’s united voice. [Col. 1098A]

No dispute arose, as we find in your same letters; no difference among the several defenders occurred, as had been supposed; no accuser and no condemner was found. Rather, one and the same judgment of all, and a clear decision concerning their restoration, was made evident, with those innocent men approved in every respect by the unanimity of everyone.

Although you did not proceed solemnly, nor, as we had decreed, disclose to the apostolic see the complete sequence of the proceedings in a full report, to such an extent that, with the acts of your council almost unknown, we were nearly deterred from deciding what should be done concerning the status of the often-mentioned clerics, had not the labor of our predecessors, found among us in written records of past events, finally encouraged us to complete the matter fully. [Col. 1098B]

You ought to have informed us unanimously, fully, and faithfully in writing of everything that had been discussed there concerning Ebbo’s deposition and restoration, the promotion of these clerics, Ebbo’s second rejection and migration to another church, and anything else whatsoever that had been debated there. You ought not merely to have informed us of it, but also to have inserted it into the records and preserved it for our fuller knowledge and certainty.

Since this was omitted through negligence, at least now take every care to gather whatever writings concerning this matter are found to have been issued both by us previously and now and by you, together with what our fellow bishop Hincmar and those deposed clerics suggested and reported to the apostolic see. Arrange these documents in a single volume in the order in which they were sent, and dispatch it with the utmost diligence to the apostolic see, while retaining their copies as is proper. [Col. 1098C]

When this has been carefully done, we shall then be able to know fully that you acted energetically in the council; and what has so far been omitted will, with Christ’s help, be recovered in this manner. In carrying this out, however, it is fitting that you undertake especially abundant care for the venerable Wlfadus.

Furthermore, we wish you to be vigilant that, if anything of this kind should happen again in the future, for which we order a gathering of priests to be held in your regions, you do not consign this matter to oblivion among the others. After everything else, make every effort to carry it out with the greatest diligence, following the custom of your predecessors.

The profession of our brother and fellow bishop Hincmar also agrees with this unanimous judgment and decision of yours. [Col. 1098D] He testifies not only that he had previously neither suspended these same brothers from office, nor judged them, nor expelled them from their grades, nor subscribed to their rejection, but also that he has now come to the synod, as we ordered, readily assented to what the other bishops agreed concerning their restoration, and took care to obey.

His name, moreover, is found written in the synodal letter, as our report indicates, together with your names—that is, the names of those who are recognized as having assembled together.

Nevertheless, it was amusing to read that the same bishop admits that he had not suspended the frequently mentioned clerics from office, judged them, expelled them from their grades, or subscribed to their rejection. This is especially remarkable since many indications prove that these assertions are not supported by truth. [Col. 1099A] We touched on them briefly above and now omit mentioning them more fully for the sake of brevity.

For unless he suspended them from office even before any hearing, when they had approached him not as accusers but as petitioners for mercy, what does it mean that the acts of his council, which he himself sent to the apostolic see, record that they had been suspended from office by him? Since he remained silent and answered nothing, what else can his silence clearly be understood to grant except that they had reported the truth?

And, conversely, against whom were they repeatedly sending their complaints to the aforementioned Pope Leo of holy memory? Whom other than him did they repeatedly reveal as the man who had driven them from their own grades and was hostile to them—someone whom, in his dealings with them, they ought to have recognized as a kindly father? [Col. 1099B]

Finally, unless he subscribed to their deposition—or rather, unless he himself wrote the entire sequence of their deposition—what does it mean that, in the privilege mentioned below, which he asked the apostolic see to confirm for him, my predecessor of blessed memory, addressing him, declares that he himself had confirmed those definitions in the synod assembled with the other bishops, by his own hand, according to his own report?

If he says that he never subscribed in that synod, then our predecessor did not confirm any synod for him by his privilege. For he expressly recalls that the synod which he established by apostolic authority had been specifically confirmed by Hincmar’s own hand.

Therefore, dearest brothers, you should know that, with all the arguments mentioned above properly assembled and the general encouragement of your unanimous consensus urging us on, we have been able to give our full consent to the restoration of the aforesaid clerics to their grades. [Col. 1099C]

But since their examination did not proceed according to our decree as a pure and complete investigation; since it was not clearly established what their promotion or rejection had been in the synodal assembly; and since this was not demonstrated to the apostolic see by a sufficient report, we therefore judged it necessary for the time being to restrain our deliberative consent from completing their restoration.

Yet since our authority preceded the decision and judgment of what had been canonically deliberated, as well as the restoration of the often-mentioned clerics and everything else that, with God leading, was fitting and required by due order, it is appropriate and honorable that, in accordance with your request, the complete integrity of our confirmation should follow. [Col. 1099D]

This is to occur in the following order: the frequently mentioned clerics, who are clearly known to have been irregularly suspended from their offices and grades and who are proved by several indications to have appealed very often to the apostolic see, shall first be restored to their former grades and offices. Thus, once returned to their former grades and orders and, as it were, reclothed in all that was theirs, they shall possess their full strength against those who attack them. An unarmed man cannot properly enter combat with an armed one.

Once they are enjoying these grades and offices, our brother and fellow bishop Hincmar shall have permission, within the course of this entire year, to prove canonically that the clerics often mentioned were expelled from their orders. [Col. 1100A] Whatever accusations he has, he shall have complete freedom to prosecute and pursue them.

But if, after the whole course of this year has elapsed, he brings no just complaint against them before the apostolic see, nor strives to accuse them of any crime or offense or condemnation whatsoever, then, while they remain in their orders, we shall certainly give ourselves over to no sluggishness and shall cease from no utmost diligence, until either he now proves that they were justly restored or himself justly demonstrates that they were once removed.

Otherwise, it will undoubtedly be fitting for us subsequently to present not only the often-mentioned clerics, who were prejudicially and without canonical basis removed from office, but also their ordainer, who was improperly and without ecclesiastical procedure deprived of episcopal governance. [Col. 1100B] On this matter, we believe, no one at all except him doubts; indeed, no one fails to proclaim it, since it is equally clear to us, as far as we can judge, and to those who are recorded as having been present at that time.

Dearest brothers, we also thought that the following matter ought not to be passed over among the others. As the sequence of your report suggests, you executed the regular provisions of our decree less cautiously than we had prescribed.

Although we decreed that the case of the clerics who had appealed to the apostolic see and provoked its judgment should be heard, or even decided, there, in order to remove from you the burden of a longer journey, we did not grant permission for any of them to be promoted or advanced to a higher order. Yet we have now learned from your favorable letters that this was done. [Col. 1100C]

We are also astonished and ask what that “supreme authority” of the matter is which you claim to have reserved to our authority. We cannot find it. What authority over the case did you reserve to us when you hastened to bring it to its conclusion so completely that, without consulting us, you even allowed pastoral responsibility to be conferred upon them? Although you needed our authority to restore them to their former grade, you did not think it necessary to await our response before promoting them.

As for how much our son, the glorious King Charles, demanded this from us, we always wrote back to him that, rightly preserving your devotion and honor—you whom we had already ordered to assemble—we would in no way give our consent beforehand, before the outcome of the matter had been made known to us through you. Brothers, since you did not observe this even in the slightest, I praise you—but in this matter I do not praise you. [Col. 1100D]

Furthermore, if anyone claims that the apostolic see, through Pope Sergius of holy memory, condemned Ebbo, the former archbishop, as unworthy of clerical communion, let him know that the apostolic see ought to have regarded Ebbo as such until his case had been examined by a synodal investigation, just as it knew that he was regarded by the others.

For he had read that the great and venerable Council of Nicaea had established that, concerning those deprived of communion, whether from the clergy or from the lay order, a regular judgment of the bishops in each province should prevail: those who are rejected should not be received by others. An inquiry must also be made, so that no one may appear to have been excluded from the congregation through the faintheartedness, contentiousness, or any other fault of a bishop. [Col. 1101A]

Until, therefore, by its own authority an examination or judgment had determined whether such faintheartedness, contentiousness, or any other fault was involved, the apostolic see ought to have done nothing except what it did—namely, it should not itself have received without investigation one who had been rejected by others.

This was especially so because the aforesaid Ebbo did not appeal to the apostolic see as someone complaining about his deposition and wishing to be lawfully restored after a prior examination. Rather, as the episcopal record indicates, having been persuaded by the contumacious and joined to them, he suddenly approached it, seeking reconciliation with them and adornment with the pallium, and requesting to communicate as a bishop among bishops, without any examination of his case having preceded. [Col. 1101B]

Having already been rejected by others, he deserved to be rejected by that same supreme see until he humbly requested its canonical assistance.

For it is established, as holy Pope Gelasius writes (Letter 11 to the Dardani), that no see ought to execute more fully than the first see the decree of any synod approved by the assent of the universal Church. The first see confirms each synod by its authority and guards it through continual moderation, in accordance with its primacy, which blessed Peter the Apostle received at the Lord’s command and which the Church, following after him, has both always held and continues to hold.

Nevertheless, whatever Ebbo may have been or whatever he may have suffered, he caused no offense whatsoever to those whom he himself ordained, since they displayed nothing except humility and obedience. [Col. 1101C]

For the most blessed Leo, writing to the Moors, gives the following instruction concerning a certain Maximus (Letter 91):

“Although Maximus was ordained reprehensibly, nevertheless, if he is no longer a Donatist and is alien to the spirit of schismatic perversity, we do not deprive him of the episcopal dignity which, in whatever manner, he attained.”

And Anastasius, bishop of that same apostolic see, demonstrates with the clearest reasoning, in a letter to the emperor Anastasius, that evil men harm only themselves when administering good things, and do not stain the sacraments of the Church.

We pray that your holy fraternity may now and always prosper in Christ. [Col. 1101D]

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of December, in the fifteenth indiction.

**(In the year 866.) CVIII. TO HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS.** Of the same subject as the preceding letter. For it exposes Hincmar’s frauds concerning the deposed clerics and concerning the letters of Pope Benedict. Near the end it also reproves him because he was said to be using the pallium beyond the proper limit.

[In Mansi, same place.]

**NICHOLAS**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy brother **HINCMAR**, archbishop of Rheims.

Receiving the letter of Your Beatitude together with the synodal letter, sent through a legate of that same sacred college of yours—namely, our brother and fellow bishop Egilo—[Col. 1102A] we have once again recognized, both from the letters themselves and from the words of that venerable man, your devotion and submissive reverence toward the Apostolic See; and we praise your perpetual goodwill, which you say you have readily shown toward the deposed brothers and sons. Certainly, you indicate that, in accordance with the Apostle, you have wept with those who weep, and now make clear that you rejoice with those who rejoice (Rom. 12).

Reason allowed us no grounds for disregarding the cry of these clerics, nor did paternal charity permit us to close our ears to their outcries, repeatedly sent to the Apostolic See even under my predecessors. For we bear the burdens of all who are weighed down; indeed, blessed Peter the Apostle bears them in us—he who, as we trust, protects and guards us in every respect as the heirs of his administration. [Col. 1102B]

Now, while we were carefully investigating certain documents delivered to the Apostolic See at various times, or issued from it, in order to discover the certainty of this matter, it happened—by God’s revealing it—that the proceedings of the council which, as is evident, separated the aforementioned men under your authority, and which you had formerly sent to us together with the proceedings concerning the venerable bishop Rothadus, came into our hands. If we wished to set out one by one the mass of reproaches found in them, paper would run out more readily than words.

There, indeed, falsehood is found immediately at the very beginning of the proceedings. Is it not falsehood when you yourself describe those deposed men as having voluntarily come to the doors of the church out of necessity, although they are proved to have come unwillingly? Especially since Wlfadus was not present there, yet his name was deceitfully recited among the names of those making petition. There it is evident that judgment had already been rendered before the time of examination and that condemnation had already been pronounced before a legitimate trial.

There, before a hearing and before a definite number of bishops had assembled, priests and deacons were subjected to deprivation of their ministries. There the metropolitan bishop at one moment lays down his rights and at another resumes them; at one moment he is subject to the synod and at another presides over it; at one moment he approaches as though accused and at another as accuser; at one moment he acts as judge, arranging everything according to his own inclination through alternating roles. Like some living creature, he does not always appear in one single and consistent form.

There, I say, men who did not wish to lodge a complaint are compelled to lodge one, and are forced, as though they were accusers, to submit a written statement of complaint, although you did not insert the text of the petition into the official proceedings according to custom, while you are shown to have inserted other matters that were even less necessary. There Wlfadus, absent and—as it is recorded there—ill, is condemned, and pain is added to pain: although absent, he is entered in the petition as though present; and, lying in bed and never lodging a protest, he is falsely alleged to have joined the protesters who were present. [Col. 1102D]

Here one must consider that, if the laws of the world do not compel a sick person to answer even concerning financial matters external to him, how much less ought any infirm servant of the Lord to have been compelled by the priests of the Lord to lodge a complaint concerning a matter that was evidently being brought against that very person and that was proved to be driving him toward the fall of deposition! Where, I ask, is there greater pain in this life?

And, to embrace almost everything in brief: there the sole obedience of subjects, which the Apostle commands them to show toward their superiors (Heb. 13), is counted as guilt; and those who did not rashly resist the judgment of their superiors but humbly submitted their necks are punished with the utmost severity. There those who committed no offense of their own incurred the condemnation of heretics as though they were heretics, and those who asked for mercy did not deserve to receive a just judgment.

But what wonder if the text and conclusion of that council were not accepted, when it was not begun in the name of the Lord according to custom? For although the Apostle commands that whatever we do in word or deed should all be done in the name of the Lord Jesus (Col. 3), and although ecclesiastical custom observes this in assembling councils, this alone was omitted, with divine judgment permitting the hidden matter. It is therefore beyond doubt that they were not assembled in the name of the Lord, and consequently did not have him in their midst—those who, contrary to the Psalmist, assembled such a council—indeed, their own gatherings—from men of blood (Ps. 15), and, imitating a certain animal, thought that they could survive only after their own offspring had been slaughtered.

Moreover, if the same council is claimed to have been approved by the Apostolic See, Your Fraternity knows how it was craftily represented as having been commanded by that See. After you had completed what seemed good to you concerning the aforementioned clerics—namely, Wlfadus and his colleagues—you sent more than once a suppliant letter to my predecessor, Bishop Leo of blessed memory, asking him to approve that council and strengthen it by apostolic authority. He not only refused to grant this, but also resolutely declined to act, saying that he had suspended your petitions for confirming the synod in which the aforementioned men had been deposed because, in order that every doubt might be uprooted from the foundation, you ought to have sent the statutes of that synod through some of the bishops who had sat in it—especially since representatives of the Apostolic See had not been present there. [Col. 1103D]

Finally, he said that these men, whom you affirmed in your letters had been deposed by the authority of the synod, had appealed by their own letters to the Apostolic See and wished to be heard again in the presence of that See; and that, if they were found guilty then, they would not refuse to undergo the Catholic censure.

Yet Your Reverence, knowing that this council—as shown above—was stained by no small number of reproaches, did not send its proceedings through any of the bishops who had taken part in it. Nevertheless, you did not cease to press your requests anew so that they might be confirmed. But as the repeated outcry of the deposed clerics grew louder, the praiseworthy bishop still did not grant what was requested.

Rather, in another letter of his decree, he ordered that you yourself should come with them to the council to which he had sent his own legate from his side—namely, Peter, bishop of Spoleto—in order to renew the judgment in his place and, with the bishops assembled again, to weigh and settle, with the Lord’s help, the case of the deposed protesters. Thus, if it should happen to those same deposed clerics that they ought to remain in their deposition and they refused to obey but again sought the Apostolic See, permission to come to it was not to be denied them, lest the privilege of that Apostolic See be dissolved.

He ordered that Your Fraternity or your representative should come with them, so that you might confer a fair judgment concerning them with your brother bishops and, when both parties had met, that the same holy See might canonically determine their cases. But you had previously withdrawn the bishop—your council’s representative—from the sight of the Apostolic See; and, by likewise withdrawing your own presence from the hearing designated by that See, you proved concerning yourself what has been said—namely, that you had established such a council as has been shown above.

Meanwhile, when the result you desired had been frustrated, Pope Leo, the pontiff of the Apostolic See and of blessed memory, who knew the intention of Your Fraternity, was taken from this light. When Benedict, the apostolic man of holy memory, had succeeded him in the order of the pontificate, Your Reverence once again prepares your weapons and secretly deceives that supreme bishop, as though he were inexperienced in your craftiness. At the very beginning of his consecration you persuaded him to confirm a council assembled at the will of one man. Yet he could in no way be deceived or persuaded into departing even slightly from the path of just judgment and exceedingly discerning moderation.

For, as can be seen—and as you yourself clearly know, since you are recognized as keeping in your possession a copy of that privilege—he strengthened the enactment of that council by the privilege granted to you in such a way that he reserved the fullness of authority to the Apostolic See. Thus it came about that what had been wrongly requested was granted by the bishop who, taught by God’s Spirit, judged wisely; and human deception accomplished nothing where divine inspiration filled the heart of so great a pontiff. Nor did anyone’s persuasion do harm where the wise and most provident moderation of the holy bishop intervened.

For in the privilege itself he prefaced the condition that the things requested were to remain unshaken only if they were in every respect as Your Holiness had reported them to him concerning that synod. He inserted an ambiguous statement, saying:

“If this is so, and as you have informed our bishopric in your letters and demonstrated in the sequence of the proceedings, we promulgate by apostolic authority that these same—and indeed the definitions—are approved.”

Although you, receiving the wording of this statement from the text of the privilege granted to you less than honestly, removed it from our sight and concealed it from the knowledge of others, inserting in addition matters that he had either never decreed or had decreed differently.

For he himself said concerning the aforementioned definitions: “We promulgate by apostolic authority that these same things are approved, and we decree that they shall always remain,” followed by the rest. But you presented it differently, adding and changing the wording, when you wrote: “We promulgate by apostolic authority that these same things are approved in every respect, and we decree that they shall always remain, so that no controversy may ever arise from them at any time.” [Col. 1105A]

You yourself can judge how greatly the words he promulgated differ from what you diminished, added, or changed.

But there is still another remarkable piece of cunning on Your Fraternity’s part, accompanied by a prudence that favors only your own desire. When our same predecessor, Pope Benedict of apostolic holiness and blessed memory, had conferred upon you the privilege of which we have just spoken, he confirmed its contents in such a way as to join to them a suspended sentence, reserving inviolate, in every respect, to the Apostolic See its privileges—as we have already said—and the rights of its own authority, which we too have followed in this matter.

Moreover, he inserted the bonds of anathema against those whom he judged must be prohibited from obstinately opposing any of the canonical constitutions and decrees of the Roman pontiffs—that is, from attempting to act against what he had granted to you or what he had reserved to the rights of his own See.

But you disclosed to everyone’s knowledge whatever you saw favored your own inclination, while concealing from everyone’s understanding what had been reserved to the jurisdiction of the Apostolic See. Copies of that same privilege, sent to the Apostolic See at different times, testify to this.

How much harm such corruption or mutilation of documents causes you could now observe, together with your brothers and fellow bishops. For, as we learned from their own report, when they saw certain provisions of that enactment at the council but did not see others, they were deterred and were on the point of abandoning the pious work begun on behalf of the oppressed in an incomplete state—unless they had been instructed by our admonitions and strengthened there by our letters. [Col. 1105C]

For this reason, perhaps, we could justly acknowledge that you have committed some fraud in such matters, had our moderation not wished to spare Your Reverence something you yourself do not expect. For the truncation of reports not only removes knowledge from people but also leads those who hear them into error.

For example, we say: “The Lord our God is just, and there is no injustice in him.” If a single syllable is removed, blasphemy against God is immediately committed without hesitation. If the removal of only one syllable produces such sacrilege against God, how great a loss do you think the cutting away of so many words can produce for those who do not know the facts?

There is, however, another matter in this deed that must be considered carefully. The insertion of the anathema strikes not only those who act against the benefits granted to you but also those who rashly dissolve the rights of the Apostolic See. Yet you, while suppressing that part of the anathema which concerns the privileges of the Apostolic See, mentioned it after the text of the command granted to you only insofar as it pleased you. It is therefore plainly evident that by this device you craftily touched upon us in such a way that, while it is certainly clear that the bond of anathema strikes those who do not observe the decree of our predecessor, the right of the Apostolic See nevertheless remains unimpaired—provided that what was reported had been proved true in every respect.

Therefore, what we did in the case of the deposed clerics belongs to the privilege of the Apostolic See, and consequently we are rightly free from liability in that matter. You, however, are held liable for violating that same privilege: for, when those clerics appealed to the Apostolic See after being expelled, you are seen to have craftily placed an obstacle in their way, and consequently are thought more appropriately to have incurred the penalty of anathema imposed in that enactment.

This is because, by your addition, truncation, and alteration, you repeatedly displayed the text and wording of the often-mentioned privilege to everyone in such a form that it could rightly instill fear and despair in the aforementioned clerics and completely turn them away from the protest they had begun.

Since you knew that we customarily preserve in the registers of the Roman Church copies of documents issued by the Apostolic See, and since you could infer that we had personally seen those documents when they were issued under my predecessor, you did not fear sending us the same enactment mutilated and corrupted. How much more corrupted and fraudulent a version might you perhaps have presented for the overthrow of those enduring oppression, who had no experience of the matter!

You ought certainly, dearest brother, to have avoided this matter with the greatest care—fearing that, if you did not appear to be acting against the privilege repeatedly mentioned as having been granted to you, or against the principal right of the Apostolic See, you might at least be found, God forbid, to be a falsifier in some respect, contrary to priestly modesty.

For in your written communication to my predecessor of outstanding memory, you reported that those same clerics had appealed to neighboring bishops, had submitted a written complaint against you, had chosen judges for themselves, and other matters too lengthy to enumerate. [Col. 1106C] But he, inspired by God, wrote back to you:

“If this is so, and as you have informed our bishopric in your letters and demonstrated in the sequence of the proceedings”—words which you entirely erased from the text—“we promulgate by apostolic authority that these same things” (that is, the definitions) “are approved”—not “in every respect,” as you yourself added—“and we decree that they shall always remain.”

It then continued with a statement which you altered entirely, writing: “so that no controversy may ever arise from them at any time.”

Now, since both we and your holy council have established that the matter was not as you had reported, what you had previously sought has rightly been annulled, since you had not obtained it straightforwardly against the deposed men.

But let us return to the matter at hand.

At last, when the often-mentioned clerics—who had always appealed to the Apostolic See—had also explained their complaint about their deposition to us in their letters, we had no freedom to dissemble or remain silent. For the zeal of the entire Christian religion rests upon us more heavily than upon all others.

Accordingly, we first sent you a letter so that you might kindly make an effort to recall the aforementioned men—namely, Wlfadus and his colleagues—to you; lay aside every trace of hostility; discuss their restoration with them as a brother; and strive to complete the matter mercifully. Otherwise, you were to come together with the other archbishops and bishops established in those regions, to whom we also wrote for this very purpose, to a council, [Col. 1107A] so that all of you, meeting together, might examine the cases of those clerics and, with God before your eyes, determine them without any dispute arising.

If any dispute should arise between the parties, both sides were to come to the Apostolic See, with persons acting in the place of each side to receive our special judgment.

When this had been accomplished with the help of God’s grace, we received a letter from all of you, worthy of our embraced affection, clearly reporting that the often-mentioned clerics had been declared worthy of recovering their ranks by the unanimous voice of the entire council.

As we find in your same letter, no dispute arose there; no difference, as had been supposed, occurred among the various defenders; no accuser and no condemner was found. Rather, one and the same judgment and decision concerning their restoration became clear, and those innocent men were approved in every way by the unanimity of all.

Therefore, if those formerly deposed men are innocent, having been approved by the unanimity of all, we do not know by what right those who deposed them can be innocent.

Your own profession also lends support to this unanimous judgment and decision of your synod—although it is not straightforward, it is nevertheless a submission. In it you testify not only that you had never previously suspended those same brothers from office, judged them, expelled them from their ranks, or subscribed to their rejection, but also that you had now come to the synod, as we commanded, had readily assented to what the other bishops had agreed concerning their restoration, and had taken care to obey it. Your name, too, as his report indicates, was found written in the synodal letter together with the names of the brothers and fellow priests who had assembled.

Yet it was amusing that Your Fraternity confessed that you had never suspended the often-mentioned clerics from office, judged them, or expelled them from their ranks—especially since numerous indications also prove that these claims are not supported by the truth.

Although above we touched briefly upon what took place, we do not wish to enlarge upon these matters fully, lest we be compelled to pass judgment on things deserving judgment. For unless you suspended them from office before any hearing at all, while they had approached you not as accusers but as petitioners for mercy, what is the meaning of their being recorded in the proceedings of your council—which you yourself sent to the Apostolic See—as having been suspended from office by you? Since you yourself answered nothing, remaining silent, what else can clearly be understood except that by your silence you openly granted that they had stated the truth?

And, conversely, concerning whom were they sending their complaints to Pope Leo of blessed memory, except you—their persecutor, hostile to them, whom they ought to have recognized as a kindly father around them—and whom they repeatedly identified as the one who had driven them from their proper ranks?

Finally, unless you subscribed to their deposition—or rather, unless you yourself wrote out the entire account of their deposition—what is the meaning of my predecessor of blessed memory stating, in the aforementioned privilege which you asked to have confirmed by the Apostolic See, addressing you, that you had strengthened those definitions with your own fingers in the synod assembled with the other bishops, as your own report indicates? [Col. 1108A]

If you say that you never subscribed in that synod, then our predecessor did not confirm any synod for you by his privilege. For he himself explicitly recalls that you had strengthened with your own fingers the synod which he established by apostolic authority.

Moreover, when you wrote to us in your letter that you had both wished and still wished, had both sought and still sought, the sound and canonical status of those same clerics, who among those who knows the course of this affair or controversy would not wonder and be astonished?

If you wished it, where is the struggle that you undertook for their recovery, as for sons? And if you sought it, where does it appear? Where is it even given to be understood?

But show us when you wished for or sought their status, and we shall show you, setting aside prolixity, in brief, that you always wished for and sought not their status but their downfall. For why do you indicate that, sometimes through legates and sometimes through letters, you wished and sought from my predecessors—Pope Leo and Pope Benedict, pontiffs of blessed memory—that their deposition be confirmed, their restoration never hoped for, their downfall strengthened forever, and their status never restored? This is how you wished for their status; this is how you sought their status.

But perhaps you will say that you wished for and sought not just any status for them, but a sound and canonical one. Very well: produce this before any witnesses you please, or show it by whatever proofs you wish. For neither your writings nor the others that lie with us indicate anything of the kind about you; rather, they plainly suggest that your disposition was continually directed toward their utter ruin.

Finally, if you did not depose them, why did you not raise them up, since they were your own? And if you could not do even that by your sole authority, why did you not seek the authority of the Apostolic See on their behalf? Would that you had not sought it against them in this way.

For where is the grief that you incurred for them, as for sons? Where is even the slight labor that you mercifully undertook for restoring them?

Perhaps, however, what you testify is true: that you grieved over their deposition and rejoiced in their status—but only in this sense, that just as you had grieved over their deposition, so now you rejoice over their restored standing; for perhaps you did not grieve over their downfall then, nor rejoice over their status now.

Amid these matters, however, we wish to turn the mind’s gaze to the words of your letter and briefly show that you did not write to us straightforwardly. It is indecent—although you may not be ashamed of it—to write craftily to the Apostolic See unless your own arguments of cunning can be understood.

For in the sustained account of that letter you said nothing about the clerics’ rejection and demonstrated absolutely nothing about how unjustly they had been deposed, although you ought to have acknowledged that those same clerics, because of the consecration conferred upon them by Ebbo, ought not to have suffered any loss of their rank.

Especially since, in the synodal letter that you and your other brothers and fellow bishops jointly sent to the Apostolic See, you yourself profess that Ebbo alone incurred the prince’s wrath in his condemnation, whatever it may have been. [Note: perhaps “only the prince’s wrath,” rather than “the prince’s wrath alone”; the printed reading is uncertain.]

But if you understood the sacred canons in this way when you judged them, you should at least have said so yourself and tried to embrace what we, as possessing greater authority, would have judged concerning it. For through such a confession as Ebbo is alleged to have made, no one is subjected to canonical condemnation.

If you remain silent, we cannot remain silent; and what everyone admits to be unjust you will not be able to prove just, however many arguments you employ.

If it was feared that their unjust condemnation would endanger its author, and that therefore what had been unjustly pronounced should be kept silent, an unsuitable policy was adopted. A person obtains pardon more easily through truth than through contrived and unsuitable inventions.

Especially since truth liberates, whereas falsehood destroys; and there is nothing to fear where there is no fear. Nor should you imagine that we bear toward you such an affection of love that we would wish you to suffer any harm, since we have always been eager for your advancement.

For concerning both Ebbo’s case and the affair of these clerics—matters whose first stages have now passed—we earnestly desire that they bring you caution, not danger. Holding to the royal road, we have resolved to help them in such a way that we would in no respect appear to harm Your Holiness; and thus, in turn, we give you security concerning this matter in such a way that we do not deprive the often-mentioned clerics of it.

Finally, there is appropriate doubt whether the letter now said to have been sent to us by you was actually yours, since you neither sent your legate to declare that it had been transmitted to us by you nor took care to seal it with your seal according to custom.

It is therefore astonishing that, although you composed a volume of no short length against the deposition of those clerics, you did not issue even one simple letter on behalf of their restoration. Here it becomes apparent how much eagerness was present there and how much negligence here.

Yet do not suppose that we have exaggerated these matters to bring any danger upon Your Holiness or dignity. You know that the wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses of hatred. But do not raise yourself so excessively in defense or exaltation of your privileges that you appear in any way to have rashly touched the rights of the Apostolic See (Distinction 8: “Bad Custom”).

For bad custom, which must be avoided no less than pernicious corruption, if it is not quickly uprooted, is appropriated by the wicked as though it were a right of privilege. Transgressions and various presumptions then begin, if not swiftly restrained, to be honored as laws and perpetually celebrated in the manner of privileges.

Therefore, concerning the restoration of the aforementioned clerics, you should recognize that we have been able to offer our complete assent, with all the arguments thus far properly assembled and the general encouragement of the unanimous support of all of you urging us on.

But because their examination did not proceed according to our decree as a pure and complete investigation; because it was not clearly established what their promotion or rejection had been in the synodal assembly; and because this was not sufficiently demonstrated to the Apostolic See by a report, we judged it necessary for the time being to restrain somewhat our deliberative assent from completing their restoration.

Since, however, in decreeing and judging what had been canonically deliberated, in restoring the often-mentioned clerics, and in all things—as God led us and order required—our authority came first, it is fitting and honorable that, according to your petition, the complete integrity of our confirmation should follow.

This must proceed in the following order: the clerics so frequently mentioned, who are evidently known to have been irregularly suspended from the offices of their ranks and are proved by several indications to have appealed repeatedly to the Apostolic See, must first be restored to their former ranks and offices. Thus, returned to their former ranks and orders and, in a certain sense, reclothed with all that was theirs, they may possess their full strength against those attacking them. For an unarmed man cannot properly enter into conflict with an armed man.

Once they are enjoying these ranks and offices, Your Fraternity is to have permission, within the whole compass of this year, to demonstrate canonically that the often-mentioned clerics had been expelled from their orders. You shall have complete freedom to pursue and carry out whatever accusations you have against them.

But if, after the entire course of this year has elapsed, you have formulated no just complaint against them before the Apostolic See, and have not sought to prosecute them for any charge, offense, or condemnation whatsoever, then, while they remain in their orders, we shall certainly not devote ourselves to any sluggishness; nor shall we in any way cease from the highest diligence until either you justly prove that they have now been restored, or justly show that they were once removed by you.

Otherwise, it will unquestionably be proper for us thereafter to present not only the often-mentioned clerics, who were prejudicially separated from office without a canon, but also their ordainer, who was improperly and without ecclesiastical procedure deprived of episcopal governance. No one at all, we believe, except you, entirely doubts this; indeed, no one fails to proclaim it, since it is equally clear to us, as far as we can judge, and to those who are remembered to have been present at that time.

Finally, we wish you to know that it has been reported to our ears that Your Fraternity does not use the pallium granted by the Apostolic See at fixed times and according to the custom established for the other metropolitan bishops.

This greatly displeases us if Your Holiness has done it arrogantly, wishing, forgetful of humility, to appear superior to his other brothers. Yet the pallium ought not to be used for empty glory, but worn as an adornment of all virtues.

When you received from the Apostolic See the use of that pallium, this was properly shown and commanded to you in writing, according to the usual form. If its use was granted to Your Fraternity by the Apostolic See for all time, although it was received contrary to the custom of the Church and therefore reasonably ought to be forfeited—for, as Pope Saint Simplicius writes, the person who abuses the power granted to him deserves to lose the privilege—nevertheless, having been suitably admonished by these words of ours, strive to use it so modestly that neither arrogance of mind invades you, nor boastfulness inflates you, nor empty glory wounds you, nor you exceed the measure of your own dignity, nor moderation—which, without it, leaves the other virtues imperfect—be consigned to oblivion.

We desire that Your Fraternity may now and always prosper.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of December, in the fifteenth indiction.

(Year 866.) CIX. TO KING CHARLES. He replies to his previous letter concerning the proceedings of the Synod of Soissons.

[In Mansi, ibid.]

[Col. 1111B] NICHOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son CHARLES, glorious king.

Since Your Glory has always shown itself such toward us, and, by frequent letters and dispatched legates, has bestowed upon our pontificate the observance of devoted attentiveness, and has submitted the lofty neck of obedience to our decrees with grateful readiness, you should know with certainty that in us you honor your beloved, the blessed apostle Peter, whose place we occupy, though our merits differ exceedingly from his; indeed, that you venerate God in his apostle, who has granted such great glory to his saints and made us heirs and successors of their solicitude. And we, rendering due thanks for your ready devotion, much more do not cease continually to offer praises to that omnipotence through whom and for whose name such things are done.

Furthermore, dearest son, we return thanks to your pious kindness because, concentrating your whole desire upon the recovery of the status of the deposed clerics, you have endeavored to erase the fault which you had incurred by giving consent to their deposition. And we believe that the reward for the eagerness which you have now shown in receiving them will outweigh the offense which you committed in their former rejection, because this was done out of love for God, whereas that was accomplished through a man's deceit. Nevertheless, we exhort you and admonish you as a beloved son not readily in future to give assent to such acts, because it is unknown whether what is committed today may ever come to amendment.

Moreover, it is fitting to recall what, among other things, the text of your letter declares concerning our brother and fellow bishop Hincmar: namely, that he would have hastened to carry everything through fully in concert with the other fellow bishops, had not the privileges of our predecessor, Lord Benedict, and our own taught him that the final decision in the undertaking of restoration was reserved to us. If Brother Hincmar had not, according to his custom, partly concealed the tenor of those privileges, and by a certain cunning denied to common knowledge some things which are inserted there, we think that no one would have been diverted by our privileges from the ordinances of the Apostolic See or from the obedience that we require. For we did not preach disobedience or decree that the decrees of the Apostolic See should not be obeyed. Rather, as those same privileges testify, while preserving in every respect the command and judgment of the Roman See, we judged that the synod which he had assembled for the deposition of the aforementioned clerics should remain established; and we confirmed to him the tenor of that privilege on the condition that he should never at any time depart from the commands of the Apostolic See.

Therefore he asserts in vain that the privileges granted him by the Apostolic See prevented him from hastening to carry out our decrees. For it is clear instead, as their text shows, that they repeatedly admonished him to hasten all the more to obey us; and that, if he wished the grants made to him to remain valid in his own case, they urged him more fully and abundantly to obey our ordinances.

Furthermore, we again thank Your Most Glorious Charity concerning Baldwin; again we praise the great inclination of your devotion displayed toward him; again we pray that, through the munificence of your kindness, what is lacking may be supplied in response to our petitions offered for him. For it is right that you should willingly strive to bring to completion the good work which, at our intervention and out of regard for God, you began, so that the reward of your obedience, generosity, and clemency may be complete.

Furthermore, dearest son, be watchful, and diligently attentive toward the holy Roman Church and the Apostolic See, just as certain writings and trustworthy men testify that your forebears, worshipers of God, were; for those confessions before the apostles concerning you and your loved ones can in no way be forgotten. What we have decreed concerning the restored clerics may be made known to the ears of your wisdom by our letter sent to our brother and fellow bishop Hincmar. We desire that Your Excellency may now and always prosper in Christ, most beloved son. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of December, in the fifteenth indiction.

(Year 866.) CX. [Note: [Col. 1111D] To Wlfadus and his associates. In the Laudunensis manuscript there is likewise a letter of Wlfadus and his associates to Nicholas, [Col. 1112D] in which they give thanks for their restoration and ask that they be permitted to advance to higher orders. JAC. SIRM.] TO WLFADUS, A CLERIC OF RHEIMS, AND HIS ASSOCIATES. He rejoices at their restoration, which he confirms, warns them not to avenge their injuries, and urges them especially to show reverence to Hincmar.

[In Mansi, in the same place.]

NICHOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable clerics—namely Wlfadus and the others who, formerly deposed with him, now by the decree of the apostolic see and the promulgation of the synod, have by God’s authority been restored.

No one who considers the riches of His goodness is wholly ignorant that the fullness of divine mercy wills no one to perish, nor anyone to fall, through any misfortune, from the consecrated number of His flock, since He did not even spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all (Romans 8). The sheep that had gone astray is carried back to the flock upon the shoulders of His compassion; and, following as best we can the entrails of His clemency, we have not allowed your appeals to be disregarded for long, nor closed the ears of our compassion to your grief and lamentation, nor passed over without renewed examination the deposition which you endured from our brother and co-bishop Hincmar, or from the other bishops, without any judgment of equity.

Therefore we ordered a synod of our brothers and co-bishops of Gaul, Neustria, and Germany to be held, and your case to be examined in that venerable council and, with God kept before its eyes, decided without any dispute arising. When this had been accomplished with the help of God’s grace, we received the synod’s letter, containing the report of all the bishops. It most clearly stated that you had been unanimously declared innocent by all and pronounced worthy of being restored to your former orders by the harmonious voice of the entire council. No dispute, no diversity among the several defenders, no accuser or condemner was found there; rather, with the agreement of the aforementioned brother and co-bishop Hincmar, one and the same judgment prevailed, and complete unanimity and an identical decision concerning your restoration were made clear.

Accordingly, know that we too have given our assent to your restoration and reception into your orders, and certainly believe that we rejoice with you over your present condition, just as we grieved over your deposition. Since our authority preceded the decision and judgment of what was canonically deliberated, and in restoring you—as was fitting and as the order of the matter required—God guiding us, it is fitting and honorable that the complete integrity of our confirmation should follow.

For this reason we rejoice with you and, as we have already confessed, congratulate you; and we confirm by the authority of almighty God, of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul, and through them by the authority of our own humility, what has been decreed concerning the recovery of your status. We gladly pray that, according to the Lord’s good pleasure, it may remain firm through God’s continual establishment.

Furthermore, we wish and exhort you to conduct yourselves henceforth in all things in such a way that you may not be found ungrateful in any respect for the benefits bestowed upon you by the Lord. Therefore give thanks to His mercy, and, since He did not abandon you to the end, always call this to mind. Keep humility continually before your eyes, and tirelessly raise your hearts to meditate upon eternal things. Above all, take careful precautions not to remember your injuries or to grow angry against those who are proved to have inflicted them upon you.

Show our brother and co-bishop Hincmar the humility due to him and the reverence appropriate to him. At no time are you to have license to fabricate a complaint against him or repay him with hostile treatment because you were suspended from office by him. For in raising you up we sought no one’s ruin, nor do we wish to establish one party in such a way that the other party suffers loss of dignity or right.

Enjoy, therefore, the decree of this our command, and use it for your protection and for the security of your orders against all your accusers. Let it always be open to you, when necessity arises, to appeal to the apostolic see and await its judgment according to the canons.

Nevertheless, we do not wish you to be unaware that we have granted our brother and co-bishop Hincmar a delay, so that within the space of this year he may, if he wishes, pursue before us a case against you concerning your deposition or restoration. We say this in order to make you vigilant and so that you may foresee how to resist him if necessary, and thus be able to prepare the weapons of your justice against his arrows.

We wish you well in Christ.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of December, in the fifteenth indiction.

(Year 866.) CXI. TO THE NOBLES OF AQUITAINE. That they should immediately restore the property of churches which they unjustly retain in any way, and thereafter abstain from such property.

[In Mansi, in the same place.]

[Col. 1114B]

NICHOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the beloved nobles and leading men, and to all the inhabitants of Aquitaine.

The necessity of the concern which we bear for all the churches of the Lord compels us to exercise diligent care for the condition of all the faithful. Therefore, as we also extend careful concern toward you, we hear—something we do not wish—that certain of your number are so uplifted against God that they do not fear to plunder His churches and various holy places, and do not hesitate to divert the property belonging to them.

This has greatly saddened us and produced in our mind a grief beyond what can be expressed. Therefore, dearest sons, we have taken care to exhort you through the words of our pontificate, so that, looking carefully to your salvation, you may cease from such great cruelty; indeed, by restoring what you have taken violently or in any unlawful way, you should take care to make proper amends.

For although the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness (Psalm 23), nevertheless the property which pious princes and faithful people have bestowed upon holy places is without hesitation believed to belong especially to the Lord, since it is seen to have been dedicated to divine worship and assigned to the use of those who serve God. Therefore, whoever does not fear to seize these possessions and claim them unlawfully for himself undoubtedly commits an offense against God and is proved to inflict injury upon Him.

For when they take property from pious places, they remove the provisions of those who serve God; and when they deprive those who continually minister to divine worship of their support, they in a certain sense draw the praises of the Lord from the very mouths of men.

Accordingly, we ask you, removed from this tyranny, to restore without delay to each of the places consecrated to God what belongs to it, retaining nothing of these things among yourselves except what you may perhaps have legally acquired by the free will of certain administrators of holy places.

You must also restore in full those things which, through the simplicity or negligence of the venerable administrators of the place, you are known to have taken improperly from the revenues which, by continual use and perpetual right, have been assigned to holy places, and which you are proved to possess to this day contrary to the laws of God.

Likewise, we exhort you to do the same concerning those possessions which kings have at some time taken from holy places in any manner and bestowed upon you as benefices. This was not right, nor is it right; and whoever claims such things for himself will undoubtedly have God as his judge and avenger.

For if rapacious and violent men of any sort, unless they correct themselves, will be punished most severely—if not now by human judgment, certainly someday by divine judgment—what punishment, do you suppose, must be imposed upon those who are most clearly proved to perpetrate robbery and violence against God Himself?

Finally, your predecessors, the ancient princes and those of more recent times, not only did not plunder the pious places dedicated to the Lord, but also contributed innumerable gifts from their own possessions. Thus those holy places were dedicated with their resources and, with God’s help, enlarged through their wealth. If you do not wish to imitate them in generosity, at least do not violently take away what belongs to God Himself.

For if someone who presumes to take anything from the king’s palace does not escape legal punishment, how much less will one who violently seizes from the dwelling of God—who is King of kings and Lord of lords—the things that belong to Him be able to escape judgment when correction follows, or leap away without punishment?

Therefore, since it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God, we admonish and exhort you, and, as though protesting in the presence of God, command you to restore without deliberately caused delay to those same holy places the property of the churches which you unjustly retain. Henceforth do not presume to steal either those possessions or any others from pious places.

But if any of you scorns to hear us and fails obediently to carry out what we strive to advise for your salvation, or takes no care to observe it without delay, let him, by the authority of almighty God and of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul—whom he despises in us—and likewise by their authority and the judgment of our own humility, remain wholly deprived of communion in the venerated body and precious blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But if he comes to his senses and strives to obey what we say in the text of this letter, may he attain communion in Christ’s mysteries, the grace of blessedness, and eternal salvation.

We wish you well in Christ.

Given in the month of December, in the fifteenth indiction.

(Year 866.) CXII. TO KING CHARLES. That he should arrange for Lothair to restore what he had taken from his sister Helletrude, the widow of Berengarius.

[In Mansi, in the same place.]

NICHOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Charles, glorious king.

Through her letters it became well known to our apostolate that Helletrude, formerly the widow of Count Berengarius, had been brought to ruin by the oppression of King Lothair and had suffered his wrongs. She brought this and other matters to our attention so that we might send apostolic letters of admonition to Lothair and direct our letter to you, dearest son, and to your brother Louis, the most excellent king.

Thus, with your assistance and support, that widow might undoubtedly obtain complete justice concerning her possessions. For he not only took away estates granted to her by her father Lothair the emperor by charter, but also deceitfully stole the properties which her parents had left to the aforementioned Helletrude, and with these he made a benefaction, in proper fashion, to the pagan Northmen, enemies of the holy Church of God.

We have been unable to send apostolic letters to the aforementioned Lothair, your nephew, because, as you have plainly heard, we have excommunicated him in order that his wicked and unlawful actions may be abolished. But to your excellence, worthy of being honored with immeasurable affection, we send this request, dearest son: out of reverence for the chief apostles, to whom she appealed in writing as to a refuge and requested justice, and because by right of kinship—or of seniority—it is fitting for you to restrain him from such unlawful acts, strive to send to the aforementioned king, through your envoy or by letter, commands based upon our authority, requests on your own behalf, or admonitions grounded in the law.

And if, together with your brother Louis, the glorious king, you should address this same nephew of yours concerning his sister’s case, as we believe you will, we earnestly ask you to pursue to the end the cause of this oft-mentioned widow Helletrude, both concerning her own property and concerning the benefices formerly granted to her by the aforesaid Lothair Augustus in his testament.

Thus, when, with God’s favor, he has corrected his former fault, let him redress that woman’s claims and not add iniquity to iniquity in his kingdom, but do justice abundantly. For it is fitting that royal tribunals should assist everyone, especially widows, whose judge is Christ.

Accordingly, in the form of this letter, we have now sent a letter concerning this matter both to you and likewise to your brother Louis. We grieve deeply, most eminent king, over those who in any way take away the estates of Christ’s faithful and, in the manner of benefices, bestow them upon the enemies of Christ the King.

Meanwhile, we ask that your royal greatness not disdain to inform our apostolate in writing, point by point, of whatever your excellence decides and accomplishes for the successful resolution of these matters.

We wish your excellence well in Christ, now and always.

(Year 867.) CXIII. PRIVILEGE FOR THE PARTHENON OF VÉZELAY.

[In Acherius, *Spicilegium*, vol. II.]

NICHOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the religious woman consecrated to God, who, by divine will and providence, has been established in the monastery which has been built and endowed in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in veneration of the most blessed Virgin Mary, mother of the same God and Lord our Jesus Christ, by you—namely our most illustrious son Gerard, the most renowned count, and the most noble daughter Berta—in the place or estate called Vézelay, in the county of Avalonnais, on the borders of Burgundy; and to all those who thereafter shall perpetually govern that monastery as abbesses.

From this monastery, with everything lawfully belonging to it, you have made this holy heir—the Roman Church—for the remedy and future recompense of your souls, and by a deed of donation you have conferred it upon blessed Peter, chief of the apostles.

When those things to which the hearts of Catholic men ought to be prompted by pontifical admonitions are, through divine mercy going before, kindled with such ardent desire that they themselves spontaneously request them, they ought to be granted with a willing and joyful spirit—how much more ought the very things they desire to have been requested if they had been unwilling to do them. Therefore, in accordance with your petition, we grant, confirm, and establish by the decree of our present apostolic authority the following privileges for the monastery founded by your religious devotion in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the diocese of the city of Augustodunum, in the place and district previously mentioned.

No king, no bishop, no person endowed with any dignity, nor anyone else, may diminish, take away, apply to his own uses, or in any way grant to others, under any pretext or appearance of a cause or occasion, anything that has been lawfully bestowed upon the monastery by you or by anyone else from his own property. Rather, we wish and, by apostolic authority, command that everything offered there, or that may happen to be offered, whether by you, by those who succeed to the office of abbess or to the religious life in that place, or by those who offer their gifts there for the remedy of their souls, be possessed from the present time intact and without disturbance.

It must in every respect benefit only those for whose support and governance it has been granted and will be granted. This condition is added: none of our successors in this holy see, which by the Lord’s authority we serve, may ever or anywhere allow anything of these possessions to be granted as a benefice to anyone, exchanged, conceded under a rent, or retained for future times.

Our successors, receiving each year only the rent specified in the deed of your donation by which you made this holy heir—the mother Church—the heir of that monastery, namely one pound of silver, should diligently strive, through the care of pastoral vigilance, to provide the monastery, its abbess, and the monks living there under the Rule of the holy Father Benedict with the support of pious fatherly protection against all who attack them.

We further establish that, when the abbess of the aforesaid monastery dies, no other woman may be appointed there through any stratagem of secret influence, except one whom the community of the monks, in accordance with the fear of God and the institution of the Rule of blessed Benedict, has chosen, and whom the pontiff of this apostolic see has foreseen should be appointed, or whom he has consented to appoint at the suggestion of the nuns.

[Col. 1118A]

We add this provision to the present chapter in order to exclude the opportunity for avarice: no priest, no king, nor any other faithful person, whether acting personally or through an intermediary, may dare to receive anything in gold or in any other form of gain or gift on account of the ordination of the same abbess, or of clerics and priests, or the dispensing of chrism, the consecration of the basilica, or any other advantage of spiritual [Note: [Col. 1117D] Read *spiritualis* (“spiritual”) instead of *specialis* (“special”), for the sense requires it. The copyist was misled by the abbreviation for writing *spalis*.] or temporal service, or for any matters whatsoever belonging to the monastery.
