Nor may that same abbess presume to give anything on account of her ordination, lest on this occasion the things offered by the faithful to the pious place, or already offered, be consumed.

Nor may the bishop of that city and parish celebrate public Masses there unless invited by the abbess of that monastery; nor may he proclaim stations in that same convent, lest the quiet of God’s servants somehow be disturbed by a public gathering. Nor may he presume to demand from there provisions or lodging dues.

As for receiving the faithful, religious men and women, and showing the benevolence which the Apostle commands to be extended to all, according to the capacity of the place and its resources, we not only do not forbid this to be done there freely, but also commend it. The size of the community, however, should be so carefully maintained that a large number cannot produce poverty, nor a small number of inhabitants bring about the abandonment of the place.

All these provisions contained in the document of this command and decree of ours we decree must be observed perpetually by all who succeed you, who retain under usufruct the same monastery built by you and handed over to the Holy Roman Church, and by those whom it may concern.

But if any priest, judge, or secular person, recognizing this document of our constitution, attempts to act against it, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power or office, struck with apostolic anathema, and acknowledge that he has made himself liable to divine judgment for the iniquity committed. Unless he restores what he has wrongly taken, corrects what he has presumed to do, or mourns his unlawful conduct through worthy repentance, let him be separated from the most sacred body of God, our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and subject to strict vengeance at the eternal judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who observe what is just toward that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

Written by the hand of Sophronius, regional officer and registrar of the Roman Church, in the month of May. Given by the hand of Tiberius, chief secretary of the apostolic see.

(Year 867.) CXIV. LETTER TO THE EMPEROR LOUIS II. Fragment.—He urges the making of peace.

[In Mansi, in the same place.]

NICHOLAS TO LOUIS, EMPEROR.

It is no offense against the Christian religion, but rather an advantage, if, with charity as your guide and with regard for God, you enter into an agreement with foreign peoples for the protection and security of Christians, since it is clear that this is done for no other reason than to restrain in some way their savage violence, which burns unanimously against the faithful.

For since, according to the account of history, we know that Solomon formed treaties of friendship with foreigners for the increase of holy glory and for the easier construction of the temple for the Lord, what is surprising if a pious emperor confirms an agreement with foreign peoples for the glory of God and the security of the holy Church, which is truly a divine temple? This is especially so since Charles, your great-grandfather, of blessed memory, is known undoubtedly to have made an agreement with their ruler solely for the relief and consolation of Christians who, in various places among them, were being beaten like grains among chaff.

(Year 867.) CXV. TO KING CHARLES [CHARLES THE BALD]. Fragment.—Concerning John Scotus, that he did not judge correctly in certain matters.

[In Mansi, in the same place.]

It has been reported to our apostolate that a certain man named John, a Scot by nationality, has recently translated into Latin the work of blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, which he composed in Greek concerning the divine names and the celestial orders.

According to custom, this work ought to have been sent to us and approved by our judgment, especially since, although the same John is said to possess much learning, it has long been frequently reported that he did not think correctly in certain matters.

Therefore, let your diligence supply what has hitherto been omitted and send us the aforesaid work without any hesitation, so that, once it has been approved by the judgment of our apostolate, it may be received by everyone with greater confidence on our authority.

(Year 867.) CXVI. TO BISHOP DONNUS. Concerning a man who had killed his brother.

[Ivo, X, 184.]

NICHOLAS TO DONNUS, BISHOP, AND TO KING CHARLES.

A certain man of your diocese, named Hugh, came and reported to our pontifical office in tearful speech how he had committed fratricide under the compulsion of the ancient enemy, and how, for so great a crime, he had been placed by your blessedness under the yoke of penance.

When we heard of so great a calamity and of the shedding of a brother’s blood, we were grieved and shed many tears. Nevertheless, since, as he said, he wished to wash away the guilt of so great a stain in a fountain of tears, with fraternal grace commanding it, we decree that he should immediately recover the possessions of his own which were taken away from him on account of this deed, lest, constrained by the want of poverty, he be driven to worse things.

Moreover, let your holiness take care that his lawful wife, from whom he has been separated, be immediately restored to him, lest, contrary to our wish, he appear to fall into the abyss of fornication. In all other respects, let him continue to perform the penance which you have prescribed for him, according to its measure.

(Year 867.) CXVII. [Col. 1120A] TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF LOUIS. No one is to be subjected unwillingly to monastic discipline.

[Gratian, *Decretum* II, 20, question 3, chapter 4.]

A certain cleric named Lambertus, together with his father, named Attho, formerly a count but now a cleric, came hastening to the threshold of the apostles and approached our presence. He asserted that while his father was still in the lay order, he had built two monasteries on his own estates, intending that after his death this son of his, Lambertus, should succeed him in his position.

While Lambertus was still a child, between his eighth and tenth year, the father mentioned above, acting on his own decision and without regular formation, put a monk’s hood upon him against his entire will. After some time had passed, Bishop Salomon himself says that, together with certain others, he caused this same Lambertus—so they say, unwillingly—to put on the monastic habit, without his father’s offering him or his having received the abbot’s blessing.

On this pretext, they now wish him to be deprived by his brothers of his paternal or maternal inheritance and to remain, as was said, a regular monk against his entire will. Concerning this matter, investigating carefully, we even questioned his father under oath as to whether he was telling the truth. But Attho, the father, replied that he had had and still had the intention that his son should become a true monk and succeed him.

Under oath he firmly testified that when he first put the hood upon him, Lambertus always resisted and never consented to become a monk. Only afterward was he forcibly clothed by those who followed with the monastic habit. He asserted that he had never promised any rule, that he, his father, had not offered him clothed in the altar pallium, and that he had never promised, after receiving the blessing—as custom requires—from any priest or abbot, that he would become subject to a rule as a monk.

The aforesaid cleric Attho also solemnly declared that if at that time he had understood the monastic rule to require such harsh observance, he would never have compelled his son Lambertus to wear the hood.

Therefore, recalling advisedly the words of the Psalmist, by which he declares that he will sacrifice to God voluntarily and asks that the willing offerings of his mouth be made in God’s sight, we have judged that the cleric Lambertus, mentioned above, should by no means be made a monk under such compulsion.

For what someone does not choose or desire, he certainly does not love; and what he does not love, he easily despises. Nothing is good, after all, unless it is voluntary. For this reason the Lord commanded that no rod be carried on the way by which violence might be inflicted upon anyone.

Accordingly, you will act more wisely if, by preaching contempt for the world and love of God through pious persuasion rather than by inflicting violence, you kindle him to heavenly love.

Therefore we have decided to send this letter of our apostolate to all of you, exhorting and commanding that, if the matter is truly as these men say, no bishop, abbot, or assembly of the other monks compel him to submit unwillingly to monastic rules. Nor should his brothers in any way be allowed, on this pretext, to deprive him of his paternal or maternal inheritance.

Rather, until, moved by divine inspiration, he submits himself to the rule of his own free will, let him be permitted, removed from worldly and secular occupations or business, to live a canonical life among religious and ecclesiastical men.

For we do not think—God forbid—that canonical religious men who are joined to the life and fellowship of the holy monks are thereby excluded, since each person, according to the Apostle, will receive his own reward according to his labor.

(Year 867.) CXVIII. TO ADÔ, ARCHBISHOP OF VIENNE. Concerning the judgments and prohibitions of the apostolic see, among other matters.

[Mansi, in the same place.]

I. That archbishops should, with the fear of God, hold canonical assemblies in the provinces entrusted to them; that all the more distinguished men of the province should gather there with the venerable bishops; and that there they should hear the integrity of the faith and the observance of the canonical rules, and be taught to subscribe to their observance, so that they cannot offer excuses for failing to keep them.

II. That metropolitans should observe ecclesiastical vigor with greater reverence, and should excel by singular authority both in life and in teaching; that they should avoid secular journeys and business; that, through zeal for piety, they should rise up more firmly and truly against the wickedness of worldly people; that they should not deceive the princes of the kingdom by flattery; and that they should take every care of their provinces, divinely entrusted to them.

III. That suffragan bishops should show due reverence and obedience to their metropolitans; that they should come obediently to the metropolitan see; that they should faithfully handle ecclesiastical cases with their metropolitan; and that from him they should receive the pattern by which they are to conduct themselves in their own churches.

IV. That archbishops and bishops should establish plebeian or baptismal churches in their dioceses according to ancient custom, and teach laypeople to avoid such places; that the titles of the remaining churches should belong to them; so that there a more distinguished assembly of the people may take place, and the teaching of the faith and of Christian life may be preached more freely to those gathered together.

V. That archbishops, supported by the authority of our fathers, should ensure that worthy persons are placed in charge of holy places, and that places dedicated or consecrated to God do not become dwellings of secular people.

For this reason we have also admonished pious princes wherever it was appropriate, that, for the honor of Christ and out of their charity, they may more diligently and more properly correct again what was corrupted and destroyed in their days. Archbishops and bishops themselves should restrain their greed, so that afterward they may chastise laypeople more freely for unlawful presumption.

Nor should they, as has hitherto been done, desire the possessions of others to the scandal and ruin of many, or demand dominion over places that do not belong by right to them or to their episcopate. Let them remain content with their own boundaries; thus they will be able to restrain the greed and carelessness of laypeople more effectively.

VI. Concerning those publicly excommunicated for a public crime: they are to be received through public penance, and, according to the nature of the deed, penance is to be prolonged for each person by canonical authority.

VII. Excommunications are not to be imposed rashly, lest episcopal authority be despised; nor are absolutions to be granted disorderly, unless an orderly satisfaction, consonant with the rules of the Fathers, has preceded them.

VIII. [25, question 2, “Si quis,” distinction.] If anyone has despised the doctrines, commands, prohibitions, sanctions, or decrees salutarily promulgated by the prelate of the apostolic see for the catholic faith, for ecclesiastical discipline, for the correction of the faithful, for the amendment of criminals, or for the prohibition of impending or future evils, let him be anathema.

(This final decree is taken from the fifth chapter of the Roman council held under the same pontiff Nicholas in the year 863.)

(Year 867.) CXIX. TO HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS. Penance imposed upon one who had killed a monk who was a priest.

[In Mansi, in the same place.]

NICHOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy brother Hincmar, archbishop.

[Note: [Col. 1121D] “With what groans.” Flodoard, book III, chapter 23, listing Hincmar’s letters to various bishops, says: “To Hilmerad, bishop of Amiens, concerning a certain monk who killed a priest and monk in the monastery of Saint Richarius: concerning him the lord pope Nicholas had sent a letter to the same lord Hincmar containing the terms of his penance.”]

We know well from your prudence how much, and with what tears, paternal affection is accustomed—and indeed ought—to grieve over the dangers of its children. Therefore, as one invested with the mitre of your zeal, nourished with ecclesiastical milk, and brought to solid progress in preaching, we wish you to know that this Eriath has fled to the threshold of the apostles, asking pardon for the guilt of homicide which he incurred.

He claimed that he had killed a certain priest and monk who had done nothing deserving death. Accordingly, he humbly showed that he wished to submit his neck to penance.

Therefore we imposed upon him that the term of the penance assigned to him should be enclosed within a limit of twelve years. During the first three of these, he is to hasten to obtain mercy from the Lord by mourning and uttering sobs before the doors of the church.

During the fourth and fifth years, let him strive to beseech the Almighty among the hearers, without receiving the body and blood of the Lord.

During the remaining seven years, let him be permitted to receive communion in the Lord’s sacrament on the most solemn feast days, but let him offer no oblations whatsoever.

Nevertheless, throughout all the periods mentioned above, except on feast days and on the Lord’s Resurrection, let him continually remain fasting until evening, in the manner of Lent. If he has occasion to travel anywhere, let him not be conveyed in any vehicle but make the journey on foot.

His penance ought, finally, to have been extended until death. But considering his devotion and faith, and because he hastened to seek the apostles’ intercession, we have dealt with him more humanely.

Meanwhile, we exhort you to instruct the most reverend Bishop Hilmerad, your suffragan, to permit the monks of his monastery to live quietly under the monastic habit and to practice the fruits of penance.

Having received these letters of our apostolate, examine the future life of his penance with spiritual eyes. Weigh with catholic compassion and the hand of discretion whatever is appropriate, and deal with him in such a way that canonical authority is observed and the Lord’s sheep, wounded by the robber’s attack, is not lost through any neglect, but may be found worthy of reward at the right hand of Christ after the examination of divine judgment.

We wish your holiness well in Christ.

(Year 867.) CXX. TO HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS. Accuser and accused must be present together.

[Gratian, II, 3, question 9, chapter 21.]

[Col. 1123C]

According to the teaching of the sacred Scriptures and the path of justice, both the accused and the accuser must be present together. One party, whatever authority and of whatever kind it may possess, must be heard in such a way that no prejudice whatsoever is inflicted upon the other party.

(Year 867.) CXXI. TO HERARD, ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS. Fragment.—He must be restored who is known to have been expelled neither after conviction nor confession.

[In Mansi, in the same place.]

(v. q. 1. “Let it be known.”) Let it be known to your fraternity [Col. 1123D] that this priest, Christophorus by name, has tearfully complained to our clemency about his distress, saying that he was attacked by false accusations and irrationally expelled from his church without having been convicted or having confessed. For, as he himself reports, after your diligence had conducted an inquiry on three occasions, no fault could be found in him—neither concerning the charge of fornication nor concerning complicity in homicide, of which he was accused—except that, because of his poverty, he either did not wish or was unable to consent to or fulfill what was demanded. Nevertheless, his rival voluntarily carried these things out and unjustly seized his church. Therefore we earnestly admonish your reverence that even those matters which appear to have been carried out, perhaps without your knowledge, through Gehazi-like [Col. 1124A] greed, be corrected by the swift amendment imposed by your fraternity’s judgment. Specifically, restore the aforesaid priest to his own church and, through your piety, return to him the former honor that he lost; and do not in any way permit the canonical ordinances to be despised through anyone’s rashness, since the same punishment binds the one who acts and the one who consents.

(Anno 867.) CXXII. TO FROTARIUS, BISHOP OF BORDEAUX. Fragment.—What penance is to be imposed on invaders of ecclesiastical property.

[In Mansi, ibid.]

(12, q. 2. “Concerning the wicked man.”) Concerning a wicked man named Burgandus, who, moved by insane rage, did not hesitate to entangle himself in the devil’s snares and, lying in ambush along precipitous paths and crossroads in the manner of the pagans, presumed with demonic audacity to inflict nefarious invasions and violent plundering upon you while you were staying in a village of your church with your clerics, striving to instruct the people with salutary admonitions of doctrine, refreshing empty human hearts with the bread of the spiritual word, and desiring to visit the sacred thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul. He gathered the followers of his malice and accomplices in iniquity. And, as the text of your letter states, he dared with polluted hands to seize the sacred altar and the sacred vessels of the Lord’s body and blood, and even the holy chrism, as though they were cheap objects suited for common use. Your true affection therefore wisely consulted us, asking what judgment of our institution should bind him—and those who had joined him in so impious and unjust a crime—if at some time, touched by divine grace, they should wish to come to penance.

Concerning them, if the matter is indeed as stated, we order that, when they hasten to return to penance, they remain outside the Church of God for one year—having dared to carry away its most sacred vessels for plunder, contrary to the rite of the Christian faith. In the second year, let them remain without Communion before the doors of the church. In the third year, let them enter the Church of God and stand among the hearers without offering, neither eating meat nor drinking wine, except on the days of the Lord’s Nativity and Resurrection. In the fourth year, if during the preceding three years their labor of penance has borne fruit, let them be restored to the Communion of the faithful; and, promising with their whole attention of mind that they will never again do such things, let them be deemed worthy to receive the Lord’s body and blood. Until the seventh year, however, let them remain penitents for three days each week, abstaining from eating meat and drinking wine.

(Anno 867.) CXXIII. TO JOHN, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA. Fragment.—Concerning the catechism of those to be baptized.

[In Ivo, I, 87.]

Pope Nicholas to John, archbishop of Ravenna.

The catechisms of those to be baptized may be conducted by the priests of each church, just as it is solemnly demonstrated that they are conducted in this holy Roman Church, in which, by God’s authority, we perform the ministry of our service.

(Anno 867.) CXXIV. TO JOHN, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA. Concerning those who, having dismissed their wives, have passed to other marriages.

[Ivo, VIII, 221.]

Nicholas to the archbishop of Ravenna.

Concerning the senator’s wife, whom you say is an adulteress and who, on account of the charge of adultery, was judged to have been separated from her husband, clothed in monastic dress, and veiled, we do not know whether this judgment was reached justly or otherwise [Col. 1125B]. If she appeared to be an adulteress, you say that the matter ought first to have been investigated by her husband; and, if it was brought forward by her husband, it should have been examined and settled in the presence of investigators or judges. After the matter had been settled, approved, and made public, the judgment in the case should then have been defined either by a legal decision or by canonical judgment. If neither of these things was done, who dared to clothe her in religious dress and cover her with a sacred veil?

Nevertheless, keeping the fear of God more carefully before your eyes, we command that, in the presence of your envoy or vicar, an examination be conducted in a true inquiry, with her husband present. If their cause appears just and reasonable, let her remain. If it appears otherwise, as we have stated above, let their case be settled according to the will and fear of almighty God [Col. 1125C].

(Anno 867.) CXXV. TO ADALWIN, ARCHBISHOP OF JUVAVUM. Fragment.—Concerning a widow who returned to marriage after taking the veil of a nun.

[In Mansi, ibid.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy brother Adalwin, archbishop of the holy Church of Juvavum.

You asked about a woman who, after the death of her husband, placed the sacred veil upon her head and pretended under that veil to be a nun, but later returned to marriage. It seems good to me that, because she wished through hypocrisy to disturb ecclesiastical order and did not lawfully remain in her vow, she should do penance for this wicked deception, return to what she promised, and begin again in the holy monastery what she had commenced [Col. 1125D]. For if we agree that anyone may counterfeit all the Church’s sacraments as he wishes without truly performing them, the whole ecclesiastical order is thrown into confusion, the rights of the catholic faith do not stand, and the sacred canons are not rightly observed.

For what did it profit Simon Magus falsely to receive holy baptism and pretend that he would remain in Christianity, when through the Apostle the decree concerning what would befall him because of his fraud was foretold? For he says: “May your money be with you for destruction, for your heart is not right before God. Therefore repent of this wickedness of yours and pray to God that perhaps this thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity” (Acts VIII, 20) [Col. 1126A]. Therefore we judge that such people, unless they repent, should be struck with the spiritual sword. For it is not lawful to lie to the Holy Spirit, just as Ananias and Sapphira lied and immediately perished.

(Anno 867.) CXXVI. TO THE SAME. Fragment.—

[Ivo, XI, 104.]

Clerics who are known to have been possessed by demons in adolescence cannot advance to a higher rank of sacred governance.

(Anno 867.) CXXVII. TO THE SAME. That a bishop or cleric should in no way devote himself to hunting.

[Ivo, V, 353.]

[Col. 1126B]

Nicholas to Adalwin, archbishop of Juvavum.

It has been reported to our ears by the account of certain faithful people that Bishop Lanfred, who is also said to be a young man, is devoted to hunting. This vice entangles many, even in the clerical order, Germans and Gauls only by birth, who are irreverent [perhaps, “reverent”]. But if what we have heard is true, he is rightly called young: occupied with youthful desires, he is restrained by none of the gravity of old age.

Again: O miserable life of human beings, and especially of priests, who, when they ought to devote themselves to winning the faithful, apply themselves to hunting wild beasts; and, although they ought to capture human beings, capture birds and animals. While they pursue the deaths of living creatures, they lose the life of their own souls! O unhappy life, beyond every other life! For in what way does anyone appear more carnal than in such a life? The life of hunters catches nothing except flesh, and no one who has persisted in it has ever been proved [virtuous]. For, as blessed Jerome said, we have never read of a hunter who was a saint.

Woe to such prelates, who, although they ought to choose Peter, Andrew, James, and John—of whom the Lord said, “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew IV and Mark I)—for imitation, and are their disciples [Col. 1126D], instead imitate the reprobate Nimrod (Genesis X), Ishmael (Genesis XXI), and Esau (Genesis XXV and XXVII), who are reported to have devoted themselves to such pursuits.

Moreover, it has been reported to our apostolate concerning this bishop that he maintains an immoderate familiarity with a certain daughter of his, and that on this account an evil reputation has arisen concerning him. For this matter he has been admonished and reproved by your holiness and by his fellow bishops, but has in no way been corrected. This is especially displeasing in the case, and makes the opinion of him increasingly worse. In this he does not obey your beatitude or the counsels of his fellow bishops, and through disobedience falls back into the guilt of the first-formed man.

Therefore your fraternity ought to convene a synodical council with your bishops and suffragans [Col. 1127A], confront this bishop with salutary words, and command him with pastoral authority to remain wholly removed from the hunting of every beast and bird, and to restrain himself in every way from immoderate familiarity with his daughter. If he should scorn to obey, and, when admonished by you, should delay obedience both in abandoning hunting and in avoiding immoderate association with his daughter, let him depart excommunicated from your college. If he should still appear contumacious in this, he ought to cease from the ministry.

(Anno 867.) CXXVIII. TO THE SAME. When a bishop is ill, another is not to be substituted unless he has departed this life, lest the beauty of the entrusted talent be destroyed.

[Ivo, V, 352.]

[Col. 1127B]

Nicholas to Adalwin, archbishop of Juvavum.

Pontiffs who are afflicted by some illness or disease are not to be cast aside, nor should others be consecrated in their place unless they have been removed from this light. If they complain about the ministry entrusted to them, let priests perform what is lawful. In matters which they are not permitted to undertake, let the assistance of neighboring bishops be supplied until they recover their health; and let this be done with vigilant caution, lest ambition of presumption sprout through the occasion of necessity.

Bishops who have undertaken the care and solicitude of the Lord’s flock ought not to withdraw from its administration, so that the beauty of the talent they received may not be destroyed, but may be healthfully increased and tripled through their struggle [Col. 1127C].

(Anno 867.) CXXIX. TO SALOMON, BISHOP OF CONSTANTIA. Fragment.—That no one is to be condemned unless he has confessed voluntarily or been canonically convicted.

[Ivo, VI, 122.]

Nicholas to Salomon, bishop of Constantia.

You assert that a priest or deacon does not wish publicly to confess his crimes, but wishes to defend himself under oath; nevertheless, it is known to the bishop that the crime was committed by him. Such a man cannot, through any penance, obtain priestly or diaconal office. But it is astonishing: if he has not confessed, how can it be known to the bishop that the crime was committed by him, unless perhaps a suitable accuser has established it through suitable witnesses?

Therefore, if, when the bishop examines the case of the priest or deacon, that priest or deacon has not been convicted through the testimony of witnesses, the crime has not been legally disclosed to the bishop, unless the priest or deacon voluntarily confesses the crime itself. If he does not do so, meanwhile we do not see that the priest or deacon ought to be deprived of his office.

Thus only voluntary confession, or a canonical number or quality of witnesses, with the bishops deciding and the accuser proving what he alleged, deprives a cleric of his proper rank [Col. 1128A].

(Anno 867.) CXXX. TO THE SAME. Whether a man may have two spiritual co-mothers.

[Ivo, I, 137.]

Nicholas to Salomon, bishop of Constantia.

Your holiness asks us whether a man may have two spiritual co-mothers, one after the other. Your fraternity ought to remember that it is written: “The two shall be one flesh” (Genesis II). Since it is established that a man and wife become one flesh through marriage, it follows that the man is made co-father (compater) to the woman to whom the wife whom he took in marriage was held to be co-mother (commater). Therefore it is clear that the man cannot be joined in intercourse to the woman who was his co-mother, with whom he had become one flesh [Col. 1128B].

(Anno 867.) CXXXI. TO THE SAME. Fragment.—Concerning the penance of parricides and incestuous persons.

[Ivo, X, 185.]

Nicholas to Solomon, bishop of Constantia.

It is established that parricides, fratricides, and incestuous persons, concerning whom you ask whether they may be joined in marriage, must do penance and therefore cannot be joined in carnal intercourse [Col. 1128C]. They ought to remain in chastity throughout their entire lives, in mind and body, with the twenty-fourth rule of the Decretals of blessed Pope Leo observed toward them also, out of mercy.

(Anno 867.) CXXXII. TO THE BISHOP OF SOLANITUM OR SOLEMONIUM. Fragment.—

[Ivo, I, 136.]

Nicholas to the bishop of Solemonium.

You wish to know whether a woman who lifted her husband’s son, born by another woman, from the sacred font may afterward be joined to that same man. We decide that they may be joined, because according to the sacred canons no spouse ought to dismiss the other under the pretext of any religious observance without the consent of both [Col. 1128D]. It is a matter of great ruin for a wife who, hating her husband or failing to consider his weakness, performs impiety as though out of pious concern—especially since the Apostle commands: “Do not defraud one another, except by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and again return to the same, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control” (1 Corinthians VII).

Therefore, if it is not proved that this was done with the consent of both spouses, they are not to defraud one another, but are to return to the same union—especially since the Apostle says: “The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife” (ibid.).

(Anno 867.) CXXXIII. [Col. 1129A] TO RODULF, BISHOP OF STRASBOURG. Fragment.—Concerning a penitent matricide.

[In Mansi, ibid.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy Rodulf, bishop of the holy Church of Strasbourg.

While throngs of believers hasten from every region of the world to the threshold of the prince of the apostles, a certain man named Thothar came bearing a letter from your beatitude, which he delivered to our pontificate. Reading its page, we learned that he was a matricide. We grieved greatly at this deed, with many sighs and tears [Col. 1129B]. Therefore we command, and establish by the judgments of the holy Fathers, that he remain under the yoke of penance, in such a way that for one year he does not enter the church, but stands before the doors of the basilica, persevering in prayer and supplication to God, so that he may be rescued from so great a sin.

When the year’s cycle has been completed, let him have permission to enter the church; nevertheless, let him stand among the hearers and not yet receive Communion. When the course of three years has been completed, let the grace of sacred Communion be granted to him. Let him not offer offerings until he has completed a further course of seven years.

Throughout all these years and periods, let him not eat meat or presume to drink wine, except on feast days and Sundays, and from Easter until Pentecost. Wherever he wishes to go, let him not be taken by any vehicle, but proceed on foot. Let him take up arms only against pagans. Let him fast three days each week until evening.

He is not to separate from his own lawful wife, lest he fall into the abyss of fornication—which we desire should not happen. If, however, the end of his life should approach before the completion of three years, let him partake of the body of our Lord Jesus Christ; otherwise, let him be dealt with as we have established above.

Nevertheless, if you see his conduct and fountain of tears flourishing in every way through fruitful actions and excellent works, let your vigilant care toward him appear more humane, and let it be shown to all as gentle. We wish you well in Christ.

(Anno 867.) CXXXIV. TO GUIFRED, BISHOP OF THEROUANNE. [Col. 1129D] Fragment.—Concerning a cleric who has killed a pagan.

[In Mansi, ibid.]

Nicholas to Guifred, bishop of the Church of Thérouanne.

A cleric who has killed a pagan ought not to be advanced to a higher rank; indeed, he must also be deprived of the rank he has acquired. For he is a homicide. Since the soldiers of the world are distinct from the soldiers of the Church, it is not fitting for a soldier of the Church to serve the world, whereby he must come to the shedding of blood.

Finally, just as it is shameful and harmful for a layman to celebrate Masses and confect the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood [Col. 1130A], so it is ridiculous and inappropriate for a cleric to take up arms and go to war, since Paul, the distinguished preacher, says: “No one serving as a soldier for God involves himself in worldly affairs” (2 Timothy II, 4). In the same way, conversely, no one serving the world involves himself in spiritual affairs.

(Anno 867.) CXXXV. TO THE ELECT AND CLERGY OF THE CHURCH OF NOYON. Fragment.—A church should not be established without the approval of the apostolic see.

[Gratian, D. III, d. 1, c. 8.]

How can the Church—that is, the assembly of Catholics—be established without the approval of the apostolic see, when, according to the sacred decrees, even a basilica which is known to embrace within itself that whole company of Catholics ought not to be newly built without the pope’s instruction [Col. 1130B]?

(Anno 867.) CXXXVI. TO RIVOLADRUS, BISHOP. Concerning the penance imposed on Wimar, who had killed his three sons.

[In Mansi, Councils, vol. XV.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy Bishop Rivoladrus.

Bishops ought to observe the care of the Lord’s flock, filled with heavenly teaching, in such a way that they incur no danger through neglect of the sheepfold entrusted to them. For very many betrayers of their crimes come from every direction; how much grief they bring to our breast we recall more through sobbing than can be written with a pen.

Among them, know that this man Wimar hastened to the threshold of the apostles and disclosed the measure of penance imposed upon him for the murder of his three sons. We moderated certain aspects of it because he hastened devoutly to seek the assistance of the prince of the apostles, our nurturer. The pressure of time recalled him when he wished to go to the shrine of the blessed archangel; and apostolic solicitude sent a letter containing the measure of the constitution imposed upon him, to be delivered to your holiness.

In that letter, therefore—that is, in this one—it was established as follows: he is to stand for three years before the doors of the church, praying for his sins, and thereafter remain among the hearers for four years [Col. 1130D]. Thus he is to pass seven years without Communion of the Lord’s body and blood, and throughout all the days of his life he is not to eat meat. During those seven years he is not to take wine except on Sundays and feast days; thereafter, for five years, he is to abstain from wine three days each week, so that the measure of his penance extends to twelve years.

He is permitted not to abandon his own wife, lest he perhaps fall into adultery and, because of the occasion of one offense, be driven by the weakness of the flesh into something worse. We have allowed him to come to you wearing shoes; thereafter he must go barefoot for three years, and he may be clothed according to the season and the temper of the weather, and enjoy milk [Col. 1131A].

For the rest, discerning his conduct in this way, consider and arrange everything so that evangelical mercy may also be recognized in him. We nevertheless permit him to eat cheese and to possess his property. After the seventh year and until the day of his death, let him persevere in the aforesaid penance, and let him bear arms only against pagans. We wish your holiness well in Christ.

(Anno 867.) CXXXVII. TO JEREMIAH, BISHOP. Fragment.—How wicked it is to join oneself to blood relatives.

[Ivo, IX, 12.]

Nicholas to Jeremiah, bishop.

Those who desire unions with blood relatives must take the greatest care lest they fall into the devil’s snare. It is evident to all who remain in the true faith of Christ how wicked it is to take as wives nuns, who have rejected worldly marriage and devoted themselves to Christ, or a female cousin, or women from one’s own blood relationship [Col. 1131B].

(Anno 867.) CXXXVIII. TO OSBALD, CHOREPISCOPUS OF QUADRANTUM. Fragment.—He who kills a pagan while defending himself must lose his priestly office.

[Gratian I, 50, 6.]

Concerning those clerics about whom you consulted us—namely, those who killed pagans while defending themselves—whether, after being corrected through penance, they may return to their former rank or ascend to a higher one, know that we give no occasion or license to them to kill anyone in any way.

But if it should happen that a cleric of priestly rank has killed even a pagan, he consults his own interests greatly if he withdraws from priestly office. It is better for him in this life to serve the Lord irreproachably under a lower status than, by wrongly seeking a higher one, to be damnably plunged into the depths [Col. 1131C].

(Anno 867.) CXXXIX. TO THE SAME OSBALD. Concerning the punishment of a priest who has struck a deacon.

[Ivo, X, 24.]

[Col. 1131D]

Nicholas to Osbald, bishop of Quadrantum.

Let your holiness persuade your bishop to associate with himself a canonical number of colleagues—namely, six brothers and fellow bishops from neighboring provinces. Joined with you, and deciding matters carefully, investigate diligently and scrutinize with every effort whether the aforesaid deacon died from the blow of the named priest or from a broken neck.

If he was not struck to death by the aforementioned priest, but fell from a horse and died with his neck broken, impose upon the priest, who acted incautiously, the penance appropriate for the blow, according to your judgment, and suspend him for some time from the solemn celebrations of Mass; afterward he is to return to priestly office [Col. 1132A].

But if that deacon truly died from any blow by this priest, we decree that he may in no way minister in the manner of a priest. For even if he did not have the intention of killing, the rage and indignation from which that deadly action arose are forbidden in every person, but especially in ministers of God, in many ways, and are condemned everywhere.

If, however, the priest should prove so harmful after your investigation, we command that such a benefice be granted to him from his church that both he and his dependents may sufficiently have the means of their support.

(Anno 867.) CXL. FROM THE DECREES OF POPE NICHOLAS.

[In Mansi, ibid.]

[Col. 1132B]

If anyone has fornicated with two sisters, or with his stepmother—that is, with his father’s widow—or with his paternal aunt, or with his maternal aunt, or with his paternal uncle’s daughter, or with his maternal uncle’s daughter, or with the daughter of his paternal aunt or maternal aunt, or with the daughter of his own daughter or son; or even with his grandmother, or even with his great-grandmother, or with his brother’s or sister’s daughter, or with his brother’s or son’s wife; likewise, if any woman has allowed herself to fornicate through the aforesaid degrees of blood relationship, each of them individually is to do penance for sixteen [years] in the following manner.

First, for that entire year let the person remain confined at the entrance of the house of God, and during that year, except on Sundays and feast days, let him or her use only bread, water, and salt [Col. 1132C].

In the second year, let them indeed enter the house of the Lord, but let them not use meat, wine, or beer, except on feast days and Sundays [editorial deletion: “in”; supplied: “except,” as below]. Thereafter, during the next two years, throughout the entire year, whenever they eat meat, let them abstain from every drink by which one can become drunk; and if they drink, let them not eat meat at all. During the week: Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday; the other weekdays are to be pure (purae)—that is, Monday, Wednesday, and Friday.

Sundays, however, are to be completely free. Then, until the end of the tenth year, let the person properly observe three weekdays during each of the three Lents of the year; but Friday, for as long as he or she lives, is to be observed with bread and water [Col. 1132D]. Let the person bear arms only against pagans. Let him or her give a kiss to no one. Let him or her receive the Sacrifice only as viaticum; and, if it should happen that the person is without a wife [f. “if it should happen”], let him or her never enter marriage.

If the person is married, he or she is not to be entirely deprived of marriage after five years of penance. Whoever commits incest within the other degrees up to the seventh line is to do penance for ten years, as stated above.

Certainly, the priest must consider whether the person sinned once, or for how long he or she persisted in the vice, and whether the incest was committed by accident, involuntarily, or unknowingly; and, having considered the quality [Col. 1133A] or quantity of the sin, let him impose penance upon the fallen person with prudent judgment.

If anyone has fornicated with his mother, or with his sister, or with his daughter, first let him live for seven years on bread and water alone, as stated above, except on Sundays and feast days; and during those same seven years let him not enter the house of the Lord at all. Thereafter, until the completion of the twenty-first year, let him observe three weekdays on bread and water. Then, throughout all the days of his life, let him observe Friday with bread and water. If he is without a wife, let him never marry. If he has a wife, let him be restored to his wife after the seventh year. Concerning arms, peace, and reception of the sacred body, let it be done as stated above.

[Col. 1133B] If with a paternal or maternal aunt; if a cousin with a female cousin, according to the ancient definition, let him do penance for twelve years [Note: [Col. 1133D] The passage is corrupt]; if excommunicated, to define the matter more humanely, ten years if with a relative by blood or kinship from the third through the seventh degree, according to the ancient and humane definition: if it is the third degree, let him do penance for twelve years; if the fourth, ten; if the fifth, eight; if the sixth, seven; if the seventh, five.

If a father-in-law with his daughter-in-law, a son-in-law with his mother-in-law, a stepfather with his stepdaughter, a stepson with his stepmother, or a kinsman with a female kinswoman who is the wife of his brother or the sister of his wife, according to the ancient and more humane definition, let him do penance for ten years; if with his wife’s second-degree relative, let him do penance for seven years; if third-degree, seven; if fourth-degree, six.

If a father and son, or two brothers, with one woman, or with mother and daughter, or with two sisters, or with two co-mothers, according to the ancient and more humane definition, let him do penance for eight years [Col. 1133C].

If with a consecrated virgin, or with a nun, or with another man’s wife; if a godfather with his co-mother, or a brother with a sister in Christ, according to the ancient definition, let him do penance for ten years. According to the humane definition of the Council of Toledo I, chapter 16, let it be seven years.

If with a consecrated woman who has changed her clothing; if with another man’s chosen widow or betrothed; if with a priest’s wife or a deacon’s wife; or if with a widow or a pagan woman, according to the ancient definition, let him do penance for ten years; according to the humane definition, seven.

If with a widow of equal status, a public prostitute, or another person’s female slave, according to the ancient and humane definition, let him do penance for five years.

If with a lay virgin, whom no one [text corrupt: “whom neither … takes as wife”] takes as a wife, according to the ancient and humane definition, let him do penance for four years [Col. 1133D].

The women who have joined in incestuous and wicked intercourse with all the persons listed above are likewise to do penance according to the order prescribed for women. The one who consented to this evil is to be treated in the same way; otherwise, according to the measure of the fault, they are to be judged by the wisest priest.

Moreover, if—God forbid—someone from the clerical order should fall with any of all the persons mentioned above who are called incestuous, it is to be noted that each one is judged as follows: a layman, five years; a subdeacon, seven; a deacon and monk, ten; a priest [Col. 1134A], fourteen; a bishop, eighteen; and similarly in the matters that follow.

(Anno 867.) CXLI. LETTER TO THADO, ARCHBISHOP OF MILAN. Concerning those who scourge and kill bishops.

[Ivo, X, 20.]

Nicholas to Thado, archbishop of Milan.

Concerning those who scourge and kill priests—namely, brigands who are not restrained by the secular arm—it has pleased us, according to the Lord’s command, that they be admonished through fraternal love a second and a third time. If they do not listen to you, let the Church convene and deprive them of the Eucharist. If they should remain in their obstinacy, despising priestly admonitions, we grant permission to cut them off from the fabric of the Church under the prohibition of anathema [Col. 1134B]. Know also that, if they repent, they can eventually be recalled to the bosom of holy Mother Church after suitable satisfaction has first been made.

(Anno 867.) CXLII. TO THE SAME THADO. That the measure of the fault is to be treated according to the degrees of kinship.

[Ivo, IX, 14.]

Nicholas to Thado, archbishop of Milan.

We establish that those who have perhaps sinned with the daughter of their paternal aunt, paternal uncle, or maternal uncle—alas!—are to have the measure of their fault treated according to the degrees of kinship, just as we formerly made known to you by apostolic letter concerning those who committed this disgrace with their spiritual [Col. 1134C] mother.

(Anno 867.) CXLIII. TO THE SAME. That a priest who commits homicide is to lose priestly office.

[Ivo, X, 29.]

Nicholas to Thado, archbishop of Milan.

Therefore, concerning priests who have committed homicide involuntarily and nevertheless incur the guilt of homicide, since they truly are homicides, we decree that, removed from priestly ministry, they be afflicted with penance according to the sacred orders; afterward, when the prescribed periods of penance have elapsed and they have offered suitable satisfaction, let them obtain the grace of Communion. In all things, however, let the sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the apostolic see remain inviolate; these permit us to grant mercy to converts and penitents and not to deny them access to the Church—indeed, they salutarily encourage and command us to do so [Col. 1134D].

(Anno 867.) CXLIV. TO JOHN, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA. That if a bishop has been killed, another is not to be substituted until the guilty have been identified and punished.

[Ivo, X, 19.]

Nicholas to John, archbishop of Ravenna.

Our apostolate grieved greatly and was struck with profound sorrow over the most savage killing of Bishop Oleobert of Gravellona. Yet again we are no less astonished at your prudence: is it true that your action sent a bishop there without our permission, when, as you say, it was not lawful for one to be sent?

Certainly, even if nothing else had prevented you, at least the crime ought to have delayed you somewhat, so that you would not quickly establish a bishop over such a people and in such a place—where diseased sheep, imitating the Jews’ crime against the Lord Savior, dared to cut down their own shepherd [Col. 1135A].

Therefore wait a little, and investigate the case, most diligently, according to blessed Job, lest, unless a worthy examination precedes it, you be found—God forbid—to have placed your hand upon a head full of blood. When the guilty have been exposed and punished, and someone worthy has appeared, and concord has been achieved among the clergy, the people, and our duke who holds our authority—and who is, of course, known to be one of that same people—let the election be celebrated. Then, just as was deliberated and established in the synod, inform us of this; and when our apostolate has been notified concerning the person elected, with the preceding sanction of the Lord’s assistance, let the bishop be consecrated by your beatitude.

(Anno 867.) CXLV. TO HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS. Those who sin not deliberately but through necessity or ignorance are to be absolved.

[In Mansi, Councils, vol. XV.]

[Col. 1135C]

Nicholas to the archbishop of Rheims.

The most excellent King Charles consulted our apostolate about what should be done concerning those who communicate with persons who communicate with the woman Ingeltrude, often condemned, since it is established that they had previously been bound by the bond of anathema together with the excommunicated and their supporters.

Therefore we now charge your beatitude to dare, relying on our authority, to take care of these matters. Since your holiness, taught by God, knows very well that one thing is done out of necessity, another out of ignorance, and another through deliberate intent—and that the latter is to be punished more strictly than the two former—let your holiness watch diligently and judge the conduct of each person with careful discernment. Thus those who sin out of necessity or ignorance may be absolved by you on our authority, provided that their ignorance or necessity is genuine and not feigned, and has not arisen from their own will, as you know well [Col. 1135D].

There are many who can know what is right but do not wish to know it. Therefore the psalmist says concerning such people: “They did not wish to understand, so that they might do good” (Psalm XXXV). Those, however, who bind themselves through deliberate intent and, out of contempt, set aside our prohibitions, we wish you to absolve only after suitable satisfaction has first been made.

(Anno 867.) CXLVI. TO QUEEN THEUTBERGA. He reproves her for writing against herself, overcome by weariness, and denies that what she suggests can be done: that she dissolve her marriage out of a desire for continence unless her husband Lothair also promises a celibate life.

[In Mansi, ibid.]

[Col. 1136A]

NICOLAUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter TEUTBERGA, most glorious queen.

We have received the letter of your petition, sent to our episcopate by your envoys, and we clearly recognized that it contained in writing nothing other than what they had indicated in words [Col. 1136B]. Yet we were equally astonished and amazed at both, and, considering how suddenly the wording of the letter and the petition had changed, we recalled that you had never at any time communicated anything of this kind to us. But why do you write and suggest such things to us, when we had long before foreseen that you would both write and make this petition to us?

Yet when we turn the eyes of our mind to the reports of nearly all the distinguished persons who are present in the regions of Gaul and Germany, we see that there is a great difference between what you now alone signify and what they indicate almost daily in words and letters. For they all testify that you are suffering unremitting affliction, intolerable oppression, and excessive violence. But you, suggesting the opposite of these things, confess that, with no one compelling you, you willingly and gladly desire and wish to be stripped of your royal dignity [Col. 1136C], as well as the other matters in which you are recognized to have proceeded in one way, while they have proceeded in another.

Thus, according to the assertions of all, you are said to have been lawfully received by King Lothar, then unjustly accused, afterward cleared, subsequently rejected again, and finally lawfully restored by our decree. But now, having brought about the opposite of all these things and having forgotten your own profession, you confess certain frivolous matters which we plainly do not wish to exaggerate, because we do not wish to labor needlessly.

Nevertheless, we have understood that the one who did harm to the holy Church of God is still doing harm, and that the one who was filthy is still becoming filthier. We have understood, I say, that he has determined to let the beasts rot in their dung; and that, although it was not enough for him to have committed adultery and to have drawn together, in the cord of vanity, the deceptions of falsehood and the devices of iniquity [Col. 1136D], he has added this also: to plunge human souls, ensnared in the nets of perjury, into ultimate destruction.

But what wonder is it if, through perjury, he has brought death upon the souls of a few, when, placed in a lofty position, by the example of his adultery he has sunk many thousands of people into the chaos of perdition?

Yet the testimony you give concerning Waldrada, saying that she was Lothar’s lawful wife, you attempt in vain to establish, since no one at all needs your testimony concerning this. Rather, we judge what is just and understand what is equitable in this way: even if you had been rejected, even if you had died, Lothar would never have been permitted, by any laws or regulations that did not endanger him, to take Waldrada, an adulteress, as his wife [Col. 1137A].

Therefore, whether Waldrada was ever a legitimate wife, the Church of God has no need of your satisfaction. Know one thing, however: neither we nor that same holy Church, by the authority of God, who will judge adulterers, will in any way leave Lothar unpunished if he ever takes Waldrada back, even if you should, as we have stated, depart this life.

As for what you say—that you wish to come to Rome and disclose to us your sufferings and certain secrets of your heart—it is not appropriate. The security of the journey which you claim is nonexistent, and, as long as Waldrada is placed beside Lothar in this way, we do not permit you to depart from him by any means. For once you have departed, she will undoubtedly be believed to have been received, and in your absence she will immediately be admitted [Col. 1137B].

As for the fact that, as you assert, you are recognized as remaining barren, this is caused not by the barrenness of your body but by the wickedness of your husband. Nevertheless, we read that, when God grants fertility, “the barren woman has borne many, and she who had many children has grown weak” (1 Kings 2).

You also assert that your marriage was not divinely ordained and therefore cannot continue, since “every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted” (Matthew 15). But remember that God planted a vineyard and, according to Isaiah, expected it to produce grapes; instead, it produced wild grapes (Isaiah 5), and, according to Jeremiah, it was turned into the bitterness of an alien vine (Jeremiah 2). God therefore planted your marriage, but through the fault of your husband it has been turned into bitterness; and while it was expected to produce grapes, alas, it produced wild grapes—or even thorns [Col. 1137C].

Of the countless matters in your letter, these alone have pleased us to mention. Yet who does not know that you have brought these things forth after being overcome by many pressures and worn down by innumerable evils, since, as we have already said, all the religious and distinguished men of Gaul and Germany testify in frequent reports that these things are so? Indeed, we recognized long beforehand that you would write this letter to us.

But setting these matters aside, we exhort you and earnestly admonish you not to lay hands upon yourself or kindle the fuel of death. It is better for you that another, speaking the truth, should kill you than that you, speaking falsehood, should destroy yourself. Stand therefore fearless and steadfast, and do not be afraid to endure death, which in any event you must experience once, especially for the sake of truth [Col. 1137D]. Since Christ is the truth, whoever dies for the truth undoubtedly dies for Christ; for this reason John the Baptist is recognized to have suffered martyrdom.

If he was killed while speaking the justice of another, how much more ought you, speaking the justice of God and bearing witness to your own truth, fear no death’s destruction? “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matthew 5)—not only for another’s righteousness, but also for their own.

Yet we do not at all accept this confession of yours as a confession, since it was force, not your will, that extorted it from you. Nor do we permit so great a vice to put down roots, since, unless it is torn out from within, it may grow to the ruin of many [Col. 1138A]. Indeed, if this were permitted, all husbands could torment the women whom they had lawfully taken in marriage with various afflictions whenever they hated them, and could compel them to confess that they had not been lawfully taken. They could even force them, by intolerable punishments, to declare a capital crime against themselves.

For who can do more harm than a civil enemy? Or who can injure another more than a husband can injure his wife? We must therefore guard against such frauds and cut them off at the very beginning of their emergence, so that they may not prevail.

Nor do we think that Lothar, your husband, would descend to such ruin of himself as to consent in any way to plot against your life, since, if he had fallen into so monstrous a crime, he would bring upon himself and his kingdom no less loss than upon you [Col. 1138B].

For, as far as human understanding can determine, you have often been shown to be not only innocent but also to have constantly sought the Church’s assistance. Moreover, you sought the protection and refuge of the holy chief of the apostles. Hence the Apostolic See began to examine your case and proposed to reserve to its own special judgment whatever question might arise.

Therefore whoever acts against you gravely injures not only the Church of God but is also plainly shown to be violently provoking against himself the Apostolic See, whose judgment may not be reopened.

Certainly, if you intend to come to Rome and wish to obtain permission to depart from your husband, we instead urge you much more strongly to make every effort to persuade that same husband to provide you first with the most certain security, so that you may nowhere fear suffering any injury at the hands of anyone [Col. 1138C]. This cannot happen unless Waldrada is first sent to Rome and a suitable decision concerning her is made. Only then should such assurance of safety follow that you suffer no harm either while coming, while staying, or while returning from here.

But if he refuses to act in order to remove the evil opinion directed against him, desist, and take every possible precaution not to yield to such treacherous snares. For both he and his satellites are craftily attempting to deceive you and are undoubtedly plotting to trip you up in the traps of their artful evasiveness.

Furthermore, if, as you claim, you seek dissolution of the marriage out of love of chastity, know that this will not be granted to you in any way unless your husband himself has genuinely pursued that same chastity [Col. 1138D]. In short, as blessed Pope Gregory says: if the wife does not follow the continence which the husband desires, or if the husband refuses the continence which the wife desires, the marriage may not be divided, because it is written: “The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the man does; and likewise the man does not have authority over his own body, but the woman” (1 Corinthians 7).

We wish Your Glory to remain well in Christ now and always, most beloved daughter.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of February, in the fifteenth indiction.

(Year 867.) CXLVII. TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF LOTHAR.

He writes for the third time concerning Waldrada’s excommunication; he censures their sluggishness and orders them to report whether Lothar is living with Teutberga and how he treats her.

[According to Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 1139A]

NICOLAUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most holy and most reverend fellow bishops, the archbishops and bishops governing the Church of God in the kingdom of King Lothar.

At last we would wish, made secure by the correction of King Lothar, to extend our pen to other matters of ecclesiastical administration. But neither his completed sins, which produce death, permit this in any way, nor does your zeal, by which so great a crime might reach its end, display the fervor of justice against it by contending with us as watchfully and episcopally as it should.

Therefore we are sufficiently astonished at your hearts, and not only wonder at them but also lament them. For who would not mourn such sluggishness of speech, such slack hands of negligence, when, amid the guardianship of so many shepherds, neither the snares of the wolf that does not spare the flock are prevented, nor the approaches of the lion seeking someone to devour are barred?

Certainly, since the zeal of God ought to consume every Christian, you ought to have used that same zeal all the more, having attained the more eminent rank and order of that same holy household—if only not to your greater peril [Col. 1139C].

Having said this by way of introduction, behold: for the third time we now inform all of you by our letters that Waldrada, the most wicked rival of our daughter Queen Teutberga, has been deprived of the fellowship and communion of Christians.

After our envoy’s threats—as you yourselves know—had taken effect, and Lothar, having rejected Waldrada, had obediently restored himself to his wife, Queen Teutberga, it could rightly have been believed that, by the most certain satisfaction of the oath he had given, he had put an end to his crime. It was therefore decreed that Waldrada should be kept farther from that same king in proportion as the cunning of the ancient enemy was shown not to be absent from such matters.

It was also decreed that the woman should remain meanwhile in Italy, awaiting the tenor of our judgment; and, if we should consider it necessary for her to come to Rome, she should appear without delay [Col. 1139D], so that, standing before us, she might either show herself innocent, if she could, or, by confessing what she had committed, obtain mercy.

Although she came to Italy under compulsion, she disdained to travel to Rome, overcome by the obstinacy of her mind. Indeed, as though possessing an irreproachable conscience, she turned back and directed her steps toward the province.

When we heard this, we understood that she wished her crime to be ended by no correction and desired no subsequent remedy by which her own wound might be healed. Therefore we pronounced against her a sentence of excommunication, to continue until her correction and her suitable satisfaction to us and to the whole Church.

How much more severely she must be punished than all others is certainly shown by this: King Lothar recognized his iniquity to such an extent that he even corrected it [Col. 1140A]. She, however, neither recognized it, nor confessed it, nor abandoned the poison of her mind. Yet, brought back from the journey she had begun, she neither grieved at having been struck nor wished, once bruised, to receive discipline. For she neither returned to the one striking her nor felt more severe wounds.

She is therefore rightly counted among the dead: she who indeed neither [the Roman edition adds: “so that, while alive, she hears the voice of the preachers, nor in her own, etc.”]—though hidden in her inner chambers, indeed now lying foul-smelling—comes forth through confession. [The printed syntax is defective.]

We have thought it right to send you again, written in our letters, the text of the sentence pronounced against this adulteress, already mentioned, admonishing you that at least you should guard yourselves and your subjects from her dead works [Col. 1140B] and, as commanded, should not touch what is polluted (Isaiah 12).

Although, as we have heard from the report of certain persons—or rather, as we learned from the fact that no benefit resulted—your brotherhood refused to receive the same letter, nor took care in this matter, for which it was sent, either to remain vigilant when aroused by us or to undertake any action.

If this matter were not supported by truth, your diligence would long ago have reported to our pontificate how much it had accomplished—or failed to accomplish—in accordance with what was fitting [for “fittingly,” HARD.]. But since it has reported nothing to us concerning this, it is plainly understood that, after being admonished, it has shown no zeal whatsoever in the matter.

From this it is clearly evident what you would do if you were not stirred by any of our exhortations—since, even when so often urged by us, you undertake no labor in ecclesiastical corrections [Col. 1140C].

But at least now begin what you have hitherto neglected, so that each of you may truly be able to say with the psalmist: “Now I have begun” (Psalm 76). And finally, with the apostle, confess confidently and joyfully: “I have fought the good fight, I have completed the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for me” (2 Timothy 4).

Perhaps wickedness would now impose an end upon itself, unless some of you sought what is their own more than what belongs to Jesus Christ. Some fear that their perishable or poisoned benefits will be taken away; some refuse to speak for justice but strive with all their strength to favor adulterers, and by this they are deprived, by the just Judge’s decision, of eternal benefits.

Nevertheless, they ought also to remember that it is by no means hidden from us how much favor they themselves have shown to adulterers—indeed, they cannot be unaware that we long ago discovered their surreptitious dealings in profane proceedings [Col. 1140D].

Although perhaps we forgave these things through apostolic moderation, we remember how those whom we spared were treated. In short, we dismissed the past in such a way as to apply suitable caution concerning the future; and they should know that they would escape the judgment thus deferred only if they knew that they would never again fall into the same crime by showing favor.

Now, therefore, since they have guarded themselves against him with insufficient caution, they have fallen under the judgment that had been postponed. Nevertheless, both for them and for those who scorned sending envoys to obtain pardon, great care must be taken lest they fall from our communion and, through it, from the structure of the universal Church, and so finally rejoice less at the end in their offices than they desire [Col. 1141A].

Moreover, if anyone, as rumor falsely claims, thinks that we have granted Waldrada permission to return to Gaul—or if there are persons to whose knowledge our letters did not come because they were concealed—if they do not refuse to learn what our unchanging intention has always been concerning this matter, let them question Counts Christian and Waltar.

Although they came to Rome at different times rather than together, we urged them not only so that Lothar might continually be admonished to cease at last from his wickedness, but also explicitly informed them that Waldrada had been excommunicated, because, intending to remain impenitent, she had not asked us, when she came to the threshold of the apostles for the remedy of her salvation, to which she had been summoned, as had been decreed [Col. 1141B].

Here it must be considered that, if Waldrada was punished by us chiefly because she did not complete the salutary journey she had begun, we do not know how she could have obtained our permission to turn back.

But now our speech is addressed to you, dearest brothers, and our pen is directed to the reverence of Your Beatitude: if your zeal is not so kindled [Roman edition: “by God”] that you seem to imitate Phinehas—that is, so that you exercise the spiritual sword as he exercised the material one—at least do not refuse, in priestly emulation or pastoral solicitude, to recall Nathan, Elijah, and the other prophets who salutarily rebuked delinquent kings.

For although once Elijah, overcome by human weakness, fled from the ruler’s fury, he nevertheless repeatedly rebuked his crimes and reproached him without fear [Col. 1141C].

Likewise, this blessed shepherd of the Church, Peter, who earlier, overcome by human frailty at the voice of a single servant girl—something brought about by the divine dispensation—denied the author of life because he feared to die, after receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit, of whose portion we rightly believe you also partake, pressed upon the strength of rulers even after threats and killings, so that he was deservedly shown to have received the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire.

For the Spirit filled those whom he made burning with ardor and at the same time made them speak, and the flame of divine zeal, together with the torches of their wondrous words, approached the hearts of the rulers of the world. Indeed, “who was weak, and I was not weak? Who was scandalized, and I was not burning?” [Col. 1141D]

But, so that we do not linger longer, we now take care to address you only with the words of that same chief of the apostles. Understand that what he said while addressing presbyters applies to you all the more; and from the sermon recited by blessed Clement, consider how great an evil adultery is and what awaits you if you are found zealous or negligent. He says:

“And what is more serious among all sins than adultery? For it holds second place among punishments, since first place belongs to those who depart from God, even if they have lived soberly. Therefore, O presbyters, cultivate the Church and adorn the bride of Christ for chastity. By ‘bride’ I mean the whole congregation of Christ’s Church [Col. 1142A]. If she is found chaste by her bridegroom, she will be honored by him with great gifts and rewards, and you, as the bride’s ministers and the bridegroom’s friends, will enjoy immense joy and gladness. But if this bride is found stained by sins, she herself, as unworthy, will be driven from the royal marriage chamber; you, however, will suffer punishment if, through your negligence and sluggishness, the savage contagion of sin has crept in. Behold: you have heard the reward, you who are zealous; behold: you have heard your peril, you who are idle.”

Having gone through these matters, we exhort Your Holiness and, by the incomprehensible Holy Trinity, earnestly beseech all of you together to inform us truthfully, by letters sent without delay through suitable envoys, whether Lothar is living with Teutberga according to the oath he swore before our envoy, or whether he treats her as a king ought to treat a queen lawfully joined to him [Col. 1142B].

Also report who those men are who, in no respect dissenting from us, refuse to grant adulterers any favor. Moreover, display this letter of ours and take care to make the text of Waldrada’s excommunication known.

Now, whoever among you postpones doing and reporting these things will openly show himself liable and a supporter of adulterers. If he neglects to obey this ordinance of ours, it will be a sign to us that he has consented to so great a crime. Accordingly, as one summoned and admonished by us, unwilling to make satisfaction to a salutary warning, but in every respect disobedient to us, we declare him removed from our communion and, through it, from that of the whole Church [Col. 1142C], having at hand, in the words of the Apostle, “the power to punish every disobedience” (2 Corinthians 10).

Certainly, whoever lacks the means to send a person should at least not regard it as unimportant to send writings indicating the same matter.

We appropriately exempt from this concession the bishop of Verdun, whom we expressly command, without any delay or excuse, to send us not only letters but also a wholly suitable person from his own clergy.

We wish Your Holiness to remain well in Christ now and always.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the fifteenth indiction.

(Year 867.) CXLVIII. TO CHARLES THE BALD, KING.

[Col. 1142D]

That Lothar is said to wish to reopen Teutberga’s judgment and decide it by single combat. He asks that Charles receive her into his kingdom and then send the letters which he is writing to Lothar and to Lothar’s bishops.

NICOLAUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son CHARLES, glorious king.

Nothing produces grief like frustrated hope; nothing wounds the mind equally with an unwelcome message arriving unexpectedly. But let us make clear what we mean.

Among the other religious defenders of the holy Church of God and vigorous champions of truth, we remember that no one was more concerned than Your Piety over the suffering of the glorious queen Teutberga, and that no one sympathized more deeply with her troubles [Col. 1143A]. So much so that, during the life of her brother, you referred her case to the Apostolic See, supported her for a considerable period through your generous munificence, and frequently urged us to provide her assistance.

Therefore, when the Apostolic See saw the great abundance of your charity toward her, and was unable to complete her case quickly because of the obstacle of perverse obstinacy, it entrusted her, as though God were watching and blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, were opposing it together with the See, to your protection and merciful defense.

But now, as we have heard, King Lothar, again armed against that same Teutberga, is said to have entered into agreements with you so that he might join your consent to this wicked intention of his [Col. 1143B]. It is widely reported that, by granting you a certain monastery of his kingdom, he obtained your approval for the destruction of the aforementioned Teutberga.

If this is true, as many report, it is a matter for intense grief and bitter lamentation: that you should now, God forbid, turn back from your earlier plan of piety and give counsel to impiety, and that you who until now were offering favor to equity should now give consent to iniquity.

O incomparable loss! O indescribable diminution of a pious king’s compassion!

But may this be far from so great a prince; may it be far from the hearts of the faithful to believe such a thing readily about so great a worshiper of Christ. Rather, we should believe that those who imitate Balaam are rightly censured: he gave counsel against the life of those whom he had asked to resemble even in death, and, when he found an opportunity through greed, immediately forgot whatever he had wished for himself concerning innocence (Numbers 22) [Col. 1143C].

But since we are not yet entirely able to believe that you have given consent to wickedness, we shall meanwhile restrain our pen in order to exhort you to complete the pious work you began concerning the aforementioned queen.

For behold, Truth says: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10). Behold, it is written concerning blessed Job, who offered a continual sacrifice: “Thus Job did all his days” (Job 1). Blessed Pope Gregory, explaining this, says: “In the sacrifice, therefore, holy action is shown; in ‘all the days,’ constancy in the action of sacrifice is shown.”

With these matters thus set forth, we do not wish Your Excellency to be unaware that King Lothar has subjected his wife Teutberga to various afflictions and, contrary to the oaths he gave, forced her under innumerable pressures to the point that she now writes to us under compulsion that she wishes to be stripped of her royal dignity and marital union and desires to be content with a private life [Col. 1143D]. We wrote to her that this could not happen in any other way unless her husband Lothar chose that same life.

But, as we have learned from the report of many, Lothar himself plans to hold an assembly and intends to subject that same Teutberga to his own examination in judgment [alternative: “and to judgment,” HARD.]. If he can, by the tricks of his falsehood or by his argumentative evasions, present her as though she had not been a legitimate wife, he also wishes to separate her entirely from himself [Col. 1144A]. But if he cannot, he wishes to admit her as his own wife, yet then accuse her as though she had committed adultery, and on that account drive his own man and Teutberga’s man into single combat. If the queen’s man falls, he intends to kill her without delay.

How contrary these actions are to every divine law and to the law of the holy Fathers, Your Wisdom has already perceived more appropriately. Nevertheless, we also wish briefly to demonstrate something concerning the matter.
