First, we assert that Teutberga, whose previous controversy has been settled, ought not to be summoned to a renewed response, since what has once been properly decided and determined by the intervention of oaths ought not to be reopened, except perhaps where there is a greater authority.

Second, since she seeks the Church as a refuge and has always desired ecclesiastical judgment, she ought not to be subjected to secular judgment [Col. 1144B].

Furthermore, since we have been appealed to as judges by both sides—that is, by Teutberga as well as by Lothar—and since we have adjudicated the controversy of both, it is not appropriate to flee to other judges concerning this matter. For, according to the sacred canons, it is not permitted to appeal from judges whom common agreement has chosen; and where an appeal is allowed, it is allowed only where there is a greater authority.

Since there is nowhere a greater authority than that of the Apostolic See, which adjudicated the case of both parties, we do not know whether anyone may judge its judgment or reopen its sentence. For, as ecclesiastical law and anciently observed custom indicate, we know that appeals have been made to that See and that it has dissolved the judgment of others; but we do not know that anyone has appealed from it or violated its sentence [Col. 1144C].

As for Lothar’s accusation that Teutberga committed adultery, who does not see that it is full of deceit and every kind of iniquity? If, as he himself boasts, she is not his wife, what concern is it of his to fabricate an accusation of adultery against her, since she could not have committed adultery if she was not anyone’s wife?

Moreover, if Lothar accuses her of adultery and punishment is prepared if she is convicted, she must necessarily be acknowledged as his wife. Why, then, does he labor and grow anxious, striving by every means and every sort of argument to discover that she was not his wife? I say again: before every other controversy, he must confess her to be his wife if he considers prosecuting her as an adulteress.

She wished to clear herself of this in the presence of our envoy, but he did not consent.

As for making single combat into a law, we have nowhere found it commanded. Although we have read that some entered into such combat, as sacred history relates concerning David and Goliath (1 Kings 17), divine authority nowhere sanctions it as a law to be observed anywhere, since those who pursue this and similar practices seem merely to be tempting God [Col. 1144D].

With these matters briefly set forth, we earnestly ask Your Devotion that the care, concern, and every form of assistance or effort which you have always shown so fervently toward this woman should never grow cold or in any way become lukewarm. Rather, insofar as the strength granted from heaven enables you, let your genuine charity never permit anyone to harm her by any device [alternative, “by any twofold means”; perhaps *genuina*, genuine, HARD.].

Otherwise, if some injury should occur, you might be compelled to render an account for her before the terrible divine judgment. For, as we said above, with God watching, we have entrusted her to your protection, in the place of the prince of the apostles, whose protection she sought.

Finally, when no security or remedy for her safety and protection can be found—as we say with grief—and her certain destruction is seen to be impending, receive her to yourselves, shelter her in your kingdom until the Lord reveals what should be determined concerning her, and provide her with the customary benefits of your piety [Col. 1145B]. Then, if anything is alleged against her, let her rivals pursue the matter only after our authority has preceded it.

But note that we permit these things to be done only when Your Prudence, or those who share our judgment, foresees that no hope of Teutberga’s salvation remains.

Moreover, whether judgment is to be pursued concerning the marriage bond or the charge of adultery, no reason permits Teutberga to enter into a lawful contest with Lothar or undertake a legitimate legal proceeding unless she is first restored for a time to her own authority and freely joined to her relatives.

Among them a place must also be provided where no violence from the crowd need be feared, and where it is not difficult to produce witnesses or the other persons whom both the holy canons and the venerable Roman laws require in such controversies [Col. 1145C].

We do not say this in order that these things should be done—for above we have shown that they cannot be done without our decree or arrangement—but to show what legal conflict Lothar supposes he can undertake, when he daily exhausts and crushes the person whom he keeps in his own inner chambers, brings her out for judgment whenever he wishes, and returns her to confinement whenever he wishes.

Once she has been brought out, unless she confesses what he had ordered, who can say how many evils are imposed upon her and to what sufferings she is subjected?

She must therefore be entrusted to her own freedom, liberated from all oppression and power of the man with whom she is to enter into conflict, allowed to use her own resources freely, and permitted to avoid suspicious persons, since she wishes to show herself free from the charges brought against her [Col. 1145D].

But now, dearest son, as we bring this letter to an end, we admonish you always to remember what we mentioned above concerning blessed Job, who acted well, and always to keep it before your eyes in the case of the aforementioned queen. For a praiseworthy deed is performed in vain if the one who performs it does not carry it out throughout all the days of his life; and the one who runs in the stadium runs uselessly if he collapses before reaching the appointed place.

For it is written: “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Ecclesiasticus 2). “Run in such a way that you may obtain the prize” (1 Corinthians 9).

You are not unaware of what we have decreed concerning Waldrada, the adulteress and excommunicated woman. Since she returned to live in Gaul without our consent, you can learn what we wrote concerning her to the bishops of the kingdom of Lothar from the letter we sent them [Col. 1146A]. Let your glory also cause a transcript of it to be given to the venerable bishops governing the Church of God in your kingdom.

Moreover, we ask that Your Sublimity promptly send, without any delay, through a faithful and prudent man, the present letter, addressed in the name of the frequently mentioned King Lothar, to that same king; behold, we have transmitted a copy of it to Your Devotion. We also ask you to do the same concerning the letter we sent to the bishops of his kingdom.

But you should know that some, out of fear or favor, make light of receiving our letter; others do receive it but fear to display it openly; others, wishing to please Lothar, most disastrously deprive it of being seen by anyone else [Col. 1146B].

Therefore we earnestly beseech Your Wisdom to send this same letter to the bishops already designated through a man who proceeds prudently and passes over absolutely none of them in such a way that it might become clear that he had failed to deliver it to him.

When this has been done carefully and impartially, we ask that, through an envoy or letters of your charity, it be reported to us immediately and with complete certainty who received it and who did not.

For although all are to be censured for the excessive slumber of their sluggishness, those who, even after being so often moved by us, refuse to awaken from the pestilential sleep of their torpor deserve much more severe rebuke or punishment.

But before we truthfully recognize them as such, justice dictates that we should decide nothing definitive concerning them in their absence—or rather, in our ignorance of the facts [Col. 1146C].

We wish Your Glory to remain well in Christ now and always, most beloved son.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the fifteenth indiction.

(Year 867.) CXLIX. TO LOTHAR, KING.

That Teutberga, wearied by her afflictions, writes against herself; nevertheless, her marriage cannot be dissolved unless Lothar also promises a celibate life.

TO LOTHAR, glorious [Roman edition: most glorious] king.

Having heard, upon the return of our messenger, what we may call the beginning of your correction, we gave God fitting thanks and prepared our mind to return suitable gratitude to you as well [Col. 1146D]. But, alas, adverse news arriving swiftly thwarted the purpose of this intention. Therefore we have been compelled to change our tone, and though we had resolved to open our mouth in thanksgiving, we are now forced to turn the service of our tongue toward mourning and rebuke.

For we received, delivered by her legates, a letter of petition sent by Theutberga, the glorious queen. In it we find nothing conveyed in writing except what they seemed to assert verbally. Yet in both respects we were equally astonished and amazed. As we considered the meaning of so sudden a change in the writing and the petition, we recalled that she had never at any time communicated anything of the sort to us [alternative reading: *quoquo*; the text is difficult].

For when we turn the eyes of our mind to the reports [Col. 1147A] of nearly all who come to Rome from the regions of Gaul and Germany for the sake of prayer, or to those of the many who reside there, we see that what she now alone signifies differs greatly from what all these people almost daily indicate in words and letters. They testify that she is enduring an unremitting affliction, intolerable oppression, and excessive violence, although she, on the contrary, admits and declares that she wishes and desires voluntarily and gladly to divest herself of the royal dignity and of the marital union.

She appears to pursue these matters in one way, and they in another, so that, according to the assertions of all, she was lawfully admitted by you, then unjustly accused, afterward manifestly purified by the judgment which pleased you and all your subjects, as well as the bishops, then rejected a second time [Col. 1147B], and finally received by right in accordance with our admonitions and decree, together with the exhortation of our son, the excellent Augustus. But she has now adopted a position contrary to all these things and, forgetting her own departure, declares—I do not know what frivolities. We do not wish to exaggerate them, because we do not wish to labor uselessly.

Nevertheless, we have learned from the report of many people and from many indications that you have turned to imitate those of whom the prince of the Apostles says:

“For if, after escaping the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, their latter condition has become worse than the former. For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. For what the true proverb says has happened to them [Col. 1147C]: ‘A dog returns to its own vomit,’ and ‘a washed sow returns to wallowing in the mud.’”

We have learned, I say, that you, who for a long time persisted in wickedness and caused no small harm to the Church of God, are still causing harm, and that you, who were in filth, are still becoming filthy.

Indeed, when we heard that you had been corrected at the return of our messenger, we rejoiced beyond what can be expressed and offered immense thanks to the almighty Lord. We thought that, having at last embraced honorable conduct, you would finally direct a fragrance of sweet odor to the Lord, rather than continue to spread throughout the world the stench of the filth arising from your repeated wickedness.

But, alas, on the contrary, instead of a sweet odor, a stench—not one toward which anyone should run, but one that must be fled with all speed—is now being spread everywhere. For, as we believe, it is not enough for you merely to have committed adultery unless you also add this: that you plunge human souls, ensnared in the snares of perjury, into final destruction.

But why should it be surprising that you have brought death upon the souls of a few through perjury [Col. 1147D], when, placed in so exalted a position, by the example of your adultery you have hurled so many thousands of people into the chaos of perdition? The greater the dignity, the greater the crimes it makes.

As for what the aforementioned queen says in something like a testimony on behalf of Waldrada—that Waldrada was your lawful wife—she attempts to establish this either unwillingly or in vain, since no testimony from that woman is needed here at all. Rather, we hold this to be just and understand this to be equitable: even after Theutberga’s death [Col. 1148A], you can neither lawfully nor permissibly take Waldrada as your wife under any law or regulation.

Therefore, whether Waldrada was ever your lawful wife is not something for which the Church of God requires Theutberga’s satisfaction. One thing, however, we know: neither we nor that same holy Church, with God as our author, who will judge adulterers, will in any way leave you unpunished if you ever take Waldrada back, even after Theutberga’s death.

As for her statement that she wishes to come to Rome and disclose to us her sufferings and certain secrets of her heart, this is not appropriate. The security of the journey which she invokes does not exist, and as long as Waldrada remains placed beside you in this way, it is clear that the devil’s cunning is not absent. While Theutberga departs, Waldrada immediately approaches [Col. 1148B]; plainly, when the law is rejected, transgression is at once introduced.

Who does not know that Theutberga claims to have made these statements against herself after being overcome by many pressures, worn down by innumerable evils, or rather fearing the danger of death, which she frequently escaped only because God guarded her? Moreover, as we said earlier, nearly all the religious and distinguished men of Gaul and Germany testify by their reports that these things are so—so much so that, long ago, we foresaw that this written statement which she has now sent us would be hers.

But we by no means accept such a confession from her as a confession, since it was forced from her not by her will but by violence. Therefore whoever acts against Theutberga is shown not only to inflict grave injury upon the Church of God, but also to stir up the apostolic see vehemently against himself. Its judgment may not be reconsidered [Col. 1148C], because that see was appealed to by both parties—that is, by you as well as by Theutberga—and has consequently become the executor [Roman edition: *interpreter*] and terminator of your affair.

Now, if Theutberga intends to come to Rome and has obtained permission to depart from you, her husband, she must be given absolutely certain security, so that, relying upon it, she need fear no harm from anyone. This cannot happen unless Waldrada is first sent to Rome and a suitable decision is made concerning her. Only then should an assurance of such immunity follow, so certain that the aforementioned Theutberga suffers no disadvantage while coming, staying, or returning.

But if you do not promise to act in this way in order to remove the unfavorable suspicion [Col. 1148D] against you, you must desist; we must take every precaution lest we yield to such treacherous snares.

You, for your part, must take the greatest care to cherish and love the aforementioned Theutberga, your wife, as your own flesh, and vigilantly ensure that you do not consent to her being separated from you in any way. Therefore, if she wishes to leave you, rebuke her—rather, correct her—and strive in every respect to recall her from such an intention.

But if she seeks separation out of love for chastity and demands the dissolution of the marital union, it is certain, as the Apostle proclaims, that “the woman does not have authority over her own body, but the man does.” Yet if you yourself, also pursuing chastity, wish to dissolve the union for the sake of religion, we grant this, provided that it is not done out of hostility.

For although it is written [Col. 1149A], “What God has joined together, let no human being separate,” God, not a human being, separates them when, out of regard for divine love and by the consent of both spouses, marriages are dissolved. If you wish to proceed in this manner, we permit it with a willing heart and readily give our assent.

Otherwise, however, we forbid your mutual separation, since we read: “The two shall be one flesh.” The divine Gregory explains this by saying:

“If, then, husband and wife are one flesh, and for the sake of religion the husband dismisses his wife, or the wife her husband who remains in this world, or perhaps goes over to illicit things, what kind of conversion is this, in which one and the same flesh partly passes into continence and partly remains in pollution? But if both agree to lead a continent life, who would dare condemn this [Col. 1149B], when it is certain that the almighty Lord, who granted lesser things, has not forbidden greater ones?”

Moreover, if barrenness is alleged, consider Sarah at ninety years of age, and likewise Hannah and Elizabeth. Yet perhaps it is not infertility but iniquity that causes this barrenness.

Finally, concerning other faults, hear what Jerome, the cultivator of the heavenly library, says:

“Wives are a heavy burden if, except for the cause of fornication, it is not permitted to dismiss them. For what if she is drunk, irascible, of evil character, extravagant, gluttonous, wandering, quarrelsome, and abusive? Must such a woman be retained? Whether we wish it or not, she must be endured. For although we were free, by our own will we subjected ourselves to servitude; and, to use the Apostle’s words, ‘Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release.’”

Therefore, most glorious king, be content with your own wife and never seek the companionship of another woman besides her. Indeed, insofar as human understanding is able to discover, this frequently mentioned woman has often been proved not only innocent, but is also known to have appealed to the aid and judgment of the Church. Moreover, she sought the protection of the holy prince of the Apostles, Peter.

For this reason the apostolic see began to examine your case through her [Col. 1149C] and proposed to reserve to its special judgment whatever question might arise. We therefore do not think that you should descend to such ruin of yourself that you consent in any way to act against our decisions or against the woman so often mentioned, who relies entirely upon the refuge of blessed Peter. If you fall into so monstrous a sin, you will bring loss upon yourself and your kingdom rather than upon Theutberga.

Accept, then, our counsel, and embrace our admonitions as those of an affectionate father. Restrain your mind, tongue, and body from every depravity, above all avoiding communion with Waldrada, your mistress and the woman whom you formerly repudiated, and consigning her companionship to perpetual oblivion.

For she has been excommunicated and, until our presence [Col. 1149D], separated from all fellowship with Christians, as the entire West already knows; and very soon the East also will by no means remain ignorant of it through our messengers, together with the other punishments.

Therefore beware lest you be struck with her by the same edge of the sentence and, for the suffering of one woman [Col. 1150A] and for the sake of sulfurous stench and a desire lasting only the briefest time, be dragged bound and fettered into everlasting destruction. For those placed over peoples commit worse offenses; consequently, they are punished more cruelly than others.

But so that you may know that we speak the truth more clearly, hear blessed Pope Gregory, who says:

“Those placed over others must know that, if they ever commit perverse acts, they are deserving of as many deaths as examples of perdition as they transmit to their subjects. Therefore they must guard themselves from guilt all the more carefully, since through the evil things they do they do not die alone.”

Let what we have now written to you suffice: our words, as it were, have passed between us and you to rebuke your excesses. But beware lest, in accordance with the Lord’s command [Col. 1150B], we ever bring two or three witnesses against you; indeed, beware lest we report this to the holy Church and—something we do not wish—you thereafter become to everyone “as a gentile and a tax collector.”

Moreover, we exhort Your Excellency to keep this copy of the letter sent to Lothair in your possession, without anyone else knowing, until you have learned that he perfectly obeys our admonitions. But if he does not yield from his obstinacy and delays carrying out what we now send to him, or if he does not retain Queen Theutberga with due honour, may Your Highness make known to all what we have determined concerning him, and disseminate it far and wide in the form of our censure transmitted to your glory.

(Year 867.) CL. TO LOUIS, KING OF GERMANY. That he should continue to urge Lothair to love Theutberga, and compel Ingeltrude to return to her husband Boso.

[In Mansi, ibid.]

[Col. 1150C]

NICOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son LOUIS, glorious king.

We entreat your beloved affection never on any account to cease admonishing King Lothair always to show the due affection to Queen Theutberga, his wife; nor should he flatter himself that he may try to compel her to impute some crime to herself and thereby be able to separate her from his company [Col. 1150D], since he himself cannot lawfully do this, nor do we permit scope for such deceptions and so fraudulent a cunning. But even if, through an abundance of iniquity, by some craft—rather, by violence—he could have contrived such a thing, no one would permit him to be joined in the bond of marriage to Waldrada, the adulteress for whose unclean desire he strives, pants, and madly seeks to attain, unless he wished to be found a contemner and violator of every law and of all rules. Therefore deal kindly with him; and because he is the son of your brother, strive to admonish, rebuke, indeed even more severely correct him, as your own bone and flesh, seeking the salvation of his soul rather than that of his body [Col. 1151A].

Finally, dearest son, we believe it has not escaped you how many and how great labours we have often endured on account of that fugitive woman, Boso’s wife; how often we have beneficially admonished her to return to the path of justice; and how we struck her with the sword of anathema when she did not repent but persisted obstinately in her wickedness. Though struck, she did not grieve; though crushed, she would not receive correction. But her husband—an innocent man—is, in her absence, wearied with no small labour here and there, since he can neither be reconciled to her while she is absent nor, while she lives, be granted marital companionship with another. Therefore, since we continually endure the insolence and recklessness of this man, who ardently wishes to rush into a second—indeed, an unlawful—marriage [Col. 1151B], we earnestly ask your affection to undertake every effort, for God’s sake, to recall her; rather, that you may win this lost and repeatedly condemned woman for the Lord. Thus, if, stirred by admonitions, she does not take the path of her salvation, she may at least repent when constrained by pressures through your diligence; and she who did not wish voluntarily to enter the Lord’s supper may at least enter, even if compelled. For perhaps the Lord speaks through the prophet concerning such a woman: “Behold, I will hedge up your way with thorns, and I will fence it with a wall, and she shall not find her paths; and she shall pursue her lovers but shall not overtake them; she shall seek them and shall not find them; and she shall say: ‘I will go and return to my former husband, for it was better with me then than now’” (Hos. 2) [Col. 1151C].

If this venerable oracle is expounded tropologically, it yields no small benefit. But for the present it must briefly be said that, if this same woman, as indeed she ought not, enjoyed communion with no one and did not obtain her sought-after pleasures; if, finally, she endured her ways hedged in with thorns; if, in earthly desires, she were worn out by impossibility, she would assuredly now bring God back to mind and return, even unwillingly, to love for her own husband. Thus this stubborn and unrepentant soul, which has long tried to persist in adultery, might perhaps—if only the necessity of the circumstances just described were imposed on her by you—decide at last to be a faithful wife, and could then rightly and truthfully say: “I will return to my former husband, for it was better with me then than now.” We wish Your Glory good health, most beloved son [Col. 1151D]. Given on the Nones of March, in the fifteenth indiction.

(Year 867.) CLI. TO ADO, ARCHBISHOP OF VIENNE. The ancient privilege of the metropolitan see of Vienne is confirmed by pontifical authority.

[In Mansi, ibid.]

NICOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother ADO, archbishop: a perpetual decree for the Church of Vienne [Col. 1152A].

The authority of this holy see has not refused what your holiness reverently requested from the apostolic see and humbly petitioned: that we renew the ancient privilege granted to the holy see of Vienne by the Fathers and by our predecessors, since the request was worthy. Therefore, just as it was granted by apostolic beneficence to your predecessors by our predecessors—namely, most blessed Leo and nearly all the rest down to our own time—that four cities or towns, namely Grenoble, Valence, Geneva, and Tarentaise, should remain perpetually subject to the right of the Church of Vienne, so our pontificate by this present decree establishes that this shall remain firm and unshaken for future times, and irrevocably determines that they belong to the authority and jurisdiction of the metropolitan see of Vienne [Col. 1152B].

Yet for this reason the Church of Tarentaise shall not lose any grant of privilege made to it. For the archbishop and primate of Vienne did not request this from our authority so that he should not ordain in those same three towns or cities which now appear to have been added and entrusted to him, or should not summon their bishops to himself when he saw fit. Rather, he is to know that he is so placed under the jurisdiction of the Church of Vienne that, by its direction, he performs all these things ecclesiastically, and, when summoned, appears at the synod of that same archbishop and primate together with those very places granted to him; and, insofar as general observance is concerned [Col. 1152C], he is not to presume to determine anything apart from the authority of the bishop of Vienne. Humbly, as was beneficially confirmed and established by our predecessors of holy memory, let him be subject to the Church of Vienne in such a manner that thereafter he may more freely possess and retain the dignity granted to him by us; lest, if he acts or presumes otherwise, he not only lose what has been granted to him, but also be more severely condemned and humbled in future for transgression and disobedience. Given on the Ides of June, in the fifteenth indiction.

(Year 867.) CLII. TO HINCMAR AND THE OTHER BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF CHARLES. He sets forth the causes of the Greeks’ hatred and envy toward the Latin Church; sends their objections for refutation; and asks that whatever they discover against them be transmitted to Rome.

[In Mansi, ibid.]

[Col. 1152D]

NICOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brothers HINCMAR and the other archbishops and bishops governing the churches established in the kingdom of the glorious King Charles.

[Note: [Col. 1151D] “To bear the burdens of all.” What Hincmar is ordered to do toward the end of this letter—namely, to ensure that it is conveyed to the other archbishops—was carefully carried out by him, as Flodoardus shows in Book III, chapter 1. “When Hincmar received this letter,” he says, “he read it aloud to King Charles, who was staying at the palace of Corbonacum with several [Col. 1152D] bishops, and endeavored to send it to the other archbishops, as he had been instructed.” He also encouraged his suffragans to respond to the objections of the Greeks, as he did Odo of Beauvais, to whom Hincmar’s Letter IV on this subject survives, written on the Kalends of January of this year. Odo, therefore, replied among others and sent Hincmar a book that he had composed, as the same Flodoardus records in Book III, chapter 23, while compiling a catalogue of Hincmar’s letters to Odo. Aeneas, bishop of Paris, also replied; his book on this matter survives in the Thuane Library. From it we present the prologue. JAC. SIRM.] Your fraternity clearly knows that we bear the burdens of all who are burdened, or rather that blessed Peter bears them in us, he who protects and guards us as heirs of his administration. Nevertheless, among the other matters that involve us in immeasurable labors, those seem especially to trouble us which are wickedly thrust upon us and indeed upon the whole western region by the Greek emperors, namely Michael and Basil, and by those who obey them.

For, inflamed with hatred and envy against us, they endeavor to fasten upon us as though they were charges of heresy the matters that we shall record below. They act from hatred because we not only did not approve but also condemned the promotion of Photius—a fornicator, an invader of the Church of Constantinople, and a neophyte—which had been carried out by men deposed and anathematized. We accepted with no assent whatever the deposition of our brother and fellow minister Ignatius, patriarch of that Church, since it had been carried out by his subjects and by imperial power. They act from envy because they heard that Michael, king of the Bulgarians, together with his people, after receiving the faith of Christ, had sought instructors and teaching from the See of blessed Peter.

For they desire, and ardently strive, to withdraw those same Bulgarians from subjection to blessed Peter and craftily to subject them to their own empire under the pretext of Christian religion. Accordingly, they make such statements about the holy Roman Church, which has neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of the kind, that the Bulgarians, still inexperienced in the faith, hearing these things, may avoid, shun, and wholly abandon us as though we were guilty and stained with the filth of various heresies.

Finally, when the outcry over the evils that had been multiplied and brought to completion in the Church of Constantinople, both by those same rulers and by those who obeyed them either through fear or through affection and according to their wishes, had grown and reached our ears, and immense sorrow over such wickedness had afflicted our heart, even at their own request and earnest entreaty we sent our legates—namely Rhadoald and Zachary, then bishops—to Constantinople to investigate the matter and report it to us. On arriving there, they condemned Patriarch Ignatius and confirmed Photius in their communion, thereby consenting to the faction of the Greeks against our prohibition.

When they had returned to Rome after perpetrating this unspeakable crime, the Emperor Michael also sent to us with them his own envoy, named Leo the Secretary. Upon their arrival, we learned both that the aforesaid Ignatius had been unjustly deposed and that Photius, an adulterer, had been irregularly established in the see of Constantinople; and we bore this most grievously. We therefore wrote a letter of our supreme authority and entrusted it to Leo the Secretary to convey to the emperor in the tenth indiction. In it we declared and firmly established, with suitable reasoning, that we would accept neither that condemnation nor such a promotion, since both had been wickedly carried out.

Afterward, when a council had been held twice and the profane acts that the aforesaid Leo the Secretary had brought had been read—containing the account of the alleged deposition of our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius—the same legates of ours were found wholly culpable both in Ignatius’s condemnation and in Photius’s communion. Therefore, desiring our Church to remain, as always, entirely without stain, so that, if those men remained unpunished, no slight occasion for mockery might arise in it, or so that we might not appear to have consented to their depravity, we condemned both men and subjected them to excommunication. We utterly rejected and condemned the condemnation of Ignatius and the promotion of Photius.

When Leo the Secretary had returned to Constantinople, the Emperor Michael learned from our letter, which we had sent through him, that we had accepted neither the deposition of Ignatius nor the promotion of Photius. He immediately sent to us one of his legates, Michael the protospatharius, with a letter full of insults, and strongly urged us to change our sentence according to his wishes.

We, however, disregarding the insults directed at us—although we had not kept silent regarding the insults directed at the Church—wrote our letter and sent it in the fourteenth indiction to the aforesaid emperor through the aforementioned Michael, his legate and protospatharius. We desired both to repel from our Church the false accusations and to lead the emperor himself and his followers in this matter onto the right path of justice.

But so that these matters might be made more fully known both to the emperor himself and to the other faithful, we summoned certain brothers and fellow bishops from neighboring regions and, following the footsteps of our predecessors, decreed and arranged what seemed to us canonical concerning these affairs. With God’s favor, we intend shortly to make this known more fully to your holiness as well.

When this had been properly arranged, as we believe, we began to seek an opportunity by which, relying upon it, we might send legates of the Apostolic See once more to Constantinople, with letters of exhortation. They would strengthen the Greeks’ welfare by suitable admonitions and openly announce what sentence the Apostolic See had pronounced concerning them, in accordance with what the great Synod of Nicaea is known to have decreed concerning those who are rejected (canon 5).

The voyage by sea seemed difficult enough to us, and, because we had experienced the treachery of those same Greeks, it had to be approached with great caution. While we were thus hemmed in on every side by these anxieties and weighed down by immense hardships, suddenly we were informed that the envoys of the aforementioned king of the Bulgarians had arrived.

Who, then, could say with what joy or what exultation we were filled? We learned of their salutary conversion through the riches of God’s goodness; and we discovered that they had sought the teaching of blessed Peter the Apostle, or of his See. Although bodily far away, they had nevertheless become present to us in faith. Moreover, we perceived that through their kingdom an easy and overland route lay open for our envoys to reach the land of the Greeks.

Having therefore arranged both the matters concerning the rudiments of the faith that we had recognized as suitable for the Bulgarian people and those that we had decided to send to Constantinople, we dispatched our envoys together with the legates of the aforementioned king, so that they might pass through his territory.

The Greek emperors not only refused to agree to receive them but also fiercely aroused their hostility against the Bulgarians because they had permitted our envoys to cross their land. They plainly implied nothing other than that, if our envoys had passed through regions subject to themselves, they would have handed them over to the dangers to which the heretical rulers of that city are often said to have delivered legates of the Apostolic See sent on matters of faith or ecclesiastical correction.

Furthermore, while our envoys were staying with the Bulgarian king and attempting to approach the city of Constantinople, those same emperors sent their letter to the Bulgarian king. After receiving it, he resolved in a devout spirit to have it conveyed to us by our legates.

When we had received it and examined it together with the other writings, it became entirely clear that those often-mentioned rulers had dipped their pens in a lake of blasphemy and had used the mud of error instead of ink.

For they endeavor to criticize both our Church in particular and, in general, the entire Church that uses the Latin language: they criticize us because we fast on Saturdays; because we say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, whereas they profess that he proceeds from the Father alone; and because, as they claim, we despise marriage since we prohibit priests from taking wives.

They also attempt to accuse us because we forbid those same priests to anoint the foreheads of the baptized with chrism—although they deceitfully suppose that this chrism is not made from river water.

They likewise endeavor to criticize us because, according to our custom, we do not abstain from eating meat for eight weeks before Easter and from eating cheese and eggs for seven weeks.

They also falsely claim, as is shown by other writings of theirs, that at Easter we bless and offer a lamb upon the altar together with the Lord’s body, after the manner of the Jews.

They even strive to criticize us because among us clerics do not refuse to shave their beards, and because among us a deacon is ordained bishop without having received the office of priest. Yet they themselves did not hesitate, as they suppose, to promote to the height of the episcopate by imperial favor and power the very man whom they call their patriarch—suddenly tonsured from the lay state and made a monk.

And, what is more serious and more insane, they endeavored to demand from our envoys, contrary to every rule and beyond all custom, a written statement of faith, if they wished to be received by them, in which both these articles and those who held them would be anathematized. They also wickedly demanded canonical letters to be given to our envoys by the man whom they call their ecumenical patriarch.

In these matters, then, after setting aside all other concerns, it is especially fitting that you, brothers, labor earnestly. Since these reproaches are shared by all and are directed against the universal Church, specifically against that part of it known to use the Latin language, as we have said, all of you who appear to be illumined by the divine priesthood ought jointly to contend so that the traditions of our fathers may not be exposed to such contempt. Whatever wicked men, in their habitual contentiousness, seek to defile by lying and error must be wholly rescued from every stain of blasphemy by the united hand of defense.

For it is ridiculous and a sufficiently shameful disgrace that in our times we should permit God’s holy Church to be falsely accused or allow the traditions that we received from our fathers in ancient times to be broken at the pleasure of those who are always in error.

Therefore we must resist their efforts and oppose the shield of truth to their false arrows. We shall not fail to do this ourselves, with the help of heavenly power, insofar as we are able; nor, when opportunity is granted from heaven, shall we be silent against them on behalf of the Church of Christ.

But it is especially fitting that your fraternity also, following the custom of your forefathers, should be found contending with us and laboring with one accord in these matters. For, unless memory has deserted me, the regions of the West—leaving aside for the moment the other parts of the world—have never been found to disagree with the See of blessed Peter in questions of this kind.

Therefore, let each one of you who has received metropolitan rights, together with the brothers and fellow bishops under him, take diligent care of these matters. Let him investigate what must be opposed to their envious disparagements; let him strive with the greatest eagerness to discover it; and let him not regard it as unimportant to send what he has discovered to us promptly. Thus we too shall be able to send it afterward against their madness, together with our other assertions.

Nothing does the visible or invisible enemy fear as much as concord. Therefore let us provoke one another to mutual zeal, and against our common enemies let us be found not wandering here and there, but arrayed like the ranks of an army.

Thus, while we incite your unanimity to a common conflict and you take part in our struggles, we shall be seen to love and fraternal­ly venerate your holiness with the affection due from the heart, and you shall be known to disagree in nothing with the head—that is, with the See of Peter.

How great is the rancor and how great the madness with which the designated Greek rulers and their satellites are armed against us, because we refused to obey their unlawful passions, is made perfectly clear by this: either the accusations they endeavor to fasten upon us are false, or else they concern practices that have long been observed without anyone’s opposition in the Roman Church and indeed throughout the whole western region.

Although great teachers of the Church have flourished among them as well, none of them criticized these practices except those who, not burning with zeal for justice but struck by the zeal of envy, seek to tear apart the traditions of the Church.

In particular, the matter of the Saturday fast was sufficiently examined and debated in the time of Saint Silvester, confessor of Christ, and it was definitively established that it should be observed everywhere. After that, no one presumed rashly to act against that decree or even to murmur against it. Rather, the institution of the Apostolic See, followed by the observance of the Roman Church, is found to have been the executor of that salutary decree down to the present.

Moreover, who does not know that distinguished men, especially Latins, have written various things concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit? Supported by their authority, we could very properly answer the madness of these men, if any custom existed either of not criticizing them or of requiring us to give an account to them while they chatter contentiously.

But what wonder if they make this claim, when they also boast and assert that, when the emperors were transferred from the city of Rome to Constantinople, the primacy of the Roman See also migrated to the Church of Constantinople, and that together with the royal dignities the privileges of the Roman Church were transferred as well? Thus Photius himself, that invader of the Church, even calls himself in his writings “archbishop” and “universal patriarch.”

Consider, therefore, brothers, whether these things do not prejudice the Church of Christ; consider whether they can be judged tolerable; consider whether they ought to inflict such derogations or disparagements upon the Roman Church. From the time when the Christian religion began to spread, that Church has preserved unaltered and taught throughout the other regions of the world without corruption whatever it once received in Peter, its patron and founder.

No one, throughout so many centuries at least, has appeared who derogated from its traditions or presumed to oppose them, although, as we have said, great teachers have often shone forth in the Church.

Nor has any Church ever been seen—not to mention the Church of Constantinople, which was established much later—that followed this Church’s teaching or authority. Rather, the Roman Church established other churches and bestowed some of its traditions upon them.

Indeed, as Boniface, prelate of the Apostolic See, testifies, the institution of the universal Church at its birth took the beginning of its honor from blessed Peter, in whom its governance and supreme authority consist.

Consider, therefore, brothers, whether these things are useful to the Church of God and whether they appear consistent with its ordinances. Consider, I ask, whether they ought to have excluded the envoys of the Apostolic See from their presence, or to have rejected either them or our letters; and strive to recall, I ask, where such a thing has ever been done. Otherwise, take every care with us to oppose so great a contempt.

For if such a custom should arise in the Church of Christ—namely, that the legates or letters of individual churches or persons should not be received at all by those to whom they are sent—we utterly do not know what place would remain for salvation. This is especially so since we know that, through the intervention of legates and letters sent to them, some have been converted to the faith, many have been recalled from error, and very many have either returned to peace and other forms of correction or have entered upon them.

And certainly, if this were permitted, no one could have led a more tranquil life than we, whom the daily influx arriving from every direction, with Christ’s approval, makes considerably anxious and repeatedly exhausts with no small labors.

Consider likewise whether a written statement should have been demanded from our legates, or what precedents for this have existed. No such thing, it is believed, can be found either inserted in writing or entrusted to memory.

Did we ever prove to be inventors of some novelty? Did we transmit anything other than what concerned their salvation and the common state of the Church? Were we ever heretics?

Although we do not deny that we are sinners, we do not, thanks be to God, recognize ourselves as polluted by the dregs of every kind of error, as are those who are never found without schism and never entirely free from error.

Custom, preserved down to the present, shows that we have both demanded and received written statements from them, but have not been accustomed to demand them from our own people.

Since, by Christ’s gift, no one is permitted to judge the judgment of the Apostolic See granted in blessed Peter on account of the primacy of the Roman Church, or to revise its sentence, it is surely evident that they possess no right to demand written statements from those whom no canon commands, and no example proves, to have the right of judging.

It belongs to superiors to demand an account forcibly from inferiors or to elicit a satisfaction from them, not to inferiors from superiors.

As for letters of recommendation, even if ancient custom had demanded that we issue such a document, we would not now send one to Photius. We had decided not to establish him in the Church of Constantinople through communion expressed by our letters, but to drive him entirely from it as an adulterer, since he had already been struck by the sword of our sentence.

For the canonical examination and proper definition of these and similar matters, we would wish to summon to us the venerable presence both of you and of our other brothers and fellow bishops, unless the various calamities of the world and our daily pressures had prevented us from doing so.

But what you would do in our presence, we exhort you to do at least in our absence. Although we continually behold you as present, embracing you within the bosom of charity—an embrace that the Psalmist calls broad (Psalm 118)—you can never be absent from our sight because of the distances between lands.

Nevertheless, if you refuse to undertake the labor of coming here [perhaps: “of coming,” HARD.], let neither the commands of an earthly ruler nor any impediments of the world restrain your pious zeal from jointly considering this ecclesiastical matter or from the necessary care it requires.

Otherwise, we shall be compelled to summon your fraternity to us and to discuss such questions together, so that, in accordance with ancient custom, we may assemble with us at Saint Peter’s for this very purpose and repel the common insults directed against the Church. Each of us, according to the character of our respective privileges, is recognized as having obtained a share in the common summit of the priesthood within the Church of Christ.

This is especially so because, not only on account of such a general matter of the Church but also because of a particular case arising in this See, your predecessors together with our predecessors were accustomed, and not without reason, to meet here.

For it is astonishing why those emperors should rage so violently, be so agitated, and break out into such insults against us. If they have acted well, they ought not to insult us but to give thanks to the Author for what is good, to possess glory in themselves, and not to reject our envoys or legation, but rather gladly to receive them as congratulating them on their good deeds and to send us appropriate replies.

If, however, they have acted badly, why do they not strive instead to be corrected and improved? Why do they become indignant, rage, and hurl so many insults against the ordinances of God and the traditions of the Church?

They appear not so much to have been indignant as terrified. For, with their consciences reproaching them, they understood that we had sent our representatives to those regions so that their obligations might be judged canonically.

For this reason they adopted the plan by which our legates would not be admitted in any way: namely, so that through them the sentence of the Apostolic See concerning our restored brother and fellow bishop Ignatius, or concerning Photius, the condemned invader, might not be made known among them; and so that it might not become more clearly known, through their testimony or through the text of our writings, that they themselves, as supporters of so great a perversity and therefore under obligation, had been excommunicated because they were in error.

Who, then, does not see that they utter those words of disparagement against us for this reason: so that they might conceal the acts of their own depravity? And why do they wish to obscure our deeds by their deceptions, unless so that they may make the works of their own darkness shine far and wide?

For what pen would suffice to write how many and how great were the praises they sent us—through both legates and letters, not to mention what they sent specifically concerning us—before our envoys were dispatched there and even after their return, concerning blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, concerning his See, and concerning the privileges of the Roman Church?

But after they had dragged the envoys of the Apostolic See into their own wickedness and, like certain prostitutes, had satisfied their lusts when those envoys consented to them, they first attempted to bend us to their most wicked deeds. They approached us with repeated praises and crafty, flattering seductions, and urged and entreated us beyond measure to grant, by our consent, firmness to the things they had perpetrated.

But when, by divine inspiration, we recognized that the acts committed had been wrongly perpetrated, we not only failed to approve them—justice having guided us, as we have already said—but also condemned them. Immediately, changing their judgment, they sharpened the plectrum of their tongue into disparagements and blasphemies; and, as though they had forgotten themselves, they argued for the opposite of what they had first maintained.

And because, by God’s authority, they found nothing particular to attack in us, they undertook to disparage the ancestral traditions strengthened by divine testimonies. What their forefathers had never dared to do, these men did not hesitate to accuse and blaspheme in polluted speech—along with the numerous churches that follow it—everything that Roman antiquity had received.

They also made every effort, in various evasive ways, to revile and disparage the privileges of the Apostolic See, by whose authority they themselves had previously asked that their own position be strengthened, because we did not favor their wickedness.

Moreover, because, thanks be to God, we know the authority of the Apostolic See and have hitherto, in a certain sense, restrained their depravity almost alone, armed with the steadfastness of our ancient custom but without your support, they deceitfully suppose that their acts displease no one but us and that no one but us condemns them.

It may therefore happen that they scatter these seeds of poisonous grass through other parts of the world and bend the hearts of simpler and pious believers to their unlawful wishes.

Indeed, as they themselves boast, they have already sent to the patriarchs of Alexandria and Jerusalem, urging them to agree with them in the deposition of Patriarch Ignatius and the promotion of the invader Photius.

In this matter, we do not fear that their agreement, perhaps imprudently joined against the statutes or traditions of the Apostolic See, will prevail, God helping us. Rather, we grieve lest, enticed by their persuasions, those men should fall away from justice to their own peril.

For they have been worn down by the terrible and continuous pressures of the Hagarenes. Consequently, it may happen that, whether deceived or because the rulers of Constantinople promise them many advantages for their relief, they may be compelled to assent—a thing we say with groaning.

Therefore your venerable diligence must henceforth show itself in such a way that those same enemies may know, more clearly than the sun, that you disagree with the See of Peter in nothing, but rather think with it in all things.

Accordingly, let your divinely inspired wisdom send writings to our episcopate, criticizing and striking with a strong denunciation the great madness of those emperors. When we receive these writings, we shall be able to send them again, together with our other assertions, to refute their own insanity.

Thus, when they know that we all think alike against the same enemies, they will not falsely claim that we desire only to avenge the insults they have inflicted upon us. For they will see us, in a certain sense, engaging them in single combat; and they will clearly understand that there are also other lovers of Christ who hate their perversities.

Then the mouths of those who speak iniquity will be entirely stopped, so that, with Christ as our leader, we may be found united in mind, speech, and strength, like energetic defenders, pressing upon and defeating the enemy ranks through common effort. With his help, we shall discover that we have completely broken their pernicious faction through allied struggle, and that, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have unanimously triumphed over and overcome in every respect both the inventors of lies and the fabricators of perverse doctrines by the definitions of our fathers and the shields of true assertions.

We wish your fraternity to be well in Christ, now and always.

As for you, brother Hincmar, when your charity has read the letter, take the greatest care to have it conveyed also to the other archbishops who are established in the kingdom of our son, the glorious King Charles. Do not neglect to urge them to ensure that each of them, in his own dioceses and together with his suffragans, wherever they may be established, properly discuss these matters and take care to report to us what they discover.

Thus, you will prove an energetic executor for them of everything contained in the scope of this present letter, and you will be found before us to be a truthful and prudent reporter through the sequence of your writings.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, in the first indiction.

**(In the year 867.) CLIII. TO KING CHARLES THE BALD.** He asks him to assist the bishops in holding assemblies concerning the matter he has entrusted to them.

[In Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 1161B]

Let your Highness know that we have ordered the metropolitan prelates of your kingdom to assemble individually, each together with his suffragans, to discuss certain ecclesiastical matters, the substance of which we ordered to be made known to your Glory. We have entrusted the principal responsibility for carrying this out to our brother and fellow bishop Hincmar.

Therefore we ask your pious affection to deign to assist such an undertaking, so that our same brothers may more easily assemble. Thus, with your support, while they properly handle the present matter, you too may receive a reward for so great an act of piety.

There will also shortly be another matter for them to examine synodically by our decree. But so that a doubled labor may not prove burdensome to them, they ought meanwhile to devote their efforts to this, so that, with God’s help, they may reach the other matter more willingly and efficiently.

We wish your Glory to be well in Christ, now and always, most beloved son.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of November, in the first indiction.

**(In the year 867.) CLIV. TO KING LOUIS OF GERMANY.** He urges him finally to stop interceding for Theutguald and Gunthar.

[In Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 1161D]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Louis, glorious king.

We have received your Serenity’s letter, in which you earnestly plead for Theutguald and Gunthar, formerly bishops, and I confess that we greatly wonder and are astonished at why your Highness undertakes so many labors on their behalf.

You have often heard, and now clearly know, how many evils we have endured and how many hardships we have suffered. Yet nowhere has it appeared that you grieved because of our cause. And, as we say with affection, you have always regarded the losses of your mother the Church as though they had no connection with you in any way, and as though you appeared in every respect not to be her sons.

How many labors and how many struggles we have endured—or rather, continue unceasingly to endure—in cutting out the evil whose authors and contrivers Gunthar and Theutguald were found to be! And how we are wearied by unceasing efforts so that it may not grow again from a revived root!

Yet you never consented in all these matters to join us in contending or collaborating. Now, however, for the reconciliation of Theutguald and Gunthar, the makers of all this evil, you strive, hasten, and trouble yourself, and you do not refuse repeatedly to send us the same request.

You even call them, I do not know how, “embittered,” although they certainly do not cease almost daily to serve us a drink of bitterness. For whenever the memory of their deed is brought before us among the other harsh matters inflicted upon us, we cannot remain without the bitterness of deep sorrow.

Let your Highness therefore cease now to press us on this matter, and finally desist from seeking what cannot be done. Since we cannot attain what we wish, it is necessary that we should wish to attain entirely what we can and ought to attain.

For the sentence of the Apostolic See is always conceived with such moderation of counsel, matured with such patience, and delivered with such gravity of deliberation that it does not require reconsideration and does not deem alteration necessary—unless perhaps it was issued in such a way that it could be reconsidered, or unless, according to the tenor of the condition previously stated, it ought to be changed.

Theutguald and Gunthar, therefore, having been struck by the sentence of this holy and Apostolic See, if they act patiently, become uprooters of the evils whose planters they were, and strive to erase them from themselves with perfect humility and fitting tears of repentance [Roman edition: “wash them away”], they may indeed hope for other benefits of ecclesiastical mercy. But they will hope in vain to recover the dignity of their former ministry or of any priestly office; they will never be able to resume it.

Since your Excellence’s charity grieves for them, we praise you. For just as we then, moved by zeal for God and justice, came to our decision with groaning, to their detriment, so now, whenever we remember them, we are inflamed with immense anguish of mind and greatly sympathize and grieve with them over their peril.

According to the Apostle, “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (1 Corinthians 12).

But if you wish, as you indicate, to be fully informed about these men, their actions, and the sentence fixed concerning them in our judgment, let your Highness’s diligence, if it pleases you, return to the tenor of the letter that we sent to the venerable bishops of your kingdom.

We wish your Glory to be well in Christ, now and always, O most beloved son!

Given on the third day before the Kalends of November, in the first indiction.

**(In the year 867.) CLV. TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN KING LOUIS’S KINGDOM.** He reproves them for wishing to restore Theutguald and Gunthar to their ranks. He explains how gravely they sinned, both in receiving Ingeltrude, the excommunicated fugitive wife of Boso, and in asserting and defending Lothair’s repudiation, and that for this reason they were rightly deposed. He therefore urges them to desist and to induce Lothair to carry out the pontiff’s commands.

[In Mansi, same place.]

[Col. 1163A]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy brothers, the archbishops and bishops established in the kingdom of the glorious [Col. 1163B] King Louis.

We rejoice, brothers, and rightly rejoice with you, because we see that, out of charity, you sympathize and grieve with Theutguald and Guntharius, long ago condemned, and that we observe you exerting yourselves considerably to restore them to their former rank of dignity. But we are saddened—indeed, very saddened, dearest brothers—because you concern yourselves so greatly with the deposition of two men that you give no thought at all to the immense multitude of the Christian people whom they have injured; because you strive so earnestly to restore the status of two men who were cast down for manifest crimes that you in no way consider the fall of so many of the faithful who followed them over the precipice.

But what wonder is this, when, even while you were living near those places where Theutguald and Guntharius [Col. 1163C] seemed to govern the Churches of Christ entrusted to them, though in fact they did not govern them—places where both Waldrada and Engeltrudis, the wife of Boso, had freely and without any prohibition prepared for themselves, in a manner of speaking, brothels for their prostitution—you neither sharpened the medicinal sword against the disease that was rising up, nor at that time hastened on the feet of charity to awaken your brothers who were oppressed by a deadly slumber, although the wisest Solomon warns and says concerning such matters: “Run, hasten, awaken your friend” (Prov. 6).

It is clear that not only did you fail to do this then, but even after we had risen up and begun to shoot the arrows of the divine quiver against such abominable wickedness far and wide, you did not diligently undertake to cooperate with us. In the end, where did your labor on this matter appear? Where was your gathering, or where did your priestly zeal become evident? When did you ascend the high mountain? When did you evangelize Zion? When did you raise your voice like a trumpet? When did you announce to anyone detained in this guilt his crimes? When did you climb up opposite it and set yourselves as a wall before the house of the Lord? When did you give barking on its behalf? When did you imitate Phinehas, so that the plague might cease? When did you follow Daniel in punishing adulterous priests? Or when did you stand with us, drawn up like an army in battle array? When did you praise the Lord with us in choir? Or when did you strive to imitate doves, advancing in a flock against the kites?

When did we sing together, “God is in his holy place, God who makes [Col. 1164A] those of one mind dwell in a house” (Ps. 67), and again, “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one” (Ps. 132)—as one, that is, in mind more than in body?

If you did none of these things, and were willing to agree with us in nothing; if, just as you did not share in our labors at different times, when we spent ourselves in destroying what the men mentioned above had built, so you also refused to become participants in our sorrows—what are you now striving and anxiously laboring to do? Why do you wish to forestall the overthrow of countless faithful people for the sake of restoring two men? Do you regard the destruction of the many as of little account, and grieve only over the fall of two men? Is the ruin of those two alone grievous to you, while our daily anxiety—and that of the whole Church, which by God’s authority we serve—and the unspeakable care and indeed intolerable vexation involved in uprooting the evils they planted seem to you light and contemptible?

But what we have endured—indeed, what we endure daily because of the origin of their deeds—we do not consider contemptible, nor can we regard it as light. We see ourselves, though not you, carrying burdens of the greatest weight. Nevertheless, we do not at all doubt that your charity, once you know our troubles, will sympathize with them, and we now believe that, when they have been set before you, you will not be able to treat them superficially.

Let us therefore begin the history of Theutguald and Guntharius—if it should not rather be called a tragedy—and, so that you too may know at least in part what we have experienced concerning them, pay attention as we set it out, insofar as we can briefly discuss it in the course of this letter, taking care to avoid excessive length. [Col. 1164C]

When Engeltrudis, the wife of Count Boso, had gone to Gaul, leaving her lawful husband behind and accompanying an adulterer as an adulteress; and when her husband had wished, with great effort, to bring her back but had been unable by any means to do so, he began to seek ecclesiastical assistance. Following the proper order, he appealed to the first see in the whole world, asking that, by an ecclesiastical decree, it command her to be rescued from those who were protecting her and restored to him.

Accordingly, our predecessor, Pope Benedict of holy memory, as long as he lived, did not cease to intervene and contend with the emperor, the king, and the princes, and to write to the bishops and all the faithful, urging and commanding by apostolic authority that she be recalled. When he died without having obtained any result, we, by the grace of Christ, were appointed to succeed him in the episcopate [Col. 1164D] and also succeeded him in this labor, although we succeeded him in honor while being far inferior to him in merits.

To have this woman recalled, we did not cease to act both by word and by frequent letters sent to every person and in every direction wherever necessity required. Yet when this produced no result for us, episcopal letters began to be sent here and there from our pontificate, suggesting that such a diseased sheep should be expelled from the Lord’s flock by ecclesiastical judgment, lest it contaminate the entire flock—especially since she had refused to be healed by so many salutary medicines of admonition.

After the decree and authority described above had been issued, it was ordered that a council of bishops be held at Milan. If she, [Col. 1165A] having been summoned, did not appear at the appointed time, she was to be bound by the bonds of anathema by that sacred college. Since she did not appear at the appointed time, this was carried out, and we too, as the sacred canons prescribe, confirmed by our consent the sentence pronounced against her by the synod convened on our authority.

Meanwhile, after learning that the same woman was living in the kingdom of King Lothair, we were not content merely with what had already been done concerning her. We added to our previous labors the task of seeking her return, remembering the Lord, who descended from heaven to earth for this very reason: to seek what had been lost, as the Psalmist confessed and asked, saying: “I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost; seek your servant” (Ps. 118).

After sending our letter [Col. 1165B] to our brothers and fellow bishops established in the kingdom of the aforesaid king—and especially to Theutguald and Guntharius, in whose dioceses this lost woman was living freely—we sharply rebuked their sluggishness and severely reproached them for failing to compel her, while she was living freely among them, to return to her own husband. We also informed them that she had been bound by us with the bond of anathema and removed from all Christian communion.

But Theutguald and Guntharius, then bishops, who held a prominent position and enjoyed intimacy with the prince, not only failed, although they could have done so, to persuade her to return to her own husband, or to compel her by canonical authority, as they had repeatedly been urged by the apostolic see—especially since the aforementioned and condemned woman was said to be residing in their dioceses—but also rashly presumed, insofar as they were able, to absolve and receive her, so that she might lawfully enjoy communion with everyone and, in her obstinate flight, might remain without anyone’s opposition or hindrance, able to obtain the support of whatever powerful persons she wished.

Even if the judgment of the apostolic see were open to reconsideration by anyone, and even if the sentence of superiors ought in every respect to be revoked by inferiors, carefully consider for yourselves how contumacious Theutguald and Guntharius were regarding the sacred canons, and especially the canons of Nicaea, which clearly indicate that those rejected by others ought not to be received by them.

But lest you doubt that they committed such an act, know that, before our entire Church, they confessed that they had done this.

Meanwhile, the outrage perpetrated by King Lothar in the deposition of Queen Theutberga and the admission of Waldrada began to grow through the encouragement of their flattery and unjust defense, and to be spread more widely. Recognizing this, we restrained it with every possible effort, lest so great a crime be committed, and we endeavored to persuade everyone faithful, both by word and by our letters.

King Lothar sent two counts to us, through whom he indicated in writing and by word that the bishops of his kingdom, together with certain others, were granting him authority to reject Theutberga and take Waldrada in marriage. Yet, he said, in order that proper procedure might be observed, he was asking us above all for such authority and judgment and awaiting our advice. On hearing this, we replied that we could not send envoys for such a matter so hastily; nevertheless, we most certainly promised that we would send them later, warning also that in the meantime no one should deliberate anything at all concerning this case. But he, relying—as later became clear—on the authority of those two men, Theutguald and Gunthar, then bishops, and not waiting for our envoys, celebrated a public and solemn wedding ceremony and joined Waldrada to himself by right of marriage.

Nevertheless, our envoys from the Apostolic See, who had already set out for Gaul and reached Lothar, told him that they had been sent to him according to our promise. They urged the king, in accordance with our command, to arrange for two men from the kingdoms of the most glorious kings—namely Louis, Charles the Elder, and Charles the Younger—to meet with them, together with the bishops of his kingdom. They also stated that we had ordered Theutberga, who had appealed to the Apostolic See, to attend that assembly, provided that King Lothar gave her adequate security.

They could not, however, have with them the letters that we had sent to you and to the bishops of your kingdoms, since it was already clear to them that these had been taken from them by Lothar’s friends. But King Lothar, employing the direction of those two men, neither wished to give Queen Theutberga an assurance that justice would be observed or violence not inflicted, nor did he await anyone else for the assembly being convened near the city of Metz, except the prelates of his kingdom—those whom he had already bent to his will either by benefits or by threats.

After corrupting, or rather winning over to his favor, our envoys, he carried out without opposition whatever pleased him. When the assembly had been held, the prelates who had gathered—among whom Theutguald and Gunthar held the foremost rank and exercised the greatest authority—anticipated, indeed usurped and claimed, our judgment. This was the judgment that, moved first by Queen Theutberga’s appeal and then by King Lothar’s petition, we had already promised to deliver, and which we plainly appeared to have initiated both through our envoys and through our letters. They considered Queen Theutberga liable and judged that she should be condemned in her absence.

They set down in a certain profane booklet what had there been drawn from an evil mouth according to the king’s will, and, thus passing judgment, confirmed it with their own subscriptions, with Theutguald and Gunthar taking precedence in those subscriptions, as in the other proceedings, and pestilently compelling the others to follow them. They promised in every respect that they would soon come to Rome and give us an account of what they had done.

At last they arrived and were brought before us in the presence of the whole Church. When we asked them how that matter had been conducted, they produced the aforementioned booklet and declared that they had done neither more nor less nor anything different from what the booklet, as presented, appeared to contain.

We accepted it and read it aloud before the assembly of our bishops who were with us and before Theutguald and Gunthar themselves. We pointed out how many things in it were objectionable, judged it objectionable in every respect, and explained more fully, while they listened, how the actions recorded in it stood opposed to justice and hateful to God. [Editio Romana: “to the bishops.”]

Although not all the places in those profane proceedings that called for criticism were then found, and although all that was found cannot now return to our memory, they were nevertheless so many and so serious that the holy synod seated with me repeatedly acclaimed that Theutguald and Gunthar deserved to undergo the canonical sentence of deposition.

Moved by divine zeal, therefore—we say this here before God—and desiring to exercise nothing but just judgment, we unanimously first annulled the adulterers’ supporting council, which we mentioned above as having been assembled near the city of Metz. Then, with grief we recall it, we pronounced against them the sentence of deposition and excommunicated them if thereafter they should perhaps touch anything of the sacred ministry, in accordance with the preceding custom.

First, because they refused to obey our salutary commands concerning Engeltrude, Theutberga, and Waldrada. For disobedience is so dreadful an evil that it is rightly compared with idolatry, as Samuel says: “To resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse obedience is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Samuel 15). Hence the Apostle rightly says: “Having readiness to avenge every disobedience” (2 Corinthians 10).

Second, because they presumed to receive and absolve that same Engeltrude, rejected and anathematized by us and by the synod—and this contrary to the canons, especially contrary to the great Council of Nicaea, which is known to have decreed that those rejected by others should not be received. Blessed Pope Gelasius also explains more than once that the one who bound must absolve, and especially that this belongs to the first See.

Third, because they were most clearly exposed as guilty of fraud or falsification. When our letters, sent through our envoys for the case of the fugitive Engeltrude and read aloud at the wicked assembly already mentioned near the city of Metz, were examined, they were found to have fraudulently removed certain passages, falsely added others, and altered still others, making the letter such as they judged could conform to their own desire.

Fourth, because they not only failed pastorally to resist those who were held in adultery, nor, as watchmen, announced the sword that was coming, but by consenting to and favoring them gave them confidence to persist in wickedness and attempted to defend so great an outrage with all their strength to the very end. Hence the Lord rightly made their tongue cling to the roof of their mouth, so that those who had not possessed a tongue with which to rebuke crime might not even be able to use it, at least, to preach what is good, according to what is sung elsewhere: “But to the sinner God said: … when you associated with adulterers, you placed your portion with them” (Psalm 49).

For he places his portion with adulterers who, by consenting to them, favoring them, or failing to rebuke them, becomes like them in vices and likewise in punishments. Thus the Apostle writes concerning such men: “Those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them.”

Fifth, because, concerning the case that had been appealed by both parties—that is, by Theutberga and by Lothar, as we have already mentioned—they rashly presumed to judge and determine it for themselves, without our authority, having seized it for that purpose. This was contrary to the canons, since the sacred regulations have entrusted the judgment of appeals made at the memory of Saint Peter to the discretion and counsel of the Roman prelate.

But these men, having no reverence for blessed Peter before their eyes, rashly determined both the judgment that each party had demanded from us and that we had begun to carry out; and they decreed that Theutberga, even though she had fled for refuge to a church, should be crushed by condemnation.

Sixth, because they carried this out in her absence, contrary to the figurative saying: “Do not curse the deaf.” He curses the deaf who condemns one who is absent. For someone placed in absence is, in a certain sense, deaf, since he does not hear what is brought against him.

The absence itself, however, was procured not through Theutberga’s design or a wounded conscience, as they suppose, but rightly through fear of the king, who was unwilling to grant her adequate security, and through suspicion of the factious council.

Seventh, because they not only subscribed themselves to the profane proceedings and, without regard for the Apostolic See, confirmed everything that had been badly compiled, but also compelled others to subscribe, thus becoming the authors of all their transgression and being made answerable for as many souls as, because of their prominence, they plunged into the precipice of transgression by word or deed.
