But if we wished to set forth at greater length in writing everything that their actions revealed to us and to the holy synod—both through the booklet they themselves submitted and through other indications—paper would fail us more readily than speech. Let it suffice that we have recalled the seven chapters that principally occasioned the deposition of Theutguald and Gunthar. For the number seven commonly signifies totality.

But who could adequately recount all the things they committed wrongly, either before or after their condemnation? How, for example, they falsely claimed that we had reproved them in vain, contrary to what is said to God: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Psalm 5). How they did not fear to attack Theutberga again after she had first been acquitted by a judgment they themselves had selected, contrary to divine and human law. How afterward—although both laws prohibited it—they condemned her without an accuser. How they admitted some witnesses whom the king could command, contrary to the public laws, for her condemnation, and others who were members of the ruler’s household.

How, contrary to priestly reverence, they committed to writing all sorts of shameful and criminal things against the Apostle, as well as words utterly nauseating and offensive to everyone’s sense of decency, and openly displayed them to all, even though, as the Lord testifies, people will have to give an account of every idle word.

Or how, after they had been condemned, they harassed the emperor’s ears contrary to the sacred regulations. Or how they resisted the ordinance of God conferred on blessed Peter for the Roman Church, wrote chapters of accusation against the privileges of his See, and spread them throughout almost the whole western region. Or how, through these very things, even after being struck down for so great a crime, they urged Lothar to be strengthened in persisting in his wickedness.

Or how they tyrannically afflicted, oppressed, and wearied us with every evil they could while we were stationed near Saint Peter, to such an extent that their men violated the sanctuary of Saint Peter and shed blood in his church. How, while we were celebrating the morning hymns there, they conspired and swore an oath at night behind the tribunal of that church, together with their accomplices and supporters, against the Council of Chalcedon.

How, in the principal places of our dioceses themselves, they factiously held assemblies, arranged individual affairs, and formed cabals against us, although the canons prohibited this, and how they devised wicked negotiations and certain fabrications even with our suffragan bishops.

Finally, how they presume to retain and occupy the churches formerly entrusted to them, but later lost together with their priesthood, and to govern them as tyrants according to their own will.

Behold what Theutguald and Gunthar have done and are doing in the Church of Christ, apart from what Gunthar specifically committed by touching the divine ministry—a matter for which the sacred regulations entirely forbid him even a place for satisfaction.

At the very beginning of their prosecution, however, when they were at the frequently mentioned pernicious assembly of Metz, they clearly displayed what sort of spirit they possessed. Although our envoys later went astray there, they began their speech in a sufficiently peaceful manner. But when these men heard even a little criticism directed against them, they immediately burst into fury and claimed that we had said words that we had not said at all. They insisted that we had called them supporters, planters, and waterers of vices.

Certainly, we did not yet know the things described above, which were grievous to report concerning them, so that we could safely confess such things about them at that time. Yet, already, with conscience goading them, they chattered that we had asserted things which, because they were unknown to us, we ought not at all to have said.

What is this except that, even while we were silent, the Holy Spirit wished to show through their own mouths—not through those of others—that they were planters and waterers of vices? Just as formerly he brought forth through Caiaphas what had to be done, so through these men, though not from their own intention, he expressed what ought to be made manifest.

Yet they utterly denied that we were saying these things about them, as though we knew their life and conduct, while taking pains to assert them with their own mouths and lips, so that they might appear in every respect to be of praiseworthy life and character.

Now, if you wish to know clearly their mockeries and theatrical performances, seek out and reread the proceedings of the aforesaid council of Metz, which we judged ought to be called a brothel because, when we annulled it, it was favoring adulterers. That brothel certainly favored adulterers, since it consented in every respect to Lothar, Waldrada, and Engeltrude according to their desire, and provided examples of adultery for others who followed them.

Behold on whose behalf you plead so often; behold on whose behalf you labor without tiring. Yet we also greatly rejoice with your charity when we see you sympathizing with grieving neighbors, since we too grieve deeply over them and are repeatedly driven to sighs on their account.

And they truly deserve grief, because although they had first been the head among their own people, by teaching falsehood they became the tail, striving to plunge the Lord’s Church into such great storms and such great labors.

We grieve for them; plainly, we grieve also for the Church of God, which through them endures so many dangers. Thus the prophet Samuel is read to have lamented Saul (2 Kings 15). Indeed, the Evangelist records that the Lord, foreseeing that Jerusalem would be utterly overthrown, chiefly because of the guilt of the priests, wept over it (Luke 9).

We do not wish to be mindful of our own injuries, since we are members, nor do we intend to repay them with retaliation, as they perhaps suppose. But because they especially provoked our Head to anger by rejecting an innocent woman and admitting an adulteress, we mourn and lament them.

Indeed, in the written record of the proceedings already mentioned, only an exchange involving them is recorded—and, to omit other matters, the same thing is found written there openly by the author: “Theutguald and Gunthar, who had examined and judged Theutberga’s case”; and again, when King Lothar asserted concerning these matters: “Whatever I did in this case, I did with the counsel of these most holy bishops.”

Furthermore, when, amid countless detestable matters in those foul proceedings already mentioned, they had presumed to compile material here and there to confirm the crime of that criminal adulteress, and the assembled bishops, by subscribing, were strengthening those same proceedings—or rather, through them, the outrage—a certain one of our brothers and fellow bishops subscribed to the proceedings only as far as our deliberation, stipulating that they were to be preserved until our decision.

When Theutguald and Gunthar saw this, they seized a knife and scraped away everything that the prudent bishop had written as needing to be preserved until our deliberation, leaving only the bishop’s name; they rashly wrote in the rest just as they wished.

That bishop reported this to us, and it is perfectly clear from the authentic proceedings themselves that it happened so—for wherever the text remains sound, the matter is most evident. They sharpened heart, tongue, and pen so greatly to strengthen the outrage that what they had once determined by word or writing in confirmation of it, they strove with all their strength to defend even before us, until they fell.

But why do we linger over so many matters and attempt to recount their proceedings, which bring upon them a decisive condemnation, when neither speech can utter them nor the memory of the mind retain them all?

Since, however, your fraternity is eager in your letters to implore mercy kindly for these men and asks that consolation be offered them once they have been restored to their former condition, we for our part endeavor not inappropriately to grant what is permitted and reasonably requested.

Therefore, if the aforesaid men, Theutguald and Gunthar, act patiently; if the evil which, through their zeal in favor of it, they allowed to be completed has been uprooted from the foundations; if they strive to erase it from themselves with complete humility and worthy tears of repentance; and if the peace which they disturbed has been restored to the Church of Christ—then, assuredly, relying on the regard of God alone and on the affection of your fraternity, they may, with our approval and assistance, obtain other benefits of service in the Church.

But they may hope in vain to recover the dignity of their former ministry or of any priestly office; they will never be permitted to resume it.

Let your fraternity’s diligence, therefore, cease pressing us any longer on this matter, and let it finally desist from seeking what cannot be done. For the sentence of the Apostolic See is always conceived with such moderation of counsel, matured with such patience, and delivered with such gravity of deliberation that it does not need to be reconsidered and does not deem alteration necessary—unless it was issued in such a form that it may be reconsidered, or unless, according to the tenor of the condition stated above, it proves to require alteration.

Let them therefore bear the disgrace of their deposition, because, as Scripture testifies, it is “a shame that brings glory” (Sirach 4). For the present, let them be a sign and portent to all whom they themselves deceived or to whom they supplied the audacity to persist in wickedness. Thus may these men, covered with such shame, hold in their hearts and preserve for salvation what they confess with their mouths; and may those others plainly recognize that they were not well served when they were secretly led into falling into so great a crime.

For the evil still threatens; it has not yet ceased to be fostered; it still awaits an opening to freedom and a time of license. The flourishing glory of Waldrada, even after her public crime of adultery, proves this, as does the deposition of Queen Theutberga, our beloved daughter, who, even after oaths had been sworn, has been cast down and not even treated as the equal of a servant girl.

Finally, when King Lothar took back Theutberga, his lawful wife, in the presence of our envoy, he ordered twelve illustrious counts, as you have heard, to pledge their oaths on his behalf that thereafter he would retain and treat Theutberga in the manner in which it is fitting for a king to retain and treat his lawful wife and queen.

But, alas, now—as perhaps you are not unaware—he subjects her to such disgrace, and to such abhorrence and, what is grievous even to say, such extreme poverty, that we will not say that she has anyone near her husband to help her in her need [read “to provide a man with bread,” Hardouin]; rather, she is unable to provide anything at all either for herself or even for her own little servants.

Waldrada, on the other hand, the adulteress deprived of all communion, although she appears to have been excluded by Lothar only bodily—and although many indications show that she is never absent from his heart—possesses both royal eminence and complete power to harm or assist whomever she wishes.

Behold, brothers, the shoots; behold the fruits that have sprung from the seed cast by Theutguald and Gunthar.

If your fraternity truly and usefully grieves over these matters and wishes to offer them some assistance, it must take care, together with us, to cut out and diligently heal the wound that they not only failed to excise with the sword of justice but also nourished with the oil of unjust flattery and persuasion, thereby causing it to grow far and wide.

Yet, as we have stated, the men themselves can have no hope of being restored with respect to the priesthood. For if we rebuilt what we destroyed in them, we would undoubtedly be made transgressors before the Lord, and would appear, as though repenting of things not well done, to have changed our sentence. [Editio Romana adds: “acting better and changing the sentence,” etc.]

Consequently, neither will these men be corrected by fearing such punishment, nor will those who still harbor the crime begun within consider it worthy of punishment. Nor will the others who might fall back into such an outrage, instructed salutarily by their example, fear more prudently to commit what they see released through such great leniency.

Return, therefore, brothers, to yourselves; return to your hearts; recognize your ministry against vices, rebuking and admonishing with more fervent zeal and greater earnestness the very man through whom the Church of God suffers such scandal—namely, King Lothar—so that he may come to the aid [Editio Romana adds: “to his own aid and to that of the wretched,” etc.] of those unfortunate women whom he bound by oath on his behalf.

Let him treat Queen Theutberga, his wife, according to the terms of the oath that was given; let him shield himself from the guilt of those who swore on his behalf; and let him also send Waldrada to us. In this way he himself may thereafter lead a secure life, and we may no longer be subjected to such great labors on his account.

For it is not just that the lawful wife should suffer such hardship and dishonor at his hands, while the adulteress steals away the glory of her dignity.

But if King Lothar refuses to act in this way, while professing that he truly wishes to hear and carry out our admonitions—as our beloved son, the illustrious King Louis, informed us on the basis of Lothar’s own statement—then let him be asked, either by you or, at your urging, by the aforesaid pious king, why, when he writes to us or gives satisfaction to others, he indicates concerning Waldrada that he did not approach her after the return of our envoy, but does not likewise indicate concerning his wife Theutberga that he treats and retains her according to the tenor of the oaths given.

The reason can only be that he has nothing of which to boast and does not act toward her in such a way that he could truthfully report it to us and thereby complete a thanksgiving to us. For not only does she enjoy no generosity from him, but she also wastes away under every disgrace and the utmost poverty.

Let the pious prince therefore tell him, or let your priestly diligence persuade him, that whenever he sends us word that he has in no way approached Waldrada contrary to our prohibition, he should also send word that he treats Theutberga, his wife, kindly according to the oaths given and retains her according to royal dignity—provided, of course, that we learn, with others also testifying, that what he reports is supported by the truth.

Finally, when that woman had been rejected and King Lothar brought back Theutberga, his wife, it is clear that it was determined that Waldrada should be sent to Italy, so that she might await the decision of our judgment as to whether she ought to proceed to Rome or not [another reading: “might be required to await it,” Hardouin].

For concerning those persons whose case the Apostolic See has specially begun to handle—as we began to pursue the dispute involving Kings Lothar and Theutberga and the concubine Waldrada—it is lawful for no one else either to remove them or to determine anything concerning them, unless perhaps the See itself has commanded it.

Waldrada, therefore, whom it is established was removed from Lothar’s side through our exhortations and decrees, must also, in particular, be submitted to our judgments for suitable satisfaction to the Church whom she injured.

As long as Lothar has not done this, just as there can be neither rest for us nor security for Theutberga, so there can be no safe peace or any confidence of salvation for him.

Therefore, work all the more zealously for his correction; admonish him all the more insistently to obey us in these matters; and exhort also our beloved son, the most excellent King Louis, to urge him always to hear our admonitions. Read attentively: “Whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (James 5).

Do not merely approach your glorious king concerning this matter; also specifically entreat him to admonish and persuade Lothar not to presume to come to Rome unless he has been cleansed and until we have given our approval.

For unless he first obeys us and takes care to wash away the filth of suspicion and evil reputation, let him beware lest, like lepers, he be driven from the Lord’s camp with the greatest disgrace.

How he can remove that filth we shall briefly explain: if he treats Theutberga, his wife, kindly according to the oaths given and retains her according to royal dignity; if he compels Waldrada to hasten to us; and if he permits bishops to be ordained in the aforesaid Churches according to the order we prescribed to him.

For as long as he allows Waldrada to remain as she is—as is clear to everyone—and fails to treat Theutberga either with royal honor or conjugal affection; and as long as he allows Theutguald or Gunthar to retain and occupy the churches formerly taken from them together with their priesthood, he cannot be free either from the leprosy of a branded crime or from the filth of the worst odor, that is, evil reputation or suspicion.

He will not be able to enter the Church with pure steps, nor will the priests of Christ have any free or secure opportunity to touch him or receive him within the camp.

Therefore, labor with us in this, dearest brothers; struggle together with us. For just as labor on earth is manifold, so a rich reward will remain for us in heaven.

There is no doubt that this young man now has many people consenting to him because of his power or rule. We shall all rejoice together over the conversion and salvation of all of them if, by God’s preceding grace, their leader is more perfectly cleansed through our common exertions.

Moreover, let your holiness know that your most exalted king has written to us concerning Theutguald and Gunthar with the same affection with which you wrote to us. Since we replied to him on this matter in a brief letter, if he wishes to know more fully what sentence concerning them has been fixed in our mind, we have directed his diligence to examine the text of this letter, which we have sent to your fraternity.

Therefore, let your sanctity ensure that it is conveyed to his pious eyes for reading, with due reverence and prompt diligence.

Furthermore, if there are perhaps some who say that Waldrada is free and therefore ought not to be compelled to come here, let them know that she is not free: overcome by sin, she has been assigned as its servant. The Apostle Peter says: “By whatever a person is overcome, to that he is enslaved” (1 Peter 2); and again elsewhere: “Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8).

Since she has not yet been freed from this, she must certainly still be regarded as its servant and therefore must be specially cleansed by our judgment, by whose decree her iniquity began to be brought under examination and, with Christ’s favor, to receive abolition.

For unless we knew that she had not yet been freed from her crime, we would in no way have arranged for her to come to Italy for her own liberation and that of her supporters—although Satan afterward prevented her through his agents from reaching this place.

But now, if she has fulfilled our commands or sanctions, she considers herself a servant. Therefore King Lothar must be called a slave, since he is known to have carried out, in some fashion, our commands; and therefore she must be held to be the mistress because she remains disobedient and rules over Lothar, who has in some fashion striven to obey our decrees. This is utterly absurd and wholly wicked.

But if King Lothar had wished to send Waldrada, the adulteress, to us with as much determination—that is, so that we might lawfully determine her case—as he wished to send Theutberga, his lawful wife, to bring forward crimes extorted against her by falsehood, perhaps by now some kind of peace or return of rest would have been granted to us.

Would that he would now strive to send Waldrada to us, so that she might disclose what she has concerning her crime, just as he was eager to send Queen Theutberga, who indeed had nothing to disclose concerning a crime but had much to recount concerning the violence and continual punishment inflicted upon her, and concerning the many unjust threats by which he compelled her to bring forward a false accusation against herself before us.

We wish your fraternity well-being in Christ, now and always.

Given on the day before the Kalends of November, in the first indiction.

*(In the year 867.)*

**CLVI. TO LOUIS, KING OF GERMANY.** He complains that Lothar is fulfilling none of the promises he made. He forbids him to come to Rome before sending Waldrada there, as he was ordered, treating Theutberga as queen, and having legitimate bishops ordained at Trier and Cologne. In the embolus, concerning the revenues of Saint Peter.

*[In Mansi, ibid.]*

**Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Louis, glorious king.**
Source/review notes: Corrected reversed subject, mistranslated oath and apparatus reading, altered biblical citations, a double negation, and the final decree’s erroneous identification and syntax.

[Col. 1175A] You have disclosed in the tenor of your letters that you came together for a common conference with our beloved son Charles, the glorious king—your brother, that is. Since King Lothar, your nephew, was absent, you report that you sent to him this same brother of yours, King Charles, accompanied by one of the bishops of your realm, so that, as we instructed you in letters addressed to you, he might admonish Lothar to be obedient in all things to our commands. Since you did this both as pious princes who love justice and as kinsmen seeking the salvation of your relative through charity, while also complying with our exhortations, we give you our due thanks. Yet how much success your or our admonitions have gained with that same King Lothar [Col. 1175B] has so far, I confess, not become clear.

But you say that, both in his absence and afterward in his presence, he kindly received this admonition from you, and then professed that he would obey all our instructions. Since we have often heard this before, yet have not perceived its effect, we groan deeply and are afflicted on this account beyond what can be expressed. For although we labor daily even for his own salvation, we accomplish nothing at all with him, since he does not complete in deed what he says in words. Above all, his words can indeed sound like the leaves of trees, but, since they are without fruit, they cannot satisfy.

Therefore, while we seek someone to whom such a man may be compared, none comes more appropriately to mind than that son of whom it is written in Matthew that his father said: “Son, go today and work in my vineyard.” But he answered, “I will, Lord,” and did not go (Matt. 21). Hence he rightly represents the figure of the Jewish people. For that people promised Moses, saying, “All that the Lord has spoken we will do” (Exod. 19), yet did not fulfill by deeds what it promised in words.

So, alas, this nephew of yours too continually declares that he wishes to hear our admonitions and always desires to fulfill them. Yet he does not strive to put into practice or exhibit by deeds what he so often professes, in speech and in writing, at every suitable and unsuitable time. He does not obey our paternal admonitions as an obedient son, but, like an ungrateful one, has retreated behind our backs.

For when has King Lothar ever appeared obedient to us? Or what have we demanded of him [Col. 1175D] except his own salvation; except the oath which he violated [perhaps: “gave”—HARD.] to the Church; except security for Queen Theutberga, his wife, who seeks refuge at the blessed Peter; and except, after so many labors, some rest for ourselves? For this reason, among countless other cares, we have labored especially and have often resolved to remove every suspicion concerning Waldrada, the adulteress and excommunicate woman.

For this reason also we ordered that new bishops be appointed for the Churches of Trier and Cologne—men who would not be advanced through the favor either of Theutgaud and Gunthar, formerly bishops, or of the aforementioned Waldrada, but who, canonically elected by the sons and from among the sons of those Churches, would be regularly ordained by those who customarily consecrate the bishops of those Churches.

But although, seeing all these things to be opportune and necessary, we repeatedly commanded King Lothar to become the executor of our decision, to consent to their completion, indeed to insist that they be accomplished entirely through his own execution, we certainly do not yet know that any one of them has been carried out. Nevertheless, he professes that he wishes to fulfill all our admonitions.

Finally, not only did Lothar fail to send Waldrada to us, as we have often urged him; he even arranged to bring her back into Gaul from Ticinum, although she had already departed there while it was thought that she was making her way to us.

As for our daughter, Queen Theutberga, who has always asked to be protected under the shelter of blessed Peter, he not only fails to treat her as queen according to the oath he gave [Col. 1176B]; he does not even acknowledge her as sharing in the smallest matters, whether from fear of God, reverence for blessed Peter, the marital bond, or even the oath he himself gave. Instead, he subjects her to every deprivation, every disgrace, and utter rejection.

Moreover, concerning the aforementioned Churches, he not only disregards our commands but tramples upon the precepts of the sacred canons, since he shows no compassion for the Churches and permits them to remain without a ruler for so long.

Behold, dearest son, how King Lothar observes our decrees; behold how true it is that he says he wishes to observe all our decisions. He still gives evidence that he wishes to hasten to us, although we have often instructed and strictly forbidden him to presume to do so without our permission [Col. 1176C].

But we are astonished if the reason why Lothar desires to go to Rome could have escaped your prudence. Let him first fulfill everything we have set out above; let him cast far from himself, or rather cut away from our minds, every source of opportunity and every sinister suspicion. Then, if he ought to come here, we shall carefully decide what is to be done.

For even if he could have shown that everything we mentioned above and ordered him to do had been completely fulfilled, he still should not have hastened to Rome against our prohibition. How much less now, when, although so often admonished by us, he is shown to have completed none of these things?

Therefore, I ask your affection to forbid him now to come to Rome [Col. 1176D]. Otherwise, believe me: if he should presume to act against our purpose, he will by no means be received here with the honor he desires, nor will he depart from here in the manner he wishes. For just as the woman who approached the Lord in faith touched him, whereas the crowd, although it also touched him, merely pressed upon him, so, alas, at this time some appear to approach us, yet their touch, because it does not arise from faith, produces pressure, and their approach brings disturbance.

It is therefore necessary that King Lothar show himself in all things such that we may first be pleased to receive him with a welcoming spirit and then embrace him with open arms when he comes. This cannot happen unless Waldrada is sent to Rome, as had been begun, so that we may bring her case to its lawful conclusion—for we once undertook to begin judging her transgression [Col. 1177A]; unless we hear from King Lothar himself, her husband, that he treats Queen Theutberga according to the terms of the oath he gave; that is, that in mind and deed he shows himself toward her as a loving king ought to show himself toward his beloved queenly wife; and unless he permits bishops to be ordained from the proper clergy in the churches of Agrippina’s Colony and Trier—men who are neither chosen nor consecrated through the favor of Waldrada, Gunthar, or Theutgaud.

These are the matters, dearest son, which, if your nephew Lothar does not cunningly carry out, will certainly show that he does not truly wish to listen to us. And if your charity is concerned for his salvation, let it urge him vigorously, and not readily believe his words resounding outside; rather, let it consider the deeds of his works according to the keenest abundance of its own discernment.

The apostle John says: “My little children, let us not love in word or in tongue, but in deed and in truth” (1 John 5).

For if your excellence wishes to know what it is on account of which Lothar boasts that he fulfills our will in all things, we shall clearly explain it. He says that, obedient to us—or rather to our God—he received back his wife Theutberga, while he rightly separated himself from Waldrada as an adulteress and did not approach her after the return of our legate.

But your glorious prudence can now perceive what benefit there is if he does not approach her with the steps of his body, yet approaches her with the steps of his mind [Col. 1177C]. What benefit is there in his being seen outwardly separated from her, when inwardly he is understood to be closely joined to her? And what benefit does it bring our beloved daughter Queen Theutberga that he is not seen to be wholly removed from Waldrada in body, when he is nevertheless in no way proved to be joined to Theutberga in mind?

What benefit does she gain from the name alone of the marital bond or royal dignity, when she lacks all the insignia that appear to belong to perfect affection and equal authority? For who but her rival—Waldrada, that is—who is bound by the chains of excommunication not only for the adultery she committed but also for her impenitent heart, possesses the heights of the kingdom with Lothar, enjoys its glory, holds its rights, and arranges everything according to her own will?

Although she appears outwardly to be separated from his conversation, through intermediaries and various attendants she has as much power with him, or even more, than she could have had if she had in any way been regarded as his legitimate wife [Col. 1177D]. No one is advanced at the royal court except through her; scarcely anyone is reported to have been harmed except because of her. She is accustomed to obtain favors from him for those who ask, and she alone is accustomed to secure benefits for whomever she prefers.

But if what we say is not so—if Queen Theutberga does not suffer such great hardship and disgrace from him, and if Waldrada the adulteress does not enjoy such great glory—why, when he writes to us or gives satisfaction to others, does he report of Waldrada that he did not approach her after the return of our envoy, but not of his wife Theutberga that he treats and retains her according to the terms of the oaths he gave? Is it not because he has nothing in this matter of which he may boast, and does not act toward her in such a way that, by truthfully reporting it to us, he could receive our thanks?

She not only receives no generosity from him; she also wastes away in every disgrace and, as we have stated, in the deepest deprivation.

Tell him, then, dearest son, and strive through your prudent conference to persuade him that, when he sends us word that after the return of our envoy he did not approach Waldrada in any way against our prohibition, he should also send us proof that he treats Theutberga, his wife, kindly according to the oaths he gave and retains her in accordance with her royal dignity. Let us know this, however, with the testimony of others as well, so that we may recognize that what he sends is supported by truth [Col. 1178B].

Let him also send us proof that bishops have been regularly ordained in the aforementioned Churches, in the order we specified above. Then we shall believe him when he asserts that he wishes to fulfill our commands, and we shall render worthy thanks to God.

For as long as he does not retain Theutberga with royal honor and marital affection, and permits Theutgaud or Gunthar to remain in possession of the Churches and priesthoods formerly taken from them and now occupied, these are steps—though plunging anyone down into the depths—by which every prudent person clearly recognizes that he is gradually making his way toward Waldrada, even if he does not see her. He cherishes those whom he clearly had as leaders into wickedness, and afflicts her whom, after the required correction had first been made, he received back with Christ’s help.

As for Lothar’s accusers, we have found that he has no accuser except the one who is called “the accuser of the brethren” in John’s Apocalypse (chap. 12), and his works, which are themselves carried out at the prompting of that same ancient enemy.

But the things your nephew, King Lothar, does require no accuser. For, as the Apostle testifies, “the works of the flesh are manifest,” namely “fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness” (Gal. 5), and the rest.

We wish your glory well-being now and always, dearest son.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of November, in the first indiction.

## Supplement

Furthermore, your excellence’s legate agreed with us that, by the middle of May in this first indiction, we should send our envoys to receive the revenues for one year from the properties of Saint Peter situated in your kingdom [Col. 1178D]. Two years have now passed since revenues from those properties ought to have been collected, and we have received nothing from them.

Moreover, if, as we have learned from many people and from this same legate of yours, Arsenius has collected anything from them, although he has brought us nothing, he collected it for past years, not for future ones.

Therefore we ask your glory, for the increase of your reward, to inform us, once all those revenues have been collected by men of your court who are coming to the threshold of the apostles for the sake of prayer, before you order them to be taken outside the borders of your kingdom. If, after they have meanwhile been stored in a place made entirely secure by your prudence [Col. 1179A], we are able to obtain from our special son, the Emperor, that we send someone there with one of his men and receive the revenues so that they may be brought to us without any loss, thanks are to be rendered to the Lord.

If not, we shall send our envoy, with God as his guide, to see with your envoy how they are stored and guarded in your kingdom. While they are meanwhile kept safe in your kingdom, he shall either report back to us or, in any case, not fail to do whatever we foresee or decree.

Or, if your glory causes whatever the revenues may be to be brought within the territory under your authority, as far as Bologna or Ravenna, provided that they are secure, we shall regard this as much more useful and agreeable. We shall then order them to be transported to Rome in whatever manner we are able [Col. 1179B].

## CLVII. To the Bishops Rhodoald and John Sent as Legates to Francia

He sends them an admonition concerning Theutberga’s case.

[At Mansi, *Councils*, vol. 15.]

To the most reverend and most holy bishops Rhodoald and John.

Just as you are faithful to the holy Roman Church and are pillars of the apostolic see, so hasten, while observing everything according to our earlier command, to carry it out; and, once a synod has been summoned at Metz by apostolic authority, fulfill our instructions.

But if the synod of bishops does not assemble there, or if Lothar delays coming [Col. 1179C], then strive to go to him and declare our commands and decisions.

Afterward, when you go to Charles on Baldwin’s case, present to that glorious king, in the presence of everyone, both the synodical letters and those that we are now sending you, together with this admonition. Do not merely make this known to him; make it known also to all the bishops and to all the faithful, and strive to read it aloud and proclaim it publicly.

Furthermore, know that we are sending your holiness two letters in place of those that were taken away: one to King Charles and the second to his wife. We have instructed that another be sent to the bishops of Gaul and Germany together with this letter now addressed to you.

## Admonition Given to the Aforementioned Legates

[Col. 1179D] **[Note: “Lothar professes.” In Ivo, part 8, chapter 334, and in Gratian, 21, q. 2, the two words “Lothar professes in the admonition” are wrongly inserted. They are redundant and belong to the title of the letter; this is correctly observed in the Roman edition of Gratian [Col. 1180D]. In the admonition, therefore, the term is used as it is in other authors: for example, Zosimus speaks of an *admonition* to the priests and deacons who are at Ravenna, and in Gregory’s *Dialogues* one reads: “Sabinus, servant of Christ, an admonition to Padu.” —Jac. Sirm.]**

Lothar professes that he received Waldrada from his father and afterward took Hucbert’s sister as his wife.

First investigate this with careful inquiry. If you find that the same glorious king received the aforementioned Waldrada with the previously stated dowry, in the presence of witnesses, according to the law and the rite by which marriages are customarily celebrated, and that Waldrada was admitted into his marriage by public declaration, then it remains for you to examine why she was rejected and the daughter of Boso admitted [Col. 1180A].

But since the same glorious king says that he admitted Theutberga through fear, recall that Gospel in which the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. 10); and again: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. 6).

In these sayings of the Lord it must be considered that, if those who kill bodies are not to be feared when they drive a person against justice, and if the gain of the whole world is of no benefit to a man who loses his soul, how much less ought so great a king, through fear of one man, to have been plunged against the divine command into such an immense precipice?

In this matter he shows himself especially blameworthy: he has placed love of the world before love of God.

Here we command you nothing else: once the same king has been convicted by his own declaration, relying on canonical authority and supported by our voice, define her case.

But if it is not at all proved that Waldrada was a legitimate wife, nor that, after a marriage celebrated according to custom—namely, with the blessing of a priest—she was joined to our son Lothar, suggest to him that he should not resent the reconciliation of a legitimate wife to him, if she appears innocent. Let him not obey the voice of the flesh in this matter; rather, obeying the divine commands, let him be ashamed—indeed, let him dread—to rot in the filth of lust and, by following his own will, to have to render a strict account before the tribunal of Christ [Col. 1180B].

Moreover, I want you to know that the aforesaid Theutberga appealed to the apostolic see two or three times. She complained that she had been unjustly expelled by the aforesaid glorious king and forced by violence to fabricate a false crime against herself.

At that time she sent a petition of appeal to the apostolic see. In it she did not yet confess anything; rather, she made known that she was being compelled to speak falsely of a crime against herself. She added:

“But if I am compelled further, know that—not from truth, but from fear of death and the desire to escape, since I cannot otherwise—I shall say whatever they wish. Remember me, who have disclosed these things to you.”

Therefore we command you: when the same Theutberga comes to the appointed synod, as we have established, deal with her case through careful examination. If it is objected to her that she confessed to having committed some crime, while she proclaims that she suffered violence, or if she testifies that her judges were her enemies [Col. 1180D], then renew the judgment according to the rule of equity, so that she is not crushed by the weight of injustice.

## CLVIII. To Rotland, Archbishop of Arles

Sent together with another letter in which Nicholas delegated his authority to Rotland.

Nicholas, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Rotland, archbishop of Arles.

[Col. 1181A] Having received your letters, filled with every gift of humility and crowned with the flowers of all virtues, we render manifold acts of thanksgiving to the author of every good. We greatly commend your devotion toward the apostolic see, recognized over many years, and we exhort your fraternity with the greatest urgency to persevere in this salutary purpose.

For thus, with the Lord’s revelation, you will be able to recognize more clearly the path of holy conduct along which you ought to proceed, and more freely foresee and avoid the darts of wicked men who come upon you. You will prevail if, following the custom of your forefathers, you place your protection upon the rock of the apostolic see and strive to adhere more closely to the teachings and decrees of its faith.

He sanctified that see by his own session—he whom the Lord Christ [Col. 1181B] wished to retain as the first and special summit of his Church. Indeed, Christ chose him to be constituted the chief doorkeeper of the heavenly court. We now raise your blessedness with fitting praises for zealously pursuing this office, not only in this matter but also because you exhort our apostolate to perseverance.

For in what matter could you show yourself more manifestly to be the guardian of our sanctions and decrees than in striving so diligently to encourage our firmness, founded upon the firm rock, to persevere in these things?

As for what your fraternity asks—that we investigate what kind of predecessors our predecessors were toward yours in ancient times—and as you request permission to learn by written reply whether you may confidently approach us frequently by letter or legates and offer whatever is appropriate at suitable times, let your blessedness know that we well understand that my predecessors, among their other benefits of honor, loved your predecessors so greatly that they consented that they retain their authority in those regions, as the fifth holy and universal synod reports [Col. 1181C].

But if you fulfill the promises of your affection, and, agreeing with us, strive to stand against every wicked or troublesome person, and refuse to deviate from the decrees, know that you will thereafter be protected by the shield of our apostolate and embraced in every way by the arms of charity and piety. The holy Church divinely entrusted to you will also, with God as author, be greatly and more perfectly increased through our care and vigilance [Col. 1181D].

You ought to send us legates or letters with as much freedom as the charity with which we burn toward your holiness permits. The Psalmist calls this charity “a broad command”; within the breadth of its bosom [Col. 1182A] it receives, cherishes, and protects all its neighbors, because, according to the Apostle Paul, it is kind and bears all things (1 Cor. 15).

Yet we necessarily ask one thing of your charity: whenever you send someone to the apostolic see, let your fraternity take care to warn him not to appear excessively hasty on his return. For, as you yourself know, we are bound by the care of all the Churches of God; and since many people come from every direction to the apostolic see seeking various things, we become slow in dealing with individuals because we wish to distribute kindness and generosity among many.

We were especially pleased—and indeed rejoiced with immense delight—by the fact that, when your holiness asked our apostolate what you ought to follow, you made a most prudent decision [Col. 1182B].

Although there are many things we could send you, for the present let your diligence pursue with vigilant care, and carry out with special zeal, only those matters that we make known to your blessedness in another letter of our apostolate.

For toward us and toward the see of blessed Peter, there is no other sign of your devotion than the obedience to and completion of our decrees and decisions. Although unworthy, we are nevertheless, through the abundance of Christ’s grace, his vicars.

Given in the month of May, on the twelfth day, in the twelfth indiction.

## CLIX. To Charles the Elder, King

Fragment: on the marriage of the younger Charles [Col. 1182C].

Your beloved son and namesake Charles has now endeavored to send word to our apostolic fatherhood, informing us that he incurred the displeasure of your fatherhood on account of a certain woman who had already been abandoned by her first marriage and whom he took as his wife without your consent, though he ought not to have done so.

Likewise. Concerning the wife joined to your son: if it is found that there is some cause contrary to divine law on account of which he ought in no way to have her, we wish your affection to inform us of it. But if no other cause is found on her side that produces grave sin, there is no authority by which their marriage ought to be severed, nor is it our place to inflict upon them the prejudice of separation without manifest guilt [Col. 1182D].

Likewise. Although we know that, if you wish, you can lawfully release your daughter to Baldwin as his wife and mercifully grant her your paternal favor, we have not sent commands; we have offered petitions.

[Col. 1183]

# Appendix: Decrees or Replies of Pope Nicholas I Collected from the Volume of Gratian by John Cochlaeus and Divided into Twenty Titles

[At Mansi, *General Councils*, vol. 15.]

## On the Constitutions of the Church, Title I

[Col. 1183A]

### I. *(Dist. 10, c. 1, “To the bishops assembled in council at Constantinople VI”)*

Ecclesiastical rights cannot be dissolved by imperial judgment; nor can the laws of emperors, to which they must be subordinate, inflict prejudice upon the Gospel, apostolic, and canonical decrees.

### II. *(Dist. 12, “Ridiculous”)*

It is ridiculous and a sufficiently abominable disgrace that we should allow the traditions which we received from the fathers in ancient times to be broken.

## On Custom, Title II

### I. *(Dist. 8, c. 8, “Evil”)*

An evil custom must be rejected and avoided no less than a pernicious corruption.

### II. *(Dist. 22, “Michael the Emperor”)*

Various constitutions or customs according to place and time do not harm the salvation of believers, provided that no canonical authority stands against them [Col. 1183B].

### III. *(Dist. 21, “Finally”)*

Those who came before us handed down a prudent custom in the Churches, and it is still observed without interruption in the Roman Church, which is the teacher of all Churches: no priest should attempt to give the blessing of anything unless his senior fellow priest gives a sign of approval.

Likewise, one who stands before the congregation to pronounce a reading first asks for a blessing, but no inferior person dares to bless him, because we read in the Epistle to the Hebrews that the lesser is blessed by the greater (Heb. 3).

## On Judgments, Title III

### I. *(Dist. 12, c. “The Inferior”)*

An inferior see cannot absolve a superior one or bind it by judgment, nor can it subject it to its own decisions [Col. 1183C].

### II. *(Ibid., c. “Do not”)*

Children ought to be so restrained and devoted toward a spiritual father, as disciples toward a teacher, that they do not rush forward in any rashness at all to judge his life or even to reprove it slightly.

### III. *(Ibid., c. “Now”)*

No one can rightly be subjected to judicial decisions by those who are of an inferior order or dignity.

Hence, at the council of bishops, no one dared to pronounce a sentence against Pope Marcellinus, who, in the time of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, had been compelled to sacrifice to idols but afterward became a distinguished martyr. Instead, everyone repeatedly said to him: “Judge your case by your own mouth, not by our judgment.” And again: “Do not be heard in our judgment, but gather your case into your own bosom,” and so forth [Col. 1184A].

### IV. *(Ibid., following chapter)*

A council is plainly headless when a matter concerning so great a person is treated without awaiting the judgment of superiors, since even in the case of a cleric of lower rank only the judgment of his own bishop is to be sought [variant: awaited].

### V. *(Ibid., following chapter)*

The holy Fathers at Chalcedon detested this presumption so greatly that, among other reasons, they condemned Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, without any restoration chiefly because, “setting his mouth in heaven, while his tongue passed over the earth,” he pronounced excommunication against holy Pope Leo [Col. 1184B].

### VI. *(2, q. 2, c. 2, “To Charles, king of the Franks”)*

All laws, both ecclesiastical and civil and public, command that everything taken away be restored to the person who has been stripped of his possessions.

### VII. *(3, q. 5, c. 2, “The Emperor Michael”)*

That suspected and hostile persons ought not to be judges is dictated by reason itself and demonstrated by many examples. For what more pleasing or welcome gift can anyone give an enemy than to entrust to him the prosecution of the person whom he may wish to harm?

### VIII. *(3, q. 9, “Truly”)*

Truly, he is not a just mediator who, while one party is litigating and the other is absent, does not fear to decide the disputes arising between them [Col. 1184C].

### IX. *(Ibid., c. “Indicating”)*

You indicate that Bishop Hermann was frequently accused concerning certain matters. Since the person of one side is absent in these matters, we certainly cannot believe one party to the danger of the other.

### X. *(Ibid., c. 6, “If perhaps”)*

According to the teaching of the sacred Scriptures and the path of justice, both the accused and the accuser must be present together. One party, whatever its authority and whatever its character, must be heard in such a way that no prejudice is inflicted upon the other party.

### XI. *(4, q. 1, c. 2, “The Emperor Michael”)*

Heretics are not permitted to bring accusations against orthodox bishops in ecclesiastical matters. By heretics we mean both those who were cast out of the Church long ago and those who have since been anathematized by us. In addition, we include those who deny sound faith or falsely pretend to confess it [Col. 1185A].

### XII. *(4, q. 4, final chapter)*

Against ecclesiastical custom and venerable laws, an accuser or witness is produced from the imperial palace, and one who can be commanded is employed to give false testimony. The judges are made suspect, and wolves are made guardians.

### XIII. *(6, q. 4, “What was rightly decided,” to Charles, king of the Franks)*

What has once been rightly decided and settled with the interposition of oaths ought not to be reconsidered, except perhaps where there has been greater authority.

### XIV. *(24, q. 1, “He says,” to Michael, Emperor Augustus)*

Pope Celestine, writing to the Eastern bishops, says:

“If anyone has been excommunicated or stripped of the dignity either of bishop or cleric by Bishop Nestorius or by others who follow him, from the time when they began to preach such things, it is evident that this person has remained and remains in communion with us [Col. 1185B]. Nor do we judge him to have been removed, because the sentence of one who had already made himself liable to removal could not remove anyone.”

### XV. *(33, q. 2, “History,” to Charles, king of the Franks)*

The ecclesiastical history composed by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, speaking of a certain woman accused by her husband concerning her chastity, says:

“The emperor enacted by law that she should first be permitted to arrange her household affairs freely for a considerable time, and only then should she answer the charges brought against her.”

All laws, both ecclesiastical and civil and public, prescribe this. If such provisions have been established for women and secular men, they have been granted much more to ecclesiastical persons and priests [Col. 1185C].

### XVI. *(Ibid., c. “Whether,” to the same person)*

Whether judgment is to be undertaken concerning the bond of marriage or the crime of adultery, reason does not permit Theutberga to enter into a contest with Lothar unless she is first returned for a time to her own authority and freely joined with her own relatives.

Therefore a place must also be provided where no violence from a crowd is to be feared, so that it will not be difficult to produce witnesses or the other persons required in such controversies both by the holy canons and by the venerable Roman laws.

## On the Roman Church and the Apostolic See, Title IV

[Col. 1185D]

### I. *(Dist. 22, c. 1, “To the Milanese”)*

The Roman Church established all things, whether the rank of any patriarchate, the primacy of a metropolitan see, the chairs of bishoprics, or the dignity of Churches of any order.

But he alone founded it and raised it upon the rock of the faith that was about to arise—he who entrusted to blessed Peter, the key-bearer of eternal life, the rights of both earthly and heavenly rule (Matt. 16).

### II. *(Dist. 79, c. 1, “If anyone by money”)*

If anyone is enthroned in the apostolic see through money, human favor, popular or military tumult, without the harmonious and canonical election of the cardinals of that Church and afterward of the other clerics who follow them, let him be regarded not as pope or apostolic but as an apostate.

Let the cardinals and other God-fearing clerics, as well as the laity, be permitted to anathematize that invader and drive him from the apostolic see by human assistance [Col. 1186A].

### III. *(Dist. 97, c. “Emperor Louis”)*

Although it has never been the practice of the apostolic see to receive a legation from anywhere without sealed letters, we nevertheless honored your highness in the person of your noble and vigorous legate. Recognizing the seriousness of his character and the truthfulness of his statements, we received him even without your letter.

### IV. *(1, q. 1 and 9, q. 3, c. “Through the principal authority,” to the Emperor Michael)*

By the right hand and power of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul [Col. 1186B], we have the authority and right, when necessary and when ecclesiastical circumstances require it, to summon not only monks but also any clerics from whatever diocese.

### V. *(2, q. 6, “Your subtle wisdom,” to the archbishop of Rheims)*

Your subtle wisdom took up grounds for deposition against Rothad, removed him from the journey to the apostolic see, repeatedly condemned him when he appealed to the apostolic see, and committed him to imprisonment.

Nevertheless, you ought in no way to have consigned the privileges of the apostolic see to oblivion. By those privileges the venerable canons command that the judgments of the whole Church be brought to this see.

### VI. *(6, q. 3, “It is clear,” to the Emperor Michael)*

It is entirely clear that the judgment of the apostolic see—than whose authority there is no greater—may be retracted by no one, and that no one is permitted to judge its judgment [Col. 1186C].

The canons have never commanded that judgment be passed upon its judgment; rather, they have established that the sentence of the see whose decrees they commanded to be followed ought not to be dissolved.

### VII. *(15, q. 6, c. 2, “To the bishops of Gaul”)*

Following the authority of our venerable predecessors, and especially of the most blessed Pope and martyr Alexander, the fifth from blessed Peter, we absolve both the archbishop of Trier and his provost, and all who at that time, while held captive, bound themselves to them in any way, from every oath and every obligation by which they bound themselves under compulsion from the violence of the wicked; and we forbid those obligations to be observed [Col. 1186D].

We do not permit them ever to suffer, with God and the holy apostles and our predecessors as witnesses, any infamy or accusation on that account, nor any sequestration of their possessions, just as the Lord says through the prophet: “Loose the bonds of wickedness,” and so forth (Isa. 58).

VIII. (17, q. 4, “To No One.” To All Bishops.) No one is permitted to judge the judgment of the apostolic see or to reconsider its sentence, namely because of the primacy of the Roman Church, divinely bestowed upon the blessed apostle Peter by Christ’s gift.

IX. (55, q. 2, “If Anyone.” Presiding over the Universal Synod.) If anyone despises the doctrines, commands, prohibitions, sanctions, or decrees beneficially promulgated by the prelate of the apostolic see for the Catholic faith or ecclesiastical discipline, [Col. 1187A] for the correction of impending or future evils, let him be anathema.

X. (35, q. 9, “The Sentence.” To Emperor Michael.) We do not deny that a sentence of the Roman see can be changed for the better, when something has been obtained from it by fraudulent concealment, or when it has decided, out of consideration for ages or times or grave necessities, to arrange certain matters by dispensation; for we also read that the distinguished apostle Paul acted dispensationally in certain matters which he is later said to have rejected. This, however, must be observed when that Roman Church has chosen to act with the most discerning consideration—not when it has wished to reconsider what it itself has well defined.

XI. (On Consecration, Distinction 1, “The Church.” To the Clergy and People of the Church of Vienne.) How can the Church—that is, the gathering of Catholics—be established without the directive of the apostolic see, when, according to the sacred decrees, even a basilica newly built, which is known to embrace within itself the whole company of Catholics, ought not to be erected without the pope’s command?

## On the Decrees of the Roman Pontiffs, Title V

I. (Dist. 11, c. 2, “What Is Sanctioned.” To Emperor Michael.) What is decreed with full authority by the rulers of the apostolic see must not be removed on the pretext of any custom.

II. (Dist. 19, c. 1, “To the Archbishops and Bishops Established throughout Gaul.”) If, by the decree of the Roman pontiffs, the writings of other interpreters are approved or rejected, so that what the apostolic see truly approved is now held as accepted, and what it rejected [Col. 1187C] is henceforth regarded as ineffective, how much more ought those things which it itself has written at different times for the Catholic faith, for sound doctrines, and for the Church’s various and manifold necessities and the customs [or: movements] of the faithful to be preferred with every honor, and reverently adopted by everyone in every necessity or opportunity, with discernment or dispensation as their guide, and so forth.

III. (Dist. 20, final chapter, “To the Clergy of Constantinople.”) If you do not possess the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, you are to be reproved for neglect and carelessness; but if you possess them and do not observe them, you are to be corrected and rebuked for rashness.

## On Emperors, Title VI

[Col. 1187D]

I. (Dist. 10, c. 1, “To Emperor Michael.”) An emperor ought to be content with his daily administration of the commonwealth and not usurp what belongs exclusively to the Lord’s priests.

II. (Dist. 96, “Where Have You Read?” To the Same.) Where have you read that your predecessors, the emperors, attended synodal assemblies, except perhaps those at which the faith was discussed—the faith that is universal, common to all, and pertains not only to clerics but also to the laity and to all Christians without exception?

III. (Same distinction, following chapter, “Finally.” To the Same.) Finally, how those to whom authority has been granted only over human affairs, not divine ones, should presume to judge those through whom divine matters are administered, we utterly do not understand.

IV. (Same distinction, “When the Truth.” To the Same.) The mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, both king and pontiff, distinguished the offices of the two powers by his own acts and distinct dignities, so that Christian emperors would need pontiffs for eternal life, while pontiffs would use imperial laws only for the conduct of temporal affairs; so that spiritual action would remain separate from carnal intrusions, and the one serving God would not become involved in secular business; and, conversely, one who was entangled in secular affairs would not appear to preside over divine matters.

V. (Same distinction, following chapter, “It Is Sufficient.” To the Same.) It is sufficiently clear that the pontiff can neither be entirely released nor bound by secular power, since it is established that the pious emperor Constantine called him “God,” while it is manifest that God cannot be judged by human beings.

VI. (1, q. 1, “Not What Sort.” To the Same.) It is of the greatest importance for you to consider not what sort of persons the Lord’s priests are, but what they say about the Lord. Nor should you attend, in the case of the vicars of the blessed apostle Peter, to what they are, but to what they strive to do for the correction of the churches and for your salvation. For you cannot say that they are inferior to the scribes and Pharisees sitting on Moses’ seat, concerning whom the Lord commanded, saying: “Whatever they tell you, do”—and so forth (Matthew XXIII).

## On Kings, Title VII

[Col. 1188C]

I. (Dist. 63, “Moreover.” To King Lothair.) It has been reported to us that whoever is to be promoted to the episcopate in your kingdom is permitted by you to be elected only if he favors you. Therefore, by apostolic authority and under the solemn appeal of divine judgment, we charge you not to allow anyone to be elected in the city of Trier or in Cologne before a report concerning this matter has been made to our apostolate.

II. (2, q. 1, “What King Lothair.” To Charles, King of the Franks.) The deeds committed by King Lothair, your nephew, require no accusation. For, as the Apostle testifies, the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, impurity, and so forth (Galatians I). In manifest cases, the accused is not oppressed by the skill of accusers, nor is his own crime concealed by evasions, since the fault thrusts itself forward openly before everyone; [Col. 1188D] and therefore judicial procedure is not required in such matters.

III. (Same, final chapter, “To the Bishops Established throughout Gaul, Italy, and Germany.”) The crime committed by King Lothair—if he can truly be called a king who restrains no bodily appetites by any salutary governance, but rather yields to their illicit impulses through slippery weakness—against the two women, namely Theutberga and Waldrada, is manifest to all. But almost the whole world, converging from every direction upon the threshold or see of the apostolic see, had long reported that the bishops Theutgaud and Gunthar had served as his guardians and supporters in such an affair. Therefore, by decree of the holy synod together with us, they are unquestionably deposed in [our] presence, excommunicated from priestly office, and removed from the governance of their bishoprics.

IV. (11, q. 3, “Especially.” To King Lothair.) Above all, avoid communion with Waldrada, your concubine, who was formerly repudiated by you. For she is excommunicated and, until she appears before us, separated from all fellowship with Christians. She is excommunicated so that you may not be struck with her by an equal sword of sentence, and so that, bound and shackled by your passion for a single little woman, you may not be dragged into everlasting destruction.

V. (Same, “Thus You Yielded to the Movements of Your Body.” To the Same.) You consented to yield so far to the impulses of your body and, loosening the reins of pleasure, cast yourself—though forbidden—into the pit of misery and the mire of filth, so that you, who had been placed in the governance of peoples, became the ruin of many. [Col. 1189B] The legitimate downfall of Theutgaud and Gunthar, formerly bishops, proves this: because they had not competently instructed you—or rather, because they strove to conceal your transgression by their arguments and, under a certain appearance of justice, to overwhelm equity with various fabricated and elaborate devices—we have, by apostolic authority, deposed them and regularly removed them from all governance of the episcopate.

VI. (Same, “The Most Excellent.” To Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims.) The most excellent King Charles consulted our apostolate about what ought to be done with those who communicate with the often-condemned woman Ingeltrude, since it is established that she, together with her communicants and supporters, is bound by the same bond of anathema. Therefore we now charge your blessedness, [Col. 1189C] relying upon our authority in this matter, to take care of them. And because your holiness, divinely instructed, knows very well that one thing is done out of necessity, another out of ignorance, and another through deliberate wrongdoing—and that the latter is to be punished more strictly than the first two—let it therefore watch diligently and judge each person’s case with cautious strictness, so that those who offend out of necessity or ignorance may be absolved through you by our authority. But those who bind themselves by deliberate purpose and, in contempt, put our prohibitions aside, we do not wish you to absolve at all unless worthy satisfaction has first been made.

VII. (24, q. 3, “Or Are You Not?” To King Lothair.) Should you not be struck with strict punishment, since you are recognized as having imitated Lamech’s adultery and wickedness in taking two wives? [Col. 1189D] The Lord erased this only after seventy-seven generations by his saving coming, whereas Cain’s fratricide was abolished in the seventh generation by the waters of the cataclysm, that is, the Flood (Genesis VI).

## On Patriarchs and Archbishops, Title VIII

I. (Dist. 63, “Bishops.” To John, Archbishop of Ravenna.) Do not consecrate bishops throughout Emilia except after the election or consent of the clergy and people.

II. (3, q. 6, “This Indeed.” To Solomon, King of the Britons.) This is the ordinance of God your Father, and this is the law of your mother the Church: namely, that you do not refuse to send all the bishops of your kingdom to the archbishop of Tours, nor disdain to seek his judgment. For he is the metropolitan, and all the bishops of your kingdom are his suffragans, as the written records of my predecessors clearly demonstrate. It is not necessary for the churches of God to suffer any losses from the divisions caused by kings’ disagreements, since, as far as lies within them, all should strive to preserve among themselves the peace they preach.

III. (9, q. 3, “He Has Complained.” To the Archbishop of Bourges.) Our brother Sigebod, archbishop of Narbonne, has complained to our apostolate that, against his will, you compel his clerics to come to your judgment and, without consulting him, dispose of matters belonging to his church as though by right of your patriarchate. Yet neither antiquity—which the holy Fathers decreed must be respected—supports this, nor does the authority of the holy canons permit it, except perhaps if, concerning cases that cannot be settled among themselves, they should appeal to you as to their patriarch, or if, after their own bishop has died, they should wish the affairs of their church to be administered by your judgment. We decree that primates or patriarchs possess no privilege over other bishops except insofar as the sacred canons grant it and ancient custom has conferred it upon them from antiquity.

IV. (11, q. 3, “Theutgaud.” To All the Bishops of Gaul and Germany.) Theutgaud of Trier, primate of the province of Belgica, and Gunthar, archbishop of Cologne, have now appeared before us and the holy synod. They presented a written account, confirmed by their own hands, of how they had investigated and judged the case of King Lothair and his two women, namely Theutberga and Waldrada; and they openly confessed in a living voice that they had violated the sentence which our most holy brother Thado, archbishop of Milan, and our other fellow bishops had asked the apostolic see to issue against Ingeltrude, the wife of Boso, and which we, inflamed by divine zeal, had canonically pronounced under the attestation of anathema. In all these matters we find that they have transgressed apostolic and canonical sanctions in many respects and wickedly violated the rule of equity. We therefore judge that they must remain entirely removed from every priestly office. Accordingly, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by the authority of blessed Peter exercised through us, we decree that they are to remain stripped of the governance of their bishoprics.

## On Sacred Orders, Title IX

[Col. 1190D]

I. (Dist. 23, “Moreover.” To Rudolf, Archbishop of Bourges.) What must be observed in consecrations and orders will be taught at length by the canonical decrees of Pope Innocent, especially the opening of the letter sent to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio.

II. (1, q. 1, “We Decree,” c. 2.) Simoniacs who have been ordained simoniacally, or those who have ordained them, are to fall from their own rank according to the ecclesiastical canons. Simoniacs who have been ordained simoniacally by non-simoniacs are likewise to be removed from the office wrongly received. But simoniacs ordained non-simoniacally by simoniacs we mercifully permit to remain in office by the laying on of hands, as the circumstances of the time require.

## On Bishops, Title X

[Col. 1191A]

I. (Dist. 34, c. 1. To Albinus, Archbishop of Genoa.) Bishops must be entirely free from every kind of hunting of beasts or birds, and must abstain from excessive familiarity with their daughters, from which a bad reputation might arise. For, as the blessed Jerome says, we read of no saint who was a hunter.

II. (Dist. 43, final chapter. To Emperor Michael.) The administration of heavenly seed has been entrusted to bishops. Woe if they do not sow; woe if they remain silent, as the chosen vessel fears and cries out (1 Corinthians IX).

III. (6, q. 3, “Finally.”) If any ambiguity or dispute had perhaps arisen concerning the examination of Suffred or his renunciation of the episcopate, it ought, according to custom, to have been referred to the apostolic see, and all of you ought to have awaited our decrees concerning every such matter. We grieve that this has been omitted until now. Therefore, beloved, I earnestly implore your glory that the aforementioned Bishop Suffred be restored to his own episcopate; and if he has done anything deserving reproach, it will afterward be determined either by correction or by worthy punishment.

IV. (7, q. 1, “Pontiffs.” To Albinus of Genoa.) Pontiffs who are afflicted by some weakness or illness must not be cast aside, nor are others to be consecrated in their place unless they have been removed from this life. If they complain about the ministry entrusted to them, let priests carry out what is lawful. But in matters they are not permitted to undertake, let the assistance of neighboring bishops be supplied until they recover their health.

[Col. 1191C]

V. (Same, same chapter. To the Same.) Bishops who undertake the care and solicitude of the Lord’s flock ought not to withdraw from its administration, so that the beauty of the talent received may not be destroyed, but their struggle may salutarily increase and the fruit be multiplied threefold.

VI. (Same, “You Ask.” To Huntfrid, Bishop of the Church of Morini.) You ask whether, when you are driven from your bishopric by the Northmen, you ought thereafter to live in a monastery. Know, dearest brother, that if it is dangerous for a helmsman to abandon a ship in calm weather, how much more so in the midst of waves. We do not mean that we should not flee the ambushes of persecutors, especially pagans, when they rage for a time and, on account of the multitude of our sins, receive from God the ability to harm us—particularly since we ought not voluntarily to go out to meet them, and it is abundantly clear that many prophets and apostles, and the Lord himself, fled such persecutors. Rather, what especially befits us is that we who, like rams, lead the flocks—or rather, who by God’s authority are their shepherds—should certainly persist with them in danger to the best of our ability. And when tranquility has been restored by divine mercy and the fury of the raging enemies has subsided, we must immediately seek out the flock, gather it together, and lift its spirits upward by proclaiming above all the peace and security of the heavenly homeland.

VII. (23, q. 8, “Reprehensible.” To Charles, King of the Franks.) It is clearly very reprehensible that you have implied that the greater part of all the bishops, day and night, keep watch with all your other faithful men against the maritime pirates, and that for this reason the bishops are prevented from coming; for it is the soldiers of Christ who must serve Christ, while the soldiers of the world must serve the world, according to what is written: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs” (1 Timothy II). If the soldiers of the world devote themselves to military service, what does this have to do with bishops and the soldiers of Christ, except that they should devote themselves to prayers?

VIII. (On Consecration, Distinction 1, “Moreover.” To Rudolf, Archbishop of Bourges.) Moreover, according to our custom, bishops ought to say “Glory to God in the highest” during the solemn celebration of Mass on the Lord’s Supper. On that same day they may use the apostolic pallium if permission to do so has been granted to them by the apostolic see.

## On Priests, Title XI

I. (Dist. 32, “No One.” To All Bishops.) No one should hear the Mass of a priest whom he knows certainly to have a concubine or a woman living with him under the pretext of companionship.

II. (Dist. 50, “Priests.” To Charles, Archbishop of Mainz, and His Suffragans.) If priests fall into the snare of fornication and the act of the crime is manifest or publicly known, they cannot retain the honor of the priesthood, according to the authority of canonical institution.

III. (Same, “Let Him Strive.” To Oswald, Fellow Bishop of Quadrantina.) If a priest strikes someone but does not kill him, let him do penance for the assault and be suspended for some time from the solemn celebration of Mass. But if anyone dies from any kind of blow inflicted by him, he must in no way minister in the manner of a priest; for although he may not have intended to kill, fury and anger are nevertheless forbidden and condemned in everyone, and especially in God’s ministers, many times over.

IV. (2, q. 1, “Let It Be Known.” To Herard, Archbishop of Tours.) This priest says that he was attacked with false accusations and irrationally expelled from his church without having been convicted or having confessed. For when your diligence conducted an inquiry on three occasions, no fault could be found in him, either concerning the charge of fornication or concerning the confession of homicide of which he was accused. Therefore we earnestly admonish your reverence that whatever appears to have been done—perhaps without your knowledge—out of Gehazi-like greed be corrected by your brotherly judgment through prompt amendment, namely by restoring the aforementioned priest to his own church and, in your mercy, returning to him the former honor he lost.

V. (15, q. 8, final chapter, “In Response to the Questions of the Bulgarians.”) You ask whether you ought to receive communion from a priest who has been caught in adultery, or who is merely besmirched by a rumor of it. We answer: No one, however polluted he may be, can pollute the divine sacraments, which exist to cleanse every contagion. Whatever sort of priest he may be, holy things cannot be defiled. Therefore communion is to be received from him, whatever judgment of bishops condemns him, because wicked people harm only themselves when administering good things. A torch, once lit, provides harm to itself but gives light to others in darkness; and from the very source of its benefit to others, it suffers loss itself. Therefore receive Christ’s mysteries fearlessly from every priest, because all things are cleansed by faith in Christ—for it is faith that conquers this world—and because the merit belongs not to the giver but to the recipient, as the blessed Jerome says: “For every believing soul baptism is complete, and in every priest the body of Christ is complete.”

VI. (17, q. 4, “Concerning the Floggers of Priests.” To Thado, Archbishop of Milan.) Concerning those who flog and kill priests—namely robbers who are not restrained by the secular arm—it is pleasing, according to the Lord’s command, that they be admonished with fraternal love a second and a third time. If, when admonished, they do not listen to you, we grant permission that, with the Church assembled, you deprive them of holy communion; and if they remain obstinate and perhaps despise priestly admonitions, you may cut them off from the structure of the Church under the prohibition of anathema.

## On Clerics, Title XII

I. (Distinction 12, “That One.” To Ado, Archbishop of Vienne.) A cleric who has lived chastely through the ecclesiastical orders up to the subdiaconate cannot take a wife. For no one is granted permission, except those to whom ecclesiastical rule permits having a wife.

[Col. 1193C]

II. (Dist. 50, “A Cleric.” To Oswald, Fellow Bishop of Quadrantina.) A cleric who kills a pagan ought not to be promoted to a higher rank, and he must also be deprived of the rank he has acquired, for he is a homicide. The soldiers of the world are distinct from the soldiers of the Church, and it is not fitting for the latter to serve the world.

III. (Same place, “Those Who Cut Down a Tree.”) Those who appear to be cutting down a tree are blameless and innocent if it happens that, when the tree falls, it kills a person, because the homicide was committed neither by their will nor by their desire. But if it is recognized that the death of the person occurred through some fault or negligence of theirs, they are to be deposed from their rank and are under no circumstances to be received into the sacred order.

## On Monastic Vows, Title XIII

[Col. 1193D]

I. (Dist. 27, “What You Asked.” To Ado, Archbishop of Vienne.) A woman who, after her husband’s death, placed the sacred veil upon her head and pretended under that veil to be a nun, but afterward returned to marriage, must do penance for her wicked deception and return to what she promised.

II. (20, q. 3, “The Present One.” To All Bishops in the Kingdom of Louis.) A present cleric named Lambert, together with his father Atto—formerly a count but now a cleric—came hastening to the threshold of the apostles and appeared before us.
