He asserted that, while his father was still in the lay order, he had built two monasteries on his own estates, intending that after his death his present son Lambert would succeed him in his place. When Lambert was still of tender age, between eight and ten years old, the aforementioned father, by his own decision and without regular formation, put the cowl upon him against his entire will. After a certain period of time, as he himself says, Bishop Solomon, together with certain others, caused the same Lambert to put on the monastic habit—so they say unwillingly—without his father’s offering him or receiving a blessing from the abbot. On this pretext they wish him to be deprived by his brothers of his paternal or maternal inheritance and, against his entire will, as has been said, to remain a supposedly regular monk. And further: [Col. 1194B] Therefore, recalling advisedly the words of the Psalmist, in which he declares that he will sacrifice himself to God voluntarily and entreats that the free offerings of his mouth may be pleasing in God’s sight (Psalm XXXIII), we judged that the present cleric named Lambert should by no means be made a monk under such coercion. For what someone neither chooses nor desires, he certainly does not love; and what he does not love, he easily despises. Therefore no good thing exists unless it is voluntary. For this reason the Lord commanded that a staff not be borne on the way (Matthew X), by which violence might be inflicted upon anyone, and so forth.

III. (27, q. 1, “The Widow.” To Charles, Archbishop of Mainz, and His Suffragans.) A widow who has placed the sacred veil upon her head, if she prays in church among other veiled women and offers offerings with them, and if she has professed that she will remain in the same habit, promising never to remove the religious veil, must not presume to depart from the observance of religion.

## On the Laity, Title XIV

I. (Dist. 18, final chapter, “In Response to the Questions of the Bulgarians.”) You, who are laymen, must neither judge priests nor investigate anything concerning their lives; whatever the matter may be, it must be reserved for the judgment of the bishops.

II. (Dist. 96, “In the Scriptures.” To Emperor Louis II.) It is related in the Scriptures that the emperor Constantine said: “Truly, if I saw with my own eyes a priest of God, or any of those who are completely wrapped in the habit of a monk, sinning, I would strip off my cloak and cover him with it, so that he might not be seen by anyone.” We say this because we wish to make you cautious: if you happen to hear something about the Lord’s priests, who are rightly called fathers of souls, that might bring confusion to pious minds, do not act without restraint; rather, imitate the modest sons of Noah and thereafter cover your father’s shame (Genesis IX), so that, as they did, you may deserve, under the Lord’s guidance, to be filled with abundant blessing.

## On Churches, Title XV

(22, q. 1, “No Buildings,” from His Decrees.)

I. No buildings are to be placed in the church courtyard except those belonging to clerics.

[Col. 1195A]

II. (11, q. 2, “Concerning Things.” To Ado, Archbishop of Vienne.) Concerning things once contributed and dedicated to God, which afterward are invaded and plundered by certain persons under the pretext of concessions by princes, we decree that you should first consult the prince, in order to suppress so presumptuous an action and determine whether it was truly his concession or the presumption of the invader. If the prince’s gift was disorderly, the prince himself must be reproved for correction; but if the invader’s presumption is established, he is to be restrained by the punishment of excommunication until he makes amends.

III. (37, q. 4, “As in Antiquity.” To All Bishops.) As was established in antiquity by the holy Fathers, we decree that the larger church shall have a surrounding area of forty [Col. 1195B] paces, and chapels or smaller churches thirty. Whoever attempts to violate their boundaries or removes from them a person or his property, unless he is a public robber, is to be excommunicated until he makes amends and returns what he has taken.

## On Baptism, Title XVI

I. (On Consecration, Distinction 4, “By a Certain Person.” In Response to the Questions of the Bulgarians, chapter 104.) You report that many people in your country were baptized by a certain Jew, though you do not know whether he was a Christian or a pagan, and you ask what ought to be done about them. If they were baptized in the name of the Trinity, or merely in the name of Christ, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles—for the two are one and the same, as Saint Ambrose explains—they must not be baptized again, because it belongs not to them but to Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1195D] Something is missing. See chapter 104, *Response to the Questions of the Bulgarians*, or Letter 97.]

[Note: [Col. 1195D] On account of this canon, the Magdeburgians accuse Nicholas I of error, but very ineptly, since he taught that one could baptize in the name of Christ for the same reason that the apostles did in fact baptize in Acts II, VIII, X, XI, and XIX. Thus Suárez, volume III, *On the Sacraments*, disputation 21, section 3. Bellarmine, book IV, *On the Roman Pontiffs*, chapter 12, says that Nicholas adhered to a false and erroneous opinion only as a private teacher. All learned authorities commonly embrace this view. SEV. BIN.]

II. (Same, “Catechisms.”) Catechisms for those to be baptized may be prepared by the priests of each church, as they are solemnly known to be prepared in this holy Roman Church, in which, by God’s authority, we perform the ministry of our service.

## On Penance, Title XVII

I. (12, q. 2, “Concerning the Wicked Man.” To Frotarius, Archbishop of Bordeaux.) Concerning the wicked man named Burgandus, who, stirred by insane rage, did not hesitate to entangle himself in the devil’s snares and, in the manner of pagans, lying in ambush along precipitous roads and crossroads, dared, with demonic audacity, to inflict nefarious invasions and violent plundering upon you in a village of your church, while you and your clerics were staying there, striving to instruct the people with salutary admonitions of doctrine, refreshing the empty hearts of human beings with the spiritual bread of the word, and desiring commendably the salvation of your own souls, as you sought to visit the holy thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul—after gathering the followers and accomplices of his wickedness. He even dared, as the text of your letter says, to seize with polluted hands the sacred altar and the sacred vessels of the Lord’s body and blood, as though they were worthless objects suitable for common use. Your belovedness therefore asks us what bond of penance ought to bind him, or those who were with him in so impious and wicked a crime, if at some time, touched by divine grace, they should wish to come to penance; and you have taken care to request the judgment of our instruction. Concerning them, if the matter is as stated, we command that, whenever they hasten to return to penance, they remain outside the Church of God for one full year, since they did not hesitate to seize and carry away its most sacred vessels outside the rite of Christian faith. In the second year they are to remain before the doors of the church without communion. In the third year they may enter the Church of God and stand among the hearers without offering, not eating meat or drinking wine except on the days of the Nativity and Resurrection of the Lord. [Col. 1196B] In the fourth year, if their labor of penance during the preceding three years has been fruitful, they are to be restored to the communion of the faithful; and, promising with complete devotion of mind that they will never again do such things, they may deserve to receive the body and blood of the Lord. Until the seventh year they are to remain penitents for three days each week without eating meat or drinking wine.

II. (26, q. 7, “Concerning Those.”) Concerning those who have done penance for crimes and turn to the military profession, it is clear that they act against the sacred rules. Yet because crimes are not equal, and you report that some of these people have fallen into despair through excessive stupidity while others have fled to the pagans for this reason, we entrust the decision to you, since you are present and able to examine the places and times of that region, the measure of the fault, and also the penance and groaning of those who come to confession.

III. (33, q. 2, “Murderers.” To Rudolf, Archbishop of Bourges.) Those who kill their wives without a trial—since you do not add “adulterous” or anything of that sort—what else are they to be regarded as but homicides, and therefore brought to penance? Marriage is entirely denied to them, except for young men, concerning whom the twenty-fifth rule—or rather indulgence—of the decretals of Pope Leo the Blessed is to be observed.

IV. (Same, c. 2, “The Bearer.” To Rathald, Bishop of the Holy Church of Strasbourg.) We have learned that the bearer of this letter is a matricide. We command that he remain under the yoke of penance, so that for one full year he may not leave the church, but must stand before the doors of the basilica, continuing to pray and beseech God that he may be delivered from so great a sin. When the year has been completed, he may enter the church, but he must stand only among the hearers and may not yet receive communion. When the course of three years has been completed, the grace of holy communion is to be granted to him. [Col. 1197A] He is not to offer offerings until a further period of seven years has been completed. Throughout all these years and periods he must not eat meat or presume to drink wine, except on feast days and Sundays and from Easter to Pentecost. Wherever he wishes to go, he must not be carried in any vehicle but must travel on foot; he must not take up arms except against pagans. He must fast three days each week until evening. He must not separate himself from his own lawful wife, lest he fall into the abyss of fornication—which we pray may not happen. But if the end of his life approaches before the course of three years is completed, he is to partake of the body and blood of our Lord. Otherwise, let what we have established above be carried out. Nevertheless, if you see his conversion and the fountain of his tears flourishing in every worthy action and good work, let vigilant concern toward him appear more humane and let mercy be shown in all things.

V. (Same, following chapter, “In Response to the Questions of the Bulgarians.” Council of Worms, chapter 33.) If anyone has fornicated with two sisters, or with those persons whom Holy Scripture prohibits, and has performed suitable penance but has not been able to maintain continence in chastity, he may take a lawful wife in marriage. Likewise, a woman who has fallen into such a crime may do so, so that she may not be led into the chaos of fornication. But we establish this only for laymen and laywomen.

## On Marriage, Title XVIII

[Col. 1197C]

I. (27, q. 2, “Let It Suffice.”) According to the laws, let the consent alone of the men or women whose consent and unions are at issue suffice. If that consent alone is lacking, all the other things celebrated together with intercourse are also rendered void.

II. (Same, chapter, “The Queen Wrote.” To Charles, King of the Franks.) Queen Theutberga wrote to us that she wished to be released from royal dignity and the marital bond and desired to be content with a private life alone. We wrote to her that this could happen only if her husband Lothair chose the same life. For although it is written, “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matthew XV), God, and not a human being, separates when, out of regard for divine love and by the consent of both spouses, marriages are dissolved. We prohibit your mutual separation from being carried out in any other way.

III. (10, q. 2, c. 1.) Where there is not the consent of both parties, there is no marriage. Therefore those who give girls to boys in the cradle, and conversely, accomplish nothing unless both children consent after they have reached the age of discretion.

IV. (30, q. 5, *Nostrates*. To the inquiries of the Bulgarians.) Our people, both men and women, do not wear on their heads a band of gold or silver, or one made of any other metal, when they enter into the nuptial contract. Rather, after the betrothal—which is the promise of the future marriage—they also celebrate the marriage contract with the consent of those who enter into it and of those under whose authority they are. After the bridegroom has betrothed his bride by giving her the pledge-ring marked with the finger of faith, and after he has delivered the dowry agreed upon by both parties, with a written document containing this agreement, in the presence of those invited by both sides, the two are brought to the nuptial contract either immediately or at the proper time, lest they presume to do such a thing before the time defined by law. First, they are placed in the Lord’s church with the offerings which they ought to offer to God, by the hand of the priest; and finally they receive the blessing and the heavenly veil.

V. (31, q. 2, *Lotharius*. To Rhadoald, bishop of Porto, and John, bishop of Ficulina.) King Lothair declares in his memorandum that he received Waldrada from her father with the dowry mentioned above, and afterward received the sister of Hucbert [Col. 1198B]. First, investigate this carefully. If you find that the aforesaid glorious king received the said Waldrada with the aforementioned dowry, before witnesses, according in every respect to the law and the rite by which marriages are customarily celebrated, and that Waldrada was admitted into his marriage by public declaration, it remains for you to examine why she was repudiated, or why the daughter of Boson was admitted. But since the same glorious king says that he admitted Theutberga through fear, so great a king ought not, through fear of one man, to have been plunged into an immense precipice against the divine commandment. In this matter especially he shows himself reprehensible: he preferred the love of the world to the love of God, although even those who kill the body ought not to be feared when they drive a man against justice. Therefore we command you nothing else [Col. 1198C], once that king has been convicted by his own declaration, except that, relying upon canonical authority and acting in our place, you determine his case, and so forth.

VI. (32, q. 1, *Quidquid*. To the inquiries of the Bulgarians.) Whatever a woman may have thought or done against you, or even if she has accused you, she is not to be rejected or utterly hated, except in the case of fornication.

VII. (52, q. 8, *Hi qui*. To Charles, archbishop of Mainz.) Those who have entered into marriage in sound health, and one of the two is afterward afflicted by dementia, madness, or some other illness, cannot have their marriages dissolved on account of this illness or circumstance. The same must be understood of those who are blinded by adversaries, mutilated in their limbs, or castrated by barbarians.

[Col. 1198D] VIII. (33, q. 2, *Inter haec*. To Alwin, archbishop of Genoa.) Among other matters, Your Holiness has taken care to add the question whether, if someone’s wife has committed adultery, it is lawful for her husband to kill her according to secular law. But the holy Church of God is never bound by secular laws. She has no sword except the spiritual one, which does not kill but gives life.

IX. (33, q. 4, *Nec uxorem*. To the inquiries of the Bulgarians.) I believe that it is in no way appropriate either to take a wife or to hold banquets during Lent.

## On impediments to marriage, title XIX

I. (30, q. 1, *Nosse*. To the bishop of Salona.) You wish to know whether a woman who has lifted her husband’s son, born of another woman, from the sacred font may afterward be joined to that same man. We determine that they may be joined for this reason: according to the sacred canons, no spouse may dismiss the other spouse under any pretext of religion unless both consent. It pertains, however, to the immense ruin of a wife when, hating her husband or disregarding his infirmity, she performs an impious act under the appearance of piety—especially since the Apostle commands: “Do not defraud one another, except by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. 7).

II. (Ibid. *De his*. To Rodulf, archbishop of Bourges.) Concerning those who hold their stepchildren before bishops for confirmation—that is, those who support the children of their wife by her former husband while the children are being chrismated by bishops—if this is done knowingly, as you assert, it is indeed a sin, but it is not to be punished by separation of the marriage. Nevertheless, let them mourn and cleanse this offense by worthy penitence, saying to the Lord: “Do not remember the sins of my ignorance” (Ps. 34).

III. (30, q. 5. To the inquiries of the Bulgarians.) A man ought to love the person who received him from the sacred font as a father. Likewise, among spiritual brothers and children there is a free and holy communion, which ought not to be called consanguinity, but should be regarded as spiritual kinship. Therefore, I think that no lawful marriage can take place between them. For even Roman laws do not permit marriages to be contracted between those who are sons by nature and those who are sons by adoption. Likewise [Col. 1199C]: if marriage is not contracted between those whom adoption joins, how much more ought those joined by the regeneration of the Holy Spirit through the heavenly sacrament to abstain from carnal intercourse with one another? (c. 2, *To the inquiries of the Bulgarians.) It is therefore far more fitting that the person whom divine grace, rather than human will, has chosen to be my father’s son or my brother should be called my father’s son or my brother, and that he should more prudently be separated from reciprocal bodily intercourse.

IV. (30, q. 4, c. 1. To Solomon, bishop of Constance.) Your Holiness asks us whether a man may have two godmothers, one after the other. In this matter he must remember that it is written: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2). Since it is therefore clear that a man and a woman become one flesh through marriage, it plainly follows that he is constituted a true fellow-parent to the woman whose fellow-parent the wife he took in marriage appeared to be.

V. (33, q. 2, *Si quis*.) If anyone has committed fornication with his spiritual mother, he is struck, as you know, by the blows of anathema. Likewise, we proclaim that the man who commits the crime of fornication with the woman whom he received from the sacred baptismal font, or with the woman whom he held before the bishop when she was anointed with the sacred chrism, is to be struck [Col. 1200A] in the same way. Nevertheless, if he has a legitimate wife, he must not dismiss her.

VI. (35, q. 2, *On consanguinity*. To the suffragans of the Church of Amalfi.) Let no one take a wife from his consanguinity until after the seventh generation, or until the kinship can be recognized. A layman who has both a wife and a concubine must not receive Communion in the Church.

## On wars, title XX

I. (2, q. 4, *Monomachiam*, from his decrees.) We do not accept single combat in the law, since we do not find that it was commanded; for those who pursue this and similar practices seem to be tempting God alone.

II. (15, q. 6, c. 2, § *Quin etiam*. To the bishops of Gaul.) Moreover, we give this command to our aforesaid brother, to the sons of the Church of Trier, and to its defenders: with the spiritual and material sword alike, let them pursue those wicked men and their supporters until the possessions, or whatever ecclesiastical goods have been alienated or plundered through this deed or by any other arrangement, are restored in their entirety.

III. (23, q. 5, *Omnium*. To the Frankish army.) We wish all of you to know, beloved, that whoever—although we do not desire it—dies faithfully in this struggle of war will by no means be denied the heavenly kingdoms.

[Col. 1200C] IV. (23, q. 8, *Si nulla*. To the inquiries of the Bulgarians.) If no necessity presses, one ought to abstain from battles not only during Lent but at every time. If, however, unavoidable urgency presses, then even during Lent one must undoubtedly not spare preparations for war in defense both of oneself and of one’s country or ancestral laws. Otherwise a man would appear to tempt God if, when he has something he can do, he does not strive to provide for his own salvation and that of others and does not guard against the losses of holy religion.

V. (24, q. 3, *Illi qui*. To all the bishops.) Those who have plundered pilgrims or envoys of any saint—whether clerics, monks, women, or unarmed poor—or have seized their possessions [Col. 1200D], or have met them with evil intent, are to be struck by the bond of anathema unless they make worthy reparation. That peace which we call the Truce of God must be faithfully observed, as it has been established by the archbishops and bishops of each province. Whoever violates it is to be subjected to excommunication.

[Note: [Col. 1199D] These matters do not seem to belong to this period.]

[Col. 1201]

# Response of the Bishops of Germany assembled at Worms concerning the faith of the Holy Trinity against the heresy of the Greeks

*(From the manuscript codex Vindobonensis, “Ecclesiastical History”; in Neutgard, “Constitutions of the Bishops.”)*

[Col. 1201A] The whole ecclesiastical discipline is to be salutarily believed by all in the faith of the undivided Trinity, so that the harmony of the heavenly orders may always and everywhere remain one among all peoples. But because we have heard that Michael and Basil, emperors of the Greeks, with their supporters, have deviated immoderately from this catholic faith in certain matters, we judge it necessary that nothing pertaining to the unity of concord and the guardianship of heavenly discipline be neglected or violated by dissension, nor disturbed by dispute, so that the structure and unity of our faith may be able to stand firm. For we know that our most holy Fathers and teachers, through the gravest assaults of hostile forces, prudently cut away many blasphemies of heretics with the divine sickle, for the sake of the peace and unity of the holy Church of God, and that all unanimously persevered in the faith of the undivided Trinity.

Therefore, from their great multitude let us choose one who will crush the blasphemies of the aforesaid emperors with divine arguments. For if he were to bring forward against them the authorities of the Old and New Testament and of all the teachers, the abundance would exceed the magnitude of the subject, and the length would produce weariness in readers and hearers. Therefore, since the aforesaid heretics have dared to say that the Holy Spirit proceeds not from the Son but from the Father alone, it must be shown what the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit possess individually and what they possess in common in the undivided Trinity; how the Holy Spirit proceeds truthfully and eternally from both; and how the holy Trinity itself exists inseparably. It must also be demonstrated that the Trinity works all things together and is coeternal, and that the Father and the Son, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds, exist as one and the same substance. It must be shown that the holy Trinity itself is one and only one true God; that the Holy Spirit is understood to be equal to the Father and the Son, is called the Spirit of both, and is understood under the name of love; and that, although the Holy Spirit is most truly God, he is called the gift of God. It must also be shown how the holy Trinity itself is neither confused [Col. 1201C] nor divided, is contained neither by a finite nor by an infinite extent of place, and is not altered by either a finite or an infinite course of time.

Augustine, in his book *On the Words of the Lord in the Gospel according to Matthew* (sermon 61):

“Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come.” Therefore, he says, the forgiveness of sins, through which a spirit not divided in itself is overthrown and the kingdom expelled [the transmitted wording is unclear], is itself the fellowship of the unity of the Church of God, outside which that forgiveness of sins does not occur, as the proper work of the Holy Spirit, with the Father and the Son cooperating. For the Holy Spirit is, in a certain manner, the fellowship of the Father and the Son. The Father is not commonly called Father by the Son and the Holy Spirit, because he is not the Father of both; and the Son is not commonly called Son by the Father and the Holy Spirit, because he is not the Son of both. But the Holy Spirit is commonly possessed by the Father and the Son, because he is the one Spirit of both.

That he is the Spirit of the Father, the Son himself says: “He proceeds from the Father”; and elsewhere: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.” That he is the Spirit of the Son, the Apostle says: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’”—that is, causing you to cry out. And by this we know, as the apostle John says, that Christ remains in us through the Holy Spirit whom he has given us; that same Spirit bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God. Hence it is written: “If, therefore, there is any exhortation in Christ, any comfort of love, any fellowship of the Spirit.”

And a little earlier:

“For the Holy Spirit does not dwell in anyone without the Father and the Son, nor the Son without the Father and the Holy Spirit, nor the Father without them. Their dwelling is inseparable, because their operation is inseparable.”

From the same book, in the Gospel according to John, concerning the one Trinity and the triune unity, Augustine says:

“By this faith we most rightly and firmly hold that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are an inseparable Trinity, one God and not three gods—yet one God in such a way that the Son is not the Father, the Father is not the Son, and the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but the Spirit of the Father and the Son. This ineffable Divinity, remaining in itself, renews, creates, recreates, sends, recalls, judges, and liberates all things.”

Thus we know this ineffable Trinity as inseparable, so that it is evident that it operates all things inseparably. A little later in the same Gospel Augustine says:

“A question therefore arises which, in the name and by the will of the Lord, we have undertaken to resolve. The Father does nothing without the Son, and the Son does nothing without the Father. The Son, he says—not the Father—was born of the Virgin Mary; yet the birth of the Son, not of the Father, from the Virgin Mary was wrought by both the Father and the Son. The Father did not suffer, but the Son; nevertheless the passion of the Son was wrought by both the Father and the Son. The Father did not rise again, but the Son; nevertheless the resurrection of the Son was wrought by both the Father and the Son.”

And afterward, because the Father brought about the birth of the Son, hear the Apostle:

“When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law.”

Does the expression “from a woman” perhaps cause difficulty? Scripture says both: from a virgin and from a woman. From a virgin: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son.” From a woman: as you have heard, this is not contrary. For the distinctive usage of the Hebrew language calls females whose virginity has not been violated “women.” You have clear evidence in Genesis: when she herself was first made, it says, “He formed her as a woman.” Scripture also says elsewhere that God commanded the women who had not known a man’s bed to be separated. The Father brought about the birth of the Son, he who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all.

We have therefore proved that the birth of the Son was brought about by the Father; let us prove that it was also brought about by the Son. For the Apostle says:

“Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.”

In this passage let us see the birth of the Son as brought about by the Son himself. The Father brought about the passion of the Son, he who did not spare his own Son [Col. 1203A] but delivered him up for us all; and the Son also brought about his own passion, as the Apostle says:

“He loved me and delivered himself up for me.”

The Father delivered up the Son; the Son delivered up himself. What did Judas do here except commit sin?

Let us pass from this and come to the resurrection. The Father brought about the resurrection of the Son, as the Apostle himself says:

“For this reason he exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name.”

The Father therefore raised the Son by exalting him and raising him from the dead. The Son raised himself, remaining in the figure of his body, when he said of the temple:

“Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”

Let us see, then, whether the Son laid down his soul and whether the Father returned his soul to him rather than he returning it to himself. Because the Father returned it, the psalm says:

“Raise me up, and I will repay them.”

And because the Son laid down his soul and took it up again, he says:

“I have authority to lay down my soul, and I have authority to take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord, and I take it up again.”

Having briefly and truthfully set forth these matters according to the undertaking of the Christian faith, it remains for us to produce, in accordance with our promise, the coeternity of the holy Trinity from the books of Saint Augustine on the Gospel according to John (sermon 117):

“In the beginning was the Word,” he speaks, saying. “What can we find, my brothers, in the Creator, when we find nothing eternal in creation? I found an eternal Father in the Creator, and I found a coeternal Son. But if you do not find what is eternal, and they surpass one another in time, it is enough that we find what is coeval by analogy. We call those coeval every day who have the same measure of time: neither precedes the other in time, although both began to exist, and we call them coeval.

“If we can find what is coeval being born from the one from whom it is born, if we can find two coeval things, the begetter and the begotten, then here we find coeval things, and there we understand coeternal things. If here I find that what is begotten began to exist from the moment when the begetter began to exist, then certainly we understand that the Son of God did not begin to exist from the moment when the Begetter did not begin to exist.

“Behold, perhaps, brothers, we have found something in creation which is born from another thing and yet begins to exist from the time when that other thing, from which it is born, began to exist. This begins from the moment when that began; that began from the moment when the other did not begin. Thus one is coeval, the other coeternal.

“Let us therefore find coeval things and be instructed by the Scriptures. In Scripture we read, by way of these analogies, concerning Wisdom itself: ‘For she is the brightness of eternal light.’ She is called the image of the Father. Let us take our analogy from this, so that we may find coeval things from which we may understand coeternal things.

“For fire gives forth light, and light is given forth from fire. Consider the person who lights a lamp. Before the lamp is lit there is not yet fire, nor yet the radiance which proceeds from the fire. Let us therefore suppose that the fire is the father of that radiance, since we have already said that we are seeking coeval things, not coeternal things. If I wish to light a lamp, fire is not yet there, nor is that radiance; but as soon as I have lit it, the radiance exists together with the fire. Give me fire here without radiance, and I will believe that the Father existed without the Son.”

And a little later:

“Let us suppose, then, that something has been born upon the water, such as a shrub or a plant. Does it not come into being together with its image? As soon as it begins to exist, its image begins to exist with it; it does not precede its image by being born. I am not shown something born upon the water and its image appearing afterward, when the thing itself did not first appear without its image. Rather, it is born with its image, and the shrub and its image begin to exist together.

“Do you not admit that the image comes from the shrub, not the shrub from the image? Therefore you confess that the image comes from the shrub; and so both the begetter and what is begotten began to exist together, and therefore they are coeval. If the shrub were always present, its image from the shrub would also always be present. But whatever is from another is certainly born. Therefore the begetter can always exist, and what is born from him can always exist with him.

“Thus the Son of God is said to be Son because he has a Father, because he has one from whom he is; not according to the notion that the Father is first and the Son afterward. Always the Father, always the Son from the Father. And because whatever is born from something is born, the Son is therefore always born, the Father is always Father, and the image is always from him.

“Just as the image of the shrub was born from the shrub, and, if the shrub were always present, the image would always be born from the shrub, so you could not find a coeternal offspring with eternal begetters, but you have found coeval offspring from temporal begetters. Understand the coeternal Son born from the eternal Begetter. For what is coeval with the temporal is coeternal with the eternal.”

Here, brothers, there is little that you need to consider because of the blasphemies. In his letter to Consentius, the same teacher writes:

“For it is clear that we have received the Word of God as the only Son of God. Hence the evangelist says: ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.’ And again: ‘The Word became flesh,’ because of the birth of his incarnate Son, which took place in time from the Virgin.

“In this he declares not only that the Word is God, but also that he is of the same substance as the Father. For after saying, ‘The Word was God,’ he adds: ‘This was in the beginning with God.’ ‘All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.’ For he does not say ‘all things’ except those which were made—that is, the whole creation.

“From this it plainly appears that he himself was not made through whom all things were made; and if he was not made, he is not a creature. If he is not a creature, he is of the same substance as the Father. For every substance that is not God is a creature, and what is not a creature is God. If the Son is not of the same substance of which the Father is, then he is a made substance, and all things were not made through him. But if all things were made through him, then he is of one and the same substance with the Father, and therefore not merely God but true God.

“The same John says this most clearly in his Epistle: ‘We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and may be in his true Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life.’

“From this it is also consequently understood that the Apostle Paul did not speak only of the Father when he said, ‘who alone has immortality,’ but of the one and only God, who is the Trinity itself. And shortly afterward the Apostle says: ‘Keep the commandment without stain and blameless until the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ, which the blessed and only powerful King of kings and Lord of lords will bring about at the proper times, he who alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see; to him be honor and glory forever and ever.’

“In these words neither the Father nor the Son nor the Holy Spirit is specifically named, but the blessed and only powerful King of kings and Lord of lords is named, who is the one, only, and true God—the Trinity itself.”

Now, having explained, to the capacity of our understanding and by the gift of God himself, the coeternity and the one and same substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in the holy and undivided Trinity, let us also set forth, concerning that one, only, and true God, how the Holy Spirit is understood to be equal to the Father and the Son, is called the Spirit of both, and is understood under the name of love; and, since the Holy Spirit is God, why he is called the gift of God. Repeated explanation makes the reasoning clearer.

Augustine, in book six, chapter nine, of *The City of God*, says, on the basis of the Lord’s testimony, that we call the Father the one true God, the Son the one true God, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the holy Trinity itself together—not three true gods but one true God.

“Or, since he added ‘and Jesus Christ whom you sent,’ should ‘one true God’ be understood? Is the order of the words therefore: ‘that they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you sent as the one true God’? Why, then, did he remain silent about the Holy Spirit? Or is it because, wherever ‘one’ is named, the Holy Spirit is already understood as clinging to the one in such peace that through this both are one, even though he is not mentioned?

“For in that passage the Apostle also seems to omit the Holy Spirit, yet he is understood where he says: ‘All things are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.’ And again: ‘The head of a woman is man, the head of man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God’—that is, the head of Christ is the Trinity, since Christ is in the Trinity, so that there may be a Trinity.

“Hence it is also said of the Holy Spirit, who is understood to be equal to the Father and the Son, is called the Spirit of both, and is understood under the name of love, although each person in the Trinity is love.”

From book fifteen, chapter eight, of *The City of God*, the same Augustine says:

“Just as, therefore, we properly call the unique Word of God by the name of Wisdom, although universally the Holy Spirit and the Father are also Wisdom itself, so the Spirit is properly named by the word ‘love,’ although universally the Father and the Son are also love.

“But the Word of God—that is, the only-begotten Son of God—is plainly called the Wisdom of God by the apostolic voice, where it says that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. We find where the Holy Spirit is called love if we carefully examine the speech of the apostle John. After saying, ‘Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God,’ he continued and added: ‘Everyone who loves is born from God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.’ Immediately, wishing to say something more openly about this matter, he says: ‘By this we know that we remain in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.’

“And the apostle Paul says: ‘The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.’

“Love, therefore, which is from God and is God, and which properly is the Holy Spirit, is the means through which God’s love is poured into our hearts and through which the whole Trinity dwells in us. Therefore the Holy Spirit, although he is God, is most rightly also called the gift of God. What should this gift properly be understood to be except love, which leads to God, and without which no other gift of God leads to God?”

It must therefore be proved that the Holy Spirit is called the gift of God according to the words of the Lord:

“If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

Then the evangelist continued and added:

“He said this about the Holy Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive.”

And the apostle Paul says:

“We were all given to drink of one Spirit.”

That the holy Trinity itself is unconfused and undivided and is moved neither through time nor through place, the same distinguished teacher expresses in book eight of *Genesis Literally Interpreted*.

We have therefore declared that the supreme, true, one, and only God—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—the true God himself, his Word, and the Spirit of both, the Trinity itself, is neither confused nor divided; that he alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see; that he is contained neither by a finite nor by an infinite extent of place, and is not altered by a finite or infinite course of time.

This is the true catholic faith, in which the Law and the Prophets, the Gospel of Christ, and all orthodox teachers agree in every respect under sacred religion. Under this faith the holy Church of God has flourished and will flourish, prevailing from beginning to end, fortified by every authority from heaven. To those who believe rightly it provides perpetual and spiritual healing, but it eternally condemns unbelievers and schismatics without any remedy unless they repent.

Therefore, since the Greeks mentioned above irrationally reproach us for not fasting on Saturdays, and for not abstaining from eating eggs and cheese for seven weeks before Easter and from eating meat for eight weeks, it seems fitting that we should answer them concerning matters that are close at hand and relevant to their satisfaction, using Augustine’s words to the priest Casulanus (Epistle 36):

“As for what you ask me—whether it is permissible to fast on Saturday—I answer: if it were in no way permissible, surely neither Moses nor Elijah nor the Lord himself would have fasted for forty consecutive days. Yet by this reasoning it is also concluded that fasting on the Lord’s Day is not unlawful. Nevertheless, whoever thinks that this day should be assigned to fasting, just as some observe the Sabbath by fasting, will be a source of no small scandal to the Church, and rightly so.

“For in matters about which divine Scripture has established nothing certain, the custom of the people of God or the institutions of our ancestors are to be held as law. If we wish to dispute these matters and condemn some on the basis of the customs of others, an interminable struggle will arise. The labor of argument will consume itself without any certain proofs of the truth. We must certainly take care lest the calm of love be clouded by the storm of contention.”

And a little later:

“Who, then, would tolerate someone saying of all the Christian peoples of the East, and of many in the West, that the countless servants and handmaids of Christ who dine soberly, justly, and modestly on Saturday are carnal, cannot please God, and that what is written of them applies: ‘Let the wicked depart from me; I do not wish to know their ways’?”

And again:

“When he pursues with such reproaches and curses the Church that bears fruit and grows throughout the world, dining on Saturday almost everywhere, I urge everyone to restrain himself.”

And afterward:

“If, then, we do wrong when we dine on Saturday, we never live rightly on any Sunday—which it is impious to say.”

And shortly afterward:

“God commanded that the man who had gathered wood on the Sabbath be stoned. But nowhere do we read that anyone was stoned or judged with any worthy punishment either for fasting on Saturday or for dining.”

And in what follows:

“On that very Sabbath day on which we read that Christ’s disciples ate, they certainly plucked ears of grain, which was not permitted on the Sabbath, because the prohibition of the ancients opposed it. Let him therefore see whether it might perhaps be more fittingly answered that God wished two things to be done by the disciples on that day—one, the plucking of ears, and the other, the taking of food—so that there might immediately be an answer against those who wish to be free from work on the Sabbath. But this is directed against those who compel fasting on Saturday,” and so forth.

And again:

“Surely, if we are not in error when we fast, and if we wash away the errors of the other six days by fasting on Saturday, then no day will be worse than Sunday and no day better than Saturday. I believe, dearest brother, that no one understands the law as this man does unless he does not understand it.”

He continues:

“Nevertheless, concerning fasting or dining on this Sabbath, nothing seems to me safer or more peaceful to observe than that the one who eats should not despise the one who does not eat, and the one who does not eat should not judge the one who eats. For neither will we abound if we do not eat, nor will we lack if we do not eat. In these matters, let the unoffending fellowship of those among whom we live and with whom we live for God be preserved.

“For just as what the Apostle says is true—that it is evil for a man to eat through giving offense—so it is evil for a man to fast through giving offense. Let us not therefore be like those who, seeing John neither eating nor drinking, said, ‘He has a demon’; nor again like those who, seeing Christ eating and drinking, said, ‘Behold, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.’

“Whatever we do, therefore, let us do everything for the glory of God, and, insofar as it depends on us, let us be without offense to Jews and Greeks and the Church of God. For all the beauty of the king’s daughter is within; those observances, however, which are celebrated in various ways are understood in her clothing. Hence it is said there: ‘She is clothed in embroidered garments with golden borders.’ But let that clothing also be varied by different celebrations in such a way that it is not torn apart by hostile disputes.”

And again:

“Reflecting upon the evangelical and apostolic writings and upon the entire work called the New Testament, I see that fasting is commanded; but on which days it is not appropriate to fast, and on which days it is appropriate by the command of the Lord or of the apostles, I do not find defined.

“Why, then, does the Church sometimes fast especially on the fourth and sixth days of the week? The reason appears to be that, according to the Gospel, the Jews are found to have made their plan to kill the Lord on the fourth day of the week. After one intervening day, on the evening of which the Lord ate the Passover with his disciples, he was betrayed during the night which already belonged to the sixth day of the Sabbath. This was the first day of Unleavened Bread, beginning at evening. Therefore that sixth day is also rightly assigned to fasting.

“Fasts signify humility, as in the words: ‘I humbled my soul with fasting.’ The Sabbath follows, on which day Christ’s flesh rested in the tomb, just as God rested on that day from all his works in the first works of the world.

“From this arose the variety in that royal clothing: some, especially the peoples of the East, prefer that the fast be relaxed on account of the significance of rest; others, on account of the humility of the Lord’s death, prefer to fast, as do the Roman Church and some Churches of the West.

“Yet on the one day on which Easter is celebrated, for the renewal of the memory of what happened, because the disciples in human grief mourned the Lord’s death, all fast in such a way that even those who dine on all other Saturdays throughout the year observe the fast of that Saturday most devoutly. In this way they signify both the mourning of the disciples on the one annual day and the blessing of rest on the other Saturdays.

“For the venerable Ambrose, when asked about this matter, said: ‘What more can I teach about this than what I myself do? When I am at Milan, I do not fast on Saturday; when I am at Rome, I fast on Saturday. And wherever you come,’ he says, ‘observe the custom of that Church, if you do not wish either to suffer scandal or to cause it.’

“But how does it happen that in one Church, or in the Churches of one region, some dine on Saturday and others fast? The custom of those to whom the governance of the gathering of those peoples has been entrusted seems to me the one that should be followed.”

Finally, so that nothing may remain unfulfilled from which the basis of the dispute might waver, it must be shown what the times of fasting are that Christ, from the Law and the Prophets, divinely ordained for Christians to observe, so that in all matters everyone may rightly and lawfully have satisfaction in the interests of concord.

Augustine, in Book One of his *Questions to Januarius*:

> “Lent certainly possesses the authority of fasting both in the ancient books, from the fasts of Moses and Elijah, and in the Gospel, because the Lord fasted for the same number of days, demonstrating that the Gospel does not disagree with the Law and the Prophets, among whom he appeared glorious on the mountain, so that what the Apostle says about him might stand out more clearly: ‘Bearing witness from the Law and the Prophets.’ In what part of the year, then, could the observance of Lent have been more appropriately established than adjoining and contiguous to the Lord’s Passion? For in it this laborious life is signified, a life that requires restraint, so that one fasts from friendship with the world itself, which certainly does not cease falsely to flatter, scatter the cosmetics of its enticements around us, and allure us.

> “I think that this life is represented by the number forty for the following reason: the number ten, in which the perfection of our blessedness consists, is expressed here as in the number eight, because eight returns to the beginning. It seems to me that this is also expressed here because the creature, represented by the number seven, clings to the Creator, in whom the unity of the Trinity is to be proclaimed temporally throughout the whole world. This world is also bounded by the four winds and raised up by the four elements, and the year is varied by four changes of season. Ten is consumed four times in Lent. When the number forty is reckoned through its parts, it adds the ten itself, and they make fifty, as the reward of labor and restraint.”

Hence Augustine says in the same book:

> “The number forty has equal parts. First, forty by ones; then twenty by twos; then ten by fours; eight by fives; five by eights; four by tens; two by twenties. Thus one, two, four, five, eight, ten, and twenty, taken together, produce fifty. Therefore, just as the number forty, reckoned through its equal parts, becomes a decade by ten up to ten, and then through the decade up to fifty becomes fifty, so the time of faith in the things accomplished and to be accomplished for our salvation, lived out with a corresponding equality of life, demands the understanding of steadfast wisdom, so that discipline may be strengthened not only by believing but also by understanding.”

Therefore blessed Gregory also says, among other things (*Homily 16 on the Gospels*):

> “From the beginning of Lent until the joys of the Easter solemnity there are six weeks, whose days amount to forty-two. When six days of the Lord’s abstinence are subtracted from these, no more than thirty-six days remain in abstinence. Since the year is reckoned by 365 days, we afflict ourselves for thirty-six days, as though we were giving God the tithes of our year.”

Thus, symbolically, we have forty-two days in Lent, because the children of Israel had that many stages when they were baptized in the Red Sea, after they had gone out from the land of Egypt and from harsh slavery, and reached the Promised Land. For there are that many successive generations of Christ, with the [uncertain reading: *hiethoxia*] counted twice, together with Christ himself. It is fitting, then, that those who are journeying toward the heavenly homeland strive through the same number of stages by which the children of Israel came to the Promised Land. And rightly those who pass over to Christ through baptism reach him through the same number by which Christ deigned to come to us, as blessed Jerome says in his book *On the Stages of the Children of Israel* (*Letter to Fabiola*):

> “It is no wonder, but rather let us reach the heavenly kingdoms through that sacramental number under which the Lord and Savior came from the first patriarch to the Virgin, as to the Jordan, which flowed in a full current and overflowed with the gifts of the Holy Spirit.”

Accordingly, we regularly keep this Lenten fast, handed down to us by Christ and the holy Apostles. The other fasts, which we undertake from Septuagesima and during the four seasons of the year, we practice voluntarily and by human judgment, not by evangelical authority or the teaching of the Apostles. Hence the reproach of those who criticize us for not abstaining from the flesh of cheese and eggs for seven weeks before Easter seems frivolous.

Indeed, so that we may not transgress the boundaries established by our fathers, we maintain in this matter the observance that we see taught and followed by the holy teachers, so that the whole body of the Church may agree with itself in one observance. For the Apostle speaks of those who presume to judge beyond ecclesiastical custom:

> “Let us no longer judge one another, but judge this rather: that you do not place a stumbling-block or scandal before your brother.”

Although the reprovers themselves do not understand it, nine weeks before Easter we offer the mortification of our pleasure. The first of these weeks we call Septuagesima, according to the headings of the Sacramentary and the Antiphonary. It begins on Sunday and ends on the seventh Saturday after Easter. It signifies the period of captivity of God’s people, who were held captive in Babylonia under the number seventy.

Hence Jeremiah says:

> “I will remove from them the voice of joy and gladness, and all these nations shall serve the king of Babylon for seventy years.”

Therefore during that period *Alleluia* is not sung among us, nor the most sweet hymn of the angels, *Glory to God in the highest*. *Alleluia* is a distinguished word because of the honor and breadth of the first language, as Jerome says in his eleventh book on Isaiah. For in comparison with the Hebrew language, both Greek and Latin speech is poor. During the days mentioned above we use the poor language:

> “Praise to you, Lord, King of eternal glory.”

The Psalm says:

> “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?”

*Alleluia* and *Glory to God in the highest* are heavenly songs. Hence John says in the Apocalypse:

> “After this I heard a loud voice in heaven saying, ‘Alleluia.’”

There is no doubt that *Glory to God in the highest* is the song of the angels. We must sit—that is, be humbled—beside the rivers of Babylon and weep while remembering Zion, and through this Septuagesima prepare ourselves for the Lenten struggle by fleeing vices.

The Apostle says to the Ephesians:

> “But fornication and every impurity or greed must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints.”

Augustine says of the seventy years mentioned above in Book Three of *On Christian Doctrine*:

> “Jeremiah’s seventy years may also be understood spiritually as the whole period during which the Church is among strangers.”

Again, in Book Twelve of *Against Faustus*, he says:

> “For what faithful Christian would not understand that, just as after seventy years, according to the prophecy of that same Jeremiah, there is a return from captivity and the Temple is restored, so after the periods have passed that run their course through the repetition of the seven-day number, we too—that is, the Church of God—must return from the pilgrimage of this world to that heavenly Jerusalem? And through whom can this occur except through Jesus Christ, truly the great priest, whose figure was borne by that Jesus, the great priest of that time, when the Temple of God was built after the captivity?”

There are sixty days from Septuagesima to the Wednesday before the Lord’s Supper. Through this number the widows who are in great tribulation are signified; and that tribulation and affliction is shown by the arrangement of the fingers that expresses the number, with the index finger placed above the thumb.

The three days that remain until the Lord’s resurrection signify the three-day fast that, according to the Septuagint translators, the people of Nineveh practiced, so that our sins, for which we are afflicted, may be wiped away in the glory of the Lord’s resurrection. Thus the mystical period of seventy signifies sympathy with captives, because “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him.”

Finally, Sexagesima, running within Septuagesima up to the Wednesday, corresponds to the fourth age of the world, in which David and Solomon reigned. In the fourth age that nation, renowned for heavenly faith and glorified by the kingdom of David and Solomon and by the height of the most holy Temple, ennobled the whole world. In our Wednesday, however, David triumphs, he who conquered the lion, and Solomon, the eternal peacemaker, reigns. Of him the Apostle says:

> “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over him.”

He builds a Temple for the most noble God the Father, to whom he will say at the end:

> “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you.”

We ought to hasten toward that kingdom through Sexagesima. For the number six, reckoned through its parts, is the first perfect number: its sixth is one, its third two, and its half three; and one, two, and three together make six. This number therefore signifies perfection.

Bede says in his *Book on Times*:

> “Here it must be noted that the number six is not perfect merely because the Lord completed the work of the world in it. Rather, as Augustine says, the Lord, who wished to create all things together, deigned to work in that number because it is perfect. Six multiplied by ten makes sixty; the number ten refers to the reward of works.”

If anyone seeks through six—that is, perfection—the reward of works, he will receive the kingdom promised to us on the Wednesday of Easter.

From Sexagesima until the holy day of the Resurrection there are eight weeks. If from each week one subtracts Thursday and the first day of the week, together with the holy day of Easter itself, only forty days remain in abstinence. We say this because of those who break the fast on those same weekdays.

Melchiades, an African by nationality and in every respect an apostolic man, the thirty-fourth after Saint Peter, whose successor blessed Sylvester was in the chair of apostolic dignity, established that no member of the faithful should presume for any reason to fast on the first or fifth day of the week. The reason why, according to his ordinance, the fast is broken on the first day need not be repeated at length.

We have judged that the fifth day was released from fasting because of the great mysteries contained in it. On that day the sacred chrism is prepared for washing away the guilt of the whole world’s first origin. On that day penitents are reconciled; on that day the Redeemer of all, dining with his disciples, broke bread and likewise gave them the cup as a figure of his body and blood, and presented to us a great sacrament for our benefit. On that same day, after many mysteries, our God and Lord Jesus Christ, in the sight of his disciples, penetrated the heavens in a glorious ascension.

But so that the discussion may not be prolonged, we recognize more about this solemnity in the writings of the venerable saints. Finally, in the Council of Laodicea, title fifty, it was decreed that the fast ought not to be broken on the fifth day. But since everyone abounds in his own understanding, whether this or something else is the case, we prejudice nothing that is consistent with faith and religion.

Finally, Quinquagesima touches the first day of venerable Easter. For just as the number six signifies the perfection of works, so fifty signifies all the works that are completed through the five bodily senses. Five times ten makes fifty. If anyone has fulfilled the ten words of the Law through outward administration in the Holy Spirit, he does not doubt that he must reach participation in the blessed resurrection celebrated at the Lord’s Easter.

As religious observance increased under Pope Telesphorus, who was the ninth to shine in the holy Church after Peter, prince of the Apostles, this period came to be devoted to abstinence. By what other name could it more reasonably have been called than Quinquagesima, according to its order?

From that point onward, by reasoning assembled in this way, those who wished to observe eight weeks gradually called the period Sexagesima. Similarly, those who observed nine weeks, after the reasoning had been established, gave it the name Septuagesima. They did not preserve these names because of the number of weeks or days, or according to the literal force of the names. Otherwise, if those who wished to add a tenth week for some just reason had been following the same pattern, they would have had to call it not Decagesima or some other name because of the number of weeks, nor Septuagesima because of the number of days, but Octogesima, proceeding in due order along the straight path of the correct names.

During these periods, therefore, we keep the measure of fasting established by the holy Fathers, according to what the Lord says through the prophet:

> “Is not this rather the fast that I have chosen: loosen the bonds of wickedness, undo the burdensome bundles, set free those who are broken, and break every burden,” and so forth.

We also observe the fast of the first month for three days—Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday—for this reason: in the Book of Exodus it is written that the Lord said to Moses:

> “For in the month of springtime you went out from Egypt.”

Egypt is interpreted as “darkness,” or it may be understood as the error of this world, in which, as long as a person remains, he abides in the darkness of ignorance or even unbelief. After renouncing the devil, his pomp, and his works before baptism through a confession of true faith and through baptism, each person goes out from Egypt—that is, from the darkness of ignorance and unbelief. Having received forgiveness of all former crimes, he reaches the true light, Christ the Lord and Savior, who said:

> “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of eternal life.”

The Lord himself also prescribed the fast of the first month and those of the other three seasons through the prophet Zechariah, saying:

> “The fast of the first month, that is … [lacuna] June; the second week, the fast of the seventh month, that is September; the third week, the fast of the tenth month: a full week before the Lord’s nativity shall be for you a time of splendid solemnities.”

As we said above, the ancient Fathers decreed that the fast of the first month, lasting three days, should be observed because it borders on the days of the Lenten fast. In this way, at least on these days, a larger gathering of the Christian people might take place, so that when gathered together, by discussing holy faith with one another face to face, greater charity and greater joy might arise among them. Also, through the holy exchange thus made with one another, each person might be stirred to strive for the perfection of the holy observance of Lent, and might merit reaching holy Easter.

The fast of the fourth month is also followed immediately by a forty-day fast observed by many, after which Pentecost is celebrated. Therefore a three-day fast was generally enjoined at a distance from this one, because at that time in certain places of the Church the first fruits of the earth’s crops are gathered. This month is called by some the barley month, because at that time our ancestors had already harvested the barley and were accustomed to offer the loaves of the first fruits to the Lord:

> “Observe the month of new fruits, and you shall celebrate feast days to the Lord your God.”

At that time the Lord should be entreated with humble prayer to bring the fruit of the earth to maturity for us and, with thanksgiving, grant us the opportunity to gather it.

As for the fact that the Greeks mentioned above criticize us for forbidding our priests to take wives, we reply that we do not wish to pass beyond the boundaries established by our fathers. Rather, in accordance with the statutes of the holy canons, we desire to preserve purity of soul and body by serving God.

Thus, in the decrees of Pope Siricius, title 12:

> “We do not permit any women to be in the houses of clerics except those whom the Synod of Nicaea permitted to live with them solely for reasons of relationship.”

Hence, in the Council of Nicaea, title 3:

> “The great synod absolutely forbade this: neither a bishop, nor a presbyter, nor a deacon, nor anyone at all who belongs to the clergy may have an introduced woman, unless perhaps she is his mother, sister, aunt, or one of those persons who avoid suspicion.”

Hence, in the decrees of Pope Leo, title 27:

> “The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for presbyters. While they were laymen or readers, they could lawfully marry wives and beget children. But when they reached the ranks mentioned above, what had been lawful for them began no longer to be lawful,”

and so forth.

Likewise, from the decrees of Innocent, title 16:

> “Because it is worthy, chaste, and honorable, the Church must preserve this in every way: priests and Levites must not have intercourse with their wives, because they are occupied with the necessities of their daily ministry. For it is written: ‘Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy.’ If Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying, ‘Abstain for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer,’ and this he certainly commanded to laymen, much more must priests, whose continual duty is both to pray and to offer sacrifice, abstain from such intercourse. If someone is defiled by carnal desire, with what shame does he presume to offer sacrifice, or with what conscience or merit does he believe that he will be heard, when it is said: ‘All things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean’; and more openly he declares: ‘Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are no longer in the flesh, but in the Spirit.’”

Hence, in the Council of Carthage, title 25, Bishop Aurelius said:

> “We add, dearest brothers, that it is also reported that certain clerics, even readers, are incontinent toward their own wives. It was decided—and this has also been confirmed by various councils—that subdeacons who handle the sacred mysteries, and deacons and presbyters, and also bishops, according to the earlier statutes, should abstain even from their wives, so that they may appear to be as though they did not have them. If they do not do this, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office.”

Likewise, in the African council, chapter 37:

> “Furthermore, since it was reported that certain clerics were incontinent toward their own wives, it was decided that bishops, presbyters, and deacons should also abstain from their wives according to the earlier statutes. If they do not do this, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office.”

Hence, in the Council of Neocaesarea, title 1:

> “If a presbyter takes a wife, he is to be deposed from the order. But if he has fornicated or committed adultery, he must be expelled still more severely and reduced to penance.”

Here let everyone consider: if every word is established by the testimony of two or three witnesses, what can or ought to be done with the assertion of so many holy Fathers, who write much more about such matters?

Furthermore, because the Greeks mentioned above falsely attempt to criticize us on the ground that our presbyters anoint the foreheads of the baptized with chrism, claiming that among us this chrism is made from river water, it seems appropriate to answer them truthfully.

Our presbyters have never presumed to do this among us. Rather, our bishops, using the oil of *xylobalsamum* (wood-balsam) and olive—which God deigned to produce from green wood, and with which he anointed priests, kings, prophets, and martyrs—pray in consecrating that it be sanctified at the appointed time by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as the oil of gladness. Hence Christ was anointed above his companions. From his holy name the chrism receives its name, so that chrism may be the salvation of all who have been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, and so that God may make them participants in eternal life and sharers in heavenly glory.

As for the false claim of the Greeks just mentioned, that among us bishops are ordained from deacons before becoming presbyters, as though by some kind of leap, we firmly reply that this has never happened among us. Rather, the canonical order and procedure of consecration is observed in every rank, whereas they customarily violate it without any necessity.

Recently, it is reported, they made a tonsured monk out of a certain layman and without delay promoted him to the archiepiscopal order, contrary to all decrees. Hence, in the Council of Sardica, chapter 13, Bishop Hosius said:

> “I also consider it necessary that you examine this most carefully: if perhaps a rich man, or a scholar from the forum, or someone from the household staff is requested as a bishop … [lacuna] having served, let him ascend through each rank, if he is worthy, to the summit of the episcopate. For through these promotions, which will certainly occupy a long period, it can be tested with what faith, modesty, gravity, and reverence he acts. If he is found worthy, let him be honored with the divine priesthood. For it is neither fitting nor permitted by reason or discipline that a neophyte should be rashly and lightly ordained either bishop, presbyter, or deacon, especially since the blessed Apostle, the teacher of the nations, appears to have warned and forbidden that this should happen. Rather, those whose life has been examined over a long period and whose merits have been proved provide more examples.”

As for the claim of the Greeks mentioned above that we offer a lamb at Easter, together with the body and blood of Christ, in the manner of the Jews, no one among us has ever been able or willing to conceive such a thing.

Regarding their criticism of why our clerics shave their beards, we reply with blessed Jerome: if holiness lies in a beard, no one is holier than a goat.

These things, then, we have composed against the heresy of the Greeks and their frivolous criticism of our belief, and concerning other matters that are more ridiculous than fit to be placed before the understanding of wisdom. Now, below, we have taken care to set forth the faith that we firmly hold and confess, and also to make it generally known.

## The Profession of Faith Found in Collections of Councils

Then:

> “This is the profession of faith of the bishops assembled in synodal gathering at the city of Worms, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June. Their names are: Adalwin, archbishop; Liutbt, archbishop; Rimbt, archbishop; Anno, bishop; SALOMON, bishop; Gunzo, bishop; Arno, bishop; Witgarius, bishop; Luitbt, bishop; Ambrico, bishop; Otgarius, bishop; Gebehard, bishop; Ratolf, bishop; Ermricus, bishop; Hessi, bishop; Hildegrimus, bishop; Theodricus, bishop; Egibertus, bishop; Erolfus, bishop; Luithardus, bishop; Lantfridus, bishop; Theoto, abbot; Adalgarius, abbot; HETTO, abbot; Brunwardus, abbot; Aschericus, abbot; Theotrocus, abbot; Egilbertus, abbot.”

**I.—That the king should place the worship of God before all things, and preserve mercy together with judgment and justice.** 611
